# [The Complete Works of Augustine of Hippo]

[Col. 0009]

## Preface to the Eighth Volume

Since a Catholic teacher has two duties—one, to illuminate and confirm the truths of the Christian religion; the other, to defend those same truths against the errors of rising heretics—no one among the ancients or the moderns fulfilled both tasks more successfully than Augustine. By universal judgment he deservedly attained the distinction of being regarded as the foremost and greatest Doctor of the Church.

Thus far we have presented his works that explain Christian doctrines. Now, in the three remaining volumes, we are to reproduce those that concern the refutation of unbelievers and heretics, works that we commonly call Polemical by their now-established name. For although in his earlier writings the holy man sometimes, as occasion arose, touched upon errors that were making headway, the purpose of those works was not the same as that which he himself set before him in the works that follow.

If readers have hitherto turned over Augustine’s occasional discussions of heretics with such pleasure, far greater fruit may be expected from the books that follow. In them, in an orderly and deliberate manner, the entire body of error is divided and dispersed into its parts; the leaders of the heretics are defeated and overthrown both in public debates and in published writings; and, finally, their chief and most important works are reduced to ashes. Thus, whereas from the first kind of writings Augustine earned the title of Catholic Doctor—a title shared also by several eminent Fathers of the Church—from these later writings he deserved from Catholics, as Jerome testifies, a distinction uniquely his own, more illustrious than any other: that he should be recognized, even while still alive and dwelling on earth, as a second founder of the ancient faith.

“Courage and virtue!” Jerome writes to Augustine. “You are celebrated throughout the world. Catholics venerate and esteem you as once again the founder of the ancient faith” (*Epistle* 195 among the Augustinian letters).

Nothing seems capable of being added to commend this title and distinction. Yet in the same place Jerome adds that it is “a sign of greater glory” that, for this very reason, “all the heretics detested” the most holy man.

Their malice and estrangement progressed so far that they attempted to remove him from the midst of the living by offering whatever reward was proposed. They did not consider it enough to increase their already conceived capital hatred unless they also tried to persuade their followers that God Himself supported the plan. To these followers they did not hesitate to promise that “one may confidently believe that all sins can be forgiven by God to those who are able to do and accomplish this” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 9).

Yet Augustine’s moderation in this matter is astonishing. Although he was attacked by his adversaries not only with private accusations but was also sought by them for execution, he bore and concealed those private hostilities with such equanimity that he scarcely mentioned them in his disputations. We would know nothing certain about the plot against his life if Possidius had not committed the matter to posterity in his *Life*.

Whenever he was forced to answer injuries inflicted upon him, he did not attribute this to righteous indignation, but to the usefulness of his readers, who might otherwise be led away from the truth by such unjust accusations. No one, however, expressed the state of so moderate a spirit on such occasions better than Augustine himself. These are his words in the third book against Petilianus, chapter 1:

> “Whenever I answer anyone, whether by speaking or writing, even when provoked by insulting accusations, insofar as the Lord grants me this, with the goads of empty indignation restrained and crushed, I look to the welfare of my hearer or reader. I do not act so as to become superior to a man by reviling him, but more beneficial by convicting him of error.”

In these disputations, therefore, the whole matter was conducted through the strong force of reasons and arguments. No sense of difficulty, insult, or personal injury diverted him from his purpose. He considered himself sufficiently vindicated if, even at the cost of his own honor, he had defended the rights of the Church and of the truth—the one thing he kept before his eyes.

In refuting the arguments of heretics, the holy Doctor conducted himself so that he took the utmost care not merely to exasperate their minds, but also, insofar as it lay within his power, to call them back to recognition of the truth through gentler and more humane words and forms of address. From the beginning of his controversies he set this manner of proceeding before himself, as he himself testifies:

> “I have asked, and I ask, God to grant me, in refuting and overcoming your heresy—which you perhaps embraced more imprudently than maliciously—a peaceful and tranquil mind, thinking more about your correction than about your overthrow. For although the Lord overturns the kingdoms of error through His servants, He nevertheless commands that the people themselves, insofar as they are human beings, be corrected rather than destroyed” (*Book against the Epistle of the Manichaeans*, chap. 1).

Would that those who handle controversies of faith were guided by the same spirit!

Although Augustine’s supreme ability shines forth in all his works, his Catholic disputations nevertheless display somewhat greater brilliance—just as the valor of soldiers is tested more in war and battle than in peace. In these writings the force and sharpness of his intellect, his learning, erudition, knowledge of Scripture, eloquence, prudence, and skill unfold their light within their proper subject, while the attacks of pressing adversaries rouse and stimulate every sinew of his mind to defeat them.

[Col. 0011]

Since Augustine’s polemical writings are too numerous to be gathered into a single volume, it was necessary to divide them among several volumes. The first of these will contain the works composed against the Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and Arians. It would be idle and superfluous to say much about them here, since Augustine’s book *On Heresies* presents itself first, and in it the reader will find a concise account of all these heresies and of the others as well.

Immediately after his baptism, Augustine, the most vigorous champion, attacked the heresy of the Manichaeans, by which he had been deceived and indoctrinated as a young man. He published five books against them: *On Free Choice of the Will*, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, *On the Customs of the Manichaeans*, and *On True Religion*. Since he composed these as a neophyte and not yet a priest, we have left them in the first volume, as in the editions previously published.

Paulinus, in Epistle 25 among the Augustinian letters, designates these books as the “Pentateuch against the Manichaeans” and praises them in this manner:

> “O lamp worthy to be placed above the lampstand of the Church! From your seven-branched lamp, fed with the oil of joy, you pour forth light over the Catholic cities far and wide; you scatter the dense darkness of the heretics, and by the splendor of your glorious discourse you clear away the light of truth from the confusion of darkness!”

Thus far Paulinus on those first writings against the Manichaeans. If he detected so much light and splendor in them, what should be expected from the later works, composed by Augustine with greater care and experience as time advanced?

The first work he composed after receiving the priesthood, for the benefit of his friend Honoratus, who was held by Manichaean errors, he entitled *On the Usefulness of Believing*. In it he used these distinguished words, which deserve to be placed at the beginning of his polemical works:

> “That these things may benefit you, or at least do you no harm, and likewise all to whose hands they may happen to come, I have asked God, and I ask Him; and I hope it will be so, if I am rightly conscious of myself, because I approached this writing with a pious and dutiful spirit, not from a desire for an empty reputation or a fondness for idle display” (chap. 1).

After this he again attacked the same Manichaeans by publishing a book *On Two Natures*. They said that one nature was a part of God and the other belonged to the race of darkness. Augustine so exposes these ravings by clear arguments drawn from natural reason that he seems to bring his adversaries back to recognition of the truth more by moving their minds than by disputing with them. Meanwhile he grieved that he had not once used those same arguments, so that he might not have fallen into the ruinous sect.

Through these writings and his serious sermons to the people, he aroused such universal admiration that everyone regarded as safe and sound the cause defended by a man of such moderation and sincerity, such learning and eloquence. Hence, when the city of Hippo had been corrupted in large part by Fortunatus, a Manichaean priest, not only Catholics but also Donatists brought the holy Doctor to a private disputation with him. Fortunatus withdrew from it so weakened and broken that thereafter all the people of Hippo were free from his most pestilential contagion.

Possidius describes the successful outcome of this conference (*Life of Augustine*, chap. 6), whose proceedings are reported here. From them we learn that the extremely talkative man was reduced to silence by one argument of Augustine—the very one he had once heard from Nebridius [Note: [Col. 0011] See *Confessions*, book 7, chap. 2]. Then, under the pretext of taking time to consult his followers and answer, he made a disgraceful flight from the city of Hippo, let alone from the conference, never to return there.

After this victory, a little later, the work against Adimantus was brought forth. In it passages of the Old and New Testaments are reconciled, and answers are given to the sophistries that this crafty man, formerly a disciple of the Manichaeans, had derived from those passages.

Augustine continued the same struggle against the Manichaeans when he was already bishop. First he refuted the *Epistle of the Manichaean called “of the Foundation”*, which contained a summary of the entire perverse doctrine—that is, “the beginning, middle, and end of the doctrine,” as Felix the Manichaean testifies (*Acts with Felix*, book 2, chap. 1).

The Manichaeans read this epistle with such reverence that it was learned only while bowed down. Thus the passage appears in two ancient copies: “It was learned by us while bowed down.” Nevertheless, we preferred another reading from the excellent Corbie manuscript: “For at that time, when it was read to us miserable people, we were said by you to have been enlightened” (*Against the Epistle of the Manichaeans*, chap. 5).

Augustine had perhaps not long before laid aside this labor when the Catholics imposed another burden upon him: namely, that he should answer the book of Faustus, bishop of the Manichaeans, whom his followers praised so greatly. “The arrival of this man,” Augustine says, “was promised to us as though from heaven, to explain everything that troubled us” (*On the Usefulness of Believing*, chap. 8).

The outcome, however, did not correspond well to such magnificent promises. Indeed, the opposite occurred: the holy Doctor could rightly be regarded as sent from heaven to refute the inventions of a most foolish deceiver, who had seduced the minds of many with pitiable trifles, and especially to defend the deeds of the ancient patriarchs, which that ill-fated heretic had attempted to disguise.

In this work, when Augustine removed from an unworthy man the name of Jesus Christ’s apostle, which the Manichaean had arrogated to himself at the beginning of his epistles, the holy man indicates the time when this heresy arose. He says that it is established that “this heresy arose not only after Tertullian but even after Cyprian” (*Book 13*, chap. 4).

Epiphanius agrees with this opinion. He traces the origin of the same heresy to the ninth year of Gallienus [Col. 0013] (*Epiphanius, On Weights and Measures*), which corresponds to the year 263 after Christ. Eusebius, however, places it in the time of Pope Felix and the emperor Diocletian (*Eusebius*, book 7, chaps. 30–32)—although Diocletian did not come to the imperial power until nearly a decade after the death of Pope Felix, which occurred in the year 275.

Leo the Great moves the same origin still farther back, to the year 260 after Christ’s resurrection, under the emperor Probus and the consul Paulinus (*Leo, Sermon 2 on Pentecost*).

The proceedings of the conference with Felix the Manichaean, who had come intending to seduce Catholics but was successfully restored by Augustine to communion with the Church, provide new trophies of Catholic truth, won under Augustine’s leadership.

The book *On the Nature of the Good* exposes the abominable crimes of certain people of that sect living “not only in Paphlagonia but also in Gaul” (chap. 47). Its purpose is to show that God is the immutable nature and the supreme good; that all other natures come from Him and, insofar as they are natures, are good; what evil is and from where it comes; how many evils the Manichaeans place in the nature of the good and how many goods in the nature of evil; and what kinds of natures their error invented.

Finally, the last book against Secundinus completely overturns the pernicious doctrines of the heresy. Its author was so pleased with it that he easily preferred it to everything that had been written against that plague.

If anyone wishes to judge the worth of all these writings, let him compare them with the works of other authors on the same subject, such as, among the Greeks, Serapion of Thmuis, bishop of that Egyptian city, “who earned the surname Scholasticus on account of the elegance of his intellect,” as Jerome says (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*); Didymus of Alexandria; Titus, bishop of Bostra; and Zacharias, bishop of Mytilene; and, among the Latins, Victorinus Afer. Of these, the latter was published by Sirmond among the dogmatic minor works of five ancient writers, while the former were published by Canisius in volume 5 of his *Ancient Readings*.

As for the other writings of this volume, a single codex, exposed for sale either by chance or deliberately in the seaside street of Carthage, provided the material for the two books *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*. It contained the book of an anonymous heretic. In this work Senator Cassiodorus writes that many questions concerning the divine Law are disentangled.

We must credit Orosius with the book against the Priscillianists and Origenists. In the book of consultation prefixed to it, we restored, with the aid of a single manuscript, an obscure reading concerning a hidden year that had troubled readers. For where it had formerly been read, “That land … if you should visit it by entrusting it to me in that hidden year,” the old copy reads as follows: “If you should visit me, depositing and replenishing for me that manna which has been laid up” [reading uncertain].

These words are addressed by Orosius to Augustine. In what follows Orosius says that he and many others with him await Augustine’s “eloquence descending upon them like dew.” Augustine opposed his innate modesty to such praise. When questioned about certain obscure questions, such as the distinction among the angels, he excused himself from solving them and frankly confessed his ignorance in these words:

> “But, so that you may despise me, whom you think a great teacher, I do not know what these things are or how they differ from one another” (*Book against the Priscillianists*, chap. 11).

Finally, the last minor works of this volume were written against the Arians. First comes the book against the *Sermon of the Arians*, which contained more than thirty articles of error and is refuted summarily, point by point.

Then follows the conference held by the holy Doctor near the end of his life with Maximinus, a bishop. It was no less glorious for the Catholic Church and destructive to the Arian heresy than the other conference held several years earlier with the count Pascentius.

This conference with Maximinus was followed by two books against the same Arian bishop. They were rightly and justly praised by Pope Agatho at the Sixth General Council, with an encomium of the outstanding Doctor.

These are followed by the books *On the Trinity*. Since they had previously occupied a place in the third volume, we have deliberately moved them here because of their close affinity with the foregoing minor works: for in these books on the Trinity the arguments of the Arians are repeatedly refuted.

As for Erasmus’s criticism of this excellent work, it sufficiently proves that he had engaged only superficially with the reading of these books. We shall not delay to refute the man’s hasty opinion, considering Cassiodorus’s judgment sufficient as an antidote. In book 16 of his *Institutions* he judged these books as follows:

> “The fifteen books that Saint Augustine composed on the holy Trinity with marvelous profundity are to be studied by you with attentive application.”

Augustine, in his customary modesty, speaks modestly about this work. He says that he would not have undertaken this subject if the works written on it by the Greek Fathers had been translated into Latin, or if someone else had wished to solve and illuminate the difficulties proposed to him.

Nothing, however, should be taken away from the worth of this work on account of such a modest declaration by its author. Certainly, those who have investigated theological matters more carefully in our own times acknowledge that before Augustine no one adequately explained the invisibility of the Son of God against the Arians, nor scattered the shadows of the difficulties they raised with such abundant light. Hence the Greeks regarded this work as so remarkable that they made it the special possession of their own people.

It remains to discuss the Appendix, which contains treatises against five heresies; against the Jews, Pagans, and Arians; *On the Faith against the Manichaeans*; and *On the Unity of the Trinity against Felicianus the Arian*. All these works had been attributed to Augustine in the editions based on the Louvain recension. The admonitions that we shall place before each treatise in its proper location will, we believe, demonstrate how wrongly this was done.

We shall append similar notices to the other works in the Appendix, in which we shall attempt, insofar as possible, to uncover their true and genuine authors.

[Col. 0015]

Having thus touched lightly upon these matters, we consider it wrong to detain any longer on this threshold the reader who is eager to hasten through the works that follow. It will certainly be far more pleasing to behold the overthrow of the heresies accomplished by Augustine through the power of Jesus Christ. Concerning this, we may say what is written in the sermon *On the Cataclysm*:

> “Among that people, brothers, among whom Moses performed many miracles by means of the rod, the magicians of Pharaoh arose, themselves also performing wonders against the servant of God, Moses. But they were permitted to perform certain marvelous deeds for this purpose: that they might be defeated more marvelously. What else did the magicians of Pharaoh signify except all heretics, servants of the devil, who under the name of Christ desire to devour the people of Christ? Now heresies swarm over this land like the serpents of the magicians, whom that serpent exalted upon the wood devoured and continues to devour …
>
> “Here, beloved, there was for our times the viperous doctrine of the Donatists: it was crushed, it was consumed. Soon the serpentine fraud of the Maximianists sprouted up: it was crushed, it was consumed. The venom of the Manichaeans had crept in like that of an asp: it was crushed, it was consumed. The new dogma of the Pelagians, aroused by the servants of the devil like the magicians of Pharaoh, challenged our serpent: it is being crushed, it is being consumed …
>
> “Behold, an Arian snake, long dead, insults us … Return, our Moses; return, O rod; return, Christ the serpent; crush the head of the dragons. Say what you are with the Father. Let us hear you teaching, not the heretic blaspheming” (chap. 5, vol. 6, cols. 696–697).

# [On Heresies]

[Col. 0015]

## Notice Concerning the Book *On Heresies*

Quodvultdeus, a Carthaginian deacon, urged and encouraged Augustine to write this book. The letters that follow concern this matter. The first is Quodvultdeus’s, asking Augustine to produce a catalogue of heresies that would briefly summarize the particular errors and rites of each. The second is Augustine’s, excusing the difficulty of the work and pointing out that the matter had already been attempted by others.

Quodvultdeus replies, earnestly insisting that Augustine not refuse this task to his request—or rather, to the universal desire. At last Augustine, overcome, undertakes the labor and responsibility of writing on heresies, insofar as his other occupations permit.

For at that time he testifies that the necessity imposed upon him of refuting Julian had diverted him even from the revision of his own minor works—a task he considered extremely necessary. He adds that he had already completed two volumes of this revision, having reviewed all his books.

We observe that these two volumes were completed around the year of Christ 427 in the first volume. Since the book *On Heresies* itself is later than them, it seems that it should be assigned to approximately the year 428.

Possidius notes in his *Catalogue*, chapter 5: “On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus the deacon, an unfinished work.” Isidore, in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9, says:

> “Primasius, an African bishop, composed in scholarly prose three books on heresies, addressed to Fortunatus the bishop, explaining in them what the blessed Augustine had formerly left unfinished in his book on heresies because death intervened.”

Indeed, at the end of the preface Augustine promises a second part of the work, intended to show what makes someone a heretic. Prevented by death, he did not reach that part.

[Col. 0015]

## Four Letters Concerning the Same Book

### Letter 221

**To the deservedly venerable lord and truly most blessed father, Bishop Augustine: Quodvultdeus, deacon.**

1. For a long time I was hesitant, and repeatedly postponed this bold undertaking of mine. But what chiefly encouraged me, as the saying goes, was Your Beatitude’s benevolence, universally acknowledged. When I considered it, I feared all the more lest I be judged by the Lord proud for not asking, sluggish for not seeking, and lazy for not knocking.

I would have thought it sufficient merely to possess such a desire, if I could not obtain its fruit. But since I know for certain that the door of divine speech, which heavenly grace has opened to Your Veneration, has made your holy mind—possessed by Christ—ready not only to open itself to all who wish to enter, but also to persuade those who do not wish to enter, so that they may not be reluctant to go in, I shall not delay Your Reverence’s occupation with excessive speech. I shall briefly indicate the desire of my petition.

2. I infer from my own case that there are some unlearned members of the clergy even in this very large city. I submit to the consideration of Your Holiness how greatly what I seek would benefit that entire order.

I presume that, by the privilege of all those who deserve this through your spiritual labors, I too, though unworthy, shall obtain it, deservedly venerable lord and truly most blessed father.

I therefore ask Your Beatitude to explain which heresies have existed and now exist since the Christian religion received the name of the promised inheritance; what errors they introduced and introduce; what they have thought and think against the Catholic Church; and what they teach concerning faith, the Trinity, Baptism, [Col. 0017] penance, Christ as man, Christ as God, the resurrection, the New and Old Testaments, and absolutely everything in which they dissent from the truth.

May you also deign to explain which of them possess Baptism and which do not; after which groups the Church baptizes, and after which it does not rebaptize; how it receives those who come over; and what it answers to each according to law, authority, and reason.

3. Nor should Your Beatitude think me so foolish as not to see how many and how enormous volumes would be required to resolve these matters. I am not asking that this be done in that manner, for I do not doubt that it has already been done in many ways.

Rather, I ask that the opinions of each heresy be set out briefly, tersely, and in summary, and that what the Catholic Church holds against it be added insofar as is sufficient for instruction. Thus, if someone wishes to know any objection or refutation more fully, more extensively, and more clearly, he may be referred—as though by a common handbook formed from all these matters—to the rich and magnificent volumes that various people, and especially Your Veneration, have demonstrably labored to produce for this very purpose.

Such a notice, I think, will suffice for the learned and the unlearned, for the idle and the busy, and for those promoted from any quarter to ecclesiastical ministry of whatever rank. The person who has read much will briefly recall the same things, while the uninstructed will be taught by the summary, so that he may know what to hold and what to avoid; what he should shun lest he do it, and what he should pursue in order to do it.

Perhaps—and if what I suppose is true—this little work will also serve, among your other marvelous works, as a testimonial crown against the malicious minds and deceitful lips of slanderers. Though their field for slander lies more open, they will be confined within the strong boundaries of faith, closed in on every side, surrounded by every kind of weapon of truth, and suddenly struck down by a single many-formed dart, so that they will not dare draw a deathly breath.

4. I see how burdensome I am to a holy old man who is contemplating better things, arranging greater ones, and enduring the complaints of the body. But through Christ the Lord I ask you—He who has granted you, without envy, a share in His wisdom—to bestow this grace upon the unlearned of the Church. You acknowledge that you are a debtor to the wise and the foolish (Rom. 1:14), and you may deservedly and rightly say:

> “See that I have not labored for myself alone, but for all who seek the truth” (Ecclus. 24:47 and 33:18).

I could still offer many and humble prayers and enlist with me whole ranks of the unlearned. But I preferred to hear you dictating rather than occupy you while you read.

### Letter 222

**To his most beloved son and fellow deacon, Quodvultdeus: Augustine, bishop.**

1. I received your letter, in which with the most ardent zeal you asked me to write something briefly concerning all the heresies that have arisen against the teaching of the Lord and Savior after His coming. As soon as an opportunity arose, I replied through my son Philocalus, chief man of the people of Hippo, explaining how difficult this was. Now another opportunity has presented itself, and I am replying to it, briefly setting forth the difficulty of the task.

2. A certain Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself saw at Milan together with Saint Ambrose, wrote a book on this subject. He did not omit the heresies that existed among the Jewish people before the Lord’s coming, and he listed twenty-eight of these, followed by one hundred and twenty-eight after the Lord’s coming.

The Cypriot bishop Epiphanius also wrote on the subject in Greek. He was widely and deservedly renowned for his teaching concerning the Catholic faith. But, collecting the heresies of both periods, he comprised eighty.

Since both men wished to do what you ask of me, you see how much they differ from one another, at least in the number of sects. This would certainly not have happened unless one of them regarded something as a heresy that the other did not.

Nor should we think that Epiphanius was unaware of some heresies known to Philastrius, since we have found Epiphanius far more learned than Philastrius. If Philastrius had included more and Epiphanius fewer, we should rather have to say that many had escaped Philastrius.

But there is no doubt that, in the question of what constitutes a heresy, the two men did not hold the same view. Indeed, it is extremely difficult to define this completely. Therefore, when we attempt to reduce them all to a number, care must be taken lest we omit some that are heresies, or count some that are not heresies.

Consider, then, whether I should perhaps send you Saint Epiphanius’s book. I think that he spoke more learnedly than Philastrius on this subject. It could be translated into Latin at Carthage more easily and conveniently, so that you might provide us with what you seek from us.

3. I strongly commend the bearer of this letter. He is a subdeacon from our diocese, from the estate of the distinguished man and our very dear friend Orontius.

On his behalf, and on behalf of his father, by whom he was adopted, I have also written to Orontius himself. When your Christian Kindness has read that letter, I ask you to deign, through your intercession, to assist it with the aforesaid man.

I have also sent with him a man of the Church, so that access to Your Holiness might not be difficult for him. I am quite concerned about him, and from this concern, as I hope, the Lord will free me through the persistence of your charity.

I also ask that you not be reluctant to write back to me concerning how that Theodosius is situated in the Catholic faith—the man through whom certain Manichaeans were exposed—and whether those whom we think were exposed by him have been corrected.

If you have also heard anything concerning the departure of the holy bishops, make it known to me.

May you live in God.

### Letter 223

**To the deservedly venerable lord and most blessed holy father, Bishop Augustine: Quodvultdeus, deacon.**
1. I have received one memorandum from Your Reverence, which you deigned to send through an ecclesiastic. [Col. 0019] For the one that Your Beatitude indicated had previously been sent through the honorable man Philocalus has not yet reached me. Yet although I have always been conscious of my own sins, I now clearly recognized that, by obtaining the task for which I pleaded, I have become an impediment to the whole Church. Nevertheless, I trust completely that he who, through the grace of his Only-Begotten, deigned to wipe away the crimes of the human race will not permit mine to prevail to the destruction of all, but rather, where sin abounded, will make grace abound (Rom. 5:20), my deservedly venerable lord and most blessed father. I had already foretold, without myself being unaware of it, the difficulty of the work which I humbly begged your benevolence to undertake for the instruction of us most ignorant men; but with a truthful heart I relied upon the abundance of the divine fountain which the Lord has granted you.

2. For although the venerable bishops Philastrius and Epiphanius are remembered to have written something of this kind—something which, without doubt, is hidden from me among all the rest, indeed as everything is—notwithstanding, I do not think that they took such care and diligence as to append contrary opinions to each individual opinion and to add the corresponding practices; and, finally, whatever the work of each of them may be, perhaps it does not possess the brevity I desire. Greek eloquence is also assigned uselessly to a man who has not learned Latin, since I asked not only for advice but also for assistance. Why should I remind Your Veneration not merely of the difficulty but also of the obscurity of translators, when you yourself judge this more fully and accurately? Moreover, it is relevant that some heresies are said to have arisen even after their deaths, of which they made no mention.

3. Therefore I flee to the particular protection of your piety and, in my own voice but with universal longing, appeal to your most holy breast, ready for mercy. Setting aside foreign flavors, and considering the text of my earlier letter, do not deny to one who comes late, knocks, and suffers hunger the African bread which our province is accustomed to regard as its finest, seasoned also with heavenly manna. For certainly I shall not cease knocking until you yourself grant it, so that what privilege does not obtain where there is no merit may at least be earned by tireless persistence.

## LETTER CCXXIV

To the sincerely beloved lord, brother and fellow deacon, QUODVULTDEUS, AUGUSTINE, bishop.

1. When this opportunity to write was offered me through the Fussalan presbyter, whom I commend to your Charity, I reread your letter, in which you ask me to write something about the heresies that may have arisen since the coming of the Lord in the flesh began to be proclaimed. I did this to see whether I ought now to undertake the work itself and send you something from it, once you had considered that it would be more difficult the shorter you wished it to be. But I could not even do this, being hindered by cares that had supervened and which I could not wholly disregard; for they turned me away even from what I had in hand.

2. This is the work in which I am replying to Julian’s books, the eight which he published after the four to which I had previously replied. When our brother Alypius received them at Rome, he had not yet copied them all, but he did not wish to let pass the opportunity that had arisen, by which he sent me five of them, promising to send the other three shortly and pressing me greatly not to delay my response. Compelled by his urgency to proceed more slowly with what I was doing, I arranged not to neglect either work: one by day, the other by night, whenever I was spared by the other occupations that kept arriving from every direction without ceasing.

I was engaged in a very necessary task. I was revising my little works, and if anything in them displeased me or might offend others, I was working to determine what ought and could be read, partly by censuring and partly by defending it. I had already completed two volumes, having revised all my books, whose number I had not known; I discovered that there were 232 of them. The letters remained, and then the popular discourses, which the Greeks call homilies. I had already read a great many of the letters, but had dictated nothing from them when Julian’s books also began to occupy me; I have now begun to answer the fourth of them.

Therefore, when I have explained this one and answered the fifth, if the remaining three have not arrived, I plan—if God wills—to begin what you request as well, carrying on both tasks together: this work, naturally, and the work of revising my little writings, distributing the two between night and day.

3. I have disclosed this to Your Sanctity so that, in proportion as your desire to receive what you request burns more ardently, you may ask the Lord more fervently to grant me the assistance by which I may serve your praiseworthy zeal and the usefulness of those whom you think will benefit from it, my sincerely beloved lord and brother. I again commend the bearer of this letter and the business for which he has gone. If you learn with whom it must be conducted, I ask that you not hesitate to help him. For we cannot abandon the needs of men who are not our tenants but, what is more important, our brothers, and who belong to our care in the charity of Christ. May you live in God.

[Col. 0021]

## THE ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON HERESIES, TO QUODVULTDEUS

[Note: Written around the year 428.]

[Note: The *Book on Heresies to Quodvultdeus* has been newly collated with five Vatican manuscripts and twelve Gallican manuscripts: namely, two Royal manuscripts, four Colbertine manuscripts, one belonging to the Dominicans of the greater Paris convent, and the Victorine, Becheron, Bec, Floriacian, and Michaelian manuscripts; also with the variant readings of seven Belgian manuscripts used by the Louvain theologians; and finally with the editions of Johann Amerbach, Desiderius Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C, S)

What you ask so often and so insistently, holy son Quodvultdeus—that I write something about heresies worthy of the reading of those who desire to avoid doctrines opposed to the Christian faith and deceptive under the shadow of the Christian name—you should know that I had long ago, before you asked, considered doing this and would have done so, unless I had carefully considered what sort and how great a task it was and felt it to be beyond my strength. But since I confess that no one has persisted in asking as you have, in your very tiresome persistence I also considered your name and said: “I shall undertake it and do what Quodvultdeus [‘God wills’] wants.”

For I trust that God wills this, if in his merciful favor he brings me to the end of this work, so that through the ministry of my tongue the great difficulty of this matter may either merely be displayed or, with his fuller assistance, even be removed. The first of these two possibilities, which I placed first, I have long revolved and reconsidered in my mind and contemplated in a kind of meditation. But concerning what I said afterward, I confess that I have not received it; and I do not know whether, while I undertake this, strive to accomplish it, ask, seek, and knock, I may perhaps receive it. Yet I know that I shall neither ask, seek, nor knock as much as is sufficient unless I have also received this desire through the gift of divine inspiration.

In this work, then, which, because you urged it so strongly, I have undertaken in accordance with God’s will, you see that, if I am to carry it through, I must be compelled not so much by your increasingly frequent petitions as assisted by the pious prayers to God of not only yourself but also of the other brothers whom you may be able to find as faithful collaborators for this purpose. To make this happen, I have taken care, with the Lord’s help, to hasten the sending to Your Charity these first parts of my labor, in which this preface occurs, so that, concerning what remains, you may know how greatly you ought to pray for me—whoever among you may come to know that I have now undertaken this great task which you desire me to complete.

You ask, therefore—as your letters indicate, the letters which you gave me when you first began asking this of me—that I [Col. 0022] explain briefly, concisely, and in summary, from the time when the Christian religion received the name of the promised inheritance, which heresies have existed and exist; what errors they introduced and introduce; what they thought and think against the Catholic Church concerning faith, the Trinity, baptism, repentance, the human Christ, the divine Christ, the resurrection, the New and Old Testaments.

But when you saw that these inquiries of yours extended without limit, you thought that a summary of a certain general kind should be applied, and you said: “And absolutely everything by which they dissent from the truth.” Then you added: “Which of them also have baptism and which do not; and after which of them the Church baptizes, yet does not rebaptize; how she receives those who come to her; and what she answers each one by law, authority, and reason.”

When you ask me to explain all this, I marvel at your brilliant intellect, which both thirsts for the truth of so many and such great matters and, already fearing weariness, asks for brevity. But you yourself also saw what I might think at this point about your letter and, as though watchfully anticipating my thought, said: “Nor should Your Beatitude suppose me so foolish as not to see how many and how immense volumes would be needed for these matters to be resolved.”

But I do not expect this to be done [Note: The printed editions read *expeto*, “I seek”; the manuscripts read *exspecto*, “I expect.”]. For I do not doubt that it has been done in many ways. And, as though offering advice about how brevity might be preserved while the truth was laid open, you add the words I quoted a little earlier and say: “But briefly, concisely, and in summary, I ask that the opinions of each heresy be set down and that what the Catholic Church holds against it be added, insofar as is sufficient for instruction.”

Look: once again you send me into length—not because these matters either cannot or ought not to be stated briefly, but because they are so numerous that, however briefly they may be stated, they demand many written pages. Yet, you say, you want it to be like a kind of memorandum conceived from all of them, so that if someone wishes to know more fully, more completely, and more clearly about any objection or refutation, he may be directed to the rich and magnificent volumes which, by different authors and especially, you say, by Your Veneration, are known to have been composed for this very purpose. In saying this, you indicate that you desire one sort of memorandum concerning all these matters. Hear, then, from what source you are to be reminded of what you ask.

A certain Celsus completed the opinions of all the philosophers who founded various schools, down to his own time—for he could not go beyond it—in six not inconsiderable volumes. He refuted no one but simply disclosed what they thought [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *quid sentiret aperuit*, “he disclosed what he thought.”], using such brevity of expression that he employed as much eloquence as was sufficient for a matter that was neither to be praised nor blamed, affirmed nor defended, but merely disclosed and indicated. He named nearly one hundred philosophers, not all of whom founded heresies of their own, since he did not think those should be passed over in silence who followed their teachers without any disagreement.

Our Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus [Note: Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia or Salamis on the island of Cyprus, died around the year 403. Of his immense work against eighty heresies, entitled *Panarion*, Augustine knew only an epitome and a summary.], who recently departed this life, also wrote six books concerning eighty heresies, recounting everything in historical narrative and engaging in no disputation against falsehood on behalf of the truth. These little books are indeed brief, and if they were reduced to one book, even it would not be comparable in length with some of our books or those of others.

If I imitate his brevity in commemorating the heresies, you will have no grounds to ask or expect anything shorter from me. But the substance of my labor does not consist there, as will become apparent to you either when I demonstrate it or even when you anticipate it, once I have completed this work. For you will see in what the bishop mentioned above did how much is lacking from the work you want to be done—and how much more is lacking from what I am to do.

For although you want the matter stated briefly, concisely, and in summary, you also want the heresies mentioned to be answered; he did not do this. I, however, want to do this all the more, if God wills, so that every heresy—both the known and the unknown—may be avoided, and so that whatever comes to light may be judged correctly.

For not every error is a heresy, although every heresy, insofar as it is classified as a fault, cannot be a heresy without some error. What, then, makes someone a heretic cannot, as I think, be encompassed by any regular definition, or can be encompassed only with the greatest difficulty. This will be explained as the work proceeds, if God directs it and brings my discussion to what I intend [Note: Most manuscripts read *perduxerit dispositionem meam*, “brings my arrangement to what I intend.”]

What benefit the inquiry itself may have, even if we cannot comprehend how a heretic is to be defined, must be seen and stated in its proper place. For if this can be grasped, who would not see how great its usefulness is?

The first parts of this work, then, will concern the heresies that arose after Christ’s coming and ascension against his teaching and that have been able, in some fashion, to become known to us. In the later parts, what makes someone a heretic will be discussed.

When, therefore, the Lord had ascended into heaven, these heretics arose [Note: A list of the heresies was added here by someone. In most manuscripts it is not found in this place but is placed at the beginning of the book before the preface, under a title such as: “This book contains the following heresies.”]

### I. SIMONIANS

The Simonians derive their name from Simon Magus, who, having been baptized by the deacon Philip, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, wanted to purchase from the holy Apostles with money the power that the Holy Spirit might also be given through the laying on of his hands. He had deceived many by magical tricks (Acts 8:9–19). He taught the detestable disgrace of using women indiscriminately. He also said that God had not made the world. He denied the resurrection of the flesh and claimed that he himself was Christ. He also wanted to be believed to be Jupiter, and a certain prostitute named Helen to be Minerva [Note: The printed editions read *Selenen*, but the manuscripts read *Helenam* or *Helenen*, more correctly. Simon was imagining that she was Helen herself, the Trojan woman, as appears from Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 34, and from Philastrius and others. Epiphanius also calls her Helenê, and so does Damascenus in his work *On Heresies.]. He had made her his partner in crimes, and he supplied his disciples with images of himself and of this same prostitute to worship. He had also publicly established these images at Rome as statues of gods. In that city the apostle [Col. 0026] Peter destroyed him by the true power of almighty God [Note: The printed editions add here: “For he had said that on Mount Sinai he had given the law of Moses to the Jews in the person of the Father; that in the time of Tiberius he had appeared apparently in the person of the Son; that afterward he had come upon the Apostles in fiery tongues as the Holy Spirit; but that Christ had neither come nor suffered anything at the hands of the Jews.”]

### II. MENANDRIANS

The Menandrians derive their name from Menander, himself also a magician and Simon’s disciple, who asserted that the world was made not by God but by angels.

### III. SATURNINIANS

The Saturninians [Note: Epiphanius and Damascenus call them Saturnilians, and name their founder Saturnilus. Justin also calls him this in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, as does Theodoret.] derive their name from a certain Saturninus, who is said to have established the Simonian disgrace in Syria. He also said that the world had been made by seven angels alone, without the knowledge [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “without the awareness”] of God the Father.

### IV. BASILIDIANS

The Basilidians derive their name from Basilides, who differed from the Simonians in saying that there were 365 heavens, the number contained in the days of the year. Hence he also commended as a sort of sacred name the word **ἄβρασαξ** (*abrasax*) [Note: The manuscripts agree here with Epiphanius and Damascenus. The printed editions read *abraxas*], whose letters, according to Greek reckoning, add up to that same number.

There are seven letters: α, β, ρ, α, σ, α, ξ; that is, one, two, one hundred, one, two hundred, one, and sixty. Together these make 365.

[Note: On the authority of the ancient manuscripts, we delete the following words, which the printed editions add concerning the Basilidian heretics: “They do not believe that this world or man was made by God, but by the 365th heaven. They diligently learn love songs. They do not believe that Christ was crucified by the Jews, but Simon of Cyrene, who was compelled to carry his cross.”]

### V. NICOLAITANS

They were named after Nicolaus, one, as is reported, of the seven whom the Apostles ordained as deacons (Acts 6:5). When he was criticized because of his zeal for his very beautiful wife, he is said, as though to clear himself, to have permitted anyone who wished to use her. His act was turned into a most shameful sect, which approves the indiscriminate use of women.

They do not separate their food from that which has been sacrificed to idols, and they do not reject other rites of pagan superstitions [Note: Louvain reads “do not oppose.” Erasmus, together with the manuscripts, reads “do not reject,” which is better]. They also tell certain fabulous stories about the world, mixing into their discussions some barbarous names of rulers, by which they frighten their listeners; these stories provoke laughter in the wise rather than fear.

They too are understood not to attribute creation to God, but to certain powers, which they either invent with astonishing vanity or believe in.

### VI. GNOSTICS

They boast that they were, or ought to have been, called Gnostics because of the excellence of their knowledge, although they are more vain and more shameful than all those mentioned above. Finally, since they are called by different names in different regions of the earth, some also call them Borborites, as if to say “muddy” or “filthy,” because of the excessive disgrace which they are said to practice in their mysteries.

Some think that they arose from the Nicolaitans; others from Carpocrates, whom we shall discuss later. [Col. 0027] They transmit doctrines full of the most fabulous inventions. They too capture weak souls with frightening names of rulers or angels, and they weave together many fabulous notions, alien to sound truth, about God and the nature of things.

They say that the substance of souls is the nature of God, and they insert into these same long and foolish fables, according to their errors, the coming of souls into these bodies and their return to God. They make those who believe them not, as they suppose, preeminent in extensive knowledge, but—as I might put it—vanishing into extensive fabulizing [Note: Erasmus’s edition reads: “They say that their coming into these bodies takes place together with other aerial souls, through which sins are committed in bodies; for those souls which proceed from God’s substance return to God undefiled. They are also said to have a good God,” and so forth. The Louvain editors restored the passage from manuscript copies.]

They are also said to have in their doctrines a good god and an evil god.

### VII. CARPOCRATIANS

The Carpocratians derive their name from Carpocrates, who taught every shameful act and every invention of sin, saying that there was no other way to escape and pass beyond the principalities and powers that delight in such things, so that one might reach the higher heaven.

He is also said to have thought that Jesus was merely human and born from both sexes, but that he had received such a soul as enabled him to know and announce the things above. He rejected the resurrection of the body together with the Law. He denied that the world was made by God, but said it was made by certain powers unknown to him.

A certain Marcellina is reported to have belonged to his sect. She worshiped images of Jesus, Paul, Homer, and Pythagoras, adoring them and placing incense before them.

### VIII. CERINTHIANS

The Cerinthians derive their name from Cerinthus; they are also called Merinthians, after Merinthus. They say that the world was made by angels, that the flesh ought to be circumcised, and that other commandments of the Law of this kind ought to be observed.

They assert that Jesus was merely human and did not rise again, but will rise. They also fabulously claim that, after the resurrection, Christ will reign for a thousand years in an earthly kingdom, in accordance with the fleshly pleasures of the belly and lust. Hence they have also been called Chiliasts—millenarians (see *City of God*, book 20, chapter 7).

### IX. NAZARENES

Although the Nazarenes confess that Christ is the Son of God, they nevertheless observe all the practices of the Old Law, which Christians have learned through apostolic tradition not to observe carnally but to understand spiritually (see *Against Cresconius*, book 1, chapter 31).

### X. EBIONITES

The Ebionites also say that Christ was merely human. They observe the carnal commandments of the Law, namely circumcision of the flesh and the other practices from whose burdens we have been freed through the New Testament.

Epiphanius joins the Sampsaeans and Elcesaeans [Note: In ancient manuscripts we find the name written with aspiration, *Helcesaeans*, and below, the sect of the *Helcesaites* or *Helceseites.] to this heresy, placing them under the same number as though it were one heresy, while nevertheless indicating that there is some difference. In what follows, however, he also speaks of them separately, assigning them their own number.

Eusebius, mentioning the sect of the Elcesaeans, writes that they taught that the faith should be denied during persecution but preserved in the heart (Eusebius, book 6, chapter 38).

### XI. VALENTINIANS

The Valentinians derive their name from Valentinus, who invented many fabulous accounts concerning the nature of things. He asserted that there were thirty Aeons, that is, ages or eternal emanations, whose beginning was Depth and Silence. He also calls Depth “Father” [Note: The Michaelian, Colbertine, and Vatican manuscripts add “Silence, the Mother.”]

From these two, as though from a marriage, Understanding and Truth supposedly proceeded, and they brought forth eight Aeons in honor of the Father. From Understanding and Truth proceeded Word and Life, and they brought forth ten Aeons. From Word and Life, in turn, proceeded Humanity and the Church, and they brought forth twelve Aeons.

Thus eight, ten, and twelve make thirty Aeons, having, as we said, their first beginning in Depth and Silence.

He says that Christ, sent by the Father—that is, by Depth—brought with him a spiritual or heavenly body; that he assumed nothing from the virgin Mary, but passed through her as through a channel [Note: Erasmus’s edition reads “as through a crack”] or a tube, without assuming any flesh from her.

[Note: The following addition found in the printed editions is absent from the manuscripts: “He says that the devil was begotten from the thirtieth age and that others were born from the devil who made this world. Therefore he attributes evil not to free choice but to the nature of the world, that is, to the devil’s race.”]

He also denies the resurrection of the flesh, affirming that salvation is received through Christ by spirit and soul alone.

### XII. SECUNDIANS

The Secundians [Note: Louvain and several manuscripts read *Sevandians*. Others, together with Erasmus, read *Secundians*, whose leader is called Secundus by Philastrius, Epiphanius, and others] are said to differ from the Valentinians in adding shameful practices.

### XIII. PTOLEMAEANS

Ptolemy, also a disciple of Valentinus, wishing to found a new heresy, preferred to assert four Aeons and four others in addition.

### XIV. MARCIANS

A certain Marcus also founded a heresy, denying the resurrection of the flesh and asserting that Christ suffered not truly but only apparently. He also thought that there were two principles opposed to each other, affirming something about the Aeons similar to what Valentinus affirmed.

### XV. COLORBASIANS

Colorbasus [Note: The printed books call him *Colarbasus*, changing the second vowel from *o* to *a*, against the ancient writings] followed these men and did not hold very different opinions, asserting that the life and generation of all human beings consist in the seven stars.

### XVI. HERACLEONITES

The Heracleonites derive their name from Heracleon, a disciple of those mentioned above. They assert two principles, one from the other, and from these two many others.

They are said to redeem their dead in a new manner, namely by means of oil, balsam, and water, together with invocations which, they say, they utter over their heads in Hebrew words.

### XVII. OPHITES

The Ophites were named after a serpent, for a serpent is called **ὄφις** (*ophis*) in Greek. They consider this serpent to be Christ. But they also keep a real serpent accustomed to lick their loaves and thus, as it were, to sanctify them as their eucharist.

Some say that these Ophites arose from the Nicolaitans or Gnostics and that, through their fabulous inventions, they came to worship the serpent [Note: This is how it appears in the manuscripts. In the printed editions this heresy is described approximately as follows: “They consider this serpent, which deceived Adam and Eve, to be Christ. But they also keep a real serpent, which they feed and venerate. At the priest’s incantation it comes out of a cave and climbs onto the altar, leaning against the cave; it licks their offerings and, winding itself around them, returns to the cave. Thus they break the offerings into the Eucharist, as though they had been sanctified by the serpent Christ, as they suppose. They report that the worship of this serpent was brought to them from the Nicolaitans or Gnostics.”]

### XVIII. CAIANS

The Caians were so called because they honor Cain, saying that he possessed the greatest power. They also consider Judas the betrayer to be in some way divine and count his crime as a benefit, asserting that he foresaw how greatly Christ’s passion would benefit the human race and therefore handed him over to the Jews to be killed.

They are also said to worship those who, having caused a schism among the first people of God, perished when the earth opened up [Note: The printed editions add after “perished”: “Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.” The manuscripts do not contain this] (Num. 16:31–33), as well as the Sodomites.

They blaspheme the Law and God, its author, and deny the resurrection of the flesh.

### XIX. SETHIANS

The Sethians received their name from Adam’s son, who was called Seth. They honor him, but with fabulous and heretical vanity. For they say that he was born from a heavenly mother, who, they claim, united with a heavenly father so that another divine seed might be born, as a race of sons of God.

They too invent many empty fables about principalities and powers. Some say that they think Shem, the son of Noah, is Christ.

### XX. ARCHONTICS

The Archontics were named after rulers or principalities. They say that the universe created by God is the work of these rulers. They also practice a certain shameful act. They deny the resurrection of the flesh.

### XXI. CERDONIANS

The Cerdonians derive their name from Cerdon, who taught two mutually opposed principles. He said that the God of the Law and the Prophets was not the Father of Christ and was not a good God but a just one, while the Father of Christ was good.

He also said that Christ himself was neither born from a woman nor possessed flesh, and that he did not truly die or suffer anything but only pretended to suffer. Some, however, report that in his two principles he spoke of two gods in such a way that one of them was good and the other evil. He denies the resurrection of the dead and also despises the Old Testament.

### XXII. MARCIONITES

Marcion, from whom the Marcionites were named [Note: The printed editions read, “from whom the Marcionists were named”], also followed Cerdon’s doctrines concerning two principles, although Epiphanius says that he asserted three principles: the good, the just, and the corrupt. Eusebius, however, writes that a certain Syneros, not Marcion, was the founder of three principles and natures (Eusebius, book 5, chapter 13).

### XXIII. APELLITES

The Apellites take their name from Apelles, their leader. He introduces two gods, one good and the other evil, but does not hold that they exist as two different and mutually opposed principles. Rather, he says that there is one principle, namely the good god, and that the other was made by him. Since this other was evil, he is said to have made the world in his own malignity.

Some say that Apelles also held such false opinions about Christ that he said Christ did not indeed bring flesh down from heaven [Note: Only the Louvain edition reads “bring down from heaven”], but received it from the elements of the world and returned it to the world when, rising without flesh, he ascended into heaven.

[Col. 0030]

### XXIV. SEVERIANS

The Severians arose from Severus. They do not drink wine because, in their fabulous folly, they assert that the vine sprouted from Satan and the earth. They too inflate their unsound doctrine with whatever names of rulers they choose, while rejecting the resurrection of the flesh together with the Old Testament.

[Note: The printed editions add: “Furthermore, this man said that a certain girl named Philumena was divinely inspired to foretell the future. Referring her dreams and the passions of his mind to her, he was accustomed secretly to receive warnings from her divinations or prophecies. The same apparition appeared to Philumena in the form of a boy, sometimes asserting that he was Christ and sometimes that he was Paul. When he questioned this apparition, she would answer what she said she had heard. She was also accustomed to perform certain miracles, among which the most notable was that she would put a large loaf of bread into a glass vessel with an extremely narrow mouth and lift it out unharmed with the tips of her fingers; content, as though this food had been divinely given to her, with that alone.”]

All of this is absent from the manuscripts. Perhaps, when someone had written it in the margin of a book concerning not Severus but Apelles, copyists, being mistaken, transferred it here. Tertullian discusses Apelles and his Philumena in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapters 6 and 30.]

### XXV. TATIANISTS

The Tatianists were founded by a certain Tatian [Note: The printed editions read “by Tatius,” but the manuscripts read “by Tatian,” the name by which ancient historians call him]. They condemn marriage and make it entirely equivalent to fornication and other corruptions. They do not admit among their number anyone who uses marriage, whether male or female.

They do not eat meat and abominate all meat. They too have certain fabulous notions about the succession of the ages. They contradict the salvation of the first human being.

Epiphanius distinguishes Tatianists and Encratites in such a way that he calls the Encratites the schismatics of Tatian [Note: The printed editions read *dicant*, “they say.” Several manuscripts more correctly read *dicat*, “he says.” Refer this to Epiphanius, who calls the Encratites a separation from Tatian in the *Epitome*.].

### XXVI. THE CATAPHRYGIANS

The Cataphrygians are those whose founders were Montanus, as though the Paraclete, and his two prophetesses, Prisca and Maximilla. The province of Phrygia gave them their name, because they arose and lived there; even now they have communities in those same regions. They assert that the coming of the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord was fulfilled in themselves rather than in the Apostles. They regard second marriages as fornication; and therefore they say that the Apostle Paul permitted them because “he knew in part and prophesied in part,” for “the perfect had not yet come” (1 Cor. 13:9–10). They deliriously claim that this perfection came in Montanus and his prophetesses.

They are said to have deadly sacraments. For they are reportedly accustomed to make something like their Eucharist from the blood of a one-year-old child, extracting it from the child’s entire body through tiny puncture wounds, mixing it with flour, and making bread from it. If the child dies, it is regarded among them as a martyr; but if it survives, as a great priest.

[Col. 0030] Two Colbertine manuscripts and one Vatican manuscript read “as a great martyr; but if it survives, as a supreme priest.” Other Vatican manuscripts, together with the oldest Floriacensis, the Becheronensis, and others, read “as a martyr; but if it survives, as a most exalted priest.” The Michaelinus manuscript reads “as a first priest.”

### XXVII. THE PEPUZIANS

[Col. 0030] In nearly all the manuscripts: “Pepudians”; and below, in place of *Pepuza*, “Pepudia” is consistently written.

The Pepuzians, or Quintillians, were named after a certain place, which Epiphanius says was a deserted city. They, however, imagining it to be something divine, call it Jerusalem.

[Col. 0031] They grant women so much authority that women are even honored among them with the priesthood. For they say that Christ appeared in the same city, Pepuza, to Quintilla and Priscilla in female form; hence they are also called Quintillians. They too make something from the blood of a child, as we said above that the Cataphrygians do; for they are said to have arisen from them.

Finally, some say that this Pepuza was not a city but a village belonging to Montanus and his prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla; and because they lived there, the place deserved to be called Jerusalem.

### XXVIII. THE ARTOTYRITES

The Artotyrites are those whom their offering gave this name. For they offer bread and cheese, saying that the first human beings celebrated offerings from the fruits of the earth and from sheep. Epiphanius joins them to the Pepuzians.

### XXIX. THE TESSARESKAIDEKATITES

They were so called because they celebrate Easter only on the fourteenth day of the moon, regardless of which day of the week it falls on.

[Col. 0031] The printed editions add here: “in the month of March.”

If it falls on a Sunday, they fast and keep vigil on that very day.

### XXX. THE ALOGI

[Col. 0031] The printed editions have *Alogiani*. The manuscripts restore *Alogi*, as do the Greek heresiographers, who call them Ἄλογοι (*Alogoi*).

They are so called as though they were “without the Word” (for *logos* [λόγος] means “word” in Greek), because they refused to accept God the Word. They reject the Gospel of John, and they do not accept its Apocalypse either, denying that these writings belong to him.

### XXXI. THE ADAMIANS

The Adamianians were named after Adam, whose nakedness in paradise they imitate—the nakedness that existed before sin. Hence they also shun marriage, because Adam neither knew his wife before he sinned nor before he was expelled from paradise. They therefore believe that marriages would not have existed if no one had sinned.

Thus men and women meet naked, hear readings naked, pray naked, celebrate the sacraments naked, and on this basis regard their Church as paradise.

### XXXII. THE ELCESAEANS AND SAMPSAEANS

Epiphanius mentions the Elcesaeans and Sampsaeans here as though in their proper order. He says that they were deceived by a certain false prophet named Elci.

[Col. 0031] Epiphanius calls him *Elkesaîos* in the *Anacephalaeosis*, *Elxai* in the *Panarion*, and *Elxa* in the *Synopsis of the Panarion*.

From his lineage, he says, two women were worshiped by them as goddesses. In other respects, he says, they hold beliefs similar to those of the Ebionites.

### XXXIII. THE THEODOTIANS

The Theodotians were established by a certain Theodotus.

[Col. 0031] The printed editions have “by Theodotion,” and shortly afterward “the same Theodotion.” These readings are corrected from a Vatican manuscript.

They affirm that Christ was merely a human being. The same Theodotus is said to have taught this because, having lapsed during the persecution, he thought he could avoid the disgrace of his fall in this way: he would seem not to have denied God, but only a human being.

### XXXIV. THE MELCHISEDECIANS

The Melchisedecians believe that Melchisedec, priest of the Most High God, was not a human being but the power of God.

### XXXV. THE BARDESANISTS

The Bardesanists were named after a certain Bardesanes, who is said initially to have been distinguished in Christian teaching. Later, however, although not in every respect, he fell into the heresy of Valentinus.

[Col. 0032] After “he fell,” the printed books added the following words: “adding this from his own teaching, so as to attribute human behavior to fate.” We did not find these words in our manuscripts.

### XXXVI. THE NOETIANS

The Noetians were named after a certain Noetus, who said that Christ himself was the Father and the Holy Spirit.

### XXXVII. THE VALESIANS

The Valesians castrate both themselves and their guests, believing that in this way they ought to serve God. They are also said to teach other heretical and shameful doctrines; but what these are, Epiphanius himself does not mention, nor have I been able to find them anywhere.

### XXXVIII. THE CATHARI

[Col. 0032] The manuscripts read: “The Cathari, or Novatians, who themselves …” In Greek they are *Katharoi*.

They arrogantly and offensively call themselves by this name, as though it referred to purity. They do not admit second marriages and deny repentance, following the heretic Novatus; hence they are also called Novatians.

### XXXIX. THE ANGELICI

The Angelici inclined toward the worship of angels. Epiphanius testifies that they have now completely disappeared.

### XL. THE APOSTOLICI

The Apostolici arrogantly called themselves by this name because they did not admit into their communion anyone who lived with a spouse or possessed private property—conditions found among the Catholic Church’s many monks and clerics.

[Col. 0032] The printed editions have “the Catholic Church.” The word “Church” is absent from the manuscripts.

They are therefore heretics because, separating themselves from the Church, they believe that those who use the things they themselves lack have no hope. They resemble the Encratites, for they are also called Apotactites.

[Col. 0032] That is, “Renunciants.”

They are also said to teach certain other distinctive heretical doctrines.

### XLI. THE SABELLIANS

The Sabellians are said to have descended from that Noetus whom we mentioned above; for some report that Sabellius was his disciple. But why Epiphanius counts these as two heresies, I do not know. It is possible that this Sabellius became more famous and that therefore the heresy received its name from him more widely. The Noetians are scarcely known by anyone, whereas the Sabellians are on the lips of many.

Some also call them Praxeans, after Praxeas; and they could likewise be called Hermogenians, after Hermogenes. Praxeas and Hermogenes are said to have been in Africa and to have held the same views. Yet these are not several sects, but several names for one sect, derived from the men who became especially well known within it—just as the Donatists are also the Parmenianists, and the Pelagians likewise the Coelestians.

How, then, it came about that the aforementioned Epiphanius listed the Noetians and Sabellians not as two names for one heresy but as though they were two heresies, I have not been able to determine clearly. If they differ from one another in any respect, he stated it so obscurely—perhaps out of a desire for brevity—that I do not understand it. For in the passage where he mentions the Sabellians so far after the Noetians, as we do, he says:

“The Sabellians, while teaching doctrines similar to those of Noetus, differ in this respect: they say that the Father did not suffer” (Epiphanius, in the *Anacephalaeosis*).

How can this be understood of the Sabellians, when they became so well known for saying that the Father suffered that they are more frequently called Patripassians than Sabellians? Or if, by the phrase “differ in this respect: they say that the Father did not suffer,” he intended this to be understood of the Noetians, who can distinguish them amid such ambiguity? Or how can either group be understood not to say that the Father suffered, when they say that he is himself the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

Philaster, bishop of Brixia, in the very extensive book he composed on heresies, in which he judged that one hundred and twenty-eight heresies should be counted, places the Sabellians immediately after the Noetians:

“Sabellius, his disciple, likewise followed the likeness of his teacher; hence those who came afterward were called Sabellians. They are also called Patripassians, Praxeans after Praxeas, and Hermogenians after Hermogenes, who were in Africa and, holding these views, were expelled from the Catholic Church.”

Certainly, he later says that the same people who held the views of Noetus were called Sabellians, and he mentions the other names of the same sect. Yet he placed the Noetians and Sabellians under two numbers, as though they were two heresies. Why he did so, he himself must know.

[Col. 0033] Perhaps, in place of “and one hundred twenty-eight,” one should read “one hundred and twenty-eight.” M.

### XLII. THE ORIGENIANS

The Origenians were named after a certain Origen—not the one known to nearly everyone, but some other person of whom Epiphanius says, speaking of him and his followers:

“The Origenians of a certain Origen …”

[Col. 0033] Lov.: “the disciples of Origen.” The word “disciples” is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts, as well as from Epiphanius’s Greek text.

“are shameful in their practices; these are the ones who commit unspeakable deeds …”

[Col. 0033] The manuscripts read “doing things impossible to describe.” The Greek is ἀρρητοποιούντες (*arrētopoioûntes*).

“and surrender their bodies to corruption.”

[Col. 0033] In the *Panarion*, heresies 63 and 64, Epiphanius openly admits that he does not know whether these shameful Origenians were named after Origen Adamantius or after another Origen. But in the *Anacephalaeosis*, which alone came into Augustine’s hands without the *Panarion*, he speaks so obscurely of both groups of Origenians that one would believe that the earlier group originated not from the same Origen Adamantius but from another.

Immediately afterward he introduces another group of Origenians:

### XLIII. THE ORIGENIANS

“Other Origenians,” he says, “who are also followers of Origen Adamantius, the teacher, and who reject the resurrection of the dead; introducing Christ and the Holy Spirit as creatures; allegorizing paradise, the heavens, and everything else.”

[Col. 0033] The printed editions read: “who are also followers of that teacher Origen Adamantius, and who deny the resurrection of the dead; who say that Christ and the Holy Spirit are creatures; who do not believe that paradise, the heavens, and the other things exist according to the letter, but in allegory.” The ancient books adhere more closely to the Greek text.

This, then, is what Epiphanius says about Origen. Those who defend him, however, say that he taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one and the same substance, and that he did not reject the resurrection of the dead—although those who have read more of his works strive to convict him on these points as well.

[Col. 0033] The printed editions alone read: “the resurrection of the dead; but those who have read more of his works disagree. Origen also held other doctrines.”

But Origen held other doctrines that the Catholic Church wholly rejects. In these matters it neither falsely accuses him nor can his defenders deceive it—especially concerning the purification and liberation, and then, after a long period, the return of the whole rational creation to the same evils.

For what learned or unlearned Catholic Christian would not recoil vehemently from the purification of evils that he teaches: that even those who ended this life in the greatest possible acts of depravity, crimes, sacrileges, and impiety—and finally the devil himself and his angels—will, though after very long periods, be purified and liberated, restored to the kingdom of God and to the light, and then, again after very long periods, all those who have been liberated will fall back into and return once more to these evils; and that these alternating cycles of blessedness and misery for the rational creation have always existed and will always exist?

Against this utterly empty impiety, and against the philosophers from whom Origen learned it, I argued at greatest length in the books *On the City of God*.

[Col. 0034] On the authority of the ancient manuscripts, we have removed what the printed editions added here:

“Origen himself also says that, when compared with holy men, the Son of God is truth; but when compared with the Father, falsehood; and that the distance between the Apostles and Christ is as great as that between the Son and the Father. Hence the Son should not be prayed to together with the Father, because he is not the author of granting petitions but their supplicant.”

(In Book 21.)

### XLIV. THE PAULIANS

The Paulianists, named after Paul of Samosata, say that Christ did not always exist; rather, they assert that his beginning was when he was born from Mary. They consider him nothing more than a human being.

This heresy once belonged to a certain Artemon. But after it had died out, it was revived by Paul and afterward confirmed by Photinus, so that they are more commonly called Photinians than Paulians.

It was indeed decreed at the Council of Nicaea that these Paulianists should be baptized in the Catholic Church. From this it must be believed that they do not retain the rule of baptism—a rule that many heretics took with them when they departed from the Catholic Church and continue to preserve.

### XLV. PHOTINUS

Epiphanius does not place Photinus immediately after Paul or together with Paul, but inserts others between them. He does not fail to mention that Photinus held similar beliefs; nevertheless, he is said to have opposed Paul in some respect. What that particular respect was, however, he does not say at all.

Philaster, on the other hand, places the two consecutively, under separate and individual numbers, as though they were two heresies, even though he says that Photinus followed Paul’s teaching in every respect.

### XLVI. THE MANICHAEANS

The Manichaeans arose from a certain Persian called Manes. Yet when his insane teaching began to be preached in Greece, his disciples preferred to call him “Manichaeus,” avoiding the name associated with insanity. Hence some of them, as though more learned—and for that very reason more deceitful—call him “Mannichaeus,” with a doubled *n*, as though he were “pouring forth manna.”

[Col. 0034] The manuscripts unanimously have this reading. The printed editions instead read: “when his name began to be preached”; for previously he was called Urbicus—or rather Cubricus, according to Epiphanius, heresy 66. “But in Greece his disciples, avoiding the name associated with insanity, called him, as though more learned and for that very reason more deceitful, Mannichaeus, with a doubled *n*, as though he were pouring forth manna, instead of Manichaeus, that is, ‘insane.’ This man established two principles …”

He constructed two principles, different and opposed to one another, both eternal and coeternal—that is, existing always. Following other ancient heretics, he posited two natures and substances, namely good and evil.
