According to their doctrines, they assert the struggle and mixture of these with one another, the purification of the good from the evil, and the eternal damnation of the good that cannot be purified, together with the evil. They tell many stories about these matters, but to weave all of them into this work would be excessively long.

From these vain and impious stories they are compelled to say that the good souls—which they believe must be liberated from mixture with the nature of evil souls, their opposite—belong to the nature of the one who is God.

Accordingly, they confess that the world was made by the nature of the good, that is, by the nature of God, but they say this occurred through the mixture of good and evil that took place when the two natures struggled against each other. They say that the purification and liberation of the good from the evil is accomplished not only throughout the whole world and from all its elements by the powers of God, but also through the food consumed by their Elect.

[Col. 0035] The printed editions have “the power of God.” The manuscripts more correctly have “the powers of God,” which, as the Manichaeans say below, are holy powers in the sun and moon, as though in two ships. The old book *On Heresies*, published by Jacobus Sirmondus under the title *Praedestinatus*, agrees here in its Augiensis copy, although it prints “the power of God” in this passage.

For they claim that God’s substance is mixed into those foods, just as it is mixed into the whole world. They believe that this substance is purified in their Elect through the way of life followed by the Manichaean Elect, as holier and more excellent than that of their Hearers. They wished their Church to consist of these two professions, namely the Elect and the Hearers.

In all other human beings, including their own Hearers, they believe that this portion of the good and divine substance—which is held mixed and bound up in food and drink—is bound more tightly and more impurely, especially in those who beget children.

Whatever light is purified from every place, they believe is returned to the kingdom of God, as to its proper dwelling places, through certain ships that they identify as the moon and sun. They likewise claim that these ships were fashioned from the pure substance of God. They say that this bodily light, which lies before the eyes of mortal animals, belongs to the nature of God—not only in these ships, where they believe it to be most pure, but also in all other luminous things, where, according to them, it is held in a mixed state and is believed to require purification.

They attribute five elements, which produced their own rulers, to the nation of darkness. They call these elements by the following names: smoke, darkness, fire, water, and wind. From smoke were born two-footed animals, from which they believe human beings derive their origin; from darkness, creeping creatures; from fire, four-footed animals; from water, swimming creatures; and from wind, flying creatures.

They say that five other elements were sent from the kingdom and substance of God to fight these five evil elements and were mixed into that struggle: air against smoke, light against darkness, good fire against evil fire, good water against evil water, and good wind against evil wind.

They distinguish those ships—that is, the two lights of heaven—in this way: they say that the moon was made from good water, but the sun from good fire. They say that holy powers are in these ships, and that these powers transform themselves into males in order to entice the women of the opposing nation, and again into women in order to entice the males of that same opposing nation.

[Col. 0035] This portion of the sentence, “and again … of that opposing nation,” is restored from the manuscripts. See *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 44.

Through this enticement, they say, the desire of those beings is aroused, and the light that they held mixed into their members escapes from them; it is received for purification by the angels of light, and, once purified, is placed upon those ships to be carried back to its proper kingdoms.

[Col. 0036] On this occasion—or rather, through a certain necessity imposed by their execrable superstition—their Elect are compelled to consume, as though it were a sprinkled Eucharist, food mixed with human semen, so that the divine substance may be purified from this also, just as from the other foods they consume.

But they deny that they do this, and claim that certain others under the name of Manichaeans do it. Nevertheless, they were exposed in the church, as you know, at Carthage, when you had already been established there as a deacon, at the time when, under the authority of Ursus the tribune, who then presided over the imperial household, some of them were brought before the authorities.

[Col. 0036] See Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 16.

There a girl named Margarita exposed this unspeakable crime. Since she was not yet twelve years old, she said that she had been violated on account of this wicked rite.

[Col. 0036] The manuscripts have “had been corrupted.” The printed editions have “had been violated.”

At that point they scarcely compelled a certain Manichaean woman named Eusebia, who was regarded as a consecrated virgin and had suffered the same thing for the same reason, to confess. At first she claimed to be intact and requested that a midwife examine her. Once examined, and when the nature of her condition had been discovered, she likewise disclosed the entire shameful crime: flour is placed beneath the intercourse of the participants to receive and mix with their semen—a detail that, because Margarita had revealed it while he was absent, he had not heard.

More recently, several of them were found and brought to the church. As the episcopal records that you sent us show, under careful questioning they confessed that this was not a sacrament but an abomination. One of them, named Viator, said that those who practice these things are properly called Catharists.

[Col. 0036] The printed editions add: “that is, purifiers or cleansers.”

Although he said that the other branches of the same Manichaean sect were divided into the Mattarii and, more specifically, the Manichaeans, he could not deny that all three forms had been propagated by one founder and that all were generally Manichaeans.

[Col. 0036] The printed editions have “Macarians,” an error followed by Sirmondus in his *Praedestinatus*. The Augiensis copy of the same *Praedestinatus*, however, has “Mattarii.” All Augustine’s manuscripts likewise have this reading. They are called Mattarii because they sleep on mats, according to Book 5 of *Against Faustus*, chapter 5.

Certainly, the Manichaean books are common to all of them without question. In these books are written those monstrous doctrines concerning the transformation of the rulers of darkness from males into females and from females into males, in order to entice and dissolve them through desire, so that the divine substance held captive within them might escape liberated from them. From this source arose the shameful practice that each of them denies belongs to his group.

For they believe that they imitate the divine powers as much as they can, in order to purify a portion of their god—though they believe that this portion is held in an impure state in all heavenly and earthly bodies, and in the seeds of all things, including human semen.

Consequently, it follows that they must purify it from human semen by eating it, just as they purify it from the other seeds that they consume in food. Hence they are also called Catharists, as though they were “purifiers,” cleansing it with such diligence that they do not abstain even from this most horrifying indecency of food.

Yet they do not eat meat, on the grounds that the divine substance has escaped from the dead or slaughtered and that so much and such a kind of it remains there that it is no longer worthy of being purified in the belly of the Elect.

They do not even eat eggs, as though the eggs expire when broken and as though one ought not to consume any dead bodies, and as though only that part of flesh lives which is received by flour lest it die.

Nor do they use milk as food, although it is milked or suckled from a living animal. They abstain not because they think that none of the divine substance is mixed into it, but because their error is inconsistent with itself. They also do not drink wine, saying that it is the gall of the rulers of darkness, although they eat grapes; nor do they drink any must, even the freshest.

They believe that the souls of their Hearers pass into the Elect, or, by a more fortunate shortcut, into the food of their Elect, so that once purified there they may never return to any bodies.

But they believe that the other souls return into animals and into everything that is fixed by roots and nourished in the earth.

[Col. 0037] The Lovaniensis edition alone has “and into everything,” omitting “into.”

For they believe that herbs and trees live in such a way that the life within them both senses and feels pain when they are harmed; and they believe that no one can pluck or tear anything from them without causing them suffering.

[Col. 0037] The manuscripts read “when it is harmed.”

For this reason they consider it a crime even to clear a field of thorns. Thus they foolishly accuse agriculture, the most innocent of all the arts, as guilty of many murders. They believe that their Hearers are forgiven for this because the Hearers provide food for their Elect, so that the divine substance, purified in the Elect’s belly, may obtain forgiveness for those whose offering supplies it for purification.

Thus the Elect themselves do no work in the fields, do not pluck fruit, and do not even tear off leaves. They wait for these things to be brought for their use by their Hearers, living, according to their own folly, from so many and such great murders committed by others.

They also instruct their Hearers that, if they eat meat, they must not kill animals, lest they offend the rulers of darkness bound together in the heavens, from whom they say all flesh derives its origin. And if they have sexual relations with their spouses, they must nevertheless avoid conception and procreation, lest the divine substance that enters them through food be bound by fleshly bonds in their offspring.

For they believe that souls enter all flesh—that is, through food and drink. Hence they unquestionably condemn marriage and, insofar as they can, prohibit it, since they prohibit procreation, which is the purpose for which marriages are joined.

They assert that Adam and Eve were born from parents who were rulers of the smoke. Their father, named Saclas, had devoured all the offspring of his associates; and whatever divine substance he had thereby absorbed, he bound together with his wife through intercourse in the flesh of their offspring as though with an extremely tenacious bond.

They affirm that Christ was the one whom our Scripture calls the serpent. They say that he enlightened Adam and Eve so that they opened the eyes of knowledge and distinguished good from evil. They claim that this Christ came in the last times to liberate souls, not bodies.

They say that he was not truly in the flesh, but presented an apparent form of flesh to deceive human senses, in which he likewise falsely pretended not only to die but also to rise again.

They hold that the God who gave the Law through Moses and spoke through the Hebrew Prophets is not the true God but one of the rulers of darkness.

They read the writings of the New Testament as though they had been falsified, accepting from them whatever they wish and rejecting whatever they do not wish; and, although treating them as wholly true, they place certain apocryphal writings above them.

They say that the Lord Jesus Christ’s promise concerning the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit (John 16:7), was fulfilled in their heresiarch Manichaeus. For this reason he calls himself in his writings an apostle of Jesus Christ, because Jesus Christ promised that he would send the Holy Spirit and sent him in Manichaeus.

Therefore Manichaeus himself also had twelve disciples, in imitation of the apostolic number—a number that the Manichaeans still preserve today. From among their Elect they have twelve whom they call teachers, and a thirteenth who is their leader. They also have seventy-two bishops, who are ordained by the teachers, and presbyters, who are ordained by the bishops. The bishops also have deacons.

All the others are simply called Elect. Yet those who appear suitable are sent out either to support and enlarge this error where it already exists, or to sow it where it does not yet exist.

They assert that baptism in water brings no salvation to anyone. Nor do they consider that any of those whom they deceive should be baptized.

During the day they pray to the sun wherever it travels. At night they pray to the moon if it is visible; but if it is not visible, they stand praying toward the northern region, the direction in which the sun returns to the east after setting.

They do not attribute the origin of sins to the free choice of the will, but to the substance of the opposing nation. Since they dogmatically assert that this substance is mixed into human beings, they claim that all flesh is the work not of God but of an evil mind, which is coeternal with God as the contrary principle.

They do not believe that carnal desire—by which the flesh desires against the spirit—is an infirmity present in us because human nature was corrupted in the first man. Rather, they regard it as an opposing substance attached to us, so that when we are liberated and purified it will be separated from us and will itself continue to live immortally in its own nature.

They say that these two souls, or two minds—one good and the other evil—are in conflict within one human being when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17).

Nor do they believe that this defect will ever be healed in us, as we say. Instead, they claim that this substance of evil, separated and shut away from us, will live after the end of this age and the conflagration of the world in a certain globe, as though in an eternal prison.

They assert that an outer covering or roof, composed of souls that are good by nature but were unable to be cleansed from contact with the evil nature, will continually approach and adhere to that globe.

### XLVII. THE HIERACITES

[Col. 0038] The printed editions have *Hierachitae*. The manuscripts, without aspiration in the fourth syllable, have *Hieracitae*. The Greek is Ἱερακῖται (*Hierakitai*).

The Hieracites, whose founder was called Hieracas, deny the resurrection of the flesh.

[Col. 0039] They admit into their communion only monks and nuns, and those who have no marriages. They say that little children do not belong to the kingdom of heaven because they have no merits from the struggle by which vices are overcome.

[Col. 0039] The manuscripts have this reading. The Lovaniensis has “by which vices are separated”; Erasmus has “by which vices are surpassed.”

### XLVIII. THE MELETIANS

The Meletians were named after Meletius. They refused to pray with those who had returned, that is, those who had fallen during the persecution, and they formed a schism.

[Col. 0039] Lovaniensis has “or they formed a schism.” The word “or” is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts.

They are now said to be allied with the Arians.

### XLIX. THE ARIANS

The Arians, named after Arius, are most widely known for the error by which they refuse to acknowledge that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one and the same nature and substance—or, to state it more precisely, essence, which in Greek is called οὐσία (*ousia*).

They wish the Son to be a creature, and the Holy Spirit to be a creature of a creature—that is, created by the Son.

They are less well known for believing that Christ assumed flesh alone, without a soul. Nor have I found that anyone ever disputed this matter against them. But that it is true, Epiphanius did not conceal, and I learned it with complete certainty from some of their writings and conversations.

We also know that they rebaptize Catholics; whether they rebaptize non-Catholics as well, I do not know.

### L. THE VADIANS

[Col. 0039] The Floriacensis manuscript has *Adiani* only in this passage; above, in the list prefixed to the work, it has *Vadiani*, together with the other manuscripts. The *Praedestinatus* in the Augiensis manuscript consistently calls them *Valdiani* in the two places where Sirmondus printed *Audiani*. In Greek they are in fact called Αὐδιανοί (*Audianoi*).

Epiphanius calls the Vadians schismatics rather than heretics. Others call them Anthropomorphites because, through carnal thinking, they imagine God in the likeness of a corruptible human being. Epiphanius attributes this to their rusticity, sparing them the designation “heretics.”

He says that they separated themselves from our communion by blaming wealthy bishops and celebrating Easter with the Jews. Nevertheless, there are some who assert that in Egypt they remained in communion with the Catholic Church.

As for the Photinians, whom Epiphanius mentions at this point, I have already said enough above.

### LI. THE SEMI-ARIANS

Epiphanius calls Semi-Arians those who say that the Son is of similar essence (ὁμοιούσιον, *homoiousion*), as though they were not complete Arians.

[Col. 0039] Lovaniensis has “who say that the Father and the Son are of similar essence.”

But it is as though Arians did not wish even to say that the Son is similar, since the Eunomians are commonly reported to have taught this.

### LII. THE MACEDONIANS

The Macedonians derive their name from Macedonius.

[Col. 0039] The printed editions add “bishop of the Church of Constantinople,” but this is absent from the manuscripts.

The Greeks call them Πνευματομάχοι (*Pneumatomachoi*), “fighters against the Spirit,” because they dispute concerning the Holy Spirit. They hold a correct belief concerning the Father and the Son, namely that they are of one and the same substance or essence. But they refuse to believe this concerning the Holy Spirit, saying that he is a creature.

Some more properly call them Semi-Arians because in this question they agree partly with the Semi-Arians and partly with us. Nevertheless, some report that they say that the Holy Spirit is not God but the deity of the Father and the Son, and that he has no proper substance of his own.

### LIII. THE AERIANS

The Aerians derive their name from a certain Aerius, who, although he was a presbyter, is said to have been distressed that he could not be ordained a bishop. He fell into the Arian heresy and added certain doctrines of his own, saying that offerings ought not to be made for the departed.

[Col. 0040] The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read: “saying that one ought not to pray or offer an offering for the dead.”

He also said that fasts established by solemn custom should not be observed, but that each person should fast whenever he wished, so as not to appear to be under the Law. He further maintained that no distinction ought to separate a presbyter from a bishop.

Some report that these people, like the Encratites or Apotactites, admit into their communion only the continent and those who have renounced the world in such a way that they possess no private property.

Epiphanius says that they do not abstain from eating meat; Philaster, however, attributes this abstinence to them as well.

### LIV. THE AETIANS

The Aetians were named after Aetius. They are also called Eunomians, after Eunomius, the disciple of Aetius, by which name they became better known.

Eunomius, skilled in dialectic and defending this heresy more sharply and famously, asserted that the Son is entirely unlike the Father and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son.

He is also said to have been so hostile to good morals that he maintained that no one would be harmed by committing and persisting in any sins whatsoever, provided that he shared in the faith he taught.

### LV. THE APOLLINARIANS

Apollinaris founded the Apollinarians. They dissented from the Catholic faith concerning Christ’s soul, saying, like the Arians, that God Christ assumed flesh without a soul.

[Col. 0040] The manuscripts have “flesh alone, without a soul.”

When they were defeated in this question by the testimony of the Gospels, they said that the mind—which is the rational faculty of the human soul—was absent from Christ’s soul, and that the Word himself was present in him in place of it.

They are also said to have departed from the true faith concerning Christ’s flesh in this way: they maintained that the flesh and the Word were of one and the same substance, asserting with extreme contentiousness that the Word became flesh—that is, that something of the Word was converted and changed into flesh—and not that he assumed flesh from Mary’s flesh.

### LVI. THE ANTIDICOMARITES

[Col. 0040] The printed editions have *Antidicomarianitae*, following the Greek. All the Latin manuscripts here have *Antidicomaritae*.

The Antidicomarites were called heretics because they contradicted Mary’s virginity so thoroughly that they asserted that after Christ’s birth she had had relations with her husband.

### LVII. MASSALIANS

Epiphanius places the Massalians last among the heresies. [Note: The printed editions have *Psallianorum* (“of the Psallians”), but most manuscripts have *Massalianorum*. A smaller number have *Massilianorum*, although these too have *Massalianos* in the list before the preface. The Greek writers agree.] This name comes from the Syriac language. In Greek they are called *Εὐχῖται* (*Euchitai*), named from praying. For they pray so much that it seems incredible to those who hear this about them. For when the Lord said, “One ought always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke 18:1), and the Apostle, “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17)—which is most soundly understood to mean that the appointed times for prayer should be omitted on no day—they carry this out to such excess that for this reason they were judged worthy of being called heretics.

[Note: In the manuscripts: “they tell some fantastical and ridiculously fabulous tale.”]

Although some say that they tell a certain fanciful and ridiculous story about the purification of souls [Col. 0041]—namely, that when a person is being purified, a sow with piglets is seen to emerge from his mouth, and that a fire which does not burn likewise enters him in visible form. Epiphanius adds to these the Euphemites, Martyrianists, and Satanianists. [Note: The printed editions have *Satamanos*, through the fault of those who edited them; all the manuscripts have *Satanianos*.] He places all of these with them as one heresy.

The Euchites are said to hold that monks may not work at anything for the sake of sustaining their lives, and thus they profess themselves monks in such a way as to abstain altogether from labor.

The aforementioned Cypriot bishop therefore brought his work on heresies down to these groups. Among the Greeks he was regarded as one of the great men, and many praised him for the soundness of his Catholic faith. In recounting the heretics, I followed not his limits but his order. For I included some things from other sources that he did not include, and omitted some things that he did include. Thus I explained some matters at greater length than he did, others more briefly, and in certain cases displayed an equal brevity, regulating everything as the purpose of my undertaking required.

Accordingly, he comprised the eighty heresies—after separating twenty which, as he judged, had arisen before the Lord’s coming—and included the remaining sixty, which arose after the Lord’s ascension, in five very brief books, making all six books part of his entire work. [Note: The printed editions have *in sex libros totius ejusdem sui operis fecit concludi* (“caused the whole of the same work to be concluded in six books”). The manuscripts, however, have neither the word *in* nor the verb *concludi*.]

I, however, since at your request I undertook to recall those heresies which after Christ’s glorification raised themselves against Christ’s teaching, even under the guise of the Christian name, transferred fifty-seven from Epiphanius’s own work into mine. Where I could find no difference, I counted two as one; and again, where he wished to make one out of two, I listed them separately under their own numbers.

But I must still recall either those which I found in other authors or those which I myself remember. I shall therefore now add those which Philaster included and Epiphanius did not.

### LVIII. METANGISMONITES

Those who assert the Metangismon may be called Metangismonites. They say that the Son is in the Father as a vessel is in a vessel, imagining them almost as two bodily objects, so that the Son enters into the Father like a smaller vessel into a larger one.

Hence this error also received its name, since in Greek it was called *μεταγγισμός* (*metangismos*). For *ἀγγεῖον* (*angeion*) means “vessel” in that language; but the entry of one vessel into another cannot be expressed by a single Latin word, as it can in Greek by *metangismos*.

### LIX. SELEUCIANS

The Seleucians, or Hermians, are named after their founders, Seleucus or Hermias. They say that the matter of the elements from which the world was made was not made by God but is coeternal with God. They do not attribute the soul to God the Creator, but hold that angels are the creators of souls, from fire and spirit.

They assert that evil sometimes comes from God and sometimes from matter. They deny that the Savior sits in the flesh at the right hand of the Father, but say that he stripped it off and placed it in the sun, taking their opportunity from the Psalm where it is written, “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 18:6).

They also deny a visible paradise. They do not accept baptism in water. They do not believe that there will be a resurrection, but that resurrection occurs daily in the generation of children.

### LX. PROCLIANITES

The Proclianites followed these people and added that Christ did not come in the flesh.

### LXI. PATRICIANS

The Patricians, named after Patricius, say that the substance of human flesh was created not by God but by the devil. They consider it so necessary to flee and detest it that some of them are said even to have wished to be rid of the flesh by inflicting death upon themselves. [Note: The manuscripts have *morte sibimet illata* (“by death inflicted upon themselves”).]

### LXII. ASCITES

The Ascites were named from a wineskin: *ἀσκός* (*askos*) means “wineskin” in Greek. They are said to go about like revelers, carrying an inflated and covered wineskin, as though they themselves were the Gospel’s new wineskins filled with new wine.

### LXIII. PASSALORYNCHITES

The Passalorynchites devote themselves to silence to such an extent that they place a finger against their nostrils and lips, lest they even rob silence itself of its due by their voice, whenever they believe that they ought to remain silent.

This is also the source of their name: *πάσσαλος* (*passalos*) means “stake” in Greek, and *ῥύγχος* (*rhynchos*) means “nose.” Why those who composed this name preferred to signify “finger” by “stake,” I do not know, since “finger” is also *δάκτυλος* (*daktylos*) in Greek, and they could certainly be called Dactylorynchites, a much clearer name.

### LXIV. AQUARIANS

The Aquarians received this name because they offer water in the cup of the Sacrament, rather than what the whole Church offers.

### LXV. COLUTHIANS

The Coluthians were named after a certain Coluthus, who said that God does not make evil, contrary to what is written: “I am God, creating evil” (Isaiah 45:7).

### LXVI. FLORINIANS

The Florinians were named after Florinus, who said, on the contrary, that God created evil, contrary to what is written: “God made all things, and behold, they were very good” (Genesis 1:31).

Thus, although they said opposite things to one another, both resisted the divine utterances. God does create evil by inflicting entirely just punishments, something Coluthus did not see; but he does not create evil natures and substances insofar as they are natures and substances, which was Florinus’s error.

### LXVII.

Philaster mentions a certain heresy without an author or a name. It says that this world will remain even after the resurrection of the dead in the same condition in which it now exists, and will not be changed so as to become a new heaven and a new earth, as Holy Scripture promises (Isaiah 65:17; 2 Peter 3:13; and Revelation 21:1).

### LXVIII.

There is another heresy of people who always walk barefoot, because the Lord said to Moses—or to Joshua [Note: The words “or to Joshua” are absent from the manuscripts]—“Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exodus 3:5; and Joshua 5:16), and because the prophet Isaiah was commanded to walk barefoot (Isaiah 20:2).

It is therefore a heresy because they walk in this way not on account of bodily hardship, but because they understand the divine testimonies in that manner. [Note: The Am. Er. edition and most manuscripts omit: “It is therefore a heresy because they walk in this way not on account of bodily hardship, but because they understand the divine testimonies in that manner.”]

[Col. 0043]

### LXIX. DONATIANS OR DONATISTS

The Donatians, or Donatists, first created a schism because Caecilianus had been appointed bishop of the Church of Carthage against their will. They accused him of crimes that had not been proved, especially that he had been ordained by traditors—those who had handed over the divine Scriptures.

But after the case had been heard and concluded with him, they were discovered to be guilty of falsehood. They then solidified their obstinate dissent and turned the schism into a heresy, as though the Church of Christ had perished from the whole world because of Caecilianus’s crimes—whether real or, as seemed more likely to the judges, false—although its future existence had been promised throughout the world, and had remained only in Donatus’s African faction, while in the other regions of the earth it had been extinguished as though by the contagion of communion.

They even dare to rebaptize Catholics. In this they have confirmed themselves still more as heretics, since the whole Catholic Church has agreed not to annul the common baptism even in heretics.

We understand Donatus to have been the founder of this heresy. Coming from Numidia and dividing the Christian populace against Caecilianus, he joined with bishops of the same faction and ordained Majorinus bishop at Carthage. Another Donatus succeeded Majorinus in the same division. By his eloquence he so strengthened this heresy that many think they are called Donatists on his account rather than on account of the first Donatus.

His writings still exist. In them it appears that he did not hold a Catholic doctrine of the Trinity, but, although he regarded the Son as of the same substance, he nevertheless thought the Son lesser than the Father and the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son. The multitude of the Donatists, however, paid no attention to this error which he held concerning the Trinity; nor is anyone among them easily found who knows that he thought this way.

In the city of Rome these heretics are called Montenses. From Africa they customarily send them a bishop, or their African bishops travel from there to Rome, if they happen to decide to ordain one there.

In Africa, those called Circumcellions also belong to this heresy. They are a rustic class of people of notorious audacity, perpetrating monstrous crimes not only against others but also not sparing themselves in the same mad ferocity. For they are accustomed to kill themselves by various forms of death, especially by throwing themselves from heights, drowning, or fire. They also lead others of either sex whom they can into this madness, sometimes threatening people with death unless they allow themselves to be killed by others.

Nevertheless, most Donatists disapprove of such people and do not think that they are defiled by communion with those who madly cast the crime of unknown Africans before the Christian world.

Many schisms also arose among the Donatists themselves, and various groups separated from them one after another. The remaining great multitude did not notice their separation.

But at Carthage, Maximianus was ordained against Primianus by nearly one hundred bishops of the same error. He was condemned by the remaining three hundred and ten, together with the twelve who had been physically present at his ordination, in a most savage prosecution. This forced them to acknowledge that the baptism of Christ could also be administered outside the Church.

For they received certain people among themselves, together with those whom they had baptized outside their Church, into their offices without requiring anyone to repeat baptism. They did not cease to use the public authorities against them in order to correct them, nor did they fear contaminating their communion by the crimes of those whom they had so severely condemned by the judgment of their council.

### LXX. PRISCILLIANISTS

The Priscillianists, whom Priscillianus founded in Spain, chiefly follow a mixture of the doctrines of the Gnostics and Manichaeans. Although filth from other heresies also flowed into them, as into a kind of sewer, in a horrible confusion. [Note: Only the Lov. edition has *in eas* (“into them,” feminine); the others have *in eos* (“into them,” masculine).]

To conceal their contaminations and shameful practices, they also have the following words among their doctrines:

> Swear, perjure yourself, do not betray the secret.

They say that souls are of the same nature and substance as God, and that they descend to the earth for a kind of voluntary contest, passing through the seven heavens and certain principalities in stages. They encounter an evil prince, by whom they wish this world to have been made, and by this prince they are sown through various bodies of flesh.

They also assert that human beings are bound by the fateful stars, and that our body is composed according to the twelve signs of heaven, as those commonly called astrologers hold. They place Aries in the head, Taurus in the neck, Gemini in the shoulders, Cancer in the chest, and, proceeding through the remaining signs by name, arrive at the feet, which they assign to Pisces, the last sign called by astrologers.

This heresy weaves together these and other fabulous, vain, and sacrilegious notions, whose examination would take too long.

It also avoids flesh as though it were unclean food, separating married couples whom it has been able to persuade of this evil—husbands from unwilling wives and wives from unwilling husbands. For they attribute the making of all flesh not to the good and true God but to wicked angels.

In this respect they are more cunning than the Manichaeans: they reject none of the canonical Scriptures, but read everything together with the apocryphal books and accept it as authoritative, while turning into their own meanings by allegorical interpretation whatever they find in the sacred books that overturns their error.

Concerning Christ, they hold the Sabellian sect, saying that he is one and the same not only as the Son but also as the Father and the Holy Spirit.

### LXXI.

Philaster says that there are other heretics who do not eat food with human beings. But he does not state whether they do this with others who do not belong to the same sect, or also among themselves.

He also says that they think correctly concerning the Father and the Son, but not in a Catholic manner concerning the Holy Spirit, since they believe him to be a creature.

### LXXII.

He says that a heresy arose from a certain Rhetorius, one of astonishingly excessive foolishness, which asserts that all heretics walk rightly and speak the truth. This is so absurd that it seems incredible to me.

### LXXIII.

There is another heresy which says that the divinity in Christ suffered pain when his flesh was nailed to the cross.

[Col. 0045]

### LXXIV.

There is another which asserts God to be so three-formed that one part of him is the Father, another part the Son, and another part the Holy Spirit. That is, it says that the one God consists of the parts which make up this Trinity, as though God were completed from these three parts and neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit were perfect in himself.

### LXXV.

There is another which says that water was not created by God but was always coeternal with him.

### LXXVI.

Another says that the human body, not the soul, is the image of God.

### LXXVII.

Another says that there are innumerable worlds, as certain Gentile philosophers have believed.

### LXXVIII.

Another says that the souls of the wicked are changed into demons and into whatever animals correspond to their merits.

### LXXIX.

Another believes that the unbelievers believed in Christ when he descended to hell, and holds that all of them were thereafter liberated.

### LXXX.

Another, failing to understand that the Son was eternally begotten, thinks that his birth began at a point in time. Yet, wishing to confess the Son as coeternal with the Father, it believes that he existed with him before he was born from him. That is, it says that he always existed, but that he was not always the Son; rather, from the time he was born from him, he began to be the Son.

I thought that these heresies should be transferred into this work of mine from Philaster’s work. He himself also mentions others, but they do not seem to me to deserve to be called heresies. Whatever I have listed without names, he likewise did not mention by name. [Note: At this point the printed editions wrongly add: “which are without the names of their authors.”]

### LXXXI. LUCIFERIANS

The Luciferians arose from Lucifer, bishop of Calaris, and became widely known. Neither Epiphanius nor Philaster placed them among the heretics. I believe that they founded only a schism, not a heresy.

Nevertheless, I read in the work of a certain author—whose name I did not find in that same little work—that the Luciferians were placed among the heretics, in these words:

> The Luciferians, although they hold the Catholic truth in all things, fall into this most foolish error: they say that the soul is generated by transmission; and they say the same concerning the flesh and that it is of the substance of the flesh.

Whether this author believed that they should be placed among the heretics because they hold this view concerning the soul—if indeed they truly hold it—and whether he believed correctly; or whether, even if they did not hold it, or do not hold it, they are nevertheless heretics because they have confirmed their dissent with obstinate determination: this is another question, and it does not seem to me that it should be treated here.

### LXXXII. JOVINIANISTS

I also found the Jovinianists in this author, though I already knew of them. This heresy arose in our own time from a certain monk named Jovinianus, when we were still young. [Note: See the Admonition in the work *On the Good of Marriage*, vol. 6.]

Like the Stoic philosophers, he said that all sins are equal, that a person cannot sin after receiving the bath of regeneration, and that fasts or abstinence from particular foods are of no benefit.

He destroyed Mary’s virginity, saying that she was corrupted by giving birth. He also equated the virginity of consecrated women and the continence of men who choose a celibate life in holiness with the merits of chaste and faithful marriages. Thus, it is said that certain consecrated virgins of advanced age in Rome, where he taught these things, married after hearing him.

He himself, to be sure, neither had nor wished to have a wife. He argued that this was not because it would contribute some greater merit before God in the kingdom of eternal life, but because it was beneficial for the present necessity—namely, so that a person would not have to endure the troubles of marriage.

This heresy, however, was quickly suppressed and extinguished, and it could not proceed as far as deceiving any priests.

### LXXXIII.

When I examined the history of Eusebius, to which Rufinus added two books concerning subsequent times after translating it into Latin, I did not find any heresy that I had not read about in those authors, except one which Eusebius places in his sixth book, saying that it had arisen in Arabia.

Since he names no founder for them, we may call them Arabians. They said that souls die and dissolve together with bodies, and that both will rise again at the end of the age. But Eusebius says that they were corrected very quickly by Origen’s disputation, when he was present and addressed them (Eusebius, book 6, chapter 37).

Now those heresies must be mentioned which were not found by us in those authors but have come to our recollection in one way or another.

### LXXXIV. HELVIDIANS

The Helvidians arose from Helvidius. They contradict Mary’s virginity to such an extent that they maintain that after Christ she bore other children from her husband Joseph.

But surely Epiphanius called these people Antidicomarites, omitting the name of Helvidius. [Note: The manuscripts have: “But without doubt Epiphanius called these people Antidicomarites.”] [Note: Epiphanius calls them Antidicomarianites.]

### LXXXV. PATERNIANS

The Paternianists believe that the lower parts of the human body were made not by God but by the devil. Granting complete license to every kind of shameful act arising from those parts, they live in the utmost impurity. Some also call them Venustians.

### LXXXVI. TERTULLIANISTS

The Tertullianists arose from Tertullian, whose many little works are read as written with great eloquence. Gradually declining, they were able to survive down to our own time in their last remnants in the city of Carthage. But when I was there several years ago—which I think you also remember—they had been completely extinguished in every respect.

For the very few who remained passed into the Catholic Church and handed over to the Catholics their basilica, which is still very well known.

Accordingly, Tertullian, as his writings indicate, says that the soul is indeed immortal, but insists that it is a body—not only the soul, but God himself as well. [Note: The printed editions have: “but insists that it is an embodied form; and he says that not only the soul but God himself is corporeal, although not embodied. Nevertheless, he is not made a heretic on this account,” and so forth. We have removed these words, which are absent from the manuscripts.]

Yet he is not for this reason said to have become a heretic. It could in some way be thought that he calls the divine nature and substance itself a body—not a body whose parts can or must be conceived as larger or smaller, such as all the things we properly call bodies; although he holds something of this sort concerning the soul. But, as I said, he could be thought to call God a body because God is not nothing, not emptiness, and not a quality of body or soul; rather, he is wholly present everywhere, divided by no intervals of place, yet remaining immutable in his own nature and substance.

Tertullian therefore did not become a heretic for this reason, but because, after passing over to the Cataphrygians—whom he had previously refuted—he began to condemn second marriages as adulteries, contrary to apostolic teaching (1 Timothy 4:3), and afterward, having separated even from them, propagated his own assemblies.

He also says that the souls of the worst human beings are changed into demons after death. [Note: On the authority of the manuscripts, we have again removed what the printed books added: “and he believes that the state of the soul is propagated by transmission.”]

### LXXXVII.

There is a certain rustic heresy in our region—that is, in the region of Hippo—or rather, there was one. For, gradually diminished, it had remained in a single small village. There were indeed very few members, but all the inhabitants were involved; now all have been corrected and become Catholics, and no one remains in that error.

They were called Abelonians, by the Punic inflection of the name. Some say that they were named after Adam’s son, who was called Abel. We may therefore call them Abelonians or Abeloites. [Note: The manuscripts have *Abeloitae*.]

They did not have sexual relations with their wives, yet the doctrine of the sect did not allow them to live without wives. Thus a male and a female lived together under a profession of continence and adopted a boy and a girl, who were to become the successors of the same union.

Whenever one of them was overtaken by death, another was substituted, provided that two people of different sexes succeeded two people of different sexes in the household’s association. For when either parent died, the children served the one who remained until that person also died. After that person’s death, they likewise adopted a boy and a girl.

They were never without people to adopt, because neighbors throughout the surrounding area had children and gladly gave their poor children the hope of another’s inheritance.

### LXXXVIII. PELAGIANS

The Pelagian heresy is the most recent of all in the present age, having arisen from the monk Pelagius. Caelestius followed him so closely as a teacher that their followers are also called Caelestians.

These people are so hostile to the grace of God—by which we were predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in him (Ephesians 1:5), by which we are rescued from the power of darkness so that we may believe in him and be transferred into his kingdom (Colossians 1:13), on account of which he said, “No one comes to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father” (John 6:66), and by which charity is poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5), so that faith may work through love (Galatians 5:6)—that they believe a human being can fulfill all the divine commandments without it.

For if this were true, the Lord would seem to have said in vain, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). [Note: In most manuscripts the following is absent: “For if this were true, the Lord would seem to have said in vain, ‘Without me you can do nothing.’”]

Finally, when Pelagius was rebuked by the brothers because he attributed nothing to the help of God’s grace in carrying out God’s commandments, he yielded to their correction only to the extent that he did not place grace above free will, but with deceitful infidelity placed it beneath free will. He said that grace is given to people so that what they are commanded to do by free will they may more easily fulfill by grace.

By saying “so that they may more easily,” he plainly wanted it to be believed that people could fulfill the divine commands without divine grace, even if with greater difficulty.

They say that this grace of God, without which we can do no good, consists only in free will, which our nature received from him without any preceding merits of its own. God helps it only through his law and teaching, so that we may learn what we ought to do and what we ought to hope for; not so that, through the gift of his Spirit, we may do what we have learned ought to be done. [Note: The manuscripts have “through the gift of his Spirit”; the printed editions have “through the gift of the Holy Spirit.”] [Note: The manuscripts likewise have: “not for this purpose through the gift of his Spirit, so that we may do what we have learned ought to be done,” and so forth.]

Thus they confess that knowledge is given to us divinely, by which ignorance is driven away, but they deny that charity is given, by which one lives piously. That is, although knowledge—which without charity puffs up—is a gift of God, charity itself—which prevents knowledge from puffing up and builds up—is not a gift of God (1 Corinthians 8:1).

They also destroy the prayers offered by the Church, whether for unbelievers and those who resist the teaching of God, so that they may be converted to God; or for the faithful, so that their faith may increase and they may persevere in it. For they insist that human beings do not receive these things from God himself but possess them from themselves, saying that the grace by which we are liberated from ungodliness is given according to our merits.

Pelagius, fearing condemnation in the Palestinian episcopal judgment, was indeed compelled to condemn it; but he is found to teach it in his later writings.

They also proceed to say that the life of the righteous in this age has no sin whatsoever, and that in this mortal condition the Church of Christ is perfected so as to be entirely “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). This is as though it were not Christ’s Church which throughout the whole world cries out to God, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

They also deny that little children, born carnally according to Adam, contract the contagion of the ancient death through their first birth. They assert that they are born entirely without any bond of original sin, so that there is absolutely nothing that ought to be forgiven them through a second birth.

They say that they are baptized for this reason: so that, being adopted through regeneration, they may be admitted into the kingdom of God, transferred from good to better, rather than liberated by this renewal from some evil bondage of the old condition. For even if they are not baptized, they promise them a certain eternal and blessed life outside the kingdom of God.

They also say that Adam, even if he had not sinned, would have died bodily, and that he died not through the merit of guilt [Note: The Lov. edition has “nor did he die through the merit of guilt,” omitting *ita* (“thus”)] but by the condition of nature.

Several other matters are also brought against them, but these are the principal ones from which the others, whether all or nearly all, are understood to depend.

Behold how many heresies we have recalled, and yet we have not fulfilled the limit of your request. Since the Christian religion, to use your words, received the name of the promised inheritance, how could I recall all the heresies that arose, when I could not know them all?

I think this is because none of those whose writings on this subject I have read included them all. I found in one author things that I did not find in another, and again in this author things which the other had not included.

I have therefore listed more than they did because I collected from all of them the things which I did not find in their individual works taken separately, adding also those which I myself remembered but could not find in any of them.

For this reason I rightly believe that I have not listed them all, since I could not read all those who have written on this subject, nor do I see that any of those whom I read succeeded in doing so.

Finally, even if I perhaps listed them all—which I do not think I did—I do not know whether they are all heresies. Therefore, what you wish to have concluded by my speaking cannot at least be comprehended by my knowledge.

I heard that Saint Jerome wrote about heresies, but we were unable to find that little work in our library, nor do we know where it might be obtained. [Note: Most manuscripts insert the following here:

> “A very learned man, well acquainted with his books, was asked about this. He said that he did not know who had spread this report, but that the person did not know what he was saying. For, he said, Saint Jerome composed no little work on heresies.”

They continue: “But if you know,” and so forth. A list of heresies under Jerome’s name was later published by Claudius Menard after Augustine’s unfinished work, but learned opinion rejects it as Jerome’s.]

If you know of it, obtain it, and perhaps you will have something better than this of ours—although I do not think that even he, learned though he was, could have investigated all heresies.

Certainly, as far as I judge, he did not know the Abelonians of our region. Thus, perhaps elsewhere there were others hidden away in obscure places, escaping his notice because of the very obscurity of their localities.

Furthermore, your letter asks us to state absolutely everything by which heretics dissent from the truth. Even if I knew everything, I could not do this; how much less can I, who cannot know everything?

For there are heretics—this must be admitted—who attack the rule of truth with one or only a few dogmas, such as the Macedonians and Photinians and others of the same kind.

But those whom I may call fabulists—that is, those who weave together empty, long, and intricate stories—are so full of many false dogmas that they themselves cannot count them, or can do so only with the greatest difficulty.

No heresy is easily known by anyone outside it as it is known by its own members. Therefore I do not claim either to have stated or to have learned all the doctrines of those I have mentioned.

Who does not see how much effort this matter requires, and how many books? Nevertheless, it is not without considerable benefit to read and recognize the errors which I have woven into this work and then avoid them.

For what the Catholic Church thinks against these errors—which you thought should be stated by me—is needlessly asked, since it is enough to know that she thinks against them and that no one ought to receive any of them into the faith. [Note: More manuscripts have “into faith.”]

How the truth opposes these errors and must be asserted and defended exceeds the limits of this work. But it greatly assists a faithful heart to know what must not be believed, even if it cannot refute it by the power of disputation.

Therefore every Catholic Christian ought not to believe these things; but not everyone who does not believe them should consequently already consider or call himself a Catholic Christian. For there may be, or may arise, other heresies not mentioned in this work, and whoever holds one of them will not be a Catholic Christian.

What, then, makes someone a heretic must next be investigated, so that, with the Lord’s help, when we avoid it, we may avoid not only the heretical poisons we know but also those we do not know—whether they have already arisen or may yet arise.

Let this now be the end of this volume. I thought it should be sent to you before I had completed the whole work, so that all of you who read it might assist me with your prayers in completing what remains, which you see to be so great. [Note: Here Augustine’s book certainly ends, although most manuscript codices add the Nestorians and Eutychians—heresies certainly not named before Augustine’s death—and some also add the Timotheans, in the following order:

> “TIMOTHEANS say that the Son of God was indeed a true man, born from the Virgin Mary, but that he did not make one person in such a way that he was not reduced to one nature. They wish the Virgin’s interior to have been a kind of melting furnace, through which the two natures—that is, God and man—were dissolved and compacted into one mass, producing one form of God and man, with the properties of the natures producing the union altered. To confirm this impiety, which asserts that God was changed from his own nature, they compel the evangelist’s testimony, ‘And the Word became flesh,’ to mean: ‘The divine nature was changed into the human.’ O abolition of that inviolable substance!

> “The beginning of this impiety was made by Timotheus, who, now exiled in the city of Biza in Bithynia, deceives many by the appearance of an austere and religious life.

> “NESTORIANS, from Nestorius, a bishop who dared to teach contrary to the Catholic faith that our Lord Jesus Christ was merely a man” [most manuscripts have: “that Christ the Lord, our God and man, was merely a man”], “and that he was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb from the Holy Spirit as the mediator between God and human beings, but that God was afterward mixed with the man. He also said that the God-man did not suffer and was not buried, seeking to empty all our salvation: for the Word of God deigned to assume man in the Virgin’s womb in such a way that there would be one person of God and man. Therefore, born in this singular and miraculous manner, he also died for our sins, paying what he had not seized; and, as God and man, rising from the dead, he ascended into heaven.

> “EUTYCHIANS arose from a certain Eutyches, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople” [one codex adds: “a monk”], “who, although he seemed to refute Nestorius, passed over to Apollinaris and Manichaeus. Denying the reality of Christ’s humanity, he attributes to the divine essence alone whatever was received by the Word from our nature, so that by denying our nature in Christ he might dissolve the mystery of human salvation, which exists only in both substances. In his foolish impiety he did not understand that whatever was lacking to the head would be taken away from the whole body.”]

[Col. 0051]

## TREATISE OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST THE JEWS

[Note: The printed editions have *Oratio adversus Judaeos* (“Oration against the Jews”). In the Cistercian manuscript it is entitled *Sermo S. Augustini contra Judaeos* (“Sermon of Saint Augustine against the Jews”). In another Cistercian manuscript and in one Vatican manuscript, *Sermo S. Aug. de Incarnatione Domini, contra Judaeos* (“Sermon of Saint Augustine on the Incarnation of the Lord, against the Jews”). In two other Vatican manuscripts, *Liber B. Aug. de Incarnatione Domini, contra Judaeos* (“Book of Blessed Augustine on the Incarnation of the Lord, against the Jews”). Bede, or Florus, also calls it the *Book Against the Jews* in his treatments of Romans 9 and 11, Galatians 6, Ephesians 2, Colossians 2, and Hebrews 7. In Possidius’s Catalogue, chapter 1, two treatises against the Jews are noted.]

[Note: The *Treatise Against the Jews* has been corrected against three Vatican manuscripts, two Cistercian manuscripts, one Victorine manuscript, and the editions of Am. Er. and Lov.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Revisions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

*(C, S)*

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0051]

1. An example of God’s severity in the cutting off of the Jews, and of his goodness in the grafting in of the Gentiles. The blindness of the Jews to be refuted from the writings of the Old Testament.

The blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, exhorting us to remain steadfast and firm in that same faith, of which he has been made a qualified minister, admonishes us by command and terrifies us by example. “You see,” he says, “the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who fell, but goodness toward you” [Note: [Col. 0051] In the printed editions, “the goodness of God.” The word “of God” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.], “if you remain in goodness.” He certainly said this concerning the Jews, who, like branches from that olive tree which, rooted in the holy Patriarchs as in a fruitful root, were broken off because of unbelief, so that the wild olive of the Gentiles might be grafted in because of faith and become a sharer in the richness of the olive tree after the natural branches had been cut off.

“But do not boast,” he says, “against the branches; for if you boast, you do not bear the root, but the root bears you.” And because some of them are saved, he immediately added: “Otherwise you too will be cut off. But they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again” (Rom. 11:18–23).

Those who remain in unbelief, however, belong to that sentence of the Lord in which he says: “But the sons of this kingdom will go into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” The Gentiles who remain in goodness belong to what he said earlier: “Many will come from east and west, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:12, 11).

Thus, while those Patriarchs live in the root, the unbelieving pride of the natural branches is broken by the just severity of God, and the faithful humility of the wild olive is grafted in by the grace of divine goodness.

2. But when these things are said to the Jews, they despise the Gospel and the Apostle, and do not listen to what we say, because they do not understand what they read. For surely, if they understood what the prophet whom they read had foretold—“I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isa. 49:6)—they would not be so blind [Col. 0052], nor so diseased, as not to recognize either the light or the salvation in the Lord Christ.

Likewise, if they understood concerning whom it had been foretold—though they sing it fruitlessly and vainly—“Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5), they would awaken at the sound of the Apostles and perceive that their words were divine.

Therefore, testimonies must be drawn from the holy Scriptures, which possess great authority even among them. Even if they do not wish to be healed by the benefit offered, they may nevertheless be convicted by the manifest truth.

## CHAPTER II

3. The books of the Old Testament belong to us, and their commandments are more fully fulfilled by us.

First, however, we must refute the error by which they think that the books of the Old Testament do not belong to us because we now observe not the old but the new sacraments. For they say to us:

“What place among you has the reading of the Law and the Prophets, whose commandments you do not wish to keep? We do not circumcise the male flesh of the foreskin” [Note: [Col. 0052] Almost all the manuscripts read, “we do not circumcise the male flesh of the foreskin,” with which the common text of Bede agrees.], “and you eat meats which the Law calls unclean; you do not observe their Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days in a carnal manner; you do not sacrifice animal victims to God; nor do you celebrate the Passover in the same way with a sheep and unleavened bread.”

And there are other ancient sacraments which the Apostle, using a general term, calls “shadows of things to come” (Col. 2:17), because they signified in their own time what was to be revealed, and what we have received now that it has been revealed, so that, when the shadow was removed, we might enjoy their unveiled light [Note: [Col. 0052] So all the manuscripts and Bede, or Florus, on Colossians 2. The printed editions instead read, “so that, when the shadow of the Jews was removed, we might enjoy the light.”].

It would be too lengthy to discuss each of these individually: how, by putting off the old person, we are circumcised “not in the removal of the body of flesh”; how, in our conduct, we avoid the foods which they avoid among animals; how we present our bodies as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God; and how, in holy desires, we intelligently pour out our souls to him as blood, while we are cleansed from every iniquity by the blood of Christ, like that of an immaculate lamb.

Because of the likeness of sinful flesh, he is also prefigured in the ancient sacrifices by a goat [Note: [Col. 0052] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “by a he-goat.”]. Nor does the one who recognizes in him the greatest victim deny that he is the bull upon the horns of the cross [Col. 0053].

When we find rest in him, we truly keep Sabbath; and the observance of the new moon is the sanctification of new life. Our Passover is Christ [Note: [Col. 0053] Here the printed editions add the word “sacrificed,” which is absent from the manuscripts and from the common text of Bede.]; our unleavened bread is the sincerity of truth, without the leaven of oldness.

And whatever other matters there are in which it is not now necessary to linger—things foreshadowed by those ancient signs—find their fulfillment in him whose kingdom will have no end. In him, indeed, everything had to be fulfilled, for he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (Matt. 5:17).

## CHAPTER III

4. Christ did not abolish the Law by criticizing it, but changed it by fulfilling it. The change of the ancient sacraments foretold in the Psalms.

Accordingly, he did not abolish those ancient signs of things by criticizing them, but changed them by fulfilling them, so that the signs announcing that Christ had already come would be different from those which foretold that he would come.

What, then, does it mean that certain psalms—which they themselves read and possess among the authority of the sacred writings—are marked in their titles with the words, “For those things which will be changed” [Note: [Col. 0053] Here and below, the printed editions read, “which will be changed” in the masculine. But all the manuscripts and Bede consistently have the feminine form, “which will be changed.”], while the text of those same psalms proclaims Christ? It means that their change was foretold as coming through him by whom it is seen to have been fulfilled.

Thus the people of God, who are now the Christian people, are no longer compelled to observe what was observed in the prophetic age—not because those things have been condemned, but because they have been changed; not so that the realities signified might perish, but so that the signs of the realities might correspond to their respective times.

## CHAPTER IV

5. Christ foretold in Psalm Forty-Four.

Finally, in Psalm Forty-Five—for it is the first of those bearing such a title, “For those things which will be changed,” and it is also entitled “A song for the beloved”—Christ is displayed most openly:

“You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.”

Although he existed in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized. There he is told:

“Gird your sword upon your thigh,”

because he was to speak with human beings in the flesh. The sword signifies speech, and the thigh signifies flesh, because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” Thus he who in divinity was beautiful in form beyond the sons of men would, through weakness, also become what another prophet says of him:

“We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his face was rejected, and his form was disfigured” (Isa. 53:2).

For in the same psalm it is shown most plainly that Christ is not merely human but also God, when it continues:

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0053] Two manuscripts and the margin of the Louvain edition read, “the rod of uprightness.” Augustine follows this reading in his exposition of the same Psalm 44.] “is the rod of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

From the anointing—for “anointing” is called χρῖσμα (*chrisma*) in Greek—he was called Christ. He is God, anointed by God, and he changed the carnal anointing itself, together with the other sacraments, into a spiritual one.

There he is told concerning the Church:

“The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed round about with varied adornment.”

This signifies the variety of languages among all the nations, though inwardly there is one simple faith:

“All the beauty of the king’s daughter is within.”

The Psalm addresses her, saying:

“Listen, daughter, and see”—

listen to the promise; see its fulfillment—

“and forget your people and your father’s house.”

Thus the new things are fulfilled; thus the old things are changed.

“For the king desired your beauty.”

The beauty which he himself made by himself, he did not find in you. For how could you have been beautiful in his eyes when you were defiled by your own sins?

But lest you think that your hope should be placed in a human being, it continues:

“For he is the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0054] The word “Lord” is not found in all the manuscripts. It is present in the Septuagint, but the word “God” is absent from it.], “your God.”

Do not despise the form of a servant; do not mock the weakness of the powerful one or the humility of the exalted one: he is your God. In what appears small, greatness lies hidden; in the shadow of death, the sun of righteousness; in the disgrace of the cross, the Lord of glory.

Although persecutors kill him and unbelievers deny him, he is himself the Lord your God, through whose body the things that were formerly prefigured by shadows are changed.

## CHAPTER V

6. The change is also foretold in the title of Psalm Sixty-Eight, which was written concerning Christ’s passion.

Psalm Sixty-Nine likewise bears in its title:

“For those things which will be changed.”

There the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is sung. In himself he also transforms certain words belonging to his members, that is, to his faithful people. For he himself had no sins, but bore ours; hence he says:

“And my sins are not hidden from you.”

There it is written and foretold—what we read as having happened in the Gospel (Matt. 27:34, 48):

“They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

Through this, therefore, the old things were changed, which the title of the Psalm had foretold would be changed.

When the Jews read these things without understanding them, they think they have something to say when they ask us how we accept the authority of the Law and the Prophets, since we do not observe the sacraments commanded there.

We do not observe them because they have been changed; they have been changed because they were foretold as going to be changed; and we believe in him through whose revelation they have been changed. We therefore do not observe the sacraments commanded there because we understand what was foretold there and hold fast to what was promised there.

But those who bring these objections against us are still bitter from the ancestors who gave gall to the Lord for food, and still old from the vinegar which they offered him to drink. Therefore they do not understand, because in them is fulfilled what follows:

“Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling-block.”

For they themselves have become gall and sourness by serving bitter and sour foods to the living Bread [Note: [Col. 0054] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “They have become gall and vinegar, serving bitter and sour food to the living Bread.”].

How could they see these things, concerning whom it was foretold:

“Let their eyes be blinded” [Note: [Col. 0054] The printed editions read, “Let them be obscured,” though below, in chapter 6, they agree with the manuscripts and read, “Let them be blinded.”], “so that they may not see”?

And how could they be upright, so as to have their hearts lifted upward, concerning whom it was foretold:

“And always bend their backs” [Col. 0055]?

These things were not said of all of them; rather, they were said of all to whom the things foretold pertain.

They do not pertain to those among them who believed in Christ then, or who believe even now, or who will believe thereafter until the end of the age—namely, to the true Israel [Note: [Col. 0055] The printed editions read, “against Israel.” We judge that this should be corrected to “the true Israel.”], who will see the Lord face to face.

“For not all who are from Israel are Israel; nor are all Abraham’s offspring his children. But,” he says, “‘in Isaac shall your offspring be called’; that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. 9:6–8).

These belong to spiritual Zion and to the cities [Note: [Col. 0055] The printed editions read, “and to the city.” The manuscripts’ “and to the cities” is better.] of Judah, that is, to the churches, concerning which the Apostle says:

“I was personally unknown to the churches of Judea which are in Christ” (Gal. 1:22).

For, as the same Psalm says shortly afterward:

“God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah will be built. And they will inhabit it, and possess it as an inheritance. And the offspring of his servants will possess it, and those who love his name will inhabit it.”

But when the Jews hear these things, they understand them carnally and think of the earthly Jerusalem, which is in slavery with her children, not of our eternal mother in heaven (Gal. 4:25–26).

## CHAPTER VI

7. The title of Psalm Seventy-Nine also foretells a change. Clearer testimonies concerning the change to be made, directed against the Jews.

Psalm Eighty is likewise marked with the title:

“For those things which will be changed.”

Among other things, this Psalm says:

“Look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vine; and perfect it, which your right hand planted, and upon the Son of man whom you established for yourself.”

This is the vine of which it is said:

“You brought a vine out of Egypt.”

Christ did not plant another vine; rather, by coming, he changed this same vine for the better.

Thus it is also read in the Gospel:

“He will destroy the wicked miserably, and will lease his vineyard to other husbandmen” (Matt. 21:41).

He did not say, “He will uproot it and plant another,” but, “He will lease the same one to other husbandmen.”

For the city of God and the assembly of the children of the promise are one and the same in the fellowship of the saints. They are to be completed through the departure and succession of mortals and, at the end of the age, will together receive the immortality owed to them.

This is signified in another way in another Psalm by a fruitful olive tree, where it says:

“But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God for ever, and for ever and ever” (Ps. 51:10).

Nor, because the unbelieving and proud—therefore fruitless—branches were broken off so that the wild olive of the Gentiles might be grafted in, could the root of the Patriarchs and Prophets perish.

“For even if,” Isaiah says, “the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. 10:22)—but through him of whom it is said:

“And upon the Son of man whom you established for yourself,”

and of whom it is repeated:

“Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the Son of man whom you established for yourself. And we will not depart from you.”

Through this Son of man, that is, Jesus Christ, and through his remnant, namely the Apostles and many others among the Israelites who believed in Christ God [Note: [Col. 0056] The printed editions read, “believed in Christ the Lord.” The old Cistercian manuscript reads, “believed in Christ of the Lord.” Most of the other manuscripts read, “believed in Christ God.”—], with the fullness of the Gentiles added—the holy vine is perfected.

Thus, in the removal of the ancient sacraments and the establishment of the new, the title of that Psalm, “For those things which will be changed,” is fulfilled.

8. Therefore we must deal with them by means of clearer testimonies, which, whether they agree or disagree, they must nevertheless understand.

“Behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord, “and I will establish a new covenant over the house of Jacob, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. 31:31–32).

This foretold change is not signified only through the titles of the Psalms to the few who understand them; it is expressed by the unmistakable proclamation of the prophetic voice.

A new covenant is openly promised, not according to the covenant made with the people when they were led out of Egypt. Since these commandments were given in that old covenant, commandments which we, as belonging to the new covenant, are not compelled to observe, why do the Jews not rather acknowledge that they have remained in a superfluous oldness, instead of reproaching us, who hold fast to the new promises, because we do not observe the old things?

Therefore, as it is written in the Song of Songs, “The day has breathed forth; let the shadows be removed” (Song 2:17). Let the spiritual meaning now shine forth; let the carnal observance now come to rest.

“The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting”—clearly, the whole earth to the new covenant, to which another Psalm says:

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.”

Therefore he did not speak, as before, from Mount Sinai to one people whom the God of gods called out of Egypt. Rather, he spoke in such a way as to summon the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.

If a Jew wished to understand this utterance, he would hear this call and would be among those to whom the same Psalm says:

“Listen, my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, and I will testify against you: I am God, your God. I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are always before me. I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks; for all the beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. I know all the birds of the air, and the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world is mine, and its fullness. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and pay your prayers to the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0056] The printed editions had, “your vows.” But all the ancient manuscripts have, “your prayers,” and Augustine himself reads it this way in his exposition of the same Psalm 49. The Greek Septuagint has τὰς εὐχάς σου (*tas euchas sou*), “your prayers.”—].

“And call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.”

Here too, certainly, the change of the ancient sacrifices is made clear. God foretold that he would not accept those sacrifices and commanded his worshipers to offer a sacrifice of praise—not because, as one in need, he seeks praise from us, but so that through it he might provide for our salvation.

For he concluded the same Psalm:

“A sacrifice of praise will glorify me; and there is the way in which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49).

What, then, is the salvation of God, if not the Son of God, the Savior of the world—day, the Son from Day, from the Father; that is, light from light—whose coming revealed the new covenant?

Therefore, where it says:

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless his name,”

he is immediately shown as the one who must be proclaimed, and it is added:

“Proclaim the good news of his salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:1–2).

He himself, therefore, both priest and victim, fulfilled the sacrifice of praise, granting forgiveness for evil works and bestowing the grace to do good works.

For this purpose a sacrifice of praise is offered to the Lord by his worshipers: “that whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

## CHAPTER VII

9. The Jews wrongly interpret certain prophecies as referring to themselves. The prophetic words fit the Jews more aptly.

But when the Jews hear this, they answer with raised necks:
