“We are they; this was said about us, this was said about us. For we are Israel, the people of God. In the words of the one speaking, we recognize ourselves: ‘Listen, my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, and I will testify against you.’”

What are we to say to this? We certainly know the spiritual Israel of whom the Apostle says:

“And upon all who follow this rule be peace and mercy, and upon the Israel of God” (Gal. 6:16).

But this Israel we know to be carnal, concerning whom the same Apostle says:

“See Israel according to the flesh” (1 Cor. 10:18).

They do not understand these distinctions, and thereby prove themselves to be carnal.

It is useful to address them for a little while as though they were present:

“Do you really belong to the people whom the God of gods called from the rising of the sun to its setting? Were you not transferred from Egypt into the land of Canaan—not called there from the rising of the sun to its setting, but scattered from there toward the rising and the setting of the sun?

Do you not rather belong to the enemies of the one who says in the Psalm:

‘My God has shown me among my enemies; do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law; scatter them by your power’” (Ps. 58:12) [Note: [Col. 0057] So the manuscripts, and Augustine likewise read this in his exposition of Psalm 58. The printed editions instead had, “Show me among my enemies.” Below they read, “scatter them in your truth.”]?

Thus, without forgetting the law of God, but carrying it about—carrying it as a testimony to the Gentiles and as a reproach to yourselves—you unknowingly minister it to the people who have been called from the rising of the sun to its setting.

Will you deny this? Will you either fail to see, through even greater blindness, things foretold with such authority and fulfilled with such clarity, or refuse to acknowledge them with astonishing shamelessness?

What, then, will you answer to what the prophet Isaiah proclaims?

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be manifest, prepared upon the summit of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills; and all the nations will come to it and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will announce to us the way of salvation, and we will enter upon it. For from Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:2–3).

Will you also say here, “We are they,” because you heard the words “the house of Jacob,” “Zion,” and “Jerusalem”?

It is not as though we deny that Christ the Lord, according to the flesh, is from the seed of Jacob—the one signified by the name of the mountain prepared upon the summit of the mountains, whose height surpasses all their heights [Note: [Col. 0058] The printed editions read, “their heights, his height surpasses.” We have removed the word “their” on the authority of the Cistercian manuscripts.].

Nor do we deny that the Apostles and those churches of Judea which immediately believed in him after Christ’s resurrection belong to the house of Jacob.

Nor is another Jacob to be understood spiritually than the Christian people themselves. Although younger in age than the Jewish people, it nevertheless surpasses them by growing, and the text adds that what was foretold figuratively of those two brothers might be fulfilled:

“The elder will serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23).

Although Zion and Jerusalem are understood spiritually as the Church, they nevertheless provide a more suitable testimony against these people, because from this very place where they crucified Christ, both the law and the word of the Lord went forth to the Gentiles.

For the law given to them through Moses—the law by which they proudly exalt themselves and by which they are more effectively convicted—is not understood to have gone forth from Zion and Jerusalem, but from Mount Sinai.

They came into the promised land, where Zion is [Note: [Col. 0058] The name “Zion,” omitted in the printed editions here, has been restored from the manuscripts.], which is also called Jerusalem, after forty years with that very Law; they did not receive it there or from there [Note: [Col. 0058] All the manuscripts omit the words, “they did not receive it there or from there.”].

But the Gospel of Christ and the law of faith certainly went forth from there.

Likewise, after the Lord had risen, he spoke to his disciples and showed that the things foretold in the divine utterances had been fulfilled in him:

“Thus it is written,” he said, “and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

There is what Isaiah prophesied when he said:

“For from Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

For there, when the Holy Spirit came down from above according to the Lord’s promise, he filled those whom one house then contained and caused them to speak in the languages of all the nations (Acts 2:1–6). From there they went out to preach the Gospel for the knowledge of all the nations.

Just as that Law which went forth from Mount Sinai was written by the finger of God on the fiftieth day after Passover had been celebrated—the finger signifying the Holy Spirit—so this Law which went forth from Zion and Jerusalem was written by the Holy Spirit, not on tablets of stone but on the tablets of the hearts of the holy Evangelists, on the fiftieth day after the true Passover of the passion and resurrection of the Lord Christ. On that day the Holy Spirit was sent, having been promised beforehand [Note: [Col. 0058] The printed editions read, “which had been faithfully promised beforehand.” The word “faithfully” is absent from the manuscripts.].

10. Go now, Israelites according to the flesh, not according to the spirit; go now and continue to contradict the clearest truth. When you hear:

“Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob,”

say, “We are they,” so that, blind, you may stumble against the mountain, striking your faces against it, and may lose your foreheads even more disastrously.

If you truly wish to say, “We are they,” say it where you hear:

“Because of the transgressions of my people he was led to death” (Isa. 53:8) [Note: [Col. 0059] The printed editions read, “because of the transgression.” The manuscripts read, “because of the transgressions,” corresponding to the Greek Septuagint.].

For this was said of Christ, whom you led to death in your ancestors. He was led like a sheep to be sacrificed, so that the Passover which you celebrate unknowingly you might fulfill unknowingly by your savagery [Note: [Col. 0059] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “unknowingly you celebrate in an animal, so that it might be consecrated for us through Christ, who is the Lamb of God; for our Passover, Christ, was sacrificed.”].

If you truly wish to say, “We are they,” say it when you hear:

“Make the heart of this people gross, stop up their ears, and weigh down their eyes” (Isa. 6:10).

Then say, “We are they,” when you hear:

“All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted me” (Isa. 65:2).

Then say, “We are they,” when you hear:

“Let their eyes be blinded, so that they may not see, and let their backs always be bent” (Ps. 68:24).

In these and similar prophetic utterances say, “We are they,” where there is no doubt that you are. But you are so blind that you say you are where you are not, and do not recognize yourselves where you are.

## CHAPTER VIII

11. The Jews’ abandonment by God foretold through Isaiah.

But pay attention for a little while to the clearer things I am about to say.

Certainly, when you hear Israel spoken of favorably, you say, “We are they”; and when you hear Jacob spoken of favorably, you say, “We are they.”

When you are asked for the reason, you answer:

“Because Jacob himself is Israel, from whom we descend through the patriarch, and so we are rightly designated by the name of our father.”

We are not, then, attempting to awaken you from a deep and heavy sleep to spiritual things which you do not understand, nor are we now trying to persuade you—deaf and blind in hearing and sight—to understand these names spiritually.

As you yourselves admit, and as the reading of the book of Genesis plainly declares, one man was Jacob and Israel (Gen. 32:28). And the house of Jacob in which you boast is the house of Israel.

What, then, does it mean that this same prophet, after foretelling that a mountain would be prepared upon the summit of the mountains, to which all the nations would come—for the law and the word of the Lord would go forth not from Mount Sinai to one nation but from Zion and Jerusalem to all nations—after this, as we most clearly see fulfilled in Christ and Christians, says shortly afterward:

“And now you, house of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord” (Isa. 2:5) [Note: [Col. 0059] So several manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed editions read, “into the light.”]?

Here surely you will say, as usual, “We are they.” But pay attention for a little while to what follows, so that when you have said what you wish, you may also hear what you do not wish to hear.

For the Prophet joins these words and says:

“For he has dismissed his people, the house of Israel” (Isa. 2:6).

Here say, “We are they”; here recognize yourselves, and forgive us for recalling these things.

If you hear them willingly, they are addressed as an appeal to you; if you hear them indignantly, they are addressed as a reproach to you. They must nevertheless be spoken, whether you wish it or not.

Behold, it is not I but the prophet whom you read—the prophet through whom you cannot deny that God spoke, and whom you cannot remove from the authority of the divine Scriptures—who cries out vehemently, as the Lord commanded him, and raises his voice like a trumpet (Isa. 58:1), rebuking you and saying:

“And now you, house of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.”

You killed Christ in your ancestors. For so long you did not believe and contradicted him. Yet you have not perished, because you have not yet departed from the body; and now you have time for repentance; now come.

You ought indeed to have come long ago, but come even now. The days of one whose last day has not yet come are not yet ended.

Or, if, as the house of Jacob, you claim to follow the Prophet and already believe that you are walking in the light of the Lord, show us the house of Israel which he dismissed.

For we point out both: those whom he separated from that house by calling them, and those whom he left behind there. He called from it not only the Apostles but also a great people after Christ’s resurrection, as we have already said above.

But he dismissed those whom you imitate by not believing, and you yourselves, who by imitating them remain in the same destruction.

Or, if you are those whom he called from there, where are those whom he dismissed? You cannot say that he dismissed some other nation, since the Prophet cries out:

“For he has dismissed his people, the house of Israel.”

Behold what you are—not what you boast yourselves to be.

He also dismissed the vineyard from which he expected grapes, but which produced thorns; and he commanded his clouds not to rain upon it. Yet even from there he called those to whom he says:

“Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isa. 5:2–6).

Concerning these the Lord also says:

“If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges” (Matt. 12:27).

And promising them this, he says:

“You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

Thus the house of Jacob, which was called and walked in the light of the Lord, will sit in judgment upon the house of Israel, that is, upon the very people whom he dismissed.

For how, according to the same prophet, did “the stone which the builders rejected become the head of the corner” (Isa. 28:16; Ps. 117:22), unless the walls formed from opposite directions—one from the circumcision and one from the uncircumcision—are joined together at the corner, as in a kiss of peace?

Hence the Apostle says:

“For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

Those, therefore, from the house of Jacob or Israel who followed the one calling them are joined to the cornerstone and walk in the light of the Lord. But those whom he left there are building ruin and rejecting the cornerstone.

## CHAPTER IX

12. The Jews’ abandonment more clearly foretold through Malachi. The sacrifice of Christians is offered everywhere on earth and in heaven.

Finally, if you attempt to twist these prophetic words into another meaning according to your own inclination, Jews resisting the Son of God to your own salvation’s harm—if, I say, you wish to understand these words so that the same people and house of Jacob or Israel were both called and dismissed, not some being called and others dismissed, but the whole people being called for the purpose of walking in the light of the Lord because it was dismissed for not walking in the light of the Lord; or if you understand them as meaning that some were called and others dismissed, but with no division of the Lord’s table, which belongs to Christ’s sacrifice, having been made, so that both groups remained under the same ancient sacraments [Note: [Col. 0061] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “which pertains.” Perhaps one should read, “those who remain under the same ancient sacraments.”]—both those who walked in the light of the Lord and kept his commandments and those who rejected righteousness and deserved to be abandoned by him—

if, then, you wish to understand these things in this way, what will you say, and how will you interpret another prophet who completely cuts off this claim from you, crying out with such clarity:

“I have no pleasure in you,” says the Lord Almighty, “and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is offered to my name, a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations,” says the Lord Almighty (Mal. 1:10–11).

With what words will you contradict such overwhelming evidence?

Why do you continue to exalt yourselves with excessive shamelessness, so that you may perish more miserably in a heavier ruin?

“It is not my pleasure in you,” he says—not just anyone, but the Lord Almighty. Why do you boast so greatly of the seed of Abraham? Whenever you hear Jacob or Israel, or the house of Jacob or the house of Israel, spoken of with some praise, you insist that this could not have been said of anyone but yourselves, while the Lord Almighty says:

“I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands.”

Certainly here you cannot deny not only that he does not accept sacrifice from your hands, but also that you do not offer sacrifice to him with your hands.

For the Law of the Lord established one place where sacrifices were to be offered with your hands and strictly prohibited offering them anywhere else.

Since, therefore, you have lost this place on account of your deserts, you do not dare to offer elsewhere the sacrifice which alone was permitted to be offered there.

Behold, what the Prophet says has been completely fulfilled:

“I will not accept sacrifice from your hands.”

For if the temple and altar had remained for you in earthly Jerusalem, you could say that this had been fulfilled in those wicked people among you whose sacrifices the Lord does not accept, while he accepts the sacrifices of others among you and within you who keep God’s commandments.

But this cannot be said where there is no one among you who can offer sacrifice with his hands according to the Law that went forth from Mount Sinai.

Nor was this prophecy fulfilled in such a way as to allow you to answer the prophetic sentence:

“We do not offer flesh with our hands, but we offer praise with our heart and mouth,” according to what is written in the Psalm:

“Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God” (Ps. 49:14).

Here too the one who says, “I have no pleasure in you,” contradicts you.

### 13. Sacrifice Offered Everywhere

Then, lest you suppose that because you do not offer sacrifice, and he does not receive it from your hands, no sacrifice is offered to God—for he certainly has no need of it, since he needs none of our goods—nevertheless, because there is no sacrifice which is not useful to us rather than to him, he adds and says:

> “For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name has become great among the nations; and in every place sacrifice is offered to my name, a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations,” says the Lord Almighty.

What do you answer to this? Open your eyes at last and see that from the rising of the sun to its setting the sacrifice of Christians is offered, not in one place only, as had been prescribed for you, but in every place—not to just any god, but to the one who foretold these things, the God of Israel. Therefore elsewhere also he says to his Church:

> “And he who redeemed you, he himself shall be called the God of Israel, of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:5).

“Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life” (John 5:39). And indeed you would have it, if you understood and held fast to Christ in them. But search through them: they themselves bear witness to this pure sacrifice, which is offered to the God of Israel—not by your one nation, from whose hands he foretold that he would not accept it, but by all the nations that say:

> “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isaiah 2:3).

Nor is it offered in one place only, as you were commanded on earthly Jerusalem, but in every place, even as far as Jerusalem itself.

[Note: [Col. 0062] Bede, on Hebrews 7: “even as far as Jerusalem itself,” that is, “even in Jerusalem itself, in heaven.”]

Nor is it according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek. For it was said to Christ, and foretold of Christ so long beforehand:

> “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

What does “The Lord has sworn” mean, except that he has confirmed it with unshakable truth? And what does “he will not repent” mean, except that he will in no way alter this priesthood? For God does not repent as a human being does. God’s “repentance” is spoken of when there is a change in some matter instituted by him, although it had been believed that the matter would remain. Therefore, when he says, “He will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” he plainly shows that he did repent—that is, that he wished to change—the priesthood he had established according to the order of Aaron. We see the fulfillment of both points: Aaron’s priesthood now exists in no temple at all, whereas Christ’s priesthood endures forever in heaven.

### 14. The Prophet Calls the Jews to the Lord’s Light

To this light of the Lord, then, the Prophet calls you when he says:

> “And now you, house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord.”

“You, house of Jacob,” whom he called and chose—not “you,” whom he abandoned. For he abandoned his people, the house of Israel (Isaiah 2:5–6). Whoever among you wishes to come from there will belong to the house whom he called, and will be without the house whom he abandoned.

The light of the Lord in which the nations walk is that of which the same prophet says:

> “I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).

To whom was this said, except to Christ? Of whom was it fulfilled, except of Christ?

This light is not in you, of whom it was repeatedly said:

> “God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so as not to see, and ears so as not to hear, even to this present day” (Romans 11:8).

This light, I say, is not in you. Therefore, in your excessive blindness, you reject the stone that has been made the cornerstone. So:

> “Come to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33:6).

What does “Come to him” mean except “Believe”? For where could you go in order to approach him, when he is the stone of which the prophet Daniel says that, growing, it became so great a mountain that it filled the whole face of the earth (Daniel 2:35)?

Thus the nations that say, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord,” do not strive to travel and arrive anywhere on earth. They ascend where they are, because in every place sacrifice is offered according to the order of Melchizedek.

And as another prophet says:

> “God will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and each person will worship him from his own place” (Zephaniah 2:11).

Therefore, when it is said to you, “Come to him,” you are not being told, “Prepare ships or pack animals, load them with your victims, and travel from so great a distance to the place where God may accept the sacrifices of your devotion.” Rather, “Come to him who is proclaimed in your ears; come to him who is glorified before your eyes.” You will not grow weary through traveling: for you approach him where you believe.

## CHAPTER X

### 15. With What Love the Jews Should Be Invited to Faith

Whether the Jews hear these things gratefully or indignantly, dearest friends,

[Note: [Col. 0063] Printed editions read, “dearest brothers.” “Brothers” is absent from the manuscripts, nor does this combination of the two words, “dearest brothers,” readily occur in Augustine, except in spurious sermons.]

we nevertheless should preach wherever we can, with love for them. Nor should we boast arrogantly against the branches that have been broken off. Rather, let us consider by whose grace, with what great mercy, and in what root we have been grafted, so that, “not thinking lofty thoughts, but associating with the lowly” (Bede or Florus, on Romans 11), we may say to them—not insulting them presumptuously, but rejoicing with trembling (Psalm 2:11):

> “Come, let us walk in the light of the Lord, for his name is great among the nations.”

For if they hear and obey, they will be among those to whom it was said:

> “Come to him, and be enlightened” (Romans 11);

and your faces will not be put to shame. But if they hear and do not obey, see and envy, they are among those of whom it was said:

> “The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away” (Psalm 111:10).

But I, says the Church to Christ,

> “like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, have hoped in the mercy of God forever and for age upon age” (Psalm 51:10).

## THE WORKS AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS FOLLOW

These works Augustine composed during the time of his presbyterate and episcopate. An index of other short works is appended, in which he expressly dealt with these same heretics before his presbyterate, as well as of the remaining works in which he criticized them incidentally at various times.

[Note: [Col. 0063] Concerning the following book, see Retractions, book 1, chapter 14, volume 1, column 605, no. 1, beginning with the words “Now indeed,” through column 608, no. 6, ending with the words “The same thing would seem to be.” M.]

[Col. 0063]

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING SHORT WORK

Augustine lists the book *On the Usefulness of Believing* as the first of those he published during his presbyterate. He assumed this office at Hippo at the beginning of the year 391, as we have already demonstrated elsewhere in the preface to the second volume, in the discussion of Augustine’s Letters 8, 9, and so forth.

He wrote this work on behalf of Honoratus, in order to recall a friend from the error of the Manichaeans, into whose snares he himself had once cast him, as he confesses at the beginning of the book. Honoratus had been deceived by those attractive promises of the Manichaeans, by which they promised to teach nothing except what could be made evident and clear by reason. He mocked the discipline of the Catholic Church because faith was imposed upon human beings and the truth was not demonstrated to them by reason.

Since, therefore, Honoratus—deceived by a false appearance of truth, and not drawn into the error for the sake of temporal advantage—clung to it, and was thus more deceived by the heretics than himself a heretic, Augustine hoped that he might bring him to true religion if he could show that the Manichaeans sacrilegiously and rashly attacked those who, following the authority of the Catholic faith, are fortified by believing and prepared for God, who will enlighten them, before they are able to behold that truth which is seen by a purified mind. In this work he accomplishes that purpose by also defending the Old Testament, which especially disturbed the uninstructed because of the criticisms the Manichaeans directed against it.

The outcome desired by Augustine’s labor and zeal on Honoratus’s behalf was achieved—if, as Rivius thinks, this is the same Honoratus who wrote to Augustine from Carthage around the year 412 and proposed various questions for him to resolve. Although this Honoratus had not yet received baptism, the questions he raises do not at all suggest a Manichaean; Augustine himself speaks of the Manichaeans only incidentally and as people whom he regarded as heretics.

Cassiodorus calls this same Honoratus, to whom Augustine writes Letter 140, a presbyter; perhaps he was later advanced to the presbyterate. In Letter 83 Augustine speaks of the death of another Honoratus, a presbyter. Toward the end of his life he also wrote Letter 228 to the Thabennensian bishop of the same name.

[Col. 0065]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO  
## ONE BOOK ON THE USEFULNESS OF BELIEVING, TO HONORATUS

[Note: [Col. 0065] Written around the year 391.]

[Note: [Col. 0065] For correcting the book *On the Usefulness of Believing*, we used five Vatican manuscripts, seven French manuscripts, and the manuscripts of Victorinus, Germanus, Corbie, Michael, Cîteaux, Laon Cathedral, and the copy belonging to Lord de Maran of Toulouse; also the various readings of three Belgian manuscripts published by the Louvain scholars, and finally the oldest and principal editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0065] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

Augustine argues against the Manichaeans and proves that they sacrilegiously and rashly attack those who, following the authority of the Catholic faith, prepare themselves by its assistance for the understanding of the mysteries, while believing what they are not yet able to grasp intellectually. Above all, however, he shows that the Old Testament is wrongly criticized by these same heretics.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The Purpose for Which He Writes This to Honoratus; A Heretic and One Who Believes Heretics Are Not the Same; The Subject of the Work; How Augustine Escaped from Deception by the Manichaeans; A Saying of the Manichaeans About Those Who Abandon Their Sect

If, Honoratus, a heretic and a person who believes heretics seemed to me to be one and the same thing, I would think that both my tongue and my pen ought to remain silent in this matter. But since there is a very great difference between the two—for, in my opinion, a heretic is someone who, for the sake of some temporal advantage, and especially of his own glory and superiority, either generates or follows false and novel opinions, whereas someone who believes such people is a person deceived by a certain illusion of truth and piety—since this is so, I did not think I ought to remain silent with you about what I think concerning the discovery and retention of truth, for which, as you know, we have burned with great love from the beginning of adolescence.

But this matter is far removed from the minds of vain people who, having advanced and fallen too deeply into bodily things, think that nothing exists except what they perceive through those five familiar messengers of the body. The impressions and images they have received through these senses they carry about with them even when they try to withdraw from the senses; and, using their deadly and most deceptive rule, they think they can measure with complete accuracy the unspeakable inner sanctuaries of truth.

Nothing is easier, my dearest friend, than not only to say but also to suppose that one has found the truth. But how difficult it actually is, you will, I trust, recognize from this letter of mine. That it may benefit you—or at least do you no harm—and likewise all in whose hands it may perhaps come, I have asked God and continue to ask him. I hope this will happen if I am rightly conscious of myself: that I approached this writing with a devout and dutiful spirit, not out of a desire for an empty reputation or a trivial display.

[Col. 0066]

### 2. The Purpose of the Work; Augustine’s Earlier Deception by the Manichaeans

My purpose, then, is to prove to you, if I can, that the Manichaeans sacrilegiously and rashly attack those who, following the authority of the Catholic faith, are fortified by believing and prepared for God, who will enlighten them, before they are able to behold that truth which is seen by a purified mind.

For you know, Honoratus, that we fell in with such people for no other reason than that they said that, once the authority that inspires fear had been set aside, they would lead those willing to listen to them to God by pure and simple reason, and free them from every error.

What else forced me for nearly nine years, after rejecting the religion instilled in me as a child by my parents, to follow those men and listen to them diligently,

[Note: [Col. 0065] See *Confessions*, book 1, chapter [number omitted], and book 5, chapter 14.]

except that they said we were terrified by superstition and commanded to believe before reason, whereas they pressured no one to believe until the truth had first been examined and unraveled?

Who would not be enticed by these promises, especially a young mind eager for truth, and proud and talkative because of the disputations of certain learned men at school? That was the sort of person they found in me: one who scorned what seemed like old women’s tales and desired to grasp and drink in the open and sincere truth they promised.

But what reason, in turn, drew me back from remaining wholly with them, so that I kept to the rank which they call that of the Hearers and did not abandon the hope and affairs of this world? It was that I noticed that they themselves were more eloquent and copious in refuting others than firm and certain in proving their own doctrines.

But what should I say of myself, who was already a Catholic Christian? What breasts

[Note: [Col. 0065] The printed editions read, “who now [drink] the breasts of the Church.” The manuscripts, however, read, “what breasts,” omitting the word “of the Church.”]

I now returned to, after having been almost exhausted and dried up by a very long thirst, with all my eagerness; and I pressed and squeezed them, weeping and groaning more deeply, so that what flowed from them might be enough to refresh me in my condition and restore me to hope of life and salvation.

What, then, should I say about myself? You were not yet a Christian. At my urging, although you vehemently detested those men, you were scarcely persuaded to listen to them and investigate whether they might be worth hearing. By what other thing, I ask you—remember, I beg you—were you attracted except by some great presumption and promise of rational explanations?

But because they spent a long time and at great length arguing most broadly and vehemently about the errors of the unlearned—a matter I learned only later is extremely easy for anyone of moderate education—if they inserted anything of their own that we had to retain because nothing else presented itself in which we could rest, we thought it necessary to hold on to it.

Thus they treated us as crafty bird-catchers do, who fix branches smeared with birdlime near water

[Note: [Col. 0067] The printed editions read, “near the water.” The manuscripts read, “because of the water,” with the same sense.]

in order to deceive thirsty birds. For they cover over, or in some way conceal, the other waters that are nearby; or they even frighten the birds away from them with terrifying contrivances, so that the birds fall into their snares not by choice but from want.

### 3. Against the Manichaean Saying, “The Light Passed Through Him”

But why do I not answer myself that these polished and witty comparisons, and criticisms of this kind, can be directed, with great urbanity and sharpness, by any opponent against everyone who teaches anything?

For this reason I thought I should insert something of the kind into my letter: to warn them to stop acting in this way, so that, as that man says, once the jokes of commonplaces have been set aside, matter may contend with matter, cause with cause, and reason with reason (Cicero).

Therefore let them stop saying what they have on their lips as though it were indispensable whenever someone who has listened to them for a longer time abandons them:

> “The light passed through him.”

You see, my greatest concern—for I am not overly anxious about them—how empty and easy this statement could be for anyone to criticize. I therefore leave its examination to your prudence.

For I do not fear that you will think I was “inhabited by the light” when I was entangled in the life of this world and carried a dark hope: hope concerning the beauty of a wife, the pomp of riches, the vanity of honors, and the other harmful and destructive pleasures. As you know, I did not cease to desire and hope for all these things while I listened to them eagerly.

Nor do I attribute this to their teaching. For I admit that they too earnestly warned people to avoid such things. But to say that I was abandoned by the light when I had turned away from all these shadows of worldly things and had resolved to be content with the nourishment necessary for the health of the body, while to say that I had been enlightened and radiant when I loved these things and was held fast in their entanglements, is, to put it as mildly as possible, the judgment of someone who does not consider very sharply the matters about which he loves to speak at length.

But let us come to the issue, if you please.

## CHAPTER II

### 4. The Manichaeans Criticize the Old Testament Before the Unlearned

For you know very well that the Manichaeans, when they criticize the Catholic faith and especially tear apart and mutilate the Old Testament, disturb the unlearned. Such people certainly do not know to what extent those passages should be accepted or how, when profitably absorbed, they descend into the veins and even the marrow of souls that are still, as it were, infants.

And because certain passages are found there that may offend the minds of the ignorant and careless—for that is the overwhelming majority—they can be attacked in popular fashion. But they cannot be defended in popular fashion by very many people, because of the mysteries contained in them. Those few who know how to do so do not enjoy public and notorious contests in debate, and for that reason they are little known except to those who seek them out most persistently.

Concerning this rashness of the Manichaeans, then, by which they criticize the Old Testament and the Catholic faith, receive, I beg you, what moves me. I desire and hope that you will receive these words in the spirit in which I speak them.

God knows—he to whom the hidden things of my conscience are known—that I am doing nothing maliciously in this discussion. Rather, I am acting, as I think one should, for the sake of proving the truth. We have long since decided to live for this one purpose, and with extraordinary anxiety: lest it be very easy for me to err together with you, while it should be very difficult for me to keep the straight path together with you.

But I presume that even in this hope—that you may attain the way of wisdom with me—the one to whom I have been consecrated will not abandon me. I try to gaze upon him day and night. And because, on account of my sins and the habit of long-standing opinions, I know that I carry a weakened eye of the soul, wounded by their blows, I often ask him with tears.

Just as, after a long blindness and darkness, when the eyes have scarcely been opened and still resist the light by blinking and turning away from it, although they desire it—especially if someone tries to show them this sun—so it is happening to me now. I do not deny that there is an ineffable and unique good of the soul, perceived by the mind; but I confess with tears and groans that I am not yet fit to contemplate it.

He will not abandon me, then, if I am not pretending, if duty guides me, if I love truth, if I cherish friendship, and if I greatly fear that you may be deceived.

## CHAPTER III

### 5. Four Ways of Treating the Scriptures of the Old Testament; History and Causation in Scripture; Analogy; Allegory; The Law Is Necessary Only for Those Who Need the Usefulness of Servitude and Fear; Mysteries Veiled in the Old Law

Every Scripture called the Old Testament is handed down in four ways to those who desire to know it carefully: according to history, according to causation (*aetiologia*), according to analogy, and according to allegory.

Do not think me foolish for using Greek terms. First, I received them in this form, and I do not dare to communicate them to you otherwise than I received them. Then you yourself notice that among us the names for these matters are not customary. If I had fashioned them by translation, I would certainly be more foolish; but if I used circumlocution, I would be less efficient in exposition.

I ask only that you believe that, however I may be mistaken, I am doing nothing out of inflated or conceited vanity.

It is handed down according to history when we are taught what was written or what was done, and what was not done but merely written as though it had been done.

According to causation, when it is shown for what reason something was either done or said.

According to analogy, when it is demonstrated that the two Testaments, the Old and the New, do not contradict each other.

According to allegory, when we are taught that certain things that have been written should not be understood literally but figuratively.

### 6. The Lord and the Apostles Used All These Methods

Our Lord Jesus Christ and the Apostles used all these methods. For the historical method is involved when it was objected that his disciples had plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath:

> “Have you not read,” he said, “what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?” (Matthew 12:3–4).

The causal method, however, applies to the passage in which Christ forbade a man to divorce his wife except on account of fornication, and the questioners reported that Moses, after giving a certificate of divorce, had permitted the right to dismiss her:

> “Moses did this,” he said, “because of the hardness of your hearts” (Matthew 19:8).

Here the reason was given why Moses had rightly permitted this for the time being, so that the commandment given by Christ might appear to indicate that other times had now arrived. It would take too long to explain the changes and succession of these periods, arranged and ordered by a remarkable disposition of divine providence.

### 7. The Analogy Between the Two Testaments

As for analogy, by which the harmony of the two Testaments is perceived, why should I say that all those whose authority they accept used it, when they themselves can consider how often they are accustomed to say that many things were inserted into the divine Scriptures by certain unknown corrupters of the truth?

This claim always seemed to me extremely weak, even when I listened to them; and not to me alone, but also to you—for I remember well—and to all of us who were trying to exercise somewhat greater care in judging than the crowd of believers.

Now, however, after many things that troubled me most have been explained and unraveled for me—those very matters in which their speech usually boasts and exults all the more extravagantly because it is more secure without an opponent—nothing seems to me to be said by them more shamelessly, or, to speak more mildly, more carelessly and weakly, than that the divine Scriptures have been corrupted. They cannot prove this by any copies surviving in so recent a memory.

If they said that they did not think those writings should be accepted at all because they were composed by people whom they did not believe had written the truth, their evasion would at least be somewhat more reasonable, or their error more human. They did this concerning the book entitled *The Acts of the Apostles*.

When I consider their decision in this matter, I cannot sufficiently marvel at it. For in this matter I do not seek human wisdom, but ordinary common sense. That book contains so much resembling the writings they accept that it seems to me sheer folly not to accept it as well, and, if anything in it offends them, to say that it is false and was inserted.

Or, if such an argument is shameless—as it is—why do they think it has any force in Paul’s Letters and in the four books of the Gospel? I do not know whether, proportionately, there could have been many more passages in those works than in the Acts that they wish to believe were inserted by corrupters.

But surely the point is this, as it seems to me; consider it with me, I ask, with the calmest and most impartial judgment.

You know that, while attempting to introduce the person of their founder Manichaeus into the number of the Apostles, they say that the Holy Spirit whom the Lord promised he would send to his disciples came to us through Manichaeus himself.

Therefore, if they accepted the *Acts of the Apostles*, in which the coming of the Holy Spirit is clearly proclaimed (Acts 2:2–4), they would find no way to say that this had been inserted. For they want certain corrupters of the divine books to have existed before the time of Manichaeus, and they say that those corrupters altered the books because they wished to mix the law of the Jews with the Gospel.

But they cannot say this about the Holy Spirit unless perhaps they assert that those people predicted the future and placed in their books something that would later be brought forward against Manichaeus, who would say that the Holy Spirit had been sent through him.

But we shall speak more clearly about the Holy Spirit on another occasion. For now, let us return to what I had undertaken.

### 8. Allegory in the New Testament

For I think it has been sufficiently demonstrated that history, causation, and analogy are also found in the New Testament. It remains to demonstrate allegory.

Our own Liberator uses an allegory in the Gospel drawn from the Old Testament:

> “This generation,” he says, “seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:39–40).

What need I say about the apostle Paul, who indicates in his First Letter to the Corinthians that the very history of the Exodus was an allegory of the future Christian people?

> “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; [Note: [Col. 0070] The printed editions read “in Moses”; the manuscripts, following the Greek, read “into Moses.” Likewise below, the agreeing ancient Greek books have “For they drank,” whereas the printed editions have “But they drank.”] and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them”—the manuscripts read, “the rock accompanying them”—“and the rock was Christ. But God was not pleased with most of them”—the printed editions read, “God was not well pleased”; the manuscripts read, “was not pleased”—“for they were struck down in the wilderness.

> “Now these things happened as examples for us, so that we might not be desirous of evil things, as they desired them. Nor should we worship idols, as some of them did, as it is written: ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.’ Nor should we commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. Nor should we test Christ, as some of them tested him, and were destroyed by serpents. Nor should we grumble, as some of them grumbled, and perished by the destroyer. All these things happened to them as examples. They were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:1–11).

There is also an allegory in the Apostle that is especially relevant to the present issue, because they themselves are accustomed to bring it forward and display it in debate.

Paul likewise says to the Galatians:

> “For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the one who was born from the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one from the free woman was born through the promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two Testaments: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, bordering on the Jerusalem that now exists, and it is in slavery with its children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all” (Galatians 4:22–26).

### 9. The Law Is Necessary Only for Those Who Still Need Servitude

These exceedingly wicked people, then, while trying to frustrate the Law, force us to approve these Scriptures. They pay attention to the statement that those who are under the Law are in slavery, and they make this, above all, the subject of their attacks:

> “You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4).

We grant that all these things are true. Nor do we say that the Law is necessary except for those for whom servitude is still useful. Therefore it was usefully given, because people who could not be recalled from sins by reason had to be restrained by such a law, namely, by threats and terrors of punishments that may seem foolish.

When the grace of Christ frees us from these things, it does not condemn that Law. Rather, it invites us to obey its love rather than serve the fear of the Law.

That is grace: the gift from God whose arrival those who still wish to remain under the bonds of the Law do not understand. Paul rightly rebukes them as faithless, because they do not believe that, through our Lord Jesus, they have now been freed from the servitude to which, at a particular time, they had been subjected by God’s perfectly just arrangement.

Hence comes the statement of the same Apostle:

> “The Law was our pedagogue toward Christ” (Galatians 3:24).

Thus he gave people a pedagogue whom they would fear, and afterward a teacher whom they would love.

Yet within the precepts and commandments of the Law—which Christians are not now permitted to practice, such as the Sabbath, circumcision, sacrifices, and anything of that kind—such great mysteries are contained that every devout person understands that nothing is more destructive than to take whatever is there literally, that is, according to the word; and that nothing is more beneficial than for it to be revealed according to the spirit.

Hence comes the statement:

> “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”

[Note: [Col. 0071] *Retractions*, chapter 14, no. 1.]

Hence also comes this:

> “The same veil remains over the reading of the Old Testament; it is not revealed, because it is abolished in Christ” (2 Corinthians 3:6, 14, 16).

It is abolished in Christ—not the Old Testament, but its veil—so that through Christ what is obscure and covered without Christ may be understood and, as it were, stripped bare.

Immediately the same Apostle adds:

> “But when you turn to Christ, the veil will be taken away.”

For he did not say, “The Law will be taken away,” or, “The Old Testament will be taken away.”

Therefore, through the Lord’s grace, these things were not removed as though useless matters had been hidden there. Rather, what was removed was the covering by which useful things had been hidden.

This is what happens with those who diligently and devoutly seek the meaning of those Scriptures, not in a disorderly or wicked manner: both the order of events and the causes of deeds and sayings are carefully demonstrated, as is the great harmony of the Old Testament with the New, so that not even a single letter that does not agree with it remains; and the mysteries of the figures are so profound that everything brought forth by interpretation compels them to acknowledge that those who wish to condemn these things before learning them are wretched.

## CHAPTER IV

### 10. Three Kinds of Error Among Readers

But, setting aside for the moment the heights of learning, let me deal with you as I think one should deal with a friend—that is, as I am able, not as I have admired the greatest scholars for being able to do.

There are three kinds of error by which people go astray when they read something. I shall discuss each of them.

The first kind occurs when what is false is thought to be true, although the writer intended something else.

The second, although it does not extend so broadly, is no less harmful: when what is false is thought to be true, but it is nevertheless thought to be what the writer himself intended.

The third occurs when something true is understood from another person’s writing, although the writer did not understand it.

There is no small usefulness in this third kind; indeed, if you consider it more carefully, the entire fruit of reading is sound.

An example of the first kind would be someone who says and believes, for example, that Rhadamanthus hears and judges the cases of the dead in the underworld because he has read this in Virgil’s poem (*Aeneid* 6.566–569). Such a person errs in two ways: he believes something that should not be believed, and the person whose work he read should not be thought to have believed it either.

The second kind can be recognized in this way: suppose someone, because Lucretius writes that the soul consists of atoms and that after death it dissolves into those same atoms and perishes, considers this true and something he ought to believe.

This person too is no less wretched if, concerning so important a matter, he has persuaded himself that what is false is certain, even though Lucretius—whose books deceived him—held that opinion.

For what does it profit him to be certain about the author’s opinion, when he has chosen an author not through whom he would avoid error, but with whom he would go astray?

[Note: [Col. 0072] In the earlier editions the negating particle was omitted here.]

The third kind is illustrated by the following case: suppose someone, after reading a passage in Epicurus’s books in which Epicurus praises self-restraint, asserts that Epicurus placed the highest good in virtue and therefore ought not to be blamed.

What harm does Epicurus’s error do to this person, if Epicurus believes the highest good of human beings to be bodily pleasure, while the reader has not adopted so shameful and harmful an opinion and approves Epicurus for no other reason than that he does not think Epicurus held an opinion that ought not to be held?

This error is not merely human; it is often also most worthy of a human being.

For what if someone reported to me concerning a person whom I loved that, although bearded, he had said in the hearing of many that he liked childhood and infancy so much that he had even sworn he wished to live in the same way? Suppose this were so proved to me that it would be shameless for me to deny it. Would I seem worthy of blame if, when he said this, I thought he meant that he approved innocence and that he kept his mind apart from the desires by which the human race is entangled, and if I loved him more and more because of it, even though perhaps he had foolishly become enamored of a certain freedom in children’s games and eating, and of lazy leisure?

Suppose that he died after this had been reported to me and that I could not question him about anything so that he might explain his meaning. Would anyone be so wicked as to be angry with me when, through those very words I had received, I praised the man’s purpose and intention?

What is more, would not a fair judge of things perhaps hesitate to praise my opinion and intention, since I approved innocence and, in a doubtful matter, judged one human being favorably concerning another, when it would also have been permissible to judge badly?

[Note: [Col. 0073] The Louvain edition reads, “would curse.” Erasmus and the manuscripts more correctly read, “when it would have been permissible to judge badly”; supply “to judge.”]

## CHAPTER V
## 11. Three possible differences among writings

The Catholic Church cannot be refuted in any respect from the foregoing considerations regarding its reading of the Old Testament. Since this is so, hear also the same number of conditions and differences among those writings. For necessarily the same number of possibilities arise. Either someone wrote usefully, but someone else understands him unprofitably; or both the writing and its interpretation are unprofitable; or the reader understands profitably, although the author whose work is being read wrote in the opposite way.

Of these three, I do not condemn the first, and I take no concern over the last. For I cannot blame a man who has been misunderstood through no fault of his own; nor can I be displeased that someone is read who did not see the truth, since I see that this does no harm to the readers. One category, therefore, is the most approved and, so to speak, the purest: when good things have been written and are taken in a good sense by the readers.

Yet this category too is still divided in two, for it does not entirely exclude error. It often happens that, although the writer has understood correctly, the reader also understands correctly—but something other than what the writer meant; sometimes better, sometimes worse, though still profitably. But when we understand what the author whom we are reading understood, and that is most suited to living a good life, truth is present in its fullest measure, and no opening remains for falsehood from any other quarter.

When the reading concerns the most obscure matters, this kind of agreement is altogether rare. Nor, in my opinion, can it be known with certainty; it can only be believed. For by what arguments could I gather the intention of an absent or dead man so as to be able to swear to it, when, even if he were present and questioned, there could be many things which—if he were not wicked—he would most conscientiously conceal? I do not think it relevant to determining the matter what sort of person the writer was. Nevertheless, the man whose writings have provided for the benefit of the human race and posterity is rightly believed to have been thoroughly good.

## 12. In what category they place the alleged error of the Catholic Church

Therefore I wish these men would tell me in which category they place the error which they think belongs to the Catholic Church. If in the first, it is certainly a serious charge; but it requires no lengthy defense. It is enough to deny that we understand matters in the way they suppose when they attack us. If in the second, the charge is no less serious; but it will be refuted by the same reply. If in the third, there is no charge at all.

Come, then, and consider the Scriptures themselves. What do they object to the books called those of the Old Testament? Is it that they are good, but are badly understood by us? Yet they themselves do not accept them. Or is it because they are neither good nor rightly understood? But the preceding defense is sufficient to overthrow this claim. Or will they say: “Although they are rightly understood by you, they are nevertheless bad”? What is this other than absolving the living opponents with whom the dispute is being conducted, [Col. 0074] and accusing men long dead, with whom no controversy exists?

For my part, I believe that those men committed everything useful to memory, that they were great and divine, and that that law was promulgated and established by God’s command and will. Although I know very little of the books belonging to that class, I can nevertheless easily persuade you of this, if a fair and wholly unobstinate mind is brought to the matter. I shall do so when we are granted access to your kindly ears and mind. But that must wait until I can do it. For now, is it not enough for me that, whatever the truth of this matter may be, I was not deceived?

# CHAPTER VI

## 13. The Scriptures should not be judged by their hostile interpreters

I call my conscience and God, who dwells in pure souls, to witness that I consider nothing wiser, chaster, or more religious than all those Scriptures which the Catholic Church preserves under the name of the Old Testament.

You are surprised; I know. I cannot conceal that we had been persuaded of something very different. But surely nothing is fuller of rashness—which was present in us when we were boys—than to abandon the interpreters of whatever books, men who profess that they can master those books and transmit them to their pupils, and to seek the meaning of those books from men who, for some reason or other, have declared the bitterest war against their founders and authors.

Who has ever thought that the obscure and hidden books of Aristotle should be explained by one of Aristotle’s enemies? And I say this even of disciplines in which a reader can perhaps go astray without sacrilege. Who, finally, would have wished to read the geometrical writings of Archimedes or learn them under the instruction of Epicurus, who argued against them with great obstinacy while understanding, as I suppose, none of them?

Or are these Scriptures of the Law so perfectly plain that these men may attack them—as though they had been publicly explained—in vain and to no purpose? They seem to me like that little woman whom these same men are accustomed to mock. Angry because the sun was being praised and recommended for worship by a certain Manichaean woman, she, being religiously simple-minded, leapt up in agitation and, repeatedly stamping her foot on the place illuminated by the sun through the window, began to shout: “Look, I am trampling on the sun, your god!” Entirely foolish and womanish—who denies it? But do not these men seem similar, when they tear apart with a great rush of speech and abuse things they do not understand—things whose reason, nature, and character they do not understand at all, although they may appear commonplace, yet are subtle to those who understand and divine—because the ignorant applaud them, and so they think they are accomplishing something?

Whatever may be found in those Scriptures, believe me, it is profound and divine. Truth is present throughout, together with a discipline most perfectly suited to nourishing and restoring souls; and it is so adapted that no one can fail to draw from it what is sufficient for him, provided that he approaches it devoutly and reverently, as true religion requires.

To prove this to you would require many arguments and a longer discourse. I must first work upon you so that you do not hate the authors themselves, and then so that you love them—and this must be done in some other way rather than by explaining their meanings and writings.

[Col. 0075]

For if we hated Virgil—or rather, if before understanding him we had not come to love him through the recommendation of our elders—we would never be satisfied with the countless questions about him with which grammarians are accustomed to be troubled and perplexed. Nor would we gladly listen to those who resolved them while praising him; instead, we would favor anyone who tried to demonstrate that through these passages Virgil had erred and raved.

But now, when many people attempt in various ways, each according to his own capacity, to explain those passages, those receive the greatest applause through whose interpretation the poet is found to be better: one who, according to them, not only committed no fault but sang nothing that was not worthy of praise—even in the judgment of those who do not understand him.

Thus, when a teacher fails over some minor question and has no answer to give, we are more likely to be angry with him than to think that mule to be due to a fault of Maro. But if, in defending himself, he should assert that so great an author had made a mistake, his pupils would scarcely remain with him, even if they had paid him their fees.

How much more, then, should we have shown a similar goodwill toward those through whom the Holy Spirit has spoken, as the passage of so many ages has confirmed? Yet, of course, we considered that nothing should be believed by us because we were very intelligent young men and remarkable investigators of arguments: we had not even read those writings through, had not sought teachers, had not blamed our own slowness to some degree, nor granted even moderate consideration to those who had wished that writings of this kind should be read, preserved, and handled throughout the whole world for so long a time. We were moved instead by the voices of those who were hostile and inimical to them—men among whom, by an unheard-of promise of rational explanation, we would be compelled to believe and worship thousands of false tales.

# CHAPTER VII

## 14. True religion must be sought

### It must be sought among those distinguished by widespread fame and the devotion of entire peoples

### The objection that truth exists among only a few and need not be sought among the multitude of Catholics is futile

### Honoratus rashly thought that certain absurdities were taught in the Catholic religion

### Nothing prevented the search for religion among the Catholics

When religion is sought, the inquiry must begin from the Catholic Church. But now I shall carry out what I have undertaken, if I can, and deal with you in such a way that I shall not yet disclose the Catholic faith itself, but shall show those whose souls are their concern the hope of divine fruit and of finding the truth as they investigate its great mysteries.

No one doubts that a person who seeks the true religion either already believes that the soul is immortal and that this religion benefits it, or at least wishes to find this very truth within that religion. Religion, therefore, exists entirely for the sake of the soul. For whatever the nature of the body may be, it causes the soul no concern or anxiety, especially after death, once the soul has attained that by which it is blessed.

Religion, then—if there is such a thing—is established either solely or chiefly for the sake of the soul. This soul—I shall see for what reason, and I confess that the reason is most obscure—nevertheless wanders and is foolish, as we see, until it acquires and apprehends wisdom; and perhaps it is itself the true religion.

Am I sending you to fables? Am I compelling you to believe anything rashly? I say that our soul, entangled and sunk in error and folly, is seeking the way—if there is a way—to the truth. If this does not exist in you, pardon me and, I beg you, share your wisdom with me. But if you recognize in yourself what I am saying, let us seek the truth together.

[Col. 0076]

## 15. Those who profess religions must be sought out

Suppose that until now we had heard no one presenting any religion. Here is a new matter and undertaking for us. The teachers of this matter, if there are any, must, I believe, be sought out.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads *si nulla est* (“if there is none”); erroneously.]

Suppose that we have found others holding different opinions and wishing to draw each person to themselves through the diversity of their beliefs; but that, among them, certain people are distinguished for the moment by widespread fame and by the occupation, so to speak, of almost all peoples.

Whether these people possess the truth is a great question. But should they not first be investigated, so that, as long as we are wandering—if indeed we are human beings—we may at least seem to wander together with the human race?

## 16. “The truth exists among a few”

“But,” someone says, “the truth exists among a few.”

Then you already know what it is, if you know among whom it exists. Did I not say a little earlier that we should inquire as though we were beginners?

But if, from the very force of truth, you infer that only a few possess it, while you do not know who they are, then—if those who know the truth are so few that they hold the multitude by their authority—from where can this small number free itself and, so to speak, filter itself out into those hidden matters?

Do we not see how few attain the highest eloquence, although the schools of rhetoricians resound throughout the whole world with crowds of young men? Do all those who wish to become good orators, frightened by the multitude of the unlearned, think that they should devote themselves to the speeches of Caecilius or Erucius rather than to those of Cicero?

Everyone desires what has been confirmed by the authority of their ancestors. The crowds of the unlearned also attempt to learn what has been accepted as something to be learned from the few who are educated. Very few attain it; fewer practice it; very few become famous.

What if true religion is something of this kind? What if a multitude of the unlearned fills the churches, but there is no reason to conclude that, for this reason, no one has been perfected in those mysteries?

And yet, if as few people studied eloquence as are eloquent, our parents would never have thought that we should be entrusted to such teachers. Since the multitude—which is abundant in its unlearned element—invited us to these studies so that we might love what only a few can attain, why do we refuse to recognize a similar situation in religion, which we perhaps disregard at great risk to the soul?

For if the truest and purest worship of God, although it exists among the few, nevertheless exists among those to whom the multitude—though entangled in desires and removed from purity of understanding—gives its assent, who could doubt that this is possible?

I ask: if someone rebuked our rashness and folly because we did not diligently investigate this religion among its teachers, when we are deeply concerned to find it, what could we answer?

Did the multitude deter me? Why did no multitude deter me from the study of the liberal arts, which bring scarcely any advantage to this present life? Why did none deter me from seeking money, from pursuing honor, from acquiring and preserving good health, or finally from desiring the blessed life—although everyone is occupied with these things, while only a few excel in them?

[Col. 0077]

## 17. The objection that absurdities seemed to be taught there

“But absurd things seemed to be said there.”

By whom were they asserted? By enemies, naturally—enemies for whatever reason and by whatever method. That is not the question now; nevertheless, they were enemies.

When I read them, I judged for myself. Is that reasonable? Without any training in poetry, you would not dare approach Terentianus Maurus without a teacher. Asper, Cornutus, Donatus, and countless others are required in order that any poet may be understood—one whose poems and theatrical applause seem to attract attention. Yet you rush without a guide upon those Books which, whatever their nature may be, are nevertheless holy and full of divine things, and which are proclaimed by the confession of almost the entire human race; you dare to pass judgment on them without a teacher.

When you encounter something that seems absurd, do you not rather accuse your own slowness and your soul, corrupted by the decay of this world, such as belongs to all fools, than accuse those who perhaps cannot be understood by people of such a kind?

You should seek someone both devout and learned, or at least someone whom many people, with common agreement, would declare to be such. Under his instruction you would become better, and through his teaching more knowledgeable.

Was he not easily found? He should be sought with effort. Was he lacking in the land where you lived? What reason could more usefully compel you to travel abroad? Was he completely hidden or unavailable on the mainland? You should sail. If he could not be found across the sea nearby, you should proceed as far as those lands where the events contained in those Books are said to have taken place.

What have we done of this kind, Honoratus? And yet we perhaps condemned, according to our own will and judgment, a religion that may be most holy—for I am still speaking as though the matter were uncertain—although its reputation has already spread throughout the whole world. We did so as most wretched boys.

What if those things in the same Scriptures that seem to offend some unlearned people were placed there so that, when matters repugnant to the understanding of ordinary people—and even more to that of wise and holy people—were read, we might seek their hidden meaning with much greater diligence?

Do you not see how people try to interpret the Catamite of the *Bucolics*, for whom the harsh shepherd “poured himself out” (*effluxit*; the reading is uncertain), and the boy Alexis, for whom Plato too is said to have composed a love poem, as signifying something grand, though it escapes the judgment of the unlearned?

[Note: Published editions have *Catamitum Bucolicum*. The manuscripts have *Catamitum Bucolicorum*. “Catamitus,” the name for a boy kept for sexual service, is to be understood here as the boy Alexis himself, about whom Virgil writes in *Bucolics*, Eclogue 2.] And yet, without any sacrilege, the most fertile of poets may be regarded as having produced little songs of lust.

## 18. Nothing prevented the inquiry

But in fact, what was recalling and preventing us from seeking—was it the sanction of some law, the power of opponents, the unworthiness of consecrated persons [Note: One Michaelinus manuscript reads *sectatorum*, “followers”], a disreputable reputation, the novelty of the institution, or some secret profession?

None of these things exists. All divine and human laws permit the Catholic faith to be investigated. To hold and practice it is certainly permitted by human law, even if, with respect to divine law, we remain uncertain while we are in error. No enemy frightens us because of our weakness—although, if truth and the salvation of the soul are not found after being diligently sought where it is safest to seek them, they ought to be pursued at whatever risk.

All ranks of dignity and power serve this [Col. 0078] divine worship with the greatest devotion. The name of religion is most honorable and illustrious. What, then, finally prevents us from examining and investigating through pious and diligent inquiry whether this is that religion which a few must know and preserve with complete sincerity, even if the will and favor of all nations should unite in its support?

## 19. The inquiry must begin from the Catholic Church

Since this is so, let us suppose that, as I said, we are now seeking for the first time to which religion we should entrust our souls for purification and restoration. Without doubt, the beginning must be taken from the Catholic Church.

There are already more Christians than there would be if the Jews were added to the worshipers of idols. Among these Christians there are many heresies, and all of them wish to appear Catholic while calling everyone except themselves heretics. Yet there is one Church, as everyone admits. If you consider the whole world, it is more numerous; and, as those who know affirm, it is also more sincere than all the others in truth.

But the question of truth is a separate one. For those seeking, it is enough that there is one Catholic Church, to which the other heresies assign different names, while each of them calls itself by its own proper designation—names which they do not dare deny.

From this it becomes clear, to judges whom no partial favor hinders, to which body the Catholic name should be assigned—the name toward which all aspire.

[Note: Some manuscripts read *quod ei sit* (“that it belongs to it”).]

But lest anyone think that this needs to be argued at excessive length or unnecessarily, there is certainly one Church in which even human laws are, in a certain manner, Christian. I do not wish any prejudice to arise from this; I consider it simply the most suitable beginning for the inquiry.

For there is no need to fear that the true worship of God, resting on no strength of its own, should appear to require support from those whom it ought itself to support. Yet it would certainly be the condition of perfect happiness if the truth could be found there where both its investigation and its preservation are most secure. If it cannot be found there, only then should we approach and examine it elsewhere, whatever the risk.

# CHAPTER VIII

## 20. The path by which Augustine came to the Catholic religion

Having established these points—which, as I think, are so just that I ought to prevail with you in this case against any opponent—I shall explain to you, as best I can, what path I followed when I was seeking the true religion with the attitude in which I have now explained that it should be sought.

When I departed from you across the sea, I was already hesitating and uncertain about what I ought to hold and what I ought to abandon. My hesitation grew day by day after I heard that man whom, as you know, we had been promised as though from heaven to explain everything that troubled us.

[Note: Faustus, from *Confessions* 5.6.]

I found him to be, apart from a certain eloquence, just like the others whom I had come to know. Once I was established in Italy, I engaged in much reasoning and deliberation with myself—not about whether I should remain in that sect into which I regretted having fallen, but about how the truth might be found. No one knows my sighs in longing for it better than you.

Often it seemed to me that the truth could not be found, and great waves of my thoughts were carried toward the position of the Academics.

[Col. 0079]

But often again, when I considered as far as I could the human mind—so lively, so discerning, so perceptive—I did not think that the truth was hidden, except that the proper method of seeking it was hidden within it. I thought that this very method had to be received from some divine authority.

It remained to ask what that authority might be, since, amid such great disagreements, everyone promised that he would provide it. There appeared before me an impenetrable forest, into which I was very reluctant finally to enter. Meanwhile, without any rest, my soul was driven by its desire to discover the truth.

Nevertheless, I was gradually and increasingly separating myself from these people whom I had already decided to abandon. Nothing remained amid such dangers except to implore divine providence with tearful and pitiable cries, begging it to come to my aid.

I did this earnestly. By then certain discussions of the bishop of Milan had almost moved me—

[Note: Ambrose. See *Confessions* 5.13–14.]

—to the point that I wished, not without some hope, to investigate many things about the Old Testament, which, as you know, we had been badly taught to regard with horror.

I had decided to remain a catechumen in the Church to which I had been entrusted by my parents until I either found what I wanted or became convinced that it should not be sought. Thus, if there had been someone capable of teaching me, he would have found me at that time extremely ready and very teachable.

If you see that you too have long been affected in this way, with a similar concern for your soul, and if you already think that you have been tossed about enough and wish to put an end to labors of this kind, follow the path of Catholic teaching, which has come down from Christ himself through the Apostles to us and will continue from us to those who come after.

# CHAPTER IX

## 21. The Catholic Church requires faith from those who come to it; heretics promise rational explanation

### There is no fault in faith, and there is a great difference between one who believes and one who is credulous—a name of blame

“Ridiculous,” you say, “for everyone claims to hold and teach this.”

All heretics claim this, I cannot deny it—but they do so by promising those whom they entice that they will provide an explanation of the most obscure matters. For this reason they chiefly accuse the Catholic Church: those who come to it are instructed to believe, whereas they boast that they do not impose the yoke of belief but [Col. 0079] open the source of instruction.

“What,” you ask, “could have been said that would contribute more to their praise?”

It is not so. They do this without any genuine strength, merely to attract a multitude under the name of reason. The human soul naturally rejoices at such a promise, without considering its own strength and health. In its appetite for food suitable for the healthy—food that is dangerous except to the strong—it rushes into the poisons of deceivers.

For true religion cannot properly be entered at all unless one believes those things which one may later attain and apprehend—if one behaves well and proves worthy—and unless one is subject to a certain grave command of authority.

## 22. The distinction between believing and being credulous

But perhaps you ask to receive some explanation of this very matter, by which you may be persuaded that you must first be taught through faith rather than through reason. This can easily be done, provided that you show yourself fair-minded.

To make the matter proceed conveniently, I want you to imagine that you are answering someone who questions you. First tell me why it seems to you that one ought not to believe.

“Belief itself,” you say, “from which people are called credulous, seems to me to be a kind of fault. Otherwise we would not customarily throw this name at someone as an insult. For if being suspicious is a fault because one suspects what one has not discovered, how much more is being credulous a fault? The credulous person differs from the suspicious one in this: the suspicious person grants some uncertainty to things unknown, whereas the credulous person grants none.”

For the moment I accept this opinion and distinction. But you also know that we do not ordinarily call someone curious without blame, whereas we call someone studious even with praise. Therefore, if you please, consider what difference you think there is between these two as well.
