You will certainly reply that, although both are driven by a great desire to know, the curious person seeks what has nothing to do with him, while the studious person seeks what concerns him.

But since we do not deny that a wife, children, and their welfare belong to a man, suppose that someone living abroad diligently asks everyone who arrives how his wife and children are and how they are doing. He is certainly driven by a great desire to know; yet we do not call him studious, although he greatly wishes to know things that concern him most directly.

You now understand, therefore, that this definition of the studious person is unstable. Every studious person wishes to know what concerns him, but not everyone who does this should be called studious. Rather, the studious person is one who most earnestly seeks what pertains to the nourishment and refinement of the soul in a liberal manner.

Nevertheless, we correctly call someone a student, especially when we add what he is studying to hear.

[Note: The printed editions generally had *impensissime requirit, eum studentem recte appellamus* (“most earnestly seeks, we rightly call him a student”). This has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

We can also call someone devoted to his family if he loves only his own family; but without some further qualification, we do not think that he deserves the common name “studious.”

I would not call someone eager to hear how his relatives were doing “studious in listening” unless, rejoicing in good news, he frequently wished to hear the same thing; but I would call him a student even if he wished to hear it only once.

Now turn your attention back to the curious person, and tell me whether, if someone willingly listened to a story that would bring him absolutely no benefit—that is, a story about matters unrelated to him—and did so neither offensively [Note: Some manuscripts read *otiose*, “idly”] nor frequently, but very rarely and modestly, whether at a banquet, in a circle, or in any gathering, he would seem curious to you.

“I do not think so.”

But surely he would seem to have concern for the matter he willingly listened to.

Therefore the definition of curiosity too must be corrected by the same rule as that of studiousness. Consider, then, whether the earlier definitions should likewise be corrected. Why should someone be unworthy of the name “suspicious” merely because he suspects something on one occasion, or of the name “credulous” because he believes something on one occasion?

Thus, just as there is a great difference between being a student of some particular thing and being studious in general, and again between having concern for something and being curious, so there is a very great difference between believing and being credulous.

# CHAPTER X

[Col. 0081]

## 23. It is not shameful to believe in religion

### Very few are capable of grasping rational explanations; faith is the safer path to religion and one that all must follow

“But now,” you will say, “consider whether we ought to believe in religion. For even if we grant that believing is one thing and being credulous another, it does not follow that there is no fault in believing in religions. What if both believing and being credulous are faulty, just as being drunk and being prone to drunkenness are?”

Anyone who considers this certain seems to me unable to have any friend. For if it is shameful to believe something, then either the person who trusts a friend acts shamefully, or I do not see how someone who believes nothing a friend says can call either the friend or himself a friend.

Here you may perhaps say: “I grant that something must sometimes be believed. Now explain how it is not shameful to believe in religion before knowing.”

I shall do so, if I can. Accordingly, I ask you which you think involves the greater fault: entrusting religion to someone unworthy, or believing what is said by those who transmit it.

If I speak of an unworthy person, you may not understand me. I mean someone who approaches with a false heart. You will grant, I think, that it is more blameworthy to disclose any sacred secrets to such a person than to believe religious men when they make some statement about religion itself. For you could not properly answer otherwise.

Therefore, imagine now that someone is present who is about to hand religion on to you. How will you convince him that you are approaching with a true heart and that there is no deceit or pretense in you regarding this matter?

You will say, with a good conscience, that you are pretending nothing, asserting this as strongly as you can—but still only with words. For one human being cannot open the hidden places of his soul to another in such a way that his innermost character is completely known.

[Note: Manuscript B has *possit* (“can”), rather than *possis*; we follow Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition.]

But suppose he says: “Look, I believe you. Is it not fair that you too should believe me, since you will receive the benefit if I possess some truth, while I will be the one who gives it?”

What will you answer, except that one must believe?

## 24. Faith is necessary even for those capable of rational understanding

“But,” you say, “would it not have been better if you had given me a rational explanation [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read *reddere*, “to give”; M.], so that I could follow it wherever it led me, without any rashness?”

“Perhaps it would. But since the matter is so important that God must be known by reason, [Col. 0082] do you think that everyone is capable of grasping the rational explanations by which the human mind is led to divine understanding—or most people—or only a few?”

“I think only a few.”

“Do you believe that you are among them?”

“It is not for me to answer that.”

“Then you think it belongs to the other person to believe even this about you; and that is what he does. Remember only that he has already twice believed you when you made uncertain statements, while you are unwilling to believe him even once when he religiously warns you.”

But suppose that this is so: suppose that you approach religion with a true heart and are among the few human beings capable of grasping the rational explanations by which divine power leads to certain knowledge. What then? Do you think religion should be denied to the other people who do not possess an intellect so calm and clear? Or do you think that they must be led gradually, by certain steps, into those highest inner sanctuaries?

You plainly see which course is more religious. For you cannot in any way think that just anyone who desires so great a thing should be abandoned or rejected.

But do you not think that, unless a person first believes that he will reach the goal he has undertaken, offers a submissive mind [Note: Four manuscripts read *simplicem*, “simple”], and, obeying certain great and necessary precepts, purifies himself through a way of life [Note: Printed editions read *perpurgetur*, “is purified”; the manuscripts read *perpurget*, “purifies himself”], he will not otherwise attain those things that are purely true?

You certainly think so.

What harm, then, will it do to those whose class I now believe you belong to—those who can most easily grasp divine secrets through certain reasoning—if they come by this path, the same path followed by those who first believe?

“I do not think it will harm them.”

“But still,” you say, “why should they need to delay?”

“Because, even if they will not harm themselves by doing so, they will nevertheless harm others by their example. Few people have as high an opinion of themselves as they are capable of having. The one who thinks too little of himself must be encouraged; the one who thinks too highly must be restrained, so that the former is not crushed by despair and the latter is not hurled headlong by presumption.”

This is easily accomplished if even those who are able to fly are compelled for a little while to walk by the path that is safe for everyone else, lest they become a dangerous inducement to anyone.

This is the providence of true religion. This was divinely commanded; this was handed down by our blessed ancestors; this has been preserved down to us. To wish to disturb and overturn it is nothing other than to seek a sacrilegious path toward true religion.

Those who do this cannot reach their intended destination even if they are granted what they want. However outstanding their intellect may be, unless God is present they crawl upon the ground.

[Note: The older books consistently read *humo repunt* (“they crawl upon the ground”), rather than *humi repunt* (“they crawl on the ground”).]

God is present when there is concern for human fellowship among those who are striving toward God. No step toward heaven can be found that is firmer than this.

For my part, I cannot resist this reasoning. How could I say that nothing should be believed without knowledge, when friendship itself would be entirely impossible unless something were believed that cannot be demonstrated by certain reasoning, and when servants are often trusted without any fault on the part of their masters?

In religion, what could be more unjust than for the priests of God to believe us when we promise a sincere heart, while we refuse to believe them when they give us instruction?

Finally, what path could be healthier than first becoming capable of grasping the truth by placing faith in those things divinely established for the cultivation and preparation of the soul? Or, if you are already completely capable, why not go around for a while by the route where it is safest to proceed, rather than making yourself an author of danger and an example of rashness to others?

# CHAPTER XI
### 25. Why Believers Are Distinct from the Rashness of Those Who Opine. Understanding, Believing, Opining

It remains, then, for us to consider why those who promise to lead us by reason ought not to be followed. For how we may follow without blame those who command us to believe has already been stated; but some think that they may approach these sponsors of reason not only without reproach but even with some praise. Yet this is not so.

There are two commendable classes of persons in matters of religion: one consists of those who have already found the truth, whom we must judge to be supremely blessed; the other consists of those who seek with the greatest diligence and correctness. The first, then, are already in possession itself [Note: [Col. 0083] So the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “are even now.”]; the others are on the road by which one nevertheless arrives most certainly [Note: [Col. 0083] *Retractations* I.14.2.].

There are three other classes of people, plainly to be rejected and detested. One consists of those who merely opine—that is, those who think they know what they do not know. The second consists of those who do indeed recognize that they do not know, but do not seek in such a way that they can find. The third consists of those who neither think they know nor wish to seek.

There are likewise three things, as it were adjoining one another, which deserve the clearest distinction in the minds of human beings: understanding, believing, and opining. If these are considered in themselves, the first is always without fault; the second is sometimes accompanied by fault; the third is never without fault [Note: [Col. 0083] The printed editions add after “never without fault”: “and this we must refer to that same blessedness. For in this life, however much it may be known,” etc. The *Retractation* itself is the later statement transferred here by scribes.].

For understanding great, honorable, or even divine things is supremely blessed [Note: [Col. 0083] *Ibid.*]. Understanding superfluous things does no harm; but perhaps learning them did harm, when they occupied the time needed for necessary matters. In the case of harmful things, it is not understanding but doing or suffering them that is wretched. For if someone understands how an enemy can be killed without danger to himself, he is guilty not because of the understanding itself but because of desire; and if that desire is absent, what could be called more innocent?

Believing, however, is blameworthy when either something unworthy of God is believed, or something about a human being is too readily believed. In other matters, if someone believes something while understanding that he does not know it, there is no fault. For I believe that the most wicked conspirators were once killed through Cicero’s courage; yet not only do I not know this, I know with certainty that I cannot in any way know it.

Opining, on the other hand, is most disgraceful for two reasons: first, because one who has convinced himself that he already knows something cannot learn it—provided, of course, that it is something that can be learned; and second, because rashness in itself is a sign of a mind that is not rightly disposed. Even if someone thinks that he knows the very thing I mentioned about Cicero, although nothing prevents him from learning it, since the matter itself cannot be possessed as knowledge, he is nevertheless mistaken because he does not understand how greatly it matters whether something is held by the mind through a certain reasoning—which is what we call understanding—or whether it is usefully commended to posterity as something to be believed on the basis of report or written testimony [Note: [Col. 0083] Most manuscripts read: “whether it seems evident to the mind through a certain reasoning.”]. No error, surely, is free from disgrace.

What we understand, therefore, we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority [Note: [Col. 0083] *Ibid.*, §3.]; what we opine, to error. Yet everyone who understands also believes, and everyone who opines also believes; not everyone who believes understands; no one who opines understands.

If these three are referred to the five classes of people that we mentioned shortly before—that is, the two commendable classes we placed first and the remaining three, which are defective—we find that the first class, the blessed, believes the truth itself; while the second class, consisting of those who earnestly love the truth, believes authority. In these two classes belief is commendable.

In the first of the defective classes—that is, those who opine that they know what they do not know—belief is plainly defective. The other two reprehensible classes believe nothing: both those who seek the truth while despairing of finding it and those who do not seek it at all. This applies only to matters belonging in some way to a discipline. For in the other activities of life, I do not know how a human being could possibly believe nothing. Indeed, even those who say that in action they follow what is probable wish to appear to know that they can know nothing rather than to believe nothing. For who believes something without approving it? Or how can what they follow be probable if it is not approved?

Accordingly, there may be two classes of opponents of truth: one consisting of those who attack knowledge alone, not faith; the other consisting of those who condemn both. Yet whether either of these can be found among human beings, I again do not know.

This has been said so that we may understand that, while retaining faith even in matters we do not yet comprehend, we are protected from the rashness of those who merely opine. Those who say that nothing should be believed except what we know avoid only the name of opining—which must be admitted to be disgraceful and most wretched. But if they carefully consider how greatly it matters whether someone thinks he knows something or believes, moved by some authority, what he understands he does not know, they will certainly avoid the charge of error, inhumanity, and arrogance.

### 26. How Necessary Belief Is in Many Matters for Human Society. It Is Safest to Obey the Wise

For I ask: if what is not known ought not to be believed, how will children obey their parents and love them with mutual affection if they do not believe that those people are their parents? This cannot be known by reason in any way. Rather, through the mother’s testimony one believes concerning the father; and concerning the mother herself, usually one believes not the mother but the midwives, nurses, and servants. For can one to whom a child may be stolen and another substituted not be deceived and then deceive others? Yet we believe, and believe without any hesitation, what we confess that we cannot know.

Who does not see that, unless this is so, reverence—the most sacred bond of the human race—would be violated by the most arrogant crime? For who, even if insane, would think that someone should be blamed for performing the duties owed to those whom he believed to be his parents, even if they were not? And who, on the other hand, would not judge someone worthy of expulsion if he had utterly failed to love his true parents, fearing lest he love false ones?

Many examples could be brought forward to show that nothing at all of human society would remain intact if we decided to believe nothing that we could not hold as directly apprehended.

### 27. Those Who Forbid Belief in Religion Are Not to Be Followed

But now accept what I am confident I shall persuade you of more easily. When the matter concerns religion—that is, the worship and understanding of God—those who forbid us to believe while promising reason most readily are less worthy of being followed. For no one doubts that all human beings are either foolish or wise [Note: [Col. 0084] *Retractations* I.14.4.].

Now by “wise” I do not mean courageous or clever people, but those who possess as firmly apprehended a knowledge of the human being and of God as much as can exist in a human being, and whose life and conduct correspond to this knowledge. All the rest, whatever skills or incapacities they possess, and whatever their manner of life—whether worthy of approval or disapproval—I would count among the foolish.

This being so, who with even moderate understanding would not see plainly that it is more useful and salutary for fools to obey the instructions of the wise than to live according to their own judgment? For every action, if it is not rightly done, is sin; and nothing can be rightly done that does not proceed from right reason. Moreover, right reason is virtue itself. But in whose mind is virtue present except in the mind of the wise? The wise person alone, therefore, does not sin.

Every fool, then, sins unless he obeys the wise in those actions in which he does obey him. For such actions proceed from right reason; and, so to speak, the fool should not be regarded as the master of his action when he is like the instrument and servant of the wise person.

Therefore, if it is better for all human beings not to sin than to sin, all fools would plainly live better if they could be servants of the wise. If no one doubts that this is advantageous in lesser matters—such as buying and selling, cultivating the land, taking a wife, having and raising children, and finally administering one’s household—it is much more so in religion. Human affairs are also easier to distinguish than divine affairs; and in whatever matters are holier and more excellent, the greater the obedience and worship we owe them, the more wickedly and dangerously we sin.

You see, then, that while we are foolish, nothing remains for us, if the best and most religious life is dear to us, except to seek wise people whom we may obey, so that by obeying them we may neither feel too greatly the domination of folly while it remains within us nor fail eventually to escape it.

### 28. One Who Lacks Wisdom Does Not Seek a Wise Person Unless He Believes That Such a Person Exists. Thus Religion Is Not Sought Unless It Is Believed to Exist

Here another extremely difficult question arises. How can we, being foolish, find a wise person, when almost no one dares to claim this title openly, yet most people claim it indirectly for themselves; and when they disagree so greatly about the very matters in whose knowledge wisdom consists that either none of them or one particular person must necessarily be wise? But who that person is, when he is sought by a fool, and how he can be clearly recognized and apprehended, I utterly fail to see.

For no one can recognize something through any signs unless he knows the very thing of which those signs are signs. Yet the fool does not know wisdom. For although it is permitted to recognize gold, silver, and other things of that kind when one sees them without possessing them, wisdom may not be seen by the mind’s eye of one who lacks it. Whatever we touch through bodily sensation is offered to us from outside; therefore it is also possible to see with one’s eyes things belonging to others, even when we possess nothing of them or of their kind.

But what is grasped by the intellect is within the mind; and to possess it is nothing other than to see it. The fool lacks wisdom and therefore does not know wisdom. He could not see it with his eyes; yet he cannot see it without possessing it, nor possess it while remaining a fool. He therefore does not know it, and while he does not know it, he cannot recognize it elsewhere. As long as he is a fool, no one can find the wise person with absolutely certain knowledge, so that by obeying him he may be freed from so great an evil as folly.

### 29. God Alone Can Remedy This Difficulty

Since, then, we are asking about religion, God alone can remedy this immense difficulty. Unless we believe both that he exists and that he helps human minds, we ought not even to seek the true religion itself. For what, after all, do we desire to investigate with such exertion? What do we hope to attain? Where do we desire to arrive? Is it at something we do not believe exists or concerns us? Nothing is more perverse than such a mind.

When you did not dare—or at least dared impudently—to ask me for a favor, you come seeking the discovery of religion while thinking that God neither exists nor, if he exists, cares for us? What if so great a matter cannot be found unless it is sought diligently and with all one’s strength? What if the very difficulty of the discovery exercises the mind of the seeker so that he may grasp what is discovered?

What is more pleasant or more familiar to our eyes than this light? Yet after prolonged darkness they cannot endure or tolerate it. What is more suitable to a body exhausted by illness than food and drink? Yet we see convalescents restrained and controlled lest they dare to surrender themselves to the fullness appropriate for the healthy, and lest through the very foods they consume they bring themselves back to the illness that rejected them.

I am speaking of convalescents. But do we not urge the sick themselves to take something? Surely they would not obey us with such reluctance if they did not believe that they would escape that illness.

When, then, will you give yourself to an investigation requiring such effort and toil? When will you dare to impose upon yourself the care and labor that so great a matter deserves, if you do not believe that what you seek exists? It was therefore rightly established by the authority of Catholic discipline that those who approach religion should first of all be persuaded to have faith.

### 30. If Nothing Is to Be Believed, Religion Itself Will Not Be Believed to Exist. All Heretics Teach That Christ Must Be Believed. Christ Himself Especially Demanded Faith

So what reason, I ask you, can that heretic offer me—if indeed we are speaking of those who wish to be called Christians? What is there by which he may call me back from believing, as though from rashness?

If he commands me to believe nothing, I do not believe that there is any true religion among human beings. Since I do not believe that it exists, I do not seek it. But he, I suppose, will show it to the seeker; for it is written, “The one who seeks will find” (Matthew 7:8). I would not therefore come to the person who forbids me to believe unless I believed something. Is there any greater folly than for me to displease him through that faith alone which is supported by no knowledge, yet which alone brought me to him?

### 31. All Heretics Encourage Us to Believe in Christ

What of the fact that all heretics urge us to believe in Christ? Can they contradict themselves more thoroughly? They must be pressed on two points.

First, we must ask them: Where is the reason they promised? Where is their rebuke of rashness? Where is their claim to knowledge? If it is disgraceful to believe anyone without reason, what are you waiting for, and why are you striving to make me believe someone without reason, so that I may more easily be led by your reason? Will your reason build anything firm upon the foundation of rashness?

I am speaking to those who object to our believing. For I judge it not merely most salutary but altogether indispensable that, before reason, faith should cultivate the mind of one who is not fit to apprehend reason, so that it may receive the seeds of truth; without this, health cannot return to diseased minds.

Since this seems to them ridiculous and full of rashness, they act impudently in urging us to believe in Christ. Moreover, I confess that I have already believed in Christ and have resolved in my mind that what he said is true, even if it is supported by no reasoning. Is this the principle by which you, heretic, are going to teach me [Note: [Col. 0087] Several manuscripts read: “by which you are going to lead me.”]?

Let me consider the matter with myself for a little while. Since I did not see Christ himself in the manner in which he wished to appear to human beings—he is said to have been visible even to ordinary eyes—let me consider through whom I believed in him, so that I may now approach you already prepared by such faith.

I see that I believed no one except the established opinion of peoples and nations and the exceedingly widespread report concerning him. These peoples, however, have everywhere embraced the mysteries of the Catholic Church. Why, then, should I not diligently seek among those people above all others what Christ commanded, since, moved by their authority, I have already believed that Christ commanded something useful?

Will you explain better to me what he said—the one whom I would not have thought to have existed or to exist if you had not urged me to believe this [Note: [Col. 0087] Four Vatican manuscripts and several Gallic manuscripts read: “if you had urged me not to believe this.”]? I believed this, as I said, on the basis of a reputation strengthened by renown, agreement, and antiquity [Note: [Col. 0087] The manuscripts read the feminine form, “strengthened,” agreeing with *fama*, “reputation.”].

But as for you, who are so few, so turbulent, and so recent, no one doubts how little worthy of authority you put forward [Note: [Col. 0087] Several manuscripts read: “how much” or “whether.”]. What sort of madness, then, is this? Believe them that Christ must be believed, and learn from us what he said. Why, I ask you?

For if they failed me and could teach me nothing, I would much more readily persuade myself that Christ should not be believed than that I should learn anything about him except from those through whom I had come to believe in him.

What immense confidence—or rather, what ineptitude! “I will teach you what Christ commanded,” says the one in whom you believe. What if I did not believe in him? Could you teach me anything about him? “But you must believe,” he says. “Because you commend him?” “No,” he says, “for we lead those who believe in him by reason.” Why, then, should I believe him? “Because his reputation is well established.” Was this through you or through others? “Through others,” he says. Am I therefore to believe them so that you may teach me?

I perhaps ought to do so, unless they especially warned me not to approach you at all; for they say that you hold pernicious doctrines. You will reply: “They are lying.” How, then, shall I believe them about Christ, whom they did not see, but not believe them about you, whom they refuse to see?

“Believe the writings,” he says. But if a writing is entirely new and unheard-of, or is commended by only a few, with no confirming reason, it is not the writing but those who produce it who are believed. Therefore, since you, so few and unknown, produce these writings, I do not wish to believe them.

At the same time you act contrary to your promise, imposing faith rather than providing a reason. Again you will refer me to the multitude and to widespread report. Put an end, then, to your obstinacy and to I know not what untamed desire to propagate your name. Instead, advise me to seek the leaders of this multitude—and to seek them with the greatest diligence and effort—so that I may learn something about these writings from those people. If they did not exist, I would not know at all that there was anything to learn.

But you, return to your hiding places, and do not lay any ambush under the name of truth, which you are trying to take away from those to whom you yourself grant authority.

### 32. Those Who Deny That Christ Must Be Believed Unless an Indubitable Reason Has Been Given Are Not Christians

But if they deny that Christ must be believed unless an indisputable reason has been provided, they are not Christians. For certain pagans say this against us—foolishly, certainly, but without contradicting themselves or arguing against their own position.

Who, however, could tolerate people who profess to belong to Christ but maintain that nothing should be believed unless they produce for fools the clearest possible reason about God? Yet we see how much the history in which they themselves believe teaches: Christ wished nothing sooner or more earnestly than to be believed, at a time when those with whom he had dealings were not yet fit to perceive divine mysteries.

For what else do so many and such great miracles accomplish, since he himself says that they were performed for no other reason than that he might be believed? He led fools by faith; you lead them by reason. He cried out that he should be believed; you cry out against it. He praised those who believed; you rebuke them.

Unless, to omit other examples, he either changed water into wine (John 2:7–9) so that people could follow one who performed such deeds, or that statement has no weight at all: “Believe in God, and believe in me” (ibid. 14:1), or the man who did not wish him to enter his house, believing solely that his servant would recover at Christ’s command, is to be blamed for rashness (Matthew 8:8).

Thus, bringing a remedy that would heal the most corrupt morals, Christ won authority through miracles; through authority he earned faith; through faith he gathered a multitude; through the multitude he established antiquity; and through antiquity he strengthened religion. Neither the most foolish novelty of the heretics, advancing by fraud, nor even the ancient error of the nations, violently opposing it, could tear it down to any significant extent.

### 33. The Wisdom of God Incarnate Is the Most Convenient Way to Religion

Therefore, although I cannot teach you, I do not cease to advise you: since many wish to appear wise, while it is not easy to discern whether they are fools, beseech God with your whole attention, with all your prayers, with groans, and even, if possible, with tears, to free you from the evil of error, if you care about a blessed life.

This will happen more readily if you willingly obey his commands, which he wished to be established by the great authority of the Catholic Church. Since the wise person is so joined in mind to God that nothing intervenes to separate him—for God is truth—and since no one is wise in any way unless he touches the truth with his mind, we cannot deny that something intermediate lies between human folly and the utterly pure truth of God: namely, human wisdom.

The wise person imitates God insofar as this has been granted. For the foolish human being, however, there is nothing closer to him for salutary imitation than a wise human being. Since, as has been said, it is not easy for the fool to apprehend the wise person through reason, certain miracles had to be brought before the very eyes that fools use much more effectively than they use their minds, so that, first, their lives and conduct might be purified through the authority of the persons who were moved by those miracles, and then they might become capable of receiving reason.

Since, therefore, a human being had to be imitated, but hope could not be placed in a human being, what could divine generosity and liberality have done more fittingly than to cause the very pure, eternal, and unchangeable Wisdom of God, to which we ought to cling, to deign to assume humanity?

He not only did those things by which we would be invited to follow God, but also suffered those things by which we would be deterred from following God. Since no one can attain the certain and supreme good unless he loves it fully and perfectly—and this cannot happen as long as bodily and accidental evils are feared—he won our love by his miraculous birth and works, and by dying and rising again he removed fear.

In all his other circumstances as well—too many to pursue here—he presented himself in such a way that we might perceive both how far divine clemency extends and how far human weakness can be raised.

### 34. Authority Established by God Moves Us to Faith Partly Through Miracles and Partly Through the Multitude of Those Who Follow It

This, believe me, is the most salutary authority; this is the first suspension of our minds from their earthly dwelling; this is the turning of our minds toward the true God and away from love of this world.

Authority alone moves fools to hasten toward wisdom [Note: [Col. 0089] Most manuscripts read: “so that they may be hastened.” Some read: “so that they may be hastened forward.”]. As long as we cannot understand pure truth, it is wretched to be deceived by authority; but certainly it is more wretched not to be moved at all.

For if divine providence does not preside over human affairs, there is no need to concern ourselves with religion. But if both the appearance of all things—which must surely be believed to flow from some source of utterly true beauty—and some inner awareness urge the better minds, publicly and privately, to seek God and serve God, we must not despair that authority has been established by that same God, using it as a firm step by which we may rise toward God.

Apart from reason—which, as we have often said, is extremely difficult for fools to understand in its purity—this authority moves us in two ways: partly through miracles and partly through the multitude of those who follow it.

None of this is necessary for the wise person; who denies it? But our present concern is that we may become wise—that is, cling to the truth. A sordid mind certainly cannot do this. The impurities of the mind, to explain briefly, are love of any things other than the mind and God. The more purified someone is from these impurities, the more easily he sees the truth.

It is therefore surely perverse and backward to want to see the truth in order to purify the mind, when it is purified so that it may see.

For the human being who is unable to contemplate the truth, authority is present so that he may be made fit for it and allow himself to be purified. As I said shortly before, no one doubts that authority derives its force partly from miracles and partly from the multitude.

I call anything a miracle that appears difficult or unusual, beyond the expectation or capacity of the person who marvels at it. In this category nothing is more suitable for the masses, and in general for foolish people, than what is brought before their senses.

But these things are again divided into two kinds. Some produce wonder alone; others also win great gratitude and affection. If someone sees a human being flying, since the spectacle brings the viewer no advantage beyond the spectacle itself, he merely wonders. But if someone afflicted with a grave and hopeless disease recovers as soon as he is commanded to do so, his wonder at his own health will be surpassed by gratitude toward the one who healed him.

Such things occurred at the time when God was appearing to human beings in the true human being, to the extent that was sufficient. The weak were healed; lepers were cleansed; the ability to walk was restored to the lame, sight to the blind, and hearing to the deaf. People of that time saw water changed into wine, five thousand people filled with five loaves, seas crossed on foot, and the dead rising again. Some of these things benefited the body through a more manifest favor; others benefited the mind through a more hidden sign; and all of them served human beings as testimonies to majesty. Thus divine authority then moved the wandering souls of mortals toward itself.

“Why,” you ask, “do such things not happen now?” Because they would not move us unless they were marvelous; but if they were customary, they would not be marvelous [Note: [Col. 0090] *Retractations* I.14.5.].

For if someone who had never seen or sensed the alternation of day and night, the unwavering order of the heavenly bodies, the fourfold change of the seasons, the falling and returning leaves of trees, the countless force of seeds, and the beauty of light, colors, sounds, smells, and tastes were able to speak with us, he would grow dull and be overwhelmed by marvels. We, however, disregard all these things not because they are easy to understand—for what is more obscure than their causes?—but certainly because we experience them constantly.

Those miracles, then, were performed most opportunely, so that through the multitude of believers gathered and increased by them, authority might be turned to the improvement of conduct.

### 35. How Advantageously Good Conduct Has Been Commended to the Peoples by Authority. The Authority of the Catholic Church

Human conduct has such power to win the minds of people that even what is wrong in it—which commonly happens when desires become dominant—we can reject and detest more quickly than we can abandon or change.

Do you think it has been of little benefit to human affairs that not only a few of the most learned people debate, but even the uneducated crowd of men and women among so many different peoples both believes and proclaims that nothing earthly, nothing fiery, and finally nothing touched by bodily sensation should be worshiped as God, but that God, whom one must approach through the intellect alone, should be worshiped?

What of the fact that self-restraint is pursued even to the most meager nourishment of bread and water, and to fasts maintained not only daily but through several consecutive days; chastity even to contempt for marriage and offspring; patience even to disregard for crosses and flames; generosity even to the distribution of one’s property among the poor; and finally contempt for the whole world even to a desire for death?

Few do these things, and fewer do them well and wisely. But the peoples approve them, hear them, favor them, and finally love them. The peoples accuse their own weakness for being unable to do such things, recognizing that they cannot do so without some advance of the mind toward God and without certain sparks of virtue.

All this has been accomplished by divine providence through the prophecies of the prophets; through the humanity and teaching of Christ; through the journeys of the Apostles; through the insults, crosses, blood, and deaths of the martyrs; through the praiseworthy life of the saints; and, in all these matters, through miracles appropriate to such great events and virtues and to the needs of the times.

When, therefore, we see such great help from God and such progress and fruit, shall we hesitate to take refuge in the bosom of his Church, which has attained the summit of authority, recognized even by the confession of the human race, through the succession of bishops from the Apostolic See, while the heretics bark around it in vain and are condemned partly by the judgment of the people themselves, partly by the authority of councils, and partly also by the majesty of miracles [Note: [Col. 0091] Erasmus’s edition, with several manuscripts, reads: “it attained the pillar of authority while condemning them.”]?

To refuse to give this Church first place is surely either the height of impiety or precipitous arrogance. For if there is no certain path to wisdom and salvation for minds except when faith prepares them for reason, what else is it than ingratitude toward divine care and assistance to wish to resist an authority commended with such labor [Note: [Col. 0091] Perhaps: “with such strength.”]?

And if every discipline, however humble and easy, requires a teacher or instructor in order to be learned, what is fuller of rash arrogance than to refuse to learn the books of the divine mysteries from their interpreters and yet wish to condemn them without knowing them?

### 36. Conclusion by Way of Exhortation. The Persian Fable

Therefore, if either reason or my speech has moved you in any way, and if you truly care for yourself, as I believe you do, I would have you listen to me and entrust yourself, with devout faith, joyful hope, and sincere love, to the good teachers of Catholic Christianity. Do not cease to pray to God himself, by whose goodness alone we were made, by whose justice we suffer punishment, and by whose mercy we are freed.

In this way you will lack neither the instructions and arguments of the most learned and truly Christian people, nor books, nor the very serene thoughts by which you may easily find what you seek. Abandon those verbose and wretched people completely—what gentler description could I give them?—who, while seeking too intently where evil comes from, find nothing except evil.

In this inquiry they often rouse their hearers to seek; but what they teach those whom they have awakened is such that it would always be better to sleep than to awaken in that manner. They turn people from lethargy into frenzy. Although both illnesses are generally fatal, the difference is that the lethargic die without troubling anyone else, whereas the frenzied person is a danger to many healthy people, especially those who wish to help.

For God is not the author of evil; he has never repented of anything he made; he is not disturbed by any storm of emotion; his kingdom is not some portion of the earth; he approves or commands no disgraceful act or crime; and he never lies.

These were the things that troubled us when those people attacked them with great denunciations and accused this of being the teaching of the Old Testament. This is entirely false. I therefore grant that they rightly criticize these matters.

What, then, did I learn? What do you think, except that when these things are criticized, Catholic teaching is not being criticized? Thus I retain what I had learned from them that was true, and reject what I had thought was false.

But the Catholic Church also taught me many other things—things to which those people, whose bodies are bloodless but whose minds are heavy, cannot rise: namely, that God is not corporeal; that no part of him can be perceived by bodily eyes; that nothing in his substance or nature can in any way be violated, changed, composed [Note: [Col. 0092] The manuscripts read: “composite” or “constructed.”], or fabricated. If you grant me these points—for it is not otherwise possible to think correctly about God—all their contrivances are overturned.

But how it can be that God neither generated nor made evil, that there never has been or is any nature or substance that God did not either generate or make, and yet that he frees us from evil—this is demonstrated by such necessary arguments that it cannot be doubted at all, especially by you and people like you, provided that sound intelligence is accompanied by piety and a certain peace of mind, without which nothing at all can be understood about such great matters.

And here there is no report of smoke, nor some Persian fable to which it is enough to lend an ear and a mind not subtle but plainly childish.

Truth is altogether, altogether different from what the Manichaeans foolishly imagine. But since this speech of ours has proceeded much farther than I thought it would, let us here bring the book to an end.

I wish you to remember that I have not yet begun to refute the Manichaeans, nor have I yet attacked those absurdities; nor have I disclosed anything of great importance about Catholic teaching itself. I have merely wished, if I could, to tear out of you the false opinion maliciously or ignorantly insinuated against us concerning true Christians, and to raise you up toward the learning of great and divine things.

Let this volume, then, stand as it is. When your mind has been made more peaceful, perhaps I shall be more ready in the remaining matters [Note: [Col. 0092] *Retractations* I.14.6.].

---

## St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo  
### One Book Concerning the Two Souls Against the Manichaeans

[Note: [Col. 0093] Written approximately in the year of Christ 391.]

### On the Book Concerning the Two Souls Against the Manichaeans

See Book 1, chapter 15, of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 608, §1, beginning with the words “After this book” [Note: [Col. 0093] Namely, after the work *On the Usefulness of Believing*, which was composed approximately in the year of Christ 391.] through col. 612, §8, ending with the words “With the help of God’s mercy.” [Note: [Col. 0093] After reviewing the present book, *Concerning the Two Souls*, Augustine immediately places his *Retractation* of the book or disputation against Fortunatus, which was held on 28 August 392. M.]

The editions of the book *Concerning the Two Souls* have been compared with the manuscript codices Arnulphensis, Michaelinus, two Victorine manuscripts, two Vatican manuscripts, and with the variant readings of three Belgian manuscripts reported by Louvain. [Note: [Col. 0093] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

The Manichaean heretics say that there are two souls in every human being: one good, from the substance of God, and the other evil, from the race of darkness and not created by God. Augustine regrets that he once adhered to this teaching so closely that he failed to attend to the arguments—so obvious and manifest—by which this delirium is overturned.

For, first, upon consideration it readily becomes clear that every soul, since it is a kind of life and an intelligible thing, and therefore superior even to visible light, which the Manichaeans confess to be from God, must be attributed to God its creator.

The passages of Scripture by which they argue that the wicked are not from God are better explained by comparison with other passages. Then, from the definition of sin and the will, from the forgiveness of sins granted to those who sin in the Church, and finally from the pious and beneficial disposition of repentance, it is demonstrated with complete clarity that sinful souls are not evil by nature.

### Chapter One
1. How the Error of the Manichaeans concerning Two Souls—One of Which Is Not from God—is Refuted. Since every soul, insofar as it is a kind of life, can come only from God, the Source of Life

With the merciful assistance of God, having broken and abandoned the snares of the Manichaeans, I now gladly consider—and at least now lament—that misery of mine, restored at last to the bosom of the Catholic Church. [Note: The Louvain editors, following the corrupt Cambron manuscript, printed “having established in the bosom, I gladly consider.”] For there were many things I ought to have done, so that the seeds of the truest religion, healthfully implanted in me from childhood, would not so easily, and within a few days, be dug out of my mind and expelled by the error or deceit of false and deceptive men.

For, first, if I had soberly and diligently considered, with a mind humble and devout before God, those two kinds of souls which they assigned such distinct and proper natures to each individual soul [Note: Some manuscripts read “which they distributed”], that they wished one to be of the very substance of God, while they refused to regard God even as the creator of the other, perhaps it would have become apparent to me, as I earnestly sought the truth, that there is no kind of life whatsoever which, by the very fact that it is life—and insofar as it is altogether life—does not belong to the supreme Source and Principle of life [Note: *Retractations* I.15.1]. This is none other than the supreme, only, and true God, as we must confess.

Accordingly, those souls whom the Manichaeans call evil must either lack life and therefore not be souls, possessing no power to will or not will, to seek or avoid anything; or, if they were alive, so that they could both be souls and perform the sort of actions they imagine, they could in no way live except by life. And if it is certain—as it is—that Christ said, “I am the life” (John 14:6), we would have no reason not to acknowledge that all souls, since they cannot exist as souls except by living, were created and made through Christ, that is, through Life.

## CHAPTER II

2. If the Light Perceived by the Senses Has God as Its Author, as the Manichaeans Admit, Much More Does the Soul, Which Is Perceived by the Intellect Alone

But if, at that time, my mind could not bear or sustain the question of life itself and participation in life—a great question indeed, requiring much calm discussion among the most learned—perhaps I could nevertheless have discerned what is most plainly evident to every person who considers himself properly and without partisan bias: everything that we are said to know and understand is grasped either through bodily sensation or through intelligence.

Bodily senses are commonly counted as five: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Who would be so ungrateful and impious as not to grant that intelligence greatly and incomparably surpasses them all? Once this has been established and firmly secured, it follows that everything perceived by touch and sight, or by any other bodily means, is inferior to what we attain by understanding, to the extent that we see the senses themselves yield to intelligence.

Therefore, since all life—and consequently every soul—can be perceived not by any bodily sense but by the intellect alone, while the sun, moon, and every light visible to these mortal eyes are said by the Manichaeans themselves to be attributed to the true and good God, it is the height of madness to proclaim that what we behold through the body belongs to God, while what we grasp not only with the mind but by the very sublimity of the mind—that is, by thought and intelligence—namely, life, however it may be described, is nevertheless life, and is to be deprived of and separated from the authorship of that same God.

For if I were to invoke God and ask myself what it means to live, how hidden it is from every bodily sense, and how wholly incorporeal it is, could I fail to answer? Or would they not also admit that the souls they detest not only live, but live immortally? And when Christ said, “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22), he was not speaking of those who do not live at all, but of sinners, for the only death of an immortal soul is sin, as Paul writes: “The widow who lives in luxury is dead” (1 Timothy 5:6). Thus he said simultaneously that she was dead and that she lived.

Why, then, should I not attend simply to the fact that the sinful soul lives, rather than to how discolored or degraded its life may be? And if I could perceive this only by understanding, I believe I would have realized that every soul, whatever it might be, ought to be preferred to the light perceived through these eyes to the same degree that we prefer intelligence to the eyes themselves.

## CHAPTER III

How It Is Also Proved That Every Body Is from God. The Soul Called Evil by the Manichaeans Is Better Than Light

They themselves also affirm that this light comes from the Father of Christ. Should I, then, finally doubt that whatever soul exists comes from him? Indeed, even concerning the soul, and also concerning any body whatsoever, I would not have doubted at all—not even then, when I was a man of such ignorance and at such an age—that it came from him, if I had devoutly and cautiously considered what form is, what is formed, what appearance is, and what is clothed with appearance; and then what is the cause of each of these. [Note: The printed editions read “this, evidently”; the manuscripts correct this to “evidently a man.”]

3. But for the moment I say nothing about the body. I complain about the soul, about its spontaneous and living movement, its activity, its life, its immortality. Above all, I complain that in my wretchedness I believed that some entity could possess all these things without the goodness of God; that I failed through negligence to attend to how great they were. This is what I ought to mourn, this to lament.

I would turn these matters over in my mind, speak with myself about them, and bring them before others. [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read “bring them before those men”; understand: the Manichaeans.] I would set forth the power of understanding and how nothing in man could be compared with this excellence. [Note: Thus according to the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts: “since there was nothing in man that we could compare with this excellence.”] I would place it first. [Note: Several manuscripts read “I would place it first.” The printed editions instead have “I would place it above,” with the following punctuation: “I would place the power of understanding first (since there was nothing in man that we could compare with this excellence).”]

When these men, if they were indeed men, had granted me this, I would ask whether seeing with these eyes means understanding. [Note: The edition of Erasmus reads “whether they saw with these eyes, that is, understood.” The Vatican manuscripts likewise have that reading. But the reading found in other manuscripts, and in the Louvain edition, is better: “whether seeing with these eyes means understanding.” [Col. 0096] The sense is whether seeing with these eyes is the same as understanding.] When they denied it, I would first conclude that the intelligence of the mind must be preferred by far to the sense of these eyes. Then I would add that what we perceive by the better faculty must necessarily be judged better.

Who would not grant this? I would therefore continue to ask whether that soul which they called evil was perceived by these eyes or understood by the mind. They would admit that it was understood by the mind. Once all these points had been agreed and established among us, I would show what followed: namely, that the soul they cursed was better than the light they worshiped, since the former is known through the intellect of the mind, while the latter is known through bodily sensation.

At this point they might perhaps become stuck and refuse to follow reason as their guide. Such is the force of opinions grown old, and of falsehood defended and believed for a long time. But I would press them still more as they hesitated—not harshly, not childishly, not obstinately. I would repeat what they had conceded and show what ought to be conceded. [Note: The printed editions read “and what ought to be conceded.” The manuscripts correct this to “and show what ought to be conceded.”]

I would urge them to deliberate together and to see clearly what they would have to deny: whether intelligence should be preferred to these bodily lights; whether they would regard as false the claim that what is known by the excellence of the mind is more excellent than what is known by a base bodily sense; whether they would refuse to admit that those souls whom they believed foreign could be known only by understanding—that is, by the very excellence of the mind; or whether they would deny that the sun and moon become known only through these eyes.

If they recognized that none of these propositions could be denied except in the most absurd and shameless manner, I would advise them that they ought not to doubt that the light they proclaimed worthy of worship was inferior to that soul which they warned people to shun.

## CHAPTER IV

4. Even the Soul of a Fly Is Superior to This Light

And if, perhaps disturbed, they asked me whether I also considered the soul of a fly superior to this light, I would answer, “Yes.” I would not be frightened by the fly because it is small, but would confirm my position by the fact that it is alive.

For the question is what animates those extremely small limbs; what moves that tiny body here and there according to its natural appetite; what moves the feet of the running creature in coordinated rhythm; what controls and vibrates its little wings in flight. Whatever its nature may be, when carefully considered, something so great stands out in something so small that it ought to be preferred to any brilliance that dazzles the eyes.

## CHAPTER V

How Even Faulty Souls, Although Worthy of Condemnation, Surpass This Light, Which Is Praiseworthy in Its Own Class

Certainly, as no one doubts, whatever this is, it is intelligible; and for that reason it surpasses every sensible thing, including this light, by the divine laws. [Note: The Louvain editors corrected the text on the authority of two manuscripts. Several other manuscripts, together with Erasmus, read: “Whatever is intelligible surpasses every sensible thing, and therefore this light also.”]

For what do we perceive by thought, I ask, if we do not perceive that understanding with the mind is one thing and sensing through the body another, and that the former differs from the latter by an incomparable sublimity? For this reason intelligible things cannot fail to be preferred to sensible things, since the intellect itself is preferred so greatly to the senses.

5. From this I might also perhaps have understood what plainly follows: since injustice, intemperance, and the other vices of the mind are not sensed but understood, how is it that even these things—which we detest and judge worthy of condemnation—can nevertheless, because they are intelligible, surpass this light, although this light is praiseworthy in its own class?

For a mind that submits itself properly to God is first reminded that not everything we praise must be preferred to everything we blame. Just because I praise the purest lead, I do not therefore value it more highly than gold, which I blame. Each thing must be considered in its own class.

I disapprove of a lawyer who is ignorant of many laws; yet I prefer him to a most accomplished shoemaker to such an extent that I do not even think the two comparable. But I praise the shoemaker because he is highly skilled in his own art, while I rightly criticize the lawyer because he performs his own profession inadequately. [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “And I praise this man.”]

From this I ought to have discovered that this light is rightly praised because it is perfect in its own class. Yet, because it belongs to the class of sensible things, and that class must yield to the class of intelligible things, it must be judged inferior to unjust and intemperate souls, since they are intelligible—even though we rightly judge such souls most deserving of condemnation.

For in these souls we seek what can be reconciled to God, not what can be preferred to this brilliance. Therefore, whoever maintained that this light was from God, I would not oppose; rather, I would say that even vicious souls ought to acknowledge God as their creator—not insofar as they are vicious, but insofar as they are souls.

## CHAPTER VI

6. Whether Even Vices, as Intelligible Things, Should Be Preferred to Sensible Light and Attributed to God as Their Author. A Vice of the Mind Is a Certain Defect, and Should Not Properly Be Counted among Intelligible Things

Even if defects themselves were counted among intelligible things, they would never be preferred to sensible things. If visible light comes from God, then much more does the soul come from him, since insofar as it lives it is an intelligible thing, even when it is vicious.

The Manichaeans’ Scriptural Proof-Texts Are Brought Forward

At this point, if one of them—cautious and alert, and now more eager to learn than stubborn—were to remind me that the question concerned not vicious souls but the vices themselves, which, since they were not known by bodily sensation and yet were known, could be regarded only as intelligible things; and if intelligible things surpass all sensible things, why should it be agreed among us that light was to be attributed to God as its author, while no one but a sacrilegious person would call God the author of vices, I would answer that man as follows.

If the solution to this question had either suddenly and immediately been divinely infused into me, as often happens with good worshipers of God, or had previously been prepared for me, I would proceed at once. But if I had deserved and been capable of neither, I would postpone the undertaking; I would confess that the matter before us was difficult and arduous to discern.

I would return into myself, prostrate myself before God, and groan deeply, asking that he not allow me to remain suspended halfway along the path by which I had advanced through certain arguments; that I not be forced by this perplexing question either to subordinate intelligible things to sensible things or to call God himself the author of vices, since either conclusion would be utterly full of falsehood and impiety. I could in no way believe that he would abandon me in such a state. Rather, by his ineffable methods, he would prompt me to consider again and again whether the vices of the mind that troubled me ought to be counted among intelligible things.

To discover this, because of the weakness of my inner eye—a weakness that had justly befallen me on account of my sins—I would devise for myself, among visible things, a kind of stairway by which I might contemplate invisible things. The former are not known to us with greater certainty, but through them our familiarity is more secure.

I would therefore immediately ask what properly belonged to the sense of sight. I would discover colors, of which this light holds the primacy. These are the things that no other sense touches. For movements of bodies, their sizes, distances, and shapes, although they can be perceived by the eyes, are not perceived by them exclusively or properly, since they can also be perceived by touch.

From this I would conclude that light surpasses the other corporeal and sensible things to the same extent that sight is more illuminating than the other senses. Having selected from all the things perceived by the body this light, on which I would rely and in which I would necessarily place that step of my inquiry, I would continue to observe what happened in the following manner, speaking thus with myself:

“If this sun, visible with such brilliance and sufficient to illumine the day, were gradually to fade before our eyes until it resembled the moon, would our eyes sense anything other than some shining light? Would we not still be seeking the light because what had been present was no longer visible, and by seeing would be taking in what remained?

“We would not, then, see the fading itself, but the light that remained after the fading. When we did not see, we would not sense; for whatever we sense by sight cannot fail to be seen. Therefore, if that fading were sensed neither by sight nor by any other sense, it could not be counted among sensible things. For nothing is sensible that cannot be sensed.

“Let us now turn our consideration to virtue, whose intelligible light we rightly say illuminates the soul. A certain defect in this light of virtue—one that does not destroy the soul but darkens it—is called vice. Vice, then, may properly not be counted among intelligible things, just as that diminution of light is rightly excluded from the number of sensible things.

“Yet what remains in the soul—that is, the very fact that it lives and is a soul—is as intelligible as whatever sensible light would continue to shine, however faintly, after the diminution of this visible light. For that reason, the soul, insofar as it is a soul and participates in life, without which it cannot possibly be a soul, is rightly preferred to all sensible things.

“Therefore it is the height of error to say that any soul is not from God, when you glory in saying that the sun and moon are from him.”

7. But if someone wished to call all things sensible—not only those that we sense, but also those that, without sensing them, we nevertheless judge through the body, as with darkness through the eyes and silence through the ears—for we know the former without seeing and the latter without hearing—and if he likewise wished to call intelligible not only those things that we behold with an illuminated mind, such as wisdom itself, but also those things from which we turn away because of the deprivation of that illumination, such as folly, which I might suitably call darkness of the mind, I would not dispute over words.

I would resolve the entire question by a simple division and immediately approve this proposition for those who paid proper attention: intelligible substances are preferred to sensible substances by the divine and incorruptible law of truth, but not the defects of those substances—even if we wished to call the former defects intelligible and the latter sensible.

Therefore, those who admitted that both these visible lights and those intelligible souls were substances would be compelled in every way to grant and attribute the higher rank to souls. But the defects of either class cannot be preferred one to another, for they merely deprive and indicate non-being; in every respect they possess the same force, like the negations themselves.

When we say, “Gold is not present,” and, “Virtue is not present,” although there is a great difference between gold and virtue, there is no difference between the negations attached to them. Yet it is worse not to possess virtue than not to possess gold; no sane person doubts this. Who does not understand that this is not because of the negations themselves, but because of the things to which they are attached? To the same degree that virtue surpasses gold, it is more miserable to lack virtue than to lack gold.

Therefore, since intelligible things surpass sensible things, we rightly find the defect of intelligible things more grievous than the defect of sensible things—not valuing the defects themselves more or less, but the things that are defective. From this it is already clear that the defect of life, which is intelligible, is far more pitiable than the defect of this sensible light, since intelligible life is far more precious than visible light.

8. Since this is so, would anyone dare, while attributing to God the sun and moon, and whatever shines among the stars, and finally whatever gleams with visible light in this earthly fire of ours, to refuse to admit that any souls whatsoever—which certainly are not souls except by living—come from God, when life so greatly surpasses this light?

And when the person who says, “Insofar as it shines, it is from God,” speaks truly, shall I finally, great God, lie if I say, “Insofar as it lives, it is from God”? May the blindness of mind and the punishments of souls not increase to such an extent that people fail to understand these things.

But however their error or obstinacy might stand, relying on and armed with these arguments, I believe that if I had brought before them the matter after considering and examining it carefully, and had discussed it with them calmly, I would have feared that any one of them might seem to me to carry some weight if he tried either to prefer intellect—or those things which were perceived by intellect without defect—to bodily sensation, or even to compare them with bodily sensation or with the things that are similarly known through that same sense.

Once this had been established, who—or anyone at all—would dare deny to me that souls, however evil they might be, nevertheless, since they were souls, belonged to the number of intelligible things and were not understood through a defect? For souls existed only insofar as they lived.

They could indeed be understood through a defect insofar as they were vicious, because they were vicious through lack of virtue; but not through a defect of soul, since they were souls by living. Nor can the presence of life be the cause of defect, since everything is defective to the extent that it is abandoned by life.

9. Since it was therefore entirely evident that no souls could be separated from the author from whom this light is not separated, whatever arguments they might bring forward I would no longer accept. Rather, I would urge them to prefer to follow with me those who proclaim that everything whatsoever, simply because it exists and to whatever extent it exists, comes from the one God.

## CHAPTER VII

How Evil Is and Is Not from God

They would recite against me those evangelical sayings: “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God”; “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:47, 44).

I too would recite in opposition: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3); and the Apostle’s statement: “One God, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6); and again from the same Apostle: “From him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory” (Romans 11:36).

I would urge these people—if indeed I found them to be people—not to presume that we had, as it were, already ascertained anything, but rather to seek teachers who could show us the peace and harmony of statements that appeared to us to conflict with one another.

For in one and the same authority of the Scriptures, while in one place it sounded, “All things are from God” (1 Corinthians 11:12), and in another, “You are not from God,” and since it would be impious rashly to condemn the books, who would not see that a learned teacher, one acquainted with the solution of this question, ought to be found? If he were a good interpreter and, as Scripture divinely calls him, a spiritual person (1 Corinthians 2:15), he would necessarily support the true arguments concerning intelligible and sensible nature that I have discussed and explained as far as I could—or rather, he himself would open them up much better and more suitably for teaching.

We would hear nothing else from him concerning this question except how it could be that no kind of souls was not from God, and yet it could rightly be said to sinners and unbelievers, “You are not from God.”

For perhaps, with God invoked for our aid, we too could easily see that living is one thing and sinning another. Although life in sins is called death in comparison with a just life (1 Timothy 5:6), both can nevertheless be found in one person, so that he is simultaneously alive and a sinner: alive, in that he is from God; a sinner, in that he is not from God.

In this division we use the one of the two aspects that suits our argument. When we wish to assert the omnipotence of God the Creator, we say even to sinners that they are from God. For we speak to those who possess some form; we speak to living creatures; we speak to rational beings; and finally—and this is most relevant—we speak to the living. All these are divine gifts in themselves.

But when our purpose is to rebuke the wicked, we rightly say, “You are not from God.” For we say this to those who have turned away from the truth, to unbelievers, criminals, and depraved people—in short, to sinners. Who would doubt that all these things are not from God?

Thus Christ, convicting sinners precisely because they were sinners and did not believe in him, should not surprise us by saying, “You are not from God,” while the other statement remains intact: “All things were made through him,” and, “All things are from God.”

For if not believing Christ, rejecting Christ’s coming, and refusing to receive Christ were certain indications of souls that were not God’s, and if for that reason it had been said, “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God,” how could the Apostle’s statement be true at that memorable beginning of the Gospel: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11)?

How were they his own if they did not receive him? Or how were they for that reason not his own, because they did not receive him? It is because sinful human beings, insofar as they are human, belong to God, but insofar as they are sinners, belong to the devil.

Thus the evangelist, who said, “His own did not receive him,” retained the aspect of nature; Christ, who said, “You are not from God,” addressed the aspect of the will. The evangelist was commending God’s works; Christ was restraining human sins.

## CHAPTER VIII

10. The Manichaeans Ask Where Evil Comes From and Think That They Have Defeated Us by This Question. Let Them First Recognize What Is Easiest: Nothing Can Live without God. The Supreme Evil Is Known Only through Knowledge of the Supreme Good, Which Is God

At this point someone might say: “Where, then, do sins themselves come from, and where does evil altogether come from? If it comes from a human being, where does the human being come from? If from an angel, where does the angel come from?” When it is said that these beings are from God, although the statement is right and true, it nevertheless appears to the inexperienced and to those unable to look sharply into hidden matters as though evils and sins were linked to God by a kind of chain.

They think that they reign by means of this question—as though asking a question were the same as knowing. If only it were! No one would be found more learned than I. But somehow, in disputes, the person who raises a great question often displays the role of a great teacher, while in the matter by which he frightens another, he is usually more ignorant than the very person he frightens.

Thus these people think they should be preferred to the multitude because they are the first to ask what they themselves do not know along with the multitude.

But if, at the time when I was dealing with them—not as I have long regretted doing—I had been bringing forward these arguments and they had raised this objection, I would have said: “Please, for the moment, recognize with me what is easiest. If nothing can shine without God, much less can anything live without God. Let us not remain trapped in such monstrous opinions as to proclaim that certain souls possess life without God.

“Perhaps this will result in our learning, either together or in some order, what you do not know along with me—namely, where evil comes from. For what if knowledge of the supreme evil cannot come to a human being without knowledge of the supreme good?

“We would not know darkness if we were always in darkness; but knowledge of light does not allow its opposite to remain unknown. The supreme good is that than which nothing higher can exist. God is good, and nothing can be higher than God. God, therefore, is the supreme good.

“Let us come to know God, and then what we are rashly seeking will not remain hidden from us. Do you really think that knowledge of God is a matter of moderate difficulty or merit? What other reward is promised to us than eternal life, which is the knowledge of God?

“For God the Teacher says: ‘This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent’ (John 17:3).

“Although the soul is immortal, its turning away from the knowledge of God is rightly called its death. When it turns back to God, it earns the attainment of eternal life, so that eternal life may be, as has been said, knowledge itself.

“But no one can turn to God without turning away from this world. I feel that this is arduous and extremely difficult for me; if it is easy for you, let that very God see to it.

“I would wish to believe you, were I not troubled by the fact that, although this world from which we are commanded to turn away is visible, the Apostle said, ‘The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal’ (2 Corinthians 4:18). You assign greater authority to the judgment of these eyes than to that of the mind, since among you it is proclaimed and believed that no shining feather exists which does not shine from God, and that there is a living soul which does not live from God.”

I would say these and similar things either to them or reflect on them with myself. For even then I might have been able, while imploring God with all my inward being and devoting myself as far as possible to the Scriptures, either to say such things or at least to think what was sufficient for my salvation. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “I could have reflected. For I would have been able either to say such things, or to think what was sufficient for salvation.”]

## CHAPTER IX

11. Augustine Was Deceived by His Familiarity with the Manichaeans and by the Success of the Victory He Had Won over Unlearned Christians. The Manichaeans Can Easily Be Refuted from Knowledge of Sin and the Will

But two things in particular, which easily ensnare an unwary youth, wore me down through marvelous circuits. One was familiarity, somehow gradually taking on the appearance of goodness, like a winding bond wrapped many times around the neck. [Note: The edition of Erasmus and the Michaelinus manuscript read “through friendly circuits.”]

The other was that a certain harmful victory almost always came to me in debates with unlearned Christians, who nevertheless strove competitively to defend their faith, each as best he could. Through this very frequent success, the boldness of the young man grew, and in its own momentum it moved imprudently toward the great evil of obstinacy. [Note: The manuscripts read: “and its impulses drove it toward obstinacy.”]

Because I had undertaken this kind of disputation after hearing the Manichaeans, whatever I could accomplish by my own ability, however slight, or through other reading, I attributed most willingly to them alone. Thus from their conversations arose a passion for contests, and from the outcome of the contests a daily growth of affection for them. [Note: Most manuscripts read “was renewed daily.”]

As a result, whatever they said I approved as true, not because I knew it to be true, but because I wished it to be true, under the influence of certain astonishing maladies. [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions read: “As a result it happened that whatever they said, through astonishing methods, etc.”] Thus it came about that, although gradually and cautiously, I nevertheless followed them for a long time—men who preferred a bright straw to a living soul.

12.
