Granted that at that time I could not distinguish and separate sensible things from intelligible things, that is, bodily things from spiritual things—this was not a matter to be acquired by age, training, a certain habit, or indeed any merits; for it is no small matter of joy and blessedness—could I finally not even grasp what nature itself has established, according to the judgment of all human beings, under the laws of the supreme God? [Note: The printed editions read: “Granted, I could not.” The Louvain edition reads: “Granted, I could not do these things.” Shortly afterward the same editions read: “Thus at last not even that.” The manuscript authority supplies the corrections.]

## CHAPTER X

Sin Comes Only from the Will. Life and the Will Are Known Most Clearly to Each Person. What the Will Is

For any human beings whose capacity for common human sense had not been shattered by some madness, whatever interests they wished to bring to judgment, regardless of their ignorance or even their slowness of understanding, I would like to test by asking them whether it seemed to them that a person had sinned if someone else wrote something disgraceful using the hand of a sleeping man.

Who could doubt that they would all deny that this was a sin and protest so strongly that they might even become angry because I had thought them worthy of such a question?

After somehow reconciling them and restoring them to a state of deliberation, I would ask them not to take offense at my asking about another matter equally clear and known to everyone. I would then ask whether, if someone had done a similarly evil thing with the hand not of a sleeping but of a conscious man—although the man’s other limbs were bound and tightly restrained—this man would be held guilty of any sin merely because he knew what was happening, even though he had absolutely not wished it.

Here too, astonished that I was asking such questions, they would all answer without hesitation that this man too had committed no sin at all.

“Why?” I would ask.

“Because no one can justly be condemned for an evil done by someone else to a person who was unaware of it or unable to resist.”

If I then questioned human nature itself in these people about why this was so, I would easily arrive at what I wanted by asking in the following way:

“What if that sleeping man already knew what the other person was going to do with his hand, and deliberately gave himself over to sleep—drinking even more so that he would not wake up [Note: Several manuscripts read “if he also drank more so that he would not wake up,” omitting *potus*, “drinking”—]—in order to deceive someone by an oath? Would sleep in any way assist his innocence?”

What else would human nature pronounce him to be but guilty? [Note: The printed editions read, “What else would they pronounce him to be?” The manuscripts omit *illi*, “him,” and have *pronuntiaret*: understand, “human nature would pronounce.”]

And if that other man willingly allowed himself to be bound in order similarly to deceive someone under the pretext of a defense, what benefit, finally, would those bonds provide him in freeing him from sin? Although bound by them, he truly could not resist; just as the sleeping man at that moment was entirely unaware of what would happen.

Would there then be any doubt that both would be judged to have sinned? Once these points had been granted, I would conclude that sin exists nowhere except in the will. [Note: *Retractations* I.15.2.] This was also supported by the fact that justice holds sinners accountable solely for an evil will, even when they were unable to carry out what they willed.

13. Could anyone say, as I dealt with these matters, that I was wandering among obscure and hidden things, where, because few people understand, suspicion of deception or display commonly arises? Let us set aside for a little while the distinction between intelligible and sensible things. Let no one envy me because I pursue sluggish souls with the goads of subtle arguments.

Let me be permitted to know that I live; let me be permitted to know that I wish to live. If the human race agrees about these matters, our will is as well known to us as our life. Nor, when we profess this knowledge, must we fear that anyone can prove us capable of being deceived. For no one can be deceived about this very point if he either does not live or wills nothing.

I do not think I have introduced anything obscure, and I fear that someone may judge me all the more blameworthy because these matters are too obvious. But let us consider where they are leading.

14. Therefore sin occurs only by the will. Our will, moreover, is perfectly well known to us; for I could not know that I willed if I did not know what the will itself is. It is therefore defined in this way: “The will is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, toward either not losing or acquiring something” [Note: [Col. 0104] *Retractions* I, chapter 15, no. 3.]. Why, then, could I not have defined it that way at the time? Was it difficult to see that unwilling is contrary to willing, just as we say that left is contrary to right, though not in the same way that black is contrary to white? For the same thing cannot be both black and white at the same time. But a person standing between two others is left of one and right of the other: one person is simultaneously both with respect to the two, but with respect to one person he cannot be both at once.

Thus one mind can be simultaneously unwilling and willing; but it cannot simultaneously both not-want and want one and the same thing. When someone does something unwillingly, if you ask whether he wants to do it, he says that he does not want to. Likewise, if you ask whether he wants not to do it, he answers that he does. Thus you will find him unwilling with respect to doing it, but willing with respect to not doing it: that is, at one time he has both attitudes in one mind, but refers one attitude to one thing and the other to another.

Why do I say this? Because if we ask again why he does it unwillingly, he will say that he is being compelled. For everyone who acts unwillingly is compelled; and everyone who is compelled, if he acts, acts unwillingly. It remains, then, that the willing person is free from the one who compels, even if someone thinks that he is being compelled. For in this way also everyone who acts willingly is not compelled; and everyone who is not compelled either acts willingly or does not act.

Since nature itself proclaims this among all human beings whom we may reasonably question—from child to old man, from the elementary school to the wise man’s throne—why did I not then see that the definition of the will ought to include “compelled by no one,” which now, with the caution born of greater experience, I have inserted? But if this is everywhere manifest and is available to all by nature, not by instruction, what remains that might seem obscure—unless perhaps it escapes anyone that, when we will something, our mind is moved toward it, and that we either have it or do not have it, wanting to retain it if we have it and to acquire it if we do not [Note: [Col. 0104] The Michaelinus manuscript reads “to receive” (*recipere*).]?

Therefore everyone who wants something wants either not to lose it or to acquire it. Why, then, if all these things are clearer than daylight, as indeed they are—gifts granted not merely to my knowledge but to the knowledge of the human race by the generosity of truth itself—could I not at that time also have said: “The will is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, toward either not losing or acquiring something”?

## CHAPTER XI

### What sin is

15. Someone will say: “And how would this help you against the Manichaeans?” Wait; let us first define sin as well, which every mind reads as divinely inscribed within itself: that sin cannot exist without the will. Sin, therefore, is the will to retain or acquire what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain [Note: [Col. 0105] *Retractions* I, chapter 15, no. 4.].

Although, if it is not free, it is not will. But I preferred to define the matter more broadly [Note: [Col. 0105] The sole edition of Louvain reads “more coarsely” (*crassius*) rather than “more broadly” (*grossius*).] rather than too precisely. Did I really need to search these obscure books as well in order to learn that no one deserves blame or punishment who either wants what justice does not forbid him to want, or does not do what he is unable to do? Do not shepherds sing this in the mountains, poets in the theaters, the uneducated in their gatherings, the educated in their libraries, teachers in their schools, bishops in sacred places, and the human race throughout the world?

If no one deserves blame or condemnation either for doing what justice has not forbidden or for not doing what he cannot do, while every sin must be either blamed or condemned, who would doubt that sin exists when the willing is unjust and the not-willing is free? For that reason, who would doubt that the following definition is both true and extremely easy to understand, and that I could have stated it not only now but also then: “Sin is the will to retain or acquire what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain”?

[Note: [Col. 0105] Erasmus’s edition reads: “Was it also necessary to define this matter in these books?” Neither do these books, and so forth. The Louvain edition reads: “to define that matter. Nor do these books,” and so forth. The text is corrected from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XII

### The definitions of sin and will completely overthrow the Manichaean heresy

16. From the just condemnation of evil souls it likewise follows that they are evil not by nature but by will. Souls are good by nature, and forgiveness of sins is granted to them.

Come now; let us see how these points would have helped us. They would have helped enormously—indeed, I would have desired nothing more—for they would have settled the whole case. Anyone who consults the secret laws of his conscience and the divine laws implanted in nature, inwardly within the mind, where they are clearer and more certain, and admits that these two definitions of will and sin are true, condemns the whole Manichaean heresy without hesitation by a few brief but wholly invincible arguments.

The matter may be considered as follows. They say that there are two kinds of souls: one good, which is so from God that it is said not to have been made by him from some material or from nothing, but to have proceeded as a certain portion entirely from his very substance; and another evil, which they believe—and urge others to believe—does not belong to God in any respect whatsoever. Thus they proclaim the former to be the highest good and the latter the highest evil; and they say that these two kinds were once separate but are now mingled.

I had not yet heard either the manner or the cause of this mingling. Nevertheless, I could already ask whether that evil kind of souls had any will before it was mingled with the good. If it had no will, it was without sin and innocent, and therefore in no way evil [Note: [Col. 0106] *Retractions* I, chapter 15, no. 5.]. But if it was evil because, although without will, it would nevertheless violate and corrupt the good if it touched it, how outrageous it is both to believe that the nature of evil has such power to change any part of God and to believe that that supreme good is corruptible and violable!

But if there was will in it, then certainly there was a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, toward either not losing or acquiring something. That something was either good or was thought to be good; for it could not otherwise be desired. Yet in the highest evil, before the mingling they proclaim, there was never any good. From where, then, could knowledge or opinion of the good have arisen there? Did they want nothing that was within themselves, but desire that true good which was outside them?

That, surely, is a will worthy of being proclaimed with the highest and greatest praise: to desire the highest and true good. How, then, could there be in the highest evil a movement of the mind so deserving of praise? Or did they desire it out of a determination to harm? The same reasoning applies at the outset. For whoever wants to harm someone wants to deprive another of some good for the sake of some good of his own. There was therefore in them either knowledge or opinion of the good, which could in no way have existed in the highest evil.

Furthermore, that good placed outside themselves, which they sought to harm—how did they know that it existed at all? If they understood it, what could be more excellent than such a mind? Is there any other object toward which the whole intention of the good is extended through great labors, except that the highest and pure good may be understood? What is now granted only with difficulty to a few good and just people—could it then have been possessed by that pure evil without the aid of any good?

But if those souls possessed bodies and had seen it with their eyes, what tongues, breasts, or intellects would suffice to praise and proclaim such eyes, to which even the minds of the just can scarcely be equal? How many goods do we discover in the highest evil?

For if it is evil to see God, then God is not good. But God is good; therefore it is good to see God, and I do not know what could be compared with this good [Note: [Col. 0106] Louvain reads “with so great a good.” The words “so great” are absent from the other books.]. Moreover, if seeing is good, how can the ability to see be evil? Therefore, whatever he made in those eyes or in those minds by which the divine substance could be seen, he made a great good, one most worthy of ineffable praise. But if it was not made, and was instead of such a nature in and of itself and eternal, it would be difficult to find anything better than this evil.

17. Finally, even if those souls possessed none of the things that, according to their arguments, they are compelled to possess, I would ask whether God condemns any souls or none. If he condemns none, there is no judgment of merits and no providence; the world is governed by chance rather than reason—or rather, it is not governed at all, for governance cannot be assigned to chance. But if it is impious for all who are bound by any religion to believe this, it remains either that some souls are condemned or that there are no sins.

But if there are no sins, there is also no evil. If they say this, they kill their own heresy with a single blow. I therefore agree with them that some souls are condemned by divine law and judgment. But if these souls are good, what kind of justice is that? If they are evil, are they evil by nature or by will?

Souls cannot possibly be evil by nature. How do we demonstrate this? From the foregoing definitions of will and sin. To say that souls are evil and yet commit no sin is sheer madness; but to say that they sin without will is gross delirium. And to hold anyone guilty of sin because he did not do what he could not do is the height of injustice and insanity.

Therefore, whatever those souls do, if they do it by nature and not by will—that is, if they lack the free movement of the mind both to do and not to do; if, finally, no power to abstain from their activity is granted to them—we cannot hold them guilty of sin [Note: [Col. 0107] *Retractions* I, chapter 15, no. 6.]. Yet everyone admits that it is just for evil souls to be condemned and unjust for souls that have not sinned to be condemned. They therefore admit that those who sin are evil. But those souls, as reason has shown, do not sin. The supposed kind of evil souls, then—some foreign kind introduced by the Manichaeans—does not exist [Note: [Col. 0107] The printed editions read “outside that” (*extra illud*). The Vatican manuscripts more correctly read “foreign” (*extraneum*).].

18. Let us now consider that good kind, which they again praise so highly that they say it is the very substance of God. How much better it is for each person to recognize his own order and merit, and not to parade himself in such sacrilegious pride that, while he feels himself changing so often, he nevertheless believes himself to be the substance of that supreme good which pious reason professes and teaches to be unchangeable!

For it is evident that souls do not sin in what they are not and cannot be. Thus it is clear that those invented souls cannot possibly sin and therefore do not exist at all. It follows that, since they admit that sins exist, they cannot find anyone to whom to attribute them except the good kind of souls and the substance of God.

They are especially pressed by Christian authority. They have never denied that sins are forgiven when someone turns to God; nor have they ever said—as they have said of many other matters—that some corrupter inserted this teaching into the divine Scriptures. To whom, then, are sins forgiven?

If sins are forgiven to those of the alien kind, then those evil souls can also become good and can possess God’s kingdom with Christ. Since they deny this, and since they have no other kind except those whom they claim to be from the substance of God, it remains that they must confess that not only these souls, but these souls alone, sin.

For my part, I do not object to their being the only ones who sin. Yet they do sin. But are they compelled by the mingling of evil? [Note: [Col. 0107] The printed editions read: “Yet they sin, for they are compelled by the mingling of evil,” and so forth. The manuscripts correct this reading.]

If they are compelled in such a way that they have no power to resist, they do not sin. If it is within their power to resist and they consent by their own will, why are we compelled, on their doctrine, to find so many goods in the highest evil and this evil in the highest good? Is it not because neither is that supposed evil truly evil, nor is that highest good what they pervert through superstition?

## CHAPTER XIII

### Deliberation toward evil and toward good does not imply two kinds of souls; even if a kind of souls enticing us to shameful things is conceded, it does not follow that these are evil by nature or that the others are the highest good

19. If I had shown them—or had at least learned myself—that they were delirious and mistaken about these two kinds of souls, what reason could remain for me to think that I should listen to them or consult them about anything? Would it be so that I might learn that the existence of two kinds of souls is demonstrated by the fact that, in deliberation, our assent inclines now toward evil and now toward good?

Why is this not rather a sign of one soul, which by that free will can be carried this way and that, and turned in either direction? For when this happens to me, I feel that I am one person considering both alternatives and choosing one of them. Yet often one thing is pleasing while another is right, and we, placed between them, waver.

Nor is this surprising. We are now constituted in such a way that we can be affected by pleasure through the flesh and by moral goodness through the spirit. Why, then, am I forced by this to acknowledge two souls? We can understand more suitably and much more easily that there are two kinds of good things, neither of which is alien to God the author, and that one soul is affected in different ways by its lower and higher parts—or, as may properly be said, by its outer and inner parts.

These are the two kinds that we discussed shortly before under the names “sensible” and “intelligible,” which we more willingly and familiarly call “carnal” and “spiritual.” But it has become difficult for us to abstain from carnal things, since our true bread is spiritual. For now we eat bread with labor. Indeed, we are under the penalty of sin, having been made mortal from immortals through transgression.

Therefore, when habit formed with the flesh and our sins begin, in a certain way, to fight against us and make things difficult for us as we strive toward better things, some foolish people, through their extremely dull superstition, imagine another kind of soul that is not from God.

20. Yet even if it is granted that we are enticed toward shameful things by another, lower kind of souls, it does not follow either that those souls are evil by nature or that these are the highest good. For it may be that those souls became evil by their own will, desiring what was not permitted—that is, by sinning—and that they may again become good, though in such a way that, as long as they remain in sin, they lead other souls over to themselves by some hidden persuasion [Note: [Col. 0108] The Vatican manuscripts read “but as happens.” The Michaelinus manuscript reads: “but as happens, as long as they remain in sin, they lead other souls over to themselves by some hidden persuasion.”].

Or perhaps they are not evil at all, but, within their own kind, although a lower one, carry out their proper work without any sin. The higher souls, on the other hand, to whom supreme justice, which governs all things, has assigned a far more excellent activity, become evil by sinning if they wish to follow and imitate those lower souls—not because the lower souls are evil, but because the higher souls imitate them badly.

The lower souls perform what is proper to them; the higher souls desire what belongs to another. Thus the former remain in their own rank, while the latter sink to lower things.

It is like human beings pursuing the behavior of animals. A horse moves beautifully on four feet; but if a human being imitated this with his hands and feet, who would think him worthy even of food made from chaff? We therefore rightly often disapprove of the imitator while approving the one whom he imitates. We disapprove of him not because he has failed to attain what he imitates, but because he wanted at all to attain it.

For in the horse we approve the very thing, and the more we rank the human being above it, the more we are offended that he pursues lower things. Again, among human beings, if a herald does well in projecting his voice, is not a senator mad if he does the same thing even more loudly and effectively than the herald?

Raise your thoughts to heavenly things. The shining moon is praised, and its course and phases please those who observe them carefully. Yet if the sun wanted to imitate it—let us suppose that the sun could have such desires—who would not rightly and supremely disapprove?

This is what I want understood. Even if there are souls—which for the moment remains uncertain—that are devoted to bodily functions by nature and not through sin, and that touch us, although they are lower, by some inner proximity [Note: [Col. 0109] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have “by an inferior proximity.”], they ought not on that account to be considered evil, because when we follow them and love bodily things, we become evil [Note: [Col. 0109] *Retractions* I, chapter 15, no. 7.].

For we sin by loving bodily things because we are both commanded by justice and able by nature to love spiritual things; and then, within our own kind, we are at our best and happiest [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid., no. 8.].

[Note: [Col. 0109] The printed editions read “alternating thoughts.” The manuscripts correct this reading.]

21. What argument, then, does deliberation heated in both directions contain—now inclined toward sin, now raised toward right action—that forces us to accept two kinds of souls, one of which is by nature from God and the other is not, when so many other causes of alternating thought can be proposed?

But anyone who is a good judge of things sees that these matters are obscure and are sought in vain by minds afflicted with poor vision. Therefore those statements about the will and sin—those, I say, which supreme justice allows no rational person to ignore; those without which nothing exists from which instruction in virtue may begin, nothing from which one may rise out of the death of vices [Note: [Col. 0109] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions commonly read “the mass” (*mole*).]—when considered again and again, prove clearly and unmistakably that the Manichaean heresy is false.

## CHAPTER XIV

### The usefulness of repentance again shows that souls are not evil by nature

22. Such a certain demonstration is opposed only through the habit of erring. I shall now say something similar about repentance. For, as all sound-minded people agree—and as the Manichaeans themselves not only admit but also prescribe—repentance for sin is useful.

Why should I now collect the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, which are spread everywhere on this subject? This too is the voice of nature: no fool is deprived of knowledge of this matter. If it were not deeply implanted in us, we would perish. Someone may say that he does not sin; but no barbarian will dare to say that, if he has sinned, he has no need to repent.

Since this is so, I ask: to which of those two kinds of souls does repentance for sin belong? I know that it can belong neither to the one that cannot do evil nor to the one that cannot do good. Therefore, to use their own language: if a soul of darkness repents of sin, it is not of the substance of the highest evil; if a soul of light repents, it is not of the substance of the highest good.

For that disposition of repentance which is beneficial testifies both that the penitent has done evil and that he could have done good [Note: [Col. 0110] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “that affection which reveals that the penitent has done evil.”]. How, then, is there nothing evil from me if I did wrong? Or how can I rightly repent if I did not do it?

Hear the other side as well: How is there nothing good from me when I possess a good will? Or how can I rightly repent if I do not possess one?

Therefore they must either deny that repentance is greatly useful, and thereby be expelled not only from the Christian name but also from every form of even imaginary reason; or they must cease to say and teach that there are two kinds of souls, one from which there is nothing evil and the other from which there is nothing good [Note: [Col. 0110] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and Louvain read “to learn” (*discere*) rather than “to say” (*dicere*). M.]. If they do this, they will no longer be Manichaeans; for that entire sect is supported by this two-headed—or rather headlong—variety of souls.

23. For my part, it is enough for me to know that the Manichaeans are in error in the same way that I know that one must repent of sin. Yet if I now addressed, by the right of friendship, one of my friends who still thinks that the Manichaeans should be listened to, and said to him, “Do you know that whenever someone has sinned, it is useful to repent?” he would swear without hesitation that he knew it.

If I were to make you know in this way that the Manichaean heresy is false, would you desire anything more? What more could he reply that he could desire in this matter [Note: [Col. 0110] The printed editions read: “what more could there be to desire in this matter.” The manuscripts read: “what more he could desire in this matter.”]?

So far, so good. But when I began to set forth certain necessary arguments that followed from that proposition, bound to it—as they say—with adamantine chains, and brought the whole matter to the conclusion by which that sect is overthrown, he might deny that he knew that repentance was useful, although no educated or uneducated person is ignorant of this. Instead, he would insist that he knew that, whenever we doubt and deliberate, two souls within us bring their own advocacy to the respective sides of the question.

O habit of sin! O companion of sin’s punishment [Note: [Col. 0110] Almost the sole edition of Louvain reads “punishment of sin.”]! At that time you turned me away from considering matters so manifest, though you harmed me when I was unaware. Now, however, you have wounded and tormented me in my closest friends, who likewise do not perceive these things, while I do perceive them.

## CHAPTER XV

### He prays for the friends who shared his error

24. Please attend to these matters, dearest friends. I know your minds well. If you now grant me whatever reason and judgment a human being possesses, they are much more certain than the things that we either seemed to learn there or were compelled rather to believe.

Great God, almighty God, God of supreme goodness, whom it is right to believe and understand as inviolate and unchangeable; Trinity in unity, whom the Catholic Church worships: I humbly ask you, having experienced your mercy in me, not to permit people with whom, from childhood onward, I shared the closest agreement in all our association to disagree with me in your worship [Col. 0112] [Note: [Col. 0112] *Retractions* I, chapter 15, no. 8.].

I see that at this point people are especially waiting to hear how I would then have defended the Catholic Scriptures when they were attacked by the Manichaeans, if, as I say, I had been cautious, or how I can now demonstrate that they can be defended. In other volumes God will assist my purpose; for, as I judge, the length of this work now demands a measured restraint from further elaboration [Note: [Col. 0112] Erasmus’s edition reads “immoderate” rather than “measured.”]

[Col. 0111]

# Acts, or Disputation, of the Holy Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, against Fortunatus the Manichaean

One book [Note: [Col. 0111] Written in the year 392.] [Note: [Col. 0111] On the following Disputation, see Book I, chapter 16 of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 612, no. 1, from the words “At the same time” through the words of no. 2, “when the most distinguished consuls were in office.” M.] [Note: [Col. 0111] The book against Fortunatus was corrected with the aid of the Vatican manuscript, the Arnulfian manuscript, and two Victorine manuscripts, in addition to the variant readings of three Belgian manuscripts formerly supplied by the Louvain scholars, and after the old editions had also been read through.] [Note: [Col. 0111] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C)

## Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter VI, on the following Disputation

At that time, in the city of Hippo, the pestilence of the Manichaeans had infected and penetrated very many citizens and visitors, through the seduction and deception of a certain presbyter of that heresy, named Fortunatus, who was living and staying there.

Meanwhile, the Christian citizens and visitors of Hippo, both Catholics and Donatists, approached the presbyter Augustine and asked that he meet that Manichaean presbyter, whom they believed to be learned, and discuss the Law with him. Augustine, as it is written, was ready to give an answer to everyone who asked him for a reason concerning the faith and hope that is in God (1 Peter 3:15), and was able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradicted it (Titus 1:9); he did not refuse at all. He did, however, ask whether Fortunatus was also willing that this should take place.

They immediately conveyed the request to Fortunatus himself, asking, urging, and imploring him not to refuse. Fortunatus already knew Augustine as a holy man from the time when Augustine was still established with him in the same error at Carthage, and he was afraid to engage with him. Nevertheless, compelled and embarrassed especially by the insistence of his own people, he promised that he would come in person and undertake the contest of debate.

Accordingly, on the appointed day and at the appointed place, they came together, with very many serious men and curious crowds gathering, and with the notaries’ tablets opened. The disputation began on the first day and was concluded on the second. In it, as the reliability of the Acts records, that Manichaean teacher was able neither to invalidate the Catholic position nor to establish the Manichaean sect by means of truth. Failing in his replies, he finally said that he would report to his superiors the matters he had been unable to refute and would consult them; and, if they should perhaps not satisfy him sufficiently, he would take thought for his own soul.

Thus, in the judgment of all those among whom he had appeared important and learned, he was found to have accomplished nothing in support of his sect. Affected by this disgrace, he later departed from the city of Hippo and never returned to it. In this way, through the aforementioned man of God, that error was removed from the hearts of all who were present or who learned, though absent, what had taken place, and the sincere Catholic religion was made known and retained.

# DISPUTATION OF THE FIRST DAY

On the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the most distinguished men Arcadius Augustus for the second time and Rufinus, a disputation was held against Fortunatus, a presbyter of the Manichaeans, in the city of Hippo Regius, at the Baths of Sossius [Note: [Col. 0112] The Louvain edition reads “Sosius.” The other books read “Sossit.”], in the presence of the people.

[Col. 0113]

### 1. Augustine said:

I now think that what I previously thought was truth is error. Whether I am right to think so, I wish to hear from you while you are present [Note: [Col. 0113] After “I wish to hear,” the Vatican manuscript adds: “Fortunatus said: ‘Explain the error with certainty.’ Augustine said: ‘First of all,’” and so forth.].

First of all, I consider it the greatest error to believe that almighty God, in whom alone our hope rests, is in any respect violable, defileable, or corruptible. I know that your heresy asserts this—not, certainly, in the words I have just used. For when questioned, you too confess that God is incorruptible, wholly inviolate, and undefiled. But when you begin to explain the remaining points, you are compelled to confess that he is corruptible, penetrable, and defileable.

You say that some other nation of darkness rebelled against God’s kingdom. But when almighty God saw how great a ruin and devastation threatened his realms unless he opposed something to that hostile nation and resisted it, he sent this Power, from whose mingling with evil and the nation of darkness the world was fashioned. This is why the good souls here labor, serve, err, and are corrupted: so that they would need a liberator who might cleanse them from error, release them from the mingling, and free them from servitude.

I consider it impious to believe that almighty God feared some hostile nation or was subjected to necessity, so that he plunged us into misery.

### Fortunatus said:

Because I know that you were once one of us—that is, that you served among the Manichaeans—these are the principal points of our faith. The matter at issue here concerns our way of life and the false charges by which we are attacked. Let these good men who are present hear from you, then, whether the things for which we are accused and prosecuted are true or false. For from your teaching, explanation, and testimony they will be able to learn our way of life more accurately, if you disclose it.

You attended our prayer service.

### 2. Augustine said:

I did. But one question concerns faith and another concerns conduct. I put forward the question of faith. But if those who are present prefer to hear about conduct, I do not avoid that question either.

### Fortunatus said:

I first wish to clear myself before your conscience, before which we are defiled [Note: [Col. 0113] The manuscripts read “before whom.”], by the testimony of a trustworthy man—one who is trustworthy for me now and will also be so at the examination of the just judge Christ in the future, if he saw or witnessed in us the things that are being alleged.

### 3. Augustine said:

You are calling me to another matter, although I put forward a question about faith. Those who are your Elect can know your conduct fully. You know that I was not one of your Elect but one of your Hearers. Therefore, although I did attend your prayer service, as you asked, whether you hold some separate prayer service among yourselves God alone can know—and you yourselves.

In the prayer service I attended, however, I saw nothing shameful being done. I noticed only something contrary to the faith, which I later learned about and approved: that you pray toward the sun [Col. 0114]. Apart from this, I discovered nothing new in your prayer service.

Whoever brings a question against you concerning conduct brings it against your Elect [Note: [Col. 0114] The printed editions read “let him bring it against.” The manuscripts’ “he brings it against” is more suitable.]. What you do among yourselves as Elect I cannot know. For I have often heard from you that you receive the Eucharist; but since the time of receiving it was hidden from me, how could I know what you receive?

Therefore, if you please, reserve the question of conduct for discussion among your Elect, if it can be discussed. You gave me a statement of faith, which I now reject. I have put forward a question about that faith; let me receive an answer to the question I have raised.

### Fortunatus said:

Our profession itself is that God is incorruptible, luminous, inaccessible, untouchable, impassible, and dwells in eternal light that belongs to him [Note: [Col. 0114] In B.: “that he is inaccessible, untouchable, impassible, and dwells in eternal light.” We have followed the Lyon, Venice, and Louvain editions. M.]. He produces nothing corruptible from himself—neither darkness, nor demons, nor Satan, nor anything hostile can be found in his kingdom.

He sent a Savior like himself: the Word, born at the establishment of the world, when he was fashioning the world [Note: [Col. 0114] In the Vatican manuscript, “when they were fashioning it.”], came among human beings after the fashioning of the world. He chose souls worthy of his holy will [Note: [Col. 0114] The Vatican manuscript reads “chose out souls.”], sanctified by his heavenly commands and imbued with faith and understanding of heavenly things. With him as their guide, those same souls will return from here to the kingdom of God, according to the holy promise of the one who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the gate,” and, “No one can come to the Father except through me.”

We believe these things because souls cannot return to the kingdom of God by any other means—through any other mediator—unless they find him to be the way, the truth, and the gate [Note: [Col. 0114] The printed editions read “there are other souls.” This has been corrected here from the Vatican manuscript. Later the Louvain editors wished “in another way before” to be read instead of “by another mediator.” But all our manuscripts resist this change.].

For he himself said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also” (John 14:6, 9); and, “Whoever believes in me will not taste death forever, but passes from death to life and will not come into judgment” (ibid. 5:24).

We believe these things, and this is the principle of our faith: to obey his commands as far as the strength of our soul permits, following the one faith of this Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

### 4. Augustine said:

What cause plunged into death these souls whom you admit come from death to life through Christ?

### Fortunatus said:

Now deign to continue and contradict this, if there is nothing besides God.

### 5. Augustine said:

Rather, deign to answer what you are being asked: what cause gave these souls over to death?

### Fortunatus said:

Rather, deign to say whether anything exists besides God, or whether everything is in God.

### 6. Augustine said:

I can answer what the Lord has willed me to know: that God can suffer no necessity and cannot be violated or corrupted in any respect. Since you too confess this, I ask by what necessity he sent here the souls whom you say return through Christ.

### Fortunatus said:

What you have said is that, insofar as God has revealed this to you, he is incorruptible—as he has revealed it to me also. The question is how and for what reason the souls came into this world, so that he might rightly free them from this world through his only-begotten and like Son, if nothing exists besides him [Note: [Col. 0115] Here, on the authority of the manuscripts, we add “how.”].

### 7. Augustine said:

We ought not frustrate so many people who are present by leaving the question proposed and going on to another matter. We both confess, and agree with one another, that God is incorruptible and inviolate and could suffer nothing. It follows that your heresy is false, since it says that, when God saw ruin and devastation threatening his realms, he sent a Power to fight with the nation of darkness, and that from this mingling our souls suffer [Note: [Col. 0115] The printed editions commonly read incorrectly: “and from this mingling he would free our souls from here.” The Vatican manuscript omits “from here” and has “suffer” instead of “would free.” Thus above, no. 1, column 113: “This is why the good souls here labor.”].

My argument, then, is brief and, as I think, perfectly clear to anyone. If God could suffer nothing from the nation of darkness because he is inviolate, he sent us here without cause to suffer hardships here. But if he could suffer something, he is not inviolate, and you deceive those to whom you say that God is inviolate. Your heresy denies this when you explain the remaining points.

FORTUNATUS said: We hold what the blessed Apostle Paul teaches us when he says: “Have this mind among yourselves which you have in Christ Jesus; who, although he was established in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself and became obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:5–8). Thus, then, we understand our own condition from that of Christ: although he was established in the form of God, he became obedient unto death in order to show the likeness of our souls. And just as he displayed in himself the likeness of death and showed that he had been raised by the Father from among the dead, so we understand that the same will happen to our souls: through him we shall be able to be freed from this death—which is either alien to God, or, if it is God’s own, then his mercy, the name of “liberator,” and the works of one who liberates cease.

**8. AUGUSTINE said:** I am asking how we came into death, whereas you are explaining how we are freed from death.

**FORTUNATUS said:** The Apostle said how we ought to understand our souls, which Christ has shown us. If Christ was in suffering and death, so were we; if he descended into suffering and death by the will of the Father, so did we.

**[Col. 0116] 9. AUGUSTINE said:** It is known to everyone that the Catholic faith holds that our Lord—that is, the Power and Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the Word through which all things were made and without which nothing was made (John 1:3)—assumed a human being for our liberation. In the human being whom he assumed, he demonstrated the things you speak of. But we are now asking about the substance of God himself and of his ineffable majesty: whether anything can harm him or cannot harm him. For if anything can harm him, he is not inviolable. If nothing can harm him, what was the nation of darkness to do against him, against which you say that God waged war before the foundation of the world, in which war we—that is, the souls whom you clearly declare now to need a liberator—were mingled with every evil and entangled in death? I return to that very brief point: if he could be harmed, he is not inviolable; if he could not, he sent us here cruelly to suffer these things.

**FORTUNATUS said:** Is the soul of God, or is it not?

*[Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead read, “God is.”]*

**10. AUGUSTINE said:** If it is right that my questions should not be answered, while I am to ask questions, I shall answer.

**FORTUNATUS said:** Does the soul act in its own proper sphere? This is what I ask you.

**11. AUGUSTINE said:** I shall answer what you asked; only remember this: you were unwilling to answer my questions, whereas I am answering yours. If you ask whether the soul descended from God, that is indeed a major question. But whether the soul descended from God or not, I answer this about the soul: it is not God. God is one thing, the soul another. God is inviolable, incorruptible, impenetrable, and undefiled; he cannot be corrupted in any respect, nor can he be harmed in any respect. But we see that the soul is sinful, that it is afflicted, that it seeks the truth, and that it needs a liberator. This change in the soul shows me that the soul is not God. For if the soul is the substance of God, then the substance of God errs, the substance of God is corrupted, the substance of God is violated, and the substance of God is deceived—which it is impious to say.

**FORTUNATUS said:** Then you have denied that the soul is from God so long as it is enslaved to sins, vices, and worldly things and is led by error. Yet it cannot be the case either that God or his substance suffers this. For God is incorruptible, and his substance is immaculate and holy. What is being asked of you here is whether the soul is from God or not.

*[Note: The printed editions read, “is being asked of us.” The manuscripts read, “is being asked of you.”]*

We confess that it is, and we demonstrate this from the Savior’s coming, from his holy preaching, and from his reading—while he has pity on souls—and the soul is said to have come according to his decision, so that he might free that same soul from death, lead it to eternal glory, and restore it to the Father.

*[Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read “reading” (*lectione*).]* But what do you yourself say or hope concerning the soul? Is it from God or not? You say that the substance of God, from which you deny that the soul exists, cannot be subject to any sufferings.

**[Col. 0117] 12. AUGUSTINE said:** I denied that the soul is the substance of God in such a way as also to deny that it is God. Nevertheless, I say that it is from God as its creator, because it was made by God. The one who made is one thing; what he made is another. The one who made it cannot be corruptible in any way; but what he made cannot possibly be equal to the one who made it.

**FORTUNATUS said:** I did not say that the soul is like God. But since you said that the soul is made, and that there is nothing besides God, I ask: from where did God obtain the substance of the soul?

*[Note: The manuscripts read “made”; the printed editions read “creation.”]*

**13. AUGUSTINE said:** Only remember that I answer the things you ask, while you do not answer the things I ask. I say that the soul was made by God, just as all other things made by God were made; and among the things that almighty God made, the soul was given the chief place.

*[Note: See *Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 16, §2.]*

But if you ask from what God made the soul, remember to confess with me that God is almighty.

*[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “remember that you confess with me.”]*

A being is not almighty if it needs some material from which to make whatever it wishes. Consequently, according to our faith, God made all things that he made through his Word and Wisdom out of nothing. For thus we read: “He commanded, and they were made; he ordered, and they were created” (Psalm 148:5).

**FORTUNATUS said:** Does the universe exist by command?

**14. AUGUSTINE said:** So I believe—but the whole universe that was made.

**FORTUNATUS said:** Created things correspond to one another; but since they are mutually incongruous, it follows that they do not consist of one substance, even though they came from the command of one being into the composition and appearance of this world.

*[Note: The sole Louvain edition reads, “into that same composition.”]* The things themselves make clear that darkness and light have nothing alike, truth and falsehood have nothing alike, death and life have nothing alike, the soul and body have nothing alike, and likewise for the other things similar to these, which differ from one another both in names and in forms. And rightly did our Lord say: “Every tree that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted and thrown into the fire, because it does not bear good fruit” (Matthew 15:13; 3:10); and that there is a tree rooted—

*[Note: The Erfurt edition reads “to be rooted.” The Louvain editors corrected it from two manuscripts to “uprooted.” We print “rooted” from our manuscripts; this word seems to refer to the good tree, distinct from the one that will be uprooted.]*

Here, then, it is truly established by the nature of things—

*[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “Here, then, it is established, and reason itself is clear, both from the forms themselves and from the distinction of things.”]*

—that there are two substances in this world, which are constituted by their forms and names: one is bodily, while the other is the eternal substance of the almighty Father, which we believe to be God.

*[Note: The sole Louvain edition reads: “one temporal, the other eternal, which we believe to belong to the almighty Father.”]*

**15. AUGUSTINE said:** These oppositions that trouble you, leading us to regard things as mutually hostile, have come about because of our sin—that is, because of the human being’s sin. God made all things good and arranged them well; he did not make sin. The only thing called evil is our voluntary sin. There is also another kind of evil, which is the punishment of sin.

Since there are therefore two kinds of evil—sin and the punishment of sin—sin does not pertain to God, whereas the punishment of sin pertains to the one who administers retribution. For just as God is good in establishing all things, so he is just in punishing sin. Since, then, all things have been arranged most excellently, the things that now seem hostile to us have rightly come about because of the fallen human being, who was unwilling to keep God’s law.

God gave free will to the rational soul that is in the human being. For we could have merit only if we were good by our will, not by necessity. Since, then, we ought to be good not by necessity but by will, God had to give the soul free will. To this soul, when it obeyed his laws, he subjected everything without hostility, so that the other things God created would serve it, if it too were willing to serve God. But if it were unwilling to serve God, the things that served it would be turned into its punishment. Therefore, if all things have been rightly arranged by God and are good, God does not suffer evil.

**FORTUNATUS said:** He does not suffer evil, but he anticipated it.

**16. AUGUSTINE said:** From whom, then, was he going to suffer it?

**FORTUNATUS said:** That is my point: he wished to anticipate it—not rashly, but by his power and foreknowledge. Otherwise, deny that evil exists apart from God, even though commandments can be shown that are carried out contrary to his will.

*[Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read, “he shows what things are other.”]*

A commandment has no place except where there is also opposition. Free power to live is not given except where there has been a fall, according to the Apostle’s reasoning, when he says:

“And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the instruction of this world, according to the ruler of the power of this air, the spirit that now works in the children of unbelief, among whom we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wishes of the flesh and its thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest. But God, who is rich in all mercy, had mercy on us. And when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved; and he raised us up together and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the abundant riches of his grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves: it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.

“Therefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision, made in the flesh by human hands; that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and being without God in this world. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of partition, abolishing hostility in his flesh, annulling the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new human being, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself. And when he came, he proclaimed peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access to the Father in one Spirit” (Ephesians 2:1–18).

**17. AUGUSTINE said:** This reading from the Apostle, which you wished to recite, if I am not mistaken, is very much in favor of my position and against your faith. First, because the very free will by which, as I said, the soul sins is clearly expressed here, when he mentions sins and says that our reconciliation with God takes place through Jesus Christ. By sinning we had turned away from God; by keeping Christ’s commandments we are reconciled to God, so that we who were dead in sins may be made alive by keeping his commandments and may have peace with him in one Spirit—from whom we had been alienated by not keeping his commands. This is precisely what our faith proclaims concerning the human being who was first created.

I therefore ask you now, according to the passage that was read: how can we have sins if a contrary nature compels us to do what we do? For one who is compelled by necessity to do something does not sin. But one who sins, sins by free will. Why, then, are we commanded to repent, if we have done nothing evil but the nation of darkness has? I also ask to whom the forgiveness of sins is given: to us, or to the nation of darkness.

But if forgiveness of sins is given to the nation of darkness, then it too will reign with God, receiving forgiveness of sins. If, however, forgiveness of sins is given to us, it is clear that we sinned voluntarily. For it is utterly foolish to forgive one who has done nothing evil. But one who has done nothing voluntarily has done nothing evil.

Today, then, if God promises the soul forgiveness of sins and reconciliation, provided that it ceases to sin and repents of its sins, suppose it should answer according to your faith and say:

“What sin have I committed? What have I deserved? Why did you drive me out of your kingdoms so that I might fight against some nation I know not what? I was crushed—

*[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “I was oppressed”; likewise below, where the text has “crushed,” it reads “oppressed.”]*

—I was mingled, I was corrupted, I was exhausted—

*[Note: Several manuscripts read “I was wearied.” Perhaps the reading should be “I was deceived, I was wearied”; the two words occur in Terence, *Andria*, act 4, scene 1, line 45.]*

—my free will was not preserved for me. You know the necessity by which I was oppressed: why do you charge me with wounds that I received? Why do you compel me to repentance, when you are the cause of my wounds; when you know what I suffered; when you, as their author, caused the nation of darkness to do these things to me, although you could not be violated, and yet, wishing to protect your kingdoms—against which nothing could be harmed by that nation—you cast me into misery?

“If indeed I am a part of you, which proceeded from your inward being, from your kingdom and from your mouth, I ought not to have suffered anything in this nation of darkness, so that I might remain undefiled and that nation might be subjected, if I was a part of the Lord. But since that nation could not be restrained except through my corruption, how am I called your part, or how do you remain inviolable, or how are you not cruel, when you wished me to suffer on behalf of kingdoms that could not be harmed by that nation?

“Answer this, if you please; and also deign to explain to me how the Apostle Paul’s statement is to be understood: ‘We were by nature children of wrath,’ whom he says were reconciled to God. If, then, they were by nature children of wrath, how can you say that the soul is by nature a daughter and portion of God?”

*[Note: We have restored the following words from the manuscripts, which are absent from the printed editions: “whom he says were reconciled to God. If, then, they were by nature children of wrath.”]*

**FORTUNATUS said:** If the Apostle had said that we are by nature children of wrath with reference to the soul, the soul would have been alienated from God by the Apostle’s own words. By this reasoning you yourself show that the soul is not God’s, because the Apostle says, “we are by nature children of wrath.”

But if he spoke with reference to the fact that the same Apostle was subject to the law and, as he himself testifies, descended from the seed of Abraham (Romans 11:1), it is clear that he was speaking bodily when he said that we had been children of wrath, as were the rest. He shows, however, that the substance of the soul is from God, and that the soul cannot be reconciled to God except through the teacher, Christ Jesus.

Once hostility had been destroyed, the soul appeared to have become unworthy of God. But because it was sent, we confess that it was sent by almighty God, deriving its origin from him and being sent to carry out his will. In the same way we believe that Christ the Savior came from heaven to fulfill the Father’s will. This was the Father’s will: to free our souls from that same hostility, after that hostility had been destroyed. If it had not been hostile to God, it would neither have been called hostility where there was unity, nor would its destruction have been spoken of or carried out where there was life.

**18. AUGUSTINE said:** Remember that the Apostle said that we were alienated from God by our conduct.

**FORTUNATUS said:** I maintain that there were two substances. God is held to be in the substance of light, as we said above, incorruptible. There was, however, a contrary nature of darkness, which I still confess is overcome by the power of God, and Christ the Savior was sent for my return, as the same Apostle says earlier.

**19. AUGUSTINE said:** Those who are listening to us imposed upon us the task of examining the faith in two natures by arguments. But since you have again taken refuge in the Scriptures, I shall descend to them, and I insist that nothing be omitted, lest, by using certain passages, we bring obscurity to those who are unfamiliar with the Scriptures.

Let us therefore begin with the passage that the Apostle has in his Epistle to the Romans. For on the first page there is something strongly opposed to you. He says:

“Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God—

*[Note: The manuscripts read, “predestined for the Gospel of God.”]*

—which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined as the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, through the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 1:1–4).

We see that the Apostle teaches us about our Lord: according to the power of God he was predestined before the flesh, and according to the flesh he was made for him from the seed of David. Since you have always denied and continue to deny this, how can you demand that we debate according to the Scriptures?

**FORTUNATUS said:** You assert that he was according to the flesh from the seed of David, while it is proclaimed that he was born from a virgin (Isaiah 7:14) and is magnified as the Son of God. For it cannot be otherwise than that what is from the spirit be understood as spirit, and what is from the flesh as flesh (John 3:6). Against this stands the very authority of the Gospel, which says that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption (1 Corinthians 15:50).

At this point the people sitting with them raised an uproar, since they wanted the matter to be conducted by arguments: they saw that Fortunatus was unwilling to accept everything written in the Apostle’s book. Then discussion began to spread among everyone, until he said that the word of God was bound in the nation of darkness. Those present were horrified at this, and the session ended.

## SECOND DAY’S DEBATE

On the following day, after a notary had again been summoned, the proceedings continued as follows.

**FORTUNATUS said:** I say that almighty God produces nothing evil from himself, and that the things belonging to him remain incorruptible, having arisen and been generated from one inviolable source. The other things that exist in this world in opposition do not flow from God, nor have they obeyed God as their ruler in this age; that is, they do not derive their origin from him. This, then, is what we have accepted in faith: that evils are alien to God.

**20. AUGUSTINE said:** Our faith too is that God is not the begetter of evils and has made no evil nature. But since both of us agree that God is incorruptible and undefiled, it is for the prudent and faithful to judge which faith is purer and more worthy of God’s majesty: the one that asserts that either God’s power, or some part of God, or God’s word can be changed, violated, corrupted, or bound; or the one that says that almighty God, and his entire nature and substance, can never be corrupted in any part, but that evils arise from the voluntary sin of the soul, to which God gave free will.

If God had not given this free will, there could be no just judgment of punishment, no merit in doing what is right, no divine command that repentance should be practiced for sins, and no forgiveness of sins itself, which God has granted us through our Lord Jesus Christ. For one who sins unwillingly does not sin. I think this is clear and evident to everyone.

Therefore, we should not be troubled if we suffer some unpleasant things among those that God has made, in accordance with our merits. For just as he is good in establishing all things, so he is just in not sparing sins. As I said, these sins would not be sins unless we had free will.

For example, if someone were bound by another in all his limbs except his hand, and something false were written by his hand without his own will, I ask: if this became evident to a judge, could the judge condemn that person on a charge of falsification? Therefore, if it is clear that there is no sin where there is no free will, I want to hear from you what evil the soul—which you call either a part, or a power, or a word, or anything else belonging to God—has done, so that it should be punished by God, repent of sin, or deserve forgiveness, when it has itself committed no sin.

**[Col. 0122] FORTUNATUS said:** I have proposed concerning the substances that God is held to be the creator only of good things, but the avenger of evils, because evils are not from him. Therefore I rightly hold that God punishes evils, because they are not from him.

But if they were from him, then either he would grant permission to sin—which is what you say when you claim that God gave free will—and would thus already be an accomplice in my offense, since he would be the author of my offense; or, being ignorant of what I would become, he would commit an offense by creating one whom he would not deem worthy of himself.

This, then, is what I have proposed, and what I now ask is whether God instituted evils or not, and whether he himself instituted the end of evils. For the things that we have said were made by him, as by their craftsman, and which, having been created and generated by him, are held to be incorruptible—these matters make evident, and the evangelical faith teaches.

These are the things I have proposed as belonging to our belief, and which can be confirmed by you in this confession of ours, provided that the authority of the Christian faith is not lacking. And since I cannot properly demonstrate that I believe rightly in any way unless I confirm this same faith by the authority of the Scriptures, this is what I have indicated and stated.

Either deign to say that evils appeared in the world with God as their author; or, if it is rightly believed that evils are not from God, then the consideration of those present ought also to follow and accept this.

I spoke about substances, not about the sin that exists among us. For if there were no origin for the thing that compels us to commit offenses, we would not be compelled to fall into sin or offense. But because we sin unwillingly and are compelled by a contrary substance hostile to us, we therefore pursue knowledge of things.

When the soul is instructed by this knowledge and restored to its former memory, it recognizes from what source it derives its origin, in what evil it is involved, and by what good things it can again correct what it sinned unwillingly. Through the correction of its offenses and the grace of good works, it can establish for itself the merit of reconciliation with God, under the authority of our Savior, who teaches us both to practice good and to flee evil.

For this is what has been proposed to us: that a human being serves righteousness or makes himself liable to sins not because of some contrary nature, but of his own accord. If no contrary nation existed, and the soul alone were situated in the body, to which, as you say, God gave free will, it would be without sin and would not make itself liable to sins.

**21. AUGUSTINE said:** I say that there is no sin if one does not sin by one’s own will.

*[Note: See *Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 16, §2.]*

From this also comes the reward, because we do what is right by our own will. Or, if one who sins unwillingly deserves punishment, then one who does good unwillingly ought also to deserve a reward. But who would doubt that a reward is not bestowed except upon one who has done something with a good will?

*[Note: The Vatican and Arnulf manuscripts read, “who has done something good by his will.” A little later they read, “who has done something evil by his will.”]*

From this we understand that punishment is also inflicted upon one who has done something by an evil will.

But since you bring me back to the earlier natures and substances, my faith is that almighty God—and this must be especially observed and fixed in the mind—almighty God, just and good, made good things. But the things made by him cannot be such as he himself, who made them, is. For it is unjust and foolish to believe that works are equal to the craftsman and created things equal to their creator.

*[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “and foolish to demand that works be equal to the craftsman, and created things to their creator.”]*

Therefore, if it is a pious faith that God made all things good, although he himself is much more excellent and far superior to them, then the origin and source of evil is sin, as the Apostle said: “Desire is the root of all evils. By following it, some have suffered shipwreck in the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:10).

If you seek the root of all evils, you have the Apostle saying that the root of all evils is desire. I cannot seek the root of the root. Or, if there is another evil whose root is not desire, then desire will not be the root of all evils. But if it is true that desire is the root of all evils, we search in vain for some other kind of evil.

As for the contrary nature that you introduce, since I have already answered your objections, I ask you to deign to tell me this: if that contrary nature is the whole of evil, and sin can exist only from it, then it alone ought to deserve punishment, not the soul, from which sin does not arise.

But if you say that it alone deserves punishment and that the soul does not, I ask to whom repentance was given and who was commanded to repent. If the soul was commanded to repent, then sin arose from it, and it sinned by its own will. For if the soul is compelled to do evil and is not the one that does the evil—

*[Note: Some manuscripts read, “and that which does evil is not in it.”]*

—is it not foolish and utterly deranged that the nation of darkness should have sinned while I repent of its sins? Is it not utterly deranged that the nation of darkness should have sinned while forgiveness of sins is given to me, who, according to your faith, can say:

“What have I done? What have I committed? I was with you; I was whole; I was contaminated by no stain. You sent me here; you suffered necessity; you protected your kingdoms when great corruption and devastation threatened them. Since you know the necessity by which I was oppressed here, by which I could not breathe freely, which I could not resist, why do you accuse me as though I were sinning? Or why do you promise me forgiveness of sins?

“Answer this without evasion, if you please, just as I have answered you without evasion.”

**FORTUNATUS said:** This is what we say: the soul is compelled to offend by a contrary nature. You are unwilling to regard that nature as the root, except for the sole reason that evil exists among us, although it is clear that, apart from our bodies, evils exist throughout the whole world.

These things that we have only in our bodies do not alone exist throughout the whole world, with the names “good” and “evil” applying to them; the evil root remains fixed. For your Dignity said that desire is the root of evils, and that this desire exists in our bodies, whereas, when the desire for evil is not from our bodies, it exists throughout the whole world from that principal contrary nature.

The Apostle named desire as a root of evils, not as one evil—the desire that you said is the root of all evils—as though it existed only in our bodies.

*[Note: In this one place, Erasmus and the manuscripts read, “in our hearts.”]*

But it is clear that the evil existing in us descends from an evil author, and that this root which you call the root is a small portion of evil, so that it is not itself the root but a small portion of the evil that exists everywhere.

Our Lord called this root a bad tree, which never bears good fruit, which his Father did not plant, and which rightly is to be uprooted and thrown into the fire (Matthew 15:13; 3:10).

As for your statement that sin ought to be attributed to the contrary nature: that nature is evil. The soul’s sin consists in this: after the warning of our Savior and his sound teaching, the soul separates itself from the contrary and hostile stock and adorns itself with purer things. Otherwise it cannot be restored to its own substance.

For it was said: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin. But now, because I have come and spoken, and they were unwilling to believe me, they will have no pardon for their sin” (John 15:22).

Hence it is clear that repentance was rightly given after the Savior’s coming and after this knowledge of things, by which the soul, as though washed in a divine fountain, may be restored to the kingdom of God—from which it proceeded—after being cleansed from the filth and vices both of the whole world and of the bodies in which that same soul exists.

*[Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads “of the world and of the body,” omitting “whole”; Erasmus instead has “rather” in its place.]*

For it was said by the Apostle that “the mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Romans 8:7). It is therefore clear from these things that the good soul appears to sin through the action of that which is not subject to the law of God, and not of its own accord.

The same argument follows from the statement that “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Galatians 5:17). He says again: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin and death. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death, except the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ?” (Romans 7:23–25). Through him, “the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

22. AUGUSTINE said: I acknowledge and embrace the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, and I shall explain briefly, as God deigns to grant me, how they accord with my faith. I say that freedom of the will existed in that man who was first formed. He was made in such a way that absolutely nothing would resist his will if he wished to keep God’s commandments. But after he himself sinned by free choice, we, who descend from his stock, were plunged into necessity.

Each of us can discover with moderate reflection that what I say is true. Today, in our actions, before we become entangled in any habit, we possess the freedom to do or not to do something. But when by this freedom we have done something, and a destructive sweetness and pleasure in the deed has taken hold of the soul, it becomes so entangled through that very habit that afterward it cannot overcome what it has fashioned for itself by sinning.

We see many people unwilling to swear oaths; but because their tongue has already acquired the habit, they cannot restrain themselves from letting words come out of their mouths which we cannot say do not belong to the stock of evil. To address you in the words which—would that they were understood in your hearts just as they do not depart from your mouths—are these: You swear by the Paraclete.

[Note: [Col. 0125] Here the Vatican manuscript adds: “You cannot say that the nation of darkness swears by the Paraclete concerning us.”]

If, then, you wish to test whether what I say is true, undertake not to swear oaths. You will see that the habit is carried along where it is accustomed to go. And this is what struggles against the soul: the habit formed in the flesh. This is indeed the “wisdom of the flesh,” which, so long as it cannot be subjected to the law of God, remains the wisdom of the flesh; but when the soul has been enlightened, it ceases to be the wisdom of the flesh.

For it was said that the wisdom of the flesh cannot be subjected to the law of God in the same way as one might say that frozen snow cannot be warm. For as long as it is snow, it cannot in any way be warm. But just as that snow is dissolved by heat and ceases to be snow, so that it can become warm, so that wisdom of the flesh—that is, the habit formed together with the flesh—when our mind has been enlightened and God has subjected the whole human being to the authority of the divine law, produces in the soul, in place of the former bad habit, a good habit.

Thus, concerning the two trees—the good tree and the bad tree—which you mentioned, the Lord most truthfully said that they bear their own fruits: that is, that the good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor the bad tree good fruits, so long as it is bad. Let us take two human beings: a good person and a bad person. As long as he is good, he cannot produce bad fruits; as long as he is bad, he cannot produce good fruits.

But so that you may understand that the Lord placed these two trees in such a way that free choice would be signified by them, and that these trees are not two natures but our wills, he himself says in the Gospel: “Either make the tree good, or make the tree bad” (Matt. XII, 33). Who can make a nature? If, then, we are commanded to make the tree either good or bad, it is ours to choose what we wish.

Concerning this sin of the human being, and concerning this habit of the soul formed together with the flesh, the Apostle says: “Let no one deceive you” (Eph. V, 6): “Every creature that has been made by God is good” (I Tim. IV, 4).

[Note: [Col. 0125] In the Vatican manuscript, after “the Apostle says,” there is added: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God.” Concerning the nature of the flesh, the Apostle says elsewhere: “Let no one deceive you.”]

The same Apostle whom you yourself mentioned says: “Just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one many will be constituted righteous” (Rom. V, 19). “For through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead.”

As long, therefore, as we bear the image of the earthly man (I Cor. XV, 21, 49)—that is, as long as we live according to the flesh, and are also called the old man—we are subject to the necessity of our habit, so that we do not do what we wish. But when the grace of God has inspired divine love in us and made us subject to his will—we to whom it was said, “You have been called to freedom” (Gal. V, 13), and, “The grace of God has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. VIII, 2)—then we are liberated.

The law of sin is that whoever has sinned should die. We are freed from this law when we begin to be righteous. The law of death is expressed in the words spoken to the human being: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19). For from him we are all born in this way, because we are earth, and for the merit of the first man’s sin we shall go into earth.

[Note: [Col. 0126] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, have: “For from her human beings are [born].”]

[Note: [Col. 0126] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, have: “For from her human beings are [born].”]

But through the grace of God, which frees us from the law of sin and death, we are converted to righteousness and liberated, so that afterward this very flesh—which afflicted us with punishments while we remained in sins—may in the resurrection be subjected to us, and no adversity may shake us so as to prevent us from keeping the law of God and the divine commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0126] Retractations I, chapter 16, no. 2.]

Since, then, I have answered your questions, please answer this question which I desire answered: How can it be that, if there is a nature contrary to God, sin is imputed to us, although we were sent into that nature not by our will but by God himself, whom nothing could harm?

FORTUNATUS said: In this respect, as the Lord also said to his disciples: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. X, 16). From this it must be understood—

[Note: [Col. 0126] The Vatican manuscript reads: “From this it must be considered.” A little later the same codex has: “which he would place in the likeness of wolves.”]
