—that our Savior did not wish to send his lambs, that is, his disciples, among wolves with an inimical purpose, unless there were some contrariety which he would set down in the likeness of wolves, among which he had sent his disciples; so that whatever souls might be deceived among the wolves could be recalled to their own substance.

From this, then, the antiquity of our ages becomes apparent—the antiquity which we trace back—as well as the antiquity of our years—

[Note: [Col. 0126] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice editions: “of our souls.” M.]

—namely, that before the foundation of the world souls were sent in this manner against the contrary nature, so that by subjecting it through their own suffering, victory might be restored to God.

For the same Apostle said that our struggle was not only against flesh and blood but also against principalities and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness, and against the dominion of darkness (Eph. VI, 12). If, then, evil is found on both sides—

[Note: [Col. 0126] In the manuscripts and in Erasmus: “if they associate with evil.”]

—and wickedness is present, evil is no longer found only in our bodies but throughout the world, where the souls that dwell beneath this heaven are seen to move and to be entangled.

23. AUGUSTINE said: The Lord sent his lambs among wolves—that is, righteous human beings among sinful human beings—for the preaching of the Gospel, at the time when he assumed human nature, through the immeasurable divine Wisdom, in order to call us from sin to righteousness.

But when the Apostle says that our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers and the other things he mentioned, this signifies the devil and his angels. They, like us, fell through sin and became fallen, and obtained earthly things—that is, sinful human beings. As long as we are sinners, we are under their yoke; but when we are righteous, we shall be under the yoke of righteousness. We struggle against them so that, migrating to righteousness, we may be freed from their dominion.

Therefore, please answer me briefly this one question that I ask: Could God be harmed, or could he not? But I ask you to answer: “He could not.”

FORTUNATUS said: He could not be harmed.

24. AUGUSTINE said: Why, then, did he send us here, according to your faith?

FORTUNATUS said: This is my profession of faith: God could not be harmed, and God directed us here. But since this is contrary to you, explain by what reason the soul appeared here, which our God now desires to liberate through commands and through the sending of his own Son.

25. AUGUSTINE said: Since I see that you have been unable to answer my questions and have wished to question me about something, behold, I shall satisfy you—provided that you remember that you have not answered what I asked.

Why the soul is here in the world, entangled in miseries, I have said not merely once but I do not know how many times just a little earlier. The soul sinned, and therefore it is miserable. It received free choice and used free choice as it wished; it fell, was cast out of blessedness, and became entangled in miseries.

For this I recited to you the Apostle’s testimony: “Just as through one human being came death, so through one human being came the resurrection of the dead.” What more do you seek? You answer, then: Since God could not be harmed, why did he send us here?

FORTUNATUS said: The reason must be sought why the soul came here, or why God desires to liberate it from here, since it lives amid evils.

26. AUGUSTINE said: I ask this reason from you: if God could not be harmed, why did he send us here?

FORTUNATUS said: We are asked why, if evil could not harm God, the soul was sent here, or by what reason it was mingled with the world. This is made clear by what the Apostle says: “Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Rom. IX, 20).

If, then, this matter requires an explanation, he should be asked why he directed the soul here, although no necessity compelled him.

[Note: [Col. 0127] The Victorinus manuscripts read: “he should be asked who directed the soul.”]

But if there was a necessity for sending the soul, then there is also a justified will to liberate it.

27. AUGUSTINE said: Is God, then, constrained by necessity?

FORTUNATUS said: That is the point. Do not provoke resentment against what was said. We do not make God subject to necessity; rather, he sent the soul willingly.

28. AUGUSTINE said: Recite what was said above.

And it was recited: “But if there was a necessity for sending the soul, then there is also a justified will to liberate it.”

AUGUSTINE said: We have heard: “If there was a necessity for sending the soul, then there is also a justified will to liberate it.” You therefore said that there was a necessity for sending the soul. But if now you wish to speak of will, I add this:

[Note: [Col. 0127] The Victorinus manuscripts read: “and I add this to it.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “and I hear this.”]

Since nothing could harm God, it was a cruel will that sent the soul into such great miseries.

Because I say this in order to refute the argument, I ask pardon from the mercy of that one in whom we have hope of liberation from all the errors of heretics.

FORTUNATUS said: You assert that we say God was cruel in sending the soul—

[Col. 0128]

—but God made the human being and breathed into him a soul which he certainly foresaw would become entangled in future misery and, through the benefit of evils, would be unable to be restored to his inheritance. This is either the act of one who was ignorant or of one who gave the soul over to the evils mentioned above.

I recalled this because shortly before you said that God adopted the soul for himself, not that it came from him; for to adopt is one thing.

[Note: [Col. 0128] The Vatican codex reads: “and breathed into him.”]

29. AUGUSTINE said: I remember that I spoke some days ago about our adoption, according to the testimony of the Apostle, who says that we were called to the adoption of sons (Eph. I, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0128] The word “days,” which had dropped out of the Louvain edition, is restored from the other printed editions and manuscripts.] That, therefore, was not my own response but the apostolic one.

Concerning this matter—that is, concerning this adoption—let us inquire at the proper time, if you please. And I shall answer concerning it without delay—

[Note: [Col. 0128] The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read: “And I shall answer concerning that breathing.” Perhaps this is because above Fortunatus had said “breathed into him” instead of “insufflated,” as the Vatican codex reads.]

—when you have answered my objections.

FORTUNATUS said: I say that the soul proceeded against the contrary nature, a nature that could not harm God in any way.

30. AUGUSTINE said: What need was there for this proceeding, when God had nothing to fear and nothing could harm him?

FORTUNATUS said: Is it acknowledged in your own conscience that Christ came from God?

31. AUGUSTINE said: Are you questioning me again? Answer the questions put to you.

FORTUNATUS said: I have received this in faith: that he himself came here by the will of God.

32. AUGUSTINE said: And I say: Why did almighty God, inviolable and unchangeable, whom nothing could harm, send the soul here to miseries, to error, and to the things we suffer?

FORTUNATUS said: For it was said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up” (John X, 18). Now he said—

[Note: [Col. 0128] The printed editions read: “he did not say.” The reading of the Victorinus manuscripts, “now he said,” appears preferable. Whether the words belong to Fortunatus or Augustine is uncertain; in the same Victorinus manuscripts Augustine’s name is placed before them: “Now he said that the soul proceeded by the will of God: but I …”]

—that the soul proceeded by the will of God.

33. AUGUSTINE said: But I am asking why, since God could not be harmed—

[Note: [Col. 0128] The Vatican manuscript reads:

“AUGUSTINE said: I ask: Since nothing could harm God, why did he send the soul here?

FORTUNATUS said: I say that it appears that the soul proceeded by the will of God.

AUGUSTINE said: But I am asking why, since nothing could harm God, he sent the soul here.”]

[The manuscript text is lacunose.]

FORTUNATUS said: We have already said that God could not be harmed, and we have said that the soul is in the contrary nature, so that he might impose a limit upon the contrary nature. After imposing a limit upon the contrary nature, God takes the soul up again. For he himself said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up. The Father gave me this power to lay down my soul and to take it up.”

Therefore, the God who was speaking in the Son—of what soul would he have spoken?

[Col. 0129]

It is clear that it is our soul, which is held in these bodies, that came by his will and is again taken up by his will.

34. AUGUSTINE said: Everyone knows why our Lord said, “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up”: because he was going to suffer and rise again.

But I ask you once more and again: If God could not be harmed in any way, why did he send souls here?

FORTUNATUS said: To impose a limit upon the contrary nature.

35. AUGUSTINE said: And did almighty God, merciful and supreme over all, therefore wish that this nature be moderated in such a way as to make us immoderate?

FORTUNATUS said: But he recalls the soul to himself for that very reason.

36. AUGUSTINE said: If he recalls it to himself from immoderation, from sin, from error, and from misery, what need was there for the soul to suffer so many evils for so long a time, until the world should come to an end, when God—from whom you say it was sent—could not be harmed in any way?

[Col. 0130]

FORTUNATUS said: What, then, shall I say?

37. AUGUSTINE said: I know that you have nothing to say, and I also know that, when I listened to you on this question, I never found anything to say. For this reason I was divinely admonished to abandon that error and to convert—or rather, return—to the Catholic faith, through the indulgence of him who did not allow me always to cling to that deceit.

But if you confess that you have no answer, then, with all who are listening and acknowledging the Catholic faith—for they are believers—if they permit and wish it, I shall expound it.

FORTUNATUS said: Without prejudice to my profession of faith, I shall say this: When I have reviewed the objections you have raised with my elders, if they give no answer to this question of mine, which you now similarly present to me, it will be part of my purpose—for I too desire that my soul be liberated by a certain faith—to come to inquire into this matter which you present to me, and which you promise to demonstrate.

AUGUSTINE said: Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0129]

SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK AGAINST ADIMANTUS, A DISCIPLE OF MANICHAEUS

[Note: [Col. 0129] Written around the year 394.]

[Note: [Col. 0129] CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK: See Book I, chapter 22, of the Retractations, vol. 1, col. 618, no. 1, from the words “At the same time”—

[Note: [Col. 0129] Namely, during his presbyterate he composed the following book. In the Retractations he places it somewhat after the sermon On Faith and the Creed delivered at the council of Hippo in the year 393, among the minor works belonging to the years 394 or 395. He also mentions this work against Adimantus at the end of Book II Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, where, after naming Adimantus, a disciple of Manichaeus, he adds: “He was also called Addas by surname.”]

—up to col. 620, no. 4, with the words “Heaven and earth.” M.]

[Note: [Col. 0129] We reviewed this work against two Sorbonne manuscripts, two Victorinus manuscripts, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Corbie, Germanus, Michaelinus, and Casalinus manuscripts; against the variant readings of four Belgian copies; and against the editions of Ambrose, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0129] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the Retractations and Confessions, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

The statements of Scripture concerning the Old and New Testaments are reconciled with one another. Adimantus had collected them as though they were mutually contradictory, arguing that the two Testaments could not come from one and the same God.

CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0129]

Concerning the statement written in Genesis, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” up to the statement, “And evening came to be, and morning came to be, one day” (Gen. I, 1–5).

The most foolish Manichaeans think that this chapter of the Law is opposed to the Gospel. They say that Genesis states that God, by himself, made heaven and earth and light, whereas the Gospel states that the world was fashioned through our Lord Jesus Christ, where it says: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John I, 10).

They are refuted in three ways.

First, when it says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” a Christian understands the Trinity itself, in which not only the Father but also the Son and the Holy Spirit are understood. For we do not believe in three gods but in one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, although the Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit. It would take too long to discuss the unity of the Trinity here.

Second, where it says, “God said, ‘Let it be,’ and it came to be,” it is necessary to understand that he made what he made through the Word. The Word, however, is the Father’s Son. Therefore this passage in Genesis, where it says, “God said, ‘Let it be,’ and it came to be,” does not conflict with the Gospel passage where it says, “The world was made through him”—that is, through our Lord—because he is the Father’s Word through whom all things were made.

Finally, if the Son is not understood in Genesis because it was not said that God made things through the Son, then in the Gospel God would not, through the Son, feed the birds or clothe the lilies (Matt. VI, 26, 30), nor do the innumerable other things which the Lord himself says God the Father does, although he does not say that he does them through the Son.

They also add the Apostle’s testimony concerning our Lord Jesus Christ: “He is the firstborn of all creation, and all things were made through him in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Col. I, 15–16). They say that this passage too is opposed to Genesis, where God is said to have made the world without the Son being specifically named there.

They are greatly mistaken. They do not see that, if this is so, the Apostle himself contradicts himself, since elsewhere he says: “From him, through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36), without naming the Son.

Just as the Son is not named here but is nevertheless understood, so he is understood in Genesis. And just as these two passages of Paul do not conflict with one another, so Genesis does not conflict with the Gospel.

CHAPTER TWO

1. Concerning the statement written in Genesis: “And God completed on the sixth day all his works which he had made, and on the seventh day he rested from all his works which he had made” (Gen. II, 2).

The Manichaeans also bring an accusation against this passage. They say that what is written in Genesis—that God rested on the seventh day from all the works he had made—is opposed to the New Testament, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now” (John V, 17).

This is in no way contradictory. The Lord is refuting the error of the Jews, who thought that God had rested on the seventh day in such a way that from then on he did absolutely nothing. He rested from all the works he had made so that he would no longer make the world together with everything in it, but not so that he would also cease administering the world.

For it is not written: “God rested from all his works so that from then on he would not work.” Rather, it is written: “God rested from all his works which he had made,” so that afterward he would work not in making the world—a work from which he had ceased after its completion—but in administering it, which is the work in which the Lord indicated that he is engaged.

Nor does that rest signify that God, as though after labor, sought a pause. It signifies that after perfecting the natures of things he ceased establishing them, although he continues to work in their administration.

2. The Jews did not understand the observances of the Sabbath. They thought that one ought to cease even from works that benefit human salvation. For this reason the Lord also rebuked them elsewhere, with a remarkable comparison, concerning an ox that had fallen into a pit and an animal that must be untied in order to be led to water (Luke XIV, 5, and XIII, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0131] The manuscripts read: “a sheep which.”]

The Sabbath, however, was not rejected but understood by Christians. It ceased to be observed carnally, but it is retained spiritually by the saints, who understand the voice of the Lord calling them to rest and saying:

“Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 28–30).

This Sabbath—that is, this rest—is signified by that Scripture which the Jews did not understand. In accordance with the unfolding of the times they followed its shadow carnally, whereas its body, that is, its truth, was to be given to us.

But just as God’s rest is signified after the world was fashioned, so we shall obtain the rest promised to us after the works we have in this world, if those works have been righteous—namely, in the seventh and final period of the age. To discuss this would take too long.

The Lord, therefore, does not abolish the writing of the Old Testament but compels it to be understood. He does not dissolve the Sabbath so that what it signified may perish; rather, he opens it so that what was concealed may appear.

CHAPTER THREE

1. Concerning the statement written in Genesis: “And God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make a helper for him.’ And God cast a sleep upon Adam, and he fell asleep; and he took one of his ribs, from which he formed Eve, whom he brought to Adam. And he said, ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife’” (Gen. II, 18–24).

The Manichaeans again bring an accusation against this passage. They say that the statement is opposed to the New Testament, since God is said both to have formed a woman and to have joined her to a man. They say this because the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who has left a house, or a wife, or parents, or brothers, or children for the sake of the kingdom of heaven will receive a hundredfold in this age, and in the age to come will possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX, 29; Mark X, 29–30; Luke XVIII, 29–30).

[Note: [Col. 0132] The manuscripts read: “will receive sevenfold.” Augustine commonly cites it thus.]

In making this accusation I am amazed that they are so blinded—or rather, I am not amazed: “Their wickedness blinded them,” as it is written (Wis. II, 21). Nevertheless, who does not see how many commands the New Testament contains concerning love for one’s wife?

Why do they say that the Old Testament is opposed to this statement of the Lord, in which he says that a wife must be left for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, rather than saying that the New Testament itself is opposed to itself? It is wicked to say this. What seem contradictory to the inexperienced must be understood, not rashly accused.

2. When the Jews asked the Lord whether it was permissible for a man, after giving his wife a certificate of divorce, to dismiss her, he answered them:

“Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’? Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

[Note: [Col. 0132] “Together” is absent from several manuscripts.]

They said to him: “Why, then, did Moses command that a certificate of divorce be given and that she be dismissed?”

Jesus said to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. But I say to you: Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and if he marries another, he commits adultery” (Matt. XIX, 3–9).

Behold, the Lord himself confirms the statement of the Old Testament against the ignorance of the Jews. At the same time, he bears witness to Moses, saying that Moses permitted divorce because of their hardness of heart.

Do they also say that the Gospel is opposed to the Gospel? If they say that this passage is false and was added by corrupters of the Scriptures—for they customarily say this whenever they cannot find an answer—what if someone else were to say that the passage they themselves produce, in which the Lord says, “Everyone who has left a house, or a wife, or parents, or children for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth, was inserted and is false?

In their misery they do not understand how, by saying such things, they attempt to overthrow the whole Christian faith. But the true faith and the discipline of the Catholic Church affirm that both statements are true and were spoken by the Lord, and that they are in no way contradictory. For the union of husband and wife comes from the Lord, and the abandonment of a wife for the sake of the kingdom of heaven also comes from the Lord.

It is not because Jesus Christ raised the dead and gave them life that this life must not be abandoned for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Thus, although the Lord gave a wife to a man, she must nevertheless be left, if necessary, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

This is not always necessary, as the Apostle says: “If a believer has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to dwell with him, he should not dismiss her” (I Cor. VII, 12). He clearly signifies that if she does not consent to dwell with him—that is, if she rejects the faith of Christ in him and does not tolerate him because he is a Christian—she must be left for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

As the same Apostle says in what follows: “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. A brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such circumstances.” If, then, someone abandons the kingdom of heaven because he is unwilling to abandon a wife who cannot tolerate a Christian husband, he is disapproved by the Lord.

Likewise, if a husband dismisses his wife by giving her a certificate of divorce when there is no cause either of fornication or of attaining the kingdom of heaven, he is similarly disapproved by the Lord.

Thus neither are these two Gospel passages found to be contradictory to one another, nor is the Gospel contradictory to the Old Testament. There, a wife is joined to a husband so that together they may deserve to possess the kingdom of heaven; and likewise the wife is commanded to be left if she hinders the husband from possessing the kingdom of heaven.

3. For this reason, when the Apostle gives instructions to Christians of both sexes, that is, to husbands and wives, does he not say: “Love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her”? And: “Let women be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the Church also is subject to Christ.”

Does not the same Apostle accept as a great mystery what these miserable people ridicule in the Old Testament—what is written, “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh”—when he says: “This mystery is great, but I am speaking of Christ and the Church”?

[Col. 0134]

Then he adds: “Nevertheless, let each man love his wife as himself, and let the woman fear her husband” (Eph. V, 25, 22, 31, 32, 33).

Does he not show elsewhere with the utmost clarity that the nature and union of both sexes exist by the Lord God, their creator and orderer, when he says: “Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman, in the Lord. For just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman; but all things are from God” (I Cor. XI, 11–12)?

If these people wished to consider this, they would not create darkness for the inexperienced by fraudulently setting certain passages apart and opposing them to one another. They would recognize that everything in both the Old and the New Testament was written and commended by one Holy Spirit.

4. For in the Old Testament, in the prophet Isaiah, they also find how much is promised to eunuchs, so that they may not think that eunuchs are praised by the Lord only in the New Testament, where he says that there are some who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and adds: “Let whoever is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12).

Isaiah says:

“Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my commandments, choose for themselves the things that I desire, and are capable of my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place of renown, much better than sons and daughters. I will give them an eternal name, and it shall never fail” (Isa. LVI, 4–5).

Before the Lord’s coming, that people who received the Old Testament was held by certain shadows and figures of realities, in accordance with the marvelous and perfectly ordered distribution of the times. Nevertheless, it contains so much proclamation and foretelling of the New Testament that no commands or promises are found in the Gospel and apostolic discipline—however demanding and divine they may be—that are lacking also in those ancient books.

[Note: [Col. 0134] Retractations I, chapter 22, no. 2.]

But the holy Scriptures desire not rash and arrogant accusers, but diligent and devout readers.

CHAPTER FOUR

Concerning the statement written in Genesis:

“And the Lord said to Cain, ‘What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth. Now you shall be cursed from the face of the earth, which has absorbed and received your brother’s blood from the slaughter by your hand. For you must work the earth, which will give you sterile fruits’” (Gen. IV, 10–12).

The Manichaeans bring an accusation against this passage of Genesis, in which Cain received a curse so that he would be punished by the sterility of the earth, and they wish to demonstrate that it is opposed to the Gospel. They do not seem to think that they are dealing with human beings, but altogether as though those who heard them or read their writings were cattle. Thus they abused their ignorance and dullness of understanding—or rather, the blindness of their minds.

For they said that this passage is contradicted by the Gospel passage in which the Lord says to his disciples: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Look at the birds of the sky, because they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns” (Matt. VI, 34, 26).

As though Cain the parricide—

[Note: [Col. 0134] Only one of the Vatican manuscripts reads “fratricide.”]

—were to be compared with Christ’s disciples, so that because he deserved the punishment of a sterile earth, it would follow that those too should suffer the same sterility who, having followed the Lord Jesus Christ, were preparing themselves to preach the Gospel.

Indeed, in these two passages, one from Genesis and the other from the Gospel, which they have set down as though hostile to each other, such friendship and harmony are found that no greater could be desired.

What could be more fitting than that the one whose crime caused his brother to be killed should also be followed by sterility while working the earth, whereas the earth should serve fruitfully those through whose ministry brothers were being liberated by the preaching of God’s word, even though they gave no thought to tomorrow?

If they shudder in the Old Testament at the earth being made sterile for a sinner by God’s curse, why do they not shudder in the New Testament at the fig tree being made dry by the curse of our Lord Jesus Christ (Matt. XXI, 19), although its owner had committed no sin?

Likewise, if they delight in the Lord’s pronouncement by which he tells his disciples not to think about tomorrow, because God cares for their sustenance, why do they not also delight in the prophetic pronouncement in which he sang:

“Cast your anxiety upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. LIV, 23)?

In this way, if they are able, these miserable people may understand that the things said about God in the Old Testament which they detest are so entirely right that they are also found in the New Testament, and that the things they praise and proclaim in the New Testament are also found in the Old.

Thus the manifest concord of both Testaments becomes clear to those who understand them rightly.

CHAPTER FIVE
## 1. Concerning the passage written in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26)

The Manichaeans say that this passage in Genesis, where it is written that man was made in the image and likeness of God, is contrary to the New Testament because the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him” (John 8:44); and because elsewhere the Jews are called “offspring of serpents and vipers” (Matthew 3:7; 23:33).

They do not understand that the former statement was spoken of man before he sinned, when he was made in the image and likeness of God, whereas the Gospel statement, “You are from your father the devil,” is addressed to sinners and unbelievers. In the Holy Scriptures the name “sons” is understood in three ways.[^c0013-1] First, according to nature, as Isaac is the son of Abraham, or as the other Jews are sons of Abraham because they come from the same ancestry. Second, according to instruction, so that each person is called someone’s son in relation to the one from whom he has learned something; thus the Apostle calls those who learned the Gospel from him his sons (1 Corinthians 4:14–15). Third, according to imitation, as the Apostle calls us sons of Abraham because we imitate his faith (Galatians 3:7).

Accordingly, the sinful and unbelieving Jews are called by the Lord sons of the devil in two ways: either because they learned ungodliness from him, as the Apostle says of the devil himself, “who now works in the sons of disobedience” (Ephesians 2:2); or because they imitate him. The latter more directly applies to what was said of him: “He did not stand in the truth,” for the Jews themselves did not stand in the truth of the Law that had been given to them. The Lord bears witness to this when he says: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). According to the venom of these same sins, they are also called offspring of serpents and vipers.

## 2. Concerning man’s being made in the image of God

Not Genesis alone, but the Apostle also proclaims that man was made in the image of God, when he says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, whereas woman is the glory of man” (1 Corinthians 11:7).

And so that it may clearly be understood that man was made in God’s image not according to the oldness of sin, which is corrupted, but according to spiritual formation, the same Apostle urges us, after stripping off our sinful practices—that is, the old man—to put on the new life of Christ, whom he calls the new man. To teach that we had once lost this condition, he calls it renewal. For he says:

“Having stripped off the old man with his practices, put on the new man, who is being renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of his Creator” (Colossians 3:9–10).

Those who have been renewed according to his image are therefore sons of God, made like him even to the point of loving their enemies, just as the Lord says that we must love our enemies in order to be like our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:44–45). Scripture teaches that this has been placed within our power by God himself when it says: “He gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12).

People are called sons of the devil when they imitate his ungodly pride, fall away from the light and height of wisdom, and do not believe the truth. The Lord rebukes such people when he says: “You are from your father the devil,” and so forth. To this Gospel passage the prophet also bears witness when he says:

“I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’; but you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Psalm 81:6–7).

# CHAPTER VI

## Concerning the passage written in Exodus: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12)

The Manichaeans say that this passage, in which God commands that parents be honored, is contradicted by the Gospel passage in which the Lord replies to a man who said, “I will go first and bury my father”: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, come and proclaim the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:59–60).[^c0013-2]

This is resolved in the same way as the earlier matter concerning the abandonment of one’s wife “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven”: we must honor our parents, yet we do not impiously despise them when proclaiming the kingdom of God. For if the Gospel is contrary to the Old Testament because of this statement, then it also becomes contrary to the Apostle, who both urges children to honor their parents and parents to love their children (Ephesians 6:2–4; Colossians 3:20–21).

Moreover, the Lord himself would appear to be contrary to himself—which it is impious to believe—for elsewhere, when a man asks him about eternal life, he says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” Among these he also mentions: “Honor your father and your mother.” Once these commandments have been fulfilled, one advances to the love of God, in which all perfection consists. Love of neighbor is a sure step toward love of God.

Therefore, when the man replies that he has kept all those commandments, the Lord tells him that one thing is still lacking if he wishes to be perfect: he must sell everything he possesses, give it to the poor, and follow him (Matthew 19:17–21). From this it is clear that the honor due to parents must be maintained in its proper place, yet in comparison with divine love—especially if parents are an impediment—they must undoubtedly be disregarded.

In the ancient Scriptures also you find the following:

“He who says to his father or mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and does not acknowledge his sons, he himself has acknowledged your covenant” (Deuteronomy 33:9).

Thus, if love of parents is commended in the New Testament and disregard of parents is commended in the Old, the two Testaments agree with each other from both sides.

# CHAPTER VII

## 1. Concerning the passage written in Exodus: “I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of the parents upon their children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me” (Exodus 20:5)

The Manichaeans say that this passage is contradicted by the Gospel statement in which the Lord says: “Be kind, as your heavenly Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matthew 5:45); and by the other statement in which the same Lord says that one must forgive a sinning brother not merely seven times, but seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22).

Yet if I ask them whether God does not punish his enemies, they will undoubtedly be confounded. They themselves say that God prepares an eternal prison for the nation of darkness, which they call God’s enemy. More than that, they do not hesitate to say that he will punish his own members together with that nation.

But when they come to the passages of the Old and New Testaments, in order to deceive the uninstructed and accuse the Testaments of contradicting each other, they pretend to be exceedingly good. Let them tell us, then, what they will say about those to whom the Lord will say: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41), if he spares everyone and condemns no one.

We must therefore understand that the statement that God repays the sins of parents upon children who hate him is also just. From the addition “who hate me,” it is understood that those are punished for their parents’ sins who have chosen to persist in the same perversity as their parents. Such people are punished not by cruelty but rather by God’s justice and by their own iniquity, as the prophet says:

“For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding, and he will be rebuked by the iniquity that overtakes him” (Wisdom 1:5);

that is, a person will be rebuked by the iniquity that overtakes him when the Holy Spirit has departed from him.

And elsewhere:

“They thought these things and went astray, for their wickedness blinded them” (Wisdom 2:21).

And elsewhere:

“Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs 5:22).

To these testimonies from the Old Testament the Apostle bears witness in agreement with the New when he says: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts” (Romans 1:24). The harmony of the two Testaments sufficiently shows that God is not cruel, but that each person acts cruelly toward himself by sinning.

## 2. Concerning the third and fourth generations

As for the statement that vengeance extends to the third and fourth generation, I believe that it signifies nothing other than this: beginning with Abraham, who became the father of the Jewish people, there are four ages, including the present one, which the evangelist Matthew distinguishes (Matthew 1:17).

The first extends from Abraham to David; the second from David to the deportation to Babylon; the third from the deportation to Babylon to the Lord’s coming; and from that point to the end the fourth is reckoned, like the old age of the world, longer than the other ages.

We believe that these ages are represented by “generations,” although each consists of many individual generations. Since the third begins with the Babylonian deportation, when the captivity of the Jews occurred, while in the fourth—namely, after the coming of our Lord—the Jewish nation was completely uprooted from its own land, this is what is meant by the statement that God will repay the sins of parents upon the third and fourth generation: specifically upon those who, persisting in their parents’ sins, preferred to hold fast to them rather than follow God’s justice.

That the sins of a father do not affect a son who lives justly is shown most explicitly by the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 18:14–17).

## 3. Concerning the statement, “Be kind as your heavenly Father”

The Gospel statement, “Be kind as your heavenly Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil,” is not contrary to the Old Testament. God does this in order to invite people to repentance, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that God’s patience is inviting you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4).

Nevertheless, we must not for that reason believe that God will not punish those who, as the same Apostle says, “are storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works” (Romans 2:5–6).

The prophet also proclaims this patience and goodness of God when he says:

“You spare all things, because they are yours, O Lord, lover of souls” (Wisdom 11:27).

There are countless other passages by which it is understood that both Testaments proclaim the mercy and justice of God both in his goodness and in his severity.

## 4. Concerning the statement, “I am jealous”

If they are disturbed by the statement, “I am jealous,” let them also be disturbed by the Apostle Paul’s statement: “I am jealous for you with God’s jealousy, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

For Holy Scripture, speaking in human words, demonstrates even through such expressions that nothing can be said worthily of God. Why should these words not also be spoken of that majesty of which whatever is said is said inadequately, since it surpasses all the resources of every language by an ineffable sublimity?

Since husbands ordinarily guard the chastity of their wives through jealousy, Scripture has called God’s power and discipline—by which he does not allow the soul to commit fornication with impunity—God’s jealousy. The fornication of the soul is its turning away from the fruitfulness of wisdom and its conversion toward the conception of temporal enticements and corruptions.

## 5. Concerning forgiveness

When the Lord says that a brother must be forgiven not merely seven times but seventy-seven times, he is speaking of one who repents. God says that he repays the sins of those who hate him, not of those who are reconciled to him through repentance.

The Lord also says through the prophet:

“I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn back and live” (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11).

From this it is easily evident that the two Testaments agree and correspond in God’s patience, which invites repentance; in his forgiveness, which pardons the repentant; and in his justice, which punishes those who refuse correction—as though both had been written by one God.

# CHAPTER VIII

## Concerning the passage written in Exodus: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exodus 21:24), and other similar passages

The Manichaeans slander this passage because the ancient Law permits equal retaliation and says that an eye is to be lost for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, as though the Lord himself had displayed these two teachings in the Gospel as mutually opposed and contradictory.

For he says:

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist evil; rather, if someone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also; and whoever wishes to bring you to court and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:38–40).

These two statements do indeed display a difference between the two Testaments, yet both were established by one God. Since carnal people at first burned with a desire to avenge themselves far more severely than the injury they had suffered, a first step toward gentleness was prescribed for them: the pain of the avenger was in no way to exceed the measure of the injury received.

Thus someone could eventually learn to forgive an injury, if he had first learned not to exceed it. Therefore the Lord, already leading the people through the grace of the Gospel toward complete peace, built another stage upon this one: those who had already learned not to return a greater vengeance than the injury they had suffered would rejoice, with a pacified mind, to forgive everything.

The prophet also proclaims this in those ancient books when he says:

“O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Psalm 7:4–5).

Another prophet speaks of a man who patiently suffers injuries and endures them with the greatest gentleness:

“He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3:30).

From this it is understood both that a measure of retaliation was rightly established for carnal people and that complete forgiveness of injury was not only commanded in the New Testament but announced long beforehand in the Old.

# CHAPTER IX

## 1. Concerning the passages in which God is said to have spoken with Adam and Eve, the serpent, Cain, and the other ancients

In many passages of Scripture God is said to have spoken with human beings and to have appeared to some of them—not only to Adam and Eve, the serpent, Cain, and the others mentioned in Genesis 3, 4, and 13, and elsewhere. The Manichaeans attack these passages and say that they are all contrary to the New Testament, because the Lord says:

“No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has proclaimed him to us” (John 1:18);

and again, speaking to the Jews:

“You have neither ever heard his voice nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you did not believe the one whom he sent” (John 5:37–38).

We answer that the Gospel statement itself—“No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has proclaimed him to us”—can resolve the entire question. For the Son himself, who is the Word of God, proclaimed the Father to whomever he wished not only in the last times, when he graciously appeared in the flesh, but also earlier, from the foundation of the world, whether by speaking, by appearing, through some angelic power, or through any creature.

He himself is the truth in all things; all things subsist in him, and all things serve him and are subject to him at his command. Thus he can also appear to the eyes through a visible creature whenever and to whomever he graciously wills. Yet according to his divinity and according to his being the Word of the Father, coeternal with the Father and unchangeable, through whom all things were made, he is seen only by the purest and simplest heart.

For this reason Scripture itself testifies in certain passages that an angel was seen where it says that God was seen (Genesis 18:1–2). Thus, in Jacob’s wrestling, the one who appeared is called an angel (Genesis 32:24–30). Likewise, when he appeared in the bush to Moses (Exodus 3:2), and again in the wilderness, after he had brought the people out of the land of Egypt, when Moses received the Law and God spoke to him (Exodus 19:3), Stephen in the Acts of the Apostles says that an angel appeared to him, both in the bush and later when he was sent and given the Law (Acts 7:30, 35).

We say this so that no one may suppose that the Word of God, through whom all things were made, can be confined to particular places or appear visibly except through some visible creature. Just as the Word of God is in the prophet, and it is rightly said, “The Lord said,” because the Word of God, who is Christ, speaks the truth in the prophet, so he himself speaks in an angel when the angel announces the truth. It is rightly said, “God said” and “God appeared”; and it is likewise rightly said, “The angel said” and “The angel appeared”: the former is spoken from the person of the indwelling God, the latter from the person of the serving creature.

Following this rule, the Apostle also says:

“Do you wish to receive proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

## 2. Concerning God’s speaking even to sinners

If it troubles them that in the Old Testament God also speaks to sinners—to Adam, Eve, or the serpent—let them consider what kind of example the Lord gave in the New Testament concerning a foolish and greedy man, and how the Lord spoke to him when he said:

“Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12:20).

When truth is spoken even to sinners, through whatever creature it may be spoken, it is spoken only by the one who alone is truthful.

As for what he says to the Jews—“You have never heard his voice”—he says this because those to whom he was speaking did not obey. He also says to them, “You have not seen his form,” because they were unable to do so. And when he says, “You do not have his word abiding in you,” this is because Christ remains in the one in whom the word of God remains, whereas they had rejected him.

For when the Lord himself had said, “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed,” a voice sounded from heaven: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him” (John 12:28; 17:5). Many of the Jews who were present heard this voice, yet they are not for that reason said to have heard it, because they did not obey by believing.

Therefore, if it is not surprising that the Word of God—that is, the only-begotten Son of God, who proclaims the Father—is manifested to whomever he wishes, either by himself or through some creature, by sounding or appearing, while he himself and the Father are seen by the pure in heart—for “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8)—then it is not surprising that all these testimonies from both Testaments harmonize.

# CHAPTER X

## Concerning the passage in which God is said to have spoken to Moses and commanded him to say to the children of Israel:

“Take offerings from every person, whatever you dedicate to me: gold, silver, bronze, purple, fine linen, scarlet, goats’ hair, red-dyed rams’ skins, unrottable wood, oil for illumination, spices for incense, precious stones—that is, beryls—and establish a tabernacle in which I may dwell among you” (Exodus 25:2–8).

The Manichaeans also raise a question from this passage and say that it is contradicted by the Gospel statement in which the Lord says:

“You shall not swear, either by heaven, because it is the throne of God, or by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet” (Matthew 5:34–35).

They argue and think they are saying something important when they ask: “How can that God, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, dwell in a tabernacle constructed from gold, silver, bronze, purple, and the hair and skins of animals?”

They also bring forward the Apostle Paul as a witness, because he says that God dwells in inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16).

We respond to them with an equivalent question, and we produce from the Old Testament what they have produced from the New. For there it is written first:

“Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, or what place will be my rest? Has not my hand made all these things?” (Isaiah 66:1–2).

There they have passages in which the books of the Old Testament proclaim that God does not dwell in temples made by human hands. Yet the Son of our God, having made a whip from cords, drove from the temple those who were selling oxen and doves, overturned the tables of the money-changers, and said:

“My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers” (John 2:15–16; Matthew 21:12–13).

If, therefore, someone were to set these two passages against each other in order to deceive the uninstructed and say that in the Old Testament God is magnified as the one whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth, and who is said not to dwell in a house made by human hands, whereas in the New Testament his house is called a temple constructed by human beings, would not the Manichaeans eventually be compelled to admit that the dwelling of God made by human hands is understood symbolically in both Testaments, and that both Testaments proclaim that God does not dwell in places built by human beings?

# CHAPTER XI

## Concerning the passage written in Exodus: “You shall not worship foreign gods,” and the statement that your God is called jealous—“for he is exceedingly jealous” (Exodus 20:5; 34:14)

When the Manichaeans attack the statement written in this chapter, “You shall not worship foreign gods,” they plainly show that they themselves approve of the worship of many gods. This is not surprising, since in their sect they enumerate and commend a very large family of gods—indeed, since they themselves have even descended to these visible things, which they venerate and worship in place of the light of that truth. This is why they dislike the statement written in Exodus: “You shall not worship foreign gods.”

They add that the statement “Your God is called jealous; for he is exceedingly jealous” was spoken for this reason: so that we would not love a jealous God, whose jealousy prevents us from worshiping foreign gods. They therefore say that these statements are contrary to the Gospel, because the Lord says:

“Righteous Father, and the world did not know you” (John 17:25).[^c0013-3]

It is as though God could not be called righteous unless he allowed us to worship foreign gods.

They argue that a righteous God and a jealous God are mutually opposed, and they deceive the wretched because they do not understand that all our hope of salvation consists in God’s jealousy. By this name Scripture signifies that aspect of his providence by which he does not allow any soul to commit fornication against him with impunity, as the prophet says:

“You will destroy all who commit fornication away from you” (Psalm 72:27).

Just as what is called God’s anger is not a disturbance of mind but the power of vengeance, so God’s jealousy is not the torment of spirit by which a husband is accustomed to be distressed against his wife, or a wife against her husband. Rather, it is the most tranquil and sincere justice by which no soul is permitted to be blessed while corrupted and, as it were, impregnated by false opinions and perverse desires.[^c0013-4]

Those who recoil from these expressions have not yet understood that no words are adequate to the ineffable majesty. They think that one ought to abstain from such language, as though those who do not use it are saying something worthy of God.

The Holy Spirit, insinuating this very point to those who understand, wished to show how ineffable the highest divine realities are by using even words that among human beings are ordinarily regarded as faults. In this way people might be warned that even those things they think they can say of God with some dignity are unworthy of his majesty, to whom honorable silence is more fitting than any human speech.

I inquire into human jealousy and find a distressing disturbance of the heart. Yet when I inquire into its cause, I find nothing other than that the jealous person cannot endure the adultery of a spouse. Jealousy is most especially and properly spoken of in relation to marriage.

Therefore, if a husband were in himself blessed, omnipotent, and just, he would punish a spouse’s sin without any distress, with complete ease, and without any injustice. Even so, in the human manner of speaking, I would call such an action jealousy—not literally, but metaphorically and correctly.

Who has ever reproached Cicero, who certainly knew how to speak Latin, when he said to Caesar: “None of your virtues is either more admirable or more welcome than mercy” (*For Quintus Ligarius*, at the end)? Yet they say that mercy is so called because it makes the heart of one who suffers from another’s misery miserable.

Does virtue, then, make the heart miserable? What would Cicero have replied to those who quibble, except that by the word “mercy” he intended to name clemency? For we rightly use not only proper words but also related ones.

I wished to mention this author because the question here concerns not the matter itself but the word. Our authors—the authors, that is, of the divine Scriptures—thought chiefly about realities, whereas almost all the concern of secular authors is with words.

But I have the Gospel and all the books of the New Testament, in which God’s mercy is very frequently commended. If these wretched people dare, let them raise the same question from those books and deny that God is merciful, lest he be understood to have a miserable heart.

Therefore, just as there can be mercy in God without misery of heart, so we should not hesitate to accept God’s jealousy without any corruption or torment of spirit. Let us tolerate the limitations of human speech in order to arrive at divine silence.

But if they say that a jealous God and a just God are contradictory, what will they say when I find in the New Testament: “I am jealous for you with God’s jealousy” (2 Corinthians 11:2), and when the Gospel also applies a testimony from the ancient writings:

“Zeal for your house has consumed me” (John 2:17; Psalm 68:10)?

Again, when in the Old Testament they read:

“The Lord is righteous, and he has loved righteousness; his face has looked upon equity” (Psalm 10:8),

will they not admit that in this way as well the two Testaments could appear contrary to the uninstructed, so that in the New Testament we find God’s jealousy and in the Old Testament God’s justice? Yet to those who understand rightly, both are harmonized in both Testaments by the great unity and peace of the Holy Spirit.

# CHAPTER XII

## 1. Concerning the command that blood must not be eaten, because “the blood of the flesh is its soul” (Deuteronomy 12:23)

The Manichaeans oppose this statement of the ancient Law with the Gospel passage in which the Lord says that one must not fear those who kill the body but cannot harm the soul (Matthew 10:28). They argue:

“If blood is the soul, how can human beings have no power over it, when they do so much with blood—whether they collect it and offer it as food to dogs and birds, or pour it out, or mix it with mud and clay? Human beings can do these and countless other things with blood without difficulty.”

Thus they mockingly ask how, if blood is the soul, a person’s killer cannot harm the soul, when he has such power over the person’s blood.

They also add the Apostle Paul’s statement: “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). They say: “If blood is the soul, as Moses says, then no soul will be found capable of attaining the kingdom of God.”

This slander must first be answered by compelling them to show where it is written in the books of the ancient Law that the human soul is blood. They will nowhere find this in the Scripture which, although they persist in attacking it, the wretched are in no way permitted to understand.

If nothing of this kind is said there about the human soul, what does it matter to us whether the soul of an animal can be harmed by its killer or cannot possess the kingdom of God? But since these people are excessively concerned about the souls of animals—for although they acknowledge human souls to be rational, they nevertheless suppose that those souls are transferred into animals—they think that the heavenly kingdoms are closed to them if they agree that they are closed to the souls of animals.

## 2. Adimantus’s attack on Israel

What of the fact that Adimantus, one of the disciples of the Manichaeans, dared to insult the people of Israel? They report that he was a great teacher of that sect.

He dared, then, to insult the Jewish people because, according to their interpretation—in which they believe that blood is the soul—the souls of their ancestors were partly devoured by serpents, partly consumed by fire, and partly dried out in deserts and in the most rugged places of the mountains.

Even if someone granted that this was true, he would nevertheless prove that it occurred without guilt on the part of those whom Adimantus wished to insult. For they themselves did not harm in any way the souls of their ancestors, whom he said had suffered all those things according to their interpretation. Therefore they may have grief because of it, but not guilt.

What, then, will Adimantus himself do according to his own belief, by which he held that even rational souls—that is, human souls—can be forced into the bodies of beasts? What will he do about such a great crime if he has beaten a sluggish beast with blows or exhausted a spirited one with the bridle, when perhaps the soul of his father was in it?

I say nothing of the possibility that he might even have killed his parents among lice and fleas, from whose destruction these people do not abstain. What benefit is it to them that they sometimes deny that human souls are transferred into creatures as tiny as these? They deny it so that they will not be held guilty of so many killings, or be compelled to spare lice, fleas, and bedbugs, and to endure such great annoyances from them without permission to kill them.

For they are hard pressed to explain why a human soul can be transferred into a fox cub but cannot be transferred into a weasel, when a fox cub may perhaps be smaller than a large weasel. Then, if it can enter a weasel, why can it not enter a mouse? And if it can enter a mouse, why can it not enter a gecko? And if it can enter a gecko, why can it not enter a locust? Then into a bee, then a fly, then a bedbug, and from there even into a flea, and into anything else that may be much smaller?

I cannot find where they establish a limit. Thus, through this foolish credulity,[^c0013-5] their consciences are overwhelmed by innumerable crimes of homicide.

## 3. The command as a sign

From the statement that the blood of an animal is its soul, apart from what I said above—that what happens to the soul of an animal does not concern me—I can also interpret that command as having been given symbolically.

For the Lord did not hesitate to say, “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26), when he was giving the sign of his body.

## 4. Concerning flesh, blood, and the resurrection

As for the Apostle’s statement, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” the Law also says:

“My spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3).

And throughout the ancient books a future reward is promised to the souls of the righteous.

Nevertheless, because the Apostle wished to indicate what the bodies of the righteous would be like through the transformation that will occur in the resurrection—since “they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30)—he therefore wished to indicate the future transformation of the bodies of the saints when he said:

“I tell you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.”

This cannot be understood by isolating one sentence and maliciously citing it, but by considering—or rather reading—the whole passage of the Epistle, for the matter is not obscure.

He says:

“This corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.”

That he is speaking about the body is made clear from what precedes, when he says:

“Not every flesh is the same flesh: one kind belongs to human beings, another to animals, another to birds, and another to fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of heavenly bodies is one thing and that of earthly bodies another. The glory of the sun is one thing, the glory of the moon another, and the glory of the stars another. For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead.

“It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body, as it is written: ‘The first man, Adam, was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a life-giving spirit.’ But the spiritual does not come first; rather, the animal, and afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven.

“Now this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor can corruption inherit incorruption.”

It is now certainly clear why the Apostle said this. What, then, does that man omit through such shameful deception except this final statement, while keeping silent about the preceding statements by which what he misinterprets could be properly understood?

Because the body of our Lord was raised into heaven after the resurrection in such a way that, for its heavenly dwelling, it received a heavenly transformation—and because we have been commanded to hope for this on the last day—the Apostle therefore said:

“As was the earthly, so are the earthly,” that is, mortal; “and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly,” that is, immortal—not only in soul but also in body.

That is why he had said above that the glory of heavenly bodies is one thing and the glory of earthly bodies another.

When he said that the body in the resurrection would be spiritual, we must not therefore suppose that it will not be a body but a spirit. Rather, he calls it a spiritual body because it will be entirely subject to the spirit, without any corruption or death.

For just as he now calls the body we possess an animal body because it is subject to the soul, we must not on that account suppose that it is not a body but a soul. Thus, just as it is now called an animal body because it is subject to the soul, but cannot yet be called spiritual because it is not yet completely subject to the spirit so long as it can be corrupted, so then it will be called spiritual when it can offer no resistance to the spirit and eternity through any corruption whatsoever.

5. Or, if it still seems insufficiently demonstrated that the Apostle uttered this statement on account of the transformation that is to come, when he says, “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor can corruption inherit incorruption,” attend to what he immediately adds:

“Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed, in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

Then he continues and says also what I mentioned a little earlier, to show what this transformation itself will be like. For he immediately says: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:39–53).

From this it is therefore evident that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, because, when it has put on incorruption and immortality, it will no longer be flesh and blood [Note: [Col. 0146] *Retract.*, chap. 22, no. 3.], but will be changed into a heavenly body.

We have treated this matter incidentally, because they also habitually plot at length against this statement, denying the resurrection of bodies. For the present question concerns not the body but the soul, which they think is to be understood in the Law as blood. We, however, understand it in no way in that manner. Yet although we have no concern for the souls of animals, with which we share no fellowship of reason, we nevertheless say that what the Law stated—that blood must be poured out and must not be taken as food, because blood is the soul—was established like many other things; and nearly all the sacraments of those Scriptures are filled with signs and figures of the preaching that was to come, which has now been made manifest through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus blood is the soul in the same way that the rock was Christ, as the Apostle says: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed [Note: [Col. 0146] The printed editions read, “that followed them.” The word “them” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.], and the rock was Christ” (ibid. 10:4).

Now it is well known that the children of Israel drank water in the wilderness after the rock had been struck (Num. 20:11); the Apostle was speaking of them when he said this. Yet he did not say, “The rock signified Christ,” but, “The rock was Christ.” And again, so that this might not be understood carnally, he calls that rock spiritual—that is, he teaches that it is to be understood spiritually.

It would be a lengthy undertaking, and not necessary at present, to explain the sacraments of that same Law, except insofar as they can be treated briefly. It is enough that those who bring accusations against these things should know that we do not understand them in the way they habitually ridicule them, but in the way the Apostles, understanding everything, explained a few matters and left the rest to be understood by later generations according to the same principles.

# CHAPTER XIII

## 1

Concerning what is written in Deuteronomy: “Take care lest you forget the covenant of your God which he wrote down, and make for yourselves carved figures and images”; he adds these words as well: “Your God is a consuming fire, and a jealous God” (Deut. 4:23–24).

Adimantus proposed these words from the Scriptures in this way. We have undertaken to refute and disprove his accusations. But earlier also, when he was bringing accusations concerning the jealousy of God, I think an adequate answer was given.

Let us nevertheless remember that both there and here he accused the Scriptures concerning God’s jealousy in such a way that he also added what is commanded in those books by the Lord our God concerning the worship of idols—not to be practiced—as though he criticized God’s jealousy for no other reason than that by this very jealousy we are prohibited from the worship of idols. He therefore wishes to appear to favor idols. They do this in order to win the goodwill of pagans for their most wretched and deranged sect.

Against this passage of the Law he sets a passage from the Gospel, where someone approached the Lord and said to him: “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” Jesus replied: “Why do you ask me about goodness? No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:17–18).

He wants us, evidently, to regard these statements as contradictory because the Law says, “God is a consuming fire” and “God is jealous,” whereas the Gospel says, “No one is good except one, God.”

## 2

The matter of jealousy has already been answered: these words are not placed in the Scriptures as though they signified some disturbance or torment in God, but because nothing worthy of God can be said about him, language has descended even to such expressions. When human beings consider these expressions unworthy of God, they are compelled to learn that even the things they think they express fittingly concerning the ineffable excellence of God are unworthy of the majesty of God. His Wisdom was going to descend even to the human body, and therefore first descended even to human words.

There: I have said, “descended.” Yet if I begin to examine that word, I do not see that I have used it properly. For only what can also move from one place to another can descend. Someone who descends appears to leave a higher place and seek a lower one. But since God’s Wisdom is wholly present everywhere, it cannot in any way migrate from place to place.

John speaks of this Wisdom in the Gospel as one who shared in the Lord’s breast. For he says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not recognize him”; yet he immediately adds: “He came to what was his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:10–11).

How was he here, and how did he come, unless the ineffable sublimity must be signified by human sounds in order to accommodate itself to human beings, while, in order to make human beings divine, it must be understood through divine silence?

An explanation can therefore be given of why it was said in this way; nevertheless, nothing worthy of God can be said about God, since the very fact that it could be said already makes it unworthy.

Remove error and suffering from jealousy: what else will remain except a will that guards chastity and avenges marital corruption? By what word, then, could it better be intimated than by “the jealousy of God” that we are called to God’s marriage, that he does not wish us to be corrupted by shameful love, that he punishes our unchastity, and that he loves chastity?

For it is not without reason that the common saying goes: “Whoever is not jealous does not love.”

## 3

The same point also concerns the expression “consuming fire.” I should not argue about it, but rather ask them what fire the Lord said that he had come to cast upon this world. This statement is found in the Gospel, which they cannot accuse—not in order to honor Christ, but in order to deceive Christians.

When this is recalled to them, namely, that the Lord said, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), the wretched men say: “But that is something else.”

We answer them: “Yes, it is something else; do not be afraid.” For Christ himself also speaks in the Old Testament when he says, “I am a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24; 9:3)—the same one who speaks in the Gospel, saying that he came to cast fire upon this world, that is, the Word of God, who is himself.

After his resurrection, he certainly explained the ancient Scriptures to his disciples, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, when those same disciples confessed that they had received fire, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us on the road, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

He is that consuming fire: divine love consumes the old life and renews the human being. Thus, because God is a consuming fire, he causes us to love him; and because God is jealous, he himself loves us.

Therefore, do not fear the fire that is God [Note: [Col. 0148] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain read, “the fire who is God.” M.]; but fear the fire that God has prepared for heretics.

## 4

As for the passage Adimantus selected from the Gospel to set against this passage of the Law as though it were contradictory, where the Lord says, “No one is good except one, God,” who could count how often God’s goodness is found in the Old Testament?

I shall mention only one example, which is sung every day in the Church: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 117:1, 29).

Certainly this too appears contrary to a jealous God, as the Manichaeans suppose, and yet it is sung in the books of the Old Testament.

Again, that king who held a wedding for his son found among those reclining at table a man who did not have a wedding garment. First addressing him as “friend,” he ordered him to be bound hand and foot and sent into the outer darkness (Matt. 22:2–13). To those who understand the passage with displeasure, he does not appear to be good.

Suppose someone were to propose this very Gospel passage and, as Adimantus does with the Old Testament, accuse the Gospel maliciously: praising instead the books of the Old Testament, where it is written, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever,” and criticizing the New because the invited guest is sent into such punishment on account of his garment. Suppose he did this repeatedly with fraudulent perversity, collecting all the passages of gentleness from the Old Testament and the passages of severity from the New, and insisting that they were opposed to one another, praising the Old and criticizing the New.

He would similarly find ignorant people, pitifully uninformed about the divine Scriptures, whom he could persuade that the Old Testament ought to be retained rather than the New.

Since these people do the same thing from the other side—that is, criticizing the Old Testament as though it were contrary to the New—I am astonished that they do not consider that someone might at some point read both and, by divine assistance, praise both in his understanding; and that one might either grieve over their fraud and malice as human beings, guard against them as heretics, or mock them as ignorant and proud.

# CHAPTER XIV

## 1

Concerning what is written in Deuteronomy: “Kill and eat every kind of flesh according to the desire of your soul, according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you. But take care not to eat blood; pour it out upon the ground like water” (Deut. 12:15–16).

Adimantus thinks that these words of the Law are contradicted by what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let not your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares” (Luke 21:34); and by what the Apostle says: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine” (Rom. 14:21); and again: “You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:21).

We, however, say that all these statements, whether written in the Old Testament or in the New, were set down for reasons demanded by their circumstances, and we show that they are not opposed to one another.

Indeed, even in the words he quoted from the Old Testament he could have noticed that the command, “Kill and eat every kind of flesh according to the desire of your soul,” does not pertain to immoderate greed, since it continues, “according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you.”

For the Lord did not give you immoderate pleasure, but only as much as is sufficient to sustain nature and preserve health. Whoever follows immoderate greed is following his own vice, not the pleasure given by the Lord. Therefore the statement in the Gospel is not contradictory: “Let not your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares.”

When someone fills himself only with the pleasure that the Lord has given—that is, with what is moderate and natural—his heart is not weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares.

## 2

As for the Apostle’s statement about not eating meat and not drinking wine: he did not command this because he considered those things unclean, as these people suppose, and by which they plunge those whom they have persuaded of such things into error. Since he himself gave the reason why he said it, we do not need to interpret or explain the statement for ourselves.

It is enough to set out the Apostle’s entire passage in his Epistle in connection with this discussion, so that both the reason why the Apostle said this may become clear, and the fraud of those who select certain fragments from the Scriptures with which to deceive the ignorant may be exposed, failing to connect what is written above and below, from which the writer’s will and intention can be understood.

Thus the Apostle says:

“Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes [Note: [Col. 0149] The printed editions read, “not for debates.” The manuscripts instead read, “not for disputes.” The Greek is *eis diakriseis*.] about his thoughts. One person believes that he may eat everything [Note: [Col. 0149] The editions read, “believes that he may eat everything.” The word “that” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek.]; but the one who is weak should eat vegetables [Note: [Col. 0149] The manuscripts read, “should eat.”]. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats, for God has accepted him.

Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. But he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

One person judges one day to be different from another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord; and the one who eats eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. The one who does not eat abstains for the Lord, and gives thanks to God.

For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.

For this reason Christ died, so that he might rule over both the dead and the living.
