But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of the Lord. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Therefore each of us will give an account for himself.

Let us therefore no longer judge one another; but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or a scandal before your brother.

I know, and am certain in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean through him, except to the one who thinks something unclean; to that person it is unclean.

For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died.

Therefore let not our good be blasphemed. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by human beings.

Therefore let us pursue what makes for peace and what contributes to mutual edification. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food.

All things are indeed clean, but it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, or to do anything by which your brother is offended.

Keep the faith that you have within yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. But the one who discerns [Note: [Col. 0150] Several manuscripts read, “judges.”], if he eats, is condemned, because he does not act from faith. Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14).

Does this require anyone’s interpretation in order to understand why the Apostle said it, and how great is the malice of those who tear definite statements from the Scriptures in order to ensnare the ignorant?

The Apostle said that all things are clean according to faith, and that they are unclean to the one who considers them unclean; and he taught that one should abstain from them when they are received in such a way as to cause offense—that is, when someone who is weak thinks that he must abstain from all meat lest he eat sacrificial meat, and therefore may suppose that the person who eats does so in honor of idols and may be gravely offended by it. Yet even sacrificial meat, if received in faith by someone who does not know its origin, defiles no one.

For this reason, in another passage the same Apostle forbids inquiry when something is bought at the market, or when someone, invited by an unbeliever, sees meat set before him at that person’s table—meat that these people consider unclean, not because it was sacrificed, but because it is meat—although the Apostle proclaims that all things are clean, that every creature of God is good, and that all things are sanctified through the word and prayer. Nevertheless, one should abstain from them if someone who is weak happens to be offended.

And in one passage he indicated these people quite explicitly when he said that in the last times certain people would arise “forbidding marriage and abstaining from foods that God created” (1 Tim. 4:1–5). He is specifically identifying those who abstain from such foods not in order to restrain their own desire or to spare another’s weakness, but because they consider the meats themselves unclean and deny that God is their creator.

Let us therefore hold to the apostolic discipline, which says that “all things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15), while preserving evangelical moderation, so that our hearts are not weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares.

## 3

As for the same statement made by the Apostle—“You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons”—I do not see why the Manichaeans thought it should be set against this passage of the Law and regarded as its opposite.

For the Law is not speaking of sacrifices when Deuteronomy says, “Kill and eat every kind of flesh according to the desire of your soul, according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you,” but of foods that belong to human nourishment.

But because the Manichaeans call it a sacrifice whenever animals are prepared even for a human meal, they thought these statements were contradictory according to their own understanding. For this reason they also cited the passage where the Apostle says, “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God,” although the Apostle was speaking quite explicitly of victims offered to demons in a temple, not of foods that people prepare for themselves.

For he says:

“What then? Am I saying that something sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? Rather, because what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

“Everything is lawful, but not everything is beneficial. Everything is lawful, but not everything builds up. Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of the other.

“Eat everything sold in the market, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. For ‘the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.’

“If one of the unbelievers invites you, and you wish to go, eat everything set before you, making no inquiry for the sake of conscience. But if someone says to you, ‘This is sacrificial meat’ [Note: [Col. 0151] Louvain reads, “sacrificed.” Erasmus and the manuscripts read, “sacrificial meat.”], do not eat it, for the sake of the one who indicated this and for the sake of conscience. I mean not your own conscience, but the other person’s.

“For why should my freedom be judged by another [Note: [Col. 0151] The printed editions read, “by another person’s.” The manuscripts instead read, “by another.” The Greek has *hypo allēs*.] conscience? If I partake with gratitude, why am I blasphemed for what I give thanks? Therefore, whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10:19–31).

Let the Manichaeans attend to these words and see how the statement in Deuteronomy is to be understood: “Kill and eat every kind of flesh according to the desire of your soul, according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you.”

The command given to the Jews concerning certain meats that were not to be eaten, which were called unclean, serves to signify unclean human beings, who are represented figuratively in the ancient Scriptures.

Just as the ox whose mouth is not to be tied while it is threshing signifies the evangelist, as the Apostle explains quite explicitly (Deut. 25:4; 1 Cor. 9:7–9; and 1 Tim. 5:17–18), so too the creatures that were prohibited signify certain forms of human uncleanness, which are not admitted into the fellowship of Christ’s body—that is, into the enduring and everlasting Church.

For insofar as foods are concerned, it is entirely clear that nothing is unclean, but that it is evil for the person who eats by causing offense.

# CHAPTER XV

## 1

Concerning what is written in Leviticus: “Separate the unclean from the clean, and let no one eat the flesh of the camel, the ass, the hare, the pig, the eagle, the kite, the raven, the vulture, or the rest” (Lev. 11).

Nowhere can the soul of this man, so completely full of deceit and fraud, be caught more clearly than here. He set passages from the two Testaments against one another as though they were opposed and contradictory, in this passage where he recalled that Leviticus says that people must abstain from the flesh of certain animals.

He thought that this statement should be opposed by the Gospel passage where the Lord says: “Nothing entering into a person defiles him; rather, the things that come out of a person defile him” (Matt. 15:11).

If he did this unwittingly, nothing could be more blind; but if he did it knowingly, nothing could be more wicked.

Had he not shortly before quoted the Apostle’s testimony: “It is good, brothers, not to eat meat or drink wine” (Rom. 14:21), while he was trying to make the New Testament hostile to the Old, where it is said, “Kill and eat every kind of flesh according to the desire of your soul” (Deut. 12:15)?

How, then, does the Lord’s statement now please him, namely, that nothing entering into a person defiles him, but that the things coming out of a person defile him? Where can this man hide from that statement? Where will he flee, tell me, when by a perverse and superstitious conception of self-denial he commands that the uncleanness of meats be avoided and kept separate from the food of the holy?

Certainly, if it is true that what enters into a person does not defile him, then the Manichaeans are greatly mistaken when they call foods unclean while human beings eat meat. But if such foods are unclean, what will they do with this testimony, spoken with evangelical and divine authority, where the Lord says that a person is not defiled by what enters into him, but by what comes out of him?

Or perhaps they will say, as they usually do when the authority of the Scriptures presses them, that this passage was inserted into the Gospel by corrupters of the Scriptures. Why, then, does Adimantus use this passage as a witness and attempt to attack the Old Testament with the very passage by which he himself is overthrown?

For when some Catholic Christian, a venerator and interpreter of both Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0152] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read, “hunter.” M.], replies to him that these passages are not contradictory—that the commands concerning the flesh of certain animals, by which the people, still carnal, were instructed not to eat them, were set down as symbols of human behavior, which the Church, being the body of the Lord, cannot receive into the permanent and everlasting bond of its unity, rejecting them as unclean foods and not converting them into its own inward substance; and that all those commands imposed upon a carnal people therefore prophesied the future discipline of a spiritual people—then it is clear that they do not conflict with the Lord’s statement, in which he most truly says that a person is not defiled by what enters into him as food.

The former statement imposes burdens upon servants; the latter removes the yoke of servitude from those who are already free. Yet the former was spoken in such a way that the burdens of servants might foreshadow the faith of the free.

For, as the Apostle says, “all these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for us” [Note: [Col. 0153] The manuscripts read, “all these things happened to them in figure for us, and so forth,” omitting the words “but they were written.”] “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

If, therefore, the things they suffered happened as a figure, then the things about which they were warned were received as a figure.

## 2

When I have given this answer and shown in this way that these two passages, one from each Testament, are not contradictory, what will this man do, against whom the witness he himself produced gives the gravest testimony?

He himself cited the Gospel testimony in which the Lord says that a person is not defiled by the foods entering into him; and yet he does not cease to advise and teach that people must abstain from meats as from unclean foods.

Nevertheless, he perceived what a blow he was inflicting upon himself and with what a stroke of recoil he was wounding himself. For, lest someone question him and say, “How then do you forbid people to eat meat if the Lord says—as you yourself recall—‘Nothing entering into a person defiles him; rather, the things coming out of a person defile him’?” he wanted, as it were, to apply medicine without cause to a mortal wound.

For this is how he presented the Gospel testimony:

“In the Gospel,” he says, “the Lord says to the crowd: ‘Hear and understand: Nothing entering into a person defiles him,’ and so forth.”

By recalling that the Lord said this to the crowd, he showed nothing other than that he acted not from ignorance but from malice. He wanted later to tell his hearers that the Lord had spoken these words to the crowd and not to the few saints, such as they themselves wish to appear to be; so that, since they permit their own hearers, as still unclean, to eat meat, while they consider it wicked and criminal for themselves, as though they were already clean, it might appear that the Lord too held this view, because he taught these things not to a few saints but to the crowds.

O utterly wicked man, secure in his reliance upon human negligence to conceal his deceptions! He did not believe that anyone would arise who would seize the Gospel, read it with understanding, and discover a man hiding snares for the unwary and the less vigilant in the very meadows where the Lord feeds his flocks.

The disciples, disturbed by these words and not believing that the Lord had spoken literally but rather figuratively when he said that a person is not defiled by what enters into him through food—for the disciples themselves were Jews and had been taught from childhood to avoid the food of certain meats—approached him and said: “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard the word [Note: [Col. 0153] The editions read, “this word.” The word “this” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Gospel.], were offended?”

But he answered and said:

“Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. And if the blind guides the blind, both will fall into a pit.”

Although he called the unbelief of the Jews a planting that the heavenly Father had not planted, Peter still thought that this was a parable, and therefore that the Jews had been rebuked and called blind because they could not understand it. He answered him and said: “Explain this parable to us.”

But the Lord, showing most clearly that it was not a parable but ordinary speech, said to them: “Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine? But the things that come out of the mouth proceed from the heart, and they defile a person. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person. But eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Matt. 15:10–20).

The Jews had raised the question about unwashed hands. On that occasion the Lord made a general statement about the things that enter the mouth, go into the stomach, and are expelled into the latrine—that is, about our foods.

Although it is written that, after calling the crowds to him, he said, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth,” it is nevertheless sufficiently clear, as was said shortly before, from what fear this man added the qualification when he recalled this testimony in his own words: he wanted something with which to answer those who asked him why the leaders of the Manichaeans considered it a crime to eat meat. Evidently, he wanted the Lord’s statement to appear to have been granted only to the crowds and not to the Elect.

But since what follows makes clear that, when Peter questioned him privately in the hearing of the disciples—whom he was certainly bringing forward to the summit of the Church—the Lord answered in such a way that he testified that he had not spoken those words as a parable and showed that they applied to everyone, these men have no means of snatching food from people’s mouths and binding those mouths in the snare of superstition [Note: [Col. 0154] The editions read, “them.” The manuscripts read, “those mouths,” namely, “mouths.”].

## 3

Perhaps one of them will say: “Then explain what the flesh of the pig, camel, hare, kite, raven, and the other animals signifies, since the Law commands that people abstain from them.”

I do not wish to do so, because it would be lengthy. But suppose that I were unable to do it; does that mean that no one can? There are already innumerable volumes in which these matters have been explained.

For refuting these people, however, it is enough that the Apostle, not I, says that those observances were a shadow of things to come. Although he forbids them to be observed in a servile manner, he nevertheless declares that they signify something, saying:

“Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or concerning a festival, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. 2:16–17).

Thus, after the future realities signified by those observances had come through the Lord Jesus Christ, the servile observances were removed; but their interpretations are retained by the free.

Whatever signified the future Church is prophecy. You have the same Apostle saying: “Do not despise the Spirit; do not extinguish prophecy; examine everything, and hold fast to what is good” (1 Thess. 5:19–21).

The divine Scripture must therefore be read, the dispensation of the Holy Spirit must be understood, and prophecy must be contemplated; carnal servitude must be rejected, and free understanding must be retained.

# CHAPTER XVI

## 1

Concerning what is written in Deuteronomy:

“Observe and sanctify the day that the Lord commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work; but on the seventh day of the Sabbath you shall celebrate a feast for the Lord your God. You shall do no work—you, or your son, or your daughter, or your male servant, or your female servant, or your ox, or your ass, or any of your livestock, or your resident alien. Thus your male servant and your female servant shall rest as you do. Remember that you were a servant in Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm. Therefore the Lord commanded you to keep the seventh day” (Deut. 5:12–15).

And again, in Genesis, it is written how he speaks to Abraham concerning circumcision:

“Keep my covenant,” he says, “you and your seed after you. This is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you and your seed: every male among you shall be circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, and this shall be the sign of the covenant between me and you. On the eighth day you shall circumcise every male in your people; you shall also circumcise those of your household and those purchased by you, except for the foreigner; and this shall be a covenant among your people. Every male who does not circumcise the foreskin of his flesh shall lose his life from the midst of his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. 17:9–14).

Adimantus sets forth all these words of the Old Testament in order to oppose them to the New Testament, and he asserts that they contradict what the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the proselyte:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when you have made him, he becomes a son of Gehenna far more than you yourselves are” (Matt. 23:15).

As though the Lord called the proselyte a son of Gehenna because he was circumcised and observed the Sabbath, rather than because he was compelled to imitate the Jews’ corrupt way of life [Note: [Col. 0155] Some manuscripts read, “the Jews’ depraved customs and their corrupt way of life.”]—not the practices by which they observe the precepts of the Law, but those by which they act against the Law.

Elsewhere he speaks of this most explicitly, saying that they reject the commandment of God in order to establish their own tradition (ibid. 15:3–6). For although the Law commanded that father and mother be honored, they themselves devised a way by which parents might be dishonored.

Again, he says to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who possess the key of the kingdom of heaven; you yourselves do not enter, and you do not permit others to enter” (Luke 11:52).

Or consider the other passage where he commanded his hearers [Note: [Col. 0155] The printed editions read, “where he commanded.” The manuscripts read more correctly, “where he commanded.”] to obey the words of the Pharisees and scribes but not to imitate their deeds. For he says:

“They sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:2–3).

In this passage the Lord both confirms the authority of the Law given through Moses and shows most explicitly that the ways of those who did not obey the Law they had received must be avoided and shunned.

By these perverse practices they caused any Gentile who passed over to their Law—that is, who became a proselyte—to acquire their customs and become a son of Gehenna, twice as much as they themselves were. For they took great pains to make someone from the Gentiles a Jew, and once he had become a Jew they compelled him to imitate their exceedingly wicked customs.

### 2.

Nor could the Manichaean Adimantus discern that what he cites from the Apostle as though it were contradictory is not contradictory at all, because his entire attention was directed not toward investigating Scripture but toward criticizing it. For he cites the Apostle saying:

> “Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not restore the foreskin. Was anyone called in the foreskin? Let him not be circumcised. For neither the foreskin is anything, nor circumcision, but the observance of God’s commandments” (1 Cor. 7:18–19).

What could be clearer than that the Apostle commands each person to remain as he was when called? For when the realities of which those observances were shadows arrived, the purpose was to show that hope should not be placed in the shadows themselves, but in the realities signified by those shadows and destined to come—namely, Christ and the Church.

Therefore all those things were already empty; yet the Apostle does not command that they be removed as harmful, but that they be disregarded as superfluous. Thus, if a Jew had believed in Christ, he was not to be prevented, on account of the offense of his fellow Jews, from remaining in those superfluous observances; yet he was not to think that his salvation was established in them. For it is not those signs, but the things signified by them, that bring people into salvation.

Therefore “the foreskin is nothing, and circumcision is nothing, but the observance of God’s commandments.” And when he says elsewhere, “Would that those who are troubling you would even mutilate themselves” (Gal. 5:12), the Apostle does not say this because circumcision is contrary to the Gospel, as the Manichaeans suppose. Rather, what is contrary to the Gospel is that someone, abandoning the reality represented by that shadow, should pursue the emptiness of the shadow itself. This is what those people wanted who imposed the yoke of circumcision upon Gentiles believing in Christ as though it were necessary for salvation, when the shadow was no longer to be represented in the body but the reality itself was to be carried in the heart.

### 3.

And when he says, “You observe days, and sabbaths, and festivals; I fear that I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. 4:10–11), it is not written as Adimantus presents it. For the Apostle does not mention the sabbath there. He says:

> “You observe days and years and seasons; I fear that I have labored among you in vain.”

But does he think this was said about the sabbath? Do we ourselves not say that these things are not to be observed, but rather the things signified by them? For those people observed them slavishly, not understanding what realities they referred to and foretold. The Apostle censures this in them and in all who serve the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1:25).

For we too solemnly celebrate the Lord’s Day and Easter, as well as whatever other Christian festivals of days there are. But because we understand what they refer to, we do not observe the seasons themselves, but the things signified by those seasons.

The Manichaeans, however, criticize these matters as though they themselves observed no days or seasons. But when questioned about them according to the opinion of their sect, they try to explain everything so as to appear to observe not the seasons themselves, but the realities of which those seasons are signs. Elsewhere it is shown that these realities are mythical and utterly false.

For the present, this point has been made so that they may be compelled by their own words to acknowledge that such celebrations can be practiced rationally. It is therefore clear that circumcision of the flesh was rightly imposed upon servants and rightly understood by free people. **[Note: Only the Lovaniensis edition has *repudiatam* (“rejected”) instead of *intellectam* (“understood”).]**

With the Apostle, then, we reject circumcision according to the flesh, and with the Apostle we approve circumcision according to the spirit. We do not observe the sabbath’s rest as a temporal observance; rather, we understand the temporal sign and direct the mind toward the eternal rest signified by that sign. **[Note: Several manuscripts read “the attention of the heart” (*aciem cordis*) instead of “the attention of the mind” (*aciem mentis*).]**

Accordingly, with the Apostle we reject the observance of seasons, while with the Apostle we retain an understanding of temporal signs. We thus affirm the difference between the two Testaments: in the former are the burdens of servants; in the latter, the glory of free people. **[Note: The old Corbeiensis manuscript reads “the joys of free people” instead of “the glory of free people.”]** In the former, the prefiguration of our possession is recognized; in the latter, the possession itself is held.

The Apostle interprets the sabbath in the Epistle to the Hebrews when he says:

> “Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God” (Heb. 4:9).  
> **[Note: Manuscripts read *sabbatismum* rather than *sabbatismus*.]**

He also interprets circumcision when he says of Abraham:

> “And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4:11).

I therefore hold spiritually to the Apostle’s interpretation. I reject the carnal observance of servitude with the freedom of contempt, while venerating God as the author of both Testaments: he who placed before the old person fleeing from him, as a lord, what that person should fear, and opened before the new person returning to him, as a father, what that person should love.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 1.

Concerning what is written in Exodus:

> “If you will truly listen to my voice and do whatever I command you, I will hate those who hate you, and I will afflict those who afflict you. My angel will go before you and bring you to the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite, and you shall kill them. You shall not worship their gods, nor do their works; but utterly overthrow them and erase their memory” (Exod. 23:22–24).

After quoting these words from the ancient Books, Adimantus sets against them, as though it were contradictory, what is written in the Gospel, where the Lord says:

> “But I say to you: Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44).

Here the first point to notice is that it ought to have been sufficient for someone wishing to demonstrate an apparent contradiction merely to point out that the Old Law speaks of killing enemies. For when the Lord commands that enemies be loved, he certainly means human beings—those whom anyone can understand may be converted to salvation through our patience and charity, as has very often been demonstrated by examples.

What, then, did he intend by adding the following words:

> “You shall not worship their gods, nor do their works; but utterly overthrow them and erase their memory”?

Could it be because the Manichaeans also compel people to love the gods of the Gentiles? They suppose that the Lord’s command in the Gospel, “Love your enemies,” applies not only to human beings but also to demons and even to idols. If that is so, who would not detest such madness? But if they do not think this, then Adimantus was profoundly mistaken when he wanted to cite the Old Testament’s command that the superstitions of the Gentiles be overthrown as though it were contradictory to the Gospel’s command to love enemies.

### 2.

We, however, do not say that what was said in the ancient Books to that people about killing human enemies is contrary to the Gospel command by which the Lord orders us to love our enemies. For that killing of enemies was suited to a people still carnal, to whom the Law had been given as a tutor, as the Apostle says (Gal. 3:24).

At that time there were very few holy and spiritual people within that nation—such as Moses and the Prophets. With what disposition they carried out the killing of enemies, and whether they loved those whom they killed, is largely hidden from the uneducated and impious, who love their own blindness. Since they are incapable of seeing these matters, they must instead be pressed by the weight of authority.

For what does the Apostle mean when he says:

> “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit, and I have already judged, as though present, the man who has done this: when you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and my spirit is present with the power of our Lord Jesus, hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Cor. 5:3–5)?

What is that destruction, which they greatly magnify and maliciously discuss, except the destruction of the flesh? But because the Apostle explained with what disposition he acted, he made it sufficiently clear that punishment against an enemy can proceed with charity.

Yet here the destruction of the flesh may perhaps also be understood in another way: the destruction that occurs through repentance.

They themselves read apocryphal writings, which they even call entirely incorrupt, in which it is written that the Apostle Thomas cursed a man who had inadvertently struck him with his hand, not knowing who he was, and that the curse immediately took effect. For when that man, who was serving at a banquet, had gone out to a spring to bring water, he was killed and torn apart by a lion. To make this known and frighten the others, a dog carried his hand to the tables where the Apostle was dining. When the ignorant guests inquired into the matter and the explanation was given to them, they were converted to great fear and great honor toward the Apostle; and this became the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel.

If someone wished to turn the Manichaeans’ teeth against themselves, how fiercely they would criticize this story! Yet because the text does not fail to state the disposition with which it was done, the love of the one who inflicted the punishment is apparent. For that writing says that the Apostle prayed for the man against whom temporal punishment had been exacted, asking that he be spared in the future judgment.

If, then, in the time of the New Testament—when charity is especially commended—fear was divinely inflicted upon fleshly people through visible punishments, **[Note: Only the Lovaniensis edition reads “carnal fear” (*carnalis timor*). This is less correct.]** how much more should it be understood that this was appropriate in the time of the Old Testament for that people, whom the fear of the Law restrained as a tutor?

For this is the briefest and clearest difference between the two Testaments: fear and love. The former belongs to the old person, the latter to the new; yet both were brought forth and joined together by the most merciful dispensation of the one God.

In the Old Scripture the disposition of those exacting punishment is left unmentioned, because the very few spiritual people who knew through divine revelations what they were to do acted so that the people, for whom terror was useful, might be subdued by the strictest authority. Thus, just as they saw impious enemies and worshipers of idols being delivered into their hands to be killed, they themselves would fear being delivered into the hands of their enemies if they disregarded the commands of the true God and fell into the worship of idols and the impieties of the Gentiles.

For punishment was similarly inflicted upon those among them who sinned in like manner. All this temporal punishment terrifies weak minds, so that, nourished under discipline, they may be instructed and turned away from eternal and ineffable punishments. Carnal people fear more what God punishes in the present than what he threatens in the future.

### 3.

There can therefore be love in one who inflicts punishment. Everyone proves this in the case of his own son when he restrains him with the strictest discipline as he falls into very bad habits—and does so all the more strictly the more he loves him, because he believes that his son can be corrected in this way.

Yet people do not kill the sons they love when they wish to correct them, because many regard this life as a great good, and place all their hopes for raising their children in this life. Faithful and wise people, however, who believe that another and better life exists, and know as much of it as they are able, do not themselves punish by killing when they wish to correct their children, because they believe that their children can be corrected in this life.

But God, who knows what he grants to each person, punishes by killing whomever he wills, whether through human beings or through the hidden order of events—not because he hates them insofar as they are human beings, but insofar as they are sinners.

For in the ancient Books we read that God was told:

> “You hated nothing that you made” (Wis. 11:25).

Yet he orders everything—whether through punishments or rewards—according to the governance of justice.

Was the Apostle Paul not speaking to faithful Christians when he said:

> “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat from the bread and drink from the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a sufficient number are asleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. When we are judged, however, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Cor. 11:28–32).

**[Note: The editions read “with this world.” The word “this” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.]**

Here it is plainly shown that God corrects with love—not only through weaknesses and illnesses but also through temporal deaths—those whom he does not wish to condemn with the world.

### 4.

Let these people take note of this and see how impious nations could have been delivered into the hands of a people who, although still carnal, nevertheless worshiped one God, so that they might be killed by that people. If there were spiritual people within that nation, they would understand, without hatred toward anyone, God’s dispensation.

Let them also see how it is not contrary to what the Lord commanded us in the Gospel, namely, that we should love our enemies. Yet he himself promises punishment for them when he introduces the parable of that judge who, although unjust and fearing neither God nor respecting human beings, could not endure the widow’s daily appeals that he avenge her. He finally heard her so that she would not trouble him further. From this comparison the Lord declared that God, who is supremely kind and just, would all the more avenge his elect against their enemies (Luke 18:2–8).

Let these people dare to raise their objection against this and say, if they can:

> “Why did you command us to love our enemies, while planning to avenge us against them? Will you perhaps act against the will of your saints by punishing and condemning those whom they love?”

Rather, let them turn from this slanderous blindness to God and understand his will in both Testaments, lest they be found on the left among those to whom the Lord will say:

> “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:41–42),

and other such words.

For these wretched people are displeased that God delivered enemies to his people to be killed; yet they themselves forbid bread to be given to a beggar—not to an enemy, but to a suppliant.

Let them instead understand that punishment can exist without hatred—a truth understood by very few. Yet as long as it is not understood, the reader must struggle through the books of both Testaments amid great difficulty or error, and imagine that the Scriptures contradict one another.

### 5.

The Apostles had not yet grasped this punishment without hatred when, angered by those who refused them hospitality, they asked the Lord whether he wished them to call down fire from heaven, as Elijah had done, so that the inhospitable people might be consumed by that fire.

The Lord then answered that they did not know whose spirit they were children of **[Note: The Louvain editors rejected the word “sons” on the authority of one manuscript. It occurs in the Erasmus edition and in all our manuscripts.]**, and that he had come to save, not to destroy (Luke 9:53–56). They had wished to destroy, with a hostile disposition, those whom they wanted consumed by fire.

Later, however, when they had been filled with the Holy Spirit and perfected, so that they could even love their enemies, they received the power to punish, because they could now punish without hatred.

The Apostle Peter exercised this power in the book that these people do not accept, because it plainly contains the coming of the Paraclete—that is, the Holy Spirit, the Comforter—whom the Lord sent to those who were mourning when he himself had ascended into heaven before their eyes.

For a comforter is sent to the sorrowful, according to that saying of the same Lord:

> “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

He also says:

> “Then the sons of the bridegroom will mourn when the bridegroom has been taken away from them” (Matt. 9:15).

In that book, where the coming of the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord had promised as Comforter, is most plainly declared (Acts 2:4), we read that, at Peter’s sentence, people fell down and died: a husband and wife who had dared to lie to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:1–10).

These people condemn this in their great blindness, although in their apocryphal writings they read with great admiration both the story I mentioned about the Apostle Thomas and the story that Peter’s daughter was made paralyzed by her father’s prayers **[Note: The Louvain edition reads “made paralytic and whole,” adding “whole”; the word is absent from the other books and ought to be absent, as the context makes clear.]**, and that a gardener’s daughter died at Peter’s request. They reply that this was beneficial for them: one was released from paralysis and the other died. Yet they do not deny that it happened at the Apostle’s prayers.

But who told them, “It was not beneficial for the impious Gentiles to be killed,” when they mockingly pretend to be astonished that those Gentiles were divinely delivered into the hands of the Jewish people?

When those other acts were performed by the Apostles not out of hatred but with a good disposition, how do these people prove that the dispositions of the spiritual men who lived among that people were hateful, when by their agency divine justice ordered certain people to be taken from this life?

Let them rather restrain their presumption and not deceive the inexperienced—those who either have no time to read, or do not wish to read, or read with a perverse disposition, and fail to observe that both God’s mercy and his severity are commended in the writings of both Testaments.

For concerning love of an enemy, so that evil may not be repaid with evil, we read in the ancient Books:

> “Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who did evil to me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:4–5).

Who would say this except someone who knew that it pleases God that no one repay evil with evil?

But this belongs to the perfect: that they hate nothing in sinners except their sins, while loving the people themselves; and that when they punish, they do so not with the harshness of cruelty but with the moderation of justice, lest the remission of sin itself harm the sinner more than the punishment of retribution.

Nevertheless, righteous people did not do such things except by divine authority, lest anyone suppose that he was freely permitted to kill whomever he wished, prosecute someone according to his own judgment, or afflict people with whatever punishments he chose.

Sometimes Scripture openly sets forth the divine authority itself; at other times it conceals it, so that the reader may be instructed by what is manifest and exercised by what is obscure.

### 6.

David received into his power King Saul, his exceedingly ungrateful and hostile enemy, so that he might do with him whatever he wished; yet he chose to spare him rather than kill him. For he had not been commanded to kill him, but neither had he been forbidden. Indeed, he had even heard from God that he could safely do whatever he wished to his enemy; nevertheless, he turned such great power toward gentleness (1 Sam. 24:3–8; 26:8–12).

Let someone tell me whom David feared when he refused to kill him. We cannot say that he feared the man whom he had received into his power, nor God, who had delivered him into his hands. Where, then, there was neither difficulty in killing nor fear, love benefited the enemy. **[Note: Several manuscripts read “he spared the enemy” instead of “love benefited the enemy.”]**

There is David, that warrior, fulfilling Christ’s command which we have received: that we should love our enemies.

Would that these people imitated him—people who have twisted the human feeling of mercy into I know not what cruel madness! For while they believe that bread weeps—which cannot happen—they do not offer it to the human being whom they see weeping.

Perhaps, as blind people are accustomed to hurl insane insults, they will say that David, who spared his enemy, was better than God, who gave him the power to kill—as though God did not know to whom he had given that power.

Certainly he knew the will of his servant. But so that the love of an enemy already known to God in David’s heart might also become known to other human beings for their imitation, he delivered into David’s power an enemy whom he did not yet wish to be killed, on account of the definite dispensation of events that had to be fulfilled through him. **[Note: The manuscripts read “arrangement” instead of “dispensation.”]**

Thus David’s goodness was commended, so that people might have something to love; and the wickedness of King Saul was postponed to a more fitting end, so that people might have something to fear.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 1.

Concerning what is written in Deuteronomy:

> “If you truly listen to the voice of the Lord your God, blessed are you in your field, blessed in your meadow, blessed is the fruit of your womb, and the fruit of your land, and the offspring of your cattle, and the herds of your oxen, and the flocks of your sheep; blessed are you when you enter and when you go out” (Deut. 28:1–6).

No one should now ask us to demonstrate how appropriately God promised these things to that people. We have said much about this matter, and anyone for whom it is still insufficient is exceedingly slow to understand.

Yet they say that what the Lord says in the New Testament is also contrary to this passage—namely:

> “Do not carry gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff, for the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Matt. 10:9–10).

What wonder if he granted these things to the Evangelists? Was the Jewish people being called to this ministry?

Nevertheless, all these matters must be examined spiritually, lest the Lord himself appear to have acted against his own commands, since he also had a money box in which money was carried for necessary expenses (John 12:6). Unless perhaps they will say that it is a sin to have money in one’s belt but not a sin to have it in a money box.

That these things were permitted rather than commanded to the Apostles is shown by the fact that the Apostle Paul worked with his own hands to obtain his livelihood and did not make use of the authority that the Lord gave the Evangelists, as he himself says (Acts 18:3; 1 Cor. 4:12; 1 Thess. 2:9; 2 Thess. 3:8–9). For what the Lord permits may also be left undone; but what he commands becomes a sin if it is not done.

### 2.

They also bring forward the case of the rich man to whom God had said:

> “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12:20).

They say that this is no less contrary to the passage of the Law. Yet in that story the emptiness of vain joy is mocked: the man regarded uncertain things as certain. To the people of Israel, however, the omnipotence of the one who made the promise rendered that promise certain.

Hence the Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy about the rich of this world—whom he knew had their place among the members of the Church—speaks as follows:

> “Command the rich of this world not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment. Let them do good, let them be rich in good works, let them give readily, let them share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may grasp the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

Who would not understand here that possessing these things is not blameworthy, but that it is blameworthy to love them, place one’s hope in them, prefer them to—or even compare them with—truth, justice, wisdom, faith, a good conscience, and love of God and neighbor? Through all these things the devout soul is rich in its secret places before the eyes of God. **[Note: Several manuscripts read “through all these things every soul” instead of “through all these things the soul.”]**

But in order that God may be loved—God who gives all these visible and invisible, eternal things to those who love him, that is, who gives himself, full of all these things, to his lovers—in order that he may be loved, even at the time when the carnal soul, entangled in the desires of the flesh, knows only how to desire temporal things, it had to be persuaded that God also gives these things to human beings. This is both true and most beneficial to believe.

This was done for the people of Israel through those promises, which wretched people mock in their profound ignorance, so that they might accustom themselves, as far as they could, to love God even in the lowest things, although fear plays the greater role there. **[Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript reads *plus* (“more”) here; the editions read *prius* (“first”).]**

All these temporal gifts, however, are figures of eternal gifts, and that victory over enemies prefigures victory over the devil and his angels.

### 3.

They also added, as though it were contrary to the Old Testament, the Apostle’s statement that God delights not in strife and dissension but in peace (1 Cor. 14:33).

Let them know that those Scriptures proclaim such a God—one whose peace no one can take away—not the god they themselves proclaim, who, fearing that war might invade his regions, sent his members far away to endure foreign wars and afterward could not free and purify them once they had been defeated and polluted.

In human nature, however, which through sin has fallen into lower things, God delights in peace in such a way that he does not abandon the balance of justice. He does not wish the peace he loves to be trampled by sinners, but to be loved by those who contend, seized by victors, and—having been represented in carnal things—revealed to spiritual people.

## CHAPTER XXI
## On What Is Written in Deuteronomy: “Cursed Is Everyone Who Has Hung on a Tree” (Deut. 21:23)

Although this question has often been debated by the Manichaeans, I nevertheless do not see what contradiction there is to this statement in what Adimantus thought should be brought forward from the Gospel, where the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you possess and distribute it to the poor, and take up your cross and follow me” (Matt. 19:21; 16:24). Here, apart from the fact that he mentions the cross, he pays no attention to anything that might seem contrary to the statement, “Cursed is everyone who has hung on a tree”—as though anyone could take up such a cross and follow the Lord. But that cross is taken up when we follow the Lord, of which the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. 5:24). For by such a cross the old person—that is, the old life—which we have drawn from Adam is put to death, so that what was voluntary in him might become natural in us. The Apostle demonstrates this when he says: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

If, then, the old life comes from Adam—and the old life is also signified by the name “old person”—what absurdity is there in the fact that a curse was pronounced against the old person whom the Lord suspended on the tree? For through that very succession he bore mortality, having been born mortally from the Virgin Mary. He had flesh that was not sinful, yet that bore the likeness of sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0166] The Corbie manuscript reads: “bearing the likeness of the flesh of sin.”] (Rom. 8:3), because he could die, and death comes from sin.

Hence there is also the statement: “Knowing that our old person was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be abolished” (Rom. 6:6). Therefore it was not the Lord, through the tongue of Moses, God’s servant, who deserved the curse; it was death itself that deserved it—the death which our Lord abolished by taking it upon himself.

That death, then, hung on the tree, which had come to humanity through the woman by the serpent’s persuasion. For this reason Moses also raised up a serpent on a tree in the wilderness, as a sign of that very death. And because we are healed from deadly desires through faith in the Lord’s cross—the cross on which death was hung upon the tree—those who were being poisoned by the bites of serpents were immediately healed when they looked upon the serpent fixed and raised up on the tree (Num. 21:9).

The Lord himself bore witness to this mystery when he said: “For just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up” (John 3:14).

By accepting the most shameful form of death in human eyes—namely, death on a cross—our Lord Jesus Christ commended his love to us, so that the Apostle might rightly say, kindling us with love for him: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’” (Gal. 3:13). Thus Christian freedom would fear not merely no kind of death, but no form of death whatsoever, unlike Jewish servitude.

## CHAPTER XXII

### On the Man Whom God Ordered to Be Stoned Because He Was Found Gathering Wood on the Sabbath (Num. 15:35)

When the Lord healed the man’s withered hand on the Sabbath in the Gospel (Matt. 12:10–13), he performed a divine work, not a human one; nor did the one who commanded and it came to pass depart from rest. Therefore this event is not comparable to that of the man gathering wood, who, when he was found doing so on the Sabbath, was stoned at God’s command.

Much has already been said about the servile observance of the Sabbath and the punishment of temporal death. For just as God’s goodness is especially commended in the time of love, so his severity is especially commended in the time of fear. And since, before the Lord’s coming, it was not yet appropriate to uncover for the people the meaning of the lawful sacramental figures, they were not invited to understand what was signified; they were compelled to carry out what was commanded. For they were not yet joined to God through the spirit, but served the Law through the flesh.

I am astonished, however, that these people lament the man who was stoned at God’s command because he gathered wood contrary to the command of the Law, yet do not lament the tree that withered at Christ’s word (Matt. 21:19), although it had violated no command—especially since they believe the soul of a tree to be of the same kind as a human soul.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### On What Is Written: “Your Wife Like a Leafy Vine, and Your Children Like Young Olive Shoots around Your Table; and You Will See Your Children’s Children, and You Will Know That This Is How the Man Who Fears the Lord Is Blessed” (Ps. 127:2–4)

The Manichaeans do not understand that this was spoken figuratively through the prophet and pertains to the signification of the Church. They think it contradicts what the Lord says in the Gospel about eunuchs, who castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:12). But we have already discussed, in the third chapter, the man, the woman, and the eunuchs, to the extent that was sufficient.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### On What Is Written in Solomon: “Imitate the Ant, and Observe Its Diligence, for from summer until winter it gathers provisions for itself” (Prov. 6:6, 8)

The Manichaeans do not understand that this too must be received spiritually. They think it is a command that we should store up treasures on earth, or even take care of these storehouses, which human beings hasten to fill in great numbers without any command.

For this reason Adimantus says from the Gospel that the following statement is contrary to this passage, where the Lord says: “Do not think about tomorrow” (Matt. 6:34). But they do not understand that this pertains to our not loving temporal things, nor fearing that the necessities of life will be lacking, nor serving either God or human beings in order to obtain those necessities.

For if this was said so that bread should not be kept for the next day, the Roman vagrants whom they call “Passives” [Note: [Col. 0167] The Vatican manuscript reads *Passiones*. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, more correctly read *Passivos*. The word is especially familiar among African writers, where it signifies a wandering, unstable, and contemptible class of people. Thus Tertullian, in *Against Valentinus*, calls the disciples “passive,” that is, wandering everywhere and attached to no single teacher. In Book 1 of *Against Marcion* he calls a gathering “passive,” meaning indifferent and promiscuous. In Book 1 of *To His Wife* he speaks of “passive permission,” that is, wandering and indiscriminate; in the same sense Jerome reads *passiva libido*—“indiscriminate lust”—in his commentary on Ezekiel 16. In the First Council of Carthage, chapter 8, there is mention of *communio passiva*, that is, indiscriminate communion; and in the same council, chapter 11, *passiva corpora*, that is, any bodies whatsoever.] fulfill this more completely than the Lord’s disciples do. The Lord’s disciples, even while walking on earth with the Lord of heaven and earth, had a money box; and the Apostle Paul, although he despised all earthly things, nevertheless administered what was necessary for the present life in such a way that he even issued an instruction concerning widows, saying: “If any believer has widows, let him provide sufficiently for them, so that the Church may not be burdened and may be able to provide for true widows” (1 Tim. 5:16).

Nevertheless, the statement about the ant is placed there so that, just as the ant gathers in summer what will feed it in winter, so each Christian, during the tranquility of worldly circumstances—which summer signifies—may gather the word of God, so that in adversity and tribulations, signified by the name “winter,” he may have spiritual nourishment. For “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4).

But if it troubles them that the ant stores on earth what it gathers, let them also be angry at the treasure which the Lord says was found in a field (Matt. 13:44).

## CHAPTER XXV

### On What Is Written in Hosea: “Give Them an Empty Womb and Dry Breasts; Kill the Seed of Their Womb, So That They May Not Give Birth” (Hos. 9:14)

This too is certainly a figurative prophetic expression. For they themselves understand that the womb mentioned in the Gospel is not a fleshly womb when they read: “Rivers of living water will flow from his womb” (John 7:38). The Apostle also had certain breasts when he said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2); and again: “I became a little child among you, like a nurse cherishing her own children” (1 Thess. 2:7). And he gives birth again to the Galatians, who are turning toward carnal things, until Christ is formed in them (Gal. 4:19).

Therefore what Adimantus adduces from the Gospel does not contradict this prophetic statement: that in the resurrection from the dead “they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, nor will they die, but they will be like the angels of God” (Matt. 22:30). For this is surely what the eunuchs also receive, concerning whom Isaiah says: “I will give them a place and a name much better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name” (Isa. 56:5).

Let these people not suppose, then, that such a reward is promised to the saints only in the Gospel. Let them understand that the empty womb, the dry breasts, and the seed killed so that it may not give birth were spoken of those concerning whom the Apostle says: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, people corrupted in mind and rejected with regard to the faith; but they will not advance further, for their folly will become manifest to all, as theirs also did” (2 Tim. 3:8–9).

When they do not advance further, they will then have an empty womb, dry breasts, and dead seed. In this statement let them deign to see themselves as in a mirror.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### On What Is Written in the Prophet Amos: “If It Is Possible for Two Walking on the Road Not to Know One Another, and for a Lion to Return to Its Cub without Prey; if a Bird Falls to the Ground without a Fowler; if They Set a Trap without Cause, So That They Catch Nothing; if a Trumpet Sounds in the City without the People Being Terrified: So Also No Evil Is Perpetrated in the City That the Lord Does Not Bring About” (Amos 3:3–6)

Here “evil” must be understood not as sin but as punishment. For “evil” is called by two names: one kind is what a human being does, and the other is what a human being suffers. What one does is sin; what one suffers is punishment. The Prophet was speaking of punishments when he said this.

For while divine providence directs and governs all things, a human being does evil as he wishes, so that he suffers evil against his will. Yet these people accuse the Prophet for saying this, as though they had not read in the Gospel: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius? And not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father” (Matt. 10:29).

Thus God brings about an evil that is not evil for God himself, but for those against whom he exercises vengeance. Therefore, insofar as it concerns him, he does good, because everything just is good, and that vengeance is just.

Accordingly, what Adimantus objects that the Lord said is not contradictory: “A good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits” (Matt. 7:17). Although Gehenna is evil for the condemned, God’s justice is good, and that punishment is itself a fruit from a good tree.

But by the evils of his sins he stores up wrath for himself for the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each person according to his works (Rom. 2:5–6).

Nevertheless, these two trees are most clearly presented as a likeness of two human beings, namely, the just and the unjust, because unless a person changes his will, he cannot do good. That this lies within our power he teaches elsewhere, where he says: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” [Note: [Col. 0169] *Retractations* I, chapter 22, no. 4.]

He says this to those who thought they could speak good things while being evil—that is, produce good fruits while being bad trees. For he also adds: “Hypocrites, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 12:33–34).

A bad tree therefore cannot produce good fruits; but it can be made good, so that it may bear good fruits. “You were once darkness,” the Apostle says, “but now you are light in the Lord.” It is as though he were saying: “You were once bad trees, and therefore at that time you could produce only bad fruits; but now you are light in the Lord”—that is, you have already been made good trees, so produce good fruits. He continues: “Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light consists in all justice and truth, testing what is pleasing to the Lord” (Eph. 5:8–10).

Indeed, in that very Gospel passage, if Adimantus had not avoided the point out of deliberate malice, he could have observed how God is said to bring about evil. There the Lord says, as Adimantus himself also recalled: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 7:19).

These are the evils that God brings about: punishments for sinners—namely, that he will throw into the fire the trees that persist in wickedness and refuse to become good, although this is evil for those trees. God, as I have often said, does not produce evil fruits, [Col. 0170] because the punishment of sin is a fruit of justice.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### On What Is Written in the Prophet Isaiah: “I Am God Who Makes Peace and Establishes Evils” (Isa. 45:7)

This too is resolved by the same principle. Adimantus does not criticize the statement that God says, “I make peace,” but the statement, “I create evil.” Yet the Apostle Paul treated these two matters similarly, and indeed more fully, in one passage, saying: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness. Otherwise you too will be cut off, and they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again” (Rom. 11:22–23).

In this apostolic statement God’s goodness is sufficiently apparent, in accordance with which Isaiah said, “I am God who makes peace”; and his severity is also apparent, in accordance with which he said, “I create evil.” At the same time, it shows that it lies within our power whether we deserve to be grafted in through his goodness or cut off through his severity [Note: [Col. 0170] *Retractations* I, chapter 22, no. 4.]

The Gospel, therefore, is not contrary to Isaiah, as Adimantus thinks—or rather, wishes others to think—where the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). Even from this passage he ought to have recognized that Isaiah too knew that the sons of God are peacemakers, since through him God said, “I am the one who makes peace.”

But because he fixed his attention on one part in order to misunderstand it, he blinded himself in the other. If another person, similarly blind, wished to say that the Old Testament was good, where God says, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. 33:11), and that the New Testament was evil, where Christ says, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41), would he not, by falling into a pit, drag down with himself all who followed him—unlearned and ignorant of the Scriptures—into the blindness of ignorance, with malice multiplying their error?

But the person who reads with a devout eye finds in the New Testament what these people accuse in the Old, and in the Old Testament what they praise in the New.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### 1. On What Is Written in Isaiah: “It Happened in the Year in Which King Uzziah Died: I Saw the Lord Sitting on a Lofty and Exalted Throne; and His House Was Full of His Glory, and Seraphim Stood Around It, Each Having Six Wings: With Two They Covered His Face, and with Two They Covered His Feet” (Isa. 6:1–2)

Adimantus opposes to this passage what the Apostle says: “To the immortal King of the ages, the invisible God, be honor and praise forever” (1 Tim. 1:17).

In this question we must ask what led him either to omit, in Isaiah’s vision, the two wings with which the Seraphim flew while saying, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,” or to fail to state the whole of the Apostle’s words. For the Apostle says: “To the King of the ages, the invisible, incorruptible, only God, be honor and glory forever and ever.”

Or perhaps he feared that the mention of the Trinity would commend the Prophet to the reader and suggest that something great lay hidden there? For it is said three times: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.”

But in the Apostle he perhaps noticed that, if he had said “to the incorruptible God,” we would answer him as we now answer these people: “What, then, could the race of darkness have done to the incorruptible God, if he had been unwilling to fight against it?”

Or perhaps he had been reading corrupt manuscripts, or perhaps the text in which we read Adimantus himself is corrupt. In that case there is no need to continue discussing an uncertain matter. We must now ask how the Prophet could have said that he saw God on a lofty throne, while the Apostle Paul spoke truly in calling God invisible.

I therefore ask these people whether invisible things can be seen. If they say that they can, why do they accuse the Prophet if he saw the invisible God? But if they say that they cannot, let them rather accuse the Apostle himself, if they dare, who says: “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are understood and seen through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20).

He himself says that they are invisible, and he himself again says that they are seen. Are they not compelled here to admit that they are invisible to bodily eyes but visible to the mind? Thus the Prophet too saw God, who is bodily invisible, not bodily but spiritually.

### 2. The Various Kinds of Vision in the Holy Scriptures

For many kinds of vision are found in the holy Scriptures. One is according to the eyes of the body, as when Abraham saw three men beneath the oak of Mamre (Gen. 18:1), Moses saw the fire in the bush (Exod. 3:2), and the disciples saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain between Moses and Elijah (Matt. 17:2–3), along with other examples of this kind.

A second is according to the way we imagine things that we perceive through the body. For when that part of us is taken up by divine action, many things are revealed—not through the eyes of the body, the ears, or any other bodily sense, but nevertheless in forms resembling these senses. Thus Peter saw a sheet being lowered from heaven with various animals in it (Acts 11:5–6).

Isaiah’s vision also belongs to this category, which the impious criticize with extreme ignorance. For God is not bounded by bodily form. Rather, just as many things are expressed figuratively and not literally, so many things are also shown figuratively.

A third kind of vision is according to the perception of the mind, by which understood things—truth and wisdom—are seen. Without this kind, the two kinds I mentioned earlier are either fruitless or even lead into error. For when the things that are shown divinely, whether to bodily senses or to that part of the soul that receives images of bodily things, are not merely perceived in these ways but are also understood by the mind, then revelation is perfect.

The vision I mentioned when quoting the Apostle belongs to this third kind: “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are understood and seen through the things that have been made.” God is seen by this vision when hearts are purified through the devoutness of faith and through knowledge of God and of good conduct.

What benefit did it bring King Belshazzar that he saw the hand writing on the wall before his eyes? Because he could not add to that vision the perception of the mind, he continued seeking to see what he had seen. Daniel, however, endowed with the sharpness of vision by which such things are understood, saw with his mind what the king had seen bodily (Dan. 5).

Again, King Nebuchadnezzar saw his dream through that part of the soul which receives images of bodies. Because he did not have a suitable eye of the mind with which to see better what he had seen—that is, to understand what he had seen—he therefore sought an external observer to interpret his vision, namely Daniel. Yet, in order to give firm credence to Daniel when he disclosed the meaning, he also required him to recount the dream itself (Dan. 2).

Through the revelation of the holy Spirit of God, Daniel saw both what the king had seen in his dream, through that part of the soul by which bodily images are received, and what it signified, through the mind.

A person is not a prophet of the true and supreme God if, when divinely offered visions, he sees them either only bodily or even through that part of the spirit which receives images of bodies, but does not see them with the mind.

Often, however, things are found set down in Scripture as they were seen, but not also as they were understood, so that the vision of the mind—in which the entire benefit lies—might be reserved for the training of readers. Yet from many things that are written plainly it is made clear to us how those who wrote them understood the things they placed in their books in the same figurative form in which they had been shown.

For figurative demonstrations belong to the first two kinds of vision. Simple and literal revelation of things understood and certain belongs to the mind—that is, to the vision of understanding.

Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit of supreme and unchangeable wisdom presents and governs all these kinds through wondrous and ineffable distributions.

But these wretched people accuse the Prophet for saying that he saw God, opposing the apostolic statement in which God is called invisible. If someone were to oppose to this apostolic statement the Gospel saying in which the Lord says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5:8), how would they answer that the invisible can be seen?

They use words to overwhelm the unlearned. Even if they understand in what sense God is called invisible, they fear allowing themselves to understand it. Such is the ruin of minds that, while wishing to conquer another person, are themselves conquered by error.

[Col. 0173]

# ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST THE EPISTLE OF MANICHAEUS CALLED THE FOUNDATION

[Note: [Col. 0173] Written about the year 397.]

[Note: [Col. 0171] ON THE FOLLOWING WORK, see Book 2, chapter 2, of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 631, from the words, “The book Against the Epistle of Manichaeus,” to the words, “one true God.” M.]

[Note: [Col. 0171] We understand that this book was written in 396 or 397 from the sequence of the *Retractations*, in which it is placed immediately after the books addressed to Simplicianus, which Augustine published at the beginning of his episcopate. Moreover, from the same Epistle of Manichaeus, whose opening principles he criticizes here, you will find a fragment below in *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 46, and certain other passages in *On Faith against the Manichaeans*, chapters 5, 7, and 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0173] In correcting the book *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus*, we collated the editions of Am., Er., and Lov. with the very ancient Corbie manuscript, the Gemmeticensis, Casalino, Colbertino, Sorbonico, two Victorine manuscripts, and two Vatican manuscripts, together with the variant readings of five Belgian manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0173] In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

He refutes the earlier portions of Manichaeus’s Epistle, showing that, in place of the manifest and certain knowledge he promised, Manichaeus offers his followers nothing but uncertain and absurd ravings.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0173]

### 1. Heretics are to be healed rather than destroyed.

I have both asked and ask the one true omnipotent God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, that, in refuting and overthrowing your heresy, Manichaeans—to which perhaps you too have adhered more imprudently than maliciously—he may give me a mind peaceful and tranquil, thinking more of your correction than of your overthrow. For although the Lord overthrows kingdoms of error through his servants, he nevertheless commands that human beings, insofar as they are human beings, be corrected rather than destroyed. And whatever is divinely punished before that final judgment—whether through wicked persons or just ones, whether through those who know or those who do not know, whether secretly or openly—must be believed to avail not for the destruction of human beings but for their healing; those who reject that healing are reserved for the final punishment.

Therefore, since in this universe of things some things avail for bodily punishment, such as fire, poison, disease, and the like; while others punish the soul inwardly, not through the afflictions of its body but through the snares of its desires, such as loss, exile, bereavement, insult, and the like; and while certain things are not torments but, as it were, fomentations and alleviations for the sick, such as consolations, exhortations, disputations, and whatever else is of this kind: the supreme justice of God works some of all these things even through evil persons who do not know, and others through good persons who know. It was therefore ours to choose and desire the better means, so that we might have access to your correction, not through contention, rivalry, and persecutions, but by gently consoling, kindly exhorting, and mildly disputing, as it is written: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting those who think differently with meekness” (2 Tim. 2:24–25). It was therefore ours to wish to seek these means; it belongs to God to grant what is good to those who will and ask.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Reasons why the Manichaeans should be dealt with more gently.

Let those rage against you who do not know with what labor truth is found, and how difficult it is to avoid errors. Let those rage against you who do not know how rare and arduous it is to overcome carnal phantasms by the serenity of a devout mind. Let those rage against you who do not know with how great sighs and groans the eye of the inner human being is healed, so that it may be able to behold its sun: not this sun, which you worship as a heavenly body, shining and radiant to the fleshly eyes of both human beings and cattle, but that one of which it is written through the prophet, “For me the sun of righteousness has arisen” (Mal. 4:2), and of which it is said in the Gospel, “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). Let those rage against you who do not know by what sighs and groans it comes about that God may be understood even in however small a measure. Finally, let those rage against you who have never been deceived by an error such as that by which they see you deceived.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. Augustine was once a Manichaean.

But I, who, after being tossed about long and much, was at last able to discern [Note: [Col. 0174] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads *perspicere*, “to discern.”] what that sincerity is which is apprehended without the narration of an empty fable; who, miserable as I was, scarcely deserved, with the Lord’s help, to overcome the vain imaginations of my mind, gathered from various opinions and errors; who submitted myself, so late, to the most merciful physician who called and gently persuaded me, in order to cleanse away the darkness of my mind; who long wept that the immutable and immaculate substance might deign inwardly to persuade itself to me through the harmonious divine books; who finally both investigated curiously, heard attentively, believed rashly, persuaded others of insistently to the extent that I could, and defended stubbornly and boldly against others all those fictions which hold you entangled and bound by long habit—I cannot rage against you at all. I ought now to bear with you as I bore with myself at that time, and to deal with you with the same great patience with which my neighbors dealt with me when I erred, rabid and blind, in your doctrine.

### 4.

But so that you may more easily become mild and may not oppose me with a hostile spirit harmful to yourselves, I must obtain from you, before any judge whatever, this: that all arrogance be laid aside on both sides. Let none of us say that he has already found the truth; let us seek it as though it were unknown to both parties. For it can then be sought diligently and harmoniously if it is not believed, through any rash presumption, to have been found and known. Or, if I cannot obtain this from you, at least grant me this: that I may now hear you as strangers for the first time and examine you for the first time. I think what I ask is just, provided that this condition is kept: that I will not pray with you, celebrate your meetings, or take the name of Manichaeus, unless you give me, without any obscurity, a clear account of all matters pertaining to the salvation of the soul.

## CHAPTER IV

### 5. Arguments for the Catholic faith.

For in the Catholic Church—to pass over the most sincere wisdom, to the knowledge of which few spiritual persons attain in this life, so that they may know it, indeed only in some small part because they are human beings, yet without doubt; for the rest of the multitude is made most secure not by keenness in understanding but by simplicity in believing—to pass over, then, this wisdom, which you do not believe to exist in the Catholic Church, many other things most justly keep me in her bosom. The agreement of peoples and nations keeps me; authority, begun in miracles, nourished by hope, enlarged by charity, and confirmed by antiquity, keeps me [Note: [Col. 0175] In the Corbie manuscript, “enlarged by charity, and confirmed by antiquity” is absent.]; the succession of priests keeps me, from the very seat of the Apostle Peter, to whom after his resurrection the Lord entrusted the feeding of his sheep, down to the present episcopate; finally, the very name “Catholic” keeps me, a name which this Church alone has obtained, not without reason, amid so many heresies, so that although all heretics wish to be called Catholics, nevertheless, when some stranger asks where the Catholic assembly is held, none of the heretics dares point out either his own basilica or his own house.
