Therefore these so many and so great, most beloved [Note: [Col. 0175] Two manuscripts read *clarissima*, “most illustrious.”] bonds of the Christian name rightly keep a believer in the Catholic Church, even if, because of the slowness of our understanding or the merit of our life, truth has not yet shown itself most openly. But among you, where there is none of these things to invite and keep me, the promise of truth alone resounds. If that truth is indeed shown so manifestly that it cannot come into doubt, it must be preferred to all those things by which I am held in the Catholic Church; but if it is only promised and not presented, no one will move me from that faith which binds my mind to the Christian religion [Note: [Col. 0175] Am. and all manuscripts read *religionis*, “of religion.”] by so many and such great bonds.

## CHAPTER V

### 6. Against the title of Manichaeus’s Epistle.

Let us see, then, what Manichaeus teaches me, and let us consider especially the book which you call the Epistle of the Foundation, in which nearly all that you believe is contained. For when it was read to us in that time of our misery, you called us “Illuminated” [Note: [Col. 0176] The printed editions Am. and Er. read, “we said, inclined, Amen”; Lov. reads, “we were led, inclined, by you”; two manuscripts read, “it was taught among us to the inclined.” Finally, the most ancient Corbie manuscript reads, “you called us Illuminated.” This reading is supported by what is read below in chapter 25 concerning the same Epistle: “which is usually very well known to nearly all who among you are called Illuminated.”]. Certainly it begins thus: “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ by the providence of God the Father.” These are wholesome words, from a perennial and living fountain. Now, if you please, attend with good patience to what I ask. I do not believe that this man is an apostle of Christ. I beg you not to be angry or begin to curse. For you know that I have resolved not rashly to believe anything put forward by you. I ask, then: who is this Manichaeus? You will answer: “An apostle of Christ.” I do not believe it. You will have nothing further to say or do, for you promised knowledge of the truth, and now you compel me to believe what I do not know. Perhaps you will read the Gospel to me and try from it to establish Manichaeus’s person. If, then, you found someone who did not yet believe the Gospel, what would you do if he said to you, “I do not believe”? For my part, I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me. Why, then, should I not obey those whom I obeyed when they said, “Believe the Gospel,” when they say to me, “Do not believe the Manichaeans”? Choose what you will. If you say, “Believe the Catholics,” they themselves warn me to give you no credence; therefore, believing them, I cannot but disbelieve you. If you say, “Do not believe the Catholics,” you will not act rightly by compelling me through the Gospel to believe Manichaeus, because I believed the Gospel itself through the preaching of the Catholics. But if you say, “You rightly believed the Catholics when they praised the Gospel, but wrongly believed them when they blamed Manichaeus,” do you think me so foolish that, without any reason being given, I should believe what you wish and disbelieve what you do not wish? For I act far more justly and cautiously if, because I have once believed the Catholics, I do not go over to you unless you do not command me to believe, but bring it about that I know something most manifestly and openly.

Accordingly, if you are going to give me a reason, leave the Gospel aside. If you hold fast to the Gospel, let me hold fast to those on whose instruction I believed the Gospel; and at their command let me wholly disbelieve you. But if perhaps you can find in the Gospel something entirely clear about Manichaeus’s apostleship, you will weaken for me the authority of the Catholics, who command me not to believe you. Once that authority is weakened, I shall no longer be able to believe the Gospel either, since I had believed it through them; thus whatever you bring forward from it will have no force with me. Therefore, if nothing manifest about Manichaeus’s apostleship is found in the Gospel, I shall believe the Catholics rather than you. But if you read from it something manifest on Manichaeus’s behalf, I shall believe neither them nor you: not them, because they have lied to me about you; nor you, because you present to me that Scripture, which I had believed through those who lied to me.

But far be it from me not to believe the Gospel. For in believing it, I find no way in which I can also believe you. For the names of the Apostles which are read there (Matt. 10:2–4; Mark 3:13–19; Luke 6:13–16) do not include the name of Manichaeus among themselves. And in the Acts of the Apostles we read who succeeded in the place of Christ’s betrayer (Acts 1:26); I must necessarily believe that book if I believe the Gospel, because the Catholic authority commends both Scriptures to me alike. In the same book we also have the widely known account of Paul’s calling and apostleship (Acts 9). Read to me now, if you can, in the Gospel where Manichaeus is called an apostle; or in some other book which I acknowledge that I have already believed. Or will you read that passage where the Lord promised the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, to the Apostles? See how many and how great are the things in that passage which call me back and deter me from believing Manichaeus.

## CHAPTER VI
7. Why he wrote that he was Christ’s apostle

For I ask why the beginning of this letter is “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ,” and not “The Paraclete, apostle of Jesus Christ.” But if the Paraclete, sent by Christ, sent Manichaeus, why do I read “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ,” and not rather “Manichaeus, apostle of the Paraclete”? If you say that the one who is also the Holy Spirit is Christ himself, you contradict Scripture itself, where the Lord says, “And I will send you another Paraclete” (John XIV, 16). But if you think that the name of Christ has rightly been included, not because he himself is Christ, who is also the Paraclete, but because both are of the same substance—that is, not because they are one, but because they are one thing—then Paul too could have said, “Paul, apostle of God the Father,” because the Lord said, “I and the Father are one” (ibid. X, 30). He nowhere says this; nor does any of the Apostles write that he is the Father’s apostle. What, then, is the point of this novelty? Does it not seem to you to give off the scent of some sort of deception?

Certainly, if he thought that it made no difference, why does he call himself the apostle of Christ in some letters and the apostle of the Paraclete in others? But I have always heard “of Christ,” whenever I have heard it; “of the Paraclete,” however, not even once. What else can we suppose to be the reason for this, except that pride—that mother of all heretics—impelled the man to avoid appearing to have been sent by the Paraclete, and instead to appear to have been received in such a way that he himself was called the Paraclete?

Just as Jesus Christ as man was not sent by the Son of God—that is, by the Power and Wisdom of God through which all things were made—but was received according to the Catholic faith in such a way that he himself was the Son of God—that is, so that God’s Wisdom itself might appear in that very man for the healing of sinners [Note: Erasmus and Louvain have *pectora* (“breasts” or “hearts”). This is corrected from Amerbach and the manuscripts to *peccatoribus* (“sinners”).]—so he wished it to appear that he had been received by the Holy Spirit whom Christ promised, so that whenever we hear “Manichaeus, the Holy Spirit,” we should understand “the apostle of Jesus Christ,” that is, one sent by Jesus Christ, who promised that he would send him. Such extraordinary audacity, such unspeakable sacrilege!

CHAPTER VII

8. How Manichaeus was believed by his followers to be the Holy Spirit

Yet I ask: since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—even as you yourselves confess—are joined together in no unequal nature, why do you not consider it disgraceful to proclaim that Manichaeus, received by the Holy Spirit, was born from the union of the two sexes, while you are afraid to believe that the man received by the only-begotten Wisdom of God was born of a virgin?

If human flesh, intercourse with a man, and a woman’s womb could not defile the Holy Spirit, how could a virgin’s womb defile the Wisdom of God?

Therefore, this Manichaeus, who boasts of the Holy Spirit and of evangelical reading, must grant you either that he was sent by the Holy Spirit or that he was received by him. If he was sent, let him call himself the apostle of the Paraclete; if he was received, let him grant to the man whom the only-begotten Son received a mother, if he grants a father to the man whom the Holy Spirit received. Let him believe that the Word of God was not polluted by Mary’s virginity, if he urges us to believe that the Holy Spirit could not have been polluted by the intercourse of his parents.

But if you say that Manichaeus was received by the Holy Spirit not in the womb or before the womb, but only after he had been born, it is enough for you to admit that he had flesh begotten from a man and a woman. For since you do not shrink from Manichaeus’s entrails and blood, originating from human intercourse, or from the intestines filled with dung that that flesh carried, and since you do not believe that the Holy Spirit, by whom you believe that man was received, was contaminated by any of these things, why should I shudder at a virginal womb and untouched genital organs? Why should I not rather believe that the Wisdom of God remained immaculate and pure within those maternal entrails when it received a man?

Therefore, whether your Manichaeus asserts that he was sent by the Paraclete or received by him, he will be able to establish none of these claims. I, now more cautious, believe neither that he was sent nor that he was received.

CHAPTER VIII

9. The feast of Manichaeus’s birth

For when he added the words “by the providence of God the Father,” what else did he intend, after naming Jesus Christ, whose apostle he says he is, and God the Father, by whose providence he says he was sent by the Son, except that we should believe the Holy Spirit himself to be the third? For this is how he writes: “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ, by the providence of God the Father.”

The Holy Spirit is not named, although he especially ought to have been named by one who commends his apostleship to us through the promise of the Paraclete, so that he might overwhelm the inexperienced with evangelical authority. When this is asked of you, you reply, of course, that, when Manichaeus the apostle is named, the Holy Spirit the Paraclete is being named, because he deigned to come in Manichaeus.

I ask, therefore—as I was saying above—why you recoil when the Catholic Church says that the one in whom divine Wisdom came was born of a virgin, while you do not recoil at all from proclaiming that the one in whom you say the Holy Spirit came was born of a woman joined to a man.

What else am I to suspect, then, except that this Manichaeus, who seeks access to the minds of the inexperienced through the name of Christ, wished to be worshiped in place of Christ himself?

I shall briefly explain the basis for my inference. When I was often asking you, at the time [Col. 0179] when I was listening to you, what reason there was for the Lord’s Easter to be celebrated in most places with no observance at all, and sometimes by only a few people with the greatest tepidity—with no vigils prescribed, no longer fast imposed on the Auditors, and, finally, no more festive preparation—while you pursued with great honors your *bema*, that is, the day on which Manichaeus was killed, with a tribunal furnished with five steps and decorated with precious linens, set out openly and placed before those who worshiped it [Note: *Bêma*, that is, “a step” or “steps”]—when, therefore, I asked about this, the reply was that the day of the passion of the one who had truly suffered ought to be celebrated; but Christ, who had not been born and had displayed to human eyes not real but feigned human flesh, had not endured a passion but fabricated one.

Who would not groan at this? People who wish to be called Christians fear that the truth might be polluted by a virgin’s womb, but do not fear falsehood.

But to return to the matter: who would not suspect, upon careful consideration, that Manichaeus denied that Christ was born of a woman and had a human body for this reason—that his passion, whose commemoration is now the most festive observance throughout the whole world, should not be celebrated by those who had believed in him, and that the solemnity they desired should instead honor the day of his death with such devotion?

For this was what pleased us most in that celebration of the *bema*: it was attended at Easter [Note: The manuscripts read “because it was attended in place of Easter” (*pro Pascha frequentabatur*)], because we desired that festive day all the more intensely once another day, which had usually been the sweetest, had been taken away.

CHAPTER IX

10. When the Holy Spirit was sent

Perhaps you will say to me: “When, then, did the Paraclete promised by the Lord come?”

If I had nothing else to believe, I would still more readily expect him to come in the future than admit that he came through Manichaeus. But now, since the coming of the Holy Spirit is most clearly proclaimed in the Acts of the Apostles, what necessity compels me to believe heretics so dangerously and so readily?

For in the book mentioned above it is written:

“We have indeed composed [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read *feci* (“I composed”); the manuscripts read *fecimus* (“we composed”).] the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and to teach on the day when he chose the Apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the Gospel. After his passion he presented himself alive to them by many proofs, appearing to them over forty days and teaching them about the kingdom of God, and how he had lived with them, and commanding them [Note: In Louvain, Venice, and Louvain editions: “how he lived with them, and commanded them.”] not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the Father’s promise, which,” he said, “you heard from my mouth. For John baptized with water, but you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, which you will also receive not many days from now, until Pentecost.”

When they had come together, they asked him, saying: “Lord, will you at this time be manifested, and when will the kingdom of Israel be restored?” [Note: Erasmus and Lyons: “Will you restore the kingdom of Israel?” Venice: “Will you present the kingdom of Israel?” Manuscript reading: “Will you be manifested?”]

But he said: “No one can know the time which the Father has placed in his own power; but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the whole earth” (Acts I, 8).

There you have the place where he reminded the disciples of the Father’s promise, which they had heard from his mouth, concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit. Now let us see when he was sent.

A little later the text continues and says:

“When the day of Pentecost had been completed, they were all together in one place with the same spirit. Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind being carried along, and it filled the whole place where they were sitting. Tongues divided as if by fire appeared to them and came to rest upon each one of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in tongues, as the Spirit gave them ability to utter them.

“Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, men from every nation under heaven. And when the sound occurred, the crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language and in his own tongues. They were astonished and amazed, saying to one another: ‘Are not all these who are speaking Galileans by nationality? And how do we each hear in the language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, Armenia and Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the regions of Africa [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “and the region of Africa.”] that is toward Cyrene; and those Romans who had arrived, and Jews, and inhabitants [Note: The manuscripts read “and Jewish inhabitants,” omitting the second *et*], Cretans, and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own tongues the great works of God.’

“They were astonished and perplexed at what had happened, saying: ‘What does this mean?’ But others mocked, saying: ‘These men are all full of new wine’” (Acts II, 1–13).

There is where the Holy Spirit came. What more do you want? If the Scriptures are to be believed, why should I not believe these writings above all, which have been confirmed by the strongest authority? Together with the Gospel, in which we likewise believe that the Holy Spirit was promised, they deserved to be made known to the peoples, commended to posterity, and proclaimed.

When, therefore, I read these Acts of the Apostles, joined to the Gospel by equal authority, I find not only that the Holy Spirit was promised to those true Apostles, but also that he was sent so manifestly that no room was left for error concerning the matter.

CHAPTER X

11. The Holy Spirit was given twice

For the Lord’s glorification among human beings is his resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven. It is written in the Gospel according to John (*κατὰ Ἰωάννην*): “But the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 39).

If, therefore, he had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified, then, once Jesus had been glorified, he necessarily was given at once. And because there was a twofold glorification, according to his humanity and according to his divinity, the Holy Spirit was also given twice: once after he rose from the dead, when he breathed upon the face of the disciples, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (ibid. XX, 22); and again after he ascended into heaven, when ten days had passed.

That number signifies perfection, since the Trinity of the Creator is added to the number seven, by which the whole created order is established. Spiritual men treat of these matters piously and cautiously in many ways.

But I shall not depart from my purpose. I previously undertook to deal with you in such a way that I would not teach you—for you might perhaps consider that arrogant—but would strive as though I myself were learning from you what I had been unable to learn in nine years.

Therefore I have writings to which I can entrust my belief concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit. If you forbid me to believe them, lest I rashly believe what I do not know—for this is how you are accustomed to admonish us—then I shall believe your writings much less. Therefore either remove all books [Note: The editions have “remove all your books.” The word “your” is absent from the manuscripts.] from the discussion and lay open through argument a truth about which I cannot doubt, or produce such books that I am not arrogantly forced to believe something, but am shown without deceit what I am to learn.

“Perhaps,” you say, “this letter too is such a book.”

I do not wish, then, to linger any longer at its threshold. Let us examine what lies within.

CHAPTER XI

12. Manichaeus promises truth but does not provide it

“These,” he says, “are saving words from an eternal and living fountain. Whoever hears them and first believes them, then keeps what they teach, will never be subject to death, but will enjoy an eternal and glorious life. For surely that person must be judged blessed who has been instructed by this divine knowledge, through which, once liberated, he will remain in everlasting life.”

And this, as you see, is a promise, not yet a presentation, of truth. You too can very easily observe that any errors whatsoever can be disguised beneath such a veil, so that they may secretly creep into the minds of the inexperienced through an ornamented doorway.

For if he had said: “These are deadly words from a poisonous fountain. Whoever hears them and first believes them, then keeps what they teach, will never be restored to life, but will be afflicted with a punitive and wretched death—for surely that person must be judged miserable who has been entangled in this infernal ignorance, through which, once plunged down, he will remain in everlasting torments”—if he had said this, he would have spoken the truth. But such a statement would not only have won no reader for this book; it would also have stirred everyone into whose hands it came to the greatest hatred.

Let us therefore proceed to what follows, and not be deceived by words that can be common to the good and the wicked, to the learned and the ignorant. What follows, then?

“May the peace of the invisible God and knowledge of the truth be with the holy and most beloved brothers who believe in and equally serve the heavenly commandments.”

So be it, as he says. For this too is a kind and most welcome wish. Let us merely remember that such words can be spoken both by good teachers and by deceivers.

Therefore, if he said nothing except things of this sort, I would grant that everyone ought to read and embrace his writing. Nor would I disapprove of what follows. For he adds:

“But may the right hand of the light also protect you and rescue you from every evil attack [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript has “from every evil incursion.”] and from the snares of the world.”

And, in general, I do not wish to criticize anything written at the beginning of this letter until we come to the argument, lest much effort be spent on minor matters. Let us now examine the man’s very clear promise.

CHAPTER XII

14. Manichaeus’s ravings. A battle fought before the foundation of the world

“Concerning this matter, then, most beloved Pattici [Note: The editions have “most beloved, you have heard.” The old Corbeiensis manuscript, written a thousand years ago, has *Pattici* in place of *audisti* (“you have heard”), perhaps the name of the person to whom Manichaeus gave the letter.], which you indicated to me when you said that you desired to know what sort of thing the generation of Adam and Eve was—whether they were brought forth by a word, or were firstborn from a body—you will receive an answer as appropriate.

“For the matter has been inserted and mentioned by many people in various writings and accounts in dissimilar ways [Note: Amerbach and several manuscripts have “revelations.”]. Therefore the truth of this matter, as it actually is, is unknown to almost all peoples and to all who have also argued about it at length and at great effort. For if the knowledge of it had become manifest to them concerning the generation of Adam and Eve, they would never have been subject to corruption and death.”

He therefore promises us manifest knowledge of this matter, so that we may not be subject to corruption and death.

And if that is still not enough, see what follows:

“Necessarily, then,” he says, “more things must first be mentioned, so that one may arrive at this mystery without any ambiguity.”

This is what I was saying: truth ought to be demonstrated to me in such a way that I arrive at it without any ambiguity. Even if he himself had not promised this, I ought nevertheless to demand and insist upon it, so that, in exchange for such a reward—the most evident and certain knowledge—I would not be ashamed to become a Manichaean from being a Catholic Christian, despite the objections of all others.

Let us now hear what he brings forward.

15. “Therefore, if it seems good to you,” he says, “listen first to what existed before the foundation of the world and how the battle was waged, so that you may distinguish the nature of light from that of darkness.”

He has now proposed things altogether incredible and false. For who would believe that any battle was fought before the foundation of the world?

And yet, if it is something credible, we have come here not merely to believe but to know. When someone says that the Persians and Scythians fought one another many years ago, he is speaking of something credible; nevertheless, it is something that we can believe after hearing or reading about it, not know through personal experience and apprehension.

Therefore, if he said something of this sort, I would reject him. For he did not promise things that would compel belief, but things that I could know without any ambiguity. How, then, shall I not reject him when he speaks not only of uncertain things but even of incredible ones?

But what if he makes these things clear and known through some arguments? Let us therefore listen, if we can, with complete patience and gentleness, to what follows.

CHAPTER XIII

16. Two contrary substances. The kingdom of light. Manichaeus presents uncertainties as certainties

“For at the beginning,” he says, “there were two substances separated from one another. God the Father held the dominion of light, eternal in his holy offspring, magnificent in power, true by his very nature, always rejoicing in his own eternity, containing within himself wisdom and living senses, through which he also comprehended the twelve members of his light—that is, the overflowing riches of his own kingdom. Within each of his members are hidden thousands of innumerable and immeasurable treasures.

“The Father himself, pre-eminent in his own praise and incomprehensible in greatness, has joined to himself blessed and glorious ages, not to be measured either by number or by duration. With them the same holy and illustrious Father and begetter dwells, with no needy or infirm being established in his distinguished kingdoms.

“His most splendid kingdoms are founded upon the luminous and blessed earth in such a way that they can never be moved or shaken by anyone.”

17. How is he going to prove these things to me, or how did he himself come to know them? Do not frighten me with the name of the Paraclete.

First, I came not to believe unknown things but to know certainties, and you yourselves have made me more cautious. You know how vehemently you are accustomed to attack those who believe rashly, especially when the very man who has now begun to tell uncertain stories recently promised complete and firm knowledge.

CHAPTER XIV

He promised knowledge of certain things but commands belief in uncertain things

Next, since, if faith is to be demanded of me, that Scripture would hold me more firmly in which I read that the Holy Spirit came and inspired the Apostles (Acts II, 1–4), to whom the Lord had promised that he would send him (John XIV, 16, 26).

Therefore either prove to me that the things he says are true, so that you may show what I cannot believe; or prove to me that the one who speaks is the Holy Spirit, so that I may believe what you cannot demonstrate.

For I profess the Catholic faith, and through it I expect to arrive at certain knowledge. But you, who are trying to undermine my faith, provide certain knowledge, if you can, so that you may convict me of having believed rashly what I believed.

You put forward two claims: one, when you say that the one who speaks is the Holy Spirit; the other, when you say that the things he speaks are manifest. I ought to know both of these from you without any doubt. But I am not greedy: teach me one of them. Show that this is the Holy Spirit, and I will believe that what he says is true, even if I do not know it; or show that what he says is true, and I will believe that he is the Holy Spirit, even if I do not know it.

Could anyone deal with you more fairly or more kindly? Yet you are able to show neither this nor that. You have chosen nothing except to praise what you believe and mock what I believe.

When, therefore, I in turn praise what I believe and mock what you believe, what do you think we ought to judge or do, except leave those who invite us to know certainties and afterward command us to believe uncertainties, and follow those who first invite us to believe what we are not yet able to see, so that, made stronger by faith itself, we may deserve to understand what we believe—not now through human beings, but with God himself inwardly illuminating and strengthening our mind?

18. Since I have asked how he can prove these things to me, I now ask how he himself came to know them.

If he says that the Holy Spirit revealed them to him and that his mind was divinely enlightened so that he could know the things he says as certain and manifest, then he himself indicates the difference between knowing and believing.

For the one to whom these things are shown most openly possesses knowledge; but to those to whom he recounts them he does not impart knowledge—he persuades them to believe. Whoever rashly assents to him becomes a Manichaean, not by knowing certainties but by believing uncertainties, just as he once deceived us, inexperienced youths.

He therefore ought not to have promised us knowledge, manifest understanding, or arrival at what is sought without any ambiguity. He ought rather to have said that these things had been shown to him, while those to whom they were recounted ought to believe him concerning things they did not know.

But if he had said this, who would not have replied: “If I am going to believe things unknown, why should I not rather believe those things that are already celebrated by the agreement of the learned and the unlearned, and confirmed throughout all peoples by the gravest authority?”

Fearing that this would be said to him, he casts a mist over the inexperienced, first promising knowledge of certain things and afterward commanding belief in uncertain ones.

Yet if he is told at least to prove that these things were shown to him, he fails in the same way, and commands us to believe this as well. Who could endure such great deception and such great arrogance?

CHAPTER XV

19. What he teaches is not only uncertain but also false. The ravings about the earth and the people of darkness beside the side of the holy earth and the substance of God. First refutation: he ascribes parts and sides to God’s nature as though it were spread through space by its bulk

But what if, with God and our Lord helping me, I demonstrate that what he says is not only uncertain but also false?

What could be found more wretched than this superstition, which not only fails to provide the knowledge and truth it promises, but says things that are profoundly opposed to knowledge and truth? This will become clearer in what follows.

For he says:

“Beside one part and side of that illustrious and holy earth there was the earth of darkness, deep and immense in extent, in which fiery bodies dwelt, namely, pestilential kinds. Here were boundless darknesses, immeasurable in their outpouring from the same nature, with their own offspring. Beyond them were muddy and turbid waters with their inhabitants; within these were dreadful and violent winds with their prince and progenitors. Again there was a fiery and corruptible region with its leaders and nations. Farther inward was a people full of gloom and smoke, in which dwelt the monstrous prince and leader of them all, having innumerable princes around him, of all of whom he himself was the mind and origin. These, then, were the five natures of the pestilential earth.”

20. If he said that God’s nature was an aerial or even an ethereal body, he would certainly be mocked by all who are able, with whatever gaze of a now more serene mind, to behold the nature of wisdom and truth as neither stretched out nor spread through any spatial intervals, great and magnificent without bulk, neither smaller in one part nor larger in another, but in every respect equal to the supreme Father, having neither one thing here nor another elsewhere, but whole everywhere and present everywhere.

CHAPTER XVI

The soul itself, although changeable, is not extended through spatial intervals, for it senses as a whole in each part of the body

But what shall I say about truth and wisdom, which surpass all the powers of the soul, when the very nature of the soul, which is found to be changeable, occupies spatial intervals in no way through any bulk of its own?

For whatever possesses any thickness whatsoever [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “whatever is extended by any thickness whatsoever.”] can only be diminished by division, possessing one thing here and another elsewhere. A finger is smaller than the whole hand, and one finger is smaller than two; this finger is in one place, that finger in another, and the rest of the hand elsewhere.

We see this not only in the bulk of articulated bodies [Note: The editions have “in the movable joints of bodies.” This has been corrected with the aid of the old Corbeiensis manuscript], but also in the earth: this part of the earth is not where that part is, because each occupies its own place. A smaller portion of moisture occupies a smaller place, and a larger portion a larger place; one part is near the bottom, another near the rim of the cup.

The same is true of the parts of the air: each fills its own place. It is impossible for the air with which this house is filled to have, simultaneously with itself in the same house, the air that the neighbors possess. One part of the light itself pours through this window, another through that; more through the larger window, less through the smaller.

Nor can there be any body at all—whether heavenly or earthly, aerial or moist—that is not smaller in a part than in the whole, or that can in any way have another part simultaneously in the place of this part. Rather, possessing one thing here and another elsewhere, it is spread through all spatial intervals, distant and divisible—or, better, as I might say, extended as a bulk capable of being cut into pieces.

But the nature of the soul, even if we consider not that power by which it understands truth but that lower power by which it contains the body and senses in the body, is in no way found to be extended through spatial intervals by any bulk.

For it is wholly present to each individual part of its body, since it senses as a whole in each part. Its part is not smaller in the finger and larger in the arm, as the finger itself is smaller than the arm. Rather, it is everywhere equally great, because it is everywhere whole.

When the finger is touched, it does not sense through the whole body, and yet it senses as a whole. That touch is not hidden from the whole soul; this would not happen unless the whole soul were present.

Nor is it wholly present when the finger is touched and it senses in the finger in such a way that it abandons the rest of the body and gathers itself into that one place where it senses.

Rather, when it senses as a whole in the finger of the hand, if another place on the foot is touched, it does not cease to sense as a whole there also. Thus, in individually distant places, it is wholly present all at once: it does not abandon one place in order to be wholly in another, nor does it hold both in such a way that it has one part here and another elsewhere. Its ability to present itself wholly to individual places at the same time—because it senses as a whole in each—sufficiently demonstrates that it is not confined by spatial intervals.

CHAPTER XVII

Memory receives images of immense places

What if we consider its memory, not of intelligible things but of these bodily things, which even animals are perceived to possess? For animals proceed without error through familiar places, beasts return to their lairs [Note: The editions have “and return to their rooms.” This is corrected from the manuscripts], dogs recognize the bodies of their masters, and while sleeping they often mutter and sometimes break into barking. They could not do this in any way unless images of things seen or somehow sensed through the body were active in their memory.

Who could worthily conceive where these images are received, where they are carried, or where they are formed?

If they could not be larger than the quantity occupied by our body, someone might say that the soul forms and preserves these images within the very spatial extent of its body, which also contains them.

But now, although the body occupies only a very small part of the earth, the mind turns over images of immense regions and of heaven and earth. As these images depart and succeed one another in crowds, the mind does not become cramped. From this it shows that it is not spread through places: it is not, as it were, captured by images of the largest places, but rather captures them—not in some recess, but by an ineffable power and capacity by which it can add anything to them or subtract anything from them, contract them into a narrow space, expand them through immensity, arrange them as it wishes, disturb them, multiply them, or reduce them to a small number or to a single image.

CHAPTER XVIII

The power of understanding judges the truth of things and thought itself

What shall I now say about that power by which truth is understood, by which one vigorously resists those very images drawn from bodily sensation when they oppose themselves as though they were truth?

By this power one sees, for example, that the real Carthage is one thing and another is the Carthage that the mind imagines, which it changes with complete ease according to its own will.

By the same ease come innumerable worlds, through which Epicurus’s thought wandered innumerably. And, not to pursue too many examples, by the same ease comes this earth of light, spread through infinite spaces, and the five caves of the people of darkness with their inhabitants, in which the phantasms of Manichaeus have dared to usurp the name of truth.

What, then, is this power that distinguishes these things? Whatever its magnitude, it is certainly greater than all these things, and it is conceived without any such imagination of things.

Find spatial intervals for it, if you can. Spread it through places; extend it by the swelling of an infinite bulk. Surely, if you think properly, you cannot.

For whatever of this sort occurs to you, you judge by thought itself that it can be divided into parts, and you make one part smaller there and another larger, as much as you please. But you see that the very thing by which you judge these matters is above them—not by the height of a place, but by the dignity of its power.

CHAPTER XIX

21. If the soul is not extended through places, God is much less so

Therefore, if you perceive that the soul—so often changeable, whether through the throng of its various desires, through emotions bending themselves according to abundance or lack of things, through the countless games of its phantasms, through forgetfulness and memory, through learning and ignorance—if, as I said, you perceive that the soul, so often changed by these and similar movements, is not spread out and extended through places, but surpasses all such intervals by the vitality of its power, what should be thought or judged concerning God himself?

He remains unshaken and unchangeable above all rational minds, assigning to each whatever ought to be assigned. The soul dares to speak of him more readily than it can see him; and it speaks of him all the less, the more purely it is able to see him.

Yet if he were extended, as the phantasms of the Manichaeans loudly proclaim, with one part bounded and with limitless space stretching out on the other sides, then however many particles there might be in him, and innumerable fragments, some larger and some smaller, would be measured according to the will of the thinker, so that, for example, a two-foot portion in him would be eight times smaller than a ten-foot portion.

For this must necessarily happen to all natures that are spread through such spaces and cannot be wholly present everywhere. But this is not found in the soul itself, although those who are unable to consider these matters believe it of the soul in a deformed and disgraceful manner.

CHAPTER XX
## 22. The Delusion about Two Earths Refuted

Nevertheless, perhaps one must not deal with carnal minds in this way, but rather descend to the thoughts of those who, by thinking, either do not dare—or are not yet able—to follow an incorporeal and spiritual nature [Note: An old Corbie manuscript reads, “to pursue by thinking.”], so that they do not even consider their own thought by that same thought, and discover that it judges all such spatial extensions without any spatial extension of its own [Note: The printed editions read, “and discover that it judges spatial extensions by spatial extensions themselves.” The reading is corrected from the Corbie manuscript.].

Let us therefore descend to their senses and ask them: alongside which part and beside which side, as Manichaeus says, was the earth of darkness situated in relation to that illustrious and holy earth? For he says, “alongside one part and side,” but does not say which part or which side, right or left. Whichever they choose, this is certainly clear: one side is spoken of only where there is also another side. But where there are either three or more sides, either the perimeter of a figure is understood to be bounded on every side, or, if it extends infinitely in some direction, it must nevertheless be bounded by those features that are called sides.

Let them therefore say what was joined to the earth of light on another side or on other sides, if the race of darkness was alongside one side. They do not say. But when pressed to say, they declare that the other sides of that earth—which they call the earth of light—are infinite: that is, that it extends through infinite spaces and is confined by no boundary. They do not understand that these are no longer sides—a matter evident even to the dullest minds. They would be sides only if they ended at their own boundaries.

“But what does it matter to me,” he says, “if they are not sides?” Yet when you said “alongside one part and side,” you compelled us to understand another part or other parts, and another side or other sides. For if there had been only one side, you should have said simply “alongside the side,” not “alongside one side.” Thus, in our own body, we correctly say that something is beside one eye, because there is another eye; or beside one breast, because there is another. But if we say “beside one nose” or “beside one navel,” since there is no other, both the learned and the unlearned will laugh at us. But I do not press you with words: perhaps you wished to call one side “one” in the sense of “unique.”

## Chapter XXI

### The Same Earth of Light, if Joined to the Earth of Darkness, Must Be Corporeal. The Shape of the Earth of Darkness Joined to the Earth of Light

What, then, was beside that side of the earth which you call illustrious and holy? “The earth of darkness,” you say. What—do you at least concede that this earth was corporeal? You must say so, since you assert that all bodies derive their origin from it.

What, then, I ask, however dull and carnal you may be, do you not at some point notice even this: that these two earths cannot be joined side to side unless both were corporeal? Why, then, were we told—by some unknown perversity of blindness—that only the earth of darkness was or is corporeal, whereas the one called the earth of light must be believed incorporeal and spiritual? [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “we were told by some unknown [source],” and so on. The preposition “by” is absent from the Ambrosian manuscript and the other manuscripts.]

Let us at last wake up, good people, and, having been reminded of something very easy, let us pay attention: two earths cannot be joined to one another side to side unless both are bodies [Note: The manuscripts read, “unless both”—masculine plural—rather than “unless both”—neuter plural.].

### 23.

Or, if we are too dense and slow even for this, I ask whether the earth of darkness itself had one side and all the others infinite, like the earth of light. They do not believe this, for they fear that it might appear equal to God.

They therefore say that it was infinite in depth and in length; but upward, above it, they assert that there were spaces of infinite emptiness [Note: The common printed editions read: “infinite in depth; and in length, upward or above it,” and so forth. The manuscripts are to be followed, since they read “but” where the editions have “or,” and they punctuate the words as follows: “infinite in depth and in length; but upward, above it,” and so forth. For this earth is compared below to a black square: downward is “in depth,” and backward is “in length,” both of them infinite.].

And lest the earth of darkness itself appear to occupy one part while the earth of light occupied two, they narrow it on two sides as well. Imagine—since what is being said can thus be seen more easily—that a single loaf were divided crosswise into four squares, three of them white and one black. Now remove the divisions between the three white squares, and make them infinite both upward and downward and infinitely backward in every direction. This, they believe, is how the earth of light exists. As for the black square, make it infinite downward and backward, while above it there is an immeasurable emptiness: this, they think, is the earth of darkness [Note: The printed editions add here, “this is how they believe the earth of light exists”; the words are absent from the manuscripts.]. But they present these matters as if they were secrets to those who pay very close and careful attention.

## Chapter XXII

### The Shape of the Earth of Light Is More Deformed

Nevertheless, if this is so, it appears that the earth of darkness touches the earth of light on two sides. And surely, if it is touched on two sides, it also touches on two sides. Certainly, the earth of darkness was alongside one side.

### 24.

Furthermore, how ugly the shape of the earth of light appears: as though a hoof were split by some black wedge compressed beneath it, bounded only along the line where it is split, while above it also gapes open and remains exposed, with the emptiness inserted between it and whatever extends infinitely upward from the surface of the earth of darkness [Note: The word “earth” had been omitted in the printed editions; it is found in the manuscripts.].

How much better, then, is the shape of the earth of darkness itself shown to be! For the one splits, while this one is split; the one is inserted, while this one lies open between; the one leaves no room in itself for any emptiness, while this one is loose only on its lower side, where it is filled from beneath by the hostile wedge.

Thus ignorant and avaricious men, assigning greater honor to a multiplicity of parts than to unity, so that they might give six parts to the earth of light—three downward and three upward—preferred that the earth of light be penetrated rather than penetrate. For even if they deny that it is mixed with the other, they cannot deny that it is penetrated by it.

## Chapter XXIII

### The Anthropomorphites Sin Less Seriously than the Manichaeans

### 25.

Now compare—not the spiritual men of the Catholic faith, among whom the mind, insofar as it can in this life, perceives that the divine substance and nature is extended through no spatial dimensions and shaped by no measurements of lines—but compare our carnal and childish people, who, when they hear certain bodily members mentioned allegorically in connection with God, as when God’s eyes and God’s ears are spoken of, commonly picture God for themselves in the form of a human body, through the freedom of their imagination.

Compare such people with those Manichaeans who customarily describe these absurdities to attentive and inquisitive people as if they were great secrets. Consider who has the more tolerable and honorable conception of God: those who think of him in human form, endowed with the highest dignity proper to that kind of form; or those who imagine him spread out as an infinite mass—not infinite in every direction, but infinite and compressed through three squares, split on one side, open, gaping, and loosened above by emptiness, while below he is wedged in by the earth of darkness; or, if this is better said, open above by his own nature, and entered below by another’s [Note: The printed editions read, “constricted below.” One Vatican manuscript reads, “stopped up.” Another Vatican manuscript, together with Victorinus and the oldest Corbie manuscript, reads, “entered below.” The participle is rare in this usage, though it is used by classical authors such as Livy and Ovid.].

Look, I laugh with you at carnal people who are not yet able to think of spiritual things and therefore imagine God in human form. And you, if you can, laugh with me at those who, with a most pitiable form of thought, imagine so deformed and shameful a split or cleft in God—so pointlessly gaping above, so dishonorably stopped up below.

There is also this difference: if those carnal people who imagine God in human form are content within the bosom of the Catholic Church, and while they still need to be nourished with milk do not rush into rash opinions, but cultivate there a pious desire to seek, ask there in order to receive, and knock there so that it may be opened to them, they begin to understand spiritually the allegories and parables of Scripture. Gradually they come to discern the divine powers, appropriately expressed in one place under the name of ears, in another of eyes, elsewhere of hands or feet, or even of wings and feathers, and also of a shield, a sword, a helmet, and countless other such things. The more they advance in this understanding, the more firmly they are established as Catholics.

But when the Manichaeans abandon the imagination of that figure, they can no longer be Manichaeans. For they attribute this as something almost proper and especially distinctive to the praises of their founder: they say that the divine mysteries which had been placed figuratively in the books of the ancients were reserved to be explained and demonstrated by this man, who was to come last [Note: The manuscripts read, “which had been placed figuratively in the books,” whereas the printed editions read, “which had been placed in books concerning the divine mysteries.”]. For this reason, they say, no teacher divinely sent would come after him, since he had said nothing through allegories and figures, but had both opened up the ancient matters that had been expressed in this way and displayed his own teachings plainly and explicitly.

They therefore have no interpretations to which they can return when they read about their founder: “Alongside one part and side of that illustrious and holy earth was the earth of darkness” [Col. 0190]. Wherever they turn, they must necessarily be driven by the misery of their fantasies into splits, abrupt cuttings-off, and joints, or into most shameful clefts [Note: All the manuscripts read “supports” or “buttresses” rather than “clefts.”], which it would be most pitiable to believe not merely of the unchangeable nature of God, but of every incorporeal nature, even though it may be changeable, as the soul is.

And yet, if I were unable to direct my attention upward, or to unfold my thoughts from the false images fixed in my memory through the bodily senses into the freedom and purity of spiritual nature, how much better it would be for me to think of God in the form of a human body than to attach that black wedge to the lower cleft in him, while, finding nothing with which to plug the vast looseness above, I left it gaping and open in such immeasurable emptiness. What could be uglier than this opinion? What could be said or imagined more dark than this error?

## Chapter XXIV

### 26. The Number of Natures in the Manichaean Fantasy

Next I want it to be explained to me: when I read of God the Father, and of his kingdoms founded above the bright and blessed earth, are the Father, his kingdoms, and the earth of one and the same substance and nature?

If this is so, then that wedge of the race of darkness does not split and penetrate some other nature that is, as it were, the body of God [Note: The manuscripts read, “some other nature that is the body of God.”]—which would itself be shameful in an indescribably deformed way—but that wedge of the earth of darkness splits and penetrates the very nature of God.

I beg you, think about these things. You are human beings. I beg you, think about them and flee the sacrileges of such fantasies. If possible, tear them out and drive them from your breasts, and eradicate them from your faith.

Or will you say that those three are not of one and the same nature, but that the Father belongs to one nature, the kingdoms to another, and the earth to another, so that each possesses its own distinct substances and natures, arranged according to degrees of excellence? If this is true, Manichaeus ought to have proclaimed not two but four natures.

But if the Father and the kingdoms have one nature, while only the earth has a different one, then three natures should have been proclaimed. Or if he preferred to speak of two because the earth of darkness does not belong to God, I ask how the earth of light belongs to God. For if it has a different nature and God did not generate it or make it, it does not belong to him, and his kingdoms have been placed in what is another’s.

Or if it belongs to him because it is near him, then the earth of darkness must also belong to him, since it touches the earth of light not merely by proximity but also by penetrating and splitting it.

But if he generated it, it ought not to be believed to have a different nature. For what God generated must be believed to be what God is, just as the Catholic faith holds concerning the only-begotten Son.

Thus necessity drives you back to that shamefulness which must be fled and detested: not that another and different earth, but that very nature of God, is split by the black wedge.

But if God did not generate it and instead made it, I ask from what he made it. If from himself, what is that other than generating it? If from some alien nature, I ask whether that nature was good or evil.

If it was good, then there was some good nature that did not belong to God—which you will in no way dare to say. But if it was evil, then the race of darkness was not the only evil nature.

Or perhaps God had already taken a part from it and converted that part into the earth of light, establishing his kingdoms above it? Then he would have done this with the whole of it, so that long ago no evil nature would exist.

But if he did not make the earth of light from an alien substance, it remains that he made it from nothing.

## Chapter XXV

### 27. The Omnipotent God Creates from Nothing Other Goods Inferior to One Another. In Whatever Form the Union of the Two Earths Is Imagined, It Always Contains Deformity or Absurdity

Therefore, if you are now persuaded that the omnipotent God can make something good from nothing, come over to the Catholic Church and learn that all the natures which God made and created, arranged in degrees of excellence from the highest to the lowest, are good, though some are better than others.

Learn that they were made from nothing, when God the craftsman worked through his wisdom, in a manner of speaking, with power, so that what did not exist might exist; and that insofar as a thing existed, it was good, while insofar as it fell short, it showed that it had not been generated from God but had been made by him from nothing.

For if you consider the matter, you will find nothing that can hold you back. You cannot say that the earth of light as you describe it is what God is, lest the very nature of God be constricted by the deformity of that square. Nor can you say that it was generated from him, lest it nevertheless be understood to be what God is, bringing you back to the same deformity [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “you return,” rather than “it returns.”]. Nor can you say that it is alien to him, lest you be compelled to say that he established his kingdoms in what is another’s, and that there are not two but three natures. Nor can you say that he made it from an alien substance, lest either there have been some other good besides God, or some evil besides the race of darkness.

It therefore remains that you must confess that God made the earth of light from nothing. And if you do not wish to believe that, if God could make from nothing some great good which was nevertheless inferior to God himself, then, because he is good and envies no good, he could also make another good inferior to the first; he could make a third to which the second would be preferred; and so on, continuing the order of created natures down to the lowest good, until the whole universe of them stood as a determinate totality, rather than dissipating into an uncertain, indefinite number.

But if you do not even wish to confess that God made this earth of light from nothing, there will be no way for you to escape such great deformities and such sacrilegious opinions.

### 28.

Or consider this at least: since carnal thought is free to imagine whatever fantasies it pleases, perhaps you can discover some other form for this conjunction of the two earths, so that such a detestable and repulsive appearance of things does not present itself to the mind.

Imagine, then, the earth of God—whether it is of the same nature as God or of a different nature, but nevertheless the place in which God’s kingdoms are founded—lying with such an immense mass through the boundlessness that its limbs extend and remain open to infinity, and that from below it receives, in the most shameful and disgraceful manner, that constricted wedge of the earth of darkness, itself of immeasurable size [Col. 0192].

But whatever other figure you may discover by which these two earths are joined to one another, you cannot erase the writings of Manichaeus. I do not mean the other writings in which he described these things more explicitly; perhaps, because fewer people know them, they may seem to involve less danger. I mean these very words now under discussion, from the Epistle of the Foundation, which is usually best known to almost all those among you who are called the Enlightened:

“Alongside one part and side of that illustrious and holy earth was the earth of darkness, profound and of immeasurable magnitude.”

## Chapter XXVI

### The Manichaeans Are Cornered, Whether They Say That the Union Was Made by a Twisting, Curved, or Straight Side

In this third kind of junction there would be a harmony and beauty suitable to both earths. What more are we waiting for? We have hold of the fact that it was alongside a side. Now invent whatever shapes you please and describe whatever lines you please: that enormous mass of the earth of darkness was certainly joined to the earth of light by either a straight side, a curved side, or a twisting side.

But if by a twisting side, then that holy earth also has a twisting side. For if it itself has a straight side and is touched by this earth’s twisting side, deep caverns, empty through infinity, remain open between them; and the emptiness was no longer only above the earth of darkness, as we used to hear.

If this is so, how much better it would have been for the earth of light to withdraw somewhat farther away, allowing so much emptiness to intervene that the earth of darkness could not touch it anywhere. Indeed, so great a space of empty depth could have been left open that, if any wickedness arose from that race, and even if the princes of darkness rashly wished to leap into it—for bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by corporeal air—they would be hurled through that emptiness. Since it extended infinitely downward, they would never reach any bottom; and even if they could live forever, they could never do harm while they were continually carried downward.

But if it was joined by a curved side, then the earth of light also received it disgracefully in a curved hollow. Or if it was curved inward, like the shape of a theater, it embraced the curved part of the earth of light received into such a hollow by no less deformed a coupling [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “curvature” rather than “coupling.”].

Or if this earth had a curved side and the other a straight one, it would not touch it along its whole side. And surely, as I said above, it would have been better if it touched it nowhere, and if enough emptiness intervened both to separate the two earths by a proper interval and to prevent the rash wicked ones from doing harm by falling headlong through infinity.

But if a straight side touched a straight side, I do not indeed see any recesses or gaps; but I plainly see such peace and such harmony between the two earths that a greater union could not exist. For what could be more beautiful, what more fitting, than for straight to be joined to straight in such a way that no hollow or curve on either side breaks or divides the natural and stable conjunction of the place through infinite space and from infinite eternity? Even if the straight sides of both earths were separated by an intervening emptiness, they would not merely be beautiful in themselves because they were so straight; with the intervening interval as well, they would correspond to one another in such a way that equal straightnesses on this side and that, even without any conjunction, would nevertheless come together into a single beauty by their very similarity [Note: The words “into a single beauty” have been added from an old Corbie manuscript.].

But when this conjunction is added, I cannot imagine or state anything more harmonious and peaceful than these two earths, or anything more beautiful than the very coupling of two straight sides.

## Chapter XXVII

### 29. The Beauty of a Straight Side Could Be Removed from the Earth of Darkness without Any Removal of Substance. So Evil Happens to the Soul without Any Substance Being Added or Taken Away

The side of the earth of darkness, insofar as it was straight, would possess something good from God its creator.

What am I to do with these most wretched souls, entangled in error and habit? These people do not know what they are saying when they say such things; they do not pay attention. I beg you: no one is forcing you, no one is pressing you into a contest, no one is taunting you with your former errors—unless he has not experienced divine mercy and has therefore been without errors. Let us simply work so that these errors may at last come to an end.

Look for a little while without hostility or bitterness. We are all human beings. Let us hate not one another, but errors and falsehoods [Note: The manuscripts read, “let us hate not us, but errors and falsehoods.” The printed editions read, “let us hate not you, but errors and falsehoods.”].

I beg you, look for a little while. God of mercies, assist those who look, and kindle inward light for those who seek the truth.

For what do we understand if we do not understand that the straight is better than the crooked? I therefore ask you, if you receive this calmly and moderately: if someone were to deform the straight side of the earth of darkness, which is joined to the straight side of the earth of light, would he not remove some beauty from it?

You must admit—if you do not wish to bark—that if it were deformed, not only would beauty be taken from it, but also that beauty which it could have shared with the straight side of the earth of light. By taking this beauty away and making the straight crooked, so that what had harmonized would fall into discord and what had corresponded would become repulsive, would he thereby take away any substance?

Learn, then, that evil is not substance. Rather, just as in the body, when its form is changed for the worse, its appearance is lost—or rather diminished—and what had previously been called beautiful is called deformed, and the body that had previously pleased becomes displeasing, so in the soul the dignity of a right will, by which one lives piously and justly, is corrupted when the will is changed for the worse. Through this sin the soul becomes wretched, although it had possessed blessedness through the integrity of a right will, with no substance added or removed.

### 30.

Next, consider also this: even if we grant that the side of the earth of darkness is evil for other reasons—because it is dark, shadowy, or whatever else may be said of it—nevertheless there is no evil in the fact that it is straight.

Just as I concede that there is something evil in its color, so you must concede that there is something good in its straightness. It is therefore impious to alienate from God the craftsman whatever amount of good this may be [Note: The printed editions read, “whatever good there is.”], from whom all good that exists in any nature comes. Unless we believe this, we are disastrously in error.

How, then, does he call this earth the supreme evil, when in the straightness of its side I find, as far as the body is concerned, a good of no small beauty? And how does he wish it to be completely alienated from the omnipotent and supremely good God, when I cannot discover to whom the very good we find in it should be attributed except to the author of all good?

“But that side too was evil,” he says. Suppose it was evil. It would certainly be worse if it were not straight but distorted. How, then, is it the supreme evil, when something worse than it can be imagined?

Furthermore, there must be some good whose absence makes any given thing worse. The side would become worse by losing its straightness. Therefore, its straightness contains some good. And you will never tell me from where that good comes unless you turn to him from whom we must confess that all things, whether great or small, are nevertheless good.

But let us now pass from consideration of this side to other matters.

## Chapter XXVIII

### 31. Manichaeus Posits Five Natures in the Earth of Darkness

“Fiery bodies,” he says, “that is, pestilential kinds, inhabited that earth.”

When he says “they inhabited,” he evidently wants them understood as animate and living. But lest we appear to wish to quibble over a word, let us observe how he distributes all those inhabitants of that earth into five living kinds:

“Here,” he says, “were immeasurable darknesses, issuing from the same nature, together with their own offspring. Beyond them were muddy and turbid waters with their inhabitants; within these were dreadful and violent winds with their prince and progenitors. Again, there was a fiery and corruptible region with its leaders and nations. Further inward was a race full of gloom and smoke, in which dwelt an enormous prince and ruler of all, having around him countless princes, of all of whom he himself was the mind and origin. These, then, were the five natures of the pestilential earth.”

We observe five natures, as though they were parts of one nature, which he calls the pestilential earth. They are darkness, waters, winds, fire, and smoke. He orders these five natures in such a way that darkness is outermost among them, and from it he begins the enumeration. Within the darkness he places the waters; within the waters, the winds; within the winds, fire; within the fire, smoke.

Each of these five natures had its own kinds of inhabitants, which likewise number five. I ask, then, whether there was one kind of inhabitant in all five natures, or different kinds, just as the natures themselves were different.

They answer that the kinds were different, and teach from other books that the darkness had serpents; the waters, swimmers such as fish; the winds, fliers such as birds; the fire, quadrupeds [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “serpents inhabited the darkness; swimmers, such as fish, the waters; fliers, such as birds, the winds; quadrupeds, such as horses and lions, the fires,” and so forth.]; and the smoke, bipeds such as human beings.

## Chapter XXIX

### 32. This Delusion Refuted

Who, then, arranged these things? Who distributed and distinguished them? Who gave them number, qualities, forms, and life? All these things are good in themselves, and no source can be found from which they could have been bestowed upon each nature except God, the author of all good.

For these men are not trying to introduce what poets too customarily describe or indicate in one way or another as chaos: some formless matter without shape, quality, measure, number, weight, order, or distinction; some confused thing entirely devoid of every quality—which certain Greek teachers call ἄποιον (“without quality”). They are not, then, trying to present in this way what they call the earth of darkness.

Rather, in a wholly different, greatly divergent, and contrary manner, they join and align side to side: they count five natures, distinguish them, arrange them, and describe them by their proper qualities. Nor do they allow them to remain deserted and barren; they fill them with their inhabitants. They assign to those inhabitants forms that are suitable and adapted to their dwellings; and, above all, they assign them life.

To enumerate such great goods and declare them alien to God, the author of all good, is to fail both to recognize in things the great good of order and to perceive in oneself the great evil of error.

## Chapter XXX

### 33. How Many Goods There Are in the Natures Which Manichaeus Places in the Earth of Darkness

“But those five kinds inhabiting those natures,” he says, “were savage and pestilential.”

As though I had praised the savagery and pestilence in them! Look, I condemn with you the things that you accuse them of having as evils. You, in turn, praise with me the good things that you yourself mention in them. In this way you will see that you wish to establish good mixed with evil as the supreme and ultimate evil.

I condemn the pestilence there with you; praise the health there with me. Those kinds could not have been generated, nourished, or inhabited that earth without some health.

I condemn the darkness there with you; praise the fecundity there with me. For you call the darkness immeasurable, and yet you add “with its own offspring.” Although darkness is not corporeal and the whole word signifies the absence of light—just as nakedness means lacking clothing, and emptiness means lacking the fullness of a body—and therefore darkness could generate nothing, a dark earth, that is, an earth lacking light, could nevertheless generate something, let us set this aside for the moment.

When offspring emerge, however, there is a fitting balance conducive to health, and a certain ordered harmony of number that arranges and builds the limbs of those being born into unity, with each part corresponding to the others in a peaceful moderation. Who does not understand that all this deserves greater praise than the darkness deserves blame?

I condemn the muddy turbidity of the waters there with you; praise with me the very form and quality of the waters, the appropriately proportioned limbs of the swimming inhabitants, the life that contains and directs the body, and the entire balance adapted to the health of its kind.

However much you may criticize the muddy and turbid waters, by saying that they were such waters as could both generate and contain living creatures, you nevertheless cannot take away the form of that body, however imperfect, or the likeness of its parts by which they are formed and harmonized into a single quality. For if you take these away, there will be no body. If you are a human being, you perceive that all these things deserve praise.

And however much you exaggerate the savagery of those inhabitants, amid their attacks, tearing apart, and devastation, you nevertheless do not take away from them the measured boundaries of their forms, by which their individual bodies are harmonized through the equality of their members, nor the balance of health, nor the governance of the soul that brings the parts of its body into the unity of friendship and concord [Note: So the Corbie manuscript. The printed editions read, “the governance of the form.”]. If you observe these things with human understanding, you see that they deserve greater praise than those things that displease deserve blame.

I condemn the horror of the winds there with you; praise with me the same winds’ breathable and nourishing nature, and the bodily form produced by the continuity and diffusion of their appropriately joined parts. By these properties they could both generate and nourish their inhabitants and preserve them in health. And in those inhabitants, in addition to the other features that have been praised above in all living creatures, praise especially their active and easy movement wherever they wished, and the harmonious exertion and balanced motion of their wings in flight.

I condemn the corruption of the fire there with you; praise with me the generative fire [Note: The printed editions read, “the genital fire.”], and its vigorous and suitably tempered character for things being born: for their growing together, for their being perfected according to their proper numerical proportions and outlines, and for their being able to live and dwell there. You recognize that all these things are worthy of wonder and praise not only in the dwelling of the fire but also in the inhabitants themselves.

I condemn the obscurity of the smoke there with you, and the enormity of the prince who, as you say, dwelt in it. Praise with me the fact that even in the smoke itself you find no part unlike the others, but that in its own kind it preserves the agreement and measure of its parts with one another, so that through a certain unity it is what it is. No one considers these things soberly without praising them with wonder.

What is more, you also attribute to the smoke the power and capacity to generate, since you assign inhabitants—even princes—to it, so that what we have never seen here, smoke may there be fertile and provide a healthy dwelling for its inhabitants.

## Chapter XXXI

### 34. On the Same Argument

Since, even in the prince of the smoke itself, you noticed only the enormity that you wished to condemn, should you not have paid attention to the other features that would compel you to praise his nature?

For he had a soul and a body: the soul giving life, the body inspired with life; the soul ruling, the body obeying; the soul going before, the body following; the soul containing, the body not flowing apart; the soul moving it according to measured numbers, the body being firmly established by the ordered structure of its limbs.

Does not either ordered peace or peaceful order move you to praise in this one prince? What has been said of one may be understood of the others as well.

“But he was savage and monstrous toward the others.” I do not praise that; I praise all the great things that you refuse to notice. If anyone, even after being admonished, observes and considers these things, anyone who rashly believed Manichaeus recognizes without doubt that, when he speaks about these natures, he is speaking about certain goods—but not the highest and uncreated goods, such as God, the one Trinity; nor about those created goods that have been sublimely ordered, such as the holy angels and most blessed powers.

Rather, he is speaking about the lowest goods, ordered at the bottom of things according to the measure proper to their kind. When they are compared with higher things, the uninstructed suppose them worthy of blame; and when one considers how much of the good that is present in higher things is absent from these, the absence of that same good receives the name of evil.

I argue in this way about these natures because the things mentioned are known to us in this world. We know darkness, waters, winds, fire, and smoke. We also know creeping, swimming, flying, quadrupedal, and bipedal animals.

Except for darkness—which, as I have said, is nothing other than the absence of light, discerned by the eyes through their not seeing, just as silence is not heard by the ears through their not hearing—not because darkness is something, but because light is absent; just as it is not because silence is something, but because sound is absent—except, then, for darkness in this enumeration, the remaining things are natures, and they are known to everyone. Since their form, insofar as it exists at all, is praiseworthy and good, no prudent person alienates it from God, the author of all good.

## Chapter XXXII
35. Manichaeus constructed his fantasies from the things he saw here. For that Manichaeus, just as he wished to arrange in his fantasies—as though in a nation of darkness—the natures he had learned here [Note: [Col. 0197] The printed editions commonly read, “which he says here.” And twenty-four lines later, it was easy to say “here” and transfer to those fantasies. Corrected from the manuscripts.], is plainly proved altogether false. First, because darkness can generate nothing, as has been said.

“But,” he says, “those darknesses were not like the darkness you know here.”

How, then, do you teach me about them? Do you perhaps compel me to believe merely because you are so verbose in promising instruction? But let me believe you. I know this nonetheless: if they had no form [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “face.”] at all, just as these darknesses have none, they could have generated nothing; but if they had some form, they were better. Yet when you say that they were not such, you seem to want people to believe in something worse.

You could also have said that silence—which stands to the ears as darkness does to the eyes—gave birth there to certain deaf or mute animals. When someone told you that silence was not some nature, you could have replied, “But that silence was not like the silence you know here,” so that you could say absolutely whatever you wished to those whom you had once deceived into believing you.

Nevertheless, the reason that led him to imagine that serpents were born in darkness could perhaps have been observed properly in the very beginnings of their birth. But there are serpents that see so sharply and rejoice so much in the presence of light that they seem to offer the strongest testimony against him.

Next, it was easy for him to learn here about creatures swimming in water and transfer them to those fantasies; likewise creatures flying in the winds, since the movement of this denser air in which birds fly is called wind. But why he thought of quadrupeds in fire, I do not know. Yet he did not say this without reason; he paid too little attention and went badly astray.

For this is the explanation they are accustomed to give: quadrupeds are voracious and burn intensely with sexual desire. But many human beings, though certainly bipedal, surpass any quadruped in their gluttony—yet he says that bipeds, not fire, but smoke, are their offspring. Nothing more voracious than geese is easily found.
