Whether he places them in smoke, because they are bipedal; or in water, because they love to swim; or in the winds, because they are feathered and sometimes fly, according to his classification they certainly do not belong to fire.

As for sexual ardor, I believe he noticed neighing horses, often dragged toward mares after biting through their bridles. But while hastening to write down this observation, he failed to notice the house sparrow, in comparison with which any stallion is found to be extremely cold.

When asked why he assigned bipeds to smoke, they reply that the race of bipeds is lofty and proud. For they say that human beings derive their origin from it; and since globular, almost swollen smoke rises into the air, they not unreasonably observed that it resembles the proud. This observation should have sufficed to provide some likeness for proud human beings, whether to form or to understand an allegory. It should not, however, have led anyone to believe that bipedal animals were in smoke or born from smoke.

They should also have been born in dust, since dust often rises toward heaven with no less breadth and elevation; and in clouds, since clouds are frequently exhaled from the earth in such a way that, to those watching from a distance, it is uncertain whether they are smoke or clouds.

Finally, in the case of water and winds, he transferred an argument from the suitability of dwelling there to the inhabitants, because we see swimming creatures live in water and flying creatures in the winds. But fire and smoke did not deter this lying man from being ashamed to establish such inhabitants there—inhabitants for whom nothing more absurd could be established. For fire burns and destroys a quadruped, while smoke chokes and kills bipeds.

Here, at least, he is forced to admit that he calls these natures better in the nation of darkness, where he wants everything to be considered worse. There, after all, fire generated and nourished a quadruped and held it harmlessly, or even most beneficially. Likewise, smoke had brought forth its bipeds in its most merciful bosom and had raised and contained them up to that principality [Note: [Col. 0198] Thus the manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads, “was raising them up to that principality.”—not merely without causing them distress, but in a life-giving and indulgent manner.

Thus these lies are exposed by observing the things visible in the world—things conceived by a less careful and less perceptive bodily sense, brought forth by fantasies, and published and written down through the recklessness of heretics, thereby increasing their number.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

36. Every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. But they should be pressed more urgently in this respect, so that, if possible, they may understand how truly it is said in the Catholic faith that God is the author of all natures [Note: [Col. 0198] The Amerbach edition and the manuscripts read “in which respect,” omitting “of.”]. I was dealing with this matter above when I said:

“I condemn with you the plague, blindness, turbid filthiness, horrifying violence, corruptibility, and the savagery of the rulers, together with things of this kind. With me, praise the form, distinction, order, peace, unity [Note: [Col. 0198] The manuscripts do not have the word “unity.”] of forms, the harmonious arrangement and measured correspondences of the limbs, vital breaths and nourishment, the balance of health, the governance and direction of the soul, the service rendered by bodies, and the likeness and harmony of the parts in each nature, whether those which inhabited or those which were inhabited, together with everything else of this kind.”

For in this way they would understand—if only they were willing to consider the matter without stubbornness—that even now good and evil are mingled when they speak of that earth in which they believed evil alone, and the highest evil, existed. Thus, if the things enumerated as evil are removed, the things praised as good remain without any blame; but if the good things themselves are removed, no nature remains.

Anyone who can see therefore sees that every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. For from one and the same thing I found something to praise and he found something to blame. If the good elements are removed, no nature will exist; but if the objectionable elements are removed, an uncorrupted nature will remain.

Remove from waters their muddiness and turbidity: pure and tranquil waters remain. Remove from waters the harmony of their parts: they will no longer be waters. If, therefore [Note: [Col. 0199] The printed editions read “thus therefore”; the manuscripts, “if therefore.”], when that evil is taken away, a purer nature remains, while when the good is taken away no nature remains, then what makes the nature a nature is the good it possesses; whereas what is evil is not nature but contrary to nature.

Remove from winds the horror and excessive force that displease you, and you can conceive of gentle and moderate winds. Remove from winds the likeness of their parts, by which their body is joined into unity and brought into peace with itself so as to be a body, and no nature at all will remain for you to conceive.

It would take too long to pursue the other examples. But it is clear to those who judge without partisan zeal that, whenever these natures are mentioned, certain features displeasing to them are added to them. When we remove those features, better natures remain. From this it is understood that, insofar as they are natures, they are good, because if you remove from them in turn everything good they possess, no natures will remain.

Observe also, you who wish to judge rightly, that savage ruler as well: if his savagery is taken away, consider how many praiseworthy things remain—the joining together of his body, the correspondence of his limbs on either side, the unity of his form, the peace of his interwoven parts, and the order and arrangement of the soul that governs and gives life, and of the body that serves and is given life.

If all these good things are removed, together with whatever I may have omitted to enumerate, no nature at all will remain.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

37. Nature is never without some good. The Manichaeans consider only the evils. But perhaps you will say that those evils cannot be removed from such natures, and therefore must be regarded as natural. The question now is not what can or cannot be removed. It is certainly a considerable illumination for understanding that all natures, insofar as they are natures, are good: those goods can be conceived without the evils, but no nature can be conceived without those goods.

For I can conceive of waters without the disturbance of mud; but without the peace of their joined parts, no bodily form presents itself to the mind or can in any way be perceived. Consequently those muddy waters could not exist without that good by which it came about that some bodily nature could exist.

When you say that those evils cannot be removed from such natures, the answer is that those goods also cannot be removed from such natures. Why, then, do you wish to call these things natural evils because of the evils which you think cannot be removed, while you refuse to call them natural goods because of the goods which you are shown cannot be removed?

38. It remains for you to ask—for this is usually your final question—from where those evils come, which I too said were displeasing to me. I might answer, if you first say from where those goods come, which you too are compelled to praise, unless you wish to be utterly irrational.

But why should I ask this, when both sides acknowledge that all goods, whatever their kind and however great, come from the one God, who is supremely good?

Therefore, Manichaeus, resist your own Manichaeus, who judged that so many and such great goods as we have mentioned and rightly praised—the peace and harmony of the parts in each nature, the health and strength of living creatures, and the other things which I am now weary of repeating—existed in that invented land of darkness in such a way that he attempted to alienate them from the God whom he confesses to be the author of all good.

He did not see those goods, because he attended only to what displeased him. It was as if someone, terrified by a lion’s roar and seeing it drag away and tear apart whatever bodies of animals or human beings it had seized, were so overwhelmed by childish weakness of mind that, looking only at the lion’s ferocity and savagery while entirely neglecting and passing over its other features, he cried out that the nature of that animal was not merely evil but a great evil—exaggerating the claim in proportion to his fear.

But if he saw a lion, its ferocity subdued, being led about tame [Note: [Col. 0200] Thus the old books. The printed editions read: “But if, its ferocity subdued, he saw a sweet and tame lion.”—especially if he had never before been terrified by that beast—he would then have leisure, secure and unafraid, to consider and praise the lion’s beauty.

I will say nothing about this except what is most relevant: it is possible for some nature to offend because of one of its features, and for hatred to arise against the whole of it [Note: [Col. 0200] The printed editions commonly read “against the whole”; corrected from the manuscripts to “against the whole [nature].”], even though it is clear that the appearance of a true and living beast, when it terrifies in the woods, is far better than that of an imitation or representation when it is praised in a painting on a wall.

Let that error, then, neither deceive us nor make us blind to the forms of natures. He criticizes certain features in them in such a way as to force everything about them to displease, although he cannot criticize everything about them. Let us therefore compose our minds for impartial judgment and now ask from where the evils come together with those goods, which I also said I disapproved [Note: [Col. 0200] The printed editions read “I was going to disapprove”; the manuscripts, “I disapprove.”]. We shall see this more easily if we can gather everything under a single name.

## CHAPTER XXXV

39. Evil is nothing other than corruption; corruption itself is not nature but contrary to nature. Wherever there is corruption, there was goodness. Who, after all, would doubt that everything called evil is nothing other than corruption?

Different evils may indeed be called by different names, but the evil of all things in which some evil can be observed is corruption. Thus the corruption of a learned soul is called ignorance; the corruption of a prudent soul, imprudence; the corruption of a just soul, injustice; the corruption of a courageous soul, cowardice; and the corruption of a calm and tranquil soul, desire, fear, sadness, or boastfulness.

Then, in an animate body, the corruption of health is pain and disease; the corruption of strength is weariness; and the corruption of rest is labor.

Then, in the body itself, the corruption of beauty is ugliness; the corruption of straightness is crookedness; the corruption of order is disorder; and the corruption of wholeness is separation, fracture, or diminution.

It would be lengthy and difficult to name individually all the corruptions both of the things I have mentioned and of countless others, since many things said of the body can also be said of the soul, and innumerable things exist in which corruption retains its own proper names.

Nevertheless, it is now easy to see that corruption harms nothing except what it undermines in its natural condition, and that it is therefore not nature but contrary to nature. If evil is found in things only as corruption, and corruption is not nature, then no nature is evil.

40. But if perhaps you are unable to understand this, observe that everything which is corrupted is diminished by some good. For if it were not corrupted, it would be uncorrupted; and if it could not be corrupted at all, it would be incorruptible. It is therefore necessary that either incorruption or incorruptibility be good, if corruption is evil.

There is no question now concerning an incorruptible nature. We are discussing things that can be corrupted, which, so long as they are not corrupted, can be called uncorrupted, but cannot be called incorruptible. Properly speaking, only that is incorruptible which is not merely not corrupted but cannot be corrupted in any respect.

Whatever, then, is uncorrupted yet capable of being corrupted, when it begins to be corrupted is diminished by that very good by which it was uncorrupted—and by a great good indeed, since corruption is a great evil. For as long as corruption can increase in it, it possesses the good by which it is diminished.

Therefore, the natures which he invents as having existed in the land of darkness either could be corrupted or could not. If they could not, they were incorruptible, a good above which nothing exists. If they could, then either they were corrupted or they were not. If they were not corrupted, they were uncorrupted—something which, as we see, cannot be said without great praise. But if they were corrupted, they were diminished by that great good. If they were diminished by a good, they possessed a good by which they could be diminished. And if they possessed a good, those natures were not the supreme evil, and the whole Manichaean fable is false.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

41. Whence evil comes: the corruption of good. Since we have asked what evil is and have learned that it is not nature but contrary to nature, we must consequently ask from where it comes. If he had done this, he might perhaps have fallen less deeply into the narrow confines of such a great error.

For he asked too hastily and in the wrong order from where it came, without first asking what it was. Therefore, when he asked, only empty fantasies could present themselves to him—fantasies from which a mind long nourished by bodily senses is removed only with difficulty.

Someone, then, who no longer wishes to quarrel but wishes not to err, may ask: “From where does this corruption come, which we have discovered to be the general evil of good but corruptible things?”

One who asks in this way quickly finds the answer if he seeks the truth with great ardor and knocks piously with steadfast perseverance. Human beings can provide some reminder through signs of words; but the one true Teacher, the incorruptible Truth itself, teaches—the interior Teacher alone. He also became external, in order to call us back from external things to interior ones; and, taking the form of a servant, he deigned to appear humble to those lying low, so that his sublimity [Note: [Col. 0202] The Louvain edition alone reads “subtlety,” less well.] might become known to those rising upward.

Let us humbly entreat in his name and, through him, imploring the mercy of the Father, seek these answers.

A very brief answer can first be given to those who ask from where corruption comes: it comes from the fact that these natures, which can be corrupted, were not generated from God but made by him from nothing. Since superior reasoning has shown them to be good, no one can rightly say, “God should not have made good things.” [Note: [Col. 0202] The printed editions read: “no one can rightly say that God did not make good things. But if he says that he made them supremely good,” and so forth. Corrected on the authority of the old manuscripts.]

But if he says, “He should have made them supremely good,” he must understand that the supreme Good is the one who made these goods.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

42. God alone is supremely good. “What evil,” you ask, “would result if these things too were made supremely good?”

And yet, if one of us asked—having accepted and believed in God the Father as the supreme Good—whether there were some other supreme good from which these things might piously seem to us to derive, we could give no correct answer except that they derive from God the Father, who is supremely good.

Let us therefore remember that what comes from him was born from him, not made by him from nothing, and that for this reason it too is supremely—that is, incorruptibly—good. We see that it is unjust to demand that the things he made from nothing should be as supremely good as the one whom he begot from himself is supremely good. For unless he had begotten one, he would not have begotten one who is what he himself is, since he himself is one.

Therefore, brothers are ignorantly and impiously sought for the only Son, through whom the Father made all good things from nothing, except on the basis of what he deigned to appear as in the human being [Note: [Col. 0202] Louvain reads: “Therefore concerning the only Son, through whom the Father made all good things from nothing, brothers are impiously sought.” Incorrectly.]

For this reason he is called both “only-begotten” and “firstborn” in Scripture: only-begotten from the Father, firstborn from the dead. “And we saw,” he says, “his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full [Note: [Col. 0202] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “full” in the singular.] of grace and truth” (John 1:14, 18). And Paul says, “So that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29).

43. But if we say, “These things made from nothing would no longer be good, and only God’s nature would be good,” [Note: [Col. 0202] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read less correctly: “These good things made from nothing would no longer exist, but only God’s nature would be good.”] we shall be envious of such great goods. It is an impious statement to consider it an injury that something is not what God is, and therefore to refuse to allow anything to be good because God is set above it.

I ask you, rational nature of the soul, allow yourself to be somewhat less than God is—and less by so much that nothing better than you exists after him. Allow this, I say, and be reconciled to him, lest he continue to thrust you down into the lowest places, where, through penal hardships, the good that you are becomes increasingly worthless to you.

You are proud toward God if you resent the fact that he precedes you; and you think of him most insultingly if you do not rejoice beyond expression that you are so great a good that only he is superior.

Once this has been established and firmly secured, do not say [Note: [Col. 0203] The printed editions add, “O human soul,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]:” “God ought to have made me the only nature; I would not want any good to be made after me.” For what is good after God need not therefore have been the last good.

This above all shows how much dignity he has granted you: the God who alone naturally rules over you made other goods over which you too would rule.

Do not be surprised that they do not now serve you in every respect and sometimes even torment you. Your Lord has greater power over the things that serve you than you have over them, just as over servants of his servants [Note: [Col. 0203] In the manuscripts “over” is absent, so that “them” refers to the rational soul itself.].

What wonder, then, if, when you sinned—that is, when you disobeyed your Lord—the things over which you ruled became penal things? For what is so just, and what is more just than God?

Human nature deserved this in Adam, though this is not the place to discuss it. Nevertheless, the just ruler is shown to be just by just rewards and just punishments: by the blessedness of those who live rightly and the punishment of those who sin.

Nor have you been abandoned without mercy. At appointed measures of things and times, you are called to return. Thus, by the right governance of the most high Creator, we have come even [Note: [Col. 0203] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “until.”] to earthly goods, which are corrupted and restored, so that you might have consolations mingled with punishment: that you might praise God, delighted by the order of good things, and flee to him, disciplined by experiences of evil.

Thus, insofar as earthly things serve you, they teach you that you are their mistress; but insofar as they trouble you, they teach you to serve your Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

44. Nature is from God; corruption is from nothing. Therefore, although corruption is evil, and although it is not from the Creator of natures but comes from the fact that they were made from nothing, even corruption itself has been so ordered under his governance and direction of all that he made that it harms only the lowest natures, for the punishment of the condemned and for the training and admonition of those returning, so that they may cling to the incorruptible God and remain uncorrupted. This alone is our good, as the prophet says: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28).

Do not say: “God should not have made corruptible natures.” Insofar as they are natures, God made them; insofar as they are corruptible, God did not make them. For corruption does not come from him, who alone is incorruptible.

If you understand these things, give thanks to God. If you do not understand them, be still, and do not rashly condemn what you do not yet understand. Humbly attend to him who is the light of the mind [Note: [Col. 0204] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “who kindles the light of the mind.”], so that you may understand.

When one says “corruptible nature,” two names, not one, are spoken. Likewise, when one says “God made from nothing,” we hear two names, not one.

Therefore assign to each of these single terms its corresponding meaning: when you hear “nature,” let it pertain to God; when you hear “corruptible,” let it pertain to nothing. Yet the corruptions themselves, although they do not arise from God’s workmanship, are nevertheless subject to arrangement under his power, according to the order of things and the merits of souls.

For this reason we rightly say that reward and punishment come from him. Thus he did not make corruption, yet he can hand over to corruption one who has deserved to be corrupted—that is, one who has begun by sinning to corrupt himself—so that one who willingly embraced it when it enticed him may unwillingly experience it when it torments him. [Note: [Col. 0204] In the printed editions the negative particle was wrongly omitted. The printed editions also add “the desire of illicit pleasure,” words absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

45. How evils come from God. It is written not only in the Old Testament, “I make good things and create evil things” (Isaiah 45:7), but more explicitly in the New, where the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more that they can do; but fear him who, after killing the body, has power to cast the soul into Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28; Luke 12:4).

The apostle Paul most clearly testifies that penal corruption is added by divine judgment to voluntary corruption when he says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are. Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

If this had been said in the Old Law, with what denunciations would these people have attacked it, accusing God as though he were a corrupter! Fearing this word, many Latin translators did not wish to say “will corrupt,” but said “God will destroy him.” Without departing from the meaning itself, they avoided the offense caused by the word.

Yet these people would have railed no less against a God who destroys, if they had found this in the Old Law or the Prophets. But they are refuted by the Greek copies, in which it is written most plainly: “Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him.”

If someone asks them how this has been said, lest God be thought a corrupter, they immediately explain that “will corrupt” means “will hand over to corruption,” or they interpret it in whatever other way they can.

If they possessed the same disposition toward the Old Law, and understood the many remarkable things found there, and if they deferred things not yet understood with reverence rather than tearing them apart with hatred [Note: [Col. 0204] The printed editions read “paid them respect”; the manuscripts more truly, “deferred them.”].

## CHAPTER XL

46. Corruption tends toward non-being. If someone does not believe that corruption comes from nothing, let him place before himself these two things—being and non-being—as though they were situated on opposite sides. This is only for the sake of understanding, so that we may walk more slowly with those who are slow.

Then let him place something, as it were, in the middle—for example, the body of a living creature—and ask himself, while that body is being formed and born, while its appearance increases, while it is nourished, grows strong, gains strength, is adorned, and is made firm, in what respect it remains and is established, toward which side it tends: toward being or toward non-being.

He will not doubt that even in its beginnings it is something, but that the more its form, appearance, and strength are stabilized and made firm, the more it comes to be and tends toward the side in which being is situated.

Now let him begin to corrupt. Let that entire condition grow weak, let its strength languish, let its vigor wither, let its form become deformed, let the joining of its limbs split apart, and let the harmony of its parts decay and dissolve. Let him ask even now, through this corruption, toward which side it tends: toward being or toward non-being.

I do not think anyone could be so blind and slow as to doubt what answer he should give himself, and fail to perceive that the more anything is corrupted, the more it tends toward destruction.

Everything that tends toward destruction tends toward non-being.

Since, then, we must believe that God exists immutably and incorruptibly, while what is called “nothing” is plainly complete non-being; and since you have placed before yourself being and non-being and recognized that the more appearance increases, the more each thing tends toward being, while the more corruption increases, the more it tends toward non-being, why do you hesitate to say, in each corruptible nature, what comes from God and what comes from nothing, when appearance is according to nature and corruption is contrary to nature?

For increased appearance compels being, and we confess that God supremely is. Increased corruption, however, compels non-being, and it is established that what is not is nothing.

Why, I ask, do you hesitate to say, in a corruptible nature—which you call both nature and corruptible—what comes from God and what comes from nothing? And why do you seek a nature contrary to God, whom, if you confess to be supremely existent, you see to have nothing contrary to him?

## CHAPTER XLI

47. Corruption comes from us with God’s permission. “Why, then,” you ask, “does corruption take away what God gave to nature?”

It takes it away only where God permits it. He permits it where he judges this to be most orderly and just, according to the ranks of things and the merits of souls.

The form of an uttered voice passes away and is destroyed by silence; yet our speech is carried on through the departure and succession of passing words, and is gracefully and pleasantly distinguished by measured intervals of silence.

So too the lowest beauty of temporal natures is constituted: it proceeds through the passing of things and is distinguished by the death of those being born. If our sense and memory could grasp the order and proportions of this beauty, it would please us so much that we would not dare to call its distinguishing deficiencies corruptions.

But we struggle in relation to part of this beauty when the temporal things we love flow away from us, when we endure the punishments of sins, and when we are admonished to love eternal things.

## CHAPTER XLII

48. He exhorts us toward the supreme good. Let us not therefore seek in this beauty what it did not receive. It is the lowest precisely because it did not receive what we seek. Let us praise God in what it did receive, because he granted even this lowest beauty so great a good of form.

Yet let us not cling to it as its lovers. Let us pass beyond it as those who praise God, so that, placed above it, we may judge it, rather than being joined to it and judged within it.

Let us hasten toward that good which neither spreads through places [Note: [Col. 0206] Some manuscripts read “is made dense.”] nor rolls through time, and from which all natures, whether local or temporal, receive their form and appearance.

To behold that good, let us cleanse the heart through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

The eyes with which this light spread through places is seen—though it is not whole everywhere, having one part here and another elsewhere—are not what must be prepared to see that good.

Rather, let us purify that vision and gaze by which, insofar as this life permits, we perceive what is just, what is pious, and what the beauty of wisdom is. Whoever sees these things places them far above the fullness of all local spaces and understands that, in order to see them, the mind’s gaze is not spread through spatial dimensions but stabilized by incorporeal power.

## CHAPTER XLIII

49. Conclusion. Since fantasies are greatly hostile to this vision—fantasies drawn from bodily sensation, which our imagination turns over and holds within itself—let us detest this heresy. It followed the faith of its own fantasies and scattered and diffused the divine substance through the dimensions of places, however infinite, as though it were an unformed mass. It cut off part of that substance in order to find a place for evil, failing to see that evil is not nature but contrary to nature.

It adorned evil itself with such great appearance, forms, and peace among the parts prevailing in each nature, because it could conceive no nature without these goods. Thus the evils it criticizes there are buried beneath the abundance of countless goods.

But let this be the end of the present volume. In the remaining volumes, with God’s permission and help, its remaining deliriums will be refuted.

[Col. 0207]

# The Thirty-Three Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Against Faustus the Manichaean

[Note: [Col. 0207] Written around the year 400.]

[Note: [Col. 0205] Concerning the work that follows, see Book 2, chapter 7, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 632, from the words: “No. 1. Against Faustus the Manichaean … I wrote a large work,” through column 633, no. 3, with the words: “There was a certain Faustus.” M.]

[Note: [Col. 0205] Augustine sent this work, together with Letter 82, to Jerome. In that letter, chapter 2, no. 17, he states that he dictated the work long before receiving Jerome’s Letter 75, which could not have been delivered to him before the year 405. In the sequence of the *Retractations*, he places this work midway between the books of the *Confessions*, printed in the first volume, and the books *On the Acts with Felix the Manichaean*, which follow later in this volume. The work should therefore be assigned approximately to the year 400. He frequently cites it in Books 15 and 16 of *The City of God*; in his *Questions on Genesis*, question 26, and *Questions on Exodus*, question 2; in Book 2 of *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, chapter 12; in Book 1 of *The Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 5; and in *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 15. Cassiodorus says of it in *Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 1: “Augustine also wrote thirty-three books against Faustus the Manichaean, in which he both clearly refuted his most wicked perversion by sound reasoning and discussed the book of Genesis again with remarkable skill.”]

[Note: [Col. 0207] The thirty-three books against Faustus were reviewed anew against six Vatican manuscripts and eighteen French manuscripts: the Remigian, Corbie, Audoen, Michael, Pratelles, Lyré, Sées, Vendôme, Fleury, Benignian, Casamari, Cistercian, Bigot, Victorine, two Dominican manuscripts of Paris at the Jacobins, one of the Bernardines’ college at Paris, and one of the abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres; also against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain edition, and against the variant readings of six Belgian manuscripts preserved at Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0207] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER I

There was a certain Faustus, an African by nation and a citizen of Milevis, pleasing in speech, clever in intellect, a Manichaean by sect, and therefore perverted by a wicked error. I myself knew the man, as I mentioned him in my books of the *Confessions* (Book 5, chapters 3 and 6).

He published a certain volume against the upright Christian faith and Catholic truth. When it came into our hands and had been read by the brothers, they desired—and rightly demanded of us, by the charity through which we serve them—that we answer it.

I shall now undertake this task in the name and with the help of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, so that all who read these things may understand how worthless a sharp intellect and polished tongue are unless the Lord directs a person’s steps (Psalm 36:23).

This same gift has also been granted, by the hidden justice of divine mercy, to many who are slower and weaker, while many who are exceptionally acute and eloquent, abandoned by God’s help, hastened and stubbornly pressed on toward the point of straying farther from the path of truth.

I think it appropriate to place his words under his name and my reply under mine.

## CHAPTER II

FAUSTUS said: Since the errors have already been brought sufficiently and more than sufficiently into the light, and the deceit of both Jewish superstition and the semi-Christians has been abundantly exposed—by Adimantus, the most learned man and the only one among us worth studying after our blessed father Manichaeus—it has seemed fitting, dearest brothers, to write these brief and well-ordered answers for you as well, on account of the crafty and cunning propositions of those who confer with us.

Thus, when these same people, following the custom of their parent, the serpent, wish to ensnare you with their deceitful little questions, you too will be carefully equipped to answer them. In this way, bound to the very questions they have proposed, they will be unable to wander any farther here and there.

And lest the minds of readers be flooded by a diffuse or confused discourse, I have set their words and ours opposite one another, as briefly and distinctly as possible.

## CHAPTER III
Augustine replied: You think that the semi-Christians must be avoided, because you say that we are such; but we avoid the pseudo-Christians, because we have shown that you are such. For that which is “half” [Note: [Col. 0208] Am. and almost all manuscripts read *semum est*.] is imperfect in some respect, but in no respect is it false. What then? If something is lacking from the faith of those whom you are trying to deceive, is what they possess therefore to be destroyed, rather than what is lacking being supplied? Thus the Apostle speaks to certain imperfect people: “Rejoicing and seeing your manner of life, and that which is lacking in your faith in Christ” (Col. II, 5). He clearly perceived a kind of spiritual structure, as he says elsewhere: “You are God’s building” (I Cor. III, 9); and in it he perceived both what gave him cause for rejoicing and what called for his efforts. He rejoiced at what he saw already built; he labored over what he understood still had to be built up to the summit of perfection.

Thus we truly are Catholics who are not yet perfect, but who are, in a certain sense—as you have said—semi-Christians whom you attack in order to deceive and seduce them by your perversity. But if any who are still such should understand that you are pseudo-Christians, although they may be unable to answer the captious propositions of your questions because of what is lacking in their faith, nevertheless they recognize that you are not to be followed but avoided. Therefore, just as your aim is to seek out semi-Christians whom you may deceive, so our aim is to show that you are pseudo-Christians, so that not only the more learned Christians may expose you by refuting you, but the less learned may advance by avoiding you.

But why did you call the serpent “our father”? Have you forgotten how you customarily disparage God, who gave the human being a commandment in paradise (Gen. II, 16–17), and praise the serpent because by its counsel it opened his eyes (Gen. III, 7)? I think it is right that you should recognize as your parent that serpent whom you have praised as the devil. For he recognizes you even now as his son, though you disparage him.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0209]

### CHAPTER ONE

Faustus said: Do you accept the Gospel?

Certainly, and above all. Therefore, do you also accept Christ as having been born?

That does not follow. For if I accept the Gospel, it does not therefore follow that I accept Christ as having been born.

Why? Because the Gospel both began from the preaching of Christ and received its name from it; yet in it Christ nowhere says that he was born from human beings. But the genealogy is so far from being the Gospel that even its own author did not dare to call it the Gospel. What did he write? “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David” (Matt. I, 1). Not therefore “the book of the Gospel of Jesus Christ,” but “the book of the generation,” since there too a star is introduced which confirms the *genesis* (ibid. II, 2) [Note: [Col. 0209] In Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov.: *ibi* (“there”). M.]; so that this may more properly be called a *Genesidion* than a Gospel.

Finally, look at Mark, who did not undertake to write a genealogy, but only the preaching of the Son of God, which is the Gospel, and see how appropriately he began: “The Gospel,” he says, “of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark I, 1). Thus it appears sufficiently and abundantly that the genealogy is not the Gospel. For even in Matthew himself, after John had been imprisoned, we then read that Jesus began to preach “the Gospel of the kingdom” (Matt. IV, 12, 17). Therefore everything narrated before this is evidently a genealogy, not the Gospel. Otherwise, what prevented Matthew from writing “The Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God,” unless he thought it improper to call a genealogy the Gospel?

Accordingly, if it is now sufficiently clear to you—something you have hitherto failed to understand—that the Gospel is something quite different from a genealogy, know that I accept, as I said, the Gospel, that is, the preaching of Christ. Whatever you now wish to ask about him, ask it while setting aside the genealogies. Or, if you wish to discuss those as well, I do not refuse, since I have abundant material for answering even on that subject; but learn to ask first about what is primary. For you seem to me now to wish to know not whether I accept the Gospel, but whether I accept the genealogies.

### CHAPTER TWO

Augustine replied: Certainly you questioned yourself as though speaking on our behalf, asking whether you accepted the Gospel; and you answered, “Certainly.” Then you again asked whether you accepted Christ as having been born; and you answered, “That does not follow,” adding as the reason that Christ’s generation does not pertain to the Gospel.

What then will you answer the Apostle, who says: “Remember that Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (II Tim. II, 8)? Surely you see how ignorant you are—or pretend to be ignorant—of what the Gospel is, and that you call something “Gospel” not according to apostolic teaching but according to your error. Or, if you call Gospel what the Apostles called Gospel, you have departed from the Gospel, since you do not believe that Christ is from the seed of David, which the Apostle testified was preached according to his Gospel.

What was the Gospel of the Apostle Paul was also the Gospel of the other Apostles and of all faithful stewards of so great a mystery. For elsewhere he says: “Whether therefore it was I or they, so we preach, and so you believed” (I Cor. XV, 11). Not all of them wrote the Gospel, but all preached the Gospel. Those who narrate the origin, deeds, sayings, and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ are properly called Evangelists. For if we ask what the very name means in Latin, *Evangelium* is said to mean “good news” or “good proclamation.” It can indeed always be said whenever something good is announced; but this term properly came to designate that proclamation of the Savior which I have mentioned.

If you announce something else, it is clear that you are outside the Gospel. Surely there are little ones opposed to you—those whom you call semi-Christians—if they hear the voice of their mother, charity, sounding from the mouth of the Apostle: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what we preached to you, let him be anathema” (Gal. I, 8–9). Since Paul himself preached, according to his Gospel, that Christ was from the seed of David, you who deny this and preach something else are anathema.

And who would fail to see the great blindness in saying that Christ nowhere says that he was born from human beings, when he scarcely ever ceases to call himself the Son of Man?

### CHAPTER THREE

But naturally, most learned men, you bring forth for us from your storeroom some “first man,” whoever he may be, who descended from the race of light to conquer the race of darkness, armed with his waters against the waters of his enemies, with his fire against their fire, and with his winds against their winds.

Why then not also with his smoke against their smoke, and with his darkness against their darkness? Instead, as you say, he was armed against smoke with air, and against darkness with light. Is it because smoke and darkness are evil, and therefore his goodness could not possess them? Then those three things—water, wind, and fire—are good. Why, then, could the evil of the opposing race possess them?

Here you reply: “But the water of the race of darkness was evil, whereas the water brought by the first man was good; its wind was evil, whereas his was good; and likewise his good fire fought against its evil fire.” Why, then, could he not also bring good smoke against evil smoke? Or is it that your lies, like smoke itself, vanish and dissipate in smoke?

Certainly your first man waged war against an opposing nature. Why, among the five elements that you imagine in the opposing race, was only one brought from the divine realms as its opposite—light against darkness? For the remaining four are not opposites. Air is not the opposite of smoke, much less water of water, wind of wind, or fire of fire.

### CHAPTER FOUR

And who could listen to those sacrilegious ravings—that your first man, in accordance with the will of his enemies, changed and transformed the elements he carried in order to capture them, so that the kingdom you call the kingdom of falsehood, while remaining in its own nature, might fight not by deception, and so that the substance of truth might appear changeable in order to deceive?

You want the Lord Jesus Christ to be believed the son of this first man. You call truth the daughter of this fabricated tale. You praise this first man because he fought against the opposing race by mutable and deceitful forms. If what you say is true, you do not imitate him; but if you imitate him, then you too are liars.

Therefore our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the true and truthful Son of God and the true and truthful son of man—both of which he himself testifies concerning himself—derived from the true God the eternity of his divinity, and from the true human being the origin of his flesh.

Apostolic teaching knows nothing of your first man. Hear the Apostle Paul: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, such are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven” (I Cor. XV, 47–49).

The first man, then, was from the earth, earthly—that Adam formed from dust; but the second man was from heaven, heavenly—the Lord Jesus Christ. For the Son of God came to the flesh, and by assuming it became outwardly human while remaining inwardly God, so that he might be both the true Son of God, through whom we were made, and the true son of man, through whom we were restored.

Why, then, do you produce your fabricated first man from I know not where, and refuse to acknowledge the first man taught by apostolic doctrine? Is it so that what the Apostle himself says may be fulfilled in you: “Turning away their hearing from the truth, they will turn to fables” (II Tim. IV, 4)?

Paul announces a first man from the earth, earthly; Manichaeus announces a first man who is not earthly, clothed in five elements of some sort of deceit. Paul says, “If anyone announces to you something contrary to what we announced to you, let him be accursed.” Therefore, lest Paul be a liar, let Manichaeus be accursed.

### CHAPTER FIVE

As for the star by which the Magi were led to worship the infant Christ, you slander it as well. You are not ashamed, although you do not place your fabricated Christ—the son of your fabricated first man—under the testimony of a star, but say that he was bound up in all the stars, because you believe that he was mingled with the rulers of darkness in that battle in which your first man himself fought against the race of darkness, so that the world might be constructed from those rulers of darkness captured by such mingling.

Hence these sacrilegious ravings compel you to say that Christ is not only fixed, bound, and condensed in heaven and in all the stars, but also on earth and in everything that grows upon it—not now your Savior, but one who must be saved by you when you eat and belch him forth [Note: [Col. 0212] The printed editions read *eum*. Certain manuscripts more suitably read *ea*.].

For, seduced by this impious vanity, you also seduce your Auditors, so that they bring you foods through which Christ, bound in them, may be assisted by your teeth and bellies. You preach that he is released and liberated by such assistance—not even entirely, but with small and filthy remnants of him still remaining in excrement, so that they may be held again and again entangled and ensnared in various other forms of bodily things. And if they cannot be released and purified while the world endures, then, in that final fire by which the world itself will burn (II Pet. III, 10–12), they will be released and purified.

Yet even then you do not say that the whole of Christ can be liberated. Rather, you say that the final and remaining particles of his good and divine nature, so befouled that they can in no way be cleansed, will be condemned forever, fixed to a dreadful globe of darkness.

Behold those who pretend to be indignant that an insult is done to the Son of God because a star is said to have shown that he was born, as though his *genesis* had been determined under a fatal constellation—when they themselves establish him not merely under the conjunction of the stars but bound in the chains of all earthly things, in the juices of all herbs, in the rottenness of all flesh, and in the corruption of all foods, so bound and polluted that he cannot be released and purified from a great, though not complete, portion except by being belched forth from leeks and their little roots by human beings, namely the Manichaean Elect.

We, for our part, place the birth of no human being under the fate of the stars, so that we may vindicate the free choice of the will—by which one lives either well or badly—from every bond of necessity, on account of God’s just judgment. How much less do we believe that the temporal birth of him who is the eternal Creator and Lord of all was made subject to the condition of the stars?

Accordingly, the star that the Magi saw, when Christ had been born according to the flesh, did not rule by decree but served as a witness; it did not subject him to its authority but indicated him by its service. Therefore it was not one of those stars that, from the beginning of creation, observe the order of their courses under the law of the Creator. Rather, at the Virgin’s new birth a new heavenly body appeared, and it displayed its appointed ministry by going before the Magi themselves as they sought Christ, until by preceding them it led them to the very place where the infant Word of God was.

Which astrologers, then, have so determined the fates of human beings born under the stars as to assert that one of the stars, when some human being was born, abandoned the order of its course and proceeded toward the one who had been born? They think that the lot of the one being born is bound to the order of the stars, not that the order of the stars can be changed on account of the day on which a human being is born [Note: [Col. 0212] In most manuscripts: “for” (*ad*)].

Therefore, if that star was one of those that complete their courses in heaven, how could it determine what the born Christ was going to do, when, at Christ’s birth, it was ordered to abandon what it was doing? But if, as is more plausibly believed, a star that had not existed arose to point out Christ [Col. 0213], Christ was not born because it appeared; rather, it appeared because Christ was born.

Thus, if one ought to speak of it, we would say not that the star was Christ’s fate, but that Christ was the star’s fate. For he, not it, brought the cause of birth to the other. If, then, there are fates so called from *fari*, “to speak,” because Christ is the Word of God, in whom all things were spoken before they existed, then the fate of Christ is not the fellowship of the stars; rather, Christ is also the fate of the stars. He assumed even the flesh created beneath heaven by that will by which he also created heaven, and laid it down and took it up again by that power by which he also commanded the stars.

### CHAPTER SIX

Why, then, is what is narrated concerning this generation not Gospel, when such good news is proclaimed to us that through it our weakness is healed? [Note: [Col. 0213] Three manuscripts read: “by which these things concerning the generation are narrated, when such good things are proclaimed to us, so that through them” (*ipsa*); Am. and Er. read: “when such good things are proclaimed to us, so that through it” (*ipsum*).]

Is it because Matthew did not begin by saying, “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ,” as Mark does, but “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ”? By this reasoning, John should not be said to have written a Gospel either, because he too did not say “The beginning of the Gospel” or “The book of the Gospel,” but “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1).

Unless perhaps Faustus was so elegant a fabricator of words that he called this beginning of John a *Verbidion*, on account of the Word, just as, on account of the *genesis*, he dared to call the other a *Genesidion*. But why do you not rather consider with what shamelessness you call those lengthy and impious fables of yours the Gospel?

What good is announced there, where it is said that God could not otherwise protect and care for his kingdom against some rebellious, opposing, and alien nature than by sending a part of his own nature to be devoured by that nature’s ravenous jaws, and thereby polluted, so that after so many labors and tortures it could not even be entirely purified? Is such a bad message the Gospel?

Certainly all who know even a little Greek interpret *Evangelium* as “good news” or “good proclamation.” How, then, is this a good message, when God himself is announced to you as mourning behind a veil placed before him until his members have been restored and cleansed from that devastation and contamination? If he should ever end his mourning, he will be cruel. For what evil did that part of him deserve which will be bound in the globe? It must surely be mourned forever, because it will be condemned forever.

But we have escaped, since whoever considers this message carefully is not compelled to mourn because it is bad, but to laugh because it is false.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0213]

### CHAPTER ONE

Faustus said: Do you therefore accept the generation?

For a long time I indeed tried to persuade myself, whatever it might be, that God had been born. But I was offended above all by the disagreement of the two Evangelists who write his genealogy, Luke and Matthew (Matt. I, 1–17, and Luke III, 23–38), and I remained uncertain which one I ought chiefly to follow. For I thought it possible that, since I am not prescient, the one whom I regarded as lying might be telling the truth, while the one whom I regarded as speaking truth might perhaps be lying.

Thus, leaving aside their interminable dispute, which was endless for me, I turned from the two to John and Mark—and not inequitably from two to two, and from Evangelists to teachers of the same name. For the time being, their openings pleased me not without reason, since they introduce neither David, nor Mary, nor Joseph. John says that the Word existed in the beginning, that the Word was with God, and that the Word was God (John I, 1), signifying Christ. Mark, however, says, “The Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark I, 1), as though reproaching Matthew, who had called him the son of David. Unless perhaps one of them announces one Jesus and the other another.

This, then, is the reason why I do not accept Christ as having been born. But if you are great enough to remove this offense from me, make the two agree with each other, and I shall yield in any event. Even then, however, it will not be fitting to believe that God—and the God of the Christians—was born from a womb.

### CHAPTER TWO

Augustine replied: If only you had read the Gospel with devout diligence, and had preferred carefully to investigate what troubled you in the Evangelists as though it were contradictory rather than rashly condemn it! Then, at least because of the very obvious contradiction that seems to meet one at first sight, you might have considered that, unless something important lay concealed there, it would have been difficult for such authority to be granted to them throughout the world, by which they subjected to themselves the minds of so many learned people.

For what is so remarkable in seeing what you have seen—that different progenitors of Christ according to the flesh are mentioned by Luke and by Matthew—when both establish Joseph, Matthew ending with him and Luke beginning from him? Because of a certain holy and virginal marriage with Christ’s mother, Joseph too deserved to be called Christ’s parent, so that on account of his masculine dignity the generations might be connected either from him or to him.

What, then, is so remarkable in what you have seen—that Joseph has one father according to Matthew and another according to Luke, and one grandfather according to the former and another according to the latter, and thereafter, ascending all the way to David through so many generations, different ancestors of Joseph are enumerated by one and by the other? Did so many acute and learned men, most diligent interpreters of the divine Scriptures, fail to see such an obvious and manifest difference? There are very few of them in the Latin language; but who could count those in Greek?

They certainly saw it. What is easier, or who could look at these things even briefly and fail to see them? But, piously considering the eminence of such authority, they believed that something was concealed there—something that would be given to those who asked, denied to those who barked accusations; found by those who sought, withheld from those who criticized; opened to those who knocked (Matt. VII, 7), closed to those who attacked. They asked, sought, knocked; they received, found, and entered.

### CHAPTER THREE

The entire question, of course, concerns how Joseph could have had two fathers. For if this is shown to have been possible, there is no reason at all to believe that either of these Evangelists told a falsehood in enumerating different generations. Once there are two fathers, it will no longer be surprising or contradictory that there could also be two grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and great-great-grandfathers, and all the ancestors above them up to David, whose sons they both were: Solomon, who belongs to the line followed by Matthew, and Nathan, who belongs to the series set forth by Luke.

Some people attend to these matters and see that a human being cannot be begotten through the mingling of flesh by two men, and therefore think that this question cannot be resolved [Note: [Col. 0215] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 7.]. They do not observe what is utterly customary and very easy [Note: [Col. 0215] Several manuscripts read “utterly customary and very frequent.”]: that a person’s father is not called only the one by whom he was begotten, but also the one by whom he was adopted [Note: [Col. 0215] *Retractations* II, chapter 7, no. 2.].

For the bond of adoption was not foreign to the customs of the ancients, since we find even women adopting sons not born from their own womb: Sarah adopted one from Hagar (Gen. XVI, 2), and Leah one from her maidservant (ibid. XXX, 9–13), while Pharaoh’s daughter adopted Moses (Exod. II, 9–10). Jacob himself adopted Joseph’s grandsons as his sons (Gen. XLVIII, 5).

The name of adoption itself, moreover, has great force in the sacrament of our faith, as apostolic teaching testifies. Thus, when the Apostle Paul was speaking of the merits of the Jews, he says: “Whose is the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law; whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever” (Rom. IX, 4–5). Again he says: “And we ourselves also groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption, the redemption of our body” (ibid. VIII, 23) [Note: [Col. 0215] “Of the sons of God” is absent from the manuscripts and from the older editions of Am. and Er.]. Elsewhere he says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Gal. IV, 4–5).

How great a sacrament this adoption is is sufficiently clear from these and similar testimonies. God has one unique Son, whom he begot from his own substance, of whom it is said: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. II, 6). We, however, he did not beget from his substance; for we are creatures, whom he did not beget but made. Therefore, in order to make us brothers of Christ in our own manner [Note: [Col. 0215] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read “our manner.”], he adopted us.

This manner by which God, when we already existed as beings not born but created and established by him, begot us by his word and grace so that we might be his sons is called adoption. Hence John says: “He gave them power to become the sons of God” (John I, 12).

Since, then, the legal right of the adoption of sons is customary among our fathers and in the holy Scriptures, what madness of impiety drives people first to accuse the Evangelists of falsehood because they have recounted different generations, as though both accounts could not be true, rather than to think, attend, and see what is easiest—that by the very frequent custom of the human race one man could have two fathers: one whose flesh begot him as a human being, and another whose will adopted him as a son when he was already a human being?

If the latter may not rightly be called a father, then neither do we rightly say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9), to him from whose substance we were not born, but by whose grace and most merciful will we have been adopted according to apostolic teaching and the most faithful truth. We have him as God, Lord, and Father: as God, because we were created by him, even through human parents; as Lord, because we are subject to him; and as Father, because through his adoption we have been born again.

It was therefore easy for devout investigators of the divine Scriptures to consider the matter briefly and see, in the different genealogies of Christ recounted by the two Evangelists, how Joseph could have had two fathers whose ancestors were enumerated differently. You too could easily see this, if the zeal for argument had not blinded you. But those men also sought out and discovered other things when they examined every part of these accounts; these matters, however, are very far removed from your understanding.

Thus, even though you are fixed in the error of Manichaeus, you could have seen by reflection—if you had read without an antagonistic disposition—that in human affairs it commonly happens that one person begets a son in the flesh while another adopts him by will, and so one person has two fathers.

### CHAPTER FOUR

Why Matthew began from Abraham and descended to Joseph, whereas Luke began from Joseph and ascended not to Abraham but to God, who made the human being and, after giving the commandment, granted the power for the believer to become a son of God; why the former enumerated the generations themselves at the beginning of his book, while the latter did so after the Lord and Savior had been baptized by John; and what is signified by the number of generations according to Matthew, arranged in three groups of fourteen, which, when counted together, seem to yield one fewer [Note: [Col. 0216] The printed editions read *tamen* (“nevertheless”). The manuscripts read *tanquam* (“as though”).]; while the number of generations according to Luke, which is mentioned at the Lord’s baptism, reaches seventy-seven—the number that the Lord himself commends for the remission of sins when he says, “Not merely seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (ibid. XVIII, 22)—you could in no way investigate unless either you heard it from some Catholic, not just anyone but one devoted to the study of the divine Scriptures and as learned as possible, or, corrected from your error, you yourselves asked in Catholic piety so that you might receive, sought so that you might find, and knocked so that you might enter.

### CHAPTER FIVE

Therefore, since what troubled Faustus about the diversity of the genealogies has been resolved by understanding nature and adoption—for the difficulty lay in understanding two fathers—he has tried in vain to turn to two Evangelists and take away from two others. He would offend more those to whom he turned than those from whom he withdrew. For the saints do not love their electors if they discover them to be deserters of their companions.

They rejoice in unity and are one in Christ. Even if one says one thing and another another, or one says it in one way and another in another way, all nevertheless speak the truth and are in no way contradictory, if a devout reader approaches, if a gentle reader reads, and if one seeks not with a heretical spirit for grounds of quarrel but with a faithful heart for means of edification.

Since, then, we have believed that the individual Evangelists undertook to narrate the genealogies of the individual fathers—of whom it is not foreign to the human race for one man to have two—our faith is not foreign to the truth [Note: [Col. 0217] Er., Lugd., and Ven. read: “Now therefore in the genealogies of the individual fathers.” M.]. Accordingly, now that the Evangelists agree among themselves, as Faustus promised, yield in any event.

### CHAPTER SIX

Does what he added still trouble you? “Even then,” he says, “it will not be fitting to believe that God—and the God of the Christians—was born from a womb.”

As though we believed that the divine nature itself came forth from a woman’s womb! Did I not just recall the testimony of the Apostle, where he says concerning the Jews: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever”?

Christ, therefore, our Lord and Savior, the true Son of God according to divinity and the true son of man according to the flesh, was not born from a woman from that which he is as God blessed forever, over all things. Rather, he was born from that weakness which he assumed from us, so that he might die in it for us and heal it in us.

He was not born from the form of God, in which, though existing, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized; he was born from the form of a servant, which he took and by taking which he emptied himself (Phil. II, 6). For he is said to have emptied himself for no other reason than by taking the form of a servant, not by losing the form of God.

That nature by which, in the form of God, he is equal to the Father remained immutable, while he assumed our mutable nature, through which he was to be born from a virgin. But you, while recoiling from committing Christ’s flesh to a virginal womb, have committed the very divinity of God—not merely to human wombs but also to the wombs of dogs and pigs! You refuse to believe that Christ’s flesh was once conceived in a virgin’s womb, in which God was not only not bound but not even changed; yet you preach that the very part of God, the divine nature, is bound, oppressed, and polluted in the male seeds and female wombs of all human beings and beasts, in every conception, throughout all lands, all waters, and all hours [Note: [Col. 0218] It may perhaps be necessary to read *auras* (“breezes” or “airs”), as the sequence of the argument seems to suggest. This is also the view of Morel, who in *Elementa Critica*, p. 309, cites nearly similar words from book 6, chapter 8: “on earth, in water, in air.”].

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0217]

### CHAPTER ONE

Faustus said: Do you accept the Old Testament?

If I have an inheritance in it, I accept it; if I do not, I do not accept it. For it is excessive impudence to seize documents that testify that one has been disinherited.

Do you not know that the Old Testament promises the land of the Canaanites (Gen. XV, 18, and XVII, 8), but that it promises it to the Jews—that is, to the circumcised, those who offer sacrifices, abstain from pork and from the other meats that Moses calls unclean, observe the Sabbaths, the festival of unleavened bread, and the other practices of this kind, which the very testator himself commanded them to observe (Lev. XI, 7, and Exod. XII and XX, 8)?

Since none of these practices has pleased the Christians—for none of us observes them—it is right that, when we refuse the inheritance, we should also return the documents. This, then, is the first reason why I think the Old Testament must be rejected, unless you teach me something wiser.

The second reason is that its inheritance is so wretched, corporeal, and so far removed from the interests of the soul that, after the blessed promise of the New Testament, which promises me the kingdom of heaven and eternal life, even if its testator were to thrust it upon me as a gift, I would disdain it.

### CHAPTER TWO

Augustine replied: None of us doubts that promises of temporal things are contained in the Old Testament, and that for this reason it is called the Old Testament; nor that the promise of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven belongs to the New Testament. But that those temporal things contained figures of future realities which would be fulfilled in us, upon whom the end of the ages has come, is not my suspicion but apostolic understanding. Paul says this when speaking of such matters: “All these things were figures of us” [Note: [Col. 0218] Er. and Lov. read *figurae nostri*. Almost all manuscripts, with Am., read *figurae nostrae*; and likewise below in several places.]; and again: “All these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (I Cor. X, 6, 11).

We therefore accept the Old Testament not in order to obtain those promises, but in order to understand in them the announcements beforehand of the New Testament; for the testimony of the Old establishes faith in the New.

Thus, after the Lord had risen from the dead and had offered himself not only to be seen by the eyes of his disciples but also to be touched by their hands, lest they think that they had been deceptively dealt with in their mortal and bodily senses, he strengthened them still more by the testimony of the ancient Books, saying: “It was necessary that all things written about me in the Law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV, 44).

Our hope, therefore, is not fixed on the promise of temporal things. For we do not believe that even the holy and spiritual men of that time—the Patriarchs and Prophets—were devoted to earthly things. They understood, through the revelation of God’s Spirit, what was appropriate to that time and in what ways God had determined that future realities should be figured and announced through all those deeds and sayings. Their desire was directed rather toward the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0219] Lov. reads: “but just as the present” (*sed sicut praesens*). The word *sicut* is absent from the other editions and most manuscripts.]; but a present bodily observance was provided through old promises in order to signify the new things that were to come. Thus the life of those people, not merely their speech, was prophetic.

The carnal people, however, clung to the promises of the present life. Yet even through that people future things were likewise signified.

But you do not understand these things; for, as the prophet said, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9). For you have not been instructed in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the true catholic Church of Christ. If you had been, from the riches of the holy Scriptures you would bring forth not only new things but also old. For the Lord himself says: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder bringing forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. XIII, 52). And so, while you think that you possess only God’s new promises, you have remained in the oldness of the flesh and have introduced novelty into error. [Col. 0220] Of this novelty the Apostle says: “But avoid profane novelties of words; for they contribute greatly to impiety, and their speech spreads like cancer. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have strayed from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and have overturned the faith of some” (II Tim. II, 16–18). Recognize from what stream of falsehood you flow, you who say that there is now only a resurrection of souls through the preaching of truth, while you deny that the resurrection of bodies, which the Apostles preached, is still to come.

But what can you think spiritually, according to the inner man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God (Coloss. III, 10), when, through the oldness of the flesh and through the images of bodily things in which your entire error is wrapped, you do not possess corporeal realities by having them, but understand them through phantasm? You boast that you despise and disdain the land of the Canaanites, which was manifest and was manifestly given to that people—as though you did not similarly describe a land of light, torn away on one side from the land of the nation of darkness, as if compressed by a wedge, so that it is neither found in the truth of things nor believed in the falsehood of your thoughts; and therefore, once given, it does not even sustain your life, and, once desired, it corrupts your mind.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0219]

## CHAPTER ONE

Faustus said: Do you accept the Gospel? You ask me whether I accept it, when the very fact that I observe what it commands makes it apparent that I accept it. Or should I ask you whether you accept it, when there seem to be no signs in you of one who accepts the Gospel? I abandoned my father, my mother, my wife, my children, and the other things that the Gospel commands (Matt. XIX, 29); and you ask whether I accept the Gospel? Unless you still do not know what is called the Gospel. For it is nothing other than the preaching and commandment of Christ.

I rejected silver and gold, and ceased to carry bronze in my belts, content with daily food, caring nothing for tomorrow and taking no concern about where my belly would be filled or my body clothed (ibid. X, 9, 10, and VI, 25–34); and you ask me whether I accept the Gospel? You see in me those beatitudes of Christ that constitute the Gospel (ibid. V, 3–11); and you ask whether I accept it? You see a poor man, you see a meek man, you see a peacemaker, one pure in heart, mourning, hungering and thirsting, enduring persecutions and hatred on account of righteousness; and you doubt whether I accept the Gospel?

It is therefore no longer surprising that John the Baptist, after seeing Jesus and likewise hearing of his works, should still ask whether he was the Christ. To him Jesus did not even deign suitably and properly to announce that he was himself the Christ; rather, he sent back to him the same works that John had already heard about: “The blind see, the deaf hear, the dead rise” (ibid. XI, 2–6), and so forth. I too would not unreasonably do the same in your case: if, when you ask me whether I accept the Gospel, I say, “I have abandoned everything of mine—father, mother, wife, children, gold, silver, eating, drinking, luxuries, pleasures.” Consider this a sufficient answer to your question, and consider yourself blessed if you have not been scandalized by me.

## CHAPTER TWO

“But,” you say, “accepting the Gospel does not consist solely in doing what it commanded, but also in believing everything written in it. The first of these is that God was born” [Note: [Col. 0220] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read, “that Jesus was born.” Lov., “God,” but in the margin, “Jesus.”].

But neither does accepting the Gospel consist solely in believing that Jesus was born; it also consists in doing what he commanded. Yet if you think that I do not accept the Gospel because I pass over the generation, then you do not accept it either—and much more plainly you do not accept it because you disregard its commandments. Accordingly, for the moment we are equals, until we examine both sides. Or, if this contempt for the commandments does not prejudice you when you claim to accept the Gospel, why should the condemned genealogy prejudice me? [Note: [Col. 0220] Lov. reads “that.” M.]

But if, as you say, accepting the Gospel consists in these two things—believing the genealogies and keeping the commandments—why do you, being imperfect, judge one who is imperfect? Each of us needs what the other possesses. If, as is more certain, accepting the Gospel consists solely in observing the heavenly commandments, you are doubly wicked, since, as the saying goes, you accuse a soldier as a deserter.

Nevertheless, let us suppose, since you wish it, that these two things are parts of perfect faith, one consisting in speech—that is, confessing that Christ was born—and the other in conduct, which is the observance of the commandments. See, then, what a difficult and arduous part I have chosen for myself; and see what a very light and easy part you have chosen. Nor is it without reason that the crowd comes to you and flees from me, not knowing, of course, that the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. Why, then, do you attack me, when I have undertaken the more difficult part of faith and, as one who is weak, left the easier part to you?

“But,” you say, “for granting salvation to souls, I consider this part of faith—the part you abandoned, namely, confessing that Christ was born—to be more effective and more suitable.”

## CHAPTER THREE

Come, then, let us question Christ himself and learn from his own mouth from what source the opportunity for salvation arises most especially. “Which human being will enter your kingdom, Christ?” “The one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven,” he says (Matt. VII, 21). He did not say, “The one who confesses that I was born.”

And elsewhere, to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (ibid. XXVIII, 19, 20). He did not say, “Teaching them that I was born,” but that they should keep the commandments.

Again, elsewhere: “You will be my friends if you do what I command you.” He did not say, “If you believe that I was born.” Again: “If you do my commandments, you will remain in my love” (John XV, 14, 10). And there are many other passages.

Moreover, when he taught on the mountain, he said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0221] The word “in spirit” is absent from nearly all the manuscripts], and then, “Blessed are the meek, blessed are the peacemakers, blessed are the pure in heart, blessed are those who mourn, blessed are those who hunger, blessed are those who suffer persecution on account of righteousness” (Matt. V, 3–10). Nowhere did he say, “Blessed are those who have confessed that I was born.”

And in the judgment, when he separates the sheep from the goats, he says that he will say to those who are on the right: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and the rest; “therefore receive the kingdom” (ibid. XXV, 35, 34). He did not say, “Because you believed that I was born, receive the kingdom.”

Nor, to the rich man who was asking about eternal life, did he say anything other than: “Go, sell everything that you have and follow me” (ibid. XIX, 21). He did not say, “Believe that I was born, so that you may live eternally.”

Behold, then, everywhere the kingdom, life, and blessedness are promised to the portion I have chosen for myself from the twofold faith, as you wish it to be; but nowhere are they promised to yours. Either show us somewhere that Scripture says that the person who has confessed that he was born of a woman is blessed, or will receive the kingdom, or will possess eternal life. For the moment, even if this too is a part of faith, it does not possess blessedness.

But when we have not even proved that it is a part of faith [Note: [Col. 0221] Lov. reads, “when we have not proved that it possesses a part.” Other printed editions and the manuscripts lack the word “possesses.”], what will happen? Clearly, you will be empty—and that too will certainly be demonstrated. For the present, however, this is enough for our purpose: that this portion of ours is crowned with beatitudes.

To it there is also added that other blessedness, arising from the confession of speech as well, because we confess that Jesus is Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus himself likewise bears witness to this with his own mouth, saying to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid. XVI, 17).
