Therefore we now possess not, as you thought, one but two valid parts of faith, and in both alike we are called blessed by Christ: we exercise one of them in works, and we proclaim the other without blasphemy.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Augustine replied: Above I have already recalled how often the Lord Jesus Christ calls himself the Son of Man, and with what great folly the Manichaeans introduce the fable of their abominable error concerning some fabricated first man—whom they proclaim, contrary to the Apostle, to have been not earthly but clothed in deceptive elements—where the Apostle says, “The first man was from the earth, earthly” (I Cor. XV, 47). I have also recalled with what care that same Apostle warned us, saying: “If anyone announces to you anything other than what we have announced to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. I, 8, 9).

It remains, therefore, that we believe Christ the Son of Man as he is proclaimed by apostolic truth, not as he is fabricated by Manichaean falsehood. Since, then, the Evangelists announce that he was born of a woman, from the house of David—that is, from the family of David—and since Paul writes to Timothy: “Remember that Jesus Christ rose from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (II Tim. II, 8), it is sufficiently clear how we ought to believe Christ to be the Son of Man: he is the Son of God, through whom we were made, and he also became the Son of Man through the assumption of flesh, so that he might die on account of our sins and rise on account of our justification (Rom. IV, 25).

Therefore he says that he is both the Son of God and the Son of Man. Thus, without going through many passages, we read in one place in the Gospel according to John: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who hear will live. For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also given the Son to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John V, 25–27).

He said, “They will hear the voice of the Son of God,” and he said, “Because he is the Son of Man.” For insofar as he is the Son of Man, he received authority to execute judgment, because he will come in that very form for judgment, so that he may be seen by both the good and the wicked. In that form he also ascended into heaven, and that voice sounded to the disciples: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11).

For insofar as he is the Son of God, he is God equal to the Father and one with the Father; he will not be seen by the wicked: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. V, 8).

Since, then, he promises eternal life to those who believe in him, and since believing in him means nothing other than believing in the true Christ, as he himself proclaims himself and as he is proclaimed by the Apostles—that is, both the true Son of God and the true Son of Man—you Manichaeans, who believe in the son of a false and deceptive man, while teaching that God himself, terrified by the tumult of the hostile nation, sent his own members to be tortured and that they are not afterward to be entirely purified, see how far you are from the eternal life that Christ promises to those who believe in him [Note: [Col. 0222] Many manuscripts omit both the conjunction “while” and the verb “teaching” that occurs below.].

“But,” you say, “he said to Peter, who confessed him to be the Son of God, ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona’” (ibid. XVI, 17). Does that mean that he promises nothing to those who would believe in him as the Son of Man, when he is himself both the Son of God and the Son of Man?

You also have eternal life plainly promised to those who believe in the Son of Man. “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness,” he says, “so it is necessary for the Son of Man to be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 14, 15). What more do you want? Believe, therefore, in the Son of Man, so that you may have eternal life; for he is also the Son of God, who can give eternal life; for he is the true God and eternal life, as that same John says in his Epistle. There he also says that the antichrist is the one who denies that Christ came in the flesh (I John V, 20, and IV, 3).

## CHAPTER FIVE

Why, then, do you boast as though you possessed perfection in his commandments, because you perform what has been commanded in the Gospel? What good would those things do, where true faith is absent, even if you truly fulfilled them? Have you not heard the Apostle say: “If I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 3)?

Why, then, do you boast as though you possessed Christian poverty, when you lack Christian love? Robbers too have among themselves what they call love, binding one another by a criminal and shameful complicity; but they do not have the love commended by the Apostle. To distinguish it from the other things that must be condemned and rejected, he says elsewhere: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I, 5).

How, then, can you possess true love arising from a feigned faith [Note: [Col. 0223] The manuscripts read, “arising from an unfeigned faith.”]? Or when will you be ashamed to stain your faith with lies [Note: [Col. 0223] Several manuscripts read, “to darken your faith with lies.” Others, along with the editions of Am. and Er., read, “to make your faith contend with lies.” Two Cistercian codices read, “on account of your faith, to contend with lies.”]—when you proclaim that your first man, together with his enemies who remain in the truth of their own nature, fought by mutable deception, and when you persuade people that Christ himself, who says, “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6), lied about the appearance of flesh, the death of the cross, the wounds of his passion, and the scars of his resurrection?

Accordingly, you wish to place yourselves before your Christ, if, while he lies, you proclaim the truth. But if you wish to follow your Christ, who would not guard against falsehood in you, so that even in those commandments which you claim to fulfill there might be nothing but deception?

For Faustus dared to say that you do not carry bronze in your belts—unless perhaps he spoke the truth for this reason: that you do not carry bronze in your belts, but do have gold in your chests and purses. These things would not be criticized in you if you did not profess one thing and live otherwise.

There is still among human affairs that Constantius—now, at least, our brother, a catholic Christian—who had gathered many of you into his house at Rome for the purpose of fulfilling the commandments of Mani, commandments sufficiently vain and foolish, yet things that you consider important. When your weakness yielded to them, you were scattered, each on his own way. Hence those who wished to persevere in them made a schism from your fellowship; and because they sleep on mats, they are called Mattarii. Faustus’s feather beds and goatskin blankets were very unlike their bedding; by such an abundance of luxury he not only disdained the Mattarii but also the household of his father, a poor man of Milevis. [Col. 0224]

Remove, then, your ruined pretense—if not from your conduct, at least from your writings—lest your tongue, together with your life, seem to be fighting with lies, not elements, like that first man with the nation of darkness.

## CHAPTER SIX

But lest anyone criticize me for saying these things against people who do not fulfill what is commanded to them rather than against the sect itself, which is the most vain of errors, I say this: the commandments of Mani themselves are such that, if you do not do them, you are deceivers; but if you do them, you are deceived.

For Christ did not command you not to pull up an herb, lest you commit murder. He did not forbid his disciples, as they passed through the grainfields while hungry, to pluck ears of grain on the Sabbath (Matt. XII, 1)—and by this he would convict both the Jews who were present and the future Manichaeans: the former because it happened on the Sabbath, the latter because it happened at all.

But Mani plainly commanded you to live, with your idle hands, from the murders of others. Those murders are indeed false murders, but yours are real, when by such a doctrine of demons you slaughter miserable souls.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

Yet that heretical arrogance and intolerable pride are present. “You see,” he says, “in me those beatitudes of Christ that constitute the Gospel; and you ask whether I accept it? You see a poor man, you see a meek man, you see a peacemaker, one pure in heart, mourning, hungering, thirsting, enduring persecutions and hatred on account of righteousness; and you doubt whether I accept the Gospel?”

If it were righteousness to justify oneself, this man, when he spoke these words, would have flown into heaven on the strength of his own speech. But I am not attacking Faustus’s luxuries, which are known to all the Hearers of the Manichaeans, and especially to those in Rome. I am presenting a Manichaean such as Constantius was seeking when he demanded that those commandments be fulfilled, not one whom he did not wish to appear to be.

And yet how do I see him as poor in spirit, when he is so proud that he believes his soul to be God and is not ashamed to be a captive [Note: [Col. 0224] Am. Er., and most manuscripts read, “and is not ashamed as a captive.”]? How do I see him as meek, when he prefers to insult such great evangelical authority rather than believe? How do I see him as a peacemaker, when he thinks that the divine nature itself—by which God is whatever he is, and he alone truly is—could not possess perpetual peace? How do I see him as pure in heart, when such sacrilegious and numerous fictions are in turmoil within him?

How do I see him as mourning, unless he mourns his god as captured and bound, until he is released and escapes—though diminished in some part, that part which will be bound by the Father in the globe of darkness and will not be mourned?

How do I see him hungering and thirsting for righteousness—a righteousness that Faustus did not add to his writings, I suppose lest it seem to be lacking in him if he confessed that he still hungered and thirsted for it? But what righteousness do these people hunger and thirst for, whose perfect righteousness will be to triumph over brothers condemned in the globe, brothers who sinned through no fault of their own but were inexpiably infected by the enemy’s corruption, against which the Father sent them [Note: [Col. 0224] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read, “against which the Father sent them.”]?

## CHAPTER EIGHT

How do you endure persecutions and hatred on account of righteousness, when it is considered righteousness for you to proclaim and persuade people of these sacrileges? Why do you not reflect on how little, or almost nothing, you suffer for this impious perversity, because of the gentleness of Christian times? But, as though you were speaking to blind and foolish people [Note: [Col. 0225] Er. Lugd. and Ven. read, “as though you were speaking”], you wish it to be regarded as a great proof of your righteousness that you endure insults and suffer persecution.

Moreover, if each person is more righteous in proportion to the severity of what he suffers, I shall not mention what is easiest to see: how much more severe are the sufferings endured by various people polluted by one crime or another and by various forms of wickedness. I say this: if anyone who suffers persecution for the name of Christ, however wrongly assumed and received, must already be called a possessor of true faith and righteousness, then grant that the person must possess the truer faith and greater righteousness whom we can show to have suffered much more grievous things than you. Let the thousands of our martyrs already come before your eyes, and above all Cyprian himself, whose writings also teach that he believed in Christ born of the Virgin Mary.

For this faith, which you detest, he proceeded all the way to the sword and death, together with the communities of Christians who at that time believed and died in this way, and even more grievously.

Faustus, however, after being convicted or confessing that he was a Manichaean, was brought to the proconsular court with several others. Through the intercession of those very Christians by whom they had been brought, he was relegated to an island under the lightest penalty—if it should even be called a penalty—which servants of God voluntarily undertake every day when they wish to withdraw themselves from the tumultuous uproar of peoples, and by which the public vows of earthly rulers customarily release the condemned through clemency. Finally, not long afterward, they were all released from there under the same customary arrangement.

Therefore, either admit that those who deserved to endure things far more atrocious than you for their faith possessed the truer faith and the more righteous life, or stop boasting that you are detestable to many. Distinguish what it means to suffer persecution for blasphemy and what it means to suffer persecution for righteousness; and carefully observe, again and again, for which of these two you suffer, even in your own books.

## CHAPTER NINE

How many people in our communion truly practice those loftier evangelical commandments, whose outward appearance you use to deceive the inexperienced? How many men and women are pure and undefiled from every sexual union? How many, having experienced marriage, afterward practice continence? How many distribute and abandon their possessions? How many, by frequent, daily, or even incredibly continuous fasts, subject their bodies to servitude?

How many fraternal communities possess nothing as their own but hold everything in common—and even this only what is necessary for food and clothing—melding one soul and one heart toward God in the fire of love?

And among all these professions, how many are discovered to be deceitful and ruined; how many also remain hidden; how many, initially walking rightly, quickly fall away through a perverse will; how many are found in temptations to have accepted such a life under an outward appearance because they undertook it with another intention; and how many, humbly and faithfully guarding their holy purpose, persevere to the end and are saved?

Among their company, those who, because of some necessity, according to the Apostle’s exhortation, have wives as though they had none, buy as though they did not possess, and use this world as though they did not use it, appear to be unlike the others; nevertheless, they are joined by the same love.

To these, according to the abundant riches of God’s mercy, are also added those to whom it is said: “Do not deprive one another, except by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and come together again for this very purpose, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by way of concession, not by command” (I Cor. VII, 29, 30, 31, 5, 6).

To such people the same Apostle says: “Now it is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another.” And, bearing their weakness, shortly afterward he says: “If, then, you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are despised in the Church” (ibid. VI, 7, 4).

For it is not only those who, in order to become perfect, sell or abandon all their possessions and follow the Lord who belong to the kingdom of heaven; rather, a kind of stipendary multitude is also attached to this Christian army through a certain commerce of love. To it, at the end, it will be said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV, 35), and the rest.

Otherwise those people must be condemned whose households the Apostle arranges with such careful and solicitous attention, instructing women to be subject to their husbands, husbands to love their wives, children to obey their parents, parents to nurture their children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord, slaves to obey their fleshly masters with fear, and masters to provide their slaves with what is just and equitable (Coloss. III, 18–IV, 1).

But far be it from the Apostle to judge such people alien from the evangelical commandments and excluded from eternal life. For where the Lord says, “If anyone does not take up his cross and follow me, he cannot be my disciple,” exhorting the stronger to perfection, there he immediately also consoles these others, saying: “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward; and whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward.”

Thus not only the person who gives Timothy a little wine on account of his stomach and his frequent illnesses (I Tim. V, 23), but also the person who gives a healthier and stronger person merely a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, as the passage continues, will not lose his reward (Matt. X, 38–42).

## CHAPTER TEN

Why do you deceive your Hearers, who serve you with their wives, children, households, houses, and fields, if anyone who does not abandon all these things does not accept the Gospel?

But because you promise them not resurrection but a return to this mortality, so that they may be born again and live the life of your Elect—a life as vain, foolish, and sacrilegious as the one you live when you are highly praised [Note: [Col. 0226] Several manuscripts read, “in which you live, in which you are highly praised.”]—or, if they are of better merit, may enter into melons and cucumbers or some other foods that you are going to eat, so that they may quickly be purified by your belchings, you rightly alienate them from the evangelical commandments. But you should also separate yourselves especially from such beliefs and teachings.

For if this vanity belonged to evangelical faith, the Lord should not have said, “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” but, “You were hungry, and you ate me,” or, “I was hungry, and I ate you.”

For according to your ravings, no one will be received into the kingdom of God on account of the merit of that ministry because he gave food to the saints, but because either he ate those for whom he longed, or he was eaten by those who longed to ascend into heaven.

Nor would those people say, “Lord, when did we see you hungry, and give you food?” Rather, they would say, “When did we see you hungry, and did you eat us?” And he would not answer them, “When you gave to one of the least of mine, you gave to me” (Matt. XXV, 35–40), but, “When one of the least of mine ate you, I ate you.”

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

While holding and teaching these monstrous doctrines and living according to them, you dare to say that you keep the evangelical commandments and to disparage the catholic Church, in which there are so many little ones together with the great—both of whom the Lord blesses—as they keep the evangelical commandments according to their several degrees and hope for the evangelical promises.

But your malevolent error leads your eye only to the chaff of our harvest. You would quickly see the wheat there as well, if you yourselves wished to be there.

Among you, both those who are falsely made Manichaeans are evil, and those who are not falsely made are vain. For where faith itself is feigned, the person who uses it deceitfully deceives, while the person who considers it true is deceived. From it a good life cannot arise, because each person lives either well or badly according to the object of his love.

But if you were burning with love for spiritual and intelligible good, rather than with desire for corporeal phantoms, to say briefly what is most widely known about you, you would not worship this corporeal sun as divine substance and as the light of wisdom.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0227]

## CHAPTER ONE

Faustus said: Do you accept the Old Testament? How could I, when I do not keep its commandments? I think, indeed, that neither do you; for I have rejected circumcision as shameful—and, if I am not mistaken, so have you. I have rejected the cessation from work on the Sabbaths as superfluous; I believe that you have as well. I have rejected sacrifices as idolatry; I have no doubt that you have also. Certainly I am not alone in abstaining from pork; you likewise do not eat pork alone.

I do so because I consider all flesh unclean; you do so because you consider nothing unclean. By both positions, then, the Old Testament is destroyed by both of us.

The weeks of unleavened-food observance [Note: [Col. 0227] Lov. reads, “the festivals, the weeks, of unleavened bread.” Am. Er. and some manuscripts read, “the weeks of things made unleavened.” Many other manuscripts read “the weeks of the Feast of Unleavened Bread” or “the weeks of unleavened-food observance.” The latter is the more correct reading], the Feast of Booths—both of us have despised them as useless and vain. Not inserting purple threads into linen garments; placing a linen-wool garment among adulterous things; yoking an ox and a donkey, if necessary, counting it among sacrileges; not appointing a bald and red-haired man, or a man of similar appearance, as a priest because such people are unclean before God—we have both despised and mocked all these things, and have regarded them neither among secondary matters nor among primary ones. Yet all these are commandments and ordinances of the Old Testament.

Whatever, then, you object to me is shared with me by you, whether it is to be considered a crime or a right action. For both of us reject the Old Testament.

Therefore, if you ask what difference there is between my faith and yours, it is this: you like to lie and to act dishonorably, so that what you hate in your mind you praise with your words; I have not learned to deceive. I say what I feel, and I confess that I hate teachers of such shameful things as much as I hate the commandments themselves.

## CHAPTER TWO

Augustine replied: Above we have already explained how and why the Old Testament is accepted by the heirs of the New Testament (Book 4, chapter 2). But because Faustus shortly before discussed its promises and now wished to discuss its commandments, I answer that these people have no understanding at all of the difference between commandments concerning the conduct of life and commandments concerning the signification of life. For example: “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX, 17) is a commandment concerning the conduct of life; “You shall circumcise every male on the eighth day” (Gen. XVII, 10–12) is a commandment concerning the signification of life.

Because of this ignorance, the Manichaeans, and all who dislike the writings of the Old Testament, observe that whatever God commanded the earlier people to celebrate is not now observed, without understanding that these things were shadows of future realities. Following the custom of the present age, they criticize things that were entirely appropriate to that time, when those things that are now manifest were being signified as future.

But what will they say against the Apostle, who says: “All these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X, 6, 11)?

Behold, he himself has made clear why those Scriptures are accepted by us and why it is no longer necessary for us to observe those signs of things. When he says, “They were written for our sake,” he unquestionably shows how carefully we must read and understand them, and with what authority we must regard them, because they were certainly written for our sake. But when he says, “They were our figures,” and, “These things happened to them as a figure” [Note: [Col. 0228] Many manuscripts throughout read, “These things happened in them as a figure.”], he shows that, now that we are dealing with the realities themselves after they have been made manifest, it is no longer necessary for us to serve the celebration of the figures that foretold them.

Hence he says elsewhere: “Therefore let no one judge you concerning food or drink, or a part of a feast, or a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Coloss. II, 16, 17).

When he says, “Let no one judge you in these matters,” he also declares that it is not necessary for these things now to be observed. But when he says, “Which are a shadow of things to come,” he shows how appropriate it was that they should be observed at that time when those things that have now been made manifest and have shone forth for us were being foretold as future through such shadows of figures.

## CHAPTER THREE
Therefore, if the Manichaeans were justified by the Lord’s resurrection—whose day, reckoned from the day of the Passion, was the third, yet after the Sabbath, that is, after the seventh day, was the eighth—they would surely strip away the carnal veil of mortal desires. Rejoicing in circumcision of the heart, they would not mock the circumcision of the flesh, which was its shadow and figure in the time of the Old Testament, although in the time of the New Testament they would no longer be compelled to perform and observe it. For in what member could the stripping away of carnal and mortal concupiscence be more appropriately represented than in the member from which carnal and mortal offspring proceeds?

But, as the Apostle says, “All things are clean to the clean, but to the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15). Thus these men, who seem excessively clean to themselves because they shun—or pretend to shun—those members as unclean, have fallen into such uncleanliness of unbelief and error that, while they detest circumcision of the flesh, which the Apostle called “the seal of the righteousness of faith” (Romans 4:11), they nevertheless believe that, in those very carnal members, the divine members of their god are bound and held in pollution. Thus, when they call the flesh unclean, they are compelled to say that their god himself has become unclean in that part of him which is held there; indeed, they assert that he must be cleansed. Until this takes place, they say that, as far as possible, he presently suffers everything that flesh suffers—not only the exertion and pain of afflictions, but also the pleasure of corruptions. For they say that they spare him by not engaging in intercourse, lest he become more tightly entangled in fleshly bonds and be polluted more shamefully.

When, therefore, the Apostle says, “All things are clean to the clean”—to human beings, certainly, who can be changed for the worse by a perverse will—how much more are all things clean to God, who always remains unchangeable and undefiled? Of his divine Wisdom it is said in those Books which you pollute by criticizing them so vehemently: “Nothing defiled enters into her, and she reaches everywhere because of her purity” (Wisdom 7:25, 24).

Why, therefore, O most unclean vanity, does it displease you that in the human member from which the human race is propagated, God—who is clean in all things—commanded the sign of human regeneration to be established, while it pleases you that, in the crimes perpetrated through that member by immodest people, your god, to whom nothing is clean, should be stained and corrupted in part of his nature? For what does he suffer in various shameful corruptions, whom you believe to be polluted even by marital intercourse?

And as to what you are accustomed to say—“Was there really no other place where God could prefigure the seal of the righteousness of faith except that member?” [Note: [Col. 0229] Quite a few manuscripts read, “Dare now to say what you are accustomed to say.”]—the answer is: Why not there also? First, because “all things are clean to the clean,” and how much more to God? Second, because the Apostle said that the seal given to Abraham of the righteousness of faith was given in such a circumcision.

But do not be ashamed, if you can help it, when you are asked: “Was there really nothing else for your god to do, so that he would not entangle a part of his nature with those members which you despise in this way?” These members are indeed called shameful by human beings [Col. 0230] because of the corruptible and penal propagation of our mortality, which proceeds from them. The chaste treat them with modesty, the immodest with wantonness, and God with righteousness.

## CHAPTER IV

We now indeed regard the cessation from Sabbath observance as superfluous, since the hope of our eternal rest has been revealed; yet we do not regard it as superfluous for reading and understanding. For in the prophetic times, when the things that have now been disclosed to us had to be prefigured and foretold not only in words but also in actions, that reality which we now possess was marked out beforehand by the sign that we read.

But I want you to tell me why you do not wish to fulfill your own cessation. The Jews, in their Sabbath—which they still understand carnally—not only gather no fruit in the field, but neither cut nor cook anything in the house. You, however, while resting, await someone among your Hearers to leap into the garden armed with a knife or a small sickle, so that he may feed you: a murderer of gourds, who, strange to say, brings you their living corpses. For if he does not kill them, what do you fear in such an act? But if they are killed when they are plucked, how can life be in them—life which you claim to assist, cleanse, and restore by eating and belching them out?

You therefore receive living gourds which, if you could, you ought to swallow whole, so that after that single wound—the wound by which your Hearer became guilty when he plucked them—he might be freed by your indulgence; and so that thereafter they might reach the workshop of your belly, where you could restore your god, shattered in that battle, intact and unharmed. But before your teeth set upon crushing them, you cut them into tiny pieces, if that pleases your palate. How, then, are you not guilty of their repeated wounds? Consider how it would benefit you to do every day what the Jews do once in seven days, and to abstain also from such domestic work.

What do gourds suffer in the fire, where certainly the life that is in them is not restored? A boiling pot cannot be compared with a holy belly; yet you mock the Sabbath rest as though it were superfluous. How much healthier it would be if you not only did not criticize that observance among the Fathers, when it was not superfluous, but even now, when it is superfluous, preferred to retain it rather than your own observance—which is acceptable neither as a signification but condemnable as an error—and which, by not fulfilling it, makes you guilty according to the opinion of your vanity, while by fulfilling it you are vain according to the judgment of truth. [Note: [Col. 0230] Amerbach, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “and vain,” omitting the word “by fulfilling.”]

For you say that a fruit feels pain when it is plucked from the tree; that it feels pain when it is cut up, crushed, cooked, and eaten. You therefore ought not to have eaten anything except what could be swallowed raw and unharmed, so that at least it would suffer one pain, when plucked—not at your hands, but at those of your Hearers.

But you say: “How do we assist so much life if we consume only what can be swallowed uncooked and soft?” If, then, by this compensation you inflict so many pains upon your foods, why do you abstain from that one act to which this necessity most of all compels you? A fruit can be eaten raw, as some of your people have trained themselves to do—not merely with apples but with all vegetables. But unless it is plucked, falls, or is removed from the earth or tree in some way, it cannot possibly become food.

That, therefore, without which you could not assist it ought easily to have been regarded as pardonable—not those many tortures which you do not hesitate to inflict on the members of your god while preparing your food. But, they say, the tree weeps when its fruit is plucked; for you are certainly not ashamed to say this. Surely the life that is there knows everything and anticipates who will come to it. When the Elect come and pluck the fruit, therefore, it ought to rejoice, not weep, compensating that passing pain with such happiness and escaping such misery as it would have suffered had it fallen to others. Why, then, do you not pluck the fruit, when after plucking it you inflict so many wounds and pains upon it? Answer, if you can.

Nor are your fasts appropriate. One must not leave idle the furnace in which spiritual gold is purified from the mixture of dung and the divine members are released from their pitiable bonds. Therefore the more merciful person among you is the one who can train himself in such a way that nothing harms his health: frequently eating raw foods and consuming much. But you both eat cruelly by inflicting such punishments upon your food, and fast cruelly by abstaining from the purification of the divine members.

## CHAPTER V

Yet you also dare to curse the sacrifices of the Old Testament, call them idolatry, and associate us with such sacrilege. We therefore first answer on our own behalf: those sacrifices are no longer part of our works, yet we embrace them in the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, so that we may understand the things foretold through them. For they too were our figures, and all such things, in many different ways, signified the one sacrifice whose memory we now celebrate.

When that sacrifice was revealed and offered at its proper time, those former practices were removed from the performance of religious observance, but they remained authoritative in their signification. For “they were written for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

But the slaughter of animals in those sacrifices troubles you, although every creature in some fashion serves human uses by divine arrangement. Yet you, who do not offer bread to a poor and hungry human being, are merciful toward animals in which you believe human souls reside. The Lord Jesus, however, was cruel toward them when he permitted the demons, at their request, to enter a herd of pigs (Matthew 8:32).

Before he had demonstrated through his Passion the sacrifice of his body, he also said to a leper whom he had cleansed: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer your gift, which Moses commanded” [Note: [Col. 0231] Erasmus and nearly all manuscripts read, “and offer for yourself what Moses commanded.”] “as a testimony to them” (Luke 5:14).

Since God often declares through the Prophets that he has no need of such a gift, and since reason readily shows that one who needs nothing has no need even of that, the human mind is compelled to inquire what he intended to teach us through these things. He certainly would not have commanded things he did not need to be offered to him without showing in them something that was useful for us to know and that ought to be prefigured by such signs.

How much better and more honorably, then, would you submit yourselves to these sacrifices—which, though no longer necessary for our time, still signify and teach something—than to command and believe that living victims of food should be offered to you by your Hearers? For when the Apostle Paul most appropriately said of certain people who preached the Gospel for the sake of meals, “Their god is their belly” (Philippians 3:19), with how much more arrogant impiety do you boast, who are not afraid to call your belly not a god but—what is even more wicked—the cleanser of your god?

What greater madness is there than to wish to appear pious because you abstain from killing animals, while declaring that all your foods possess the same souls, and, while you think those souls are alive, inflicting such wounds upon them with your hands and teeth?

## CHAPTER VI

If you do not wish to eat meat, why do you not slaughter the animals offered to your god, so that those souls—which you believe not merely to be human but so divine that you regard them as the very members of God—may be released from the prison of flesh and, lest they return again, be commended through your prayers? Do you assist them more with your belly than with your mind? Is that nature of God saved which has deserved to be exhaled through your entrails, rather than that which is commended through your prayers?

You therefore do not sacrifice livestock to your belly because you cannot consume them alive and thereby liberate their souls through the intervention of your stomach. O blessed vegetables, which, after being torn out by hand, cut with iron, tortured by fire, and crushed by teeth, are nevertheless permitted to arrive alive at the altars of your intestines! And O wretched livestock, which, although they leave their bodies sooner, cannot enter your bodies!

Thus, still raving, you think that we are enemies of the Old Testament because we consider no flesh unclean, holding to the Apostle’s statement, “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15), and to the Lord’s saying, “It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out” (Matthew 15:11).

The Lord did not say this only to the crowds, as your Adimantus—whom Faustus praises above all after Manichaeus—wanted it understood when he slandered the Old Testament. Rather, when he was away from the crowds, he spoke the same thing to his disciples more clearly and explicitly. [Note: [Col. 0232] Against Adimantus, chapters 14 and 15.]

When Adimantus opposed this saying of the Lord to the Old Testament, because certain unclean meats are written there from which that people was commanded to abstain, he feared that someone might say to him: “Why, then, do you consider not merely certain meats but all meats unclean, and abstain from eating all of them, when you yourself produce the Gospel testimony that a person is not defiled by what enters the mouth, goes into the stomach, and is expelled into the latrine?”

Accordingly, in trying to escape these extremely narrow difficulties that were strangling his falsehood with the most manifest truth, he said that the Lord had spoken this to the crowds—as though he spoke the truth privately to a few but proclaimed falsehoods to the crowds. Yet it is sacrilegious even to believe this about the Lord, and all who read know that he spoke this more plainly to his disciples when the crowds were absent as well. [Note: [Col. 0233] The Louvain edition reads, “he said this to the crowds, and when the crowds were absent.” Other printed editions and manuscripts do not contain “to the crowds.”]

Therefore, because at the beginning of his work Faustus marvels at Adimantus in such a way that he prefers only Manichaeus to him, I ask briefly whether this saying of the Lord—that a person is not defiled by what enters his mouth—is true or false.

If they say it is false, why did their great teacher Adimantus, asserting that Christ uttered it, bring it forward to overthrow the Old Testament? But if it is true, why do they believe that they are defiled by it if they eat any kind of meat? Unless perhaps they wish to give the true answer and say that the Apostle did not say, “All things are clean to heretics,” but, “All things are clean to the clean.”

For why these things are not clean to them, the same Apostle goes on to say: “But to the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15). Hence, in truth, nothing at all is clean to the Manichaeans, since they contend that even the very substance or nature of God not only could have been defiled but has actually been defiled in part; and not only that it has been defiled, but also that it cannot be recovered and cleansed in its entirety.

It is therefore astonishing that they say they consider all flesh unclean and abstain from it for that reason, as though they believed anything to be clean—not merely among foods but among all creatures. For they declare that vegetables, fruits, all crops, the whole earth, and heaven itself have been polluted by mixture with the race of darkness.

Would that they were consistent with their error in the case of other foods as well, and that by abstaining from everything they call unclean they would die of hunger rather than persist in uttering such blasphemies! For who does not understand that this would be more beneficial for those unwilling to correct and amend themselves?

## CHAPTER VII

In the Old Testament, where certain meat foods are prohibited, why is this saying of the Apostle not contrary—“All things are clean to the clean” and “Every creature of God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4)? If they can, let them understand that the Apostle spoke of the natures themselves, whereas those Scriptures, because of certain prefigurations appropriate to their time, called certain animals unclean not by nature but by signification.

Thus, for example, if the question concerns a pig and a lamb, both are clean by nature, because every creature of God is good. But by a certain signification the lamb is clean and the pig unclean. It is as though you were to say “foolish” and “wise”: both words, considered as sounds, letters, and syllables of which they consist, are naturally clean; but by signification one of these words—the word “foolish”—may be called unclean, not by its own nature but because it signifies something unclean.

Perhaps what the pig is among the figures of things, the fool is among the classes of things; and both that animal and those two syllables forming the word “foolish” signify one and the same thing.

That animal was designated unclean in the Law because it does not chew the cud; but this is not its fault—it is its nature. There are human beings signified by this animal who are unclean by their own fault, not by nature: they gladly hear words of wisdom, but afterward give them no thought at all. For when you recall something useful that you have heard, bringing it back from the inner storehouse of memory, as it were, to the mouth of thought through the sweetness of recollection, what is this other than, in a spiritual sense, chewing the cud? Those who do not do this are represented by the class of those animals.

Thus even abstinence from such meats warned us to avoid this fault. Since wisdom itself is a desirable treasure, Scripture says elsewhere of this cleanness of chewing the cud and uncleanness of not chewing it: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it” (Proverbs 21:20).

These likenesses of things, expressed in figurative speech or observances, beneficially and pleasantly move rational minds through the exercise of seeking and comparing. But the earlier people were commanded not merely to hear many such things but also to observe them. For it was a time when what would later be revealed had to be prophesied not only in words but also in deeds.

Once these things were revealed through Christ and in Christ, the nations were not burdened with the observances of faith, but the authority of the prophecy was commended. We have now explained why, although according to the saying of the Lord and the Apostle we consider no animal flesh unclean, we do not oppose the Old Testament, where certain things are called unclean. Now let them explain why they consider flesh unclean.

## CHAPTER VIII

According to your error, because of the mixture with the race of darkness, it is not flesh but your god himself who is unclean in that part which he sent and mixed in order that it might be absorbed and polluted, as though enemies were to be conquered and captured. Moreover, because of that same mixture, everything else you eat is also unclean.

But you say: “Meat is much more unclean.” Why meat should be more unclean would require a lengthy account of their ravings on this subject. I shall touch briefly on enough to enable readers to see that the critics of the Old Testament are so worn out by the old age of their folly that, as accusers of flesh, they are shown to understand only flesh, without any spiritual truth.

Perhaps this somewhat lengthy answer will so instruct the reader against them that in our other responses we shall not be required to use so many words.

These empty talkers and seducers of minds say that in that battle, when their first human being ensnared the race of darkness in deceptive elements, the rulers of both sexes were captured from that same race. As the world was constructed from them, many of them were bound in the heavenly structures, among whom were also certain pregnant females. When the heaven began to revolve, they were unable to endure the same rotation and expelled their conceptions by miscarriage. These aborted offspring, both male and female, fell from heaven to earth, lived, grew, engaged in intercourse, and produced offspring.

They say that from this comes the origin of all flesh that moves on earth, in water, and in air.

Therefore, if the origin of flesh is from heaven, it is utterly absurd to consider it more unclean on that account—especially since, in the very structure of the world, they say that those same rulers of darkness were bound through all the interweavings, from the highest to the lowest, in such a way that the more good each possessed in mixture, the more highly he deserved to be placed. Accordingly, the flesh whose origin is from heaven ought to be cleaner than the crops that arise from the earth.

Moreover, what could be said more insane than that fetuses conceived before the mixture of life were so much more vigorous that, although miscarried and falling from heaven to earth, they lived, while once life was mixed in, they could not live unless born at the proper time and, if they fell from even a somewhat greater height, immediately died?

If the kingdom of life fought against the kingdom of death, mixed life ought to have made them more vigorous, not more corruptible. But if each thing retains its own incorruptibility more fully according to its nature, they ought to have proclaimed not two natures, good and evil, but two good natures, one of which was better.

Why, then, do they assert that the flesh whose origin they claim to derive from heaven is unclean—flesh known to everyone as such? For they think that the first bodies of the rulers of darkness arose from trees growing there, like little worms, and that the trees themselves arose from those five elements.

Therefore, if the bodies of animals have their first origin from trees and their second from heaven, why should they be considered more unclean than the fruits of trees?

If it is because, when they die, they lose their soul, so that whatever remains after life has departed is now unclean, why are vegetables and fruits not unclean in the same way? When they are plucked or torn away, they too surely die, as was said above. Yet they do not wish to be guilty of these murders when they pluck anything from the earth or from a tree.

Furthermore, since they assert that there are two souls in the body of one living creature—one good, from the race of light, and the other evil, from the race of darkness—when an animal is killed, does the good soul flee while the evil one remains? If this were so, the slaughtered animal would live as it lived among the race of darkness, when it possessed only the soul of its own race, by which it had also rebelled against the divine kingdoms.

Since, therefore, at the death of any animal both souls, good and evil, leave the flesh, why is the flesh called unclean, as though it were abandoned only by the good soul? For even if some remnants of life remain, they remain from both; they do not even say that the dung itself remains without some tiny remnants of the members of God.

They therefore find no reason for asserting that meat is more unclean than crops.

But, evidently, while trying to display their deceptive chastity, they consider flesh more unclean because it originates from intercourse—as though they were not thereby compelled all the more urgently to assist that divine member by eating, the more tightly they think it is bound there.

Finally, if this is the reason for the greater uncleanness of meat, let them eat the bodies of animals that do not originate from intercourse, such as the countless kinds of worms, some of which certain regions of Venetia commonly eat, since they arise from trees.

They ought also to take frogs—which the earth suddenly generates from a single rainfall—as food, in order to liberate the members of their god mixed in such forms, if they detest the flesh propagated through intercourse. They would thereby condemn the human race for its error, since people eat chickens and pigeons, produced by the intercourse of males and females, while rejecting the cleaner daughters of heaven and earth, the frogs.

For according to their tale, the first rulers of darkness, whose parents were trees, are cleaner than Manichaeus himself, whom his father and mother produced through intercourse. Their lice, which arise without intercourse from the sweat or exhalation of flesh or body, are also cleaner than these wretched men themselves, who were born from parents who engaged in intercourse.

Or if they now consider whatever is born from flesh, even without intercourse, unclean because flesh itself derives from intercourse, then vegetables and crops which have grown more abundantly and fruitfully from dung will be unclean. Let them see what they are doing, or what answer they can give, when they say that crops are cleaner than meat. For what is expelled from flesh is more unclean than dung, and what is applied to crops is more fertile?

They themselves certainly say that through the crushing and digestion of foods life departs from them, and that only something very small remains in the dung. Why, then, where only a little life remains, do your foods—that is, the fruits of the earth—arise from dung both better, larger, and more numerous?

Flesh is nourished not by the refuse of the earth but by offspring; the earth, however, is fertilized by the refuse of flesh, not by offspring. Let them choose what is cleaner—or, now corrected, let them cease to be unclean and unbelieving, to whom nothing is clean, and join us in embracing the Apostle’s statement: “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15).

“The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Psalm 23:1). “Every creature of God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4). Everything that exists naturally is good in its own order, and no one sins in these things except the person who, failing to maintain his own order in obedience to God, also disturbs their order by using them wrongly.

## CHAPTER IX

Our Fathers, who pleased God, maintained their own order in that obedience, so that whatever God distributed by command at appropriate times, they observed in the manner in which he distributed it.

Thus they not only refrained from eating certain meats given as food—which were all clean by nature but were nevertheless unclean at that time by a certain signification—during the period when they were commanded not to eat them, so that by such significations the future revelation of things might be prefigured; they also observed unleavened bread and other practices of the same kind, in which the Apostle says that there was “a shadow of future things” (Hebrews 10:1). The people of that time would have been just as guilty if they had refused to observe them, when those things had to be performed in that way and the realities now revealed had then to be foretold in that manner, as we would be foolish if, now that the New Testament has been revealed, we thought that those prophetic observances could benefit us.

Likewise, we would be sacrilegious and impious if, recognizing that the same Books were written for us so that we might understand that the things now revealed and proclaimed openly to us had long before been foretold to them through figures, we nevertheless thought those Books should be rejected because the Lord now commands us not to observe physically what is written there but to understand and perform it spiritually.

For “they were written for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come,” as the same Apostle says again (1 Corinthians 10:11). “Whatever was written beforehand was written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4).

Therefore, in the time of the Old Testament it was a sin not to eat unleavened bread for the appointed seven days (Exodus 12:15); in the time of the New Testament it is not a sin. But, in the hope of the future age that we have in Christ—who, clothing our soul with righteousness and our body with immortality, renews us wholly—it is always a sin, so long as these seven days through which time proceeds are passing, to believe that we will suffer or do anything out of the necessity and want of the old corruption. This was concealed in figure from certain holy people in the time of the Old Testament; in the time of the New Testament it has been revealed openly and is preached to the peoples.

Thus that Scripture was then a commandment; now it is a testimony.

At one time it was a sin not to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:34); now it is not a sin. But not to be joined to the tabernacle of God, which is the Church, is always a sin. At that time this was performed under a figurative command; now it is read in a revealed testimony. For what was then done would not be called the tabernacle of testimony unless, through an appropriate signification, it bore witness to some truth that was to be declared in its own time.

At one time it was a sin to mix purple with linen garments and to wear clothing woven of linen and wool together (Deuteronomy 22:11); now it is not a sin. But to live disorderly and to wish to mix professions of different kinds—so that either a religious woman wears the adornments of married women or a woman who married because she could not remain continent presents herself as a virgin—is altogether a sin; and so is anything that is inappropriately woven from different kinds in anyone’s life. What was then represented in clothing is now declared in conduct. That was the time of signification; this is the time of manifestation.

Therefore, the same Scripture which was then an exactor of significant works is now a witness to the things signified; what was then observed as a foretelling is now recited as a confirmation.

At that time it was not permitted to yoke an ox and a donkey together for work (Deuteronomy 22:10); now it is permitted. This was explained by the Apostle when, recalling the Scripture concerning the ox that treads grain and should not be muzzled, he said: “Is God concerned about oxen?” Why, then, is it read now, when what it prohibited is now permitted? Because the same Apostle goes on to say: “For our sake Scripture says this” (1 Corinthians 9:9–10).

It is certainly impious for us not to read what was written for us. Indeed, it was written more for us, to whom it is manifested, than for those in whom it was figured.

If necessary, anyone may yoke an ox and a donkey together without impairing the work. But no one can, without scandal, make a wise person and a fool companions—not so that one commands and the other obeys, but with equal authority—that they might proclaim the word of God together.

Thus we hold to the same Scripture: then, by the authority of a commandment, it ordered that what is now opened should be covered by shadows; now, by the authority of testimony, it attests that what was then covered is open in the light.

As for the bald man and the person whose hair has fallen out (Leviticus 13:40), Faustus had paid too little attention to the fact that the Law called them unclean, or he had encountered a corrupt manuscript. But would that he himself had wished to have a bald forehead [Note: [Col. 0238] The printed editions commonly read this way. Many older manuscripts, however, read: “But would that he himself had not wished to have a bald forehead.”] and had not been ashamed to set the cross of Christ upon it! Surely he would then have believed that Christ, crying, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), neither died with false wounds nor rose with false scars.

He even says: “I have not learned to deceive; I speak what I feel.” He is therefore not a disciple of his Christ, whom in his madness he supposes to have displayed false scars to his doubting disciples; and he wants to be believed, as though he himself did not deceive, not only concerning his other vanities but also concerning Christ’s very deception.

Is he better than Christ, since when he deceives, he himself does not deceive? [Note: [Col. 0238] Amerbach, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read this way. The Louvain edition reads: “Let whoever wishes decide whether he is better than Christ.”] Or is he, precisely in this, a disciple not of the truthful Christ but of the deceitful Manichaeus, since he deceives even in the matter in which he boasts that he has not learned to deceive?

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0237]

## CHAPTER I

Faustus said: Why do you not believe in the genealogy of Jesus? There are indeed many reasons, but the chief one is that he himself nowhere confesses with his own mouth that he has a father or lineage on earth. On the contrary, he says that he is not of this world, that he proceeded from God the Father, that he descended from heaven, and that he has no mother and brothers except those who do the will of his Father, who is in heaven.

Moreover, those very people who ascribe these genealogies to him do not seem to have known him before his birth. Nor do they appear to have joined him immediately after he was born, so that they could be believed to have written what they had seen him do with their own eyes. Rather, they joined him when he was already young and mature, at about thirty years of age; for even an age may be ascribed to the divine without blasphemy [Note: [Col. 0238] The Amerbach edition alone among all editions reads, “cannot be ascribed.”]

Since, then, in every testimony to truth it is customary always to ask whether someone heard a matter or saw it, while these men do not admit that they heard this order of his generation from him himself—or even that he was born at all—and did not see it with their eyes, since they came to know him only much later, namely after his Baptism, it seems to me, and to everyone who judges correctly, just as foolish to believe this as to summon a blind and deaf witness to court.

## CHAPTER II
AUGUSTINE replied: In the very place where he declares the “decisive reason” why he does not accept the genealogy of Jesus Christ, he is most plainly shown to be defeated, if readers consider what we said above about the Son of Man—how frequently Christ attests that he is this (Matt. 8:20)—and about the Son of God, and how he is himself also the Son of Man (ibid. 9:6); how, according to his divinity, he has no earthly lineage, but according to the flesh is from the seed of David, as apostolic teaching testifies (Rom. 1:3; 2 Tim. 2:8).

Accordingly, he must be believed and understood both to have come forth from the Father (John 16:28) and to have come down from heaven (ibid. 6:41), and yet here, among human beings, the Word made flesh dwelt (ibid. 1:14). But if they think that for this reason he had neither a mother nor a lineage on earth, because he said, “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” (Matt. 12:48), it remains for them also to assert that his disciples, to whom he gave this example in his own person—that for the sake of the kingdom of heaven they should despise earthly kinship—had no fathers, because he said to them, “Do not call anyone your father on earth; for one is your Father, God” (ibid. 23:9). What, then, he taught these men about fathers, he himself first did regarding his mother and brothers, just as he did many other things in which he deigned to offer himself to us for imitation and to go before us for following.

Therefore, since this man is so decisively defeated in the point on which he thinks he has the decisive argument, we must observe how he lies prostrate and entangled in the rest. For he says that the Apostles are not to be believed because they announced not only Christ’s divine birth but also his human [Col. 0240] birth, since they attached themselves to him only later, when he was already a young man, and neither saw him being born nor said that they had heard this from him.

Why, then, do they believe John when he says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3), and the rest, which please them even though they do not understand them? Let them say where John saw this, or where he said that he had heard it from the Lord himself. Whatever they say as to how John could have known this, from the same source we believe that all those who announced Christ’s birth could have known what they announced.

Next I ask: Why do they believe that the Lord said, “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” If it is because the Evangelist narrated this, why do they not also believe him when he says, “Because his mother and brothers were seeking him” (Matt. 12:48, 46)? But if he lied about what they do not wish to believe, how do they believe him when he says that Christ spoke what they do not wish to understand?

Furthermore, if Matthew could not have known that Christ was born because he had attached himself to him only when he was already a young man, how could Manichaeus, born so many years later, have known that Christ had not been born? They will say: “The Holy Spirit knew this, and he was in Manichaeus.” Certainly, if he had been the Holy Spirit, he would have spoken the truth. But why do we not rather believe Christ’s disciples, who also attached themselves to him bodily? If anything concerning human affairs lay hidden, they could have learned it not only through the Holy Spirit imparted by him, but also, with memory so recent and immediate, through ordinary human perception alone: namely, Christ’s lineage according to the flesh and his entire origin.

And yet the Apostles are called blind and deaf witnesses. Would that you had been not merely blind and deaf, lest you learn such empty and sacrilegious things, but also mute, lest you say such things!

## BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0239]

### CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: Why do you not accept the Old Testament? Because I have already been anticipated by the New; but the Old and the New do not agree, as Scripture testifies. For, it says, “No one sews a piece of new cloth onto an old garment; otherwise a greater tear will result” (Matt. 9:16; Luke 5:36). Since, therefore, I take care not to make a greater tear, as you do, I do not mix Christian novelty with Hebrew antiquity.

[Note: [Col. 0239] Almost uniquely, the Louvain edition reads: “as you know. It would make a tear; I take care not to mix Christian novelty with Hebrew antiquity.”]

Who would not also judge it disgraceful, when dressed in new clothes, not to give the old ones to inferiors?

[Note: [Col. 0239] In Erasmus’s Lyon edition, “the old ones.” M.]

Therefore, even if I had been born a Jew, as the Apostles were, it would nevertheless have been proper for me, after accepting the New Testament, to reject the Old, as they did. But now, since by nature’s gift I have attained the benefit of not being born under the yoke of servitude, and since Christ immediately came to meet me with the full gift of liberty, how miserable, foolish, and, moreover, ungrateful I would be if I should subject myself to servitude any longer!

[Col. 0240] For Paul rebukes the Galatians precisely because, falling back into circumcision, they were returning to the weak and beggarly elements, to which they wished to be enslaved again (Gal. 4 and 5). How, then, could I admit something in which I see another being reproved? It is shameful to return to servitude, but it is even more shameful to go into it.

### CHAPTER TWO

AUGUSTINE replied: Above we have already shown sufficiently why and how we hold the authority of the Old Testament—not in imitation of Jewish servitude, but as testimony to Christian liberty. For it is not my voice but the Apostle’s: “All these things happened to them symbolically, but they were written for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

Therefore, we do not perform in servitude the things commanded to foreshadow us; rather, in freedom we read the things written to strengthen us. Who, then, does not now understand what the Apostle recalls the Galatians from—not their religious reading of the Scripture of circumcision, but their superstitious desire to be circumcised again (Gal. 4 and 5)?

Thus we do not sew a [Col. 0241] new piece of cloth onto an old garment; rather, we are instructed in the kingdom of heaven, like that householder whom the Lord mentions bringing forth from his treasure new things and old (Matt. 13:52). But the person who wants spiritual continence while he has not yet laid aside carnal hope is the one who sews a new piece of cloth onto an old garment.

For read carefully and see that, when the Lord was asked about fasting, he answered, “No one sews a piece of new cloth onto an old garment” (ibid. 9:16). At that time the disciples still loved the Lord carnally, since they even feared losing him if he were killed. Hence he calls Peter, who was trying to turn him away from his passion, “Satan,” because he did not understand the things of God but those of human beings (ibid. 16:23).

Therefore, consider in that fantasy of yours concerning the kingdom of God what sort of carnal hope [Col. 0242] you possess, since you love and worship this light of the sun, visible to the flesh, as though it had been set before you as an example. You will find that your fasts are sewn onto carnal wisdom as onto an old garment.

Nevertheless, since a new piece of cloth does not fit an old garment, how could the members of your God have adhered to the rulers of darkness—not joined and sewn together, but, more strongly still, mixed and fused with them? Or is everything old because everything is false, and everything derives from carnal wisdom?

Unless perhaps you wish to prove that one was new and the other old because a greater tear was made: that the miserable piece of cloth was cut away from the kingdom of light and fastened to the mass of darkness for eternal punishment. And yet, like a tailor in the filth of such fables—or a beggar putting them on—he thinks he is cleverly piercing the supports of the divine Scriptures with the needle of his tongue.

[Note: [Col. 0242] Thus the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain have “compingere” instead of “compungere.”]

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0241]

### CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: Why do you not accept the Old Testament? If the Apostles were permitted to depart from it, though they were born under it, why should I not be permitted not to appropriate what I was not born under? For all of us are born Gentiles, not Jews and, finally, not Christians. The Old Testament brings some people from the same Gentile condition to itself and makes them Jews; the New brings others and initiates them as Christians. It is as though two trees, one sweet and one bitter, draw into themselves from the roots of a single soil a power that changes according to their own qualities.

Since the Apostles passed from the bitter tree to the sweet, how foolish shall I be if I am changed from the sweet to the bitter?

### CHAPTER TWO

AUGUSTINE replied: Why, then, does the Apostle—whom you say passed from bitterness into sweetness after leaving Judaism—say that those who refused to believe in Christ from among that very people were broken-off branches, while the Gentiles were grafted in, like a wild olive, into the root of the olive tree itself—that is, into the origin of the holy Hebrews—in order to become sharers in the richness of the olive?

When he was warning the Gentiles against pride because of the fall of the Jews, he spoke as follows:

“For I say to you Gentiles: Inasmuch as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some of them. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? If the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches. But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, remember that you do not support the root; the root supports you. You will say, then, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Very well: they were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear; for if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise [Col. 0242] you too will be cut off. And they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut from a wild olive tree that was natural to you and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will those who are natural branches be grafted into their own olive tree? For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: a partial blindness has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel is saved” (Rom. 11:13–26).

You see, then, that you who do not wish to be grafted into this root are not indeed like branches that were broken off, as is the carnal and impious Jewish people; rather, you have remained in the bitterness of the wild olive. For what does worshiping the sun and moon signify, if not the character of the Gentile wild olive?

Unless perhaps you no longer think that you are in the Gentile wild olive because you have added thorns of a new kind and fashioned a false Christ—whom you worship with the sun and moon—not by a craftsman’s hand but in a perverse heart.

Be grafted, then, into the root of the olive tree, to which the Apostle rejoices that he has been restored. He was once among the branches broken off through unbelief. For he says that he was freed from this when he rejoices that he passed from Judaism to Christ, because Christ was always proclaimed in that root and in that tree. Those who did not believe in the one who came were broken off from it; those who believed were grafted into it. To prevent them from becoming proud, it is said: “Do not be high-minded, but fear; for if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.”

But lest anyone despair concerning those very branches that were broken off, he says shortly afterward: “And they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut from a wild olive tree that was natural to you and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will those who are natural branches be grafted into their own olive tree?”

See from where he too boasts that he has been freed from being broken off and restored to the richness of the root. Therefore, let those among you whom impiety broke away from that root return and be grafted in again. Those who have never been there, however, should come, cut off from their natural barrenness, to become sharers in its fruitfulness.

## BOOK TEN

[Col. 0243]

### CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: Why do you not accept the Old Testament? Because both from it itself and from the New we have learned not to desire what belongs to another. But, you ask, what does the Old Testament have that belongs to another? Rather, what does it have that does not?

It promises riches, fullness of belly, sons and grandsons, a long life, and, along with these, the kingdom of the Canaanites—but all this to those who are circumcised, observe the Sabbaths, offer sacrifices for themselves, abstain from pork, and observe the other practices of the same kind.

Since I disregard these things, as does every Christian, judging them foolish and having no relevance at all to the salvation of the soul, I therefore recognize that what it promises no longer concerns me either. Remembering the commandment, “You shall not desire what belongs to another” (Exod. 20:17; Rom. 7:7), I willingly and deliberately allow the Jews to have their own blessings, being content with the Gospel alone and with the splendid inheritance of the kingdom of heaven.

For just as, if a Jew appropriated the Gospel for himself, I would rightly rebuke him by saying, “Wicked man, what have you to do with something whose commands you do not keep?” so I fear that a Jew may rebuke me in the same way for holding the Old Testament while disregarding its commandments.

### CHAPTER TWO

AUGUSTINE replied: He is not ashamed to repeat the same empty arguments so often, but I am weary of repeatedly answering the same things, even when they are true. Therefore, whoever seeks a response to these arguments as well should read what we said above (Book 6, chapter 2).

If a Jew says to me, “Why do you hold the Old Testament, whose commandments you do not keep?” I answer that Christians keep, even from those very Books, the commandments concerning the conduct of life; but the commandments concerning the signification of life were rightly observed at the time when they foretold the things that have now been revealed.

Therefore, I do not observe these matters religiously in the same way, though I retain them for the sake of testimony, just as I retain the carnal promises contained there, from which the Testament is properly called “Old.” For although eternal things have been revealed to me as things to be hoped for, I also read those things that happened to them symbolically: “They were written for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

So, if you have heard what we answer the Jews, hear also what we object to the Manichaeans.

### CHAPTER THREE

Certainly Faustus said that we could be thrown into confusion if Jews said to us: “Why do you hold the Old Testament, whose commandments you do not observe?” To them we respond by revering and maintaining the authority of that same Scripture.

[Col. 0244] What do you answer when you are told: “Why do you hold the evangelical Books, whose followers you pretend to be in order to deceive the ignorant, and whose contents you not only do not believe but also attack with all the strength you can muster?”

Surely you see that you are less able to answer objections concerning the New Testament than we are those concerning the Old. For everything written in the Old Testament we declare to be true, divinely commanded, and assigned to appropriate times.

But when the things written in the books of the New Testament are brought against you—things that you do not accept—you fail in your response and, with your throats constricted by manifest truth, gasp out in a wounded breath that they have been falsified. What else could suffocated mouths of liars exhale? Or rather, what else could the pierced corpses of the dead give off but stench?

And yet Faustus confessed that he had learned not to desire what belongs to another not only from the New Testament but also from the Old—something he certainly could not have learned from his own god. For if that god did not desire what belonged to another, why did he construct new ages upon the land of darkness, where they had never existed?

Will he say: “The nation of darkness first desired my kingdom, which was alien to it”? Then he imitated the nation of darkness, so that he too might desire what belonged to another. Or was the kingdom of light previously too narrow? Then war ought to have been desired, so that victory might acquire a wider realm of rule. If that is good, it could have been desired beforehand; but it was awaited until the hostile nation first burst into war, so that it might be conquered as though more justly.

But if it is not good, why, after defeating the enemy, did he wish his kingdom to grow upon another’s land, when previously he had lived in complete happiness, content with his own boundaries?

Would that these people truly wished to learn from those Writings the very commandments concerning the conduct of life—one of which is that we should not desire what belongs to another! They would surely become gentle and would understand with mildness that the commandments concerning the signification of life, at which their offense snarls, were appropriate for observance at that time.

But how do we desire the Old Testament as something belonging to another, when we read that its contents happened to them symbolically and were written for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come? I think that a person does not desire what belongs to another if he reads what was written for him.

## BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0243]

### CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: Do you accept the Apostle?

“Very much so.”

Why, then, do you not believe that the Son of God was born from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3)?

I certainly would not believe that the Apostle of God could have written contradictory things about himself, holding now one opinion and now another concerning our [Col. 0244] Lord. But since this pleases you—people who never hear without irritation that something has been interpolated into the Apostle—know that we do not regard even this as contradictory.

For this may seem to be Paul’s old and ancient opinion concerning Jesus: that he [Col. 0245] himself, like the others, thought him David’s son. But when he learned that this was false, he alters and weakens it, writing to the Corinthians: “We know no one according to the flesh; and if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Cor. 5:16).

You must therefore consider how great the difference is between these two passages: one affirms that Jesus is the son of David according to the flesh, while the other says that he now knows no one according to the flesh. If both are Paul’s, they will be so for the reason I have stated; otherwise one of them is not Paul’s.

Finally he continues: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, everything has become new” (ibid. 5:17). You see, then, that he calls the earlier faith old and transitory—the faith by which he formerly believed Jesus to be from the seed of David according to the flesh—but calls this latter faith new and permanent, by which he now knows no one according to the flesh.

Therefore elsewhere also he says: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (1 Cor. 13:11).

[Note: [Col. 0245] Erasmus and Louvain have “I abolished” instead of “I put away.” The Lyon edition has: “the things of a child I put away and abolished.” M.]
