If this is so, what disgrace is it for us if, holding Paul’s new and better confession, we cast away the old and inferior one? Or, if you wish to believe what he writes to the Romans, why should it not be permitted to us to teach according to what he writes to the Corinthians?

Although I have answered you in this way because of your stubbornness, nevertheless, far be it from us to suppose that the Apostle of God ever destroyed what he had built, thereby making himself a transgressor, as he himself testifies (Gal. 2:18). Still, if that earlier opinion is also his, it has now been corrected; but if it is not permissible for Paul ever to have said anything in need of correction, then it is not his.

### CHAPTER TWO

AUGUSTINE replied: This is what I said shortly before: when these people are so strangled by manifest truth that, hemmed in by the clear words of the holy Scriptures, they cannot find an escape for their deceit, they answer that the testimony produced is false.

O voice fleeing from truth and obstinate in madness! The things brought against you from the divine Books are so invincible that you have nothing else to say except that they have been falsified. What authority of writings could then be opened, what sacred book unfolded, what evidence from any Scripture brought forward to refute your errors, if this voice is admitted and regarded as having any weight?

It is one thing not to accept the books themselves and not to be bound by any authority of theirs—as the pagans do with all our Books, as the Jews do with the New Testament, and, finally, as we ourselves do with the writings of you and of other heretics, if they possess any books that are considered their own and proper, or with those called apocryphal—not because they ought to be held in any authoritative esteem, but because, having been made known by no light of testimony, they were produced from some unknown secrecy through the presumption of unknown persons.

It is one thing, then, not to be held by the authority of certain books or persons, and another to say: “This holy man wrote everything truthfully, and this [Col. 0246] letter is his; but in that very letter this statement is his and that one is not his.”

When you hear in reply, “Prove it,” do not flee to more reliable copies, or to the greater number of manuscripts, or to older ones, or to the earlier language from which the text was translated into another language. Instead, say: “I prove that this belongs to him and that does not because this supports my position and that opposes it.”

Are you, then, the rule of truth? Whatever opposes you is not true? What if another person, possessed by a similar madness but with a stubbornness strong enough to crush yours, should arise and say: “Rather, what supports you is false, while what opposes you is true”? What will you do, unless perhaps you produce another book in which everything you read can be understood according to your position?

If you do this, the other person will contradict you and cry out, not merely about some part of it but about the whole book: “It is false.” What will you do? Where will you turn? What origin, antiquity, or succession of transmission of the book you have produced will you cite as a witness?

For if you try to do this, you will accomplish nothing. And in this matter you see what authority belongs to the Catholic Church, which is confirmed from the most firmly established seats of the Apostles down to the present day by the succession of bishops following one another and by the agreement of so many peoples.

Therefore, if the question concerned the reliability of copies—as it does in certain variations of wording, which are few and well known to students of the sacred Scriptures—our uncertainty would be resolved either from manuscripts of other regions, from which the teaching itself had come, or, if the manuscripts there too differed, the greater number would be preferred to the fewer, the older to the more recent. If the variation still remained uncertain, the earlier language from which the text had been translated would be consulted.

This is how those who wish to discover what troubles them in the holy Scriptures, established by such great authority, investigate the matter: they seek material from which they may be instructed, not grounds for quarrelling.

### CHAPTER THREE

But the statement brought against your impiety from the Epistle of the Apostle Paul—that the Son of God is from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3)—is found in all manuscripts, new and old; all Churches read it; all languages agree.

Therefore, cast off the cloak of deceit in which Faustus was clothed. When he had posed to himself the question, as though someone were asking, “Do you accept the Apostle Paul?” he replied, “Very much so.” Why did he not instead answer, “Not at all,” unless, being deceitful, he could not reply with anything other than what was false?

What part of the Apostle Paul does he accept? Not the first man, whom Paul says is “of the earth, earthly.” Of this man he also says, “The first man Adam became a living soul.”

Faustus, however, announces some other first man—not earthly and of the earth, nor made into a living soul, but existing from the substance of God and identical in being with what God is. He says that this man plunged his members, garments, or weapons—that is, the five elements, which themselves were nothing other than God’s substance—into the nation of darkness, so that they might be seized after being polluted.

Nor does he accept the man whom Paul says is from heaven,

[Note: [Col. 0246] Louvain has “heavenly from heaven.” “Heavenly” is absent from the other printed editions and from the manuscripts.]

whom he also calls the last [Col. 0247] Adam, a life-giving spirit (1 Cor. 15:47, 45); whom he says was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, made from a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law (Gal. 4:4–5).

Of him Paul says to Timothy: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (2 Tim. 2:8). On the example of his resurrection he also proclaims our resurrection, saying: “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures.”

A little later he adds why he said this: “But if Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Cor. 15:3–4, 12).

This man, however, when asked whether he accepts the Apostle Paul, answers, “Very much so,” yet denies all these things. He does not wish to accept Jesus as being from the seed of David, nor as having been made from a woman—Paul calls her a woman not because she was corrupted either through intercourse or childbirth, but according to the usage of the Scriptures, which customarily call the female sex by this name. Thus in Genesis it is written of Eve, “He formed her into a woman” (Gen. 2:22), although she had not been joined to a man.

Nor does he accept Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection, since he says that Christ did not have a mortal body in which there could be a true death, nor were the scars genuine that he showed to the disciples after his resurrection, when he appeared to them alive, as Paul also recalls (Luke 24:39–40; 1 Cor. 15:5).

Nor does he accept that our own flesh will rise again, changed into a spiritual body, as the same Apostle says most plainly: “The natural body is sown; the spiritual body rises.”

[Note: [Col. 0247] Almost only the Louvain edition has “to be changed” (*mutandam*) instead of “changed” (*mutatam*).] Distinguishing between the natural body and the spiritual, he then connected this with what I have already mentioned about the first Adam and the last Adam.

Next he added: “But this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.” And lest anyone should believe that the visible form and substance of the flesh itself cannot rise, he wished to make clear what he had called “flesh and blood”—namely, that he meant the corruption itself, which will not exist at the resurrection of the righteous—and immediately continued: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

And lest anyone should still think that it is not what was buried that will rise, but that one garment is laid aside and another, better one is received, he wished to declare most plainly that the very same thing will be changed for the better. Thus Christ’s garments on the mountain were not put aside and others taken up; rather, the garments that had been there were themselves glorified for the better (Matt. 17:2).

Accordingly, he continues and says: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” And lest it remain uncertain who those are who will be changed, he says: “In an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

Perhaps they will still say that we are not changed at the resurrection according to this mortal and corruptible body, but according to the soul. Yet the [Col. 0248] Apostle did not begin by proposing this subject; from the very beginning of the question he spoke about the body, as his opening statement itself shows: “But someone will say, ‘How do the dead rise? With what kind of body do they come?’”

He then points to the subject of which he is speaking as though with a finger and adds: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:35–53).

Since, then, this man denies all these things, and since he also proclaims as corruptible the very God of whom Paul says, “To the immortal, incorruptible, only God, be honor and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17)—for he dreams up his detestable and abominable fable that God’s substance, nature, and entire being were afraid of being corrupted by the nation of darkness, and that part of it was corrupted so that the rest might be protected—what is he trying to do even here but deceive the ignorant and those less educated in the divine Scriptures?

When asked whether he accepts the Apostle Paul, he answers, “Very much so,” yet is found to accept him not at all.

### CHAPTER FOUR

“But,” he says, “there is a certain sound argument by which I shall show either that the Apostle Paul changed his opinion as he progressed and, when writing to the Corinthians, corrected what he had written to the Romans, or that he did not write at all what is presented as his: that the Son of God is from the seed of David according to the flesh.”

By what argument does he prove this? “Because,” he says, “both cannot be true: what is written in the Epistle to the Romans, ‘Concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh’ (Rom. 1:3), and what he says to the Corinthians, ‘Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh; and if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him’ (2 Cor. 5:16).”

It remains, then, for us to demonstrate how both can be true and how these two statements are not contradictory. We cannot possibly say that one of them is not Paul’s, since the authority of the manuscripts does not vary in this matter.

Even if in certain Latin copies one reads not “made” but “born from the seed of David,” while the Greek copies have “made,” so that the Latin translator wished to render the sense rather than the word by saying “born,” nevertheless the authority of all books and languages agrees that Christ is from the seed of David according to the flesh.

Far be it from us to say that Paul ever erred in this matter and changed his opinion as he progressed. Faustus himself perceived how shameful and impious such a claim would be, and preferred to say that Paul’s Epistle had been corrupted by the falsification of others rather than that it was defective through Paul’s own error.

### CHAPTER FIVE

For it can be said of these books that they may perhaps contain something not in harmony with a more hidden and more difficult-to-discern truth, whether it remained that way or was later corrected. Such writings are composed by us not with the authority of giving commands, but as an exercise in progress.

For we are among those to whom the same Apostle says: “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal that to you as well” (Phil. 3:15). This kind of writing is to be read not with the necessity of believing but with the freedom of judging.

Yet, so that this place might not be closed off and the salutary labor of language and style in treating and examining difficult questions might not be denied to later generations, the excellence of the canonical authority of the Old and New Testaments has been distinguished from the books of later [Col. 0249] writers. That canonical authority, confirmed in the times of the Apostles through the succession of bishops and the spread of the Churches, has been established, as it were, in an exalted seat, to which every faithful and devout understanding must submit.

If something there should seem absurd, one may not say, “The author of this book did not possess the truth.” Rather, one must say: either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator has erred, or you do not understand.

In the later writings, however, which are contained in countless books but are in no way equal to the most sacred excellence of the canonical Scriptures, even where the same truth is found in them, their authority is nevertheless far inferior.

Therefore, if some passages in them happen to seem discordant with the truth because they are not understood as they were spoken, the reader or hearer has the freedom of judgment to approve whatever pleases him or reject whatever offends him. For that reason, unless such matters are defended either by sound reasoning or by canonical authority—so that it may be shown either that they are entirely so or that what is there discussed or narrated could have happened—no one is reproached if he dislikes them or refuses to believe them.

But in the supreme canonical authority of the sacred Scriptures, even if the confirmation of the canon declares that a single prophet, apostle, or evangelist placed something in his writings, it is not permissible to doubt that it is true. Otherwise there will be no page by which the weakness of human ignorance may be governed, if the salutary authority of the canonical Books is either wholly despised and abolished or confused without limit.

### CHAPTER SIX

Therefore, whoever you are whom these apparently contradictory statements have troubled—one place saying that the Son of God is from the seed of David, and another saying, “If we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him”—even if both were not produced from the writings of one Apostle, but one had been said by Paul and the other by Peter, Isaiah, or any other Apostle or prophet, since all things in the canonical authority agree with one another as though spoken with one voice, and are believed with the most just and prudent devotion, discovered by the clearest understanding, and demonstrated with the most diligent care, it would not be permissible to doubt either one.

Therefore, since both statements are produced from the canonical writings of the Apostle Paul—that is, from Epistles truly belonging to Paul—we cannot say either that the manuscript is corrupt, for all corrected Latin copies have the same reading, or that the translator has erred, for all corrected Greek copies have the same reading.

It remains, then, that you do not understand, while reason is required of me to show how neither statement differs from the other, but both agree within the same sound rule of faith. If you too were seeking this piously, you could discover how these matters become clear when carefully examined.

### CHAPTER SEVEN
For the Son of God was made man from the seed of David, and not only does the same apostle say this in one place, but the other holy Scriptures proclaim it most explicitly. But as for what he says, “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him,” the very context of the passage in Scripture sufficiently shows what the Apostle is discussing. For, in his customary manner, he contemplates our future life—which has already been completed in the man Christ Jesus, our Head, having risen—as though it were already present and possessed with certainty. That life, of course, will not be according to the flesh, just as Christ’s life is no longer according to the flesh.

For in this passage he does not mean “flesh” as the very substance of our body, which the Lord also calls flesh after his resurrection, saying, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). Rather, he means the corruption and mortality of the flesh, which will then no longer exist in us, just as it no longer exists in Christ. He was speaking of this specifically as “flesh” even when he was speaking quite clearly about the resurrection itself and saying what I have already quoted above: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

When, therefore, what he goes on to say there has come to pass—“Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. In an instant, that is, in a moment, at the last trumpet—for the trumpet will sound—and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:50–53)—then, according to his use of “flesh” to mean not the substance of the body itself but the corruption of mortality, there will no longer be flesh, since, once changed, it will not possess the corruption of mortality. According, however, to the origin of the substance and body itself, it will be the same flesh, because it will rise and be changed—the same flesh—for this too is true, which the Lord said after he had risen: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have”; and this too is true, which the Apostle said: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.”

The former statement was made according to the substance itself, which will also exist then, since it will be changed; the latter was made according to the carnal quality of corruption [Note: [Col. 0250] Several manuscripts read *carnalis* (“carnal”) instead of *carnis* (“of flesh”).], which will then no longer exist, since the changed flesh will not decay. Thus we once knew Christ according to the flesh—that is, according to the mortality of the flesh—before he rose; but now we no longer know him in that way, because, as the same Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him” (Romans 6:9).

For if you cling to the literal propriety of the words, he was lying when he said, “We once knew Christ according to the flesh,” if Christ was never according to the flesh; for no one knew what did not exist. Yet he did not say, “We thought Christ was according to the flesh,” but “We knew.” Nevertheless, so that I may not press the point verbally, lest someone assert that the Apostle spoke by an abuse of language, saying “we knew” instead of “we thought”—I am astonished that blind people do not notice this; or rather, I am not astonished that blind people do not see it. For if Christ did not have flesh because the Apostle said that he no longer knew Christ according to the flesh, then neither did those people have flesh of whom he says in the same passage, “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh.”

For if he wanted this to be understood only of Christ, he could not have said, “We know no one according to the flesh.” Rather, because he was contemplating as already present the future life of those who will rise and be changed, he says, “From now on we know no one according to the flesh”—that is, we hold so certain a hope of our future incorruption and immortality that already now we rejoice in that very knowledge.

Hence elsewhere he says: “But if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2). Certainly we have not yet risen as Christ has; nevertheless, on account of the hope that is ours in him, he testified that we have already risen with him. Hence he also says: “According to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5). Who does not understand that in the washing of regeneration the hope of future salvation was given to us, not salvation itself, which is promised? Yet because the hope is certain, he says, as though that salvation had already been given, “He saved us.”

Elsewhere he says most clearly: “We groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body. For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:23–25). Therefore, just as here he did not say, “We shall be saved,” but, “From now on we have already been saved,” although not in reality but in hope—for he says, “In hope we were saved”—so also what is said there, “From now on we know no one according to the flesh,” is to be understood not in reality but in hope. For our hope is in Christ, because in him what we hope will be given to us has already been completed.

He has already risen, and death will no longer rule over him. And although we once knew him according to the flesh, while he was still destined to die—for that mortality which the Apostle specifically calls “flesh” was present in his body—now we no longer know him in that way. For his mortal nature has already put on immortality, and therefore, according to his former mortality, he can no longer be called flesh.

## CHAPTER VIII

Let us therefore consider the context of the passage in which this statement occurs, the statement they criticize, so that what I am saying may become clearer. “The love of Christ,” he says, “compels us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them. Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh; and even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.”

Surely it is now apparent to everyone that the Apostle said this because of Christ’s resurrection, since these words were preceded by: “So that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them.” For what else does it mean to live not for oneself but for him, except that one should not live according to the flesh in the hope of earthly and corruptible goods, but according to the spirit in the hope of the resurrection, which has already taken place in Christ from among the dead?

Therefore the Apostle knew no one according to the flesh among those for whom Christ died and rose, and who now live not for themselves but for him, because of the hope of future immortality in expectation of which they lived—a hope that in Christ was already not hope but reality. And although he had known Christ according to the flesh while Christ was still destined to die, he no longer knew him in that way, because he knew that Christ had risen and that death would no longer rule over him.

And because all of us are already in him—not yet in reality, but in hope—the Apostle continues and says: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation. The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:14–18).

Every new creation, therefore—that is, the people renewed through faith, so that for the present they may possess in hope what will later be perfected in reality—already has in Christ what it hopes to have in itself. Thus the old things have now passed away according to hope, because the time of the Old Testament has now ended, when a temporal and carnal kingdom was expected from God. And all things have become new according to that same hope, so that we may hold fast to the promise of the kingdom of heaven, where there will be neither death nor corruption.

At the resurrection of the dead, however, the old things will pass away not according to hope but according to reality, when the last enemy, death, is destroyed; and all things will become new when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:26, 53). This has already taken place in Christ, whom Paul, according to reality, no longer knew according to the flesh. But among those for whom Christ died and rose, he knew no one according to the flesh yet in reality, but only according to hope, because, as the same Apostle says to the Ephesians, we have been saved by his grace.

That passage itself also bears witness to this interpretation: “But God,” he says, “who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ; by whose grace we have been saved.” What he says here, “He made us alive together with Christ,” he says to the Corinthians in these words: “So that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them.” And when he says here, “By whose grace we have been saved,” he speaks as though what he holds in hope were already complete.

For, as I mentioned shortly before, he says elsewhere with complete clarity: “In hope we were saved.” Therefore here too he continues, and counts as though already complete what is still future: “And he raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:4–7). Certainly Christ already sits in the heavenly places, but we do not yet. Yet because we hold with certain hope what will be, he says that we sit together in the heavenly places—not yet in ourselves, but already in him.

And so that you would not think that what is spoken of in hope as though it were complete is already complete, and so that you might understand that it is still future, he continues: “So that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.”

This is also the meaning of what he says elsewhere: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which are through the Law, were at work in our members so as to bear fruit for death” (Romans 7:5). He said, “When we were in the flesh,” as though they were no longer in the flesh. This is to be understood as: “When we were in hope of carnal things.” At that time the Law, which cannot be fulfilled except through spiritual love, was upon them for this purpose: that through transgression sin might abound, so that afterward, when the New Testament had been revealed, grace might abound through forgiveness (Romans 7:20).

Similarly, elsewhere he says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” And lest anyone think that he meant those who had not yet died, he immediately added: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit” (Romans 8:8–9). That is: those who are in hope of carnal goods cannot please God; but you are not in hope of carnal goods, but in hope of spiritual goods—that is, of the kingdom of heaven, where the body itself too, through that transformation, will be spiritual in its own particular manner, although now it is natural. “The natural body is sown,” as the same Apostle says to the Corinthians; “it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44).

If, then, the Apostle already knew no one according to the flesh among those who were therefore said not to be in the flesh because they were not in hope of carnal things, although they still carried corruptible and mortal flesh, how much more explicitly would he say of Christ that he no longer knew him according to the flesh, since in Christ’s body the reality itself had already been perfected which they held as promised in hope?

How much better, how much more reverently, therefore, are the divine Scriptures treated when, after all their passages have been examined, they are found to agree, than when human weakness, faced with a question it cannot solve, accepts them as true in one part and condemns them as false in another! For even when the Apostle was a child and understood the things that belonged to childhood (1 Corinthians 13:11)—although he said this by way of comparison—he was not yet spiritual in the manner in which he already was when he wrote writings that were to be handled in the hands of students, not as an exercise in progress, but read in the ecclesiastical canon with the authority of precept, for the edification of the Churches.

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0253]

## CHAPTER I

**FAUSTUS said:** Why do you not accept the Prophets?

**FAUSTUS continued:** Rather, you should say, if you have anything to say, why we ought to accept the Prophets.

“Because of the testimonies,” you say, “which they previously gave concerning Christ.” I myself have found none, although I have read them with great attention and the utmost curiosity. Yet even this is a confession of weakened faith [Note: [Col. 0253] Erasmus reads *inertis fidei* (“of sluggish faith”).]: not to believe in Christ without a witness and evidence.

You yourselves are accustomed to teach that nothing should be investigated too inquisitively, because Christian belief is simple and unqualified. Why, then, are you now destroying the simplicity of faith by supporting it with proofs and witnesses—and with Jewish ones at that?

Or, if you dislike your first position and therefore pass over to another, who ought to be a more reliable witness for you than God himself concerning his Son? He did not speak through a seer or an interpreter, but, of his own accord, with a voice sent down from heaven, said when he sent him to earth: “This is my most beloved Son; believe him” (Matthew 3:17; Luke 9:35).

And Christ himself says concerning himself: “I proceeded from my Father and came into this world” (John 16:28), along with many other statements of this kind.

To these words the Jews responded angrily [Note: [Col. 0253] Erasmus reads *respondentes* (“responding”). Manuscript reading: *ringentes* (“gnashing” or “rearing angrily”).]: “You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.” He replied to them: “Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, because I am not alone. For it is written in your Law, ‘The testimony of two men is true.’ I am the one who bear witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me” (John 8:13–18). He did not say, “The Prophets.”

He also calls his very works to bear witness for him, saying, “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38). He did not say, “If you do not believe me, believe the Prophets.”

Therefore we need no testimonies from the Prophets concerning our Savior. In the Prophets we seek only examples of honorable life, prudence, and virtue. I perceive that you are not unaware that none of these existed among the Jewish seers. For when I asked you why you thought they should be accepted, you proceeded neither unwisely nor discourteously, passing over their deeds in silence and moving directly to their predictions [Col. 0254]. You surely forgot that it is written: “You will never gather grapes from thorns, nor figs from thistles” (Matthew 7:16).

Thus, for the moment, I have answered your question briefly and concisely: why do we not accept the Prophets? Otherwise, it has already been sufficiently demonstrated in the books of our ancestors that they prophesied nothing concerning Christ.

I will add this: if the Hebrew seers knew Christ and proclaimed him, yet lived so shamefully, then what Paul testifies concerning the wise men of the Gentiles may rightly be said also of them: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; rather, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Romans 1:21).

You see, then, that it is not a great thing to have known great matters, unless one lives according to the dignity of what one knows.

## CHAPTER II

**AUGUSTINE replied:** In all these words Faustus is trying to make us believe that the Hebrew Prophets neither foretold anything concerning Christ, nor—if they did foretell him—that their testimonies benefit us, nor that the Prophets themselves lived in accordance with the dignity of those testimonies.

We shall therefore demonstrate both their predictions concerning Christ, how greatly they have served us in establishing and strengthening the truth of the faith, and how they lived in a manner appropriate and suitable to their prophecy.

In this threefold discussion, the first point—that the Prophets foretold Christ—is too lengthy to prove by producing testimonies from all those books through which I could show that Christ was predicted. But I shall crush this man’s frivolity beneath the tremendous weight of authority.

For he does not accept the Hebrew Prophets, yet he professes that he accepts the Apostles. Let us hear what the Apostle Paul—whom, when he asked himself as though speaking from the opposing side whether he accepted him, he answered, “And especially so” (above, Book 11)—says about their prophecy.

“Paul,” he says, “a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised through his Prophets in the holy Scriptures [Col. 0255] concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:1–3).

What more does he want? Unless perhaps he wishes this to be understood as having been said about some other Prophets, not about our Hebrew Prophets. But although it was said through any Prophets whatsoever, the Gospel was nevertheless promised concerning that Son of God who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh; and the Apostle says that he was set apart for this Gospel.

It is contrary to the perfidy of these people that we believe, according to this Gospel, that the Son of God was made from the seed of David according to the flesh. Let them nevertheless recognize clearer statements, by which the Hebrew Prophets are given the most evident testimony through that Apostle whose authority should break the necks of these arrogant men.

## CHAPTER III

“I speak the truth in Christ,” he says, “I do not lie; my conscience bears witness with me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself could wish to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kindred according to the flesh, who are Israelites, whose are the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:1–5).

What could be said more abundantly, declared more explicitly, or commended more sacredly?

For what is the adoption of the Israelites except through the Son of God? Hence he says to the Galatians: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5).

And what is their glory, except especially that of which the same Paul says to these same Romans: “What advantage, then, has the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Romans 3:1–2).

Let these people inquire what the utterances of God entrusted to the Jews are, and let them show us any others besides those of the Hebrew Prophets.

Why did he say that the covenants belonged especially to the Israelites, except because the Old Covenant was given to them and the New Covenant was prefigured in the Old?

These people, in their furious ignorance, are accustomed to criticize the giving of the Law that was given to the Israelites because they do not understand its dispensation, since God now does not want us to be under the Law but under grace. Let them therefore yield to apostolic authority, which, while praising and commending the excellence of the Israelites, also counted among their privileges that the giving of the Law belonged to them. If the Law were evil, it would certainly not have been included in their praise.

And if it did not proclaim Christ, the Lord himself would not have said: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). Nor, after his resurrection, would he have testified to this by saying: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44).

## CHAPTER IV

But because the Manichaeans proclaim another Christ—not the Christ proclaimed by the Apostles, but their own deceitful Christ, deceitfully—and because the followers of this falsehood fittingly lie along with it, except that they shamelessly demand to be believed while confessing themselves disciples of one who lies, what the Apostle says about those unbelieving Jews has happened to them: “When Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.” For this veil, through which they do not understand Moses, is not removed unless they turn to Christ—not the Christ they have invented, but the one whom the Hebrew Fathers foretold.

For the same Apostle says: “But when you turn to the Lord, the veil will be taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:15–16).

It is no wonder that these people do not want to believe the risen Christ when he said, “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled.” For Christ himself recounted what Abraham said to a certain merciless rich man while the man was being tormented in the underworld and asking that someone be sent from there to his brothers to teach them, lest they too should come to that place of torment.

For this was said to him: “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.” And when he replied that they would not believe unless someone rose from the dead, the truest answer was given: “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead” (Luke 16:27–31).

Therefore, because these people do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they do not merely refuse to believe Christ who rose from the dead; they do not believe at all that Christ rose from the dead. For how can they believe that he rose, when they do not believe that he died? And how can they believe that he died, when they do not believe that he had a mortal body?

## CHAPTER V

We, however, do not believe those deceitful preachers: they preach not a Christ who was deceitful, but one who did not exist at all. For we have the true and truthful Christ, foretold by the Prophets and proclaimed by the Apostles, who bring forward testimonies of their proclamation from the Law and the Prophets, as they show in countless passages.

Paul expressed this most briefly and most truthfully when he said: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, testified to by the Law and the Prophets” (Romans 3:21).

Which Prophets, except the Israelites, whose, as he most explicitly said, are the covenants, the giving of the Law, and the promises (Romans 9:4)? Promises concerning whom, except Christ? He briefly specifies this elsewhere when speaking of Christ: “For however many are the promises of God, in him they are also” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Paul tells me that the giving of the Law belongs to the Israelites. He also says: “For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). Speaking of Christ, he also says: “For however many are the promises of God, in him they are also.” And you tell me that the Prophets of the Israelites foretold nothing concerning Christ!

What remains, then, except that I must choose whether to believe the Manichaean, telling a long and empty tale against Paul, or Paul, who warns: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8–9)?

## CHAPTER VI

Perhaps they will say here: “Show us where Christ was foretold by the Prophets of Israel.”

As though it were a small authority when the Apostles say that the things we read in the writings of the Hebrew Prophets were fulfilled in Christ—or when the Lord himself says that those writings were composed concerning him.

Therefore, whoever cannot demonstrate this does not understand it; it is not the Apostles, or Christ, or the holy books that are lying.

Nevertheless, without collecting many passages, let me recall this one statement which the Apostle goes on to make in the same passage: “But it is not possible for the word of God to have failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all children because they are the seed of Abraham. Rather, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’ That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed” (Romans 9:6–8).

What will they answer to this, when elsewhere the promise concerning this seed is plainly made to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 26:4)?

For if we were discussing this at the time when the Apostle explained it by saying, “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed”—he does not say “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “and to your seed,” which is Christ (Galatians 3:16)—perhaps someone would have been unwilling to believe this so shamelessly before seeing all the nations believing in Christ, who is proclaimed as coming from the seed of Abraham.

But now, when we see fulfilled what we read was foretold so long ago, when all the nations are already being blessed in the seed of Abraham, to whom it was said thousands of years earlier, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed,” who could be so obstinately mad as either to introduce another Christ who is not from the seed of Abraham, or to think that the Hebrew Prophets foretold nothing concerning this true Christ, whose ancestral father Abraham is?

## CHAPTER VII

Who could recount—not in one brief answer, such as we are constrained to give in this work, but in any volume, however immense—all the proclamations of the Hebrew Prophets concerning our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ?

For everything contained in those books was either said about him or written on his account. Yet for the exercise of the seeker and the delight of the one who finds, much more is conveyed there through allegories and riddles: some things are intimated by words alone, while others are also related as deeds.

Nevertheless, unless some things there were clear, the meaning by which the obscure passages too might be illuminated would not be grasped. Indeed, even among those passages wrapped in figures, if certain ones are set down as though woven together under a single view, they join their voices in bearing witness to Christ so harmoniously that the deafness of even the dullest person would blush.

## CHAPTER VIII

In six days God completed all his works in Genesis, and on the seventh he rested (Genesis 2:1–2).

In this age, through the succession of times, the works of God mark out six ages of the human race. The first is from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth, from that time to the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now taking place, until the Most High comes for judgment.

The seventh is understood as the rest of the saints—not in this life, but in another, where that rich man saw the poor man resting while he himself was being tormented in the underworld (Luke 16:23). There evening does not occur, because there is no decline of anything there.

On the sixth day in Genesis the human being is formed in the image of God (Genesis 1:27); in the sixth age of the world our renewal is manifested in the newness of the mind, according to the image of him who created us, as the Apostle says (Colossians 3:10).

A wife is made for the sleeping man from his side (Genesis 2:22); for the dying Christ the Church is made from the sacrament of the blood that flowed from the side of the dead man (John 19:34).

Eve is called “life” and “the mother of the living,” because she was made from her husband’s side. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone does not eat my flesh and drink my blood, he will not have life in himself” (John 6:53).

Everything that is read there, when treated carefully and in detail [Note: [Col. 0258] Ambrose, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *intelliguntur* (“are understood”).], speaks beforehand of Christ and the Church, whether in good Christians or in bad ones.

For the Apostle did not say without reason, “Adam, who is a type of the one to come” (Romans 5:15), and: “A man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh. This mystery is great,” he says; “but I am speaking of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:31–32).

Who does not recognize that Christ left the Father in this manner: although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7)? He also left his mother, the synagogue of the Jews, which clung carnally to the Old Testament, and clung to his wife, the holy Church, so that in the peace of the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0258] The manuscripts read “so that in the peace of the New Testament,” omitting *in*. This may perhaps be preferable.] the two might be one flesh.

For although he is God with the Father, through whom we were made, he became through the flesh a participant in us, so that we might be the body of that Head.

## CHAPTER IX

Just as Cain’s sacrifice from the fruits of the earth is rejected, while Abel’s sacrifice from the sheep and their fat is accepted, so the faith of the New Testament, praising God through the innocence of grace, is preferred to the earthly works of the Old Testament.

For although the Jews previously performed those works rightly, they are nevertheless guilty of unbelief because, when Christ came, they did not distinguish the time of the New Testament from the time of the Old Testament.

For God said to Cain: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” If he had obeyed God, who said, “Be still; for its turning is toward you, and you will rule over it,” he would have turned his sin toward himself, attributing it to himself and confessing it to God. Thus, aided by the grace of forgiveness, he himself would have ruled over his sin; instead of being ruled by it and becoming its slave, he would not have killed his innocent brother (Genesis 4:3–8).

So too the Jews, in whom these things were prefigured, if they had ceased from their disturbance and, recognizing the time of salvation through grace for the forgiveness of sins, had listened to Christ saying, “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:12–13), and, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin”; and, “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:34, 36)—if they had turned their sin toward themselves in confession, as it is written in the Psalm, saying to the physician, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40:5), and, as long as sin still remained in their mortal body, had ruled over it freely through the hope of grace—

But now, because they did not know the righteousness of God and wished to establish their own (Romans 10:3), lifted up by the works of the Law and not humbled by their sins, they did not remain still. While sin reigned in their mortal body so that they obeyed its desires (Romans 6:12), they stumbled against the stone of stumbling (Romans 9:32) and burned with hatred against him whose works they saw to be acceptable to God.

They grieved when the man who had been born blind and now saw said to them: “We know that God does not hear sinners; but whoever worships him and does his will, he hears” (John 9:31). It was as though he were saying to them: “He does not look upon Cain’s sacrifice, but he looks upon Abel’s sacrifice.”

Thus Abel, younger in age, is killed by his older brother; Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, older in age: the one in the field, the other at the place of Calvary.

## CHAPTER X

God asks Cain where his brother is—not as someone ignorant who seeks information from him, but as a judge questioning the guilty man whom he is about to punish.

Cain replies that he does not know and that he is not his brother’s keeper.

What do the Jews still answer us when, with God’s voice—that is, with the voice of the holy Scriptures—we ask them about Christ, except that they do not know the Christ of whom we speak? Cain’s deceitful ignorance is the Jews’ false denial.

They would in a certain sense be keepers of Christ if they had been willing to accept and preserve the Christian faith. For whoever keeps Christ in his heart does not say, like Cain, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”

God says to Cain: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.”

Thus the divine voice accuses the Jews in the holy Scriptures. The blood of Christ has a great voice upon the earth, when, having received it, all the nations respond, “Amen.” This is the clear voice of the blood, which the blood itself expresses from the mouths of the faithful who have been redeemed by that same blood.

## CHAPTER XI
God says to Cain: “And now you are cursed by the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand; because you will work the earth, and it will no longer give you its strength: groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth” (Gen. 4:9–12). He did not say, “Cursed be the earth,” but, “You are cursed by the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand.” For the unbelieving Jewish people is cursed by the earth—that is, by the Church—which has opened its mouth in the confession of sins to receive Christ’s blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins, from the hand of the persecutor who was unwilling to be under grace but under the Law. Thus he was cursed by the Church—that is, so that the Church might understand and show him to be accursed—for the Apostle says, “For all who are of the works of the Law are under the curse of the Law” (Gal. 3:10).

Furthermore, after saying, “You are cursed by the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand,” he did not say, “Because you will work it,” but said, “Because you will work the earth, and it will no longer give you its strength.” Hence it is not necessary to understand that Cain works the same earth which opened its mouth to receive his brother’s blood from his hand. Rather, he is understood to be cursed by that earth because he works the earth which will no longer give him its strength. That is, the Church recognizes and shows the Jewish people to be accursed because, after Christ was killed, they still work an earthly circumcision, an earthly Sabbath, earthly unleavened bread, and an earthly Passover. All this earthly observance contains the hidden power of understanding Christ’s grace, which is not given to the Jews while they persist in impiety and unbelief, because it has been revealed through the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0260] Three manuscripts read, “which [is] from the New [Testament].”]. And when they do not turn to the Lord, the veil that remains in the reading of the Old Testament is not taken away from them, since it is removed only in Christ—not the reading itself of the Old Testament, which possesses a hidden power, but the veil by which it is concealed (2 Cor. 3:14–16). Therefore, when Christ suffered on the cross [Note: [Col. 0260] Two manuscripts read, “when he was placed on the cross.”], the veil of the temple was torn (Matt. 27:51), so that through Christ’s passion the secrets of the sacred mysteries might be revealed to the faithful who, passing over to drink his blood with an open mouth in confession, receive them.

Therefore that people, like Cain, still works the earth and still practices the works of the Law carnally, which does not give it its strength because it does not understand Christ’s grace in it. For this reason, in the very earth that Christ bore—that is, in his flesh—they themselves worked our salvation by crucifying Christ, who died for our sins. Yet that same earth did not give them its strength, because they were not justified by the power of his resurrection, who rose for our justification (Rom. 4:25). For although he was crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God, as the Apostle says (2 Cor. 13:4). This, then, is the power of that earth, which it does not show to the impious and unbelieving. Hence, even after rising, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified, just as Cain was working the earth so that that grain might be sown, while the same earth did not show the fruit of its strength [Note: [Col. 0260] The Vatican manuscript reads, “while the same earth did not show.”]: “Because you will work,” he says, “the earth, and it will no longer give you its strength.”

## CHAPTER XII

“Groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth.” Now, who does not see, who does not recognize throughout the whole earth, wherever that people has been dispersed, how it groans in grief over the loss of its kingdom and trembles with fear beneath innumerable Christian peoples? Therefore Cain answered and said: “My guilt is greater, if today you cast me away from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face, and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth; and it shall come to pass that everyone who finds me will kill me.” Truly he groans and trembles lest, having also lost his earthly kingdom, he should be killed by this visible death. He calls this a greater guilt than the fact that the earth does not give him its strength, lest he die spiritually. For he thinks carnally, and he does not consider it serious to be hidden from the face of God—that is, to have God angry with him—unless he should be found and killed. He thinks carnally, like one working the earth whose strength he does not receive. But to think according to the flesh is death (Rom. 8:6). Since he does not understand this, he groans over the loss of his kingdom and trembles at bodily death.

But what does God answer him? “Not so,” he says, “but whoever kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance”—that is, not as you say; the impious race of carnal Jews will not perish by bodily death [Col. 0261]. Whoever destroys them in this way will pay sevenfold vengeance—that is, he will remove from them the sevenfold vengeance by which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s death. Thus, throughout all the time that revolves in the number of seven days, because the Jewish nation does not perish, it may clearly appear to faithful Christians what subjection they deserved, since in their proud kingdom they killed the Lord [Note: [Col. 0261] Several manuscripts read, “in the kingdom of the proud.”].

## CHAPTER XIII

“And the Lord God set a sign upon Cain, lest everyone who found him should kill him” (Gen. 4:13–15). This is truly a matter of great wonder: how all the nations that were conquered by the Romans passed over into the rites of Roman sacrifices and undertook to observe and celebrate those sacrileges, while the Jewish nation, whether under pagan kings or under Christian ones, did not lose the sign of its Law, by which it is distinguished from the other nations and peoples. Every emperor or king who found them in his kingdom found them with that same sign and did not kill them; that is, he did not make them cease to be Jews, distinguished from the fellowship of the other nations by a certain distinctive sign of their observance.

This is so unless one of them has passed over to Christ, so that he is no longer found as Cain, no longer goes out from the face of God, and no longer dwells in the land of Naid [Note: [Col. 0261] The manuscripts read, “in the land of Naim.”], which is said to be interpreted as “Commotion.” Against this evil God is entreated in the Psalm: “Do not let my feet be moved” (Ps. 65:9); and, “Let not the hands of sinners move me” (Ps. 35:12); and, “Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved” (Ps. 12:5); and, “The Lord is at my right hand; I shall not be moved” (Ps. 15:8); and innumerable passages of this kind. All who go out from the face of God—that is, from the mercy of his love—suffer this.

Hence it is said in a certain Psalm: “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall not be moved forever.’” But see what follows: “Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty; but you turned your face away, and I became troubled” (Ps. 29:7–8). From this it is understood that every soul is beautiful, comely, and endowed with strength through participation in God’s light, not through itself. If these Manichaeans considered and understood this, they would not fall into such great blasphemy by thinking that they are the nature and substance of God. But they cannot do so because they do not rest; for they do not understand the Sabbath of the heart. If they rested, they would, as was said to Cain, turn their sin back upon themselves—that is, attribute it to themselves—not to some unknown race of darkness. In this way, through God’s grace, they would gain mastery over that same sin.

But now both they and all who, stubborn in various errors, resist the truth and go out from the face of God, dwell like Cain, like the lost Jews, in the land of commotion—that is, in carnal disturbance, opposed to the delight of God, that is, opposed to Eden (Gen. 4:16), which is interpreted as “Delight,” where paradise was planted. I shall now briefly touch upon a few of the many remaining points, lest the purpose of this work and of my reply be impeded by excessive length of discourse.

## CHAPTER XIV

For, to omit matters which, although they are contemplated with greater sweetness the more they are drawn out from hidden places, nevertheless require an extended exposition because they need numerous testimonies—to omit such matters, then—who would not be moved to saving faith, and to seek and understand Christ in those Books, by the fact that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, pleased God and was translated (Gen. 5:24), and that a seventh rest is proclaimed, to which everyone is translated who, as on the sixth day and in the sixth age of the world, is formed by Christ’s coming?

Who would not be moved by the fact that Noah and his companions were saved through water and wood (Gen. 7:23), just as the household of Christ is marked by the Baptism of the cross’s passion [Note: [Col. 0262] In B., “was marked.” We have followed Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice. M.]. The same ark was constructed from squared timbers, just as the Church is built from holy people, always prepared for every good work (2 Tim. 2:21). For a square stands firmly whichever way you turn it.

The ark’s length, six times its breadth and ten times its height, displays the likeness of the human body, because Christ appeared in a human body. Its breadth is extended to fifty cubits, as the Apostle says, “Our heart has been enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11). By what, except spiritual love? For this reason he likewise says: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). For on the fiftieth day after his resurrection Christ sent the Holy Spirit, by whom he enlarged the hearts of believers (Acts 2:1–4).

The ark is three hundred cubits long, so that six times fifty may be completed. This signifies that the whole period of this world extends through six ages, in all of which Christ never ceased to be proclaimed: in five ages he was foretold through prophecy, and in the sixth he was spread abroad through the Gospel.

Its height rises to thirty cubits, a number contained ten times in the three hundred cubits of its length. For Christ is our height: at the age of thirty he consecrated evangelical teaching, bearing witness that he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17). The heart of the Law is recognized in the Ten Commandments. Hence the ark’s length is completed by ten times thirty; hence Noah himself is counted as the tenth from Adam (Gen. 5; Luke 3:36–38).

The timbers of the ark are joined with pitch inside and outside (Gen. 6:14–15), so that in the structure of unity the endurance of love may be signified, lest, when scandals assail the Church—whether from those within or those outside—the fraternal bond yield and the bond of peace be dissolved. For pitch is an extremely hot and powerful adhesive, signifying the ardor of love, which through great strength endures everything in order to preserve spiritual fellowship [Note: [Col. 0262] Ambrose and Erasmus read, “the ardor, through great strength, for preserving fellowship.”].

## CHAPTER XV

The fact that every kind of animal is shut inside the ark signifies that the Church contains all nations, which are also represented by the disk shown to Peter. There are both clean and unclean animals there (Acts 10:11–12), just as both good and evil people are present in the Church’s sacraments [Col. 0263]. The clean are present by sevens and the unclean by twos (Gen. 7:2), not because there are fewer evil people than good, but because the good preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Holy Scripture commends the Holy Spirit in a sevenfold operation: wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of God (Isa. 11:2–3). Hence the number of fifty days associated with the coming of the Holy Spirit is completed in seven times seven, which makes forty-nine, with one added. For this reason it is said: “Eagerly preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3). The evil, however, are shown by the number two to be prone to schisms and, in a certain sense, divisible.

Noah himself is counted as the eighth together with his companions, because in Christ the hope of our resurrection appeared. He rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath, on the first day—this being the third day from his passion, but in the number of the days that revolve through all time both the eighth and the first.

## CHAPTER XVI

The ark is completed above by being gathered together to a single cubit. This signifies that the Church, gathered into unity as the body of Christ, is raised up and perfected [Note: [Col. 0263] Two Vatican manuscripts and nearly all Gallican manuscripts read: “Just as it raises up and perfects the Church, the body of Christ, gathered into unity.”]. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30).

An entrance is made for it in the side. No one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the remission of sins; and this flowed from Christ’s opened side.

The lower parts of the ark are constructed with two and three chambers (Gen. 6:16), just as the Church gathers from all nations either a twofold multitude, because of circumcision and foreskin, or a threefold one, because of Noah’s three sons, whose descendants filled the world. These lower parts of the ark are so called because in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations, whereas in the highest place we are all perfected into one. This variety is not a contradiction, because Christ is all things and in all things, perfecting us in one cubit above through heavenly unity.

## CHAPTER XVII

After seven days from the time Noah entered the ark, the flood occurred. This signifies that we are baptized in the hope of the future rest, which was signified by the seventh day.

All flesh that the earth sustained was destroyed by the flood apart from the ark. This signifies that outside the fellowship of the Church, the water of Baptism, although it is the same water, not only does not avail for salvation but rather avails for destruction.

It rained for forty days and forty nights (Gen. 7:17–23), because every guilt of sins admitted under the Ten Commandments is washed away throughout the whole earth, which is contained by its four quarters. For ten multiplied by four makes forty. Whether that guilt, with respect to the days, was contracted through prosperity, or, with respect to the nights, through adversity, it is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly Baptism.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord spoke to him and commanded him to make an ark, and he was six hundred years old when he entered it (Gen. 5:31; 7:6). Hence it is understood that the ark was built over one hundred years. What else do these hundred years seem to signify here except the individual ages of the world?

Thus this sixth age, signified by the completion of five hundred years and the arrival of six hundred, builds the Church through the manifestation of the Gospel. Therefore whoever takes thought for his life should be like squared timber, prepared for every good work, and should enter the holy structure. The second month of Noah’s six-hundredth year, in which he enters the ark, likewise signifies this same sixth age.

For two months are concluded in the number sixty; from the number six come the names sixty, six hundred, six thousand, sixty thousand, six hundred thousand, six hundred times, and whatever number thereafter rises through the same numerical progression into infinite increases.

## CHAPTER XIX

The mention of the twenty-seventh day of the month also pertains to the meaning of the square, which has already been expounded in connection with the squared timbers. Here, however, the matter is clearer, because the Trinity perfects us, prepared for every good work—that is, squared in a certain sense—in memory, by which we remember God; in understanding, by which we know him; and in will, by which we love him.

Three times three, and that again three times, make twenty-seven, which is the square of the ternary number.

The fact that the ark came to rest—that is, rested—in the seventh month (Gen. 8:4, 14) returns us to the signification of that seventh rest. And because the perfected rest, the number of that square is repeated there as well. For this sacrament was commended on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, and again the same commendation was confirmed on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, when the ark came to rest. What is promised in hope is exhibited in reality.

Furthermore, because that seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection—for the rest that receives the saints after this life does not end when the body is restored, but rather receives the whole human being, renewed in every respect not yet in hope but already in reality, with both spirit and body perfected in the salvation of immortality, into the gift of eternal life—because, then, the seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection, this too is a profound and lofty mystery in the sacrament of our regeneration, that is, in Baptism.

The water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains (Gen. 7:20). This signifies that the sacrament surpasses all the wisdom of the proud. Seven and eight joined together make fifteen. And because seventy is named from seven, and eighty from eight, the water rose for one hundred and fifty days when the two numbers were joined together, commending and confirming to us the same height of Baptism in consecrating the new person to hold fast the faith of rest and resurrection.

## CHAPTER XX

The raven sent out after forty days did not return, either because it was caught by the waters or because it was enticed by some floating corpse. This signifies people made exceedingly filthy by the uncleanness of desire and therefore excessively intent upon the things outside, in this world, whether being rebaptized or being deceived and held by those whom Baptism outside the ark—that is, outside the Church—has killed [Col. 0265].

The dove, when sent out and finding no place of rest, returned. This shows that through the New Testament rest has not been promised to the saints in this world. It was sent out after forty days, a number signifying the life lived in this world.

Finally, after seven days it was released and brought back a fruitful olive branch, because of that sevenfold spiritual operation. This signified that some who have been baptized outside the Church, if they have not lacked the richness of love, may at a later time, as it were toward evening, be led into the fellowship of unity in the mouth of the dove, as in the kiss of peace.

When it was released after another seven days, it did not return (Gen. 8:6–12). This signifies the end of the world, when the rest of the saints will no longer be in the sacrament of hope by which the Church is joined together in the present time, as long as what flowed from Christ’s side is being drunk, but already in the perfection itself of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father (1 Cor. 15:24), so that in the clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we will need no bodily mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXI

It would take too long even to touch upon all these matters as briefly as I have raced through them. Why, in the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life—that is, after six hundred years had been completed—the roof of the ark is opened, and what had been a hidden sacrament is, as it were, revealed. Why it is said that on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the earth dried [Note: [Col. 0265] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have “dried the earth.”] (Gen. 8:13–14), as though the necessity of baptizing had already been completed in the number fifty-seven of the days. For this is the twenty-seventh day of the second month, a number formed from the joining of spirit and body: seven times eight, with one added because of the bond of unity.

Why those who entered separately come out of the ark joined together. For it had been said that Noah and his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons entered the ark (Gen. 7:7); the men and women were mentioned separately. In the present time of this sacrament, the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17). But Noah and his wife, his sons and the wives of his sons came out (Gen. 8:18), males and females now mentioned together, because at the end of the world and in the resurrection of the righteous, in complete and perfect peace, the body will cleave to the spirit, with no need or desire of mortality resisting.

Why, although clean and unclean animals were in the ark, after leaving the ark they are offered to God in sacrifice only if they are clean (ibid., 20).

## CHAPTER XXII

What, then, is intended by God’s speaking to Noah and, as it were, beginning again from the outset, commending the figure of the Church, since the same things had to be signified in many ways? His offspring is blessed so that they may fill the earth, and all the animals are given to them as food, just as it is said to Peter in that disk: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

They are commanded to eat after the blood has been poured out, so that their former life may not remain held, as though suffocated, in the conscience, but may have something like an outpouring through confession.

God established a covenant between himself and human beings and every living soul, so that he would not destroy it by a flood, and set the bow that appears in the clouds (Gen. 9:1–17). The bow never shines except from the sun. Those do not perish in the flood, separated from the Church, who recognize Christ’s glory in the Prophets and all the divine Scriptures, as in God’s clouds, and do not seek their own glory.

But lest the worshipers of this sun grow more swollen with pride, let them know that Christ is sometimes signified by the sun, just as by a lion, a lamb, or a stone, on account of a certain similarity, not because of an identity of substance.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Now, as for the fact that Noah, drunk from the vine he had planted, was stripped naked in his house (ibid., 20–23), to whom is it not apparent that Christ suffered among his own people? For then the mortality of his flesh was exposed: to the Jews, a stumbling block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to those called from Jews and Gentiles, like Shem and Japheth, the power of God and the wisdom of God. “For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:23–25).

Accordingly, in the two sons, the eldest and the youngest, two peoples are represented. Carrying one garment on their backs—that is, the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, already past and completed—they do not look upon the nakedness of their father, because they do not consent to Christ’s death; and yet they honor it with a covering, as though knowing whence they were born [Note: [Col. 0266] The printed editions read, “they cover the nakedness of their father.” The word “cover” is absent from the manuscripts.].

The middle son, that is, the Jewish people, is called middle because it held neither the primacy of the Apostles nor the last place in believing among the Gentiles. He saw the nakedness of his father because he consented to Christ’s death, and he reported it outside to his brothers. Through him what had been secret in prophecy was made manifest and, in a certain sense, made public. Therefore he becomes the servant of his brothers.

For what else is that nation even today except a kind of book-chest of Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as a testimony supporting the Church’s assertion, so that we honor through the sacrament what it proclaims through the letter?

## CHAPTER XXIV

Who would not be stirred, instructed, or strengthened in faith by the fact that those two who honored their father’s nakedness, although they turned away, are blessed—as though they had been displeased by what happened in the wicked vineyard? “Blessed,” he says, “is the Lord God of Shem.” Although he is the God of all nations, in a certain way, even among the Gentiles, he is called by the proper name “God of Israel.” And how did this happen except through Japheth’s blessing?

For in the people of the Gentiles the Church occupied the whole world. This was plainly foretold when it was said: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the houses of Shem” (Gen. 9:26–27).

See, Manichaeans, see: the whole world is before your eyes. This is what amazes and grieves you among our peoples, because God enlarges Japheth. See whether he does not dwell in the houses of Shem—that is, in the churches which the Apostles, the sons of the Prophets, built.

Hear what Paul says to the Gentiles who already believe: “You were at that time,” he says, “without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants and without hope of the promise, and without God in this world.” These words show that Japheth did not yet dwell in the houses of Shem [Col. 0267]. But observe how he concludes shortly afterward: “Therefore,” he says, “you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2:12, 19–20).

See how Japheth is enlarged and dwells in the houses of Shem. Yet you possess, read, and proclaim the Apostles’ Letters in which all these things are attested. Where should I place you, unless in that accursed middle portion for which Christ is not the cornerstone? For we recognize you neither in the wall that believed in Christ from circumcision, from which the Apostles came, nor in the wall that is from the foreskin, from which all the others among the Gentiles come, converging into the same unity of faith, as into the peace of the corner [Note: [Col. 0267] So most manuscripts read. Others, with Ambrose and Erasmus, read, “into the peace of the corner.” The Lyons edition has, “in the corner of peace.”].

And all who accept and read any books of our canon, in which Christ is shown to have been born and to have suffered mortally, but who do not honor that same mortality, exposed in his passion, with the reverent covering of the sacrament of unity, and who proclaim without knowledge of piety and love that from which we were all born—although they disagree among themselves, Jews from heretics and heretics from one another—are nevertheless useful to the Church under one condition of servitude, either for some testimony or for some proof.

For it was also said concerning heretics: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19).

Go now and heap accusations upon the ancient sacred Letters. Do this, servants of Ham. Go, you to whom the exposed flesh from which you were born has become vile. For there would be no basis on which you could in any way be called Christians unless Christ, as he was foretold by the Prophets, had come into the world, had drunk from his vineyard that cup which could not pass away, had slept in his passion as in the drunkenness of a foolishness wiser than human beings, and had thus exposed the weakness of mortal flesh through the hidden plan of God, stronger than human beings. Unless the Word of God had assumed it, the Christian name in which you too glory would not exist at all on earth.

But do as I said: mockingly bring forth what we honor reverently. Let the Church use you as subjects to her, so that those who are approved may become manifest in her. So completely did those Prophets leave nothing unsaid that either was to befall or be endured that we even find you there, each in your proper place: harmful vanity for ensnaring the reprobate, but useful [Note: [Col. 0267] The printed editions read, “useful.” The manuscripts have “useful,” with “vanity” understood.] for making the approved manifest.

## CHAPTER XXV

You say that Christ was not foretold by the Israelite Prophets. Yet all those pages are vigilant in proclaiming him, if only you preferred to search them with piety rather than attack them with levity.

Who else is represented in Abraham leaving his land and his kindred so as to become rich and prosperous among foreigners (Gen. 12:1–3), except the one who, having left the land and kindred of the Jews—from whom he was born according to the flesh—so greatly prevails and rules among the Gentiles, as we see?

Who else in Isaac carried wood for himself to the sacrifice (Gen. 22:6), except the one who himself carried the cross for his passion?
