Who else was the ram to be sacrificed, caught by its horns in a thornbush, except the one who was to be offered for us and fastened to the cross’s gallows [Note: [Col. 0268] Here the Lyons edition adds, “first crowned with thorns.” These words are absent from the other printed editions and from our manuscripts.]?

## CHAPTER XXVI

Who else wrestled with Jacob in the angel, allowing himself to be overcome by him, and, as the weaker one, conquered yet victorious, partly blessed him and partly made the breadth of his thigh lame (Gen. 32:24–31), except the one who allowed the people of Israel to prevail against him and blessed in them those who believed?

The breadth of Jacob’s thigh, however, became lame in the multitude of the carnal people.

Who else is the stone placed at Jacob’s head, so that in a certain sense it might be explicitly named, and which was also anointed, except Christ, the head of the man? For who does not know that Christ is named from anointing?

When he recalled this very matter in the Gospel and bore the clearest witness that it had been represented in himself, after calling a certain Nathanael a true Israelite in whom there was no deceit, and after Nathanael, as though he had that stone at his head, confessed him to be the Son of God and King of Israel—thereby in a certain sense anointing the stone, that is, confessing him to be the Christ—the Lord appropriately recalled there also what Jacob saw when he was called Israel through the blessing:

“Amen, I say to you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:47–51).

Israel had seen this when he had that stone at his head: a ladder from earth to heaven, upon which the angels of God ascended and descended (Gen. 28:11–18). In these angels the evangelists, preachers of Christ, were signified. They ascend when, in order to understand his utterly transcendent divinity, they rise above the whole creation and find him “in the beginning God with God,” through whom all things were made (John 1:1–3). They descend when they find him made from a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law (Gal. 4:4–5).

In him the ladder extends from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit, because in him carnal people, by making progress as though ascending, become spiritual. To nourish those who are still infants with milk, even spiritual people descend in a certain way when they cannot speak to them as spiritual people but as carnal people (1 Cor. 3:1–3).

Thus one ascends and descends upon the Son of Man. For the Son of Man is above in our head, which is the Savior himself, and the Son of Man is below in his body, which is the Church.

We understand him himself also to be the ladder, because he said, “I am the way” (John 14:6). Therefore one ascends to him so that he may be understood in the heights, and one descends to him so that the little ones may be nourished in his members [Note: [Col. 0268] Ambrose, Erasmus, and nearly all manuscripts read this way. The Lyons edition has, “so that he may be nourished as a little one in his members.”].

Through him one ascends and descends. For his preachers, following his example, not only raise themselves up so as to contemplate him in sublimity but also humble themselves so as to proclaim him with moderation.

See the Apostle ascending: “Whether we have been beside ourselves,” he says, “it is for God.” See him also descending: “Whether we are moderate,” he says, “it is for you.” Let him also say through what he has ascended and descended: “For the love of Christ,” he says, “constrains us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them” (2 Cor. 5:13–15).

## CHAPTER XXVII

Who is not delighted by these holy spectacles in the sacred Scriptures? Whoever cannot endure sound teaching turns to fables (2 Tim. 4:3–4). Those fables, indeed, entice souls that remain childish at every bodily age with a varied kind of pleasure. But let us now, as the body of Christ, recognize our voice in the Psalm and say to him: “The unjust have told me of delights, but not such as your law, O Lord” (Ps. 118:85).

As I travel through and pant after Christ everywhere in those Books, everywhere in those Scriptures, amid that sweat of human condemnation, he encounters and refreshes me, whether openly or secretly. He himself also kindles in me, through the difficulty of finding him, a desire by which I eagerly swallow what I discover and keep it safely stored in my inmost depths.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

He himself is suggested to me in Joseph, who, after his brothers persecuted and sold him, was honored in Egypt after his labors (Gen. 37–47). For we have learned of Christ’s labors in the world of the Gentiles, which Egypt signified, through the various sufferings of the martyrs. Now we see Christ’s honor in that same world, as he subdues all things to himself by distributing his grain.

He himself is suggested to me in Moses’ staff, which, when it became a serpent on the ground, represented his death coming from the serpent. But when its tail is grasped and it is restored again as a staff, this signifies that later, after everything has been accomplished at the end of the action, he returns by rising again to what he had been [Note: [Col. 0269] Some manuscripts read this way. Others, with the printed editions of Ambrose and Erasmus, read: “but when its tail is grasped, this signifies that later”—omitting the words “it is restored again as a staff.” The Lyons edition likewise omits these words and reads: “but when its tail is grasped, it signifies that later, after everything has been accomplished, at the end of the action.”]. There, with death destroyed through the restoration of life, no trace of the serpent appears.

We too, being his body, are rolled about in that same mortality amid the slippery courses of time. But at the final end, like the tail of the world, we will be restored by the hand—that is, by the power of judgment—when it is grasped so that it may slip no farther. Rising again after the last enemy, death, has been destroyed (1 Cor. 15:26), we will be the staff of the kingdom in the right hand of God.

## CHAPTER XXIX
Now concerning the exodus of Israel from Egypt, let not I but the Apostle speak: “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (ibid. X, 1–4). By explaining one thing, he has introduced an understanding of the others. For if the rock was Christ because of its firmness, why not also the manna—Christ as the living bread that came down from heaven (John VI, 42)? Those who truly feed on him live spiritually. For those people, receiving the ancient figure carnally, died. But when the Apostle says, “They ate the same spiritual food,” he shows that the food too is to be understood spiritually in Christ; and why he called the drink spiritual he made clear when he added, “But the rock was Christ.” Once this was disclosed, everything shone forth.

Why, then, should the cloud not also be Christ, and the pillar, because he is upright and steadfast and supports our weakness—shining by night and not shining by day, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John IX, 39)? The cloud and the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0270] Thus Am. and Er. Most manuscripts and Lov. instead read: “The cloud is red, and the Red Sea.”]; baptism, certainly consecrated by the blood of Christ: enemies pursue from behind; past sins die.

## CHAPTER XXX

The people are led through the desert (Exod. XVII, 1). All who have been baptized, not yet enjoying the promised homeland, but hoping for what they do not see and awaiting it with patience (Rom. VIII, 25), are as though in the desert. There too are difficult and dangerous temptations, lest they turn back in their hearts toward Egypt. Yet Christ does not abandon them there, for that pillar too does not depart (Num. XIV, 14). Bitter waters are made sweet by wood, because the enemies of the people are tamed when the sign of Christ’s cross is honored. And the twelve springs watering seventy palm trees (Exod. XV, 23–27) prefigure apostolic grace, watering peoples in the number seven multiplied by ten, so that through the sevenfold gift of the Spirit the Decalogue of the Law may be fulfilled.

And when the enemy attempts to block the way, he is overcome by Moses’ outstretched hands, through the sign of the Lord’s cross (ibid. XVII). The deadly bites of the serpents are healed when the bronze serpent is lifted up and gazed upon. This is explained by the words of the Lord himself: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life” (Num. XXI, 9; John III, 14).

Do these things, too, not cry out? Is there such deafness in hardened hearts? Passover is made in the slaughter of a sheep: Christ is slain, of whom it is said in the Gospel, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29). Those who celebrate Passover are forbidden to break the bones: the Lord’s bones are not broken on the cross. The Evangelist testifies that this was spoken of him: “You shall not break his bone” (Exod. XII, 46; John XIX, 39). The doorposts are smeared with blood so that destruction may be driven away (Exod. XII, 22–23); the people’s foreheads are marked with the sign of the Lord’s passion as a safeguard of salvation.

The Law is given there on the fiftieth day after Passover has been celebrated (ibid. XX); the Holy Spirit comes on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s passion (Acts II, 1–4). There the Law is said to have been written by the finger of God (Exod. XXXI, 18); the Lord says of the Holy Spirit, “By the finger of God I cast out demons” (Luke XI, 20). And Faustus cries out with his eyes closed that he has found nothing in those Scriptures relating to the announcement of Christ!

What wonder, though, if he has eyes for reading but no heart for understanding—if, placed before the closed door of the divine mystery, he does not knock with the faith of piety but assails it with the arrogance of impiety? Let it plainly be so; let it happen so, for it is just. Let the door of salvation be closed to the proud. Let the meek one come, the one whom the Lord teaches his ways (Ps. XXIV, 9); let him see these things in those Books, and the rest—either all of them or some of them—of such a kind that he may believe them all.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Let him see Jesus introducing the people into the promised land (Josh. III). For he was not called this name rashly from the beginning; rather, through that very dispensation, his name was changed and he was called Jesus. Let him see a cluster of grapes hanging upon wood from the land of promise (Num. XIII, 24).

Let him see in Jericho, as in this mortal age, a prostitute—one of the sort of whom the Lord says that they go before the proud into the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XXI, 31)—sending out scarlet through the window of her house, as through the mouth of her body (Josh. II). This is plainly a sign of blood: to confess for salvation, because of the remission of sins.

Let him see the walls of that city, as the mortal fortifications of this age, fall when the ark of the Testament has been carried around them seven times (ibid. VI). So now, through the ages that pass in the succession of seven days, the Testament of God circles the whole world [Note: [Col. 0271] Some manuscripts omit “the whole.” The printed editions read “throughout the whole world.”]; so that at the end of the ages the last enemy, death, may be destroyed, and from the destruction of the impious a single household, as the single Church, may be delivered—cleansed from the shame of fornication through the window of confession, in the blood of remission.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Let him observe the periods: first of the Judges, afterward of the Kings—just as there will first be judgment and afterward the kingdom—and let him observe how, throughout those periods of the Judges and Kings, Christ and the Church are again and again prefigured in many different ways.

Who was it in Samson, killing the lion that met him as he went among foreigners to seek a wife (Judg. XIV), except the one who, intending to call the Church from the Gentiles, said, “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33)? What does the honeycomb constructed in the mouth of that slain lion (Judg. XIV, 8) signify, except that we now see the very laws of the earthly kingdom—which formerly raged against Christ—now, their savagery having been destroyed, even furnishing defenses for the preaching of evangelical sweetness?

What is that woman full of confidence, driving a peg through the enemy’s temple with wood (ibid. IV, 21), except the faith of the Church, destroying the kingdoms of the devil through Christ’s cross?

What do the fleece drenched while the threshing floor remained dry, and afterward the threshing floor drenched while the fleece remained dry (ibid. VI, 37–40), signify, except first the single nation of the Hebrews, secretly possessing in its holy mysteries the mystery of God, which is Christ, while the whole world was empty of that mystery; but now, in its manifestation, the whole world possesses it, while that nation has been emptied?

## CHAPTER XXXIII

And during the times of the Kings—to mention a few things from that period as well—does not the priesthood itself, changed to Samuel when Eli was rejected (I Kings II, 27–36), and the kingdom, changed to David when Saul was rejected (ibid. XVI, 1–14), proclaim that a new priesthood and a new kingdom were to come in our Lord Jesus Christ, the old having been rejected, since it was a shadow of what was to come?

When David himself ate the bread of the Presence, which no one was permitted to eat except the priests (ibid. XXI, 6), did he not, in one person, prefigure what was to come—namely, kingdom and priesthood in the one Jesus Christ?

When ten tribes were separated from the temple and two were left behind (III Kings XII, [Col. 0272] 16, 20), does this not sufficiently indicate what the Apostle says about that entire nation: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. XI, 5)?

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Elijah is fed in a time of famine, with ravens bringing him bread in the morning and meat in the evening (III Kings XVII, 6). Yet the Manichaeans do not understand Christ in those Books—Christ who in a certain manner hungers for our salvation—to whom sinners confess faith, now possessing the firstfruits of the Spirit and, at the end, as though at the evening of the age, also the resurrection of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0272] Am., Er., and most manuscripts read *habentem*, “possessing,” instead.].

Elijah is sent to be fed by a foreign widow who intended to gather two pieces of wood before she died. Here the sign of the cross is expressed not only by the name of wood but also by the number of the pieces of wood. Her flour and oil are blessed (ibid. 9–16): the fruit and joy of charity, which, when expended, does not fail; for “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7).

## CHAPTER XXXV

Boys insult and shout at Elisha, “Baldhead, baldhead,” and beasts devour them (IV Kings II, 23–24): in childish folly they mock Christ crucified at the place of Calvary, and, attacked by demons, perish.

Elisha sends his servant to place a staff upon a dead man, but he does not revive. He himself comes, joins and fits himself to the man’s corpse, and the man revives (ibid. IV, 29–37). The Word of God sent the Law through his servant, and it did not benefit the human race, dead in sins; yet it was not sent without reason, for the one who sent it knew that it had first to be sent. He himself came, conformed himself to us, became a participant in our death, and we were given life.

When wood was being cut with axes, the iron flew from the axe, sank into the depths of the river, and, when Elisha threw wood upon it from above, returned to the wood (ibid. VI, 4–7). So, when Christ’s presence operating through his body was cutting down the impious Jews as unfruitful trees—for John had said of him, “Behold, the axe has been laid to the root of the trees” (Matt. III, 10)—then, with his passion intervening, he abandoned the body itself [Note: [Col. 0272] The edition of Lov. reads, “the spirit departed from the body.” “The spirit” is absent from the other books; in its place “Christ’s presence” is understood.], descending into the depths of hell. When, in burial, it had been placed above, he rose, as though the spirit were returning to its handle.

How many things I omit, constrained by the need for brevity, those who read know.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

And the very migration into Babylon—to which the Spirit of God, through the prophet Jeremiah, commands them to go and to pray for those in whose kingdom they are living as strangers, since in their peace there would also be peace for them, and to build houses, cultivate vineyards, and plant gardens (Jer. XXIX, 1–7)—who would fail to recognize what it prefigured, if he considered the true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit (John I, 47), having migrated through the apostolic dispensation, together with the evangelical mystery, into the kingdom of the Gentiles?

Thus the Apostle, as though repeating Jeremiah, says to us: “I therefore urge, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and charity. For this is good and acceptable before our Savior God, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II, 1–4).

From this, once they believed, dwellings of peace were built for them: the basilicas of Christian assemblies, the renewed vineyards of the faithful people, and the planted gardens. There, among all the vegetables, that grain of mustard also reigns; beneath its far-spreading branches even the lofty pride of the Gentiles, like the birds of heaven, takes refuge and rests (Matt. XIII, 31–32).

For since, according to the prophecy of that same Jeremiah, after seventy years there is a return from captivity and the temple is renewed (Jer. XXIX, 10; and Ezra I), what faithful Christian would not understand that, after the ages have passed—ages that run their course through the repetition of the number seven, as in the days of the week—we too, that is, the Church of God, must return from our pilgrimage in this age to that heavenly Jerusalem?

Through whom, unless through Jesus Christ, the true great priest, whose figure was borne by that Jesus, the great priest of that time when the temple was built after the captivity? The prophet Zechariah saw him in filthy clothing, while the devil who stood to accuse him was defeated; his filthy garment was taken away and a garment of honor and glory was given him (Zech. III). So the body of Jesus Christ, which is the Church, after the adversary has been overcome through judgment at the end of the ages, is taken up from the mourning of pilgrimage into the glory of eternal salvation.

This is also sung most clearly in the Psalm of the dedication of the house: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and not be pierced” (Ps. XXIX, 12–13).

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Who could, while engaged in another work, touch upon with however much brevity all the things in those ancient books of the Law and the Prophets that figuratively announce Christ? Unless perhaps someone thinks that it happens through ingenuity that things which proceeded through their own times in the order of events can be turned, by interpretation, into signs of Christ.

Jews or pagans may perhaps say this. But apostolic authority weighs upon the necks of those who wish to be thought Christians, saying, “All these things happened to them in a figure,” and, “All these things were figures for us” (I Cor. X, 10, 6).

For if Ishmael and Isaac, men who were born, signify the two Testaments (Gal. IV, 22, 24), what are we to believe about so many events that occurred with no natural necessity and no practical requirement? Do they signify nothing?

If one of us, who do not know Hebrew letters—that is, the actual shapes of the words—were to see them written on a wall in some honored place, who would be so witless as to think that the wall had merely been painted in that fashion? Would he not rather understand that something had been written, so that, even if he could not read it, he would nevertheless not doubt that those marks signified something? [Note: [Col. 0273] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read *ac non*, “or rather.”]

So, before anything else, whoever reads all those things contained in the ancient instrument of the holy Scriptures without a perverse disposition ought to be moved in this way: he should not doubt that they signify something.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

For example: if woman had to be made as a helper for man, did any necessity or useful purpose compel or recommend that she be made from the side of a sleeping man (Gen. II, 18, 21–22)? If an ark had to be built to escape the flood, what need was there for its measurements, or for those particular measurements, or even for their being recorded in writing so that they might be transmitted to posterity as a religious matter?

If animals had to be enclosed for the preservation of the race, what need was there for precisely that number—seven each of the clean animals and two each of the unclean? Necessity certainly compelled an entrance to be made into the ark; but what compelled it to be made in the side, or even to be commended to memory in writing (ibid. VI, 14–VII, 3)?

Abraham is commanded to sacrifice his son. He may have been commanded this so that his obedience, tested by such an examination, might become known to posterity. The son may appropriately have carried the wood, lest his aged father carry it. The father was afterward not permitted to strike the son, lest he strike himself with the gravest bereavement. But if they were to return without any blood being shed, would Abraham have been proved less faithful? Or if the sacrifice now had to be completed, did the ram that appeared caught by its horns in a thornbush (ibid. XXII) contribute anything to the increase of the victim?

When all these things are considered, and things apparently superfluous are found woven together with necessary things, they admonish the human mind—that is, the rational mind—that the first question is what they signify, and the second what precisely they signify.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Therefore even the Jews themselves, who mock Christ—the Christ whose passion we have recognized—do not wish him to appear to have been foretold by such figures of events, not only spoken but also enacted. They are compelled by us to say what those things signify [Note: [Col. 0274] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read “to say” instead of “to learn.”]. Unless they concede that those things signify something, they cannot defend Books of such divine authority from the disgrace of foolish fables.

A certain Philo saw this, a man of exceptionally liberal learning, one of their number, whose eloquence the Greeks do not hesitate to rank with Plato’s. He attempted to interpret some things—not in order to understand Christ, in whom he did not believe, but so that it might become still clearer how great the difference is between referring everything to Christ, for whom these things were truly spoken, and pursuing any conjectures whatsoever, with whatever keenness of mind, apart from him; and how powerful is what the Apostle says: “When you turn to the Lord, the veil will be taken away” (II Cor. III, 16).

To mention one example from this same Philo: wishing the ark of the flood to be understood as constructed according to the proportions of the human body, he examined everything limb by limb, as it were. When he consulted the rules of numbers with great subtlety, everything that came before him fit appropriately and did not hinder an understanding of Christ, since the Savior of the human race also appeared in a human body; yet these correspondences did not compel such an interpretation, because the human body is also the body of other human beings.

But when he came to the door made in the side of the ark, every conjecture of human ingenuity failed. Nevertheless, to say something, he dared to believe, dared to say, and dared to write that the door signified the lower parts of the body through which urine and excrement are expelled. It is no wonder that, having failed to find the door, he went astray in this way.

If he had turned to Christ and the veil had been removed, he would have found the sacraments of the Church flowing from the side of that man (John XIX, 34). For since it was foretold, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24), some things in the ark are therefore referred to Christ and others to the Church, for the whole is Christ.

The same may be considered in the other interpretations of figures throughout the entire text of divine Scripture, and one may compare the understandings of those who recognize Christ there with those who, apart from Christ, attempt to twist those things toward any other interpretation whatsoever.

## CHAPTER XL

The pagans, too, do not obstruct us in this matter. For they do not dare to contradict our figurative interpretation of those things—not only spoken but also enacted—in order to understand Christ. This is especially because we also demonstrate that the things we understand to have been foretold have been fulfilled.

While attempting to give their own fables some sort of justification, they try to refer them by interpretation to certain physiologies or theologies—that is, natural or divine explanations. In part they plainly reveal what such things are [Note: [Col. 0275] Am., together with many manuscripts, reads “they judge sufficiently clearly” instead of “they sufficiently indicate.”]; in part they conceal it, laughing in the theaters at things they venerate in the temples—excessively free in their indecency, excessively enslaved in their superstition.

## CHAPTER XLI

But if anyone says to us that those things were neither done nor written for the purpose of understanding Christ in them, then, apart from the very great harmony between the things prefigured and those now fulfilled, he will be struck by other clear and manifest prophetic predictions.

Such is the saying, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” This was said to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob (ibid. XXII, 18; XXVI, 4; XXVIII, 14). Therefore he rightly says, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III, 6), since he would certainly fulfill, in the blessing of all nations, what he promised would come from their seed.

Nor was it without reason that Abraham himself, when his servant swore an oath to him, ordered him to place his hand under his thigh (Gen. XXIV, 2, 9), knowing that from there the flesh of Christ would come. In Christ all nations would be blessed—not something we merely announce as having been foretold then, but something that had been foretold then and that we now see.

## CHAPTER XLII

I would like to know—or, better, I would prefer not to know—with what blindness of mind Faustus read the passage where Jacob called his sons and said: “Gather yourselves together, so that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days. Gather yourselves together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel, your father.”

Here surely no one doubts that the person of a prophet is clearly revealed. Let us therefore hear what he says to his son Judah, from whose tribe Christ came from the seed of David according to the flesh, as apostolic teaching testifies (Rom. I, 3).

“Judah,” he says, “your brothers shall praise you” [Note: [Col. 0275] Thus the manuscripts, following the Septuagint. The printed editions read, “your brothers will praise you.”]; “your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies; your father’s sons shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the sprouting, my son, you have risen. Reclining, you have slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who will rouse him? A ruler shall not be lacking from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things that have been reserved for him come; and he himself is the expectation of the nations, binding his colt to the vine and his donkey’s colt to the vine-shoot. He shall wash his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are bright with wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX, 1–2, 8–12).

Let these things be false, let them be obscure, if they have not shone forth with the clearest light in Christ; if his brothers—the Apostles and all his fellow heirs—do not praise him, seeking not their own glory but his; if his hands are not upon the backs of his enemies; if those who still oppose him are not brought down and bent toward the earth as the Christian peoples increase; if the sons of Jacob did not worship him in the remnant that has been saved according to the election of grace (Rom. XI, 5).

Let him not be the lion’s cub, since he was made small by being born; for this reason it was added, “From the sprouting, my son.” The reason is given why he is a cub; elsewhere it is written in his praise, “A lion’s cub is stronger than beasts” (Prov. XXX, 30)—that is, even when small, he is stronger than the great.

Let him not go up upon the cross, reclining, when, with his head bowed, he gave up his spirit; let him not have slept like a lion, because even in death itself he was not defeated but conquered; and like a lion’s cub, because he died from the same source from which he was born.

Let the one whom no human being has seen or can see (I Tim. VI, 16) not have raised him from the dead. For in the question “Who will rouse him?” the meaning of someone unknown is sufficiently expressed.

If a ruler from Judah and a leader from his thighs were lacking until the things promised as though reserved for him came at the appointed time, there are very reliable historical writings even among the Jews themselves, by which it is shown that Herod, a foreigner, was the first king among the Jewish people at the time when Christ was born (Matt. II, 3, 7). Thus a king from the seed of Judah was not lacking until the things reserved for him came.

But because what was promised benefited not only faithful Jews, see what follows: “And he himself is the expectation of the nations.” He himself bound his colt to the vine—that is, his people—preaching and crying out in sackcloth, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid. III, 2).

We know that the people of the Gentiles, subjected to him, are compared to the donkey’s colt; upon it he also sat, leading it into Jerusalem (ibid. XXI, 2–10)—that is, into the vision of peace—and teaching the meek his ways.

Let him not have washed his robe in wine. For this is the glorious Church that he presents to himself, “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27). To her it is also said through Isaiah, “If your sins are as scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. I, 18). From what, if not from sins being forgiven?

In what wine, then, except that of which it is said that it “will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI, 28)? For he is that cluster of grapes which hung upon the wood (Num. XIII, 24). Therefore see what he adds here as well: “And in the blood of the grape his garment.”

Now, as for his eyes shining with wine, those members of his body recognize them—those members to whom it has been granted, in a certain holy drunkenness of the mind’s being carried away from the temporal things flowing below, to behold the eternal light of wisdom. Hence we recalled shortly before a statement of Paul: “Whether we have been beside ourselves, it is for God.” These are the eyes shining with wine.

Yet because what follows is, “Whether we are self-controlled, it is for you” (II Cor. V, 13), the little ones who still must be nourished with milk are not abandoned (Heb. V, 12), since here too it follows: “And his teeth are whiter than milk.”

## CHAPTER XLIII

What do you answer to these things, madmen? Surely they are clear; surely they drive away not only every accusation of contradiction but even every cloud of doubt.

First seek such things in those Books; first believe such things—things which now cannot all be mentioned by me, because that would be too much; nor many, because it would be too long; nor would I wish to mention only a few, lest those who do not read them think that these alone exist, and lest a faithful and diligent reader reproach me when he discovers more evident passages, asking why I chose precisely those that happened to occur to me at the present moment.

For you will find many passages that do not require even such an admonition as the one I have just used in discussing Jacob’s words. Who, when reading, “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter,” and all the things said there in many and evident ways—“By his bruising we were healed,” “He himself bore our sins” (Isa. LIII, 7, 5)—would still seek an interpreter?

Who would not think that this was being sung almost as a Gospel: “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and gazed upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots”?

Who, unless excessively blind, would not now see the fulfillment of this: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence” (Ps. XXI, 17–19, 28)?

What of the words in the Gospel, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38), and, “Now my soul is troubled” (John XII, 27)? Did not the Psalm first sound forth, “I slept in turmoil”? And how did it come about that he slept? Was it not through the voices by which “Crucify, crucify” was shouted (Luke XXIII, 21–22)? Did not the Psalm also continue by foretelling, “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword”?

But what did they do? What harm did they cause to one who was going to rise again, ascend above the heavens, and possess the whole world through the glory of his name? See whether the Psalm had previously kept silent about this. For it continues: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Ps. LVI, 5–6).

Who has ever doubted that this was spoken of Christ: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth’” (Ps. II, 7–8)?

Who was permitted to understand anyone else when Jeremiah says—plainly speaking of Wisdom—“He gave her to Jacob, his servant, and to Israel, his chosen one. Afterward she appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 37–38)?

## CHAPTER XLIV

Who would not recognize the same Savior in Daniel, when the Son of Man is presented to the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom without end, so that all nations may serve him (Dan. VII, 13–14)?

Now, if anyone reads and examines that passage which the Lord cited from the prophecy of that same Daniel—“When you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by Daniel” [Note: [Col. 0278] “By Daniel” is absent from the manuscripts], “standing in the holy place, let the reader understand” (ibid. IX, 27; Matt. XXIV, 15)—and also calculates the periods of the weeks, he will find not only Christ but also the time at which Christ had to come and suffer.

Indeed, even without calculating the periods, we are accustomed to press the Jews with the manifest results of events. Our dispute with them is not whether our salvation is in Christ, but whether he has already come and suffered. They are refuted by the clearest facts—not only by all the nations, which the same Scripture, to which they are compelled to yield, foretold would serve him, and whose faith now shines throughout the whole world so brightly that it strikes the eyes of all who evade the truth; but also by what has already happened among the Jewish people themselves: the sanctuary has been destroyed, the sacrifice, the priesthood, and the former anointing have ceased. Daniel foretold all these things at the time when he clearly prophesied that the Holy of Holies would be anointed (Dan. IX, 24–27).

Since all those things have now happened, the anointed Holy of Holies is also demanded of them, and they find nothing to answer.

How could they dispute with us not about Christ but only about his coming, unless they knew well that he had been prophesied in their Books? Why do they ask John whether he is the Christ (John I, 19)? Why do they themselves say to the Lord, “How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (ibid. X, 24)? Why do Peter, Andrew, and Philip say to Nathanael, “We have found the Messiah,” which means Christ (ibid. I, 41), unless that name was both known and awaited among that people through those Scriptures?

For no other nation had kings and priests whom it called its christs, whose symbolic anointing could rightly cease only when the one whom they prefigured had come (I Kings X, 1–2; and Exod. XXIX). The Jews knew those christs of theirs in such a way that they nevertheless awaited one through whom they would finally be liberated. But, blinded by the hidden justice of God, while thinking only of his power, they did not understand the weakness in which he died for us.

Hence we recognize those words in the Book of Wisdom as foretold about them: “Let us condemn him to a shameful death, for there will be regard for his words. If he is truly the Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his adversaries.” They thought these things and went astray, “for their wickedness blinded them” (Wis. II, 18–21).

This can also be said most truly of those who, amid such a multitude of testimonies, such an arrangement of things foretold, and such a manifestation of things fulfilled, still say that Christ was not prophesied in those Scriptures. If they say this again and again, we too can produce the proofs again and again, with the help of the one who supplied such an abundance against the slanders of human error—though without repeating what we have already mentioned.

## CHAPTER XLV

Furthermore, I am reluctant even to refute another evasive argument of Faustus. I believe that, when he too was struck by the most brilliant light of prophecy, he thought he had discovered a remarkably clever device. I hesitate to refute it lest he be thought to have said something merely because it was considered worthy of an answer.

What utterly insane person would say that faith is weak because one does not believe in Christ without a witness? I wish these people would answer me: whom did they themselves believe concerning Christ? Did they hear that voice from heaven, “This is my Son” (Matt. III, 17; XVII, 5)?

Faustus commands us to believe that voice, even though he does not want human witnesses to be believed concerning Christ—as though knowledge of that same voice had reached us without a human witness. Yet it is clear that it reached us in such a way that the Apostle says: “How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things’” (Rom. X, 14–15)?

You surely see how the preaching of apostolic doctrine is accompanied by prophetic testimony. The Apostles’ announcements were not to be despised or regarded as fables; therefore the Prophets demonstrated that these things had been foretold beforehand. For although miracles bore witness, there would not have been lacking those who—as some still mutter today—would attribute all those things to magical power, unless such an idea had been defeated by prophetic testimony.

No one, surely, would say that by magical arts, long before they were born, prophets had been provided for them to foretell those things. Yet Faustus forbids us to believe the Hebrew Prophets as witnesses to the true Christ, even though he himself believed the errors of the Persians concerning a false Christ.

## CHAPTER XLVI

Catholic teaching therefore teaches that the Christian mind must first be nourished by simple faith, so that it may be made capable of understanding heavenly and eternal things. Thus the prophet also says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9).

This very simple faith is the faith by which we believe before we know the surpassing knowledge of the charity of Christ, so that we may be filled with all the fullness of God (Eph. III, 19). It is not without reason that the dispensation of his humility—through which he was born and suffered as a human being—was foretold so long beforehand by the Prophets, through the prophetic race, the prophetic people, and the prophetic kingdom.

For in that foolishness which is wiser than human beings, and in that weakness which is stronger than human beings (I Cor. I, 25), something great lies hidden for our justification and glorification. And there are hidden in it “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 3). These treasures are opened to no one who despises the food conveyed to him through a mother’s flesh—that is, the nourishment of milk through apostolic and prophetic breasts—and who, disdaining infant nourishment as though he were too old for it, rushes first into the poisons of heretics rather than into the food of wisdom, for which he rashly considers himself ready.

Therefore, saying that simple faith is necessary is not contrary to saying that the Prophets must be believed. Indeed, it contributes precisely to this: that the Prophets should be believed before the purified and strengthened mind can understand the one who spoke in this way through the Prophets.

## CHAPTER XLVII
But if they prophesied Christ, they did not live in a manner worthy or consistent with their prophecy. “How do you know this? Are you yourselves able to judge what it means to live well or badly—your justice being rather that one should come to the aid of a melon that does not feel, so that you may eat it, than of a hungry beggar, so that you may give him something to eat?”

For the Catholic little ones, however, before they know what perfect justice of the human soul is, and how great the difference is between that justice for which one longs and the justice by which one lives here, it is enough to think of those men what the soundness of apostolic teaching commends: “The just person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17). “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” For Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations by faith, foretold to Abraham, saying, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gal. III, 6, 8). These are the Apostle’s words.

If only you would awaken from your most deceitful dreams at this clear voice, so well known to all, and follow the footsteps of our father Abraham, and be blessed in his seed together with all the nations. For, as the Apostle says, he received “the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that righteousness might be counted to them also; and the father of circumcision—not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised” (Rom. IV, 11–12).

Since, then, the righteousness of faith has been set before us as an example to imitate, so that we too, justified by faith, may have peace with God, we ought to understand how he lived, not to condemn him. Otherwise, before we are formed and brought to perfection through a firm conception, we may fall by miscarriage from the womb of Mother Church.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

This is the brief answer I would give Faustus concerning the conduct of the Patriarchs and Prophets, speaking as one of our little ones. I would count myself among them, provided that I do not condemn the life of the holy men of old, even if I do not understand how mystically they lived—men whose life the Apostles commendably proclaimed to us in their Gospel, just as those men, through their prophecy, foretold the future Apostles, so that the two Testaments might cry out to one another, like two Seraphim: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI, 3).

But when Faustus begins to accuse the Patriarchs and Prophets not by the general and indefinite condemnation he has used here, but by recalling their specific deeds, the Lord God of those men—and therefore also our God—will help me to answer each point suitably and appropriately.

For now, however, the Manichaean Faustus condemns those men, while the Apostle Paul praises them. Let each person choose whom to believe.

# BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 0281]

## CHAPTER I

**FAUSTUS said:** How do you worship Christ while rejecting the Prophets, from whose predictions it is understood that he was to come? That some Hebrew Prophets announced our Christ—that is, the Son of God—I do not know whether anyone can prove, once the matter is examined. Nevertheless, even if this is so, what does it have to do with us? This condemnation falls upon those who, having perhaps been converted from Judaism to Christianity under the testimony, as you claim, of the Prophets, later disregarded them as ungrateful for their benefits.

We, on the other hand, are Gentiles by nature—that is, what Paul calls “the uncircumcision” (Eph. II, 11)—born under another law [Note: [Col. 0281] Many manuscripts read, “alienated from the law.”], and under other foretelling authorities whom the Gentiles call prophets. From these we were later converted to Christianity. We did not first become Jews, so that we might rightly follow the faith of the Hebrew Prophets in going over to Christianity; rather, we were stirred only by the report and reputation of the virtues and wisdom of our Liberator, Christ Jesus.

Therefore, if, while I was still living in the religion of my fathers, a preacher came and wished to introduce Christ to me from the Prophets, I would immediately consider him insane: he would be trying to establish doubtful matters by means of still more doubtful ones for me, a Gentile and a man of an entirely different religion. What, then, was necessary except that he first persuade me that the Prophets should be believed, and then lead me through the Prophets to Christ? For this very purpose, other prophets were also needed, who could establish the credibility of these Prophets.

Consequently, if you think Christ must be received through the Prophets, through whom will you receive the Prophets? Will you say, “Through Christ,” so that in turn—that is, so that each commends the other—Christ commends the Prophets and the Prophets Christ? But a Pagan, free from the condition of both, would believe neither the Prophets speaking about Christ nor Christ speaking about the Prophets.

Thus, whoever from among the Gentiles becomes a Christian owes the whole matter to no one but his own faith. To make what we are saying clearer by an example, let us suppose that a Gentile is now being catechized by us, and that, as we sit beside him, we say, “Believe in Christ, because he is God.” But he says, “How do you prove this to me?” And we answer, “From the Prophets.” Again he asks, “Which Prophets?” and we reply, “The Hebrews.” Then, smiling, he says, “But I do not believe them at all.”

We answer, “What about the fact that Christ confirms them?” And he, laughing much more, says, “What about the fact that I do not believe him either?” What will happen after matters have reached this point [Note: [Col. 0281] Some manuscripts read, “after matters have been discussed”?] Shall we not be stuck, while he laughs at us as fools and returns to his former beliefs?

Thus, as I said, the testimonies of the Hebrews contribute nothing to the Christian Church, which consists more of Gentiles than of Jews. Certainly, if there are—as is commonly reported—some predictions of the Sibyl concerning Christ, or of Hermes, whom they call Trismegistus, or of Orpheus and other Gentile prophets, these may help us somewhat toward faith, since we become Christians from among the Gentiles. But the testimonies of the Hebrews, even if true, are useless to us before faith and superfluous after faith: before faith, we could not believe them; now, we believe them unnecessarily.

## CHAPTER II

**AUGUSTINE replied:** Let the preceding, very lengthy reply serve us here for the sake of brevity. I think that anyone who has read it now laughs at this man’s ravings, since he still says that the Hebrew Prophets did not foretell Christ the Son of God. Yet among that one people alone the very name “Christ,” which means “the Anointed,” was most sacredly applied both to king and priest (Exod. XXIX; I Kings X, 1; and Exod. XIX); nor was it removed from there before the one whom those figures represented had come (Dan. IX, 24).

Let them answer for themselves, then: from where did they learn the name of Christ? If they learned it from Manichaeus, I ask Manichaeus himself how they came to believe him—Africans believing a Persian—to say nothing of the rest. Faustus criticizes Romans, Greeks, and other nations if they believe in Christ on the testimony of the Hebrew Prophets as though they were foreigners, and says that the prophecies of the Sibyl and Orpheus, or perhaps those of other Gentile prophets, are more suited to them as grounds for believing in Christ. Yet he does not notice that these are recited in no churches, whereas the Hebrew Prophets resound throughout all nations and lead such great multitudes of believers to Christian salvation.

To say that Hebrew prophecy is unsuitable for Gentiles as a means of believing in Christ, when he sees all nations believing in Christ through Hebrew prophecy, is ridiculous madness.

## CHAPTER III

You dislike the Christ who was foretold through the Hebrews. Yet all the Gentile peoples, among whom you suppose that Hebrew prophecy has no weight of authority, believe in such a Christ as was foretold through the Hebrews—namely, by receiving the Gospel that God had previously promised, as the Apostle recalls, “through his Prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 2–3).

Therefore the prophet Isaiah said, “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Isa. XI, 10); and, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel” (ibid. VII, 14), which is interpreted as “God with us” (Matt. I, 23). Nor should these people [Note: [Col. 0282] In Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov.: “ne”; M.] suppose that the Hebrew Prophets foretold Christ merely as a human being. Faustus seems to have touched on this point when he said, “our Christ, the Son of God,” as though the Hebrews did not call their Christ the Son of God.

Behold, we demonstrate from Hebrew prophecy that Christ, the Son of the Virgin, is God. For even the carnal Jews, lest they should think that Christ was only what he became for our sake—human, from the seed of David—the Lord himself admonishes from the prophecy of that same David. He asks them what they think concerning Christ, whose son they say he is. When they answered, “David’s,” lest Christ should be thought to be only this, as I have said, and they should fail to look toward Emmanuel, which is interpreted “God with us,” he said to them: “How then does David himself, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet’?” (Matt. XXII, 42–44).

Behold, I say, we demonstrate from Hebrew prophecy that Christ is God. You produce some prophecy of your own from which you learned the name of Christ.

## CHAPTER IV

Your Manichaeus was not a prophet of the coming Christ. He calls himself his apostle, with an utterly shameless falsehood; for it is established that this heresy arose not only after Tertullian but even after Cyprian. Nevertheless, all his letters begin in this way: “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ.”

Why did you believe this man concerning Christ? What witness did he bring you for his apostleship? And the very name of Christ—which we know was instituted only in the kingdom of the Jews, among priests and kings, so that not merely this or that individual, but the entire people and the whole kingdom might become a prophecy of Christ and the Christian kingdom—why did this man seize and usurp it, when he forbids you to believe the Hebrew Prophets, so that a false and deceitful apostle may make you false and deceitful disciples of a false Christ?

Finally, lest he be told, “You are lying,” suppose that he brought forward for you certain prophets who, according to his claim, foretold Christ. What will you do with the sort of person Faustus proposed as an example to be catechized—someone unwilling to believe either those prophets or Manichaeus? Will he call our Apostles as witnesses on his behalf? No, I think he will produce not men but books—and will find that those books have been opened not for him but against him.

For there we read and teach that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, and that the Son of God was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (ibid. I, 22–25; Luke II, 7; and Rom. I, 3). If he says that those books have been falsified, he will attack the credibility of his own witnesses. But if he produces other books which he claims belong to our Apostles, how will he himself give them the authority that he did not receive through the churches of Christ established by those Apostles, so that it might pass from them to later generations with its endorsement firmly established?

How can a man whom I do not believe produce Scriptures for me through which I am to believe in him, and then try to give those Scriptures authority when I do not believe him himself?

## CHAPTER V

But if you believed the report concerning Christ—for Faustus, pressed by great difficulties, briefly touched on this point in passing, lest he be forced either to produce books that have no authority or to bind himself to books whose authority is opposed to him—then, if you believed the report concerning Christ, consider carefully whether a report is a trustworthy witness, and where you are rushing headlong.

For much bad report is spread about you, and you do not want it to be believed. What, then, is the reasoning by which you wish this report about Christ to be truthful, while you wish the report about yourselves to be false?

Moreover, you contradict even the report about Christ. That report, clearer and more powerful, holds the ears, minds, and tongues of all nations. It proclaims Christ, spread abroad as descended from the seed of David according to the Hebrew Scriptures, and fulfills what is written there, what was promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18; XXVI, 4; and XXVIII, 14).

What, then, do you answer when asked whose report about Christ you believed, since foreign witnesses do not satisfy you? The authority of our Books, strengthened by the agreement of so many nations and by the succession of Apostles, bishops, and councils, stands against you. Your books, however, have no authority, since they are produced by so few, and by people who worship a lying God and Christ. How is their lying doctrine refuted unless they too are regarded as liars, imitators of their God and Christ?

The report itself, when examined, both proclaims you to be exceedingly wicked and does not cease to preach Christ, descended from the seed of David, against you.

You did not hear the Father’s voice from heaven (Matt. III, 17; XVII, 5); you did not see the works of Christ by which he bore witness concerning himself. You accept the books in which these things are written, as though receiving them under the appearance of Christianity, so that they will not be read against you; yet you say that they have been falsified.

From them you produce Christ saying, “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John X, 38), and, “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (ibid. VIII, 18). But you do not want these words to be produced from the same books against you:

“Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life; they themselves bear witness concerning me”; and, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me”; and, “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them” (ibid. V, 39, 46); and, “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead” (Luke XVI, 29, 31).

Where have you come from, then? Where do you place your confidence? You reject Scriptures established and commended by such great authority, and you perform no miracles. If you did perform them, we would still be on our guard against them, since the Lord warns us in advance, saying, “Many false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will perform many signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. Behold, I have told you beforehand” (Matt. XXIV, 24–25).

He wished nothing to be believed against the confirmed authority of the Scriptures, which proves its faith by the facts themselves, demonstrating through the succession of ages that these things have been fulfilled and accomplished—things it foretold long before they occurred.

## CHAPTER VI

It remains for you to say that you can offer a proof so certain and invincible that, once the truth has declared itself, it requires neither the authority of a witness nor the truth of a miracle. What do you say? What do you produce? What proof, what truth?

That story is long and empty—a childish jest, a woman’s diversion, and an old woman’s ravings [Note: [Col. 0284] Most manuscripts read, “a distraction.”]—containing a truncated beginning, a rotten middle, and a ruined ending.

For when you are asked, from its beginning, “What was the race of darkness going to do with the immortal, invisible, incorruptible God, if he had not wanted to fight it?”; and from its middle, “How is God incorruptible and undefiled, when you crush his members by eating and digesting them in fruits and vegetables, in order to purify them?”; and from its end, “What did the wretched soul do to deserve punishment by an everlasting bond in the sphere of darkness, when it was stained not by its own fault but by another’s, and could not be cleansed because its God, who sent it into pollution, failed it?”—when you hesitate and cannot find what to answer, your many great [Note: [Col. 0285] In the manuscripts, “and so very ancient.”] and precious books are spat upon [Note: [Col. 0285] Most manuscripts read, “are seen.”]; and the labors of copyists, the little bags of the wretched, and the bread of the deceived are deeply lamented [Note: [Col. 0285] Lov. reads, “are erased.” Am. and several manuscripts more correctly read, “are lamented”; others have, “are to be lamented.”].

If, then, neither the antiquity of scriptural authority, nor the power of miracles, nor soundness of conduct, nor the truth of reason supports you, depart in confusion and return acknowledging that he is Christ, the Savior of all who believe in him. His name and his Church are displayed by the present age just as the past announced them—not through some random person emerging from hidden caves, but through a certain people and a certain kingdom propagated and established for this purpose: there, everything concerning him was marked out beforehand in figures, so that it might now be recognized in its fulfillment; and there, through the Prophets, the things that were to come were foretold in writing, so that they might now be presented as proclaimed through the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0285] Am., Er., and some manuscripts read, “might now be furnished.”].

## CHAPTER VII

Therefore, imagine for yourselves a Gentile being catechized—the person in whom Faustus mocked our failure, although it was he himself who failed, deserving not laughter but lamentation.

If we say to a Gentile, “Believe in Christ, because he is God,” and he replies, “Why should I believe?”; and, when the authority of the Prophets is produced, says that he does not believe them because they are Hebrews while he is a Pagan, we demonstrate the faithworthiness of the Prophets from what they sang would come and what is seen to have come.

I believe he would not be unaware of how many persecutions the Christian religion had previously endured from the kings of this world. Or, if he were unaware, this could easily be demonstrated to him through the history of the nations and the imperial laws committed to writing and memory. When he recognized that this had been foretold long beforehand by the prophet who said, “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ?”—it would be clear from that same psalm that this was not spoken about David himself.

For there it also says what confounds people, however stubborn, by the very manifestation of events: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession’” (Ps. II, 1–2, 7–8). No one doubts that this was not granted to the Jewish nation over which David ruled, but was fulfilled when all nations were occupied far and wide by the name of Christ.

I believe he would be moved when he heard many other passages from the Prophets, which it would take too long to pursue here. He would also see the very kings of the earth already salutarily subjected to Christ’s rule, and all nations serving him. He would hear read from a psalm, foretold long beforehand, “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI, 11).

And if he wished to read the whole psalm itself, which is figuratively spoken as though about Solomon, he would find Christ truly to be the peaceful king—for this is what the name “Solomon” is interpreted to mean. In Christ he would recognize the fulfillment of everything said there, things far removed from that man Solomon, king of Israel.

He would likewise consider the psalm in which God is said to be anointed by God, and Christ is plainly shown to be God, since he is indicated as God anointed by God (Ps. XLIV, 8). If he wished to consider what is said there about Christ and about the Church itself—what he would read as foretold there and observe as fulfilled throughout the world—he would also see the very idols of the nations perishing from the world through the name of Christ, and would learn that this too had been foretold by the Prophets.

He would hear Jeremiah say, “Thus you shall say to them: ‘The gods that did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from beneath heaven’” (Jer. X, 11).

Again, elsewhere, when he heard the same prophet say, “Lord, my strength, my help, and my refuge in the day of troubles: to you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth, and they shall say, ‘Our fathers possessed false idols, and there is no profit in them! Can a human being make gods, when they are not gods?’ Therefore, behold, I will show them at that time; I will show them my hand and my power, and they shall know that I am the Lord” (ibid. XVI, 19–21)—when he heard these words from prophetic Scripture and saw them throughout the whole earth, what should I say about how he would be moved to faith? For we prove this by the facts themselves, when we recognize that the hearts of believers are so strengthened through a prophecy written long beforehand and fulfilled in these times.

## CHAPTER VIII

And now, lest he suppose Christ to be merely a human being, however great such human beings may have been, the same prophet would remove this thought from his mind. For he continues and says:

“Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, and makes flesh the strength of his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He shall be like a tamarisk [Note: [Col. 0286] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read, “a shrub.”] in the desert; he shall not see good when it comes, and he shall dwell among the wicked in a deserted land, in a salty land that shall not be inhabited.”

And:

“Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his hope. He shall be like a fruitful tree beside water, and in moisture he shall send out his roots. He shall not fear when the heat comes, and its branches shall be leafy; in the year of drought he shall not fear, and he shall not cease to produce fruit.”

When this prophet said that the one who places his hope in man is cursed, explaining that curse through prophetic images, and that the one who trusts in the Lord is blessed, weaving that blessing likewise through fitting images, the Gentile might perhaps be troubled. How, he might ask, could we proclaim Christ as God so that hope may be placed in him with complete security, and then say that he is human—not by his own nature, but by the mortality he assumed from us?

For some have erred by believing Christ to be God and denying him to be human. Others, again, by supposing him to be human and denying him to be God, either despised him or, placing their hope in a human being, fell under that curse.

If this Gentile were troubled, he might say that this prophet had spoken against our faith, since according to apostolic teaching we say not only that Christ is God, so that hope may be placed in him with complete security, but also that he is “the man Christ Jesus, Mediator between God and human beings” (I Tim. II, 5). Yet, he might say, this prophet speaks only of God and makes no mention of human nature.

At that very point he would hear the voice of the same prophet admonishing and correcting him: “The heart is unsearchable above all things, and it is a man; who will know him?” (Jer. XVII, 5–9).

He is therefore human, so that those whose hearts are weighed down might be healed through faith by the form of a servant and recognize him as God, who for their sake became human, so that their hope would not be in a human being but in the human God.

And yet: “The heart is deep in every way, and he is a human being”—receiving the form of a servant. “And who will know him?” He who, “although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. II, 7, 6).

“And he is a human being,” because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” “And who will know him?” Because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 14, 1).

And truly, “the heart is deep in every way.” For even in his disciples there was that heaviness of heart when he said to them, “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me.” What does “I have been with you for so long” mean except what is said here, “And he is a human being”? And what does “You have not known me” mean except what is said here, “And who will know him”? Whom, except the one who says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (ibid. XIV, 9)?

Thus our hope is not in a human being, because of the curse proclaimed through the prophet [Note: [Col. 0287] Am., Er., and some manuscripts read, “the pronounced curse.”], but in the human God—that is, in the Son of God, our Savior Jesus Christ, Mediator between God and human beings: the one whom the Father is greater than because of the form of a servant, and who is equal to the Father because of the form of God.

## CHAPTER IX

Isaiah also says:

“The insolence of human beings shall be humbled and fall [Note: [Col. 0287] Some manuscripts read, “the defiance of human beings.”], and the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day. And all things made by human hands they shall hide in caves, in clefts of rocks, and in caverns of the earth, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the majesty of his power, when he rises to shatter the earth. On that day a human being shall cast away the abominations of gold and silver that they made in order to worship useless and harmful things” (Isa. II, 17–20).

Perhaps this Gentile whom we are catechizing—the one whom Faustus, laughing, said would declare, “I do not believe the Hebrew Prophets”—has hidden some hand-made idols in a cave, or in a cleft of rock, or in a cavern of the earth. Or perhaps he knows that one of his friends has done this, or that in his city or on his estate something of this sort has been done, because of the fear of the Lord, who, through the kings of the earth—already serving and worshiping him according to the same prophecy—now shatters the earth by the strictest laws; that is, he breaks the boldness of the earthly heart.

How, then, can he say, “I do not believe the Hebrew Prophets,” when he may recognize that what was once foretold by the Hebrew Prophets has been fulfilled even in himself?

## CHAPTER X

It was more to be feared that, surrounded by such clear evidence of events, he might say that, after these things began to occur throughout the world, Christians had composed these writings so that they might be thought to have been divinely foretold in advance, lest they be despised as though they had been produced merely by human effort.

This would indeed be something to fear if the Jewish people were not widely dispersed and widely known: that Cain, who received a sign so that no one would kill him (Gen. IV, 15), and Ham, servant of his brothers (ibid. IX, 25), should carry the Books by which others are instructed while being burdened by them himself [Note: [Col. 0288] II Retractations, chapter 7, no. 3.].

For through their books we prove that these writings were not composed by us as though we had been prompted by the occurrence of events, but were foretold and preserved long ago in that kingdom, and are now revealed and fulfilled.

In those writings, even the things that are less clear there—because they happened to those people in symbolic form, but were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (I Cor. X, 11)—are now illuminated and disclosed in their fulfillment. What was still obscured by the shadows of future events is now made manifest by the light of events already accomplished.

## CHAPTER XI

Perhaps he would also say that he was moved by this: that those very people in whose books these events are found foretold, and now visibly fulfilled, do not share with us in the fellowship of the same Gospel.

But when he was taught that this too had been foretold by the same Prophets, who could fail to see how greatly he would be moved to faith? Who could be so mad as not to see it, or so shameless [Note: Am. and several manuscripts read, “so foolish.”] as to pretend that he did not?

Who doubts that this was prophesied concerning the Jews, when Isaiah says, “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel does not know me, and my people does not understand me” (Isa. I, 3)? Or when the Apostle recalls, “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people that does not believe and contradicts” (Rom. X, 21; Isa. LXV, 2)? And especially when he says, “God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they might not see, and ears so that they might not hear and understand” (Rom. XI, 8; Isa. VI, 10)—along with many similar passages?

If he were to say, “What sin, then, did the Jews commit, if God blinded them so that they would not recognize Christ?” we would show, as far as we could, by instructing this inexperienced man, that the just punishment of this blindness arises from other hidden sins known to God.

The Apostle not only said this about certain people: “For this reason God handed them over to the desires of their hearts,” or “to a debased mind, to do what is improper” (Rom. I, 24, 28), wishing to show that certain manifest sins arise as punishment for certain hidden ones; we would also demonstrate that the Prophets themselves did not leave this unmentioned.

For, without going further, in the very passage where Jeremiah says, “He is a human being, and who will know him?”—lest the Jews should seem to have been excused on this very ground because they did not know him, since, as the Apostle says, “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8)—the prophet continues and shows that it was the consequence of their hidden merit that they did not know.

For he says: “I am the Lord, examining hearts and testing the inner parts, to give to each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his practices.”

## CHAPTER XII

Further, if that Gentile were troubled by the question why those who are called Christians themselves also separate into many different heresies, we would teach him that this too was not omitted by the Hebrew Prophets.

For, as though it followed that, once the Jews had been shown in their blindness, this thought would occur to him—that many people under the Christian name also deviate from the Christian fellowship itself—the prophet Jeremiah, as though indicating to us the order of catechesis, immediately added:

“The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch, making its wealth without judgment.”

The partridge is a very quarrelsome animal, and it is well known with what eagerness it runs into the snare of its own contentiousness. Heretics do not love disputation; rather, with the most shameless obstinacy, they seek to prevail by any means, so that they gather, as the prophet said here, what they did not hatch.

They find Christians—those whom they chiefly seduce under the name of Christ—already born through the very Gospel of Christ, and they make them their wealth, not with judgment, certainly, but with inconsiderate recklessness. They do not understand that the true, saving, and in a certain sense genuine and foundational Christian fellowship is there, from which they have separated those whom they gathered into their own wealth.

And because the Apostle says of such people, “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth—people corrupted in mind, rejected with regard to the faith. But they will not progress further, for their folly will become evident to all, as theirs also did” (II Tim. III, 8–9), the Prophet here too continues and says of the partridge that gathered what it did not hatch:

“In the middle of its days they will abandon it, and at its end it will be foolish.”

That is, the one who at first seduced people by promising and displaying superior wisdom will be foolish—that is, he will be shown to be foolish. To those for whom he was wise at first, he will then be foolish, when it becomes evident that his folly is known to everyone.

## CHAPTER XIII

And as though the person whom we are catechizing were to ask, “By what manifest sign, while I am still a little one and not yet able to distinguish clear truth from so many errors, by what unmistakable indication shall I recognize the Church of Christ, in whom I am already compelled to believe by the manifestation of so many things foretold beforehand?”—the same prophet continues and, as though receiving the movement of his mind in the proper order, teaches him that the Church of Christ itself was foretold, since it stands out and appears to everyone.

It is itself the seat of glory, of which the Apostle says, “For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (I Cor. III, 17). Hence the prophet says, “But the seat of glory has been exalted: our sanctification” (Jer. XVII, 10–12).

Because of these movements of the little ones, who can be led astray by human beings, the Lord too, foreseeing the manifestation of the Church’s glory, says, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V, 14). For certainly “the seat of glory has been exalted: our sanctification,” so that those who lead people away into religious divisions may not be heeded when they say, “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there.”

They point out parts, saying, “Behold, here; behold, there.” But that city is upon a mountain. What mountain, except the one that, according to Daniel’s prophecy, grew from a small stone and became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole earth (Dan. II, 34–35)?

Nor should those be heeded who, under the name of a supposedly secret and apocryphal truth and a supposedly tiny group of people, say, “Behold, he is in the inner rooms; behold, he is in the desert” (Matt. XXIV, 23, 26). For a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, because “the seat of glory has been exalted: our sanctification.”

## CHAPTER XIV

When, therefore, this Gentile saw, through these and other such testimonies of the Prophets, the persecution by kings and peoples, the faith of kings and peoples, the abolition of idols, the blindness of the Jews, the confirmation of the books preserved by the Jews themselves, the madness of heretics, and the excellence of the holy Church of true and genuine Christians—all foretold beforehand and now fulfilled—what could he find more worthy of faith than those Prophets, through whom he might choose to believe in the divinity of Christ?

Indeed, if before these things happened I were to present a Gentile with the Hebrew Prophets, asking him to believe that they foretold events he did not yet see, he might reasonably say, “What have I to do with these Prophets? You have not shown me how to prove that they are truthful.”

But when so many and such great things as they foretold have already been brought to fulfillment and manifestation, then, if he did not wish to be perverse, he would plainly neither despise these events, which deserved to be commended for foreseeing and proclaiming them so long beforehand and with such solemn preparation, nor despise those by whom they could be foreseen and proclaimed.

For we believe no one more wisely—whether concerning past events that happened long ago or future events that have not yet happened—than those who have proved the credibility of their words to us through so many and such great events that they foretold and that have now occurred.

## CHAPTER XV
Furthermore, as for the Sibyl—or the Sibyls—and Orpheus, and some Hermes or other whom I do not know, and any other seers, theologians, sages, or philosophers among the Gentiles who are reputed to have foretold or spoken something true about the Son of God or God the Father: this is indeed useful for refuting the vanity of the pagans, but not for embracing the authority of such people. For we demonstrate that we worship that God about whom even those men could not remain silent who either dared partly to teach their fellow Gentile peoples to worship idols and demons, or dared not forbid them to do so.
