But our holy authorities propagated and governed, under God’s rule and assistance, that people, that commonwealth, and that kingdom in which the very thing that was a religious observance for these men would have been sacrilege. Accordingly, if anyone there fell into the worship of images and demons, they were either punished according to the laws of their own commonwealth or restrained by the prophetic voices with the freest thunder.

[Note: [Col. 0290] So in the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain instead read “most freely,” omitting the word “thunder.”]

For the one God who made heaven and earth was worshiped by them, in a prophetic rite—that is, one signifying future events. This rite was to be abolished when those things had come which it signified would come. For the kingdom itself was a great prophet, in which a king and a priest were anointed with mystical significance (Deut. XVIII, 15; Ps. II, 6; Ps. CIX, 4; I Kings X, 1, and Exod. XXIX). This was not taken away until that one had come—although even the Jews themselves did not know it and therefore resisted it—the God anointed with spiritual grace above his companions, the Holy of Holies (Dan. IX, 24, and Ps. XLIV, 8), at once the true king, by providing counsel for us, and the true priest, by offering himself for us.

Therefore, as great as the difference concerning Christ’s coming between the angels’ proclamation and the demons’ confession, so great is the difference between the authority of the Prophets and the curiosity of sacrilegious men.

CHAPTER XVI

When these and similar points, which we now touch on briefly, had perhaps then been discussed at somewhat greater length as the need to drive away an age-old error required, and had been asserted with the strength of fuller proof, that Gentile whom Faustus proposed for us to catechize would surely have been moved to faith, if he preferred his salvation to his sins. Once instructed in the faith and placed in the bosom of the Catholic Church to be nurtured, he would consequently also be taught what manner of life he ought to maintain.

Nor would he be disturbed by the multitude of those in whom he did not find the things he was commanded to observe, although they were bodily gathered with him in the Church and received the same Sacraments. He would know that God’s inheritance is shared with the few, but his seals with the many; that with the few he shares holiness of life and the gift of charity poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5), to that inner fountain no outsider having access; but that with the many he shares the holiness of the Sacrament. Whoever eats and drinks it unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (I Cor. XI, 29), while whoever refuses to eat it will not have life within him (John VI, 54), and therefore will not attain eternal life.

He would also understand that these same people are called few in comparison with the multitude of the wicked, but that, considered in themselves, they are numerous, spread throughout the whole world, growing among the weeds, and remaining with the chaff until the day of harvest and winnowing (Matt. XIII, 25–26; III, 12).

This was spoken in the Gospel; this was foretold beforehand by the Prophets. It was foretold beforehand: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song II, 2). It was foretold beforehand: “I dwelt in the tents of Kedar; with those who hated peace I was peaceable” (Ps. CXIX, 5, 7). It was foretold beforehand: “Mark those on their foreheads who groan and mourn over the iniquities of my people which are committed in their midst” (Ezek. IX, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0291] Louvain reads: “Mark Tau on their foreheads.” “Tau” is absent from the other editions and the manuscripts, as well as from the Greek Septuagint.]

Thus this Gentile, whom we would strengthen with such an address, already made a citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household, no longer a stranger to Israel (Eph. II, 19, 12), but a true Israelite in whom there was no deceit (John I, 47), would also learn to speak from a sincere heart the words which that same Jeremiah next joins together:

“Patience of Israel, Lord; let all who forsake you be terrified.”

For when he had spoken of the partridge,

[Note: [Col. 0291] Erasmus reads “which”; manuscripts read “who.”]

which cries out and gathers what it has not hatched, he commended the excellence of the city set upon a mountain, which cannot be hidden, so that heretics might not separate a man from the Catholic Church,

[Note: [Col. 0291] The Ambrosian edition and Erasmus read “that he might not separate a heretical man.” Several manuscripts read “that he might separate a heretical man.”]

saying: “But the throne of glory has been exalted; our sanctification.”

Then, as though the question had occurred to him, “What, then, are we to do about so many wicked people, who are mixed everywhere in such greater numbers as Christ’s glory in the unity of all nations is more exalted?” he immediately added: “Patience of Israel, Lord.”

For we must patiently endure what he says: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. XIII, 30), lest, through impatience in tolerating the wicked, the good—who properly constitute Christ’s body—be abandoned; and therefore, when they are abandoned, he is abandoned.

Thus he continued and added: “Let all who forsake you be put to shame; let those who have departed into the earth be confounded.” For the earth is a person who presumes upon himself and induces others to presume upon him. Therefore it follows: “They shall be overturned, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living water.”

For what else does the partridge cry out except that the fountain of life is in itself and is given by itself, so that those who have gathered around it may depart from Christ, deceived by Christ’s promise, though they were already held and instructed in his name? For it does not gather those whom it has hatched; rather, in order to gather those whom it has not hatched, it says: “The salvation which Christ promised is with me; I will give it.”

But see what this man says: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved.” Hence the Apostle says: “Let no one glory in man” (I Cor. III, 21); and this man adds: “For you are my glorying” (Jer. XVII, 13–14).

By such means we instruct a man from apostolic and prophetic doctrine, so that he may be built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets (Eph. II, 20).

CHAPTER XVII

But how would Faustus persuade a Gentile of Christ’s divinity when he has him say: “I believe neither the Prophets about Christ nor Christ about the Prophets”? Would he believe Christ speaking about himself, while he would not believe him testifying about others? It is truly ridiculous to suppose this. Once he had judged someone unworthy of belief, he would either believe nothing he said, or would more likely believe him when testifying on behalf of others than on his own behalf.

Perhaps, if Faustus had been mocked, he would have read to the man the Sibyls, Orpheus, and others of that kind, if he found any other Gentiles who had foretold something about Christ? But he would not do so. He confessed that these authors were unknown to him, saying:

“Certainly, if there are—as rumor has it—some prophecies about Christ by the Sibyl or Hermes, whom they call Trismegistus, or Orpheus or other Gentile seers.”

Since, therefore, he did not know the writings of these men, and thought on the basis of rumor that there were such authors, he certainly would not read them to the man who said, “I believe neither the Prophets nor Christ.”

What, then, would he do? Would he bring forward Manichaeus and commend Christ from him? They never did this. Rather, concerning Christ, whose name is now sweetly renowned everywhere, they have always tried to commend Manichaeus, so that with this honey they might anoint the lips of their poisoned cup.

For when Christ promised his followers that he would send the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter or Advocate, the Spirit of truth (John XIV, 16)—taking advantage of this promise, they say that this Paraclete is Manichaeus, or is in Manichaeus, and so creep into the minds of ignorant people, who do not know when the Paraclete promised by Christ was sent.

But those who have read the canonical book entitled Acts of the Apostles see that Christ’s promise is mentioned there again and most clearly fulfilled there (Acts I, 8; II, 1–4).

But for the moment we are asking how he would establish faith in Christ for that Gentile. For I think no one is so blind as to wish to say, “I believe Manichaeus,” while saying, “I do not believe Christ.”

Then, if he were not laughing but at least irritated, he would say: “Do you really order me to believe Persian books, when you told me not to believe the Hebrew ones?”

[Note: [Col. 0293] So in the Ambrosian edition and most manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain instead read, “when I told you not to believe.”]

How, then, will you capture this man, heretic, unless you find him already in some way subject to the name of Christ, so that, because he no longer doubts that Christ must be believed, he may be deceived into accepting Manichaeus as one who preaches Christ better?

Behold the partridge gathering what it has not hatched. Do you not yet forsake him, you whom he gathers? Does it not yet become apparent to you that he is foolish when he says that the testimonies of the Hebrews are useless to us before faith, even if they are true, and superfluous after faith?

[Note: [Col. 0293] The Ambrosian edition and Erasmus read “to you.”]

CHAPTER XVIII

Let those who have believed, then, throw away all the books through which they came to believe. For if this is true, I do not see why the very Gospel of Christ should be read by the faithful. Before faith it is useless, because that Gentile whom Faustus introduces laughing—and who ought rather to be mourned—does not believe Christ. After faith it is superfluous, if one already believes the true proclamations about Christ superfluously once one has believed in him.

Perhaps you will say: “But the believer ought to read the Gospel so that he does not forget what he believed.” In that case, madmen, let him also read the true testimonies of the Prophets, so that he does not forget why he believed; for if he forgets that, what he believed will not be firm in him.

Or throw away the books of Manichaeus, on whose testimony you believed that light fought against darkness, although that light was God himself; and that, so that light might bind darkness, light first had to be devoured by darkness, bound, defiled, and torn apart—light which you restore by eating, release, cleanse, and heal, so that a reward may be repaid to you, lest you be condemned in an eternal globe together with that part which could not be liberated.

You sing this little story every day, both in your conduct and in your words. Why do you still seek testimony for it in books, so that in matters that are superfluous, and in the production of your books, another substance may be consumed and your god’s bound substance may be held captive?

[Note: [Col. 0294] Louvain reads “his bound members may be held captive.” The word “members” is unnecessarily added; it is absent from the other editions and the manuscripts, although “substance” is understood in each place.]

Burn all those parchments, and their elegant bindings, carefully fashioned from beautiful skins,

[Note: [Col. 0294] So the Ambrosian edition, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Louvain reads “made smooth.”]

so that neither a superfluous thing may burden you and your god may be released from them—your god who, like a slave under punishment, is held bound even in a book.

For if you could eat your books after boiling them, what a benefit you would provide to the members of your god! Or, if it could be done, would the uncleanness of flesh prevent the pages from being included in your feasts? Let the cleanliness of the encaustic paint take responsibility for itself, since it has adhered to lambskin.

But you have done this also: as though in your first battle, by writing you attached to the uncleanness of parchments what had been clean in the reed pen.

[Note: [Col. 0294] The Louvain edition reads “as though in your first little book you attached what was unclean.” The reading is corrected on the basis of the other editions and the manuscripts.]

Except that the colors themselves accuse you with contrary testimony. For you rather came into the light of white pages together with the darkness of ink.

Should you be angry with us for saying such things, or with yourselves for believing such things, so that, whether you wish it or not, these consequences follow?

But we, both to recall our faith, to console our hope, and to encourage our charity, read the prophetic and apostolic books, whose voices harmonize with one another. By that harmony, like a heavenly trumpet, they both rouse us from the torpor of mortal life and stretch us toward the prize of the heavenly calling.

For after the Apostle had recalled something from the prophetic books—“The reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me” (Ps. LXVIII, 10)—he immediately adds the benefit of divine reading:

“For whatever was written beforehand,” he says, “was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope in God” (Rom. XV, 4).

But Faustus contradicts this:

“Let what Paul says happen to him: ‘If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed’” (Gal. I, 9).

FOURTEENTH BOOK

[Col. 0293]

CHAPTER I

[Col. 0293]

FAUSTUS said: Why do you not accept Moses?

Because of the love and devotion by which we worship Christ. For who is so irreligious as willingly to look upon one who cursed his own father?

[Note: [Col. 0293] Several manuscripts read “receive.”]

Therefore we too execrate Moses, although he never spared any of the human or divine beings in his blaspheming; but we execrate him more for this reason: that he assailed Christ, the Son of God, who hung upon the tree for the sake of our salvation, with the dreadful insult of a curse.

[Note: [Col. 0293] The Ambrosian edition, Erasmus, and certain manuscripts consistently read “devotion” instead of “curse”; likewise a little later, at Col. 0295, “not so harsh an insult of devotion.” The Antwerp edition of the Benedictine Fathers has “devotion.”]

Whether he did so intentionally or by accident, you may decide. For he will be excused or commended on neither ground, so as to deserve acceptance. For he says that everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed (Deut. XXI, 23).

Do you therefore wish me to accept this man and believe him, when, if he was divine, it is clear that he knowingly and willingly cursed Christ; but if he cursed him unwillingly and unknowingly, it is clear that he was not divine?

Choose, then, whichever you like: either that Moses was not a prophet and sinned through ignorance, so that, while cursing others according to his custom, he unknowingly blasphemed God; or that he was indeed divine and did not fail to know that this would happen, but nevertheless, envious of our salvation—which was to come through the tree—uttered the poisons of his cursing mouth against its author.

Who, then, would believe that this man had seen or known the Father, when he so tore apart the Son? How could he have foretold the Son’s coming when he did not know the outcome of his ascension?

Moreover, I consider how widely that insult was spread and how many it includes and dishonors, so that it even touches all the righteous and martyrs who ended their lives in a passion of the same kind, such as Peter, Andrew, and the rest of the same lot. Unless Moses, as a non-prophet, was ignorant of them, or, as a malicious man, hated them if he was a prophet, he would not have torn them apart with such a cruel insult of cursing.

For he does not merely call them accursed in the ordinary sense—that is, accursed among human beings—but accursed by God. If that is so, what hope of blessing will remain for Christ, or for the Apostles, or for us ourselves, if we happen to be crucified for the sake of his name?

[Note: [Col. 0295] Almost only the Louvain edition reads, “if all of us happen to be crucified for his sake.”]

Finally, how foolish and devoid of divine inspiration he was, that he could not consider that people might be hanged upon a tree for different reasons: some for an evil deed, but others for justice and for God’s sake; and that therefore he indiscriminately and without any distinction cast them all under the same curse.

He should have said, if he possessed any wisdom—not to mention prophecy—and if the cross had so offended him that it alone was excluded and rejected from every kind of punishment: “Accursed is every criminal and impious person who has hung upon a tree,” so that there might be some distinction between the righteous and the unrighteous.

Yet even then he would not have spoken truly, since Christ brought the thief with him from the tree into the paradise of his Father (Luke XXIII, 43).

Where, then, is “Everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed”? Or was that notorious robber Barabbas—who was not only not hanged upon a tree but was also released from prison at the Jews’ request (Matt. XXVII, 26)—more blessed than the one who ascended from the cross into heaven with Christ?

Finally, what of the fact that he also calls accursed anyone who worships the sun or the moon (Deut. XVII, 3)? If, then, placed under a Gentile king, I am forced to worship the sun, and, when I resist, am ordered to be crucified for fear of this curse, I fall under another curse of his, which he pronounced against the one who hangs upon a tree.

Or is it his habit to curse every good thing? We should value his curses as highly as the curses of angry old women. For in the same way he pursues all God’s boys and girls with an equal curse, saying that everyone who has not raised up seed in Israel is accursed (Deut. XXV, 5–10).

This insult likewise touches Jesus principally, who, as you say, was himself born from the Jews, yet raised up no offspring among them for the preservation of posterity. Then it also touches his disciples, some of whom he separated from their wives—those whom he found joined to them—and others whom he forbade to marry, finding them untouched.

Concerning this matter, you may rightly recognize that we execrate Moses’ unpunished tongue, which assails Christ—light, holiness, and all things divine—with the darts of its curses.

And lest you perhaps think that there is much difference between being hanged and being crucified—for you often take this also as a defense—listen to Paul prescribing these arguments against you:

“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us; for it is written: ‘Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree’” (Gal. III, 13).

CHAPTER II

AUGUSTINE replied: The devout Faustus grieves that Christ was cursed by Moses, and therefore hates Moses because he loves Christ.

For the moment, before I explain with what great sacramental meaning and with what piety it was said, “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. XXI, 23), I ask these devout men why they are angry with Moses, since his curse did not reach the Christ of these men.

For if Christ hung upon a tree, he was certainly fastened with nails. For this reason he even showed the scars themselves after his resurrection to the disciple who was slow to believe (John XX, 27). If that is so, he certainly had a vulnerable and mortal body, which these men refuse to admit.

If, then, those wounds and scars were false, it is also false that he hung upon a tree. That curse therefore could not reach him, and they have no reason to be angry with the one whose mouth uttered it.

Thus, if they pretend to be angry with the one who cursed Christ’s false death—as I have said according to their own position—how must we flee those who do not curse Christ but, what is more detestable, accuse him of a crime? For if one who imposes a curse upon mortality is not to be accepted, how is one to be detested who attributes deceit to the truth?

But now, taking the opportunity provided by the calumnies of the heretics, let us see how that sacramental meaning is to be explained to the faithful.

CHAPTER III

Human death is the punishment of sin, and therefore death itself is also called sin—not because a person sins while dying, but because it came about through sin.

In one sense, “tongue” properly means the flesh that moves within the teeth beneath the palate; in another sense, “tongue” means what is done through the tongue, in which sense we speak of one tongue as Greek and another as Latin.

Likewise, in one sense “hand” properly means the bodily member which we move in order to work; in another sense “hand” means the writing produced by the hand. For we say: “His hand was brought forth”; “His hand was read against him”; “I have your hand”; “Take back your hand.”

The hand is certainly properly a human bodily member. Yet I do not suppose that writing is a human bodily member, and nevertheless it is called a hand because it is made by the hand.

So too “sin” means not only the evil deed itself, which deserves punishment, but also death itself, which came about through sin and has been called sin.

[Note: [Col. 0296] Erasmus and most manuscripts read “has been called.”]

Christ did not commit that sin by which he would be guilty of death; but he accepted for us the other thing—that is, death, which was inflicted upon human nature because of sin. He hung this upon the tree; this was cursed through Moses. There death was condemned so that it would not reign, and cursed so that it would perish.

Therefore, through Christ’s such sin, our sin too was condemned, so that we might be freed and not remain condemned while sin reigned.

CHAPTER IV

Why, then, does Faustus marvel that sin is accursed, that death is accursed, that the mortality of flesh without Christ’s sin is accursed, although it came about even in Christ through human sin?

For he took a body from Adam, because Mary the Virgin, who bore Christ, was descended from Adam. God had said in paradise: “On the day you touch it, you shall surely die” (Gen. II, 17). This is the curse that hung upon the tree.

Let him deny that Christ was accursed who denies that he died. But whoever confesses that he died, and cannot deny that death comes from sin and is therefore itself also called sin, should hear the Apostle saying: “Our old man was crucified together with him” (Rom. VI, 6), and should understand whom Moses called accursed.

Therefore the Apostle confidently says of Christ: “He became a curse for us” (Gal. III, 13), just as he did not fear saying: “He died for all” (II Cor. V, 15).

For “he died” means the same as “he was accursed,” since death itself comes from a curse, and every sin is accursed—whether the sin itself which is committed, so that punishment follows, or the punishment itself, which in another sense is called sin because it comes about through sin.

Christ accepted our punishment without guilt, so that from it he might release us from our guilt and also bring our punishment to an end.

CHAPTER V

I would be speaking these things from my own ingenuity if the Apostle did not repeat them so often that he both awakens the sleeping and silences the slanderers.

“God,” he says, “sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and, concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. VIII, 3).

That flesh, therefore, was not sinful flesh, because it had not come into Mary through the transmission of mortality by a male. Yet because death comes from sin, and that flesh, although from a virgin, was nevertheless mortal, precisely because it was mortal it bore the likeness of sinful flesh.

He also calls this “sin,” saying accordingly: “So that, concerning sin, he might condemn sin in the flesh.”

Again, in another place he says: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (II Cor. V, 21).

Why, then, would Moses fear calling accursed what Paul did not fear calling sin? Clearly, this the Prophet ought both to have foreseen and to have foretold, prepared to be criticized by heretics together with the Apostle.

For whoever criticizes the Prophet for saying “accursed” is compelled to criticize the Apostle for saying “sin”; for a curse is certainly the companion of sin.

CHAPTER VI

Nor is the charge more serious because he added “by God,” saying: “Everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed by God.”

Unless God hated sin and our death, he would not have sent his Son to accept and destroy it. Why, then, is it surprising that what God hates is accursed by God?

For the more willingly he grants us immortality, which is to come when Christ comes, the more mercifully he hates our death, which hung upon the tree when Christ died.

As for the addition of “everyone,” so that it says, “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree,” Moses did not fail to foresee that the righteous too would be upon the cross. Rather, he correctly foresaw that heretics would deny the true death of the Lord and would therefore wish to separate Christ from this curse, in order to separate him from the reality of death as well.

For if that death was not real, no curse hung upon Christ crucified on the tree, because he was not truly crucified.

But against the heretics who would come from far in the future, Moses cries out from far away:

“You are evading the issue for no reason, you who are displeased by the truth of Christ’s death: ‘Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree’”—not this one or that one, but absolutely everyone.

“Even the Son of God?”

“Yes, certainly. For this is what you do not want; this is what you strive to avoid; this is where you deceive others. For you are displeased by the one who was accursed for us because you are displeased by the one who died for us.”

Only if he is outside Adam’s death is he then outside Adam’s curse. But when he accepted death from man and for man, he did not disdain to accept from him and for him also the curse that accompanies death—not even he, absolutely not even he, the Son of God, always living in his own righteousness but dead because of our offenses (Rom. IV, 25), in flesh assumed from our punishment.

Thus he was always blessed in his own righteousness, but accursed because of our offenses, in the death accepted from our punishment. For this reason “everyone” was added, lest Christ be said not to belong to true death if, through foolish honor, he were separated from the curse joined to death.

CHAPTER VII

Whoever is faithful through the truth of the Gospel understands that there is no insult to Christ in Moses’ mouth when Moses called him accursed—not because of the divinity of his majesty but because of the condition of our punishment, on account of which he was suspended upon the tree.

Nor is there praise of Christ in the mouth of the Manichaeans when they deny that he had mortal flesh in which he would suffer a true death. From that prophetic curse, praise of humility is understood; from this heretical semblance of honor, an accusation of falsehood is brought.

If, then, you deny the curse, deny the death. If you deny the death, you are no longer fighting against Moses but against the Apostles.

But if you confess the death, confess that he accepted the punishment of our sin without our sin. Now, when you hear of the punishment of sin, believe either that it comes from a blessing or from a curse.

If the punishment of sin comes from a blessing, wish always to remain in the punishment of sin. But if you wish to be freed from it, believe that it came through the justice of the divine sentence from a curse.

Confess, therefore, that he accepted a curse for us whom you confess to have died for us. And confess that Moses wished to signify nothing other than this when he said, “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree”: “Every mortal person, and everyone who dies, who hangs upon a tree.”

For he could have said, “Accursed is every mortal person,” or “Accursed is everyone who dies.” But this is what the Prophet asserts,

[Note: [Col. 0298] The manuscripts read “prophecy.”]

because he knew that Christ’s death would hang upon the cross and that heretics would arise who would say: “He did hang upon a tree, but only in some appearance, not so that he would truly die.”

By crying out, therefore, “Accursed,” he cried out nothing other than that he truly died, knowing that human death, which he accepted without sin, came from that curse concerning which it was said: “If you touch it, you shall surely die” (Gen. II, 17).

The serpent suspended upon the tree also pertains to this, signifying that Christ did not feign a false death but suspended upon the tree of his passion that true death into which the serpent cast man by its evil counsel.

These people do not wish to see that true death. Therefore they are not healed from the serpent’s poison, just as in the wilderness all who looked upon it were healed (Num. XXI, 9).

CHAPTER VIII

Accordingly, the unlearned say that being fastened to a tree is one thing and hanging upon a tree another. Certain people think that this is how the question should be resolved: by saying that Judas was cursed by Moses because he hanged himself with a noose—as though they first knew whether he hanged himself from a tree or from a stone.

But what Faustus also recalled is true: the Apostle does not allow us to understand anything other than that this was foretold about Christ.

Yet the ignorance of certain Catholics of this kind is a hunting ground for the Manichaeans. Such people they customarily attack; such people they entangle in their deceptions. We had fallen among such people and remained caught among them; from such people we were rescued, not by our own strength but by God’s mercy.

CHAPTER IX

What divine things did Moses attack, as Faustus accuses him, saying that he never spared any human or divine things?

He said it and moved on. He made no effort to prove anything and took no care to demonstrate anything.

But we know that Moses truly and devoutly praised all divine things, and that, in accordance with the circumstances of his time and the grace of his dispensation, he rightly governed human affairs.

Let these men demand that I teach this when they too have tried to prove what Faustus alleges—a claim made cautiously, as he was clever, but incautiously because by his cleverness he was destroying himself.

A heart clever for the truth is fortunate; against the truth, unfortunate.

He did not say that Moses had spared none of human beings and gods, but “human and divine things,” he says.

If he had said that Moses had not spared God, he would easily be convicted of false accusation, since Moses would everywhere be found honoring and proclaiming the true God who made heaven and earth.

But if he said that Moses had spared none of the gods, he would expose himself as worshiping, for Christians, those gods from whose worship Moses forbids them. Thus, while the chicks flee beneath the wings of the Catholic mother, he would not gather what he had not hatched.

Therefore, in order to set a trap for the little ones, he said that Moses had spared none of the divine things, so that Christians could not flee from the impiety of these men—an impiety utterly alien to Christian religion—by openly worshiping the gods, and so that pagans might favor them against us, knowing that Moses had spoken many true and worthy things against idols and against the gods of the Gentiles, which are demons.

CHAPTER X

If this displeases these men, let them openly admit that they are worshipers of idols or demons—though they would be such worshipers unknowingly, simply because they are heretics.

The Apostle spoke of such people:

“In the latter times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons through the hypocrisy of liars” (I Tim. IV, 1–2).

For who but demons, to whom deceit is congenial, would persuade these men that Christ suffered deceitfully, died deceitfully, and deceitfully displayed his scars; that is, that he did not truly suffer, did not truly die, and that those scars did not truly come from real wounds?

What doctrines of lying demons are more evident than these, by which people are persuaded that the Son of God—that is, truth itself—is a liar?

Yet these men also have in their doctrine an open worship—not indeed of demons, but nevertheless of a creature—which the Apostle condemns, saying: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. I, 25).

CHAPTER XI

Accordingly, without knowing it, these men worship idols and demons in the phantoms of their stories. But in the sun and moon they know that they serve a creature; and because they think that they also serve the Creator, they are greatly deceived.

For they serve their own phantom, but they do not serve the Creator at all when they deny that God created those things which the Apostle clearly demonstrates belong to God’s creation.

Speaking about food and meats, he says: “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (I Tim. IV, 4).

See what sound doctrine is, which you could not endure and therefore turned to fables.

Just as the Apostle praises God’s creature and nevertheless forbids religious worship to be offered to it, so too Moses—who, as you think, spared none of the divine beings, and whom I suspect you accuse for no other reason than that he forbade the sun and moon to be worshiped (Deut. XVII, 3), toward whose circuit you turn in every direction so that you may worship them—praised the sun and moon with true praise.

He narrated, as is true, that they were made by God and placed in the heavenly order to perform their appointed works:

“The sun for the authority of the day, the moon for the authority of the night” (Gen. I, 16; Ps. CXXXV, 8–9).

The sun and moon do not rejoice in your false praises. The devil, the rebellious creature, knows how to rejoice in false praise.

But the powers of heaven, which have not fallen through sin, wish their craftsman to be praised in them. Their true praise is that by which no injury is done to their Creator.

Injury is done when it is said that they are his parts, or his members, or something of his substance. For he is perfect, lacking nothing, nowhere flowing away, neither divided nor extended through space, wholly immutable in himself, sufficient to himself, blessed in himself.

Because of the abundance of his goodness, he spoke through his Word, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. CXLVIII, 5).

Therefore, if earthly bodies are good—those about which the Apostle was speaking when he declared that no food is unclean—because “every creature of God is good,” how much more are heavenly bodies good, among which the sun and moon excel?

For the Apostle himself says: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and that of the earthly another” (I Cor. XV, 40).

CHAPTER XII

Moses therefore does not insult the sun and moon when he forbids them to be worshiped; rather, he praises them as heavenly creatures.

But he praises God as the Creator of heavenly and earthly things, and he does not wish God to be offended when those are worshiped in place of him who are praised because of him and from him.

But how cleverly Faustus seemed to reproach Moses for calling accursed even the man who had worshiped the sun and the moon. “If, then,” he says, “while living under a pagan king, I am compelled to worship the sun, and when I resist I am ordered to be crucified, fearing this curse, I shall fall under another curse which he pronounced against the one who hangs on a tree.”

No pagan king compels you to worship the sun—and the sun itself would not compel you to do so if it ruled on earth, since even now it does not wish this to be done by you. But just as the Creator himself endures his impious blasphemers until the judgment, so too the heavenly bodies themselves tolerate their vain worshipers until the judgment of their Creator [Note: [Col. 0301] *II Retractationes*, chapter 7, no. 3.]. Nevertheless, remember that a Christian king cannot compel anyone to worship the sun. Faustus proposed an example involving a pagan king, knowing perfectly well that what you do belongs to the pagans, since you worship the sun.

This, then, is not Christian. But everywhere the partridge now places the name of Christ, “to gather what she did not hatch” (Jer. XVII, 11). See, nevertheless, how easily truth answers, and how readily sound doctrine tears apart this snare of your question, which seems inescapable and two-headed.

Suppose, then, that some man armed with royal power threatened a Christian, saying that if he refused to worship the sun he would be hanged on a tree. “If I turn aside,” you say, “I shall fall under the curse which the Law pronounced upon the worshiper of the sun, and under the curse which that same Law pronounced upon the one who hangs on a tree.”

You will indeed be thrown into confusion—but you, or rather not even you, since you worship the sun without anyone compelling you. A Christian, however, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets (Eph. II, 20), considers each cause and each curse separately. He sees that one pertains to the mortal body, which is hung on a tree, and the other to the soul, by which the sun is worshiped. For even if the body is bent down in worship, the soul either worships what it adores or pretends to do so; and either course is destructive.

Therefore, since death has been deserved under both curses, just as the death of the body consists in hanging on a tree, so the death of the soul consists in worshiping the sun. The curse involved in bodily death must therefore be chosen—a curse by which the body itself will be freed in the resurrection. But the curse involved in the death of the soul must be avoided, lest the soul be condemned with its body in everlasting fire.

For the Lord resolved this question for us when he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who has power to destroy both soul and body in the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28). It is as though he were saying: “Do not fear the curse of bodily death, which is dissolved in time; but fear the curse of spiritual death, through which the soul is tormented eternally with its body.”

Behold, this is not an old woman’s curse but a prophetic prediction: “Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Thus Christ takes a curse away through a curse, just as he takes death away through death and sin away through sin.

Moses therefore did not blaspheme when he said, “Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Nor did the Apostles blaspheme when they said, “He died” (II Cor. V, 14–15), and “Our old man was crucified with him” (Rom. VI, 6), and “Concerning sin, he condemned sin” (ibid. VIII, 3), and “Him who knew no sin he made sin for us” (II Cor. V, 21), together with many similar statements?

But when you shudder at Christ as accursed, you admit that you shudder at Christ’s death. Here your curse appears—not an old woman’s curse but a diabolical pretense: through the death of your own souls, you do not believe in the death of Christ’s body. Yet you persuade people that Christ’s death was not real but simulated, as though you did not dare to deceive people under the name of Christianity unless you made Christ himself the master of deception.

## CHAPTER XIII

As for the fact that Moses seemed to Faustus envious of continence or virginity because he said, “Accursed is everyone who will not raise up offspring in Israel” (Deut. XXV, 7), let them read Isaiah crying out:

“Thus says the Lord to all the eunuchs who observe my commandments, choose what I desire, and keep my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a named place, better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name, and it shall not fail them” (Isa. LVI, 4–5).

Or, if they think Isaiah contradicts Moses, let them accept this passage if they reject the other; it is no small argument against them. For us it is enough to know that one God spoke both through Moses and through Isaiah, and that “accursed is everyone who will not raise up offspring in Israel”—whether at that time, when the people were to be propagated according to the flesh and the activity of bodily procreation in conjugal chastity belonged to civic duty [Note: [Col. 0302] The Lov. edition reads *ad officium conjugum* (“to the duty of spouses”). But the manuscripts, together with Am. and Er., read *ad officium civicum* (“to civic duty”), or *ad officium civium* (“to the duty of citizens”).]; or now, lest anyone born spiritually suppose that this alone ought to suffice for him and fail to strive for the Lord’s gains, by which each person, preaching Christ according to his capacity, ought to generate Christians.

Thus that divine pronouncement embraces the times of both Testaments with marvelous brevity: “Accursed is everyone who will not raise up offspring in Israel.”

# BOOK FIFTEEN

[Col. 0301]

## CHAPTER I

**FAUSTUS said:** Why do you not accept the Old Testament? Because no vessel, once full, receives what is poured over it, but spills it; and a satisfied stomach rejects what is put into it. Accordingly, the Jews, already filled in advance with the Old Testament of Moses, rejected the New; and we, filled beforehand with the New through Christ, reject the Old.

You accept both because you are full in neither but only half-full; and one is not so much filled from the other as corrupted by it. For half-filled vessels are never filled with a dissimilar material, but only with one of the same kind and like to it—wine with wine, honey with honey, and vinegar with vinegar. If you pour in dissimilar substances that are not of the same kind—gall into honey, water into wine, and garum into vinegar—this will not be called filling but adulteration.

This, then, is why we accept little of the Old Testament. Moreover, since our Church, the bride of Christ, though poorer, has been married to one who is rich and is content with the goods of her husband, she disdains the wealth of low-born lovers. The gifts of the Old Testament and of its author are contemptible to her, and, most diligent guardian of her reputation, she accepts no letters except those of her bridegroom.

Let your Church make use of the Old Testament, since, like a wanton virgin forgetful of modesty, she delights both in the gifts and the letters of another husband. That lover of yours, then, and corrupter of your modesty, the God of the Hebrews, promises you by his stone diptych gold and silver, fullness of belly (Deut. VIII, 7–9), and the land of the Canaanites (Exod. XXIII, 23).

Such sordid profits have delighted you that you are willing to sin after Christ, so as to prove ungrateful for his immense dowry. These things entice you, so that after Christ’s marriage you pine for the God of the Hebrews. Learn, then, even now that you are being deceived and misled by his false promises. He is poor and needy, and cannot even provide what he promises. For if he provides none of these things to his own wife—I mean the Synagogue—which in every respect obeys him and serves him more submissively than a slave, what can he provide for you, who are alien to him and reject the yoke of his commandments with proud necks?

But go on as you have begun: join a new patch to an old garment; entrust new wine to old wineskins (Matt. IX, 16–17); serve two husbands, pleasing neither; and finally make the Christian faith into a Hippocentaur, neither a complete horse nor a human being. Allow us to serve Christ alone, content only with his immortal dowry and imitating the Apostle who says, “Our sufficiency is from God, who made us competent ministers of a new covenant” (II Cor. III, 5–6).

The condition of the God of the Hebrews and ours is entirely different: he cannot fulfill what he promises, and we disdain to accept it. Christ’s generosity has made us proud in the face of his blandishments.

And lest you think I have made this comparison improperly, Paul was the first to apply this image of conjugal discipline to us when he said: “A woman who is under a husband, while her husband is alive, is bound by the law of her husband; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man; but if her husband dies, she is not an adulteress if she is joined to another man” (Rom. VII, 2–3).

By this he showed that those commit spiritual adultery who do not first repudiate the author of the Law and, in a certain sense, regard him as dead, and only then join themselves to Christ. This statement applies especially to those who have believed from among the Jews, so that they themselves may forget their former superstition.

But what need have we of this commandment, since we have turned from paganism to Christ? The God of the Hebrews ought not to seem dead to us, but not even born. Certainly, to a Jew, if he believes, Adonai ought to seem dead; to a Gentile, an idol; and to each person, whatever he worshiped before coming to know Christ. For if, after divorcing himself from idolatry, a Jew worships both the God of the Hebrews and Christ, he differs in no way from a woman of worn-out modesty who, after the death of one husband, has married two.

## CHAPTER II

**AUGUSTINE replied:** Hear these words, you whose hearts Christ possesses, and see whether you can endure them—unless he himself is your endurance. Faustus, full of new honey, rejects old vinegar; and Paul, full of old vinegar, poured out half of it so that he might receive the new honey that was poured in—not to preserve it but to corrupt it.

You see that what the Apostle Paul says—“Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God”—comes from the new honey. But what follows—“which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 1–3)—comes from the old vinegar.

Who could endure hearing this, unless the same Apostle consoled us by saying, “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19)?

But why repeat what has already been said sufficiently above (Book 8)? Let whoever can remember, or whoever wishes consult the passage again, that the new patch and the old garment, and the new wine and the old wineskins, signify not the two Testaments but two lives and two hopes. For understanding the two Testaments, the Lord gave this comparison: “Therefore every scribe who has been instructed in the kingdom of God is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. XIII, 52).

If anyone thinks that two hopes are to be held, so that he may serve God both for earthly happiness and for the kingdom of heaven, the one hope cannot contain the other; and when the former is disturbed by some tribulation, the failing person will lose the latter as well. Hence also the saying, “No one can serve two masters,” which he explained by adding, “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (ibid. VI, 24).

To those who understand it rightly, the Old Testament is a prophecy of the New Testament. Thus, even among that first people, the holy Patriarchs and Prophets who understood what they were doing, or what was being done through them, possessed in the New Testament this hope of eternal salvation. For they belonged to what they understood and loved; although it had not yet been revealed, it was already being represented in figures.

Those belonged to the Old Testament who desired nothing more than the temporal promises contained there, and did not understand that eternal realities had been represented and prophesied in them. But these matters have already been stated sufficiently and more than sufficiently in our earlier replies.

## CHAPTER III

There is, however, astonishing shamelessness in the fact that the sacrilegious and filthy society of the Manichaeans does not hesitate to boast that it too is the chaste bride of Christ. What does this accomplish against the truly chaste members of the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0304] The Lov. edition alone reads “the chaste members of the truly catholic Church.”] except to bring to mind that apostolic admonition against such people: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2–3)?

For what are these people doing when they evangelize us with something beyond what we received, except corrupting the chastity which we preserve for Christ? They blame God’s Law under the name of antiquity and praise their own error under the name of novelty, as though every old thing were to be avoided or every new thing desired. Yet the Apostle John commends an old commandment (I John II, 7), while the Apostle Paul commands that profane novelties of words be avoided (I Tim. VI, 20).

Therefore I too shall address you, the true bride of the true Christ, the Catholic Church, and, as best I can, as whatever sort of son and servant of yours, placed within you to distribute food to my fellow servants. Always beware, as you do beware, of the impious folly of the Manichaeans, which you have already tested at the peril of your own people and refuted by your deliverance.

That error once shook me from your bosom. Having tested it, I fled what I ought not to have tested. But let my dangers also benefit you, since my deliverance now serves you. For unless your true and truthful bridegroom, from whose side you were made, had placed the forgiveness of sins in his true blood, the abyss of deception would have swallowed me, and the serpent that had become earth would have devoured me beyond recovery.

Do not be deceived by the name of truth. You alone possess it—in your milk and in your bread. But in that other communion there is only its name; truth itself is not there. Among your mature members you are secure; but I appeal to your little ones—my brothers, sons, and masters—whom you cherish either like eggs beneath anxious wings or nourish like infants with milk, a fruitful virgin mother.

I appeal to these tender offspring of yours within you, lest they be led astray from you by babbling curiosity. Rather, let them anathematize anyone who preaches to them a gospel beyond what they received in you (Gal. I, 9). Let them not abandon the true and truthful Christ, in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. II, 3), and the great abundance of whose sweetness he has hidden for those who fear him but perfected for those who hope in him (Ps. XXX, 20).

How, then, can the words of the truthful one be present in a preacher of Christ who is himself false? Despise their insults, for you know well that you have loved the promise of eternal life in the gifts of your bridegroom—that is, your bridegroom himself, since he is eternal life.

## CHAPTER IV

You have not, as they foolishly suppose, been led astray to another god who promises fullness of belly and the land of the Canaanites. For you understand that even within those promises you were already represented and prophesied, and that they gave birth to the foreknowledge of the saints.

Nor should you be disturbed by the miserable mockery directed against the stone diptych, since you do not have the stone heart signified by those tablets among the former people. You are a letter of the Apostles, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the fleshly heart (II Cor. III, 2–3).

Those foolish people rejoice in these words, thinking that the Apostle criticized the dispensation of the Old Testament suited to that time, and not understanding that he spoke this from the Prophet. For these words, which they incompetently embrace, were foretold long before they were spoken and fulfilled through the Apostles by the Prophets whom they reject.

The Prophet had said: “I will take away from them their heart of stone, and I will give them a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XI, 19). Let them see whether this is not the meaning of “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of hearts of flesh.” For neither there, where “heart of flesh” is said, nor here, where “fleshly tablets” are mentioned, is the intention that we should think in a fleshly manner [Note: [Col. 0305] The Lov. edition reads *sapiamus ista* (“that we should think these things”). *Ista* is absent from the other books.]. Rather, because flesh has sensation in comparison with stone, which lacks sensation, the insensitivity of stone signifies a heart that does not understand, while the sensitivity of flesh signifies a heart that understands.

You should instead laugh at those who say that earth, wood, and stones possess sensation and live with a more intelligent life, while flesh is more foolish and dull. Hence they are compelled, not by the truth but by their own folly, to admit that the Law written on stone tablets is cleaner than their treasure in the skins of corpses.

Or perhaps, because in their fable they also say that stones are the bones of the rulers, they do not hesitate to place lambskins above them? In any event, the ark of that Testament covered the stone tablets more cleanly than a goatskin covers the book of these people.

Laugh at this mercifully, so that you may commend to them what they ought to laugh at and flee. For in that stone diptych you, who no longer have a stone heart, understand what suited that hard-hearted people; and yet in it you recognize the rock, your own bridegroom—the one whom Peter calls “a living stone rejected by human beings but chosen and honored by God.”

“For them,” therefore, “he was a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; but for you, the stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” [Note: [Col. 0306] The manuscripts read “at the head of the corner” (*in capite anguli*).] (I Pet. II, 4–8). The Apostle Peter explains all this, and recalls that the whole matter was foretold by the Prophets, from whom these condemned people alienate themselves.

Read that diptych as well; do not fear it. It plainly belongs to your bridegroom. To others that stone signified harsh stupidity; to you it signifies firm stability.

Those tablets were written by the finger of God (Exod. XXXI, 18). By the finger of God your bridegroom cast out demons (Luke XI, 20). By the finger of God, cast out the doctrines of demons who speak lies and cauterize the conscience [Note: [Col. 0306] Lov. reads *cauteriatam habentium* (“having a cauterized conscience”). But the other printed editions and the manuscripts have *cauteriantium* here.] (I Tim. IV, 2).

By means of this diptych you drive away the adulterer who calls himself the Paraclete, so that he may seduce you by the holy name. For those tablets were given on the fiftieth day after Passover (Exod. XX); and on the fiftieth day after the passion of your bridegroom, which that Passover prefigured, the finger of God—the Holy Spirit, the promised Paraclete—was given (Acts II, 1–4).

Do not, then, fear the diptych through which things once written for you, things that you would now recognize, were sent to you. Only do not live under the Law, lest you fail to fulfill it through fear; live instead under grace, so that the fullness of the Law—love—may be in you.

For the friend of your bridegroom was reviewing no other diptych when he said: “You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love does no evil to the neighbor. Therefore love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. XIII, 9–10).

There are the two commandments, love of God and love of neighbor, set out on the separate tablets. This, then, is the diptych that was set forth by the one who came and commended these two commandments to you, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. XXII, 37–40).

In the first commandment is the chastity of your marriage; in the second, the unity of your members. By the first you embrace divinity; by the second you gather society. These two commandments are themselves ten: three pertain to God and seven to the neighbor.

O chaste diptych, in which, under the old figure, your lover and beloved foretold to you a new song on the ten-stringed psaltery (Ps. XCI, 4), as though he would also stretch out his own sinews for you on the tree, so that “by sin he might condemn sin in the flesh, and the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in you” (Rom. VIII, 3–4). O nuptial diptych, which the adulteress hates for no small reason!

## CHAPTER V

Now my speech is addressed to you, deceitful Manichaean assembly, wrapped in deceits. Do you, married to so many elements—or rather, a prostitute whoring with demons and impregnated with sacrilegious vanities—dare to tear apart your Lord’s Catholic marriage by the charge of unchastity?

Show us your adulterers: your *splenditenentem* (“splendor-holder”), the weigher [Note: [Col. 0307] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read *splendide tenentem* (“holding splendidly”).], and your burden-bearing Atlas. You say that the former holds the elements’ heads and suspends the world; the latter, with bent knee and powerful shoulders, supports such a massive weight beneath him—plainly so that the former does not fail.

Where are these figures? If they really existed, when would they come to you, occupied as they are with so great a task? When would they enter into you, so that with your gentle, idle, and entirely delicate hand you could rub the fingers of the one and the shoulders of the other after so much labor? [Note: [Col. 0307] Good-quality manuscripts read this way. Others, together with the printed editions, read “and with idle bread, delicate.”]

But evil demons deceive you. They prostitute themselves with you, so that you conceive lies and give birth to phantoms.

Why, then, do you not reject the diptych of the true God, which is hostile to your parchment, when in your wandering mind you have fallen passionately in love with so many false gods through the fabrications of your thoughts? All the lies of the poets would be found more weighty and honorable than these—or at least this difference: among the poets no one is deceived, because they openly profess falsehood; but in your books such a crowd of deceits, under the name of truth, corrupts childish souls and the souls of old men [Note: [Col. 0307] Lov. reads “childish and aged souls.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts more suitably read “childish souls and the souls of old men.”] with pitiable errors, when, as the Apostle says, “having itching ears and turning away their hearing from the truth, they turn to myths” (II Tim. IV, 4).

How, then, could you endure the sound doctrine of those tablets, whose first commandment is, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. VI, 4), when you roll about in the fornication of your most shameful heart, delighted by the names of so many gods? Do you not remember your love song, in which you describe the greatest reigning king, an everlasting scepter-bearer, surrounded by flowered crowns and radiant in face?

If you loved only such a figure, you ought to be ashamed. Even one man surrounded by flowered crowns would displease a modest wife. Nor can you say that this was spoken or represented with some mystical meaning, since you especially praise Manichaeus for no other reason than that, removing the coverings of figures, he himself speaks to you the naked and proper truth.

You therefore sing, in the proper sense, of a scepter-bearing god crowned with flowers. Let him at least set aside his scepter when he is encircled with flowered crowns; such softness of luxury is unfitting for the severity of a royal rod.

Furthermore, he is not loved by you alone. For you continue your song and add twelve ages, clothed in flowers, full of songs, and casting their flowers into the face of their father. There you also profess twelve great gods, three through each of four regions, by which that one god is surrounded.

Since you say that he is enclosed in this way, you have never been able to discover how you make him infinite. You also add innumerable kings of kingdoms, hosts of gods, and cohorts of angels, all of which, you say, God did not create but generated from his own substance.

## CHAPTER VI

You are thus convicted of worshiping innumerable gods, because you do not accept the sound doctrine which teaches that the Son was born one from the one God, and the Holy Spirit from both. Yet it is not lawful to call them not only innumerable gods but even three gods, since they possess not only one and the same substance but also one and the same operation, through that one and identical proper substance; while through bodily creation there is also a manifestation of the individual persons.

You do not understand or grasp this. I know you: you are full, intoxicated, and stuffed with fabulous sacrilege. At some point digest what you exhale, and cease overwhelming yourself with such things. Meanwhile, sing what you sing, and look, if you can, upon the disgrace of your fornication.

The doctrine of lying demons invited you to imaginary houses of angels, where a health-giving breeze blows, and to fields [Note: [Col. 0308] Perhaps “to the field.”] where spices spring up, whose trees and mountains, seas and rivers pour sweet nectar throughout all the ages. You believed these things and fashioned them in your heart, where you toss about luxuriantly and dissolutely amid empty recollections.

When such things are said about the ineffable abundance of spiritual delights, they are of course said in an enigma. Thus the mind that is exercised by such things knows that something else is to be sought and understood there. Either something of this kind is demonstrated in truth through bodily senses and bodily reality, as with the fire in the bush (Exod. III, 2), the serpent from the staff and the staff from the serpent (ibid. IV, 2–4), the Lord’s tunic not divided by his persecutors (John XIX, 24), the woman’s service in anointing his feet or head (Matt. XXVI, 7; John XII, 3), and the branches of the crowd going before and following his donkey (Matt. XXI, 7–9);

or such things are shown figuratively in the spirit through images of bodies, in a dream, or in ecstasy, as with Jacob’s ladder (Gen. XXVIII, 12), the stone cut without hands and growing into a mountain shown to Daniel (Dan. II, 34–35), that sheet shown to Peter (Acts X, 11), and the many things shown to John (Rev. I and following);

or they are represented by speech alone in the same manner, as in the Song of Songs (Song I and following), in the householder’s wedding feast for his son in the Gospel (Matt. XXII, 2–14), in the story of a man who had two sons, one frugal and one profligate (Luke XV, 11–32), and in the story of a man who planted a vineyard and leased it to farmers (Matt. XXI, 33).

But you especially praise Manichaeus on the grounds that he came last not to speak such things but rather to explain them: that, with the figures of the ancients made clear and his own narratives and arguments brought forth in evident light, he would conceal himself in no enigma.

You add this reason for such presumption: the ancients, you say, knew that he would later come, through whom everything would be revealed, and therefore, whether they saw, enacted, or spoke such figures, they expressed them; but he, knowing that no one would come after him, did not weave his pronouncements into any allegorical obscurities.

What, then, is your inclination, soiled by carnal desires, doing amid fields and wooded mountains, flowered crowns, and spices springing up? If these are not enigmas of reason, they are phantoms of thought or madness of frenzy. But if they are said to be enigmas, why do you not flee from the adulterer who promises open truth in order to entice you, and then mocks those whom he has enticed with fabulous deception?

Do not his ministers—and those wretched people themselves, poisoned by such vanities—usually place this bait from the Apostle Paul upon their hook, where he says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is in part will be done away;” and, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 9–10, 12)?

The implication, of course, is that the Apostle Paul knew in part and prophesied in part, seeing through a mirror and in an enigma; all this would be taken away when Manichaeus came and brought what is perfect, so that truth might be seen face to face [Note: [Col. 0309] The word “truth” is absent from several manuscripts.].

O wanton and unclean woman, shamelessly you still chatter such things! You still feed on winds; you still embrace the idols of your heart! Have you really seen face to face the reigning scepter-bearing king, surrounded by flowered crowns; the hosts of gods; and the great *splenditenentem* bearing six faces and mouths and flashing with light [Note: [Col. 0309] Er. and Lov. read *splendentem Agnum* (“the shining Lamb”). Am., together with several manuscripts, reads *splendide tenentem magnum* (“holding the great one splendidly”). Certain other good-quality manuscripts read *splenditenentem magnum* (“the great *splenditenentem*”).]?

And another king of honor surrounded by armies of angels; another adamantine warrior-hero holding a spear in his right hand and a shield in his left; another glorious king driving three wheels—of fire, water, and wind; and the great Aulantes carrying the world on his shoulders and supporting it with both arms, one on either side, while kneeling [Note: [Col. 0309] Some codices read “with both [arms]” (*utrisque*).]?

Did you see these and a thousand other monstrosities face to face? Or does the doctrine of lying demons sing these things to you through the mouths of deceivers, while you remain unaware?

Woe to you, unhappy woman! Behold the phantasms with which you are defiled; behold the vanities which you lick in place of truth. Drunk from serpentine cups, you dare insult the matronly modesty of the wife of the only Son of God on account of the stone diptych, because she no longer lives under the pedagogy of the Law [Note: [Col. 0309] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead read “under the pedagogue of the Law.”], but under the instruction of grace.

She lives by faith, hope, and love, neither proud because of works nor broken by terrors. She has become Israel, “in whom there is no deceit” (John I, 45), and hears what is written there: “The Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. VI, 4). You, however, refusing to hear this, have spread your fornication among so many fabricated gods.

## CHAPTER VII
How, then, can those Tablets not be hostile to you, in which the second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. 20:7), when you have even placed Christ himself—who, in order to cleanse the carnal from carnal vanity, appeared also to carnal eyes, truly in the reality of flesh—in the vanity of falsehood? How can the third commandment, concerning rest on the Sabbath, not be opposed to you, when your restless soul is tossed about by so many illusory fantasies? When will you understand, when will you grasp, when will you love, that these three commandments pertain to the love of God?

You are immoderate, foul, and contentious: you have swollen with pride, become empty, become worthless, and gone beyond your proper measure; you have defiled your beauty and disturbed your order. Such was I among you; I know you. How, then, am I now to teach you that these three commandments pertain to the love of God, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist (Rom. 11:30)? How can you understand this, when your detestable perversity of error does not even allow you to know and observe those seven commandments that pertain to love of neighbor, by which human society is held together?

Among these the first commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother”—a commandment that Paul also recalls as the first commandment with a promise, himself likewise enjoining the same thing (Exod. 20:12; Eph. 6:2). But you have learned from demonic teaching [Note: [Col. 0310] The manuscripts have *daemonica* (“demonic”).] to regard your parents as enemies, because through sexual intercourse they have bound you in the flesh and have thereby, as you suppose, imposed unclean fetters upon your god.

From this follows the commandment: “You shall not commit adultery.” You violate it in such a way that you chiefly detest in marriage the procreation of children; and thus, while your Hearers take care that the women with whom they have intercourse do not conceive, you make them adulterers of their own wives. For they take these women in accordance with the law of marriage, the marriage contracts publicly declaring that the purpose is the procreation of children. But under your law, fearing that they may defile a particle of their god with the filth of flesh, they unite with women in an indecent coupling merely to satisfy lust; they receive children unwillingly, although the sole reason for joining in marriage is the procreation of children.

How, then, do you not forbid marriage, which the Apostle predicted so long beforehand concerning you (1 Tim. 4:3), when you attempt to remove from marriage the very thing from which marriage derives its nature? Once this has been removed, husbands will be disgraceful lovers, prostitutes will be wives, bridal chambers will be brothels, and fathers-in-law will be pimps.

Accordingly, by the perversity of the same error you also fail to observe the commandment: “You shall not kill.” While you fear that a member of your god might be bound in flesh, you do not give bread to the hungry: here you fear a false homicide, while there you commit a real one [Note: [Col. 0310] B has *perpetrans verum* (“committing the real one”). We have followed Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice; M.].

Thus, if you encounter a hungry person who may die unless you help him by supplying food, you will already be held a murderer either by the law of God, if you do not give it, or by the law of Mani, if you do. What of the remaining commandments of the Decalogue? How will you observe them?

Will you refrain from theft, so that some person may devour bread—or any other food—to be slaughtered in his entrails, rather than your stealing it from him, if you can, and running with it to the workshop of the bellies of your Elect, so that by your theft your god may neither fall into a more grievous bondage nor be released from the bondage into which he had fallen? Moreover, if you are caught in that very theft, will you not swear by your god himself that you did not take it?

For what can such a god do to you when you say to him: “I swore falsely by you, but for you; unless you wished me to bring destruction upon you while rendering you honor”?” In the same way you will also disregard the commandment of the Law, “You shall not bear false witness,” for the sake of the members of your god, freeing them from their fetters not only by testimony but also by a false oath [Note: [Col. 0311] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice have *contemnis* (“you disregard”). M.].

As for the commandment that follows, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. 20:13, 16, 17), it ought to be fulfilled by you; and this is the one thing I see that you are not compelled to violate by any necessity of your error. But if it is wicked to covet another man’s wife, consider what it means to offer oneself to be coveted by others. Recall your handsome gods and beautiful goddesses, presenting themselves so as to be ardently desired: the male gods by the female rulers of darkness, and the female goddesses by the males. When these beings have been aroused to the lust of enjoyment and burn greedily for one another’s embraces, they extract from them that god of yours, everywhere bound in fetters and in need of so much of his own shame in order that he may be released.

As for not coveting your neighbor’s property, which is the final commandment of the Decalogue, how can you fulfill it, wretched woman? Does not your own god falsely claim that, in a foreign land, he is fashioning new ages for himself, in which you will swell with pride in a false triumph after a false victory? When you desire this now with insane vanity and believe that the land of the nation of darkness will be joined, by the greatest proximity, to the substance of your own nature, you are surely coveting your neighbor’s property.

Small wonder that the diptych is hostile to you, since it contains such good commandments, so greatly opposed to your error. Those three commandments that pertain to the love of God you utterly ignore and utterly fail to observe. As for the seven commandments by which human society is not harmed, whenever you do observe them, either shame restrains you lest you be disgraced among human beings; or fear breaks you lest you be punished by public laws; or you shrink from an evil deed because of some good custom; or you take heed of the natural law itself, according to which you should not do to another what you do not wish another to do to you. Yet you perceive how your error compels you to go in the opposite direction, both when you follow it and when you do not follow it: either when you do what you do not wish to suffer, or when you refrain from doing something only because you do not wish to suffer it.

## CHAPTER VIII

But this true bride of Christ, whom you attack with the most shameless forehead from the stone diptych, understands the distinction between letter and spirit (2 Cor. 3:6)—the two things that are otherwise called Law and grace. Serving God not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit (Rom. 7:6), she is no longer under the law but under grace.

She is not blinded by contentiousness; rather, in gentleness she attends to the Apostle’s words, so that she may understand what he calls “the law” under which he no longer wishes us to be, because it was imposed on account of transgression until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made (Gal. 3:19), and because it entered in order that the trespass might increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Rom. 5:20).

Yet he does not therefore call the law itself sin, because without grace it does not give life. Rather, it increases guilt by adding transgression: “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). Thus, in itself, when it is only the letter without the spirit—that is, law without grace—it merely makes people guilty. But he sets before himself what those of lesser understanding might suppose and explains what he means when he says:

“What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Did, then, what is good become death to me? By no means! Rather, sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (Rom. 7:7–13).

The one whom you attack understands these things, because she asks with groaning, seeks in humility, and knocks in gentleness. Thus she sees that the law is not condemned when it is said, “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6), just as knowledge is not condemned when it is said, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” For he himself had said, “We know that we all possess knowledge”; and then he adds, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

Why, then, did he have something by which he might be puffed up, unless it is because, when accompanied by love, knowledge not only does not puff up but also strengthens? In the same way, when the letter is joined to the spirit and the law to grace, the letter and the law are no longer called by that name in the same sense as when, standing by themselves, they kill by increasing sin.

Thus the law is also called “the power of sin” (1 Cor. 15:56), because through severe prohibition it increases the harmful pleasure of sin. Yet even in this respect it is not evil; rather, “sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death through what is good.” In this way many things are harmful to certain people although they are not evil. When your eyes hurt, you too close the windows even against the sun, your god.

This bride of Christ, then, having died to the law—that is, to sin, which becomes more abundant through the prohibition of the law when the law commands without helping—has died to such a law in order to belong to another, who rose from the dead. She distinguishes these matters without injuring the law, lest she commit sacrilege against its author. You, however, commit sacrilege against the one whom you do not understand to be the author of good, although you hear the Apostle saying: “Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.”

Behold: the author of good is the one who, in your view, is one of the rulers of darkness. Attend to the truth—it strikes your eyes. Behold, the Apostle Paul says: “The law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.” Behold whose author he is, the one who introduced that diptych, which you foolishly ridicule, as part of the administration of a great sacrament [Note: [Col. 0312] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have *dispensatione* (“by the administration”) rather than *dispensationem* (“as the administration”).].

For the same law that was given through Moses was made grace and truth through Jesus Christ (John 1:17), when the spirit was added to the letter, so that the righteousness of the law might begin to be fulfilled—the law which, when unfulfilled, made people guilty even through transgression. There is not one holy, just, and good law, and another through which sin works death, to which we must die in order to belong to the one who rose from the dead: it is the very same law.

Look, follow, read. “But sin,” he says, “so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment.” Deaf woman, blind woman, hear and see! “Through what is good,” he says, “it worked death in me.” Therefore the law is always good: whether it harms those who lack grace or benefits those who are filled with grace, it is always good.

So too the sun is always good, because every creature of God is good (1 Tim. 4:4), whether it harms diseased eyes or delights healthy ones. Accordingly, what health in the eyes is for seeing the sun, grace is for minds in fulfilling the law.
