And just as healthy eyes do not die from the sun’s delight but from the harsh blows of its rays, when, struck by them, they are driven into denser darkness, so the soul, made safe through the love of the spirit, is said not to have died to the righteousness of the law but to the guilt and transgression that the law produced through the letter when grace was absent.

Thus both statements are made concerning the law: “The law is good, if one uses it lawfully”; and what follows: “Knowing this, that the law is not laid down for the just” (1 Tim. 1:8–9), because the person who delights in righteousness has no need of a terrifying letter.

## CHAPTER IX

This bride of Christ, rejoicing in the hope of her full salvation, wishes you also a good conversion from fables to truth, lest, fearing Adoneus as an adulterer, you remain with the most cunning adulterous serpent.

For *Adonai* is a Hebrew word and is interpreted as “Lord,” in the sense in which God alone is called Lord. Likewise *latria* is a Greek word and is interpreted as “service”—not service of every kind, but that by which God alone is served. So too *Amen* is interpreted as “true,” not in just any place or in just any manner, but in a mystical religious sense.

If you are asked where you too obtained these words, you will find them nowhere except among Hebrew writings or things derived from Hebrew. The Church of Christ therefore does not fear the objection based on these names. She understands and loves them; she does not care about an ignorant attacker. And what she does not yet understand, she believes to be of the same kind as certain things she has already experienced, which were of that kind even before she understood them.

Let someone object to her that she loved Emmanuel: she laughs at that person’s ignorance and embraces the truth of the name. Let someone object that she loved the Messiah: she repels the extinguished adversary and holds fast to the anointed teacher.

In the same way she wishes you also to be healed of your vain errors and to be built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Eph. 2:20). You call him a Hippocentaur, not knowing what you are saying and not considering what your own fable has fashioned for you, since in your heart you have fabricated a false world partly from your god and partly from the land of darkness.

Is he not, then, a Hippocentaur—half-beast and half-god? Indeed he is not to be called a Hippocentaur at all. But pay attention to what he is, and blush and grow gentle, so that you may recoil from your corruption by the adulterous serpent. If you did not think that his cunning was to be believed in the case of Moses, you ought at least to have guarded against it in the case of Paul. Wishing to present the true Church as a chaste virgin to Christ, Paul says:

“I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2–3).

Yet when you heard this, you were so utterly foolish, and became so deranged by his poisonous incantations, that the same serpent has persuaded many other heresies of one thing or another, but has persuaded you even that he himself is Christ.

Now, if many have gone astray, ensnared by his varied and manifold deceptions, although they nevertheless acknowledge this warning of the Apostle as true, how adulterated are you, how far have you prostituted yourself, since you regard as Christ himself the one whom the Apostle of Christ declares to be the deceiver and corrupter of Eve, and by this warning seeks to protect Christ’s virgin bride from him?

He has darkened your heart, the one who rolls about with you amid fantasies of shining groves. Where are they? What are they? From where are his faithful promises? O woman drunk—not with wine! (Isa. 51:21).

## CHAPTER X

You have indeed insulted, with sacrilegious shamelessness, the God of the prophets, because he did not provide what he had promised to the Jews who served him. Yet you have not said what he promised and failed to provide, lest you be convicted there either because it has already been provided, though you do not understand it, or because it is still future, though you do not believe it.

What has been promised and presented to you that would make you believe that you will receive triumphs of new ages over the land of darkness? If you produce some prophets in whom we may read that the future Manichaeans were foretold with praise, so that you may think that something has already been presented to you simply because we see that you exist, you must first prove that it was not Mani himself who fabricated the prophets for you, wishing you to believe him.

For he does not think lying a disgrace—or can he hesitate to display false prophets in sheep’s clothing, when, while praising Christ, he asserts that Christ displayed false scars upon his limbs?

But I clearly read that you were foretold, not only by the prophets in more obscure terms at some earlier time, but also more explicitly by the Apostle. “The Spirit,” he says, “clearly says that in the latter times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, forbidding marriage and abstaining from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:1–4).

How these words have been fulfilled in you is so clear that it strikes the eyes of all who know you; and we have already shown this above, as the occasion required [Note: [Col. 0314] The Louvain editors wanted *oculos tangant* (“may strike the eyes”), but this is less correct.].

## CHAPTER XI

This Church, whom apostolic teaching urges to beware of the serpent’s deception—by which you have been corrupted—by presenting her as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ, acknowledges the God of the prophets, the true God, her own God. She confidently believes his final promise, since she already possesses the fulfillment of so many of his promises. No one says that the prophets whom she cites from the books of the Jews were fabricated for the present occasion.

For what more incredible promise could have been made than the one spoken to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18)? And what do we now possess with greater certainty as having been fulfilled?

Certainly this is his final promise, which the prophet briefly recalls in these words: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you forever and ever” (Ps. 83:5). When every need has ended and the final enemy, death, has been destroyed (1 Cor. 15:26), the perpetual praise of God will be the occupation of those who are at rest. No one will then enter from elsewhere, and no one will then depart.

The prophet recalls this elsewhere in the following words: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you” (Ps. 147:1–2). Once the gates are closed, no one will enter and no one will leave. The bridegroom himself also says this in the Gospel: he will not open to the foolish virgins, even when they knock (Matt. 25:12).

This Jerusalem—the holy Church, the bride of Christ—is described more fully and abundantly in the Apocalypse of John. Let the chaste virgin not believe this prophetic promise if she does not already possess what the same prophecy promised would happen to her in the present time:

“Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. For the king has desired your beauty, because he is your Lord; and the daughters of Tyre will worship him with gifts. The rich among the people will entreat your favor. All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, adorned with golden fringes and varied ornaments. Virgins will be brought to the king after her; her companions will be brought to you. They will be led in joy and exultation; they will be brought into the king’s temple. In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth. They will remember your name throughout every generation and generation. Therefore the peoples will confess you forever and for ages of ages” (Ps. 44:11–18).

But you, unhappy woman corrupted by the serpent, when do you even attempt to consider what the inner beauty of the king’s daughter might be? It is the chastity of the mind itself, where you have been violated, so that your eyes might be opened to love and worship the sun and moon. Thus, by the just judgment of God, you were separated from the tree of life, which is eternal and inward wisdom. You called and thought nothing else to be truth and wisdom except this light, which you handled through eyes wrongly opened, magnifying it beyond measure and twisting it in an indecent mind through multifarious images of fables.

These are your utterly detestable fornications. Yet think of them patiently and return to me, says Truth. “Return to me, and you will be cleansed; you will be restored” [Note: [Col. 0316] Only the Louvain edition and Belgian manuscripts omit *reparaberis* (“you will be restored”).]—if you are ashamed before yourself and pour yourself back into me. Hear this; true Truth says it: she did not fight against the nation of darkness through deceptive forms, nor redeem you by deceptive blood.

# BOOK SIXTEEN

[Col. 0315]

## CHAPTER I

**FAUSTUS said:** Why do you not accept Moses, when Christ says: “Moses wrote about me; and if you believed Moses, you would believe me also” (John 5:46)?

For my part, I should like not only Moses to have written about Christ, but also all the prophets of the Jews and of the Gentiles. What harm would this do to our faith—or what benefit would it not rather provide—if from every side we gathered testimonies congruent and consistent with our god?

In that case it would still be open to us, while our hatred and abhorrence of their superstition remained, to select from them only the prophecies concerning Christ. It surely cannot be contrary to me if Moses, although alien to Christ, nevertheless appears to have written something about Christ.

Who would not wish to gather a flower from every thorn, fruit from every plant, and honey from every fly, even though we neither use flies as food, nor grass as nourishment, nor thorns as material for a crown? Who would not wish pearls to grow in every depth, gems in every land, and fruit in every forest? Or, if eating a fish from the sea does no harm while drinking its water does harm, and people know how to take what is useful and reject what is harmful, would it not be permitted to us, after condemning the practice of any religion as useless to us, to accept from it only the prophecies concerning Christ?

Nor would this benefit errors by enabling them to seize us and reduce us to their own slavery. For even the unclean spirits did not benefit from the fact that, when they openly and unreservedly confessed Jesus to be the Son of God (Matt. 8:29), they consequently ceased to be hateful to us.

Therefore, if Moses too wrote something about Christ in accordance with this testimony, I shall accept it—but in such a way that this will in no respect benefit Moses in taking me captive under his own law, which I see as differing in nothing from paganism.

Accordingly, there is absolutely no reason for you to suppose that, if this is proved, I shall not rejoice that every spirit prophesied about Christ.

## CHAPTER II

I shall certainly be grateful to you if, just as you show that Christ testified that Moses wrote about him, you also teach what those writings are. For I have searched through his Scriptures, as I was commanded [Note: [Col. 0316] Louvain has “as it seemed”; Erasmus and the older edition have “as was right.” The manuscripts more correctly have “as I was commanded,” evidently referring to John 5:39: “Search the Scriptures,” and so forth.], and have found no prophecies about Christ there—either because there are none, or because I myself could not understand them.

Thus, placed in great perplexity, reason compelled me to one of two conclusions: either I had to declare this passage false, or Jesus a liar. But to regard God as having lied was incompatible with piety. It therefore seemed more reasonable to attribute falsehood to the writers than lying to the author of truth.

Indeed, I also heard him say that all who came before him were thieves and robbers (John 10:8). By this statement I see Moses struck first of all. Moreover, when the Jews indignantly objected to the same speaker’s declaration of his majesty, in which he called himself the light of the world, saying, “You testify about yourself; your testimony is not true,” I do not see him going on to say, at the point where it would have been most appropriate, that Moses had prophesied about him. Instead, as though he were truly alien to them and had no testimony from any of their ancestors, he replied:

“It is written in your law that the testimony of two persons is true. I am the one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me” (John 8:13, 17–18).

He reminded them of what all had heard spoken from heaven: “This is my beloved Son; believe him” (Matt. 3:17; Luke 9:35).

Nor does it seem likely to me that the Jews could have remained silent when Christ said that Moses had written about him. Being malicious and astute, they would immediately have asked what it was that Moses had written about him. Their complete silence on every side therefore indicates no less clearly that Jesus said no such thing.

## CHAPTER III

Although these points too may seem significant for confirming the suspicion that the passage is false, I am held still more firmly by the fact that, as I said, I searched through the whole of Moses’ writing and found no prophecies about Christ there.

Now, however, having discovered that you are a reader of better understanding, I believe that I shall achieve something, and I confess that I shall be grateful if you do not frustrate the hope of progress and instruction that your confidence in rebuking me promises. Teach me, then, whether there is something that I may have overlooked while reading about God and our Lord in Moses’ writing.

Please do not say, as the ignorant commonly do, that this ought itself to be sufficient for faith, because Christ said that Moses had written about him. I do not want you now to look to me, whom my profession has made bound to believe, so that I cannot fail to believe the one whom I follow. Rather, suppose that we are dealing with a Jew; suppose that we are dealing with a Gentile. When we say to them, “Moses wrote about Christ,” they will ask us for proofs [Note: [Col. 0317] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read *erant* (“they were”). M.]. What shall we offer them? Can we say, “Christ said this,” when they do not yet believe in Christ at all? Clearly, we shall have to show them what Moses wrote.

## CHAPTER IV

What, then, shall we show them [Note: [Col. 0317] B has *ostendimus* (“what have we shown?”). We have followed Erasmus and Lyon–Louvain. M.]? Shall we show them what you customarily bring forward, where your god speaks to Moses and says: “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you” (Deut. 18:15, 18)?

But that this does not at all refer to Christ is known even to a Jew, nor is it advantageous for us to believe it in this way. Christ is not a prophet, nor is he a prophet like Moses. Moses was a human being; Christ is God. Moses was a sinner; Christ is holy. Moses was born from sexual intercourse; Christ, according to you, was born from a virgin, but according to me, not even from a virgin. Moses was killed on a mountain after offending his god (Deut. 34:5); Christ, pleasing to the Father, suffered by his own will (John 10:18).

How, then, will he himself be a prophet like Moses? Surely the Jew will immediately either mock us as ignorant or convict us as liars.

## CHAPTER V

Shall we offer him the passage that you likewise habitually introduce: “They will see their life hanging, and will not believe in their own life” (Deut. 28:66)? You add “on the wood,” although that wording is not found in the text.

But it is equally obvious that this does not refer to Christ. Among the savage curses that he pronounced upon his people if they should abandon his law, he also added this: they would be in captivity among their enemies and would contemplate the end of their life day and night, so that they would have no confidence even in the life itself that had been spared them by their conquerors, since it would hang uncertainly, fearful and anxious, always beneath the threat of swords.

This passage, then, does not refer to Christ either; other passages must be sought. For I can scarcely believe that you think the following was said about Christ: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23). Nor can I believe that you think it refers to Christ when it says that a prophet or ruler of the people who wished to turn them away from their god or to weaken any of his commandments was to be put to death (Deut. 13:5).

I certainly cannot deny that Christ did this. But you, on the other hand, cannot openly admit that these words were written about him, lest, if this were the case, we should again begin to ask in what spirit Moses prophesied—whether he was pronouncing a curse upon Christ or commanding that he be killed.

For if Moses possessed the Spirit of God, he did not say these things about Christ; if he said these things about Christ, he did not possess the Spirit of God. The divine Spirit would not curse Christ or command him to be killed.

Therefore, in order to free Moses from this charge, you must acknowledge that he did not write even these things about Christ. But if he did not write these things about Christ, you must produce other passages, or there will be none. If there are none, Christ could not have asserted what exists nowhere. And if Christ did not assert this, it will be established that the passage is false.

## CHAPTER VI

Nor is the statement that follows at all plausible: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also” (John 5:46). For the teaching of Moses and that of Christ are exceedingly dissimilar and entirely different, so that if the Jews believed one of them, they would necessarily oppose the other.

Moses teaches, above all, that one must abstain from every work on the Sabbath. He gives this as the reason for the religious observance: when God fashioned the world and everything in it, he devoted six days to work but ceased on the seventh, which is the Sabbath. Therefore he blessed it—that is, sanctified it—as a harbor of his own tranquility, and in addition gave the law that anyone who violated it should be killed (Exod. 20:8–11; 31:13–17).

The Jews therefore believed this very firmly, Moses being their teacher. Accordingly, they thought that Christ should not even be listened to when he affirmed that God is always at work and has appointed no day of cessation, since his power is continuous and untiring, and that he himself therefore ought never to cease—not even on Sabbaths: “For my Father is always working, and I must work” (John 5:17; 9:4).

Again, Moses counts circumcision of the flesh among sacred things beloved by God. He commands every male to be circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, and teaches that this is the necessary sign of the covenant that their god established with Abraham. He declares that any male who does not bear it will be cut off from his tribe and will have no share in the inheritance promised to Abraham and his seed (Gen. 17:9–14).

The Jews therefore believed this too very strongly, Moses affirming it. Consequently, they could not believe Christ when he weakened these requirements and further asserted that the circumcised person would become a son of Gehenna twice over (Matt. 23:15).

Again, Moses makes a careful distinction among bodily foods. He sits as an assessor among fish, birds, and four-footed animals, after the manner of a glutton’s arbiter, commanding that some be eaten as clean but others be regarded as unclean and not even touched. Among the latter he expressly counts the pig and the hare, as well as anything among fish that lacks scales, or among quadrupeds that does not have a divided hoof and does not chew the cud (Deut. 14:3–20).

The Jews therefore also believed these things firmly, since Moses wrote them. Consequently, they could no longer believe Christ when he taught the indiscriminate character of foods, removing all foods entirely from his own disciples but commonly allowing secular people everything that could be eaten, and asserting that nothing entering the mouth defiles them; for only the things that proceed shamelessly from the mouth defile a person (Matt. 15:11–20) [Note: [Col. 0319] The manuscripts have *imprudenter* (“thoughtlessly”) rather than *impudenter* (“shamelessly”).].

No one can be unaware that Jesus taught these and many other things contrary to Moses.

## CHAPTER VII

Since it would take too long to go through each of these individually, I shall point out one example in place of many: the fact that the majority of Christian heresies and, most obviously, the Catholics take no care to observe any of the things that Moses writes.

If this does not arise from some error but from that true tradition of Christ and his disciples, you must openly acknowledge that Jesus and Moses taught things mutually opposed to each other. Consequently, Christ was not believed by the Jews because they wished to show faith in Moses.

Why, then, would it not be false that Jesus said to them, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also,” when it is perfectly clear that they believed Moses and therefore believed Jesus all the less, whereas they could have had faith in Christ if they had ceased to believe Moses?

Nevertheless, as I said, please teach us where Moses wrote anything about Christ.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Elsewhere,” he says, “if you are a Christian, believe Christ when he says that Moses wrote about him. If you do not believe, you are not a Christian.”

This is always an inept and feeble response from people who have nothing to show. How much better you would have done if you had simply acknowledged the matter! Yet you could indeed say this to me, knowing that, for the sake of the religion in which I serve Christ, I am bound to believe. Even so, it is still under investigation whether this testimony is really Christ’s, so that it ought to be believed without qualification, or the writer’s, so that it ought to be carefully examined.

And if we do not believe false things, we do not offend Christ by this, but the falsifiers.

Still, this may somehow be brought against Christians. But what shall we do with those whom I mentioned—the Jew and the Gentile—to whom we cannot say, “If you are a Christian, believe; if you do not believe, you are not a Christian”?

Indeed, you could not properly say this even to a Christian, since Christ did not disdain the Apostle Thomas when he doubted concerning him. Rather, to heal the wounds of Thomas’s soul, he showed him the scars of his body. He did not say, “If you are a disciple, believe; if you do not believe, you are not a disciple.”

Say this to me, then, not when I doubt Christ, but when I am considering whether the statement belongs to him or has been introduced by someone else.

“But,” you say, “he calls blessed those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:27, 29). If you think this was said so that we should believe everything without reason or judgment, then be more blessed than I in your lack of understanding. I shall be content to have heard it, blessed with reason.

## CHAPTER IX

**AUGUSTINE replied:** You cunningly claim to be prepared to accept any prophecies about Christ that you find in the books of Moses, just as one might eat a fish from the sea while rejecting the water from which the fish is caught.

But because everything Moses wrote concerns Christ—that is, pertains entirely to Christ—whether it foretells him through figures of things done or spoken, or commends his grace and glory, you, who have believed in a fictitious and deceitful Christ from the writings of Mani, refuse to believe Moses just as you refuse to eat the fish.

There is, however, this difference: you attack Moses with hostility, but praise the fish deceitfully. If, as you yourself said, eating a fish from the sea does no harm, why do you proclaim it harmful in such a way that, if no other food is available, you would waste away from hunger before eating fish?

Moreover, if all flesh is unclean, as you say, and if in every water and every plant that wretched life of your god is held captive and must be cleansed through your foods, does not your detestable superstition compel you both to throw away the fish you praised and to drink seawater and eat the thorns you condemned?

As for your comparison of God’s servant with demons, so that, just as they were when they confessed Christ (Matt. 8:29), this man too should be accepted if something should be found in his books that proclaims Christ—he certainly does not disdain the reproach of his lord. For if the master of the household was called Beelzebul, how much more his household members? (Matt. 10:25).

But consider from whom you learned these things—surely from people more wicked than those who hurled such abuse at the Lord. For they did not believe that he was Christ and therefore thought him deceitful. You, however, think no doctrine truthful unless it dares to proclaim Christ deceitful.

## CHAPTER X
From where, then, does it seem to you that the law of Moses differs in no respect from Paganism? Is it because it commends a temple, sacrifice, altar, and priest? Yet all these terms are also found in the New Testament. “Destroy this temple,” he says, “and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19); and, “When you offer your gift at the altar” (Matthew 5:24); and, “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for yourself the sacrifice which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them” (Matthew 8:4). Whose figures these things were, the Lord himself partly demonstrates, when he compares the temple of his body with that temple; and partly we learn from apostolic teaching: “For the temple of God is holy,” says the Apostle, “which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17); and, “I appeal to you therefore, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1); and other passages of this kind. Accordingly, all those things were our figures (1 Corinthians 10:6), as the same Apostle says—and this must often be recalled—for they were not offered to demons, but to the one true God, who made heaven and earth; not as though he needed such things, but because he was distinguishing the ages and commanding present things through which he might signify future things.

But you, who pretend to detest Paganism in order to lead astray and deceive ignorant and imperfect Christians, produce for us the authority of Christian books in which you were commanded to worship and adore the sun and moon. Your error, therefore, is rather like Paganism, since you do not worship Christ, but something—I do not know what—which you have fabricated for yourselves by lying under Christ’s name; and you adore gods, either visible in this conspicuous heaven or other innumerable fictitious gods. To these phantasms, as though they were empty and vain images, you have built not little shrines but made your own hearts temples.

## CHAPTER XI

You demand that I show what Moses wrote about Christ. Much has indeed already been demonstrated above; but who could demonstrate everything? Especially since, if I mention certain passages, this perverse man seems ready either to twist them into another meaning, or, if he is overwhelmed by the evidence of clearer truth, to say that he is taking from the salty sea a sweet fish—as though he were not thereby compelled to drink the whole of Moses’ Scripture, like seawater. Therefore I think it sufficient for this work to show that the very passages which he selected from the Scripture of the Hebrews for criticism [Note: [Col. 0321] American and Manuscripts: *secerpit*, “has culled”; the printed editions: *decerpsit*, “has plucked out.”] pertain to the proclamation of Christ if they are rightly understood. From this it will sufficiently appear that the remaining passages, whether pronounced immediately or diligently and faithfully examined, accord much more with the Christian faith—if the very things which the enemy brings forward for ridicule and condemnation are themselves used to prove that he must be condemned by Christian truth.

Therefore, O man filled with every kind of deceit, when the Lord said in the Gospel, “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me; for he wrote about me” (John 5:46), there is no reason for you to pretend that you are placed in a great dilemma and seem forced to choose one of two alternatives: either to declare this passage false or Jesus a liar. For just as this passage is true, so Jesus is truthful. “It seemed preferable,” he says, “to attribute falsehood to the writers than a lie to the author of truth.” Do you really believe Christ to be the author of truth, when you proclaim him to have been a pretender to flesh, death, wounds, and scars? I want you to show me how you learned that Christ is the author of truth, if you dare to attribute falsehood to those who wrote about him, whose authority, commended and confirmed by recent memory, has passed down to later generations.

You did not see Christ, nor did he speak with you as he did with the Apostles, nor did he call you from heaven as he called Saul (Acts 9:3–7). What can we think or believe about him except what Scripture testifies? Moreover, if the Gospel, disseminated and known among all nations and established in every church from the beginning of the preaching of Christ’s name at such a pinnacle of holiness, is a lie, what writing can be produced to which faith concerning Christ should be given? What written document could you produce which one who does not wish to believe this would not call fabricated, if such universal knowledge of the Gospel is brought into doubt?

## CHAPTER XII

Next you add that you yourself heard him say that all who came before him were thieves and robbers (John 10:8). From where did you hear him say this, unless from the Gospel? But if someone insists that this statement—which you believe from the Gospel so firmly that you say you heard it as though from the Lord’s own mouth—is false, and denies that Christ said it, where will you turn? What will you do? Will you not proclaim the authority of the Gospel with all the strength you can muster? Wretched man, it is written there that which you do not wish to believe—the very place where you learned what you believe so firmly that you say you heard it from Christ himself.

Behold, we believe both statements because we believe the holy Gospel, where both are written: that Moses wrote about Christ, and that all who came before Christ were thieves and robbers. He wishes “came” to be understood in this way: they were not sent. For those who were sent, such as Moses and the holy Prophets, came not before him but with him; they did not wish to precede him through pride, but humbly bore him, speaking through them. [Note: [Col. 0322] An old codex of the Bernardines of Paris here contains some not unsuitable insertions, namely: “They did not come apart from him, because they came with him. He was sending heralds who were to come,” etc. But these are taken from Augustine’s Tractate 45 on John.]

But you, who understand these words of the Lord in this way, thereby openly confess, according to your own understanding, that you have no prophets who prophesied that Christ would come; and for that reason you fashioned him as you wished. For if there are any of your people—who certainly ought not to be believed because they are produced by you alone—yet if there are some whom you dare to say prophesied that Christ would come in false flesh, would suffer a false death, and would offer false scars to his doubting disciples, I will not even speak of how detestable and avoidable they are, or how they cannot be truthful when they delight in Christ’s falsehood. Without saying this, let me return to my point: according to your understanding, they were thieves and robbers because they came before Christ—those who in some manner proclaimed that he would come.

But if that interpretation is correct, according to which those are said to have come before Christ who refused to come with Christ, that is, with the Word of God, and who, since God did not send them, brought their falsehoods to human beings, then you yourselves are also thieves and robbers. Although you were born into this world after Christ’s passion and resurrection, you wished to come before him, before he himself enlightened you so that you might proclaim his truth, in order to parade your own deception.

## CHAPTER XIII

But in that passage where the Jews said to him, “You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true,” it is not surprising that you did not see him pursuing the matter until he said that Moses had prophesied about him. You do not possess the pious eye by which you could see this. For behold, what he answered them—namely, “In your law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me” (John 8:13, 17–18)—what does this signify to those who understand rightly, except that the number of witnesses was consecrated and commended in the law by the prophetic Spirit, so that in this way also the future revelation of the Father and the Son might be foretold, whose Spirit in that inseparable Trinity is the Holy Spirit?

Therefore it is written, “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Otherwise, one witness often speaks the truth, and several often lie; indeed, at the beginning of the faith of the Gentiles, one evangelizing Apostle was believed rather than the erring crowds by whom he himself was persecuted. This number of witnesses, then, was not consecrated without reason. And when the Lord gave this answer, he also wished it to be understood that Moses had prophesied about him.

Or do you slander him because he did not say, “In the law of God,” but, “In your law,” it is written? Who does not recognize here the customary expression of Scripture? He said “in your law,” that is, the law given to you (2 Timothy 2:8; Galatians 1:11–12), just as the Apostle calls the Gospel “his,” though he testifies that he received it not from a human being but through the revelation of Jesus Christ.

Do you also claim that Christ denied that God was his Father wherever he did not say “our Father” but “your Father” (Matthew 6:26, 32, and elsewhere)? As for that voice which you mentioned as having come from heaven—“This is my beloved Son; believe him” (Matthew 3:17; 17:5)—because you did not hear it, do not believe him. But if you believe it because you found it in the holy Scriptures, there too is the statement which you refuse to believe: that Moses wrote about Christ. There are also many other statements there from which you likewise withdraw faith.

And are you not afraid, wretched men, that some profane person might say that this voice did not sound from heaven at all? Just as you argue against the salvation of the human race, which is conferred on all nations by evangelical authority, even to your own destruction, when you say that Christ’s statement that Moses wrote about him should not be believed because, if he had said this, the Jews—being wicked and cunning—could not have failed immediately to ask what he thought Moses had written about him, so that same foolish and ruined person might say: “If that voice had sounded from heaven, would not all the Jews who heard it have believed?”

Why, then, insane men, do you not consider that just as the Jews’ hard unbelief could have remained even after that heavenly voice, so it could also have happened that, when Christ said Moses had written about him, they avoided asking altogether what Moses had written about him out of malicious cunning, fearing all the more the grounds on which they would be convicted?

## CHAPTER XIV

Faustus himself understands that this argument is not only sacrilegious against evangelical holiness but also feeble and powerless; and he directs his attention instead to the point which, he says, troubles him more, because he has searched all Moses’ writings and found no prophecies there concerning Christ. I answer him briefly: he does not understand. And if someone asks why he does not understand, I will answer: because he reads with a hostile and adverse disposition [Note: [Col. 0323] The Erasmian edition reads: “turned away” (*averso*).]; because he does not search in order to know, but thinks he knows what he does not know.

This presumption of swollen arrogance either closes the eye of the heart so that it sees nothing at all, or distorts it so that it sees perversely and approves or condemns one thing in place of another.

“You teach me,” he says, “what it is that I may perhaps have overlooked while reading, which is mentioned in the Scripture of Moses concerning God and our Lord.” I answer him briefly here: You overlooked everything, because he wrote everything about Christ [Note: [Col. 0323] Printed editions: “that whole thing” (*illud*); manuscripts: “he” (*ille*).]. But since we cannot examine and treat everything in detail, I will reserve for this work, if the Lord assists me, what I said above: to show that the very passages you choose for criticism were written about Christ.

You even ask me not to say, as the ignorant commonly do, that this ought to be sufficient for faith because Christ said that Moses wrote about him. If I say this, I say it not as an ignorant man but as a believer. I also admit that it is not sufficient to convince a Gentile or a Jew. But against you, who in whatever manner boast in the Christian name, it is sufficiently valid and exceptionally powerful. Even though you delayed and evaded for a long time, you were nevertheless compelled to confess this when you said:

“I do not wish you now to consider me, whom my profession has made bound to believe, so that I cannot fail to believe him whom I follow; but suppose that we are dealing with a Jew, suppose that we are dealing with a Gentile.”

By these words you showed that, for the moment, you yourself—whom I am now addressing, since your profession has bound you to believe—are sufficiently convicted that Moses wrote about Christ. For it is written in the Gospel that Christ himself said this, and you do not dare to undermine the Gospel’s such distinguished and holy authority. Even when you dare to do so indirectly, pressed by the constraints of your difficulty and seeing what ruin overwhelms you when one says to you: “If you do not think that such a universally and holily known Gospel should be believed, then demand what Scripture concerning Christ’s deeds and words ought to be believed”—and fearing that, once the cloak of the Christian name has been removed, your naked vanity will remain exposed to everyone’s contempt and hatred, you try once again to gather yourself, wounded as you are, and say that your profession has now made you bound to believe the words of the Gospel.

Thus, for the moment, I hold you, the man with whom I am dealing; I strike and destroy your error and deception—that is, I compel you to confess that Moses wrote about Christ, because the Gospel records that Christ said this, and your profession has bound you to believe the Gospel. If it becomes necessary for me to dispute with a Jew or a Gentile, I have already shown above how I think I ought to act, according to my limited abilities, for the sake of my little ones.

## CHAPTER XV

Nor do I deny that what you selected as easy to refute was foretold about Christ, where God speaks to Moses, saying: “I will raise up for them a Prophet from among their brothers, like you” (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18). Nor do your polished and witty antitheses, with which you attempted to color and paint your muddy speech, deter me in any way from this truth of faith.

For, comparing Christ with Moses and wishing to demonstrate that they are unlike, so that what is written—“I will raise up for them a Prophet like you”—might not appear to be understood of Christ, you set against one another many opposites: Moses was a human being, Christ is God; Moses was a sinner, Christ is holy; Moses was born from sexual intercourse, whereas Christ, according to us, was born from a virgin—and according to you, not even from a virgin; Moses was killed on the mountain after offending God, whereas Christ suffered by his own will, pleasing the Father completely.

As though, when something is said to be similar, it must be understood to be similar in every respect and in every way! For not only things of one and the same nature are said to be similar to one another—such as twin human beings, children to their parents, or all human beings to all human beings insofar as they are human, as is readily observed also in other animals, or among trees, as an olive is said to resemble an olive and a laurel a laurel—but many things of different natures are also similar and are said to be so: for example, the wild olive resembles the cultivated olive, and spelt resembles wheat.

I am speaking of things that are still closely related and touching one another. For what is as far removed from the Son of God, through whom all things were made (John 1:3), as an animal or a stone? Yet we read in the Gospel, “Behold, the Lamb of God” (ibid., 1:29), and in the Apostle, “Now the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). No one would rightly say these things if Christ in no way assumed any likeness to them.

What wonder, then, if Christ did not disdain to become like Moses himself, who became like the sheep which God, through Moses himself, commanded his people to eat in anticipation of him, and whose blood he commanded to be used for the protection of salvation, and to be called the Passover (Exodus 12)—which no one is permitted to deny has now been fulfilled in Christ?

Therefore, from the Scriptures I acknowledge that Christ is unlike Moses; from the Scriptures acknowledge with me also that he is like Moses. He is not unlike him for the same reason that he is like him, but for one reason he is unlike him and for another he is like him, while I demonstrate both.

Christ is unlike a human being because he is God; for it is written of him, “Who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5). Christ is like a human being because he is human; for it is likewise written of him, “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

Christ is unlike a sinner because he is always holy; and Christ is like a sinner because “God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3).

Christ is unlike a human being born from sexual intercourse insofar as he was born from a virgin; but Christ is like a human being born insofar as he too was born from a woman, to whom it was said, “What will be born from you as holy will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Christ is unlike a human being who died because of his own sin, insofar as he died without sin and by his own authority; but again Christ is like a dead human being insofar as he too died a true bodily death.

## CHAPTER XVI

Nor should you disparage Moses, the servant of God, because you said that he was a sinner and was killed on the mountain after offending his God (Deuteronomy 34:5). He himself knew how to glory in the Lord, so that he might be saved by him—as was also the one who says, “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1 Timothy 1:15).

Moses is reproved by the divine voice because his faith hesitated somewhat when he was to bring water from the rock [Note: [Col. 0325] American and Manuscripts: *ejiciendam*, “to drive out”; the printed editions: *eliciendam*, “to draw out.”] (Numbers 20:10–12). This may be compared with Peter’s sin, who, in the midst of the waves, doubted through a similar failure of faith (Matthew 14:30–31).

But far be it from us to believe that Moses was thereby separated from the eternal fellowship of the saints, since, together with the holy Elijah, he was found worthy, as the Gospel says, to stand beside the Lord when he was glorified on the mountain (Matthew 17:1–5). For, as we read in the ancient Books, even after that sin the extent of his merit before God is apparent.

But what was the reason that God spoke of avenging his sin with such a death? Since I promised to demonstrate that the very things you selected for criticism pertain to the foreshadowing of Christ, I shall do what I can, with the Lord’s help, to show those who understand rightly that what you criticized in Moses’ death was also a prophecy concerning Christ.

## CHAPTER XVII

For, as is customary with the divine mysteries in the holy Scriptures, the same person at different times assumes one role and then another in order to signify different things. At that time Moses represented the people of the Jews placed under the Law and figured them in prophetic anticipation.

Therefore, just as Moses, striking the rock with his staff, doubted the power of God, so that people held under the Law given through Moses, fastening Christ to the wood of the cross, did not believe that he was the Power of God. But just as water flowed from the struck rock for the thirsty, so the wound of the Lord’s passion became life for believers. We have an especially clear and trustworthy statement of the Apostle on this matter, when he spoke of it and said, “Now the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

Thus God commands this carnal despair concerning Christ’s divinity to die upon Christ’s own height, when he commands Moses’ bodily death to take place on the mountain. For just as Christ is the rock, so Christ is also the mountain: the rock is humble strength, the mountain exalted greatness.

For just as the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ,” so the Lord himself says, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14), asserting that he is the mountain and that his faithful people, founded in the glory of his name, are the city.

The wisdom of the flesh lives when Christ’s humility is despised on the cross, as though the rock had been struck; for “Christ crucified is a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.” And the wisdom of the flesh dies when Christ is recognized as exalted, like the height of a mountain; for “to those who are called, Jews and Greeks, Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).

Moses therefore ascended the mountain so that, with the flesh dead, he might be received alive in spirit. Faustus had not ascended there, so that with a dead mind he might speak carnal accusations.

Did Peter not shrink, through the wisdom of the flesh, from striking that very rock, when he said to the Lord who foretold his passion, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you; be gracious to yourself”? The Lord did not spare him for this sin when he answered him, “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me. For you do not think the things of God, but the things of human beings” (Matthew 16:22–23).

Or when did this carnal distrust die, except in Christ’s glorification, as though upon the height of a mountain? It was certainly alive when Peter fearfully denied him; and it was certainly dead when he proclaimed him openly.

This distrust was alive in Saul when, detesting the stumbling block of the cross, he ravaged the Christian faith (Acts 8:3). And where but on that mountain did it die, when Paul could already say, “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20)?

## CHAPTER XVIII

What, then, do you possess, heretical vanity, by which you think you can prove that the statement, “I will raise up for them a Prophet from among their brothers, like you,” was not foretold about Christ, when you cannot do so even on the basis of your claim that he is unlike Moses? We too demonstrate that he is like Moses, for other reasons.

Is it because he is called a prophet, since he deigned to become human and foretold so many future things? Unless perhaps a prophet is something other than a human being who proclaims future events beyond human conjecture. Hence he also said of himself, “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matthew 13:57).

But I shall leave you aside for the moment—you who shortly before admitted that you were convicted when you said that your profession had made you bound to believe the Gospel. Let the Jew himself come forward, who wickedly lifts his neck from the yoke of Christ and therefore still thinks himself entitled to say, “Your Christ lied; Moses wrote nothing about him.”

## CHAPTER XIX

Let him tell me which prophet God promised when he said to Moses, “I will raise up for them a Prophet from among their brothers, like you,” or “similar to you.” Many prophets arose afterward, but surely God wished one particular person to be understood.

I believe the successor of Moses will immediately occur to him: the man who led the people liberated from Egypt into the promised land. When he thinks of this man, he may perhaps still laugh at me for asking of whom it was said, “I will raise up for them a Prophet like you,” since I read who succeeded Moses in the same office of governing and leading that people after Moses’ death.

When he laughs at me as though I were ignorant—for Faustus also portrays him as such—I will not cease to address the man further and call him back from carefree laughter to the responsibility of answering. I will ask and insist on knowing why Moses changed the name of this very future successor, in comparison with whom Moses himself was disqualified so that he would not introduce the people into the promised land—lest the Law given through Moses, not for saving but for convicting the sinner, should be thought to introduce people into the kingdom of heaven (John 1:17), whereas grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

I will ask the Jew, then, why Moses changed the name of that very future successor. He was called Ause [Note: [Col. 0327] Thus the Manuscripts, following the Septuagint. The American and Erasmian editions, following the Vulgate, read: “For he was called Osee.” Lovaniensis reads: “For he was called Josue.”], and Moses called him Jesus (Numbers 13:9; 14:6).

Why, finally, did Moses call him this at the very time when he sent him ahead from the valley of Pharan to that same land into which the people were to come under his leadership? For the true Jesus himself said, “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself” (John 14:3).

I will also ask whether the prophet does not bear witness to this figure when he says, “God will come from the South, and the Holy One from Pharan” (Habakkuk 3:3)—as though he were saying: “The holy God will come bearing the name of the one whose name was borne by him who came from the South, from Pharan”—that is, Jesus.

Furthermore, the same Word of God is understood to speak when he promises this very successor of Moses, through whom the people would be sent into the promised land, calling him by the name of an angel—just as human beings who announce something are also commonly called angels in divine Scripture. He says:

“Behold, I am sending my angel before your face, to guard you on the way and to bring you into the land which I swore to you” [Note: [Col. 0327] Lovaniensis reads: “which I prepared for you.” The other printed editions and the Manuscripts read: “which I swore to you.”]. “Pay attention to him and obey him; do not disbelieve him, for he will not take anything away from you; for my name is in him” (Exodus 23:20–21).

What does this mean? Let him search those Scriptures—not now as a Manichaean but even as a Jew—and see whether God said of any angel, “My name is in him,” except of this one whom he promises as the one who would bring the people into the promised land.

Then let him ask among human beings who introduced the people after Moses, and he will find Jesus—not called by this name from the beginning of his life, but called by it after his name had been changed.

Therefore, the one who said, “My name is in him,” in that Jesus is the true Jesus, the ruler and leader of the people into the inheritance of eternal life, according to the New Testament, of which the Old Testament was a figure. Thus, as far as the prophetic preparation is concerned, nothing could be done or said more strikingly, since the matter was carried as far as the very expression of the name.

## CHAPTER XX

It remains for that Jew, if he wishes to be a Jew in secret—not according to the letter but according to the spirit (Romans 2:29), and if he wishes to be reckoned a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit (John 1:47), to remember that in the figure it was the dead Jesus who introduced the people into the land of the dying, and to recognize in truth the living Jesus, under whose leadership he may enter the land of the living.

Such a person will no longer resist this obvious prophecy bitterly. Recalling Jesus who introduced the people into that promised land, he will become gentle and hear the one whose name that earlier Jesus bore, now introducing people more truly and saying, “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:4).

At this point even the Gentile, if he did not have a heart too stony—or if he were made from those stones from which God raises up children for Abraham (Matthew 3:9)—would surely marvel that in the ancient Books of the same people from whom Jesus was said to have been born, such an evident prophecy concerning him was written that even his name was expressed.

At the same time he would notice that the Jesus foretold was not some ordinary human being, but certainly God, since God said that his own name was in that man who was appointed to rule and introduce the people into the kingdom, and called him an angel. By the very fact that he was sent after his name had been changed, he announced something great and divine. Who, even with only a slight acquaintance with that language, does not know that “messenger” is called *angelos* in Greek?

Therefore, any Gentile who did not wish to be perverse and obstinate would not despise those Books because they were Hebrew and because he was not bound by the law of that people. Rather, he would value the books of any people precisely because he found in them, written so long beforehand, things which he recognized as fulfilled in his own times.

He would not reject Christ Jesus because he saw him foretold in Hebrew writings; instead, he would judge that the one who, before he was born among human beings, had merited to be foretold and commended through so many volumes and ages—partly by clearer testimonies, partly through figures and mysteries of deeds and words—ought to be followed and revered with immense wonder and devout religious observance [Note: [Col. 0328] All Manuscripts read: “and with due religious observance.”].

Thus, from the already-present effects of Christian realities, the truth of the Books’ prophecy would be demonstrated to him; and from the prophecy of the Books, Christ would be recognized as worthy of worship. Let them call me a speaker of vanity if this did not happen, if it is not happening, if people throughout the whole world are not converging upon this faith through the reading of these same Books.

## CHAPTER XXI

Hence the senselessness of these people is wonderfully deserving of ridicule. They ask us, as though it were impossible, how a Gentile could wish to learn the Christian faith through the Books of the Jews, even though he sees all nations becoming disciples of these Books with such devotion and such public renown [Note: [Col. 0329] The American edition and most manuscripts read *cernat* (“he sees”); the Erasmian and Lovaniensian editions read *cernant* (“they see”).].

This happens all the more powerfully and firmly because so many testimonies concerning Christ are produced from the hands of his enemies. The nations that believe can therefore think that nothing concerning him was fabricated for the moment, since they find Christ in those Books to which, for so many ages, those who crucified Christ have been subject, and which those who blaspheme Christ every day hold at such a pinnacle of authority.

For if prophecies concerning Christ were produced by those who preach Christ, they would be thought to have fabricated them themselves. But now the one who preaches explains what the one who blasphemes recites.

All the blindness of the ungodly is ordered toward some use for the saints by the Most High God, who, in the equity of his government, makes good use even of evil things, so that those who live unjustly according to their own will may be justly disposed according to his judgment.

Therefore, so that the testimonies prophesying that Christ would be born, perform marvelous deeds, suffer unworthy things, die, rise again, ascend, and disseminate the Gospel of eternal life among all nations might not be thought fabricated by those who announced him to the peoples, something great was accomplished for our benefit through the Jews’ unbelief: the very people who did not possess these things in their hearts for their own sake possessed them in their books for our sake.

Nor is the authority of those Books diminished because they are not understood by the Jews; rather, it is increased. Their very blindness was foretold there. Thus, by failing to understand the truth, they bear witness to the truth even more: since they do not understand the Books in which they were foretold as not understanding, they show by this also that those Books are truthful.

## CHAPTER XXII

This is also the source of that passage by whose ambiguity Faustus is deceived: “You will see your life hanging, and you will not believe your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66).

Someone may say that these words can be understood in another way. But Faustus did not dare to say that they cannot be understood of Christ, nor will anyone dare to say so unless he denies either that Christ is life, or that he was seen hanging by the Jews, or that they did not believe him.

Since Christ himself says, “I am the life” (John 14:6), and it is certain that he hung before the eyes of the Jews who did not believe him, I do not see why we should doubt that Moses wrote this also about Christ—Moses of whom Christ says, “For he wrote about me” (John 5:47).

Therefore, if Faustus attempted to show that the statement, “I will raise up for them a Prophet from among their brothers, like you,” cannot be understood of Christ because Christ is not like Moses, and yet he has been convicted on every side, what need is there to labor over this testimony? Or, just as he said that Christ is not like Moses in order to refute that prophecy, let him likewise say, in order to refute this one, that Christ is not life or that he did not hang in the sight of the Jews who did not believe him.

But since he has not said this, and none of them today dares to say it, there is no reason for us, servants of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, to hesitate to embrace this prophecy also.

“But,” he says, “this too was placed among other curses.” Is it therefore not a prophecy, when the other things among which it was placed are themselves nothing other than prophecies? Or is it not a prophecy about Christ because the preceding and following words woven into that reading appear to have nothing to do with Christ?

As though anything worse could occur among the curses which prophetically befell the Jews for the merit of their proud impiety than that they should see their life—that is, the Son of God—hanging and not believe their life [Note: [Col. 0330] Printed editions read *superbiae* (“of pride”); manuscripts read *superbae* (“proud”).]. For when curses are spoken from prophecy, they do not express the evil wish of one invoking harm, but the announcement of one who foretells through the Spirit.

Those curses which arise from an evil wish are forbidden when it is said, “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12:14). Yet such words are often found in the speech of the saints. Thus the Apostle Paul says, “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works” (2 Timothy 4:14).

In another passage, as though angered and provoked, the Apostle even appears to have wished evil upon them: “Would that those who trouble you would cut themselves off!” (Galatians 5:12). Yet if you consider the identity of the writer, you will understand that through a most elegant ambiguity he wished them well. For there are eunuchs who have cut themselves off for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:12).

Faustus would have understood this in these words too, if he had brought a pious palate to the Lord’s food.

For perhaps this statement—“You will see your life hanging, and you will not believe your life”—sounded to the Jews as though, amid the threats or deceptions of their enemies, they would see their own life hanging in uncertainty and would not believe that they would survive.

But the son of the Gospel, when he hears, “For he wrote about me,” sees in this very ambiguity of the sentence what the Prophets cast before swine and what they intimate to human beings: immediately he recognizes Christ, the life of human beings, hanging, and the Jews who did not believe him precisely because they saw him hanging.

Another person might quickly say that, among the other curses in that reading—which do not pertain to understanding anything about Christ—this one statement alone concerns Christ: “You will see your life hanging, and you will not believe your life.” For it certainly could have happened that, among the various curses prophetically foretold against the impious people, this too was included.

But I, and those who reflect with me somewhat more attentively upon that evangelical and dominical statement—which does not say, “He also wrote about me,” as though he were believed to have written other things unrelated to Christ, but says, “For he wrote about me,” so that by searching we might understand the whole purpose of that Scripture only in relation to the grace of Christ—we recognize that the other curses in that reading were also foretold because of Christ.

To demonstrate this now would take too long.

## CHAPTER XXIII
Therefore, it is very far from being the case that what Faustus cited does not pertain to Christ because it was placed among other curses; indeed, those other curses themselves do not have a correct interpretation unless they are understood as prophecies referring to Christ’s glory, through which provision is made for the human race—how much more, then, does this particular passage have such an interpretation? Even if Moses had been such a man that, contemplating one thing in his heart, he uttered another with his mouth, I would more readily say that he prophesied unknowingly than deny that the words, “You shall see your life hanging, and you shall not believe your life,” spoken to the Jewish people, were a prophecy about Christ. For Caiaphas too did not contemplate in his mind what was understood from his words when, persecuting Christ as an enemy, he said that it was expedient for one man to die lest the whole nation perish. There the Evangelist added that he had not said this on his own, but, because he was high priest, had prophesied (John 11:49–51). But Moses was not Caiaphas. Therefore, when he said to the Hebrew people, “You shall see your life hanging, and you shall not believe your life,” he not only spoke about Christ—for even if he had said it unknowingly, it ought to be understood as having been said about no one else—but he also said it knowingly. For he was the most faithful steward of the prophetic mystery, that is, of that priestly anointing from which we recognize the name “Christ.” By virtue of this mystery even Caiaphas, although a very wicked man, was able to prophesy without knowing it. The prophetic anointing accomplished this in him, that he prophesied; his impious life accomplished this, that he prophesied unknowingly. With what face, then, can it be said that Moses prophesied nothing about Christ—the one from whom that anointing began, through which the name “Christ” became known, and through which even Christ’s persecutor prophesied about Christ, though unknowingly?

## CHAPTER XXIV

As for the curse concerning one hanging on a tree, we have already said above as much as seemed sufficient. It is also sufficiently clear, from the many points we have already discussed, that Moses did not give a command against Christ when he ordered that a prophet or ruler of the people who wished to turn the children of Israel away from their God, or to violate any of the commandments, should be put to death. This will become increasingly clear to anyone who considers more and more carefully the words and deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ, because Christ did not wish to turn any of them away from their God. The God whom Moses had commanded them to love and worship is certainly the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—the very God whom the Lord Jesus Christ also recalls with the same commendation, and by whose authority refutes the error of the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, when he says: “But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what God spoke to Moses from the bush: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:31–32; Luke 20:37–38); for all of them are alive.

Appropriately, then, the Manichaeans are now refuted by the same saying by which the Sadducees were then refuted, since these people too, though in another way, nevertheless deny the resurrection itself. Likewise, when praising the faith of the centurion, he said, “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel”; he added: “But I say to you that [Col. 0332] many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the children of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (Matthew 8:10–12). If, then—and Faustus cannot deny this—Moses commended to the people of Israel no God other than the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Christ himself without doubt commends that same God in these and other testimonies, Christ did not try to turn that people away from their God. Rather, he threatened that they would go into the outer darkness because he saw them turned away from their God, in whose kingdom he says that the Gentiles, called from the whole world, will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—not for any other reason than that they would have kept the faith of the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Hence the Apostle also says: “And Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the Gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you all the nations shall be blessed’” (Galatians 3:8)—that is, those would be blessed in Abraham’s offspring who imitated Abraham’s faith. Therefore Christ did not wish to turn the Israelites away from their God; rather, he reproved them because they were turning away from him.

As for anyone who thinks that the Lord violated one of the commandments given through Moses, it is no wonder if he thinks this as the Jews did; but he is mistaken because the Jews were mistaken in this matter. When Faustus mentions the particular commandment that he wants people to believe the Lord violated, it is necessary for us to show how he is deceived, just as we have already shown above where appropriate. For now I say this: if the Lord had violated any one of those commandments, he would not also have reproved the Jews for that very thing. When they accused his disciples of eating with unwashed hands, and therefore of transgressing—not God’s commandment, but the traditions of the elders—he said to them: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God in order to establish your traditions?” He then recalls the very commandment of God that we know was given through Moses. For he continues: “For God said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall die the death’” [Note: Am., Er., and the Cistercian manuscript read “shall die.”]. “But you say, ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, The gift that is from me will benefit you’” [Note: Er., Lyon, and Venice editions: “The gift that is from me will benefit you.” The Vulgate: “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you.” M.], “shall not honor his father; and you have made void the word of God for the sake of your tradition” (Matthew 15:3–6).

Observe how many things he teaches us in this passage: that he did not turn the Jews away from their God; that he not only did not violate his commandments, but also reproved those by whom they were violated; and that it was none other than God who gave these commandments through Moses.

## CHAPTER XXV

Therefore, since we believe that everything Moses wrote pertains to the commendation of Christ—and since in this work we cannot demonstrate this in its entirety, we promised to show it in those passages that Faustus selected for refuting or condemning that Scripture—it is rightly demanded of us that we also show how Moses’ command to put to death a prophet or ruler who wished to turn them away from their God, or to violate any of the commandments, pertains to preserving the faith taught in the Church of Christ.

For Moses saw, through the prophetic Spirit [Col. 0333] and with God speaking to him, that many heretics, teachers of various errors, would arise against the teaching of Christ—men who would not preach the Christ who is the true Christ. For the true Christ is the one who was foretold through the prophecies issued by Moses himself and by the other holy men of that nation. Therefore, whoever wished to teach another Christ, Moses commanded should be put to death.

What else does the Catholic tongue now do except put to death, with the spiritual sword of the two-edged line of both Testaments, all who wish to turn us away from our God or to violate any of the commandments? Among these, Manichaeus himself is especially struck down, when his error is destroyed by the asserted truth of the Law and the Prophets. He wishes to turn us away from our God—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom Christ commends—and to violate the commandments of the Law, in whose figures we also recognize that Christ was prophesied.

## CHAPTER XXVI

As for that argument of his, whether I should call it extremely dull [Note: In the manuscripts, “extremely dull” is spelled with an additional n. Elsewhere too, the form with the additional n occurs instead of “dull.”] or extremely fraudulent, I do not know. Faustus had intelligence; for this reason I am more inclined to think that he wished to cast a fog before the less attentive reader than that he failed to see what I am about to say [Note: Am. and one Vatican manuscript read “what he might say.”]. For he says: “If these things were not written about Christ, either you will produce others, or there will be none.”

This proposition is true, but it was incumbent upon him to show both that these things were not written about Christ and that no others could be produced. He did none of this, since we have shown how these things can be understood as referring to Christ, and above we produced many others that cannot be understood as referring to anything but Christ. Therefore, Faustus, you have no reason to conclude that nothing about Christ was written by Moses.

Pay attention to what you say: “If these things,” you say, “were not written about Christ, either you will produce others, or there will be none.” You speak truly. Therefore, since we have shown that these things were written about Christ or on account of Christ, and have produced many others, your argument will instead amount to nothing.

As for the passages you cited, although you did not succeed in your case, at least you attempted to show that they were not written about Christ. But when you added, “Either you will produce others, or there will be none,” you first ought to have demonstrated that we could not produce others, so that you might safely infer that there were none. Instead, as though your little book were going to have deaf hearers or blind readers, so that no one would notice what you had omitted, you rushed on to say: “If there were none, Christ could not have asserted what is nowhere found; and if Christ did not assert this, it will be established that this passage is false.”

What a man you are, who thinks himself a speaker, and thinks the other does not think as an opponent! Where is your acumen? Or could you not have acted otherwise in a bad cause? But your bad cause compelled you to speak foolishly; no one, however, compels you to have a bad cause.

For what if we produce others? Certainly there will not be none, because there will be some. And if there are some, Christ could have asserted what exists. Thus, if Christ could have asserted this, it does not follow that the Gospel passage is false.

Return, then, to your proposition, in which you said, “Either you will produce others, or there will be none [Col. 0334],” and observe that you have not shown that we will produce no others. Observe also how many others we have already produced above, and note what follows from this: namely, that what we read Christ said in the Gospel is not false: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me.”

The authority of the Gospel is so eminent and its truth so firmly established that, even if, because of the slowness of our understanding, we found nothing written by Moses about Christ, we ought nevertheless to believe not only that there are some such passages, but that everything he wrote pertains to Christ, because he did not say, “And he wrote about me,” but, “He wrote about me.”

But now, even if—God forbid—we had to doubt this Gospel passage, the discovery of so many testimonies about Christ in the writing of Moses would remove all doubt. And because there is no reason to doubt the Gospel passage, even if those testimonies had not been discovered, we would nevertheless have to believe that they exist.

## CHAPTER XXVII

As for your further claim that the tradition of Christ was unlike that of Moses, and that therefore it was not plausible that if they believed Moses they would also believe Christ; rather, that the natural conclusion would be that if the Jews believed one, they would necessarily oppose the other—you certainly would not say this if you raised the eye of your consideration a little and looked upon the whole world without the blindness of contentiousness: educated and uneducated, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, to whom the Apostle declared himself a debtor (Romans 1:14), believing in both Moses and Christ at the same time.

If, then, it was not plausible that the Jews should believe Moses and Christ equally, it is much less plausible that the whole world should believe Moses and Christ equally. Yet when we see all nations believing both, and holding with the strongest and most widespread faith that Moses’ prophecy agrees with Christ’s Gospel, one nation was not being called to something impossible when it was told, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also.” Rather, we should marvel at and rebuke more vehemently the hardness of the Jews, who did not do what we see the whole world has done.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

As for whatever you say about the Sabbath, the circumcision of the flesh, and the distinction among foods—that Moses handed down one tradition, while Christians learned something else through Christ—we have already shown above that, as the Apostle says, “All these things were figures of us” (1 Corinthians 10:6). The doctrine, then, is not different; the time is different.

There was one time when these things had to be foretold through figurative prophecies, and there is another time when they must now be fulfilled through manifest truth, once that truth has been revealed. But what wonder is it if the Jews, understanding the Sabbath carnally, resisted Christ, who was already intimating its spiritual meaning?

Answer the Apostle, if you can, who testifies that the observance of that day was a shadow of things to come (Colossians 2:16–17). But if they resisted Christ because they did not understand the true Sabbath, do not resist him, and understand true innocence.

For in that very passage where Jesus is regarded especially as a destroyer of the Sabbath—when his disciples, passing through a grainfield and being hungry, plucked ears of grain and [Col. 0335] ate them—he declared them innocent, answering the Jews: “If you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy’” [Note: Lov. reads “I prefer mercy.” Other editions and the manuscripts read “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice,” in accordance with the Greek and Hosea 6.] “rather than sacrifice, you would never have condemned the innocent” (Matthew 12:7). They ought rather to have had mercy on the hungry, because the disciples did this under the compulsion of hunger.

But among you, whoever plucks ears of grain is counted a murderer—not according to the tradition of Christ, who calls this innocence, but according to the tradition of Manichaeus. Or perhaps the Apostles showed mercy to those same ears of grain, so that by eating them they might cleanse the members of God, as your fable has it? Then you are cruel because you do not do this.

But of course Faustus knows how to destroy the Sabbath, because he knows that the power of God is always and tirelessly at work. Let those who understand that God, without any temporal change of will, creates all times say this. This is far beyond you, who assert that the repose of your god was shaken by the rebellion of the race of darkness and disturbed by the sudden assault of its enemies.

Or, since he foresaw this from eternity, did he never have repose because he was never secure, as he was thinking that he would have to wage so great a war, with such grave loss and ruin to his own members?

## CHAPTER XXIX

Furthermore, that Sabbath which you foolishly and impiously deride would not itself have had a meaning among the prophecies written about Christ unless Christ had also borne witness to it in this way. When, by his own will—as you yourself have stated in his praise—he suffered, and therefore had the times of his passion and resurrection within his power, he arranged for his flesh to rest in the tomb on the Sabbath from all its works. Then, rising on the third day, which we call the Lord’s Day and which is counted as the eighth after the Sabbath, he also declared that the circumcision of the eighth day pertained to the prophecy concerning him.

For what does circumcision of the flesh signify? What, unless the stripping away of the mortality that we carry from carnal generation?
