For this reason the Apostle said: “Stripping off the flesh, he made a display of principalities and powers, triumphing over them confidently in himself” (Colossians 2:15).

When he says that he stripped off the flesh, in that passage we understand “flesh” to mean the mortality of the flesh, according to which this body is properly called flesh. This mortality is properly called flesh because it will not exist in the immortality of the resurrection. Therefore it is written, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

You are accustomed to slander our faith on account of these words, since we believe that this body will rise again—a resurrection that has already taken place beforehand in the Lord himself—while concealing what follows, where the Apostle plainly explains what he means by “flesh” in that passage. For, wishing to show what he had meant by “flesh,” he immediately added: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” He says that this body, which because of its mortality is properly called flesh, will be changed in the resurrection, so that it will no longer be corruptible and mortal.

And so that this may not be thought to be our own conjecture, consult the very words that follow. “Behold,” he says, “I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. In an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet—for the [Col. 0336] trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:50–53).

Therefore, in order to be clothed with immortality, it is stripped of mortality. This is the mystery of circumcision, which was commanded to be performed on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12), and which on the eighth day—that is, on the Lord’s Day after the Sabbath—was already fulfilled in reality by the Lord.

Hence it is said, “Stripping off the flesh, he made a display of principalities and powers.” For through this mortality the devil’s powers, envious of us, held dominion over us. He is said to have made a display of them because, in himself, our head, he provided the example that will be completed in the final resurrection throughout his whole body, that is, the Church, which is to be delivered from the devil’s power. This is our faith.

And because, as Paul recalls in prophetic testimony, “The just shall live by faith” (Romans 1:17; Habakkuk 2:4), this is our justification. The pagans too believe that Christ died; but that Christ rose again is the distinctive faith of Christians. For “if you confess,” the Apostle says, “with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9).

Therefore, since we are justified by faith in this resurrection, that apostolic statement too concerns Christ: “He died for our sins, and rose again for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

And because this resurrection, which justifies us when believed, was prefigured by the circumcision of the eighth day, the Apostle says of Abraham, to whom it was first given: “And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith” (Romans 4:11). Thus Moses also wrote this circumcision among the other prophetic figures about Christ—Moses of whom Christ himself says, “He wrote about me.”

But when the Lord says, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and dry land to make one proselyte; and when you have made him, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves,” he did not say this because the proselyte was circumcised, but because he imitated their conduct. He restrains his own disciples from imitating them when he says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matthew 23:15, 2–3).

In these words of the Lord you ought to notice both how great an honor was accorded to the teaching of Moses—for even evil men, sitting in his seat, were compelled to teach good things—and how the proselyte became a son of Gehenna: not by hearing the words of the Law from the Pharisees, but by following their deeds.

Thus one might say to the circumcised proselyte what Paul says: “Circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the Law” (Romans 2:25). But because he imitated the Pharisees in failing to keep the Law, he became a son of Gehenna. Therefore, as I think, he became twice as much one as they were, because he neglected to fulfill what he had voluntarily undertaken—not having been born a Jew, but having become a Jew of his own accord.

## CHAPTER XXX

What did you intend to say—disrespectfully and without consideration—when you said that Moses, like a glutton, sits as an arbiter and orders some things to be greedily devoured as clean, while others, as unclean, are not even to be touched? [Col. 0337] It would rather be characteristic of a glutton to make no distinctions; or, if he does distinguish, to choose the more flavorful things.

Or do you say this so that, to the uneducated, your abstinence may appear admirable from your earliest years—as though you did not know, or had already forgotten, how much more pleasant pork tastes than mutton?

But because Moses too wrote these things about Christ through prophetic figures, signifying by the flesh of animals human beings who are either to be incorporated into Christ’s body, which is the Church, or to be rejected, he also represented you among the unclean animals. You do not agree with the Catholic faith because you neither ruminate on the word of wisdom nor, distinguishing the two Testaments—the Old and the New—in harmony, possess the divided hoof.

Who, moreover, could tolerate the fact that you were not ashamed to follow the deceitfulness of your own Adimantus?

## CHAPTER XXXI

You too say that Christ taught the indifference of foods in such a way that he entirely removed all meats from his own disciples, while granting secular people generally everything that could be eaten; and that he asserted that nothing entering the mouth defiles them, because only the things that shamelessly come out of the mouth defile a person.

These are your words, drawn out and expressed with a lie all the more shameless because it is all the more obvious.

First, according to Christ’s judgment, if only those things defile a person that proceed from the mouth as evil, why did the disciples of Christ not also become defiled only by those things, so that it would not be necessary to prohibit them as though from unclean meats? [Note: The printed editions read “so that he would prohibit them”; the negative particle, supplied from manuscripts of good authority, has been added here.]

Or are secular people not defiled by what enters the mouth, but by what comes out of it? Then they are better protected against defilement than the saints, if both what enters and what comes out can defile the saints.

I would like these people to tell me what Christ ate and drank, since, in comparison with John, who neither ate nor drank, Christ declared himself to be one who ate and drank. For when he was rebuking the perversity of people who sought accusations in both cases, he said: “John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker’” [Note: Er., Lyon, and Venice read “a wine-drinking woman.” M.], “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:18–19).

We know John’s food and drink. It was not said that he drank nothing at all, but that he did not drink wine or strong drink (Luke 1:15); therefore he drank water. His food too was not entirely nonexistent, but consisted of locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3:4).

Why, then, was he called one who neither ate nor drank, unless it was because he did not use the kind of food by which the Jews lived? Therefore, unless the Lord used such food, he would not be called one who ate and drank in comparison with John.

Or perhaps the reason is that the Lord ate bread and vegetables, which John did not eat? It would be strange to call someone who ate locusts and honey “one who does not eat,” while calling someone who was content with bread and vegetables “one who eats.”

But speculate about the food as you wish. Certainly he would not have been called one who drank and was a wine-drinker unless he drank wine. Why, then, do you also consider this unclean? [Col. 0338] For you do not prohibit contact with these things on the grounds of temperance and the discipline of subduing the body, but because you say that they are unclean. You claim that they are filth and gall from the race of darkness, contrary to the Apostle, who says, “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15).

Behold those who dare to say that Christ was the teacher of the indifference of foods, yet claim that he prohibited his disciples from those things which they themselves consider unclean. Show us where he removed these things from his disciples, deceitful and wicked men. Yet the providence of God, who avenges the truth, has blinded you in such a way that you even remind us of the passage by which you are convicted.

For I cannot restrain myself from inserting the entire Gospel passage that this man wished to oppose to Moses, so that we may see there how false it is that the earlier Adimantus and now Faustus said that the Lord Jesus removed meats from his disciples’ diet and granted them to secular people generally [Note: Above, in the book Against Adimantus, chapter 15].

When he had answered those who accused the disciples of eating with unwashed hands, the Gospel continues in this way: “And he called the crowds to him and said, ‘Hear and understand. It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth that defiles a person.’ Then the disciples approached and said to him, ‘Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this saying, were scandalized?’”

Here, certainly, when questioned by his disciples, he ought, according to these people’s interpretation, to have explicitly taught them to abstain from all meats, so that his earlier statement—“It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth”—would appear to have been spoken to the crowds in one sense.

Let the Evangelist continue, then, and tell us what the Lord answered now—not the crowds, but his disciples. He answered: “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. And if the blind leads the blind, both will fall into a pit.”

This was evidently because, wishing to establish their own traditions, they did not understand the commandments of God. But the disciples had not yet asked their Teacher how they themselves should understand what he had said to the crowds.

Now this too takes place. For the Evangelist continues: “But Peter answered and said to him, ‘Explain this parable to us.’”

From this we understand that Peter thought the Lord had not spoken literally and openly when he said, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth,” but that, as usual, he wished to signify something through the obscurity of a parable.

Let us see, then, whether, when the disciples now question him more privately, he says what the Manichaeans want: that all meats are unclean and that they ought not to touch any of them.

What follows? He reproaches them for not yet understanding his plainly spoken words, and for thinking that what he had said literally was a parable. For the passage continues: “But he said, ‘Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the belly and is discharged into the latrine? But the things that proceed from the mouth come from the heart, and those are what defile a person. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person’” (Matthew 15:10–20).

## CHAPTER XXXII

Certainly now the exposed deceit [Col. 0339] departs convicted. Certainly it is now clear that the Lord did not teach one thing to the crowds about this matter and another thing privately to his disciples. Certainly it is evident without any doubt that the Manichaeans, not Moses, not Christ, are liars and deceivers; that the doctrine of both Testaments is there figured and here revealed, there foretold and here presented.

How, then, do they think that Catholics observe none of the things Moses wrote, when they observe absolutely everything—not now in figures, but in the realities that those figures foretold by signifying them?

For if there were one time for writing and another for reading, we would not rightly say that a reader failed to observe that Scripture because he himself did not form those written characters. Those characters had been figures of sounds, whereas he now uttered the sounds themselves; nevertheless, he was not occupied with forming those figures, but was reminded of them by looking at them.

The Jews did not believe Christ because they did not observe even those things that Moses had commanded not figuratively but openly. Hence Christ says to them: “You tithe mint and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the Law, mercy and judgment; straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel. These things you ought to do, and not omit the others” (Matthew 23:23–24).

This is also the meaning of the passage in which, by their traditions, they taught how God’s commandment was to be weakened—the commandment by which he had ordered honor to be shown to parents. On account of this pride and wickedness they deserved to be blinded, so that they would not understand the other things, because they impiously despised the things they did understand.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0339]

Do you see that I am not telling you, “If you are a Christian, believe Christ when he says that Moses wrote about him; and if you do not believe this, you are not [Col. 0340] a Christian”?  [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The editions of Erasmus and Louvain read: “Do you see? I certainly will not say this to you now.” The manuscript reading is preferable.]

You yourself must see what you think about yourself, since you ask to be instructed about Christ as though you were a Gentile or a Jew. Nevertheless, I have neither avoided this nor left any entrance to error open to you, insofar as I could close them all.

Nor have I allowed to remain open that precipice into which you blind people cast yourselves when you say that something in the Gospel is false wherever your heresy finds no way out—so that nothing remains for you by which you could return to the place where you might believe Christ, and where this voice of pestilence could not be brought against you.

Indeed, you wish to be instructed in the manner of the Christian Thomas, whom Christ did not reject when he doubted about him, but, in order to heal the wounds of his soul, showed him the scars of his body. These are your words. It is good that you demand to be instructed in this way. For I was very much afraid that you would also insist that this passage in the Gospel was false.

Believe, then, in Christ’s scars. For if those scars were real, those wounds too had been real; and real wounds could not have been possessed except by real flesh. This one truth overturns your entire error.

But if Christ displayed false scars to a doubting disciple, then you call him a deceiver for teaching in this way, and you wish to be deceived by learning in this way. But since no one wishes to be deceived, while many wish to deceive, I understand you to wish rather to teach deceitfully by Christ’s example than to learn deceitfully by Thomas’s example.

Therefore, if you believe that Christ deceived the doubting disciple with false scars, who would wish to believe you as a teacher, rather than beware of you as a deceiver? But if that disciple touched Christ’s real scars, you are compelled to confess the reality of Christ’s flesh also.

Thus you will not remain a Manichaean if you believe as Thomas did; but you will remain an unbeliever if you do not believe even as Thomas did (John 20:27–28).

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

[Col. 0339]

## CHAPTER I

Faustus said:

Why do you not accept the Law and the Prophets, since Christ said that he had not come to abolish them but to fulfill them (Matthew 5:17)?

Who testifies that Jesus said this? Matthew.

Where did he say it? On the mountain.

In whose presence? In the presence of Peter, Andrew, James, and John—only these four. For he had not yet chosen the others, nor Matthew himself.

So, of these four, did one—namely John—write a Gospel?

Yes.

Does he mention this anywhere himself?

Nowhere.

How, then, did Matthew write what John, who was on the mountain, does not testify, when Matthew followed Jesus only after a considerable interval, after Jesus had descended from the mountain?

Accordingly, the first question is whether Jesus said anything of this sort, since a reliable witness is silent while a less reliable one speaks. For the moment, let us allow that Matthew has done us an injury, until we also prove that he did not write these things, but that someone else—whoever he was—wrote them under his name. This is also shown by the indirect narrative in Matthew’s own reading.

For what does he say? “And as Jesus was passing by, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew, and he called him; and he immediately rose and followed him” (Matthew 9:9).

Who, then, writing about [Col. 0340] himself, would say, “He saw a man, and called him, and he followed him,” rather than say, “He saw me, and called me, and I followed him”? This can only be because it is evident that Matthew did not write these things, but someone else under his name.

Therefore, even if Matthew had written this, it would not be true, because he was not present when Jesus spoke these words on the mountain. How much less should it be believed when Matthew did not write them either, but someone else under the names both of Jesus and of Matthew?

## CHAPTER II

Moreover, from the very speech in which he commands people not to think that he came to abolish the Law, it may rather be understood that he did abolish it. For the Jews could not have suspected anything of the sort if he had done nothing of the kind.

But he says, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law.” Very well, then: suppose the Jews had said to him, “But what are you doing that could lead us to suspect this?” Is it because you deride circumcision, violate the Sabbath, reject sacrifices, and confuse the foods?

This, then, is the meaning of “Do not think so.” And what could have been done more extensively or more clearly for the destruction of the Law and the Prophets?

Or if this is to fulfill the Law, what would it be to abolish it?

Furthermore, the Law and the Prophets do not even rejoice in being fulfilled, so complete and consummate do they seem to themselves. Their author and father is no less indignant when anything is added to them than when anything is taken away, so that, writing in Deuteronomy, he says: “These commandments that I give you today, Israel, you shall observe; and take care not to turn away from them, neither to the left nor to the right; do not add anything to them, nor take anything away; but you shall persevere in them, so that your God may bless you” (Deuteronomy 5:32; 12:32).

Therefore, whether Jesus added something to the Law and the Prophets in order to fulfill them, he appears to have fallen to the right; or whether he removed something in order to destroy them, he appears to have fallen to the left. In either case he certainly offends the author of the Law. Thus this statement either signifies something else, or it is false.

## CHAPTER III
AUGUSTINE replied: O astonishing madness [Note: [Col. 0341] Some manuscripts: “O pitiable madness!”]—to refuse to believe Matthew when he recounts something about Christ, yet to insist on believing Manichaeus! If Matthew was not present when Christ said, “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17), and therefore he is not to be believed, was Manichaeus present, or had he even been born, when Christ appeared among human beings? According to this rule of your faith, then, you ought not to have believed him when he testified about Christ. We, however, do not say that Manichaeus is not to be believed because he was not present at Christ’s words and deeds and was born long afterward, but because he speaks about Christ against Christ’s disciples and against the Gospel, which has been established on their authority.

For we have the testimony of the Apostle, who saw in the Holy Spirit that such people would come. Hence he said to the faithful: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9). For if no one speaks truthfully about Christ except one who saw and heard him while he was present, then today no one speaks truthfully about him. But if truth is spoken about him today to his faithful because those who saw and heard him disseminated these things either by preaching or by writing, why could Matthew not have heard true things about Christ from the mouth of John, his fellow disciple, when John was present and Matthew was not, if from John’s book we can speak truthfully about Christ—not only we, born so long afterward, but also others who will be born after us? For this reason not only Matthew’s Gospel, but also those of Luke and Mark, who followed the same disciples, have been received with no lesser authority.

Furthermore, the Lord himself could have narrated to Matthew what he had done with those whom he had called earlier, before he called Matthew. But, someone may object, John himself ought to have included this in his Gospel if he had heard the Lord say it, since he was present when it was said. As though it could not have happened that, although he could not write down everything he had heard from the Lord, he omitted this among the other things he passed over, while he was occupied with writing other matters. Did he not conclude his Gospel in this way: “Jesus did many other things, which, if they were written down one by one, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would be written” (John 21:25)? Here he plainly shows that he knowingly omitted many things.

But if you take pleasure in John’s authority concerning the Law and the Prophets, [Col. 0342] believe John when he bears witness to the Law and the Prophets. He wrote that Isaiah saw Christ’s glory (John 12:41). In his Gospel you also find the passage we discussed shortly before: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). Your evasions are beaten down on every side. Say openly that you do not believe Christ’s Gospel; for when you believe in the Gospel what you wish and refuse to believe what you wish, you believe yourselves rather than the Gospel.

## CHAPTER IV

What an ingenious point Faustus thought he had made when he wished Matthew not to be believed to have written this, because, when speaking of his own calling, he did not say, “He saw me and said to me, ‘Follow me,’” but, “He saw Matthew and said to him, ‘Follow me’” (Matthew 9:9). I do not know whether he said this out of an error of ignorance or according to his customary deceit. I would not consider him so ignorant that he had neither read nor heard that writers of historical events, when they come to their own person, commonly describe themselves as though they were narrating the story of someone else.

I therefore think that he wished to cast a fog before the ignorant—not as an ignorant man, but in the hope of catching more people who did not know this. Examples of this kind of narration are indeed found in secular histories; but there is no need for me to remind our people or refute him by appealing to another literary genre. Shortly before this, he himself cited certain testimonies from the books of Moses in such a way that he did not deny Moses had written them—in fact, he affirmed it—but argued that they did not pertain to Christ.

Let him therefore read in those same books what Moses wrote about himself, and see whether he wrote, “I said,” or “I did this or that,” rather than, “Moses said” (Exodus 3:3), and “Moses did” (Exodus 7:6); or, “The Lord called me,” or “The Lord said to me,” rather than, “The Lord called Moses” (Leviticus 1:1), and “The Lord said to Moses” (Exodus 4:19)—and everything else in the same manner.

Thus Matthew also wrote about himself as though about someone else. John did the same. Near the end of his book he speaks in this way: “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved, who had reclined at the supper on his breast and had said to the Lord, ‘Who is the one who will betray you?’” Did he perhaps say here, “Peter turned and saw me”? Or do they perhaps therefore think that John did not write this Gospel either? Yet shortly afterward he says: “This is the disciple who bears witness about Jesus and who wrote these things; and we know that his testimony is true” (John 21:20, 24). Did he say, “I am the disciple who bear witness about Jesus and who wrote these things; and we know that my testimony is true”? It is plainly evident that this was the custom of writers when they narrated events.

Who would be able to enumerate how many things the Lord himself says about himself in the same manner? “When the Son of Man comes,” he says, “do you suppose he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8). He did not say, “When I come, do you suppose I will find it?” Again: “The Son of Man came eating and drinking” (Matthew 11:19); he did not say, “I came.” And: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25); he did not say, “My voice.” There are many examples of this kind.

Hence I now think that what has been said [Col. 0343] is sufficient both to admonish the earnest and to convict the slanderous.

## CHAPTER V

Who does not see how weak is the argument that he makes when he says that Christ could not have said, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them,” unless he had already done something that could give rise to such a suspicion? It is as though we denied that Christ could have appeared to Jews who did not understand him to be a destroyer of the Law and the Prophets. Yet this is precisely why he, who is truthful and is the Truth, could not have been speaking of another Law and other Prophets when he said that he would not abolish them, but of those whom they suspected him of abolishing.

This is sufficiently confirmed by what follows there, where he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things come to pass. Therefore whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

When he said this, he was thinking of the Pharisees, who abolished the Law by their deeds and taught it by their words. Concerning them he says elsewhere: “Whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matthew 23:3). Therefore he continues here in this way: “For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:17–20)—that is, unless you do and teach what they do not do but teach, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, the Law that the Pharisees taught but did not practice is the very Law that Christ says he did not come to abolish but to fulfill. For it pertains to the chair of Moses, in which the Pharisees sit. Since they speak but do not act, they are to be heard, but not imitated.

## CHAPTER VI

Faustus does not understand—or perhaps pretends not to understand—what it means to fulfill the Law, since he thinks it must be understood as an addition of words, because it is written that nothing should be added to God’s Scripture or taken away from it (Deuteronomy 12:32). Hence he says that what is commended as so complete that nothing may be added or subtracted ought not to be fulfilled.

Such people do not know how the Law is fulfilled: by living as the Law commanded. “The fullness of the Law is love,” as the Apostle says (Romans 13:10). The Lord was pleased both to display and to grant this love by sending the Holy Spirit to his faithful. Hence the same Apostle also says: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). The Lord himself says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35).

The Law, then, is fulfilled either when the things commanded there are done, or when the things prophesied there are manifested. For “the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). When the Law is fulfilled, it becomes grace and truth. [Col. 0344] Grace pertains to the fullness of love; truth pertains to the fulfillment of the prophecies.

And because both come through Christ, he did not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them—not so that what was lacking might be added to the Law, but so that what had been written might come to pass. His own words bear witness to this. He did not say, “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until what is lacking is added,” but, “until all things come to pass.”

# BOOK EIGHTEEN

[Col. 0343]

## CHAPTER I

FAUSTUS said: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17). But unless this means something else, you should know that believing this was said by Christ is no less contrary to you than it is to me. Both of us are Christians under this belief, because we have thought that Christ came for the destruction of the Law and the Prophets. Even if you do not wish to confess this for the moment in words, you indicate it by your actions.

For this is why you yourself disregard the commandments of the Law and the Prophets; and this is why we both admit that Jesus established the New Testament. What else do we thereby admit than the destruction of the Old Testament? Since this is so, how shall we believe that Christ said this unless we first condemn ourselves for our former foolish opinion, return to repentance, submit ourselves again to the Law and the Prophets, and take care to observe their commandments, whatever they may be?

When we have done this, then at last we shall truly believe that Jesus said he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. But now it is false, since you do not believe it any more than I do, though you alone accuse me.

## CHAPTER II

But let us grant that it was permissible to have erred in the past. What now, finally? Is it agreeable to place oneself under the Law, if Christ did not so much [Note: [Col. 0344] Perhaps: “now.”] abolish it as fulfill it? Is it agreeable to be circumcised—that is, to mark one’s shameful parts with a shameful sign—and to believe that God delights in such sacraments? Is it agreeable to undertake the rest of the Sabbaths and to insert one’s hands into Saturnian chains?

Is it agreeable, for the gluttony of the Jewish demon—for it is not the gluttony of God [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Lovaniensis has: “for the gluttony of the Jewish demons, for it is not of God”]—to slaughter now bulls, now rams, now even goats, not to mention human beings, with knives; and, for the sake of which we have hated idols, to practice this even more cruelly under the Prophets and the Law?

Finally, is it agreeable to regard some of the foods of beasts as clean, and to count others among the unclean and polluted, among which the Law and the Prophets declare pork to be especially defiled?

You will certainly deny that any of these things ought to be done if we wish to remain what we are, since you hear Christ saying that the one who has been circumcised becomes a son of Gehenna twice over (Matthew 23:15). You see that he himself neither kept the Sabbath nor commanded it to be kept anywhere. Likewise, you hear him affirming concerning foods that a person is not defiled by any of the things that enter the mouth, but rather by the things that proceed from the [Col. 0345] mouth (Matthew 15:11).

You also hear him frequently speaking about sacrifices: “God desires mercy, not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). If these things are so, where will be that claim that he did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them? If he said it, he either said it meaning something else, or—God forbid—he said it while lying, or he did not say it at all.

But let no one, at least no Christian, say that Jesus lied. Therefore it was either said differently, or it was not said at all.

## CHAPTER III

Nevertheless, the Manichaean faith has already made me safe against the difficulty of this chapter. At the outset it persuaded me not to believe indiscriminately everything that is read as having been written in the name of the Savior, but to test whether such things are true, sound, and uncorrupted. For there are very many weeds that some nocturnal sower has scattered through nearly all the Scriptures, to infect the good seed (Matthew 13:25).

Therefore this saying will not frighten me either, even though it bears the inscription of a revered name, because I am still permitted, according to my established purpose, to test whether it belongs to the sower of the day and to the good seed, or to that nocturnal and most evil one.

But what will you do, since you believe everything recklessly, condemn reason as a gift of nature because it comes from human beings, regard judging between truth and falsehood as a religious offense, and fear separating good from its opposite no less than infants fear bogeys? [Note: [Col. 0345] Erasmus and Lovaniensis here and later, chapter 7, read *lamiae* (“lamias”). Ambrosianus and nearly all the manuscripts consistently read *maniae*. These are commonly called things that frighten children, and in Isidore’s Glossary they are described as images of terrors. It is evident that *lamiae* has the same meaning here.]

What will you do when necessity forces you into the narrow confines of this chapter, when a Jew—or someone else who understands this statement—confronts you and asks why you do not observe the commandments of the Law and the Prophets, since Christ says that he did not come to abolish them but to fulfill them? You will necessarily either submit to empty superstition, declare the chapter false, or deny that you are Christ’s disciple.

## CHAPTER IV

AUGUSTINE replied: Since you repeat what has so often been exploded and refuted, we too, who have refuted these things, will not be reluctant to repeat our answer. Christians do not perform the things from the Law and the Prophets that were signs of the things they do perform. Those things were figures of future realities, and once those realities had been revealed and presented through Christ, the figures had to be removed, so that precisely by their removal the Law and the Prophets might also be fulfilled.

For it was written there that God would give a New Testament: “Not like the one I gave to their fathers,” he says (Jeremiah 31:32). That people, because of their stony heart, had received many commandments more suited to them than intrinsically good, though these too foreshadowed and prophesied future things. At that time they were observed by people who did not understand them.

But when the realities they signified came and were disclosed, those things are no longer commanded to be performed; they are read so that they may be understood. Hence it is also said there concerning a future event: “I will take away their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19)—that is, not a heart without understanding, but a heart with understanding.

From this the Apostle [Col. 0346] drew his statement: “Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). What else did he say than “a heart of flesh”? Since this too had been foretold, the Law and the Prophets would rather not be fulfilled if these observances were not removed from our practice, because what they had foretold would not take place. But when this also takes place, they are understood to be fulfilled precisely where you think they are not fulfilled.

## CHAPTER V

Nor does your taunt frighten us when you call the Sabbath rest Saturnian chains. It is empty and foolish; you would not have thought of saying this unless you worship the sun on the day you call the day of the Sun. But just as we call that same day the Lord’s Day and venerate in it not the sun but the Lord’s resurrection, so the Sabbath rest was observed by the fathers without worship of Saturn, when it was proper for it to be observed in that way. For it was a shadow of future things, as the Apostle testifies (Colossians 2:17).

The Gentiles gave the days whose number, seven, returns in a cycle the names of their gods. Concerning them the Apostle says that they “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25). In this respect you imitate them as well, except that you worship with them the two brighter luminaries, while you do not worship the other stars with them.

They also gave the months the names of their gods. Out of honor for Romulus, whom they believed to be the son of Mars, they dedicated the first month to Mars and called it March. From this they called the second April, not from the name of any god, but from the thing itself, as though *Aperilem*, because at that time a great deal of growth opens into flower. The third month they called May because they worship Maia, the mother of Mercury, as a goddess. The fourth they called June after Juno. The remaining months, down to December, they named from numbers.

Among these, Quintilis and Sextilis were renamed July and August after men to whom they had decreed divine honors. For the seventh month is September, and the remaining months, as I said, are designated in order by names derived from numbers, down to December. January was named after Janus; February after the Februa, the sacred rites of the Luperci.

Do you therefore want people to say that you worship Mars in the month of March? For in that month you celebrate your Bema with great festivity. [Note: Compare the book *Against the Epistle of Fundamen­tus*, chapter 8.] But if you think that in March you are permitted to consider something other than Mars, why do you try to introduce Saturn into the divine Scriptures because the Gentiles called the seventh day, which was named Sabbath from rest, the day of Saturn? Surely you now see how impiously you rave.

## CHAPTER VI

As for sacrifices of animals, who among us does not know that they were imposed more appropriately on a perverse people than offered to a God who desired them? Yet even in these sacrifices there were figures of us, because there is no cleansing for us and no reconciliation with God for us without blood. But Christ is the reality of those figures; by his blood we have been redeemed and cleansed.

For in the figures of the divine utterances the bull was named on account of the power of the cross, with whose horns he scattered the ungodly; the ram on account of the primacy of innocence; and the goat on account of the likeness of sinful flesh, so that by sin he might condemn sin (Romans 8:3). If you recall any other kind of sacrifice more explicitly, I shall show you that Christ too was prophesied in it.

Accordingly, whether circumcision, the Sabbath, distinctions among foods, or the offering of sacrifices, all these were figures and prophecies concerning us. Christ came not to abolish them but to fulfill them, when he brought to completion the things announced beforehand through them. Consider whom you are contradicting: the Apostle—or rather, I speak from the Apostle—who says, “All these things were figures of us” (1 Corinthians 10:6).

## CHAPTER VII

For just as Manichaeus taught you impious perversity, so that you accept from the Gospel whatever does not obstruct your heresy and refuse whatever does obstruct it, the Apostle taught us pious foresight, [Col. 0347] so that anyone who announces to us anything beyond what we received should be accursed (Galatians 1:8–9).

Therefore Catholic Christians also count you among the weeds, because the Lord explained what the weeds are: not certain falsehoods inserted into true Scriptures, as you interpret it, but human beings who are sons of the evil one—that is, imitators of diabolical falsehood (Matthew 13:39).

They do not believe everything recklessly; and for this reason they do not believe Manichaeus or the other heretics. They do not condemn reason as coming from human beings; rather, they prove that what you call reason is error. They do not regard judging between truth and falsehood as impious; [Col. 0348] therefore they judge your sect to be most false and the Catholic faith to be most true.

They do not fear separating good from its opposite; rather, they understand that evil is not a nature, because it is contrary to nature. They do not believe in some nation of darkness that arose from its beginning against the divine kingdoms and rebelled against them—a nation that truly brought more fear to your god than bogeys bring to infants, since you say that he placed a veil before himself so as not to behold his own members captured and ravaged by that power.

Therefore they suffer no difficulty from this chapter on the grounds that they do not observe the commandments of the Law and the Prophets. For through the grace of Christ they possess the lawful love of God and neighbor, on which two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew 22:40). And whatever was prophetically foreshadowed there—whether through historical events, the celebration of sacraments, or forms of speech—they recognize as fulfilled in Christ and in the Church.

Thus we neither submit to empty superstition, nor say that this Gospel chapter is false, nor deny that we are Christ’s disciples. For, according to the reasoning of truth that I have explained so often to the best of my ability, he did not say that Christ came to abolish and fulfill any Law or any Prophets other than those upheld by Catholic authority.

# BOOK NINETEEN

[Col. 0347]

## CHAPTER I

FAUSTUS said: “I have not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets, but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). Behold, I now agree that this was said. Yet we must ask why Jesus said it: whether to flatter the fury of the Jews, because they were indignant when they saw their sacred institutions trampled by him and considered him, as though he were impious and insane, not even worthy to be heard, much less followed; or whether he said it to instruct and train us Gentiles who believed in him to submit patiently and obediently to the yoke of the commandments that the Law and the Prophets of the Jews would impose upon our necks.

But I do not think that even you believe that Jesus uttered this statement in order to bind us to the Law of the Hebrews and to the Prophets. Therefore, if that was not the reason for his saying it, the other reason I mentioned must be intended.

No one who is aware of it is unaware that the Jews were always intensely hostile to Christ in words and deeds. When they inferred from these things that he was abolishing their Law and Prophets, they necessarily became indignant. Therefore, in order to restrain their fury, it was not inappropriate for him to say that they should not think he had come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it. Nor was he lying or deceiving in this, since he named the Law without qualification and absolutely. [Note: [Col. 0347] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read, “so that they might reckon it.” M.]

## CHAPTER II

There are three kinds of law. One is the law of the Hebrews, which Paul calls the law of sin and death (Romans 8:2). Another is the law of the Gentiles, which he calls natural: “For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, [Col. 0348] do by nature the things of the law, they are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written on their hearts” (Romans 2:14–15).

The third kind of law is truth. Signifying this in the same way, the Apostle says: “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has liberated me from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2).

Since there are three laws, and Jesus assures us that he did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, considerable care and diligence are required to understand which of these laws he meant. Likewise, there are three groups of Prophets: some are Jewish, some Gentile, and some prophets of truth.

No one will ask about the Jewish prophets; they are well known. If anyone doubts that the Gentiles have prophets, let him listen to Paul, who, writing to Titus about the Cretans, says: “One of their own prophets said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies’” (Titus 1:12). Therefore there can be no doubt that the Gentiles too have their prophets.

That truth has its own prophets is indicated both by Paul and by Jesus. Jesus says: “Behold, I send you wise men and prophets, and some of them you will kill in various places” (Matthew 23:34). Paul says: “The Lord appointed some first as apostles, then prophets” (1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11).

## CHAPTER III

Since the Law is divided into three parts, and the Prophets likewise, it is not entirely clear which of them Jesus meant. Nevertheless, it can be inferred from what follows.

For if he had immediately mentioned circumcision, Sabbaths, sacrifices, and Hebrew observances, and had introduced something concerning their fulfillment, there would have been no doubt that he was speaking of the Law and Prophets of the Jews, [Col. 0349] that he had not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.

But when he mentions none of these things and instead lists only the more ancient commandments—“You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not swear falsely”—and these had existed from ancient times among the nations, as can readily be demonstrated, having formerly been promulgated through Enoch, Seth, and the other righteous men like them, to whom illustrious angels entrusted the same commandments in order to restrain human savagery—who would not think that he was speaking of the law of truth and its prophets?

Finally, his fulfillment is also proved by what he promised concerning these same commandments. What does he say? “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; but I say to you, do not even become angry.” This is fulfillment. “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you, do not even lust.” This is fulfillment. “It was said, ‘You shall not swear falsely’; but I say to you, do not swear at all.” This too is fulfillment.

In these sayings he confirms the earlier commandments and adds what was lacking. But when he seemed to mention certain Jewish commandments, he not only did not fulfill them but utterly uprooted them by prescribing their opposites.

What follows? “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth’; but I say to you, whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also.” This is now destruction. Again: “It was said, ‘You shall love your friend and hate your enemy’; but I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” This too is destruction.

Again: “It was said, ‘Whoever wishes to divorce his wife, let him give her a writ of divorce’; but I say, whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery, and he will be an adulterer if he later marries another” (Matthew 5:21–44).

These, then, are plainly commandments of Moses, and for that reason they were destroyed. The earlier commandments of the ancient righteous were, for that reason, fulfilled.

If you too are pleased to understand it in this way, it will not be unreasonable to say that Jesus said he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. If this explanation does not please you, seek another; only do not be forced to say that Jesus lied, or to become a Jew. Do not continue even now to abolish the Law that he himself did not abolish.

## CHAPTER IV

Yet if some Nazarene—whom others call Symmachian—had brought this objection against me, namely, that Jesus said he had not come to abolish the Law, I would for a time have remained uncertain what answer to give him. And not without reason: he came bearing the Law and the Prophets upon both body and mind.

For the people I have mentioned carry circumcision, observe the Sabbath, and abstain from pork and other such things prescribed by the Law, while professing, at least in name, to be Christians. They too have been deceived, as may be understood, by this very chapter, because Christ said that he had come not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

Therefore, while I would have had, as I said, a considerable struggle with such people until I had demolished the difficulty of this chapter, I do not fear engaging you. I rely on no strength, but on the fact that you challenge me more through shamelessness than through argument; I consider myself more likely to be tested by you than compelled to believe that Christ said something I do not see you believing either.

For you do not bring forward [Col. 0350] any of the things by which the Law and the Prophets appear not to have been abolished but fulfilled. Yet on the basis of this chapter you reproach me as sluggish and a prevaricator.

Or do you now boast of that obscene sign of mutilated groins, like a Jew or a Nazarene? Or do you raise your brow over observing the Sabbaths? Or do you rejoice inwardly in abstaining from pork? Or, finally, do you exult that by the blood of victims and the odors of burnt offerings you have sated the God of the Jews?

If you have done none of these things, why do you insist that Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it?

## CHAPTER V

For this reason I give unending thanks to my teacher, who held me back when I was similarly slipping, so that I might be a Christian today.

When I was imprudently reading this chapter, I too, like you, had almost decided to become a Jew. And not without reason. For if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, and fulfillment is never spoken of in relation to an empty vessel but to one that is full, it seemed to me that only an Israelite could become a Christian—one who came to Christ filled for the most part with the Law and the Prophets, so that he might be filled with what he still appeared capable of containing, provided that Christ did not abolish the earlier things. Otherwise this would not be fulfillment in relation to him, but exhaustion.

But as I came from the Gentiles, I thought that I had approached Christ in vain, because I brought nothing of the kind that he could fulfill in me by adding to it. Seeking, therefore, what that earlier measure might be, I found the Sabbaths, circumcision, sacrifices, new moons, baptisms, eating of unleavened bread, distinctions among foods and drinks, regulations concerning clothing, and other matters too numerous to review.

I therefore thought that this was what was meant, and nothing else, by Christ’s saying that he had not come to abolish these things but to fulfill them. And not without reason: for what is the Law without commandments? What are the Prophets without their prophetic utterances? [Note: [Col. 0350] One Paris manuscript reads, “without prophetic utterances” with a different spelling.]

Furthermore, I found there a bitter curse pronounced against those who did not persevere in all the things written in the book of that Law, so as to do them (Deuteronomy 27:26). Fearing that curse as God’s curse on the one hand, and hearing Christ, as though he were God’s son, say on the other that he had not come to abolish those same things but to fulfill them, consider whether anything could still have prevented me from becoming a Jew.

But the venerable faith of Manichaeus rescued me from this danger.

## CHAPTER VI

Yet I ask what confidence you have when you raise these objections, or why you think that only this is contrary to me when it seems no less contrary to you. If it is not Christ’s role to abolish the Law and the Prophets, then neither is it the role of Christians. Why, then, do you abolish these same things?

Or do you secretly admit that you are not Christians? Why do you profane by every kind of work that sacred Sabbath day which, as the Law and all the Prophets testify, even God himself, the maker of the world, kept as a day of rest (Genesis 2:2), without fearing either the death penalty that he established against those who violate it or the disgrace of the curse?

Why do you also protect your loins from that disgraceful sign of circumcision, honored by the entire Law and the Prophets, and [Col. 0351] especially by Abraham after his reputed faith? Especially since the God of the Jews declares that everyone from his people who has not been marked with this disgrace will perish (Genesis 17:9–14).

Why do you despise the lawful sacrifices, which neither Moses and the Prophets under the Law nor Abraham under his faith regarded as secondary? Why do you pollute your souls by indifference toward foods, if, as you believe, Christ did not come to abolish any of these things but to fulfill them?

Why do you profane the annual right of unleavened bread and the sacred slaughter of the lamb, which the Law and the Prophets command to be observed forever? Why, finally, do you not carefully avoid violating the new moons, baptisms, the Feast of Booths, and the other carnal sacraments of the Law and the Prophets, if Christ did not destroy them at all?

Therefore I would not unreasonably say that if you want the rationale for your contempt of these things to stand, you must either deny that you are Christ’s disciples or finally admit that he first destroyed all these things.

Once you have confessed this, it follows that you must either falsely admit that it was written that he said he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, or acknowledge that he signified something quite different from what you think.

## CHAPTER VII
AUGUSTINE replied:

Since you now admit that Christ said, “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them” (Matt. 5:17), for it seems difficult to you to oppose the authority of the Gospel, let it also seem difficult to you to oppose the Apostle, who says, “All these things were figures for us” (1 Cor. 10:6); and who likewise says of Christ, “For he was not Yes and No, but Yes was in him: for however many the promises of God are, in him is Yes” (2 Cor. 1:19–20)—that is, in him they were presented and fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed editions read *Quia non fuit in illo* (“For there was not in him”); *in illo* (“in him”) is absent from the manuscripts.] Then, without obscurity, you will see both what Law he came to fulfill and in what manner he fulfilled it.

Nor will you continue to stretch yourself across three kinds of law and three kinds of Prophets, looking for a way out and finding none. For it is manifest—and the writing of the New Testament often bears witness to this more clearly than daylight—which Law and which Prophets Christ did not come to abolish, but to fulfill. It is that very Law which was given through Moses; grace and truth came into being through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). It is, I say, that very Law given through Moses, concerning whom Christ says, “For he wrote about me” (ibid. 5:46).

Certainly it is that very Law which “entered in so that the trespass might increase” (Rom. 5:20)—a statement which, understanding nothing, you are accustomed to keep on your lips as a reproach against it. Read there, therefore, and see that it is the same Law of which it is said: “So then, the Law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good. Therefore, did what is good become death to me? By no means. But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (ibid. 7:12–13).

For the Law did not command sin, so that sin might increase when it entered in. Rather, the addition of a holy, righteous, and good commandment made proud people, who attributed much to themselves, also guilty of transgression. Thus, having been humbled in this way, they might learn that they belonged to grace through faith, so that they would no longer be subjected to the Law through guilt, but joined to the Law through righteousness.

For the same Apostle says: “Before faith came, we were kept confined under the Law, shut up until the faith that was later to be revealed. Therefore,” he says, “the Law was our pedagogue toward Christ Jesus; but after faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue” (Gal. 3:23–25), because the guilt of the Law no longer binds us, since we have been liberated by grace.

Before we had been humbled and received spiritual grace, the letter did nothing but put us to death, commanding what we could not fulfill. Hence he also says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Again, these are the words of the same Apostle: “For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the Law; but Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:21–22).

His words are also these: “For what was impossible for the Law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit” (Rom. 8:3–4).

[Note: [Col. 0352] Lov. reads *Legi* (“for the Law”); the other printed editions and the manuscripts read *Legis* (“of the Law”), in accordance with the Greek.]

[Note: [Col. 0352] The printed editions read *quae* (“which”); several manuscripts read *quia* (“because”).]

There you have what is meant by, “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.” Because the Law, by increasing sin when it commands what people cannot fulfill, also bound the proud under the guilt of transgression, the righteousness of the Law is fulfilled through the grace of the Spirit in those who learn from Christ to be meek and humble in heart—Christ, who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

Furthermore, since even for those who live under grace it is difficult in this mortal life to fulfill in every respect what is written in the Law, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17), he, having been made a priest through the sacrifice of his flesh, obtains forgiveness for us, fulfilling the Law also in this respect: whatever we are less able to accomplish through our weakness is restored through the perfection of him whose members we have become.

[Note: [Col. 0352] Some manuscripts read *recuretur* (“may be restored”), rather than *recuperetur* (“may be recovered/restored”).]

Hence John says: “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2).

## CHAPTER VIII

He fulfilled the prophecies when the promises of God became reality in him. I mentioned this shortly before from the Apostle, who says, “For however many the promises of God are, in him there is Yes.” He says the same thing again: “For I say that Christ became a servant of circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers” (Rom. 15:8).

Whatever, therefore, was promised in the Prophets—whether openly, or through figures in words or actions—was fulfilled in him, who did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets, but to fulfill them.

You do not understand this because, if certain deeds and observances that were figures announcing what was to come were still performed by Christians, nothing would be signified except that what was then announced through those figures had not yet come. For what is still announced as future either has not yet come, or, if it has already come, is announced in vain or falsely.

Therefore, precisely where it seems to you that Christ did not fulfill the Prophets—because Christians do not perform certain things that the Prophets instituted for the Hebrews to perform—it is rather proved that he did fulfill them. Indeed, everything that was prophesied through such figures has been fulfilled to such an extent that it is no longer prophesied through them.

This also pertains to what the Lord himself says: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). The Law, which confined transgressors under an increasing guilt until the faith that was later revealed, became grace through Jesus Christ, through whom grace abounded beyond measure. Thus it was fulfilled through liberating grace, whereas it was not fulfilled through the commanding letter.

Likewise, within the Law itself, the whole prophecy that promised the coming of the Savior—not only in words but also through the figures of certain actions—became reality through Jesus Christ. For “the Law was given through Moses; but grace and truth came into being through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

From his coming onward, therefore, the kingdom of God began to be proclaimed, because “the Law and the Prophets were until John”: the Law, to make people guilty who would desire salvation; the Prophets, to promise the Savior.

But who does not know that other prophets arose in the Church after Christ’s ascension? Concerning them Paul says: “And God has appointed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers” (1 Cor. 12:28), and so forth.

The statement “The Law and the Prophets were until John” was not spoken about those prophets, but about those who prophesied Christ’s first coming. Once that coming had been fulfilled, it could not still be prophesied as future.

## CHAPTER IX

Accordingly, when you ask why a Christian is no longer circumcised in the flesh, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: rather, a Christian is no longer circumcised for the very reason that Christ has already fulfilled what was prophesied through circumcision itself.

The stripping away of carnal generation, which was represented in that act, has already been fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection; what is to occur in our resurrection is commended to us through the sacrament of Baptism. For the sacrament of new life was not to be entirely removed, since the future resurrection of the dead still remains for us; nevertheless, it had to be changed for the better through the succeeding sacrament of Baptism, because what had never before occurred had now occurred: an example of future eternal life was given to us in Christ’s resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0353] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read: “that is, with Baptism succeeding.”]

When you ask why a Christian does not observe the Sabbath rest, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: rather, a Christian does not observe it for the very reason that Christ has already fulfilled what was prophesied through that figure.

For in him we have the Sabbath-rest, who said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

## CHAPTER X

When you ask why a Christian does not observe the distinction among foods prescribed in the Law, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: rather, a Christian does not observe it for the very reason that Christ has already fulfilled what was prophesied through those figures, not admitting into his body—what he predestined in his saints for eternal life—whatever was signified through those animals in human conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0354] The printed editions read *quod corpus* (“what body”); the word *corpus* (“body”) is not repeated in the manuscripts.]

When you ask why a Christian does not offer to God sacrifices of flesh and blood from slaughtered animals, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: rather, a Christian should no longer offer these things for the very reason that Christ fulfilled through the offering of his flesh and blood what was prophesied to them through such figures of things.

When you ask why a Christian does not observe unleavened bread as the Jews do, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: rather, he does not observe this for the very reason that Christ fulfilled what was prophesied through that figure, demonstrating new life after the leaven of the old life had been purged (1 Cor. 5:7).

When you ask why a Christian does not celebrate Passover with the flesh of a lamb, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: rather, a Christian no longer celebrates Passover in this way for the very reason that Christ, the spotless Lamb, fulfilled through his passion what was foretold by that figure.

When you ask for what reason a Christian does not celebrate the new moons commanded in the Law, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: rather, a Christian no longer celebrates them for the very reason that Christ has already fulfilled what they were celebrated to announce.

For the celebration of the new moon announced the new creation, about which the Apostle says: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17).

When you ask why a Christian does not observe the baptisms prescribed in the Law for each kind of impurity, if Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, I answer: the Christian does not observe these things precisely because they were figures of things to come, which Christ fulfilled.

For he came to bury us with himself through Baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life (Rom. 6:4).

When you ask why the Feast of Tabernacles is not a Christian solemnity, if the Law was fulfilled rather than abolished by Christ, I answer: the faithful are God’s tabernacle, in whom, joined together by charity and somehow compacted into one, he deigns to dwell. Therefore, it is all the more fitting that Christians do not observe that feast, because Christ has already fulfilled in his Church what that figure prophetically promised.

## CHAPTER XI

For the present, in accordance with the task undertaken, we have touched on these matters briefly, as far as we could, so that they might not be passed over in silence. When examined part by part and point by point, they have made many large books, showing nothing other than Christ as the subject of prophecy.

[Note: [Col. 0354] Some manuscripts read *facerent* (“would make”) rather than *fecerunt* (“have made”).]

Thus everything from that Scripture which you think is not observed by Christians because Christ abolished it is found, for that very reason, not to be observed by Christians because Christ fulfilled it.

The very observance of such figures was a prophecy of Christ. Therefore, what is surprising, what is absurd—or rather, what is not fitting and appropriate—if, after his coming, whatever was done for the purpose of announcing his coming ceased?

The figures of things that were observed so that, through their very observance, the coming Christ might be prophesied ought not, therefore, to be thought unfulfilled by Christ’s coming merely because they are not observed when he has come. Indeed, unless they were already fulfilled through Christ’s coming, they would still be observed.

People cannot be united into any name of religion, whether true or false, unless they are joined by some fellowship in visible signs or sacraments. The power of these sacraments is ineffably great, and therefore contempt for them makes people sacrilegious. For that without which piety cannot be perfected is impiously despised.

## CHAPTER XII

Nevertheless, since visible sacraments of piety can also exist among the impious—as we read that even Simon the Magician possessed holy Baptism (Acts 8:13)—such people become like those of whom the Apostle says: “Having the form of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5).

The power of piety, however, is the end of the commandment, namely, “love from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

Thus the Apostle Peter, speaking about the sacrament of the ark in which Noah’s household was saved from the Flood, says: “In the same way, Baptism now saves you by a corresponding figure.” And lest they think that the visible sacrament was sufficient for them—through which they possessed the form of piety—while by living wickedly they denied its power, he immediately added: “Not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience” (1 Pet. 3:21).

## CHAPTER XIII

Accordingly, the first sacraments, which were observed and celebrated according to the Law, were announcements of Christ who was to come. When Christ fulfilled them by his coming, they were removed—and removed for the very reason that they had been fulfilled. For he did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.

Other sacraments were instituted, greater in power, better in usefulness, easier in practice, and fewer in number, as the righteousness of faith was revealed and the sons of God, called to liberty, were freed from the yoke of slavery (Gal. 5:1, 13)—a yoke that was suited to a harsh people devoted to the flesh.

## CHAPTER XIV

Nevertheless, if the ancient righteous, who understood that the revelation of faith to come was being announced through those sacraments—and who, although it was still covered and hidden, nevertheless understood it by the gift of piety—already lived by it at that time, since in this life no one can be righteous except one who lives by faith (Rom. 1:17);

if, therefore, the ancient righteous were prepared to endure—and many of them did endure—all harsh and terrifying things for the sake of those anunciatory sacraments and figures of things not yet fulfilled;

if we praise the three youths and Daniel because they did not wish to be defiled by the king’s table (Dan. 1:8), although this ran counter to the sacramental practice of that time;

if we hold the Maccabees in the highest admiration because they refused to touch foods that Christians now lawfully eat (2 Macc. 7), since at that time such things were forbidden in accordance with the prophetic period;

how much more ready ought a Christian now to be to endure all things for Christ’s Baptism, Christ’s Eucharist, and Christ’s sign, since those things were promises of realities to be completed, whereas these are signs of realities already completed?

For what is still promised to the Church—that is, to the body of Christ—is both proclaimed in its manifestation and has already been completed in the very head of the body, the Savior, that is, in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5).

For what is promised except eternal life through the resurrection from the dead? This has already been completed in that flesh in which “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

At that time, therefore, faith was also hidden. For all the righteous and holy people of those times believed and hoped for the same things; and all those sacraments and that entire rite of sacred observances were promises.

Now, however, the faith in which the people were confined when they were kept under the Law has been revealed (Gal. 3:23). What is promised to the faithful in the judgment has already been completed in an example, through him who did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them.

## CHAPTER XV

Accordingly, among investigators of the holy Scriptures the question is raised whether the faith of the ancient righteous in Christ who would suffer and rise again—which they learned either through revelations or understood in the Prophets—benefited them as much as faith in him who has now suffered and risen benefits us; or whether the shedding of the blood of the Lamb of God, which occurred—as he himself says—for many, for the forgiveness of sins (Matt. 26:28), provided or added some benefit and purification even for those who, believing that this would happen, had departed from this life before it occurred; and whether his death also visited the dead for their liberation.

But to examine this question fully now, or to establish with confirmation whatever answer may be found in it, would be lengthy and unnecessary for this work.

## CHAPTER XVI

Meanwhile, it will be sufficient, against Faustus’s slanderous ignorance, to demonstrate how greatly those people are deluded who think that, when the signs and sacraments have been changed, the realities themselves are also different—although the prophetic rite announced and promised those realities, while the evangelical rite announced them as fulfilled.

The same error belongs to those who think that, although the realities are the same, they ought not to be announced as completed through sacraments different from those through which they had previously been announced as still to be completed.

For if the sounds of the words by which we speak are changed according to the times, and the same reality is announced differently as something to be done and as something already done—as in the case of the two words I have just spoken, *facienda* (“to be done”) and *facta* (“done”), which did not sound with equal intervals of duration or with the same or the same number of letters or syllables—what is surprising if Christ’s passion and resurrection were promised as future through one set of mystery-signs, and are announced as having already occurred through another, since the very words *futurum* (“future”) and *factum* (“done”), *passurus* (“about to suffer”) and *passus* (“having suffered”), *resurrecturus* (“about to rise”) and *resurrexit* (“he rose”), could neither be extended equally nor sound alike?

For what else are bodily sacraments except certain visible words—sacred indeed, yet changeable and temporal? God is eternal; yet the water and the entire bodily action performed when we baptize are not eternal: the action occurs and passes away.

[Note: [Col. 0357] Some manuscripts read: “when Baptism takes place and passes away.”]

Likewise, those syllables that sound and pass swiftly—when “God” is said—do not consecrate anything unless they are spoken. All these things occur and pass away; they sound and pass away. Yet the power that operates through them remains continually, and the spiritual gift signified through them is eternal.

Therefore, someone who says, “If Christ had not abolished the Law and the Prophets, the sacraments of the Law and the Prophets would remain in the assemblies and celebrations of Christians,” may also say, “If Christ had not abolished the Law and the Prophets, he would still be promised as one who would be born, suffer, and rise again.”

But he did not abolish them; rather, he fulfilled them precisely because he is no longer promised as one who will be born, suffer, and rise again—the things once proclaimed by those sacraments. Instead, it is announced that he has been born, has suffered, and has risen, which is what the sacraments performed by Christians now proclaim.

Therefore, he who came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them removed, through the fulfillment itself, those things by which what had already been established as fulfilled was still being promised. It is as though he removed the words “about to be born,” “about to suffer,” and “about to rise,” which were rightly spoken when these things were still future, and instituted the words “he was born,” “he suffered,” and “he rose,” which are rightly spoken once those things have been completed and, for that reason, removed.

## CHAPTER XVII

Just as these words were changed, so also those sacraments of the earlier people, because they had already been fulfilled through him who did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them, had to be removed and changed.

The Apostles allowed the first Christians who had believed from among the Jews to preserve their ancestral rite and tradition for a time, until they could gradually be persuaded to overcome so long-standing a custom and be brought to full understanding. Since they had been born and formed in this way, the Apostles also instructed those for whom it was necessary to act in a manner accommodating their slowness and customs.

This is why the Apostle circumcised Timothy, who had a Jewish mother and a Greek father, for the sake of those to whom he had come with Timothy (Acts 16:1–3). He himself also observed such a custom among them—not through deceitful pretense, but through prudent judgment.

For these practices were not harmful to people born and formed in this way, although they were no longer necessary for signifying future things. It was much more harmful to prohibit them as though they were harmful in people among whom they had to continue for a time.

Christ, who had come to fulfill all those prophecies, had found them initiated into these practices. But thereafter, those who were not held by such a necessity, and who came to him from the opposite wall, so to speak—that is, from uncircumcision—to the cornerstone that is Christ (Eph. 2:14, 20), were not to be compelled to any such practices.

If those who came from circumcision and were still devoted to such sacraments voluntarily wished, like Timothy, to provide a point of agreement, they were not to be prohibited. But if they thought that their hope and salvation were contained in such works of the Law, they were to be forbidden them as though they were being protected from certain destruction.

Hence the Apostle’s statement: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2)—that is, if you are circumcised as they themselves wished, and as certain corrupt people had persuaded them, claiming that they could not be saved without these works of the Law (Acts 15:1).

When the Gentiles came to faith in Christ—as they ought to come, especially through the preaching of the Apostle Paul—without being burdened by such observances, those observances, especially circumcision, would have frightened away people advanced in age who feared things unfamiliar to them. And people who had not been born to be instructed in such sacraments, if they became proselytes according to the former custom, would have thought that Christ was still being promised through those mysteries.

When they came to the faith in the manner appropriate for Gentiles, those who had come from circumcision did not understand why such practices had been permitted to themselves but were not to be imposed on the Gentiles.
