They began to disturb the Church through certain carnal disputes, because Gentiles approaching the people of God were not solemnly made proselytes through circumcision of the flesh and the other observances of the Law.

Among them were people who insisted especially strongly that this be done because they feared the Jews among whom they lived. Against these people the Apostle Paul wrote much. Indeed, because of their hypocrisy, he corrected even Peter by a brotherly rebuke (Gal. 2:14).

But after the Apostles had assembled together and had also determined by their common judgment that the Gentiles were not to be compelled to such works of the Law (Acts 15:6–11), certain Christians from the circumcision were displeased. They could not mentally distinguish that only those who had already been formed by these practices when the revealed faith found them were not to be prohibited from them.

In such people the prophetic action was now to be completed. They had already been held by it before the fulfillment of prophecy. For if it were removed even from them, it would appear to have been rejected rather than brought to an end. But if it were imposed also on the Gentiles, people would either think that it had not been instituted to promise Christ, or that it was still promising Christ.

Thus, before Christ came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, the first people of God were commanded to observe all those things that promised him: among them, those who understood what these things signified were free, while those who did not understand were slaves.

The later people, coming to the faith in which Christ was already proclaimed as having come, suffered, and risen again, were neither compelled nor prohibited from observing these things if the same faith found them already formed by such sacraments.

But those who believed without such practices—held by no necessity of lineage, custom, or conformity—were even prohibited from observing them. Through them it was to begin to appear that all those things had been instituted to promise Christ; and when he came and fulfilled those promises, they ought now to cease.

When this arrangement and moderation of the Holy Spirit working through the Apostles displeased certain believers from the circumcision who did not understand it, they remained in such perversity that they also compelled Gentiles to Judaize.

These are the people whom Faustus mentioned under the name of Symmachians or Nazarenes. They continue down to our own times, now indeed in small numbers, but nevertheless still surviving even in that small remnant.

## CHAPTER XVIII

What basis, then, do these people have for slandering the Law and the Prophets, claiming that Christ came to abolish them rather than to fulfill them because Christians do not observe what is commanded there?

Christians do not observe only those things through which Christ was promised. They do not observe them precisely because Christ has already fulfilled those promises, and what has already been fulfilled is no longer promised. Their signs of promise had to come to an end among those whom the faith of Christ, which fulfilled these things, found already formed by them.

Do Christians not observe what is written in that Scripture: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4)? “You shall not make an idol for yourself,” and other commandments of this kind?

Do Christians not observe what is said there: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”?

Do Christians not observe the Sabbath itself, which pertains to understanding true rest?

Do Christians not honor their parents, as it is commanded there?

Do Christians not restrain themselves from fornication, murder, theft, false testimony, coveting their neighbor’s wife, or coveting their neighbor’s property—all of which are written in that Law (Exod. 20:4–17)?

These are commandments concerning conduct; those are sacraments concerning promises. The former are fulfilled through assisting grace; the latter through the truth that has been delivered. Both are fulfilled through Christ, who has always given grace and now also reveals it, and who then promised this truth and now presents it, because “the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came into being through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Finally, these commandments, which are preserved in the conscience of one who lives rightly, are fulfilled through faith working by love (Gal. 5:6). But those that consisted in promising signs have passed away when the realities were delivered.

Thus they too were not abolished but fulfilled, because Christ showed that they were neither invalid nor deceptive when he presented what had been promised through their signification.

## CHAPTER XIX

Therefore, it is not the case, as Faustus thinks, that the Lord Jesus fulfilled some commandments that had already been stated by the ancient righteous before the Law of Moses—such as “You shall not kill”—which he did not refute by contradiction but rather confirmed when he also withdrew people from anger and insult (Exod. 20:13; Matt. 5:21–22); while he abolished others that seemed proper to the law of the Hebrews—such as “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”—which he appears rather to have removed than confirmed when he said, “But I say to you, do not resist evil; rather, if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Exod. 21:24; Matt. 5:38–39), and so forth.

We say that even these commandments, which such people think Christ abolished by presenting them as contrary, were properly instituted for their time, and that now they have not been abolished by Christ but fulfilled.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0360]

I ask them first whether those ancient righteous people—Enoch and Seth, whom Faustus especially mentions, and any others who lived not only before Moses but even before Abraham—were angry with their brother without cause or said to their brother, “Fool.”

For if they did not do these things, why did they not also teach such matters? But if they did teach them, I ask how Christ fulfilled either their righteousness or their teaching by adding: “But I say to you, if anyone is angry with his brother; or if anyone says, ‘Raca’; or if anyone says, ‘Fool,’ he will be liable to the judgment, the council, or the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22), since those ancient righteous people lived in the same way and advised others to live in the same way.

Or did those righteous people not know that anger had to be restrained and that a brother must not be provoked by insolent abuse? Or did they know this but were unable to abstain from such things?

Then they were guilty of Gehenna. How, therefore, were they righteous?

Surely you would not dare to say that their righteousness consisted in ignorance of matters belonging to their duty, or in lack of self-control, to such an extent that it made them guilty of Gehenna.

Why, then, would Christ fulfill that law according to which the ancient righteous lived by adding these things, when their righteousness could not exist without them either?

Or will you say that reckless anger and an abusive tongue began to belong to iniquity only after Christ came, whereas before that it was not wrong either to commit these things in the heart or to utter them with the mouth?

As in certain matters instituted in accordance with the circumstances of the times, we find that something is now forbidden which was formerly permitted, or that something is now permitted which was formerly forbidden.

You are not so foolish as to say this. But even if you did, you would be answered that, according to this interpretation, Christ did not come to fulfill what the ancient Law lacked, but to institute a law that had not existed.

If Christ wished saying “Fool” to one’s brother—when it had not been unjust among the ancient righteous—to be unjust now, so that whoever said it would be guilty of Gehenna, then you have still not found the law that once lacked these things which Christ would fulfill by adding them now.

## CHAPTER XXI

Or perhaps the law against adultery was only half-complete among those ancient righteous people until it was fulfilled by the Lord, who added that no one should look at a woman in order to desire her?

For you quoted the very statement in this way: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you, do not even desire.”

“It is a fulfillment,” you say. Explain the Gospel’s actual words plainly. Do not weaken what was said by your own additions, and consider what you have thought about those most ancient righteous people.

“You have heard,” he says, “that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you, whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Exod. 20:14; Matt. 5:27–28).

Is it really the case that those righteous people, Seth or Enoch, or any who were like them, committed adultery in their hearts? Did this mean either that their heart was not the temple of God, or that they committed adultery in the temple of God?

If you do not dare to say this, how did Christ fulfill in this matter the law of those people, which was already complete among them at that time?

## CHAPTER XXII

Regarding the prohibition against swearing (Exod. 20:7; Matt. 5:33–37), since you have also said that Christ fulfilled their law in this matter, I cannot affirm that the ancient righteous did not swear. For we find that the Apostle Paul swore (Rom. 1:9; Phil. 1:8; 2 Cor. 1:23).

But frequent swearing does not leave your own mouths, since you swear by the Light, which you love together with flies. For you do not know how to think, even partially, about that Light which is not entirely foreign to these eyes and which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9).

You also swear by your lord Manichaeus, who was called Manes in his native language. But to avoid the name of madness among the Greeks, as though by altering and lengthening the name, you added something like a fusion, so that you might fall even more deeply into error.

One of you explained to me why he was called Manichaeus: supposedly, in the Greek language he appeared to pour forth manna, since “to pour forth” is expressed in Greek by χέειν (*kheein*). I do not know what you have accomplished there, except that you have made yourselves dream of madness more explicitly.

For you did not add one letter to the first part of the name so that *manna* might be recognized. Instead, you added two syllables to the second part, calling him not *Mannichaeus* but *Manichaeus*, so that, amid all his lengthy and empty speeches, the name would sound as though he poured forth nothing but madness.

You swear very frequently also by the Paraclete—not, of course, by the one whom Christ promised and sent to his disciples (John 14:16, 26; 16:7; Acts 2:2–4), but by that one whose name, if I interpret it into Latin, means *insanifusor*, “the pourer-forth of madness.”

[Note: [Col. 0361] Several manuscripts read *insaniae fusorem* (“the pourer-forth of madness”).]

Since you never stop swearing, I should like to know how you understand this part of the Law as well—the part that you want to be regarded as most ancient—which you claim the Lord fulfilled for you, especially in view of the oaths of the Apostle.

For what authority do your own writings possess, either for you yourselves—much less for me or for any human being?

From this, I think, it is already clear how differently Christ’s statement must be understood: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.” He did not mean these additions, which either belong to the exposition of the ancient statements under discussion or to conduct, rather than to fulfillment.

[Note: [Col. 0361] The manuscripts read *et per domnum* (“and by the lord”); the printed editions read *et per dominum* (“and by the Lord”).]

[Note: [Col. 0361] Most manuscripts read *vobis somniaretis* (“you might dream for yourselves”). Am. and certain other manuscripts read *vobis somniaremini* (“you might dream for yourselves”); Er. and Lov. read *nobis somniare videremini* (“you might seem to dream for us”). Morel, *Éléments de critique*, p. 316, considers *ominaremini* (“you might divine/forebode”) to be the correct reading.]

## CHAPTER XXIII
Because they did not understand “murder” except as the destruction of a human body, by which life is taken away, the Lord made clear that every unjust impulse to harm one’s brother is to be reckoned as murder. Hence John also says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

And because they thought that only bodily intercourse with a woman was called adultery, the Teacher demonstrated that such desire too is nothing other than adultery. Again, since committing perjury is a grave sin, while not swearing—as also swearing truthfully—is no sin; and since the person who never customarily swears is farther removed from false swearing than one who is inclined to swear truthfully, the Lord preferred that we, by not swearing, should not depart from the truth rather than, by swearing truthfully, draw near to perjury.

Accordingly, the Apostle too, in the speeches he is said to have delivered, never swore, lest through the habit of swearing he should at some time, [Col. 0362] even unknowingly, slip into perjury. In his writings, however, where there is greater and more deliberate reflection, he is found to have sworn in several places, lest anyone should think that even swearing truthfully is sinful, but rather understand that the hearts of human beings are more safely preserved from perjury by not swearing. When these matters have been considered, we find that those things which Faustus thinks have been destroyed—and which he wants to belong specifically to Moses—have not been destroyed at all.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Here too I ask these people why they want the statement addressed to the ancients, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (Leviticus 19:18), to be peculiar to the Law of Moses. Did the Apostle Paul not also say that certain people are hateful to God (Romans 1:30)? And surely, in this exhortation, the Lord himself urges us to imitate God: “So that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.”

We must therefore ask how, following the example of God, to whom Paul said certain people are hateful, enemies are to be hated, and again, following the example of God, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, enemies are to be loved. Thus it will become apparent that, by the statement “You shall hate your enemy,” the Lord intended to introduce to those who misunderstood it something they had entirely failed to recognize, so that they might love their enemies.

How both commands are to be observed would require a lengthy discussion. For the moment, however, we have an argument against these people, who universally disapprove if anyone hates his enemy. It presses upon their shamelessness when we ask them whether their god loves the nation of darkness. Or, if enemies are now to be loved because they possess a share of the good, why should we not for that reason also hate them because they possess a share of evil?

That rule resolves the matter and shows that there is no contradiction between what is said in the ancient Scripture, “You shall hate your enemy,” and what is said in the Gospel, “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:43–45). Every unjust person, insofar as he is unjust, is to be hated; but insofar as he is a human being, he is to be loved. Thus we may condemn in him what we rightly hate—that is, his vice—so that, once the vice has been corrected, what we rightly love in him—that is, human nature itself—may be set free.

This, I say, is the rule by which we both hate our enemy for what is evil in him, namely, his iniquity, and love our enemy for what is good in him, namely, his social and rational nature. The difference is that we prove him to be evil not by his own nature or by another nature, but by his own will.

They, however, think that human beings are evil by the nature of the nation of darkness—a nature which, according to them, their whole God feared before it was conquered in part, and by which he was so defeated in part that he could not be wholly liberated.

Thus, having heard but not understood the statement made to the ancients, “You shall hate your enemy,” people were carried into hatred of a human being, when they ought to have hated nothing except vice. The Lord corrects them by saying, “Love your enemies.” Since he had already said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it,” he did not abolish the Law’s statement concerning hatred of one’s enemy by commanding us to love our enemies. Rather, [Col. 0363] he compelled us to understand how one and the same person can be hated on account of guilt and loved on account of nature.

But this is too much for their perverse minds to understand. They must simply be pressed to defend, according to the ruined logic—or rather the madness—of their slander, their god, whom they cannot call a lover of the nation of darkness. Therefore, following his example, they have no way to urge each person to love his enemy.

Indeed, they could more readily attribute love of an enemy to the nation of darkness itself than to their god. For that nation, as they rave, desired the light near and adjacent to it, wished to enjoy it, and devised an assault in order to enjoy it. Nor is this considered a fault when a true and blessed good is desired. Hence the Lord also says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

There you have it: according to their vanity, the nation of darkness wished to use force and seize the good it had loved, delighted by its brightness and beauty. Yet God did not in turn love it; rather, he hated and abominated it and attempted to eradicate it utterly when it wished to enjoy him.

If, then, the wicked love the good in order to enjoy it, while the good hate evil so as not to be defiled by it, answer, Manichaeans: which of them fulfills the Lord’s command, “Love your enemies”? If you want these statements to be individually contradictory, your god did what is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall hate your enemy,” while the nation of darkness did what is written in the Gospel, “Love your enemies.”

Yet even in your inventions you have not been able to discover how to settle the dispute between light-loving flies and light-fleeing cockroaches—for you insist that both are offspring of the nation of darkness. Why, then, do the former love a light foreign to them, while the latter, by turning away from this light, take delight instead in their own origin? Are flies born more cleanly in foul sewers than cockroaches in dark bedrooms?

## CHAPTER XXV

Now, as for the statement made to the ancients, “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,” how is it contrary to what the Lord says: “But I say to you, do not resist evil; rather, if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Exodus 21:24; Matthew 5:39), and so forth?

Indeed, that ancient command was also given to restrain the flames of hatred and curb the uncontrolled impulses of those raging with anger. [Note: [Col. 0363] Er. and Lugd. read, “is from the command.” M.] Who, after all, is easily content to return exactly as much vengeance as he has received injury? Do we not see people who have been lightly wounded plotting murder, thirsting for blood, and scarcely finding enough in the misfortunes of their enemy to satisfy them?

Who, when struck with a fist, either does not bring legal charges to secure the condemnation of the person who struck him, or, if he wants to strike back himself, does not batter the whole man with fists and kicks, perhaps even seizing some weapon? Against this immoderate—and therefore unjust—vengeance, the Law established a just measure by instituting the penalty of retaliation: that is, that each person should suffer a punishment equal to the injury he inflicted.

Accordingly, [Col. 0364] “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” is not fuel but a boundary for fury. It was imposed not to rekindle what had been quieted, but to prevent what was burning from spreading farther. [Note: So read the Ambrosian and Erasmian editions and several manuscripts; the Lyon edition has, “from spreading farther. For a certain [limit] was imposed.”]

There is, in fact, a certain just vengeance, and it is justly owed to the person who has suffered injury. Thus, when we forgive, we in a certain sense give away something that belongs to us. Hence the debts that we are humanly instructed to forgive in the Lord’s Prayer are also called “debts,” so that our debts may be divinely forgiven (Matthew 6:12).

What is owed, even if generously forgiven, is not unjustly reclaimed. But just as, in the matter of swearing, even the person who swears truthfully draws near to perjury, while the one who does not swear at all is far removed from it—and although the person who swears truthfully does not sin, the one who does not swear is farther removed from sin—so the admonition not to swear preserves us from the sin of perjury.

Similarly, although the person who unjustly seeks vengeance without measure sins, while the person who seeks just vengeance within proper limits does not sin, the one who does not want vengeance at all is farther removed from the sin of unjust vengeance.

The person who demands more than is owed sins; the person who demands what is owed does not sin. Yet the one who does not demand the debt at all is much safer from the sin of the unjust creditor, especially lest he himself be compelled to repay a debt to one who has no debt.

I could therefore formulate the matter in this way: “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not avenge yourself unjustly’; but I say, ‘Do not avenge yourselves at all.’” This is a fulfillment, just as Faustus says concerning swearing: “It was said, ‘You shall not commit perjury’; but I say, ‘Do not swear at all.’” That too is a fulfillment.

I could therefore have spoken in this way if I thought that, through these added words, Christ had supplied what was lacking in the Law, rather than that what the Law intended to accomplish—namely, that no one should sin by taking unjust vengeance—is more safely preserved if one does not take vengeance at all, just as what it intended to accomplish—namely, that no one should sin by committing perjury—is more safely preserved if one does not swear.

For if “An eye for an eye” is contrary to “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, turn to him the other also,” why is “You shall fulfill your oath to the Lord” not contrary to “Do not swear at all” (Exodus 20:7; Matthew 5:33–37)? And yet Faustus considers the latter not an abolition but a fulfillment. He ought to have considered the former in the same way.

For if “Swear truthfully” is fulfilled by saying, “Do not swear,” why is “Take just vengeance” not fulfilled by saying, “Do not take vengeance”? Thus, in both cases, I too regard the command as preserving us from the sin by which either falsehood is sworn or unjust vengeance is taken. Moreover, the matter of entirely relinquishing vengeance also applies to this: by forgiving such debts, we may deserve to have our own debts forgiven.

But a stubborn people first had to be subjected to a rule by which they might learn not to go beyond what was owed. Once their anger—which drives them toward immoderate vengeance—had been subdued, anyone who wished could calmly consider what he himself owed and desired the Lord to forgive him, and by this reflection forgive the debt of his fellow servant.

## CHAPTER XXVI

As for the Lord’s command concerning not dismissing one’s wife, while it was said to the ancients, [Col. 0365] “Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce” (Deuteronomy 24:1; Matthew 5:31–32), if we examine the matter carefully, we shall see that the two are not contradictory.

The Lord explained what the Law intended when it commanded anyone who dismissed his wife to give her a bill of divorce. It did not say, “Let whoever wishes dismiss his wife,” which would be contradicted by the command not to dismiss her. Rather, it certainly did not want a wife to be dismissed by her husband, since it inserted this delay so that a mind rushing headlong toward separation might be checked by the writing of the bill and might reflect on the evil of dismissing a wife.

This was especially so because, as they report, among the Hebrews no one was permitted to write Hebrew letters except the scribes. They professed superior wisdom, and those among them who possessed equity and piety not only professed wisdom but also practiced it.

The Law therefore intended the husband who dismissed his wife to go to those who ought to be wise interpreters of the Law and just opponents of divorce, and commanded him to give a bill of divorce if he had dismissed his wife. The bill could not be written except by those who, on this occasion, would receive him as one compelled by necessity into their hands and, by offering good counsel, would turn him back, conducting themselves peacefully between him and his wife and urging affection and harmonious agreement.

If the hatred between them was so great that it could neither be extinguished nor corrected, then the bill would indeed be written, because it would be futile to prevent him from dismissing the woman whom he hated so intensely that no prudent persuasion could recall him to the marital affection he owed.

For if a wife is not loved, she must be dismissed. Since she must not be dismissed, she must be loved. Love, however, can be brought about through admonition and persuasion; it cannot be imposed by coercion upon one who is unwilling.

A just and wise scribe, such as a person in that profession ought to be, was to do this. To ensure that the husband came to him, the discontented husband was commanded to have a bill written. A good and prudent husband would not have it written unless, in a mind excessively estranged and perverse, counsel for reconciliation had proved ineffective.

Nevertheless, I ask you, in the sacrilegious vanity of your error, why you disapprove of dismissing a wife whom you believe should be regarded not as an instrument of marital fidelity but as an occasion of lustful crime. Marriage, after all, is called *matrimonium* because a woman ought to marry for no other reason than to become a mother—and that is hateful to you. For you think that in this way a portion of your god, defeated and subdued in battle by the nation of darkness, is also bound in fetters of flesh.

## CHAPTER XXVII

But to explain more directly what is now under discussion: when Christ, after presenting certain statements made to the ancients, added, “But I say to you,” he neither fulfilled the law of the first human beings by adding these words nor destroyed the Law given through Moses by setting up an opposition of contraries.

Rather, he commended everything cited from the law of the Hebrews in such a way that whatever he further spoke in his own person served either to require an interpretation, if the Law had stated something obscurely, or to preserve more securely what the Law had intended.

You therefore see how differently we must understand his statement that he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it: not as though these words completed something only half-finished, [Col. 0366] but so that what could not be accomplished through the commanding letter, because of the presumption of the proud, might be fulfilled through grace persuading people because of the confession of the humble—by the work of deeds, not by an addition of words.

“For faith,” as the Apostle says, “works through love” (Galatians 5:6). Hence he also says, “Whoever loves another has fulfilled the Law” (Romans 13:8).

Because Christ, when he came, bestowed this love through the Holy Spirit whom he promised and sent, and because only through this love could the righteousness of the Law be fulfilled, he therefore said: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.”

This is the New Testament, in which the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven is promised to this love, which was concealed in figures in the Old Testament according to the distribution of the ages. Hence he also says: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Accordingly, either all or nearly all the things that he admonished or commanded when he added, “But I say to you,” are also found in those ancient Books.

There it is said against anger: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6:8); and, “The one who conquers anger is better than the one who captures a city” (Proverbs 16:32).

There it is said against harsh speech: “The stroke of a whip will make a bruise, but the stroke of the tongue will break bones” (Sirach 28:21).

There it is said against adultery of the heart: “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20:17). For it does not say, “You shall not commit adultery,” but, “You shall not desire.” Hence the Apostle recalls this from the Law, saying: “I would not have known desire unless the Law had said, ‘You shall not desire’” (Romans 7:7).

There, concerning the patience of not resisting, a man who offers his cheek to the one striking him and is filled with reproaches is praised (Lamentations 3:30).

There, concerning loving an enemy, it is said: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Proverbs 25:21). The Apostle recalled this from there (Romans 12:20).

And in the Psalm: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable” (Psalm 119:7), along with many other passages.

As for imitating God by restraining vengeance and loving even the wicked, there is an extensive passage in those Books concerning God himself doing this. It is written there:

“For it is always yours alone to possess great power, and who can withstand the strength of your arm? [Note: [Col. 0366] Some manuscripts read *supererat* (“belonged”); the printed Vulgate has this reading, but our manuscript Bibles read *superat* (“belongs”). The Greek has *parestin* (“is present”).] For the whole world before you is like a speck on a balance, and like a drop of morning dew that descends upon the earth. But you have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook human sins so that they may repent. For you love all things that exist, and you hate nothing that you have made; for you would not have created anything while hating it. How could anything endure if you had not willed it, or be preserved if it had not been called by you? But you spare all things, because they are yours, Lord, lover of souls. For your good spirit is in all things; therefore you rebuke those who go astray little by little, and admonish them concerning the things in which they sin, and speak to them so that, abandoning wickedness, they may believe in you, Lord” (Wisdom 11:22–12:2).

[Col. 0367] Christ urges us to imitate this gracious patience of God, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, so that we may neglect to avenge our injuries and do good to those who hate us, in order to be perfect, as our heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:44–48).

That remitting to others these debts of vengeance benefits us toward the remission of the debts of our sins, and that we must beware lest, if we do not do this, the obligation of sin be not forgiven us even when we pray for forgiveness, is written in those ancient Books as follows:

“Whoever wants vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord, and he will surely confirm that person’s sins. Forgive your neighbor who has injured you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven. Does one human being preserve anger against another, yet seek healing from the Lord? Does he have no mercy on a person like himself, yet pray for his own sins? Though he is flesh, he preserves anger and asks the Lord for reconciliation? Who will plead for his sins?” (Sirach 28:1–5).

## CHAPTER XXIX

Now, concerning the command not to dismiss one’s wife, what more appropriate passage—or what other passage—from those Books could I recall than the one from which the Lord himself answered the Jews when they questioned him about this matter?

When they asked whether it was lawful to dismiss one’s wife for any reason, he said to them:

“Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’? Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

[Note: The Lyon edition reads, “he who made the human being from the beginning.” Other printed editions and manuscripts, agreeing with the Greek, do not have “the human being”; this word is also absent from the ancient Corbie manuscripts of the Vulgate, or Latin edition.]

There the Jews are refuted from the books of Moses themselves: they believed that they were acting according to the will of the Mosaic Law when they dismissed their wives, yet those books prove that a wife should not be dismissed.

At the same time, with Christ himself bearing witness, we learn that God made and joined together male and female. The Manichaeans condemn this by denying it. [Note: In the manuscripts and in Am., the reading is “are condemned.”] They are no longer merely resisting the book of Moses but the Gospel of Christ.

Furthermore, if what they themselves believe and proclaim is true—namely, that the devil made and joined together male and female—by what diabolical cunning does Faustus rebuke Moses as though he were dissolving marriages through the bill of divorce, while praising Christ as though, according to the command of the Gospel, he were confirming that same kind of bond?

According to their foolish and sacrilegious opinion, Faustus ought instead to have praised Moses for separating what the devil had made and joined together, and blamed Christ for strengthening the devil’s creation and bond.

Now consider what the good Teacher reveals about why Moses himself, whose book contains that holy account of the first union of male and female—a union not to be violated by any separation—afterward permitted a wife to be dismissed.

When they replied to him, “Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and that the wife be dismissed?” he said to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives” (Matthew 19:4–8).

This is what we explained above (chapter 26). For how great was the hardness that could not be dissolved or bent toward recovering or restoring marital affection even through the insertion of the bill of divorce, when an opportunity for dissuasion was granted to just and prudent [Col. 0368] men?

Thus the Lord, by the testimony of the same Law, made clear both what the Law commanded the good and what it permitted the hard-hearted. From that same Scripture he recalled the union of male and female to admonish that a wife should not be dismissed, explained the divine authority of that union, and showed that the bill of divorce was to be given because of the hardness of a heart that either had to be subdued or remained unsubdued.

## CHAPTER XXX

Since all those excellent commandments of the Lord which Faustus wanted to show as contrary to the ancient Books of the Hebrews are also found in those same Books, why did the Lord come not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it?

Was it not so that, apart from the figures of the promises—which, once the reality had been given, were fulfilled and removed—[Note: [Col. 0368] Am. reads, “except from the commandments”; Er. reads, “except from things perceived.”]the commandments themselves, through which that Law is holy, just, and good (Romans 7:12), might be fulfilled in us not through the oldness of the letter that commands and increases the guilt of the proud by adding transgression, but through the newness of the Spirit that gives assistance and, by the grace of salvation, liberates the confession of the humble?

For just as all these sublime commandments are not absent from those ancient Books, so the end toward which they are directed is hidden there. Nevertheless, the saints lived according to that end: they saw its future revelation and, in accordance with the character of the ages, either concealed it prophetically or wisely understood it when prophetically concealed.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Finally—and I do not say this rashly—I do not know whether anyone finds the name “kingdom of heaven” in those Books, a phrase that the Lord mentions so frequently.

It is indeed said there: “Love wisdom, so that you may reign forever” (Wisdom 6:22). And if eternal life were not proclaimed there openly, the Lord would not say even to the wicked Jews: “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life; it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39).

To what else could the following passages refer? “I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the Lord” (Psalm 118:17); and, “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Psalm 13:4); and, “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment shall touch them”; and shortly afterward, “They are in peace. Though in the sight of human beings they suffered torments, their hope is full of immortality, and, after being disciplined in a few things, they shall be greatly rewarded” (Wisdom 3:1–5).

And elsewhere: “The righteous shall live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and their concern is with the Most High. Therefore they shall receive the kingdom of splendor and the crown of beauty from the hand of the Lord” (the same work, 5:16–17).

These and many other testimonies to eternal life, some very clear and others somewhat obscure, are found there.

The prophets were not silent even about the resurrection of the bodies. Hence the Pharisees fought most fiercely against the Sadducees, who did not believe in it. This is evident not only in the canonical Acts of the Apostles—which these people do not accept, lest they be convicted by it concerning the coming of the true Paraclete whom the Lord promised (Acts 23:6–9)—but also in the Gospel, where the Sadducees pose to him the question concerning a woman who had married seven brothers one after another, as each succeeded the brother who had died: whose wife would she be in the resurrection? (Matthew 22:23–28).

That Scripture is therefore abundant in testimonies to eternal life and the resurrection of the dead. But the name itself—“the kingdom of heaven”—does not occur to me in any passage there. This belongs properly to the revelation of the New Testament, because those bodies which had been earthly will, in the resurrection, through the transformation that Paul describes more openly, become spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and therefore heavenly, in which we shall possess the kingdom of heaven.

That name was reserved to be spoken by the mouth of the one whom the [Col. 0370] entire apparatus of the Old Covenant—through its genealogies, deeds, words, sacrifices, observances, festivals, and all the proclamations of its sacred writings, as well as its historical events and symbolic representations—was bringing forth as the king who would rule his faithful and the priest who would sanctify them.

He, being “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14)—helping us by grace to carry out the commandments and accomplishing the promises through truth—came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

# BOOK TWENTY

[Col. 0369]

## CHAPTER ONE

Faustus said: Why do you worship the sun, unless because you are pagans and a schism of the Gentiles rather than a sect? It will therefore not be irrelevant to ask this question as well, so that we may see more clearly which of us ought to be called by this name.

If I now state my faith to you simply, as I would to a friend, you may perhaps think that I am fabricating this as an excuse, or—God forbid—that I am ashamed of worshiping the divine lights. But accept it as you wish. I shall not regret having said it, at least for the sake of those who will thereby learn that our religion has nothing in common with the Gentiles.

## CHAPTER TWO

We worship one and the same divine power under the threefold designation of the Father, God almighty, Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit. But we believe that the Father himself dwells in the highest and principal light, which Paul elsewhere calls inaccessible (1 Timothy 6:16).

We believe that the Son exists in this second and visible light. Since he too is twofold—as the Apostle recognizes when he says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24)—we believe that his power dwells in the sun and his wisdom in the moon.

As for the Holy Spirit, who is the third majesty, we confess that the entire circuit of the air is his seat and dwelling place. Through his powers and spiritual outpouring, the earth also conceives and gives birth to the passible Jesus, who is the life and salvation of human beings, suspended from every tree.

Therefore, in relation to all things, we have a religion equal to yours with respect to bread and the cup, although you hate their authors most fiercely.

This is our faith. If you think that it should be examined on another occasion, you shall hear it, although for the present there is also this no less firm argument: if you or anyone else were asked where you believed your god dwells, he would not hesitate to answer, “In the light.” Thus my worship is confirmed by the testimony of almost everyone.

## CHAPTER THREE

But now to the matter of your calling us not a sect but a schism of the Gentiles.

A schism, unless I am mistaken, consists in holding the same opinions as others and worshiping in the same rite as they do, while taking pleasure merely in the division of the congregation. A sect, however, consists in holding opinions very different from those of others and establishing for oneself a worship of divinity with a different and wholly dissimilar rite.

If this is so, then for the moment both my opinion and my worship are very different from those of the pagans. [Col. 0370] We shall consider yours afterward.

The pagans dogmatically assert that good and evil, foul and splendid, perpetual and perishable, changeable and certain, bodily and divine things all have one and the same source. I think very differently. I acknowledge God as the source of all good things, but for contrary things I acknowledge Hyle—thus our theologian calls the source and nature of evil.

Again, the pagans think that God should be worshiped with altars, shrines, images, victims, and incense. Here too I proceed very differently from them. I regard myself, if I am worthy, as the rational temple of God; I accept Christ, his Son, as the living image of the living majesty; I regard the mind imbued with good arts and disciplines as an altar; and I place divine honors and sacrifices in prayers alone, and in prayers that are pure and simple.

How, then, am I a schism of the pagans?

## CHAPTER FOUR

Up to this point you could also have called me a schism of the Jews, since I worship the omnipotent God—a claim that every Jew boldly makes for himself—if you had not considered the difference in the rites by which I worship the Omnipotent and those by which the Jews do, assuming that the Jews worship the Omnipotent at all.

For the moment, however, we are discussing the opinion that has deceived both the pagans concerning the worship of the sun and the Jews concerning the Omnipotent.

Nor is it true if you call me a schism of your own people, although I revere and worship Christ, because I worship him with a different rite and in accordance with a different faith from yours.

A schism either ought to change nothing—or very little—from that from which it arose. Consider, for example, yourselves: when you broke away from the Gentiles, you first separated from them the doctrine of monarchy, that is, the belief that all things come from God. But you transformed their sacrifices into love-feasts, their idols into martyrs, whom you worship with similar vows; you appease the shades of the dead with wine and food; and you celebrate the solemn days of the Gentiles with them, such as the Kalends and the solstices.

As far as life is concerned, you have changed nothing. You are indeed a schism, differing from your mother only in your assembly.

Your predecessors, the Jews, likewise separated from the Gentiles, abandoned only sculpted images. Temples, sacrifices, altars, priesthoods, and the entire ministry of sacred rites they practiced according to the same rite—and much more superstitiously than the Gentiles.

As for the doctrine of monarchy, they too differ from the pagans in no respect. Thus it is clear that you and the Jews are schisms of paganism: holding its faith and [Col. 0371] rites, though moderately altered, you think that you are sects merely because of the division of your assemblies.

If you ask about sects, there will be no more than two: that of the Gentiles and ours, because we hold opinions very different from theirs. We are opposed to one another as truth is to falsehood, day to night, poverty to abundance, sickness to health.

You, however, are neither a sect of error nor a sect of truth, but merely a schism—and not even a schism of truth, but of error.

## CHAPTER FIVE

Augustine replied: O ignorant pest and deceitful vanity! Why do you throw at yourself an accusation which, if someone throws it at you, shows that he does not know whom he is dealing with?

We do not call you pagans, or a schism of the pagans. We say that you have a certain similarity to them because you worship many gods. In reality, you are far worse than they are. They worship things that exist, though they ought not to be worshiped as gods—for idols too exist, but they are nothing with respect to salvation.

Someone who worships a tree—not by cultivating it but by adoring it—does not worship something that exists nowhere, but something that ought not to be worshiped in that way.

The demons too, concerning which the Apostle says, “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Corinthians 10:20), certainly exist, since he says that they sacrifice to them and does not want us to be partners with them.

Moreover, heaven and earth, sea and air, sun and moon, and the other heavenly bodies—all these appear plainly to the eyes and are present to the senses themselves. When the pagans worship these things as gods, or as parts of one great god—for some of them think that the entire universe is the greatest god—they worship things that exist.

When we deal with them to persuade them not to worship these things, we do not tell them that they do not exist, but that they ought not to be worshiped. We urge them to worship instead the invisible God, the creator of all these things, through participation in whom alone a human being can become blessed—for no one doubts that everyone desires blessedness.

Some of them do worship an invisible and incorporeal creature, namely the human soul and mind. Yet since a human being does not become blessed through participation even in such a creature, the invisible and immutable God—that is, the true God—must be worshiped.

He alone must be worshiped, because the one who enjoys him alone becomes blessed as his worshiper, while every mind that does not enjoy him alone is miserable, whatever other thing it may enjoy.

But since you worship things that do not exist at all and are fabricated by the vanity of your deceitful myths, you would be closer to true piety and religion if you were at least pagans—or among those who worship bodies: things that ought not to be worshiped, but that nevertheless exist.

For this reason I should more truly say that you do not even worship this sun, around whose circuit your prayer revolves.

## CHAPTER SIX

You make claims about the sun itself that are so false and detestable that, if it avenged its own injuries, you would already be burning alive in its flames.

First, you say that it is a certain ship. Thus you are not merely, as the saying goes, wandering through the whole heaven—you are swimming through it as well.

Then, although it shines round before everyone’s eyes and its shape is perfect in accordance with the position of its order, you declare it to be a triangle: that is, you say that this light radiates into the world and upon the earth through a certain triangular window of heaven.

The result is that you bend your back and neck toward this sun, [Col. 0372] but you do not worship the sun itself, which is visible in such a bright roundness. Instead, you worship I know not what ship, flashing and shining through a triangular opening, which you have fabricated in your imagination.

That ship, surely, would not be made by a craftsman if words, by which the myths of heretics are fabricated, were bought in the same way as the timbers by which ships are assembled.

Still, these ideas of yours can more tolerably be laughed at or pitied. What is intolerably wicked is your claim that beautiful girls and boys are placed upon that ship, so that the rulers of darkness may be inflamed by their most beautiful bodies—the male rulers by the females and the female rulers by the males—and that, amid this burning lust and gaping desire, the members of your god may be released from their dark and filthy fetters as though from chains.

And with these most obscene rags of yours you attempt to sew together the ineffable Trinity, saying that the Father dwells in a certain secret light, the power of the Son in the sun, his wisdom in the moon, and the Holy Spirit in the air!

## CHAPTER SEVEN
In this tripartite—or rather now quadripartite—fable of yours, concerning the Father’s secret light, what shall I say to you except that you cannot conceive of light except as the kind you are accustomed to see? For, gazing upon this visible light, familiar to every creature of flesh—not only to human beings but also to beasts and little worms—you habitually enlarge without limit the fantasy conceived from it in your hearts and call it the light in which God the Father dwells with his subjects in the kingdom. When have you distinguished the light by which we see from the light by which we understand, since you have never thought understanding to be anything other than conceiving bodily forms, whether finite or infinite in some of their parts—forms which you do not realize are empty phantasms?

Accordingly, since there is so great a difference between the thought by which I think of your land of light, which exists nowhere at all, and the thought by which I think of Alexandria, which I have never seen but which nevertheless exists; and since there is again so great a difference between the thought by which I think of unknown Alexandria and that by which I think of known Carthage; from the thought by which I think of certain and familiar bodies there is, in turn, a far greater and incomparable distance to the thought by which I understand justice, chastity, faith, truth, love, goodness, and everything of this kind. Tell me, if you can, what sort of light that thought is by which all things that are not this light are faithfully recognized, distinguished both from one another and from it, and their distance from it is known.

Yet even this light is not that Light which God is. This one is a creature; he is the Creator. This one was made; he made it. Finally, this one is mutable, since it wills what it did not will, knows what it did not know, and remembers what it had forgotten; whereas he remains in immutable will, truth, and eternity. From him we have the beginning of our existence, the principle by which we know, and the law by which we love. From him all living creatures, including those without reason, receive the nature by which they live, the vigor by which they sense, and the movement by which they desire. From him, too, all bodies receive measure by which they subsist, number by which they are adorned, and weight by which they are ordered.

That Light, therefore, is the inseparable Trinity, the one God, whose incorporeal, spiritual, and immutable substance you divide spatially, although it has no body joined to it. You do not even assign three places to the Trinity, but four: one to the Father—that is, the inaccessible light, which you do not understand at all; two to the Son, namely the sun and the moon; and one again to the Holy Spirit, namely this entire expanse of air. Concerning the Father’s inaccessible light, since for those who hold the true faith the Son and the Holy Spirit are not separated from it, let this suffice for the present.

**CHAPTER VIII**

But what led your vanity to place the Son’s virtue in the sun and his wisdom in the moon? Since the Son remains inseparable within the Father himself, how can his wisdom be separated from his virtue, so that the one is in the sun and the other in the moon, when bodies alone can be divided and separated by such spatial locations? If you understood this, you would never weave such enormous fables out of a foolish and insane phantasm.

Yet even within that falsehood and deception of yours, how incongruously and perversely you say that the seat of wisdom shines less than the seat of virtue, when working and effecting seem to belong to virtue, while teaching and displaying belong to wisdom! Thus, if heat prevailed in the sun while light prevailed in the moon, your inventions might somehow have found a cloud of plausibility with which to deceive carnal and animal people who think that nothing exists except what they have conceived bodily. For heat operates violently in moving things, and would therefore be attributed to virtue; while the clear brilliance of light serves to reveal, and would therefore be assigned to wisdom.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the commonly printed editions, less correctly, read: “For the violence of heat is an operation for moving.”]

But since light is far more splendid in the sun, how can virtue be there, while wisdom is here, where there is so much less light? O sacrilegious folly! And since Christ is one, the Virtue of God and the Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24), while the Holy Spirit is not himself Christ, how is Christ separated from himself, when the Holy Spirit is not separated from him?

You claim that the air, which your fable assigns as the seat of the Holy Spirit, fills the entire structure of the world. Hence the sun and the moon, completing their circuits, are always with him. But the moon withdraws from the sun and again approaches the sun. Thus, according to you authors—or rather deceivers—the wisdom withdraws from virtue through half the circle and again approaches it through the other half. When the moon is full, wisdom is then farthest from virtue; for the two lights are then separated from each other by so great an interval that, when the sun inclines toward the west, the moon rises from the east. It follows that, since everything abandoned by virtue becomes weaker, wisdom is weaker in proportion as the moon is fuller.

But if, as truth teaches, the wisdom of God always has the same power and the virtue of God always has the same wisdom, why do you speak of these two in such a way as to separate them by the positions and intervals of their places, while you also say that these very seats are of the same substance? You are people of blind and insane minds, never withdrawing from the phantasm of bodies, and so lacking both virtue and wisdom that you cannot think anything with strength or possess strength with wisdom.

Is this truly the case, detestable and accursed folly: that Christ is stretched between the sun and the moon, dwelling here as virtue and there as wisdom—neither perfect and complete here, nor wise in the sun, nor mighty in the moon—and that in both places he arranges handsome boys to be desired by the female rulers of darkness, and girls by the males? You read these things, believe them, and teach them. You live by this faith and doctrine, and you wonder that you are so abominable!

**CHAPTER IX**

But if you err concerning these pre-eminent and most familiar lights so greatly that you worship in them not what they are but what you insanely invent them to be, what shall I say about the rest of your fables? For who is the splendor-bearer who suspends the world, and who is Atlas who supports it together with him? These things, and countless others about which you rave in the same way, do not exist at all, yet you worship them.

In this respect we call you worse than the Pagans: you resemble them only in worshiping many gods; but you differ from them for the worse in that they worship as gods things that exist, although they are not gods, whereas you worship things that are neither gods nor anything else, since they do not exist at all.

They too have certain fabulous inventions, but they know that those inventions are fables. They either assert that poets made them up for the sake of entertainment, or try to interpret them in relation to the nature of things or the customs of human beings. Thus they explain Vulcan as lame because the movement of earthly fire is of that kind; Fortune as blind because things called accidental happen uncertainly; and the three Fates at the distaff and spindle, twisting a thread from wool with their fingers, as representing the three times.

The past is what has already been spun and wound around the spindle; the present is what passes between the fingers of the spinner; and the future is in the wool attached to the distaff, which still has to pass through the spinner’s fingers to the spindle, just as the present passes into the past. They explain Venus as the wife of Vulcan because pleasure naturally arises from heat, and as the adulteress of Mars because she is incongruous with warfare. They explain Cupid as a flying and arrow-shooting boy because irrational and unstable love wounds the hearts of the wretched, and they interpret many other things in this manner.

Consequently, what we ridicule in them is that they worship these things after interpreting them. Had they worshiped them without understanding, their worship would have been damnable but more excusable. For by their very interpretations they are convicted of not worshiping that God through participation in whom alone the mind becomes blessed, but rather a creature formed by him—not only the virtues of that creature, such as Minerva, whose fable of being born from Jupiter’s head they interpret as prudence in counsel, which belongs properly to reason and to which Plato likewise assigned the seat of the head, but also vices, as we have said of Cupid.

Hence one of their tragedians says:

> Lust, favoring shame and vice,  
> fashioned Love as a god.

(Seneca, *Hippolytus*, act 1, scene 2, lines 194–195.)

The Romans even consecrated images of bodily vices, such as Pallor and Fever.

To pass over, then, the fact that worshipers of images are emotionally attached to the actual forms of bodies, so that they fear those very shapes, elevated in honored places where they see such homage being offered to them, as though they were gods: those interpretations themselves, by which these mute, deaf, blind, and lifeless objects are defended, are more deservedly condemned. Nevertheless, even these things exist in some manner, although, as I have already said, they are nothing for salvation or any useful purpose; and the realities interpreted through them are found in actual things.

But you claim that the first man fought with the five elements; that a powerful spirit, fashioned from the captive bodies of the nation of darkness—or rather [Note: In B, “or rather not.” We have followed Lugd. and Lov.] from the conquered and subjugated members of your god—constructed the world; that the splendor-bearer holds in his hand the remnants of those same members of your god and mourns all the other captured, oppressed, and polluted parts; that he carries with him beneath his shoulders the enormous Atlas, lest Atlas, exhausted, throw everything down; and that your fable cannot reach, as though across a theatrical tapestry, the *catastolium* of that final sphere.

[Note: The printed editions read *tabula vestra* (“your board/table”), but the manuscripts read *fabula vestra* (“your fable”). Shortly afterward, two manuscripts have *castatolium* instead of *catastolium*, and another codex has *catastolum*. From the verb καταστέλλω (*katastellō*) comes καταστολή (*katastolē*), “clothing,” and *catastolium*, which has the same meaning as *coopertorium*, “covering.” This is the term used in the *Book on Heresies*, chapter 46, at the end, where, according to the Manichaeans, the final sphere is a covering composed of souls naturally good that could not be cleansed from contact with the evil nature; after the end of the age, the substance of evil will be enclosed within this covering as in an eternal prison.]

You neither depict nor sculpt nor interpret these and countless other equally foolish and insane notions; yet, although they do not exist at all, you believe and worship them. In addition, you insult Christians whose pious minds are cleansed by sincere faith, as though they were rashly credulous.

To avoid pursuing the many arguments by which it could be shown that these things do not exist—for although it would not be difficult for me to discuss the construction of the world more subtly and profoundly, it would certainly be too lengthy—I say this: if these things are true, the substance of God is mutable, corruptible, and capable of pollution. To believe this is the height of sacrilegious madness.

All those things, therefore, are vain, false, and nonexistent. In this respect you are altogether worse than those Pagans who are commonly known and who existed in ancient times, but who now blush at what remains of them: they worship things that are not gods, whereas you worship things that do not exist at all.

**CHAPTER X**

Therefore, if you think that you possess the truth because you are vastly unlike the error of the Pagans, while we are supposedly in error because we are perhaps farther from you than from the Pagans, let the dead man be called healthy simply because he is no longer sick, and let the healthy man be blamed because he is nearer to the sick man than to the dead.

Or, if most Pagans are to be regarded not as sick but as dead, let shapeless ash in the tomb be praised because it no longer retains even the form of a corpse, and let living limbs be condemned because they resemble a corpse more than they resemble ash. In the same way, these people think that we should be blamed because they say we resemble the funeral bier of the Pagans more than the ashes of the Manichaeans.

[Note: The manuscripts have *sicut nos ideo* (“just as they think that we…”).]

[Note: Erasmus, the Aldine edition, and several manuscripts read *quam favillae* (“than embers/ashes”). Some other manuscripts read *quam fabellae* (“than little fables”).]

Although things are habitually divided for purposes of distinction in different ways, so that what belonged to one class under one distinction may be found under another distinction in a different class where it was not previously found: for example, if someone divides all flesh into flying creatures and those unable to fly, quadrupeds are more similar to human beings than to birds under this distinction, since neither quadrupeds nor human beings can fly. But if someone divides them according to another distinction, saying that some are rational and others irrational, quadrupeds are then more similar to birds than to human beings, since quadrupeds and birds are alike without reason.

Failing to consider this, Faustus says: “Moreover, if you seek sects, there are no more than two: that of the Gentiles and ours, since we think entirely differently from them.” This was evidently because he had said that the Gentiles differ most from the Manichaeans in claiming that everything comes from one principle, whereas the Manichaeans deny this and add the principle of the nation of darkness.

Under this distinction, it must be admitted, many Pagans agree with us. But he did not see that someone might likewise divide those who adhere to some religion by saying that some approve of worshiping one God, while others approve of worshiping many. Under this distinction the Pagans are separated from us, while these people are counted with the Pagans, and we with the Jews. Someone could therefore, according to this distinction, likewise suppose that there are only two sects.

Perhaps you will say that you claim your many gods to be of one substance—as though the Pagans did not likewise assert that their many gods were of one substance, although they assign them different duties, works, and powers. So, too, among you one god defeats the nation of darkness, another constructs the world from what has been captured from it, another suspends it above, another carries it below, another sets the wheels of fire, wind, and water in motion at the bottom, and another, circling in heaven with his rays, even gathers the members of your god from sewers.

Who could count all the fabulous duties of your gods, displayed by no truth and represented by no allegories?

Again, if someone divides all human beings by saying that some believe God cares for human affairs, while others entirely deny this, then under this distinction the Pagans and the Jews agree with us, as do you and all heretics who are called Christian in some manner. Under the other category are found the Epicureans and any others who have held this opinion.

Is this a small distinction? Why, then, should only two sects not be said to exist according to this distinction also, so that you would be with us in one of them? Or will you dare, under this distinction, to separate yourselves from us, who proclaim that God cares for human affairs, and to be with the Epicureans, who deny it? At this point, plainly rejecting them, you run to us.

Thus, through different distinctions, they are found now here and now there: joined in one respect, separated in another; in turn, all of them with us and we with all of them, and again none of them with us and we with none of them. If Faustus had considered this, he would not have raved so eloquently.

**CHAPTER XI**

What shall I say here about his claim that, through the powers of the Holy Spirit and a spiritual outpouring, the earth itself conceives and gives birth to the suffering Jesus, who is the life and salvation of human beings, hanging entirely from a tree?

O madman! Without for the moment examining your empty talk on this subject, can the earth conceive from the Holy Spirit and give birth to the suffering Jesus, while the Virgin Mary could not? Compare, if you dare, the virgin womb sanctified by such purity with all the places of the earth where trees and grasses grow.

Do you shudder at that woman—or pretend to shudder—at a womb dedicated to chastity, while you do not shudder at Jesus being born in every garden around every city from water flowing out of sewers? For what muddy fluid does not produce and nourish countless sprouts?

Thus you proclaim that the suffering Jesus is born from something which you declare unworthy of belief when it is said to have been born from a virgin. If you think flesh is unclean, why does that seem to you less unclean which the very nature of flesh purifies from its own sustenance? Is flesh unclean while the dung expelled from flesh is clean? Do you not pay attention? Do you not see that fields rejoice in manure so that they may be made more fertile?

Your madness comes back to this: the earth conceives of the Holy Spirit—whom you say disdained Mary’s flesh—more abundantly and more joyfully the more diligently it has been enriched with the filth and squalor of flesh.

Or, to defend this, will you say that the Holy Spirit possesses an uncontaminated presence everywhere? We answer you: Why, then, not also in the virgin womb?

But let us now set aside the conception and consider the birth itself. You say that the earth, conceiving from the Holy Spirit, gives birth to the suffering Jesus, whom you nevertheless claim hangs from every tree, so contaminated by fruits and apples that he is further polluted by countless animals that eat flesh, and that he must be cleansed from that pollution solely in the part to which your hunger has come to his aid.

We, for our part, believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that Christ, the Son of God and Word of God, was clothed with flesh without contamination, because that substance cannot be contaminated by flesh—or by anything else. But according to your fable, you say that Jesus, while still hanging on the tree, is already contaminated before he enters the flesh of anyone who eats him. Or, if he is not contaminated, how do you purify him by eating him?

Furthermore, since you say that all trees are his cross, and Faustus therefore proclaims that he hangs from every tree, why do you not, just as that good man Joseph of Arimathea took the true Jesus down from the cross in order to bury him (John 19:38), pluck the fruits so that, having taken Jesus down from his suspension on the tree, you may bury him in your belly? Or why is it pious to place Christ in a tomb but impious to take him down from the tree?

Or, so that the words of the Apostle concerning the prophet may also apply to you: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. 5:10; Rom. 3:13)—do you wait with open mouth for someone to bring Christ into your jaws as though into the finest of tombs?

Finally, tell us how many Christs you claim there are. Is the one whom the earth, conceiving from the Holy Spirit, gives birth to as the suffering Jesus—hanging not only from every tree but also lying in the grass—different from the one whom the Jews crucified under Pontius Pilate, and from the third, the one stretched between the sun and the moon? Or are they one and the same, bound in one part of himself to the trees and free in another, assisting the part that is bound and captured?

If this is so, then concerning the one whom you admit suffered under Pontius Pilate, although you say that he was without flesh, I will not yet ask how such a death could have been endured without flesh. I ask instead: to whom did he leave those ships, so that, descending from them, he might suffer such things as could not occur without some kind of body?

According to spiritual presence, he could in no way suffer those things; according to bodily presence, he could not be simultaneously in the sun, the moon, and on the cross. Therefore, if he had no body, he was not crucified. But if he had a body, I ask where he obtained it, since you say that all bodies come from the nation of darkness, although you have never been able to conceive of divine substance except as bodily.

Thus you are forced either to say that he was crucified without a body, than which nothing more absurd or insane can be said; or to say that he appeared to be crucified in a phantasm rather than in reality, an impiety surpassed by nothing worse; or to admit that not all bodies come from the nation of darkness, but that there is also a body belonging to the divine substance, which nevertheless is not immortal but can be fastened to wood and killed—an assertion no less full of madness; or to say that Christ had a mortal body from the nation of darkness, and thus, while fearing to believe that Mary the Virgin was the mother of that body, not fear the nation of demons.

Finally, according to Faustus’s opinion—which he extracted from your very lengthy fable and touched upon as briefly as he could—if the earth, conceiving from the Holy Spirit, gives birth to the suffering Jesus, who is the life and salvation of human beings, hanging from every tree, why does the Savior correspond to the one who hangs by hanging, but not to the one who is born by being born?

But if you say that Jesus is in the trees, that Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and that Jesus is stretched between the sun and the moon because all this comes from one and the same substance, why do you not include the other thousands of your divinities under this name as well? Why should that splendor-bearer not also be Jesus, and Atlas, and the king of glory, and the powerful spirit, and the first man, and everything else that you proclaim under innumerable different names and through different functions?

**CHAPTER XII**

Finally, why is the Holy Spirit placed as the third person, when he is one among countless persons? Or why is he not also Jesus?

And what does Faustus’s deceptive weaving of words mean when, attempting to appear to agree with true Christians—though he is separated from them by an immense distance—he says:

“Therefore we worship the one and the same divinity under three names: the Father, God Almighty; Christ, his Son; and the Holy Spirit.”

Why “under three names,” and not rather under many—not merely in name but also in reality—if there are as many persons as names?

You cannot say, as you can with weapons, that one thing has three names—sword, blade, and saber—and likewise say that the moon, the lesser ship, the luminary of the night, and whatever other name you assign to the same thing are one thing. Nor can you say that the same person is the first man, the powerful spirit, the splendor-bearer, and the enormous Atlas. Rather, one is this person, another that, and another still another, and you are not accustomed to call any of them Christ.

Or how can there be one divinity if there are different works? Or why is the whole not simultaneously one Christ, if, because of one substance, Christ is in the trees, Christ in the persecution by the Jews, and Christ in the sun and moon?

Clearly, your phantasms have lost every path. Clearly, they are nothing other than visions of people gone mad.

**CHAPTER XIII**

I do not know why Faustus thinks that our religious practice concerning bread and the cup is equal to yours, since among the Manichaeans tasting wine is not religion but sacrilege. They recognize their god in the grape but refuse to recognize him in the vat, as though something about his being trodden and enclosed had offended them.

Our bread and cup, however, are not just any bread and cup—as though on account of Christ bound in the ears of grain and in the vine-shoots, as they foolishly imagine—but become mystical for us through a specific consecration.

[Note: Five manuscripts read *certa consideratione* (“through a specific consideration”). This is incorrect.]

[Note: The Louvain edition adds here *corpus Christi* (“the body of Christ”), but this is absent from the manuscripts.]

They do not come into being as such. Therefore, what is not made in this manner, even though it is bread and a cup, is food for bodily nourishment, not a sacrament of religion—except that we bless and give thanks to the Lord for every gift of his, both spiritual and bodily.

But according to your fable, Christ, bound in every kind of food, is set before you, still to be bound in your entrails and released through your belchings. For when you eat, you refresh yourselves by the wasting away of your god; and when you digest, you waste him away through your refreshment. When your recovery makes you full, your fullness presses upon him.

This would indeed be attributed to mercy, since he suffers something for you within you, if he did not once again leave you empty so that, liberated from you, he might escape.

How, then, do you compare our bread and cup with yours and call the two religious practices equal, although one error is far removed from the truth? In this you are more foolish than certain people who think that we worship Ceres and Liber because of the bread and cup.

I have thought it necessary to mention this so that you may recognize the same vanity in your belief that our fathers were dedicated to Saturn on account of the Sabbath. For just as we are far from Ceres and Liber, the Pagan gods, although we embrace according to our rite the sacrament of bread and cup, which you praised so highly that you wished to be our equals in it, so our fathers were far from the Saturnian chains, although for the time appropriate to prophecy they observed the Sabbath rest.

**CHAPTER XIV**

But why did you not also say that you shared with the Pagans an equal religion on account of *Hyle*, which frequently appears in some of their books? Indeed, you wanted to be understood as unequal and very different from them for this reason: because your theologian calls the principle and nature of evil by this name.

Here your great ignorance is exposed, because you do not know what Hyle is, yet you affect to inflate yourselves as though learned by using the name of a reality you entirely fail to understand.

For when the Greeks discuss nature, they define *Hyle* (ὕλη) as a certain matter—entirely unformed, but capable of receiving all bodily forms. This is in some way recognized in the mutability of bodies; in itself, however, it can neither be sensed nor understood.

Certain Gentiles err in joining it to God as coeternal, so that it does not come from him, although it is formed by him. That this is contrary to the truth, the truth itself teaches.

Yet observe which Pagans you are found to resemble concerning this very Hyle: you too claim that it has its own principle and does not come from God. And in this respect you said that you differed from them, without knowing what you were saying.

But in the point that Hyle has no form proper to itself and can be formed only by God, they agree with our truth and disagree with your falsehood. For, not knowing what Hyle is—that is, what the matter of things is—you call the nation of darkness Hyle, although you establish there not only countless bodily forms distinguished into five kinds, but also a mind that fashions those bodies. More ignorant—or rather more insane—still, you call that mind itself Hyle, even though you say that it is not formed but forms.

For if there were there some mind that formed, and bodily elements that were formed, those elements would have to be called Hyle—that is, the matter which the same mind, which you wish to be the principle of evil, would form.

If you said this, you would not be very far wrong about what Hyle is, except that those elements themselves, although destined to be formed into other shapes, would not be Hyle, since they would already be elements distinguished by their proper kinds. Hyle is altogether formless.

Nevertheless, your ignorance would be tolerable, because you would call Hyle that which is formed, not that which forms. Even so, however, you would still be held as vain and sacrilegious, because, while not knowing that every mode of nature, number of forms, and order of weights can exist only from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, you would attribute so much goodness to the principle of evil.

But now, since you know neither what Hyle is nor what evil is, if only I could persuade you to restrain yourselves from misleading the ignorant!

**CHAPTER XV**

Now, because you also wish to be better than the Pagans for this reason—that they think God should be worshiped with altars, shrines, images, victims, and incense, whereas you do none of these things—who would not laugh?
