As though it were not better to set up an altar even for a stone, which exists in some fashion, and to offer a victim, than to worship what does not exist at all in the delirium of a phantasm!

But you, who have said that you are the rational temple of God, how will you explain this? Do you approve of God’s having a temple in which the devil has fashioned some part?

Are you not the people who say that all your members and your entire body were fashioned by the evil mind whom you call Hyle, and that a part of that very fashioning power dwells there together with a part of your god?

Since that part is held there, as you claim, chained and enclosed, should you have called yourself the temple of God or the prison of God?

Unless perhaps you call your soul the temple of God because you possess it from the land of light. But you are accustomed to call that part, or member, of God—not the temple of God.

It follows, then, that you could not have called yourself the temple of God except on account of the body which, according to you, the devil fashioned.

See how you blaspheme the temple of God: you say not only that it is not holy, but also that it is the devil’s contrivance and God’s prison.

But the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.” And so that you may not think this refers only to the soul, listen to the more explicit statement: “Do you not know,” he says, “that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 3:17; 6:19.)

Yet you call the work of demons the temple of God, and there you place the living Christ, as Faustus says, “the image of the living majesty,” the Son of God.

Let your phantasmal Christ dwell in such a temple of sacrilegious vanity. He can be called an image not from resemblance but from simulation.

**CHAPTER XVI**

Thus you have made your mind an altar as well—but see whose altar it is. For the very arts and disciplines with which you said it was imbued reveal this.

Those arts and disciplines forbid you to offer bread to a hungry human being, so that on your altar you may burn with a sacrifice of cruelty. The Lord destroys such an altar when he recalls from the Law the kind of odor in which God delights, saying: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6).

Now observe where the Lord recalled this. He did so when he was passing through a grainfield and his hungry disciples were plucking ears of grain—an act which, according to the discipline with which you have imbued your mind, you call murder.

It was an altar not of God but of lying demons, whose doctrines brand and sear the evil conscience as with a hot iron (1 Tim. 4:2), calling murder what the Truth declares to be innocence.

For he said to the Jews—and in doing so he struck down and destroyed the place you too would occupy: “If you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy rather than sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent” (Matt. 12:7).

**CHAPTER XVII**

What simple and pure prayers will you be able to offer as divine honors and sacrifices, when you hold such unworthy and shameful opinions about the very nature and substance of God that the true God is not only not appeased by your sacrifices, but your god is actually sacrificed in the sacrifices of the Pagans?

For you think that he is bound not only in wood, grass, and human members, but also in the flesh of animals, which contaminates and pollutes him.

And your own soul—to which god can it give praise? It loudly declares that it is itself a particle of that god, held captive in the nation of darkness. What does it do other than revile the god whom it testifies to have been unable to provide for itself against its enemies in any other way than through such corruption and such shameful captivity of his own parts?

Hence your prayers to your god could not be religious but envious. What evil had you committed against him that you now groan to him under this punishment, when you did not abandon him by sinning of your own will, but were handed over by him to his enemies so that peace might be secured for his kingdom?

Nor were you handed over as hostages who are customarily guarded with honor. Nor does a shepherd set a trap in order to catch a beast: he normally places his own sheep in that snare, not one of his own members, and usually does so in such a way that the beast is caught before the sheep is harmed.

But you, members of your god, were handed over to his enemies, unable to restrain their ferocity by your god except by being contaminated by their foulness. You had no sin of your own, but were wasted away by the poison of the enemy.

Therefore you cannot say in your prayers: “For the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us, and be merciful to our sins for your name’s sake” (Ps. 78:9). Instead you say: “Deliver us by your art, because, so that you may now mourn securely in your kingdom, we are here oppressed, torn apart, and polluted.”

This is an accusatory voice, not a prayer of supplication.

Nor can you say what the Teacher of truth taught: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). For who are your debtors who have sinned against you? The nation of darkness? Do you forgive its debts when you eradicate it completely and enclose it in an eternal prison?

And what debts can he forgive you, when he rather sinned against you by sending you into these circumstances than you sinned against him by obeying the one who sent you?

Or, if he did not sin because he acted under necessity, your necessity is greater now that you lie defeated in battle than his was before you fought. For you are already suffering from evil mingled with you, whereas he suffered nothing of the kind when he nevertheless endured the necessity of sending you.

Thus either he himself owes you something that you should forgive, or, if he owes you nothing, you owe him even less.

Where, then, are your sacrifices? Where are your simple and pure prayers, when they are deceitful and impure blasphemies?

**CHAPTER XVIII**
And yet I want you to tell me by what names you call all those things which you praise in yourselves, so that you say “temple,” “altar,” and “sacrifice.” For if these things are not truly owed to the true God, why are they proclaimed laudably in the true religion? But if a true sacrifice is rightly owed to the true God—and hence divine honors are also rightly so called—then the other things called sacrifices are made in imitation of a certain true sacrifice.

Some of these are imitations of false and deceptive gods—that is, demons—who arrogantly demand divine honors from those whom they have deceived, as is the case, or was the case, with everything in the temples and idols of the Gentiles. Others are proclamations of the one most truly future sacrifice that would have to be offered for the sins of all believers, such as were the divinely given commandments to our ancient fathers, among which was that mystical anointing by which Christ was prefigured; hence even his name is derived from *chrisma* (“anointing”).

Accordingly, the true sacrifice owed to the one true God, with which Christ alone filled his altar, the demons arrogantly demand for themselves in the form of animal victims. Hence the Apostle says: “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God” (1 Cor. 10:20)—not blaming what was offered, but because it was offered to them. The Hebrews, however, in the animal victims that they offered to God, celebrated in many and varied ways, as was fitting for so great a matter, a prophecy of the future victim whom Christ offered.

Therefore Christians now celebrate the memory of that same accomplished sacrifice through the most holy offering and participation in the body and blood of Christ. But the Manichaeans, not knowing what must be condemned in the sacrifices of the Gentiles, what must be understood in the sacrifices of the Hebrews, or what must be held and observed in the sacrifice of Christians, offer their vanity as a sacred offering to the devil who deceived them. They depart from the faith and attend to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, in the hypocrisy of liars.

## CHAPTER XIX

Let Faustus learn—or rather, let those who take pleasure in his writings learn—that we do not derive the doctrine of monarchy from the Gentiles. Yet the Gentiles have not fallen so completely into false gods that they lost the belief in one true God, from whom every kind of nature derives.

For their wise men—because, as the Apostle says, “the invisible things of God, from the foundation of the world, are understood and seen through the things that have been made; his eternal power and divinity also,” so that they are without excuse—although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks. Instead, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents.

These are the idols of the Gentiles. In interpreting them, they find no way out except toward the creature whom God created. Thus, even in their interpretation of idols—the interpretation in which their more learned men customarily boast and puff themselves up—what the same Apostle says shortly afterward comes to pass in them: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:20–25).

But you are vain both in what makes you unlike them and in what makes you like them—you are worse. [Note: [Col. 0383] Ambrosian, Erasmian, and several manuscripts read: “and in what makes you like them, you are vain; and in what makes you unlike them, you are worse.”] For you do not believe in monarchy together with them because they believe what is true, so that you may believe the substance of that one God to be vulnerable and corruptible; and that is impious vanity. But in the worship of many gods, the doctrine of lying demons persuaded them to have many idols, while it persuaded you to have many phantasms.

## CHAPTER XX

We do not, as Faustus says, turn their sacrifices into love-feasts. Rather, we understand that sacrifice which I mentioned shortly before, when the Lord says, “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice.”

For our love-feasts feed the poor, whether with grain or with meat. God’s creature is fed from God’s creature that is suitable as human food. But because lying demons have persuaded you—not to govern the flesh but to exercise blasphemy—to abstain from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have come to know the truth—for “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:2–4)—you are ungrateful to the Creator and repay his abundant benefits with sacrilegious insults.

Because meat is often distributed to the poor even at love-feasts, you call the mercy of Christians similar to the sacrifices of the pagans, some of whom you resemble in this respect also. For you consider it unlawful to kill animals because you imagine that human souls pass into them; this belief is found in the books of certain Gentile philosophers, although it is said to have been understood differently by later writers. Yet in this respect also you err much more grievously. They feared to slaughter their fellow human beings in the form of animals; you fear to slaughter your god, whose members you imagine the souls of animals to be.

## CHAPTER XXI

As for what Faustus also accuses us of on this matter—namely, that by honoring the memorials of the martyrs we have turned them into idols—I am not so much moved to answer this accusation as to show that Faustus, in his eagerness to slander, wished to stray even from the vanities of Mani himself and somehow fell unawares into the common and poetic opinion of the pagans, from whom he wants to appear utterly alien.

For after saying that we had turned idols into martyrs, whom, he says, we worship with similar vows, he adds: “You appease the shades of the dead with wine and food.” Then, are there shades of the dead? We have never heard this in your discussions, never read it in your writings. Indeed, you are accustomed to contradict such opinions, asserting that the souls of the dead who are evil or less purified [Note: [Col. 0384] The Erasmian edition has *animas mortuorum magis minusve purgatas* (“the souls of the dead, more or less purified”).] either enter into cycles of reincarnation or undergo some more severe punishments, while the good are placed in ships and, sailing through heaven, pass from here into that phantasm of the earth’s light for which they had perished in battle. Thus no souls are detained around the tombs of their bodies. Where, then, are the shades of the dead? What is their substance? What is their place?

But in his eagerness to curse, Faustus forgot what he was professing. Or perhaps, drowsing, he dictated this while dreaming of shades; and when he read his own words, he did not wake up.

The Christian people, however, solemnly celebrate the memorials of the martyrs, both to arouse imitation and to be joined to their merits and assisted by their prayers. Yet we establish altars not to any of the martyrs, but to the God of the martyrs himself, even though they are established at the memorials of the martyrs. For which bishop, standing at an altar in the places of the holy bodies, has ever said, “We offer to you, Peter,” or “Paul,” or “Cyprian”? What is offered is offered to God, who crowned the martyrs, at the memorials of those whom he crowned, so that from the reminder provided by those places a greater devotion may arise, sharpening our love both for those whom we are able to imitate [Note: [Col. 0384] Most manuscripts here and in the following passage read *possimus* (“whom we can imitate”).] and for him by whose help we are able to do so.

We honor the martyrs, therefore, with that worship of love and fellowship with which holy human beings of God are also honored in this life—those whose hearts we perceive to have been prepared for such suffering on behalf of the truth of the gospel. But we honor the martyrs with greater devotion because they are safer after their struggles have been overcome [Note: [Col. 0384] Ambrosian, Erasmian, and several manuscripts read *post incerta omnia superata* (“after all uncertainties have been overcome”).], and we proclaim them with more confident praise because they are now victors in a happier life, whereas in this life they were still fighting.

But with that worship which is called in Greek *λατρεία* (*latreia*)—which cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word, since it is a service owed properly to divinity—we neither worship nor teach that anyone should be worshiped except the one God. Since the offering of sacrifice belongs to this worship, and since *idololatria* is the name for those who offer this also to idols, we offer nothing of this kind and prescribe nothing of this kind to be offered either to any martyr, any holy soul, or any angel. Whoever falls into this error is corrected by sound doctrine, either so that he may be corrected [Note: [Col. 0385] Lovaniensis adds here, “or so that he may be condemned.” This is absent from Ambrosian, Erasmian, and the manuscripts.] or so that others may be warned against it.

For the saints themselves, whether human beings or angels, do not wish to have rendered to them what they know is owed to the one God. This was evident in Paul and Barnabas when the Lycaonians, stirred by the miracles performed through them, wished to sacrifice to them as gods. They tore their garments, declared and urged that they were not gods, and forbade this to be done to them (Acts 14:7–17). It was also evident in the angels, as we read in the Apocalypse: an angel forbade himself to be worshiped and said to his worshiper, “I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Rev. 19:10; 22:8–9).

The proud spirits—the devil and his angels—plainly demand these things for themselves, as they do throughout all the temples and sacred rites of the Gentiles. Their likeness has also been manifested in certain proud human beings, as we remember from the accounts preserved about certain kings of Babylon. Hence the holy Daniel endured accusations and persecution because, after an edict had been issued that no one was to ask anything from any god except the king alone, he was discovered worshiping and praying to his God—that is, the one true God (Dan. 6).

But how can those who become drunk at the memorials of the martyrs be approved by us, when sound doctrine condemns them even if they do this in their own homes? Yet one thing is what we teach, another what we tolerate, another what we are commanded to prescribe, and another what we are commanded to correct—and until we correct it, are compelled to tolerate. Christian discipline is one thing; the dissipation of wine-drinkers or the error of the weak is another.

Nevertheless, even in this matter the guilt of drunkards and of sacrilegious people differs greatly. It is a much lesser sin to return drunk from the martyrs than to sacrifice to the martyrs while sober. I said “to sacrifice to the martyrs”; I did not say “to sacrifice to God at the memorials of the martyrs”—something we do very frequently, but only in that rite by which the manifestation of the New Testament commanded sacrifice to be made to him. This belongs to the worship called *latria*, which is owed to the one God.

But what am I to do? When will I show these heretics, blind as they are, what force there is in what is sung in the Psalms: “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I will show him my salvation” (Ps. 49:23)?

Before Christ’s coming, the flesh and blood of this sacrifice was announced through sacrificial likenesses [Note: [Col. 0385] Two manuscripts read *per victimarum similitudinem* (“through the likeness of victims”).]; in Christ’s Passion it was rendered through the truth itself; after Christ’s ascension it is celebrated through the sacrament of remembrance. Accordingly, the difference between the sacrifices of the pagans and those of the Hebrews is as great as the difference between an erroneous imitation and a prophetic prefiguration.

Just as the virginity of consecrated women is not for that reason to be despised or detested because there were also Vestal virgins, so the sacrifices of the Fathers are not for that reason to be condemned because there are also sacrifices of the Gentiles. For just as there is a great difference between those forms of virginity—even though the only difference may be whom each is vowed and rendered to—so there is a great difference between the sacrifices of the pagans and those of the Hebrews, precisely because the one difference is whom the sacrifices were immolated and offered to.

The former were offered to the proud impiety of demons, who arrogantly claim the very thing for themselves so that they might be regarded as gods, since sacrifice is a divine honor. The latter were offered to the one God, so that a likeness promising the truth of the sacrifice might be offered to him—the very truth that was to be rendered in the Passion of the body and blood of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXII

For it is not true, as Faustus said, that our predecessors, the Jews, separated from the Gentiles, though they possessed a temple, sacrifices, altars, and priesthoods, abandoned only the sculptures—that is, the idols. They could have sacrificed, like some people, even without sculpted idols: to trees, mountains, and finally even to the sun, moon, and other stars.

If they had done this through that worship called *latria*, serving the creature rather than the Creator and thereby wandering in the grave evil of impious superstition, the demons would nevertheless have offered themselves to deceive them and to take from them what they had offered in this way. Those proud and impious spirits are fed not by scent and smoke, as some foolish people imagine, but by the errors of human beings—not by the nourishment of their bodies, but by malicious delight [Note: [Col. 0386] Ambrosian, Erasmian, and some manuscripts read *dilectione* (“affection”) instead of *delectatione* (“delight”).] when they deceive them by whatever means, or by the arrogant ostentation of a pretended majesty when they boast that divine honors are rendered to them.

Our fathers, therefore, did not abandon only the idols of the Gentiles. They offered nothing to the earth, to anything earthly, to the sea, to the sky, or to the host of heaven; instead, they offered victims to the one God, creator of all. He wished these victims to be offered because, through their likeness, he promised the true victim by which, in Christ Jesus our Lord, he reconciled us to himself through the remission of sins.

Paul addresses the faithful, who have been made the body of this head, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12:1).

But the Manichaeans say that human bodies are the handiwork of the nation of darkness and prisons in which God, having been conquered, is confined. Thus Faustus announces one thing and Paul another. But since “if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9), Christ speaks the truth in Paul: let the Manichaean be accursed in Faustus.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Faustus also says that we have changed nothing in the customs of the Gentiles, not knowing what he is saying. Since “the just shall live by faith” (Rom. 1:17), and since “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5), and since these three remain for shaping [Note: [Col. 0386] Thus the manuscripts. Ambrosian and Erasmian: “for confirming”; Louvain: “for forming.”] the life of the faithful—faith, hope, and love (1 Cor. 13:13)—how can someone have the same customs as another who does not share these three with him? One who believes one thing, hopes for another, and loves something else must live differently.

Even if the use of certain things appears similar among us and the Gentiles—food and drink, houses, clothing, and baths—and even if some of our people live married lives, taking and keeping wives, begetting children, raising them, and leaving them inheritances—the person who directs the use of these things toward a different end uses them very differently. So does the person who gives thanks for these things to God, about whom he does not hold perverse and false beliefs.

For just as, in your own error, although you eat the bread that other human beings eat, live on fruits and springs, and clothe yourselves in wool and linen woven in the same way, you nevertheless do not lead the same life as they do—not because you eat, drink, or wear something different, but because you think and believe something different and direct all these things toward another end, namely, the end of your error and vanity—so we, both in these things and in others that we use in the same way, do not live with the Gentiles in the same way. We do not direct the same things toward the same end, but toward the end of the lawful and divine commandment: love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Some have strayed from these and turned aside to empty talk.

In this matter you certainly hold first place, since you do not observe or consider how much, in possessing and doing the same things, a different faith contributes to a different life. Your Hearers have wives and children, even though they receive the children unwillingly; they accumulate or preserve inheritances for them; they eat meat, drink wine, bathe, reap, harvest grapes, conduct business, and administer public offices. Yet you count them among your own people, not among the Gentiles, although their actions appear more like those of the Gentiles than like yours.

Indeed, the actions of certain Gentiles come closer to yours than those of some of your Hearers. For some Gentiles abstain from wine, meat, and sexual intercourse in their sacrilegious rites. Yet you count Hearers who use all these things—and who differ from you in this respect—among the followers of Mani, rather than counting those Gentiles who do the same things you do. You call a woman who has believed in Mani your own, even if she gives birth, but you do not call the Sibyl your own, although she did not even marry.

But, you say, many Catholics are called Christians, and are adulterers, robbers, greedy, drunkards, and guilty of whatever else is opposed to sound doctrine. What about among you? In your very small and almost nonexistent number, are there not many such people? And are there not some among the pagans who are not such? [Note: [Col. 0388] Many manuscripts read: *et plerique in Paganis* (“and most among the pagans”).] Do you therefore call those pagans who are not such better than yourselves? Yet because of the sacrilegious vanity of your sect, even those among you who are not such are worse than pagans who are such.

It is therefore clear that sound doctrine, which alone is Catholic, is not discredited because many wish to be counted by its name but refuse to be healed through it. We must recognize that small number which the Lord especially commends amid the vast and innumerable multitude spread throughout the whole world (Matt. 20:16). Yet this number of saints and faithful is called small—something that must often be emphasized—like a quantity of grain in comparison with the multitude of chaff. In itself, however, it forms so great a mass of wheat that it surpasses by an incomparable multitude all your worthy and unworthy members whom the truth equally rejects.

Behold, we are not a schism of the Gentiles, since we differ from them very greatly for the better. But neither are you this, since you differ from them very greatly for the worse.

# BOOK TWENTY-ONE

[Col. 0387]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0387]

**FAUSTUS said:** There is one God, or two? Clearly, one. How, then, do you assert two? The name of two gods has never, at least in our own assertions, been heard. But from where you suspect this, I would like to know.

**AUGUSTINE:** Because you teach two principles of good and evil.

**FAUSTUS:** It is true that we confess two principles, but we call one of them God and the other Hyle—or, to speak in the ordinary and customary way, the demon. If you think that this signifies two gods, then when a physician discusses illness and health you could also think that these are two healths; when someone names good and evil, you could think these two things are both good; and when you hear of abundance and poverty, you could think these are two abundances.

If, while I was discussing white and black, cold and hot, and sweet and bitter, you said that I had shown two whites, two hots, and two sweets, would you not appear to be out of your mind [Note: [Col. 0387] Ambrosian, Erasmian, and some manuscripts read *incompos* (“disordered”) instead of *mentis impos* (“out of one’s mind”).] and entirely unsound in brain? In the same way, when I teach two principles, God and Hyle, I should not on that account already appear to you to be displaying two gods.

Or, because we assign every evil power to Hyle and every beneficial power to God, as is fitting, do you therefore think it makes no difference whether we call both of them God? If so, then when you hear of poison and an antidote, you could think it makes no difference whether both are called antidotes, because each has its own power and each does and accomplishes something. Likewise, when you hear of a physician and a poisoner, you will call both physicians; and when you hear of a just man and an unjust man, you could call both just, because each of them does something.

If it is absurd to do this, how much more absurd is it to think God and Hyle two gods merely because each of them does something? Accordingly, this argument is foolish and entirely feeble: since you cannot answer me concerning the matter itself, you manufacture hostility from names alone.

I do not deny that we sometimes call the adverse nature a god, but we do so not according to our faith; rather, we use the name already applied to it by its worshipers, who foolishly think it a god. In the same way the Apostle says, “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (2 Cor. 4:4). He calls it “god” because it was already so called by its own followers, but he adds that it blinds minds, so that from this it may be understood not to be the true God.

## CHAPTER II

**AUGUSTINE replied:** In your discussions we commonly hear of two gods. Although you first denied this, shortly afterward you yourself confessed it, as though explaining why you say this: because the Apostle also says, “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers.”

Many of us punctuate this sentence so as to say that the true God blinded the minds of unbelievers. For when they read, “Among whom God,” they pause; then they add, “has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age.” Even if you do not punctuate it this way, but, for explanatory purposes, change the word order thus—“Among whom God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age”—the same sense emerges as in that punctuation.

For even such an action, by which the minds of unbelievers are blinded, can in a certain manner belong to the true God. He does this not through wickedness but through justice, just as Paul says elsewhere: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” (Rom. 3:5). Elsewhere also he says: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. For he says to Moses, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’”

After he had first stated what must be held without hesitation—namely, that there is no injustice with God—pay attention to what he says shortly afterward: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that were prepared for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory,” and so forth (Rom. 9:14–15, 22–23).

Here it cannot in any way be said that the God who shows wrath and demonstrates his power in vessels prepared for destruction is one God, and the God who shows his riches in vessels of mercy is another. Apostolic teaching testifies that one and the same God does both.

This is also the meaning of the passage: “For this reason God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves.” Shortly afterward: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions.” And again shortly afterward: “Since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind” (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28).

Behold how the true and just God blinds the minds of unbelievers. For in these words of the Apostle that I have recalled, no other God has ever been understood than the one who sent his Son, who said: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

Here too it is sufficiently evident to faithful minds how God blinds the minds of unbelievers. Something hidden precedes in the hidden places, where God carries out the most just examination of his judgment, so that the minds of some are blinded and those of others enlightened. To him it is most truly said: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7). Astonished at the unfathomable depth of this, the Apostle exclaims: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments,” and so forth (Rom. 11:33).

## CHAPTER III

But because you cannot distinguish what God does by gracious benefit from what he does by judgment—and because our Psalter is far from both your heart and your mouth, where it says, “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Ps. 100:1)—whatever offends you through the weakness of human mortality, you remove entirely from the will and judgment of the true God. You have ready another evil god, whom truth has not shown you but vanity has invented, to whom you attribute not only everything you do unjustly but also everything you suffer justly.

Thus you attribute to God the benefits of gifts while taking away from him the judgments of punishments, as though Christ had said that someone other than the one who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil and sends rain on the just and the unjust had prepared eternal fire for the wicked (Matt. 25:41; 5:45).

Why do you not understand that such great goodness here and such great severity there belong to one God, unless it is because you do not know how to sing of mercy and judgment? Is it not the same God who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil and sends rain on the just and the unjust, yet breaks the natural branches and grafts in the wild olive contrary to nature?

Does the Apostle not say of this one God: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness” (Rom. 11:17–24)? Surely you hear and understand how he neither takes judicial severity away from God nor free will from the human being.

It is hidden, it is deep, and it is shut away from human thought in an inaccessible secrecy, how God both condemns the wicked and justifies the wicked. Scripture’s truth speaks of both as belonging to him. Does it therefore please you to chatter against divine judgments because they are unsearchable?

How much more fitting and appropriate to our limited capacity it is to be awestruck where Paul was awestruck and to exclaim: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways!” How much better it is to marvel at what you are not sufficient to investigate than, for that reason, to wish to invent another evil god because you could not comprehend the one good God! For the issue is not the name but the work.

## CHAPTER IV

Faustus seems to defend himself quickly when he says: “We do not say two gods, but God and Hyle.” But when you ask what he means by Hyle, you will plainly hear another god being described.

If by Hyle they called an unformed matter capable of bodily forms—the matter called Hyle by the ancients—none of us would object to its being called a god. But what an error, what madness, either to call the matter of bodies the maker of bodies or to deny that the maker of bodies is God [Note: [Col. 0390] Several manuscripts read, “or to deny God to be the matter of bodies.”]!

Since, then, you say that someone else does what the true God does—that is, produces the qualities and forms of bodies, elements, and animals, so that they are bodies, elements, and animals—whatever name you give him, you are rightly said, in your error, to introduce another god.

In this one matter you err twice with sacrilegious error. First, because you say that the one who makes the things God makes is someone whom you are ashamed to acknowledge as God; but you will in no way make him not God unless you deny that he makes such things as only God makes. Second, because you suppose that the things the good God makes good are made by an evil being and are themselves evil. With childish judgment, you shudder at what does not suit the weakness of mortal punishment and love what does suit it.

Accordingly, you call the one who made the serpent evil. But you consider this great sun so great a good that you believe it was not made by God but brought forth or sent out. The true God—in whom I grieve exceedingly that you have not yet believed—made both the serpent among other lower things and the sun among other higher things. And in realms still higher—not bodily heavenly things, but spiritual ones—he made many things far better than all this light, things that no carnal person perceives.

How much less do you perceive them, since, although you detest the flesh, you detest nothing except your own rule by which you measure good and evil? For you cannot have a thought of evil except of things that offend the carnal sense, or a thought of good except of things that delight the carnal eye.

## CHAPTER V

When, therefore, I consider these works of God at the lowest level of things—earthly, weak, and mortal, yet nevertheless works of God, such as we are able to see—I am moved beyond words to praise their Creator, who is so great in great works that he is not less great in the smallest.

The divine art by which heavenly and earthly works are made is itself alike in all things, although those works differ from one another, because in perfecting each according to its own kind it is everywhere perfect. God does not create the universe in each individual thing; rather, while creating individual things as part of the universe’s whole, he presents his universal art to each of them, making and arranging everything suitably according to its places and orders and assigning to all things what is fitting both particularly and universally.

Look here, in this lowest foundation [Note: [Col. 0391] Some manuscripts read “in this lowest world.”] of the entire creation, at the animals that fly, swim, walk, and crawl. Surely they are mortal; surely their life, as it is written, is “a vapor that appears for a little while” (James 4:15).

They contribute this measure, received from the best Creator, as though contributing it in common to the universe, each according to its kind, so that together with these lowest things all the good things exist in which the higher things are better than they are.

Nevertheless, pay attention and give me any most despised animal whose soul hates its flesh and does not instead nourish and cherish it, enliven and govern it by vital movement, and in a certain way administer, according to the smallness of its kind, a certain universe of its own that has been secured for its preservation.

When a rational soul disciplines its body and subjects it to servitude, so that it is not hindered by an immoderate appetite for earthly things from perceiving wisdom [Note: [Col. 0391] Most manuscripts read, “so that the perception of wisdom is not hindered by an earthly appetite.”], even then it certainly loves its flesh, which it rightly subordinates and orders to obedience.

Finally, you yourselves, although through carnal error you detest the flesh, can do nothing but love your flesh and care for its health and safety. You avoid every blow, accident, and excess by which it is harmed, while desiring the protections and well-being by which it is preserved. Thus you show that the law of nature prevails against the opinion of your error.

## CHAPTER VI

What do the vital organs within the flesh itself—fitting harmoniously into the whole form—the limbs for action, the vessels for sensation, everything distinguished according to its places and functions and woven together in harmonious unity, the moderation of measurements, the equality of numbers, and the order of weights—not indicate their maker, the true God, to whom it was rightly said: “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21)?

If, therefore, you had hearts that were not perverted and corrupted by empty fables, you would perceive his invisible things through the things made in this weak and carnal creation (Rom. 1:20). From whom do these things I have mentioned derive their nature, if not from him by whose unity every measure is established, by whose wisdom every beauty is formed, and by whose law every order is arranged? But if you lack the eye with which to look upon these things, let apostolic authority guide you.

## CHAPTER VII

When the Apostle was giving instructions about holy love—what a husband’s love toward his wife ought to be—he took his example from the soul of one who loves [Note: [Col. 0392] The editions of Ambrosius and Erasmus read “from the soul of a living creature.”]. “He who loves his wife,” he says, “loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church” (Eph. 5:28–29).

Behold, all bodily substance is before your eyes. See how, in every animal, this communion of nature extends toward what has been joined to it for its preservation, so that it loves its flesh.

This is not found only in human beings, who, when they live rightly, not only care for the health of their flesh but also tame and restrain bodily impulses for the use of reason. Wild animals too flee pain and fear death; whatever can tear apart and separate that joined structure and bond of limbs, flesh, and spirit from harmonious union, they avoid with all the agility they possess, themselves also nourishing and cherishing their flesh.

“No one has ever hated his own flesh,” he says, “but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.” See from where this has risen and to where: contemplate, if you can, how great a force is drawn from the Creator through creation, extending from the heavenly arrangements themselves all the way to the flesh and blood that complete the fullness of the universe, adorned with a variety of forms and ordered by degrees of being.

## CHAPTER VIII
Again, when the same apostle was teaching us about diverse spiritual gifts that nevertheless harmonize toward unity—a truly great, divine, and hidden subject—he gave us an analogy from this very flesh of ours, and in speaking of it he certainly did not leave its craftsman, God, unmentioned. Although the passage is long [Col. 0393], because it is exceedingly necessary I shall not hesitate to insert the entire passage from his Epistle to the Corinthians into this work:

> Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know how, when you were Gentiles, you were led to voiceless idols. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus”; and no one can say, “The Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit.
>
> There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministrations [Note: In the manuscripts, “there are divisions of ministries”; *ministeriorum sunt*.], yet the same Lord; and there are divisions of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all people. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in one Spirit; to another, workings of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of words. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each person his own gifts as he wills.
>
> For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free; and we were all given one Spirit to drink. For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body,” would it therefore not be of the body? Or if the ear should say, “Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body,” would it therefore not be of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If it were entirely hearing, where would the sense of smell be? But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed. If they were all one member, where would the body be? But now there are many members, yet one body.
>
> The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you”; nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.” Rather, those members of the body that seem to be weaker are more necessary; and those members of the body that seem to be less honorable, we surround with greater honor; and our less honorable members have greater dignity, whereas our honorable members have no need of this. But God has composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there might be no division in the body, but that the members might be mutually concerned for one another. If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it [Note: Thus Am., Er., and most manuscripts. Lov. has “if one member boasts,” *sive gloriatur*.] (1 Cor. 12:1–26).

If you possess any faith—not, I say, Christian faith, so that you may believe the apostle, but any human understanding, so that you may see what is evident—let each person observe and consider these things in himself: how true and certain they are, how great they are in what is small, and how good in what is humble. For the apostle places these things among objects of praise, so that through these lowly bodily realities that are seen, those lofty spiritual realities that are not seen might more easily be understood.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0394]

Whoever, then, denies that God is the craftsman of these members and of our body, which the apostle so commends and praises, you see whom he contradicts, proclaiming to you something beyond what we have received [Note: Several manuscripts have “to us,” *nobis*.] (Gal. 1:9). Why, then, must he be refuted by me rather than anathematized by all Christians?

The apostle says, “God has composed the body”; this man says, “Matter” (*Hyle*). What could be more obvious than that these enmities should be anathematized before they are refuted? Did the apostle, when he said “God,” add “of this age” (2 Cor. 4:4)? Even if someone understands the devil as blinding the minds of unbelievers, we do not deny that he does so through evil persuasions. Those who consent to them lose the light of righteousness, God repaying them with what is just.

We read all these things in the holy Scriptures. For it is also said concerning seduction coming from outside:

> I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that are in Christ (ibid. 11:3).

The following is similar:

> Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15:33).

And this passage says that each person may also be his own seducer:

> Whoever thinks that he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself (Gal. 6:3).

And concerning God’s vengeance, which I mentioned above:

> God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting (Rom. 1:28).

Likewise, in the earlier Books, after saying, “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1:13), Scripture shortly afterward says:

> Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world (ibid. 2:24).

And again, concerning death itself, so that people might not place themselves outside guilt:

> The impious summoned it by their hands and words; and, considering it their friend, they wasted away (ibid. 1:16).

Elsewhere, however:

> Good things and evil things, life and death, riches and poverty, are from the Lord God (Sir. 11:14).

Here, confused people do not understand that, in one and the same evil act—not through something else that follows afterward and will be evident, but through a certain punishment accompanying it continuously—one thing comes from the cunning of the persuader, another from the wickedness of the one who wills, and another from the justice of the one who punishes: the devil suggests, the human being consents, and God abandons him.

Therefore, in an evil act—that is, in the blinding of unbelievers—if the devil is understood as involved because of his malignity in persuading, so that “the god of this age” may be distinguished in this way, it does not seem absurd to me. For he is not called simply “God” without an addition, since “of this age” is attached: that is, the god of impious human beings who desire to flourish only in this age. Accordingly, “an evil age” is also mentioned, as it is written:

> To rescue us from the present evil age (Gal. 1:4).

The same applies to the statement:

> Their god is the belly (Phil. 3:19).

If “their” were not there, it would in no way say “the god is the belly.” Nor could demons be called gods in the Psalm unless “of the nations” were added. For it is written:

> The gods of the nations are demons (Ps. 95:5).

But here there is neither “the God of this age,” nor “their god is the belly,” nor “the gods of the nations are demons.” Rather, it simply says, “God has composed the body,” and this can be understood only of the true God, the creator of all. Those statements are made with condemnation; this one is made with praise.

Unless perhaps Faustus understands “God has composed the body” not as an arrangement of members—that is, as fashioning and constructing [Col. 0395] it—but as a mingling of his own light, so that another being placed these members, distinguished and located in their seats—he who fashioned this body [Note: Lov. reads “fashioned these things.” Am., Er., and the manuscripts read “fashioned this,” with “body” understood.]—while God, by mixing in his goodness, tempered the malice of this construction. For with such fables they dull childish minds.

But even this they were not permitted to say, because God came to the aid of little ones through the mouths of the saints. For a little earlier you have:

> God placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed.

Who, then, cannot understand that in this passage God is called the composer of the body because he fashioned the body from many members, preserving the functions of diverse operations within the structure of unity?

## CHAPTER X

Let the Manichaeans say whether the animals which, according to their ravings, Matter had fashioned among the nation of darkness—before God had mingled his light with them—did not possess that harmony of members which the apostle so praises. Did the head there say to the feet, “I have no need of you,” or the eye to the hand, “I have no need of you”?

They never said this, nor could they have said it. For they attribute to them such actions and activities: they crept, walked, swam, flew—each according to its kind; they also saw and heard, perceived through their other senses, and nourished and sustained their bodies with suitable foods and temperaments.

From this they also possessed fertility of offspring, for they attribute marriages to them. Certainly, all these things which the Manichaean condemns as works of Matter cannot occur without the harmony of the members, which the apostle praises and assigns to God.

Do you still doubt whom you should follow and whom you should anathematize?

What of the fact that there were certain creatures there that even spoke, so that, while they preached, all the serpents, quadrupeds, flying creatures, and swimming creatures might hear, understand, and obey? What marvelous and altogether divine eloquence! They had heard no grammarian or rhetorician, nor had they learned these things amid tears under the schoolmaster’s rod and the birch.

Indeed, this Faustus, in order to babble eloquently about such vanities, came rather late to the discipline of composing speech [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven. have “later,” *serius*. M.]; and although he was sharp-witted, he burst his stomach through reading, so that when he spoke, so few agreed with him.

O miserable man, who was born in this light and not in those darknesses! There, while he preached against the light, every two-footed creature, every many-footed creature, and every serpent, from the dragon to the snail, would gladly hear him and eagerly obey. Here, however, while arguing against the darkness, many called him eloquent rather than learned, and many called him a most perverse seducer. Among the few Manichaeans who applauded him as a great teacher, not one animal nodded assent to him; nor did even his horse know anything from that doctrine—as though the divine portion had been incorporated into all animals for the purpose of making them stupid.

What is this, I ask? Wake up at last, wretched men, and compare, within your own fable, the earlier condition of all living creatures with their present condition: then in their own land, now in this world; then their bodies were strong, now they are weak; then their eyes had a keen vision for seeing with delight as they invaded the region of God, now their sight is so dull that they turn away from the sun’s rays; then the minds of the animals were enlarged so as to understand the speech of the preacher, now they are dull and entirely incapable of such understanding; then they possessed a natural eloquence so great and powerful, now, with so much effort and labor, scarcely a small and meager eloquence is attained [Col. 0396].

How great were the goods that the nation of darkness lost through the mingling of the good!

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0396]

This same Faustus, in the very speech to which I am now replying, seemed elegantly to set many opposites against one another: health and weakness, abundance and poverty, white and black, heat and cold, sweetness and bitterness. Here I shall omit saying anything about white and black—or, if there is any element of good and evil in colors, and they say that white belongs to God but black to Matter, when they claim that Matter created every kind of flying creature, if God sprinkled white color upon their feathers, where were the ravens when the swans were covered with whiteness?

Nor is it necessary to argue about heat and cold. Each, when used temperately, is healthful; when used intemperately, harmful.

Let us examine the rest. Good and evil, which he perhaps ought to have placed first among these opposites, he seems to have arranged in such a way that he wanted them understood as general categories: namely, that health, abundance, white, heat, and sweetness belong to the good, while weakness, poverty, black, cold, and bitterness belong to the evil. Anyone who can should observe how ineptly and thoughtlessly he has done this.

But, lest I seem to be slandering the man, I raise no objection concerning white and black, heat and cold, sweetness and bitterness, health and weakness [Note: Thus Am., Er., and several manuscripts. Lov. has “lest I make a pronouncement concerning sweetness and bitterness, health and weakness,” *ne dulci et amaro, sanitati atque infirmitati praescribam*.].

For if white and sweet are two good things, while black and bitter are two evil things, how is it that a great many grapes, and every olive, become sweet by turning black—that is, become better by possessing more of what is evil?

Likewise, if heat and health are two good things, while cold and weakness are two evil things, why do bodies become sick as they grow hot? Or are healthy things perhaps feverish?

I therefore do not raise these objections, since perhaps he mentioned them carelessly, or rather as examples of whatever opposites, not of good and evil—especially since they have never said that the fire of the nation of darkness was cold, but have certainly called its heat evil.

## CHAPTER XII

But let us set these matters aside and consider those things which he so mentioned as good among these opposites that he does not want anyone to doubt that they were present: health, abundance, and sweetness.

Was there no health of bodies in that nation in which those animals were able to be born, grow, reproduce, and continue to live—so that, after some of them had been captured while pregnant, according to their folly, and bound in heaven, even premature fetuses falling from such a height to the earth were able to live and grow and propagate these now innumerable kinds of creatures of flesh?

Or was there no abundance there, where trees were able to grow not only in water and wind but also in fire and smoke, and to become so fertile that animals of their respective kinds were generated from their fruits and preserved, nourished, and fed by the fertility of those trees—whose well-fed condition was also attested by the fertility of their offspring? [Col. 0397] Especially since there was no agricultural labor, nor any harshness of summer and winter. For the sun did not revolve there, so that the seasons of the year might pass in alternation.

Accordingly, the trees possessed perpetual fertility. The element and nourishment proper to their kind, just as it had been present for their generation, was likewise perpetually available for their fruitfulness, and ensured that their fruits never failed. So we see citrus trees produce flowers and fruit throughout the whole year if they are continually irrigated.

There was therefore great abundance there, and great security in possessing it. For hail was not feared there, where there were no exactors of light whom, as you imagine, thunder would disturb.

## CHAPTER XIII

If their foods were not sweet and pleasant, they would never desire them, nor would their bodies be invigorated by them. The matter is arranged in such a way that, according to the suitability of each body, food either delights or offends. If it delights, it is called sweet or pleasant; if it offends, it is rejected as bitter, harsh, or otherwise disagreeable.

Are we human beings not ourselves such that one person often desires a food that another finds abhorrent—whether because of the constitution of nature, the use of habit, or the condition of health?

How much more can bodies of animals, whose kinds are so different from ours, find pleasant what is bitter to us? Otherwise, why would goats hang themselves up to gnaw the wild olive? Just as honey is bitter to some people because of illness, so the wild olive is pleasant to that kind of animal.

Thus the order of things reveals itself to those who wisely investigate them, when what is suited to each is supplied and returned to it, and how great this good is—from the lowest things to the highest, from bodily things to spiritual things.

Therefore, in the nation of darkness, when an animal of one element fed upon food that was produced in its own element, the very suitability undoubtedly made it pleasant. But if it happened upon food belonging to another element, the incompatibility itself would offend the taste of the one eating it. That offense, whether called bitterness, harshness, unpleasantness, or something else—or, if it is so excessive that by an alien force it breaks apart the structure and harmony of the body and thus kills it, or removes its strength—is also called poison. It is poison only because of incompatibility, although through compatibility it is food for another kind.

Thus, if a hawk takes the bread that is our daily food, it dies; and we die if we take hellebore, which most animals feed upon, although a certain quantity of that herb is also a medicine.

If Faustus knew or considered this, he would certainly not set poison and antidote before us as examples of two natures, evil and good—as though God were the antidote and Matter the poison—since one and the same thing, and one and the same nature, when taken or applied suitably or unsuitably, may either benefit or harm.

Accordingly, according to their fable, it could be said that their god was poison to the nation of darkness, whose bodies, though so strong, he corrupted so that he made them exceedingly weak. But because the light itself was also captured, oppressed, and corrupted, they were poison to one another.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0398]

Why, then, do you not call these two good things or two evil things—or rather, both two good things and two evil things: two good things in themselves, and two evil things in relation to one another?

Later, if necessary, we shall ask which of these is better or worse. For the present, since there were two good things in themselves, consider the matter thus: God reigned in his own land, and Matter reigned in its own. The health of the rulers existed in both places; abundance of fruits existed in both; fertility of offspring existed in both; and the sweetness of their proper pleasures existed among both.

“But that nation,” they say, “apart from being evil in relation to the neighboring light, was also evil in itself.”

I have already mentioned many of its goods. If you can also demonstrate its evils, there will be two good kingdoms, but the one will be better where no evil existed. What evils, then, do you say this kingdom had?

“They devastated one another,” he says; “they injured, killed, and consumed one another.”

If they were occupied there only with this, how could such great multitudes be generated, nourished, and brought to maturity? Therefore there was also rest and peace there.

Nevertheless, let us concede that the kingdom where there was no discord was the better one. Yet I should much more appropriately call these two things good than call one good and the other evil: the former would be better, where individuals harmed neither themselves nor one another; the latter would be an inferior good, where, although they opposed one another, each animal nevertheless preserved its own health, safety, and nature.

Yet that prince of darkness can at least be compared with your god: no one resisted him, everything served him while he reigned, and everything followed him while he preached. This could not have happened without great peace and harmony. For kingdoms are happy where rulers are obeyed with the full consent of all.

Moreover, not only creatures of his own kind—that is, the two-footed beings whom you call the parents of human beings—but also every other kind of animal was subject to that prince and turned at his command, doing what he ordered and believing what he persuaded them to believe.

When you say these things, do you suppose human hearts are so deaf that they must wait for you to name another god, when they plainly and openly see one being described?

If this prince possessed such powers, then he possessed great power; if honor, great glory; if love, great harmony; if fear, great discipline. If there were certain evils amid all these goods, does that mean that the nature itself must already be called evil—except by those who do not know what they are saying?

Furthermore, if you consider it the nature of evil because it was not only evil in relation to the other nature but also contained evil in itself, do you not think the harsh necessity suffered by your god before the commingling of the opposing nature was an evil? He was compelled to fight it and to send his members into its jaws to be so crushed that he could not cleanse the whole of them [Note: Lov. has “so that they could not.” But the manuscripts have “so that it could not.” The editions of Am. and Er. also have the singular, “so that it cannot”; supply “the nature of God.” This too refers to what follows immediately: “Behold, there was also a great evil in it.”].

Behold, there was also a great evil in that nature before what alone you call evil was mingled with it.

For either it could not be injured and corrupted by the nation of darkness, and through its own folly it suffered that necessity; or, if its substance could be corrupted, you do not worship an incorruptible God such as the apostle proclaims (1 Tim. 1:17). [Col. 0399]

What, then? Does not even that corruptibility—which had not yet corrupted that nature, but by which it could be corrupted—seem to you an evil in your god? [Note: The editions have “but by another.” The manuscripts more suitably read, “but by which it could be corrupted,” that is, it was of such a character that it could be corrupted.]

## CHAPTER XV

Who would not also see that either foreknowledge did not exist there—in which case it is for you to consider whether it is not a defect in God to lack foreknowledge and to be entirely ignorant of what threatens—or, if foreknowledge did exist there, security could not exist there, but only eternal fear? And surely you recognize how great an evil this is.

Did he not fear that the time would come at any moment when his members would be so devastated and polluted in that battle that they would scarcely be liberated and cleansed, even with such great labor, and not even entirely?

But if this did not pertain to him personally—which, you see, is a harsh thing to say—surely his very members, which were destined to suffer such great evils here, were afraid. Did they themselves not know that this would happen?

Then foreknowledge was certainly lacking in some part of the substance of your god. Count the evils present in your supreme good.

Or did they not fear because they foresaw equally that they would obtain their own liberation and triumph? Certainly they feared at least for their companions, whom they knew would be separated from their kingdom and bound in eternal chains within that sphere.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0400]

Was there no charity there, so that there was no fraternal compassion for those who, despite no preceding sin of their own, were destined to suffer eternal punishments?

What of those very souls that were to be bound in the sphere—were they not also members of your god? Were they not of one kind and one substance? Surely those souls, foreknowing their future eternal bondage, were afraid and grieved.

Or, if they did not know that this would happen, then one part of your god was provident and another improvident. How, then, could they be one and the same substance?

Since such great evils therefore existed there too before the commingling of another evil, what are you boasting about him as though he were pure, simple, and the supreme good?

Therefore, even with respect to these two natures in themselves, you are compelled to confess either two goods or two evils.

We grant you this: if you call them two evils, call whichever you wish the worse. If, however, you call them two goods, call whichever you wish the better; we shall afterward examine the matter more carefully. Let only that error of yours be removed, by which you say that there are two principles of two natures, a good and an evil one, and plainly two gods, one good and the other evil.

Now, if something is evil because it harms another, these two harmed one another. One part may have been more blameworthy because it first desired what belonged to another. One therefore wished to inflict evil, while the other returned evil for evil—not according to the law of retaliation, “an eye for an eye” (Exod. 21:24), which you are accustomed to criticize foolishly, but much more grievously.

Choose, then, which you will call worse: the one that first wished to harm, or the one that both wished and was able to harm more greatly.

The former desired to enjoy the light according to its measure; the latter uprooted it completely. If the former had fulfilled what it desired, it would certainly have harmed nothing of itself; but the latter, in order to destroy its hostile adversary completely, also gravely harmed its own part.

It is like that well-known mad saying preserved in the memory of certain writings:

> Let friends perish, so long as enemies perish together  
> (Cicero, *For Deiotarus*).

For a part of the god was sent into an inexpiable contamination, so that there might be something with which the sphere could be covered, in which the living enemy was to be buried eternally. The conquered enemy would be feared so greatly, and the imprisoned one would inspire such terror, that the perpetual misery of the divine part would grant the remaining god some sort of security.

O great innocence of goodness! Behold, your god will also do what you horribly accuse the nation of darkness of doing: harming both his own and those belonging to another. That final sphere itself proves the same thing against your god, since the enemy is enclosed in it and the citizen is fastened to it. Indeed, the portion that you call god surpasses Matter in inflicting harm upon both others and its own.

For Matter did not wish to uproot the kingdom of another, but to possess it. Although it consumed and killed some of its own by means of certain others of its own, it nevertheless changed them again into other forms, so that by dying and being reborn they might at least enjoy the pleasure of their own life at intervals.

But God, whom you describe as omnipotent and supremely good, eternally uproots those belonging to another and condemns his own. And what is believed with even more astonishing madness is that Matter injures its animals in its battle, while God punishes his members in his victory.

What is this, foolish men? Surely you remember Faustus’s words about God as an antidote and Matter as poison. Behold, your antidote does more harm than the poison.

Would Matter have enclosed God in such a dreadful sphere for eternity, or fastened its own entrails there? And what is more criminal, it accuses those same remnants so that it may not appear to have failed because it could not cleanse them [Note: Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. have *affligeret*, “would afflict,” instead of *affigeret*, “would fasten.”].

For the Manichaean says in the *Epistle of the Foundation* that those souls are made worthy of such punishment because they allowed themselves to stray from their former luminous nature and became hostile to the holy light—although he himself sent them into that error, so that they would become so darkened that light would become hostile to the light. If he sent them unwillingly, he was unjust, compelling them; if willingly, he was ungrateful, condemning them [Note: Er. and Lov. have “so that he might condemn them,” *ut damnaret*. Am. and the manuscripts have “so that he condemns them,” *ut damnet*.].

If they could foresee that they would become enemies of their own origin, then before the war they were tormented by fear, in the war they were inexpiably stained, and after the war they were condemned eternally—never blessed. But if they could not foresee it, then before the war they were improvident, in the war weak, and after the war miserable—never divine.

And whatever they are, God is, according to the unity of substance.

Do we suppose that you notice how monstrously you blaspheme? Yet at times, wishing as though to defend the goodness of God, you even say that Matter possesses something good, so that, enclosed within itself, it may not rage [Note: Am. and Er. have “rage against itself,” *in semetipsam non saeviat*. This may be preferable.].

Then it will possess something good when no good is mingled with it? Or perhaps, just as God before the war possessed the evil of necessity without any commingling of evil, so Matter after the war will possess the good of cessation without any commingling of good?

Say, then, either that there are two evils, one worse than the other, or two goods that are not supreme, one better than the other. But let it be in such a way that you call the better one the more miserable. For if the outcome of that great war is that, after Matter has been overcome [Note: Am. and eight manuscripts have “separated,” *separata*.] by its own devastation and God’s members have been fastened in the sphere, something good is provided for the enemies and so much evil inflicted upon the citizens, consider who has won.

But of course Matter is the poison, which was able to form, strengthen, nourish, and invigorate its animals; and God is the antidote, who was able to condemn his members but was unable to heal them.

Madmen, neither is that Matter, nor is this God. Thus rave those who, unable to endure sound doctrine, turn to fables (2 Tim. 4:3).

# BOOK TWENTY-TWO

[Col. 0401]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0401]

**FAUSTUS said:** Why do you blaspheme the Law and the Prophets?

We are certainly not enemies or foes of the Law and the Prophets—or of anyone at all—to such an extent that, if only you yourselves would permit it, we would be ready to admit that all those things written about them are false, and that it is because of them that they seem hateful to us.

But you resist us, and by agreeing with your writers you perhaps bring innocent prophets under accusation, disgrace the patriarchs, dishonor the Law, and—what is more foolish—want both your writers not to be liars and those people whose crimes and shameful lives they have written down to be religious and holy.

Since both positions cannot stand together equally, one or the other must be true: either these men were evil, or those writers were liars and false.

## CHAPTER II

Come, then, if you wish, let us condemn the writers by common agreement and undertake the defense of the Law and the Prophets.

When I now speak of the Law, I do not mean circumcision, Sabbaths, sacrifices, and the other things of this kind belonging to the Jews. I mean the Law that truly is the Law: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not swear falsely” (Exod. 20:13, 14, 16), and the rest.

Because this Law had long been publicly known among the nations—that is, from the time when the creation of this world was established—the Hebrew writers attacked it and, like leprosy and scabies, mingled with it these detestable and most shameful commandments of theirs, which pertain to circumcision and sacrifices.

Come, then: if you are truly a friend of the Law [Note: Er., Lugd., and Ven. have “certainly,” *pro certo*. M.], condemn with me those who dared to violate it by this commingling of precepts that do not belong with it.

Unless you also knew that these precepts are not the Law, nor part of the Law, you would either strive to observe them after professing righteousness, or openly admit that you are not righteous.

But now, while you who wish to live rightly are concerned about those commandments that forbid crimes, no mention is made of the matters that belong to the Jews. How will this be excused to you, unless it becomes clear that the latter are not the same Law?

Finally, if, just as you would burn with indignation, judging it an intolerable insult, if someone called you negligent of the commandment that says, “You shall not kill,” or “You shall not commit adultery,” so you would also flare up if someone called you uncircumcised and negligent of the Sabbath, it would plainly be understood that both were the Law and commandment of God [Note: Er., Lugd., and Ven. read this passage as follows: “Finally, if, just as you would burn with indignation . . . so you would also flare up if someone called you uncircumcised and negligent of what belonged to the Sabbath; you understand plainly that both were the Law and commandment of God.” M.].

But now you seek praise and glory from the former if you preserve them, while you fear no loss of the same good from the latter because you despise them.

Therefore, as I have said, it is clear that these things are not the Law but rather blemishes and scabies upon the Law. If we condemn them, we condemn them as false, not as lawful.

This insult touches neither the Law nor God, the author of the Law, but those who have inscribed him and it with their wicked religious practices.

But if at times, while attacking Jewish commandments, we assail the venerable name of the Law, this is your fault, because you do not want there to be any distinction between the Hebrew institutions and the Law.

Otherwise, restore to the Law its proper dignity; cut away the Israelite obscenities from it as though they were warts; attribute the charge of its disfigurement to the writers [Note: Only the Lov. edition has “to your writers.”]; and you will immediately see that we have been enemies of Judaism, not of the Law.

The name “Law” deceives you, because you do not know to whom it ought rightly to be attributed.

## CHAPTER III

As for the Prophets and Patriarchs whom you suppose us to blaspheme, I do not see why you think so.

If these things which those same men are said to have committed had been written or dictated by us, your accusation against us would not be unreasonable. But when either the men themselves wrote these things contrary to the standards of morality, seeking glory from their vices, or their associates and equals wrote them, what fault is ours?

We condemn, abhorring them, the wicked acts which they freely confessed about themselves, though they were not questioned. Or, if the malice of the writers fabricated these things against them out of envy, let the writers be punished, let their books be condemned, let the prophetic name be cleansed of an undeserved reputation, and let the authority of the patriarchs be restored to their dignity and moral seriousness.

## CHAPTER IV

And indeed it could have happened that, just as these same writers shamelessly invented such things about God—now saying that he had dwelt in darkness from eternity and later marveled when he saw the light; now ignorant of the future, so that he gave Adam that commandment which Adam would not obey; now improvident, so that after Adam’s nakedness had been discovered he could not see him hiding in a corner of paradise; now envious and afraid that, if his man tasted from the tree of life, he would live forever; now desiring the blood and fat of every kind of sacrifice, and jealous if the same offerings were made to others as to himself; now angry with outsiders, now also with his own; now killing thousands of human beings for slight or even nonexistent offenses; now threatening that he would come with a sword and spare no one, neither the righteous [Col. 0403] nor the sinner—so, I say, it could have happened that they also lied about the men of God, since they lied about God himself with such insolence.

But agree with us, if you want the writers to bear the guilt, so that the Prophets may likewise be freed.

## CHAPTER V

[The supplied source ends here, at the heading “Chapter V.”]

Otherwise, we did not write those things about Abraham: that, burning with an insane desire to have offspring and placing no trust in God, who had already promised him this concerning Sarah his wife, he lay with a concubine while his wife knew of it (which makes the matter more disgraceful) (Gen. 16:2–4). Nor did we write that, as the most infamous trafficker in his marriage, for the sake of greed and his belly, he twice—at different times—lied to two kings, Abimelech and Pharaoh, saying that Sarah his wife was his sister (Gen. 20:2; 12:13), and sold her into intercourse because she was exceedingly beautiful. Nor did we write that Lot, Abraham’s brother, after being rescued from Sodom, lay with his two daughters in the mountain (Gen. 19:33, 35)—a man who would have burned more honorably in Sodom by a stroke of lightning than he burned in the mountain with the forbidden flame of lust.

Nor did we write that Isaac did the same things as his father, and comparable things, toward Rebekah his wife, himself also pretending that she was his sister (Gen. 26:7), so that through her he might live dishonorably. Nor did we write that Jacob, his son, wandered like a he-goat between Rachel and Leah, two sisters, and their respective maidservants, being the husband of four wives; so that every day there might be a contest among four prostitutes as to which of them would seize him first for intercourse when he came in from the field, and that at times they even hired him from one another for the night in exchange for payment (Gen. 29–30).
