Likewise, we did not write that his son Judah slept with his daughter-in-law Tamar after the marriages of both his sons, having been deceived, as they say, by the clothing of a prostitute (Gen. 38)—the disguise into which she had transformed herself, though she knew well that her father-in-law always had dealings with this class of women.

[Note: Am. and Er. read *cum omni genere feminarum*: “with every class of women.”]

Nor did we write that David, after so many wives, committed adultery with the little wife of his soldier Uriah and had him killed in battle (2 Sam. 11:4, 15). Nor did we write that his son Solomon had three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines, as well as the daughters of kings without number (1 Kings 11:1–3). Nor did we write that Hosea, the first of the prophets, fathered children by a prostitute—a disgrace to which, to make it worse, the counsel of God is also attributed (Hos. 1:2–3).

Nor did we write that Moses committed murder (Exod. 2:12), that he plundered Egypt (Exod. 12:35–36), that he waged wars, that he both commanded and committed many cruel deeds (Exod. 17:9, etc.), or that even he was not content with one marriage. These things, I say, and things like them, which are found in various books of theirs, were neither written nor dictated by us. Either these are false inventions of your writers, or the crimes of the fathers are true. Choose which alternative you want: for we must detest either the one group or the other alike, since we hate them as much for being wicked and disgraceful as for being liars.

## CHAPTER VI

Augustine replied: You understand neither the sacraments of the Law nor the deeds of the Prophets, because you do not know how to conceive either holiness or justice. But we have already said often and at length concerning the precepts and sacraments of the Old Testament, so that it might be understood that one thing was there to be fulfilled by being put into practice through the grace of the New Testament, and another thing was there to be shown as fulfilled by being removed through the truth that had been revealed. The commandment of the Law was undertaken for fulfillment through love of God and neighbor, while the Law’s promise, having been discharged, was shown by the cessation of circumcision and the other sacraments of that time.

For the commandment made them guilty, so that they would desire salvation; but the promise celebrated its figures, so that they would await the Savior. Thus, through the coming of the New Testament, the grace bestowed would free those people, while the truth fulfilled would remove those figures. For the Law itself, which was given through Moses, came through grace and truth by Jesus Christ (John 1:17): grace, namely, so that, forgiveness of sins having been given, what was commanded might be kept through God’s gift; and truth, so that, the observance of shadows having been taken away, what had been promised might be presented in accordance with God’s faithfulness.

## CHAPTER VII

Accordingly, those who criticize what they do not understand and call the promised figures of the sacraments the leprosy, scab, or warts of the Law are like people who dislike things whose usefulness they do not grasp. It would be as though a deaf person, seeing the lips of speakers move, criticized them as superfluous and misshapen movements of the mouth; or as though a blind man, having heard a house praised, wished to test by touch what had been said, and, running his hand over the smoothness of the walls, collided with the windows and condemned them as unsuitable to that evenness, while thinking the recessed openings were ruined places.

[Note: Am. and several manuscripts read *lenitatem* (“softness, gentleness”) instead of *laevitatem* (“smoothness”).]

## CHAPTER VIII

Now, as for the deeds of the Prophets themselves having also been prophetic and mystical, what am I to do so that those may understand whose minds vanity has occupied—so much so that they think we even believe that God himself was at some time dwelling in darkness, because it is written, “Darkness was over the abyss” (Gen. 1:2)? It is as though we called the abyss God, where darkness was because light was not there, before God made light by his word.

But because they do not distinguish between the Light which God himself is and the light which God made, they think it follows that he himself was in darkness before he made light, since darkness was over the abyss before he said, “Let there be light”; and light was made (ibid., 3). For just as both statements are made about him in the New Testament—for there we read both, “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5), and, “The God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts” (2 Cor. 4:6)—so also in those ancient Books it is said of the Wisdom of God, “She is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26). That Wisdom certainly was not made, because all things were made through it (John 1:3).

And concerning a certain light that can be made only through that Wisdom, it is said there in this way: “You will light my lamp, Lord; my God, you will enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17:29). Likewise, in the beginning, when darkness was over the abyss, God said, “Let there be light”; and light was made. He would not have made it unless the light that gives light—which is God—had made it.

## CHAPTER IX

For just as God is sufficient for himself in eternal blessedness, and from this abundance makes others blessed, so he is sufficient for himself in eternal light, and from this abundance makes others enlightened. He desires the good of no one, since every good will enjoys him; he fears no one’s evil, since every evil will abandons him. For the one who is blessed by his gift does not increase him, nor does the one who is wretched by his judgment terrify him.

Such a God, Manichaeans, you do not worship. You have gone far from him while pursuing your phantasms, which, through manifold invention, have expanded and diversified your vain and wandering heart as it drinks in this light of the heavenly bodies through the eyes of the flesh. This light, although God himself also made it, is far and incomparably inferior even to that light which God made in the minds of the devout, whom he enlightens from darkness just as he justifies them from ungodliness—how much more inferior, then, to that inaccessible Light which makes all these things?

Yet it is not inaccessible to everyone: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all”; but the ungodly “shall not see the light,” as Isaiah says (Isa. 59:9–10). To such people, therefore, that light which gives light is inaccessible—the light that made not only the spiritual light in the minds of the saints but also this bodily light, not in order to forbid the wicked to approach it, but because it makes it rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5:45).

## CHAPTER X

When, therefore, darkness was over the abyss, he who was light said, “Let there be light.” It is clear what light made light, for it is plainly written, “God said.” What sort of light he made, however, is not equally clear. For whether God then made that light which is in the minds of the angels—that is, the rational spirits themselves—or some bodily light, remote even from our sight in the lofty regions of this world, is a matter debated with agreement among students of the divine Scriptures.

For on the fourth day he made these visible lights of heaven. It is likewise asked whether they were made simultaneously with their light, or whether they were somehow kindled from the light that had already been made. Whatever kind of light was made when, while darkness was over the abyss, God said, “Let there be light,” no one who becomes worthy to understand the holy Scriptures through devout reading doubts that created light was made by the creative Light.

## CHAPTER XI

Nor should one therefore think that God lived in darkness before he made light, because “the Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (Gen. 1:2), when it had already been said, “Darkness was over the abyss.” For the abyss is the immeasurable depth of the waters. Hence it may occur to carnal understanding that the Spirit of God dwelt in those darknesses that were over the abyss, since it was said, “He was moving over the waters”—to someone who does not understand how light shines in darkness, and darkness does not comprehend it (John 1:5), unless through God’s word they become light and are told, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

If rational minds, darkened by an ungodly will, cannot comprehend the light of God’s wisdom, which is nowhere absent, because they are far from it in disposition, not in place, what wonder is it if the Spirit of God, who was moving over the waters, was also moving over the darknesses of the waters—at an incomparable distance, certainly, but a distance of substance, not of place?

## CHAPTER XII

I know that I am singing these things to ears as deaf as theirs; nevertheless, I do not despair that the truth of my song will find its ear when the Lord opens it—the Lord from whom come the truths we speak. But what sort of judges of the divine Scriptures do we have to endure in these people, who even dislike the fact that God’s works pleased him? They criticize him as though he had been astonished by an unfamiliar light, because it is written, “And God saw that the light was good” (Gen. 1:4).

He approves his works because what he made pleases him, and this is what it means to see that they are good. For he is not compelled to do something unwillingly, so that he does what does not please him; nor does he stumble unwisely into making something, so that he is displeased that it has been made.

But why should it displease these people that our God saw his work to be good, when their god, after plunging his own members into darkness, placed a veil before himself? He did not see what he had made to be good; rather, he did not wish to see it because it was evil.

## CHAPTER XIII

Faustus did indeed say that our God had been astonished, although Scripture does not say this. Nor does it at all follow that, when someone sees that something is good, he must also be said to have been astonished. We see many good things without being astonished, as though they were contrary to expectation; we merely approve them as things that ought to be as they are.

Nevertheless, we have shown them—not in the Old Testament, which they maliciously slander, but in the New Testament, which they accept in order to deceive the uninstructed—that God was astonished. They confess that Christ is God, and they place this in their snare as an exceedingly sweet bait by which to capture those devoted to Christ. God, therefore, was astonished when Christ was astonished. For it is written in the Gospel that, after hearing the faith of a certain centurion, he was astonished and said to his disciples, “Truly I tell you, I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:10).

Behold, we have explained as best we could, “God saw that it was good.” Perhaps better people offer a better explanation of these words. Let these people also explain why Jesus was astonished at something that he knew before it happened and certainly knew before he heard it.

Although there is a great difference between someone seeing that a thing is good and being astonished at it, there is nevertheless some similarity here: Jesus was also astonished at the light of faith that he himself had made in the heart of that centurion—he who is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9).

## CHAPTER XIV

Certainly some impious pagan could slander and criticize Christ in the Gospel in the same way that Faustus criticizes God in the Old Testament. He might call Christ improvident, not only because he was astonished at the centurion’s faith, but also because he chose Judas among his disciples, although Judas was not going to keep his commandments (John 6:71)—just as this man criticizes why a command was given in paradise to a human being who would not carry it out (Gen. 2:16–17; 3:6).

He might also criticize the fact that Christ could not know who had touched him when a woman suffering from a flow of blood touched the fringe of his garment—just as this man criticized God for not knowing where Adam was hiding. I suppose that pagan would say, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9), just as Christ said, “Who touched me?” (Luke 8:44–45).

He might call Christ envious and fearful that, if the other five virgins entered his kingdom, they would live forever; and that he shut the door against them so that he would not open it even when they knocked pitifully (Matt. 25:11–12), as though forgetting what he himself had promised when he said, “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). This would be like the charge this man brings against God for having refused to admit the sinner to eternal life.

He might call Christ desirous—not of the blood of animals but of the blood of human beings—because he said, “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it for eternal life” (Matt. 10:39), just as this man wished to slander the sacrifices of animals, by which the sacrifice of blood through which we were redeemed was promised in figures.

He might criticize Christ as jealous because, after driving the buyers and sellers from the temple with a whip, the Evangelist recalled that it had been written of him, “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (John 2:15–17)—just as this man accused God of jealousy because he had forbidden sacrifices to be offered to others.

He might call Christ angry with his own and with outsiders: with his own, because he said, “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is appropriate will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47);

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “and does things deserving of blows will be beaten with many blows.”]

and with outsiders, because he said, “If anyone does not receive you, shake the dust from your feet. Truly I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matt. 10:14–15). This would be like the charge this man brings against God for being angry, now with outsiders, now with his own—both of whom the Apostle mentions when he says, “All who have sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law, and all who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Rom. 2:12).

He might also call Christ one who slaughtered and shed the blood of many for slight or no offenses. To a pagan, it might seem a slight or nonexistent offense either not to have a wedding garment at the wedding feast, for which our King in the Gospel ordered that a man be thrown, with hands and feet bound, into the outer darkness (Matt. 22:11–13), or to refuse to have Christ reign over him, for which sin he said, “But as for those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and kill them in my presence” (Luke 19:27). This would be like the charge this man brings against God in the Old Testament, whom he thinks slaughtered thousands of people for slight or nonexistent offenses.

But as for the final charge Faustus makes against God—namely, that he threatened to come with a sword and spare no one, neither the righteous nor the sinner—how would that pagan criticize it when he heard the Apostle Paul say concerning our God, “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32)? What would he say when he heard Peter, speaking of the great tribulations and killings of the saints and exhorting them to endure, say, “It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not obey the Gospel of God? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. 4:17–18).

For what is more just than the Only-Begotten, whom nevertheless the Father did not spare? And what is clearer than the fact that he does not spare even the righteous, correcting them through varied tribulations, since it is plainly said in this matter, “If the righteous person is scarcely saved”?

Not only is it written in the Old Testament, “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he accepts” (Prov. 3:12), and, “If we receive good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?” (Job 2:10); it is also written in the New Testament, “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. 3:19), and, “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Cor. 11:31–32).

But if a pagan were to criticize such things in the New Testament as these people criticize in the Old, would they not themselves undertake to defend them? If they could do so, with what madness do they criticize here things of this kind while defending them there? But if they could not, why do they concede that in only one Testament—and not rather in both—what would seem perverse to the impious who do not understand is to be believed by the devout who do not understand as something right, though hidden?

[Note: The printed editions read *idem intelligentibus* (“the same to those who understand”), omitting the negative particle. The sense requires the manuscripts’ reading, *idem non intelligentibus* (“the same to those who do not understand”).]

## CHAPTER XV

Or perhaps they even dare to say that the similar passages we have brought forward from the New Testament are false and perverse, by that diabolical privilege of theirs whereby they insist and persuade others that whatever in the Gospel or the canonical Epistles seems useful to their heresy was spoken by Christ and the Apostles, while whatever sounds against them from those same books they do not hesitate, with an impudent and sacrilegious mouth, to declare was inserted by falsifiers.

To this madness of theirs—which seeks to extinguish and abolish the authority of all the books—I have already given no small response above, as far as the scope of the work undertaken allowed.

## CHAPTER XVI

Now I wish to point out that, while they attempt to cloak their insane and sacrilegious fables with the mantle of the Christian name, they should nevertheless recognize that, when they argue against the Christian Scriptures, we are defending the truth of the divine books of both Testaments not merely against pagans but also against Manichaeans.

As for these matters that Faustus has just presented in his speech as unworthy of God from our ancient Scriptures, if I were defending them against a pagan who criticized such things in the Gospel or apostolic writings, I might perhaps do so by recalling comparable statements from the pagan authors themselves, just as our Paul did among the Athenians (Acts 17:28).

For I might perhaps find in their writings a god who is the creator and maker of the world, and the founder of this light, who nevertheless did not lie in darkness before he established it; and that he was filled with joy at his completed work—which is certainly more than “he saw that it was good”; and a giver of law, so that if a human being followed it, he would do so for his own good, but if he rejected it, for his own harm.

[Note: Erasmus reads *quem si homo sequeretur* (“whom, if a human being followed”). The other books more correctly read *quam*, referring to the law: “which, if a human being followed it.”]

They would not call him ignorant of the future merely because he gave a law to those who would later despise it. Nor would they call him improvident because he asked a question. In their books, many things are asked for no other reason than that each person may be convicted by his own answers; and the one who asks not only knows what he wants the other to answer, but also knows that the other will give that answer.

If they wished to call God envious because he did not permit the wicked to become blessed, they would find their own books full of discussions on this matter, which pertains to divine providence.

[Note: Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *pertinentes* (“pertaining”), agreeing with the plural *libros* (“books”).]

## CHAPTER XVII

As for sacrifices, the pagan would object to me only by asking why we criticize such practices among them when we read that our God commanded such things to be offered to him in our ancient Books.

Here I might perhaps give a fuller account of the true sacrifice and demonstrate that it is owed to the one true God alone—the sacrifice offered to him by the one true Priest, the Mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5). The promised figures of this sacrifice had to be celebrated in the victims of animals, to commend the flesh and blood that were to come, through which alone forgiveness would be accomplished for sins contracted through flesh and blood. Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, because that same bodily substance will be changed into a heavenly quality. Fire in the sacrifice signified this, as though it were swallowing up death in victory (1 Cor. 15:50–54).

These rites were properly celebrated among that people whose kingdom and priesthood were a prophecy of the King and Priest who was to come, to rule and consecrate the faithful among all nations, and to lead them into the kingdom of heaven, the sanctuary of the angels, and eternal life. Thus, just as the Hebrews celebrated the religious proclamations of this true sacrifice, so the pagans celebrated sacrilegious imitations of it. “What the Gentiles sacrifice,” the Apostle says, “they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Cor. 10:20).

For the sacrificial offering of blood is an ancient act of prophecy, testifying from the beginning of the human race to the future passion of the Mediator. In the holy Scriptures, Abel is the first person found to have offered this sacrifice (Gen. 4:4). It is therefore not surprising if the transgressing angels—whose two greatest vices are pride and deceit—flying about through the air, demanded for themselves from their worshipers what they knew was owed to the one true God, wishing to be regarded as gods. Human vanity gave them the opportunity, especially since images were made out of desire for the dead, from which the use of idols arose (Wis. 14:15). Divine honors were paid to them with even greater flattery, as though they had been received into heaven; and in their place demons were set up to be worshiped on earth, while they demanded sacrifices from the deceived and ruined.

Sacrifice, therefore, whether the true God justly commands it or a false god arrogantly demands it, sufficiently shows to whom it is owed. If these matters were more difficult for that pagan to believe, I would also persuade him by the prophecy in which, written so long beforehand, I would show what has now been fulfilled. If he also despised this, I would acknowledge that rather than be astonished, since I would recall, in accordance with the truth of that same prophecy, that not everyone would believe.

## CHAPTER XVIII

If he objected to Christ or God being jealous in both Testaments and attacked the very word, he would merely show himself either ignorant of all literature or careless in reading it.

For although their learned writers distinguish between will and desire, joy and gladness, caution and fear, clemency and mercy, prudence and cleverness, confidence and boldness—and in many similar pairs, assigning the former terms to virtues and the latter to vices—their books are nevertheless full of the abusive use of these names, which properly signify vices, even when virtues are also called by them. Thus desire is used for will, gladness for joy, fear for caution, mercy for clemency, cleverness for prudence, and boldness for confidence.

Who could list all the cases in which ordinary usage employs language with similar freedom? To this must also be added the particular character of each language. For I do not recall that in ecclesiastical writings “mercy” is ever used as a reproach. Everyday speech agrees with this usage as well.

The Greeks call two things that are indeed closely related but nevertheless distinct—labor and pain—by one name, *ponos*.

[Note: Greek *ponos* (πόνος), “labor” or “pain.”]

We express them with separate words. Likewise, we use one word for “life,” whether in the sense in which we say, “He lives,” meaning that he is not lifeless, or in the sense in which we say, “He is a man of good life.” The Greeks signify these two meanings with two different words as well.

[Note: Greek *zōē* (ζωή) and *bios* (βίος).]

Thus it is possible that, apart from the abusive use of words—which is widespread in all languages—there may also be some characteristic of the Hebrew language by which “jealousy” is used in both senses: whether when a mind, troubled by a wife’s adultery, wastes away—which cannot happen to God—or when careful vigilance is exercised to preserve marital chastity. It is useful for us to confess, without any hesitation and indeed with thanksgiving, that God acts in this way when he addresses his people as a wife and does not wish them to commit fornication with many false gods.

I would say the same concerning the anger of God. God is not disturbed when he inflicts anger; rather, “anger” is used for vengeance, either through an abusive usage or through some characteristic inherited from an earlier language.

## CHAPTER XIX

As for the thousands of people who were killed, the pagan would not be astonished if he did not deny God’s judgment. Even pagans do not deny this, since they concede that the universe is ruled and governed by God’s providence from the highest things down to the lowest.

If he denied this as well, he would be refuted either more easily by the authority of his own writers or, with somewhat greater delay, through an argument based on sound reasoning. Or, as someone excessively obstinate and foolish, he would be left to the divine judgment concerning the very thing he refused to believe.

But if he explicitly mentioned the slight or nonexistent offenses on account of which God killed people, we would show that they were neither nonexistent nor slight. For example, in the case of the wedding garment (Matt. 22:11–13), we would demonstrate how great a crime it was to approach the sacred wedding seeking glory there not for the bridegroom but for oneself. Or, if that garment should be found, by a better interpretation, to signify something else.

As for those who are killed before the eyes of the king because they did not want him to reign over them (Luke 19:27), it would perhaps become clear without a lengthy discussion that, just as it is no fault for a human being to refuse to have another human being reign over him, so it is no slight or nonexistent fault to refuse to have reign over oneself the one in whose kingdom alone one lives rightly, happily, and forever.

## CHAPTER XX

As for the final point Faustus raised, lying in ambush against the ancient Books as though they insulted God because he threatens a sword with which he will spare no one, neither the righteous nor the sinner: if this were explained to a pagan as it should be understood, perhaps he would not resist either the New or the Old Testament, and he would approve the Gospel comparison that either does not appear to those who wish to be regarded as Christians, as though they were blind, or displeases them, as though they were perverse.

For that supreme vinedresser (John 15:1) prepares the pruning knife differently for fruitful branches and for fruitless ones. Nevertheless, he spares neither the worthy nor the rejected: the former he prunes for cleansing, the latter he cuts off.

There is no human being endowed with such great righteousness that the trial of tribulation is not necessary for him, whether to perfect, strengthen, or test his virtue. Unless perhaps they do not even count the Apostle Paul among the righteous. Although he humbly and truthfully confesses his former sins, he nevertheless gives thanks that he was justified through faith in Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 1:13).

Or did the one who, as these foolish people do not understand, said, “I will spare neither the righteous nor the sinner,” spare him? Let them listen to Paul himself: “So that I might not be exalted because of the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I pleaded with the Lord three times that he might take it away from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

Behold, he did not spare even the righteous person, so that he might perfect his virtue in weakness—the one who had given him an angel of Satan to buffet him—unless you say that the devil gave him. The devil, then, was working to prevent Paul from being exalted because of the greatness of his revelations and so that his virtue might be perfected. Who could say such a thing?

The righteous man, therefore, was handed over by the one who handed him over to the angel of Satan to be buffeted; and through Paul he also handed over the unrighteous to Satan himself. Concerning these Paul likewise says, “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20).

Do you now understand how the one above does not spare either the righteous or the sinner? Or are you more horrified because a sword is mentioned there? To be buffeted is one thing; to be killed is another. As though thousands of martyrs had not been struck down by various kinds of death, or as though their persecutors truly possessed this power unless it had been given to them from above by the one who said, “I will spare neither the righteous nor the sinner.” The Lord of the martyrs himself, whom the Father did not spare—his own Son (Rom. 8:32)—says most openly to Pilate,

[Note: Am. reads *quia Filio*; Er. and Lov. read *qui Filio*. The text is corrected from the manuscripts.]

 “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

Paul himself says that these afflictions and persecutions of the righteous are an example of God’s judgment (2 Thess. 1:5). The Apostle Peter explains this judgment more fully, as I recalled above, when he says that it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God: “And if it begins with us,” he says, “what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. 4:17–18).

From this it is understood how the ungodly are not spared, like branches cut off for burning, when the righteous are not spared for the sake of perfecting their purification. Peter himself also testifies that these things happen by the will of the one who says in the ancient Books, “I will spare neither the righteous nor the sinner.” For he himself says, “It is better, if the Spirit of God so wills, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil” (1 Pet. 3:17).

When, therefore, those who do good suffer by the will of the Spirit of God, the righteous are not spared; and when those who do evil suffer, sinners are not spared. Nevertheless, both occur according to the will of the one who says, “I will spare neither the righteous nor the sinner”: one he chastises as a son, the other he punishes as an ungodly person.

## CHAPTER XXI

Behold, I have shown, as far as I could, that we do not worship a God who dwelt from eternity in darkness, but the one who is light and in whom there is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5), and who dwells in himself in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6:16), whose eternal light is the coeternal Wisdom (Wis. 7:26).

We do not worship one who was astonished by unexpected light, but the creator of light that was made, so that it might exist, and its approver, so that it might remain.

We do not worship one ignorant of the future, but the giver of the commandment and the condemner of sin, so that the punishment justly pronounced against disobedience might restrain those living in the present and terrify those yet to come.

We do not worship one who, being improvident, seeks by not knowing, but one who judges by questioning.

We do not worship one who is envious and fearful, but one who justly forbids the transgressor eternal life, which is given to the one who obeys rightly.

We do not worship one who desires blood and fat, but one who, having imposed suitable sacrifices upon a carnal people, promised through certain figures the true sacrifice.

We do not worship one who is jealous through dark perturbation, but one who, in tranquil goodness, is jealous lest the soul that owes chastity to the one God be defiled by being corrupted and prostituted among many false gods.

We do not worship one who rages turbulently with a human sort of anger, but one who renders a different, divine, severe, and just recompense.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit *alia divina* (“a different, divine”).]

This recompense is called “anger” through an established usage of speech, not because of a desire for vengeance but because of the forcefulness of judgment.

We do not worship one who kills thousands of people for slight or nonexistent offenses, but one who, through a most equitable judgment, imposes upon peoples the salutary usefulness of fear through the temporal deaths of mortals.

We do not worship one who punishes the righteous and sinners in blind confusion, without any discrimination, but one who distributes wholesome correction to the righteous for the sake of perfection and due severity to sinners for the sake of justice.

Thus it is evident, Manichaeans, that you have been deceived by your suspicions. Through misunderstanding our Scriptures—or through encountering interpreters who misunderstand them—you believe false things about Catholics. And so, abandoning sound doctrine, you have turned to sacrilegious fables, becoming excessively perverse and alienated from the fellowship of the saints. Nor do you wish to be corrected by the New Testament, from which we bring forward passages of the same kind as those you criticize in the Old.

Consequently, we are compelled to defend both Testaments against you just as we defend them against the pagans.

## CHAPTER XXII
But suppose someone were so utterly foolish in a carnal manner as to worship a god—not the kind of God whom we worship, who is one and true, but the kind of god whom you say we worship, a god fabricated by your calumnies or suspicions: would not even such a person worship a better god than you do? I ask you, pay attention and open whatever eyes you have. No great intellectual acumen is needed to see what I am about to say. I appeal to all, wise and unwise alike: listen, pay attention, judge.

How much better would it have been if your god had dwelt in darkness from eternity, than if he had plunged into darkness a light coeternal and kindred with himself? How much better would it have been if, marveling at a new light that had arisen for him to dispel the darkness, he had praised it, rather than being unable to avoid the ancient darkness rushing upon him except by having his own light darkened? Miserable, if he did it troubled; cruel, if he did it unconcerned.

Certainly it would have been better for him to see and marvel that the light had been made by him and was good [Note: [Col. 0413] Several manuscripts read, “seeing the light, he marveled that it was good.” Some read, “he saw the light was good,” omitting “and marveled.”], than to make what was begotten by him evil: a light that repelled the hostile darkness from him in such a way that it became hostile to him. For this will be counted as their fault, when those remnants are condemned in the globe: that they allowed themselves to stray from their former luminous nature and became hostile to the holy light. Before this happened to them, they endured from eternity either the everlasting darkness of ignorance, if they did not know that this would happen to them, or the everlasting darkness of fear, if they did know it.

Behold, truly a part and substance of your god dwelt in its own darkness from eternity. Nor did it afterward marvel at a new light; rather, it encountered other, alien darknesses [Note: [Col. 0413] Almost only the Louvain edition reads, “and alien darknesses”], which it had always feared. Moreover, the god himself, whose part it was—if he feared that so great an evil would befall his own part—was himself already possessed by the darkness of fear; but if he did not know that this would happen, he was blinded by the darkness of ignorance. If, however, he knew that this would happen to his part and did not fear it, the darkness of such great cruelty is worse than either ignorance or fear.

For your god did not possess what the Apostle praises in the very flesh which you madly believe was made not by God but by Hyle: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26). Yet we do not accuse him [Note: [Col. 0413] More manuscripts read, “but let us not accuse him.”]: he foresaw, feared, and grieved, but had no means of acting. Thus he dwelt in the darkness of his own misery from eternity. Nor did he afterward marvel at a new light that would dispel darkness from him; rather, he experienced, to the great detriment of his own light, the other darknesses that he had always feared.

How much better would it have been—not to say that he should give a command, as God, but that he should receive a command, as man—which he might keep for his own good or disregard for his own harm, while in either movement of the soul he exercised free will, rather than being forced against his will by unavoidable necessity to darken his own light! For it would certainly have been much better for him to give a command to a human nature whose future sin he did not know than, compelled by necessity, to force his own divine nature [Note: [Col. 0413] The Louvain edition reads, “divine.” The reading has been corrected on the basis of other editions and manuscripts] to sin.

Awake, and tell us: how does one conquer darkness whom necessity conquers? Necessity was already a greater enemy within him, by which he was overcome and commanded to fight against the lesser enemy. How much better would it have been for Adam not to know where he might flee from the face of that god, than for the god himself first to have no place to flee from the face of harsh and dreadful necessity, and afterward no place to flee from the face of a different and hostile race?

How much better would it have been for him to begrudge human nature its blessed life, than to consign his divine nature to misery; to desire the blood and fat of sacrifices, rather than himself to be so often sacrificed to idols, mingled with the fat and blood of every victim; to be disturbed with jealousy if those sacrifices were offered to other gods, rather than himself to be bound—not only in all fruits [Note: [Col. 0414] Am. and Er. and several manuscripts read, “grains”—frugibus] but also in all flesh—on every altar and offered to every demon?

How much better would it have been for him, moved and agitated by human indignation, to grow angry with sinners, his own and others’, than for him himself to be agitated not only in all who are angry but also in all who are afraid, to be defiled in all sinners, and punished in all the condemned—bound everywhere in that part of himself which he himself condemned, though innocent, to such disgrace, so that through it he might conquer what he feared; himself also condemned to so destructive a necessity that his condemned part might forgive him, if, now miserable, he would at least be humble?

But now, who could tolerate your reproving God for becoming angry with his own and others’ sins, when the god whom you invent later condemns his own members—the members whom he forcibly compelled to enter the jaws of sin—in the globe? Yet when, according to you, he does this, he will not be angry. I wonder whether he will have the audacity to inflict something resembling vengeance upon those from whom he ought to ask forgiveness and say: “I beg you, forgive me; you are my members. When could I have done this to you except after being overcome by necessity?”

You yourselves know that at the time when I sent you here, a dreadful enemy had broken out; but now that I bind you here, I fear that he may break out again.

Surely you also now admit that it is much better to kill thousands of human beings by temporal death for no fault or for a slight fault than to hand over his own members—that is, the members of God, the substance of God, plainly God himself—to the gulf of sin and condemn them to everlasting punishment by binding them there. For if those members had free choice whether to sin or not to sin—although, in the case of the substance of God, which truly is God’s substance and therefore wholly unchangeable, it is impossible to see how this could be said—God cannot sin at all, just as he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13). Man, however, can sin and deny God; but if he does not wish to do so, he does not.

Therefore, if those members of your god had, as I have said, free choice of will to sin or not to sin, like a human and rational soul, perhaps they would rightly be punished for serious crimes by the penalty of the globe. But you cannot say that those particles possessed freedom of will when the god as a whole did not possess it. For if he did not send them into sin, he himself, entirely overrun by the race of darkness, would be forced to sin. But if they could not be forced, then he sinned when he sent them to a place where they could be forced. Therefore he himself is more deserving of that supposedly parricidal sack, since he did this by free command, than are they, who obeyed and went to the place where they lost the free choice of living rightly [Col. 0415].

But if he himself could be compelled to sin after being invaded and possessed—unless he had first provided for himself through the crime and afterward the punishment of his own part—then there was no free will either in your god or in his parts. Let him not pretend to be a judge, but acknowledge himself guilty—not because he suffered what he did not wish, but because he pretends to distribute just retribution by condemning those whom he knows suffered evil rather than committed it. He pretends to do this merely so that he may not be found defeated—as though it benefited any wretched person to be called happy or fortunate.

Indeed, it would already have been better for your god to spare neither just nor sinners without any examination of justice—a course which Faustus, understanding nothing in his attack on our God, placed last in his indictment—than for him to rage against his own members in such a way that it was not enough for him to offer them, irredeemably to be poisoned [Note: [Col. 0415] The Vatican manuscript reads, “that he offered them to be poisoned in expiation of himself”], to their enemies, unless he also falsely accused them of the crime of iniquity.

For this reason, he rightly says that they endure such an immense and endless punishment: because they allowed themselves to stray from their former luminous nature and became hostile to the holy light. Why, unless because, as he himself says, they were so deeply embedded in the first appetite of the princes of darkness that they could neither recall their origin nor distinguish themselves from the hostile nature?

Thus souls of this kind themselves did nothing evil, but merely suffered great evil while innocent. Who caused this, unless the one who first commanded them to proceed from him into so great an evil? They therefore experienced a father worse than an enemy. The father sent them into so great an evil; the enemy desired them as something good, wishing to enjoy them, not to harm them. The one harmed them knowingly; the other unknowingly.

But the weak and helpless god could find no other way to provide for himself, first against the wicked enemy and then against the enemy shut within him. At least, then, let him not accuse those whose obedience made him safe and whose death made him secure. If he was compelled to fight, was he also compelled to slander?

For when they allowed themselves to stray from their former luminous nature and became hostile to the holy light, they were certainly compelled to do this by the enemy. If they could not resist him, they are condemned though innocent. But if they could resist and would not, why do you continue to introduce, in such a fabulous manner, a nature of evil, when the origin of sin lies in the will itself? They certainly did this through their own fault, not through another’s force: although they could resist evil, they did not wish to.

If they had done so, they would have acted well; but if they did not, they sinned gravely and monstrously. If they were able to do it and did not, then plainly they were unwilling. If they were unwilling, the fault lies in the will, not in necessity.

The beginning of sin, therefore, lies in the will. From where the beginning of sin comes, there also comes the beginning either of evil-doing against a just command or of suffering according to a just judgment. Consequently, there is no reason for you, while seeking the origin of evil, to rush into so great an evil of error as to call a nature abounding in so many good things the nature of evil, and to place the dreadful evil of necessity in the nature of the supreme good before the commingling of the nature of evil [Col. 0416].

The cause of this error of yours is pride. You would not have it if you did not wish to. But while you wish to defend in some fashion the error into which you have rushed, you remove the origin of sin from the freedom of the will and place it in a vain and false fable about a nature of evil.

It remains, therefore, for you to say that those souls too are to be condemned in the horrible globe by eternal bondage: not because they willed it, but because necessity made them hostile to the holy light. You would thus establish your god as a judge before whom you could accomplish nothing for those whose cause you defend by demonstrating necessity; and as a king from whom you could obtain no mercy for your brothers, his sons and members, whose hostility toward you and toward him you affirm arose not from their will but from necessity.

O monstrous cruelty!—except that you turn yourselves to defending him, excusing him as well for doing these things out of necessity. If, then, you could find another judge who, free from the bond of necessity, governed with equity, he would certainly not fasten this god externally in the globe but would shut him within it together with that terrible enemy. For why should the one who is first in the crime of necessity not also be first in the punishment of condemnation?

How much better, therefore, would it be for you to choose, in comparison with a worse god, not the one whom we worship, but another whom you either pretend or suppose that we worship—a god who would spare neither his servants [Note: [Col. 0416] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read, “would not spare in his servants.”], whether just or sinful, without any examination of equity and without any distinction between condemnation and discipline—rather than one who would not spare his members, whether they were innocent, if necessity is not a crime, or became harmful by obeying him, if necessity is a crime.

Then they would be condemned by him eternally together with the one with whom they ought either to be acquitted together, if freedom recovered its breath after victory, or condemned together, if even after victory necessity retained at least enough power for equity to have some power as well.

Just as you fabricate another god—not the true and supreme God whom we worship—a false god of some sort whom you either think or slander us into worshiping, though even he is much better than your god—for neither exists, and both are fabricated by you—so you fabricate as better the god whom you accuse as though he were ours than the god whom you worship as your own.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Likewise, you do not reproach the Patriarchs and Prophets as they are honored by us, but as you have maliciously and vainly fabricated them to be, because you do not understand our books. Yet even the people you suppose them to have been, it is not enough for me to say, were better than all your Elect who keep all the Manichaean commandments, unless I also show that they were better than your god himself. I shall not undertake to demonstrate this until, with the Lord’s help, I have first defended our holy fathers, the Patriarchs and Prophets, against your accusations by clear reasoning, against carnal minds [Note: [Col. 0416] Thus several manuscripts. The printed editions read, “by discourse”].

And indeed, Manichaeans, it would be enough to answer you by teaching that even the faults you attribute to our people are preferable to the praises of yours. To complete your confusion, we could add that your god himself would prove far worse than the human beings whom you claim our fathers to have been.

Thus, as I have said, it would be enough to answer you. But since some people are moved of their own accord even apart from your empty talk, comparing the life of the Prophets in the Old Testament with the life of the Apostles in the New Testament, and unable to distinguish the custom of that period, when the promise was veiled, from the custom of this period, when the promise is revealed, I am compelled to answer especially those who dare to prefer their own temperance to that of the Prophets, or who seek from the Prophets a defense for their own wickedness.

## CHAPTER XXIV

On this matter I say first that those men’s life, no less than their speech, was prophetic; and that the entire kingdom of the Hebrew people was a great prophet, because it was also the prophet of something great.

Accordingly, as concerns those who were instructed there in the wisdom of God in their hearts, prophecy must be sought not only in what they said but also in what they did. As concerns the rest, and all the people of that nation together, prophecy must be examined in the things that were divinely done in them or concerning them, prophecy of the Christ and of the Church to come. For all those things, as the Apostle says, “were figures of us” (1 Cor. 10:6).

## CHAPTER XXV

Thus these people criticize certain deeds—deeds whose height they are far from attaining—as though they were the lust of the Prophets, just as some sacrilegious pagans criticize Christ as though it were stupidity, or rather madness, because at an inappropriate season of the year he sought fruit on a tree (Matt. 21), or because, displaying some childish foolishness, he bent his head and wrote with his finger on the ground, and, after answering the people who questioned him, began doing the same thing again (John 8).

They understand nothing and perceive nothing: in great souls certain virtues resemble the faults of little ones in some outward appearance, but not at all in a fair comparison [Note: [Col. 0417] Several manuscripts read, “with no comparison of equality.” One reads, “with no equality of comparison.”].

Those who criticize such things in great people are like ignorant children in school. Having learned as an important rule that a singular noun must be accompanied by a singular verb, they criticize the most learned author of the Latin language because he said, “The part cut into pieces” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.212). “He ought,” they say, “to have said, ‘The part cuts.’” And because they know that *religion* is spelled with one *l*, they blame him for writing, “With the religion of the fathers” (ibid. 2.715), with the letter doubled.

Thus it might not absurdly be said that, within their respective categories, the difference between the figures and metaplasms of learned writers and the solecisms and barbarisms of the ignorant is as great as the difference between the figurative deeds of the Prophets and the lustful sins of the wicked. Accordingly, just as a boy who had been rebuked for a barbarism and tried to defend himself by appealing to Virgil’s metaplasm would be beaten with rods, so whoever, after lying with his wife’s maidservant, takes Abraham’s act of begetting offspring from Hagar as an example in his defense—may he be corrected, not indeed with rods, but at least with clubs, lest he be punished with the other adulterers by everlasting punishment.

Those matters are very small, whereas these are great; nor has the comparison been introduced to equate a figure with a sacrament or a solecism with adultery. Nevertheless, in proportion to the nature of each category, what expertise or ignorance accomplishes in certain virtues or faults of speech is accomplished in these matters by wisdom or folly concerning virtues or faults of conduct, although the categories are very different.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Therefore, so that we may not rush rashly into praising or reproving, accusing or defending, restraining or permitting, condemning or absolving, desiring or avoiding anything—for sins or right actions are involved in all these matters—we must first consider what sin is. Then we must examine the deeds of the Saints recorded in the divine books, so that, if we find any sins among them, we may carefully determine, as far as we can, for what benefit those deeds themselves were committed to writing and entrusted to memory.

When we find that foolish or malicious people regard as sins things that are not sins, and yet those things do not display any outstanding examples of virtue, we must also consider why they were inserted into the Scriptures, which we rightly believe were composed for the benefit of guiding the present life and attaining the life to come.

Whatever lessons of justice shine forth in the deeds of the Saints, no one—not even the ignorant—doubts that they ought to have been recorded. The question, then, concerns those things that may seem to have been written pointlessly if they appear neither to be right actions nor sins; or even harmfully, if they are shown to be sins and might therefore encourage imitation—whether they were not reproved in the books themselves and could consequently be thought not to be sins, or whether they were reproved there as well but are committed in the easy hope of forgiveness because they were also found among holy people.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Sin, therefore, is a deed, word, or desire contrary to the eternal law. The eternal law is the divine reason or the will of God, commanding the natural order to be preserved and forbidding it to be disturbed.

What, then, is the natural order in man? This must be investigated. Man plainly consists of soul and body, but so does an animal. No one doubts that, by the natural order, the soul must be placed above the body. Yet the human soul possesses reason, which an animal does not possess.

Therefore, just as the soul is placed above the body, so, by the law of nature, the reason of the soul itself is placed above its other parts, which animals also possess. And within reason—which is partly contemplative and partly active—contemplation unquestionably excels.

In contemplation is the image of God, by which we are re-formed from faith unto sight. Rational action, therefore, ought to obey rational contemplation, whether contemplation commands through faith [Note: [Col. 0418] Am., Er., and most manuscripts read, “works.”], as it does so long as we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), or through vision, as it will when we are like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Then, also made equal to his angels in a spiritual body by his grace (Matt. 22:30), we shall have received again the first robe of immortality and incorruption, with which this mortal and corruptible body of ours will be clothed, so that death may be swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:53–54), in perfect justice through grace.

For the holy and exalted angels also have their contemplation and their action. They command themselves to do what the one whom they contemplate commands; they serve his eternal command freely, because they serve it gladly.

But we, whose body is dead because of sin, live justly according to the measure of our weakness and according to the eternal law by which the natural order is preserved, before God gives life to our mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in us (Rom. 8:10–11), if we live by sincere faith, which works through love (Gal. 5:6). We possess in a good conscience a hope laid up in heaven: the hope of immortality and incorruption, and of the completion of perfect justice unto a certain ineffably sweet satisfaction, which must be hungered and thirsted for during this pilgrimage, so long as we walk by faith and not by sight (2 Cor. 5:7).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Accordingly, man’s action, serving faith, which serves God, restrains all mortal pleasures and confines them within their natural measure, preferring what is better to what is inferior through ordered love.

For if nothing illicit were pleasing, no one would sin. Therefore, the person who relaxes the pleasure of what is illicit rather than restraining it sins. What is illicit is whatever that law forbids by which the natural order is preserved.

Whether there is any rational creature that cannot be pleased by anything illicit is a difficult question. If such a creature exists, neither man nor that angelic nature which did not remain in the truth was made in that category. Rather, these rational creatures were made in a category in which they possessed the possibility of restraining pleasure from what is illicit; by failing to restrain it, they sinned.

Great, therefore, is the human creature, since through it that possibility is restored—a possibility by which, had it wished, it would not have fallen. Great, therefore, is the Lord, and greatly to be praised (Ps. 47:2), who created it.

He created lower creatures, which cannot sin; he also created better creatures, which do not wish to sin. The animal nature does not sin, because it does nothing contrary to the eternal law. It is so subject to that law that it cannot participate in it.

Again, the exalted angelic nature does not sin because it participates in the eternal law in such a way that God alone pleases it, and it obeys his will without undergoing any experience of temptation.

But man, whose life upon earth is temptation because of sin (Job 7:1), should subject to himself what he shares with animals and subject to God what he shares with angels, until, having attained perfect justice and immortality, he is raised above the animals and made equal to the angels.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Mortal pleasures, insofar as they serve the restoration or preservation of mortal health—whether of an individual person or of the human race itself—are to be either stimulated or relaxed. But if they go beyond this and, breaking loose, carry away a person who is not governing himself according to the rule of temperance, they will certainly be illicit and shameful desires, worthy of being corrected through suffering.

If they also plunge a disturbed ruler into so deep a gulf of corrupt habit that, either believing that they will go unpunished and neglecting the remedy of confession and repentance by which he might emerge corrected, or applying to them, against that eternal law of providence, the blasphemous protection of a defense based on an even worse death of the heart, he reaches the end of his life, that irreproachable law judges him worthy no longer of correction but of condemnation [Col. 0420].

## CHAPTER XXX

Having consulted the eternal law—which commands the natural order to be preserved and forbids it to be disturbed—let us see what Father Abraham sinned in, that is, what he did contrary to this law, in the matters that Faustus brought forward as great crimes.

“He was burning with an insane desire to have offspring,” Faustus says, “and, not believing at all in the God who had already promised him this offspring from his wife Sarah, he lay with a concubine.”

But Faustus, blinded by an insane desire to accuse, has both exposed the crime of his heresy and, through ignorance and error, praised Abraham’s intercourse. For just as the eternal law—that is, the will of God, the creator of all creatures, caring for the preservation of the natural order—permits the pleasure of mortal flesh to be relaxed by the rule of reason into intercourse solely for the propagation of offspring, not for the satisfaction of lust but for the welfare of the race, so, conversely, the perverse law of the Manichaeans commands those who have intercourse above all to avoid offspring, lest their god, whom they mourn as bound in every seed, be bound more tightly in the conception of a woman. They prefer their god to be poured out through a shameful fall rather than bound by a cruel bond.

Abraham, therefore, was not burning with an insane desire to have offspring; rather, the Manichaean was raving with the insane folly of avoiding offspring. Accordingly, Abraham, preserving the order of nature, did nothing in human intercourse except that a human being might be born. The Manichaean, observing the perversity of his fable, feared nothing in any intercourse except that the god might be captured.

## CHAPTER XXXI

But where Faustus, in Abraham’s action, censures what he supposes to have been his wife’s complicity, there, although with an evil mind and an intention to reproach, he nevertheless unknowingly and unwillingly praises both of them.

Nor did she involve her own conscience in the disgrace of her husband, by which he might satisfy his lust through a shameful and illicit pleasure. Rather, she too, desiring children according to the natural order and knowing herself to be sterile, lawfully claimed the fertility of a servant’s womb for the exercise of her right—not yielding to a lustful husband but commanding an obedient one (Gen. 16:2–4).

Nor was this an act of disordered pride. Who does not know that a wife ought to serve her husband as her lord? But with regard to the members of the body by which sex itself is distinguished, the Apostle says: “Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. 7:4). Thus, while in other actions pertaining to human peace the woman owes service to the man, in this one matter—by which the two sexes are distinguished according to the lot of the flesh and joined through the mingling of the flesh—the man and the woman possess equal authority over one another.

Sarah therefore wished to have from her servant the offspring whom she could not have from herself, yet from the seed from which she ought also to have had offspring from herself, if she had been able [Note: [Col. 0420] In the manuscripts, “desired.”].

A woman would never do this if she were held by carnal desire for her husband’s body. She would be jealous of the concubine instead and would not make her a mother. But in this case her intention to propagate was pious precisely because her intention to have intercourse was not lustful [Note: [Col. 0421] Thus Am. Er. and several manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads, “lustful pleasure.”].

## CHAPTER XXXII

Certainly, that cannot be defended if Abraham, as Faustus alleged, wished to receive offspring from Hagar because he did not at all believe God, who had already promised him offspring from Sarah. But this is plainly false: God had not yet made that promise.

Let those who wish to do so review the earlier passages of that Scripture. They will find that a land and an abundance of an innumerable multitude had already been promised to Abraham’s seed (Gen. 12:3), but that it had not yet been revealed how the propagation of that seed would occur—whether from Abraham’s flesh, if he himself were to beget a child, or by his will, if perhaps he were to adopt someone. Furthermore, if from his flesh, it had not yet been made clear whether the child would come from Sarah or from some other woman altogether.

Let them read, I say, if they wish, and they will find that Faustus either is innocently mistaken or shamelessly deceives. Thus, when Abraham saw that he was not having children but nevertheless held fast to the promise made concerning his seed, he first thought of adoption.

This is indicated by the fact that, speaking with God, he said of his household servant, “This man shall be my heir,” as though he were saying: “Because you have not given me offspring from myself, fulfill in this man what you promised to my seed.”

For if anyone’s seed were called only what was born from his flesh, the Apostle would not call us the seed of Abraham (Gal. 3:29). We certainly do not derive our bodily origin from him, but we have become his seed by imitating his faith, believing in Christ, whose flesh was propagated from Abraham’s flesh.

Then Abraham heard from the Lord: “This man shall not be your heir, but one who shall come from your own body shall be your heir” (Gen. 15:3–4).

At that point [Note: [Col. 0421] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read, “now.”], once the thought of adoption had been removed and Abraham was hoping for offspring from himself, it remained uncertain whether the child would come from Sarah or from another woman. God wished to conceal this from him until the Old Testament had first been prefigured through the servant.

What wonder, then, if Abraham, seeing that his wife was sterile and wishing for the offspring that she herself could not bear, but that could come from her servant and from her husband, did not yield to his own carnal desire but obeyed his marital authority? He believed that Sarah had wished this by God’s direction, since God had already promised him an heir from himself but had not foretold from which woman.

Faustus therefore rushed madly to bring this charge, accusing Abraham as an unbeliever in an unbelieving manner. In his blindness, born of refusal to believe, he could not understand the other matters; in his lust for calumny, he neglected even to read this one.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

As for Faustus’s claim that Abraham—calling this just and faithful man the most infamous broker of his own marriage—lied to two kings, Abimelech and Pharaoh, at different times, saying that Sarah his wife was his sister, and that because she was very beautiful he had sold her for intercourse: with a slanderous mouth he does not distinguish honesty from disgrace but turns everything into a crime.

Abraham’s action may appear similar to procuring prostitution, but only to those who are unable, by the light of the eternal law, to distinguish right actions from sins. To such people constancy may appear obstinacy, the virtue of confidence may be judged the vice of audacity, and whatever similar charges are brought against those who are acting rightly may seem justified to those who do not see rightly [Col. 0422].

Abraham did not consent to his wife’s disgrace or sell her adultery. Rather, just as Sarah did not surrender her servant to her husband’s lust [Note: [Col. 0422] Am. and Er. read, “did not surrender her servant to her husband out of lust.”] but freely offered her for the duty of procreation, without disturbing the natural order where she possessed authority—commanding an obedient man rather than yielding to a lustful one—so Abraham, too, kept silent about his chaste wife, who was joined to him with a chaste heart and whose mind, in which the virtue of chastity dwelt, he did not doubt in the least.

He said that she was his sister and kept silent that she was his wife, lest, after he had been killed, she be held captive by foreign and impious men. He was certain concerning his God that God would not allow her to suffer anything shameful or disgraceful.

Nor did faith and hope deceive him. Pharaoh, terrified by prodigies and afflicted with many evils on her account, returned her unharmed and with honor when he learned by divine revelation that she was Abraham’s wife. Abimelech, likewise warned and instructed in a dream, did the same (Gen. 12 and 20).

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Some people who are not, like Faustus, slanderous and malicious, but who give due honor to the same books—which Faustus either criticizes because he does not understand them or does not understand because he criticizes them—have considered this action of Abraham and concluded that he fell short and faltered somewhat in the firmness of faith. They thought that, through fear of death, he denied his wife just as Peter denied the Lord (Matt. 26:70–74).

If this had to be understood in that way, I would acknowledge the man’s sin, but I would not therefore consider all his merits erased and obliterated, just as I do not consider those of that Apostle erased—although the fault of denying one’s wife is not equal to the fault of denying the Savior.

But now that I have a reason for understanding the matter otherwise, I am compelled by no cause to slip rashly into censuring someone whom no one proves to have fallen through fear into lying.

For when he was asked whether she was his wife, he did not answer that she was not. Rather, when he was asked what that woman was to him, he identified her as his sister; he did not deny that she was his wife. He kept silent about something true; he did not say something false.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Are we so utterly foolish as to follow Faustus here, when he says that Abraham lied about her being his sister, as though he had learned the lineage of Sarah from some other source, although Holy Scripture has not disclosed it?

I think it is right that, in a matter Abraham knew but we do not, we should believe the Patriarch speaking about what he knew rather than the Manichaean accusing him of what he does not know.

Since Abraham was living among human beings at a time when it was no longer permitted for brothers born of the same two parents, or of either the same father or the same mother, to be joined in marriage, but custom joined the children of brothers and other blood relatives of a more distant degree without any law or authority forbidding it, what is surprising if he had his sister—one born from the blood of his father—as his wife?

For when the king returned her to him, Abraham himself said that she was his sister from his father, not from his mother. Certainly, at that point he was no longer compelled by fear to lie that she was his sister, since the king had learned that she was his wife and, terrified by divine intervention, was returning her with honor.

Scripture testifies that among the ancients “brothers” and “sisters” were customarily used as general terms for male and female blood relatives.

Tobias, for example, says to God, when he prayed before joining himself to his wife: “And now, Lord, you know that I take my sister not for lust” (Tob. 8:9). She was not born from the union of the same father, nor from the womb of the same mother, but had arisen from the same family stock (ibid. 6:11; 7:2).

Lot is also called Abraham’s brother (Gen. 13:8), although Abraham was his uncle (ibid. 11:31). From this usage of the term, the Lord’s “brothers” are also called brothers in the Gospel—not, of course, those whom the Virgin Mary bore, but all the relatives connected with him by blood (Matt. 12:46).

## CHAPTER XXXVI
Someone may say: Why did Abraham not rather presume so much upon his God that he would not be afraid to acknowledge her as his wife? For surely God could have driven away the death which he feared, and could have protected him with his wife from every danger during that journey abroad, so that no one would desire his wife, beautiful though she was, and he himself would not be killed on her account. God certainly could have accomplished this—who would be so foolish as to deny it? But if Abraham, when questioned, had identified that woman as his wife, he would have entrusted two things to God’s protection: his own life and his wife’s chastity. Yet it belongs to sound doctrine that, when a person has something he can do, he should not tempt the Lord his God (Deut. VI, 16).

For even the Savior himself could have protected his disciples, yet he said to them: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X, 23). He first supplied an example of this conduct. For although he had power to lay down his life, and would not lay it down unless he wished (John X, 18), nevertheless, as an infant, he fled to Egypt when his parents carried him there (Matt. II, 14). And he went up to the festival not openly but secretly, although at other times he spoke publicly to the Jews, who were enraged and listening with the utmost hostility; yet they could not lay hands on him, because his hour had not yet come (John VII, 10, 30)—not because the necessity of some hour would compel him to die, but because the fitting opportunity of his hour would allow him to be killed.

Thus, by teaching and rebuking openly, while nevertheless not allowing the fury of his enemies to have any power over him, he demonstrated God’s power. Yet by fleeing and hiding he also instructed human weakness, so that one should not dare to tempt God when one has something one can do, and thus escape what ought to be avoided. Nor had the apostle Paul despaired of divine help and protection, or lost faith, when he was lowered through a wall in a basket in order to escape the hands of his enemies (Acts IX, 25). He did not therefore flee in this way because he did not believe in God; rather, he would have been tempting God if he had refused to flee in this way, when he could have done so.

Accordingly, when, among strangers, Sarah’s exceptional beauty placed both her chastity and her husband’s life in danger, and Abraham could not protect both, though he could protect one of them—that is, his life—he did what he could so as not to tempt his God, and entrusted what he could not protect to him. Thus, because he was unable to conceal that he was a human being, he concealed that he was a husband, lest he be killed; but he entrusted his wife to God, lest she be violated.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Although the matter could be argued with greater subtlety—whether that woman’s chastity would have been violated even if someone had had intercourse with her, since she would have permitted this to happen for her husband’s life, not without his knowledge but at his command, in no way abandoning conjugal fidelity and not rejecting her husband’s authority—just as that man was not an adulterer when, obeying his wife’s authority, he consented to beget a child by a maidservant [Note: [Col. 0424] See Book 1 of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapters 16, §§49–50]. Nevertheless, because of the force of first principles—for a woman is not subjected to intercourse with two living men in the same way that two women are subjected to one man [Note: [Col. 0424] Am. and Er., “in that way”; that is, *qua*]—we accept as much more true and honorable the view that Abraham, the father, did not tempt God, since as far as he could, being human, he took care of his own life and placed his wife’s chastity in God’s hands.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Now, in this deed that was accomplished, set down in the divine books, and faithfully narrated, who would not also delight to investigate the prophetic significance of the event and to knock with devout faith and eagerness at the door of its mystery, so that the Lord might open it and show whom that man then represented, and whose wife she is who, during this journey and among foreign peoples, is not permitted to be polluted or stained, so that she may be without spot or wrinkle for her husband?

For the Church rightly lives unto the glory of Christ [Note: [Col. 0424] Thus the better manuscripts; the printed editions have “in the glory”], so that her beauty may be an honor to her husband, just as Abraham was honored among foreign peoples because of Sarah’s beauty. To her of whom it is said in the Song of Songs, “O beautiful among women” (Song I, 7), kings offer gifts because of the excellence of that beauty—just as King Abimelech offered gifts to Sarah, admiring in her all the more the splendor of a beauty which he could love but could not violate.

For the holy Church is also, secretly, the wife of the Lord Jesus Christ. Secretly, inwardly, in the hidden spiritual mystery, the human soul clings to the Word of God, “so that the two may be one flesh”: this great sacrament of marriage the Apostle commends in Christ and in the Church (Eph. V, 31–32). Accordingly, the earthly kingdom of this age, whose figure was represented by the kings who were not permitted to violate Sarah, neither experienced nor recognized the Church as the spouse of Christ—that is, as one who faithfully clung to him, her first husband, in submission [Note: [Col. 0424] The printed editions commonly read “her chief husband.” Some manuscripts have “her first principle and husband.” Better manuscripts read “her first husband”: shortly before he said that, by the force of first principles, a woman is not subjected to two living men as two women are to one man.]—until it attempted to violate her, yielded before the divine testimony through the faith of the martyrs, and, rebuked, honored her with a gift under the later kings, whereas it had not been able to subject her to its rebuke under the earlier kings. For what was then represented first and later in the same king is fulfilled in this kingdom through its earlier and later kings.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

When the Church is said to be Christ’s sister by the father, not by the mother, kinship is being affirmed not according to an earthly generation that will pass away, but according to the heavenly grace that will remain forever. According to this grace we shall no longer belong to mortal generation, having received the power to be called and to be children of God (1 John III, 1).

For we received this grace not from the Synagogue, the mother of Christ according to the flesh, but from God the Father. Christ taught us to deny and not acknowledge this earthly kinship, which generates for temporal death, when he called us into another life in which no one dies, saying to his disciples: “Do not call anyone your father on earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XXIII, 9).

He supplied an example of this when he himself said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand over the disciples, he said: “These are my brothers.” And lest anyone should understand this expression as referring to earthly kinship, he added: “Whoever does the will of my Father, he is my brother, and mother, and sister” (Matt. XII, 48–50)—as though he were saying: “I call this kinship from God the Father, not from the Synagogue, the mother. For now I call them to eternal life, where I was born immortal, not to the temporal life from which I became mortal in order to call them.”

## CHAPTER XL

The reason why the Church’s identity as wife is concealed from foreign peoples, while her identity as sister is not concealed, readily presents itself: it is hidden and difficult to understand how the human soul is joined or united to the Word of God—or whatever better and more suitable expression may be used—since the Word is God, while the soul is a creature. In this respect Christ and the Church are called bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife.

But by what kinship Christ and all the saints are brothers—by divine grace, not earthly consanguinity; that is, from the father, not from the mother—is expressed more eloquently and heard more intelligibly.
