For all the saints are also brothers to one another through the same grace; but the bridegroom is not one of them in the fellowship of the others.

Accordingly, although Christ was a man of outstanding justice and wisdom, foreign peoples much more easily and readily believed him to be a man—not falsely, certainly, in believing that he was a man; but they did not know how he was also God. Hence Jeremiah too says: “He is a man, and who will recognize him?” (Jer. XVII, 9). “He is a man,” because what is disclosed is that he is a brother. “And who will recognize him?” because what is concealed is that he is the bridegroom.

Let this suffice concerning Father Abraham against the most shameless, ignorant, and slanderous statement of Faustus.

## CHAPTER XLI

His brother Lot, however, a just and hospitable man in Sodom, pure and undefiled by every contamination of the Sodomites, deserved to escape safely from that conflagration which was a likeness of the future judgment. He bore the type of the body of Christ, which now groans among the wicked and impious in all the saints, does not consent to their deeds, and will be freed from their fellowship at the end of the age, while they are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.

Another class of people was represented in Lot’s wife: those, namely, who, called by God’s grace, look backward—not like Paul, who forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what lies ahead (Phil. III, 13). Hence the Lord himself says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke IX, 62).

Nor did he omit that example by which he seasons us, as it were, with salt, so that in our foolishness we might not neglect this evil but, in our prudence, beware of it. Thus, to give this warning, she was turned into a pillar of salt. For when he was commanding each person, with the most persevering attention to what lies ahead, to rescue himself from what lies behind, he said: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII, 32).

Likewise, in Lot himself, when his daughters had intercourse with him, something other than what was represented when he was rescued from Sodom was signified. At that time Lot himself seems to have borne the character of the future Law; certain people begotten from it and placed under the Law, by misunderstanding it, intoxicate it in a certain manner [Note: [Col. 0426] Er., Lugd., Ven., “intoxicating it”; M.], and by using it improperly produce works of unbelief. “The Law is good,” the Apostle says, “if one uses it lawfully” (1 Tim. I, 8).

## CHAPTER XLII

Yet we do not therefore justify this deed, whether of Lot himself or of his daughters, because it signified something that foretold the future perversity of certain people. They intended one thing in doing this, while God, who permitted it to happen in order also to disclose something through it, intended another; his righteous judgment upon the sin of the people then living remained in force, while his providence watched over the signification of future things.

Accordingly, when that deed is narrated in Holy Scripture, it is prophecy; but when it is considered in the lives of those who committed it, it is a crime.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Nor is the matter worthy of so great a reproach and accusation as Faustus, its hostile and blind opponent, spewed forth against it. For that eternal law which commands the natural order to be preserved and forbids it to be disturbed takes account of the matter. It does not judge this deed as though Lot had burned with wicked lust for his daughters in order to enjoy their violated bodies or to have them as wives; nor does it judge the women as though they had burned with execrable love for their father’s flesh.

For reason, in judging rightly, considers not only what was done but also why it was done, so that it may examine deeds in proportion to their causes on the scales of equity. Since they were seeking offspring for the preservation of the race—and the affection in them was certainly human and natural—and since they did not believe they could find other men, as though the whole earth had been consumed in that conflagration—for they could not determine how far that fire had raged—they wished to have intercourse with their father.

They ought rather never to have become mothers than to have used their father in this way. Nevertheless, it makes a great difference that they acted from this motive rather than from a desire for such a dreadful pleasure.

## CHAPTER XLIV

They felt such revulsion toward that act with their father that they did not believe they could accomplish it unless they secured his ignorance. For, as it is written, “they made him drunk, and had intercourse with him without his knowing” (Gen. XIX).

Therefore he is indeed to be blamed, but not as much as that incest deserves; rather, as much as that drunkenness deserves. For the eternal law also condemns this, since it admits food and drink into the natural order only for the preservation of health.

Although there is a great difference between a drunkard and a drunken person—for a drunkard is not always drunk, and not everyone who is drunk on some occasion is consequently a drunkard—nevertheless, in the case of a righteous man, the cause of this very thing, even if not of habitual drunkenness, certainly of drunkenness on that occasion, must be sought.

What, after all, compelled him to consent or to believe when his daughters repeatedly mixed wine for him, or perhaps repeatedly offered it even unmixed? [Note: [Col. 0427] Some manuscripts, “yielded.”] Did he perhaps wish to console his daughters, who were pretending to excessive grief, in such a way that the pain of their desolation and maternal bereavement would be driven from the mind of the drunken man—believing that they themselves were drinking an equal amount while using some trick to avoid drinking it? But even if this was their sorrow, we do not see how it was fitting for a just man to offer them such consolation.

Or could they, by some especially wicked Sodomite art, have so intoxicated their father with only a few cups that they committed that sin with him while he was unaware—or rather, against him in his ignorance? Yet it would be astonishing if divine Scripture had kept this silent, or if God had allowed his servant to suffer this without some fault of his will.

## CHAPTER XLV

We, however, are defending the Holy Scriptures, not the sins of human beings. Nor do we labor to excuse this deed as though our God had either commanded it to happen or approved it once it had happened; nor are righteous people called such in those books in such a way that, if they should wish to sin, they would be unable to do so.

Since, then, in the writings that these people criticize, God gave no testimony of righteousness to this deed, with what madness and recklessness do they try to accuse those writings on this account, when elsewhere in them they find such things expressly prohibited by divine commands?

Accordingly, in the account of the event, the deed of Lot’s daughters is narrated, not praised. Some matters ought to be narrated with God’s judgment explicitly stated, and others with it left unspoken: when what God judged about them is brought forth, our ignorance is instructed; when it is left unspoken, either our understanding is exercised, so that we recall what we learned elsewhere, or our laziness is shaken, so that we seek what we do not yet know.

God, therefore, who knows how to bring good works even out of the evil deeds of human beings, propagated from that seed the nations he wished; he did not condemn his Scriptures because of human sins. He disclosed these things; he did not commit them. He warned us to avoid them; he did not set them before us for imitation.

## CHAPTER XLVI

With truly astonishing shamelessness [Note: [Col. 0427] Several manuscripts, “ignorance.”] Faustus also accused Isaac, Abraham’s son, of pretending that Rebekah, who was his wife, was his sister (Gen. XXVI, 7). Rebekah’s lineage is not concealed, and it is clear that she was his sister through a very well-known relationship (Gen. XXIV).

As for his keeping silent about the fact that she was his wife, what is surprising, or what is insignificant, if he imitated his father, since he is defended by the same justice by which his father was found innocent when accused of a similar matter? What we said in defense of Abraham against the accusing Faustus, insofar as this matter is concerned (above, chapters 33–36), applies equally to his son Isaac, and it is not difficult to review it.

Unless perhaps one of those eager to investigate asks in what sacramental figure we should understand the fact that the foreign king recognized Rebekah as her husband’s wife when he saw him playing with her; he would not have recognized this unless Isaac had been playing with her in a way that it would not be proper to play with a woman who was not one’s wife.

When holy married people do this, they do not do it pointlessly but prudently. In a certain way they descend to the weakness of the female sex, so as to say or do something with gentle cheerfulness; they do not weaken manly firmness but temper it [Note: [Col. 0428] Most manuscripts, “strength.”]—though what someone says or does in this way to a woman who is not his wife is shameful.

I say this concerning human manners, lest some harsh and unfeeling person accuse the holy man of the very fact that he played with his wife. Such inhuman people, if they see some serious man chatting playfully even with small children, in order to soothe their childish minds with friendly and nurturing kindness, rebuke him as though he were delirious. They forget from what condition they themselves grew, or show no gratitude that they grew at all.

But what this signifies sacramentally concerning Christ and the Church is surely evident to anyone who carefully examines the mystery of her husband in the Holy Scriptures, lest by error he commit some sin against the Church. He finds that Christ temporarily concealed his majesty, by which in the form of God he is equal to the Father, in the form of a servant (Phil. II, 6–7), so that human weakness might be capable of receiving him, and that in this way he might fittingly adapt himself to his wife.

For what is absurd—or rather, what is not suitably adapted to the foreshadowing of future things—if God’s Prophet played in a bodily manner in order to win his wife’s affection, when the very Word of God became flesh in order to dwell among us (John I, 14)?

## CHAPTER XLVII

Now, as for the four wives attributed to Jacob, Isaac’s son, as a grave crime (Gen. XXIX and XXX), the matter is cleared up by a general preliminary statement. When it was customary, it was not a crime; and now it is a crime precisely because it is not customary.

For some sins are against nature, others against customs, and others against commandments. Since this is so, what crime is there in the charge brought against the holy man Jacob because he had several wives at the same time? If you consult nature, he used those women not for wantonness but for begetting children. If you consult custom, this was commonly done at that time and in those lands. If you consult commandment, no law forbade it.

But now, why is it a crime if someone does this, unless it is because both custom and law forbid it? Whoever despises these two things, even if he can use several women solely for the purpose of begetting children, nevertheless sins and violates human society itself, which requires the propagation of children.

But because people, now that customs and laws have changed, cannot take pleasure in a multitude of wives except through the magnitude of lust, they err and think that it was altogether impossible for a man to have many wives unless he was inflamed by carnal desire and sordid pleasure.

For when they compare themselves—not with others, whose virtue of mind they cannot possibly know, but, as the Apostle says, “with themselves and among themselves” (2 Cor. X, 12)—they do not understand. Since they themselves, even if they have only one wife, approach her as men not merely driven by the duty of begetting children but often dragged weakly along by the stimulus of intercourse, they seem to themselves to infer with certainty how much more powerfully others must be seized by this disease when they see that they cannot maintain self-control with one woman.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Yet we ought not entrust judgment concerning the conduct of holy men to those who do not possess this virtue, any more than we allow fever patients to judge the sweetness and healthfulness of food. Rather, we prepare nourishment for them according to the judgment and prescription of healthy physicians [Note: [Col. 0429] Printed editions, including Am. and Er., and many manuscripts, “and according to prescribed medicine”; some, “and prescribed medicines.”], not according to the feelings of their illness.

Therefore, if these people wish to receive healing—not of a false and shadowy chastity, but of true and solid chastity—let them trust the divine Scriptures as medical books. It was not without reason that such great honor of holiness was attributed to certain men who also had several wives, unless it is because it is possible for the mind, the ruler of the flesh, to prevail with such power of self-control that it does not permit the movement of genital pleasure, implanted in mortal nature, to exceed the laws imposed by the providence of begetting children.

Otherwise these men, who are more rightly called slanderous accusers than truthful judges, could also accuse the holy Apostles, claiming that they preached the Gospel to so many peoples not from the charity of begetting children for eternal life but from a desire for human praise.

For those evangelical fathers were not lacking a splendid reputation acquired throughout all the Churches of Christ, with so many tongues praising them. Indeed, it was so great that human beings ought not to bestow greater honor and glory on other human beings.

The fallen Simon desired this glory in the Church with perverse intention, when in his blindness he wished to buy with money from them what they had obtained through divine and equally gratuitous grace (Acts VIII, 18–20).

The man who wanted to follow the Lord in the Gospel is understood to have been greedy for this glory, but the Lord restrains him, saying: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have shelters; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII, 20). He saw that the man, darkened by deceitful pretense and puffed up by empty arrogance, had no place of faith in which he could receive the teacher of humility when he bowed down; for in discipleship to Christ he was seeking not Christ’s grace but his own glory.

Those whom the apostle Paul censures were corrupted by this love of glory, because they proclaimed Christ not purely but through envy and rivalry. Yet the Apostle rejoices when they preach (Phil. I, 15–18), knowing that, while they pursued the desire for human glory, believers could nevertheless be born through hearing them—not from their envious desire, by which they wished either to equal or surpass the glory of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0430] The Vatican manuscript, “apostolic grace”; certain other manuscripts, “apostolic teaching.”], but through the Gospel, which they proclaimed, though not purely. Thus God brought good out of their evil, just as it can happen that a man approaches intercourse not from the will to beget children but is seized by lust for pleasure; yet a human being is born, a good work of God arising from the fertility of seed, not from the shamefulness of vice.

Therefore, just as the holy Apostles took pleasure together with hearers who admired their teaching, not from eagerness to obtain praise but from love of sowing the truth, so the holy Patriarchs had intercourse with their wives when the latter received their seed, not from lust for pleasure but from providence for propagating offspring. Consequently, neither did the multitude of peoples make the Apostles ambitious, nor did the multitude of wives make the Patriarchs lustful.

But why should I speak of the men, to whom divine speech bears such outstanding testimony, when it is sufficiently clear that the women themselves desired nothing else in intercourse but children? For when they saw that they were not giving birth, they gave their maidservants to their husband so that they might make them mothers in the flesh, while they themselves became mothers by intention [Note: [Col. 0430] Lov., “they gave them to their husbands.” Other printed editions and manuscripts, “they gave them to their husband.” Thus the following *facerent* refers to the wives themselves who gave them.].

## CHAPTER XLIX

As for the claim that Faustus made with his utterly false accusation—that the four women had competed among themselves like prostitutes over which of them would drag him to intercourse—I do not know where he read this, unless perhaps in his own heart, as though in a book of wicked falsehoods, where he himself truly played the prostitute, together with that serpent of whom the Apostle was afraid for the Church, which he desired to present as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ, lest, just as the serpent had deceived Eve by its cunning, so it might corrupt their minds by turning them away from the chastity of Christ (2 Cor. XI, 2–3).

For these people are so friendly toward this serpent that they contend it benefited rather than harmed humanity [Note: [Col. 0430] Lov. adds here, “the human being.”]. It plainly persuaded Faustus, pouring seeds of falsehood into his adulterated heart, so that his most filthy mouth might give birth to these ill-conceived accusations and his audacious pen might also commit them to memory.

None of the maidservants dragged Jacob away from another; none quarreled with another over intercourse with him. Therefore there was greater order because there was no lust, and the rights of conjugal authority were preserved all the more firmly because the injury of carnal desire was avoided more chastely.

For the fact that he was also procured by one wife reveals our position clearly; there the truth itself cries out in its own defense against the curses of the Manichaeans. Why would one woman need to procure him unless it was the other woman’s turn for her husband to enter her? For he would not have failed ever to go to Leah unless she had procured him; but he certainly went to her at the proper times, since he had fathered so many children by her and had obeyed her so as to father a child also by her maidservant, and later fathered another child when she did not procure him.

At that time Rachel had the night by right, so that she might remain with her husband; at that time she possessed the authority of which the voice of the New Testament certainly did not remain silent through the Apostle, saying: “Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.” Thus she had already made an agreement with her sister, so that, having become her debtor, she would transfer her to her own debtor.

For the Apostle calls it by this name: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife” (1 Cor. VII, 4, 3). Therefore, to whichever sister the husband was indebted, he had already received from the other what she had chosen by her own will, so that he might give her what was under her authority.

## CHAPTER L

Now consider this man, whom Faustus accuses as though he were impure, with his eyes closed—or rather extinguished. If he had been a servant of lust rather than of justice, would he not have burned throughout the entire day with desire for that night on which he was to sleep with the more beautiful woman—whom he certainly loved more, and for whom he had paid fourteen years of labor without wages?

When the day had ended and he was going into her embrace, when would he have turned away from her if he had been the kind of man the ignorant Manichaeans imagine? Would he not, disregarding the women’s agreement, have entered instead the chamber of his beautiful wife, who owed him that very night not only by the custom of marriage but also by the right of the arrangement?

He himself would rather have exercised his marital authority, since the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and the reciprocal arrangement of their service at that time worked in his favor. Therefore he would have used his conjugal authority all the more forcefully if he had been overcome by desire for her beauty.

But the women would have been better if they had competed for the conception of children while he competed for the pleasure of intercourse. Thus, being a thoroughly self-controlled man—and truly a man, because he used women so manfully that he was not subjected to carnal pleasure but ruled over it—he considered what he ought to render rather than what was owed to him. He did not wish to misuse his authority for his own pleasure; he preferred to be the one who paid the debt rather than the one who exacted it.

It followed that he should render himself to the woman whom the one to whom he was indebted had chosen to receive that debt on her behalf. When he learned of their agreement, and was suddenly and unexpectedly recalled from his most beautiful wife and summoned to the less beautiful one, he did not flare up in anger, grow clouded with sadness, or make weakly flattering efforts between them to have Rachel return the night to him.

Rather, as a just husband and provident father, when he saw that they were concerned with offspring and that he himself sought nothing else from intercourse, he judged that he ought to obey their will, since each of them desired children by him and nothing of his was diminished, because both were giving birth to his children [Note: [Col. 0431] Er., Lugd., and Ven. have “to herself”; M.].

As though he were saying: “Yield and concede to one another as you wish, deciding which of you will become a mother. Why should I compete, when whoever is born from one side or the other will have no father but me?”

If Faustus had been as perceptive as he was sharp in attack, he would have understood and praised in those writings this modesty, this restraint of desire, and this sole pursuit of human posterity in the union of married bodies. Instead, his intellect was corrupted by a detestable sect; he looked for something to criticize and considered the one honorable purpose of the marital union—that men and women are joined for the purpose of begetting children—the greatest crime.

## CHAPTER LI

Now that the conduct of the Patriarch has been defended and the crime that wicked error brought against him has been refuted, let us, as best we can, explore the secrets of the mysteries freely [Note: [Col. 0432] Lov., “from the book”; the other printed editions and manuscripts more correctly have “freely,” that is, “of one’s own accord.”], and let us knock with the piety of faith, so that the Lord may open to us what was represented by these four wives of Jacob, two of whom were free women and two maidservants.

We see that the Apostle understands the two women whom Abraham had, one free and one a maidservant, as representing the two Testaments (Gal. IV, 22–24). But there, what is said is more readily apparent because there is one of each; here, however, there are two and two. Moreover, there the son of the maidservant is disinherited, whereas here the sons of the maidservants receive the promised land together with the sons of the free women. Therefore something else is undoubtedly signified here.

## CHAPTER LII

Although I think that Jacob’s two free wives pertain to the New Testament, to which we have been called into freedom, they are not two without reason—unless perhaps because, as I have observed and found in the Scriptures, two lives are proclaimed to us in the body of Christ: one temporal, in which we labor, and the other eternal, in which we shall contemplate the delight of God.

The Lord made the first known through his passion and the second through his resurrection. The names of these women also urge us to understand this. For they say that Leah is interpreted as “Laboring,” while Rachel is “The Vision of the Beginning,” or “The Word through which the beginning is seen.”

The activity, then, of human and mortal life, in which we live by faith, performing many laborious works whose outcome for the benefit of those for whom we wish to care is uncertain, is Leah, Jacob’s first wife. Hence she is also said to have weak eyes. “For the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our planning is uncertain” (Wis. IX, 14).

But the hope of the eternal contemplation of God, possessing a certain and delightful understanding of the truth, is Rachel. Hence she is also said to have a beautiful face and attractive appearance. Every devout lover of wisdom loves her, and for her sake serves God’s grace, by which our sins, even if they have been like scarlet, are made white like snow (Isa. I, 18). For Laban is interpreted as “Whitening,” and Jacob served him for Rachel (Gen. XXIX, 17, 30).

No one turns under the grace of the remission of sins to serve righteousness except in order to live peacefully in the Word through which the beginning is seen, who is God. Therefore one serves for Rachel, not for Leah [Note: [Col. 0432] The printed editions add here *servitur*, “one serves”; the word is absent from the manuscripts.].

Who, after all, would love the labor of activity and suffering in works of righteousness for its own sake? Who would desire that life for itself, just as Jacob did not desire Leah? Yet when she was substituted for him at night, he embraced her for the purpose of begetting children and experienced her fertility.

For the Lord, because she could not be loved for her own sake, first caused her to be endured so that Rachel might be reached, and afterward commended her because of her children. Thus every useful servant of God, established under the grace of the whitening of his sins, what else has he meditated upon in his conversion, what else has he carried in his heart, what else has he loved, except the teaching of wisdom?

Many think that they will immediately acquire and obtain this once they have exercised themselves in the seven commandments of the Law concerning love of neighbor, so that no harm is done to any human being: “Honor your father and mother”; “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not kill”; “You shall not steal”; “You shall not bear false witness”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX, 12–17).

When these commandments have been observed as far as possible, and when, for a person who longs for and hopes for the most beautiful delight of teaching, the endurance of labor has attached itself through various temptations, as through the night of this age, then Leah has unexpectedly been joined in place of Rachel. He endures her in order to reach Rachel, if he perseveringly loves her, after receiving the other seven commandments, as though it were said to him: “Serve another seven years for Rachel,” so that he may be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and a peacemaker (Matt. V, 3–9) [Note: [Col. 0433] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov., “may you be.”].

A person would wish, if it were possible, to reach immediately the delights of beautiful and perfect wisdom without any endurance of labor, which must be embraced in doing and suffering. But this cannot happen in the land of the dying.

This is apparently signified by what was said to Jacob: “It is not customary in our place for the younger to marry before the elder” (Gen. XXIX, 27, 26). For the woman who is earlier in time is not inappropriately called “elder.” In the proper education of a human being, the labor of doing what is just comes first, before the pleasure of understanding what is true.

## CHAPTER LIII
The following is relevant to this: “You desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide it for you” (Ecclus. 1:33). These commandments obviously pertain to justice—justice, moreover, which comes from faith and exists amid the uncertainties of temptations, so that by piously believing what it does not yet understand, the soul may also attain the merit of understanding. For just as much as the passage I have now recalled is worth: “You desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide it for you,” so, I think, is that other passage also worth: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9). Thus it is shown that justice pertains to faith, while understanding pertains to wisdom.

Accordingly, in those who burn with an immense love of manifest truth, their zeal should not be condemned but brought back into proper order, so that it may begin from faith and strive by good morals to arrive where it is tending. For in that with which it is occupied there is laborious virtue; but in that which it desires there is luminous wisdom. [Note: Col. 0433. Lov.: “in that which is opposed.” One Vatican manuscript: “which is opposed.” Other manuscripts, with Am. and Er.: “in that which it is occupied.”] “Why,” it says, “is it necessary for me to believe what is not shown to me plainly? Offer me some word by which I may see the principle of all things.” This is what a rational mind chiefly and first kindles toward, if it is devoted to truth. To it the answer should be: What you desire is indeed beautiful and most worthy of love; but Leah marries first, and Rachel afterward.

[Col. 0434] Let that ardor therefore serve to prevent the order from being rejected, and rather to make it bearable; for without it one cannot arrive at what is loved with such ardor. When one has arrived there, one will possess in this age not only splendid understanding but also laborious justice. However keenly and sincerely mortals may discern the unchangeable good, “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things” (Wis. 9:15). We must therefore strive toward the one goal, but for its sake many things must be endured.

## CHAPTER LIV

Jacob has two free wives: both are daughters of the remission of sins—that is, of the whitening which is Laban. Nevertheless, one is loved and the other endured. But the one who is endured is the first to bear fruit, and bears it more abundantly, so that, if not for her own sake, at least for the sake of her children, she may be loved.

For the labor of the righteous bears its greatest fruit in those whom they beget for the kingdom of God by preaching the Gospel amid many temptations and tribulations. Those for whose sake they are more abundantly in labors, exceedingly in beatings, and frequently in deaths (2 Cor. 11:23), for whose sake they have “fighting without and fears within” (ibid. 7:5), they call their joy and crown (Phil. 4:1).

They are born to them more readily and abundantly from that word of faith by which they preach Christ crucified (1 Cor. 1:23), and whatever of his humanity is more quickly grasped by human thought; this does not disturb even Leah’s weak eyes. Rachel, however, beautiful in appearance, is beside herself for God (2 Cor. 5:13), and sees “in the beginning the Word, God with God” (John 1:1); she wishes to give birth but cannot, “for who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

Accordingly, the life suited to the pursuit of contemplation—in order that it may behold, through the things that have been made, what is invisible to the flesh, understood not by the mind’s weak eyes, and may ineffably contemplate the eternal power and divinity of God (Rom. 1:20)—wishes to be free from every occupation, and for that reason is barren. In seeking the leisure by which the pursuits of contemplation are kindled, it does not accommodate itself to the weakness of human beings, who desire to be helped in their various hardships. But because it too burns with the love of bearing children—for it wishes to teach what it knows, and does not wish to make its way while wasting away through envy (Wis. 6:25)—it sees its sister abounding in children through the labor of action and suffering. It grieves that people hasten toward that virtue by which provision is made for their weaknesses and needs rather than toward the virtue by which something divine and unchangeable is learned.

This grief appears to be represented in what is written: “Rachel became jealous of her sister” (Gen. 30:1). Therefore, because a clear and pure understanding of that substance which is not body, and thus does not pertain to the sense of the flesh, cannot be expressed in words produced by the flesh, the teaching of wisdom chooses to insinuate the divine, so far as it can be conceived, through all kinds of bodily images and likenesses rather than cease from the duty of teaching such things. Rachel likewise chose to receive children from her husband through her maidservant rather than remain altogether without children.

For Bala is said to be interpreted as “Aged” [Inveterata]. Rachel had this woman as her maidservant. From the old life, devoted to bodily senses, bodily images are aroused—even when something is heard concerning the spiritual and unchangeable substance of divinity. [Note: Col. 0435. Nearly all manuscripts read “are conceived/thought” (*cogitantur*) rather than “are aroused” (*concinantur*).]

## CHAPTER LV

Leah also receives children from her maidservant, kindled by love of having a more numerous offspring. We find that her maidservant Zilpah is interpreted as “Mouth agape” [Os hians]. Therefore, whenever in the preaching of evangelical faith we notice people whose mouth is open but whose heart is not, this woman is understood to be Leah’s maidservant.

For it is written of certain people: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). And to such people the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. 2:21–22).

Nevertheless, so that through this dependent maidservant the free wife of Jacob, laboring, might also receive children as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord says: [Note: Col. 0435. Lov. reads “condition” (*conditionem*); Am., Er., and all our manuscripts read “dependent [woman]” (*conditionalem*): understand, the maidservant “Mouth agape.”] “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3).

Hence, amid the labor of apostolic bonds: “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice” (Phil. 1:18)—as though the maidservant too had rejoiced at bearing a more numerous offspring.

## CHAPTER LVI

There is, moreover, a child of Leah produced through Rachel’s assistance, when Rachel permits her husband to lie with her sister on the night appointed for him to sleep with his wife, in exchange for the mandrakes obtained from Leah’s son. [Note: Am. Er. and our manuscripts read, “permits him to lie with her.”]

I know that some people suppose of this kind of fruit that, when eaten by barren women, it produces fertility; and therefore they think that Rachel was altogether eager to obtain it from her sister’s son because she desired to bear children. I would not think so, even if she had then conceived. [Note: The Erasmus edition alone reads, “which I too would suppose, if she had then conceived.”]

But since, after Leah had borne two other children from that night, the Lord gave Rachel offspring, there is no reason for us to suspect something about the mandrake such as we have experienced in no other woman. I shall therefore say what I think; perhaps the more learned will offer better explanations later.

When I myself had seen these fruits and, because I had encountered them on account of this very passage of sacred reading—which is a rare occurrence—had rejoiced, I carefully investigated their nature as far as I could: not through some science remote from common understanding, which teaches the properties of roots and powers of herbs, but as much as sight, smell, and taste reported to me and to any other person.

Accordingly, I found the object beautiful and sweet-smelling, but tasteless. I confess that I do not know why the woman desired it so greatly, unless perhaps because of the rarity of the fruit and the pleasantness of its smell.

But why holy Scripture did not wish to pass over the event in silence—since it would certainly not take pains to present such feminine desires to us as something of great importance unless it were prompting us to seek something great in them—I cannot conjecture anything beyond what common understanding suggests to me: namely, that by that mandrake fruit I should understand a good reputation—not the reputation conferred when a few just and wise people praise someone, but the popular reputation by which a greater and more conspicuous renown is also acquired. This reputation is not to be sought for its own sake, but is absolutely necessary to the intention of good people by which they provide for the human race.

Hence the Apostle says: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3:7). Although such people may possess little wisdom, they nevertheless usually return to those whose labor serves their interests both the splendor of praise and the fragrance of a good reputation.

Those who are in the Church do not first attain this popular glory unless they are engaged in the dangers and labor of action. Therefore Leah’s son finds the mandrakes when he goes out into the field—that is, when he walks honorably before those who are outside.

But that teaching of wisdom, which is most remote from the noise of the crowd and is fixed in the contemplation of truth with sweet delight, would not attain even this small measure of popular glory except through those who preside over peoples amid the surrounding tumult, acting and persuading—not in order to rule, but in order to benefit them.

For while these active and occupied people, through whom the welfare of the multitude is administered and whose authority is dear to the people, also bear witness to the life of leisure devoted to seeking and contemplating truth, the mandrakes somehow reach Rachel through Leah.

They reach Leah herself through her firstborn son—that is, through the honor of her fertility, in which lies all the fruit of laborious action exposed to danger amid the uncertainties of temptations. Many people endowed with good ability and burning with zeal, although they may be capable of governing peoples, nevertheless avoid this because of its turbulent occupations and devote themselves wholeheartedly to the leisure of teaching, as though embracing beautiful Rachel. [Note: Col. 0436. Lugd. and Ven. read *tanquam in speciosae* (“as though into [that] of the beautiful …”; reading materially uncertain). M.]

## CHAPTER LVII

But because it is good that this life, too, as it becomes more widely known, should earn popular glory, it is unjust for it to obtain that glory if it keeps in leisure a lover who is suitable and capable of administering ecclesiastical responsibilities and does not contribute him to the governance of the common good.

Therefore Leah says to her sister: “Is it not enough for you that you have taken my husband, but do you also wish to take my son’s mandrakes?”

By the one husband she signifies all those who, although capable through their active virtue and worthy of being entrusted with the governance of the Church for dispensing to it the sacrament of faith, are inflamed by devotion to teaching [Note: Col. 0436. Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read: “for dispensing the sacrament of faith: they, inflamed,” etc. M.] and to investigating and contemplating wisdom, and wish to withdraw from all the troubles of action and hide themselves in the leisure of learning and teaching.

Thus the words mean: “Is it not enough that the life of study keeps in leisure people necessary for the labor of practical affairs, but does it also seek popular glory?” [Note: Col. 0436. Several manuscripts read “the life of scholars” rather than “the life of study.”]

## CHAPTER LVIII

Accordingly, so that Rachel may acquire it justly, she gives her husband to her sister on that night: namely, so that those who are suited by their laborious virtue to the governance of peoples, even if they had chosen to devote themselves to knowledge, may undertake the burden of the experience of temptations and responsibilities for the common good.

This is so that the very teaching of wisdom, to which they had decided to devote themselves, may not be blasphemed, and so that it may obtain from uneducated peoples a good reputation—signified by those fruits—which is necessary for exhorting learners.

But they are plainly compelled by force to undertake this responsibility. This too is sufficiently signified by the fact that, when Jacob came from the field, Leah went out to meet him and, detaining him, said: “You shall come in to me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes” (Gen. 30:14–16).

It is as though she said: “Do you wish a good reputation to be conferred upon the teaching that you love? Do not flee the labor required by duty.”

Anyone who pays attention can see these things being done in the Church. We experience them in examples, so that we may understand them in books. Who does not see this happening throughout the whole world: people coming from the works of the world and entering the leisure of learning and contemplating truth, as though into Rachel’s embrace, and then being intercepted by ecclesiastical necessity [Note: Col. 0437. The manuscripts read “people coming”; the printed editions read “all people coming.”] and appointed to labor, as though Leah were saying, “You shall come in to me”?

When, in the night of this world, they chastely dispense the mystery of God in order to beget children of faith, the people also praise that life whose love caused them to be converted and to abandon their worldly hope, and from whose profession they were taken up to govern the people in mercy.

For in all their labors they act so that the profession to which they had converted—because it has given such leaders to the peoples—may be glorified more widely and more splendidly. This is like Jacob’s not refusing Leah’s night, so that Rachel may enjoy the sweet-smelling and brightly shining fruits.

At times Rachel herself also gives birth through God’s merciful assistance, although only with difficulty and at last; for it is exceedingly rare that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1), and whatever is said about this subject piously and wisely can be grasped, without the phantasm of carnal thought, even in part and with salutary effect.

## CHAPTER LIX

What has been said about the three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—whom God, whom the Catholic Church worships, chose to call himself their God, should suffice against Faustus’s calumnies.

This is not the place now to discuss the merits and piety of these three men, or the prophetic elevation so far removed from the judgment of carnal people. In the present work they needed only to be defended against the crimes with which a slanderous tongue hostile to the truth attacked them [Note: Col. 0437. Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read “had needed” (*fuerant*). M.], lest those who read the holy and salutary Scriptures with a perverse and hostile mind should appear to be saying something against them, while they pursue with insolent insults those who are proclaimed there with such great honor.

## CHAPTER LX

Lot, moreover, Abraham’s brother—that is, his kinsman—is by no means to be compared with those of whom God says, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6). Nor is he to be counted among those to whom that Scripture bears witness to righteousness to the end.

Nevertheless, he lived piously and chastely among the Sodomites, was commended also for the merits of his hospitality, and was rescued from the burning of that land. For Abraham’s sake, because Abraham had been his uncle, the land was given by God as a possession to his descendants (Gen. 19). [Note: Lov. reads “the land of promise.” The other printed editions and nearly all manuscripts more correctly read “the land of possession.” Perhaps “their own” should be added. The land given for possession to Lot’s descendants—namely, the Moabites and Ammonites—is discussed in Deuteronomy, chapter 2.]

These are the merits set before us for praise in those books, not drunkenness or incest (Deut. 2:9). But when we find both a right deed and a sin written of the same man, one is presented for imitation and the other for avoidance.

Now, if Lot’s sin—of whom a testimony to righteousness had been given before he sinned (Wis. 10:6)—not only does not discolor the divinity of God or the truth of that Scripture, but even commends it as worthy of praise and love, because, like the brightness of a faithful mirror, it reveals in the persons placed before it not only what is beautiful and whole but also what is deformed and vicious, how much more does Judah’s deed, when he had intercourse with his daughter-in-law (Gen. 38:13–18), contribute nothing whatsoever by which sacred authority may be blamed?

That authority, firmly founded in those books, rightly disregards not only the slanderous sophistries of a very few Manichaeans but also the terrible hostility of so many great pagan peoples. By divine right it has nearly subdued them all from the wicked superstition of idols to the worship of the one true God through Christian rule, with the world conquered not by the violence of armed conflict but by the power of unconquered truth.

Where, then, is Judah praised in those writings? What good does that Scripture testify about him, except that in the prophecy of Christ—who was foretold as destined to come in the flesh from his tribe—he was distinguished above the others by his father’s blessing (ibid. 49:8–12)?

## CHAPTER LXI

Moreover, concerning what Faustus recalled—that Judah committed fornication—we add another fact: he sold his brother Joseph into Egypt (ibid. 37:26–28).

Does anyone’s distorted limb corrupt the light that reveals everything? In the same way, no one’s evil deeds make the Scripture evil by which they are disclosed to its readers.

For that eternal law, consulted by us, which commands the natural order to be preserved and forbids it to be disturbed, establishes that intercourse between human beings is to take place only for the sake of procreation, and then only within a socially ordered marriage that does not overturn the bond of peace. Therefore divine and eternal law condemns the prostitution of women who are offered not to provide offspring but to satisfy lust.

For saleable shame dishonors every purchaser. Accordingly, although Judah would have sinned more gravely if he had knowingly wished to have intercourse with his daughter-in-law—for if, as the Lord says, a man and his wife are no longer two but one flesh (Matt. 19:6), a daughter-in-law must be regarded no differently from a daughter—it is nevertheless beyond doubt that, so far as he was concerned, he lay disgracefully with a prostitute.

But she who deceived her father-in-law did not sin out of desire for his flesh or from a craving for a prostitute’s payment. Rather, seeking offspring from the same blood from which she had already been married to two brothers but could not have a child because a third had been denied to her, she fraudulently offered her body to their father, her father-in-law, for the begetting of a child, having received a pledge of payment which she kept not for adornment but as evidence. [Note: Am. Er. and the manuscripts read as above. Lov. reads, “she could have no child from the third, who had been denied to her.”]

It would indeed have been better for her to remain childless than to become a mother without the right of marriage. Nevertheless, she sinned with a very different intention: she provided a father for her children in her father-in-law, rather than desiring him as an adulterer.

Finally, when, at his command, she was brought out to be put to death, she produced the staff, the necklace, and the ring, saying that she had conceived by the man whose pledges these were. When he recognized what he had given, he declared that she was more justified than he, because he had not wished to unite his son to her in marriage. Driven by that rejection, she had sought offspring in that manner rather than not at all, and from no other stock than the same lineage.

In this statement, when he says that she was not justified but more justified than he, he does not praise her but places her above himself. He blamed less the desire for offspring, which had led her to offer herself to her father-in-law, than the ardor of lust by which he had entered as though to a prostitute, overcome by desire.

So it is said to certain people: “You have justified Sodom” (Ezek. 16:52)—that is, “You have sinned so greatly that, compared with you, Sodom appears righteous.”

Even if this woman is understood not merely to have been blamed less by comparison with a worse deed but to have been praised outright by her father-in-law, nevertheless, when the eternal law of justice is consulted—the law that forbids the natural order to be disturbed, not merely the order of bodies but above all and first of souls—she is rightly found blameworthy, because she did not preserve an ordered union in the begetting of children. What wonder, then, if a sinner is praised by a sinner?

## CHAPTER LXII

Faustus, or the Manichaean perversity itself, judges this to be contrary to us, as though, in venerating and worthily praising that Scripture, we were obliged to approve the vices of the people whom it records.

Rather, the more devoutly we receive it, the more confidently we must condemn those things which through its truth we have learned should more certainly be condemned. For there fornication and every unlawful intercourse are condemned by divine law (Exod. 20:14, 17). Consequently, when it records the deeds of certain people concerning whom it does not state its judgment in that place, it permits us to judge them; it does not prescribe that they be praised.

Who among us does not detest Herod’s cruelty in the Gospel, when, troubled about Christ’s birth, he ordered so many infants to be killed (Matt. 2:16)? Yet that deed is not there reproved but merely narrated.

But lest the insane shamelessness of the Manichaeans claim that this is false because they also deny Christ’s birth, let them read about the brutality and blindness of those very Jews: let them observe how it is merely narrated there, not reproved, and yet is detested by everyone.

## CHAPTER LXIII

“But,” they say, “this Judah, who had intercourse with his daughter-in-law, is counted among the twelve patriarchs” (Gen. 35:22–26).

What then? Was not that Judah who betrayed the Lord also numbered among the twelve Apostles, and was he not sent with them as one of them to preach the Gospel, even though he was a devil (Matt. 10:2–5; John 6:71–72)?

But they continue to respond and say: “After such a crime, that one killed himself by hanging and was removed from the number of the Apostles (Matt. 27:5). This one, however, after such a disgrace, was specially blessed and praised above all his brothers by that father to whom God bears such great testimony (Gen. 49:8–12).”

On the contrary, this makes it more evident that the prophecy pertains not to Judah himself but to Christ, who was foretold as destined to come in the flesh from his tribe. Therefore divine Scripture ought not to have passed over his crime in silence, just as it did not pass over it, so that in the words of his father—by which he is praised in such a way after that disgrace, although Judah himself is not recognized—another person might be sought.

## CHAPTER LXIV

Although Faustus may be understood to have wished to attack this very point with his slanderous tooth: namely, that we proclaim Christ to have come from Judah’s tribe. This is especially so because among the genealogies of his fathers, which the evangelist Matthew records, there is also found Zerah, whom Tamar bore from that union (Matt. 13; Gen. 38:30).

For if he wished to criticize Jacob’s lineage rather than Christ’s genealogy, he had the firstborn Reuben available, who violated his father’s bed by wicked lust (Gen. 35:22)—a form of fornication which the Apostle says was not even heard of among the Gentiles (1 Cor. 5:1). Jacob himself, their father, did not pass over this deed in silence when he blessed them, but accused and condemned it over his head (Gen. 49:3–4).

Faustus would therefore have brought forward this crime instead, in which there is evident not an error arising from the occupation of a prostitute but an entirely voluntary defilement of his father’s bed—unless he hated Tamar even more because she desired nothing other than to bear a child through that intercourse than he would have hated her had she burned solely with lust for carnal pleasure; and unless, by blaming Christ’s ancestors, he wished to diminish faith in his Incarnation.

Poor man, he did not know that the truest and most truthful Savior had become a teacher not only by speaking but also by being born. For his faithful people, who were to come from all nations, had to learn even from the example of his flesh that the iniquities of their ancestors could not harm them.

Accordingly, that bridegroom suited to his invited guests—he who was going to call good and bad to the wedding (Matt. 22:10)—also wished to be born from good and bad. Thus he confirmed that the Passover prophecy, in which the accepted lamb was commanded to be eaten from sheep and goats (Exod. 12:3–5), had gone before as a figure of him, as of the just and the unjust.

For, preserving everywhere the signs of God and humanity, he did not reject good and evil ancestors because of the fittingness of his humanity; but because of the miracle of his divinity he chose birth from a virgin.

## CHAPTER LXV

Faustus therefore attacks in vain, and with a sacrilegious tooth directed rather against himself, the holy Scripture which the whole world now rightly venerates. As I said above, like the brightness of a faithful mirror, it does not accept any person for flattery, but either judges the deeds of human beings, whether worthy of praise or blame, or sets them before its readers for judgment.

It does not merely disclose people themselves as either blameworthy or praiseworthy; it also does not remain silent about certain things worthy of praise in blameworthy people and things worthy of blame in praiseworthy people.

For although Saul was a blameworthy man, his deed is not therefore unworthy of praise when, obedient to God who had forbidden it, he investigated so carefully what had been tasted from the ban and attempted to avenge it so severely (1 Sam. 14:24–45). Nor is the fact that he eradicated the spiritists and ventriloquists from his kingdom unworthy of praise (ibid. 28:3).

Conversely, although David was praiseworthy, his sins—which God himself also reproved through the prophet (2 Sam. 12:1–14)—are not thereby worthy of approval or imitation.

Nor is it blameworthy in Pontius Pilate that, against the accusations of the Jews, he judged the Lord innocent (John 19:4, 6). Nor is it praiseworthy in Peter that he denied that same Lord three times (Matt. 26:70–74), or that he was called Satan by him because, not understanding the things of God, he wished to turn him away from his passion—that is, from our salvation. A little earlier he had been called blessed; shortly afterward he was called Satan (ibid. 16:22–23, 17). But what prevailed in him is shown by his apostleship and the crown of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER LXVI

In the same way, we read of King David’s sins, but we also read of his right deeds. What prevailed in him, and over what he gained victory, is readily apparent—not to the malevolent blindness with which Faustus attacked the holy books and holy men, but to religious prudence, by which both divine authority and human merits can be discerned and distinguished.

Let them read and see that God reproved more things in David than Faustus did (2 Sam. 12 and 24). But there is also the sacrifice of repentance. There is that incomparable gentleness toward the most savage and atrocious enemy, who, as often as he was delivered into David’s powerful hands, was as often released unharmed by those devout hands (1 Sam. 24 and 26).

There is the memorable humility beneath God’s scourge, and the royal neck so subjected to the Lord’s yoke that, armed and accompanied by armed men, David most patiently endured bitter insults from the mouth of his enemy. He restrained with the greatest moderation his companion, who was inflamed with anger because his king was hearing such things and was already advancing to strike the insulter’s head with an avenging hand. He added the weight of fear of God to his royal command, saying that this had been repaid to him according to his merits by the heavenly judgment, by which that insulting man had been sent to hurl such reproaches against him (2 Sam. 16).

There is such great pastoral love for the flock entrusted to him that he himself wished to die for them, when God chose to punish his sin of pride after the people had been counted by reducing that same number through the death of many—the very multitude of which had provoked the king’s heart to pride.

In this hidden judgment God, with whom there is no injustice (Rom. 9:14), removed from this life those whom he knew to be unworthy of it; and in the one who had exalted himself because of the multitude of human beings, he healed the swelling of the human spirit by diminishing that multitude.

There is such religious fear of God that he preserved the sacrament of Christ in the holy anointing: his heart trembled with devout concern when he secretly cut off a small piece of Saul’s garment, so that he would have evidence by which to persuade him that he did not wish to kill him when he could have done so.

There is such prudence and clemency toward his sons that, although he had prayed to the Lord for the innocent child who was ill, casting himself down with many tears and signs of humility, he did not mourn the child when it died; yet he wished to preserve and wept over the young son who had rushed forward in murderous fury, had stained his father’s bed with abominable acts, and had waged a wicked war against his father.

David foresaw the eternal punishments of a soul entangled in such crimes, and for the sake of escaping them he wished his son to live, humbled and corrected through repentance (2 Sam. 18).

Many other things worthy of praise and imitation are found in that holy man, if a perverse mind does not scrutinize the Scripture that speaks of him—especially if, with a submissive, devout, and wholly faithful mind, we follow the judgment of God, who knew the secrets of his heart. In the sight of the one who cannot be deceived, David was so pleasing that God even set him before his sons for imitation.

## CHAPTER LXVII

What else did the Spirit of God see but the depths of his heart when David, rebuked through the Prophet, said, “I have sinned,” and immediately deserved to hear, in response to this one statement alone, that he had received forgiveness?

For what purpose, if not for eternal salvation? The discipline of the paternal scourge was not omitted in him, in accordance with God’s threat, so that, having confessed, he might be freed eternally, and, having been afflicted temporally, might be tested.

It was no slight strength of faith, nor a small indication of a meek and obedient spirit, that, when he heard from the Prophet that God had forgiven him, yet saw the things God had threatened subsequently occur, he did not say that the Prophet had deceived him with a lie, nor murmur against God as though the Prophet had announced a false pardon for his sins.

For that profoundly holy man understood—lifting his soul not against God but toward God—that unless the Lord were merciful to one who confessed and repented, his sins deserved how great eternal punishments. While he was being burned by temporal corrections for those sins, he saw that forgiveness remained toward him and that the remedy was not being neglected. [Note: Some manuscripts read “used”; Am. has “feared”; Er. has “was scourged.”]

But why did Saul, when rebuked by Samuel and himself saying, “I have sinned” (1 Sam. 15:24), not deserve to hear what David heard—that the Lord had forgiven him? Is there partiality with God? Certainly not (Gal. 2:6). But beneath a similar expression heard by human ears there was a dissimilar heart, which the divine eye discerned.

What are we taught by such examples except that the kingdom of heaven is within us (Luke 17:28), and that we ought to worship God from our inmost selves, so that the mouth may speak from the abundance of the heart (Matt. 12:34), rather than so that, like the people, we may honor him with our lips while our heart is far from him (ibid. 15:8)?

Nor should we dare to judge differently concerning people whose inner selves we cannot see than the God who can see them and cannot be deceived or corrupted. Since divine Scripture contains such lofty authority and so clear a judgment concerning David, is not human rashness that thinks otherwise greatly deserving of ridicule—or rather, of lamentation?

For we must believe those divine books concerning the men of ancient times who foretold such distant future events that they now appear as present realities.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

What else do we learn in the Gospel when the same voice is heard from Peter confessing Christ as the Son of God (Matt. 16:16), and from demons also uttering equivalent words but from a heart utterly different (Luke 8:28)?

Thus, in a similar utterance Peter’s faith is praised, while the demons’ impurity is restrained. By whom, if not by the one who knew how to inspect the inner roots of those utterances—not with a human ear but with a divine mind—and to distinguish them without any falsehood?

How many other people also say that Christ is the Son of the living God and yet are not comparable to Peter’s merits—not only those who will say on that day, “Lord, Lord,” and hear, “Depart from me” (Matt. 7:22–23), but also those who will be separated to the right hand (ibid. 25:33)?

Among them are many who have never denied Christ even once, who have not disapproved of his passion for our salvation, and who have not compelled the Gentiles to practice Judaism (Gal. 2:14). Yet they will appear inferior to Peter, who did these things, when he sits on twelve thrones and judges not only the twelve tribes but also the angels.

Likewise, many people may desire no one’s wife and may pursue no husband who has been desired by them even to the point of death, yet they cannot possess before God the merit of David, who did such things.

How much it matters what each person dislikes in himself, and to what extent he dislikes it, so that it may be utterly uprooted—and what fruitful and abundant growth rises in its place with immense fertility! Farmers, too, prefer fields which, after even large thorns have been uprooted, produce a hundredfold, to those which have never had any thorns and scarcely reach thirtyfold.

## CHAPTER LXIX

In the same way, we read of Moses, the most faithful servant of God in all his house, the minister of the holy, just, and good commandment and law, to whom the Apostle bears witness (Heb. 3:5; Rom. 7:12)—for these are his words that I have quoted.

Moses was also the minister of the sacraments, which did not yet bestow salvation but still promised the Savior. The Savior himself confirms this when he says: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me; for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). We have therefore discussed him in its proper place, to the extent that seemed sufficient, against the shameless calumnies of the Manichaeans.

This Moses, then, servant of the living God, the true God, the supreme God, maker of heaven and earth—not from some other substance but from nothing, not under the pressure of necessity but from overflowing goodness, not through the punishment of one of his members but through the power of his Word—

this Moses, I say, humble in refusing so great a ministry (Exod. 4:10), submissive in accepting it, faithful in preserving it, energetic in carrying it out; vigilant in governing the people, forceful in correcting them, ardent in loving them, patient in enduring them; who interposed himself before God when He was providing for those over whom Moses presided, and opposed Him when He was angry—

such a great and remarkable man must not be assessed by us from the slanderous mouth of Faustus, but from the mouth of the entirely truthful God, who truly knew the human being whom he had made. For God recognizes the sins of human beings, which he himself does not commit, as judge in those who deny them, and forgives them as father in those who confess them.

From his mouth, Moses, God’s servant, is one whom we both love and admire, and whom, as far as we can, we imitate, although we are far inferior to his merits—even though we have neither killed nor despoiled any Egyptian and have waged no war. Moses did the one as a foreshadowing of the defender who was to come, and the other under God’s imposed command.

## CHAPTER LXX
In the meantime, let me pass over the fact that, when he struck the Egyptian (Exod. II, 12), although God had not commanded him to do so [Note: [Col. 0444] According to Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, *praeciperet* (“had commanded”). M.], it was nevertheless divinely permitted in the prophetic person for the purpose of prefiguring something future. I am not dealing with that now; rather, I examine those deeds as though they signified nothing at all. Consulting the eternal law, I find that a man ought not to have been killed by one who held no duly established authority, even though he was injurious and wicked.

Nevertheless, souls capable of and fertile in virtue often put forth beforehand certain faults by which they indicate to what virtue they are especially suited, if they are cultivated by instruction. For just as farmers, when they see what sort of soil, however unproductive, produces enormous weeds, declare it suitable for grain; and when they see fern [Note: [Col. 0444] Louvain edition: *felicem*. Corrected from other printed editions and manuscripts.]—even though they know it must be uprooted—they recognize that the soil is suited to vigorous vines; and when they see a mountain overgrown with wild olive trees, they do not doubt that it will be useful for olives once cultivation is applied; so that movement of spirit by which Moses could not endure to leave unpunished a foreigner suffering injury from a wicked citizen, without observing the order of authority, was not useless for the fruits of virtue. It was still uncultivated, but it was displaying signs—indeed faulty signs—of great fertility.

Finally, through his angel, God Himself called Moses with divine words on Mount Sinai, through whom the people of Israel would be delivered from Egypt; and by the miraculous vision of the bush blazing without being consumed, together with the Lord’s words, He prepared him for the fruit of obedience (ibid. III, 4). In the same way He called Saul, who was persecuting the Church, from heaven, struck him down, raised him up, and filled him—just as though He had struck, cut off, grafted in, and made fruitful (Acts IX, 4).

For Paul’s ferocity, when he persecuted the Church in accordance with zeal for the traditions of his ancestors (Gal. I, 14), thinking that he was performing a service for God, was like a wild vine, but an indication of great fruitfulness. The same was true of Peter when, wishing to defend the Lord with a drawn sword, he cut off the ear of the persecutor. The Lord restrained this deed with sufficiently threatening words, saying, “Put the sword away; for whoever uses the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI, 51–52).

He uses the sword who arms himself against another’s blood without the command or authorization of a superior and legitimate authority. Certainly, the Lord had commanded that His disciple carry iron, but He had not commanded him to strike with it.

What, then, is incongruous if Peter, after this sin, became the shepherd of the Church, just as Moses, after striking the Egyptian, became the ruler of that Synagogue? Neither exceeded the rule of justice through detestable savagery, but through an amendable impetuosity. Each sinned out of hatred for another’s wickedness—Moses out of brotherly love, Peter out of love for his Lord, though still carnal. This fault had to be cut away or uprooted; nevertheless, so great a heart, like soil for crops, had to be cultivated for the bearing of virtues.

## CHAPTER LXXI

What, then, does Faustus now object concerning the Egyptians who were despoiled, when he does not know what he is saying? Moses sinned so little by doing this that he would have sinned by not doing it. For God had commanded it (Exod. III, 21–22; XI, 2; XII, 35–36)—God, who certainly knows not only according to people’s actions but also according to their hearts what each person ought to suffer, and through whom.

That people was still carnal and occupied with desire for earthly things. The Egyptians, on the other hand, were sacrilegious and unjust. They used that gold—that is, God’s creature—in an evil way, serving their idols to the injury of the Creator; and they had unjustly and violently oppressed foreign people with unpaid labor. Therefore both the Hebrews, to whom such commands were given, and the Egyptians, who suffered such things, were deserving: the former of the commands, the latter of the suffering. Perhaps, according to their own wishes and thoughts, the Hebrews were permitted to do these things rather than commanded to do them; but God wished to make His permission known to them through His servant Moses, when He commanded him to say so.

There may, however, be other very secret reasons why this was divinely said to that people. But divine commands must be obeyed by compliance, not resisted through argument. The Apostle said: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?” (Rom. XI, 34).

Whether, then, this is the reason I have proposed, or whether some other reason lies hidden in the secret and concealed disposition of God for which He told that people through Moses to ask the Egyptians for the things they were to take away from them, I nevertheless affirm this: it was neither said without reason nor unjustly, and Moses was not permitted to act otherwise than God had said. The decision to command belonged to the Lord; the duty of carrying it out belonged to His servant.

## CHAPTER LXXII

“But,” Faustus says, “the true and good God must in no way be believed to have commanded such things.”

On the contrary, no one rightly commands such things except the true and good God, who alone knows what ought to be commanded to each person and who alone permits no one to suffer anything incongruous. Otherwise, this ignorant and false human goodness [Note: [Col. 0445] The Louvain edition alone reads *contradicit* (“contradicts”).] would contradict Christ, lest, when the good God commands, the wicked should suffer something evil, even though He will say to the angels: “Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to be burned.” Yet He forbade the servants, who wished to do precisely this at an inappropriate time [Note: [Col. 0445] The printed editions read *importune* (“inopportunely”). Corrected from the manuscripts.], saying: “Lest, while you wish to gather the weeds, you uproot the wheat also with them” (Matt. XIII, 30, 29).

Thus the true and good God alone knows what He should command or permit to be done, when, to whom, and through whom. This human quality—which is not goodness but plainly vanity [Note: [Col. 0446] Seven manuscripts read *improbitas* (“wickedness”).]—could also have contradicted that same Lord when, at the demons’ harmful desire, He permitted them to enter the pigs, as they wished and requested (ibid. VIII, 31–32). Even though the Manichaeans believed that not only pigs but also small and despised animals possessed human souls, once that vanity has been rejected and cast aside, this nevertheless remains certain: our Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God and therefore the true and good God, permitted the death of another’s animals [Note: [Col. 0446] Ambrose, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “by the death of another’s animals.”], the destruction of creatures of whatever kind, and serious loss to human beings, at the desire of demons.

What madman would say that He could not have excluded them from human beings even if He had not wished to grant the destruction of the pigs to their wicked will? Furthermore, if the fierce and unjust desire of condemned spirits, already destined for eternal fire, was released by the Creator and Governor of all natures, under a hidden but everywhere just moderation, into the thing toward which it had inclined, what is absurd if the Egyptians deserved to be deprived by the Hebrews—unjustly ruling people by free people—of earthly possessions to which they were entitled as payment for their own harsh and unjust labor, and which the Egyptians themselves used in sacrilegious ritual to the injury of the Creator?

If Moses had commanded this on his own authority, or if the Hebrews had done it on their own authority, they would certainly have sinned. Nevertheless, the Hebrews may have sinned by desiring such things, though not by doing what God had either commanded or permitted them to do. But because they were permitted to do this by divine dispensation, they were permitted by the just and good judgment of Him who knows how either to restrain the wicked through punishments or to educate those subject to Him; who gives stronger commands to the healthier and arranges certain medicinal stages for the weaker.

Moses, however, should be accused neither of desire concerning those coveted possessions nor of defiance concerning any divine commands that he disregarded.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

For that eternal law, which commands the preservation of the natural order and forbids its disturbance, placed certain actions before human beings in such an intermediate position that boldness is rightly condemned when they are undertaken by unauthorized initiative, while obedience is rightly praised when they are carried out in compliance with command. In the natural order, it makes all the difference who acts, by whose authority, and under whose authority each person acts.

If Abraham had sacrificed his son voluntarily, what would he have been except horrifying and insane? But when God commanded him, what did he appear to be except faithful and devoted? (Gen. XXII, 10.) The truth itself proclaims this so loudly that Faustus, frightened by its voice, although he searched with claws and teeth for something to say against Abraham, went so far as to make a slanderous falsehood, yet did not dare to criticize this deed—unless perhaps the famous act did not occur to him [Note: [Col. 0446] Some manuscripts read *non ei venerit in mentem* (“did not occur to him”).], either because he had not read it or because he did not seek it with attention; an act sung in so many tongues and depicted in so many places that it would strike the ears and eyes even of one who pretended not to see.

Therefore, if voluntary impulse in killing a son is execrable, but obedient service when God commands is found to be not merely blameless but even praiseworthy, why do you criticize Moses, Faustus, because he despoiled the Egyptians? If the wickedness of a human agent irritates you, as though he were acting on his own, let the authority of the divine commander terrify you. Or are you prepared to condemn God Himself for wishing such things to be done?

“Get behind me, Satan! For you do not set your mind on the things of God, but on the things of human beings” (Matt. XVI, 23). Would that you had been worthy to hear this as Peter did, and that afterward you had proclaimed what, through your weak understanding, you criticize in God—just as Peter later announced to the nations with glorious proclamation what had displeased him at first, when the Lord wished it to happen.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

Therefore, if human stubbornness and a perverse and distorted will in matters that are right finally understand how greatly it matters whether something is undertaken through human desire or recklessness, or whether God is obeyed—God who knows what He permits or commands, to whom, and when, and what it is fitting for each person to do or suffer—then let such a person neither marvel at nor shudder over the wars conducted through Moses. For in those wars also he followed divine commands: he was not raging but obeying.

Nor was God raging when He commanded these things. He was repaying what was due to those who deserved it and terrifying those who deserved terror [Note: [Col. 0447] Some manuscripts read “and terrifying those who did not deserve it.”].

What is blamed in war? Is it that those who will eventually die sometimes die, so that those who are to live in peace may be subdued [Note: [Col. 0447] Ambrose, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read *ut dominentur* (“so that they may rule”)]? To criticize this is the attitude of cowards, not of religious people. The desire to inflict harm, the cruelty of revenge, an unrestful and implacable spirit, the savagery of rebellion, the lust for domination, and similar things—these are what are rightly condemned in wars. Often, so that they may also rightly be punished, wars themselves are undertaken by good people against the violence of those who resist, whether God or some legitimate authority commands it, when the order of human affairs is such that that very order justly compels them either to command such things or to obey in such matters.

Otherwise, when soldiers came to John to be baptized and said, “And what shall we do?” he would have answered them: “Lay down your arms; abandon this military service; strike no one, wound no one, throw no one down” [Note: [Col. 0447] Lyons and Venice repeat *neminem* three times: “strike no one, wound no one, throw no one down.” M.]. But because he knew that, in doing these things as soldiers, they were not murderers but ministers of the law, and not avengers of their own injuries but defenders of public safety, he answered them: “Extort from no one, accuse no one falsely; let your pay be sufficient for you” (Luke III, 14).

But because the Manichaeans are accustomed openly to blaspheme John, let them hear the Lord Jesus Christ Himself commanding that this pay be rendered to Caesar, which John says ought to suffice the soldier. “Render,” He says, “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII, 21). For taxes are also paid for this purpose: so that, on account of the wars that are necessary, pay may be provided for the soldier.

He rightly praised the faith of the centurion who said, “I also am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (ibid. VIII, 9–10); He did not command him to abandon military service [Col. 0448].
