But to discuss now the just and unjust causes of wars would be lengthy and unnecessary.

## CHAPTER LXXV

It matters for what reasons and under whose authority people undertake wars that must be waged. Nevertheless, the natural order, adapted to the peace of mortals, demands that the authority and deliberation for undertaking war belong to the ruler, while soldiers ought to perform the military commands as a service for peace and the common welfare.

There can be no doubt that a war undertaken with God as its authority is rightly undertaken, whether to terrify, crush, or subjugate the pride of mortals. For even what is conducted through human desire can harm neither the incorruptible God nor His saints, and it is instead found to benefit them by exercising their patience, humbling the soul, and enabling them to bear paternal discipline.

“No one has any power over them except what has been given from above. For there is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII, 1), whether He commands or permits it.

Therefore, if a just man happens to serve under a human king, even a sacrilegious one, he rightly asks to fight at that king’s command, preserving the order of civic peace. What is commanded to him [Note: [Col. 0448] In the manuscripts: “when what is commanded to him.”] is either certainly not contrary to God’s command, or it is not certain whether it is. Thus the king’s injustice in commanding may make the king guilty, while the order of obedience shows the soldier to be innocent.

How much more innocently does one conduct himself in the administration of wars when he wages war at God’s command, since no one who serves God is unaware that He cannot command anything evil.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

If they think that God could not have commanded a war because the Lord Jesus Christ later said, “But I say to you, do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the left also” (Matt. V, 39), let them understand that this readiness is not in the body but in the heart. There is the holy dwelling-place of virtue, which also lived in those ancient righteous fathers of ours.

But the ordering and distribution of events required that the order of the times first make it evident that even earthly goods—among which are reckoned human kingdoms and victories over enemies—belong only to the power and decision of the one true God. It is precisely for these earthly goods that the city of the impious, spread throughout the world, generally supplicates idols and demons.

Thus the Old Testament covered and, in a certain way, shaded more obscurely the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, which was to be opened at the proper time, with earthly promises. But when the fullness of time came, so that the New Testament might be revealed—the reality veiled by the figures of the Old—it had to be demonstrated by clear testimony that there is another life, for the sake of which this life ought to be despised, and another kingdom, for the sake of which all the adversities of earthly kingdoms must be endured with the greatest patience.

Therefore, through the confessions, sufferings, and deaths of those by whom God chose that this should be attested, they are called martyrs, which in Latin means “witnesses.” Their number flourished so greatly that if Christ, who called Saul from heaven and transformed him from a wolf into a sheep, had wished to gather them together, arm them, and help them fight in the same way that He helped the Hebrew fathers, what nations would have resisted? What kingdoms would not have yielded? (Acts IX.)

But in order that a most glorious testimony might be given to the truth—that it had now to be taught [Note: [Col. 0449] Some codices read *quia jam* (“because now”).] that God should be served not for temporal happiness in this life but for eternal happiness after this life—the condition commonly called unhappiness had to be undertaken and endured for the sake of that happiness.

And so, in the fullness of time, the Son of God, made from a woman and made under the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law (Gal. IV, 4–5), made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. I, 3), sends His disciples like sheep into the midst of wolves. He warns them not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; He also promises that the integrity of the body itself will be renewed, down to the restoration of every hair (Matt. X, 16, 28, 30).

He recalls Peter’s sword into its sheath; He restores the severed ear of the enemy to its former shape. He says that He could have commanded legions of angels to destroy His enemies, unless the cup that the Father’s will had given Him to drink had to be drunk (ibid. XXVI, 52–53; Luke XXII, 51, 42; John XVIII, 11). He drinks first and offers the cup to those who follow. By His command He reveals the power of patience; by His example He confirms it [Note: [Col. 0449] Ambrose, Erasmus, and the Cistercian manuscript read “raises up” rather than “reveals.”].

For this reason God raised Him from the dead and gave Him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II, 9–11).

The Patriarchs and Prophets therefore reigned in this world, so that it might be shown that God gives and takes away earthly kingdoms. The Apostles and martyrs did not reign here, so that the kingdom of heaven might instead be disclosed as the object of desire.

Those kings [Note: [Col. 0449] Ambrose and Erasmus read *illi regi bella* (“that king waged wars”); some manuscripts, *illi regum bella* (“those wars of kings”).] waged wars, so that it might be clear that such victories too are granted by God’s will. These were killed without resisting, so that they might teach that the better victory is to be killed for the faith of the truth.

Yet the Prophets also knew, in that earlier period, how to die for the truth, as the Lord Himself says: “From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matt. XXIII, 35). And here, after what had been prophesied under the figure of Solomon—whose name in Latin means “Peaceful”—began to be fulfilled concerning the Lord Christ, “For He Himself is our peace” (Eph. II, 14), as it was foretold in the Psalm: “All the kings of the earth shall adore Him; all nations shall serve Him” (Ps. LXXI, 11)—Christian emperors too, placing complete confidence in devotion to Christ, gained a most glorious victory over sacrilegious enemies who had placed their hope in the sacred rites of idols and demons.

This happened with the clearest and best-known proofs, some of which have already been committed to writing for remembrance: the prophecies of demons deceived the former, while the predictions of the saints strengthened the latter.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

If this seems strange to these vain people—that at one time God commanded one thing to the stewards of the Old Testament, when the grace of the New Testament was veiled, and another thing to the preachers of the New Testament, when the obscurity of the Old Testament was revealed—let them observe the Lord Christ Himself changing what He had said and saying something different:

“When I sent you,” He said, “without purse, bag, or sandals, did you lack anything?” They replied, “Nothing.” Therefore He said to them: “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever has no sword, let him sell his tunic and buy one.”

If these people found such differing instructions in the separate Testaments, the Old and the New, they would cry out on this basis also that the two Testaments were opposed to each other. What, then, will they answer now, when the same person says: “Previously I sent you without purse, bag, or sandals, and you lacked nothing; but now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever has a tunic, let him sell it and buy a sword”?

Do they now understand how, without any inconsistency in the one giving commands, commands, counsels, or permissions may be changed according to the diversity of times, through the reasoning of the one who orders events? If they say that He spoke of taking a purse and bag and buying a sword for the sake of some particular mystery, why do they not admit that the one God commanded the Prophets to wage wars at one time and prohibited the Apostles from doing so at another, for the sake of a particular mystery?

For in the Gospel passage we have recalled, it was not merely the Lord’s words that followed; the deeds of the disciples who obeyed also followed. At that earlier time they went without purse and bag, and they lacked nothing, as His question and their answer made clear. And now, when He commanded them to buy a sword, they said to Him, “Look, here are two swords.” And He answered, “That is enough.”

This is why Peter was found armed when he cut off the ear of the persecutor. There his spontaneous boldness was restrained (Luke XXII, 35–36, 38, 50–51), because just as he had been commanded to take the sword, he had not been commanded to strike with it.

Certainly the Lord’s will was hidden as to why He had commanded them to carry weapons which He did not wish them to use. Nevertheless, it belonged to Him to command with reason, and to them to carry out the commands without hesitation.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

Thus Moses is criticized by Faustus through slanderous ignorance because he waged wars, although he would have deserved less criticism if he had waged them on his own initiative than if, when God commanded him, he had not waged them.

But to dare to criticize God Himself for having commanded such things, or not to believe that the just and good God could have commanded such things, is—if I may speak mildly—the thought of a person unable to consider the divine providence that extends through all things, from the highest to the lowest. Under that providence, what arises is neither new, and what dies does not perish; rather, each thing in its own order, whether of natures or of merits, either gives way, succeeds, or remains.

The right will of human beings is joined to the divine law, while disordered desire is restrained by the order of the divine law, so that the good person desires nothing other than what is commanded, and the wicked person can do nothing beyond what is permitted—though he cannot do with impunity what he has unjustly desired.

Accordingly, in all the things that human weakness dreads or fears, only iniquity is rightly condemned. The rest are either conditions belonging to natures or consequences deserved for faults.

A person becomes unjust when, for their own sake, they love things that ought to be sought for the sake of something else, and for the sake of something else they desire things that ought to be loved for their own sake. For, insofar as it lies within that person, this disturbs within them the natural order that the eternal law commands to be preserved.

A person becomes just when they do not seek to use things for any purpose other than that for which they were divinely instituted; when they enjoy God Himself for His own sake; and when they love themselves and their friend in God, for the sake of that same God. For the person who loves God’s love in a friend loves the friend for God’s sake.

Whether iniquity or justice is involved, neither would exist in our power unless it existed in the will. And if it were not in our power, no reward and no punishment would be just—something no one understands except one who is out of his mind.

Ignorance and weakness—by which a person either does not know what he ought to desire or cannot do everything he desires—arise from a hidden order of punishments and from those inscrutable judgments of God, with whom there is no iniquity (Rom. IX, 14).

The sin of Adam has been handed down to us through the faithful word of God; and because all die in Adam, and because through him sin entered this world, and through sin, death, it is truthfully written (ibid. V, 12–19). Because through this punishment the body is corrupted and weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts (Wis. IX, 15), this is most true and most familiar to us. And because only merciful grace delivers us from this just punishment, that too is certain.

For this reason the Apostle cries out with a groan: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24–25).

But the distribution made by God, who judges and shows mercy—why one person is treated this way and another that way—takes place for hidden reasons, though they are just. Nevertheless, we do not for that reason fail to know that all these things occur by the judgment or mercy of God, even though they are arranged according to hidden measures, numbers, and weights, by which all things are ordered by God, the Creator of all that exists naturally (Wis. XI, 21). He is not the author of sins, but He is their governor and orderer, so that things would not be sins unless they were contrary to nature, and yet are judged and ordered in such a way that they are not permitted to disturb or disfigure the nature of the universe, being assigned to the places and conditions proper to their merits.

Since these things are so, and since, through this secret judgment and movement of human wills, some are corrupted by the same prosperity while others use it temperately, and some are weakened by the same adversity while others are strengthened; and since human mortal life itself is a trial upon the earth (Job VII, 1)—what human being knows whom it benefits or harms to reign or serve, to be at leisure or to die in peace, and to command, fight, conquer, or be killed in war?

Nevertheless, this remains certain: whatever benefits a person benefits them only through divine favor, and whatever harms a person harms them only through divine judgment.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

Why, then, do we rush into rash criticisms—would that they were criticisms of human beings and not of God? Let the stewards of the Old Testament, who were also foretellers of the New Testament, have served God by killing sinners; and let the stewards of the New Testament, who were also interpreters of the Old Testament, have served Him by dying at the hands of sinners.

Both nevertheless served the one God, who, in different and appropriate periods, taught that temporal goods are both to be sought from Him and despised for His sake, and that temporal troubles can both be imposed by Him and ought to be endured for His sake.

What cruelty, then, did Moses command or commit when, zealously caring for the people entrusted to him and wishing them to be subject to the one true God [Note: [Col. 0452] The Corbie manuscript reads “and to the one true man of God.”], after he learned that their minds had slipped away to make and worship an idol and had prostituted themselves to demons, he punished some of them with the sword—those whom God Himself, whom they had offended, in His deep and secret judgment had wished to be struck down immediately [Note: [Col. 0452] Most manuscripts read “had wished punishment to be inflicted”; the particle *mox* (“immediately”) is omitted. The Corbie manuscript reads “had wished to be taken away.”]—and thereby both terrified them beneficially in the present and established discipline for the future?

Who would not recognize from his words, when he prayed for their sin and said, “If You forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of Your book” (Exod. XXXII), that he did what he did not through cruelty but through great love?

Anyone who compares that slaughter with this prayer in pious wisdom sees with complete clarity—sees how great an evil it is for the soul to commit fornication with demons through images, since the one who loves so greatly displays such fury.

In the same way the Apostle, not cruelly but lovingly, handed a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus (I Cor. V, 5). He handed others over as well, so that they might learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. I, 20).

The Manichaeans read apocryphal writings composed under the name of the Apostles by certain unknown makers of fables—writings that would have deserved to be received into the authority of the holy Church if the holy and learned men who were then living and able to examine such matters had recognized their authors as speaking the truth.

Yet in those writings they read that the Apostle Thomas, while he was a stranger and entirely unknown at a certain wedding feast, was struck on the face by a servant and invoked upon the man a continual and savage vengeance. For when the servant had gone out to the spring to bring water to the guests, a lion attacked and killed him; and the dog carried to the tables at which the Apostle himself was reclining the hand with which the man had struck the Apostle’s head with a light blow, in accordance with the Apostle’s own words, by which he had desired and invoked this.

What could appear more cruel than this? But because, unless I am mistaken, it is also written there that he sought forgiveness for the man in the future age, a greater benefit was thereby set against the deed: the Apostle’s dearness to God was commended to strangers through this fear, and the man’s eternal welfare was secured after this life, which would eventually end.

Whether that story is true or fabricated is of no concern to me now. Certainly, however, the Manichaeans—who accept as true and sincere those writings rejected by the ecclesiastical canon—are at least compelled by this to admit that the virtue of patience taught by the Lord when He says, “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the left also” (Matt. V, 39), can exist in the preparation of the heart even when it is not displayed through bodily gesture or verbal expression.

For when the Apostle was struck on the face, he apparently prayed that God would spare the injurious man in the future age, while in the present he did not leave the injury unpunished, rather than either offering the other side to the one striking him or urging him to strike again.

He kept inwardly the affection of love, while outwardly he sought an example of correction.

Whether this story is true or fabricated, why do they refuse to believe that the servant of God Moses, with such a disposition, struck down with the sword the makers and worshipers of the idol, when his words sufficiently show that he prayed for forgiveness for that sin in such a way that, if he did not obtain it, he wished to be blotted out of God’s book?

And what comparison is there between an unknown man struck on the face and the God who freed His people from Egyptian slavery, led them across by dividing the sea, covered the pursuing enemies with its waves, and was abandoned and despised when an idol was preferred to Him?

If we compare the punishments themselves, what comparison is there between being killed by the sword and being slaughtered and torn apart by wild beasts? Public judges serving the laws order those guilty of the greater crimes to be exposed to beasts rather than struck with the sword.

## CHAPTER LXXX

There remains, among Faustus’ slanderous and sacrilegious criticisms to which I now respond, the matter of what the Lord said when He spoke to the prophet Hosea: “Take for yourself a wife of fornication, and have children by a woman of fornication” (Hos. I, 2).

In this Scripture their impure hearts are so blinded that they do not understand even the clearest evangelical words of the Lord when He says to the Jews: “Prostitutes and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXI, 31).

What is contrary to the clemency of truth, what is hostile to the Christian faith, if a prostitute abandons fornication and is changed into a chaste marriage? And what is so incongruous and foreign to the faith of the Prophet as refusing to believe that all the sins of an immodest woman are forgiven when she is changed for the better?

Therefore, when the Prophet made the prostitute his wife, the woman was provided with the means of correcting her life, and the sacramental meaning of the figure—which we shall discuss shortly—was expressed.

But who does not see what more particularly offends the error of the Manichaeans in this deed? Namely, that prostitutes are accustomed to take care not to become pregnant. Thus they preferred the woman to remain a prostitute, so that she would not bind their god, rather than to become the wife of one man and bear children.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

What shall I say about Solomon, except that he is refuted more seriously by the faithful and holy testimony of Scripture itself than by Faustus’ wanton and frivolous insults?

Scripture spoke about him truthfully and faithfully: both about what good he had possessed earlier and about how, by doing evil, he abandoned the good in which he had first stood (III Kings III, XI; Ecclesiasticus XLVII). Faustus, however, with his eyes closed—or rather extinguished—did not proceed by the light that revealed the way; he rushed forward where malevolence drove him headlong.

By this very account the holy Books more strongly indicated to their religious readers and followers [Note: [Col. 0453] Some manuscripts read “and lovers.”] how chastely many holy men had several wives. Solomon, who did not have them in that manner but rather for lust than for the propagation of offspring, was disapproved and censured in these words, being called a “lover of women.” From there he fell and was plunged into the depths of idolatry, and the same truth exposed him without showing partiality to any person.

## CHAPTER LXXXII
Now, therefore, having already dealt with all the persons through whom Faustus thought the Scriptures of the Old Testament should be censured, and having given each its appropriate reply—by which either the men of God have been defended against the calumnies of heretics and carnal-minded people, or, when men have been censured, Scripture has nevertheless been shown to be praiseworthy and venerable—let us next examine, in order, what the very deeds of the persons whom Faustus mentioned in his accusations signify, and what prophecies they contain and what future things they foretell. We have already done this with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom God wished to be named in this way (Exod. 3:15), as though He were the God only of those men, although He is the God of the whole creation. He would surely not have granted them so great an honor without reason, unless He knew in them that sincere and preeminent charity which He alone could also know perfectly and supremely.

In those three Fathers, in a certain manner, He completed the great and wondrous mystery of His future people: they were begotten through free women not only into freedom, as through Sarah (Gen. 21:1–2), Rebekah (ibid. 25:21), Leah, and Rachel (ibid. 29 and 30), but also into slavery, as Esau was born through that same Rebekah, to whom it was said, “You shall be the servant of your brother” (ibid. 27:40); and through slave women they were begotten not only into slavery, as through Hagar (ibid. 16:15), but also into freedom, as through Bilhah and Zilpah (ibid. 30).

For likewise, in the people of God and through spiritual free persons [Note: [Col. 0454] Some manuscripts read, “and through spiritual men.” The better printed editions and other manuscripts read, “and through spiritual free persons,” so that it forms an antithesis to what is said later, “and through carnal slaves.”], people are born not only into praiseworthy freedom, as those to whom it is said, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:16), but also into damnable slavery, as through Philip, Simon (Acts 8:13); and through carnal slaves people are born not only into damnable slavery, namely, those who imitate them, but also into praiseworthy freedom, namely, those to whom it is said, “Whatever they tell you, do; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3).

Whoever wisely recognizes this great mystery in the people of God preserves the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace to the end, cleaving to some and bearing with others. We did this also concerning Lot, showing what Scripture relates as praiseworthy and blameworthy in him, and what it signifies should be understood from the whole event (Gen. 19).

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

Next we must consider the deed of Judah, who had intercourse with his daughter-in-law (ibid. 38), and what it signified concerning future things. But first something must be said, lest a person of limited understanding be offended that certain future things, not evil but good, are signified in the sacred Scriptures [Col. 0455] by certain evil deeds of human beings [Note: [Col. 0454] Thus read the manuscripts of Amerbach, Erasmus, and most others. Lovaniensis reads, “of faulty understanding.”].

For divine providence everywhere preserves the power of its goodness, so that, just as from the intercourse of adulterers a human being is formed and born, and from an evil human act there comes a good work of God—as we already said in the preceding discussion (above, chap. 48)—through the fertility of the seed and not through the shamefulness of the vice, so also in the prophetic Scriptures, which narrate not only the good deeds of human beings but also their evil deeds, because the narration itself is prophetic, something concerning future good things may be signified even through the evil deeds of human beings—not by the deed of the sinner, but by the act of the writer.

For when Judah, overcome by desire, went in to Tamar, he did not intend his lustful purpose to signify something that would contribute to human salvation. Nor did that Judas who betrayed the Lord intend that something should result from his deed that would contribute to the same human salvation. Yet if the Lord made so good a work from that Judas’s so evil deed that He redeemed us by the blood of His own passion, what wonder if His Prophet, of whom He Himself says, “For he wrote about me” (John 5:46), signified something good from this Judah’s evil deed, so that through his ministry he might instruct us?

The Prophet who narrated these deeds of human beings collected them under the arrangement and inspiration of the Holy Spirit; their insertion was not without reference to the foreshadowing of the things he intended to prophesy. For the purpose of signifying some good things, it makes no difference whether the deeds by which they are signified are good or evil. What difference does it make to me, when I wish to learn something by reading, whether I find black Ethiopians written in vermilion and white Gauls in ink? Yet if I saw such a thing not in writing but in a painting, I would certainly condemn it.

Thus, in the deeds of human beings that are proposed for imitation or avoidance, it makes a great difference whether they are good or evil. But in deeds written or spoken for the purpose of signifying something, it does not matter, with respect to the character of those who perform them, what praise or blame they deserve, provided only that they possess some necessary appropriateness for prefiguring the matter under discussion.

For just as, in the Gospel, Caiaphas’s words were evil insofar as they reflected his harmful and destructive intention—and, finally, insofar as the words themselves are considered in relation to the speaker’s will, since he was arranging for a just man to be unjustly killed—nevertheless, without his knowing it, they signified a great good when he said, “It is better that one man should die, and not that the whole nation perish.” And it was said concerning him, “He did not say this from himself; but, being high priest, he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the nation” (ibid. 11:50–51).

Thus Judah’s deed was evil according to his lust, but, without his knowing it, it signified a great good. He committed the evil from himself, but he did not signify the good from himself. What I have thought necessary to say by way of preface applies not only to Judah’s deed but also to any other evil deeds of human beings that may occur, through which the narrator prophetically signified something good.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

In Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, the people of the kingdom of the Jews are understood; kings from the tribe of Judah were joined to that people as husbands. Her name is rightly [Col. 0456] interpreted as “Bitterness,” for she gave the Lord a cup of gall (Matt. 27:34).

Two kinds of rulers who did not act rightly among the people are signified by Judah’s two sons: one kind consisted of those who caused harm, the other of those who were of no benefit. One of them was evil, or savage, before the Lord; the other spilled his seed upon the ground so that he would not give seed to make Tamar fertile.

There are no more than two kinds of useless people in the human race: one consists of those who cause harm; the other of those who refuse to be of service and who lose in this earthly life whatever good they possess, as though spilling it upon the ground. And because the one who causes harm is worse than the one who is of no benefit, the first is called the greater evil, while the other follows as the one who spilled his seed upon the ground.

The name of the elder, who was called Er, is interpreted as “Pellicius,” referring to the kinds of tunics in which the first human beings were clothed as punishment when they were expelled from paradise (Gen. 3:21). The name of the younger, who was called Onan, is interpreted as “Their sorrow.” Whose sorrow could this be, if not that of those who, possessing the means to be useful, benefit no one and lose that capacity upon the earth?

The greater evil is the taking of life, signified by “Pellicius,” than the failure to assist, signified by “Their sorrow.” Nevertheless, God is said to have killed both, by which it is symbolized that He removed the kingdom from such people.

The third son of Judah, because he was not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which kings began no longer to come from the tribe of Judah for the people of the Jews. He was indeed Judah’s son, but Tamar did not receive him as her husband, because the tribe of Judah still existed, but no one from it any longer ruled the people. Hence his name, that is, Shelah, is interpreted as “His dismissal.”

Holy and just men do not belong to this signification. Although they lived during that period, they belong to the New Testament, for which they were knowingly useful by prophesying; David was such a man.

When Judea had already begun to have no kings from the tribe of Judah, Herod the elder must not be counted among its kings as Tamar’s husband. He was a foreigner, and he was not joined to her by that sacramental bond of mystical anointing, as by a marital covenant. Rather, he ruled as an outsider, having received that power from the Romans and from Caesar.

The same is true of his sons, the tetrarchs, one of whom was called Herod after his father and who agreed with Pilate in the Lord’s passion (Luke 23:12). These foreigners were not counted as part of that mystical kingdom of the Jews, to such an extent that the Jews themselves publicly cried out, gnashing their teeth against Christ, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

Nor was this statement true except because of the universal domination of the Romans. Caesar, too, was not properly king of the Jews. But in order to deny Christ and flatter Caesar, they condemned themselves by making such a declaration.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

At that time, therefore, when the kingdom had already failed from the tribe of Judah, the true Savior, our Lord Christ, had to come—one who would not cause harm but would greatly benefit. For it had been prophesied:

> “The prince shall not fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he is [Col. 0457] the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10).

By this time, all the authority of the Jews, and the mystical anointing from which they were called “christs,” had also failed, according to the prophecy of Daniel. Then He came to whom it had been reserved, the expectation of the nations, and the Holy of Holies was anointed (Dan. 9:24–27) with the oil of gladness above His companions (Ps. 44:8).

He was born during the time of Herod the elder (Matt. 2:1), but suffered under the tetrarch Herod the younger [Note: [Col. 0457] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “the tetrarchy.”] (Luke 23:7, 46).

The figure of this coming Lord, who came to the sheep of the house of Israel that had perished (Matt. 15:24), was enacted by Judah himself when he went to shear his sheep at Timnah, which is interpreted as “Failing.” For the prince had already failed from Judah, as had all the authority and anointing of the Jews, so that He might come to whom it had been reserved.

He came with his Odollamite shepherd, whose name was Hira. “Odollamite” is interpreted as “Testimony in water.” The Lord plainly came with this testimony, possessing a testimony greater than John’s (John 5:36), yet He used this testimony in water on account of the weak sheep.

For Hira, the name of that shepherd, is interpreted as “The vision of my brother.” John surely saw his brother—his brother according to the seed of Abraham and according to the kinship of Mary, His mother, and Elizabeth, John’s mother. He also saw Him as his Lord and God, because, as John himself says, he received from His fullness (ibid. 1:16).

John truly saw Him, and therefore no one born of women arose greater than he (Matt. 11:11), because among all those who foretold Christ, John saw what many righteous people and prophets desired to see but did not see (ibid. 13:17). He greeted Him from the womb (Luke 1:44), recognized Him more perfectly through the dove, and therefore, like an Odollamite, truly bore testimony in water (ibid. 3:21–22).

The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to relieve them of burdensome loads—so that the teeth of the Churches praised in the Song of Songs might be like a flock of sheep that have been shorn (Song 4:2).

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

Now let Tamar change her clothing, for Tamar is also interpreted as “Changing.” Yet let the name “Bitterness” remain entirely in her—not the bitterness in which she offered gall to the Lord, but that in which Peter wept bitterly (Matt. 26:75).

For Judas in Latin means “Confession.” Let bitterness, therefore, be mixed with confession, so that true repentance may be prefigured. By this repentance the Church, established among all nations, is made fruitful. For it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in His name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:46–47).

The prostitute’s clothing itself also signifies confession of sins. Tamar already bears the type of the Church, called from the nations, sitting in this clothing at the gate of Enaim, or Enam, which is interpreted as “Fountains.” For she ran like a deer to the springs of water, in order to reach the seed of Abraham. There she was made pregnant by one who did not recognize her, because it was prophesied concerning her, “The people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17:45).

She secretly received a ring, [Col. 0458] a necklace, and a staff. By these are signified calling, adornment through justification, and exaltation through glorification:

> “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30).

But these things, as I said, are still hidden, where the conception of holy fruitfulness also takes place.

A promised kid is sent to her as though she were a prostitute—a kid signifying the reproach of sin—through the same Odollamite, as though he were rebuking her and saying, “Brood of vipers” (Matt. 3:7). But the reproach of sin did not find her, because the bitterness of confession had changed her.

Later, after the signs—the ring, the necklace, and the staff—had been made public [Note: [Col. 0458] Thus read certain manuscripts together with Amerbach and Erasmus. Lovaniensis reads, “after the public signs.”], she overcame the Jews who judged rashly. Judas himself already represented their person; even today they say that this is not the people of Christ and that we do not possess the seed of Abraham. But when the most certain proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification have been brought forth, they will undoubtedly be confounded and will confess that we have been justified more than they have.

I would examine and expound these matters more precisely, almost section by section and articulately, insofar as the Lord might assist my purpose, if concern for bringing this work to an end—which has already become longer than I wished—did not restrain me from such laborious diligence.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

I shall now touch upon David’s sin (2 Sam. 11) and what it signified prophetically, with as much brevity as I can. The very interpretations of the names sufficiently show what this deed also prefigured.

David is interpreted as “Strong of hand,” or “Desirable.” What is stronger than that Lion of the tribe of Judah, who conquered the world (Rev. 5:5)? And what is more desirable than the one of whom the prophet says, “The Desired One shall come to all nations” (Hag. 2:8)?

Bathsheba is interpreted as “Well of satiety,” or “Seventh well.” Whichever of these interpretations of her name we adopt for the point we intend to make, it fits sufficiently well. For in the Song of Songs the bride is the Church, which is called “a well of living water” (Song 4:15). To this well the name of the number seven is joined as a sign of the Holy Spirit, because of Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit came, sent from heaven (Acts 2:1–4).

The Scripture of Tobit also testifies that this same feast consists of weeks (Tob. 2, according to the Septuagint). To forty-nine, which is seven times seven, one is added, by which unity is commended. In this arithmetic lives that apostolic statement:

> “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

By the spiritual gift, that is, the gift of the number seven, the Church became a well of satiety, because in her there was made a spring of water leaping up into eternal life; whoever possesses it will never thirst (John 4:14, 13).

What else does Uriah, who had been her husband, signify by the interpretation of his name than the devil? All those whom the grace of God liberates [Col. 0459] were bound to him by a most evil marriage, so that the Church might be joined to her own Savior, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27).

For Uriah is interpreted as “My light is God.” “Hittite” [Note: [Col. 0459] Lovaniensis reads “Hethite.” The manuscripts have “Chettite,” as it is written in the Septuagint, or “Cethite,” as in Amerbach and Erasmus.] is interpreted as “Cut off”: either because he did not stand in the truth (John 8:44) but, through the merit of his pride, was cut off from the heavenly light that he had from God; or because, having fallen and lost his true powers, he nevertheless transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14), still daring to say, “My light is God.”

Thus this David did indeed sin grievously and wickedly. God reproved his crime through the prophet’s rebuke, and David himself washed it away through repentance. Nevertheless, that Desired One of all nations loved the Church, which was washing herself on the roof—that is, cleansing herself from the filth of the world and transcending and trampling upon the earthly house through spiritual contemplation. After beginning with her an initial acquaintance, He later killed the devil, who had been utterly separated from her, and joined her to Himself in an everlasting marriage.

Let us therefore hate the sin, but let us not extinguish the prophecy. Let us love that David as much as he ought to be loved—the one who mercifully freed us from the devil. Let us also love this David, who healed so great a wound of iniquity in himself through the humility of repentance.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

What shall I now say about Solomon, whom holy Scripture vehemently censures and condemns (1 Kings 11), and concerning whose repentance or God’s forgiveness toward him it mentions absolutely nothing?

I cannot at all see what good this lamentable downfall of his signifies, even allegorically—unless someone should say that the foreign women whose love inflamed him signify the chosen Churches from the nations. This interpretation might perhaps be understood without absurdity if, on Solomon’s account, they had abandoned their gods and worshiped his God. But since he offended his God on their account and worshiped their gods, we cannot infer any good from it.

Yet I do not think that it signifies nothing. Rather, it signifies evil, as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters. For in the person of this Solomon there appears both extraordinary excellence and extraordinary downfall.

What therefore existed in him at different times—first good, and later evil—is displayed in the Church during this present age at one and the same time. By his goodness, I think, the good members of the Church are signified; by his evil, the evil members—just as, in the unity of one threshing floor, the good are in the grain and the evil in the chaff; and, in the unity of one harvest, the good are in the wheat and the evil in the weeds (Matt. 3:12; 13:30).

If, on more careful examination of what has been written about him, something more persuasive should become clear either to me or to more learned and better interpreters, nevertheless I have not now dismissed the matter in such a way that it interrupts the chain of the argument as my purpose hastens toward other subjects.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

There is no need for me to explain what the command or deed concerning the prophet Hosea signifies, when the Lord said to Hosea, “Go, and take for yourself a wife of prostitution, and have children of prostitution,” [Col. 0460] since Scripture itself sufficiently shows why and for what reason this was said.

For it continues:

> “Because the land, by committing fornication, will commit fornication against the Lord. And he went and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived and bore him a son. And the Lord said to him: Call his name Jezreel, because in a little while I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Judah, and I will bring to an end and turn away the kingdom of the house of Israel. And it shall come to pass that on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.
>
> “And she conceived again and bore a daughter. And the Lord said to him: Call her name ‘Without mercy,’ because I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; yet I will have mercy on the house of Judah and will save them by the Lord their God. I will not save them by bow, sword, war, horses, or horsemen.
>
> “And she weaned the one who was called ‘Without mercy,’ and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to him: Call his name ‘Not my people,’ because you are not my people, and I will not be your God.
>
> “And the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they shall be called ‘Children of the living God.’ And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head, and they shall go up from the earth, because great is the day of Jezreel.
>
> “Say to your brothers, ‘My people,’ and to your sister, ‘She who has obtained mercy’” (Hos. 1:2–2:1).

Since the Lord Himself so clearly discloses through the same Scripture the figure represented by this command and deed, and since the apostolic writings testify that this prophecy was fulfilled in the preaching of the New Testament, who would dare say that the command and deed did not take place for the very reason for which He who gave the command explains in the sacred writings that He commanded it and that the Prophet carried it out?

For the Apostle Paul says:

> “In order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—us, whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the nations—as he says through Hosea: ‘I will call the one who was not my people, my people; and the one who was not beloved, beloved’; and ‘In the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, there they shall be called children of the living God’” (Rom. 9:23–26).

Paul thus shows that this was prophesied concerning the nations. Hence Peter, writing to the nations, although he does not name the Prophet, incorporates his prophecy into his own words, saying:

> “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, so that you may proclaim the mighty works of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light; once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Pet. 2:9–10).

From this it is evident that what was said through the Prophet—“The number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted”—and what is added immediately afterward—“In the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, they shall be called children of the living God”—was not said entirely concerning that Israel which is according to the flesh, but concerning the Israel of whom the Apostle says to the nations, “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:29).

Yet since many of the Jews also believed and will believe in that Israel [Note: [Col. 0460–0461] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “from that Judea.” The manuscripts read, “from that [Israel] of the Jews,” that is, from that Israel according to the flesh which is that of the Jews.]—for from them came the Apostles, and from them came the many thousands who joined the Apostles in Jerusalem (Acts 3:41; 4:4), and from them came the Churches concerning which he says to the Galatians, “I was unknown by face to the Churches of Judea that are in Christ” (Gal. 1:22)—and since he therefore interprets the Lord, who is called the cornerstone in the Psalms (Ps. 117:22), as having joined two walls in Himself, namely circumcision and uncircumcision, so that He might create the two in Himself into one new man, making peace and reconciling both in one body to God through the cross, killing hostility in Himself, and coming to preach peace to those far away and to those near—that is, to the nations who were far away and to the Jews who were near—for He is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2:11–22). It is therefore rightly said that this prophet, putting the children of Judah for the Jews and the children of Israel for the nations, declares:

> “And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head, and they shall go up from the earth.”

Whoever contradicts this prophecy, so clearly declared by the fulfillment of events, contradicts not only the prophetic writings but also the apostolic writings—not merely writings of any kind, but writings fulfilled by events and illuminated by the clearest light. Such a person contradicts it most shamelessly.

Perhaps, then, Judah’s deed required more careful attention, so that this prostitute, who signifies the Church gathered from the prostitution of Gentile superstitions, might be recognized in the clothing of that woman who was called Tamar. But here, since Scripture itself opens the matter and the harmonious writings of the Apostles illuminate it, why do we linger any longer instead of now considering what remains concerning God’s servant Moses, and what the very things Faustus objected to signify?

## CHAPTER XC

That Moses killed the Egyptian while defending his brother is readily understood by anyone: it signifies that the Lord Christ killed, while defending us, the devil who wrongs us in this pilgrimage.

But that he buried the man he had killed in the sand (Exod. 2:12) clearly signifies that the already dead presence of the devil lies hidden in those who have no firm foundation.

Hence the Lord builds the Church upon a rock. He compares those who hear His word and do it to a prudent man who builds his house upon a rock, so that it may not yield to temptations and collapse. But those who hear and do not act He compares to a foolish man building upon sand; when his house is tested, its ruin is great (Matt. 7:24–27).

## CHAPTER XCI

As for Moses’s stripping the Egyptians by the command of the Lord his God (Exod. 3:22; 11:2; 12:35–36), what this signifies—apart from the justice of the One who commanded it—I recall having set down, insofar as it occurred to me at the time, in certain books that I entitled *On Christian Doctrine* (Book 2, chap. 40).

The gold, silver, and clothing of the Egyptians signify certain branches of learning that can be acquired through useful study within the customs of the nations themselves.

But whether this is what it signifies, or whether it signifies that precious souls from the nations, like vessels of gold and silver, together with their bodies [Col. 0462]—which the clothing signifies—join themselves to the people of God so that together they may be liberated from this age as from Egypt; whether this or that, or something else, was represented here, it remains certain to those who devoutly read these Scriptures that those commands, deeds, and written accounts did not occur without reason or without a foreshadowing of future things.

## CHAPTER XCII

As for the wars fought through Moses, it would take too long to examine them all. It is enough, therefore, that concerning the war fought against Amalek (Exod. 17:8–16), I have already explained earlier in this same work, in which I am answering Faustus, as much as seemed sufficient for the matter undertaken, what prophecy it anticipated and what mystery it contained.

Now let us consider what prophetic significance there was in the event concerning which those hostile to these Scriptures, or those ignorant of all learning, commonly accuse Moses of cruelty. Faustus did not state this explicitly when he said that Moses both commanded and carried out many cruel deeds. But because I know what they are accustomed to proclaim most insistently and maliciously [Note: [Col. 0462] Thus read the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “what he is accustomed to proclaim.”], I mentioned this matter myself and defended it earlier, so that no Manichaean who might be corrected, nor any other ignorant or impious person, would think that there was any crime in that deed.

Now, however, we must inquire what prophetic significance there was in his ordering the execution, without distinguishing any relationship, of many of those who had fashioned an idol for themselves while he was absent (ibid. 32).

It is easy to understand the killing of those men as signifying the pursuit of such vices as led them to that same idolatry [Note: [Col. 0462] The manuscripts omit the word “pursuit.”]. The Psalm commands us to rage against such vices when it says, “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). The Apostle commands us to rage against such vices when he says:

> “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5).

## CHAPTER XCIII

But what does it mean that Moses first caused the calf itself to be burned in the fire, crushed into tiny pieces, scattered upon the water, and given to the people to drink? This calls for more intense attention in searching out its significance.

If he broke the tablets that he had received, written by the finger of God—that is, by the working of the Holy Spirit—because he judged the people unworthy to read them; and if, finally, he burned that calf so that it might be completely destroyed by them, crushed it, scattered it in water, and submerged it, why did he also give this water to the people to drink?

Who would not be stirred by this deed to seek and understand its prophetic significance?

Let the meaning now present itself to attentive minds: the body of the devil is represented in the calf, that is, human beings among all the nations, for whom the devil is the head—that is, the author—of these sacrileges.

It was golden because the rites of idolatry appear to have been instituted by wise people. Concerning them the Apostle says:

> “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged [Col. 0463] the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Rom. 1:21–23).

From this supposed wisdom came the golden calf, like the images that even the leading Egyptians and supposedly learned men were accustomed to worship.

The calf therefore signified the whole body—that is, the entire society—of the nations devoted to idolatry.

The Lord Christ burns this sacrilegious society with that fire of which He says in the Gospel, “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). Since no one can hide from its heat (Ps. 18:7), while the nations believe in Him, the devil’s form in them is dissolved by the fire of His power.

Then the whole body is crushed: that is, torn away from the evil fusion of its conspiracy, it is humbled by the word of truth. Once crushed, it is cast into water, so that the Israelites—that is, preachers of the Gospel—may transfer them from baptism into their own members, that is, into the Lord’s body.

To Peter, concerning these very nations, it was said, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). If it says, “Kill and eat,” why should it not also say, “Crush and drink”?

Thus, through the fire of zeal, the sharpness of the word, and the water of baptism, that calf was swallowed by those whom it had been trying to swallow.

## CHAPTER XCIV

If, then, these passages of Scripture also—passages over which heretics slander the same Scriptures—when carefully examined and, in a certain sense, questioned, respond that the more obscure they appear, the more wondrous are the treasures of mysteries hidden within them, how much more ought the blasphemous mouths of the impious to fall completely silent?

They are stopped by the clearest truth, against which they cannot find anything to mutter with strangled breath. Wretched people that they are, they would rather have their throats closed by its revelation than have their hearts filled by its sweetness.

All these things, therefore, proclaim Christ: that Head who has already ascended into heaven, and this body of His that labors on earth until the end. The whole purpose of those who wrote the truly sacred Scriptures gave birth to these things.

Nothing should be believed to have been narrated in the sequence of the prophetic books that does not signify something concerning future things—except those matters that have been inserted so that, through them, the things that foretell that King and His people, whether through proper or figurative expressions or events, might in some way be joined together.

For just as in lyres and similar musical instruments, not everything that is touched produces a melodious sound, but only the strings, while the other parts have been fashioned in the whole body of the lyre so that the strings might have something to which they could be fastened and from which and toward which they could be stretched, and which the musician could tune and strike for the sweetness of the song, so in these prophetic narratives, which are selected from human deeds by the prophetic Spirit, some things already sound forth by signifying future events. If they signify nothing of that kind, they are inserted so that there may be something by which those significant elements, like sounding strings, can be connected.

## CHAPTER XCV

If heretics do not wish to accept these allegorical narratives of events as we explain them, or even insist that they signify nothing except what they literally express, there is no need to struggle with people who say, “What you say tastes good to your palate [Col. 0464], but not to mine.”

Let it nevertheless be believed or understood that the things divinely commanded either form morals and piety, or signify something figuratively, or preferably both rather than neither. Let even those things that are understood to have been said or done figuratively be referred to the same good morals and piety.

Accordingly, even if the Manichaeans or anyone else finds our understanding, reasoning, or interpretation of these figures drawn from historical events displeasing, it should be sufficient that our fathers—of whom God bears witness to the goodness of their life and their obedience to His commandments—are defended by that rule of truth which can displease none but crooked and distorted hearts.

It should also be sufficient that the Scripture to which the perversity of that error is hostile remains itself blameless and venerable in all the deeds of human beings that it either praised, censured, or merely set before us in its narrative for our judgment.

## CHAPTER XCVI
What more useful and salutary counsel could have been provided for pious readers or hearers of those sacred Scriptures than that they should be presented not only with admirable people to imitate and blameworthy people to avoid, but also with certain departures of good people and falls into evil—whether they are corrected again and return to the path, or remain unremedied—and, conversely, with certain changes in evil people and advances toward goodness—whether they will persevere or relapse again into their former condition? Thus the righteous may not be lifted up by security into pride, nor the wicked hardened by despair against the remedy. But those human actions which belong neither to imitation nor to avoidance, and which nevertheless occur in Holy Scripture, have either been included as links in the narrative, by which the circumstances lead to matters that are necessary, or, precisely because they seem superfluous, sufficiently warn us that we ought to seek in them the oracle of some mystical signification. For we are not speaking of those books in which the divine authority is attested by the most faithful and splendid light of truth—books in which not a few, or only few and not many, things foretold in the clearest prophetic spirit have now also been fulfilled in the events themselves. Anyone who thinks that such books speak superfluously or foolishly is utterly senseless: for he sees that every kind of human being and every kind of human intellect is subjected to them, and he reads and recognizes that this very fact was foretold by them and brought to completion.

## CHAPTER XCVII

If, then, someone, while reading about David’s deed—of which he repented when the Lord reproved and threatened him—should derive from it an incentive to sin, is the fault to be attributed to that Scripture? Or should he not rather be condemned all the more severely, since he wished to misuse for his own wounding or destruction something that was written for healing and deliverance? Because people who have fallen into sin either neglect the medicine of repentance through pride, or perish utterly through distrust of receiving salvation and obtaining forgiveness, the example of so great a man has been set before them so that the sick may be healed, not so that the healthy may be wounded. Nor is it a fault of medicine if either the insane kill themselves or the malicious kill others with surgical instruments.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

Yet these fathers of ours—the Patriarchs and Prophets—to whom that Scripture bears so distinguished a testimony of holiness and piety, Scripture which no one denies to have been divinely administered for the salvation of the human race unless he is ignorant of it or has lost every capacity for rational judgment—even if they had been lustful and cruel, as the error, or rather madness, of the Manichaeans accuses them of being, would they not even then be shown to be better not only than their Elect, but also than their very god?

Is it better for a man to roll about with a concubine than to be the utterly pure light and, by mingling with darkness, become defiled? Look: a man, for the sake of greed and his belly, falsely claimed that his wife was his sister and sold her to the embraces of others. How much worse and more execrable is the one who pretended that his own nature was adapted to the lust of those desiring it, and subjected it freely to be polluted and corrupted by them?

Again, would one who knowingly had intercourse with his daughters not perpetrate less evil than one who mingles his own members with the lusts of every such and even worse disgrace? For what such thing is committed by the unclean and depraved in which your god, Manichaeans, is not polluted by every kind of disgrace?

Finally, if Jacob truly, as Faustus says, wandered among four wives in foul desire like a goat, seeking no care for offspring but only wanton pleasure, how much less wretched would he be than your god, who not only endured all that disgrace of lust in Jacob and his four wives, being incorporated into all their bodies and movements, but also endures all that generative movement and heat in the very goat whom he sordidly compared to that man: being everywhere mixed in a shameful condition, inflamed in the male goat, sown in the female goat, and generated in the kid?

Accordingly, even if Judah had been not merely a fornicator but also knowingly a wicked incestuous violator of his daughter-in-law, your god would likewise cling to, be soiled by, and burn in the lust of that incest. David, however, repented of his iniquity: he had loved another man’s wife and ordered her husband to be killed. But when will your god repent that, having been loved by the male and female rulers of the dark realm, he surrendered his members to their lust—not the husband whose wife he had loved, but his own sons in the members of the demons by whom he himself had been loved, he killed?

But even if David had not repented and had not recovered the health of righteousness through such medicine, he would still have proved better than this god of the Manichaeans. Let us suppose that this god, by one single deed—and by however many similar deeds one man might commit—had done only that much; whereas he is shown to be disgraced and polluted by the mingling of his members in all the similar deeds of all people.

Faustus also accuses the prophet Hosea. If Hosea, captivated by shameful desire, had loved and married a prostitute, you certainly proclaim that the souls of both—the wanton lover and the obscene prostitute—are parts, members, and the very nature of your god. That prostitute, then—why should I evade the word instead of speaking plainly?—that prostitute would be your god. For you cannot say that, while his nature remained holy and undefiled, he entered into that prostitute’s body without being bound to it, merely presenting himself to it. You admit instead that these members of your god are most polluted and therefore require extensive purification. That prostitute, then, whom you dare to accuse the man of God, would be your god, even if she had not been changed into a chaste marriage; or, if you do not wish to say that, you certainly do not deny that the soul of that prostitute was a particle—however small—of your god.

She, therefore, would already be better than your god, since she would herself be only one prostitute, whereas he, by the condition of that commingling of his, is prostituted throughout the entire race of darkness in all prostitutes; indeed, he rolls about, is dissolved, and is bound in all males and females who fornicate and corrupt themselves in manifold ways, only to be rolled about, dissolved, and bound again in their offspring, until at last the most polluted part of your god is brought to the final globe like an unexpiable prostitute.

These, then, are the evils, these the disgraces, these the dishonors that your god could not remove from his members; compelled by the necessity imposed by the monstrous enemy, he arrived at such things. For he was unable to destroy the injurious and violent enemy while preserving his own citizens or members.

How much better, therefore, is the one who, after killing an Egyptian, defended his brother unharmed—this is the man whom Faustus accuses with astonishing frivolity, while in his still more astonishing blindness he does not consider his own god? How much better would he have been to take vessels of gold and silver from the Egyptian people than to have his members plundered by the nation of darkness?

And yet, although he himself had waged such a wretched war, his worshippers charge the servant of our God with having waged wars in which he always triumphed victoriously over his enemies with all his people. During Moses’ warfare, no male or female captives could be led away from the people of Israel—something your god would certainly have done if he had been able. This, then, is not an accusation of the wicked but envy of the more fortunate.

And what cruelty was Moses guilty of when he punished with the sword the people who had grievously sinned against God? Yet he entreated forgiveness for that sin, offering himself even to divine vengeance on their behalf. But if he had done this not mercifully but cruelly, he would still have been better than your god. For if any innocent and obedient person of his own had been sent to break through an enemy line and had been captured, he would never, after winning, have condemned that person. Yet this is what that god will do to his own part, which he will fasten upon the globe, because it obeyed his command and, for the salvation of his kingdom, advanced into the enemy lines with its own death as the price.

“But in this succession of ages,” he says, “after it had been mixed and incorporated with evils, it did not obey the commands.” Let us ask why. If it acted by its own will, then there is true guilt and a just punishment. But if the will is already guilty, no nature opposed to sin exists; and thus the whole falsehood of the Manichaeans is convicted and overthrown. If, however, it was overcome by the enemy to whom it had been sent, defeated by an alien evil that it had been unable to resist, then the punishment is unjust and the cruelty great.

But the necessity of God is brought forward as an excuse. Let those who refuse to worship God worship such a god. To be sure, what must be admitted is that even his worshippers themselves, although they are wicked because they worship such a god, are still better than he is, because at least they exist; whereas he is nothing except a fiction of falsehood and an imagining of vanity.

But let us now examine the remaining ingenious ravings of Faustus.

# BOOK TWENTY-THREE

[Column 0467]

## CHAPTER I

Faustus said: Once, while I was engaged in discussion, someone from the large crowd replied to me: “Do you accept Jesus born of Mary?” I answered him: “Which Jesus do you mean? For there were several Jesuses among the Hebrews: one was the son of Nave, the disciple of Moses (Exodus 33:11; Sirach 46:1); another was the son of Josedech, the high priest (Haggai 1:1); another was called the son of David (Romans 1:1–3); and another was the Son of God (Mark 1:1). Which of these, then, are you asking me whether I accept as born of Mary?”

“Certainly,” he said, “the Son of God.”

I replied: “On what authority, and under the instruction of what teacher, am I to accept this?”

“Matthew,” he said.

I asked again: “What, then, did Matthew write?”

He answered: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham, and so forth” (Matthew 1:1).

Then I said: “I had supposed that you were going to say, ‘The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, Son of God,’ and I had prepared myself to object. But since you have now faithfully remembered the heading, you need only be reminded to consider what you recited. For Matthew does not here admit that he undertook to write the generation of the Son of God, but of the son of David.”

## CHAPTER II

For the moment, then, let me believe this man when he says it: the one born of Mary will be, for me, the son of David. As yet, throughout this entire account of the generation, no mention is made of the Son of God, namely until the baptism; and you bring a false charge against the writer, as though he had enclosed the Son of God in a woman’s womb.

But here, as it seems, he cries out and by the very title of his work completely absolves himself from this sacrilege, declaring that he wrote of one descended from that stock as the son of David, not as the Son of God. For if you consider the mind and purpose of this writer, he does not so much wish us to understand the Jesus who is the Son of God as having been born from the virgin Mary, as having been made at some point through baptism beside the waters of the Jordan. There, he says, the one whom David designated as his son at the beginning was baptized by John and was at some point made the Son of God (the same, 3:16–17), only after, according to Luke’s testimony, nearly thirty years, when a voice was also heard saying to him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Luke 3:23, 22).

You see, therefore, that what, as this man understands it, was born of Mary thirty years earlier is not itself the Son of God, but what was afterward made at the Jordan through baptism—that is, a new human being, just as in us when, having been converted to God from the error of paganism, we believe. Yet I do not know whether this agrees sufficiently with the faith that you call catholic. For the moment, however, this is what Matthew seems to say, if these words are indeed his.

For nowhere in the accounts of Mary’s labor is the statement found: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” or, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” It occurs at his purification beside the Jordan. If you too believe as it is written, you will indeed be a follower of Matthew; for this is how I must put it. But you will certainly not be a catholic.

For we know the catholic faith, which is as far removed from this profession of Matthew as it is from the truth. Indeed, if your creed is such that you believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was born of the virgin Mary, then it is your position to receive the Son of God from Mary; Matthew’s, from the Jordan; ours, from God. Accordingly, Matthew, if these teachings are certainly his, is as contrary to you in this profession as he is to us—except that he has proved somewhat more prudent than you, in that he attributed the origin from the female sex to the son of David rather than to the Son of God.

Therefore you must confess one of two things: either this is not Matthew, who seems to assert these claims, or you do not hold the apostolic faith.

## CHAPTER III

Although no one at all can dislodge us from believing that the Son of God is received from God, nevertheless, to concede a great deal to imprudence and to force us even to believe falsehoods, Jesus will have been made the Son of God for us from the Jordan rather than born from a woman’s womb.

Yet even the one whom Mary bore—if there was such a person—could not rightly be called the son of David unless it is established that he was conceived from the father Joseph. Since you deny this, you must also admit that he is not even the son of David. For the genealogy from Abraham to David, and from David to Joseph, is traced through all the Hebrew fathers. Since Jesus, as we read, was not conceived in this way, he will not be the son of David; and he is utterly insane who, intending to say that one born of Mary without intercourse with Joseph was born, nevertheless placed him at the beginning as the son of David.

Since not even the one generated from Mary can rightly be called David’s son because he was not born from Joseph, how much more is this true of the Son of God?

## CHAPTER IV

Moreover, the virgin’s own origin is not shown to have been from that tribe from which David is known to have come—I mean Judah, from whom the Jewish kings descended—but from the tribe of Levi, from which the priests came. This is clear because she had as her father a certain priest named Joachim, yet no mention of him is found anywhere in this genealogy.

How, then, can Mary be said to belong to this lineage of David, when you see that she has neither a father nor a husband in it? Accordingly, neither will anyone born from her be the son of David, unless you attach this mother of his to Joseph in such a way that she is proved either to have been his daughter or his wife.

## CHAPTER V

Augustine answered: The catholic and likewise apostolic faith is that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is both the Son of God according to divinity and the son of David according to the flesh. We prove this from the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures in such a way that no one can contradict our proofs except one who contradicts those very Scriptures—not as this Faustus proposed to himself: that someone, I know not whom, had spoken a few words, while afterward he offered no testimony against the craftiness of that deceitful Faustus.

When I have done so, nothing will remain for him to answer except the device by which he tries openly to mock and evade the force of the clearest truth in the holy Scriptures: namely, to reply that those false statements were inserted into the divine books. I have already refuted this madness, this frenzied presumption and audacity, earlier in this work, to the extent that seemed sufficient; nor is it necessary to repeat the same arguments, so that we may also give some thought to the proper length of our discourse.

What need, then, is there to search for and gather testimonies scattered throughout all the Scriptures by which we may prove against him, in books of the greatest divine authority, that the same person is always called the only-begotten Son of God, God with God, who is also called the son of David because he received the form of a servant from the virgin Mary, the wife of Joseph?

For the present, since he chose to argue about Matthew, and since the whole book of Matthew cannot be inserted into this discussion by me, let whoever wishes read it and observe how Matthew carries the one whom he says is the son of David when he is about to enumerate his parents all the way through to the Passion and Resurrection. Let him observe that Matthew speaks of no other than this same person as conceived and born of the virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit.

To this he adds the testimony of the prophet: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). He likewise says that after being baptized by John, the same person heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17)—the one of whom it had already been said from the virgin’s birth, “God with us.”

Unless perhaps Faustus thinks that it is less to be called God than to be called the Son of God. For from this he has tried to infer that Matthew did not think that he became the Son of God until baptism, because there a voice from heaven said, “This is my Son,” although the same evangelist had already introduced the divine testimony from the prophet, where the virgin’s child himself was called “God with us.”

## CHAPTER VI

We ought to look upon and take note of this wretched, raving chatterer Faustus, who never misses an opportunity to cast clouds of falsehood over his empty talk, even by means of testimonies from the Scriptures. Thus he said of Abraham that he had not believed God when God promised him a son from Sarah, because he had intercourse with the slave woman, although Scripture testifies that the birth of Sarah’s child had not yet been promised to him (Genesis 16:4; 17:17).

Or he says that Abraham falsely called his wife his sister, although he has nowhere read the lineage of Sarah in those writings on which faith must be based in this matter (the same, 12:13; 20:2, 12). And he says of Abraham’s son Isaac that he too falsely called Rebekah his sister, although her lineage is plainly written there (the same, 26:7; 24).

And he says of Jacob that there was a daily contest among his four wives as to which of them would seize him first for intercourse when he came from the fields—something which he is demonstrably nowhere to have read there.

Look at the sort of man who boasts that he hates lying writers of the divine books, yet dares to lie about the Gospel, known to everyone for the height of its authority, in such a way that he wants it to be thought that not Matthew—lest he be constrained by the weight of the apostolic name—but some other person, I know not whom, writing under Matthew’s name, composed what he does not wish to believe about Christ and attempts to refute with that slanderous cunning.

[Note: Some editions, along with numerous manuscripts, read “from the known Gospel” rather than “from the Gospel known to everyone for the height of its authority.” Among those same manuscripts, some read: “from the Gospel, known to everyone for so great a height of authority.”]

## CHAPTER VII

Thus a voice from heaven was spoken over the water of the Jordan: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” just as it was spoken on the mountain as well (Matthew 17:5). The fact that the same voice also sounded from heaven there does not mean that he was not previously the Son of God. For it was he who, while existing in the form of God and not considering equality with God something to be seized, received from the virgin’s womb the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7, 6).

Finally, the apostle Paul himself says most clearly elsewhere: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law” (Galatians 4:4), calling her a woman—*mulier*—in accordance with the Hebrew manner of speaking, by which a female is so designated.

He, therefore, is the Son of God who is also the Lord of David according to divinity; and he is the same person who is the son of David, from the seed of David according to the flesh. If it were not beneficial for us to believe this, that same apostle would not so earnestly commend it to Timothy, saying: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (2 Timothy 2:8).

Against this Gospel, he carefully warned the faithful, whoever should announce another, “let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8–9).

## CHAPTER VIII

What, then, should now trouble a follower of the holy Gospel—that Christ, born of a virgin without intercourse with Joseph, is nevertheless called the son of David—when the evangelist Matthew traces the sequence of generations not to Mary but to Joseph?

First, because Joseph was her husband, his person ought rather to be honored on account of the male sex.
