For the fact that he did not have intercourse with her does not mean that he was not her husband, since Matthew himself reports that Mary was called his wife by the angel, while also reporting that she had conceived not through intercourse with him but from the Holy Spirit.

But if it was not the apostle Matthew who wrote these true things, and if someone else wrote them falsely under his name, as the Manichaeans suppose, would that person have contradicted himself in matters so clear and so closely connected, saying that the one born of the virgin Mary without intercourse with any man was the son of David, and then, while enumerating his parents step by step, carrying the genealogy to the very person whom he himself had said was not joined to Mary?

For if one person were to enumerate Christ’s ancestors from David to Joseph, calling him the son of David, while another said that he was born of the virgin Mary without intercourse with any man and did not call him the son of David, even then we should not immediately suppose that they had spoken contradictions against one another, so that either both or one of them would be convicted of falsehood. We ought to consider that it could have happened that both spoke the truth: Joseph could be called Mary’s husband because he had her as his wife in continence—not through intercourse but through affection, not through bodily union but through the union of souls, which is more precious.

For this reason, the husband of the virgin mother of Christ ought not to have been separated from the series of Christ’s ancestors; and Mary herself could have drawn a line of blood from some branch of David, so that Christ’s flesh, although produced from a virgin, could not be without the seed of David.

But when one and the same narrator says both things and commends both the husband of Mary, Joseph, and Christ’s virgin mother, both Christ as descended from the seed of David and Joseph in the series of Christ’s ancestors from David, what remains for someone to believe who wishes to believe the divine Gospel rather than the fables of heretics? He must believe that Mary was not foreign to David’s lineage; that she was not called Joseph’s wife without reason, on account of the order proper to the male sex and the covenant of their souls, even though he was not joined to her in the flesh; and that Joseph, rather, because of the dignity of the male sex, ought not to have been separated from that genealogical sequence, lest by this very separation he appear to have been separated from the woman to whom he was joined by the affection of his mind.

This was also so that faithful Christians would not consider the bodily union of spouses so essential to marriage that they would not believe people to be spouses without it. Rather, they were to learn that faithful marriages adhere much more intimately to the members of Christ to the extent that they are able to imitate Christ’s parents.

[Note: Lovianus reads “who prefers,” while other printed editions and manuscripts read “who wishes,” as above. Augustine uses this wording repeatedly.]

## CHAPTER IX

We therefore believe that Mary too belonged to David’s kinship, because we believe those Scriptures which say both that Christ is from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3; 2 Timothy 2:8) and that his mother Mary was a virgin, not having intercourse with a man (Matthew 1:18; Luke 1:27).

Whoever therefore says that Mary did not belong to David’s blood relationship is plainly resisting the outstanding authority of these Scriptures. Let him prove that she did not belong to David’s seed, and let him demonstrate this not from writings of just any kind, but from ecclesiastical, canonical, catholic writings.

For other writings have no authoritative weight among us in these matters. These are the writings that the Church, spread throughout the whole world, receives and holds—and by which the Church itself was prophesied, just as it was promised and, in the same way, granted.

Accordingly, what Faustus claimed about Mary’s ancestry—that her father was a certain priest named Joachim from the tribe of Levi—does not bind me, because it is not canonical. But even if I believed it, I would rather say that Joachim himself had in some way belonged to David’s bloodline, and in some way had been adopted from the tribe of Judah into the tribe of Levi—whether he himself, one of his ancestors, or certainly someone born in the tribe of Levi who nevertheless derived some blood relationship from David’s stock.

For Faustus himself admits that it could have happened that Mary was from the tribe of Levi, although it is established that she was given in marriage to a man who was from David’s stock, that is, from the tribe of Judah. He also says that Christ could be understood as the son of David if Mary had been Joseph’s daughter.

[Note: The words “if Mary had been Joseph’s daughter” are absent from the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus and from some manuscripts.]

Accordingly, if Joseph’s daughter had married into the tribe of Levi, it would not be absurd to call anyone born from her in the tribe of Levi also the son of David. Thus, if the mother of that Joachim whom Faustus mentions as Mary’s father had married into the tribe of Levi from the tribe of Judah and from David’s lineage, then Joachim, Mary, and Mary’s son could also truthfully be said to be from David’s seed.

If I were constrained by the authority of that apocryphal writing in which Joachim is read to be Mary’s father, I would therefore believe this, or something similar, rather than that the Gospel lied—the Gospel in which it is written both that Jesus Christ, our Savior, the Son of God, is from the seed of David according to the flesh, and that he was brought forth through the virgin Mary.

This is sufficient for us: the Scriptures that say these things, and in which we believe, cannot be convicted of any falsehood by their enemies.

## CHAPTER X

Let him not reply to me in turn: “Although I do not show that Mary was not of David’s kinship, you show that she was.” I do show it, and with an entirely clear and powerful proof: Scripture, whose authority is thoroughly confirmed, says both that Christ is from the seed of David and that his mother Mary was a virgin without intercourse with any man.

How exceedingly modest a detester of some supposed disgrace Faustus seemed to himself when he said: “You bring a false charge against the writer, as though he had enclosed the Son of God in a woman’s womb!”

The catholic faith, which believes that Christ the Son of God was born according to the flesh from a virgin, certainly does not enclose that same Son of God in a woman’s womb as though he were not outside it, as though he had abandoned the governance of heaven and earth, or as though he had withdrawn from the Father.

But you, Manichaeans, with that heart by which you can think only of bodily phantoms, do not understand at all how the Word, Power, and Wisdom of God, while remaining in himself and with the Father and ruling the entire creation, “reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things well” (Wisdom 8:1).

By the marvelous and ineffable ease of this ordering, he prepared a mother for himself on earth, and, in order to free his servants from slavery to corruption, received in her the form of a servant—that is, a mortal body. Having received it, he displayed it; having displayed it and been brought low by death, he raised it up through the Resurrection.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “raised it up again.”]

And, like a temple that had been destroyed, rebuilt it again.

Yet you, who fear to believe these things as though they were sacrilegious, enclose the members of your god not in a virgin’s womb but in the wombs of all carnal females, from elephants to flies.

Or does the true Christ seem inferior to you for this reason: that we say the Word became flesh in a virginal womb, while remaining inviolably in his own nature without any alteration of himself and joining a human being to himself as a temple? And is your god dear to you for this reason: that he is bound and polluted by so many bonds of flesh in that part which is also to be fixed upon the globe, and that he either begs for aid without cause or, being utterly overwhelmed, is not even permitted to beg?

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

[Column 0473]

## CHAPTER I

Faustus said: Why do you deny so completely that a human being is made by God? We certainly do not altogether deny that a human being is made by God; but we ask who is made, when he is made, and how he is made.

For according to the Apostle there are two human beings. One he sometimes calls outward, but more often earthly, and at times also old; the other he calls inward, heavenly, and new (Romans 6 and 7; 1 Corinthians 15; 2 Corinthians 4; Ephesians 3 and 4; Colossians 3). We therefore ask which of these is made by God.

For there are also two times of our birth: one is that by which nature, having entangled us in bodily bonds, brought us forth into this light; the other is when Truth, after we have been converted from error, regenerates us to itself and initiates us into the faith.

Signifying this time of second birth in the Gospel, Jesus says: “Unless someone has been born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” When Nicodemus, understanding this inadequately, hesitated and asked how it could happen—for a grown man could not enter his mother’s womb and be born again—Jesus answered him: “Unless someone has been born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” And he continues: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the spirit is spirit” (John 3:3–6).

Therefore, if birth is not only that by which we are generated in the body but also that other birth by which we are reborn in the spirit, it is no less important to ask in which of these births God makes us.

The manner of birth is also twofold. One is proper to fury and intemperance, by which we are shamefully and lustfully begotten by our parents. The other belongs to honor and holiness, by which, in Christ Jesus through the Holy Spirit, we have been trained under good teachings toward faith.

[Note: The Amerbach edition and all our manuscripts read “we have become disciples.”]

For this reason every religion, and especially the Christian religion, calls those who are inexperienced in the sacrament “infants.” Signifying this also, the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

The question, therefore, is no longer whether God makes a human being, but when, whom, and how he makes him. For if it is when we are fashioned in the womb—as is generally pleasing to pagans, Jews, and yourselves—that God forms us in his image, then he makes us old and creates us through fury and lust; I do not know whether that is compatible with his divinity.

But if we are formed by God when we believe and are converted to a better state of life—as is generally pleasing to Christ, his Apostles, and us—then God makes us new, and he does so honorably and purely. What could be more consonant or more appropriate to his holy and venerable majesty?

If you do not reject Paul’s authority, we will show you from Paul himself whom, when, and how God makes a human being. He says to the Ephesians: “You must put away, with respect to your former way of life, the old human being, who is corrupted through the desires of error; but be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who has been created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:22–24).

[Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “through desires”; Lovianus reads “according to desires.”]

You see, then, when a human being is created in the image of God. Here you also see another human being, another birth, and another manner of being born. For when he says, “Put off and put on,” he clearly signifies the time of belief. But when he testifies that the new human being is created by God, he then indicates that the old human being is neither from God nor formed according to him.

And when he continues, saying that the new human being is made in holiness, justice, and truth, he then designates and demonstrates the other manner of birth that I said is entirely unlike this one, which sowed our bodies through the frenzied embraces of our parents. He also shows that this former birth is not from God, when he demonstrates that only the new human being is from God.

Again, in the Letter to the Colossians he says the same thing: “Strip off the old human being with his practices, and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him in you.”

[Note: Some manuscripts here and below read “into the knowledge of God” rather than “in the knowledge of God.”]

From this, then, he not only shows that the new human being is the one whom God makes, but also teaches when and by what means he is formed: namely, “in the knowledge of God,” by which the time of belief is signified.

And further, he says, “according to the image of him who created him,” so that from this it becomes clear that the old human being is neither the image of God nor formed by him.

For the statement that follows also—“where there is neither male nor female, Jew nor Greek, barbarian nor Scythian” (Colossians 3:9–11)—shows more and more clearly that the birth which made us males and females, Greeks and Jews, Scythians and barbarians is not the birth in which God acts when he forms a human being. Rather, it is that birth which strips us of every diversity of nation, sex, and condition and makes us one, after the likeness of the one who is one, namely Christ.

As the same Apostle says again: “All who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither male nor female; there is neither slave nor free; but all are one in Christ” (Galatians 3:27–28).

Therefore a human being is made by God when he becomes one out of many, not when he is divided from one into many. Our first birth, the bodily one, divided us; the second, intelligible and divine, unites us. For this reason we have rightly attributed the former to bodily nature and assigned the latter to the majesty above.

Accordingly, the same Apostle says again to the Corinthians: “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4:15). And to the Galatians, speaking of himself: “When it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb to reveal his Son in me so that I might announce him among the nations, immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood” (Galatians 1:15–16).

You see, therefore, that everywhere he insists that in this second birth of ours—namely, the spiritual one—we are formed by God, not in that first birth, obscene and disgraceful, which conceived, formed, and brought us forth in our mother’s womb no more nobly or cleanly than the other animals.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “of spiritual things only.”]

If you wish to take note of this matter, you will find that in this respect we differ from you less in profession than in interpretation. For you may be pleased to attribute the old, outward, and earthly human being to God as having been formed by him; whereas we, on the contrary, assign this to the heavenly, inward, and new human being.

We do not do so rashly or presumptuously, but by learning from Christ and from his Apostles, who are shown to have been the first to teach these same things in the world.

## CHAPTER II
AUGUSTINE replied: The apostle Paul indeed wants the inner person to be understood as being in the spirit of the mind [Note: [Col. 0475] Ambrose, Erasmus, and the manuscripts: “through the spirit of the mind.”], and the outer person as being in the body and in this mortal life. Yet nowhere in his Letters is it read that he called these two together two persons; rather, he called them one person, whom God made wholly—that is, both what is inward and what is outward. But he made that person in his own image only according to what is inward: not merely incorporeal, but also rational, something not present in animals.

Thus he did not make one person in his image and another not in his image. Rather, because these two—the inner and the outer—together constitute one person, he made this one person in his image, not according to what he possesses as body and bodily life, but according to what he possesses as a rational mind, by which he may know God and, through the same excellence of reason, be set above all irrational creatures.

But Faustus concedes that the inner person is made by God: “when he is renewed,” he says, “in the knowledge of God, according to the image of the one who created him.” I plainly recognize this as the apostolic teaching (Col. III, 10). Why, then, does he not acknowledge the other statement: “God placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed” (I Cor. XII, 18)? Behold, the same apostle also proclaims God to be the maker of the outer person. Why does Faustus select from this what he thinks serves his case, while keeping silent about or rejecting what cuts away the Manichaean fables?

Again, when that same Paul was discussing the earthly and heavenly person, distinguishing between the mortal and the immortal, between what we are in Adam and what we shall be in Christ, he brought forward, from the very Law, from the very book, and from the very passage, testimony concerning the earthly—that is, the animal—body, where it is written that God also made the earthly person. For when he was dealing with how the dead rise and with what kind of body they will come, after giving the example of seeds of grain—that bare grains are sown, and that God gives them a body as he wills, to each seed its own body—he nonetheless proceeded to overturn the Manichaean error. The Manichaeans say that grains, herbs, and all roots and shrubs are created by the race of darkness, not by God; and they believe that God is rather bound within those forms and kinds of things than that he performs any of these works.

After speaking against the sacrilegious folly of Manichaeus even in these matters, Paul came to the differences among fleshly bodies: “Not every flesh is the same flesh.” From there he proceeded to heavenly and earthly bodies, and then to the transformation of our body by which it may become spiritual and heavenly: “It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.” Then, wishing to show the origin of the animal body, he said: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual body; as it is written: ‘The first man Adam was made into a living soul’” (I Cor. XV, 35–45).

This is written in Genesis (Gen. II, 7), where it is related how God made the human being and gave life to the body he had formed from the earth. The apostle calls the old person nothing other than the old life, which is in sin, in which one lives according to Adam. Of this he says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

Therefore that whole person—that is, both in his inner and outer part—grew old because of sin and was subjected to the punishment of mortality. But he is now renewed according to the inner person, where he is reformed according to the image of his Creator, putting off injustice—that is, the old person—and putting on justice—that is, the new person.

Then, when the spiritual body that is sown as an animal body rises, the outer person too will receive the dignity of heavenly condition, so that everything that was created may be recreated and everything that was made may be restored: by the one who recreates because he created, and restores because he made. He explains this briefly where he says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of justice. But if the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, the one who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. VIII, 10, 11).

For who, instructed in Catholic truth, is unaware that according to the body some human beings are male and others female, but not according to the spirit of the mind, in which we are renewed according to the image of God? Nevertheless, because God made both, the same apostle again bears witness when he says: “Neither is woman without man, nor man without woman, in the Lord. For just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman; but all things are from God” (I Cor. XI, 11, 12).

What does the foolish deceitfulness of people alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their hearts (Eph. IV, 18) say in response to these things, except: “In the apostolic Letters whatever we want is true, and whatever we do not want is false”? This is how the Manichaeans rave. But let them come to their senses [Note: [Col. 0476] In the manuscripts: “Thus may the Manichaeans rave, and let them come to their senses.”], and let them cease to be Manichaeans.

If they are asked [Note: [Col. 0476] The Lyons edition alone reads “how”; less well.]—for they admit that the inner person is renewed in the image of God, and even voluntarily bring forward this testimony—since Faustus says that God makes the human being when the inner person is renewed in the knowledge of God, whether the one who restores him is the one who made him, and whether the one who renews him is the one who created him, they will answer: “He is.”

But if we add to their answer the question of when he formed the one whom he is now reforming, they will look for somewhere to hide, lest they be compelled to expose the disgrace of their fable. For they do not say that he was formed, created, or established by God, but that a part of God’s very substance was sent against the enemies; nor that he grew old through sin, but that he was taken captive by necessity and disfigured by enemies, along with the other claims that it is now tiresome to repeat.

There too they mention the first human being—not the one whom the apostle calls “earthly, from the earth” (I Cor. XV, 47), but some unknown being of their own, leaping forth from the ark of lies. Faustus says nothing at all about him when he has proposed to himself a question concerning the human being, fearing that he might somehow become known to those against whom he is arguing.

# BOOK TWENTY-FIVE

[Col. 0477]

## CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: Does God have an end, or is he infinite? If your prayer does not deceive, the prayer that says, “God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob” (Exod. III, 15), then God has an end—unless perhaps the one about whom you are asking is one god and the one whom you worship is another. Otherwise, the boundary of circumcision, which separates Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob from the fellowship of the remaining nations (Gen. XVII, 9–14), also limits God’s own power with respect to them. But whatever has finite power is itself not without an end.

Finally, in this prayer you do not even mention the ancients who lived before Abraham—Enoch, I mean, and Noah, and Shem (Gen. V), and the rest like them. You do not deny that they were righteous in uncircumcision, but because they lacked the mark of circumcision, you do not even wish them to have God as their God, but only Abraham and his seed.

Therefore, if there is one infinite God, what does this most careful and anxious precision in your invocation mean? You are not content to name God, but add whose God he is—namely, Abraham’s, Isaac’s, and Jacob’s—as though your prayer, wandering or suffering shipwreck amid some crowd of gods, could not reach its destination unless it sailed by Abraham’s signal.

It is certainly not absurd [Note: [Col. 0477] Some manuscripts read: “And these indeed.”] for Jews to pray to this God for a definite reason, since they are circumcised; for in this way they indicate that they invoke the God of circumcision, on account of the gods of the uncircumcision. But why you do this I scarcely understand, since you do not at all bear the sign that Abraham had, whose God you invoke.

Indeed, as can be understood, it seems that the Jews and the God of the Jews imposed such identifying marks upon one another for the sake of mutual recognition, so that they would not stray from one another [Note: [Col. 0477] The Cistercian manuscript reads “alternate [alternas]” rather than “alternately [alternis].”]. He marked them with the obscene character of circumcision, so that wherever they might be, in whatever nation, they would nevertheless be recognized through circumcision as belonging to him. They, in turn, marked their God with the name of their ancestors, so that wherever he might be, even amid a great multitude of gods, whenever he heard “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob,” he would immediately recognize that he was being invoked.

This is almost what commonly happens among people who share one name: none of them responds when called unless his surname is heard. In the same way, shepherds and cattlemen brand identifying marks upon their animals, lest any one of them claim another’s animal as his own.

Since you do something similar—saying “God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob”—you show not only that God has an end, but also that you yourselves are alienated from him, lacking his sign and sacrament, which is the mutilation of the male organs by which he recognizes his own.

Therefore, if this is the God whom you worship, it is perfectly clear from this that he has an end. But if you want God to be infinite, you must first renounce this god and, with your prayer altered, express repentance for your former error.

This statement is made in such a way that we may seem to have defeated you on your own ground. Otherwise, if the question is whether the supreme and true God is infinite or not, the opposition between good and evil can briefly instruct us on this point. For if evil does not exist, God is certainly infinite; but he has an end if evil exists. Yet it is established that evil exists. Therefore God is not infinite, for evils are understood to exist where good comes to an end.

## CHAPTER TWO

AUGUSTINE replied: Let no one who knows you ask you this question, or engage in discussion about this matter with people like you. First you must be cleansed of your carnal and bodily notions by devout faith and by whatever small measure of truth you possess, so that you may be able to think, in some way and to some extent, about spiritual things.

So long as you cannot do this—for your heresy knows nothing except how to extend both body and soul and God through finite or infinite intervals of space, although only the body occupies such spaces or is occupied by such spaces—you would be acting more prudently if you did not involve yourselves in this question [Note: [Col. 0478] Lyons and some manuscripts read “did not commit yourselves to this question.”]. You cannot teach anything true here, any more than in other matters; nor are you capable of learning what perhaps you could learn in other matters, if you were not proud and quarrelsome.

When people begin to ask how God can be finite, whom no place contains; how infinite, whom the Son knows wholly; how finite, yet immeasurable; how infinite, yet perfect; how finite, yet having no limit; how infinite, yet the limit of all things—every carnal thought vanishes. And if it wishes to become what it is not yet, it must first grow ashamed of what it is.

Therefore, you do better to end this question that you put to us concerning a finite and infinite God by keeping silent, until you cease to stray so far from the end of the Law, which is Christ.

As for the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, since he is the true God of every creature, we have already said as much as was sufficient about why he wished to make himself known to his people by that name. Concerning circumcision, too, we have often responded in the earlier parts of this work to your ignorant slanders.

If these people would think about this divinely given sign on the appropriate part of the body, by which the stripping away of the flesh was symbolized, with a Christian rather than a heretical mind, in accordance with the saying, “Everything is clean to the clean,” they would by no means ridicule it.

But because what follows is also true—“For the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Tit. I, 15)—we gently admonish them as they laugh and mock with witty insults: if, according to their own principles, circumcision is shameful, they have nothing there to laugh at, but something to mourn over, because their god is bound up with and contaminated by both the little piece that is cut off and the blood that drips from it.

# BOOK TWENTY-SIX

[Col. 0479]

## CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: If Jesus was not born, how did he die? This is plainly a conjecture; but no one uses conjectures unless proofs have failed him. Nevertheless, we shall also answer this, bringing examples from none other than the things you are accustomed to believe. If these examples are true, they will confirm us as well; if false, they will destroy you too.

You say, then: “How did Jesus die if he was not a human being?” And I ask you in return: “How did Elijah not die, since he was a human being?” Was it permitted for him, contrary to his mortal condition, to seize the right of immortality, but not permitted for Christ, who is immortal, to appropriate something from death, if that was necessary?

And if Elijah lives forever contrary to nature, why should you not all the more grant that Jesus could have died for only three days, contrary to nature? Especially since you believe this not only about Elijah, but also about Moses and Enoch—that they are immortal and were themselves taken up into heaven with their bodies.

Therefore, if the argument correctly establishes that Jesus was a human being because he died, the same argument can nevertheless establish that Elijah was not a human being because he did not die. But it is false that Elijah was not a human being, although he is believed immortal. It will likewise be false that Jesus was a human being, although he is thought to have died.

And if you are willing to believe me when I speak the truth, both of them, among the Hebrews, acquired a false reputation: Jesus concerning death, and Elijah concerning immortality. For the one did not die, and the other did not fail to die. But you believe whatever you wish, while referring whatever you do not wish to believe back to nature.

Therefore, if the question is what belongs properly to nature, nature neither wishes an immortal being to die nor a mortal being not to die. But if we are asking about God’s and humanity’s power to accomplish whatever they wish, I think that Jesus could more easily have died than Elijah could have failed to die, for greater power exists in Jesus than in Elijah.

And if you raise the weaker one—Elijah—into heaven against nature’s allowance and consecrate him to perpetual existence, forgetting his nature and condition, why should I not grant that Jesus could have died if he wished, even if I agree that that death was truly a death and not a figure of death?

For just as from the beginning, having assumed the likeness of a human being, he simulated all the experiences of human condition, so it would not have been inappropriate if at the end, too, for the sake of confirming the divine plan, he had appeared to die.

## CHAPTER TWO

Moreover, this too must be mentioned: if the question is what nature permits each thing, that question ought to be asked concerning everything Jesus did, not only concerning his death.

Nature does not permit a person blind from birth to see light. Yet Jesus is seen to have powerfully accomplished this for the blind of this kind [Note: [Col. 0480] The edition of Erasmus and one Vatican manuscript read, “is seen to have accomplished it.” Hence: “to have given light to the blind of this kind,” and so forth.], to such an extent that even the Jews exclaimed that from the beginning of the world it had never been seen that someone opened the eyes of one born blind (John IX).

Who would not be brought to astonishment, and compelled in some way not to believe while considering what nature permits or does not permit, by the healing of a withered hand; the restoration of voice and speech to people deprived of them by nature; and the restoration of vital breath to the dead, whose bodies had already dissolved into decay, after their structure had been reassembled?

Yet we Christians commonly believe that all these things were done by him, not now by consideration of nature, but solely by the power and might of God.

It is also read that, once hurled from the brow of a mountain by the Jews, he departed unharmed. Therefore, since he was thrown down from a lofty mountain and did not die because he did not wish to, why could he not also have died when he wished?

This, then, is our answer for the present, because you like to argue and are attempting to use foreign weapons, wishing to dispute dialectically. Otherwise, for us Jesus did not die, nor is Elijah immortal.

## CHAPTER THREE

AUGUSTINE replied: Whatever Holy Scripture, placed at the highest summit of authority by certain and great proofs of its faith, testifies concerning Enoch, Elijah, and Moses, we believe—not what Faustus suspects that we believe.

But people who err as you do cannot know what is according to nature and what is contrary to nature. We do not deny that, in human terms, what is contrary to the customary course of nature is called contrary to nature among mortals. Thus the apostle says: “If you were cut from the naturally wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, grafted into a good olive tree” (Rom. XI, 24). He called that contrary to nature which is contrary to nature’s customary course as human understanding comprehends it: namely, that when a wild olive is grafted into an olive tree, it bears not the berries of a wild olive but the richness of an olive.

God, however, the creator and founder of all natures, does nothing contrary to nature. For what he has made will be natural to each thing—he from whom come every measure, number, and order of nature.

Nor does a human being himself do anything contrary to nature except when he sins; yet through punishment he is brought back to nature. For it belongs to the natural order of justice either that sins not be committed or that they not be able to remain unpunished. Whichever of these occurs, the natural order is preserved, whether by the soul or certainly by God.

Sins torment the conscience and harm the mind itself, since through sin it is deprived of the light of justice, even if the pains do not follow—pains that are imposed for correction or reserved as a final punishment for those who are not corrected.

But we may appropriately say that God does something contrary to nature when he acts contrary to what we know in nature. We also call nature the familiar and customary course of nature known to us; when God does something against this course, such deeds are called great works or miracles.

Against that supreme law of nature, however, which is remote from the knowledge of the impious and of those who are still weak, God does nothing at all—just as he does nothing against himself.

The spiritual and likewise rational creature, of which kind the human soul also is, participates in that unchangeable law and light to a greater or lesser degree. The more it participates, the more it sees what can and cannot happen; the farther it is removed from that law and light, the more it marvels at unusual things, because it sees less of what lies ahead.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Accordingly, we do not know what happened to Elijah. Nevertheless, we believe about him what truthful Scripture testifies. We do know this: what happened to him is what God’s will contains; and what God’s will does not contain cannot happen to anyone at all.

Therefore, if I am told that it can happen, for example, that the flesh of this or that human being may be changed into a heavenly body, I concede that it can happen, but I do not know whether it will happen. I do not know because God’s will concerning this matter is hidden from me. Yet I do know that it will certainly happen if this is what God’s will contains.

But if I hear that something was going to happen, and that God prevented it from happening, I shall answer with complete confidence: what God did was going to happen, not what—if it had been going to happen—he would have prevented [Note: [Col. 0481] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice editions: “would not have prevented this.” Manuscript M.]. For God certainly knew what he was going to do, and therefore at the same time knew that what he was going to prevent would not happen. Without doubt, what God knows is truer than what a human being supposes.

Therefore future events cannot fail to occur any more than past events can fail to have occurred, since it is not in God’s will that something be false in the respect in which it is true. Accordingly, everything that is truly future will certainly happen; but if it did not happen, it was not future. Likewise, everything that is truly past has certainly passed away.

## CHAPTER FIVE

Whoever says, then, “If God is omnipotent, let him make what has happened not to have happened,” does not see that he is saying: “If he is omnipotent, let him make what is true, in the very respect in which it is true, false.”

For he can make something that was cease to be. He makes it cease to be when he finds that it exists and makes it cease to exist—for example, when he causes someone who began to exist by being born to cease to exist by dying. He found something that existed, from which he could make it cease to exist.

But who could say that he should make something that no longer exists cease to exist? Whatever is past no longer exists. If something can also be done to the past itself, then there is still something there from which it may be done; and if it exists, how is it past?

Therefore, the thing that we truly say existed does not exist now. Yet it is true that it existed because that is true in our judgment, not in the thing that no longer exists. The judgment by which we say that something existed is true precisely because the thing about which we speak no longer exists.

God cannot make this judgment false, because he is not opposed to truth. If you ask where this true judgment exists, it is first found in our mind, when we know and say that something is true. But even if it is removed from our mind, when we have forgotten what we know, it will remain in truth itself [Note: [Col. 0482] Most manuscripts, with Ambrose and Erasmus: “truth itself will remain.”].

It will always be true that what existed but no longer exists did exist. And it will be true that what existed has already existed in the place where it was true, before it came to be, that what did not exist would be future.

God cannot oppose this truth, since in him is the supreme and unchangeable truth itself, by which whatever is true in any person’s soul or mind is illuminated so that it may exist.

We do not call God omnipotent as though we believed that he could also die; nor, because he cannot do this, should he therefore not be called omnipotent. He alone is truly called omnipotent who truly is and from whom alone comes whatever exists in any manner, whether spiritual or bodily.

He uses his entire creation as he pleases. Yet what pleases him accords with true and unchangeable justice, which he himself is. All things are changeable, while he is unchangeable, changing them according to the merits either of their natures or of their deeds [Note: The sole edition of Erasmus: “to change.”].

Are we therefore going to say that Elijah, since he was a creature, could not be changed either for the worse or for the better, or that he could not be changed in a way unusual for the human race, according to the will of almighty God? Who could say this, even if utterly foolish?

Why, then, should we not believe what is recorded about him in the most truthful Scripture—unless we suppose that God can do only what we are accustomed to see?

## CHAPTER SIX

“But,” he says, “if Elijah was a human being and could fail to die, why could Christ not die, since he was not a human being?”

This is as if someone said: “If human nature could be changed into something better, why could divine nature not be changed into something worse?” Fool! Human nature is changeable, whereas divine nature is unchangeable.

Some equally insane person might say: “If he can grant a human being the ability to reign forever, why can he not also make himself be condemned forever?” “I am not saying that,” he replies, “but I compare God’s three-day death with the human being’s eternal life.”

Certainly, if you understood God’s three-day death in this way—that the flesh he assumed from the mortal race died in him—you would have sound judgment. For evangelical truth proclaims that Christ’s three-day death was accomplished for the eternal life of human beings.

But when you want a three-day death, with no mortal creature assumed, to be believed—not absurdly—in the divine nature itself merely because human nature can be granted immortality, then you are plainly raving like someone who knows neither God nor God’s gifts.

Moreover, why do you not say and believe what I stated above [Note: [Col. 0482] Ambrose, Erasmus, and most manuscripts: “that God did not make for himself.”]: that God made for himself the means by which he would be condemned forever, when that part of your god is fixed forever in the globe? Or will you also say that, because a part of the light is light, a part of God is not God?

Finally, so that you may hear from us without any reasoning and with the plain truth of faith why we believe that Elijah, born a human being, was divinely taken from the earth, but that Christ was truly born from a virgin and truly died on the cross: we believe these things because Holy Scripture testifies both to the one concerning Elijah and to the other concerning Christ (IV Kings II, 11; Matt. I, 25, and XVII, 50). No devout person believes this Scripture except one who believes; no one fails to believe it except an impious person [Note: Lyons edition: “no one is impious except one who does not believe.” This is false and should be corrected from the manuscripts as follows: “no one who is not impious fails to believe.”].

You deny the matter concerning Elijah because you pretend everything. But concerning Christ, you do not say that he could not be born and could die; rather, you maintain that his birth from a virgin was nonexistent, while his death on the cross was false—that is, that it too was nonexistent, merely simulated to deceive human eyes, for no other purpose than that those who believed these things might also pardon you when you lied about everything.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

Who would propose to you what Faustus, as though speaking in the person of a Catholic, proposes to himself—“If Jesus was not born, how did he die?”—except someone who gives little consideration to the fact that Adam himself was not born, and yet died?

Therefore, if the Son of God had wished to form for himself true human flesh from the same source from which he formed it for that first human being—for all things were made through him (John I, 3)—who would dare say that he could not do so?

Finally, if he had wished to take a body from a heavenly, aerial, or watery creature and change it into the true quality of human flesh, in which he could live as a mortal human being and also die, who would deny that the omnipotent Son of the omnipotent Father could do this?

If, at last, he had wished to assume a body from none of the bodily elements created through him, but to create true flesh for himself entirely from nothing, just as through him all things that did not exist were created, who among us could object? Who among us could contend that this could not happen?

We therefore do not believe that he was born from the virgin Mary because he could not otherwise exist in true flesh and appear to human beings. We believe it because this is written in that Scripture: unless we believe it, we can be neither Christians nor saved.

Therefore we believe that Christ was born from the virgin Mary because this is written in the Gospel. We believe that he was crucified and died because this is written in the Gospel. And we believe that he was truly born and truly died because the Gospel is truth.

Why he wished to undergo all those sufferings in the flesh assumed from the womb of a woman belongs to the highest counsel, which rests with him. Perhaps he judged that both sexes, which he had created, should also be commended and honored in this manner, by assuming the form of a man and being born from a woman. Or perhaps there was some other reason; I would not rashly say what it was.

This, however, I shall say confidently: it did not happen otherwise than evangelical truth has taught, nor ought it to have happened otherwise than the wisdom of God judged. We place faith in the Gospel above all the arguments of heretics; and we praise the counsel of God’s wisdom above every counsel of any creature.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

Nevertheless, Faustus urges us to believe him, saying: “And if you are willing to believe me when I speak the truth, both of them, among the Hebrews, acquired a false reputation: Jesus concerning death, and Elijah concerning immortality.” Yet shortly afterward he says: “For just as from the beginning, having assumed the likeness of a human being, he simulated all the experiences of human condition, so it would not have been inappropriate if at the end, too, for the sake of confirming the divine plan, he had appeared to die.”

You most wicked and deceitful human being, how am I to believe you as though you were speaking the truth, when you say that Christ could have pretended to die? So he was lying when he said, “The Son of man must be killed and rise on the third day” (Luke XXIV, 7); yet you are not lying when you say that we should believe you as one speaking the truth?

Peter, then, was more truthful when he said to him, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen,” and therefore deserved to hear, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. XVI, 22, 23). And he did not hear this without benefit, since afterward, corrected and perfected, he proclaimed the truth of Christ’s death until his own death.

But if Peter deserved to hear “Satan” merely because he thought that Christ would not die, what do you deserve to hear, since you do not deny that he died but even say that he pretended to die?

“But,” you say, “he should be believed to have pretended even to die because he simulated all the experiences of human condition.”

Who will grant you, against the Gospel, that he simulated all the experiences of human condition? Certainly, if [Note: [Col. 0484] Ambrose, Erasmus, and more manuscripts omit the particle “if” here and in the following occurrence. A little later, Lyons and the manuscripts read, “and if anything else”; Ambrose and Erasmus, “and other such things.”] the evangelist said, “Jesus slept” (ibid. VIII, 24); if he said, “He was hungry” (ibid. IV, 2), “he thirsted” (John XIX), “he was sorrowful” (Matt. XXVI, 37), “he rejoiced,” and other things of this kind—then all these things are true, since they are narrated in such a way that he did not merely pretend them, but plainly did or displayed them. Yet he did so not from the compulsion of his condition, but by the will of his teaching office and also by divine power.

For a human being often becomes angry even if unwilling; becomes sorrowful even if unwilling; sleeps even if unwilling; hungers and thirsts even if unwilling. But he did all these things because he willed to [Note: [Col. 0484] The printed editions read, “he did them because he willed to”; “he did them” is absent from the manuscripts.].

Human beings are likewise born and suffer not because they wish to, nor at the time they wish to [Note: Most manuscripts: “nor when they wish to.”]; but he underwent even these things because he willed to.

Nevertheless, these events were truly and faithfully recorded concerning him, so that whoever believed his Gospel might be instructed in truth and not deceived by lies.

# BOOK TWENTY-SEVEN

[Col. 0483]

## CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: If Jesus was not born, he did not suffer; but if he suffered, then he was also born. Believe me, it is not advantageous for you to seek the sequence of nature in these matters; otherwise all your faith will be weakened.

For you believe that Jesus was born from a virgin without intercourse with a man. If what follows is to prove what came before, this will be false. For one could answer you in this way: if Jesus was born from a woman, then he was also conceived from a man; but if he was not conceived from a man, then he was not born from a woman.

Yet, as you believe, he could be born without being conceived. Why, then, could he not also suffer without having been born?

## CHAPTER TWO

AUGUSTINE replied: No one proposes to you what you propose to yourself except someone unlearned whom you deceive, not someone instructed by whom you are refuted [Note: In the manuscripts, “by whom you may be convicted.”].

For Jesus could both be born without being conceived and suffer without having been born. But he willed one of these and did not will the other. He willed to be born without being conceived, but did not will to suffer without having been born, because he did suffer after being born.

You ask me: “How do you know?” Because I read this in the Gospel of truth. But if I ask you, “How do you know the things you say?” you bring the authority of Manichaeus against me and say that falsehood exists in the Gospel.

But I would not believe Manichaeus when he said these things, even if he did not praise to me Christ’s having lied. In fact, he found no such thing in Christ; rather, he revealed what he himself loves.

# BOOK TWENTY-EIGHT

[Col. 0485]

## CHAPTER ONE

FAUSTUS said: But he could not die unless he had been born. And I reply: Nor could he be born unless he were not God. Or, if he could both be God and be born, why could he not also fail to be born and die?

You see, then, that it is not at all useful to seek a sequence in these matters or to rely upon arguments when the subject concerns things pertaining to Jesus. Rather, one must ask what he himself proclaimed about himself and what his apostles proclaimed about him.

Indeed, his genealogy itself must be examined in detail, and it must be seen whether it is consistent with itself. The truth of his birth should not be sought from a conjecture based on his suffering, because he could suffer without having been born, and he could be born without suffering—especially since you yourselves admit that nothing is impossible for God. That admission itself will also be false if it is established that one who was not born could not die.

## CHAPTER TWO
Augustine replied: Again and again you propose to yourself what you do not hear from those by whom you are refuted. No one says to you, “He could not die unless he had been born,” since Adam died although he had not been born. Rather, this is said to you: He was born because this is what the holy Gospel says—not some unknown heretic; he died because this is read in the holy Gospel, not in the book of some heretic.

But when you forbid argument in matters that concern Jesus, and think that we should inquire what he himself preached about himself and what his Apostles preached about him, as soon as I begin to recite the Gospel of his apostle Matthew, where the whole account of his birth is set out, you will immediately say that this account is not Matthew’s—although the whole Church declares it to be Matthew’s, a certainty handed down in an unbroken succession from the apostolic sees to the bishops of the present day.

What will you read against me? Perhaps some book of Manichaeus, in which Jesus is denied to have been born of a virgin. Just as I believe that book to be Manichaeus’s because, from the very time when Manichaeus lived in the flesh, it has been preserved and handed down through his disciples, in an established succession of your leaders, down to your own times, so you should believe this book to be Matthew’s, since from the time when Matthew himself lived in the flesh the Church has transmitted it down to these times through an unbroken succession of ages and a firmly connected chain.

And tell me whose book we ought rather to believe: that of the apostle who had clung to Christ while he was still on earth, or that of some Persian [Col. 0486] who was born so much later? But perhaps you will produce another book bearing the name of some apostle whom it is certain Christ chose, and there you will read that Christ was not born of Mary.

Since one of these two books must necessarily be false, whom do you think we ought rather to trust? The book which that Church—begun by Christ himself, advanced through the Apostles in a sure succession, and spread throughout the whole world—recognizes and approves as handed down and preserved from the beginning? Or the book which that same Church rejects as unknown, even though it is produced by people so truthful that they praise Christ for having lied?

## Chapter III

You will say that the genealogy itself in the two Gospel books should be examined to see whether it agrees with itself. We have already said elsewhere in this work what needed to be said on this matter (above, book 3, chapter 3). What troubles you is only how Joseph could have had two fathers. If the distinction between one who begot him and another who adopted him had not occurred to you, even then you ought not lightly to have delivered a rash judgment against such great authority. But now, if you think about how this could have happened, once reminded of it, simply believe the Gospel and cease, rather, to argue so badly and perversely.

## Chapter IV

But when Faustus thinks that we should inquire what Jesus himself preached about himself, who could regard this as unjust? Yet can this be known except through the testimony of his disciples? If they are not believed when they announce that he was born of a virgin, how will they be believed when they announce what he himself preached about himself?

For if some writings were produced and declared to be properly Christ’s own, without any other narrator reporting them, how could it happen that, if they truly were his, they would not be read, accepted, and distinguished by the highest authority in his Church—the Church that, propagated and enlarged by him through the Apostles and their successive bishops, extends down to the present day, with many things already fulfilled that had earlier been foretold, and with the remaining things undoubtedly destined to occur until the end?

Even if such writings were produced, it would certainly be necessary to consider by whom they were produced. If they came from him, they could undoubtedly first have been produced by those who at that time remained attached to him, and through them could also have reached others. If that had happened, [Col. 0487] they would shine forth with the most firmly established authority through the successions of leaders and peoples that I mentioned.

*[Note: Some manuscripts read “leaders and Apostles” instead of “leaders and peoples.”]*

Who, then, is so mad as to believe today that there is a letter of Christ produced by Manichaeus, and not believe that Christ’s deeds or words were written by Matthew? Or if he even doubts whether Matthew himself wrote these things, why should he not believe concerning Matthew himself what he finds in the Church, which is attested from Matthew’s own time down to the present through a firm succession? Why should he instead believe some unknown person arriving unexpectedly from Persia two hundred or more years later and persuading us that we ought rather to believe what Christ said and did according to him?

When the apostle Paul himself, called from heaven after the Lord’s ascension (Acts 9), would not have been believed at all by the Church if he had not found Apostles in the flesh, associated himself with them, and conferred with them about the Gospel, thereby showing that he belonged to the same fellowship. But when the Church recognized that he was announcing what they also announced, living in their fellowship and unity, and when signs such as those they performed were also accomplished through him, he deserved authority, with the Lord commending him, so that his words are now heard in the Church as though Christ himself were heard speaking in him, just as he most truly said (2 Cor. 13:3).

And yet Manichaeus thinks that the Church of Christ ought to believe him when he speaks against the Scriptures, which are supported by such great and orderly authority—Scriptures through which he was especially commended to us: “If anyone should preach to you something other than what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8–9).

## Chapter V

[Col. 0488]

But, he says, I present an argument by which I can demonstrate that those Scriptures should not be believed.

Certainly you are not arguing? And yet even in this very argument you are defeated. For your entire argument is reduced to this: that the soul should finally believe that it is wretched in this world because, through its wretchedness, it came to the aid of its god, lest he be deprived of his kingdom; and that his nature and substance are so changeable, corruptible, violable, and defileable that one part of him cannot even be cleansed and, although he knowingly mixed it into such great contamination—he who knew it to be innocent and to have committed no sin against him—is punished by an eternal torment in the globe.

This is the end of all your arguments and fables. Would that it were the end of them in your hearts and mouths, so that at last you might cease believing and uttering such detestable blasphemies.

“But,” he says, “from the writings themselves I prove that they should not be believed everywhere, since they speak contradictions against one another.”

Why, then, do you not rather say that they should nowhere be believed, as inconsistent witnesses who attack one another?

“But this,” he says, “is what I choose, because I see it to be in agreement with the truth.”

With what truth? With your fable, of course: a fable that has a war against God at its beginning, God’s contamination in its middle, and God’s condemnation at its end.

“And nowhere,” he says, “are writings that oppose and contradict one another to be believed.”

This seems so to you because you do not understand. Everything you have brought forward that appeared to be such has been shown to reveal your lack of understanding; and whatever you bring forward will likewise be shown to do so.

There is therefore no reason why we should not believe those Letters endowed with such great authority. Indeed, this is the strongest reason why we should anathematize those who preach something else.

# BOOK TWENTY-NINE

[Col. 0487]

## Chapter I

Faustus said: Then his having been seen and having suffered was magic, if he was not born. The same argument is turned back upon you in reply: his being carried in the womb, or his being born, would likewise have been magic if he was not generated.

It is established that a virgin’s giving birth is outside the law of nature, and still more so that she was found to remain a virgin even after giving birth. Why, then, are you unwilling that this also should have happened contrary to nature: that he was able to suffer by his own will, without the condition of birth?

Believe me: so far as the matter itself is concerned, we both profess something contrary to nature here. But the difference is that we do so honorably and you dishonorably. We offer some account of his suffering, and one that is plausible; you offer no account at all of his birth, or else a false one.

In the end, we confess that he suffered only in appearance and did not truly die; whereas you believe that there was a genuine childbirth and that he was carried in a woman’s womb. Or, if this is not so, admit that this too happened only imaginatively, so that he appeared to be born, and our entire dispute will be destroyed.

For what you often assert—that he necessarily had to be born because otherwise he could not have appeared or spoken to human beings—is ridiculous, since, as has already been proved by [Col. 0488] our people, Angels have repeatedly been shown both to have appeared to human beings and to have spoken to them.

*[Note: The Erfurt edition and several manuscripts read “by your people” instead of “by our people.”]*

## Chapter II

Augustine replied: You are not told that it is magic for one who has not been born to die; for we have already mentioned above that this happened in Adam. But even if it had never happened, and the Lord Christ had wished to come in such a way that, though he was not taken from a virgin, he nevertheless appeared in true flesh and redeemed us by a true death, who would dare to say that he could not have done so?

Yet what he did was better: he was also born of a virgin, and he deigned, by being born, to commend both sexes—for whose liberation he was going to die—by being generated in the flesh as a male from a woman. By this very deed he spoke most forcefully against you and overturned you, since you proclaim that male and female are the work not of God but of the devil.

But what you are said to assert as resembling magic is that his passion and death took place only in appearance [Col. 0489] and were deceptively shadowed forth, so that he seemed to die although he did not die. It follows from this that you also call his resurrection shadowy, imaginary, and deceptive; for the resurrection of one who did not truly die cannot be true.

Thus it follows that he showed false scars to his doubting disciples, and that Thomas, confirmed not by truth but deceived by a falsehood, cried out, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). And yet you try to persuade people that you speak the truth with your tongues, while saying that Christ lied with his entire body.

These are the charges brought against you, who have fashioned for yourselves such a Christ that you cannot be his true disciples unless you too become liars.

Nor can flesh born of a virgin be considered magic merely because Christ’s flesh alone was born in this way, just as it is not magic that Christ’s flesh alone rose on the third day, never again to die. Otherwise all God’s miracles would be magic, because they were performed uniquely. But they truly happened and revealed what was true; they did not deceive human eyes with fraudulent tricks.

Such events are often called contrary to nature—not because they oppose nature, but because they surpass the course of nature familiar to us. Therefore may the Lord drive from the minds of his little ones what Faustus has tried, as though by way of admonition, to persuade them of: that we too should profess an imaginary rather than a true birth of Christ.

Let the whole dispute between us therefore end in this—or rather, let our struggle on behalf of the truth against them remain, instead of our agreeing with them in falsehood.

## Chapter III

Nevertheless, I ask them: if our dispute ends when we say this, why do they themselves not say it? Why do they affirm that Christ’s death was not real but imaginary, while choosing to say that his birth was not even such a thing, but altogether nonexistent?

If they were ashamed because of the weight of evangelical authority, and therefore did not dare to say that Christ did not suffer even imaginatively,*

*[Note: Thus Am., Er., and several manuscripts of good authority. Four Vatican manuscripts read, “If they were ashamed of the weights of evangelical authority.” Another Vatican manuscript and the Cistercian manuscript read, “But they were ashamed to be pressed by the weight of evangelical authority.” The Louvain edition reads, “If they were ashamed to answer evangelical authority.”]*

that same evangelical authority also bears witness to his birth. For although two Evangelists narrated Mary’s actual delivery (Matt. 1:25; Luke 2:7), none of the Evangelists was silent about Jesus having a mother (Matt. 2:11; Mark 3:32; Luke 2:33; John 2:1).

Or were they reluctant to proclaim even this as simulated because Matthew traces one set of generations and Luke another, so that they appear not to agree with one another? But present someone who does not understand, and he will think that the Evangelists also disagree in many matters relating to Christ’s passion. Present someone who does understand, and they agree everywhere.

Or is it because simulating death is honorable, whereas even simulating birth is shameful? Why, then, does he urge us to confess what could bring our dispute to an end? Why, then, did he seem to me to wish to preach that Christ’s birth was not even simulated as his death was, but entirely nonexistent? This will become clear in the speech that follows, where we shall answer the other question.

## Chapter IV

[Col. 0490]

Far be it from us to suppose that there is any shame even in the genital members of the saints. They are indeed called dishonorable because they do not possess the same visible beauty as the members placed in public view.

*[Note: Retractations II, chapter 7, section 3.]*

But observe what the Apostle says when, from the very unity and structure of the members of our body, he persuades the Church to love:

“Those members of the body that seem to be weaker are much more necessary; and those members of the body that seem to be less honorable, we surround with more abundant honor; and our dishonorable members have more abundant dignity, whereas our honorable members have no need of it. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there might be no division in the body” (1 Cor. 12:22–25).

Therefore it is the illicit use of those members, not subject to the laws of temperance, that is shameful—not the members themselves. They are preserved not only in eminent integrity by celibates and virgins, but are also used by holy married fathers and mothers, who employ them solely for the sake of generation, so that the natural impulse itself is in no way shameful when it serves reason rather than lust.

How much more, then, in the case of the holy virgin Mary, who conceived Christ’s flesh through faith, did the members have nothing shameful about them—members that served not even a lawful human conception, but only a divine birth?

She was rightly honored in such a way that, while preserving her integrity bodily, she might transmit Christ to us, whom we conceive by believing with undivided hearts and, in a certain sense, give birth to by confessing him.

For Christ could in no way make his mother worse by being born, taking away the honor of virginity from the one to whom he had brought the gift of fertility. These things truly happened, not deceptively; but they are new, unusual, and contrary to the familiar course of nature because they are great, wondrous, and divine—and for that very reason all the more true, certain, and confirmed.

*[Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venice edition read “firm” instead of “confirmed.”]*

“And Angels,” he says, “appeared and spoke, although they were not born.” [Col. 0490] As though we were saying that Christ could neither have been seen nor spoken if he had not been born of a woman. He could have—but he did not wish to; and what he wished is better.

That he wished this is certain because he did it—he who, unlike your god, would do nothing out of necessity, but everything by his will. We do not doubt that he did this because we believe not some heretic but his Gospel.

# BOOK THIRTY

[Col. 0489]

## Chapter I

Faustus said: Paul wrote long ago concerning you that some would depart from the faith, giving attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, [Col. 0490] speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage, and abstaining from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful [Col. 0491] (1 Tim. 4:1–3).

I would never agree with you that these words were spoken by the Apostle unless you first confess that Moses and the Prophets brought forward doctrines of demons and were interpreters of a deceitful and evil spirit, since they carefully teach abstinence from pork and from the other kinds of flesh that they call unclean.

You must therefore first deliberate about this and think long and hard about how these things should be understood: whether Moses and the Prophets themselves appear to have spoken them in God or in a demon. For on this point either Moses and the Prophets will be condemned along with us, or we will be acquitted along with them.

Your present judgment cannot be just: you regard us—who hold that only the priestly class among the people should abstain from flesh—as followers of demonic doctrine, while you think that your own Prophets, and Moses himself above all, who first forbade not only priests but the entire human race indiscriminately to eat pork, hare, hedgehog flesh, cuttlefish, squid, and all other kinds of fish without scales (Lev. 11),*

*[Note: The Louvain edition reads “goat flesh” (*hircina*) for “hedgehog flesh” (*hericina* or *ericina*); the other editions and manuscripts more correctly have the latter reading.]*

spoke not under the influence of a deceitful spirit or in accordance with demonic doctrine, but rather in God and in the Holy Spirit.

So, even if I grant for the moment that Paul said this to you, you will nevertheless not have defeated me until you condemn Moses and the Prophets. Thus, what you perhaps never would have done when conquered by reason and truth, you now appear ready to do for the sake of your belly: to blaspheme Moses.

*[Note: The Lyon and Venice editions read “whether anything should be accepted.” The Louvain edition reads “what should be accepted.”]*

## Chapter II

There is also another matter concerning the three boys in Daniel, by which you will likewise be thoroughly confounded if it is established that abstaining from foods is a religious practice of demons. For they are said to have abstained not only from what the Law prohibited, but also from what it permitted (Dan. 1:12).

You greatly admire them and count them among the martyrs, although they too would have adopted demonic doctrine if this is what the Apostle’s testimony means.

Moreover, Daniel himself reports that he fasted for three weeks, eating no meat and drinking no wine, while he was pleading for his people (Dan. 10:2–3). Why, then, does he too boast in the doctrine of demons and seek glory from the invention of a deceitful spirit?

## Chapter III

But what shall I say about you—that is, about the more Christian people among you? Some of them abstain from pork, most from every four-footed animal, and others from every living creature altogether. For this reason the whole Church holds them in esteem and receives them with the greatest reverence, scarcely failing to regard them as gods.

And yet you do not see, foolish people, that if this testimony is true and was spoken by the Apostle, they too have been deceived by demonic doctrines.

What, moreover, shall we say about that practice [Col. 0492] which surely no one would dare to frustrate or deny, since it is universally recognized and is celebrated every year throughout the world with great zeal in the Catholic assembly? I mean Lent. Anyone among you who thinks it should properly be observed must necessarily abstain from all those things which this chapter says were created by God for us to receive, and which it further calls abstinence from the aforesaid foods a doctrine of demons.

What, then, about you, my dear friends? Do you live according to demonic practice when these mysteries of Christ’s passion are celebrated by you? Are you then captured by the fraud of a deceitful spirit, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having your conscience seared?

If none of this applies to you, neither does it apply to us. What, then, does this chapter mean? Who shall we think wrote it, and against whom, since it confirms neither the traditions of the Old Testament nor the decrees of the New?

The former is observed by all, as is evident from your own practices; the latter, although it teaches some people to abstain, is nevertheless observed by certain persons. But this statement of yours wants all abstinence from bodily foods to be doctrines of demons.

If you also believe this, I shall say again what I have said so often: condemn Moses, renounce the Prophets, and pass the same judgment on yourselves. For just as they always abstain from certain foods, so you sometimes abstain from all foods.

## Chapter IV

But if Moses and the Prophets seem to you, when distinguishing foods, to establish God’s law rather than that of demons; if Daniel observed three weeks in the Holy Spirit; if the boys Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, moved by divine inspiration, preferred to use vegetables and legumes; if, finally, all those among you who abstain do so not because they are impelled by demons; if Lent is kept by you without wine and meat not superstitiously but according to divine law—then consider, I beg you, consider carefully, lest it be the height of madness to think that Paul said abstinence from all foods and the prohibition of marriage are doctrines of demons.

The same applies to what he says about consecrating virgins to Christ. You read this just as thoughtlessly as the other passages and then turn your attention to us. Yet you do not see that this marks your own virgins as captured by demonic doctrine and marks you as priests of demons, since you continually urge them by your exhortations to make this profession, so that now in almost all the churches the number of virgins among you is greater than the number of women.

Why, then, do you not also cease from such undertakings? Why do you lead unfortunate daughters of human beings into a trap, if it is not Christ’s will that is fulfilled in them but the will of demons?

Yet first I would like you to answer this: is it altogether a doctrine of demons to make virgins, or is it only making them virgins by forbidding marriage?

If it is by prohibition, this has nothing to do with us. We ourselves consider it just as foolish to restrain one who wishes as it is altogether unlawful and impious to compel one who does not wish it.

But if you think that even favoring this purpose and not resisting one who wishes it is a doctrine of demons, I shall say nothing now about the danger you face; I already fear for the Apostle himself, lest he appear to have introduced demonic doctrine at Iconium when, through his speech, he inflamed Thecla—already betrothed and destined for the marriage chamber—with love for perpetual virginity.

What shall we say about the teacher himself, Jesus, the author of all holiness and the celestial bridegroom of girls who make this very profession?*

*[Note: The manuscripts read “celestial bridegroom” (*coelite sponso*) for “celibate bridegroom.”]*

In the Gospel, when he identifies three kinds of eunuchs—one natural, another made so by human action, and a third voluntary—he nevertheless assigns the palm to those who, he says, “made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:12).

By this he signifies virgins and boys who, having cut out from their hearts the very desire to marry, live perpetually in his Church as eunuchs, as though in a royal palace.

What, then? Does this too seem to you a doctrine of demons, spoken under the influence of a deceitful spirit? And who else will be found speaking in God if Paul and Christ are proved to have been priests of demons?

I leave aside the other Apostles of our Lord—Peter and Andrew, Thomas, and that blessed John, who among the others was untouched by Venus—for, throughout different places, they proclaimed this good profession among virgins and boys by divine preaching, leaving us, and indeed you yourselves, an example for making virgins.*

*[Note: The manuscripts read “possession” (*possessionem*) for “profession” (*professionem*).]*

But I pass over them, as I said, because you have excluded them from the canon, and in the sacrilegious state of your minds you can easily attribute demonic doctrines to them.

Will you then also be able to say the same things about Christ, or about the apostle Paul, who is everywhere known likewise to have consistently preferred the unmarried to the married in word, and to have shown this also in his conduct toward the most holy Thecla?

If this was not a doctrine of demons—if Paul announced it to Thecla and the other Apostles announced it to others—who can now believe that the matter was mentioned by Paul himself as though the persuasion of holiness were the will and doctrine of demons?

There is therefore no reason for you to think that you alone make virgins by exhortation and not by prohibition of marriage. We too have this conviction implanted in us. For a person would be utterly mad, not merely foolish, if he thought that private law could prohibit what public law permits—namely, marriage.

Therefore we too exhort those who wish to remain virgins, but we do not compel unwilling people to join them. We know how powerful the will is, and how powerful the force of nature itself can be even against public law, let alone against private law, to which one may freely reply, “I do not wish it.”

If, then, making virgins in this way is blameless, we too are free from guilt; but if making virgins in any manner is a crime, you too are guilty. I do not see with what attitude or purpose you produce this chapter against us.

## Chapter V

[Col. 0493]

Augustine replied: Listen, then, to what you confess you do not see: with what attitude or purpose we produce this chapter against you.

It is not because you abstain from flesh, for our earliest fathers also did this in certain cases, as you recall. They did not do so in order to condemn those foods, but to signify something that you do not understand, and about which I have already spoken at sufficient length, as it seemed, in the earlier parts of this work.

Christians—not heretics, but Catholics—abstain, for the discipline of the body [Col. 0494] and to humble the soul more deeply in prayer, not because they believe those foods to be unclean, not only from flesh but also from certain fruits of the earth. Some do so always, as a few do; most do so on particular days and at particular times, as during Lent. Each does so to a greater or lesser degree, according to what he wishes or is able to do.

But you deny that the creature itself is good and call it unclean, saying that the devil produces flesh from a more polluted material of evil. Consequently, you reject it with horror as though it were one of the more unclean and savage bonds of your god.
