To your hearers, whom you said were distinguished from the priestly class, you permit such foods to be eaten as a concession—just as the Apostle permits certain people, by way of concession, not every form of marital intercourse, even that undertaken solely for the purpose of procreation, but intercourse undertaken because of lack of self-control, though still with one’s spouse (1 Cor. 7:5–6).

For nothing is granted by way of concession except a sin. This is what you think about every kind of fleshly food; this is what you yourselves learned from your heresy, and what you teach your hearers. You grant them this concession because they must be forgiven, since they provide you with the necessities of life, as I said—not saying that it is not a sin, but granting pardon to sinners. You yourselves, however, abstain from every such food as though from an evil and unclean contamination.

Consequently, the words of the Apostle that follow the passage with which you ended your recollection of this chapter are precisely what compel us to bring this testimony against you. I think you knew this, and that is why you first omitted those words and at the end said to us, “I do not see with what attitude or purpose you produce this chapter against us,” although you preferred to conceal rather than mention our very purpose.

For after the Apostle had said, “Abstaining from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful,” he continued: “and by those who know the truth, because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. 4:3–5).

These are the things you deny. You abstain from such foods with this intention, this will, and this belief: that they are evil and unclean by nature, not merely that they signify something.

In this matter you undoubtedly blaspheme their Creator. This is what belongs to the doctrine of demons. Do not, therefore, be surprised that the Holy Spirit prophesied this about you so long ago.

## Chapter VI

If you exhorted people to virginity in the manner in which apostolic teaching exhorts them—“He who gives in marriage does well, and he who does not give in marriage does better” (1 Cor. 7:38)—so that you declared marriage to be good but virginity better, as the Church does, the Church that truly is Christ’s Church, the Holy Spirit would not have foretold you in this way by saying, “forbidding marriage” (1 Tim. 4:3).

For the one who forbids marriage is the one who says that it is evil, not the one who places something better before this good.

In fact, you especially detest that sexual intercourse which alone is honorable and marital, and which is expressly set forth in marriage contracts: “for the purpose of begetting children.” Thus you truly forbid not so much intercourse as marriage.

Intercourse can also occur for the sake of lust, but marriage occurs only for the sake of children.

Nor should you say that you do not forbid marriage because you tolerate many of your hearers who are unwilling or unable to obey in this matter, while preserving your friendship with them. You have this tolerance in the necessity of social relations, but you have the prohibition in the doctrine of your error.

This is why earlier I postponed saying why Christ’s death seemed to you something to be proclaimed as deceptive and simulated, while his birth was not to be treated in the same way. [Col. 0495]

You proclaim and praise his death as the separation of the soul—that is, of your god’s nature—from the body of its enemies, namely, from the devil’s creation. Consequently, you believed that this was a thing worthy for Christ to commend, even if he did not die, by simulating death.

But in his birth, because you believe that your god was not released but rather bound, you did not wish to believe that Christ even imagined or simulated it. Thus Mary would not have displeased you so much if she had had intercourse and not conceived as she displeases you because she did not have intercourse and nevertheless gave birth.

You therefore see that there is a great difference between exhorting people to virginity by placing a greater good before a lesser good, and forbidding marriage by attacking more vehemently the intercourse of procreation, which alone is properly marital.

There is also a great difference between abstaining from foods because of the sacramental signification [Col. 0496] or for the discipline of the body, and abstaining from foods that God created on the claim that God did not create them.

The former, therefore, is the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles; the latter is the doctrine of lying demons.

*[Note: The manuscripts read “because of the sacramental signification.” The printed editions read “because of the sanctified signification.”]*

# BOOK THIRTY-ONE

[Col. 0495]

## Chapter I

Faustus said: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and contaminated nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled.”

It must also be considered whether it is advantageous for you to believe that this was said by Paul. For until now it has been evident not only that Moses and the Prophets were driven by demons when they enacted so many laws concerning distinctions among foods, but also that they themselves were impure and defiled in mind and conscience, so that what follows could appropriately be applied to them as well: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:15–16).

To whom could this apply more than to the Prophets and Moses, who are shown to have lived in a manner very different from what was fitting for those who knew God?

Until now, however, I had thought that, apart from adulteries, frauds, and murders, there was nothing else for which Moses and the Prophets might appear to have possessed polluted consciences. But now, since this passage demonstrates it, we are given to understand that their minds were also defiled in this respect: they thought that something was defiled.

Why, then, do you think that such people could even now have been granted a vision of the divine majesty, since it is written that no one except those pure in heart can see God (Matt. 5:8)?

Even if they had been free from unlawful crimes, this superstition alone—their abstinence from certain foods—could, if it contaminates the mind, have denied them the vision of divinity.

Daniel’s boast, and that of the three boys, has therefore also vanished and been extinguished. In Judaism they too had been regarded, until this preaching that nothing is unclean, as exceedingly chaste and sound-minded young men because, mindful of their ancestral traditions, they had diligently kept themselves undefiled from the banquets of the Gentiles, especially from sacrificial foods (Dan. 1:12).

Now at last it has become clear that they too were defiled in mind and conscience, especially when they kept their mouths from blood and savage foods.

*[Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts omit “their mouths.” Other manuscripts have “all” in its place.]*

## Chapter II

Perhaps ignorance excuses them, since this Christian faith, which teaches that all things are pure for the pure, had not yet appeared. They may themselves have thought that certain things were not pure.

But what excuse do you now use? [Col. 0496] Paul cries out that nothing is unclean, calls abstinence from foods a doctrine of demons (1 Tim. 4:1, 3), and calls those whose minds are polluted because they think something is defiled themselves polluted. Yet, as we have said, you not only abstain; you also seek glory from it and think that you are more acceptable to Christ the more abstinent you are from foods—that is, according to this judgment, the more and more defiled in mind and polluted in conscience.

Moreover, since there are three religions in the world that alike place the purification of the mind in chastity and abstinence, though according to very different rites—I mean the Jews, Christians, and Gentiles—from which of these religions does this statement come, the one that teaches that nothing is unholy?

Certainly it does not come from Judaism. Nor does it come from paganism, since paganism too distinguishes among foods. The only difference is that the Hebrew disagrees with the pagan about certain animals.

The Christian faith remains. If you think that this is its distinctive teaching—that nothing should be considered polluted—then you must first admit that there is not a single Christian among you. For, to say nothing of the rest, everyone among you considers carrion and sacrificial foods to be a significant defilement (Acts 15:29).

Or, if you practice this according to the law of Christianity, then this too is not the judgment of a religion that removes all abstinence from unclean foods.

Why, then, could Paul have said something that accords with no religion? For when the Apostle became a Christian from being a Jew, he did not so much cast off religion as change its rite.

But the person who wrote this chapter seems to me to have been supported by no religion whatsoever.

## Chapter III

*[The supplied source ends here, at the heading of Chapter III.]*
Therefore, if in the future, while searching the Scriptures for anything that harms our faith, you should find something, remember to bring it against us only when you have clearly seen that it is not contrary to you—just as you are accustomed to cite that passage concerning Peter, as though he once saw a vessel lowered from heaven containing every kind of animal and serpents; and, when he was astonished and marveling, a voice was heard saying to him: “Peter, whatever you see in the vessel, kill and eat.” He replied: “Lord, I will not touch anything common or unclean.” And again the voice said to him: “What I have sanctified, do not call unclean” (Acts 10:11–15).

Although this passage may perhaps signify something else allegorically, rather than an indifference regarding foods, nevertheless, since you are also pleased to understand it in this way, you must therefore eat indiscriminately every beast, as well as vipers [Note: [Col. 0497] Several manuscripts read “and hedgehogs”], and snakes, and every other kind of serpent, in accordance with Peter’s vision. For only then will you truly prove that you are obedient to the voice he is said to have heard. Yet remember always this as well: on account of that voice’s pronouncement, Moses and the Prophets have been condemned, since they thought that many things were polluted which God had sanctified.

## CHAPTER IV

AUGUSTINE replied: When the Apostle says, “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15), he intended the natures themselves that God created to be understood, in accordance with what Moses wrote in Genesis: “And God made all things, and behold, they were very good” (Genesis 1:31); not the symbolic meanings according to which, through that same Moses, God distinguished clean things from unclean things (Leviticus 11). Since we have already said much about this in many places, it will be enough for the present to have given this brief reminder.

Accordingly, those who, even in the time of the revelation of the New Testament, still thought that the shadows of future things had to be observed in such a way that they insisted that the Gentiles could not receive the salvation that is in Christ without them—these, the Apostle calls unclean because they had carnal opinions, and unbelieving because they did not distinguish the time of grace from the time of the Law. He says that nothing is clean to them because they used neither the things they rejected nor the things they consumed in a holy and righteous manner. Thus all unbelievers are included, but you especially, Manichaeans, for whom absolutely nothing is clean.

For even the food you eat, although you separate it with great care, as though from contact with flesh, is not clean for you, since you say that it was created by no one except the devil. You even claim that, by eating it, you cleanse your god, who is bound and polluted within it. At least you yourselves would seem clean to yourselves, since he supposedly deserves to be cleansed in your bellies. But you also maintain that your bodies are the nature and handiwork of the nation of darkness, while your souls are still polluted by those very bodies.

What, then, is clean for you? Not the things you consume; not the place into which you put what you consume; not even you yourselves, who cleanse what you have consumed. You see, therefore, for whose sake the Apostle then uttered this statement. Yet he uttered it in such a way that it applied to all unbelievers and unclean persons, while exposing and convicting you especially and above all.

“All things, then, are clean to the clean” according to the nature in which they were created. Yet not all things were clean according to their symbolic meaning for the first Jewish people; nor are all things suitable for us, either for the health of the body or for the customs of human society. But when each thing is assigned what belongs to it and preserves the natural order, all things are clean to the clean; whereas to the unclean and unbelieving, such as you especially are, nothing is clean.

You would yourselves profitably say the Apostle’s remaining words, if you wished your seared conscience to be healed. For he continues: “But both their mind and their conscience are polluted.”

# BOOK THIRTY-TWO

[Col. 0497]

## CHAPTER I

FAUSTUS said: If you accept the Gospel, you must believe everything written in it. What then? Because you accept the Old Testament, do you therefore believe indiscriminately everything written in it? Surely you extract from it only those prophecies that indicated that a king would come for the Jews, because you think that he is Jesus, together with a few common precepts of civic morality, such as “You shall not kill” and “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:13–14). You pass over the rest and consider it no less than those things that Paul regarded as refuse (Philippians 3:8).

What, then, is strange or surprising if I too, reading from the New Testament only the purest things and those compatible with my salvation, pass over what was deceitfully introduced by your predecessors and disfigures both its majesty and its grace?

## CHAPTER II

If the Father’s Testament contains certain matters in which it ought to be heard only sparingly—for you wish the Jewish Law to belong to the Father, and we know how many things in it cause you horror and how many cause you shame, so that, as far as your mind is concerned, you yourselves long ago judged it not to be sincere, although, as you believe, the Father himself wrote part of it with his finger and Moses, faithful and upright, wrote part—do you think that the Son’s Testament alone could not have been corrupted, and that it alone contains nothing that ought to be rejected?

Especially since it is not established that it was written either by him or by his Apostles, but long afterward by certain men of uncertain name. To ensure that their writings would not be denied credibility because they were writing things they did not know, they placed at the head of their writings partly the names of Apostles and partly the names of those who seemed to have followed the Apostles, asserting that they had written according to them.

For this reason they seem to me to have inflicted a particularly grave injury upon the disciples of Christ: they attributed to them writings that were discordant and mutually contradictory, and professed to write according to them Gospels filled with so many errors and so many contradictions in both their narratives and their opinions that they agree neither with themselves nor with one another.

What else is this than slandering good men and bringing the harmonious company of Christ’s disciples under accusation of discord? Since we, in reading these writings, have noticed this with a perfectly sound perception, we judged it entirely reasonable to accept from them what is useful—that is, what builds up our faith and advances the glory of Christ the Lord and of his Father, almighty God—and to reject the rest, which agrees neither with their majesty nor with our faith.

## CHAPTER III

Accordingly, as I began to say, you do not believe that circumcision in the Old Testament is to be understood carnally, although it is written that way (Genesis 17:9–14); nor that the Sabbath is to be honored in idleness and rest, although it is read that way (Exodus 31:13); nor that God is to be appeased by sacrifices and offerings, as Moses seems to teach (Leviticus 1). You have despised these practices as wholly alien and far removed from Christian observance, and as in no respect credible.

Some of them, however, you have divided into two, embracing part and rejecting part. Thus, with regard to Passover—which is itself an annual sacred observance of the Old Testament, and concerning whose celebration it is written that you must not only slaughter and eat a lamb at night, but also abstain from leaven for seven days and be content with unleavened bread and bitter herbs (Exodus 12)—you accept Passover but omit that observance and custom by which it was decreed that the same practice should be maintained.

Likewise, you observe the seven-week period—that is, Pentecost—which Moses likewise judges should be marked by a particular kind and number of sacrifices (Leviticus 23); but you reject the condemned part of it, namely, the very rites and sacrifices, because these do not agree with the Christian faith.

Regarding the command to abstain from ordinary foods, you considered it appropriate and firmly believed that carrion and sacrificial meat are certainly unclean (Acts 15:29). But you did not wish to hold the same belief about pork, nor about the hare or hedgehog, nor about mullets and squids, nor about the other kinds of fish that suited your taste, although Moses testifies that all these things are unclean (Leviticus 11).

## CHAPTER IV

As for the following matters from the Old Testament, I believe you are now unwilling even to hear them, much less to admit them: fathers-in-law sleeping with daughters-in-law, as Judah did; fathers with daughters, as Lot did; Prophets with prostitutes, as Hosea did; husbands selling the nights of their wives to lovers, as Abraham did; one husband joining himself to two sisters, as Jacob did; rulers of the people, and those whom you would consider especially inspired, consorting by the thousand and the hundred with prostitutes, as David and Solomon did.

Or consider also what is prescribed by the law concerning marriage in Deuteronomy: that the wife of a deceased brother, if he died without children, must marry the surviving brother, and that he must raise up offspring from her in place of his brother, giving the child born from her his brother’s name. If the man refused to do this, the woman was to bring before the elders a complaint about this impiety of her kinsman, so that they might summon him and restrain him with censorial severity. If he persisted in his refusal, he was not to escape punishment before them, but was to be stripped of the shoe from his right foot, struck in the face by the woman mentioned above, spat upon, and cursed; and he was to depart bearing this perpetual disgrace in his posterity (Deuteronomy 25:5–10).

These, then, and other things of this kind, are both examples and laws of the Old Testament. If they are good, why do you not imitate them? If they are bad, why do you not condemn their author—that is, the Old Testament itself? Or if you too think that these things were inserted into it falsely, just as we believe that such things were inserted into the New Testament, then we are equals.

Stop, therefore, demanding from us in the New Testament what you yourselves do not observe in the Old.

## CHAPTER V

For my part, as far as I judge, since you have wished it already to be accepted that the Old Testament too is from God, it is much more convenient and excusable for you, while not observing its commandments, to admit that it has been corrupted by inappropriate additions than to despise it as inviolate and uncorrupted.

Accordingly, I have always held, and still hold, this opinion concerning you whenever the question is asked why you violate the commands of the Old Testament: either, as wise men, you despise its false statements, or, as obstinate and irreligious men, you neglect its true ones.

Meanwhile, since you compel me to believe everything inserted in the records of the New Testament if I accept it as a whole, know that you too, as far as your mind is concerned, do not believe many things contained in the Old Testament, although you profess to accept it as a whole.

For you do not even count among the acknowledged and credible statements of that book that everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed (Deuteronomy 21:23), since this certainly applies also to Jesus; nor that the person who has not raised up offspring in Israel is to be held accursed, since this would include all virgins and the children of God; nor that the person who has not circumcised the flesh of his foreskin is to be utterly cut off from his people (Genesis 22:14), since this too applies to every Christian; nor that the person who has violated the Sabbath is to be killed by stoning (Numbers 15:35); nor that no one who has broken any one commandment of the Old Testament is to be spared.

If you believed all these things and firmly held that they were equally commanded by God, believe me, you would have been the first to lay hands upon Christ; nor would you now be angry with the Jews, who pursued him with heart and strength and thereby fulfilled the commandments of their god.

## CHAPTER VI

I certainly know that you do not dare to call these things false, but say that they were commandments given to the Jews for that particular time, namely, until the coming of Jesus. Since he has come, having been foretold, as you wish, by the Old Testament, he himself now teaches us what we should accept from it and what we should leave aside.

But whether the Prophets foretold Jesus we shall see later. For the present I must answer this: if Jesus, announced through the Old Testament, now judges and sifts it [Note: [Col. 0500] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “brings to an end.” Some manuscripts read “determines.”], teaching that little of it should be accepted but very much rejected, and if the Paraclete promised to us from the New Testament likewise teaches what we ought to accept from it and what to reject—for Jesus himself, when promising him, says in the Gospel, “He will lead you into all truth, and he will announce all things to you and remind you of them” (John 16:13)—then we too should be permitted, through the Paraclete, as much freedom in the New Testament as you show yourselves permitted, through Jesus, in the Old.

Unless perhaps that Testament of the Son seems more valuable to you than the Father’s, if indeed it belongs to the Father: so that, while so many things are rejected from the Father’s Testament, there is nothing in this one that ought not to be approved, especially since, as we have said, it is established that it was written neither by Christ nor by his Apostles.

## CHAPTER VII

Therefore, just as you admit from the Old Testament only the prophecies and those civil precepts pertaining to the discipline of common life that we mentioned above, while you have set aside circumcision, sacrifices, the Sabbath and its observance, and unleavened bread, what is unreasonable if we too, accepting from the New Testament only what we find to have been spoken in honor and praise of the Son’s majesty either by him himself or by his Apostles—but by Apostles already perfected and faithful—have passed over the rest, whether it was spoken simply and ignorantly at that time by inexperienced men, or presented obliquely and maliciously by enemies, or asserted imprudently by writers and handed down to later generations?

I mean such matters as this very claim that he was shamefully born of a woman, circumcised in the Jewish manner, offered sacrifice in the Gentile manner, humbly baptized, led by the devil through the wilderness, and most miserably tempted by him.

With these matters excluded, and with anything falsely introduced by the writers from the Old Testament under the guise of testimony likewise excluded, we believe the rest—especially the mystical crucifixion of his cross, by which the wounds of our soul’s passion are displayed; then his saving precepts; then his parables; and his entire divine discourse, which chiefly sets forth the distinction between the two natures and is beyond doubt his own.

There is therefore no reason why you should now think that I must believe everything contained in the Gospels, when you, as has been shown above, scarcely touch the highest liquor of the Old Testament with your fingertips, as the saying goes.

## CHAPTER VIII

AUGUSTINE replied: We rightly praise all the Scriptures of the Old Testament as true and divine. You attack the Scriptures of the New Testament as falsified and corrupted [Note: [Col. 0501] Some manuscripts read “blame.”].

We not only say that the things we do not now observe from the books of the Old Testament were nevertheless appropriately commanded at that time and for that people, and that in those very things we do not observe meanings are signified for us to understand and hold spiritually; we also demonstrate and teach this in the apostolic writings.

But you criticize everything in the books of the New Testament that you do not accept, and assert that it was spoken or written neither by Christ nor by his Apostles. You see, therefore, how great the difference is between us and you in this matter.

When you are asked why you do not accept everything in the books of the New Testament, but in those books in which you approve certain things reject, criticize, and accuse many others, claiming that they were inserted by corrupters, do not take as an example the distinction found in our faith or observance. Instead, give an account of your presumption.

## CHAPTER IX

For if we are asked why we do not worship God by the rite in which the Hebrew fathers worshiped him during the time of the Old Testament, we answer that God commanded something else for us through the fathers of the New Testament. This is not contrary to the Old Testament, since the same thing was previously foretold in it.

For this very matter was foretold through the Prophet: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a New Testament over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah, not according to the Testament that I made with their fathers, on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt” (Jeremiah 31:31–32).

Behold: this too was prophesied—that the former Testament would not continue, but that a New Testament would come.

If someone objects that we do not belong to the house of Israel and the house of Judah, we defend ourselves by apostolic teaching, because the Apostle teaches that Christ is the seed of Abraham and says to us, who belong to his body: “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed” (Galatians 3:29).

Further, if we are asked why we hold to the authority of a Testament whose rite we do not observe, we answer this also from the apostolic writings. For the Apostle says: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of future things” (Colossians 2:16–17).

In this way he shows both why these things must be read and accepted—namely, so that we do not extinguish the prophecy, since they were made as shadows of future things—and why we should not concern ourselves with those who wish to judge us on this account, because we no longer observe them physically.

Elsewhere he said something similar: “These things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Therefore, when something is read in the instrument of the Old Testament which in the New Testament we are either not commanded to observe or are even forbidden to observe, we must inquire what it signifies, not criticize it. For by the very fact that it is no longer observed, it is shown not to have been condemned but fulfilled. We have already said this often and at length.

## CHAPTER X

Consider, for example, the very matter that Faustus, in his ignorance, has now brought against the commandments of the Old Testament as a crime: that a brother was commanded to marry his brother’s wife so that he might raise up offspring not for himself but for his brother, and that the child born from her should be called by his brother’s name (Deuteronomy 25:5–10) [Note: [Col. 0502] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “which would be born from her there.”].

What else does this prefigure in symbolic form except that every preacher of the Gospel ought to labor in the Church in such a way that, when his brother—that is, Christ, who died for us—has died, he raises up offspring for him, and that what has been raised up should receive his name?

Accordingly, in fulfilling this—not now carnally in the foregoing symbolism, but spiritually in the completed reality—the Apostle, recalling that he had begotten them in Christ Jesus through the Gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15), rebukes and corrects them when they wish to belong to Paul: “Was Paul crucified for you?” he says, “Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (Ibid. 1:13).

It is as though he said: “I begot you for your deceased brother; you are called Christians, not Paulians.”

But anyone chosen by the Church for the ministry of evangelization who refuses it is deservedly and rightly despised by the Church herself. This is why the woman is commanded to spit in his face—not without the sign of this disgrace that the shoe of one foot is removed, so that he may not belong to the lot of those to whom the Apostle himself says, “and having your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6:15), and concerning whom the Prophet says, “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isaiah 52:7)!

The person who holds the evangelical faith in such a way that it benefits him and he does not refuse to benefit the Church is rightly understood to be shod on both feet. But the person who thinks that, because he has believed, sufficient provision has been made for himself, while he avoids the task of winning others, will not merely symbolize the disgrace of the unshod man but will bear that disgrace fulfilled in himself.

## CHAPTER XI

What of the fact that he also objects to our celebrating Passover, while mocking us because we do not celebrate it in the manner of the Jews? We possess the sheep rather in the reality of the present Gospel, not in the shadow of what was to come. We commemorate its slaughter, both daily and especially in our annual solemnity; we do not foretell something still to come, but commemorate what has already happened.

For this reason the day of our solemn Passover does not coincide with the day of the Jews’ shadowy celebration, so that we might also include the Lord’s day on which Christ rose.

Those who are Christians of sound faith observe unleavened bread not in the leaven of the old life, that is, of wickedness, but in the truth and sincerity of the faith itself (1 Corinthians 5:8)—not for seven days, but every day. This was signified by the number seven, since every day revolves in a seven-day cycle.

Although this is somewhat laborious in the present age, because “the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted” (Matthew 7:13), a sure reward is nevertheless reserved. For that labor itself was signified by the bitter herbs, since they are somewhat bitter.

## CHAPTER XII

We also celebrate Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day from the Lord’s passion and resurrection—on which he sent us the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete whom he had promised (Acts 2:1–4).

This future event too was signified through the Jews’ Passover, when, on the fiftieth day after the celebration of the slaughtered sheep, Moses received on the mountain the Law written by the finger of God (Exodus 19–31).

Read the Gospel and notice that there the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God (Luke 11:20).

The things that were accomplished with outstanding excellence on particular days are celebrated annually in the Church, so that a festival celebrated by all may preserve their necessary and beneficial remembrance.

If you wish to know why we celebrate Passover: because Christ was sacrificed for us at that time.

If you wish to know why we do not celebrate it according to the Jewish rite: because that was a prefiguration of the true one that was to come, whereas this is a commemoration of the one already fulfilled. What is future and what is past are not expressed in the same way even in our own words. We have already spoken sufficiently about this in the present work.

## CHAPTER XIII

But if you also ask why, among all the foods from which that people was forbidden in the shadow of future things, we do not eat meat from carrion or sacrificial offerings, hear this as well, and at last place truth before the calumnies of vanity.

Why is it not expedient for a Christian to eat sacrificial meat? The Apostle says: “I do not want you to become partners with demons.” He does not criticize the sacrifice itself, which the fathers performed as a prefiguration of the blood of the sacrifice by which Christ redeemed us. Rather, he says: “The things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.” Then he added what I have just said: “I do not want you to become partners with demons” (1 Corinthians 10:20).

For if the nature of sacrificial meat itself were unclean, it would contaminate even someone who was unaware of what he was eating. It would be no less unclean because it was received unknowingly rather than knowingly. But the concern is conscience, so that no one may appear to have shared in the things of demons.

As for carrion, I think that its use as human food was not admitted because it is the diseased flesh of animals that have died rather than been slaughtered, and is not suitable for the health of the body, for whose sake we take nourishment.

The command given in symbolic form to the ancients concerning the pouring out of blood—that is, the command given to Noah himself after the flood (Genesis 9:6)—we have already shown what it signified, as many understand (Acts 15:29).

In the Acts of the Apostles, this command is also said to have been given as a law by the Apostles: that the Gentiles should abstain only from fornication, from sacrificial offerings, and from blood—that is, that they should eat no flesh whose blood had not been poured out.

Others do not understand it in this way, but think that the command to abstain from blood meant that no one should pollute himself by homicide. It would take too long, and is not necessary, to discuss this now. For even if the Apostles at that time commanded Christians to abstain from the blood of animals, so that they would not eat strangled meat, they seem to me to have chosen, for that period, something easy and in no way burdensome to observe. In this way the Gentiles might observe something in common with the Israelites on account of that cornerstone which makes the two into one (Ephesians 2:11–22).

At the same time, they were reminded that in Noah’s ark, when God gave this command, the Church of all nations had been symbolized, a prophecy of which was beginning to be fulfilled as the Gentiles came to the faith.

But when that period had passed during which those two walls—one coming from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision—although united in the cornerstone, still stood out as distinct through certain peculiarities of their own, and when the Church of the Gentiles had become such that no carnal Israelite appeared within it, what Christian now observes this rule: that he does not touch thrushes or smaller birds unless their blood has been poured out, or that he does not eat a hare if it has been killed by a blow to the neck without a bleeding wound?

And if a few people still happen to fear touching such things, they are mocked by the rest. Thus that statement of truth has taken possession of everyone’s mind in this matter: “It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out” (Matthew 15:11). It condemns not any kind of food admitted by human society, but the sins committed by wickedness.

## CHAPTER XIV

We have already shown in a sufficiently full discussion why the deeds of the ancients were written down, preserved, and commended with such reverence for Scripture itself—both those that appear to foolish and uneducated people to be sins although they are not, and those that truly are sins.

We have also already answered, in its proper place, the matter concerning the curse upon the one who hangs on a tree and the one who has not raised up offspring in Israel, when we previously disposed of these objections (above, Book 22).

Indeed, we defend all these matters—both those about which we have discussed individually in the earlier parts of this work and those similar matters that Faustus included in the discourse to which we are replying—with one most firmly established principle of truth, which we have received from the authority of the holy Scriptures.

We praise, accept, and approve everything written in those books of the Old Testament as having been written most truly and most usefully for eternal life. But the commandments in them that we do not observe through bodily practice we understand to have been rightly commanded at that time; we have learned that they were shadows of future things; and we now recognize that they have already been fulfilled.

Accordingly, whoever at that time failed to observe even those practices that were commanded to be performed for the sake of signification paid the penalties established by God according to the strictest justice, just as now, if anyone dares with sacrilegious presumption to violate the sacraments of the New Testament, which have been distinguished according to the requirements of the present age.

Just as the righteous men of that time, who did not refuse even death for the sake of those sacraments, are rightly praised, so now the holy martyrs are praised for the sake of these sacraments.

And just as a sick person ought not to criticize medical treatment if it prescribes one thing for him today and another tomorrow, even forbidding what it had prescribed earlier—for this is how the method of healing his body proceeds—so the human race, from Adam to the end of the age, as long as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15), is sick and wounded. It ought not to criticize divine medicine if God commands that in some matters one thing be observed first and in others something else later, especially since he promised that he would prescribe something else.

## CHAPTER XV

There is therefore no comparison in the analogy Faustus puts forward: that the Paraclete, since he was prophesied in the New Testament, selected from it what you should believe and showed what you should reject, just as Christ did for us from the Old Testament, in which he likewise was prophesied.

This argument would have some appearance of plausibility if there were anything in the books of the Old Testament that we said had not been rightly spoken, divinely commanded, or truthfully written.

We say none of this. We accept everything: both what we observe, so that we may live rightly, and what we do not observe, so that we may nevertheless see that those things, once commanded and observed in prophecy, are now being fulfilled.

Furthermore, just as we read that the Paraclete was promised in those books, not all of which you wish to accept, so we read that he was sent in the book whose very name you fear to mention.

For in the Acts of the Apostles, as I have often recalled, including shortly before, it is stated most clearly that the Holy Spirit was sent on the day of Pentecost. He also demonstrated by his work who he was. For those who first received him spoke in all languages (Acts 2), so that by this sign he might also promise that the Church would exist in all languages—that is, among all nations—and would proclaim him with complete truth as Father and Son.

## CHAPTER XVI

You must therefore now say why you do not accept everything from the books of the New Testament. Is it because they are not the writings of Christ’s Apostles, or because the Apostles of Christ taught something wicked?

You reply: “Because they are not the writings of Christ’s Apostles.” For the other statement—that the Apostles of Christ did not teach correctly—is the claim of pagans.

What, then, do you say? From where do you show that those Scriptures were not delivered by the Apostles? You reply: “Because many things in them are contrary both to one another and to themselves.”

This is entirely false; you do not understand. For whatever Faustus has brought forward that seemed to you to be of this kind, it has been shown not to be so; and whatever of this kind you bring forward, we shall demonstrate the same.

Who, then, would tolerate a reader or hearer daring to accuse a Scripture of such authority more readily than he would accuse the defect of his own dullness?

Or do you say that the Paraclete taught you that these Scriptures are not the Apostles’ but were written by others under their names? At least, then, show that this Paraclete himself is the one from whom you learned that these writings are not the Apostles’.

Will you say, “Christ promised him and sent him”? You are answered: Christ certainly neither promised nor sent this person, and at the same time it is shown when he sent the one whom he promised.

Prove, then, that Christ sent him. From where do you assert the identity of your author—or rather, your deceiver? You reply that you prove it from the Gospel.

From which Gospel? The one you do not accept in its entirety, the one you say has been falsified. Who, then, first declares his own witness to have been corrupted by falsehood and afterward produces him for testimony?

If we believe that witness when you wish us to and do not believe him when you do not wish us to, then we are no longer believing him but you. But if we were willing to believe you, we would not demand a witness from you.

Furthermore, the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, was promised in such a way that it was said: “He will lead you into all truth” (John 16:13). How, then, will he lead you into the truth if he teaches you that Christ is a deceiver?

Moreover, even if you could demonstrate that all the things read in the Gospel concerning the promise of the Paraclete were such that they could be understood only of your Manichaeus, just as it is shown that the Prophets spoke of Christ things that could not possibly apply to anyone else, nevertheless, when you brought these statements from the codices that you say were falsified, we would say that this very passage was false and had been inserted there by your earlier corrupters: that you read there something written about Manichaeus in such a way that we could not understand it of anyone else.

Tell me, what would you do except cry out that you could not possibly have falsified codices that were already in the hands of all Christians? As soon as you began to do so, you would be convicted by the truth of older copies.

Therefore, for the very reason that you could not corrupt them, no one else could have corrupted them either. For whoever had first dared to do this would have been refuted by comparison with many older codices, especially since the same Scripture was contained not in one language but in many.

Even now, certain errors in codices are corrected either from older copies or from the preceding language.

Thus you are forced either to acknowledge those codices as truthful—and they immediately overturn your heresy—or, if you call them deceptive, you cannot establish the Paraclete by their authority, and you overturn your own heresy.

## CHAPTER XVII
To this must be added the fact that these words were spoken in the promise of the Paraclete, so that they completely exclude Manichaeus, who came after so many years, from this suspicion. For since the Holy Spirit was going to come immediately after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, John stated most plainly: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). If, then, this was the reason he was not given—because Jesus had not yet been glorified—then, plainly, once Jesus had been glorified, there was already reason for him to be given at once.

For the Cataphrygians also claimed to have received the promised Paraclete, and on this account they deviated from the Catholic faith, attempting to prohibit what Paul permitted and to condemn second marriages, which he allowed. They lay in ambush under these words: “He himself will lead you into all truth,” as though Paul and the other Apostles had not taught all truth, but had reserved a place for the Paraclete of the Cataphrygians. They also applied to this purpose what Paul says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when perfection has come, what is in part will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13:9–10). Thus, supposedly knowing and prophesying only in part, the Apostle said, “Let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if he marries” (ibid. 7:36), and therefore the perfection of the Phrygian Paraclete abolished this.

When it is said to them that they have been condemned by the authority of Churches promised so long beforehand and spread throughout the whole world, they reply that this too has been fulfilled in themselves: namely, what was said of the Paraclete, “The world cannot receive him.” Are these not also the words you customarily quote: “He himself will lead you into all truth”; “When perfection has come, what is in part will be abolished”; and “The world cannot receive him” (John 14:17)—claiming that they were foretold of your Manichaeus? What heresy, finally, could arise under the name of the Paraclete that would not dare plausibly to apply all these statements to itself? Is there any heresy that does not call itself the truth—and, the more arrogant it is, call itself perfect truth as well—so that it promises to lead people into all truth and attempts to abolish the teaching of the Apostles, which contradicts its error, as though through that teaching perfection had come?

And since the Church holds what the Apostle most emphatically commended: “If anyone proclaims to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9), when someone begins, by proclaiming something else, to be accursed by the whole world, will he not immediately say, “This is what was written: ‘The world cannot receive him’”?

## CHAPTER XVIII

How, then, will you be able to prove what is demanded of you: that the Paraclete is the one from whom you learned that the Gospel writings are not those of the Apostles? For we too prove that the Holy Spirit is not the Paraclete except the one who came immediately after Jesus had been glorified. For this reason he had not yet been given: because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

We also prove that he himself leads people into all truth, because no one enters into truth except through love. “The love of God,” the Apostle says, “has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

We further teach that Paul did not say, “When perfection has come,” except of that perfection which will exist in the attainment of eternal life. For when he was speaking of this, he said: “For now we see through a mirror, in a riddle; but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:10, 12). Here, unless you plainly wish to be insane, you will admit that you do not see God face to face. Therefore that perfection has not come to you.

In this way the Apostle clearly explained what he thought about the matter; nor will this be granted to the saints until what John also says has come to pass: “We are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Then the Holy Spirit will lead us into all truth; of him we have now received a pledge.

But the statement “The world cannot receive him” was certainly spoken of those who in the Scriptures are accustomed to be called “the world”: lovers of the world, or the ungodly, or the carnal. Of such people the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:14). They are said to belong to this world so long as they cannot understand anything beyond those bodily things that they have perceived in this world. So also you understand nothing else: when you marveled at this light of the sun and moon, you imagined all divine things to be of such a kind, following that empty talker whom, deceived and deceiving others, you call the Paraclete.

Therefore, since you are in no way able to show how he is the Paraclete, you have no basis for teaching that you discovered by some firm authority how these Gospel writings—which you do not wish to accept in their entirety—are not those of Christ’s Apostles. It remains, then, for you to say that you discovered this because they contain things that tarnish Christ’s glory: namely, because they relate that he was born of a virgin, circumcised, that a sacrifice was offered for him—the kind that was offered at that time—that he was baptized, and that he was tempted by the devil.

## CHAPTER XIX

Apart from these matters and the testimonies from the Old Testament inserted into those writings, you admit, in accordance with what Faustus says, that you accept the rest—and especially his mystical nailing to the cross, by which the wounds of your soul’s suffering are displayed.

“Next,” he says, “come his salutary commandments and parables, and his entire divine discourse, which chiefly sets forth the distinction between two natures; there can be no doubt that it is his.”

You see, then, what you are doing: removing all authority from the Scriptures, so that each person’s own mind becomes the authority for what he approves or rejects in each Scripture. That is, faith is not subjected to the authority of the Scriptures; rather, he subjects the Scriptures to himself. Something does not please him because it is read as written in a sublime authority; instead, it appears to be correctly written because it has pleased him.

Where are you committing yourself, wretched soul, wrapped in carnal clouds? Where are you committing yourself? Remove authority; let us see. Remove authority; give an account. Is your reasoning brought to this point: that your long theatrical story cannot find an ending unless God’s nature is believed to be violable and corruptible?

Finally, how do you know that there are eight earths and ten heavens, that Atlas bears the world and Splenditenens [“Light-holder”] suspends it, and innumerable things of this kind? How do you know these things?

“Clearly,” you say, “Manichaeus taught me.”

But miserable one, you believed him; for you did not see them. If, then, you subjected yourself to an utterly unknown and insane authority concerning thousands of fabulous fantasies with which you have been shamefully impregnated, so that you believed all these things simply because they were written in those books which, in pitiable error, you decided must be believed—even though none of them is demonstrated to you—why do you not rather submit yourself to the authority of the Gospel, so firmly founded, so stable, so widely proclaimed with such glory, and commended by the most certain succession from the time of the Apostles down to our own days, so that you may believe, see [Note: Am. and the manuscripts read: “live”], and learn even that all those things which offend you offend you because of a vain and perverse opinion?

Would it not rather be true that the immutable nature of God assumed something from mortal creation, and, remaining immutably within it, truly rather than deceptively did and suffered whatever it was fitting for that creature to do and suffer for the salvation of the human race from which it had been taken, than that you should believe God’s nature to be violable and corruptible, unable to be wholly liberated and cleansed once polluted and oppressed, but condemned by the supreme necessity of God to the eternal punishment of the universe?

## CHAPTER XX

“But,” you say, “I believed what he did not show me because, in this very world, he clearly showed me two natures, namely, that of good and that of evil.”

But this very thing, miserable one, is the reason you were deceived: because, just as in that Gospel Scripture, so also in this world you could regard nothing as evil except what offended your carnal sense—such things as a serpent, fire, poison, and the like—and nothing as good except what caressed that same carnal sense with some pleasure, such as the pleasantness of flavors, the sweetness of scents, the sight of this light, and whatever else may similarly have delighted your ears, eyes, nostrils, palate, or sense of touch [Note: “or the sense of touch” (vel palpatui) has been added from the manuscripts].

But if you had first contemplated the whole creation in such a way that you attributed it to God the Creator, as though reading a great book of the nature of things; and if, whenever anything there offended you, you had rather believed that its cause might be hidden from you as a human being than dared to criticize anything in God’s works, you would never have fallen into those sacrilegious absurdities and blasphemous fictions by which, not understanding the origin of evil, you attempt to fill God with every evil.

## CHAPTER XXI

Now, if you ask us how we know that these writings belong to the Apostles, we answer you briefly that we know it in the same way that you know those writings to belong to Manichaeus, which you pitiably place above this authority.

For if someone were to raise this question against you and cast in your way the scruple of contradiction, saying that the books you produce are not Manichaeus’ books, what would you do? Would you not rather laugh at the madness of someone who, against a matter confirmed by so extensive a chain and succession, should utter such an impudent assertion?

Therefore, just as it is certain that those books belong to Manichaeus, and one who comes from elsewhere, born so much later, is entirely deserving of ridicule if he brings against you a dispute of this kind, so it is certain that Manichaeus—or the Manichaeans—are deserving of ridicule, or even pity, for daring to say anything of this kind against an authority so firmly established, preserved and carried forward by certain successions from the time of the Apostles down to the present.

## CHAPTER XXII

The authority of Manichaeus must therefore now be compared with the authority of the Apostles. For it is just as certain that these writings belong to the Apostles as those belong to him.

Who compares Manichaeus with the Apostles except one who separates himself from Christ, who sent the Apostles? Or who has ever conceived, in the words of Christ, two natures mutually opposed and deriving from their own principles, except one who does not understand the words of Christ?

The Apostles, as disciples of the truth, proclaim Christ’s birth and true passion. Manichaeus, however, boasts that he leads people into all truth, and wishes to lead them into such a Christ that he proclaims the falsity of Christ’s own passion.

The Apostles proclaim that Christ was circumcised in the flesh which he received from Abraham’s offspring; Manichaeus proclaims that God himself, in his very nature, was cut to pieces by the race of darkness.

The Apostles proclaim that, in place of the infant Christ’s flesh, a sacrifice was offered—the sacrifice that was then piously performed [several manuscripts omit “for the infant”; Erasmus’ edition has “while making an offering” in its place]; Manichaeus proclaims that not a member of flesh, but a member of the divine substance itself, was presented to be sacrificed to all the demons and delivered over to the nature of the opposing race.

The Apostles proclaim that Christ was baptized in the Jordan in order to provide an example; Manichaeus proclaims that God himself was submerged by himself in the pollution of darkness, and would not emerge whole, but that whatever part of him could not be cleansed would be punished with eternal condemnation.

The Apostles proclaim that Christ’s flesh was tempted by the leader of the demons; Manichaeus proclaims that a part of God was possessed by the race of demons. The Apostles say that Christ’s flesh was tempted so that he might teach resistance to the tempter; Manichaeus says that it was possessed so that it could not be restored to the Father or to the victor.

Finally, Manichaeus announces something else from the teaching of demons, as though he were more eminent; but the Apostles commend their teaching from the doctrine of Christ, so that whoever announces anything else is to be accursed (Galatians 1:8–9).

# BOOK THIRTY-THREE

## CHAPTER ONE

Faustus said:

“It is written in the Gospel: ‘For many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 8:11). Why, then, do you not accept the Patriarchs?

“Let it be far from us to envy any mortal whom God, perhaps looking upon him with compassion, has at some time brought back from destruction to salvation. But we attribute this to the mercy of the one who showed mercy, not to the merit of the one whose blameworthy life you cannot deny.

“Accordingly, if this testimony of Christ that you cite is certainly about the fathers of the Jews—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—although they themselves were extremely disgraceful, as Moses, their descendant, more or less indicates, or whoever else was the author of this history called Genesis, who wrote accounts of their lives worthy of every hatred and disgust, nevertheless let them also now be in the kingdom of heaven; let them be in a place which they had neither believed in nor hoped for, as is more or less evident from their own books—provided, however, that this is established: even by your own admission, they were released by Christ our Lord, after a long interval, from the gloomy and punitive custody of hell, where the merits of their lives were holding them, and through his mystical passion they were able, if they did arrive there, to reach the very place of which this is written about them [perhaps: ‘if they arrived at the place of which this is written’].

“For since our same Lord also freed a certain thief from the cross and said that on that very day he would be with him in the paradise of his Father (Luke 23:43), surely no one would envy him, nor could anyone be so inhuman as to be displeased by an act of such great kindness.

“Yet we will not therefore say that the lives and conduct of thieves ought to be approved by us, simply because Jesus granted forgiveness to a thief; nor, because he forgave publicans and prostitutes their sins and said that they would even precede into the kingdom of heaven those who behaved arrogantly (Matthew 21:31). When the Jews accused a woman caught in injustice and adultery, he himself acquitted her, instructing her to cease sinning (John 8:3–11).

“Therefore, if he did something of this kind also with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, thanks be to him. It is fitting that he should act in such ways toward souls who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).

“But one thing nevertheless troubles me in your opinion: why do you hold this only concerning the fathers of the Jews, and not concerning the other patriarchs of the Gentiles as well—that they too at some time experienced this grace of our Liberator? Especially since the Christian Church is more clearly established from their children than from the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

“But you will surely say that those men worshiped idols, whereas these worshiped the omnipotent God, and that for this reason Jesus took care of these alone. Thus the worship of the omnipotent God thrusts one into Tartarus, while the Son needs the help of the one who worshiped the Father?

“But you may have it your way. Let us agree, I say, that they have been brought back to heaven—not because they deserved it, but because divine mercy overcomes the force of sins.”

## CHAPTER II

Nevertheless, whether this too was said by Christ, the very variation among the writers makes us doubtful and uncertain. For two Evangelists, Matthew and Luke, tell together the story of a certain centurion whose servant was then ill, and on whose account Jesus appears to have said this very thing: namely, that he had not found such great faith in Israel as in that man, although he was a Gentile and pagan. He had said that he was not worthy for Jesus to enter under his roof, but asked only that Jesus give the command by a word and his servant would be healed.

Matthew alone, however, adds that Jesus continued by saying:

“Truly I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will be sent into the outer darkness.”

By “many” he indicated the pagans who would come, on account of the centurion, since he too was a Gentile and yet such faith had been found in him [perhaps: “apart from the centurion”]. By “the children of the kingdom” he meant the Jews, in whom no faith had been found.

Luke, however, although he too thought this event necessary and memorable enough to insert among Christ’s miracles in his Gospel, makes no mention there of Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob. If someone says that he omitted this because Matthew had already said it sufficiently, why, then, does he relate the event itself concerning the centurion and his servant, which Matthew’s diligence had likewise already made abundantly known to us?

But this is false. For concerning the request that Jesus come, Matthew indeed says that the centurion himself came to him to ask for healing; Luke, however, does not. Rather, he says that the centurion sent Jewish elders to him. Perhaps the centurion feared that Jesus would reject him as a Gentile—since they plainly wish Jesus to be a Jew [Note: Lov.: “since here some people”; Am. and Er.: “since these indeed”; the manuscripts: “since indeed,” omitting “here.”]—and the elders began to persuade Jesus, saying that the man was worthy for him to grant this, because he loved their nation and had built the synagogue for them (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:2–10).

It was as though this too pertained to the Son of God: that the Jews should have deserved the construction of their synagogue from a pagan centurion.

Luke nevertheless did not entirely suppress this statement. I think he remembered that it might indeed have been genuine, but he changes its setting and applies it to another cause entirely unlike it. He says that Jesus told his disciples:

“Strive to enter through the narrow door, for many will come seeking to enter, and they will not be able. But when the master of the household has entered and shut the door, you will begin to stand outside and knock, saying, ‘Lord, open to us.’ And answering, he will say, ‘I do not know you.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets and synagogues.’ And he will say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.’ There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all the Prophets entering into the kingdom of God, while you are cast out. And they will come from east and west and south and north, and recline in the kingdom of God” (Luke 13:24–29).

Matthew also did not fail to write this very thing: that many will be excluded from the kingdom of God—those, namely, who will have borne Christ’s name only, but will not have done his works (Matthew 7:21). Yet there too he makes no mention at all of Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob.

Likewise, Luke did write about the centurion and his servant, but he too bears no testimony there whatever concerning Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob. Since it cannot be established with certainty where this was said, there is nothing to prevent us from not believing that it was said.

## CHAPTER III

Nor is it without reason that we never bring our ears to such discordant and varied Scriptures without judgment and reasoning. We examine everything, compare one passage with another, and weigh whether each statement could have been spoken by Christ.

For many words of our Lord have been inserted by your predecessors into their discourses [or: “into the sayings of our Lord”], and although marked with his name, they do not agree with his faith. This is especially so because, as we have often already proved, these writings are neither his nor written by his Apostles. Rather, long after their assumption, they were gathered from reports and opinions by certain half-Jews—who themselves did not agree with one another. Yet by attaching the names of the Lord’s Apostles, or of those who appeared to have followed the Apostles, to all the same material, they falsely claimed that they had written their errors and lies in accordance with them.

But have it your way. For the moment, as I say, I will not contend with you too vigorously over this chapter, since the point I stated earlier is sufficient defense for me—and one which you yourselves cannot deny: before the coming of our Lord, all the Patriarchs of Israel and the Prophets lay in the darkness of Tartarus according to their merits.

Therefore, if they were ever liberated by Christ and brought back to the light, what bearing does this have on hatred of their lives? We hate and reject not what they were—that is, human beings—but what they were like—that is, evil people. Nor do we reject what they now are—that is, purified—but what they once were—that is, impure.

Thus, for the present, however much you may wish this chapter to mean otherwise, it causes us no difficulty: whether it is true, in which case Christ’s mercy and goodness are commended here; or false, in which case the crime remains with its writers. Either way, we are safe, as always.”

## CHAPTER IV

Augustine replied:

“How are you safe, wretched man? How are you safe when you say that you hate the Patriarchs as impure, while you still lament that your god is impure?

“You have granted that those Patriarchs were purified and given blessed rest after the Savior’s coming. But your god, even after the Savior’s coming, still lies in darkness, is still immersed in every disgrace, and still wallows in every impurity. Thus not only was the life of those men better than your god, but even their death was happier.

“In what abodes the righteous were dwelling who had departed this life before Christ came in the flesh, and whether Christ’s passion transferred them also to something better—since they had believed not only that he would come, suffer, and rise again, but had also foretold these very things, as was fitting, through the prophetic Spirit—must be investigated in the holy Scriptures, if it can in any way be investigated clearly. We must not pursue the rash opinions of just anyone, much less the perversities of so execrable a heresy, whose adherents wander so far from the truth [some manuscripts: ‘the perversity of those who wander so far from the truth’].

“Faustus vainly promises himself, through this evasive argument, that something can be granted to anyone after this life which he did not secure for himself in this life. It is good for you, while you are living here, to abandon this error and to know and hold the truth of the Catholic faith. Otherwise, what the unjust man promises himself will be far from him, when what God has threatened against the unjust begins to occur.”

## CHAPTER V

Concerning the life of the Patriarchs, I have already answered the slanderous man at sufficient length, as I judged. The Lord bore witness to them—not as though they had been corrected only in death or justified after his passion—when he admonished the Jews that, if they were Abraham’s children, they should do the works of Abraham; and when he said that Abraham desired to see his day and rejoiced when he saw it (John 8:39, 56).

He also bore witness to them when he said that the angels carried the poor man, despised by the wealthy man in his misery, into Abraham’s bosom—that is, into some great and hidden secret of peaceful blessedness (Luke 16:23).

What shall I say about the Apostle Paul? Surely he too praises Abraham as justified after death, because before he was circumcised he believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Romans 4:3). Paul values this so highly that he says we became his children, although we were not propagated from his flesh, for no other reason than that we follow the footprints of his faith.

## CHAPTER VI

But what am I to do with you, whose iniquity has so deafened you against the testimonies of Scripture that you dare to say that whatever is brought forward from them against you was not spoken by the Apostle, but was written under his name by some unknown falsifier?

The doctrine of demons that you preach is so openly alien to Christian teaching that you cannot defend it under the name of Christian doctrine in any way unless you say that the Apostles’ Scriptures are false.

Wretched enemies of your own soul! What writings will ever possess the weight of authority if the Gospel and Apostolic writings do not? Of what book will it be certain who its author is, if it is uncertain whether the writings which the Church says and holds were propagated from the Apostles themselves are truly theirs, while it is to be regarded as certain that the Apostles wrote what heretics opposed to this Church produce under the names of their authors, men who existed long after the Apostles?

As though, even in secular writings, there were not authors whose identity was entirely certain, although many works were later produced under their names and rejected for that reason: either because they did not at all agree with what was known to be theirs, or because they had not become known at the time when those authors wrote, nor deserved to be brought forth and commended to later generations by those authors themselves or by their closest associates.

To omit others, were not certain books produced under the name of Hippocrates, the most distinguished physician, but not received by physicians as authoritative? Some similarity of subject and language did not help them, since, when compared with those works that were known to be genuinely Hippocrates’, they were judged unequal; and because, unlike his other writings, they had not become known from the time at which he wrote.

But the writings by comparison with which those that are produced from elsewhere are rejected—how is it established that they are Hippocrates’, and if someone denies this, how is he refuted, or at least laughed at, except because a continuous chain of succession has commended them as his from Hippocrates’ own time down to the present, so that it would be madness to doubt it?

How do people know that the books of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Varro, and other such authors are theirs, except through the same continuous testimony of successive generations?

Many people have written many things about ecclesiastical writings—not indeed with canonical authority, but out of some desire either to help or to learn. How is it established who wrote each work, except that, in the times when each person wrote, he made his work known and published it as he could; and from there, through a continuing awareness passed on to others, spread more widely, and strengthened among later generations, it reached even our own times? Thus, when asked whose book a particular work is, we do not hesitate over what answer we ought to give.

But why should I go back into the distant past? Look at these writings that we now have in our hands. If, after some time had passed from our present life, someone were to claim that either those writings were Faustus’ or these were mine, how could he be refuted except because those who now know these facts will convey their knowledge to people far in the future through continuing successions of descendants?

Since this is so, who could be blinded by such madness as to say—unless he has been overthrown by consenting to the wickedness and deceit of lying demons—that the Church of the Apostles did not deserve to have so faithful and numerous a concord of brothers transmit their writings faithfully to later generations, when they have preserved their sees in the most certain succession down to the present bishops, even though the same thing happens with the writings of all sorts of people, whether outside the Church or within it, with such ease?

## CHAPTER VII

“But,” he says, “their writings are found to contradict one another.”

You read with malicious intent; in your folly you do not understand; in your blindness you do not see. What great difficulty would there have been in examining these matters carefully and discovering the great and salutary agreement among the same writers, if contention had not perverted you and piety had not been lacking?

When has anyone, reading two historians who write about the same event, judged that both—or either—must be deceiving or deceived merely because one said something the other omitted? Or because one treated something more briefly, while nevertheless preserving the same meaning whole and intact, whereas the other arranged everything member by member, so as to explain not only what happened but also how it happened?

Faustus attempted to slander the truth of the Gospels on this very point, because Matthew said something which Luke omitted when relating the same event—as though Luke had denied that Christ said what Matthew wrote that he said.

There has never been any question at all about this, and no one except people who are utterly imprudent and unwilling or unable to consider such matters can raise it as an objection.

There is, however, a matter that believers often investigate and unbelievers often object to—unless, once admonished, they recover their senses—whether they are poorly educated or excessively contentious.

Matthew says: “A centurion approached him, asking him and saying.” Luke, however, says that he sent Jewish elders to Jesus, asking this very thing concerning his sick servant, so that Jesus might heal him; and when Jesus was approaching the house, the centurion sent others through whom he said that he was not worthy for Jesus to enter his house, nor was he himself worthy to come to Jesus.

How, then, according to Matthew, did he approach him, asking and saying, “My servant lies at home paralyzed and is grievously tormented” (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:2–10)?

This is understood as follows: Matthew briefly embraced the true and complete meaning [Note: Lov. alone reads “full”], saying that the centurion approached Jesus, without saying whether he approached by himself or through others; and saying that he spoke to him about his servant, without specifying whether he spoke by himself or through others.

What then? Is human speech not full of such expressions, when we say that someone has approached a matter very closely even though we do not yet say that he has reached it? Do we not also very commonly speak of reaching someone through others, although reaching seems to be something to which nothing more could be added? We often say, “He conducted his case and reached the judge,” or, “He reached this or that powerful person,” although he usually does so through friends and does not see at all the person whom he is said to have reached.

For this reason, such people—who somehow reach the inaccessible minds of the powerful, whether by themselves or through others, through the art of ambition—are now even commonly called “reachers” [perventores].

What then? When we read, do we forget how we customarily speak? Or was God’s Scripture going to speak with us in a manner different from our own usage?

This, then, is how I would answer the stubborn and disorderly, on the basis of ordinary speech.

## CHAPTER VIII

But those who investigate these matters not contentiously but calmly and faithfully should approach Jesus—not in the flesh, but in the heart; not by bodily presence, but by the power of faith, like that centurion. Then they will better understand what Matthew said.

To such people it is said in the Psalm: “Approach him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm 33:6).

Thus the centurion approached Christ more closely—the centurion whose faith Christ praised—than did those through whom he sent his words.

Something similar is also found in what the Lord said: “Someone touched me,” when the woman who suffered from an issue of blood touched the fringe of his garment and was healed.

He seemed to say this astonishingly to his disciples: “Who touched me?” and “Someone touched me,” while the crowd pressed around him. Finally, they answered him: “The crowds press around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” (Luke 8:43–46).

Therefore, just as they pressed against him but she touched him, so they had been sent to Christ, but the centurion approached him more closely.

Thus Matthew both preserved a mode of expression that was not altogether unusual and communicated something mystical. Luke, on the other hand, also showed how the event happened, so that from this we would be compelled to notice how Matthew expressed it.

I wish that one of these empty-headed people who maliciously raise such petty questions as though they were great objections against the Gospel would himself tell the same story twice—not falsely or deceptively, but with the full intention of conveying and explaining it—and that his words were taken down in writing and recited back to him.

Would he not say something more or less, or place something in a different order—not only words but also events? Would he not state something from his own interpretation as though another person had said it, when he had not heard that person say it but clearly knew what he had wished and intended? Would he not briefly embrace the truth of some meaning whose details he had previously explained more explicitly?

And if there is anything else that can perhaps be comprehended by definite rules, how does it happen that, whether in the separate accounts of the same event by two people or in two accounts by one person of one and the same event, many differences are found, yet none is contradictory; many variations, yet none is opposed?

In this way everything is resolved over which these wretched men tie their own necks, so that they keep the spirit of their error within and admit no breath of salvation from outside.

## CHAPTER IX

Therefore, after all Faustus’ slanders have been refuted—at least those in the chapters to which, so far as the Lord has deigned to assist me, I have replied sufficiently, as I think, and at considerable length—I briefly admonish you who are held by that utterly impious and detestable error.
