If you wish to follow the authority of the Scriptures, which must be preferred above all else, follow that authority which, from the time of Christ’s own presence, through the arrangements of the Apostles and the certain successions of bishops from their sees [Am., Er., and most manuscripts: “and the other successions”], has been preserved, commended, and glorified throughout the whole world and has reached the present day.

There you will see both the obscure things of the Old Testament revealed and the things foretold fulfilled.

But if you are moved, as though by reason, first consider who you are and how little qualified you are to comprehend the nature—not to mention God’s nature—of your own soul: to comprehend it, that is, as you claim to wish or have wished, by the most certain reasoning rather than by utterly empty credulity.

Since you have been completely unable to do so—and undoubtedly, as long as you remain as you are, you will be entirely unable to do so—at least consider, or believe, what is naturally implanted in every human mind, provided it has not been disturbed by the perversity of a corrupt opinion: that God’s nature and substance are wholly immutable and wholly incorruptible.

Then you will immediately cease to be Manichaeans, so that at some time you may also be Catholics.

# Two Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Concerning the Proceedings with Felix the Manichaean

[Note: [Col. 0520] Written in the year of Christ 404, on December 7 and 12.]

[Note: [Col. 0517] CONCERNING THE SUBSEQUENT DISPUTATIONS AGAINST FELIX. See book 2, chapter 8, of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 633, at the words “Against a Manichaean,” through col. 634, at the words “On December 7.” M.]

[Note: [Col. 0519] We have corrected the *Proceedings with Felix* against the manuscripts of Victorinus, Floriacensis, and Casalensis; against the various readings of three Belgian manuscripts; and against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0519] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

## NOTICE

[Col. 0517]

Concerning these same disputations against Felix, Possidius writes in chapter 16 of Augustine’s *Life*:

> “When the blessed Augustine also disputed publicly in the church at Hippo, with the notaries recording the proceedings and the people standing by, with a certain Felix—one of the number whom those same Manichaeans call the Elect, who had come to Hippo to sow the same error—after the second or third conference that Manichaean, his foolishness and the error of that sect having been frustrated, was converted to our faith and to the Church, as the document itself, when reread, will be able to show.”

When Possidius indicates that three conferences were held, he includes the one that Augustine held with Felix on the preceding day without notaries, before the official proceedings. Hence, at the beginning of the first book he says: “Yesterday you know that you said you could defend the writings of the Manichaeans.” Felix refers to that earlier conference also when he says in book 1, chapter 14: “If you bring me the writings of the Manichaeans, the five authorities whom I mentioned to you.” Understand this as, “Yesterday I mentioned”: for on the actual day of the official proceedings nothing is recorded as having been said by Felix about those five authorities.

Compare Augustine’s Letter 79, written to a certain Manichaean presbyter, whom in the preface to the second volume we conjectured to be Felix. The following public profession, made by a certain Felix who had been converted from the Manichaean heresy, appears to concern this same man. Baronius published it in the Appendix to volume 5 of the *Annals*, transcribing it from a manuscript of the Gervasian College in Paris. After the book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, the following is written there:

> “I, Cresconius, one of the Manichaeans, have written this: if I should depart before the proceedings are signed, I am to be regarded as though I had not anathematized Manichaeus. I, Felix, converted from the Manichaeans, declare under God’s attestation that I truthfully confess everything concerning those Manichaeans or Manichaean women whom I know to be in the Caesarean districts: Maria and Lampadia, the wife of Mercurius the silversmith, with whom we also prayed together with Eucharistus the Elect; Caesaria and her daughter Lucilla; Candida, who lives at Tipasa; Victorina the Spaniard; Simplicianus, the father of Antoninus; Paul and his sister, who are at Hippo. Through Maria and Lampadia I also learned that these women were Manichaeans. This alone I know: if anything else should be discovered that I knew beyond what I have said, I myself confess that I am guilty.”

## BOOK ONE. PROCEEDINGS OF THE FIRST DAY

[Col. 0519]

### CHAPTER ONE

In the sixth consulship of the Emperor Honorius, on December 7, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church of the people of Hippo Regius [Note: [Col. 0519] Perhaps “of the people of Hippo Regius.”], said:

“Yesterday you know that you said you could defend the writings of the Manichaeans and assert that they contain the truth. If you are willing, or presume yourself able, to do this today, speak.”

Felix the Manichaean said:

“I do not deny that I said I would defend my law, if the authorities of my law are brought forward publicly.”

When Bishop Augustine had produced the letter of Manichaeus called *The Letter of the Foundation*, he said:

“If I read from this codex, which you see me carrying, the letter of Manichaeus that you call *The Letter of the Foundation*, can you recognize whether it is that letter itself?”

Felix said:

“I recognize it.”

Augustine said:

“Take it yourself and read.”

When Felix had received the codex, he read:

> “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ by the providence of God the Father. These are saving words from the eternal and living fountain. Whoever hears them and first believes them, and then keeps what has been conveyed, will never be subject to death but will enjoy eternal and glorious life. For surely that person must be judged blessed who has been instructed in this divine knowledge, through which, having been liberated, he will remain in eternal life.”

Bishop Augustine said:

“You certainly recognized the letter of your Manichaeus?”

Felix said:

“I recognized it.”

Augustine said:

“Prove to us, then, how this Manichaeus is an apostle of Jesus Christ. For we never read of him in the Gospel among the Apostles; and we know who was appointed in the place of Judas the betrayer, namely Saint Matthias (Acts 1:26). Everyone recognizes who was afterward called by the Lord’s voice from heaven, namely the apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0519] Erasmus, the Lyons edition, and the Venice edition: “this is the apostle Paul.” M.] (Acts 9). Prove to us, then, that this Manichaeus is an apostle of Christ, which he dared to place at the beginning of his letter.”

### CHAPTER TWO

Felix said:

“Let Your Holiness prove to me that it is written in the Gospel, Christ saying, ‘I go to the Father, and I will send you the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who will lead you into all truth’ (John 16:13). Prove to me from outside this writing that this is the writing of the Holy Spirit, which Christ promised, where all truth is to be found. And if I find the truth in other books that do not belong to Manichaeus, and Christ handed them down, for Christ said that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, would himself lead into all truth—according to Christ’s saying, I reject the writings of Manichaeus.”

Augustine said:

“Since you have been unable to prove how Manichaeus is an apostle of Christ, and you demand that I prove how he sent the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom he promised, so that you may then reject the writings of Manichaeus if you find Christ’s promise fulfilled apart from those writings—although you ought first to have answered my questions, nevertheless I shall answer first and show you when the Holy Spirit whom Christ promised was sent.”

And he turned to the Gospel and to the Acts of the Apostles.

### CHAPTER THREE

When he had received a Gospel codex, he recited:

> “While they were speaking these things, Jesus stood in their midst and said to them, ‘Peace be with you; I am he, do not be afraid.’”

As he was reading, he said:

“This occurred after the resurrection.”

And after saying this, he read:

> “But they were troubled and terrified, thinking that they saw a spirit. And he said to them, ‘Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, for I myself am he; touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.’ And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. While they still did not believe and were marveling for joy, he said, ‘Do you have anything here to eat?’ They offered him a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb. When he had eaten before them, he took the remains and gave them to them, and said to them: ‘These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.’” [Col. 0521] “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures, and said to them: ‘Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things. And I will send upon you the promise of my Father; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high’” (Luke 24:36–49).

When he had returned the Gospel codex, he took the Acts of the Apostles and said:

“We have heard that the holy Evangelist mentioned in the Gospel Christ’s promise, which is in the Gospel according to John, whom Felix here has mentioned. For when the Lord said, ‘I send you the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete’ (John 16:7), the evangelist John wrote this. But what I have just read was attested by the evangelist Luke, and agreed with the truth of the apostle John. Let us also see how what the Lord promised was completed and fulfilled, so that when the fulfillment of the Lord’s promise has been demonstrated from the canonical books of the holy Church, we may not seek another Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, and fall into the snares of deceivers.”

### CHAPTER FOUR

And he recited from the Acts of the Apostles:

> “I made my first account, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day on which he chose the Apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the Gospel. To them he presented himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and teaching them about the kingdom of God. He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the Father’s promise, ‘which,’ he said, ‘you have heard from my mouth; for John baptized with water, but you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you will also receive not many days from now,’ until Pentecost. Accordingly, when they had come together, they asked him, saying, ‘Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?’ But he said: ‘No one can know the time which the Father has placed in his own power; but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.’ When he had said these things, a cloud received him, and he was lifted up from them. And while they were watching him go into heaven, behold, two men stood beside them in white clothing. They said to them: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.’ Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. When they had entered, they went up to the upper room where Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James were staying. They all persevered with one accord in prayer, together with the women, Mary who had been the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter rose in the midst of the disciples [Note: [Col. 0521] The printed editions have “in the midst of the brothers.” The manuscripts have “in the midst of the disciples.” The Greek is *mathētōn*.], and said”—there was a crowd of about one hundred and twenty men [Col. 0522]—“‘Brothers, it was necessary that this Scripture be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of holy David concerning Judas, who was the guide of those who arrested Jesus, because he was numbered among us and had received a share in this ministry. He acquired a field from the reward of his injustice, and, having hanged himself, he fell headlong, burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out. This became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their language *Aceldemach*, that is, Field of Blood. For it is written in the Book of Psalms: “Let his estate become desolate, and let there be no one dwelling in it”; and, “Let another receive his episcopate.” Therefore, from these men who have accompanied us throughout the whole time in which the Lord Jesus Christ came upon us [Note: [Col. 0522] The printed editions have “among us.” The manuscripts have “upon us.” This agrees with the Greek, *eph’ hēmas*.], beginning from John’s baptism until the day on which he was taken up from us, one must become with us a witness to his resurrection.’ And he appointed two: Joseph, who was called Barsabas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. And he prayed, saying: ‘You, Lord, knower of all hearts, show which of these two you have chosen to receive the place of this ministry and apostleship from which Judas departed to go to his own place.’ And they cast their lots [Note: [Col. 0522] We have added “their,” from the manuscripts. The Greek has *autōn*.], and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven Apostles as the twelfth.”

When he had read this, he said:

“We have heard who was appointed in the place of Judas the betrayer, as I mentioned shortly before, so that no one might secretly intrude into the number of the Apostles and deceive the uninstructed by the title of apostleship.”

### CHAPTER FIVE

“Now let us see what we promised: how Christ’s promise concerning the Holy Spirit was fulfilled.”

And after saying this, he read at the appropriate place:

> “When the day of Pentecost had been completed, they were all together in one place. And suddenly a sound came from heaven, as of a violent wind being carried along, and it filled the whole house in which they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them, as of fire, which also rested upon each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit granted them utterance. Now there were inhabitants of Jerusalem, Jews, men from every nation under heaven. When the sound occurred, the crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language. They were amazed and wondered, saying to one another: ‘Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how do we each hear the language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, and Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia [Note: [Col. 0522] The printed editions had “Armenia and Cappadocia.” The manuscripts are corrected here in agreement with the Greek and Latin text of the Vulgate.], Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own languages the mighty works of God’” (Acts 1–2:11).

As he recited this, he said:

“Have you now heard how the Holy Spirit was sent? I have proved what you demanded of me. It remains for you to do what you promised: since we have found when the Holy Spirit whom Christ promised was sent, reject that writing which, under the name of the Holy Spirit, sought to defraud either reader or hearer.”

### CHAPTER SIX

Felix said:

“I do not deny what I said: when it has been proved to me that the Holy Spirit taught the truth that I seek, I shall reject that writing. For Your Holiness has just read to me the place where the Apostles received the Holy Spirit, and among those Apostles I seek one who will teach me about the beginning, the middle, and the end.”

Augustine said:

“If you read that the Lord said, ‘I send you the Holy Spirit, who will teach you the beginning, the middle, and the end,’ you rightly compel me to show whom the Holy Spirit taught.”

Felix said:

“Since Your Holiness says that the Apostles themselves received the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, I say again: let whichever of the Apostles you wish teach me what Manichaeus taught me, or let whichever of the Twelve you choose abolish his teaching.”

Augustine said:

“Far be it from the faith of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0523] The word “Apostles” is absent from the manuscripts.] that they should teach the sacrilegious doctrine of Manichaeus. But since you say that one of them ought to abolish the doctrine of Manichaeus, while the holy Apostles are no longer in the body, I, the least—not only of all the Apostles but of all bishops—for how could I aspire to the merits of the Apostles?—to the extent that the Lord has deigned to grant me from his own Spirit, abolish the doctrine of Manichaeus, when the sequel of that letter which you yourself do not deny to be Manichaeus’s begins to be read.”

Felix said:

“You said that the Apostles have departed from the body, but that their writings remain valid to this day. And because Your Holiness said, and because you gave permission to say whatever we wished without any fear, you said, ‘I abolish the law of Manichaeus.’ I also say, ‘Every human being is a liar; God alone is truthful’ (Psalm 115:2; Romans 3:4). The Scriptures of God speak.”

### CHAPTER SEVEN

Augustine said:

“You are indeed a human being, and, as the matter itself will now show, a liar. Since you have spoken what you wished—not from the Scripture of God—it is necessary that I too speak what I wish. If the teaching of your Manichaeus is true, it cannot be destroyed by me; if it is false, what difference does it make by whom it is destroyed? Nevertheless, since you spoke about the writings of the Apostles, saying that although they are not in the body, their writings are here, the Apostles were taken up before the error of Manichaeus had arisen in the world. Therefore, writings of the Apostles explicitly arguing against Manichaeus are not found. Yet what the apostle Paul, in this Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom he had received, foresaw would come concerning men such as Manichaeus was, and such as you are, I shall recite, so that you may recognize it.”

And having received the apostle Paul’s Epistle to Timothy, he read:

> “But the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer. By teaching these things to the brothers, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ” (1 Timothy 4:1–6).

As he read, he said:

“I say that this refers to you and to those who say that some creature of God is unclean, and who say that every sexual union, including that which takes place with one’s wife, is fornication. For this is what he says: ‘Forbidding marriage.’ I say that this has been designated and expressed through the spirit of prophecy. But if you deny that every sexual union is fornication, or if you say that every human food permitted and granted to human beings for eating is clean, you are not among those whom the Apostle prophesied. But if you are found to be among those whom I have described, behold, you have the apostle Paul destroying and abolishing the doctrine of the future Manichaeus. Therefore answer what I ask: Is every sexual union fornication, or is sexual union with one’s wife not a sin?”

### CHAPTER EIGHT

Felix said:

“Let what the Apostle said be recited to me again.”

And it was recited:

> “But the Spirit expressly says,”

and the rest as above.

Felix said:

“Manichaeus did not depart from the faith, as Paul says, in the way that others departed from the faith, as though into their own sect. Manichaeus departed from no sect, so that it could be said that he departed from the faith.”

Augustine said:

“Since I see that you do not wish to answer what you are asked, lest you be found either not to possess the Holy Spirit, whom we have already proved to have been sent to the Apostles, or not to belong to the number of those whom Paul designated as future, where he also prophesied about you yourselves, I shall answer briefly. To understand what you said according to your own meaning—‘They will depart from the faith’—only those depart from the faith who had been in some faith. But Manichaeus was in no faith from which he could depart; rather, he remained in the faith in which he was. This is what I ask you: whether Manichaeus—or rather, the doctrine of deceitful demons who spoke lies and who were in Manichaeus—has led any Catholic Christians astray, so that they departed from the faith.

“For if many are led astray by you, through you, and through that doctrine, so that they depart from the faith and pay attention to deceitful spirits such as existed in Manichaeus; and if they begin to say that every sexual union is fornication, which is why the Apostle says, ‘Forbidding marriage’; and if they begin to say that the flesh people eat is not God’s creation but the work of demons and is unclean, then it is clear that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who was in the apostle Paul, foretold these things concerning them: that they would depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits such as existed in Manichaeus.

“Since I have now answered, it is right that you answer what I asked: whether you do not say that every sexual union is fornication. Or, if you do not wish to answer this, answer what I asked first, so that you may prove Manichaeus [Col. 0525] to be an apostle of Christ. Or, if you do not wish to do that either, permit me to abolish his doctrine, as I promised when his letter, which you call *The Letter of the Foundation*, was being read.”

### CHAPTER NINE

Felix said:

“I answer what Your Holiness says, namely that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, came in Paul.”

Augustine said:

“Not in him alone.”

Felix said:

“I am speaking of him: because if in him [Note: [Col. 0525] The manuscripts have “because also in him.”], then in all. And if in him—for Paul says in another Epistle: ‘We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished’ (1 Corinthians 13:9–10).

“We heard Paul say this. Then Manichaeus came with his preaching, and we received him according to what Christ said: ‘I send you the Holy Spirit’ (John 16:7). Paul came and said that he too would come, and afterward no one came; therefore we received Manichaeus. Since Manichaeus came and through his preaching taught us the beginning, the middle, and the end; taught us about the world’s construction—why it was made, from what it was made, and who made it; taught us why there is day and why night; taught us about the course of the sun and moon—we believe that he is the Paraclete, because we did not hear this from Paul or in the writings of the other Apostles.

“Therefore I say again what I said above: if I hear in another writing, where the Paraclete speaks—that is, the Holy Spirit—about whatever I wish to ask, and you teach me, I shall believe and renounce my former belief.”

### CHAPTER TEN

Augustine said:

“You say that you do not believe that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, was in the apostle Paul because Paul says, ‘For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.’ From this you suppose that the Apostle, by these words, foretold someone else who would come after him and preach everything that he himself could not, because he spoke only in part; and you believe that this person is Manichaeus.

“First, I shall show from the Apostle’s own passage what the Apostle was speaking about. Then, since you said that Manichaeus taught you the beginning, the middle, and the end, and how and why the world was made, about the course of the sun and moon, and about the other matters you mentioned, it is not written in the Gospel that the Lord said, ‘I send you the Paraclete, who will teach you about the course of the sun and moon.’ He wished to make Christians, not astronomers. It is enough for human beings to know about such matters as much as they have learned in school, for ordinary human uses.

“But Christ said that the Paraclete would come, who would lead into all truth. Yet he did not say there, ‘the beginning, the middle, and the end’; he did not say, ‘the courses of the sun and moon.’ Or, if you think that this teaching belongs to that truth which Christ promised through the Holy Spirit, I ask you how many stars there are. If you have received that Spirit of which you speak, whose task, you say, is to teach the things about which I say that they do not belong to Christian discipline and teaching, you must state it and answer me.

“You have made yourself liable: if I ask you something about such matters and you do not answer, that Spirit of which it was said, ‘He will lead into all truth’ (John 16:13), will not appear to be in you—if these things belong to that truth. Therefore choose whether you wish and are prepared to answer me about these matters, as a man who has received the Spirit that leads into all truth, and who says that knowledge of these worldly things belongs to that very truth.

“I can tell you what belongs to Christian teaching. But you, who think that how the world was made and what occurs in the world belong to it, must answer me about everything. Clearly, once you have answered, you will have to prove your answer.

“But before you begin to speak, if perhaps you have something fabricated by the one whom you followed, I shall first teach what I promised: what the Apostle meant when he said, ‘We know in part, and we prophesy in part.’”

### CHAPTER ELEVEN

“For he was saying—as the reading itself will immediately show—that in this life, while a human being is here, he cannot attain everything; rather, in this life he attains only in part. But the Holy Spirit himself, who teaches in part in this life, will lead him into all truth after this life. To make this absolutely clear, hear the Apostle.”

And as he spoke, he read from the Apostle:

> “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished—for we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I abolished the things that belonged to childhood. For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:8–12).

As he read, he said:

“Now tell me: if the Apostle was predicting the future times of Manichaeus, do you now see God face to face?”

### CHAPTER TWELVE

Felix said:

“I cannot contend against your power, since the episcopal rank possesses remarkable power; and then there are the laws of the Emperors. Above, I asked you briefly [Note: [Col. 0526] The Lyons and Venice editions have *contendive*, “contentiously.” M.] to teach me what truth is. If you teach me what truth is, it will become clear that what I hold is false.”

Augustine said:

“It has become clear that you have been unable to prove that Manichaeus is an apostle of Christ. I shall briefly explain why you have been unable to do so.

“You said that you proved Manichaeus to be an apostle of Christ because Christ promised that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, would come; and because you did not find when the one whom Christ promised had come, you therefore believed that he was Manichaeus. But when I proved from the holy, ecclesiastical, canonical Scriptures the time when the Holy Spirit whom the Lord Christ promised would come—proved it with complete clarity—you turned aside and said that it had to be shown what he taught and whether he abolished the doctrine of Manichaeus.

“When I answered that Manichaeus came in the flesh after the Apostles, but that the Apostles themselves had preached their doctrine before Manichaeus was born, I nevertheless said that one of the Apostles, Paul, through the Holy Spirit who had come upon all the Apostles, had also prophesied about this doctrine of yours, since it was to come, and had called it the doctrine of deceitful demons who speak lies.

“I showed that the things Paul said would occur in that doctrine pertain to your profession: namely, the prohibition of marriage, since you say that every sexual union, even with one’s wife, is fornication; and abstinence from foods that God created, since I know that some among you call certain foods unclean, although Paul himself continues and says, ‘Every creature of God is good’ (1 Timothy 4:1–4).

“When I demanded that you answer this, you said that Manichaeus teaches you the beginning, the middle, and the end, the course of the sun and moon, and other such matters. When I showed that these things do not belong to Christian teaching, you answered that the apostle Paul himself said that he knows in part and prophesies in part.

“I said that we cannot know divine things while we are in this life, and that here we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face. I asked you whether you thought the apostle Paul meant that Manichaeus would come to teach what Paul could not, and whether this applied to you, who say that you have received that very Spirit and now see God face to face.

“Since you cannot do this, it is clear that the apostle Paul was speaking of that other life, concerning which John also says:

> ‘Beloved, we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is’ (1 John 3:3).

“When you heard this, you said that you were unable to withstand my power. But this power is not mine; if I possess any, it was given to me by him for refuting errors—he who is the power of all his faithful, who presume upon him with a full heart.

“You also said that the authority of the episcopal office frightened you, although you see with what peace we converse, with what calmness we dispute, and how the people present use no force against you and inflict no fear upon you, but listen with complete tranquility, as is fitting for Christians.

“You also said that you feared the laws of the Emperors. One whom the Holy Spirit filled would not fear them on behalf of the true faith. The apostle Peter too was afraid during the Lord’s passion and denied him three times. But when the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit whom Christ had promised, filled him, he was crucified for the Lord’s faith. The man whose first denial sprang from fear afterward fulfilled the most glorious passion of confession.

“Therefore, from the very fact that you have said you fear the laws of the Emperors—although the other matters are also sufficient—it is clear that you have not found the Spirit, the Paraclete, of truth. Even if you did not fear, you would be convicted on other grounds.”

Felix said:

“The Apostles were also afraid.”

Augustine said:

“They were afraid in order to take precautions, not so as to hesitate to proclaim their faith after being arrested. But from this point you ought already to have been afraid, so that we would not find you here. You are already in the midst of the proceedings. Why are you afraid, unless you have nothing to say? Even if you had feared the Emperors, you would have kept silent beforehand. But yesterday, when you gave a petition to the Curator and loudly proclaimed publicly that you were ready to be burned with your books if anything evil were found in them, you demanded the laws like a brave man; today you flee from the truth like a coward.”

### CHAPTER THIRTEEN

Felix said:

“I am not fleeing from the truth.”

Augustine said:

“Then say whether you see God face to face, according to your promise, since you said [Col. 0528] that the apostle Paul spoke of you, saying that you would receive the complete truth, so that we may understand—or believe—that the Apostle possessed it in part, while you possess it in its entirety.”

Felix said:

“I am not fleeing from the truth, but seeking the truth. What you say—that I do not possess it—must now be proved to me from the divine Scriptures. This is what I seek.”

Augustine said:

“First acknowledge that you have been unable to prove Manichaeus to be an apostle of Jesus Christ. Then, insofar as I am able, when all that is contrary has been uprooted from your heart through my ministry, with the Lord granting it, I shall implant in you the knowledge of truth, which leads to God, beginning with faith.”

Felix said:

“Since you say this in order that I should deny my law and accept another—one that is at least better, which is what I seek—I do not answer in such a way as to deny my law before I accept another.”

Augustine said:

“First, what is contrary is poured out of a vessel, and then what is good is put into it. Or, if you still hesitate to pour it out, defend what fills you. For, with the Lord’s help, I shall show you how full of impurity and blasphemies the doctrine of Manichaeus is, if you permit the letter whose beginning we have already discussed to be read. You were unable to prove that Manichaeus is an apostle of Christ, and for that reason you are delaying, so that the remainder may not be read, where your sacrileges are openly exposed. Or, if you permit it, let it be read.”

Felix said:

“I permit it, because you said that everything unclean must be poured out, and then good things are put in. This is what Your Holiness said. To this I reply: no one pours out water unless someone else has filled it.”

Augustine said:

“You see how thoughtlessly you have spoken—to put it mildly, and without calling it insane. I gave you an analogy from a vessel: no one can put anything into a vessel that is full unless what filled it is poured out.”

Felix said:

“You said one thing, and I said two.”

Augustine said:

“If you meant two vessels, shall we pour out and fill your equal [Note: [Col. 0528] He perhaps calls Cresconius Felix’s equal; we reported Cresconius’s words above in the Notice prefixed to these proceedings.], so that you may be able to pour out what you have?”

Felix said:

“We both have the same water.”

Augustine said:

“Since you are both full of your own water, what shall we fill you with in order to teach you, unless one of you pours out what he has? Or, if it is good and therefore ought to be retained, and that letter ought to be read in its defense, let us see whether even the remainder can be defended, if you failed at the very beginning. Or, if you say that you did not fail there, prove to us how Manichaeus is an apostle of Christ.”

### CHAPTER FOURTEEN

Felix said:

“Christ said that he would send the Holy Spirit, who would lead into all truth.”

Augustine said:

“If you possess that Spirit, attend to what I asked you long ago. You said that knowing even these worldly things belongs to his doctrine. Tell me how many stars there are, if you have been led into this entire truth.”

[Col. 0529] Felix said:

“I also say that if the Paraclete spoke through the Apostles and through Paul, I ask Your Holiness to show me the things I have already mentioned.”

Augustine said:

“Admit that you have been unable to show what I asked, and I shall show from the Scriptures what pertains to the Christian faith.”

Felix said:

“And I say that if you bring me the writings of Manichaeus, the five authorities whom I mentioned to you, I shall prove to you whatever you ask me.”

Augustine said:

“This letter, whose beginning we have opened, belongs to those five authorities. There we found written, ‘Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ.’ And I see that you do not explain that very beginning to me, because you do not prove how Manichaeus is an apostle of Jesus Christ.”

Felix said:

“If I do not prove it in this one [Note: [Col. 0529] The Louvain edition has “in this one.” The other books have “in this,” with *letter of the Foundation* understood.], I shall prove it in the second.”

Augustine said:

“In which second?”

Felix said:

“In *The Treasure*.”

Augustine said:

“Who wrote this *Treasure*, which you call by that name in order to deceive the wretched? Manichaeus? I do not want you to prove it to me from him, because that Manichaeus lies by saying that he is what he is not.” [Note: [Col. 0529] Erasmus, the Lyons edition, and the Venice edition present the passage as follows: “Augustine said: Who wrote this *Treasure*, which you call by that name in order to deceive the wretched? Felix said: Manichaeus. Augustine said: I do not want you to prove it to me from him, because Manichaeus lies by saying that he is what he is not.” M.]

Felix said:

“Prove it to me through another.”

Augustine said:

“What do you want for yourself—”

Should I prove it?

Felix said: “Because Manichaeus lies.”

Augustine said: “Because you cannot prove that Manichaeus speaks the truth, is it necessary for me to prove that Manichaeus lied?”

Felix said: “Why could I not prove it? Were the Scriptures I requested brought forward, and did I not prove it?”

Augustine said: “But you are requesting Manichaeus’s Scriptures, which we do not accept as authoritative. Prove it from another source. Yet from that very Scripture of Manichaeus I prove to you that Manichaeus lied and blasphemed.”

Felix said: “Let the books be brought.”

Augustine said: “The letter of Manichaeus that you call *The Foundation* is present. There is no beginning in a building except the foundation. If I show that he brought about a collapse in the very foundation, why should we investigate the rest of his construction?”

## CHAPTER XV

Felix said: “You say this while showing that there is a collapse in it [Note: [Col. 0529] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: ‘show in it that there is a collapse.’]; and I say: provide as many arbiters as you have here, and I will prove to you that he does not lie.”

Augustine said: “May it never be that we, or the human race, should regard as Manichaeans as many people as you see here.”

Felix said: “Provide those whom I requested from you.”

Augustine said: “Whom, then, do you want me to provide?”

Felix said: “Whomever you wish.”

Augustine said: “I provide these men. If you have better ones, ask for them.”

[Col. 0530] Felix said: “How do you provide these men?”

Augustine said: “Those present who are listening to us.”

Felix said: “These men do not favor me.”

Augustine said: “Then you are looking for people who will favor you, not people who will favor the truth?”

Felix said: “People who will listen to me—and not merely to me, but also to the Scripture itself—in order that it may be proved whether he speaks the truth or lies.”

Augustine said: “You see, then, that they are listening. Let us read the rest, since you have confessed that this letter belongs to Manichaeus.”

Felix said: “I do not deny it.”

Augustine said: “Then let it be read.”

## CHAPTER XVI

Felix said: “I have no arbiters.” And he added: “Let the chapter of that book be read.”

When it was being read and they had reached the passage where the same letter says:

“May the peace of the invisible God and the knowledge of the truth be with his brothers and beloved ones, who alike believe in and serve the heavenly commandments. And may the right hand of the Light guard you and rescue you from every evil assault and from the snare of the world; and may the devotion of the Holy Spirit open the innermost recesses of your heart, so that with your own eyes you may see your souls”—

Felix said: “Provide a Scripture that refutes this.”

Augustine said: “So far we have heard nothing evil, except that Manichaeus dared to call himself an apostle of Christ. The things he has said thus far still belong to the plasterwork of deception and to the sheep’s skin by which he first speaks good words to them, so that he may introduce evil. But let us see what he intends to introduce by these words. For if he introduces something evil, then these words too will be evil and deceptive; but if in what follows he says something good and true, we shall necessarily grasp the matter [Note: [Col. 0530] In the manuscripts: ‘we are refuted.’]. Permit, therefore, that the following passages be read.”

Felix said: “If, then, you assert that good things are placed first and evil things introduced afterward, how can I believe you, when you first say good things to me?”

Augustine said: “Thus far I have called these things neither good nor evil. I said, ‘So far we have heard nothing evil’; I did not say, ‘We have already heard something good.’ For I called only this evil: that he dared to say that he was an apostle of Christ. The words he has spoken in what follows will be evil if they introduce something evil; they will be good if they introduce something good. Permit, then, that the following passages be read. Why are you afraid?”

Felix said: “I am not afraid.”

Augustine said: “Permit them, then, to be read.”

Felix said: “Let them be read.”

## CHAPTER XVII

When it was being read and they had reached the passage where it says:

“Now his most splendid kingdoms were founded above the bright and blessed land in such a way that they could never be moved or shaken by anyone”—

Augustine said: “This land of which he speaks: where did he get it? Did he make it, or beget it, or was it equal and coeternal with him? I mean this bright and blessed land of which he speaks.”

[Col. 0531] Felix said: “How is it written: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the earth was invisible, capable of being defiled, and formless’? I understand it in this way: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the earth was.’ It seems to me that there are two earths, corresponding to what Manichaeus says about the two kingdoms.”

Augustine said: “Since you have recalled our Scripture, which you usually blaspheme, it is my responsibility to explain it and to show you that what is written there is free from blasphemy and accords with the truth, not with Manichaeus. Then you may answer me, on the second point, concerning what I asked.”

Felix said: “I will answer.”

Augustine said: “The words ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’ briefly summarize what God made. Then, because this earth that he had made was not yet visible before he distinguished and adorned it, the following passage explains what sort of earth God had made—the earth of which it had said, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth.’ It is as though, when we heard, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth,’ we asked, ‘What sort of earth?’ The text added and said: ‘But the earth’—that is, the earth God had made—‘was invisible and formless’ (Gen. I, 1–2). Thus it did not speak of two earths, but explained what that one was like.

“Now, then, answer me briefly concerning what I asked: this bright and blessed land of which Manichaeus speaks, above which the kingdoms of God were founded—was it made by God himself, or begotten from him, or coeternal with him? Answer one of these three without evasion, unless it troubles you.”

Felix said: “The Scripture itself interprets itself.”

Augustine said: “If, then, you know of a passage here where Scripture says that God either begot that land, made it, or that it was coeternal with him, open the passage you know and read it to me.”

Felix said: “It is not in this Scripture, but in another.”

Augustine said: “I believe you, because if that Scripture exists, you remember what it says there. Therefore answer me, since you know that Scripture; and if I say that it does not say this, you will convict me. But if I discover that it does say this, I shall argue on the basis of your own answer. So tell me whether God made this land, begot it, or whether it was coeternal with him—you who have read some book or other in which you say this is written.”

Felix said: “Since Your Holiness has just interpreted your Scripture as you wished, and I accepted your interpretation, you should likewise accept whatever I say.”

Augustine said: “For the present, if nothing in what I ask moves me to objection, I accept it. But if something does move me, I will indicate my objection to you, so that you may answer that.”

Felix said: “I have not answered what you said.”

Augustine said: “It is necessary first for you to answer what I asked. Nevertheless, I also answered you first, in case what I said did not move you; perhaps what you answer will not move me either. Answer, then, what I asked.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0532]

Felix said: “I will answer.” And he added: “You asked about that land in which God dwells: whether it was made by him, whether he generated it, or whether it is coeternal with him. I say that, just as God is eternal and there is no created thing with him, so everything is eternal.”

Augustine said: “Then he did not beget it, nor make it?”

Felix said: “No; it is coeternal with him.”

Augustine said: “But if he had begotten it, it would not be coeternal with him.”

Felix said: “What is born has an end; what is unbegotten has no end.”

Augustine said: “For whom, then, was he a father, or whose father was he—the one whom he has just called ‘father’? For if he had begotten nothing, he could not be a father.”

Felix said: “But there are other things that he generated.”

Augustine said: “Then those things that he generated are not coeternal with him—or are they also coeternal?”

Felix said: “Whatever God generated is coeternal with him.”

Augustine said: “Then you were mistaken when you said above, ‘Everything that is born has an end.’”

Felix said: “At the time I was speaking according to the generation of the flesh; I was mistaken.”

Augustine said: “You have confessed your error with great modesty; may you therefore deserve to understand the truth.”

Felix said: “May God bring that about.”

Augustine said: “Pay attention, then, so that you may begin to recognize the error of this doctrine. If the things God begot are not coeternal with him, then that land which God did not beget, in which all the things God begot dwell, is better than the land which you say was not begotten by him.”

Felix said: “All things are equal to one another, both those he generated and those he did not generate—that is, that land where he dwelt.”

Augustine said: “What, then? Is the one who generated them equal to all of them, or is he greater than they?”

Felix said: “The one who generated them, those whom he generated, and the place where they were set [Note: [Col. 0532] Er., Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read *posita sunt* (‘were placed,’ neuter) instead of *positi sunt* (‘were placed,’ masculine). M.]—all are equal.”

Augustine said: “Then they are of one substance?”

Felix said: “They are of one substance.”

Augustine said: “What God the Father is, that are his sons, and that also is that land?”

Felix said: “All are this one thing.”

Augustine said: “Then he is not the father of this land, but merely its inhabitant?”

Felix said: “Yes.”

Augustine said: “Thus he neither begot nor made it. I do not see how it belongs to him except by mere proximity—just as, if someone had a good neighbor, there would now be two things, both unbegotten: the land and the father.”

Felix said: “Rather, there are three: the unbegotten father, the unbegotten land, and the unbegotten air.”

Augustine said: “Is all this one substance?”

Felix said: “One.”

Augustine said: “And was it founded in such a way that it could never be moved or shaken by anyone?”

[Col. 0533] Felix said: “Movement and shaking are different.”

Augustine said: “Let them be different. But nevertheless, were they such that they could never be moved or shaken by anyone?”

Felix said: “There is a difference between being moved and being shaken.”

Augustine said: “That is not what I am asking you.”

Felix said: “But that is precisely how you want to hold me.”

Augustine said: “Understand it as you wish. Could it not be moved?”

Felix said: “I am not saying that it could not be moved; I am saying that movement is different.”

Augustine said: “But I said, ‘Neither moved nor shaken.’ I did not say, ‘It can indeed be moved, but cannot be shaken,’ or, ‘It can indeed be shaken, but cannot be moved.’ I spoke of both things: that it could neither be moved nor shaken.”

Felix said: “There is a difference between being moved and being shaken in both matters.”

## CHAPTER XIX

Augustine said: “Let us read the following, then, and see whether this god who had his kingdoms founded above the bright and blessed land—which could never be moved or shaken by anyone—feared no one, as he ought not to have feared anyone, since his kingdoms were founded in such a way that they could never be moved or shaken by anyone.”

And he read the following:

“Beside one part and side of that illustrious and holy land…”

As he read, he asked: “Which side? The right or the left?”

Felix said: “I cannot interpret this Scripture for you or explain what is not there. It interprets itself; I cannot say, lest I perhaps fall into sin.”

Augustine said: “Then let what follows be read.”

When it was being read and they had reached the passage that says:

“But the most blessed Father of the Light, knowing the great corruption and devastation that would rise from the darkness and threaten his holy realms, unless he set against it some excellent and glorious divine power, mighty in virtue, by which he might at once overcome and destroy the offspring of darkness, whose extinction would prepare perpetual rest for the inhabitants of the Light”—

Augustine said: “Now that open blasphemies have begun, if you think they should be defended, tell me: what harm could this race of darkness—which God appears to have feared, lest great corruption and devastation from the darkness break into his kingdoms—have done to God? Especially since he said above that his kingdoms were founded in such a way that they could never be moved or shaken by anyone. What, then, was this race going to do to him? Could it harm him, or could it not? Answer one of the two.”

Felix said: “I answer: If there is nothing opposed to God, according to what Manichaeus said in his Scripture—that there is another kingdom—for what reason was Christ sent, to free us from this snare of death? Whose snare and death is this? If there is no adversary opposed to God, why were we baptized? Why the Eucharist? Why Christianity, if nothing is opposed to God?”

Augustine said: “I see that you do not want to answer what I ask, but instead ask me questions so that I may answer you. I do not refuse to answer, provided that you remember that when you asked me, I answered you, whereas when I asked you, you did not want to answer me. But since you have asked me, hear the answer to your question.

“We say that Christ the Liberator came, and we say that we are freed from our sins, because we were not generated from the substance of God but were made by God through his Word. There is a great difference between something born from the substance of God and something made by God that is not from the substance of God.

“Whatever God made can be mutable; God himself, however, is not mutable, because the works cannot be equal to the craftsman and creator. But you said a little earlier, in answer to my question, that the Father who generated the sons of the Light, the air, the land itself, and the sons themselves are one substance and are all equal. You must therefore tell me how the race of darkness could harm this substance, which is surely incorruptible.

“For if it could harm it, it was not an incorruptible nature. But if it could not, there was no reason for battle to be stirred up or for the divine power of which he speaks to be sent here.”

Felix said: “I ask for a postponement, so that I may be able to answer.”

Augustine said: “When? Is an adjournment until tomorrow sufficient?”

## CHAPTER XX

Felix said: “Give me three days’ adjournment—that is, today, tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow—or until the day after Sunday, namely, the day before the Ides of December.”

Augustine said: “I see that you have asked for a postponement in order to answer. It is human to grant it to you. But if you cannot answer by the appointed day, what will happen?”

Felix said: “I will be defeated.”

Augustine said: “What if you flee?”

Felix said: “I will be liable before this city, everywhere, and before my own law.”

Augustine said: “Rather, say this: ‘If I flee, let me be regarded as though I had anathematized Manichaeus.’”

Felix said: “I cannot say that.”

Augustine said: “Then tell us openly that you are thinking of fleeing; no one is holding you.”

Felix said: “I am not fleeing.”

Augustine said: “As I see it, you do not want to depart as one defeated. But at least say this: ‘If I flee, I am defeated.’”

Felix said: “I have said it.”

Augustine said: “And how will it be evident that you fled because of the Proceedings?”

Felix said: “Order that I remain with whomever I choose.”

Augustine said: “Choose for yourself one of these brothers present here, who are standing by the barrier.”

Felix said: “Let me remain with the one who is in the middle.”

Augustine said: “As you have chosen, you shall remain with him until that day.”

Felix said: “Yes, and I agree to this.”

Boniface said [Note: [Col. 0534] Er., Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read these words and the preceding ones as follows: “Augustine said: ‘Choose for yourself one of these brothers present here who are standing by the barrier.’ Felix said: ‘Yes, and I agree to this—but with the one who is in the middle.’ Augustine said: ‘As you have chosen, you shall remain with him until that day.’ Boniface said, etc.” M.]: “Christ will grant that, if I come with him, he is a Christian.”

[Col. 0535] I, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church of Hippo Regius, have subscribed to these Proceedings, held in the church before the people.

[Col. 0536] I, Felix, a Christian and worshiper of the law of Manichaeus, have subscribed to these Proceedings, held in the church before the people.

# BOOK TWO: PROCEEDINGS OF THE SECOND DAY

[Col. 0535]

## CHAPTER I

When the appointed day had arrived—that is, the day before the Ides of December—the proceedings began in the Church of Peace.

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church of the regions of Hippo Regius, said: “You remember that, when we were speaking some time ago, you asked for a postponement because you could not answer at that time what I had asked. If, then, during so long an interval of time—after the fifth day, that is—you have thought of something, answer.

“This was what I asked you then: If nothing could harm God, why did he wage war against the race that you call the race of darkness, in that war mixing with the nature of the demons his own substance, which is what he himself is, as you said when questioned? But if that race could harm him, then you do not worship an incorruptible God, such as truth and apostolic teaching attest.”

Felix said: “After I left Your Holiness in order to return on the appointed day and answer your question—whatever you wished to ask—the appointed day arrived. Since I had no Scripture in my hands, because the books from which I could have instructed myself were not returned to me—for no one goes out to battle unless he has first been equipped [Note: [Col. 0535] Am. and the manuscripts: ‘having served as a soldier’ (*militatus*).], and no litigant can litigate without his documents—I likewise cannot answer without my Scripture.”

Augustine said: “You have thought up this evasion during all these days. It will not help you, since you have no answer to give in a lost cause and sacrilegious error. It is known to everyone who was present—and I see that those same people are still present—that you asked only for a number of days’ postponement. You should also have requested the codices when you asked for the postponement, if you thought that they could equip you to answer; but you did not do so.

“I know that you requested the codices, but not to inspect them for instruction. You requested them long before you asked for the postponement. When you asked for the postponement, however, you made no mention of having the codices returned to you for examination, so that you might be better prepared.”

Felix said: “Now I ask for the codices. Let them be returned to me, and I will come to the contest after two days. If I am defeated, I will submit to whatever you decide.”

Augustine said: “I do not think that you are inexperienced in this wicked sect, as you yourself admit. Everyone can already see that you have no answer, even if you do not admit it. But since you are asking again for your codices, which are being kept under the public seal, and say that after examining them you will be able to come prepared after two days, recall this established fact: you were unable to answer the questions put to you. Take your codices, then, and say what you want to have produced from them that you can examine now and answer.”

[Col. 0536] Felix said: “All the Scriptures that were taken from me. For this letter of *The Foundation* is the one that Your Holiness knows well—and I also said this—it contains the beginning, middle, and end. Let it be read, and whatever evil is alleged against my law, let it be proved. I deny it if those crimes alleged against my law are proved.”

Augustine said: “Since you admit that this is the letter in which the beginning, middle, and end of your doctrine are contained, consider how sacrilegious this beginning is: you say that God fought against the race of darkness and mixed with the nature of the demons a part of his own substance, which was to be polluted and bound, and which is what he himself is. It is so sacrilegious that it can scarcely be endured by those who hear it.

“This is alleged first against your sect, whether you call it the beginning, the middle, or the end—I do not greatly care about that distinction. What matters is that you do not deny that this has been read from the letter that you admit belongs to Manichaeus. This is what is alleged against you. Defend it, if you can, so that we may proceed to the other matters.

“Therefore I ask again: If you worship an incorruptible God, what could harm him—the unknown opposing race that you invent? If nothing could harm him, there was no reason for him to mix a part of his own substance with the nature of the demons. But if it could harm him, then you do not worship an incorruptible God.”

## CHAPTER II

Felix said: “Manichaeus says that there are two natures, and he is now accused precisely because he said that there are two, a good one and an evil one. Christ says in the Gospel that there are two trees: ‘A good tree never produces evil fruit, and an evil tree never produces good fruit’ (Matt. VII, 17). There are the two natures.

“Then it is written in the Gospel: ‘Did you sow good seed in the field? From where, then, did the weeds appear?’ ‘An enemy did this’ (Matt. XIII, 27–28). If this enemy is not foreign to God, let it be proved to me. If this enemy belongs to God, what sort of seed did he sow?

“Again, it is written in the Gospel, Christ saying that at the end of time he will place his throne in the midst of the world and send his angels to the east and west, north and south. He will gather all nations before him and separate them, just as a shepherd separates the lambs from the goats. To speak briefly, he will say to the lambs: ‘Go into the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’ To the goats on the left he will say: ‘Depart from me, you who have practiced iniquity; for you had my name, but did not perform the works. Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matt. XXV, 31–41).

[Col. 0537] “Who are those who bear the name of Christ and are sent into the eternal fire with the devil and his angels? To what side do they belong—those with whom Christ does not mingle, yet who bear his name? For Manichaeus says that those whom Christ condemns do not belong to him.

“For the apostle Paul says: ‘The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be’ (Rom. VIII, 7). Manichaeus says that what is hostile to God does not belong to God. But if it does belong to God, then he made an enemy for himself. Manichaeus does not say this.

“Again Paul says: ‘The god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that they may not behold the light of the Gospel of Christ, who is the image of God’ (II Cor. IV, 4). Paul says again: ‘There was given to me a thorn of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0537] The printed editions have: ‘a thorn of my flesh.’ The word ‘my’ is absent from the manuscripts], an angel of Satan, to buffet me day and night. For this I pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and he said to me: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is proved in weakness”’ (II Cor. XII, 7–9).

“See what the Apostle said; see what the Evangelist said. Since Manichaeus maintains that the one who fought against God is foreign to God—whether because Christ was crucified, or because all the Apostles [fragment: ‘on account of God’s command’]—let Your Holiness tell me whether the one who crucified them, to whom God’s command is displeasing, belongs to God.”

## CHAPTER III

Augustine said: “You have wished to recall the holy Scriptures, which you greatly depart from the truth by failing to understand them, as though you were bringing them forward as a defense of your empty talk. Yet among everything you recalled—some passages as they are truly written, others differently from what is written—you have nowhere been able to show that God, wishing to drive away a hostile nature threatening his kingdoms so that he might have rest, caused a part of himself, which is what he himself is, to be mixed with the opposing nature of the demons and bound and polluted by them.

“This is what is alleged against you. Since you have no answer to give, you recalled passages of the divine Scriptures in which it is said concerning sinners that they do not belong to the blessed life that God grants to the good and faithful. You wanted to take these as though they were two natures, according to the ravings of Manichaeus.

“But the truth says that all these things that we see and do not see, which exist by nature, were made by God. Among them, rational creation—also itself made—received free will, whether in angels or in human beings. By this free will, if it wished to serve God according to God’s will and law, it would possess eternal happiness with him. But if it did not wish to submit to his law and instead used its own power against his command, it would be subject, according to his justice, to the punishment it deserved.

“This is God’s omnipotence in creating all things [Note: [Col. 0537] The printed editions have: ‘in creating human beings.’ The manuscripts read better: ‘in creating all things.’]; this is his justice in requiting sinners.

“I also prove that there is free will—and that anyone sins if he wishes and does not sin if he does not wish—not only from the divine Scriptures, which you do not understand, but also from the words of Manichaeus himself. For, hemmed in, he perceives the power of truth. Against that truth he had attempted to introduce another nature, one that God did not make, in opposition to God—not with substantial truth, but with an empty fantasy. Nevertheless, in confessing the truth about free will, the human nature in which God made him proved stronger in him than the sacrilegious fiction he invented for himself.”

## CHAPTER IV

“Hear, then, first the Lord himself concerning free will, where he recalls the two trees that you yourself mentioned. Hear him say: ‘Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad’ (Matt. XII, 33).

“When he says, ‘Either do this or do that,’ he indicates power, not nature. No one except God can make a tree. But each person has it in his will either to choose what is good and be a good tree, or to choose what is evil and be an evil tree—not because the evils that are chosen possess any substance in themselves, but because God created all the things he established according to their grades and distinguished them according to their kinds: heavenly and earthly, immortal and mortal. He created all things good in their own kind.

“He placed the soul possessing free will beneath himself and above the other things, so that if it served what is higher, it would rule what is lower; but if it offended what is higher, it would experience punishment through what is lower.

“Thus, when the Lord says, ‘Either do this or do that,’ he shows that it lies within their power what they would do. He himself is secure and certain in himself as God. If they chose good, they would receive its reward; if they chose evil, they would experience its punishment. He is always just, whether as rewarder or as condemner.”

## CHAPTER V

“Hear now how Manichaeus himself—so perverse and so proud that, by introducing another nature, he made himself equal to God and brought God down to his own level—nevertheless confessed that there is free will.

“In your *Treasure*, to which you gave this name in order to deceive people, he certainly speaks as follows, as you yourself know:

‘But those who, through their own negligence, have by no means allowed themselves to be cleansed from the pollution of the spirits mentioned above, and who have obeyed the divine commandments only inadequately and not completely, and have not wished to observe fully the law given to them by their liberator [Note: [Col. 0538] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: ‘given by God the liberator.’], nor governed themselves as was fitting, etc.’

“You see that in these words free will has been confirmed even by one who did not know what he was saying. For one who does not wish to observe the law has it in his power to do so if he wishes. He did not say, ‘They were unable’; he said, ‘They were unwilling.’

“Certainly, they are not compelled by the race of darkness not to observe the law. If they are compelled, they are not unwilling but unable. If they are unwilling, they are not compelled not to do it; rather, they are unwilling by their own choice.

“Thus, the fact that it lies within their will to be unwilling is certainly sin, without any necessity imposed by the race of darkness. Recognize that this is sin without any necessity imposed by the race of darkness. From this you see where all faults come from, where the merits of faults come from, and where the distribution of punishments comes from.”

## CHAPTER VI

“You also have this in the apocryphal writings [Col. 0539], which the Catholic canon certainly does not admit, but which are all the more weighty for you because they are excluded from the Catholic canon. Let me recall something from them as well—not because I am bound by its authority, but because you will be convicted by it.

“In the *Acts* written by Leucius [Note: [Col. 0539] In the Victorine codices it is written ‘Levitio.’ In Am. and Er., ‘Lenticio.’ See below, *The Book on Faith against the Manichaeans*, chapter 5], which he presents as though they were the Acts of the Apostles, you find the following:

‘For elegant fictions, simulated display, and the compulsion of visible things do not proceed from their own nature, but from that human being who, through his own agency, became worse through deception.’

“See how he says both ‘through his own agency’ and ‘through deception.’ The devil was indeed the deceiver of the human being—not a sinner by nature, but first a sinner by will.

“But because it lay within the human being’s power not to consent to the deceiver, the text therefore says both ‘through his own agency’ and ‘through deception’: in the words ‘through his own agency,’ understand free will; in the words ‘through deception,’ understand the devil—not an oppressor of one unwilling, but a tempter of one willing.”

## CHAPTER VII

“Therefore, since I have answered and, insofar as I could, proved that the things written in the holy books concerning sinners and the just pertain not to a diversity of natures but to a distinction of merits—and since in those merits it is not nature that produces necessity but the will that produces guilt—you answer what I have already asked.

“If nothing could harm God, why did he mix his own part, his own substance, that which he himself is, with the demons, to be polluted and bound—something that you have been unable to find in any canonical divine Scripture? But if it could harm him, then you do not worship an incorruptible God, of whom the Apostle says:

‘To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, incorruptible, to God alone, be honor and glory for ages of ages’ (I Tim. I, 17).

“Finally, the same Apostle says: ‘God dwells in inaccessible light’ (I Tim. VI, 16). Do the saints not approach that light, concerning whom it is written: ‘Approach him, and be enlightened’ (Ps. XXXIII, 6)? Do those not approach that light of whom it is said: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ [Note: [Col. 0539] Er., Lyons, Venice, Louvain, and some others omit certain words here; they have this reading: ‘Be enlightened,’ and then: ‘Blessed,’ etc. M.] (Matt. V, 8)?

“But because no one can approach it unless God himself grants that he approach, it is inaccessible in itself. No one can approach it unless God wills that he approach it. But whoever receives this gift will approach.

“How, then, could that race of darkness approach the dwelling of God, where there is inaccessible light, which no one approaches unless God grants it? Or if God had given it the gift of approaching, he would not have given it to attack God’s kingdom, and he would not have feared it.

“But if he had not given it such a gift that it could approach, he was secure in his own kingdom, dwelling in inaccessible light. What could he fear from the race of darkness, so as to mix with it his own part, his own substance, that which he himself is, to be bound, oppressed, and polluted—where it would not only be held in misery, but also cleansed in disgrace?

“For you say that, in order for it to be cleansed from there—and it is sacrilegious even to hear this, but we cannot remain silent about it in order to confound you [Col. 0540] and perhaps save you—you say that the part of God is cleansed from there in the ship of light, which you call the sun, thereby committing an injury against the Creator of the sun and against the sun itself, which you say was made in such a way that so great an obscenity is performed there.

“For you say that God placed there turns his powers into males, to arouse the desires of the female demons, and then turns those same powers into females, to arouse the desires of the male demons. When they arouse lust in the demons, who are inflamed by the forms fashioned by God, their limbs are released, and thus the part of God that had been bound there escapes.

“You have dared to believe this immense disgrace and sacrilege, and you do not hesitate to preach it. These are the middle doctrines of your teaching.

“What, then, is the end? What else but that God was unable to cleanse everything? And because he was unable, you say that he will make of what remains a kind of plasterwork for the race of darkness, so that what could not be cleansed may be condemned there forever, although it committed nothing by its own will.

“Thus your god—who is not the true God but a fabricated one, not established anywhere but imagined in your heart—mixes his own part in misery, cleanses it in disgrace, and condemns it cruelly.

“Answer these points, then, and begin with what I said: why did God mix this part of himself, when nothing could harm him? Or, if it could, how is he incorruptible?”

## CHAPTER VIII

Felix said: “You assert that Manichaeus is cruel for saying these things. What, then, do we say about Christ, who said, ‘Go into the eternal fire’ (Matt. XXV, 41)?”

Augustine said: “He said this to sinners.”

Felix said: “Why, then, were these sinners not cleansed?”

Augustine said: “Because they were unwilling.”

Felix said: “You said that because they were unwilling?”

Augustine said: “I said it because they were unwilling.”

Felix said: “Why were they unwilling? Is there anyone who does not wish to be healed? Is there anyone who does not wish to be cleansed? Is there anyone who does not wish to be enlightened? What sick person does not wish to come to health?

“If it is cruel that Manichaeus said that some part of God, which could not cleanse itself, was bound in a sphere, is it not also cruel that Christ, who said, ‘I came on account of sinners,’ should now send into eternal fire those who bore his name? But, I suppose, they were unable to fulfill the commandments.

“If this is cruel, then the other is even more cruel. If the other is more cruel—because God was unable to cleanse them and bound them in a sphere—and if it seems even more cruel to send into eternal fire those whom Christ was unable to cleanse, let Your Holiness explain this cruelty to me.”

AUGUSTINE said: If you had either understood what I have already said, or admitted that you understood it—for perhaps, having nothing to say, you pretended not to understand what is clear—you would not say these things. For we have already said and proved from the divine Scriptures that there is free will; and that God is the just judge of free will, rewarding the faithful who submit themselves to him and wish to be healed, but condemning the proud and ungodly. Since, then, he came to heal sinners, he certainly heals those who confess their sins and those who repent. No one, however, repents when someone else has sinned; but if repentance is just and genuine, then repentance itself shows that whatever we may perhaps do wrong belongs not to another nature but to our own will. For if one person repents when another has sinned, that is not wise repentance but insane repentance.

According to you, however, there are no sins at all. The nation of darkness does not sin, because it does what its own nature makes it do; the nature of light does not sin, because it is compelled to do what it does. Thus you find no sin that God condemns, and no sin that repentance can heal. But if there is repentance, there is also guilt; if there is guilt, there is also will; and if there is will in sinning, then it is not nature that compels one to sin.

But if those who cannot fulfill what they will suffer some weakness, as the Apostle Paul says, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7:23), it is clear that this came from the transmission of Adam’s first sin and from evil habit. Even today [Note: The editions of Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain read *hodie* (“today”). M.] people freely form a habit; once they have formed it, they cannot easily overcome it. Thus they themselves have made, out of themselves, the condition that a contrary law should dwell [Note: In the manuscripts: “that it should dwell against them.”] in their members.

But those who conceive the fear of God and, through free will, submit themselves for healing to the excellent physician—and, as to a good healer, so also to a merciful creator—are healed through the humility of confession and repentance. The proud, however, who say that they are righteous, or who say that they themselves do not sin but that something else sins in them, and that another nature sins through them, become incurable through that very pride of theirs. They experience the just judgment of God, who “resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

It is therefore not unfitting that God should say, “Go into eternal fire,” to those who by free will rejected his mercy; and should say, “Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:41, 34), to those who by free will accepted his faith, confessed their sins, did penance, were displeased with what they had been, and were pleased with what they had become through him.

Now answer what I asked you; but let me obtain from you that we do not cause unnecessary delays: If nothing could harm God, why did he send us here? If it could harm him, God is not incorruptible.

## CHAPTER IX

FELIX said: If nothing could harm God, why did he send his Son here?

AUGUSTINE said: See how you are always asking questions and do not wish to answer the questions that have been put to you. Listen to what you asked, but remember that you do not answer the things I say, whereas I do answer. Nothing can harm God; but he sent his Son so that he might be clothed in flesh and appear to human beings, heal sinners, and in that very flesh suffer for us—the flesh he took from us.

For in his own nature he could suffer nothing, since “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” In this nature, because the Word was God, he could suffer nothing. But so that he might suffer for us, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14). “The Word became flesh” by assuming flesh, not by being changed into flesh: he assumed humanity but did not lose divinity.

Thus the same one is both God and human: in the nature of God, equal to the Father; in the nature of humanity, made mortal; among us, for us, and from us; remaining what he was and assuming what he was not, so that he might free what he had made, not what he was. Christ’s suffering, therefore, arose not from necessity but from mercy. He offered us an example of patience from among us—from human being to human being, from flesh to flesh. Yet he himself did not become worse in that flesh; rather, flesh became better in him.

But your god’s portion, without assuming any flesh—for there was no flesh among the nation of darkness for which it could suffer—descended to be seized, bound, defiled, and cleansed in a manner more shameful than the manner in which it was bound. I have already spoken of its cleansing. The more disgraceful all these things are, the easier they are to understand as things that cannot befall the nature of God.

Far be it from a pious and faithful mind to believe such things about God—the good God, the true God—as you believe: not the God you found, but the one you invented. Answer now: If nothing could harm God, why, according to your empty tales, was that pure substance of his sent here, without assuming any flesh in which it might suffer, if it was to suffer at all?

## CHAPTER X

FELIX said: If God could not be harmed at all by the opposing side, and Christ could not be harmed at all by the opposing nature, to whom did Christ come in order to set it free?
