For, as you say, he came on account of our freedom; therefore we were in captivity. If we were held in captivity, and Christ came for that reason, to free us from captivity, then the one who held us was either foreign to God or a power of God.

If it was a power of God that held us, why did the one who held us send Christ? If it was within his own discretion to release us whenever he wished, why was Christ crucified? No one is unaware that Christ was crucified. Why did they crucify him? If it is a power of God, it did us no harm. If it was a power of God, we were not captives in its possession, but as though we were with our own ruler, as a son with his parents—not as Romans with barbarians.

Therefore, since we were established with the power of God, it was not necessary for God to send his Son so that it might be said that our liberator had come. If, then, it appears that we were established with the power of God, the Apostle said [Note: Venice reads, “as the Apostle said,” adding *ut* (“as”). M.], “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, because it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23). This is what the Apostle says. If the one who curses everyone who hangs on a tree is the power of God—for Christ hung on a tree, as did all his Apostles who were condemned on account of his command—who, then, is this one who curses everyone who hangs on a tree?

## CHAPTER XI

AUGUSTINE said: Those whom Christ redeemed from the devil were held by the devil through their consent and were placed under his dominion by the just judgment of God, since they had consented to their deceiver through free will.

Just as it was within human power to consent to the devil and thereby be taken captive, so it was within the devil’s power, when he was an angel, to sin and thereby be changed for the worse. Thus the sinful angel, through free will, persuaded a human being possessing free will to sin; so that, if the devil had not wished to sin, he would not have sinned, and if the human being had not wished to consent, he would not have consented.

Once the human being was held by the one to whom he had consented, this was not because the devil had any power, but because it was the just judgment of God, and because the human being had refused to obey God’s law. Since, therefore, Christ found sinners in this condition under sin, he redeemed those who confessed their sins from the one who was exalting himself.

As for what was established in the Law—“Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree”—of which the Apostle says, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us,” for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree”: he did not criticize the Law but commended mercy.

Because Adam had sinned, and that entire mass and offspring of sin had been cursed, the Lord wished to assume flesh from that very mass, so that by assuming the mortality that had come from punishment, he might destroy death, which came from grace. Therefore the Law says, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” For death itself hung on the tree, and that death came from the curse.

Just as, then, by assuming death he killed death, so by assuming the curse he dissolved the curse. Hence the Apostle also says, “Knowing that our old self was crucified together with him” (Romans 6:6). From our old self—that is, from the condition of death that came as the result of sin—he graciously assumed mortal flesh from the virgin Mary, in which he might offer us an example both of suffering and of resurrection: suffering, to strengthen repentance; resurrection, to awaken hope.

Thus he showed us two lives in the flesh he assumed from our mortal life: one laborious, the other blessed—the laborious life, which we must endure; the blessed life, which we must hope for. We endure the laborious life as the consequence of our sin; he showed it in his flesh, not as the consequence of his own iniquity but as the work of his mercy.

To show you that the Law is good, although you wished to criticize it, the Apostle Paul himself said in one place, “The Law entered so that transgression might abound.” He still seems to criticize it; but listen to what follows: “But where transgression abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

The Law was given to proud human beings who attributed everything to their own strength, so that, when they could not fulfill the Law that had been given, they might be found transgressors and, having become liable under the Law, seek mercy from the Law’s author.

Accordingly, a little later the same Apostle says, “Therefore the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.” But lest you say that he is speaking of another commandment, and so fail to see that he is speaking of the one about which he had just said, “The Law entered so that transgression might abound,” he immediately posed this question to himself: “What then? Did that which is good become death to me? By no means! But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through that which is good” (Romans 7:12–13).

Sin existed, but it did not appear as sin. The Law was given to the proud person; he acted against the Law, and the sin that existed but had not appeared became manifest. Once sin had appeared, it humbled the proud person; the humbled proud person became repentant, and through repentance he obtained mercy.

You have heard the answer to what you asked; now answer what I ask: Nothing could harm God from the nation of darkness. Why, then, did he send his portion here to be mixed with and polluted by the nature of demons?

## CHAPTER XII

FELIX said: If we are under our own will, let no one compel anyone: whenever I wish, I will be a Christian. Whether to be a Christian or not to be one lies within our will.

AUGUSTINE said: That the will lies within us is clear, and I have taught this from the divine Scriptures; even the one who led you into this error was compelled to say it, though unwillingly.

But when you say, “Let no one be compelled; whenever I wish, I will be a Christian,” no one is compelling you at all. Whenever you wish, be one, since you came here by your own will and disputed these things by your own will. Woe to an evil will, if it is evil; peace to a good will, if it is good. Whether it is evil or good, it is still will. A crown follows a good will; punishment follows an evil one. God is the judge of wills, but the creator of natures.

If, then, you think you are being compelled to be a Christian, hear from us that you are in no way being compelled. Rather, consider what you hear; weigh it carefully; you are acting according to your own will. Examine, as a prudent person—if indeed there is any human prudence in you—whether what has been said is supported by truth; whether you yourself have failed in defending your Manichaeus, as is apparent. And whenever you wish, become what you are not yet, and cease to be what you are.

## CHAPTER XIII

FELIX said: Now let us proceed briefly, as Your Holiness said; let us not pile up papers [Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain, omitting punctuation, read: “as Your Holiness said, let us not pile up papers.” M.], if it pleases you, but grant what I asked earlier: come here; show me the truth, so that what I hold may be shown not to be the truth, and you will find me ready to believe.

AUGUSTINE said: It is already sufficiently clear that what you hold is not the truth. For far be it from the hearts of those who seek or hold the truth to believe that God, compelled by necessity, plunged his own substance so that it might be bound and polluted by the nature of demons. Far be it from the faithful to believe that God changed himself into males against females and into females against males in order to arouse their desire. Far be it from the faithful to believe that God would later condemn forever his own substance, which he himself plunged among the demons.

That this, therefore, is not the truth is clear. But since you wish the truth to be made manifest to you after this falsehood has been exposed and refuted, if anything still troubles you concerning knowledge of the Catholic faith, you can be instructed from the beginning of the faith. For pious faith makes a person fit to apprehend immutable truth. Whoever refuses to begin with that faith will remain outside in pride and will not be brought to what he seeks or to where he wishes to arrive.

But since that falsehood is now manifest, anathematize the falsehood [Col. 0545], so that you may begin to be fit to know the truth.

## CHAPTER XIV

FELIX said: When it has appeared to me—for it does not appear to me, since the other matter has not been shown to me—I cannot anathematize it.

AUGUSTINE said: Is the error that says God is corruptible to be anathematized, or is it not to be anathematized?

FELIX said: Say it again.

AUGUSTINE said: Is the error that says God is corruptible to be anathematized, or is it not to be anathematized?

FELIX said: It will be investigated whether it says that.

AUGUSTINE said: This is what I asked: Is the person who says that God is corruptible to be anathematized, or not?

FELIX said: The person who says that God is corruptible is to be anathematized—is this what you are charging me with?

AUGUSTINE said: This is what I am asking.

FELIX said: You say that God is corruptible, not what you said at first, that he gave his portion to his adversaries?

AUGUSTINE said: For the moment answer what I am asking: Is the person who says that God is corruptible to be anathematized, or not?

FELIX said: Very much so.

AUGUSTINE said: Is the person who says that the nature and substance of God are corruptible to be anathematized, or not?

FELIX said: I did not understand what you said.

AUGUSTINE said: I am saying what every person understands who does not pretend not to understand: Is the person who says that the nature and substance of God—that is, God himself, whatever God is—are corruptible to be anathematized, or not?

FELIX said: He is also to be anathematized, if it should be proved to be true.

AUGUSTINE said: I have not yet told you that Manichaeus says that God’s nature is corruptible; I have told you only that whoever says this is to be anathematized.

FELIX said: And I answered, “Yes.”

## CHAPTER XV

AUGUSTINE said: Is that portion which has been mixed with the nation of darkness from God’s nature, or from some other nature?

FELIX said: From God’s.

AUGUSTINE said: Is what comes from God’s nature what God is, or something else that is not God?

FELIX said: It is so: what comes from God is God, according to what is written: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). For “God is light, and there is no darkness in him” (1 John 1:5).

AUGUSTINE said: You have answered well, because whatever comes from God’s nature is God, and God is light, and there is no darkness in him, and such a light shone in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

Let us see, then, whether Manichaeus does not say that a portion of God was comprehended by the darkness, and also held bound, and also stained and polluted, so that it needs the mercy of a liberator and purifier. But if he says these things, then, according to you and according to your true confessions, he is to be anathematized, because he says that the portion and nature of God—which is God himself—was comprehended by the darkness, bound [Col. 0546], and polluted.

You yourself, speaking according to the Gospel, could not say this; rather, you rightly said that the light shines in the darkness and that the darkness did not comprehend it. Manichaeus, then, is to be anathematized, because he said that the light was darkened in the darkness and that the darkness comprehended it.

FELIX said: But what is polluted and held bound is set free; and if we have been polluted, we are cleansed.

AUGUSTINE said: But this is not rightly said of God’s nature; it is rightly said of that which can be polluted, because it is polluted and cleansed. But with regard to that which cannot be polluted, you see with what great sacrilege it is said, “It is polluted and cleansed”—especially since you say that a certain portion of God has been polluted and therefore is bound forever in a globe of darkness, because it could not be cleansed.

Whoever does not anathematize the person who says this answered falsely a little earlier, since everyone who says that God is corruptible is to be anathematized.

## CHAPTER XVI

FELIX said: Your Holiness said that the portion that did not cleanse itself from the defilement of the nation of darkness—and so Manichaeus says—was not sent into the kingdom of God. You assert that this portion was condemned; but Manichaeus does not say that it was condemned [Note: In the manuscripts: “but Manichaeus says that it was not condemned.”]; rather, he says that it was placed to guard that nation of darkness.

AUGUSTINE said: I am arguing with you about the portion that you say is polluted and cleansed; afterward, if necessary, we shall discuss the portion that is fixed in its globe. For the present, the portion that is cleansed was polluted.

FELIX said: What is polluted is also cleansed.

AUGUSTINE said: Then is the person who says that God’s nature and substance, and that which God is, can be polluted, bound, and defiled by the nation of darkness not to be anathematized?

FELIX said: From what did Christ cleanse us? From what did he set us free?

AUGUSTINE said: Christ did not set free a portion of God or God’s nature; he set free, by his mercy, the creature he had made, which had fallen into sin through free will. He cleansed that which could be polluted; he set free that which could be taken captive; he healed that which could become sick.

But now we are speaking about God, about God’s nature, about God’s substance, about that which God is. Could it be polluted, or could it not?

## CHAPTER XVII

FELIX said: Is our soul, which has been polluted, from God? If it is not from God, why was Christ crucified for it? If, then, it is clear that Christ was crucified on account of our soul, it is clear that the soul is from God, that it was polluted, and that he himself cleansed it.

AUGUSTINE said: I say that not only our soul but also our body and every creature, both spiritual and bodily, is from God, because this is what the Catholic faith holds. But one thing is what God begot from himself, which is what he himself is; another is what God made.

What God begot is equal to the Father; what God made is not equal to the creator as something created. We say that one thing is from God—or, more properly, is “of God”—because it is what he himself is, as the only-begotten Son, his Word, through whom all things were made (John 1:3). Of other things we say that they are from God because “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were established” (Psalm 148:5).

The soul belongs among the things God made; it is not what God begot from himself. Therefore the Word whom he begot from himself could not, cannot, and will not be polluted. But the soul, which he made to rule the body—to serve what is above and rule what is below, that is, to serve God and rule the body—was polluted by sin when it despised God’s law.

God, however, extending mercy to what he had made, sent the Son through whom he had made it, and through him remade it. When what did not exist was to be created, it was created through the Word; when what had been corrupted was to be restored, a creature was taken from the virgin Mary, so that through what was human it might be shown to humanity both what must be endured and what must be hoped for.

Thus the nature of the Word, the substance of God’s only-begotten Son, suffered nothing either from the Jewish persecutors or from the devil, the evil angel who persecuted him. But because he clothed himself with flesh, he clothed himself with a mortal, passible, mutable thing. In that with which he clothed himself, he suffered whatever he wished as an example of patience, and restored it as an example of righteousness.

Now tell me concerning God’s portion, which is God himself, whether it can be polluted or not. If it can, God is not immutable, and the person who says this is to be anathematized. But if it cannot, you see that Manichaeus is to be anathematized, because he says that God’s portion, God’s nature, that which God is, came here pure to the nation of darkness, bound and polluted, so that it needed to be released and cleansed.

## CHAPTER XVIII

FELIX said: You said this about the soul: that it is not from God.

AUGUSTINE said: I did not say that; I said that it is from God, as something made by God, not as something born from God.

FELIX said: You said concerning the soul that it is not from God but is God’s creation, because without God it is nothing. For this is what you say, and you do not wish to affirm that the soul is from God.

AUGUSTINE said: It is from God, but it was made by God.

FELIX said: Whether made, sent, or given, it is from God. Therefore, if it is from God, and it was polluted, and Christ came to free it from pollution, why do you blame Manichaeus?

AUGUSTINE said: Because I say that the soul is not God’s nature but was made by God; that it sinned through free will; that it was polluted by sin; and that through God’s mercy it was freed in repentance. But you say that God’s very nature—what God is, God from God—was captured and polluted in the nation of darkness.

There is a great difference between what God begot from himself and what he made not from himself but from nothing—that is, what, when it altogether did not exist, it received from God so as to exist, that is, so as to be established.

FELIX said: Therefore it is a portion of God.

AUGUSTINE said: It has already been told you that it is not a portion of God. Now understand how you are to conceive of God as omnipotent creator.

Everything that comes to be, and everything that anyone makes, is either from himself, from something, or from nothing. Because a human being is not omnipotent, he makes a son from himself; from something, as a craftsman makes a chest from wood or a vessel from silver. He can make a vessel but cannot make silver; he can make a chest but cannot make wood. No human being can make something exist from nothing—from what altogether does not exist.

But God, because he is omnipotent, both begot the Son from himself, made the world from nothing, and formed the human being from clay, so that through these three powers he might show that his activity is effective in all things.

What he made from himself should not be said to have been made but to have been begotten. What he made from something, such as the human being from earth, he did not make in the way that another had made the earth for him from which to make the human being, as God made silver for a silversmith from which to make a vessel. Rather, he himself made both what did not exist, so that it might exist, and what would exist from it, which he himself had already created from nothing so that it might exist.

Thus the body, the soul, and the whole creation are understood to have been made by God—not begotten from God, so as to be what God is.

Perhaps, then, you will now choose what you should hold and what you should reject. Choose what is better. Since we see many mutable things that are nevertheless good, although mutable, and many mortal things that are nevertheless good, although mortal, while God alone is wholly immutable good, choose which it is better for you to hold: that God is mutable, or that what God made is mutable.

For it is necessary that you say one of these two things. If you refuse to admit that what God made is mutable, it remains for you to say that God himself is mutable. But in order to cleanse yourself of this sacrilege and blasphemy, so that you do not say that God’s substance is mutable, why do you not concede that the God who truly is and is immutable—since he himself also said, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14)—made all things good, but not equal to himself?

Therefore, since he himself is immutable, it is not surprising that what he made, because it is not equal to him, is not immutable but mutable. Thus it could sin and be polluted through free will, and be freed through his mercy.

## CHAPTER XIX

FELIX said: You said that a human being made a son for himself; there is no difference between father and son. Since Your Holiness has brought this forward, I answer that God and the things he makes are equal to him.

AUGUSTINE said: What you refused to understand is that when a human being makes a son, he is not properly said to “make” him but properly to “beget” him. So too, I told you, God begot his only Son; he did not make him. He made that which is not equal to him; what he begot is equal to him.

Therefore choose for yourself whether you wish to say that God’s creation is mutable or that God’s nature is mutable.

FELIX said: Just as God is immutable, so too what he begot is immutable; and what he made, if it is from his own nature, does not change—but he made it from nothing, because a work does not change [Note: The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from our manuscripts.].

AUGUSTINE said: But it has already been told you that what he made is not from his own nature; rather, he made it from nothing, because he is omnipotent. It did not exist, and he made it—not from himself [Col. 0549], nor from some thing that he himself had not made, but from nothing.

FELIX said: I did not say that. I said that God is immutable, that what he begot is immutable, and that what he made is immutable. I did not say where he made it from; I did not ask from where he made it.

AUGUSTINE said: But you heard from me what you did not ask, so that you might now cease speaking foolishly. Almighty God could both beget from himself, make from nothing, and form something from what he had already made: from himself, a Son equal to himself; from nothing, the world and the whole creation; from something, a human being from earth—for he is omnipotent.

What is from himself can never be polluted, just as he himself cannot. But what was made by him and is not from him can be polluted through free will and cleansed through his mercy, by condemning what has sinned and acknowledging him who created it.

But you, who a little earlier said that whoever calls God’s portion corruptible and defilable is to be anathematized, cannot deny that Manichaeus said that a portion of God was seized and polluted in the nation of darkness. It is evident that by these words he blasphemed him—perhaps in a manner that could scarcely be worse. Either anathematize him for saying such things, or you yourself, together with him, are to be anathematized and rejected.

## CHAPTER XX

FELIX said: Manichaeus says that God’s portion was polluted, and Christ says that the soul was polluted and came to free it from pollution.

AUGUSTINE said: But the soul is not a portion of God. For you have already confessed that Manichaeus said that a portion of God was polluted. We, however, say that the soul was polluted through the will to sin; but the soul is not a portion of God, nor was it begotten from God, but it was made by God.

Thus the soul is said to be from God in the same way that some work of a craftsman is said to be from his craftsmanship or made by him, though it was not begotten from him as his son was.

Since, then, you have already confessed that Manichaeus said that a portion of God was polluted, and you said earlier that the person who says that God, or his nature, is corruptible or defilable is to be anathematized, you have already anathematized him, though you do not wish to admit it.

For when you said that it is polluted and cleansed, by saying “cleansed” you yourself made clear that it is polluted; and you have no way to escape. Both Manichaeus [Note: Erasmus and Venice read, “whence Manichaeus may escape.” Louvain reads “you may escape”; the words “and Manichaeus” are absent. M.] and you have said that a portion of God is polluted. Therefore either anathematize Manichaeus, or, holding these views, you are to be anathematized together with Manichaeus.

FELIX said: I did not learn from Manichaeus that a portion of God was polluted; I learned from Christ that he came on account of the soul, which had been polluted.

AUGUSTINE said: You did not learn from Christ that the soul is a portion of God.

FELIX said: I learned from Christ that the soul is from God.

AUGUSTINE said: And we have learned that the soul is from God, but it is not a portion of God. For the soul is from God in the same way that a product is from a craftsman—not from God as a son is from a father.

[Col. 0550] FELIX said: We are discussing pollution. If the soul, which is from God, was polluted and can be cleansed by Christ, who came for it, then that portion of God which Manichaeus speaks of can also be polluted and cleansed through the command of God himself.

AUGUSTINE said: There you go again saying that a portion of God, having been polluted, is cleansed, although a little earlier you said that the person who calls it corruptible is to be anathematized. Now you say that it could be polluted, and you say that it can be cleansed, thereby confirming that it could be polluted.

We do not say this about a portion of God; we say it about the soul, because it is from him as his work, not as offspring from him. Return, then, to what you are saying and distinguish what we say. The soul is neither God nor a portion of God.

But you say that Manichaeus said that a portion of God was polluted, and that he says it is cleansed in order to confirm that it is polluted. It remains, therefore, either that you anathematize him or that, holding these views, you yourself be anathematized.

## CHAPTER XXI

FELIX said: Does the soul that has been defiled by sin belong to God, or does it not?

AUGUSTINE said: It belongs to him, but it is not a portion of him.

FELIX said: I did not ask that.

AUGUSTINE said: What did you ask?

FELIX said: Does it belong to God or not?

AUGUSTINE said: I have already said both that it belongs to him and how it belongs to him.

FELIX said: I am asking whether it truly is from God.

AUGUSTINE said: It is from God, not of God.

FELIX said: If sin is nothing, and the soul is from God, and it was polluted, and Christ came to free it, and freed it from sin, why do we blame Manichaeus, who says that a portion of God was polluted and was again cleansed?

AUGUSTINE said: Because you have already confessed that Manichaeus said that a portion of God was polluted, and you say that it is not a sin to pour forth such blasphemy against God.

We, however, say that the soul did sin through free will and is cleansed through repentance by the mercy of its Creator, because it is not from God as his portion or as his offspring, but is from God or made by God as his work.

The difference between our faith and your faithlessness is clear to everyone. Therefore, according to your earlier words, since you conceded that the person who says that God’s nature is corruptible is to be anathematized—and since it is clear that Manichaeus says this—you refused to anathematize him. You will therefore be anathematized together with him.

## CHAPTER XXII

After they had discussed the matter at length:

FELIX said: Tell me now: what do you want me to do?

AUGUSTINE said: That you anathematize Manichaeus, whose are these great blasphemies. But if you do it sincerely, then do it; for no one compels you against your will.

FELIX said: God sees whether I do it sincerely; a human being cannot see that. But I ask you to strengthen me.

AUGUSTINE said: In what do you wish me to strengthen you?

FELIX said: You anathematize him first, so that afterward I too may anathematize him.

AUGUSTINE said: See, I am even writing it with my own hand; for I want you also to write it with your own hand.

[Col. 0551] FELIX said: But anathematize him in such a way that you anathematize the very spirit that was in Manichaeus and spoke these things through him.

Augustine, having received a sheet of paper, wrote these words:

“I, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, have already anathematized Manichaeus and his teaching, and the spirit that spoke such execrable blasphemies through him, because it was a spirit of seduction, not of truth but of wicked error; and now I anathematize the aforementioned Manichaeus and the spirit of his error.”

After he had given the same sheet to Felix, Felix too wrote these words in his own hand:

“I, Felix, who had believed Manichaeus, now anathematize him, his teaching, and the seductive spirit that was in him, which said that God had mixed his own portion with the nation of darkness and had freed it in so shameful a manner that he transformed his powers into females against males, and those same powers again into males against female demons, so that afterward he might fix the remnants of his portion forever in a globe of darkness. I anathematize all these and the other blasphemies of Manichaeus.”

I, Augustine, bishop, have subscribed to these Proceedings held in the church before the people.

I, Felix, have subscribed to these Proceedings.

[Col. 0551]

**SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: ONE BOOK ON THE NATURE OF THE GOOD AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS** [Note: Written after the year 404. In the *Retractations* it is placed immediately after the books on the Proceedings with Felix, which were written toward the end of the year 404.]

[Note: Concerning the following short work, see Book 2, chapter 9, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 634, from the words “The book *On the Nature of the Good*” through the words “God is.” M.]

[Note: The book *On the Nature of the Good* was revised against four ancient Vatican manuscripts; nine Gallican manuscripts; the Victorine, Sorbonnian, Corbie, Fossat, Cistercian, Casal, Bigot, and Laon manuscripts of the major church; one Augustinian manuscript of the major Parisian convent; variant readings transcribed by the Louvain editors from Belgian manuscripts; and the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C, S)

## CHAPTER ONE
God is the supreme and immutable good, from whom all other spiritual and bodily goods derive. The supreme good, above which there is nothing, is God; and therefore it is immutable good, and thus truly eternal and truly immortal. All other goods exist only from him, but are not from his substance. For what is from him is what he himself is; but what has been made by him is not what he is. Therefore, since he alone is immutable, everything he made is mutable, because he made it from nothing. For he is so almighty that he can make good things even from nothing—that is, from what altogether does not exist—both great and small, heavenly and earthly, spiritual and bodily. But because he is also just, he did not make what he made from nothing equal to what he begot from himself.

Since, therefore, all things are good, whether great or small, through whatever degrees of being, they can exist only from God; and since every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good, no nature can exist except from the supreme and true God. For all things—not only the highest goods [Col. 0552], but also those close to the supreme good, and again all the lowest goods, which are far removed from the supreme good—can exist only from that supreme good. Every spirit, therefore, even a mutable one, and every body are from God; and this is the whole of created nature [Note: [Col. 0552] Er., Lugd., and Ven. read *et hoc est omnis* (“and this is the whole”); Lov. reads *et haec omnia* (“and all these things”). M.]. For every nature is either spirit or body. The immutable Spirit is God; mutable spirit is created nature, but is better than body. Body, however, is not spirit, except when wind is called spirit in another sense because it is invisible to us, although its considerable force is felt.

## CHAPTER II

### How this may suffice for correcting the Manichaeans

For the sake of those who, unable to understand that every nature—that is, every spirit and every body—is naturally good, are disturbed by the wickedness of spirit and the mortality of body, and therefore attempt to introduce another nature of evil spirit and mortal body, which God did not make, we think that what we say can be brought within their understanding in the following way. They admit that no good can exist except from the supreme and true God. This is true, and, if they are willing to take note of it, it is sufficient to correct them.

## CHAPTER III

### Measure, form, and order as universal goods in things made by God

For we Catholics and Christians worship God, from whom all goods come, whether great or small; from whom comes every measure, whether great or small; from whom comes every form, whether great or small; from whom comes every order, whether great or small. For the more measured, formed, and ordered things are, the better they are; and the less measured, less formed, and less ordered they are, the less good they are.

These three things, therefore—measure, form, and order—to say nothing of the innumerable things shown to belong to these three—these three, measure, form, and order, are as it were universal goods in things made by God, whether in spirit or in body. God, therefore, is above every measure of creation, above every form, and above every order—not spatially above them, but by his ineffable and singular power, from whom come every measure, every form, and every order.

Where these three are great, there are great goods; where they are small, there are small goods; where they are absent, there is no good. And again, where these three are great, there are great natures; where they are small, there are small natures; where they are absent, there is no nature. Every nature, therefore, is good.

## CHAPTER IV

### Evil is the corruption of measure, form, or order

Accordingly, when the origin of evil is sought, one must first ask what evil is. It is nothing other than the corruption either of natural measure, or of natural form, or of natural order. A nature is therefore called evil when it has been corrupted; for an incorrupt nature is certainly good. Yet even the corrupted nature is good insofar as it is a nature, and evil insofar as it is corrupted.

## CHAPTER V

### A nature of higher order, even when corrupted, is sometimes better than an inferior nature even when incorrupt

It can happen that a nature which is more excellently ordered in its natural measure and form, even when corrupted, is still better than another which is incorrupt but ordered at a lower level with a lesser natural measure and form. Thus, according to the quality apparent to the senses in human estimation, corrupted gold is certainly better than incorrupt silver, and corrupted silver better than incorrupt lead.

So too, among more powerful and spiritual natures, a rational spirit corrupted by an evil will is still better than an incorrupt irrational spirit; and any spirit, even a corrupted one, is better than any incorrupt body. For that nature which, when present to a body, supplies it with life is better than the nature to which life is supplied. However corrupted the spirit of life that was made may be, it can still supply life to a body; and therefore a corrupted spirit is better than that body, although the body is incorrupt.

## CHAPTER VI

### The nature that cannot be corrupted is the supreme good; the nature that can be corrupted is some good

If corruption were to remove every measure, every form, and every order from corruptible things [Col. 0554], no nature would remain. Therefore every nature that cannot be corrupted is the supreme good, as God is. Every nature that can be corrupted is itself also some good; for corruption could not harm it except by taking away or diminishing what is good.

## CHAPTER VII

### The corruption of rational spirits is partly voluntary and partly punitive

God granted the most excellent creatures—that is, rational spirits—the following privilege: if they do not wish it, they cannot be corrupted; that is, if they preserve obedience under the Lord their God and thus cleave to his incorruptible beauty. But if they do not wish to preserve obedience, then, because they are corrupted willingly in sins, they are corrupted unwillingly in punishments.

God is such a good that no one who abandons him can fare well. Among the things made by God, rational nature is so great a good that there is no good by which it can be blessed except God. Sinners, therefore, are ordered in punishments. Since this ordering is not suited to their nature, it is punishment; but since it is suited to their guilt, it is justice.

## CHAPTER VIII

### From the corruption and destruction of inferior things comes the beauty of the universe

The other things that were made from nothing, which are certainly inferior to rational spirit, can be neither blessed nor miserable. But because they too are good according to their measure and form, and because even the lesser and least goods could exist only from God, the supreme good, they have been so ordered that the weaker yield to the stronger, the less powerful to the more powerful, and the less capable to the more capable; and thus earthly things harmonize with heavenly things as subjects with what excels them.

As things pass away and are succeeded by other things, a certain temporal beauty arises in its own kind, so that even those things which die, by ceasing to be what they were, neither disfigure nor disturb the measure, form, and order of the whole creation. It is like a well-composed speech, which is certainly beautiful, although its syllables and all its sounds pass by as if being born and dying.

## CHAPTER IX

### Punishment is established for the sinful nature so that it may be rightly ordered

What kind and how great a punishment is owed to each fault belongs to divine judgment, not human judgment. When punishment is remitted to those who have turned back, there is great goodness with God; and when what is owed is exacted, there is no injustice with God. For nature is better ordered when it suffers justly in punishment than when it rejoices in sin with impunity.

Yet even a nature in such a condition, possessing some measure, form, and order, retains some good, however extreme its condition may be. If these were wholly removed and entirely consumed, there would be no good, because no nature would remain.

## CHAPTER X

### Corruptible natures are so because they were made from nothing

All corruptible natures, therefore, would not be natures at all if they did not come from God; nor would they be corruptible if they were from him, because then they would be what he himself is. They possess whatever measure, form, and order they have because God is the one by whom they were made; but they are not immutable because they were made from nothing [Col. 0555].

It is sacrilegious audacity to equate nothing with God, if we wish what was made from nothing by God to be of the same nature as what was born from God.

## CHAPTER XI

### Neither God nor any other nature can be harmed except by his permission

Therefore the nature of God cannot be harmed in any way, nor can any nature under God be unjustly harmed. For even when some people harm others unjustly by sinning, their unjust will is imputed to them; but the power by which they are permitted to cause harm comes only from God, who knows, even without their knowing it, what those whom he permits them to harm ought to suffer.

## CHAPTER XII

### All goods come only from God

If those who introduce another nature which God did not make were willing to attend to all these things, so clear and certain, they would not be filled with such great blasphemies as to place so many goods in the supreme evil and so many evils in God.

As I said above, it is sufficient for their correction, if they are willing to attend to it, that the truth compels them—even against their will—to confess that absolutely all goods come only from God. Great goods do not therefore come from one source and small goods from another; both great and small goods come only from the supreme good, which is God.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Individual goods, whether small or great, come from God

Let us therefore recall as many goods as we can, which we ought rightly to attribute to God as their author; then, when these have been removed, let us see whether any nature will remain.

Every life, great and small; every power, great and small; every health, great and small; every memory, great and small; every virtue, great and small; every understanding, great and small; every tranquility, great and small; every abundance, great and small; every sensation, great and small; every light, great and small; every pleasantness [Note: [Col. 0555] The manuscripts read this way; printed editions have *sanitas* (“health”).], great and small; every measure, great and small; every beauty, great and small; every peace, great and small—and whatever similar things may occur to us, especially those found throughout all things, whether spiritual or bodily—every measure, every form, and every order, great and small, come from the Lord God.

Whoever wishes to use all these goods badly will pay the penalty according to divine judgment. But where none of these exists at all, no nature will remain.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Small goods are called by contrary names in comparison with greater goods

In all these matters, whatever things are small are called by contrary names in comparison with greater things. Thus, since human beauty is greater, the beauty of a monkey is called ugliness in comparison with it. This deceives the unwary, as though one were good and the other evil. They fail to observe in the monkey’s body its proper measure, the symmetry of its limbs on both sides, the harmony of its parts, the preservation of its soundness, and the other features which it would take too long to enumerate.

## CHAPTER XV

### The good of beauty exists in the body of a monkey, though to a lesser degree

To make what we are saying understood, and to satisfy those who are extremely slow—or even to compel those who obstinately resist the clearest truth to confess what is true [Col. 0556]—let them be asked whether corruption can harm the body of a monkey. If it can, making the body uglier, what does it diminish except the good of beauty? Something will therefore remain for as long as the nature of the body subsists. Accordingly, if the nature is consumed when the good is consumed, then the nature is good.

Similarly, we call slowness the opposite of speed; yet someone who does not move at all cannot even be called slow. We call a deep voice the opposite of a high voice, and a harsh voice the opposite of a melodious one. But if every form of voice is completely removed, there is silence, where there is no voice; and yet silence, precisely because there is no voice, is customarily set against voice as its contrary.

Likewise, light and darkness are called two contraries; yet even darkness has something of light. If it were completely without light, it would be darkness as the absence of light, just as silence is the absence of voice.

## CHAPTER XVI

### Privations in things are fittingly ordered by God

Yet even these privations of things are so ordered in the totality of nature that, for those who consider wisely, they occupy their turns without impropriety. By not illuminating certain places and times, God made darkness as fittingly as he made day. If, by restraining our voice, we fittingly introduce silence into our speech, how much more fittingly does he, the perfect craftsman of all things, create the privations of certain things?

Hence, in the hymn of the three youths, both light and darkness praise God (Dan. III, 72); that is, they produce his praise in the hearts of those who consider them rightly.

## CHAPTER XVII

### No nature is evil insofar as it is nature

No nature, therefore, is evil insofar as it is nature; for each nature’s evil consists only in a diminution of its good. If, by being diminished, that good were consumed, then, just as no good would remain, no nature would remain either—not merely the kind of nature introduced by the Manichaeans, in which so many goods are found that their excessive blindness is astonishing, but any nature that anyone might introduce.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Hylen, which the ancients called the formless matter of things, is not evil

Nor should that matter which the ancients called *hylen* be called evil. I am not speaking of what the Manichaean, in utterly senseless folly and without knowing what he is saying, calls *hylen*, the fashioner of bodies. It was rightly said to him that he introduces another god, for no one but God can fashion and create bodies. Nor are bodies created unless measure, form, and order subsist in them; and I think that by now even they confess that these goods can exist, and can exist only, from God.

Rather, I call *hylen* a certain entirely formless and qualitatively indeterminate matter from which these qualities that we perceive are formed, as the ancients said. For this reason wood is also called *hylē* (ὕλη) in Greek, because it is suitable for those who work with it—not because it itself makes something, but because something is made from it.

This *hylē*, therefore, should not be called evil. It can scarcely be perceived through any form, but may be conceived through the complete privation of form. Yet it too possesses a capacity for forms. For if it could not receive a form imposed by an artisan, it would not properly be called matter.

Moreover [Col. 0557], if form is some good—whence those who excel in form are called well-formed, just as those who excel in beauty are called beautiful—then without doubt the capacity for form is also some good. Since wisdom is a good, no one doubts that it is good to be capable of wisdom. And since every good comes from God, no one ought to doubt that this matter too, if it exists, comes only from God.

## CHAPTER XIX

### True being is proper to God

Magnificently and divinely, therefore, our God said to his servant, “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14). For he truly is because he is immutable. Every change makes what was cease to be what it was. He, therefore, truly is who is immutable; but the other things made by him received from him, according to their measure, the being they possess.

To him who supremely is, therefore, nothing can be contrary except what is not. Accordingly, just as everything good comes from him, so everything that exists naturally comes from him [Note: [Col. 0557] The manuscripts have only *quod naturale est* (“what is natural”).], since everything that exists naturally is good. Every nature, therefore, is good, and every good comes from God; therefore every nature comes from God.

## CHAPTER XX

### Pain exists only in good natures

Pain, which some regard as the chief evil, whether it occurs in the soul or in the body, cannot itself exist except in good natures. For that which resists in order to suffer pain, by that very resistance in some way refuses to cease being what it was, because it was some good [Note: [Col. 0557] The manuscripts read *restitit* (“resisted”).]. But when it is compelled toward something better, the pain is useful; when toward something worse, it is useless.

In the soul, therefore, pain is caused by a will resisting a greater power; in the body, pain is caused by sensation resisting a more powerful body. There are evils without pain that are worse. For it is worse to rejoice in iniquity than to grieve over corruption. Yet even such joy can arise only from the attainment of inferior goods; iniquity, however, is the abandonment of better goods.

Likewise, in the body a wound with pain is better than painless putrefaction, which is specifically called corruption. Dead flesh did not undergo this corruption—that is, it did not see it—as had been foretold in prophecy: “You will not give your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10). For who denies that he was wounded by the fastening of nails and pierced by a lance (John XIX, 18, 34)?

But even what human beings properly call bodily corruption—that is, putrefaction itself—if it still has something on which to consume itself, increases as it diminishes the good. If it consumes everything completely, then, just as no good remains, no nature remains, because there will no longer be anything for corruption to corrupt; and therefore putrefaction itself will no longer exist, since there will be no place where it can exist at all.

## CHAPTER XXI

### Small things are named from measure

Small and slight things are therefore also called *modica* (“moderate” or “small”) in common usage because some measure has remained in them; without it they would no longer be small, but altogether nothing. Those things called immoderate because of excessive extension are condemned for that excess. Yet even they must necessarily be restrained in some way under God, who has ordered all things “in measure, number, and weight” (Wis. XI, 21) [Col. 0558].

## CHAPTER XXII

### Whether measure can in any sense be attributed to God himself

God should not be said to have measure, lest he be thought to have an end. Yet he is not therefore immoderate, since he is the one who grants measure to all things so that they may exist in some way. Nor should God again be called measured, as though he had received measure from someone else.

If we call him the supreme measure, perhaps we say something appropriate—provided that, in calling him the supreme measure, we understand the supreme good. For every measure, insofar as it is measure, is good. Hence “measured,” “moderate,” and “regulated” cannot be said without praise, although in another sense we use “measure” for “end” and say that there is no measure where there is no end. This too is sometimes said with praise, as in the words, “And of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke I, 33).

One could also say, “There shall be no measure,” understanding measure as an end. For one who does not reign at all does not truly reign.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### Why measure, form, and order are sometimes called evil

Evil measure, evil form, or evil order is therefore spoken of either because something is less than it ought to be, or because it is not suited to the things to which it ought to be suited. In that case it is called evil because it is alien and incongruous.

Thus one might say that someone acted in a bad manner because he did less than he ought to have done, or because he acted in a way inappropriate to the matter at hand—either doing more than was fitting or acting incongruously. What is criticized as having been done in a bad manner is rightly criticized for no other reason than that measure was not observed there.

Likewise, form is called bad either in comparison with something more well-formed and more beautiful, so that one form is lesser and the other greater—not in bulk, but in beauty—or because it does not suit the thing to which it has been applied, making it appear alien and inappropriate. Thus a naked man walking in the marketplace is offensive, whereas seeing him naked in a bath does not offend.

Order is similarly called bad when order itself is observed to a lesser degree. In such a case it is not order but rather disorder that is bad, whether something is less ordered than it ought to be or is not ordered as it ought to be.

Nevertheless, wherever there is some measure, some form, and some order, there is some good and some nature. Where there is no measure, no form, and no order, there is no good and no nature.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Scripture proves that God is immutable and that the Son of God was begotten, not made

The truths held by our faith and in some measure traced out by reason must be fortified by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures. Thus those who cannot attain them through a lesser degree of understanding may believe the divine authority and thereby become worthy to understand. Those who do understand them but are less familiar with ecclesiastical writings should not suppose that we are presenting them from our own understanding rather than that they are found in those books.

That God is immutable is written in the Psalms: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Ps. CI, 27). And in the Book of Wisdom, concerning Wisdom itself: “Remaining in herself, she renews all things” (Wis. VII, 27). Hence the apostle Paul says: “To the only invisible and incorruptible God” (1 Tim. I, 17). And the apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James I, 17).

That what he begot from himself is what he himself is is stated briefly by the Son himself: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

That the Son was not made, since all things were made through him, is written as follows: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1–3)—that is, nothing was made without him.

## CHAPTER XXV

### Some misunderstand the Gospel statement, “Without him nothing was made”

Nor should we listen to the ravings of people who think that the word “nothing” in this passage must be understood as “something,” and who suppose that someone can be compelled to this absurdity because *nothing* is placed at the end of the sentence.

“Then,” they say, “it was made; and because it was made, this nothing is something.” They have lost their senses through their eagerness to contradict, and they do not understand that it makes no difference whether one says, “Without him was made nothing,” or “Without him nothing was made.” For even if it were said in the latter order, “Without him nothing was made,” they could still say that this nothing is something because it was made.

For something that truly exists, what difference does it make whether one says, “Without him was made a house,” or “Without him a house was made,” provided that it is understood that something was made without him, namely, a house?

Thus, since it is said, “Without him was made nothing”—because *nothing* is certainly not something when it is used in its true and proper sense—it makes no difference whether one says, “Without him was made nothing,” or “Without him nothing was made,” or “Nothing was made.” What sensible person would wish to argue with people who can say of the very statement I have made, “It makes no difference,” “Then something makes a difference, because this very nothing is something?”

If such people ask someone, “What have you done?” and he replies that he has done nothing, they will accordingly accuse him, saying, “Then you have done something, because you have done nothing; for this nothing is something.”

They even have the Lord himself placing this word at the end of a sentence, when he says, “I have spoken nothing in secret” (John XVIII, 20). Let them read it, then, and be silent.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Creatures were made from nothing

Since God made all things that he did not beget from himself but made through his Word—not from things that already existed, but from things that did not exist at all, that is, from nothing—the Apostle says: “Who calls those things which are not as though they were” [Note: [Col. 0559] The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have *tanquam ea quae sunt* (“as though they were things that exist”).] (Rom. IV, 17).

More explicitly, it is written in the Book of Maccabees: “I beg you, my son, look upon heaven and earth and all that is in them; see and know that they did not exist, from which the Lord God made us” (2 Macc. VII, 28).

And the statement written in the Psalm, “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5) [Col. 0560], clearly shows that he did not beget these things from himself, but made them by his word and command. Since they were not made from himself, they were made from nothing.

For there was nothing else from which he could make them. Of this the Apostle says most explicitly: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36).

## CHAPTER XXVII

### “From him” and “of him” do not signify the same thing

“From him” does not signify the same thing as “of him.” What is of him can be called from him; but not everything that is from him is properly said to be of him.

Heaven and earth are from him because he made them, but they are not of him because they are not from his substance. Thus, if a human being begets a son and makes a house, both the son and the house are from him; but the son is of him, while the house is from earth and wood.

This is because a human being cannot make something from nothing. God, however, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, did not need any matter that he himself had not made to assist his omnipotence.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Sins come not from God but from the will of sinners

When we hear, “All things are from him, and through him, and in him,” we must understand all natures that exist naturally. Sins are not from him, for they do not preserve nature but corrupt it. Holy Scripture testifies in many ways that sins arise from the will of sinners, especially in the passage where the Apostle says:

“But do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and patience and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s kindness is leading you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. II, 3–6).

## CHAPTER XXIX

### God is not defiled by our sins

Although all the things he created are in God, they do not defile him when they sin. Of his wisdom it is said: “She reaches all things because of her purity, and nothing defiled enters into her” [Note: [Col. 0560] The printed editions have *per suam munditiam* (“through her purity”); the manuscripts, in accordance with the Vulgate, have *propter*, etc.] (Wis. VII, 24–25).

Just as we must believe God to be incorruptible and immutable, so consequently we must believe him to be undefiled.

## CHAPTER XXX

### Even the smallest and earthly goods come from God

Since he himself also made the smallest goods—that is, earthly and mortal things—this is understood without doubt from the passage where the Apostle speaks of the members of our flesh. After saying, “If one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it; and if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it,” he also says there:

“God placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed”; and, “God has composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there might be no division in the body, but that the members might care for one another” (1 Cor. XII, 26, 18, 24–25).

What the Apostle praises here in the measure, form, and order of the members of the flesh is found in the flesh of all animals, both the greatest and the smallest; for all flesh is counted among earthly goods and therefore among the smallest goods.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### Both the punishment and the forgiveness of sins equally belong to God

Since what kind and how great a punishment is owed to each fault belongs to divine judgment, not human judgment, it is written: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

Since sins are forgiven by God’s goodness to those who turn back, the fact that Christ was sent sufficiently demonstrates this. He died for us not in his own nature, in which he is God, but in ours, which he assumed from a woman. The Apostle proclaims God’s goodness and love toward us as follows:

“God demonstrates his love toward us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Rom. V, 8–10).

Since, when the deserved punishment is also rendered to sinners, there is no injustice with God, he says: “What shall we say? Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” (Rom. III, 5).

In another passage he briefly indicates that both goodness and severity come from God, saying: “See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness” (Rom. XI, 22).

## CHAPTER XXXII

### The power to cause harm also comes from God

Since even the power of those who cause harm comes only from God, Wisdom speaks as follows: “Through me kings reign, and tyrants hold the earth through me” (Prov. VIII, 15). The Apostle also says: “There is no power except from God” (Rom. XIII, 1).

That this can happen fittingly is written in the Book of Job: “He makes a hypocrite reign,” it says, “because of the perversity of the people” (Job XXXIV, 30). And God says concerning the people of Israel: “I gave them a king in my wrath” (Hos. XIII, 11).

It is not unjust that when the wicked receive the power to cause harm, the patience of the good is tested and the iniquity of the wicked is punished. For through the power given to the devil, Job was tested so that his righteousness might be revealed (Job I–II); Peter was tempted so that he would not presume upon himself (Matt. XXVI, 31–35, 69–75); Paul was struck so that he would not exalt himself (2 Cor. XII, 7); and Judas was condemned so that he might hang himself (Matt. XXVII, 5).

Although God himself therefore did all these things justly through the power he gave the devil, the devil will not receive punishment at the end on account of these just deeds, but on account of the wicked will to cause harm, which belonged to the devil himself. Then it will be said to the wicked who have persisted in consenting to his evil:

“Go into the eternal fire prepared by my Father for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### The evil angels became evil by sinning, not by being created evil by God

Since the evil angels too were not created evil by God but became evil by sinning, Peter says in his Epistle:

“For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but thrust them down into the prisons of darkness [Note: [Col. 0561] The manuscripts read *trudens* (“thrusting”);] and delivered them to be kept for punishment in the judgment” (2 Pet. II, 4).

Here Peter shows that punishment at the final judgment is still owed to them, concerning which the Lord says: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Although they have already received this lower darkness as a punishment—that is, the lower, darkened air—as a prison [Note: [Col. 0562] The manuscripts have *poena* (“punishment”) in place of *poenaliter* (“as a punishment”).], it is nevertheless also called heaven. This is not the heaven in which the stars are, but the lower heaven, in whose gloom clouds gather and where birds fly. For the cloudy sky is also called heaven, and birds are called the birds of heaven.

In this sense the Apostle Paul calls these same wicked angels, against whom we struggle by living devoutly, “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12). To prevent this from being understood of the higher heavens, he says elsewhere explicitly: “According to the prince of the power of this air, who now works in the sons” [Note: [Col. 0562] The printed editions have *in filios* (“in the sons”); the manuscripts have *in filiis* (“among the sons”). The Greek is *en huiois* (“among the sons”).] “of disobedience” (Eph. II, 2).

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### Sin is not desire for an evil nature but abandonment of a better one

Since sin or iniquity is not desire for evil natures but abandonment of better ones, Scripture says: “Every creature of God is good” (1 Tim. IV, 4). Accordingly, every tree that God planted in paradise was also good.

When the human being touched the forbidden tree, therefore, he did not desire an evil nature. Rather, by abandoning what was better, he himself committed the evil deed. The Creator is better than any creature he made. His command should not have been abandoned in order to touch what was forbidden, even though it was good; for, after abandoning the better, the good of the creature was desired and touched against the Creator’s command.

God had not therefore planted an evil tree in paradise; rather, the one who forbade it to be touched was himself better.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### The tree was forbidden to Adam not because it was evil, but because it was good for humanity to remain subject to God

God forbade it in order to show that the nature of a rational soul ought not to be in its own power but subject to God, and that it preserves the order of its salvation through obedience and corrupts it through disobedience.

For this reason he called the tree whose fruit he forbade to be touched “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II, 9). When Adam touched it against the prohibition, he would experience the punishment of sin and thus learn the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### No creature of God is evil; evil consists in using a good thing badly

Who could be so foolish as to think that God’s creature—especially one planted in paradise—should be condemned, when even the thorns and thistles that the earth produced for the sinner to crush in his labor, according to God’s judicial will, should not rightly be condemned [Note: [Col. 0562] The printed editions have *conterendos* (“to be crushed”); the manuscripts more plausibly have *conterendo* (“in crushing”).]?

Such plants too have their own measure, form, and order, and anyone who considers them soberly will find them worthy of praise. Yet these things are evils for that nature which ought, by the merit of sin, to have been restrained in this way.

Sin is therefore not, as I said, desire for an evil nature but abandonment of a better one. The evil is in the act itself, not in the nature that the sinner uses badly. For it is evil to use a good thing badly.

Thus the Apostle condemns certain people judged by God who “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. I, 25). He does not condemn the creature—for whoever does that wrongs the Creator—but those who used a good thing badly, having abandoned what was better.

## CHAPTER XXXVII
The evils of sinners God uses well. Therefore, if all things preserve the measure, form, and proper order of their nature, there will be no evil; but if anyone wishes to use these goods badly, even then he does not overcome the will of God, who knows how to order even the unjust justly: so that, if they themselves through the iniquity of their will have misused his goods, he through the justice of his power may use their evils well, rightly ordering in punishments those who have perversely ordered themselves in sins.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

The eternal fire that torments the wicked is not evil. For the eternal fire itself, which is going to torment the impious, is not an evil nature, since it has its own measure, form, and order, corrupted by no iniquity; rather, the torment is evil for the condemned, whose sins have made it their due. Nor, indeed, is this light an evil nature merely because it torments those with sore eyes.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

The fire is called eternal, not in the same way as God, but because it is without end. The eternal fire, however, is not called eternal in the same way as God is eternal; for although it is without end, it nevertheless is not without a beginning [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition have this passage as follows: “The eternal fire, however, is not properly called eternal in the same way as God is eternal, because the fire is eternal precisely because it is without end, although it is not without a beginning.” M.]. God, on the other hand, is also without a beginning. Moreover, although it is applied to the perpetual punishments of sinners, its nature is nevertheless changeable. True eternity is that which is true immortality—that is, that supreme unchangeableness which God alone possesses, since he cannot be changed in any way. For it is one thing not to change although one can be changed; it is another thing to be wholly unable to be changed.

Thus a human being is called good, but not in the same way as God, of whom it is said, “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18); and a soul is called immortal, but not in the same way as God, of whom it is said, “Who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16); and a human being is called wise, but not in the same way as God, of whom it is said, “To the only wise God” (Romans 16:27). So the fire is called eternal, but not in the same way as God, whose immortality alone is true eternity.

## CHAPTER XL

Neither God nor anyone else can be harmed except by God’s just ordering. Since these things are so according to the Catholic faith and sound doctrine, and according to the truth evident to those who understand, no one can harm God’s nature, nor can God’s nature unjustly harm anyone, nor does it permit anyone to harm another with impunity. “For the one who does wrong,” says the Apostle, “will receive what he has done wrong; and there is no partiality with God” (Colossians 3:25).

## CHAPTER XLI

How many good things the Manichaeans place in the nature of evil, and how many evils in the nature of good. If the Manichaeans wished to consider this without the pernicious zeal of defending their error, and with fear of God, they would not most wickedly blaspheme by introducing two natures, one good, which they call God, and the other evil, which God did not make. They err, rave, indeed they are so insane that they do not see that, in what they call the nature of the supreme evil, they place so many good things: life, power, health, memory, understanding, equilibrium, virtue, abundance, sensation, light, sweetness, measures, numbers, peace, measure, form, and order.

In what they call the supreme good, however, they place so many evils: death, sickness, forgetfulness, ignorance, disorder, weakness, poverty, stupidity, blindness, pain, iniquity, disgrace, war, lack of restraint, deformity, and perversity.

For they say that the princes of darkness both lived in their own nature and were safe in their own kingdom, and that they remembered and understood. They describe the prince of darkness as having preached in such a way that he could neither have uttered such things himself nor been heard by those to whom he spoke without memory and understanding. They also say that he possessed a constitution suited to his mind and body, that he ruled by the strength of his power, that he possessed the abundance and fruitfulness of his elements [Note: Several manuscripts have “fruitfulness” in the singular.], and that they perceived one another, as well as the light near them, and had eyes with which they could see it from afar. Those eyes, certainly, could not see light without some light; hence they are rightly also called “lights” [Note: The Louvain edition alone here omits “light.”]. They say that they enjoyed the sweetness of their pleasure and were bounded by measured limbs and dwellings.

But unless some kind of beauty had also existed there, they would not love their marriages, nor would their bodies be constituted by the fitting agreement of their parts. Where that agreement did not exist, the things they insanely claim to have happened there could not happen. And unless some peace existed there, they would not obey their prince. Unless there were proportion there, they would do nothing other than eat, drink, rage [Note: The Cistercian manuscript has “or thirst”; four Vatican manuscripts have “or serve.”], or do some other thing without any society [Note: The manuscripts have “without any satiety.”]. Indeed, even those who did these things would not be bounded by their forms unless proportion existed there. Yet they describe them as doing such things that they cannot deny that they possessed appropriate proportions in all their actions.

If form had not existed there, no natural quality would have subsisted there. If no order had existed there, some would not dominate while others were subject; they would not live fittingly in their elements; finally, their limbs would not be arranged in their proper places, so that they could perform all the things these people foolishly imagine.

But if they do not say that God’s nature was dead, what is it that Christ raises up according to their foolishness? If they do not say that it was sick, what does he heal? If they do not say that it had forgotten, what does he recall? If they do not say that it was foolish, what does he teach? If they do not say that it was disturbed, what does he restore? If it was not conquered and captured, what does he liberate? If it does not lack, whom does he assist? If it has not lost sensation, what does he revive? If it has not been blinded, what does he illuminate? If it is not in pain, what does he refresh? If it is not unjust, what does he correct through his commandments? If it has not been disgraced, what does he cleanse? If it is not at war, to whom does he promise peace? If it is not without restraint [Col. 0565], upon whom does he impose the measure of the law? If it is not deformed, what does he reform? If it is not perverse, what does he amend?

For they say that all these things are provided by Christ not to that entity which God made and which was corrupted by sinning through its own free choice, but to the very nature, the very substance of God—which is identical with God.

## CHAPTER XLII

The Manichaeans’ blasphemies concerning God’s nature. What can be compared with these blasphemies? Nothing at all. But if the errors of other perverse sects are considered, and if this error is compared with the other aspect of it, about which we have not yet spoken, it is shown to blaspheme against God’s nature still more grievously and abominably.

For they also say that certain souls—which they wish to be of God’s substance and altogether of the same nature, and which did not sin voluntarily but were overcome and overwhelmed by the nation of darkness, which they call the evil nature, against which they descended not of their own accord but at the Father’s command—are fastened eternally to a dreadful globe of darkness.

Thus, according to their sacrilegious empty talk, God freed himself in one part from a great evil, and again condemned himself in another part, which he was unable to free from the enemy; and, as though he had conquered that enemy, he even celebrated a triumph over himself. O wicked and unbelievable audacity—to believe such things about God, to say such things, and to preach such things!

When they try to defend this and rush, with closed eyes, into worse things, they say that the mixture with the evil nature causes these things, so that God’s good nature suffers such evils; for, they claim, it could not and cannot suffer any of these things within itself [Note: The printed editions have: “lest they rush into worse things, they say with closed eyes.” The manuscripts correct the reading as translated here.].

As though an incorruptible nature should be praised because it does not harm itself, rather than because nothing can harm it. Moreover, if the nature of darkness harmed God’s nature, and God’s nature harmed the nature of darkness, then there are two evils that harmed one another; and the nation of darkness had the better disposition, because, even if it inflicted harm, it did so unwillingly. For it wished not to harm but to enjoy God’s good.

God, however, wished to extinguish it, as Manichaeus most plainly raves in his letter called *The Ruin of the Foundation*. For, having forgotten what he had said shortly before—“Its most splendid kingdoms were founded above the bright and blessed earth in such a way that they could never be moved or shaken by anyone”—he later said:

> “The Father of the most blessed Light, knowing the great stain and devastation that would rise from the darkness and threaten his holy ages, unless some outstanding and glorious divinity, powerful in virtue, were set against it, so that it might at once overcome and destroy the stock of darkness, after whose extinction perpetual rest might be prepared for the inhabitants of the light” [Note: Most manuscripts have “a light might be set against it.”].

Behold, he feared the stain and devastation threatening his ages. Surely, then, they were founded above the bright and blessed earth in such a way that they could never be moved or shaken by anyone? Behold, out of fear he wished to harm the neighboring nation, which he attempted to destroy and extinguish so that perpetual rest might be prepared for the inhabitants of the light.

Why did he not add, “And a perpetual bond”? Were those souls whom he fastened eternally within the globe of darkness not inhabitants of the light [Col. 0566]—souls of whom he plainly says that they allowed themselves to stray from their former bright nature? There he was even unwillingly compelled to say that they sinned by free choice, although he does not wish to place sin anywhere except in the necessity of the contrary nature. Everywhere he does not know what he is saying, as though he himself were already enclosed in the globe of darkness that he invented, seeking a way out and finding none.

Let him say what he wishes to the deceived and miserable people, by whom he is honored much more than Christ, so that at this price he may sell them such long and sacrilegious fables. Let him say what he wishes; let him enclose the nation of darkness in the globe as in a prison, and fasten the nature of light outside it, promising it perpetual rest after the enemy has been extinguished. Behold: the punishment of the light is worse than that of the darkness; the punishment of the divine nature is worse than that of the opposing nation.

For even if the nation of darkness is inside the darkness, dwelling in darkness belongs to its nature. But the souls that are identical with God will not be received, as he says, into those peaceful kingdoms; they will be excluded from the life and freedom of the holy light, and will be fastened in the dreadful globe mentioned above. Hence, he says, “the same souls will cling to those things that they loved, left in that same globe of darkness, acquiring this for themselves by their own merits.”

Surely, then, there is no free choice of the will? See how, in his madness, he does not know what he is saying, and by speaking contradictions wages a worse war against himself than against the god of that nation of darkness.

Moreover, if the souls of light are condemned because they loved darkness, the nation of darkness is unjustly condemned, since it loved the light.
