Indeed, the nation of darkness loved the light from the beginning; although it wished to possess it violently, it did not wish to extinguish it. The nature of light, however, wished in the war to extinguish the darkness; thus, having been defeated, it loved the darkness.

Choose whichever you wish: were they compelled by necessity to love the darkness, or were they seduced by their will? If by necessity, why is it condemned? If by will, why is God’s nature found involved in such great iniquity? If God’s nature was compelled by necessity to love the darkness, then it was conquered, not victorious. If by will, why do the miserable hesitate to attribute the will to sinning to the nature that God made from nothing, lest they attribute it to the light that he begot?

## CHAPTER XLIII

The Manichaeans attribute many evils to God’s nature before the mixture with evil. What if we also show that, before the mixture with evil—which they insanely believe to have been fabulously invented—in the very nature of light as they describe it there were great evils? What will seem capable of being added to these blasphemies?

There was, before the battle began, a harsh and unavoidable necessity of fighting. Behold, then, a great evil already existed before evil was mixed with good. Let them say where this came from, since no mixture had yet taken place.

But if there was no necessity, then there was will. From where, then, came so great an evil that God himself wished to harm his own nature, which could not be harmed by the enemy, by sending it to be cruelly mixed, shamefully cleansed, and unjustly condemned? Behold how great was the evil of a pernicious, harmful, and utterly savage will before any evil from the opposing nation had been mixed in.

Or perhaps he did not know that this would happen to his members: that they would love the darkness and become enemies of the holy light, as he himself says—that is, enemies not only of their god but also of the Father from whom they came? Where, then, did such a great evil of ignorance in God arise before any evil from the opposing nation had been mixed in?

But if he knew that this would happen, then either there was eternal cruelty in him, if he felt no grief over the future pollution and condemnation of his nature, or eternal misery, if he did grieve. Where, then, did such a great evil of your supreme good arise before any mixture with your supreme evil?

Certainly, that particular portion of his nature which is fastened in the eternal bond of that globe—if it did not know that this threatened it—was nevertheless subject to eternal ignorance within God’s nature. But if it did know, there was eternal misery. Where, then, did such a great evil arise before any evil from the opposing nation had been mixed in?

Or perhaps it rejoiced with great love because, through its punishment, perpetual rest was being prepared for the other inhabitants of the light? Whoever sees how wicked it is to say this, let him anathematize it [Note: The Ambrosian and Erasmus editions have: “Whoever hears how wicked it is to say that God’s nature is thus aided, let him anathematize it,” and the Louvain edition has: “Whoever hears how wicked it is to say that God’s nature is thus aided by God’s nature, let him anathematize it.” The manuscripts of better quality, omitting “that God’s nature is thus aided by God’s nature,” have the reading translated here. But if he did at least act in this way, supply: “that particular portion of God’s nature.”].

But if it had at least acted in such a way that it did not itself become hostile to the light, it might perhaps have been praised not as God’s nature but as some human being who wished to suffer something for his homeland—something that could indeed have been temporary, not eternal. But now they say both that its fastening in the globe of darkness is eternal and that it is not the fastening of just anything but of God’s nature. And certainly, if God’s nature rejoiced that it would love the darkness and become an enemy of the holy light, that joy was utterly unjust, execrable, and ineffably sacrilegious.

Where did such an enormous and wicked evil arise before any evil from the opposing nation had been mixed in? Who could endure such perverse and impious madness: attributing so many goods to the supreme evil, and so many evils to the supreme good, which is God?

## CHAPTER XLIV

Incredible obscenities devised by Manichaeus concerning God. They say that this very portion of God’s nature is everywhere mixed—in the heavens, on the earth, beneath the earth, in all bodies, dry and moist, in all flesh, and in all the seeds of trees, plants, human beings, and animals. They do not say that it is present in all things, administering and governing them without any bond, undefiled, inviolate, and incorruptible, by the power of divinity, as we say of God. Rather, they say that it is bound, oppressed, and polluted, and that it is released, liberated, and cleansed not only through the courses of the sun and moon and the powers of light, but also through their Elect.

It is horrifying to say what sacrilegious and incredible obscenities this kind of utterly wicked error urges upon them, even if it does not persuade them. For they say that the powers of light are transformed into beautiful males and presented to the females of the nation of darkness, and that the same powers of light are again transformed into beautiful females and presented to the males of the nation of darkness. Thus, through their beauty, they inflame the most filthy lust of the princes of darkness [Col. 0568], and in this way the vital substance—that is, the nature of God—which they say is held bound in their bodies, escapes from their limbs when loosened by that very desire, and, once released and received or cleansed, is liberated.

The wretched read this, say this, hear this, and believe this. In the seventh book of their *Treasury*—for so they call a certain writing of Manichaeus in which these blasphemies are recorded—it is set down as follows:

> “Then that blessed Father, who possesses luminous ships, dwelling places, habitations, or expanses, moved by the clemency inherent in him, offers assistance by which his vital substance is stripped and liberated from the impious restraints, confinements, and anguish [Note: Several manuscripts have “his vital substance” in the nominative rather than “of his vital substance.”].  
>   
> “Therefore, by his invisible nod he transforms those powers of his that are contained in this most brilliant ship, and makes them submit to the opposing powers that have been arranged in the several regions of the heavens. Since these consist of both sexes, male and female, he therefore commands the aforementioned powers partly to submit, in the form of beardless boys, to the opposing race of females, partly in the form of radiant virgins to the opposing race of males. He knows that all the hostile powers, because of the deadly and most filthy desire innate in them, are easily captured, enslaved by those most beautiful forms that appear, and in this way dissolved.  
>   
> “Know also that this same blessed Father of ours is identical with his powers, which, for a necessary reason, he transforms into the undefiled likeness of boys and virgins [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts have “unrestrained” rather than “undefiled.”]. He uses these as his own weapons and through them accomplishes his will.  
>   
> “These divine powers, which are set up in the likeness of marriage against the infernal races, and which accomplish at the very moment, with alacrity and ease, whatever they have conceived, fill the luminous ships. Therefore, whenever reason requires that the same holy powers appear to males, they immediately display their own image in the guise of the most beautiful virgins. Again, when they come to females, they set aside the forms of virgins and display the appearance of beautiful boys.  
>   
> “At this decorous sight, their ardor and desire increase, and in this way the bond of their worst thoughts [Note: Two manuscripts have “passive thoughts.”] is loosened. The living soul that was held in their limbs is released on this occasion and escapes, mingling with its own purest air. There, when thoroughly washed, the souls ascend to the luminous ships that have been prepared to carry them and convey them across to their homeland.  
>   
> “But whatever still bears the stains of the opposing race descends little by little through the heats and warmth, and is mixed with trees, other plants, and all seeds, and is affected by different heats [Note: Most manuscripts have “and is impressed by different colors.”].  
>   
> “In this way, from that great and brilliant ship, the forms of boys and virgins appear to the opposing powers that dwell in the heavens and possess a fiery nature; and at this decorous sight the portion of life held in their limbs is released and carried through the heats into the earth. In the same way, that highest power which dwells in the ship of the vital waters appears through its angels in the likeness of holy boys and virgins to those powers whose nature is cold and moist and which have been arranged in the heavens. To those that are female the form of boys appears; to the males, that of virgins.  
>   
> “By this change and diversity of divine and most beautiful persons, the male and female princes of the moist and cold stock are loosened, and what is vital within them escapes. Whatever remains is released and carried through the cold into the earth [Note: Several manuscripts of good quality have “before the cold.”], and is mixed with all the kinds of earth.”

Who could endure this? Who could believe it—not that it is so, but that it could even be said? Behold those who fear anathematizing Manichaeus as a teacher, yet do not fear believing that God both does and suffers these things!

## CHAPTER XLV

Certain abominable obscenities rightly believed concerning the Manichaeans themselves. They say that this same mixed portion and nature of God is cleansed through their Elect, namely by eating and drinking, because they say that it is held bound in all foods. When it is taken by the Elect, as though by holy men, in eating and drinking for the nourishment of the body, they say that it is released, marked, and liberated through their holiness.

The wretched do not notice how fittingly it has been believed concerning them that they do what they vainly deny—unless they anathematize those same books and cease to be Manichaeans. For if, as they say, God’s portion is bound in all seeds and is cleansed by the Elect through eating, who would not rightly believe that they do what they read in their *Treasury* is done between the powers of heaven and the princes of darkness? For they say that their own flesh comes from the nation of darkness, and they do not hesitate to believe and affirm that the vital substance, the portion of God, is held bound in it.

If this substance must be released and cleansed by eating, as their fatal error compels them to confess, who would not see, who would not shudder, at the great obscenity and abomination that follows?

## CHAPTER XLVI

The wicked doctrine of the *Letter of the Foundation*. They also say that Adam, the first human being, was created by certain princes of the nation of darkness so that the light would not escape from them but be held fast.

For in the letter that they call the *Foundation*, Manichaeus wrote how the prince of darkness—whom they present as the father of the first human being—spoke and acted toward the other princes of darkness, his companions:

> “Then, with wicked schemes, he said to those who were present: ‘What do you think of this great light that is arising? Look at how it moves the heavens and shakes many powers. Therefore, it is more fitting that you surrender to me the light that you possess in your powers. For thus I shall fashion an image of that great one who has appeared in glory, through which we shall be able to rule once we have been freed from our association with darkness.’  
>   
> “When they heard this and deliberated among themselves for a long time, they considered it most just to provide what was requested. For they had no confidence that they would retain the same light forever. Therefore they judged it better to offer it to their prince, by no means despairing that in the same way they themselves would rule [Note: The Vatican manuscript has “in the same act.”].”

How, then, they provided that light which they possessed must be considered [Note: The manuscripts have “that same light.”]. For this too has been scattered throughout all the divine Scriptures and heavenly mysteries. It is not difficult for the wise to know how it was given; indeed, it is openly and clearly understood by anyone who wishes to look upon it truly and faithfully.

Since the multitude of those who had gathered was mixed—female and male—he compelled them to come together with one another. In that intercourse some sowed seed, while others became pregnant. The offspring were like those who had begotten them, possessing very great powers, as their parents had possessed them first.

Their prince took these offspring as a special gift and rejoiced. And just as even now we see the evil nature that fashions bodies, drawing its powers from that source and giving them shape, so the aforementioned prince, receiving the offspring of his companions—offspring that possessed the perceptions and prudence of their parents, together with the light generated in them at birth—ate them. Having taken in many powers from such food, in which there was not only strength but, even more, cunning and corrupt perception from the savage race of their parents [Note: Several manuscripts have “from the mind.”], he summoned to himself a consort flowing from the stock from which he himself had come. Having had intercourse with her, he sowed, like the others, the abundance of evils that he had devoured, adding something from his own thought and power so that his perception might be the shaper and delineator of all that he had poured forth. His female counterpart received these things, as cultivated earth is accustomed to receive seed with great care.

For within her were constructed and woven images of all the heavenly and earthly powers, so that what was being formed might evidently obtain the likeness of the entire universe.

## CHAPTER XLVII

He compels the perpetration of horrifying obscenities. O wicked monster! O accursed destruction and defilement of deceived souls! I pass over what it means to say that a portion of God’s nature is bound in this way [Note: The Ambrosian and Erasmus editions read “is read”; the Louvain edition has “will be read.” The manuscripts correct the reading as translated here.].

Let the miserable, deceived, and fatally poisoned at least attend to this: if, through the intercourse of males and females, the portion of God is bound—a portion that they profess to release and cleanse by eating—then the necessity of this utterly wicked error compels them not only to release and cleanse the portion of God from bread, vegetables, and fruits, which alone they appear openly to accept, but also to release and cleanse it from whatever can become bound through intercourse if it has been conceived in a woman’s womb.

Some are reported to have confessed publicly that they do this, not only in Paphlagonia but also in Gaul, as I heard from a Catholic Christian at Rome. When they were asked by whose scriptural authority they did these things, they are said to have disclosed this passage from their *Treasury*, which I mentioned shortly before.

When this is charged against them, they usually reply that some enemy of theirs from their own number—that is, from among their Elect—deserted and created a schism, founding this kind of utterly filthy heresy. It is therefore clear that, even if these people do not do it, whoever does do it does so from their books.

Let them therefore reject the books if they abhor the crime which, if they retain the books, they are compelled to commit; or, if they do not commit it, let them try to live more purely in opposition to their books.

But what do they do when they are told: “Either cleanse the light from whatever seeds you can, so that you do not reject even that which you assert you do not do; or anathematize Manichaeus, who says that a portion of God is in all seeds and is bound through intercourse, and that whatever light—that is, whatever portion of God—has reached the food of the Elect is cleansed by eating”? You see what he urges you to do, yet you hesitate to anathematize him?

What, I ask, do they do when this is said to them? To what evasions do they turn, when either such a wicked doctrine must be anathematized or such a wicked obscenity must be committed? Compared with this, all those evils that I mentioned shortly before as intolerable—namely, that they say of God’s nature that it was compelled by necessity to wage war; that it was either secure in eternal ignorance or troubled by eternal pain and fear, awaiting the corruption of the mixture and the bond of eternal condemnation; that, after waging war, it was captured, oppressed, and polluted; and that, after a false victory, it was destined to be fastened eternally in a dreadful globe and separated from the happiness of its origin—all these seem tolerable, although, considered by themselves, they cannot be endured.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Augustine prays for the Manichaeans’ repentance. O your great patience, Lord, merciful and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in mercy and truth (Psalm 102:8); you who make your sun rise upon the good and the evil and rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45); you who do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn back and live (Ezekiel 33:11); you who, correcting in portions, give room for repentance [Note: The printed editions have “correcting a portion, giving room.” The manuscripts have the reading translated here, as in the sacred Scriptures, Wisdom 12:2.], so that, abandoning wickedness, they may believe in you, Lord (Wisdom 12:2); you who by your patience lead people to repentance, although many, according to the hardness of their heart and their unrepentant heart, store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of your just judgment, when you repay each person according to his works (Romans 2:4–6); you who, on the day when a person turns from his wickedness to your mercy and truth, forget all his iniquities (Ezekiel 18:21):

Grant us, give us, that through our ministry—by which you wished this execrable and utterly dreadful error to be refuted—as many have already been liberated, so others too may be liberated; and that, whether through the sacrament of your holy Baptism or through the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart (Psalm 50:19), in the sorrow of repentance they may deserve to receive forgiveness of their sins and blasphemies, by which through ignorance they offended you.

For your surpassing mercy and power, and the truth of your Baptism, and the keys of the kingdom of heaven in your holy Church, are so effective that one must not despair even of those who, while they live on this earth through your patience, remain in that evil profession because of some habit or acquisition of temporal and earthly advantage—even though they know how great an evil it is to think or speak such things about you—if, at least, when reproved by your corrections, they flee to your ineffable goodness and prefer heavenly and eternal life to all the enticements of the flesh [Note: The manuscripts add “Amen.”].

# [AGAINST SECUNDINUS THE MANICHAEAN]

[Col. 0571]

## THE LETTER OF SECUNDINUS THE MANICHAEAN TO AUGUSTINE

[Note: For the following writings, see Book 2, chapter 10 of the *Retractions*, volume 1, column 634, from the words “A certain Secundinus” up to the words “Your benevolence toward me.” M.]

[Note: The book *Against Secundinus*, once unsuccessfully sought in the Belgian manuscripts through the efforts of the Louvain scholars, has now been discovered by us in an excellent Gallican manuscript preserved in the abbey of Saint Peter in the valley of Chartres. With its help it has been cleansed of many errors.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

He commends and defends the doctrine of Manichaeus while criticizing the Catholic faith. He is indignant that Augustine attacks it in writing, alleging that Augustine abandoned Manichaeus out of a certain fear and desire for honor, and exhorting him to return at last to that sect.

[Col. 0571] **1.** I give thanks and express gratitude to the ineffable and most sacred Majesty, and to its firstborn, the king of all lights, Jesus Christ. I give thanks and humbly offer thanks to the holy Spirit, because they have given and provided the opportunity by which I, in safety, might greet your excellent Holiness, my lord, deservedly praiseworthy and uniquely worthy of devotion.

[Note: In Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition, the following is a preamble to Secundinus’ letter to Augustine: “To the deservedly honorable and praiseworthy, uniquely revered Augustine, Secundinus. I give thanks,” and so forth. M.]

Nor is this surprising. For they are fully capable of providing every good and warding off every evil; they defend your benevolence with their ramparts and rescue you from that evil which is not nothing, nor is generated by the conspiracy and suffering of mortals, but is prepared to come. Woe, however, to the one who offers himself as an occasion for it. For you are worthy to receive such gifts from them, and for them to become the nourishers of your truth—truly the lamp that the right hand of truth placed upon the candlestick of your heart, lest, at the thief’s arrival, the patrimony of your treasure be squandered.

May they command that house to remain without falling, the house that you established not upon the sand of error but upon the stone of knowledge. May they drive away from us that savage spirit which instills fear and faithlessness in human beings, so that it may turn souls away from the narrow path of the Savior. All its assault is poured forth through those princes against whom the Apostle confesses that he has entered into combat in the Letter to the Ephesians. For he says that his struggle is not against flesh and blood but against princes and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12).

And truly, who would have weapons against anyone except against one who is armed, against one who is in motion? For just as human bodies are weapons of sin, so salutary commandments are weapons of righteousness (Romans 6:13). This Paul testifies; this Manichaeus himself also testifies.

### 2

It is therefore not a battle of weapons, but of spirits, who make use of those same weapons [Note: [Col. 0573] Thus the old Carnotensis codex, of excellent quality. The printed editions, however, read “which make use.”]. They fight for the sake of souls. In their midst stands the soul, to which from the beginning its nature gave victory. If it acts together with the spirit of the virtues [Note: [Col. 0573] The printed editions here and in the following book, chapter 8, read “if it performs virtue together with the spirit.” The Carnotensis manuscript is better: “if it acts together with the spirit of the virtues.” For Secundinus opposes “the spirit of the virtues” to “the spirit of the vices.”], it will have eternal life with it and will possess that kingdom to which our Lord invites us. But if it begins to be drawn along by the spirit of the vices, and consents, and after consenting shows repentance, it will have a fountain of pardon for these filths. For it is led on by the mingling of the flesh, not by its own will. But if, once it has come to know itself, it consents to evil and does not arm itself against the enemy, it has sinned by its own will. If it is afterward ashamed that it has gone astray, it will find the author of mercies ready. For it is not punished because it sinned, but because it did not grieve over its sin.

But if it departs with that same sin unforgiven, then it will be excluded; then it will be compared with the foolish virgin; then it will be an heir of the left hand; then it will be driven by the Lord from the wedding feast because of its black garments, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; and it will go with the devil to the fire of his own origin—that devil whom your remarkable wisdom either records as having been made from an archangel or declares to be nothing.

Why, then, will the righteous reign? Why will the apostles and martyrs be crowned? Entirely because they conquered nothing? O how greatly the power of the victor is frustrated when the adversary is proclaimed to possess no virtue! Change your opinion, I beg you; lay aside the treachery of the Punic people, and turn your withdrawal to the truth—which was brought about through fear. Do not excuse yourself with these lies [Note: [Col. 0573] The old Carnotensis codex reads, “Do not excuse yourself with these lies”; supply “your retreat.”].

### 3

For my meagre and whatever sort of Roman talent has read some of the writings of your Revered Dignity [Note: [Col. 0573] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read, “and whatever sort of talent a Roman possesses.” Manuscript reading.] [Col. 0574], in which you rage against truth as Hortensius does against philosophy. Thus, when with suspended mind and alert eye I had gone over them again and again, I found everywhere a supreme orator and almost the god of all eloquence; but nowhere did I find a Christian. You are armed, indeed, against everything, but affirm nothing, although you ought to have shown yourself learned in knowledge rather than in speech.

Yet I cannot keep silent about this before your most patient Holiness: it seemed to me—and so it certainly is—that you were never a Manichaean and could not have learned the unknown secrets of his mystery, and that under the name of Manichaeus you are persecuting Hannibal [Note: [Col. 0574] The printed editions commonly read *humilem* (“humble”) in place of *Hannibalem* (“Hannibal”). The reading is corrected from the Carnotensis manuscript.] and Mithridates. For I confess that the marbles of the Anician house do not glitter with such diligence and such labor as your writings shine with eloquence. If you had been willing to reconcile this eloquence with the truth, it would certainly have been a great adornment to us.

Do not, I beg you, act against your own nature; do not be the spear of error with which the Savior’s side is struck. For you see that he is crucified both in the whole world and in every soul—a soul that has never possessed a nature inclined to anger [Note: [Col. 0574] Thus the Carnotensis codex. The Louvain edition, however, reads, “which never possessed a cause and a nature inclined to anger.” The Amsterdam edition reads, “which never possessed an end and a nature inclined to anger.”]. You, therefore, who are from that very soul, abandon, I beg you, your now empty accusations and leave aside your superfluous controversies.

For so long a time, standing with your parent in the midst of darkness, you never mocked; once you had been brought into the midst of the sun and moon, you became an accuser. Who, then, will be your advocate before the just tribunal of the Judge, when you begin to be convicted by your own testimony both in speech and in deed? Persa, whom you accused, will not be present. Apart from him, who will console you as you weep? Who will save the Punic man?

Has the Gospel been corrected so that the broad way does not lead to destruction (Matt. 7:13)? Is Paul wrong in saying that each person will have to give an account of his own deeds (Rom. 14:12)? O, if in departing from Manichaeus you had gone to the Academy, or had interpreted the wars of the Romans, who conquered everything! How great and splendid things you would have discovered there—and then, as a chaste man, wholly devoted to purity and poverty, you would not have gone to the barbarous peoples of the Jews in their morals, while inserting fables into their commandments [Note: [Col. 0574] In the Carnotensis manuscript: “you would have gone to the nation of the Jews, barbarous both in morals and in commandments, inserting fables”; and you bring in a wife, etc.], and bringing in a prostitute as a wife; and, “You shall make sons of a prostitute”; and, “The land shall commit fornication away from the Lord” (Hos. 1:2); and, “You shall not wash your hands after intercourse with your wife”; and, “Place your hand upon my thigh” (Gen. 24:2; 47:29); and, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13); and, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28).

Did you perhaps enjoy the lions in the pit (Dan. 6:16), because there were no cages? Did Sarah’s barrenness grieve you, although her husband, pretending that she was his sister, had become the agent of the dispersal of her chastity (Gen. 12:13; 20:2)? Or perhaps, after the contest of Dares and Entellus (Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.362–484), you wished to await Jacob and his own wrestling match (Gen. 32:24–25)? Or the number of the Amorites (Josh. 10:5)? Or had you planned to behold a collection of every kind in Noah’s ark [Col. 0575] (Gen. 7)?

I know that you have always hated these things; I know that you have always loved great things—things that would leave the earth behind, seek the heavens, mortify bodies, and give life to souls. Who, then, is he who has suddenly changed you?

### 4

Yet it would be exceedingly absurd to say such things to your Holiness. You yourself are not unaware how wicked he is, how malicious, and how cunningly he wages war against the faithful and the greatest men: he compelled Peter, in a single night, to deny the Lord three times, and did not allow Thomas to believe the risen Lord. Yet these wounds were healed by the medicine of pardon.

Consider how boldly he attempted this: while the Lord was sowing the best seed, he mixed in weeds; he snatched Judas Iscariot from so great a shepherd; and, in order that the punishment of the cross might ultimately be reached, he stirred up the scribes and Pharisees against him to his destruction, so that they cried out for Barabbas to be released and Jesus to be crucified.

We therefore escaped because we followed the spiritual Savior. For his audacity burst forth to such an extent that, if our Lord had been carnal, all our hope would have been cut off. Yet even the disgrace of the cross could not satisfy him. In his madness he compelled him, on one side, to be crowned with thorns and, on the other, to be given vinegar to drink; on one side, to be struck by a soldier’s lance and, on the other, to be blasphemed by the mouth of the wicked thief (Matt. 26–27; Luke 22–23; John 18–20).

Afterward his wickedness grew so great that, when he himself and his apostles had ascended there, he composed various controversies under their names—what is worse, dividing the dignity of the Catholic name among all the superstitious. I pass over how he armed each disciple against his teachers, how he deceived Hymenaeus [Note: [Col. 0575] The Carnotensis codex reads *Hermogenem* (“Hermogenes”) instead of *Hymenaeum* (“Hymenaeus”).], how he deceived Alexander (1 Tim. 1:20), and what he perpetrated at Antioch, Smyrna, and Iconium. I now add what the present multitude is practicing, from which virtue is as far removed as it is shut away from the crowd. For that to which the crowd has attained is not virtue—and the crowd is composed chiefly of women.

But I fear making their secret deeds public, lest crimes begun by others should be doubled. Yet it is the mark of the wise to endure and laugh at both, and to strive only for that which brings blessedness and gives birth to life.

### 5

And yet, again and again, as a suppliant I beseech you; I ask and entreat you repeatedly: first, deign to grant pardon if by any expression your golden breast has been tickled or irritated. For I did this in excessive ardor because I do not want you to be torn away from our flock—from which I myself, while wandering, nearly perished, unless I had quickly withdrawn myself from the wicked nature of that communion.

Next, reconcile yourself to her who has done you no wrong. Return to her who, if you return, will not be angry with you even on account of the faults of your life [Note: [Col. 0575] The same Carnotensis codex reads, “who, if you return to her, will not be angry with you on account of your fault.” Perhaps *ob culpam* (“on account of the fault”) should be read.]. For she knows how to forgive not merely seven times; indeed, she possesses the power both to bind and to loose.

Do not pretend to grope your way, you who saw long ago; do not wish to learn, you who are able to teach. Abandon human glory if you wish to please Christ [Col. 0576]. Renew Paul in our times: although he had been a teacher of the Jewish law, after receiving from the Lord the grace of apostleship, he regarded as refuse the things he had considered gains, in order to gain Christ (Phil. 3:8).

Come to the aid of your soul, so luminous—for you do not know at what hour the thief will come. Do not adorn the dead, since you are the adornment of the living. Do not be a companion of the broad road, for it awaits the Amorite; hasten instead to the narrow way, so that you may attain eternal life.

Cease, I beg you, to enclose Christ in the womb, lest you yourself should again be enclosed in the womb. Cease to make two natures one, because the Lord’s judgment is drawing near. Woe to those who receive and transform what is sweet into bitterness.

### 6

But if you doubt about the beginning, if you are uncertain about the origin of the battle, an explanation can be given through a day-long discussion and a peaceful conversation. Yet I make this known to your exceedingly discerning goodness: there are certain matters that cannot be expounded in such a way that they can be understood. Divine reason exceeds mortal hearts—for example, this very question: how there can be two natures, or why one who could suffer nothing should have fought; and likewise the matter of the new age, which he also mentions, saying that it is built after the great earthquakes of that earth have been cut away [Note: [Col. 0576] Thus the Carnotensis manuscript. The printed editions read, “after the earthquakes of that great earth have passed away.”].

But who would admit that something has been cut away among divine things—unless you make it a figure of an interpreter addressing a hearer [Note: [Col. 0576] The Carnotensis codex reads, “unless you make it a figure adapting things to a hearer”; that is, words are cut off from one person and composed in another.], because words are cut off from the former and arranged in the latter? And although the interpreter may have said many things that the hearer retains within himself, they have not departed from the interpreter—unless you think similarly about that age and regard what is said as sufficiently foolish and inept.

The same applies to the battle. Unless you first infer that God is entirely justice, while the ultimate crime is to invade what belongs to another, the following point will not be clear: when the opposing nature came against him, he could indeed suffer nothing, because he knew beforehand; yet he would have appeared to consent to the crime unless he had fought. Therefore he opposed the one who came with great virtue, so that his justice would not be polluted by consenting to sacrilege.

For the Just One was defined by him in such a way [Note: [Col. 0576] Thus the Carnotensis manuscript. The printed editions read, “Thus the just man was brought to an end.”], that he himself neither ever sins nor ever consents to the sinner. This too is to be understood: God was powerful in his kingdom by nature, as omnipotent and judge.

These things have been said not as he was made, but as I was unable to grasp them [Note: [Col. 0576] Perhaps read, “as I was able,” deleting *non* (“not”).]. Yet they still do not satisfy unbelief; the sun has not risen for the blind, the voice has not been heard by the deaf, and food has not been prepared for the dead.

That places cannot be assigned to natures is what the human condition calls indescribable and ineffable. But the Savior, for whom everything is easy, calls these two things right and left, within and without, “Come” and “Depart” (Matt. 25). But you make a turn and set down a foot, as in: “World, life, salvation, light, law, order, power.” If you call a vowel mute and call a long syllable short, these things do not sound according to nature; nevertheless, the two certainly signify something, separated from one another [Col. 0577].

### 7

But when such matters are expounded by me to your admirable and lofty wisdom, it is like the Jordan lending water to the Ocean, a lamp lending light to the sun, or a people lending holiness to a bishop. For this reason one must endure whatever this letter contains.

Indeed, if I had not known your divine patience—which readily pardons everyone—I would never have written in this manner, although you can see that I have touched upon the most important ideas only in outline and have taken great care not to seem tiresome to you.

Accordingly, let these matters find credence with your Holiness, and let them show how we are saved. Otherwise, you will be able to produce thousands of volumes from them, O lord deservedly worthy of praise and uniquely deserving of honor. Farewell.

[Col. 0577]

## One Book of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Against Secundinus the Manichaean

[Note: [Col. 0577] In the *Retractationes*, the work *On the Nature of the Good* follows immediately; it is appended to the books written against Felix at the end of the year 404. This book therefore belongs approximately to the year 405.] (C)

Augustine explains why he abandoned the sect of the Manichaeans and refutes it by arguments drawn from Secundinus’s own letter.

## Chapter One

Your goodwill toward me, which appears in your letter [Note: [Col. 0577] In B., “Your goodwill toward me,” etc.; but Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read, “Your goodwill toward me.” This reading is supported by the Benedictine edition, *Retractationes* 2.10. Manuscript reading.], is pleasing to me. Yet, as much as I ought to return your love, since you love me, so saddened am I that you have clung stubbornly to false suspicions, partly against me and partly against truth itself, which cannot be changed.

But because what you think about my mind is untrue, I easily disregard it. For you think something which, although I do not recognize it in myself, nevertheless may exist in a human being. Therefore, even if you are mistaken about me, you are not so mistaken as to remove me from the number of human beings by your opinion. You believe of me what can occur in the human mind, even if it has not occurred in mine.

It is not therefore necessary for me to make a great effort to remove this suspicion from you. For your hope does not depend upon me, nor can you be good only if I am good. Think of Augustine whatever you wish; may conscience alone not accuse me in the sight of God. For the Apostle says, “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Cor. 4:3).

I, for my part, will not repay you in kind by daring to form a sinister opinion about your mind—something I cannot see. Nor do I say that you wished to wound me deceitfully; I think of you only as much as you disclose about yourself in your words.

Therefore, although you suspected me of evil—namely, that I abandoned the Manichaean heresy through a carnal fear of some disadvantage that might have come upon me from your society, or through desire for the honor that I obtained in the Catholic Church—I do not in turn think ill of you. I believe that your suspicion is benevolent, and I judge that you wrote this not to accuse me but from a desire to correct me.

If you would extend to me the goodwill of believing me, since you accuse me concerning the hidden recesses of my mind [Col. 0578], which I certainly cannot bring forth and display before your eyes, you would easily change your opinion of me and would no longer rashly affirm what you do not know.

## Chapter Two

For I confess that I abandoned the Manichaeans through fear—but fear of those words spoken through the Apostle Paul:

> “The Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars, having their own conscience branded, forbidding marriage, abstaining from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:1–4).

Although by these words he may perhaps have briefly and clearly described other heretics as well, he described the Manichaeans above all. Because of this fear, when I possessed only a child’s understanding [Note: [Col. 0578] In the Carnotensis codex, “when I possessed a servant’s understanding.” Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 188–189, thinks the reading should be: “When, as an African, I scarcely possessed understanding in a childish intellect.”], I tore myself away from that society.

I also confess that I burned with a love of honor, so that I might depart from it—but with love of the honor of which the same Apostle says, “But glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good” (Rom. 2:10). Who, however, will attempt to do good if he believes that evil exists not in a changeable will but in an unchangeable nature?

For this reason the Lord himself says to those who thought they were speaking good things although they were evil: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12:33). But to those who had already been changed from evil to good, the Apostle says: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

But if you do not wish to believe me concerning my mind, think as you please; only take care what you think about the truth itself [Col. 0579]. “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10:13). For it is a human error to believe that something occurred in my mind merely because it could have occurred, even if it did not.

But when you think that a sacrilegious—and not merely utterly false but also utterly deceptive—Persian fable, woven and fabricated from the most contaminated lies, is the truth concerning not just any human being but the supreme God, this must not be passed over, nor must so great a death of the soul be disregarded.

There is something that can be discussed with you. For just as, concerning my mind [Note: [Col. 0579] The printed editions read, “because, as concerning my mind,” omitting the negative particle, which we restore from the Carnotensis codex.], I can say nothing more than “believe me,” and if you are unwilling, I do not know what to do, so also, when you judge something false concerning that very light of minds—which rational minds behold more peacefully the purer they are—you can be shown, if you listen patiently, how far from the truth your opinion is.

For just as I cannot experience the sensation of your eyes, nor you mine, and we can only believe or disbelieve one another about this matter, while we are able to show one another the visible form that lies before both our eyes, so too, concerning the affections of our minds, which belong personally to us, let us believe one another if we wish; but if we do not wish, let us not believe one another. Let us attend together, however, with minds cleared of the darkness of obstinacy, to the rational ground of truth, which belongs neither to me nor to you but is set before both of us for contemplation.

## Chapter Three

I shall bring you no other proofs by which the error of the Manichaeans becomes apparent than those found in your own letter. You write that you give thanks to the ineffable and most sacred Majesty and to his firstborn, the king of all lights, Jesus Christ.

Tell me: of what lights is Jesus Christ king? Of those which he made, or of those which he begot?

For we say that God the Father begot the Son, equal to himself, but through him created—that is, established and made—the inferior creature, which certainly is not what he is who made it and through whom he made it. Therefore, since through him he made the ages, he is rightly called by the Apostle “King of the ages” (1 Tim. 1:17), as superior to inferior things, powerful to rule them, ruling those that require governance.

But when you call Jesus Christ king of the lights, if he begot them, why are they not equal to the one who begot them? If you say that they are equal, how is he their king, since a king must rule, and it is wholly impossible for those who are ruled to be equal to the one by whom they are ruled [Note: [Col. 0579] Thus the Carnotensis manuscript. The printed editions read, “similar.”]?

But if he did not beget these lights and instead made them, I ask from what he made them. If he propagated them from himself, why are they inferior? Why did they degenerate [Note: [Col. 0579] We add, “Why did they degenerate?” from the same manuscript.]? But if they are not from himself, tell me from where they are.

Or perhaps he neither made nor begot the lights over which he reigns? Then they possess an origin and nature of their own, but certainly a weaker one, so that they either endure being ruled by a more powerful neighbor or desire it.

Do you not recognize that, if this is so, apart from the race of darkness there are already two natures, one requiring the aid of the other, but neither deriving its origin from the other? You will certainly reject this opinion, because it is especially opposed to Manichaeus, who attempts to persuade us not of two natures—the king of lights and the lights that are ruled—but of two natures, the kingdom of light and the kingdom of darkness.

You will therefore flee to the position that you should call these lights begotten. But when I ask why they are weaker, you may perhaps try to assert that they are equal. When I reply, “What reason is there for their being ruled?” you will deny that they are ruled. Then I shall answer, “Why do they have a king?” Here I do not see what remains for your candor except regret that you placed such an opening in your letter, through which you yourself cannot escape.

But even when you regret it and say that Manichaeus ought not to be considered defeated merely because you carelessly wrote something in your letter, I shall cite from innumerable passages in the books of Manichaeus that he calls the kingdom of light that which he holds to be naturally opposed to the kingdom of darkness—and not one kingdom but kingdoms. For in the very letter of the ruinous *Foundation*, when he speaks of God the Father, he says: “With none being needy or weak in his kingdoms.”

But where there are kingdoms, who is so blind as not to understand that kings absolutely cannot be equal to those over whom they reign?

What, then, if you are willing to attend, is so close and so appropriate to the honor of your heart as that you should not regret having put that expression in your letter? For Jesus Christ is most truly king of the lights—not lights in any way equal to him, but subject to him—and their blessed ruler.

Rather regret that you were a Manichaean, whose every deceptive stratagem the truthful face of your letter has overthrown with a single blow. For because Christ is king of the lights, he neither begot from himself the inferior beings over whom he would reign, nor took up as neighboring beings those over whom he would rule—beings whom he himself had neither begotten nor made—lest there be two kinds of good, neither of which derives from the other, and lest one should be in need of the other, which is alien to the path of truth.

It remains, therefore, that the lights over which he reigns—which are certainly good—were not begotten by him, because they are inferior; he did not seize them as his own, because they are his own proper possession; but God made and established them.

## Chapter Four

If you wish to ask from what he made them, and begin to imagine the assistance of matter—which he himself did not make—so that God does not seem able to make whatever he wished unless some thing he had not made assisted him, you will again suffer the impenetrable darknesses of error.

But by joining the prophetic words to the sublime and ineffable Majesty with sober understanding, you will see most appropriately: “He spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5) [Note: [Col. 0580] The printed editions read, “They are joined most openly: ‘He spoke,’ they say, ‘and they came to be.’”].

In this way you will see how it is said in the Catholic faith that God made all things very good from nothing (Gen. 1:31). For if he made them from something, then he made them either from himself or not from himself. But if from himself, then he did not make them but begot them. Why, then, did he beget inferior things? For unless they were inferior, he could not be their king.

If not from himself, then certainly not from something that he himself did not make. Otherwise, he made them from what belonged to another, and there was already something good that he had not made, from which he might establish a kingdom for himself. If this is so, he begins not to be the creator of good things, because there was something good that he had not created. For he would not make the lights over which he would reign from another’s evil.

It follows, then, that if he made them from some thing, he made them from that which he had already made himself.

## Chapter Five

Thus we acknowledge that God made the first origins of things to be established from nothing—unless perhaps you have said that Jesus Christ is the firstborn of the ineffable and most sacred Majesty, not according to the assumption of humanity, in which he graciously judged those called by adoption, as the Apostle says and as the Catholic faith believes, to be brothers who should have him as firstborn (Rom. 8:29), but rather according to the very excellence of divinity.

You wish him to be understood as firstborn so that the lights over which he reigns may be his brothers—not made by the Father through him, but begotten by the Father after him—so that they are themselves those begotten afterward, while he is the firstborn, all nevertheless deriving from the Father’s own one substance.

If you believe this, you first contradict the Gospel, where he is also called the only-begotten:

> “And we saw his glory,” it says, “as of the only-begotten from the Father.”

This could in no way be true if his eternal power and divinity, by which he is of one substance with the Father and exists before every creature, had brothers from the same substance [Note: [Col. 0581] In the printed editions, *fratres* (“brothers”) was absent. A little later, instead of *fratres ejus sint* (“may be his brothers”), *semper ejus sint* (“may always be his”) was read. Likewise, the Louvain edition gave approximately the following text below: “Since eternal power also and his divinity, by which he is consubstantial with the Father and is before every creature, would in no way be truly spoken of unless he always had [brothers] from the same substance.” We correct these and other passages throughout from the Carnotensis manuscript.].

Since the divine utterances testify that he is both only-begotten and firstborn—only-begotten because he has no brothers, firstborn because he has brothers—you will not find how both can be understood of him according to the same nature of divinity.

The Catholic faith, however, which distinguishes between the Creator and the creature, encounters no difficulty in understanding these two names. It accepts him as only-begotten according to what is written:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:14, 1);

and as firstborn of all creation according to what the Apostle says:

> “That he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Col. 1:18).

The Father begot these brothers for fellowship with him—not by equality of substance but by adoption through grace.

Read the Scriptures, then. Nowhere will you find it said of Christ that he is the Son of God by adoption. But concerning us it is very often read:

> “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons”;  
> “awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:15, 23);  
> “that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4:4);  
> “He predestined us for adoption as sons” (Eph. 1:5);  
> “a holy nation, a people for adoption” [Note: [Col. 0581] Ambrose also reads this way, in *Sermon 6 on Psalm 118*. The Greek is **λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν** (*laos eis peripoiēsin*), “a people for possession.”] (1 Pet. 2:9);  
> “He called you through our Gospel to the adoption of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thess. 2:12–13);

and any other passages of this kind that may occur to one remembering or reading.

For it is one thing to be the only Son of God through the Father’s excellence, and another to receive, through merciful grace, the power to become sons of God—those who believe in him. “He gave them,” it says, “the power to become sons of God.”

They were therefore not sons by nature, since they received the power to become so by believing in him, the only Son whom he did not spare but handed over for us all (Rom. 8:32), so that he might be only-begotten with the Father and firstborn among us.

According to that in which he is only-begotten, he was born not from flesh, not from blood, not from the will of a man, nor from the will of the flesh, but from God. According to that in which he became firstborn in the Church among his brothers, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:12, 14).

We too, insofar as we were naturally children of wrath (Eph. 2:3)—that is, children of punishment, bound by the chain of mortality—were born from flesh and blood and from the will of the flesh, although it was he who created and established us, who unquestionably arranges and forms all things from the highest to the lowest in measure, number, and weight (Wis. 11:21).

But insofar as we received the power to become children of God, we too are born not from flesh and blood, nor from the will of a man, nor from the will of the flesh, but from God—not by nature making us equal, but by grace adopting us.

## Chapter Six

Next, even if I were now to grant that Jesus Christ is not the only-begotten of the Father according to the divinity of the same substance, but has brothers born after him, for whom he is firstborn, how could he be their king?

I ask you: would you dare say that one is born stronger because he is born earlier? You would certainly be ashamed to think so. But you do not think so. What, then, do you think? Calm your mind and make yourself willing to consider the truth without obstinacy.

I shall also ask you this: how do you understand Jesus Christ as firstborn in that divine, perfect, and eternal substance? Do you understand him to be begotten first in time, so that we are to conceive of others born later in that kingdom, for whom he is firstborn—without being able to say by how many hours, days, months, or years the one born earlier is older, yet still imagining that these generations are separated by some temporal interval and span?

Or should we understand him as firstborn not in time but in the very excellence of a superior majesty, by which he deserved to be king even of his brother-lights—firstborn, as though begotten into a kind of primacy?

If you answer that he is earlier and greater than his brothers in time, and contend that the kingdom was conferred upon him over his brothers on this account, because by being born he preceded them and once existed when they did not yet exist, what do you say, brother? Will you hurl your heart into this precipice of impiety, so as to imagine that temporal mutability falls upon that divine and supreme nature, and to believe that something exists there which previously did not exist?

Or, because the lights had to advance from there against the race of darkness, do you call those advances generations, imagining that they occurred in time so that the battle might be waged in time?

Could one light, then, not have been sufficient to accomplish the whole of that military undertaking by divine power? Or, if many were needed, is this to be thought about spiritual beings [Note: [Col. 0583] Thus the Carnotensis manuscript. The printed editions read, “Is this now to be thought about spiritual beings?”]—that the passage was so narrow that they could not all go out together, and that because one of the brothers had gone out first, he deserved to be called firstborn and to become king of the others?

I do not wish to pursue every detail, lest I become too burdensome to your capable intellect, which can perceive everything from a few points. Raise, then, the power of your mind and wipe away the clouds of contention.

I see clearly that neither spatially nor temporally can motions, advances, risings, settings, or any changes take place except in a mutable creature [Note: [Col. 0583] The old Carnotensis codex reads, “or those changes.”]. Yet unless the creature came from God the craftsman and creator, the Apostle would not have said:

> “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:25).

## Chapter Seven

For in this position there are two matters above all which I ask you to consider with me.

The first is that, if the creature were foreign to God, God would not be called its creator by the Apostle. The second is that, if the Creator and the creature were of one and the same substance, they would not be rebuked for serving the creature rather than the Creator, since, whoever they served, they would not have departed from the same nature and substance.

For just as no one can serve the Son without serving the Father, because the two have one substance, so no one can serve the creature without serving the Creator, if the two had one substance.

Therefore, if you now discern and understand, you would pay the greatest attention to the distinction between the Creator and the creature. You must understand that the offspring of the Creator is not a creature. For if it were, it would not be inferior but equal, of the same substance [Note: [Col. 0583] The printed editions read, “and could not be inferior to him, but equal and of the same substance.” We have restored here the more accurate reading of the old Carnotensis codex.]. Consequently, whoever worshiped it and served it would at the same time offer worship and service to its Creator and Father.

But when those who worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator are rebuked by the Apostle and regarded as detestable, it is sufficiently shown that the substance of the one differs from that of the other.

For just as the Son cannot be seen—that is, understood—without the Father also being understood in him, since he himself says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), so the Son cannot be worshiped without the Father also being worshiped in him.

And therefore, if the Son were a creature, he would not be worshiped without the Creator, nor would those who worshiped the creature rather than the Creator be condemned.

You see, then, I think, that it is not fitting for you to call Jesus Christ the firstborn of the most secret and ineffable Majesty and the king of all lights unless you cease to be a Manichaean and distinguish the creature from the Creator.

Then Jesus Christ is both only-begotten, according to the fact that he is the Word of God, God with God (John 1:1), equally unchangeable and equally eternal, “not considering equality with God something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6); and firstborn of all creation, according to the fact that all things were created in him, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.

For I think you recognize the Apostle’s words to the Colossians (Col. 1:15–16).

## Chapter Eight
Therefore, when I ask you from what source the whole of creation was made—although it is good in its own order, yet inferior to the Creator, who remains immutable while it is mutable—you will find no answer unless you confess that it was made from nothing. And for that reason creation can tend toward nothing when it sins, as can that part of creation which is capable of sinning—not so that it becomes nothing, but so that it has less vigor and is less firm. For to have less vigor and less strength, if carried altogether to the extreme, leaves nothing.

It voluntarily loves vanity, then, when, having abandoned the solidity of truth, it follows things that are matters of opinion—that is, mutable things. But when it pays the penalties it has deserved for this, it is subjected to vanity against its will, just as it has been subjected in the sinful human being. For this reason the Apostle says, “Every creature has been subjected to vanity, not willingly” (Rom. 8:20), because this is also the case in the human being. There is in a human being something invisible, according to the soul, and something visible, according to the body; and every creature is partly visible and partly invisible. Yet not everything is present in an animal, since an animal does not possess an intellectual mind.

He says, however, that it has been subjected in hope, because of the mercy of the one who liberates through the remission of sins and the adoption of grace. But if you refuse to confess that creation was made from nothing by the Father through the Son in the goodness of the Holy Spirit—the Trinity, consubstantial, eternal, and always immutable—you will necessarily be driven to sacrilege: you will have to say that God generated from himself something that is not equal to its begetter and that can be subjected to vanity.

Or, if you say that it is equal, then both will be mutable. What greater impiety is there than to believe and say such things, and, through a perverse opinion, to prefer to change God for the worse rather than, through sound reasoning, to change oneself for the better? But if you fear saying that God is mutable—for truly that is a great and utterly manifest impiety—and if you say that creation is immutable, so as to make it equal to the Creator and of one and the same substance, your own letter will once again answer you.

From where, then, is that soul which you place among the spirits, and to which you say that its nature was given victory from the beginning? You propose to it a law and a condition: if it acts together with the spirit of the virtues, it will have eternal life with that spirit and will possess the kingdom to which our Lord invites it; but if it begins to be drawn by the spirit of vices, and afterward repents, it will have a fountain of pardon for these impurities. When these words of your letter are thus recalled, you also acknowledge that you have established the soul’s nature as mutable. For what else is it to consent at one time to the spirit of vices and afterward to repent than to be changed now for the better, now for the worse? And the clearest truth compelled you to say this. For your own soul, if you wished to dissemble, would force you to attend to its mutability; changed so many times since the day you were born through various wills, teachings, forgettings, and acts of consent, it would become its own witness and would seek no proofs from outside.

[Note: So in the old manuscript. In the printed editions, “unless you wished to dissemble.” The latter is less correct.]

## CHAPTER IX

Unless perhaps you think you are helped by saying that the soul is immutable because you added these words: “For it did not sin by its own will, but under the direction of another; for it is led through the commixture of the flesh, not by its own will.” Perhaps in this statement you want it understood that the soul is immutable in its own nature, but mutable through its commixture with another nature—as though the question were not why it is so, but merely whether it is so.

By this reasoning the bodies of Hector and Ajax—or, indeed, of all human beings and animals—could also be called invulnerable if blows and accidents, by which wounds could be inflicted upon them, were absent. But Achilles’ body was called invulnerable—whether by poetic fiction or through some more hidden force in the nature of things—for the very reason that, even when weapons attacked it, they did not penetrate it; and in whatever part it could be penetrated, in that part it was plainly not invulnerable.

So, if the soul were immutable, it would be changed by no commixture with anything, just as a body that is invulnerable is wounded by neither contact nor assault of anything. Therefore, because we say that the Word of God is undefiled, we do not fear believing that he was born of a virgin, even after assuming mortal and vulnerable flesh, so that he might teach us to despise both death and every bodily affliction. But because you, through impious perversity, believe the Son of God contaminable, you fear allowing him to enter flesh. Yet you declare his substance to be the nature of the soul, and assert that he was so mingled with flesh that you do not hesitate to hold that he was even changed for the worse.

[Note: The Ambrosian edition and the Carnotensis manuscript read: “whose substance is said to be in the nature of the soul,” and so forth.]

Choose, then, what you wish: either to say or believe that God is mutable, and thus to believe likewise that a mutable offspring was generated from the substance of a mutable Father—the impiety of which you surely perceive—or to say that God is immutable but nevertheless generated from his substance an offspring that is mutable, which you likewise see to be said impiously and absurdly.

Or rather, confess God to be immutable in such a way that what he generated from his substance is also equally immutable, equally the highest and most excellent good, and possesses supreme being in the same manner, through inviolable permanence. The remaining, inferior goods—which we call creation—he did not make from himself, for then they would be equal to him; but, because they are good, he made them from nothing. If you believe this, you will not be impious, you will forget the Persians, and you will be one of us.

## CHAPTER X

But the Apostle says, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6:12), who, by turning through an impious will toward the love of their own pride and honor, begrudge pious souls their return.

[Note: This is the reading of the printed editions; the manuscripts read “which.”]

The difference between your opinion and our faith is this: you think that these same principalities arose from some nature of their own, which God neither generated nor made, but which he had beside him, contiguous through eternal proximity; and that they waged war against God and brought war upon him before the commixture of good and evil.

[Note: The printed editions read “inflicted by art”; the Carnotensis manuscript reads “brought before”: supply “war.”]

What a great evil of necessity this would have been at the outset: God would have been forced to mingle with them his substance, to be afflicted and disturbed, changed in error, and utterly plunged into self-forgetfulness, so that he would need a liberator, corrector, reformer, and teacher. You see how foolishly and fabulously this is said, and how great a crime of impiety it entails.

For us, however, Christian faith has made us certain that nothing is opposed to the God who supremely is except that which altogether is not. Whatever in any way exists has received from him who supremely is the fact that it exists in whatever way it does, and is good in its own order; some things are more, others less. Thus all the good things made by God the Creator have been arranged in definite and distributed degrees: some by intervals and positions of place, as with all bodily things; some by natural merits, as when the soul is placed above the body; some by the merits of rewards and punishments, as when the soul is either raised to rest or subjected to sufferings.

Accordingly, those principalities against whom the Apostle says that we struggle first endure the punishment of their sins before they are able to do harm. For no envious person harms another without first being a torment to himself. The stronger harm the weaker, since no one overcomes another except by being more powerful; yet the wicked principalities are weaker in the present than they would be if they had remained in their former condition and righteousness.

[Note: The old Carnotensis manuscript omits “in the present.”]

It matters from what source one person is stronger than another: whether in body, as horses are stronger than human beings; in the nature of the soul, as the rational is stronger than the irrational; in the disposition of the mind, as the virtuous is stronger than the unjust; or in the order of power, as an emperor is stronger than a soldier or provincial.

[Note: The same Carnotensis manuscript reads “as the just is stronger than the unjust.”] Power, however, is believed to be granted altogether from the supreme power of God, often even to worse people over better ones—that is, to the unjust over those who already possess justice or strive to attain it. It is granted so that those who have been tested may be revealed through endurance (1 Cor. 11:19), either for their own hope or for the imitation of others.

The Apostle says: “Knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope” (Rom. 5:3–4). This is the kind of conflict involved when a faithful human being struggles against the principalities and powers of transgressing angels, and against spiritual forces of wickedness: they receive the power to tempt, while he receives the command to endure. Thus they overcome in an inferior sphere and are overcome in a more powerful one. They often overcome the weaker body, but are overcome by the stronger mind.

[Note: The printed editions of Erasmus and Louvain read, “The weaker body is often overcome, and he is overcome by one who holds more firmly.” The text has been corrected with the help of the Carnotensis manuscript.]

Their violence is resisted by endurance, their snares by prudence, so that they may neither bend us by force into a destructive consent nor deceive us by trickery. Since the virtue and wisdom of God is that through which all things were made, therefore, in created things, when superior things decline toward inferior ones—where every sin and everything called evil is found—force imitates virtue and deceit imitates wisdom.

[Note: The printed editions read, “Since virtue is rightly …,” and, a little later, “therefore the things that are made become nothing, when superior things …”; these readings are corrected from the same Carnotensis manuscript.] But when those things that have declined turn back and return, greatness of soul imitates virtue and instruction imitates wisdom.

Sinners also imitate God the Father through impious pride, while the righteous imitate him through pious generosity. Finally, the desire of the wicked imitates the Holy Spirit, while the love of the upright imitates him. Both, however, depart from imitation of God, by whom, through whom, and in whom the natures themselves were made: the former through a blameworthy imitation, the latter through a praiseworthy one. Nor is it surprising that, when those who are making progress and those who are failing come into conflict, the imitation of those who are failing is overcome by the imitation of those who are making progress. The former are hurled down by exaltation; the latter rise through humility.

But if it troubles you that those who are stronger in mind are weaker in body, this is not surprising: having been freed through the remission of sins, they are exercised by the mortality of the body, with whose immortality they will be crowned. For punishment is not easily avoided unless the one who is released from it has conquered it by merit.

[Note: The printed editions read, “unless he who releases them has conquered”; the Carnotensis manuscript has the better reading, “unless he who is released from it has conquered.” It also seems that the following should read, “unless he has lived better.”]

Hence the Apostle says: “But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11).

Therefore, if the soul, bearing mortal flesh because of the punishment of sin, is changed for the better and does not live according to mortal flesh, it also changes that flesh for the better and will deserve to have an immortal body. But this will occur at the end, when death, the last enemy, will be destroyed, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption. It will not occur through that fabulous sphere of yours, but through the change of which he says, “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.”

After expressing this by saying, “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed,” he then continued, showing what kind of change he meant: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.” He was discussing the body of those who rise, having posed the question in this way: “But someone will say, How do the dead rise? And with what kind of body do they come?” (1 Cor. 15:26, 51–53, 35).

Read the whole passage, then, with devout attention and without being disturbed by obstinate contention. With God assisting your intellect, and without needing any interpreter, you will find nothing there other than what I am saying. Then turn your mind back to the matter we had begun to discuss, and see, if you can, that I am not saying that the righteous struggle against nothing, but against those substances that have failed by not standing in the truth.

## CHAPTER XI

To fail, however, is not yet to be nothing, but to tend toward nothing. For when things that are more decline toward things that are less, it is not those toward which they decline but those that decline that fail and begin to be less than they were. They do not become the things toward which they have declined, but become less in their own order.

When the mind declines toward the body, it does not become a body; nevertheless, through a certain defective desire, it becomes bodily in a manner of speaking. In the same way, a certain angelic sublimity, when it took greater delight in its own dominion over itself, inclined its affection toward what is less, began to be less than it had been, and, in accordance with its rank, tended toward nothing. For the less anything is, the nearer it is to nothing.

When these failures occur voluntarily, they are rightly reproved and called sins. But when disadvantages, troubles, pains, and adversities follow upon these voluntary failures—all of which we suffer against our will—the sins are rightly punished by penalties or cleansed through exercises. If you are willing to contemplate these matters with a tranquil mind, you will certainly cease accusing natures and bringing substances themselves to trial.

If you desire a fuller and clearer explanation of this matter, read the three books of ours entitled *On Free Will*, which you can find in Campania, at Nola, in the possession of Paulinus, that noble servant of God.

## CHAPTER XII

Now I must remember to answer your letter, although it is much longer, with a letter of my own. For that reason I did not remain silent on other matters, lest I should be forced to say the same things everywhere. But I had promised to persuade you from your own writings how false were the things you had believed and how true is the assertion of the Catholic faith.

The whole distinction between us is this: you say that there is a certain substance that is evil; we say that evil is not a substance but a tendency away from what is greater toward what is less.

Listen, then, to this very point.

[Note: The Carnotensis manuscript reads, “Listen also to this very point.”]

In your letter you state and say of the soul that it is led into sin through its commixture with flesh, not by its own will. And immediately afterward, I believe because you saw that, if this were so, the omnipotent God would have to come to the aid of every soul without exception, and that none at all ought to be condemned, since it would sin unwillingly—and because this would overturn the doctrine that Mani, in a terrifying voice, proclaims concerning the punishments of souls that come even from the portion of light—you very carefully added:

“But if, when it has come to know itself, it consents to evil and does not arm itself against the enemy, it has sinned by its own will.”

It is good that you sometimes confess that it is possible for the soul to sin by its own will. But to what evil, after all, does it consent and thereby sin by its own will? Certainly to that which you say is a substance.

## CHAPTER XIII

But I already see three things; and you too, I think, see them with me. The soul that consents to evil, the evil to which it consents, and the consent itself are three things. For you do not say that this consent too is the soul, but that it belongs to the soul.

Of these three, then, the soul is a substance; and that evil to which the soul voluntarily sins by consenting is also, according to your opinion, a substance. I ask, therefore, what the consent itself is: do you say that it is a substance, or that it exists in a substance?

If you say that it is a substance, you will no longer hold two substances but three. Or do you hold there to be two because the soul’s consent, by which it consents to evil, is of the same substance as the soul itself?

I ask, then, whether this consent is evil or good. If it is good, the soul certainly does not sin when it consents to evil. Yet not only does the truth cry out against this; you yourself write that it sins by its will at that moment. This consent, therefore, is evil, and consequently the soul’s substance is also evil, if the consent is the substance of the soul and both are one substance.

Do you see where you have been driven? You are forced to declare that the soul and that evil are not one good substance and one evil substance, but two evil substances.

Perhaps here you will try to attribute the blameworthy consent not to the soul that consents to evil, but to the evil itself to which it consents, so that in this way there may be two substances, one good and one evil: the soul is said to be from the good side, while its consent, by which it consents to evil, together with the evil itself to which it consents, is constituted from the other side, and both are assigned to the evil substance.
