Who could rave more absurdly? The soul does not consent if the consent is not its own; but it does consent. The consent, therefore, belongs to it. Further, if the consent belongs to it, and this consent is evil, then this evil belongs to it. For if this evil also belongs to the evil to which the soul consents, the evil did not need to exist before the soul consented to it.

What kind of good, then, is the soul, by whose arrival that evil is either doubled or, to put it more mildly, increased?

## CHAPTER XIV

Furthermore, if this consent is a substance, and it is established that it is evil, we find that it lies within the soul’s power whether some evil substance exists or does not exist, since this consent lies within the soul’s power. For if it is not within its power, then it does not consent by its own will. Yet you have said that, because of this consent, it sins by its own will.

The soul therefore has, as I have said, the power to make some evil substance exist or not exist. But what else is substance than nature? There will therefore be some nature that is neither natural to the soul—for if the soul does not wish it, it will not exist—nor natural to the evil to which the soul voluntarily consents. For you cannot say that the evil of the nation of darkness is natural when it is established there by another’s will, that is, by the soul’s will.

To what nature, then, will this nature—that is, this consent—be assigned, if it is a nature that is natural neither to the soul nor to the nation of darkness? The only possibility is that, contrary to Mani, you should argue that there are not two natures but three. For even if there were once two, after this consent arose there are now certainly three.

You will be forced to say that this third nature, born from the consenting soul and from the evil to which it consents, is like a daughter of both. But since it was born from two natures, one good and the other evil, I ask why something neutral was not born from them. For just as what is born from a horse and a donkey is neither horse nor donkey, so what is born from a good nature and an evil one, if it too is a nature, ought to be neither good nor evil.

Yet you confess that the consent is evil. For you say that the soul sins by its own will when it consents to evil. Or do you perhaps suppose that the good nature and the evil nature are like two sexes, male and female, so that, just as from a male and a female something neutral is not born but either a male or a female, so from good and evil you insist that a third thing was born that is not neutral but evil?

If this is so, where is that victorious nature of the soul? Has it been so separated—or perhaps overcome [Note: Perhaps “overcome” should be read.]—that something good did not rather arise from it?

Furthermore, do you not see that you are now speaking of different sexes, not different natures? For if there were a difference of natures between good and evil, nothing could arise from both except some third thing that could be neither good nor evil. Or at least the commixture itself would be sterile, and no third substance would be born from it.

If, indeed, from those animals I mentioned above, when they mingle with one another, nothing other than a mule, male or female, is born—something that is neither the one nor the other—how much more ought this to have happened in so great and supreme a difference between good and evil?

Or if no new nature arose from their commixture, it would not be evil, even though it could not be good. We are therefore left with no way to avoid such incredible ravings unless we confess that the consent which is clearly evil and blameworthy is not a substance, but exists in some substance.

## CHAPTER XV

Let us then investigate most carefully in what substance it exists. For who does not see that, just as persuasion occurs only in the one who persuades, so consent exists only in a consenting nature? When the soul consents to evil, therefore, the soul itself is a substance, but its consent is not a substance.

[Note: So the Carnotensis manuscript. The printed editions read, “when it consents, it is itself an evil substance.”]

You now see, I think, in what substance it exists. That is, you plainly see that this consent exists in the soul, and you do not doubt that this consent is a sin and consequently an evil.

From this you now understand that it is possible for some evil that is not a substance to exist in a good substance, such as the soul; and because of this evil the soul itself may also be called evil. For the sinful soul is certainly evil, and it sins when it consents to evil.

Thus one and the same thing—the soul—is good insofar as it is a substance; but insofar as it has some evil that is not a substance, namely this consent, it is evil. It has this consent not through progress but through failure. For it fails when it consents to evil, and begins to be less and therefore to have less strength than it had when, consenting to no one, it stood in virtue. It is all the worse insofar as it inclines away from what supremely is toward what is less, so that it too becomes less.

The less it is, the nearer it becomes to nothing. For whatever becomes less tends toward not being at all. Although it does not reach the point where, by utterly perishing, it becomes nothing, it is nevertheless clear that every failure is the beginning of perishing.

Open, then, the eyes of your heart and observe, if you can, that every substance is good, and therefore that the failure of substance is evil, because being a substance is good. Yet not every failure is blameworthy, but only voluntary failure: that by which the rational soul, abandoning its Creator, inclines its affection toward things created below it. This is what is called sin.

Other failures, however, which are not voluntary, are either punishments, by which sins are punished under the guidance and ordering of supreme justice, or they belong to the measures of the lowest things, so that what precedes yields to what follows and the whole temporal beauty is completed through its successive turns and according to its own order.

A speech, for example, unfolds as though its syllables were dying and being born. They are extended through fixed intervals of duration, and, when their periods have been completed, they pass away in an ordered succession of what follows, until the whole discourse is brought to its conclusion. The measure of how long a syllable is prolonged or shortened, or the form in which individual letters preserve the moments proper to their places, lies not in the sounds as they pass but in the regulation of the speaker. The art that produces speech itself neither resounds with the sounds nor rolls and varies with time.

[Note: The Carnotensis manuscript reads “nor is rolled along.”]

In the same way, through the rising and setting, passing away and succession of temporal things, along fixed and determined courses until they return to their appointed end, temporal beauty is woven together. It is not evil for this reason, that in spiritual creatures we can understand and admire better things; rather, it possesses its own beauty in its own order and reveals to those who live well the supreme wisdom of God, hidden on high above all temporal limits, its maker and governor.

## CHAPTER XVI

Come now, attend to that which you said was the evil to which the soul voluntarily sins by consenting. Is it some substance, or can you not even there accuse a substance?

For I ask what attracts the soul’s consent. Does that thing rush upon it without reason, and is it therefore said to receive consent because the soul is moved by some pleasure in it toward enjoyment? If this is so, it does not follow that the thing should be called evil merely because it is not loved rightly.

If I show that something is loved wrongly, while the fault lies not in the thing loved but in the one who loves it, you will certainly admit that the appearance of a thing is not immediately vicious merely because the consent of one who desires it slips toward it viciously. How much this helps me will become clear afterward.

But in order to show what I have promised, what better example could I choose, when an abundance of examples surrounds me? What, I ask, could I choose rather than that which we praise as a heavenly creature, while you adore it as a portion of the Creator himself?

For among all visible things, what is more splendid than this sun? Yet if someone desires its light beyond measure, he inflicts wars of quarrels upon his own eyes, if he happens to possess the power to satisfy his desire: he looks at houses opposite his open windows, so that the sun may less fully flood his inner rooms beneath a more open sky.

[Note: Perhaps “he inflicts wars of quarrels upon his vices” should be read. In the Carnotensis manuscript: “through the windows of his soul, so that the sun may not …” The passage is obscure and corrupt.]

Is the sun therefore at fault because that person loved its light so much that he dared to prefer it to the light of justice, and, wishing to receive a greater abundance of the light of bodily eyes into the dwelling of the body, closed the door of his heart and the vision of his mind against the light of equity?

You see, then, that a good thing can be loved with a bad love. Therefore, while you call evil the thing to which the soul consents and thereby sins, I call it good in its own order, but a good of such a kind that it is not fitting for a soul to consent to it insofar as the soul is better.

Since the soul is superior to the body and has God above itself, although bodily nature is good in its own order, the soul nevertheless sins and becomes evil by sinning if it attaches to an inferior body the consent of love that it owes to the superior God.

## CHAPTER XVII

But if you say that you do not call the consent blameworthy when the thing is loved that does not act so as to receive consent, but that the soul consents only when the one to whom it consents either persuades it of something or forces it to something, and that the evil lies in the fact that it persuades or compels the commission of some evil, then this is a second question, which must now also be treated in its proper order.

Let us first remember the first sin, about which, I think, enough has been said: it has become clear that something can be good in its own order and yet be loved wrongly, while the lover is blamed and the thing itself is not reproved.

[Note: So the old Carnotensis manuscript; the printed editions read, “while the love is blamed.”]

For what if a sinful and vicious soul, already corrupted by such a love, persuades another person to commit the same sin? Is not the one who consents to the persuader corrupted by the same vice by which the one whom it follows has been corrupted?

[Note: Perhaps “is not that one” should be read, following Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 300.]

The first sin, then, is to prefer a good creature in love to the Creator. The second is to attempt to lead another to do the same, either by persuasion or by force. No one wishes to lead another into depravity without first having been depraved himself.

Those who desire to lead others into sin sin voluntarily.

[Note: Perhaps: “because he sees that …”]

They do so either through foolish benevolence or through malicious envy. For what father advises his children to regard no profit as dishonorable, but to acquire abundant money from any source, unless he loves them perversely? Certainly he does not hate them, yet he persuades them to their ruin.

He himself has already been corrupted by such a love, since gold and silver are not evil—just as the sun we discussed above is not evil—but the lover of a good thing is at fault when his love is disordered.

In envy, when someone wishes another to sin, he loves honor with immoderate pride, desires to excel in it and surpass everyone else, and, seeing that honor is more fully and truly attributed to virtue, wishes others to be cast down

[Note: The same Carnotensis manuscript reads, “But those who sin wish …”]

 from the citadel of equity into the abyss of iniquity, lest he be surpassed in that respect.

In this way the devil attempts to persuade or compel people to sin. But is honor itself at fault because the devil, loving it perversely and impiously, became impious? Or is the angelic substance of that same devil, which God created, evil for the reason that it is a substance?

But when he abandoned love of God and turned excessively toward himself, wishing to appear equal to God, he was cast down by the swelling of pride. He is therefore not evil insofar as he is a substance, but because, although he was made a substance, he loved himself more than the one by whom he was made. He is evil for this reason: he is less than he would have been if he had loved what supremely is. The failure, therefore, is evil.

Every failure from what is tends toward not being, just as every progress from what is less tends toward being more.

The highest honor, such as the piety of the devout offers, is owed to God. Whoever loves honor, therefore, imitates God. Humble souls wish to be honored in God; the proud wish to be honored above God. The humble, in relation to God, become more exalted than the unjust; the exalted, in opposition to God, become lower than the just. This occurs through the dispensation of rewards and punishments: the former have loved God above themselves, the latter have loved themselves in place of God.

## CHAPTER XVIII

By now, I think, it is easy for you to understand from the very words of your letter—in which you said that, when the soul consents to evil, it sins by its own will—that no evil is either an evil nature or the love of an evil nature. Rather, since all natures are good in their own order, evil is the sin committed by the soul’s will when it loves a creature in place of the Creator, whether by its own inclination, when it is evil, or through another’s persuasion, when it consents to evil.

Nevertheless, the soul also becomes evil through the punishments that follow, so that all things may be ordered according to their merits by the supremely good Creator in good creation, though not supremely good, because he did not beget it from himself but made it from nothing.

But you have established two natures, one of which you wish to be good and the other evil—or rather, one belonging to good and the other to evil, since an evil nature also becomes evil from a good one by sinning.

Yet you admit that the nature which you call good does evil by consenting to evil, that is, by sinning voluntarily. I, on the other hand, assert that both are good, but that one does evil by persuading and the other by consenting.

Just as the consent of the one is not a nature, so the persuasion of the other is not a nature. If the former does not consent, it will remain good, preserving the integrity of its nature; likewise, if the latter does not persuade, it will be more upright. If it also does not commit the sin it does not persuade another to commit, both will remain intact and praiseworthy in their own order.

Although the one who both commits and persuades sins twice, while the one who merely consents to wrongdoing sins once, they become evil through their sins; they are not evil by nature.

Or, if this nature is evil because of its persuasion, then the other is likewise evil because of its consent. But if persuading seems to you worse than consenting, let this one be evil and that one worse. Nevertheless, do not show such partiality or such unjust favoritism in judgment that, when both sin—although one more gravely and the other less gravely—you call one the nature of evil and the other the nature of good. Rather, either both are good, with the one who sins less being the better, or both are evil, with the one who sins more being the worse.

## CHAPTER XIX

But from where, then, did the evil called sin come, if there is no evil nature? Tell me from where that evil consent exists in the nature which you acknowledge and proclaim to be good.

For whatever suffers in order to consent to evil would certainly not suffer unless it were capable of suffering. I therefore ask from where it has the very capacity to suffer. It would be better if it did not possess it. It is therefore not the nature of the supreme good, since something better could exist.

Furthermore, if it has the power either to consent or not to consent, then it does not consent because it has been overcome. I ask, therefore, from where it has this evil consent when no contrary nature compels it.

But if it is compelled to consent, so that it is not within its power to act otherwise, then it does not sin, as you were saying, by its will, since it does not consent by its will.

Yet I continue to ask from where it has the capacity to be deceived, if it is deceived. Before it was deceived, unless it had within itself the capacity to undergo this, it certainly could never have undergone it.

Although it consents in no way except voluntarily, if it is compelled, it should rather be said to yield than to consent. But whatever name you give this, I ask you, an acute and astute man who boasts of his Roman intelligence, from where this good nature has the capacity to suffer what it suffers, so that it consents to evil.

For just as wood contains fragility before it is broken—without which it could not be broken at all—and is not for that reason not fragile if no breaker approaches, so I ask where in this nature there is a certain fragility or flexibility before it is either broken by force or bent by persuasion toward an evil consent.

Or, if fragility already existed because of its proximity to evil, just as bodies are commonly corrupted by the exhalation of a neighboring marsh, then it was already corruptible, since the pestilential contagion of that proximity could corrupt it. I therefore ask from where it had that corruptibility.

Please attend to what I am saying, and yield to evident truth. For I am not asking where corruption comes from; you would answer, “From the corrupter,” and you maintain that this same corrupter is some prince of the nation of darkness, so wrapped in fabulous coverings that he can scarcely be uncovered and grasped. Rather, I am asking where corruptibility came from, even before the corrupter approached; for unless it existed, either no corrupter would exist, or the approach of any corrupter would do no harm.

When, therefore, you have discovered where this corruptibility existed in a good nature before it was corrupted by the contrary nature—or, if you do not wish to say that it was corrupted, where this changeability existed before it was changed by hostile opposition—for a nature is certainly changed for the worse when it becomes foolish from being wise and forgets itself: you yourself added these words, saying, “If, when it has come to know itself, it consents to evil.” It is therefore changed for the worse when it forgets, so that it again recognizes itself when recalled to mind.

[Note: [Col. 0594] The American edition and the Carnotensis manuscript read: “if so that it recognizes itself.” Perhaps one should read: “when it forgets itself, so that it again recognizes itself.”] Yet it could not possibly have been changed unless it had been changeable before it was changed. When, therefore, you have discovered where this changeability existed in the substance of the highest good before any mixture of good and evil had occurred, you will certainly cease asking me where evil comes from.

Although, if you consider the nature of the highest good correctly, no changeability at all in time can be found in it, whether arising from itself or from the approach of anything else, as it can in that nature which Manichaeus invents and considers supremely good, or even persuades those who believe him to regard as such. Ask and answer, if you can: where did this changeability come from—a changeability not discovered but exposed when delay came?

[Note: [Col. 0594] Perhaps: “which was not introduced but exposed when the enemy—that is, the corrupter—approached.”]

For it could not be changed by the enemy either, if it could not be changed at all. But when it could be changed, it showed that it had not been immutable. When, therefore, this changeability is believed to exist in the substance of the highest good, that is, in the substance of God, you see, if you are not contentious, how great an act of folly is involved in blaspheming it. But when something of this kind is said of a creature, which God neither begot nor brought forth from his substance, but made from nothing, the matter does not concern the highest good, though it does concern a good of such a kind that it could not have been instituted except by the highest good, who is God.

For God, supremely good and immutably so, made all things not supremely good and not immutable, but nevertheless good: from the angels of heaven down to the lowest beasts and plants of the earth, all things ordered in fitting places according to the dignity of each nature. Yet when rational creation remains joined to its Creator—that is, to its Maker and Founder, God—through obedient love, it preserves its nature in his eternity, truth, and love. But when it abandons him through defiant disobedience, it entangles itself in sins through its free will; and through his just judgment it is afflicted with punishment and misery. This is the whole of evil: partly what it does unjustly, and partly what it suffers justly.

Do not ask me where this comes from, since you have already answered yourself when you said that, when the soul has come to know itself, if it consents to evil, it sins by its own will. There, then, is the source of evil: plainly, from its own will. But this is not a nature; it is guilt. Consequently, it is also contrary to nature, since it harms nature by depriving it of the good by which it could have been blessed had it been unwilling to sin.

You do not think that this will to sin is moved in the soul except by another evil which you believe to be a nature—a nature which God did not make—and you insist that this soul is God’s nature. Consequently, if this supposed nature of evil, by persuading the soul to sin, casts it down when overcome by sin—

[Note: [Col. 0595] Perhaps: “the will to sin.”]

—then God is overcome.

## CHAPTER XX

See with what impiety, and with what unspeakable and dreadful blasphemies, you refuse to free yourself, by placing in a nature that God did not make life, sensation, speech, measure, form, order, and countless other goods; and by placing in God’s own nature, before any mixture with evil, the very changeability by which it could be captured and which it was compelled to fear, as it saw a great ruin and devastation threatening its holy realms unless some outstanding and glorious divine power, strong in virtue, were set against it.

(From Manichaeus’ Letter, which they called *The Foundation*.)

And why all this, unless it is so that this nature and substance of God may hold the enemy subject to itself, so that, while sinning, it may bear him bound; and, once purified, may not wholly escape him defeated; and, once condemned, may keep him enclosed?

You have indeed found a splendid excuse for the necessity of war in your god,

[Note: [Col. 0595] Thus the Carnotensis manuscript; the printed editions read “exclusion.”]

in answer to the challenge put to you: what would the nation of darkness have done to God if he had refused to fight it? If you say that it would have caused him some harm, you will admit that God was corruptible and violable. But if you say that it could not harm him, you will be asked: Why, then, did he fight? Why did he hand over his substance to its enemies to be corrupted and violated and compelled to every sin? Against this dilemma you have never been able to escape.

[Col. 0596]

You seem to yourselves to have found something great and secure when you answer: “It is a great injustice to desire what belongs to another; God would have consented to that injustice if he had refused to conquer the nation that dared to do this.” This answer would have some appearance of justice if, at least in the war itself, the nature of your god had preserved itself whole and undefiled, and, when mixed with hostile members, had done nothing unjust, whether compelled or seduced. But when you say that it consented while captive to such enormous crimes and abominations; when, finally, you do not even maintain that it can be wholly purified from that monstrous impiety by which it became hostile even to the holy light, of which it is a portion, and for which you believe it deservedly receives the eternal punishments of that dreadful mass—who would not see how much better it would have been to leave the hostile enemy in its own iniquity, striving after empty things, than to hand over to it a portion of God, whose powers it would drain and whose corrupted beauty it would associate with its own iniquity?

Who could be so obstinately blinded as not to perceive and consider that the nation of darkness would have acted with far less injustice by vainly attempting to invade a nature belonging to another than God did by handing over his own nature to be invaded, compelled to iniquity, and even partly condemned to punishment?

Is this, then, what it means to have refused to consent to iniquity—to have committed such enormous iniquity without any necessity? Or was there a necessity, a claim that Manichaeus himself was not ashamed to make, though you are ashamed of it? For he says that God saw a great ruin and devastation threatening his holy realms unless some outstanding divine power, strong in virtue, were set against it.

But you reason more cleverly, of course. For if you say that God fought from necessity, lest the nation of darkness harm him, you call God violable and corruptible, since something could harm him if he had refused to fight.

[Note: [Col. 0596] The Ambrosian manuscript and the Carnotensis read *quasi*, “as if,” instead of *quam si*, “than if.”]

Therefore drive away and expel from your hearts and from your faith even the war itself, and finally condemn and anathematize that entire story, woven from the horror of impious and filthy blasphemies.

For what is the meaning, I ask you, of your not fearing—as was said above—to call that nature violable and corruptible, so that the nature of your god, if it could not exercise the strength by which it could not be captured, was at least unable to preserve justice while captive? Daniel was able to do so: he dared to mock the lions, and, through his piety, without being compelled by any terror, he did not consent to the injustice of those by whom he had been led captive. He did not lose the equity and freedom of a patient and wise mind while enduring bodily servitude (Dan. VI and XIV).

But the nature of God was led captive and made unjust; it cannot be wholly purified and is compelled at the end to be condemned. If it knew from eternity that this evil would befall it, no divinity was owed to it. But if the kingdom of light and the nation of darkness were adjacent to one another, whether in lands or in regions contiguous to themselves—

[Note: [Col. 0596] The printed editions read: “in places of the kingdom situated next to one another in the city,” and so forth. There are many errors here, which it was not possible to correct entirely with the help of the Carnotensis manuscript.]

—and you have said that the things which Manichaeus recounts, and which prudent and understanding people ought to laugh at, are ineffable, and that Christ calls them the right and the left hand, we know that Christ uses “right” and “left” to mean not bodily places but the blessedness and misery corresponding to each person’s merit.

But your carnal thought is so unwilling to depart from bodily places that you say that this visible sun—and therefore corporeal, since it cannot be contained except in a bodily place—is both God and a part of God. But it is foolish to discuss these matters with you. For what incorporeal reality could you understand, when you do not yet believe God to be incorruptible?

## CHAPTER XXI

But, as if you were a good and kindly friend, you rebuke me for abandoning the Manichaeans and turning to the books of the Jews. These are the very books that suffocate your error and deceit. In them Christ was prophesied as the truth of God presented him, not as the vanity of the Manichaeans invented him.

Yet, as a most urbane person, you attack the ancient Scripture because it is written in the prophet: “And make children of fornication, because the earth will fornicate against the Lord” (Hos. I, 2), while you hear in the Gospel: “Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXI, 31).

I know where your indignation comes from. It is not the prostitute’s fornication that displeases you so much as the fact that she has been changed into marriage and converted to marital chastity. For you believe that your god is bound by tighter bonds of flesh in the begetting of children. You think that prostitutes spare him because they take care not to conceive, so that, freed from the duty of bearing children, they may serve lust. For among you a woman’s conception is a prison and a bond for God.

This also is why the words “The two shall become one flesh” displease you, although the Apostle commends this as a great mystery in Christ and the holy Church (Gen. II, 24; Eph. V, 31–32).

[Note: [Col. 0597] The Carnotensis manuscript reads: “although the Apostle commends this sacrament in Christ and the Church as a great mystery.”]

This is why “Be fruitful and multiply” displeases you (Gen. I, 28): lest the prisons of your gods be multiplied.

But I confess that in the Catholic Church I learned that, just as the soul and the body—one endowed with authority, the other subject—are good, so too the good of the soul and the good of the body come only from the highest good, from whom all good things come: whether great or small, heavenly or earthly, spiritual or bodily, temporal or eternal. These things are not therefore to be condemned because the others are to be preferred.

## CHAPTER XXII

As for the words that you include among the things to be condemned, “Kill and eat” (Acts X, 13), they too are used spiritually in the Acts of the Apostles. Nevertheless, even when understood bodily, it is not food that is blameworthy but gluttony.

These words ought especially to have pleased you, even in their carnal sense, so that you might slaughter the flesh and thus, once the prisons had been broken, your god might flee from his wretched confinement; and, if any remnants of him remained there, you could cleanse them by eating them in the workshop of the belly.

You mock me because I grieved over Sarah’s barrenness. I did not grieve over this at all, since she too was a prophetic figure. But your sacrilegious fables properly lead you to grieve not over Sarah’s barrenness but over her fertility, since every woman’s fertility is a harsh calamity for God.

[Col. 0598]

It is therefore no wonder that among you the statement made about such people is fulfilled most fully: “Forbidding marriage” (1 Tim. IV, 3). For you do not detest intercourse so much as marriage, because in marriage intercourse undertaken for the propagation of children is not a vice but a duty. Holy men and women are free from that duty through continence—not because they avoided it as an evil, but because they chose something better.

Nevertheless, the marital duty of fathers and mothers such as Abraham and Sarah were should be considered not as arising from merely human society but from divine dispensation. For since Christ had to come in the flesh, Sarah’s marriage served the propagation of that flesh, just as Mary’s virginity served it.

[Note: [Col. 0598] The printed editions read: “to which Mary’s virginity is preferred.” The added words “is preferred” are superfluous and absent from the Carnotensis manuscript, since “served in its place” is understood.]

## CHAPTER XXIII

This is also why you mockingly mentioned, with praiseworthy ignorance, the words: “Place your hand under my thigh,” which Abraham said to his servant when requiring an oath of allegiance. “Place,” he said, “your hand under my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven” (Gen. XXIV, 2–3).

The servant swore by obeying. But Abraham prophesied by commanding, namely, that the God of heaven would come in that flesh which would be propagated from that thigh.

You, chaste and pure men, reject, detest, and abominate this—men who fear a single virgin womb for the Son of God, whom no contact with flesh could have changed, while you entangle the nature of your living god,

[Note: [Col. 0598] Perhaps: “your.”]

changed and polluted, in the wombs of every kind of woman—not merely of human beings but also of beasts.

And so, while you shudder at the thigh of a single patriarch, what thighs, I will not say of prophets but of any prostitutes, can you find in which you would not have to swear by your god so shamefully fettered there?

[Note: [Col. 0598] Erasmus and the editions of Louvain read: “in which you would not have to avoid your god, so shamefully fettered there.” The text has been corrected from the Carnotensis manuscript.]

Unless perhaps you are not ashamed to touch a member of the human body chastely, but are ashamed to swear by a god bound there so shamefully.

With such grotesque deformity you attack Noah’s ark, in the name of your captive *pancarpus*, which is customarily served at theatrical banquets because it contains animals of every kind.

[Note: [Col. 0598] Morel, in *Elementa Critica*, pp. 330–331, judges that this passage should be restored as follows: “But you are ashamed to swear by a god so shamefully bound there, so grotesquely captive. In the name of *pancarpus*.”]

The ark represented the future Church from all nations through its inclusion of every kind of animal (Gen. VII). Here I congratulate you for having used an appropriate word, whether knowingly or unknowingly: for *pancarpus*—Greek πάγκαρπος (*pánkarpos*)—means “bearing every fruit,” which is spiritually true of the Church.

Yet you do not consider how much happier Noah and his companions were among those wild beasts, entering unharmed and leaving unharmed, than your god, who was torn apart and devoured by the savage fury of the nation of darkness. Thus he was not made *pancarpus*, “bearing every fruit,” but plainly *compartus*, “torn apart.”

[Note: [Col. 0598] The old Carnotensis manuscript reads *comparcus*.]

You mock Jacob’s struggle with the angel (Gen. XXXII, 24–25), in which the future struggle of the people of Israel with Christ’s flesh was prophetically represented. But however you understand it, how much better it would have been for your god to wrestle with a human being than to be defeated, captured, and carried away by the nation of demons.

You falsely accuse Abraham of selling his wife’s chastity. He did not lie about his sister but prudently kept silent about his wife, entrusting the preservation of her chastity to his God. If he had not done what he could do, he would have been judged to trust not in God but to tempt God (Gen. XII and XX).

Yet you do not consider your god, who handed over not a wife but his own members to his enemies to be polluted, corrupted, and disgraced—not selling them, but giving them away for nothing. If it were possible, you would surely wish that the glorious nature of your god return from his enemies as undefiled as Sarah was returned undefiled to her husband.

## CHAPTER XXIV

You praise my former conduct and studies and ask who suddenly changed me. Then, by circumlocution, you mention the ancient enemy of all the faithful and holy, and of the Lord Jesus Christ himself—the one whom you evidently wish to be understood as the devil.

What should I say to you about my change? Unless I believed that it had taken place for the better in that way, I certainly would not have abandoned, detested, and condemned your error and transferred myself to the Catholic Church and faith.

Whether I did this rightly—that is, whether I was changed from evil to good—you yourself resolve for me in the very word you used concerning my change. For if my soul were, as you say, God’s nature, then whether it were changed for the better, as I trust, or for the worse, as you accuse me of being, it could not be changed at all—neither by itself nor by the impulse of anyone or anything else.

Therefore, when I abandoned this error and chose the faith in which God’s nature is devoutly believed, and understood wisely, to be wholly immutable, my change displeases no one except those who are displeased by the immutable God.

The devil is the adversary of the saints, not because he rises against them as an enemy from a contrary principle of another nature, but because he envies them the heavenly honor from which he himself was cast down. Having himself been changed, he attempts to change others.

For according to the extended account of that Persian fable which you give, if he changes others without having been changed himself, he is plainly greater and victorious. But if, as you assert, he is of the holy light, then he is not an enemy of God but his friend, and better than those whom he deceives, since he makes them enemies of the holy light of which he himself is a friend.

[Note: [Col. 0599] Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read *effecit*, “made,” instead of *efficit*, “makes.”]

This is why Manichaeus says that souls are to be condemned to eternal punishment in that dreadful mass: because they allowed themselves to wander from their former luminous nature and then became enemies of the light. Yet he insists that the very mind of the nation of darkness, burning with love of the light it wished to possess, created the bodies of animals.

Free yourself, then, from these utterly empty and sacrilegious fictions, changing for the better through the help of him who is changed neither for the better nor for the worse.

## CHAPTER XXV

“We have escaped,” you say, “because we followed a spiritual Savior. For only his audacity went so far that, if our Lord were carnal, all our hope would have been cut off.”

If you say this because you do not believe that Christ had flesh, you ought not to place your hope in Manichaeus, whom you admit to have had flesh, having been begotten from a man and a woman like other human beings. Why, then, do you place such hope in him?

For in this very letter of yours, when you sought to frighten me, you yourself said:

“Who, then, will be your advocate before the just tribunal of the Judge, when you begin to be convicted by your own testimony, both from your speech and from your conduct? The Persian whom you accused will not be present. Apart from him, who will console you as you weep? Who will save the Punic man?”

You therefore said that, apart from Manichaeus, no one could be a consoler and savior. How, then, when you were discussing Christ’s sufferings, did you say that you had escaped because you followed a spiritual Savior, lest the enemy be able to kill him if he had been embodied in flesh?

If the enemy killed your Manichaeus, then, in whom he found flesh, so that he could already be your savior, how can you say, “Apart from him, who will console you as you weep? Who will save the Punic man”?

You see what it is to be in heresy and the doctrines of demons, in the hypocrisy of liars (1 Tim. IV, 1–2).

[Note: [Col. 0600] Perhaps: “what you are.”]

You want Manichaeus to be truthful about Christ while Christ is deceitful. Thus, if Christ acted wholly deceitfully and falsely in displaying his flesh, his death, his resurrection, and finally the places of his wounds and nails, which he showed to his doubting disciples (John XX, 20), then Manichaeus spoke truthfully about Christ. But if Christ displayed true flesh, and therefore a true death, a true resurrection, and true scars, then Manichaeus lied about Christ.

Accordingly, the difference between you and me in this matter is that you chose to believe Manichaeus truthful by believing Christ deceitful. I, however, prefer to believe Manichaeus a liar—as in other matters, so also concerning Christ—rather than believe Christ a liar about anything, and especially about that matter in which he placed the chief hope of believers: his passion and resurrection.

For whoever says that, when Christ appeared to his hesitant disciples after what was thought to be his death, while they thought they were seeing a spirit, and when he said, “Touch my hands and feet, and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV, 39); and when he said to the one who did not believe, “Put your finger into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John XX, 27)—whoever says that Christ did not display all this truthfully but deceitfully is not Christ’s preacher but his accuser.

“But,” you say, “Manichaeus preaches Christ and calls himself his apostle.” For this very reason he should rather be detested and avoided. For if he said these things in order to accuse Christ, he could at least boast that he loved truth by exposing another’s falsehood. But now, unaware and incautious, he betrays himself and clearly shows those who look carefully what he himself does and what he loves, by praising and proclaiming the one who lies.

Flee, then, my friend, such a great plague, lest Manichaeus, by deceiving you—which cannot truly be done—wish to make you faithful, like the disciple whom Christ wished to appear to have made faithful when he said to him, “Put your fingers into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing.”

For as the sweetest truth teaches, what else did Christ say to the disciple than this? “Touch what I bear; touch what I bore; touch true flesh; touch the traces of true wounds; touch the true places of the nails; and by believing what is true, do not be unbelieving but faithful.”

But as the sacrilegious vanity of Manichaeus speaks foolishly, what else did Christ say to the disciple than this? “Touch what I pretend; touch what I counterfeit; touch false flesh; touch the deceptive places of false wounds; and do not be unbelieving toward my lying limbs, so that by believing what is false you may be faithful.”

Such are the faithful whom Manichaeus possesses: followers of every doctrine of demons and of lying speakers.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Flee these things, I beg you. Do not let the appearance of their small number deceive you, since the Lord himself said that the way is narrow and belongs to the few (Matt. VII, 14).

You wish to be among the few, but among the worst. It is true that the completely innocent are few in every respect; but among the guilty there are fewer murderers than thieves, fewer incestuous persons than adulterers. Finally, even the old fables and histories themselves contain fewer Medeas and Phaedras than women guilty of other crimes and abominations, and fewer Ochi and Busirises than men guilty of other impieties and crimes.

See, then, whether perhaps among you an excessive horror of impiety produces the merit of being few. For such things are read, said, and believed there that it is astonishing that more than a few should rush into that error or remain in it.

The small number of the saints, whose way is narrow, is contrasted with the multitude of sinners. This small number is indeed hidden among a much greater quantity of chaff; but within the threshing floor of the Catholic Church it must now be gathered and threshed, and at the end winnowed and purified (Matt. III, 12).

You ought to turn to that Church if you desire faithfully to be faithful, lest, by trusting in falsehoods, you “feed on the wind,” as it is written (Hos. XII, 1)—that is, lest you become food for unclean spirits.

For if the Apostle Paul, whom you mention, counted not the Scriptures of the wise men of the Old Testament and that entire prophetic dispensation of words and deeds as refuse, but rather the carnal distinction of Jewish descent; and, on behalf of the synagogues of his ancestral people, which were wandering and did not recognize Christ, counted as refuse his zeal for persecuting Christians—a zeal with which they were inflamed as though it were praiseworthy—and the righteousness that comes from the Law, in which the Jews proudly glory because they did not understand God’s grace there, in order to gain Christ (Phil. III, 8–9), how much more ought you to cast away, not as refuse but as poison, those Scriptures filled with the most unspeakable blasphemies, in which the nature of truth, the nature of the highest good, and the nature of God are described as so often changeable, so often defeated, so often corrupted, and partly polluted in an inexplicable manner and finally condemned by truth itself?

You ought to abandon them and pass to the Catholic Church, which was prophesied so long beforehand and revealed in its own time, now that the dispute has ended.

I say this to you because your mind is neither the nature of evil, since no such nature exists at all, nor the nature of God, since otherwise I would be speaking in vain to one who is immutable. Rather, because your mind was changed by abandoning God, and because this change itself is evil, let it be changed by turning toward the immutable good, with the help of that immutable good; and such a change will be its liberation from evil.

If you disregard this admonition, continuing to believe that there are two natures—one, a mutable nature of good which, when mixed with evil, was able to consent to injustice; the other, an immutable nature of evil which, though mixed with good, was unable to consent to justice—you will chatter the familiar shameful fable, sowing execrable and disgraceful blasphemies among those whose ears itch for fornication, so that you may belong to the company of those of whom it was foretold that a time would come when they would not endure sound doctrine but, according to their own desires, would heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears, and would turn their hearing away from truth toward fables (2 Tim. IV, 3–4).

But if you receive this admonition wisely and turn to the immutable God, through this praiseworthy change you will become one of those of whom the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

This could not be said of God’s nature, since it was never evil and never worthy of being called darkness; nor of the nature of evil, since, if it existed, it could never be changed or become light. Rather, it is rightly and truthfully said of that nature which is not immutable but, after abandoning the immutable light by which it was made, is darkened in itself. When it turns toward that light, it becomes light—not in itself but in the Lord.

For it is not light from itself, since it is not the true light, but shines because it has been illuminated by him of whom it is said: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I, 9).

Believe this, understand this, hold fast to this, if you wish to be good through participation in the immutable good, which you cannot be through yourself. You could neither lose it if you were immutably this good, nor receive it if you were immutably not this good.

[Col. 0601]

# INDEX OF OTHER SHORT WORKS OF AUGUSTINE IN WHICH HE DEALS, EITHER DIRECTLY OR INCIDENTALLY, AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS

## IN VOLUME I

Three books *On Free Will*.

Two books *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*.

Two books *On the Morals of the Catholic Church and the Morals of the Manichaeans*.

One book *On True Religion*.

Much against them in the books of the *Confessions*.

## IN VOLUME II

Letters LXXIX and CCXXXVI.

## IN VOLUME IV

Exposition of Psalm CXL.

## IN VOLUME V

Sermons I, II, XII, L, CLIII, CLXXXII, and CCXXXVII.

## IN VOLUME VI

The book *On Christian Combat* and the book *On Continence*.

Moreover, see in the Appendix to this eighth volume the book *On Faith against the Manichaeans* and the *Admonition concerning the Reception of Manichaeans Who Are Converted*.

[Col. 0603]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: TWO BOOKS AGAINST AN ADVERSARY OF THE LAW AND THE PROPHETS

[Note: [Col. 0603] Immediately before the books recently reviewed, *On the Soul and Its Origin* and *On Adulterous Marriages*, which belong to the year 419, Augustine indicates that the following books against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets were written by him at approximately the same time. Cassiodorus speaks of this work with praise in book 1 of *On the Institution of Divine Literature*, chapter 1. The individual chapters of the Adversary’s book, each of which had to be refuted here, are listed before the end of book 2, in chapter 10.]

[Note: [Col. 0603] “For the work that follows, see book 2, chapter 58, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 654, beginning with the words ‘Meanwhile the book’ and continuing to the words ‘Beloved brothers.’”]

[Note: [Col. 0603] Written approximately at the beginning of the year 420.]

[Note: [Col. 0603] We have collated this work *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets* with eleven Gallican manuscripts: the Germanensis, Corbeiensis, Remigianus, Michaelianus, Fiscamnensis, Pratellensis, Cisterciensis, Casalensis, Sorbonicus, Colbertinus, Regius, and one Vatican manuscript; also with the editions of Ambrosius, Erasmus, and Louvain, and with the variant readings of Belgian manuscripts reported by Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0603] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1.]

(C)

# BOOK ONE

## In this book, passages of the Old Testament maliciously criticized are defended

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0603]

### 1

When, most beloved brothers, I found the book of some heretic that you sent me—as you wrote—in a seaside marketplace, where the book itself was being offered for sale and was being read by crowds rushing together with dangerous curiosity and pleasure, I first asked whose error it was, so that I might answer with as much brevity as possible.

For the Manichaeans are not the only ones who condemn the Law and the Prophets. The Marcionites do so as well, along with certain others whose sects have not become so widely known among Christian peoples.

But this man, whose name I did not find in the same book, detests God, the Maker of the world. The Manichaeans, although they do not accept the book of Genesis and blaspheme against it, nevertheless confess that the good God made the world, even if from a foreign nature and material.

Although it has not become clear to me to which sect this blasphemer belongs, divine Scripture must be defended against his tongue, since he attacks it with slanderous arguments. And since he wishes in some manner to appear a Christian, and for this reason adduces certain testimonies from the Gospel and the Apostle, he must also be refuted by the Scriptures belonging to the New Testament, so that it may be shown that in criticizing the ancient writings he rages more thoughtlessly than craftily.

## CHAPTER II

### 2

First, this impious man asks with a sacrilegious mouth what a pious person could have asked in a religious spirit: how the words “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” should be understood (Gen. I, 1), although he did not add the word “earth,” about which he speaks afterward.

He therefore asks: “In what beginning? Was it the beginning in which that same God began to exist, or the time when he grew weary of being empty?”

The answer is that God neither began to exist nor grew weary of his idleness. He never was not, never became sluggish through inactivity, and never grew weary through working. He did not need a dwelling because heaven did not yet exist, nor, once heaven had been made, did he find a dwelling as a traveler who had reached the end of his wanderings.

For he is able to remain supremely blessed in himself and to impart his dwelling to his temple—which is all the saints, angels, and human beings—in such a way that they receive from him the good by which they can be blessed, rather than he receiving from them a dwelling without which he could not be blessed.

[Note: [Col. 0604] Almost only the Louvain edition reads: “all the holy angels and human beings.”]

Either, then, the words “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” should be understood to mean that the beginning was the point from which they began to exist. They were not always co-eternal with God, but, being made, they received a beginning from which they would begin to exist.

Or certainly, because God made heaven and earth in a beginning co-eternal with himself, the meaning is that he made them in the Only-Begotten Son. For he is the Wisdom of whom the Apostle says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I, 24). And to the God who made heaven and earth it is said in the Psalm: “You made all things in Wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24).

Or, if this man does not wish to accept testimony from the Psalm, let him hear the Apostle speaking about Christ: “Because in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Col. I, 16).

### 3

God, therefore, neither began to exist nor will cease to exist. But some of his works, having begun, cease to exist at a fixed end, such as times and temporal things. Others, having begun, will remain, such as the eternal life of the holy human beings, which they will receive.

This man did not see this. He thought that it had to be said and defined that no beginning can exist without an end. Nor could he consider the number whose beginning is from one and whose end is in none. For no number, however large—whether it is spoken or, if it can no longer be spoken, conceived—exists to which one cannot add something so that it becomes greater.

And I suppose that, whatever heresy he holds under the name of Christ against Christ, he promises himself life in Christ—certainly a blessed life—whose beginning can be at the point when the end of this miserable life has come.

Let him answer, then: will that blessed life—which he does not deny will have, or does not deny to have, a beginning—have an end or not? If he says that it will have an end, how will he dare call himself a Christian? If he says that it will not have an end, where is the truth of what he dared to say, that no beginning exists without an end?

## CHAPTER III
4. He also asks: “If this world is something good, why was that which was better not made by him long ago, from the beginning?” As though God had made the world better than himself, or as though this good ought not to have been made because it is not equal to its maker. But as for his question why this was not made long ago, from the beginning, let him receive this answer: Indeed, it was made long ago, from its own beginning—not from God’s, for God has no beginning. If, however, this beginning could be indicated by the words, “In the beginning God made” [Genesis 1:1], why does he bring an accusation, as though asking in which beginning he made it, when he himself again asks why it was not made long ago, from the beginning? Accordingly, his own words must be repeated to him.

For just as, because it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” he argues and says, “In which beginning, then? The beginning in which this same God began to exist, or the beginning from which he became weary of being empty?”—so, in response to his statement, “Why was this not made long ago, from the beginning, by him?” we too should say to him: “In which beginning, then? The beginning in which this same God began to exist, or the beginning from which he became weary of being empty?” For what displeases him is that God did not make heaven long ago, from the beginning, when he asks, “Why not long ago, from the beginning?” It is as though he ought to have begun making it from that beginning from which the maker himself exists.

Why did he not fear that, by saying “from the beginning from which God himself exists,” he would be told: “Then God has a beginning, and consequently, according to your own opinion, he will also have an end; for you said that no beginning exists without an end”? Moreover, if God has no beginning, how could he make something from the beginning from which he himself exists [Note: The printed editions read, “from which he himself is not.” The manuscripts lack the negative particle.]? Therefore, he made it from the beginning from which he made it—that is, from the beginning at which what he made began to exist.

Thus either their god never made anything good; or, according to this man, whatever good he made, he made from the beginning from which he himself exists—and for whatever has a beginning, an end must be feared; or he ought to submit to the words of holy Scripture and understand that God, who began to exist from no beginning, made heaven “in the beginning,” that is, at the beginning from which heaven began to exist, or in the Son. When the Jews asked who he was, the Son answered that he was the Beginning [John 8:25].

[Col. 0606]

5. Unless perhaps he is going to say that “beginning” and “origin” are different things. If it had therefore been written, “In the origin God made heaven and earth,” this man, who said, “Why was it not made long ago, from the beginning?” would have raised no objection, since he would have read, “In the origin God made”—not considering it impious to believe that God has an origin but not a beginning.

If that is so, let this author correct the Gospel, where it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” [John 1:1]. Why does he not say here too, “In which beginning, then? The beginning in which this same Word began to exist?” And since the Word was God, he can also say it in the form in which he spoke in this book: “The beginning in which this same God began to exist?”

Let him say here, if he wishes, also his own definitive pronouncement when he hears, “In the beginning was the Word.” Let him say here too, if he dares, “No beginning exists without an end,” so that even the Manichaeans themselves—who perhaps read him with the greatest eagerness because they find him hostile to the Law and the Prophets—may judge him insane.

But if the God who made the world displeases him, why does the one through whom the world was made not displease him? For it is written of Christ: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” [John 1:10, 1].

## CHAPTER IV

6. Let him understand, indeed [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “therefore”], that God can make good things, but cannot need the good things he has made. Thus he did not need the things he was to make, since he does not need the things he has made. The supremely good God made all things—things unequal to himself, certainly, but nevertheless good. For even what is not supremely good, indeed even what is lowest, could not exist as good except from the supreme good.

But anyone who denies that something is good because he recognizes that it is not equal to God thinks very badly of God. For God would not be the supreme good but the lowest good if whatever is less than him were no longer good. Moreover, among the things he created, even the highest goods are vastly unequal to the Creator, because he made them and they were made. Clearly, then, since he did not need such things to increase his blessedness, he must be thought even less to have needed lower and altogether least things. Yet he made them as the author of all good things.

For the Lord Jesus [Note: In the manuscripts: “For the Lord God, through whom …”], through whom the world was made, indicates that God created not only heavenly things but also earthly things, including those earthly things that appear insignificant, when he says: “If therefore God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?” [Matthew 6:30].

There is therefore one and the same God, author of heaven and earth, of the stars and the plants—of everything in heaven and on earth that exists with its own measure, form, and order; of everything in heaven and on earth that lives; of everything in heaven and on earth that senses; and of everything in heaven and on earth that understands.

These things ought not to have been equal either to the one by whom they were created or to one another—and therefore they are all good. For if they were equal, there would be one kind of good things, not all things. As it is, they are all good because some are better than others, and the goodness of the lower adds [Note: Thus the better manuscripts; the Louvain edition reads “is added”] to the praise of the better. In the inequality of good things itself there is a pleasing gradation, in which the comparison of the lesser commends the greater.

[Note: The Louvain edition adds here “good.” This is superfluous.]

## CHAPTER V

7. But the things called evil are either defects of good things, which cannot exist anywhere by themselves wholly outside good things [Note: In the Louvain edition: “outside all good things.” “All” is absent from the other editions and the manuscripts]; or punishments for sins, which proceed from the beauty of justice.

Yet defects themselves also bear witness to the goodness of natures. For what is evil through defect is certainly good by nature. A defect is contrary to nature because it harms nature; and it would not harm it unless it diminished its good. Evil, therefore, is nothing other than the deprivation of good. Consequently, it exists nowhere except in some good thing—and, although not in the supremely good, since the supremely good remains incorruptible and unchangeable, as God is, nevertheless only in something good, because it harms only by diminishing what is good.

Thus good things can exist without evils, as God himself can, and as all the higher heavenly things can; but evils cannot exist without good things. For if they harm nothing, they are not evils; but if they harm, they diminish something good. And if they harm more greatly, they still have some good to diminish. If they consume it entirely, no nature will remain for them to harm; consequently, there will be no evil by which it can be harmed, once the nature whose good is diminished by the harm has ceased to exist.

## CHAPTER VI

8. Whether any nature—that is, any substance—can be reduced altogether to nothing is a very subtle question. But the truest faith [Note: The printed editions read “most truly”; the manuscripts, “truest”] sings to God: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” [Psalm 101:27–28]. Therefore, it is only the unchangeable good, which is God, that both made and governs changeable goods.

Changeable goods are good because they were made by the supreme good; they are changeable because they were made not from him but from nothing. Consequently, mortal things too, although in some respect they are punishments for those for whom only immortality can fulfill the measure of perfect blessedness, nevertheless possess their proper place of beauty in the beauty of temporal things. Yet the sense by which such beauty is perceived is greater than human understanding [Note: The editions read “but greater”—*sed majorem*. The manuscripts, “but greater”—*sed major*, which is preferable].

Nevertheless, that faith which says to its God, “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight” [Wisdom 11:21], although it recoils from mortality out of love for life, still praises the Creator of all good things even for mortal goods.

For this very man who criticizes—and who does not believe that God exists, although he sees that God’s earthly works are mortal—could not complete the very argument that pleased him so greatly that he committed it to writing and memory, except through words belonging to his several statements, words that themselves both begin and come to an end. Thus he could not explain the beauty of the argument by which he wishes to persuade us that whatever arises and dies cannot be good, except through syllables that arise and die.

What wonder, then, if in so great a totality of nature there is some lowest good in the orders of time—a thing beautiful not through the permanence of things, as certain sublime spiritual things are, but for the adornment of its own kind, indeed of its earthly origin and passing away?

[Col. 0608]

9. Since these things are so, let him not bring accusations against the Scripture that says, “God saw the light, that it was good” [Genesis 1:4]. For not only did the supremely good God create the light that he called day, the firmament that he called heaven, the sun and moon and the other stars; he also created trees and plants, and all mortal things in the waters and on the earth, and he saw that they were good in their own kind and order.

Nor did the one who wrote this book under the revelation of God’s Spirit fear that impious critics, men who speak vanity and seduce minds—first their own, then those of others who delight in blasphemous loquacity—would arise. For God saw that they too were good insofar as they are human beings; insofar as they consist of body and a rational soul; insofar as the members of their bodies are distinguished by their proper functions and, through a wonderfully ordered and perfectly harmonious difference, agree in the unity of their peace; insofar as the soul, by its natural excellence, surpasses and governs them; insofar as the five senses of the flesh, distributed into their several parts, fulfill and animate them with unequal power and social harmony; and insofar as, through mind and reason—something of which a beastly soul is incapable—they can know and understand [Note: The manuscripts read thus. The editions have: “they cannot know and understand,” followed by “God saw, etc.”]. Therefore God saw that they were good, and for that reason he created them.

For he did not merely see them after they had been created; he also foresaw them before they were to be created. And although through perverse will and blind error they are evil, he did not therefore see that they were not to be created. He foresaw where they were to be ordered. Thus, from the same mass of the first transgression, justly condemned, he made them vessels of wrath—if they persist in this wickedness to the end—in order that they might benefit the vessels of mercy [Romans 9:22–23], so that through their sharpness in vanity the latter might seek the secrets of truth more diligently.

“For great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” [Psalm 110:2]. What wonder, then, if human folly dislikes what divine wisdom finds pleasing in its works? For what else is meant by “He saw the light, that it was good” than that it pleased him?

[Note: Several manuscripts read “except that it pleased him,” omitting “that.”]

## CHAPTER VII

10. But this empty-speaking blasphemer, who wrote a book full of sacrilegious insults—would that he had found his own work displeasing and had not thought it good, but had seen that it was evil—see what he said:

“So completely,” he says, “did he previously not know what light was that, seeing it for the first time only now, he judged it to be extremely good.”

Then the Lord Jesus too, when he marveled at the centurion’s words and said to his disciples, “Amen I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” [Matthew 8:10], previously did not know what that faith was, so that when he saw it for the first time then, he judged it to be extremely good.

Or was it someone else who worked that faith in the centurion’s heart, rather than the one who marveled at it? Certainly, the foolish and unbelieving have even greater grounds for blasphemy in the fact that Jesus marveled at whatever faith a human being possessed than in the fact that God saw that the light was good.

Anyone can see even familiar things and recognize that they are good—that is, approve them as pleasing to himself. But whoever marvels at something, according to the ordinary manner of human speech, indicates that what he marvels at was unexpected and unforeseen by him. Yet Jesus, who knew all things beforehand, praised by his marveling what he commended to others as worthy of wonder.

But what did God see that he himself had made which he had not first seen as something to be made in the light—which is himself? And what does holy Scripture so repeatedly and necessarily affirm except that God saw that the things he made were good, so that the piety of the faithful might learn from this not to judge visible and invisible creation according to human perception—which is often offended even by good things whose causes and order it does not know—but to believe God when he praises his works and to learn [Note: The better manuscripts read this way. The editions have “to believe and yield”].

For everyone makes progress in knowledge more easily in proportion as he has believed God more reverently before he came to know.

God therefore saw the light that he had made, that it was good, because what pleased him to be made pleased him when made, so that it might remain according to the measure of existence or continuance established for each thing by so great a craftsman.

But the light that is God is one thing, and the light that God made is another. Incomparably better is the light who made it, needing in no way [Note: Manuscript B reads “would need.” We restore “needing” on the authority of the editions of Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, Louvain, and Maurists.] the light he made.

And from this accusation of his—why God did not make these good things as long ago as he himself existed [Note: The Louvain edition has “as long ago as he himself who made them existed.” “Who” is absent from our manuscripts and from the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus]—we should instead understand that God did not make them because he needed them, without which he could exist in his perfect blessedness eternally and without beginning.

The sole cause for making these things was therefore God’s goodness, because he had no necessity. Thus, whatever this man rails at God for—as though God, who had been ignorant of light, had seen it for the first time then—he would recognize as foolish and empty if he himself possessed any light within.

## CHAPTER VIII

11. He even attributes it to the writer’s foolishness that he said the darkness had always existed without beginning, whereas the light received its beginning from the darkness—as though he had read in the book he criticizes that the darkness was eternal. Yet what is written is: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss.”

Darkness therefore began from the time when the confused mass of heaven and earth began to exist, before the light was made by which what had been dark without light would be illuminated.

What is inappropriate, then, if the beginnings of the world’s material were dark, so that, when light was added, what had been made might be rendered better, and the disposition of a human being who was later to progress might in this way be signified?

Nevertheless, anyone who, by God’s gift, has been able to examine these matters more perceptively may perhaps discover in the creation—which is narrated as having been made without intervals of temporal delay—a wonderfully ordered sequence of things.

For matter is not altogether nothing, concerning which it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “You who made the world from unformed matter” [Wisdom 11:18]. Therefore, because it is called unformed, it is not altogether nothing. Nor was it coeternal with God, as though it had been made by no one; nor did someone else make it so that God would have something from which to make the world. Far be it from us to say that the Almighty could not make anything unless he first found the material from which to make it.

Therefore God made matter itself as well. Nor should it be considered evil because it is unformed; rather, it should be understood as good because [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts omit “because”] it is formable—that is, capable of formation.

For if form is something good, then being capable of good is itself something good. A confused voice is a shout without words, whereas an articulated voice comes into being when it is formed into words. The former, then, is formable; the latter, formed. The former receives form; the latter possesses it. For it is readily apparent which of these is made from which.

No one would say that a vocal sound is made from words. Rather, who would not understand that sounding words are made from the voice?

[Note: We have removed a gloss absent from the manuscripts but inserted in the printed editions: “but rather that the sound of a word is made from the voice; or rather that sounding words are made from the voice,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER IX

12. God should not therefore be thought first to have made unformed matter and, after some interval of time, to have formed what he had previously made unformed. Rather, just as sounding words proceed from one who speaks—not as though an unformed voice first receives form afterward, but as a formed utterance is produced—so God should be understood to have made the world from unformed matter while creating that matter together with the world.

Yet it is not useless first to narrate from what something is made and afterward what is made from it. For although both can occur simultaneously, both cannot be narrated simultaneously.

## CHAPTER X

13. Whether, then, under the names “heaven and earth,” or “the invisible and unformed earth” and “the dark abyss,” the unformed matter itself was first signified by terms drawn from familiar things—for it is utterly unknown to the human senses and scarcely comprehended at all when things are changed for the worse, as though everything more deformed were approaching it without ever reaching that unformed state, however little visible or intelligible form may remain—or whether spiritual and bodily nature was first indicated generally through “heaven and earth”—or whether something else is meant, which can here be understood without violating the rule of faith—in any case, there can be no doubt that the true, supreme, and good God made all that we see and all that we do not see that is better, although the manner in which he made these things cannot be grasped by the human mind.

But these uneducated blasphemers of the sacred writings should not be addressed with the subtle reasoning by which such matters ought to be sought and discussed among the peaceful children of God.

## CHAPTER XI

14. But if this man thinks that, against the books of the Law and the Prophets, he knows what he says he knows—that the supreme God is an incomparable splendor of incomprehensible light—I should first like to hear from him: of what light does he think the supreme God is the splendor? Is the light itself also God? Does he understand the Father as light and his only-begotten Son as that light’s splendor, while nevertheless confessing the Son to be the supreme God?

If that is what he believes, I approve and praise it. But if he does not believe that the one whom he believes to be light from light, or the incomparable splendor of incomprehensible light, is the maker of the world, I reject and condemn it, since he reads there: “The world was made through him,” where he also reads: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” [John 1:10, 9].

I reject it also if he is ignorant of this; and I reject and detest it still more if he knows it and lies in wait to deceive the ignorant, although it was written earlier in the old divine Scriptures: “Come to him, and be enlightened” [Psalm 33:6]; and, “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” [Psalm 18:9]; and, “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” [Psalm 12:4].

For this mortal human being was not praying that he might never die bodily, nor was he asking that sleep never come to his bodily eyes. Rather, he was asking that those eyes be enlightened of which the Apostle says: “The eyes of your heart having been enlightened” [Ephesians 1:18].

15. Moreover, if he dislikes the idea that the light received its beginning from darkness—for he attacks this too with the words of his chattering vanity—let him say the same thing to that Apostle who, writing to the faithful, says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” [Ephesians 5:8].

For who brought this about except the one who, when darkness was over the abyss, said, “Let there be light,” and there was light [Genesis 1:3]? The same Apostle expressed this more clearly elsewhere, saying: “God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts” [2 Corinthians 4:6].

But if he thinks that the prophetic Scriptures lack the teaching that the Son is light from light, or the splendor of light [Note: After “or the splendor of light,” the Louvain edition adds “eternal,” but unnecessarily], let him read what is written in those same Scriptures concerning Wisdom: “For she is the radiance of eternal light” [Wisdom 7:26]. Or let him read this in the prophetic Psalm: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord and bless his name; announce his salvation from day to day” [Psalm 95:1–2].

For what is “day from day” except the Son, light from light? Let him read in the Gospel that Christ is the salvation of God, when the aged Simeon recognized him in his mother’s arms—small in the flesh, great in spirit—and, taking him into his arms, said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation” [Luke 2:29–30].

## CHAPTER XII

16. If he answers here that the light of which it is said, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord,” is one thing—namely, the spiritual light of the mind, not of the flesh—and that the light of which it is written, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light,” is another, belonging to bodily eyes, then first he will confess that from the supreme light, which is God himself, it was possible for some sort of very low light to be made, though nevertheless a good one.

Next, how does he know what kind and what magnitude it had? Finally, was it spiritual or bodily?

Unless perhaps faithful people, who as long as they are in the body are away from the Lord [2 Corinthians 5:6], can already rightly be called light because of their faith, while the angels cannot—although they always see the face of the Father [Matthew 18:10]. How, then, does he know whether such a light was made first? How does he know how evening and morning can be understood in that light? How, finally, does he know how it was presented in the number six through God’s works, and how God rested in the seventh, from which a kind of form of that number seven was transferred to those days familiar to us, which revolve through the sun’s course?

But even if the light was bodily, how does he know how it could exist before the sun and before the firmament, which was afterward called heaven—removed from the sight of earthly beings in the higher regions of the world, so that God alone divided it from the darkness?

For between the darkness that makes for us the night so familiar to us and the light that makes for us the day so familiar to us, God commanded visible luminaries to divide them.
