Who could endure this man’s claim—although it should be laughed at rather than treated with indignation—that hours designate the day, while the sun distinguishes and separates the hours, and his demand that we believe Moses did not know this, and therefore named the day before the sun was made?

Let people gather to hear this man’s book, and let it be placed before them which is more credible: that this man did not know a certain light and a certain day that Moses knew, or that Moses did not know this light and day, which not only this man but even those who do not understand his words know.

## CHAPTER XIII

17. What shall we say of the question that some utterly ignorant person raises concerning the gathering of the waters? Indeed, it is not a question but a criticism, as though it had not rightly been said: “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” [Genesis 1:9], on the ground that the waters held everything.

He does not understand how water, thinned into airy vapors, becomes rarefied and occupies a great amount of space in a cloudy mist, but, when gathered together, becomes condensed in a small space [Note: The manuscripts read *denseatur*, “is condensed”], no longer floating lightly but flowing heavily. It is no wonder, then, if in its rarefied state it covered the earth but, when thickened, uncovered it.

What if, moreover, by divine command it settled into the earth’s great hollows [Note: The better manuscripts read “of the earth.” The editions have “into the earth”], and thus whatever of the watery nature lay spread throughout it, flowing together into concave regions, withdrew from the other parts and uncovered what it had covered [Note: Several manuscripts read “appeared”], gathering into lower depressions through which the sea might flow between and around them, while abandoning the higher places where the globe rises?

I leave aside the possibility that this may signify that the unformed matter was indicated by the terms “water” or “abyss,” and received the forms of these two heavy elements, moisture and soil [Note: In manuscripts of good quality: “moisture and the moist element”]. For this reason it was said, “Let the water be gathered,” because it was given a fluid and mobile form; and “Let the dry land appear,” because it is immobile and fixed [Note: The editions read “immobile and fixed.” On the authority of the manuscripts, we have removed the conjunction “and”].

For the point that the author of this prophetic book intended more fully—that his narrative of things made should also be a prefiguration of things to come—should not be forced upon contentious and unbelieving minds.

Since so many outcomes lie open to those who seek devoutly, let no one rashly attack so great an authority. Why, then, except by diabolical instigation, does this man choose to bring accusations against matters that he is not competent to investigate?

## CHAPTER XIV

18. As for the way this blind and ungrateful man attacks God, the creator of humanity, and dares to say to the one who fashioned him, “Why did you make me like this?”—although he entirely ignores how he was made—this is the audacity of a mind rushing headlong.

Yet the vessels of wrath are permitted to chatter in this way, so that, as though roused from the sleep of negligence, the vessels of mercy may be awakened [Romans 9:20–23] and, in their zeal to answer pernicious curses, may devote care to words that bring healing.

For consider what this man criticizes in the Creator of humanity: that he forbade the human being to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil [Genesis 2:17], as though he had wished to make him like cattle, which do not know how to distinguish these things, and had denied this to one to whom he had given power over beasts, by which capacity alone a human being surpasses beasts.

How necessary it is for a well-ordered life that we learn [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “that we say”] that some things are unhappily learned and that certain things are more happily left unknown! For how much happier would we be if we did not know diseases and pains?

Suppose, then, that a physician forbade us some food which he foresaw would make us ill if we ate it, and for that reason called it the food of the knowledge of health and weakness, because through it a human being, when he began to fall ill, would learn by experience the difference between contracted illness and lost health [Note: In the printed editions: “and good health lost.” “Good” is absent from the manuscripts]. He would certainly have been better off not knowing this and remaining in the health he lost, believing the physician through obedience rather than illness through experience. Would we say that such a physician begrudged us this kind of knowledge?

Who doubts that sin is evil? Yet the Lord Jesus Christ is praised because “he knew no sin” [2 Corinthians 5:21]. He therefore did not know this evil, and for that reason he did not possess the knowledge of good and evil from which Adam was forbidden.

If someone asks how he could condemn what he did not know—for he certainly did condemn sins—the Apostle says: “All things that are reproved are made manifest by the light” [Ephesians 5:13]. How, then, could the things he reproved be unknown to him?

The most correct answer would be: He both knew and did not know. Entirely correct. He knew through wisdom; he did not know through experience.

Adam therefore ought to have believed this divine wisdom, so that, obedient to God’s command, he might refrain from that knowledge of evil which comes through experience. For he would not have known evil unless he had done it. But he did it to his own hurt, not to God’s. For by the will of disobedience he could do nothing except what he himself was to suffer under the law of justice.

This is the punishment rendered to disobedient humanity within itself: that it should in turn not be obeyed even by itself. We have discussed this matter more fully elsewhere, especially in the fourteenth book of *The City of God*.

19. For now, however, I will answer briefly what this man says: that the one who established humanity prohibited the person he had made from the supreme good, wishing him to be like an animal without the knowledge of good and evil.

This knowledge is not the wisdom of a blessed human being but the experience of a miserable one. The tree therefore received its name from the food of which the human being was forbidden to eat, so that obedience might be commended—obedience, which is the greatest virtue and, so to speak, the origin and mother of all virtues in a nature to which free choice of the will was given, yet which must nevertheless live under the authority of a superior.

Still, there have been some who thought that the knowledge of good and evil was a great good [Col. 0614]. Those who seized it against the prohibition were not yet capable of it, and sinned through disobedience.

20. Those who think that the human being ought to have been made so as not to wish to sin should not object to his having been made so that he could refrain from sin if he wished. For if the one who could not sin were better, was the one who could sin and yet did not sin therefore not made well?

Or must one be so utterly foolish as to see that something better ought to have been made and not think that God saw this; or think that he saw it but believe that he did not wish to make it; or believe that he wished to make it but could not?

May God turn this away from the hearts of the devout.

If right reason demonstrates that the rational creature which never abandons God through disobedience is better than the one that did abandon him, let anyone who understands this know that the heavenly beings who never abandon God are not lacking from the order of things, nor was humanity made in such a way that it was compelled by some necessity to abandon God.

And because it abandoned him by its will, nothing was diminished from the most wise arrangements of God, who makes good use of evil things and right use of the perverse, and who declares that from the human race, justly and deservedly condemned, he will transfer to the eternal kingdom a holy and numerous family made not by its merit but by his grace.

21. Since these things are so, God ought not to have hidden the tree which, because of the misery that would follow for humanity if it seized and ate from it contrary to the prohibition and thereby learned from what good it had fallen and into what evil it had fallen, he called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Why would he hide the tree concerning which he gave a command and through which he commended obedience? He was not ignorant that the human being would sin. Rather, in his supreme divinity, he foresaw at the same time what just and good things he would do with the sinner.

He did not establish something harmful, if the human being had not wished to harm himself; rather, he established something beneficial. For if the human being had kept obedience, he would not have done so without a good reward; and if he had paid the penalties of disobedience, this would not have been without a useful example, so that his holy descendants might keep it.

He did not will what he could not accomplish. For what he willed was that the human being should either be obedient or not remain unpunished in disobedience.

Nor did he command fruitlessly what the human being was not going to keep, since the punishment of the one who despised the command taught others to obey.

Nor did a part of God resist God in the human being. For if the human soul were a part of God, it could not be deceived either by itself or by anyone else, could not be compelled by any necessity to do or suffer anything evil, and could not be changed at all for better or worse.

22. The breath of God by which he gave life to the human being [Genesis 2:7] was made by God himself, not from God himself [Note: The Louvain edition reads “not from himself,” which is less satisfactory].

For even a human being’s breath is not a part of the human being; nor does a human being make it from himself, but from the airy breath that he takes in and expels. God, however, could make from nothing what was living and rational, which a human being cannot [Note: Here Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts add “could.” Some codices have “to restore.” The Louvain edition, with certain other codices, has “to make.” The principal manuscripts omit the phrase].

Although some believe that the first human being was not then animated when God breathed into his face and he became a living soul, but that he then received the Holy Spirit—whichever of these interpretations may be shown to be more credible, it would take too long to discuss here—it is nevertheless impermissible to doubt that the soul is not a part of God, nor created or brought forth from his substance and nature, but made from nothing.

## CHAPTER XV

23. Therefore, contrary to what this blasphemer says, the serpent is not found in a better place than God simply because it prevailed in deceiving the human being whom God had made [Genesis 3:1–6].

The human being would in no way have been deceived if, with his heart lifted up in pride, he had not withdrawn from God. For that saying is true, since it is divine: “Before destruction the heart is exalted” [Proverbs 16:18].

Wherever the heart is exalted against God, there it is abandoned by him and enveloped in darkness within itself. What wonder, then, if, while it is in darkness, it does not know what follows? It is not light from itself but is illuminated by the one who is light.

The fact that God is always unconquered is shown even by the human being’s defeat, for he would not have been defeated if he had not withdrawn from the unconquered one.

How, then, is the deceiver victorious over the human being when he himself too has been deceived by himself? Thus both the one who deceived and the one deceived were deceived by withdrawing from the one who cannot be deceived; and both were defeated by withdrawing from the one who cannot be defeated.

Whoever withdraws farther from him is more thoroughly conquered, because he is more inferior in proportion as he is worse. Therefore, the one who appears to prevail by first inflicting evil on another must himself be conquered more greatly by losing the good. It is impossible for his place to be better when his cause is worse.

And although the devil appeared for a time to prevail over the human being after overcoming him, even so he was defeated forever when the human being was restored.

The words “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” [Genesis 3:22] are not the words of God confessing something but rather reproving something. The same is true when the Apostle says, “Forgive me this injury” [2 Corinthians 12:13]: in the presence of an educated speaker, he certainly intends the opposite meaning, not the meaning imposed by an uneducated accuser.

24. Moreover, whoever is displeased that the sinner was forbidden the tree of life—what does he want except to live wickedly with impunity? It was not difficult for God, by any other means, to take life away from the human being whom he did not wish to live. But because rational souls live by wisdom, and their death is folly, the tree of life was placed in paradise to signify this reality: by its fruit it would not even have allowed a human being to die bodily. Thus, the fact that he was separated from it and handed over to death, to be consumed by age—a fate that would by no means have befallen him if he had always enjoyed that same food—signified that, because of sin, his soul had first been excluded from the tree of spiritual life and had thus already died by a certain inner death. [Col. 0615] For it is written concerning wisdom: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Prov. III, 18).

Not understanding this, he says: “How, then, could immortal man have lived forever before the curse, since he had not yet eaten from this tree?” As though someone had told him, or he had read somewhere in that book, that Adam had not yet eaten from the fruit of the tree of life. Rather, he must be understood in this way: because life in the body was continually supplied to him from that tree, so that he would not be consumed by the decay of age [Col. 0616], he was therefore forbidden it, so that, as punishment for sin, the necessity of death would now be imposed upon him.  
[Note: Am. and several manuscripts read *ista* (“this”) here.]

25. “How,” he says, “did he begin to die through God’s curse, when life itself never had its beginning from him?” As though God had wished him dead, as one human being might wish another dead, and as though God’s words did not belong to the sentence of one who punishes rather than to the anger of one who curses. To punish him with bodily death was to separate him from the tree of life, since he had already died spiritually, being separated in soul from the nourishment of wisdom. God therefore wished to signify what had happened to him in his soul by separating him from the tree of life, by which wisdom was signified.

26. “But this tree,” he says, “which bore the fruit of life in paradise—for whose benefit was it?” For whose, except those first human beings, male and female, who had been placed in paradise? After these people had been expelled from paradise on account of their wickedness, the tree remained as a memorial signifying the spiritual tree of life—that is, as we have said, wisdom itself, the unchanging food of blessed souls.

Whether anyone now feeds upon that food, except perhaps Enoch and Elijah, I do not think should be asserted rashly. Yet unless the souls of the blessed were nourished by that tree of life which is in the spiritual paradise, we would not read that, as a gift of piety and of the most faithful confession, the believing soul of the thief who trusted in Christ was granted paradise on that very day: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). To be there with Christ is to be with the tree of life. For he himself is Wisdom, of whom, as I mentioned above, it is written: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her.”

## CHAPTER XVI

27. Must this also be refuted—that which he mocks as though it were a clever argument, at least as it seems to him? [Note: The manuscripts read *quo velut acute* (“which, as though cleverly”).] First, that God did not foresee what happened; second, that he was unable to accomplish what he had earnestly intended; third, that, having been defeated, he resorted to cursing.

How does he know that God did not foresee what happened? Is it because it happened? Indeed, if it had not happened, he could in no way have foreseen that it would happen, because it would not have been going to happen. Or, if he thinks that God did not foresee it because, had he foreseen it, he would have taken precautions to prevent it [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read *praevidisset* (“had foreseen”); corruptly.], he can say the same thing about Christ, who gave a talent to a man who would acquire nothing. He had certainly given it so that his money might be increased, whatever that money signifies. Therefore, because it happened that the man, through his own laziness, acquired nothing, did the one who gave it fail to foresee this? He can also say that Christ did not fulfill what he had earnestly intended concerning this profit. [Note: On the authority of the Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions, *potest* (“can”) is restored; it is omitted in B., whose margin nevertheless notes, “supply *potest*.”] He can likewise make the third accusation: that, having been defeated, he resorted to cursing, since he said, “Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXV, 15–30), just as it was said concerning Adam, so that, separated from the tree of life, he might also be punished by bodily death (Gen. III, 24, 19).

To this eloquent man, the curse of one who is failing seems to be the command of one who is powerful. [Col. 0617] [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read *definientis* (“of one determining”) for *deficientis* (“of one failing”). They also read *impotentis imperium* (“the command of one powerless”) for *potentis imperium* (“the command of one powerful”), the reading found in the better manuscripts and in Am. with several manuscripts.] Let him therefore call Christ powerless, since he could not accomplish what he desired concerning the acquisition of spiritual wealth. Let him call him jealous and malicious, because he begrudged his servant light and salvation and ordered him cast into darkness, where there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

But if he does not say these things about Christ, lest he thereby reveal that he is not a Christian, why does he dare to say of the creator of humanity and the condemner of sin what he does not dare to say of humanity’s redeemer—the very same one, of course, who, if his commands are despised, avenges them with the punishment of eternal death? [Note: The Louvain editors, on the authority of some manuscripts, add *plectetur* (“will be punished”); it is rightly absent from the other editions and manuscripts.] For against whom else, unknowingly, does this man hurl such curses except against Christ himself? For Christ says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote about me” (John V, 46). What did the Father ever do, or do at any time, without the Son?

Therefore, if Holy Scripture commendably teaches not only God’s goodness but also his severity, since God is beneficially loved and feared, and the Apostle mentions both in the same passage, saying, “Behold, therefore, the goodness and severity of God” (Rom. XI, 22), What is this mad and reckless man doing, who, while boasting that he is a Christian, censures in the God of the Prophets what he finds in the God of the Apostles, since the God of both is the same?

28. Concerning the one whom I mentioned—the severity of God that sent the lazy servant into the outer darkness—the faithful reader ought to observe the same in all punishments of people recorded as inflicted on sinners in the prophetic books: God is not called ignorant of the future because he entrusted his money to such a man; nor powerless because he did not himself direct him to act rightly but corrected him; nor jealous and malicious because he sent him, separated from the light, into darkness. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain corrupt the sense by adding *est*, making “the severity of God is [that which] sent ….” Elsewhere the reading is “nor is God said to be ignorant even of future things”; and Am. and Erasmus omit *ipse rexit* (“he himself directed”), though it is present in the manuscripts.]

This applies also to the flood. For the Lord Jesus did not fail to foretell that something of this kind would occur at his coming, when he said: “As it was in the days of Noah: they were eating, drinking, planting, building, marrying, and giving in marriage; the flood came and destroyed them all. So will the coming of the Son of Man be” (Luke XVII, 26, 27).

This applies also to the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart. For the writings of the New Testament likewise say of certain people: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. I, 28).

This applies to the lying spirit whom God, who makes good use even of evil things, sent by a most just judgment to deceive the wicked king, as the prophet Micaiah testifies that this was shown to him in a prophetic vision (III Kings XXII, 19–23). Nor did the Apostle Paul hesitate to say something of this kind, although he knew that he was speaking with complete truth, when he said: “God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie, and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” [Col. 0618] (II Thess. II, 10, 11).

This applies to what was done through Moses, to whom God said: “Take all the leaders of the people and sacrifice them to the Lord before the sun” (Num. XXV, 4)—that is, openly, in the daytime. Or it applies to the way Moses avenged the making of the idol, so that no one spared even his neighbor but slew the wicked with the sword (Exod. XXXII).

Nor did the Lord Jesus fail to say: “But as for those who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and kill them before me” (Luke XIX, 27). Since this plainly signifies the death of souls, it is certainly more horrifying and fearful to the faithful than the death of bodies. Hence the same Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

29. If anyone considers with a faithful mind, as is fitting, the deaths of this kind, by which souls are sent into Gehenna, he will regard as utterly insignificant any enormous slaughter and rivers of the blood of mortal bodies, however and whenever they may die. [Note: The editions read *vili*; the manuscripts read *viliter* (“very cheaply” or “as utterly insignificant”).] By exaggerating these killings and describing them with scholastic vanity in order to blaspheme God, who scourged with such deaths those for whom this kind of terror had been useful, this man strikes horror into mortal senses and thinks that he is accomplishing something, kicking against the goad—so that, while accusing God’s providence on account of the death of the flesh, he may be sent into Gehenna by the death of his heart.

What human being, of either sex, would not prefer to be slain by the sword—even in the manner in which the priest Phinehas slew the fornicators in the very embrace of their wicked pleasure (Num. XXV, 8), setting up a terrifying example of punishment against accursed lusts, which was therefore especially pleasing to God? Who, I ask, would not prefer to be killed by such a kind of death, or finally consumed by fire, or torn apart by the bites of wild beasts through the very private parts, rather than be sent into the Gehenna of eternal fire?

Why, then, does the God of the Christians punish sinners with such deaths, so that after the transitory death of the body [Note: Manuscripts read “after the transitory death of the body.”] there follows in Gehenna punishment without end, unless because the God of both Testaments is one? For the Jews could say against this man’s impiety—however much he exaggerates wars, slaughter, wounds, corpses, and blood—that, in comparison with our God, they have a God who is far gentler, plainly one who punishes much more mildly with transitory deaths of the body than with the everlasting flames of Gehenna.

30. Yet, he says, the God of the Law and the Prophets, who is the one true God, seems to deserve accusation of cruelty because he inflicted the punishment of death, bodily death, for very trivial or even shameful reasons: because David counted the people (II Kings XXIV); and because, as this man says, the infants—the sons of Eli the priest—had tasted something from the pots or cauldrons prepared for God.

In this matter I do not discuss how great and how pernicious a vice of pride crept into so holy a man that he wished to count God’s people, and how he was scourged by the deaths—not eternal, but already imminent according to human condition and soon to pass [Col. 0619]—of those whose multitude had inflated him. Nor do I say that the sons of Eli were not infants [Note: The printed editions read “that the sons of Eli were infants,” omitting *non* (“not”); we restore *non* from the manuscripts], as this man says, not knowing what he is saying. Rather, they were of an age at which they could and ought to have been restrained by punishment deserved for their sacrilegious presumption, by which, in the sacrifices, they placed themselves before the Lord God. God avenged this neglect even by war—not consulting his own interests, but those of the people whom religion and piety would have benefited [Note: The principal manuscripts read “whom the piety of religion would have benefited.”]—a punishment in which the fear of God could be increased among those who would live on through the deaths of men who, although they were growing old, would in any case have died after no very long period of time.

For we read that others also died bodily because of sins not their own but another’s (I Kings II–IV). In such cases the wound is more truly in the grief of the hearts of the living than punishment in the dissolution of the flesh of the dying. Souls departing from bodies have their own causes, whether good or bad; they are not burdened merely because they have been stripped of the body. But no one is punished in the death of souls on behalf of another.

I ask only this: how great does this man think the sin was of the person found at a wedding feast without a wedding garment? If we measure the matter by human judgment, I think it should have been enough for him to feel some embarrassment; at most, the indignation of the inviter might have gone so far as to compel him to change his garment. Yet it was said: “Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII, 11–13).

But he will say: “Not having a wedding garment does not signify a slight fault, since small things are signs of great realities.” So too, then, visible sacrifices, although insignificant in earthly matters, are signs of great and divine realities: in them the priest’s sons placed themselves before God, whose honor is considered in the sacrifices. The wedding guest, however, did not place himself before the bridegroom; he merely failed to be suitably dressed because he did not have a wedding garment.

Nevertheless, among the punishments by which both matters were avenged, the person who observes the difference understands how greatly one surpasses the other, namely, the person who prefers spiritual and eternal things to bodily and temporal things.

31. But why is it necessary to press upon carnal minds a discourse about the mystical meanings of sacrifices and of the wedding garment, when it does not suit them? Let us bring forward something clearer.

Comparing the Gospel with the ancient Law, the Lord testifies that it is not the evil thing people had previously learned, but what he himself taught, that is more perfect: “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you: Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment; whoever says, ‘Racha,’ shall be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V, 21, 22).

What is as small among sins as saying to one’s brother, “Fool”? What is as great among punishments as the fire of Gehenna? If this man had found in the Law or the Prophets that someone had been divinely ordered to be stoned because he had said to his brother, “Fool,” how greatly he would accuse God of cruelty! Who would not prefer—not merely to be stoned, but to be torn apart and consumed alive and conscious, limb by limb [Col. 0620], indeed piece by piece, slowly and minutely—rather than be consigned to the fires of Gehenna? [Note: Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read: “Who, moreover, would not have preferred …”]

Yet let no one say that the God of the Gospel is more cruel than the God of the Law, when he understands that the God of both is one and the same: in the Law he terrifies with bodily punishments, in the Gospel with spiritual punishments; in both places he is faithful, nowhere cruel.

32. What of this? If Christ were to find a tongue foreign to him and blaspheming against him, condemned for impious chatter such as this man’s, would he not be chastised more harshly and bitterly than he indignantly complains that a bodily and temporal punishment was inflicted for sacrilege because someone had tasted beforehand from sacrificial food? There the Lord threatens that he will come and say to those placed on his left: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41, 42).

Are you asking the reason for such a great punishment? “I was hungry,” he says, “and you did not give me food” (ibid., 41, 42). Behold: for temporal food, not taken away but not given, he threatens an eternal and dreadful punishment. And rightly so, if you consult the truth. What is given in alms is very small; but when it is given piously, an eternal reward is thereby acquired. Therefore, precisely because what is given is small, it is not given with great impiety. Hence it is not surprising that the punishment of eternal fire is prepared for such great barrenness, as for unfruitful trees.

But if you consult the human being, so that he may answer you from his own perspective—“Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 11)—he dismisses the guilt and exaggerates the punishment. He does not see the former with his carnal mind, while he shudders at the latter with his mortal flesh.

Such is this man concerning all the human beings who are punished or corrected in the Old Testament with bodily punishments that are far milder than those read of in the Gospel. For what flood can be compared with eternal fire? What slaughter, what wounds, what deaths of bodies can be compared with everlasting torments? The madman swells with such a great noise of his cheeks over the twenty-four thousand who fell, as though countless thousands did not die every day throughout the whole world. But this is transitory death of the body. Who, however, can estimate how many thousands from all nations will stand on the left, destined to be condemned to everlasting fire?

33. Let him go on shouting with open mouth and closed eyes, as though God had confessed his own cruelty, because he says through the prophet: “I will sharpen my sword like lightning; I will intoxicate my arrows with blood, and my sword will devour flesh from the blood of the wounded” (Deut. XXXII, 41, 42).

From these words he accuses God as though God were always hungering for human blood, as though he had said, “I will intoxicate myself with blood,” or, “I will devour flesh from the blood of the wounded.” But however much this empty and deranged man may shudder at this useful threat of God as though it were eager for crime and, as he says, gloried in evil only through sheer cruelty, what force does it have when compared with the words of the one who says: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire [Col. 0621] which has been prepared for the devil and his angels”?

There the arrows will not be intoxicated with blood; rather, the flames will not be satisfied with all their limbs. Nor will the sword devour flesh, removing the sensation of pain from the dead more quickly than it inflicts wounds upon the wounded. Instead, no one will be withdrawn from the torments even by dying, lest the punishment itself also die together with the dying person.

Why does he not say here: “Shall we call this being one to be worshiped, or rather one to be abhorred and fled?” Does he fear to say such things about Christ, lest he fail to escape the punishment of that eternal fire into which Christ prepares to send the impious? In his misery, does he not understand that, by saying these things about the God of the Prophets, he is speaking about the very one whose terrifying severity in the Gospel he fears to offend?

## CHAPTER XVII

34. He also censures the statement that God says the punishments of the impious—signified by the grape of gall and the cluster of bitterness, and by the fury of dragons and asps—are gathered up with him and stored away in his treasuries, to be repaid at the appointed time, when their foot slips (Deut. XXXII, 32–35). He does not understand that “treasuries” here means the hidden dispositions of God, who determines to repay each person according to his works.

Hence the Apostle says: “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each according to his works” (Rom. II, 5, 6). With whom does an impenitent heart store up wrath for itself, except with the one who will judge the living and the dead?

Nor are those ancient books unaware of the desirable treasure of which it is written there that it rests in the mouth of the wise (Prov. XXI, 20, according to the Septuagint). And in Proverbs we read that God treasures up salvation for those who love him (Prov. VIII, 21). The prophet Isaiah says: “In the treasuries is our salvation; there are wisdom, discipline, and piety toward the Lord. These are the treasuries of righteousness” (Isa. XXXIII, 6).  
[Note: The printed editions read, “In the treasuries is [*est*] …” The manuscripts lack the word *est*, which is also absent from the Septuagint. In the same manuscripts, “and piety” is omitted; nevertheless, the Greek has *kaì eusébeia* (“and piety”) corresponding to it.]

But empty talkers and deceivers of the mind, who oppose the sacred Scriptures because they do not wish to understand them, select from those Scriptures the harsh passages that commend God’s severity, and from the Gospel and apostolic writings the mild passages that commend God’s goodness. Among the uninstructed they thus introduce horror from one side and seek favor from the other.

It would be easy for someone equally blasphemous and impious to oppose the New Testament in the way this man opposes the Old: selecting from the Old those passages in which God’s goodness is commended, and, conversely, from the New those in which his severity is commended. He could then shout, enviously and venomously:

“Behold the God who is to be worshiped: merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy; he will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant eternally; he has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our sins from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him” (Ps. CII, 8–13). He says, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 23; XXXIII, 11). [Col. 0622]

Not that one who, on account of greed for profit, ordered even the servant who had not lost the talent he had received to be bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness merely because he had not acquired more, where there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XXV, 14–30); nor that one who removes from his banquet a man without a wedding garment and punishes him with the same punishment after having him bound (ibid. XXII, 11–13); nor that one who responds to those who come to him, knock, and say, “Lord, open to us,” “I do not know you,” merely because they did not bring with them oil to pour into their lamps (ibid. XXV, 1–2); nor that one who sends a person into Gehenna for a single insulting word (ibid. V, 22); nor that one who condemns someone to eternal fire for temporal food not received (ibid. XXV, 41, 42).

If some sacrilegious person, in a deranged state of mind, gathered mild passages from one side and harsh passages from the other, and in this way tried to turn the uninstructed away from Christ as savage and cruel and convert them to the merciful and gentle God of the Prophets, would he not himself appear impure and impious—he who does to the Old Testament what a similarly sacrilegious person could do to the New?

But whoever rightly worships God discovers that the God of both Testaments is certainly one, and loves the goodness of that one God in both, while fearing his severity in both: in the former understanding Christ as promised, in the latter receiving Christ as given.

35. Was it not first read in those ancient books that evil should not be repaid with evil, where it is commanded that, if anyone finds his enemy’s animal wandering, he should lead it back to its owner, and, if he sees it fallen on the road, he should not pass it by but raise it up with him (Exod. XXIII, 4, 5)?

Was it not first written there that which the Apostle quotes: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Prov. XXV, 21; Rom. XII, 20)?

Was it not there first that the man of God says to his God what he certainly knows to be pleasing to him: “Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil” (Ps. VII, 4, 5)?

Was it not there first that the prophet Jeremiah describes the patience of the holy man, offering his cheek to the one who strikes him (Lam. III, 30)?

Was it not there first commanded through another prophet that no one should remember the malice of his brother (Lev. XIX, 18)?

What, then, is this blasphemer doing, gathering these things from the New Testament as though they were contrary to the Old—either because he does not know both Scriptures, or because, in order to deceive the uninstructed, he pretends to know them?

If he were asked whether the one who sends a person into eternal fire for food not received is not repaying evil with evil, he would certainly be confused. He would be reminded that it is incomparably milder to take away a person’s eye for an eye or a tooth for a tooth (Exod. XXI, 24), where the measure of vengeance does not exceed the measure of the injury, than to repay so great a severity for humanity not shown, where the offense is transitory but the punishment has no end. In this way, if he is not obstinate, he will learn that in both Testaments of the one God goodness must be loved and severity feared.

Although in the Old Testament, because of the promise of temporal goods and the threat of temporal evils, temporal Jerusalem gives birth to slaves [Col. 0623], while in the New, where faith obtains love by which the law can be fulfilled not merely through fear of punishment but through love of righteousness, eternal Jerusalem gives birth to free people (Gal. IV, 22–31) [Note: Most manuscripts read *delectatione justitiae* (“through delight in righteousness”).], nevertheless in those earlier times there were spiritual righteous people whom the letter commanding did not kill but whom the Spirit, assisting, gave life (II Cor. III, 6).

Thus faith in the coming Christ certainly dwelt in the Prophets, who foretold that Christ would come. And now there are many carnal people who either create heresies by failing to understand the Scriptures, or, within the Catholic Church itself, are still little ones nourished on milk, or, like enduring chaff, are being prepared for future fires.

Just as the one true God is the creator of both temporal and eternal goods, so he himself is the author of both Testaments, because the New Testament was prefigured in the Old, and the Old was revealed in the New.

36. The merciful gentleness of forgiveness, on account of which it was said that sins must be forgiven a brother not merely seven times but seventy times seven, does not mean that iniquity should go unpunished, or that discipline should become sluggish and asleep—something that would do more harm than attentive and vigilant punishment.

For Christ gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven to the Church in such a way that he not only said, “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven,” by which the Church most clearly repays good, not evil, for evil; he also added, “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven,” because the justice of punishment is good.

That saying, “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector,” is more severe than if he were struck with the sword, consumed by flames, or torn apart by wild beasts [Note: Some manuscripts read *subjiceretur* (“be subjected”).]. For there too he added: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 17–22), so that it might be understood how much more severely punished is the person who seems to have been left unpunished.

Let this man say, if he wishes: “Is this how we have received the Savior’s commands? He orders us, ‘Repay evil to no one with evil; but if someone strikes you on one cheek, offer the other also’; and, ‘Forgive the injuries of your brothers’” (Matt. V, 39–44; XVIII, 35).

Behold: by people who do not repay evil with evil, a person is bound by the keys of the Church more bitterly and unhappily than by any of the gravest and hardest bonds of iron or adamant.

“Far be it,” he says, “from me to say this, since I am a Christian.”

If that were truly so, he would not have said those other things either. For the God of the Prophets, whose writings he blasphemes, is himself the God of the Apostles, whose writings he is afraid to blaspheme.

## CHAPTER XVIII

37. “But David,” he says, “asked God, and was not heard until he had offered a sacrifice, so that mercy might be shown to people who had not sinned” (II Kings XXIV). “Therefore the true God cannot be believed to be one who takes pleasure in sacrifices.”

We have already answered above concerning the punishment of the people who were killed—a death that, since they were destined to die at some point, did them no harm—and concerning the fact that their deaths rightly chastened the heart of the king who was exalting itself.

As for sacrifice, this man understands nothing at all. He is therefore mistaken because, after the one sacrifice arrived whose shadows all those sacrifices were, God’s people no longer offer such sacrifices to God. Those sacrifices did not reject this one but signified it. Just as one thing can be signified by many expressions and in many languages, so one true and unique sacrifice was previously signified by many figures of sacrifices.

You see how long it would be to discuss each of them here. Yet let the ignorant—slow to understand and quick to criticize—know this one thing: the demon would not demand sacrifice for himself unless he knew that sacrifice was owed to the true God.

A false god wants to be honored by those whom he deceives in the way the true God is honored by those for whom he cares. Above all, sacrifice is what is especially owed to God. For other services offered to divinity, human beings have even dared, in the arrogance of pride, to claim for themselves. But very few are mentioned who, although they could command sacrifice by royal power, dared to order it for themselves. Whoever did dare this wished thereby to be regarded as a god.

Who does not know that God has no need of sacrifices? But neither does he need our praises. Yet just as praising God is useful to us, not to him, so offering sacrifice to God is useful to us, not to him.

Because Christ’s blood was poured out for us in the one unique and true sacrifice [Note: The manuscripts read *vere* (“truly”) for *vero* (“true”).], God commanded sacrifices of spotless animals to be offered to him in the earliest times, so that this sacrifice might be prophetically signified by such signs. Just as those animals were without bodily blemish, so it might be hoped that the one who alone was without sin would be offered for us.

Those times were foretold by the prophet in this manner:

“The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; from Zion comes the beauty of his splendor.”

And shortly afterward in the same psalm:

“Hear, my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, and I will testify against you: I am God, your God. I will not accuse you concerning your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are always before me. I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. For all the beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High.”

And again, at the end of the same psalm:

“A sacrifice of praise,” he says, “will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX).

I have already mentioned and demonstrated above that this salvation of God is Christ himself (above, §15). What sacrifice of praise is more sacred than thanksgiving? And from what source are greater thanks owed to God than for his grace through Jesus Christ our Lord? The faithful know all of this in the Church’s sacrifice, of which all the earlier kinds of sacrifices were shadows.

As for these empty-talking critics of the Old Testament, even if they understand little of the other things I have mentioned from this psalm, it should be enough for them, as far as the present question is concerned, that the God of the Prophets, who is also the God of the Apostles, does not eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats. [Col. 0625] The holy people who spoke these words, filled with his Spirit, knew him to be such. [Col. 0625]

Therefore, what David offered so that the people might be spared was a shadow of the future. It signified that through the one sacrifice [Note: All our manuscripts read “through the true sacrifice.”], of which that was a figure [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read *illa figura erant* (“those were a figure”).], the people are spiritually spared for salvation.

For it is Christ Jesus himself who “was handed over for our offenses and rose again for our justification,” as the Apostle says (Rom. IV, 25). For this reason he also says: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V, 7).

## CHAPTER XIX
**38.** But in attempting to prove that holy David had plainly served demons, because by sacrifices he won their favor, this man showed still more clearly how fraudulently he lies in wait for the minds of the uninstructed. For he brought forward the Apostle as a witness, because he had said: “Consider Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What then? Am I saying that an idol is something? But those who sacrifice, sacrifice to demons.” This is not how it is written. Rather, it reads: “Consider Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat from the sacrifices partners in the altar? What then? Am I saying that something sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? But because what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons.”

[Note: The printed editions add only here the word “Gentiles”; the manuscripts consistently omit it here and below.]

It could happen, however, that owing to variation among translations, not in the matters themselves but in the words, some manuscripts have “according to the flesh,” where I said “carnally”; and where I said “those who eat from the sacrifices,” some have “those who eat the sacrificial victims”; and where I said “partners in the altar,” some have “participants in the altar”; and where I wrote, “What then? Am I saying that something sacrificed to idols is anything?” he may have written less, or his manuscript may have contained less, and therefore he wrote only, “because an idol is something.”

What follows, however, is very relevant, because he rendered it differently. The Apostle says: “But because what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.” This man, on the other hand, said: “But those who sacrifice, sacrifice to demons,” as though all who sacrifice sacrifice only to demons. The Apostle did not say, “Those who sacrifice,” but “what they sacrifice,” or, as I rendered it, “they sacrifice”—namely, those who worship idols. What they sacrifice, they sacrifice, or offer, to demons and not to God. Therefore he added: “I do not want you to become partners with demons,” for he was prohibiting them from idolatry.

For this reason he wished to show them that they become partners with demons if they eat sacrificial food offered to idols, just as carnal Israel was a partner of the altar in the temple by eating from the sacrifices. He therefore added “carnally,” or “according to the flesh,” because there is also an Israel spiritually, or according to the spirit, which no longer follows the ancient shadows but the reality signified by those preceding shadows.

For this was the starting point from which he began to say this: “Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols.” Then, continuing, he showed to what sacrifice they ought now to belong, saying: “I speak as to prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless—is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break—is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all share in the one bread” (1 Cor. 10:14–20).

And for this reason he added: “Consider Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat from the sacrifices partners in the altar?”—so that they might understand that they were now partners in the body of Christ in the same way that those people were partners in the altar.

And because, in saying this, he was prohibiting idolatry—and, as I have mentioned, this was the origin of this passage in his discourse—lest they should think that it did not matter if they ate from the sacrifices of idols, on the grounds that an idol is nothing and that such things, as though superfluous, could not harm them, he himself indeed confirmed that an idol is nothing. Yet he was not prohibiting these things because sacrifices are offered to idols, which possess no understanding, but because, he says, what they sacrifice—that is, the worshipers of idols—they sacrifice to demons and not to God. “I do not want you to become partners with demons.”

The truth itself makes this meaning clear, because in the temple served by carnal Israel an idol was certainly not worshiped. For if the sacrifices offered to God in that temple according to the ancient Law were condemned as sacrifices to idols, or as sacrifices offered to demons, the Lord Christ would certainly not have said to the leper whom he had cleansed: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded as a testimony to them” (Matt. 8:4). For he had not yet offered, in place of all those sacrifices, the sacrifice of his own body; nor had he yet raised up the temple of his own body.

Nor, when he drove from that temple those who were selling oxen and doves, would he have said [Note: Most manuscripts have “had said”]: “My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. 21:13).

### CHAPTER XX

**39.** This man also brought forward testimonies from apocryphal writings composed under the names of the apostles Andrew and John. If those writings had truly been theirs, they would have been received by the Church, which has endured from their times through the most certain succession of bishops down to our own age and onward, and which offers to God, in the body of Christ, a sacrifice of praise. The God of gods has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.

This Church is Israel according to the spirit. It is distinguished from that Israel according to the flesh, which served amid the shadows of sacrifices; those sacrifices signified the one unique sacrifice now offered by Israel according to the spirit. To this Israel it was said and foretold: “Hear, O my people, and I will speak to you; O Israel, and I will testify to you” (Ps. 49:2, 7), together with the rest that I have already mentioned above.

For from this house he does not receive calves, nor from its flocks goats. This Israel offers God a sacrifice of praise, not according to the order of Aaron but according to the order of Melchizedek.

This is set forth in the psalm which the Lord Jesus, in the Gospel, testifies was written about himself, when he asks the Jews, who answered that Christ was the son of David—a fact they knew only carnally—how David could call him Lord in the Spirit. At that time he recalled the beginning of this psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1). There it is also said: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Matt. 22:42–45; Ps. 109:4).

Those who read know what Melchizedek brought forth when he blessed Abraham (Gen. 14:18–19); and if they are already participants in that offering, they see such a sacrifice now being offered to God throughout the whole world.

God’s oath is a rebuke of the unbelieving. And the statement that God will not repent signifies that this priesthood will not be changed. The priesthood according to the order of Aaron, however, was changed.

Therefore another prophet says to the one who is Israel according to the flesh: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty” (Mal. 1:10–11).

There is what belongs to the order of Melchizedek. For the incense—which in Greek is θυμίαμα (*thymiama*)—as John explains in the Apocalypse, is the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8).

That God, as it is sung in the psalm, who summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting, would say to this earth—that is, to this people spread from the rising of the sun to its setting—“I will not receive calves from your house; offer a sacrifice of praise to God” (Ps. 49:2, 9, 14). He himself, through this prophet, already proclaiming as accomplished what was most certainly going to happen, says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations.”

**40.** For God does not repent as a human being does, but as God does—just as he does not become angry as a human being does, nor show mercy as a human being does, nor feel jealousy as a human being does, but does all things as God.

God’s repentance is not subsequent to an error. God’s anger does not contain the heat of a disturbed mind. God’s mercy does not contain the sorrowful heart of one who suffers with the wretched, from which mercy received its name in Latin. God’s jealousy does not contain the resentment of the mind.

Rather, God’s repentance is the unforeseen change, for human beings, in things established under his power. God’s anger is the punishment of sin. God’s mercy is the goodness that comes to help [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have “the goodness of one who helps.”]. God’s jealousy is the providence by which he does not allow those subject to him to love with impunity what he forbids.

Therefore let this man, who has attacked God’s repentance with such loquacity, first learn that it is scarcely possible to find anything that can worthily be said about God. We say many things, almost everything, about him from the necessity of speech, measuring them more by human beings and from human beings; but how they ought to be understood of him is scarcely understood except by a few spiritual people.

For this reason divine Scripture, speaking most providently about the ineffable God, also descends to certain expressions that, when spoken of God, already seem absurd and unworthy even to human beings who are carnal. It does this so that, when people fear that such expressions should be understood as they ordinarily are among human beings, and investigate how they may rightly be understood of God, they may also learn that the expressions which in those same Scriptures seemed worthy of God to human understanding must not be understood or believed according to human customs.

It is quickly perceived that repentance, as it occurs among human beings, cannot belong to God. But it is not as quickly perceived that mercy, as human beings show mercy, cannot belong to God either. From the matter, therefore, which he admits must be investigated, a person learns to investigate this also—something he had thought sufficient already.

Thus, when God repents, he is not changed but changes; when he becomes angry, he is not moved but punishes; when he shows mercy, he does not suffer but liberates; and when he is jealous, he is not tormented but torments.

**41.** Are such expressions absent from the books of the New Testament—expressions which, if understood as they ordinarily are among human beings, would in no way befit divinity and would cause grave offense?

When the evangelist says with complete truth about Christ that he did not need anyone to testify to him about human beings, “for he himself knew what was in a human being” (John 2:25), why does Christ himself say to certain people, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12)?

Moreover, since he foreknew and chose his saints before the foundation of the world, what does the Apostle mean by saying, “But now that you have come to know God—or rather, to be known by God” (Gal. 4:9), as though he had only now come to know those whom previously he did not know?

And when he says, “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19), as though the Spirit could be extinguished, who could endure it [Note: The ancient manuscripts have “who could rescue it?” Perhaps the intended reading is “who could preserve it?”] unless he understands these expressions wisely?

Is it not written in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever is disobedient to the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36)? Let this blasphemer bring a charge against this expression also and say: “What sort of being is one who becomes angry, when it is written, ‘The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God’” (James 1:20)?

Let him likewise bring a charge against the Apostle, who says: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” (Rom. 3:5).

Furthermore, if someone were to say, “Christ will be put to shame,” and to say this of the time when he will judge the living and the dead, what Christian would listen to him patiently? Yet in the Gospel Christ says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels” [Note: In B., “in glory.” “In glory” is better, with Erasmus and the Vulgate; the Greek reading, *en tē doxē*, supports it. M.] (Mark 8:38).

Why, then, do we pray, “May your name be sanctified” (Matt. 6:9), if it is always holy—unless what is written about certain people is also true, namely, that “they profaned the name of the Lord their God” (Ezek. 43:8)?

And why was it said to the Lord, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42), if he forgets nothing—unless it is said to him not foolishly but intelligently: “Will you forget our poverty and our tribulation?” (Ps. 43:24)?

Therefore he knowingly does not know; what he has always known, he knows at a certain time; when he is extinguished by those who deny him, he remains inextinguishable; he becomes angry calmly; he cannot be put to shame even when he is put to shame; his name cannot be profaned even when it is profaned; he cannot forget even when he is said to forget; and he remembers even when he is reminded.

Thus he is ineffable. For these things are said of him, of whom nothing can be said by human beings—or about whom nothing can be said sufficiently worthily and appropriately by human beings.

Since this is so, what religious person would not blow this man away like dust, which the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:4)? Inflated, elated, and rushing into the eyes of the weak, disturbing them, he thinks that he is saying something by attacking words in the Old Testament that he does not understand, while failing to consider the things in the New Testament that he does understand.

**42.** This discussion of God’s repentance arose when, in recalling the prophecy about Christ in which it is said, “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” we were commending the saving sacrifice in which sacred blood was poured out for us—whose shadows were the sacrifices commanded to be offered from unblemished animals.

Thus, regarding God’s repentance, lest he think it should be understood in such a way that, because of what he does not understand, he might rage madly in the barking of blasphemies, this man had something nearby by which he could have been warned.

For he himself recalled that God said: “I repent that I have anointed Saul as king” [Note: The manuscripts have “into the kingdom.”]

This is written as having been said to holy Samuel, through whom God rebuked Saul because he had spared a man whom God had commanded to be killed, displaying what seemed to be mercy while disregarding obedience—as though he knew better what ought to be done with a human being than the one who made the human being.

Here we learn something supremely salutary: that the divine command must always prevail in us over human affection.

Yet that same Samuel to whom God had said, “I repent that I have anointed Saul as king,” clearly says that God does not repent. For it is written:

“And the word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying, ‘I repent that I have made Saul king, because he has turned away from me and has not kept my words.’”

And shortly afterward Samuel himself said to Saul:

“The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today, and he will give it to your neighbor, who is better than you; and Israel will be divided into two. And he will not turn back, nor will he repent, because he is not like a human being, that he should repent” (1 Sam. 15:11, 28–29).

Behold the one who knew how to understand God as showing mercy without misery [Note: The manuscripts have “who knew”; the printed editions have “without mercy.”], becoming angry without anger, being jealous without jealousy, forgetting without forgetfulness, not knowing without ignorance, and repenting without repentance.

This man does not understand how to speak according to God’s word, does not consider his Scriptures, and does not attend to their expressions; he has become a mute barker, a blind reader, and a deaf hearer.

**43.** “Forgetful,” he says, “and with a dead memory, God placed the bow in the clouds, which is called the rainbow, so that he might be reminded not again to destroy the human race by a flood” (Gen. 9:12–17)—as though he had no knowledge at all of what he was doing, and therefore rightly needed a constant reminder.

But if, in matters that are more obvious, this man, who possesses not a memory but a dead soul and does not know what he is saying, brings charges, how much more does he grow dark [Note: The manuscripts have “is enveloped in darkness.” Am. has “grows dark.”] among the clouds and is compelled to rave?

To answer him briefly, I say that God wished to be reminded, although he had not forgotten, just as Christ wished to be informed where Lazarus had been laid, although he was not ignorant.

I do not wish to say whom that bow signifies [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “what that bow signifies.”]—shining from the clouds with splendor and with rays of light by which the dewy darkness is illuminated, responding in a way with a pleasing confession; nor how God does not destroy the world by a spiritual flood while he remembers those whose illuminated clouds are a figure—for their names are written in heaven, so that the Father who is in heaven may remember them, since they know that they shine not from themselves but from the Sun of righteousness, just as those clouds shine from the visible sun.

But he must be challenged, on the basis of what I have mentioned, as to how he understands the Lord saying of Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:34), and having the place shown to him as though he did not know it.

For unless we admit that he signified something by this inquiry, in which he appeared not to know, how do we proclaim that Christ not only knew the present but also foreknew the future? Especially since this man, with remarkable blindness, rushed into the position of saying, “No one asks a question except one who is ignorant.”

Could he not consider how often Christ asked questions? Is one who says, “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” (Matt. 22:42) not asking a question? What testimony could be clearer than this?

And if he is excessively obstinate, will he deny that Christ asked a question even where Christ himself declares that he is asking, saying: “I will ask you one question; if you tell me, I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?” (Matt. 21:24–25)?

Where now will this most loquacious and desperate disputant against God hide? Where is what he said: “No one asks a question except one who is ignorant”? Behold, Christ is not ignorant, and yet he asks a question.

With these eyes he censures the God of the Prophets—eyes that do not see Christ. Yet in such questions Christ is most plainly a teacher.

But when he says, “Where have you laid him?” and, “Who touched me?” (Luke 8:45), and if anything of this kind is recorded as having been said, he appears to wish to be taught what he does not know, and yet he knows.

Thus, in those books too, God is reminded as though he had forgotten, but far be it from us to suppose that he ever forgets anything.

**44.** And what of the very statement the Lord made to his disciples, “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20)? Does it not seem as though God were reminded by letters in heaven, as it were by that bow shining from the clouds?

Unless these things are received piously, until faith obtains the ability to understand them, are they not laughed at as fables? And who laughs at them except the foolish—and, by the very fact that they think themselves wise, increasingly deranged?

Who can consider how those who follow the Lord are written in heaven for the memory of God, while those who abandon the Lord are written on the earth—of whom the prophet Jeremiah says: “All who abandon you shall be put to shame; those who depart [Note: The printed editions add “from you,” which is absent from the manuscripts and from the Septuagint] shall be written upon the earth” (Jer. 17:13)?

Jesus is rightly understood to have signified these people when the Jews, defeated and put to shame, after hearing, “Let the one who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her,” withdrew one after another. Then, to show to what number they belonged, he was writing with his finger on the earth (John 8:7–9).

### CHAPTER XXI

**45.** “If,” he says, “we think that the people of the flood deserved the sentence they received because of their manner of life, and that righteous Noah was preserved for the restoration of a better creation, why do worse people arise afterward, and why does the human race even now continue to be born into the same acts of filthy living?”

He says this as though he had lived with those who perished in the flood and knew from that experience that worse people now arise.

But whether the human race after the flood is engaged in a worse, the same, or a better way of life, I think judgment must be left to God [Note: The printed editions have, “judgment must be left to God’s judgment.” The manuscripts’ reading, “judgment must be left to God,” is more harmonious], who knows how to repay each person according to his merits—not to this rabid dog barking against its master, or to this foolish ass kicking against the goad.

The Apostle cries out: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33–34). Yet this man dares to be an adversary of the one who has no counselor.

What difference does it make, since all must die, as far as bodily death is concerned, whether they die one by one or all together at once? Except that when individuals die, everyone experiences death and everyone suffers grief over the dead; but when one destruction carries everyone away together, at least no one is left to mourn.

Indeed, God’s purpose in that flood was deeper than the heart of unbelievers either knows or comprehends.

But I do not wish this man to listen to me; let him listen instead to the Apostle Peter, who says: “In the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, eight souls were saved through water; and this,” he says, “prefigures baptism, which now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but an appeal to God for a good conscience through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 3:20–21).

Behold, the sacrament of the flood has been explained. The words “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” were added so that we might understand the eighth day, which was signified by the number of people in the ark. For on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath—the Lord rose again.

Thus, if someone understands the events whose occurrence is recounted, they were also prophecies.

But this man, stationed outside the ark—that is, outside the Church—was submerged in the flood, not cleansed.

### CHAPTER XXII

**46.** He also brings a charge against and blasphemes the testimony of the prophet Isaiah, because it says: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me”; and shortly afterward calls those same people “a wicked seed” (Isa. 1:2–4). He does this as though presenting God as the begetter of evil people, whose sons are a wicked seed.

He does not understand that they are called a wicked seed because, by sinning, they became degenerate from the grace of God by which they had been made his sons, becoming the sons of those whom they chose to imitate.

Therefore they are told elsewhere: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16:3)—because they followed the impiety and wickedness of those nations, although they did not derive their physical origin from them.

Let him solve the Gospel’s problem, where the Lord says: “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13).

Let him explain how God can be the good Father of evil people. The Truth said both things. Were those to whom he said, “Although you are evil,” not evil? Did they not have the good God as their Father, to whom he said, “How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him”?

Furthermore, if they were called evil because of their sins—for in this weakness of mortality there is no human life, even among the righteous, without sin—how much more appropriately would that be called a wicked seed which was born from an impious will and sprouted into execrable conduct?

**47.** “But,” he says, “the Lord Christ called this God a bad tree producing bad fruits.”

Rather, this very blasphemous speech of one who thinks such things, like the fruit of a bad tree, is itself bad fruit.

For the Lord plainly testifies that when he called a human being a bad tree whose bad fruits were bad works, and a good human being a good tree whose good fruits were good works (Matt. 7:15–20), he meant that human wills themselves—the bad will of a bad person and the good will of a good person—are different trees bearing different fruits. He says: “The good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure” (Matt. 12:35).

How could he say, “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12:33), unless a person could turn now in one direction and now in another by a changed will?

### CHAPTER XXIII

**48.** “But,” he says, “God himself confesses through the same prophet and says, ‘I am God, making good things and creating evil things’” (Isa. 45:7).

Exactly so. For he is the God of whom the Apostle says: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God” (Rom. 11:22).

His severity is evil for those deserving condemnation, because it brings upon them the evil of condemnation. Yet because it is just, it is found to be good in another sense; for everything just is good.

How cleverly this man thinks he examines and distinguishes the words, without knowing what he is saying! For he has deliberately presented the testimony in this form—not “making good things and evil things,” nor “creating good things and evil things,” nor “creating good things and making evil things,” but “making good things and creating evil things”—and wishes to turn this into a charge.

He tries to show that what is made is made externally, while what is created exists within the creator himself and proceeds from him, so that the God of the Prophets may appear to have been at some time a maker of good external to himself, but a creator of evil as an evil nature producing from itself what it created.

If we consider these words according to ordinary human speech, both “made” and “created” are said not only of sons whom each person begets from himself, but also of magistrates and cities, and of anything else that does not come out of the one who gives birth but is made externally.

But if we examine how the holy Scriptures, against which this man lies in wait, are accustomed to speak, then either “to make” is the same as “to create,” although it is distinguished from “to beget”; and the expression “making good things and creating evil things” could have been used merely to vary the verb, without implying any difference among things, just as one could say “creating good things and making evil things.”

Or, if the prophetic Spirit intended there to be some distinction here, the words would much more suitably be understood in this way: that “to make” refers to what would not exist at all if it were not made; while “to create” refers to establishing or arranging something out of what already existed, just as we said that magistrates and cities are created.

For magistrates are appointed from among people who already existed, when they are created as magistrates; and the wood and stones from which cities are constructed already existed, but had not yet arrived, through a certain order and arrangement, at the form of things that we see in cities. When this occurs, cities are said to be created.

What the Greeks call κτίζειν (*ktizein*), our writers sometimes translate as “to create,” sometimes as “to establish,” and sometimes as “to found”; and in those writings it very often means the same as “to make.”

For we read both, “God made the human being in the image of God,” and, “God created the human being incorruptible” (Wis. 2:23). And if the words are sometimes used with some distinction, the difference may more properly be the one I have stated: “to make” is to bring into existence what did not exist at all; “to create” is to establish something from what already existed by arranging it.

For this reason God is said in this passage to be “creating evil things”: by the arrangement of his severity he turns into evil for sinners things that were made good by the generosity of his goodness.

Hence the Apostle Paul says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” [Note: Lov. has “We are the good fragrance of God in every place.” “Of God” is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts], “both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, a fragrance of life leading to life; to others, a fragrance of death leading to death.” But since he immediately adds, “And who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Cor. 2:15–16), are we not in a way intrusive when we thrust these matters upon carnal people who are not earnest but contentious, utterly incapable of grasping them—and who, if only they would cease, might at least cease attacking them?

**49.** He perhaps does not know how great a conflict was stirred up against the Arians, lest they should say that the only-begotten Son was a creature, since they thought “created” meant the same as “begotten.”

But so that his false and twisted rule may be struck down and broken by the very prophetic and Gospel testimony he himself produced, God speaks through the prophet as follows: “I create light and make darkness; I make peace and create evil” (Isa. 45:7).

He did not quote this either in full or as it is written there. It is easy enough to overlook that he substituted “good things” for “peace,” since peace is good.

But this must not be passed over: by deceit he was able to omit the first part of the sentence, so that he would not say “creating light.” For although light is certainly good—something he himself admits—he did not wish to confess that it was created by the one whom he wishes to make a creator of nothing except evil.

We must therefore understand “create” and “make” as used without distinction. His rule of distinction, however, is broken, because the God of the Prophets—whom he blames for a word he does not understand—is there read as the creator of good things, which he denies.

Likewise, consider the Gospel. He set before us, as though it strongly favored his own side, what the Lord says: “A good tree makes good fruits, and a bad tree makes bad fruits” (Matt. 7:17).
