Why, then, did he not say “creates” rather than “makes,” according to this man’s theory? If his distinction is true, by which he separates the maker from the creator, saying that what is made is alien to the maker because it comes from outside [Note: The manuscripts have “because it happens from outside”; below they have “would happen externally”], while what is born belongs to the one who begets, let him see that his rule has been broken and restrain his tongue.

For he thinks that God is the begetter of evil because it is said, “creating evil,” supposing—as the Arians supposed—that in those Scriptures it makes no difference whether something is said to be begotten or created.

But since the Lord did not say that the good tree “creates” good fruits and the bad tree “creates” bad fruits, but that it “makes” them, let him see that his rule is broken.

What could be more foolish than to say that the God of the Prophets is a bad tree, and to want this understood in what the Lord says, “A bad tree makes bad fruits,” and then to say, “He does not make evil things but creates them,” because if he made them they would be alien to him and would come to him from outside; whereas when he creates them, he himself produces them from himself, as though from the root?

Therefore the Lord did not say of this God, “A bad tree makes bad fruits,” because this God creates evil things rather than making them.

Behold the man who dares to accuse the Prophets, while the witnesses he himself has produced from the Gospel contradict him.

### CHAPTER XXIV

**50.** He attacks certain words from the book of Deuteronomy, recoiling from them as though they were impure, although he himself is impure—as though God ought to be ashamed to inflict or foretell shameful torments upon the impious, and ought not to threaten them in these words:

“The woman among you who is tender and exceedingly delicate, whose foot has not learned by experience to walk upon the ground because of her tenderness and delicacy, will begrudge her husband, her son, her daughter, and her afterbirth; and she will eat what comes out between her thighs” (Deut. 28:56–57).

Indeed, the more horrifying it is, the more terrifying it is.

For this was not said by the prophet as an admonition but as a threat—not so that human beings would do these things, but so that they would not do what a perverse mind practices and would not reach what the human mind abhors.

Who could express worthily how much more execrable is the foulness of the mind that recoils from the punishments of its deeds but does not avoid the deeds that deserve punishment?

Let the undefiled and undefilable Holy Spirit plainly say what an unclean soul refuses to hear but refuses to be without. For the soul recoils from the uncleanness of the flesh when its bodily senses are offended, but loves its own uncleanness when the senses of the heart have been extinguished.

Let the Spirit of God say these things, and through the horror of suffering such evils let him instill fear of doing evil.

## 51

For that same Spirit, speaking also through the Apostle, was not ashamed to offend impious minds while wishing to instruct the godly. After mentioning the impiety of certain people, who worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, he added and said: “For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions. Their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature; and likewise the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned with desire for one another, males committing indecency with males and receiving in themselves the due recompense for their error” [Romans 1:26–27].

If some enemy of the Apostle wished to derive from these words the sort of things that this blasphemer derives from certain passages of the Old Books, would he not have abundant material over which to rave loquaciously? And the more eloquent the statements seemed to him, the more detestable curses would he hurl [Note: [Col. 0635] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “would seem to speak more eloquently.”]—especially since it is said: “receiving in themselves the due recompense for their error.” For the Apostle was not afraid to say that it was due that those who served the creature rather than the Creator should receive the recompense for their error, not unwillingly by suffering these shameful things, but willingly by committing them. This was by the judgment, not of some utterly impure human being whom such things would delight, but of the most just God, who handed them over to dishonorable passions, so that crimes might be punished by crimes and the punishments of sinners might not be torments but increases of vice.

But when a wise person hears this, he fears more greatly that very wrath of God in this life, by which a person does not suffer what he sharply dreads but does what he shamefully desires; and he disregards the deranged words of the one who dislikes such judgments, because in him he recognizes Pharaoh’s punishment—that is, a hardened heart [Note: [Col. 0635] The printed editions read, “because he recognizes it as proceeding from him.”].

For if God handed certain people who did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge over to a depraved mind, so that they might do what is improper (Romans 1:28), what wonder if God also handed this man, who blasphemes the divine utterances, over to a depraved mind, so that he might say what is improper?

“For there must also be heresies,” says the Apostle, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19). Thus the vessels of wrath are appointed in fitting places and times, so that even through them God may make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, which, by his grace and not by their merits, are made for honor from the same mass of condemnation (Romans 9:22–23). For he grants that what benefits us is not only what truth teaches but also what vanity clamors, so that when the most restless vanity is answered, the most sincere truth may be heeded.

## 52

Vanity brings an accusation concerning an obscene curse [Note: [Col. 0635] Some manuscripts read, “Vanity accuses God.”]. But merciful truth shows that it is not obscene to point out, by naming certain obscene things, what obscenity must be avoided; and senseless vanity is defeated.

For the Apostle Paul himself can be criticized by verbose impious people on account of an obscene curse, when he says: “Would that those who are troubling you would also cut themselves off!” (Galatians 5:12). Although to those who understand it rightly this appears rather as a blessing—that they might become eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven—garrulous blindness can nevertheless criticize even this in the Apostle, arguing that he ought not to have expressed an honorable matter by an obscene word.

They can also criticize the Lord himself, who, commending the gift of that same continence, says: “There are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12).

These little scribblers read such things—for they ought to be called little scribblers rather than literate men, since by reading literate men they have learned to understand nothing. They read something of this sort in Cicero, from which they imagine that they can learnedly censure Christ’s words, being ruined rather than learned. For when Cicero was teaching that obscenity should be avoided in metaphorical expressions, he said: “I do not want it said that the republic was castrated by the death of Africanus” (Cicero, *On the Orator*, book 3).

But if he did not avoid the very word that he wished to be avoided, in order to show that it should be avoided, and if he was compelled to say what he did not want said, how much more is a matter that is rightly signified by that same word expressed by its proper word, so that it can be understood by the hearer?

And to return to what this man criticizes in Deuteronomy: if Cicero, the most eloquent of men and the most watchful examiner and measurer of words, said what he did not want said in order to prevent it from being said, how much more did God, who seeks the beauty and purity of conduct rather than of words, speak of something shameful not shamefully but threateningly, so that it might be dreaded and the other thing not committed [Note: [Col. 0636] The Old Latin translation and the manuscripts read, “so that another thing might not be committed.”]—the thing that would lead to what is horrifying to hear?

And yet, when it is read, unbelief closes its ears, turns its face away, hardens its expression, brandishes its tongue, and hurls blasphemies. See whether these people do not belong to the class of those who, when Christ was speaking about the sacrament of his body and blood, said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John 6:60). Except that those people are more excusable who could not bear the divine words they did not understand—not as a curse, but as a blessing.

For it is not surprising that a curse is dreaded when heard; nor should it be required that what is said for the purpose of making the hearer fear should be expressed in words that do not inspire dread. The Lord, however, was saying things that he commanded to be loved, not feared, and yet what unbelief can endure? “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink; unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:55, 53).

If, therefore, the Wisdom of God, nourishing the believing soul with words appropriate to the sacrament, did not concern itself with the nausea of foolishness, how much more did that same Wisdom, where the occasion and time called for fear rather than love, wishing to bring a salutary terror, not concern itself with the error of a fool, even though it foresaw his dread?

Who among these people knows how to dread the spiritual foulness of the soul, when, as though driven by a certain hunger and destitution of their own, they are compelled to eat what proceeds from their carnal thoughts as though from their thighs? The result of that curse which this man criticizes as obscene is rare [Note: [Col. 0636] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice editions read, “the result is equal.” M.]; for famine is scarcely ever so great that it compels anyone to those unspeakable acts. But everything is everywhere full of this other hunger, by which the souls of the wretched, deprived of truth, eat as truth what their carnal senses produce—so much the more unhappily because it causes greater harm and is dreaded less.

## 53

But I think that I ought to answer one book of the one you sent me with not merely one of ours, so that it may not become too lengthy. Therefore let us make this the end of the present book, so that another may begin from the matters that remain to be examined. Somehow, the reader’s attention is refreshed by the end of a book just as a traveler’s labor is refreshed by an inn.

# BOOK TWO

## In Which the Passages of the New Testament That the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets Collected as Though Contrary to Them Are Examined

[Col. 0637]

# CHAPTER ONE

### 1

The matters must now be examined that this man imagines can support him from the books of the New Testament against the prophetic Scriptures, as though Christ’s Apostles had condemned them by their own judgment.

He thinks, therefore, that the Apostle called the divine utterances of the Law and the Prophets “profane and old-womanish fables and endless genealogies,” because he said: “Avoid profane and old-womanish fables” (1 Timothy 4:7), and elsewhere: “Do not attend to Jewish fables and endless genealogies, which provide questions rather than edification” (1 Timothy 1:4). Who, except a very blind heretic, could go so far astray?

For why did the Apostle himself not do this, if he judged these to be old-womanish fables? Why does he say to the Galatians: “Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law, have you not read the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman; these things are allegorical, for these are the two Testaments” (Galatians 4:21–24)?

And to the Corinthians: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink—for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them [Note: [Col. 0637] Lovaniensis reads, “but they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them.” The manuscripts, omitting “them,” have, “for they drank,” in agreement with the Greek text]; and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:1–4)?

### 2

He does not know that, besides the canonical and prophetic Scriptures, the Jews have certain traditions of their own, which they do not possess in writing but retain by memory, passing them verbally from one to another; these they call *deuterosis* (“second tradition”). There they even dare to say and believe that God created two women for the first man. From these they weave genealogies truly “endless,” as the Apostle says, producing utterly fruitless questions.

But if this man had never happened to hear such things, should he therefore have become so deaf even against the Gospel that he failed to notice the words of the Lord Christ, by which he reproved the Jews for teaching their children impiety concerning the failure to honor their parents?

There he also recalled, in confirmation, God’s command written in the Law. He reproved them for no other reason than that they were rejecting God’s command in order to establish their own traditions.

For when the Pharisees and scribes had asked, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with common hands?” he answered them: “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.’ For abandoning the commandment of God, you hold to the tradition of men—washings of pitchers and cups—and you do many other things like these.”

And he said to them: “You make God’s commandment completely void in order to establish your tradition. For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall die the death.’ But you say, ‘If a man says to his father or mother, Corban’—which means ‘gift’—‘whatever from me might benefit you,’ you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, nullifying the word of God through [Note: [Col. 0638] The printed editions read, “on account of.” The manuscripts read, “through.”] your tradition, which you have handed down; and you do many other things of this kind” (Mark 7:1–13).

Here Christ clearly shows both that the Law of God which this profane man blasphemes is truly God’s Law and that the Jews possess traditions foreign to the prophetic and canonical Books. A Catholic reader, rather than a heretic, understands that the Apostle called these traditions profane and old-womanish fables and interminable genealogies.

Moreover, if I wished to gather all the testimonies by which I could show how both the Lord himself and his Apostles used the Law and the Prophets—which this man considers old-womanish fables—when would I be finished? Or to whom would what we have said not be sufficient?

# CHAPTER TWO

### 3

This man is not so blind and deaf to the light and voice of the Lord and of the Apostles that he does not know how, in the books belonging to the New Testament, the authority of the Law and the Prophets is confirmed and commended by Christ and the Apostles.

Accordingly, he imagines that he has devised a way to evade the mass of testimonies drawn from the Old Books and placed in the evangelical and apostolic writings—testimonies by which, whether he wishes it or not, his stiff-necked tongue is crushed.

For he says that the Apostle spoke according to the varieties of human understanding in five persons. “When he was introducing the things of God,” he says, “to a people still uneducated, he ought not to begin with the more perfect, nor, excluding the custom of antiquity from them, begin with difficult matters, lest perfect doctrine should disturb those who were still new to the faith.”

Then, wishing as it were to prove what he had said, he recalls the same Apostle saying: “Although I am free from all, I made myself subject to all, so that I might win more” [Note: [Col. 0638] The printed editions read, “I made myself a servant.” “Servant” is absent from the manuscripts]. “I became to the Jews as a Jew, so that I might win the Jews; to those under the Law, as one under the Law—although I myself am not under the Law—so that I might win those under the Law; to those without the Law, as one without the Law—although I am not without the Law of God but am within the Law of Christ—so that I might win those without the Law; I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak. I became all things to all, so that I might win all” (1 Corinthians 9:19–22).

He wants four persons to be understood in whom he thinks the Apostle spoke: one of the Jews, another of those under the Law, a third of those without the Law, and a fourth of the weak. A fifth is required, since he had promised five. To add this fifth, he says: “In another passage he already said above, ‘We speak wisdom among the perfect’” (1 Corinthians 2:6), so that the person of the perfect may appear to be the fifth.

He contrived all this for the purpose of saying that, whenever something is produced from an apostolic Letter in which the Law and the Prophets bear witness to the Gospel, the Apostle was speaking not to the wise and perfect but to Jews as a Jew, or to those under the Law as though he himself were under the Law—and thus that he was slyly and falsely pretending to build up the imperfect by what he would destroy among the perfect, not by lying but by speaking the truth.

Some Fabricius, whom he boasts of having found in Rome as a teacher of truth, evidently constructed this machinery of error for him. Who would not recoil from this monstrosity—not merely a Christian understanding, but any human understanding at all?

### 4

First, one must consider how fraudulent and mendacious he declares himself to be when he thinks and praises the Apostle as a liar. What the Apostle said not through the trickery of one deceiving but through the affection of one who shares another’s weakness—for he came to the various illnesses of souls with as merciful a heart as he would have wished others to bring to him if he himself suffered from a similar error or weakness—this man turns into a detestable deception.

Next I ask: how did the Apostle speak to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, and Thessalonians? In which of those five persons did he classify them? Beyond doubt, they were Gentiles in uncircumcision, not Israelites in circumcision.

For he testifies that the ministry had been assigned to him among them when he says that Peter, James, and John gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that he and Barnabas should go to the Gentiles, while the others should go to the circumcision (Galatians 2:9). Elsewhere he says most explicitly: “As long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles” (Romans 11:13), and in many other passages he testifies that he is the teacher of the Gentiles by a special commission.

Since there were so many Gentiles without the Law to whom he preached the Gospel, why did he need to introduce the Law and the Prophets to them as witnesses of Christ and impose upon the ignorant, as this plague supposes, the bond of error from which he ought rather to have been glad that they were free?

Why did he begin his letter to the Romans in this way? “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised through his Prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:1–3).

Why did he not instead assume their persona? Why did he make himself as one under the Law to those who had been without the Law?

Why does he say to them: “For I speak to you Gentiles: inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will glorify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some of them. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? If the first-fruit is holy, so is the whole lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches”?

He says this about the Israelites, concerning whom he had already said: “What advantage, then, has the Jew, or what benefit is there from circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them. What if some did not believe? Surely their unbelief will not nullify the faithfulness of God?” (Romans 3:1–3) [Note: [Col. 0640] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “Did their unbelief nullify it?”].

Then the passage I had begun to recall continues:

“But if some of the branches were broken off, while you, though a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root you. You will say, then, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ They were broken off because of unbelief [Note: [Col. 0640] The printed editions read, “broken off in unbelief.” The particle “in” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle]. But you stand by faith; do not be proud, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you [Note: [Col. 0640] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “lest perhaps he spare you not.”].

“See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off, and they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut from a wild olive tree by nature and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will they, who are natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree?

“For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation: blindness has occurred in part to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved [Note: [Col. 0640] Many manuscripts read, “will be saved.” Some others read, “may be saved.”], as it is written: ‘The one who comes from Zion will deliver and turn away impiety from Jacob; and this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins’” (Romans 11:13–27).

It would take too long to go through everything, or to gather into one view what is scattered everywhere throughout the apostolic Scriptures. Why did he need to say these things to the Gentiles? Why did he not rather become to them as one without the Law, just as they were without the Law?

Why did he not rather praise their gods and proclaim their sacrifices, if both the Scripture received by the people of Israel and the sacred rites of the Gentiles belonged to demons, as this man says?

What is more, the wretched man dares to say that the God of Israel is not only a demon but worse than the other demons [Note: [Col. 0640] The older codices read, “more cruel.”]. Why, then, did the Apostle, who became all things to all—not through compassionate mercy, as truth shows, but through deceptive cunning, as this man foolishly imagines—not pretend to be a servant of those demons whom the Romans worshiped, whom this man considers more gentle, so that he might become like them and thus win them?

### 5

Does he not likewise say to the Ephesians:

“Therefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision, performed in the flesh by hand; that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the community of Israel and strangers to the covenants and the promise, having no hope and being without God in this world. But now, in Christ Jesus, you who once were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ.

“For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of the barrier, the hostility, in his flesh, nullifying the Law of commandments in decrees [Note: [Col. 0640] The printed editions read, “nullifying the Law of commandments by decrees,” omitting the particle “in,” which all the manuscripts here preserve in agreement with the Greek text], so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself. And coming, he preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

“Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:11–20).

Let this blasphemer say how he can call the Israelites “near,” when they were serving the worse demon—as he blasphemously claims—and call the Gentiles “far away,” although they had been subject to gentler demons.

How can he say that the Gentiles had been alienated from the community of Israel and were strangers to the covenants and the promise, when they had no hope and were without God in this world, if Israel was not the people of God [Note: [Col. 0641] Here the printed editions add, “and of Christ,” which is absent from the principal manuscripts]?

Against this clearest and most exalted trumpet of truth, the madman makes a din and heaps abuse, saying that the Apostle spoke in five persons, so that through some roles he might deceive by means of others, pretending to be what he was not [Note: [Col. 0641] The printed editions read, “so that he might deceive others.” The manuscripts read, “so that he might deceive some other”—that is, “persons,” understood].

Yet he sees the Apostle preaching to the Gentiles who had been far from the God of the Israelites the same God, the same Law, the same Prophets, and the same covenants.

Who first spoke of the cornerstone? Was it not the prophet, filled with the Spirit of God, whom this plague blasphemes [Note: [Col. 0641] The manuscripts read, “whom this plague”—feminine—“blasphemes.”]? For he says: “Behold, I place in Zion a chosen, precious cornerstone; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isaiah 28:16). The Apostle Peter also recalled this testimony (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:6–8).

Was it not first said in the Psalm belonging to the sacred writings of the former people: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 117:22)?

Instructed by these Scriptures, the Apostle Paul wrote what I recalled shortly before: “with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone.”

Therefore the Lord himself convicted the Jews, in whom blindness had occurred in part, and put them to shame, saying: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this has come from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” (Matthew 21:42).

So, according to this man’s blasphemy, all these things were brought forward falsely by Christ from the Law and the Prophets, and falsely by the Apostles, because the weak supposedly could not yet grasp solid truth?

Is he so blind that he does not understand that nourishing little children is one thing and deceiving the gullible another; feeding them so that they may grow one thing and acting so that they may not live another?

This is what he says and thinks about the God of the Law and the Prophets and about those Scriptures themselves. According to the opinion he holds of them, when the Apostles preached to believers the God of the Law and the Prophets and confirmed the authority of such Scriptures, they appear, in his view, to have given little children not milk to drink but poison. Whoever believes this about them is foolish, empty-minded, and insane.

### 6

“Then,” someone may say, “did the Apostle say in vain: ‘I could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able’ (1 Corinthians 3:1–2); and, ‘We speak wisdom among the perfect’; and, ‘The natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God’ (1 Corinthians 2:6, 14)?”

Far be it from us to think that he said these things without purpose or falsely. Yet are we for that reason to believe that he wished to deceive any of those who believed him?

He therefore gave infants small things, not false things; things like milk, not harmful things; things that nourish, not things that destroy.

But if it is not true that the Son of God was made according to the flesh from the seed of David; if it is not true that the natural branches were broken off because of unbelief so that the faithful wild olive coming from the Gentiles might be grafted into the holy root of the Israelites and become a sharer in the richness of the olive tree; if those are not the utterances of God but, as this man blasphemes, of some exceedingly wicked demon, concerning which the Apostle says, “First, indeed, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Romans 3:2)—then surely the one who gave these things to infants, who proclaimed them as true, and who wanted them to be believed was destroying wretched people, not nourishing them.

But because we know that this is foreign to the faith and teaching of Christ’s truthful Apostles, it remains for us to detest this man most vehemently as a plague and enemy of the Christian faith. He is so blinded and driven headlong by madness that he does not see that even Timothy himself—whom he thinks was commanded by apostolic authority to avoid the ancient Law and the Prophets as old-womanish fables—was not to be deceived by that same Apostle, but was to be counted among the fifth person, the perfect, so that the Apostle would not speak falsely to him when he said:

“Remember that Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (2 Timothy 2:8).

If Christ is preached as coming from the seed of David through old-womanish fables, how is Timothy commanded to avoid those things which he is commanded to believe and remember?

But if Christ is truthfully preached as coming from the seed of David, there is the root into which the wild olive is grafted [Note: [Col. 0642] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “where is the root into which the wild olive is grafted? Nor are they old-womanish fables,” and so forth]. Nor are the old-womanish fables anything except the ravings of the Jews belonging to what they call the *deuterosis*, apart from those utterances of God that were entrusted to the circumcision.

In those utterances, even carnal Jews had learned that Christ would come from the seed of David, as they answered the Lord when he asked them (Matthew 22:42), although they were unable to understand him as the Lord of David himself—not according to the flesh but according to divinity.

Yet both things are contained in those utterances: what they believed and what they did not understand—“From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne” (Psalm 131:11), on account of Christ from the seed of David; and, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109:1), on account of Christ, who is also the Lord of David himself.

### 7

Was the Apostle really speaking deceitfully when he said:

“I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself could wish to be accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong adoption, glory, the covenants, the giving of the Law, worship, and the promises; to whom belong the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen” (Romans 9:1–5)?

At the beginning of this statement the Apostle loudly declares that he is speaking the truth—and this in Christ, who is truth itself—his conscience bearing witness in the Holy Spirit; and at the end he concludes the statement with “Amen.”

Yet this man says: “What the Apostle says here is not true. He deceives the weak because they cannot grasp the truth; he feeds infants on vanities and pours the poison of diabolical falsehoods into hungry children so as to nourish them.”

What a monstrosity, to be banished not only from Christian ears but even from the boundaries of the Christian world!

Are adoption, glory, covenants, the giving of the Law, worship, promises, and the fathers from whom Christ is according to the flesh—Christ who is God over all, blessed forever—old-womanish fables?

What he is especially commanded to hold fast, while he is commanded to avoid old-womanish fables—are these old-womanish fables?

### 8

But what wonder that he raves with such impiety, since he wishes to be a destroyer of the Law, when the same Apostle says that certain people who wish to be teachers of the Law—not destroyers but teachers—understand neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions?

But let us hold fast, against both groups, what he immediately added. So that no one might think that they failed to understand what they said and the things about which they made assertions because they wished to be teachers of a bad law, he immediately continued:

“We know that the Law is good, if one uses it lawfully” (1 Timothy 1:7–8).

This statement refutes both those who use the Law badly and those who think it is bad.

Moreover, if it is good, with what madness is the good God denied, who gave the good Law? What condemnation could be sufficient for people who accuse, under the name of old-womanish fables, the Law that the Apostle praises in this way—and who think that they do so on the authority of that same Letter, in which the Apostle praises it by saying that they wish to be teachers of the Law, but are not teachers, rather blasphemers, understanding neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions?

# CHAPTER THREE

### 9

“But it could not have happened,” he says, “that the coming of our Savior was announced by the Prophets of the Jews.”

Why could it not have happened, when the Apostle says: “The utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Romans 3:2)?

“But before the Savior’s coming,” he says, “the holy and divine Spirit was not upon the earth.”

Vanity speaks this, not truth. For by what Spirit except the Holy Spirit did the Lord fill his Prophets, concerning whom it was said to the Romans at the beginning of the Letter—as I recalled above:

“Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised through his Prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:1–3)?

This testimony was also included by this man himself, although he forbids the person to whom he writes to believe in other Prophets concerning Christ besides those whom the Apostle calls his Prophets in the letter to the Romans. I suppose he does not think that these were Prophets of the Jews.

But whatever nation he supposes them to have belonged to, why does he not notice the words, “which he had previously promised through his Prophets”? If, through whatever Prophets of his own, he previously promised the Gospel concerning his Son, what becomes of this man’s claim that the holy and divine Spirit was not upon the earth before the Savior’s coming?

And yet how could they have been prophets announcing Christ as coming according to the flesh from the seed of David, unless he belonged to the nation of which David was a member, from whose seed Christ was promised by God’s Prophets as one who would come?

### 10

“But the Law,” he says, “was given through Moses, whereas truth is from Christ Jesus.”

It is not written that way. Rather, it is written: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

The Law, therefore, was given through Moses. But grace came through Jesus Christ, when, through his Spirit and the love poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5), what the Law commands comes to be fulfilled.

For what is commanded through the letter is fulfilled not by the letter but by the Spirit. Thus what is written, “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17), is the Law through Moses, because it is commanded; but grace comes through Christ when what is commanded is fulfilled.

Truth, however, came through Christ on account of those things that were promised in the prophecy of the Law, because in Christ they are conspicuously fulfilled.

### 11

But when the Apostle says to the Romans, “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard?” he was speaking about the Gentiles, not about the Jews, as this man dreams.

The Teacher of the Gentiles wished to refute those who thought that the Gospel should be preached only to the nation of the Jews and not also to the uncircumcised Gentiles.

Wishing to show that it concerned not only the Jews but all nations, he first introduced the testimony of the prophet: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” Then, after saying, “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard?” he immediately added: “And how will they hear without someone preaching? Or how will they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:12–15).

Thus he refuted those who denied that preachers of Christ should be sent to the uncircumcised Gentiles.

## 12.

That passage too he does not understand, being utterly unlearned: “First Apostles, then Prophets” (1 Cor. 12:28). For he supposes that there were no Prophets before the Apostles, not knowing that the Apostle is there referring to Prophets who existed after Christ’s coming [Note: [Col. 0644] Manuscripts: “who came after Christ’s coming.”]. Whoever wishes to know who they were should read the Acts of the Apostles, and also what he says to the Corinthians: “Let two or three Prophets speak” (ibid. 14:29).

But if there were no Prophets before the Apostles, who were those through whom God formerly promised the Gospel concerning his Son, “who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:2–3)? Who was it that said, “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22)? Who was it that said, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:7–8)? How is God, whose throne is forever and ever, anointed by God, unless this is Christ Jesus, who received the name Christ from that very anointing? For *chrisma* means “anointing,” and Christ means “the Anointed One.”

Who was it that said what Christ himself testifies was foretold about him: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet”? David also confirms that he spoke this in the Spirit (Ps. 109:1; Mark 12:36)—the Spirit whom this man denies was upon the earth before the Lord’s coming.

What does the Apostle mean when he says, “Isaiah also says, There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Rom. 15:12)? What Spirit was it who, through that same Isaiah, so long beforehand foretold:

“This one bears our sins and suffers for us; and we regarded him as being in pain, in a wound, and in affliction. He was wounded because of our sins and weakened because of our iniquities; the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; each person has gone astray in his own way, and the Lord handed him over because of our iniquities. And he, because of his affliction, did not open his mouth; like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away; who will declare his generation? For his life shall be taken from the earth. He was led to death because of the iniquities of my people” (Isa. 53:4–8);

and the other things that it would take too long to set out in sequence?

There too the Church was foretold so long beforehand, as we read mentioned by the Apostle and now see fulfilled:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

For the Lord said:

“Enlarge the place of your tent and your curtains; drive in your stakes, do not spare; extend your ropes and strengthen your stakes. Enlarge still farther to the right and to the left; your offspring shall possess the nations, and you shall make desolate cities inhabited” [Note: [Col. 0645] Some ancient manuscripts: “you shall make.”]. “Do not fear, because you have been confounded; do not be ashamed, because you have been reproached. For you shall forget eternal confusion, and you shall not remember the disgrace of your widowhood. For the Lord who made you—the Lord of hosts is his name—and your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:1–5; Gal. 4:27).

Who was it that said:

“I was seeing in a night vision, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven; and he reached the Ancient of Days, and was brought before him. And to him were given dominion, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7:13–14)?

From where, then, were these and the many other clear prophecies concerning Christ and the Church, which we see fulfilled in this way and, in harmony with the Evangelical and Apostolic Scriptures, also hope to see fulfilled, if the Spirit of God was not upon the earth before Christ’s coming; or if Christ’s coming was not foretold by the Prophets of Israel, as this man foolishly claims? By denying that Christ was promised beforehand, he has no grounds for asserting that he was sent. And deservedly so, because the one whom he proclaims was neither sent nor promised: he is not real, but fabricated.

# CHAPTER IV

### 13.

I am not surprised that this uneducated man thinks the statement of the Apostle, “One of their own, their proper prophet, said, Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies; this testimony is true” (Titus 1:12–13), was spoken about the Jewish Prophets. He does not know that it was said about a certain Epimenides, who was a Cretan, and in whose books this statement is found. He is not counted among the Prophets of God, nor does he belong to those utterances of God entrusted to the Jews by him who does not lie.

For this reason the Apostle did not mention his name, as he customarily mentions the Prophets of God, sometimes saying, “As David also says” (Rom. 4:6); “But Isaiah boldly says” (ibid. 10:20); “As Hosea also says” (ibid. 9:25); or, while leaving their names unmentioned, saying, “As it is written” (ibid. 1:17). In such cases the Scripture intended is understood to be one possessing the authority of God.

At other times he explicitly asserts that God is speaking, when he introduces a testimony from the Law or from God’s Prophets, as in the statement, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain. Is God concerned about oxen?” he asks. “Or does he say this entirely for our sake?” (1 Cor. 9:9–10). By this he clearly shows that God is speaking in that same Scripture.

Or consider this statement: “Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the nations by faith, foretold to Abraham, saying, In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gal. 3:8). He put Scripture itself in the place of God, because it is God’s Scripture.

Or the statement about Abraham: “He did not waver in unbelief at the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that what he had promised he was also able to do” (Rom. 4:20–21). Contrary to this divine and apostolic declaration, that rabid dog, barking angrily, dared to say that Abraham did not believe his God when he promised him offspring. He does not understand the statement, “If a son will be born to me who am a hundred years old” (Gen. 17:17): these words express astonished joy, not the doubt of one who distrusts.

Or consider this: “The word of God cannot fail. For not all who are from Israel are Israel; nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are they all children [Note: [Col. 0646] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions: ‘nor are those who are’]. But, In Isaac shall your seed be called—that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed” (Rom. 9:6–8).

Or the statement about Elijah: “But what does the divine answer say to him? I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (ibid. 11:4).

By these and similar testimonies the authority of the Apostle commends those Scriptures as belonging to the good and true God—those Scriptures which this man blasphemes.

But whenever the Apostle also cites something from Gentile authors, he does not call them Prophets of God, nor does he say that God is the author of those writings, even though he finds some truth in them. Thus, concerning this Cretan, he says, “One of their own, their proper prophet, said, Cretans are always liars” (Titus 1:12). He was therefore not the proper prophet of the Jews but of the Cretans; and this was certainly said so that he would not be thought to be a prophet of God.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, when he was speaking to the Athenians, he said concerning God: “For in him we live and move and exist, as some of those who are among you have also said” (Acts 17:28).

### 14.

“But,” he says, “when our Lord was questioned by the Apostles about what judgment should be formed concerning the Prophets of the Jews, who were thought to have sung something in the past about his coming, he was angered that they still held such opinions and answered them: ‘You have abandoned the living one who is before you and are talking about the dead.’”

What wonder is it—since he produced this testimony from I know not what apocryphal writings—if heretics, who do not accept those same writings, have invented such statements about the Prophets of God?

For in the Gospel, which is not apocryphal but known to all in the light of truth [Note: [Col. 0647] Several manuscripts: “but under the guidance of truth.”], the Lord, even after his resurrection, accompanied his disciples on the road and, beginning with Moses and proceeding through all the Prophets, showed that the things concerning himself which had occurred had been foretold (Luke 24:27).

### 15.

“Again,” he says, “he argues about himself when he says:

‘Many will say to me on that day, “Lord, in your name we cast out demons, and in your name we prophesied, and in your name we performed many mighty works.” And then I will say to them, “Depart from me, for I never knew you, because you have worked iniquity”’” (Matt. 7:22–23).

Far be it from us to suppose that the Lord spoke this about the holy Prophets, among whom were Moses and the others. Rather, he spoke about those who, after his Gospel had been preached, think that they speak in his name, while not knowing what they are saying. This man, destined for destruction, has found a place among them.

### 16.

He also says that the Lord said: “I am the door of the sheep; all the others, as many as came before me, are thieves and robbers.”

But it is not written that way. Rather, it says: “All who came are thieves and robbers” (John 10:8). Here “came” means those who had not been sent. Jeremiah also reproves such people, saying: “Thus says the Lord concerning the Prophets who prophesy in my name, though I did not send them” (Jer. 14:15).

But those whom this madman blasphemes were sent by the Lord; they did not come on their own initiative. The Lord also makes this clear in a parable, though with the most explicit meaning, when he says:

“Hear another parable. There was a landowner who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, leased it to tenants, and went away to a distant country. When the time of the fruits drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to receive his fruits. But the tenants seized his servants, struck one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more numerous than the first, and they treated them in the same way. Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’ And they seized him, threw him outside the vineyard, and killed him.

“When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?”

“They say to him, ‘He will destroy those evil men evilly and lease his vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons.’”

Jesus says to them:

“Have you never read in the Scriptures:

‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone; this was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?

“Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:33–43).

What could be more open, clearer, or more evident than this? But this man belongs to the number of those who stoned the servants of this landowner. He does so not with blows from stones, but with harsh curses.

For the parable testifies that the vineyard of God was first planted among the Jewish people, and that Prophets were sent before the coming of the Savior himself. And when it says, “The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits,” what kingdom does it mean except the one they hoped for, not the one they had received—that is, eternal life?

Therefore elsewhere he says: “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life; they themselves bear witness about me” (John 5:39). And elsewhere: “Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you hindered” (Luke 11:52).

Are these enormous masses of testimony not enough to grind down his shameless vanity? Who listens to this man except one who does not listen to the holy Scriptures, or listens so badly that, like this blind man, he rushes against them?

# CHAPTER V

### 17.

“But,” he says, “the Lord said concerning them, ‘Your fathers ate manna and died’” (John 6:49), teaching that none of them belonged to the Lord, since death ruled over them.

Certainly none—but he meant those fathers of the people to whom he was speaking. For whose fathers were they except those of unbelievers, whom he wanted to be understood as unbelievers?

Hence elsewhere he says:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the Prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the Prophets.’ Thus you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the Prophets.”

He called them sons in the imitation of their crime, not in the descent of their lineage. For the fact that they had been born from those people according to the flesh could not itself be a crime charged against them; rather, it was that they showed themselves like them through unbelieving cruelty.

Therefore he continues and says:

“And you, fill up the measure of your fathers. Serpents, brood of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” [Note: [Col. 0648] In the manuscripts: “how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?”]

“Therefore, behold, I send you Prophets, wise men, and scribes; some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues, and you will persecute them from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Truly I say to you, all these things shall come upon this generation” (Matt. 23:29–36).

It is entirely certain and manifest that these people are sons of the wicked by imitation. From the holy and righteous Prophets—from Abel himself, whom his brother killed, all the way to Zechariah, whom these people killed—they endured the most impious and criminal persecutions.

For how will the blood of those who lived long before these people were born come upon them [Note: [Col. 0649] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, Louvain: “comes upon them.” M.], unless it is because the wicked form one kind, one mixture, one mass, joined to one another by imitation?

At the same time it is made clear that there were righteous people and Prophets of God within that same people, whose tombs these men, to whom the Lord speaks, built and whose monuments they adorned.

This man, therefore, is worse and more savage: he tears with his slanderous tongue those who were dead and to whom even the impious paid honor. He savagely rages against his own soul and blasphemes those whom Christ asserts to have been Prophets and righteous men, while he himself wants to appear Christian.

### 18.

Now, when he wished to add the holy Patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—to those concerning whom the Lord says, “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died,” on the grounds that these patriarchs too had died, it is uncertain whether he should be judged fraudulent or blind. But whichever alternative he chooses, he is detestable.

For he wanted to establish this point by recalling those same patriarchs, concerning whom the Lord says, “He is not the God of the dead but of the living,” whereas the Lord rather said that they were alive. After introducing the testimony from the Law where it is written, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” he added, “He is not the God of the dead but of the living.” And he added, “For all live to him” (Matt. 22:32; Luke 20:37–38)—that is, they possess the true life by which the righteous live even when they die bodily.

But when would this man say such things, if he were alive?

### 19.

He also wants the Lord’s statement to the Jews to be understood in this sense: “You know neither me nor my Father; and you do not have the word of God remaining in you” (John 8:19).

This is certainly not contrary to what he said: “You have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you hindered” (Luke 11:52).

They did not have the word of God within themselves, but they had it in the Scriptures that they read. For if they had possessed it within themselves, they too would have entered and would have allowed others to enter.

Not entering means not understanding. This is why they knew neither him nor his Father: they did not understand what they were reading, not because they had failed to proclaim the God and Christ whom they read about.

To enter, therefore, means not to be content with the surface of the letter, but to reach the interior meaning.

### 20.

He also argues from John the Baptist, because the Lord says: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist; but the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matt. 11:11). Thus he reasons as though John did not belong to the kingdom of heaven, and therefore the other Prophets of that people belonged there even less, since John is greater than they are.

These words of the Lord can be understood most correctly in two ways.

Either in that passage the Lord called “the kingdom of heaven” the kingdom that we have not yet received and in which we are not yet present. Hence at the end he will say, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (ibid. 25:34). And because the holy Angels are there [Note: [Col. 0649] Several manuscripts: “and those Angels who are there.”], even the least among them is certainly greater than any holy and righteous person bearing a body that is subject to corruption and weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15).

Or, if in that saying he wanted “the kingdom of heaven” to be understood in the sense in which it also signifies the Church in the present age—whose children are all those, from the establishment of the human race until now, who have been able to be righteous and holy—then surely the Lord was referring to himself. At the time of his birth he was younger than John, but in the eternity of his divinity and in his lordly power he was greater.

Accordingly, under the first interpretation the sentence is punctuated as follows:

“Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist; but the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven”—and then follows, “is greater than he.”

Under the second interpretation it is punctuated this way:

“Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist; but the one who is lesser”—and then follows, “in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

But whichever interpretation agrees with the truth, it is sufficient to refute this man’s vanity.

Whether it is an Angel who is lesser than the other Angels but greater than John, or whether the Lord himself is understood—at the time of his birth younger than John his forerunner, but greater in majesty—nothing is thereby taken away from the other Prophets. Some of them could have been John’s equals, others lesser than he; but none could have been greater, because of the Lord’s statement. Yet all of them were holy, righteous, and good.

# CHAPTER VI

### 21.

“But Moses,” he says, “destroyed all hope of a future resurrection among human beings when he declared that the soul is mortal and said that it is blood.”

Then, reasoning with great effort, he attempts to demonstrate that the soul is not blood, laboring over an obvious matter because he does not understand the Law [Note: [Col. 0650] Earlier manuscripts: “so that we may not understand the Law.”].

For this is how the statement is to be understood: “The soul of every flesh is its blood” (Lev. 17:14), just as it is said, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4)—not because the rock actually was Christ, but because Christ was signified by it [Note: [Col. 0650] Manuscripts: “but because it signified him.”].

The Law did not wish to signify the soul through blood without reason—that is, an invisible reality through a visible one. Blood, diffused through all the veins from the heart itself, exercises greater dominion in our body than the other fluids, so that wherever a wound is inflicted, it is not another fluid but blood itself that flows.

Thus, because the soul invisibly surpasses all the elements of which we consist, it is better signified by that which visibly surpasses all the elements of which we consist.

### 22.

As for what the Apostle says—and this testimony too was introduced by the man—“Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0650] The Louvain edition alone has “shall not possess,” plural.], this raises a question not about the soul but about the resurrection of the body.

This too, however, can be resolved in two ways.

Either by “flesh and blood” he meant the corruption of flesh and blood, which will not exist in the resurrection; or by “flesh and blood” he meant people devoted to all the enticements of worldly pleasures and enslaved to flesh and blood—people who shall not possess the kingdom of God.

But if the whole passage of the Apostle’s discourse where it is written, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God,” is considered more carefully, it will more strongly persuade us that he wished to call the corruption of flesh as it now exists by these names, and that, to explain what he meant, he added: “Neither shall corruption possess incorruption.”

For when that change takes place which is hoped for in the resurrection, no corruption will remain. Although, therefore, after the resurrection the Lord said to his disciples, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39), there will indeed be flesh according to its substance, but not according to the corruption that now gives flesh this name.

Hence the Prophet says, “All flesh is grass.” Surely he does not mean the flesh of the Lord, which he raised into heaven. In what sense, then, did the Prophet call it flesh when he said, “All flesh is grass,” and was about to add, “The grass withered” (Isa. 40:6–7)? In the same sense the Apostle says, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God”: corruption will not be there, by which the nature of flesh now withers like grass.

The statement “Neither shall corruption possess incorruption” is not a different assertion. It is a repetition that explains the preceding statement: where “flesh and blood” was said, we are to understand corruption, not the substance of flesh; and where “the kingdom of God” was said, we are to understand incorruption.

Thus we should understand the statement “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” as saying nothing other than, “Corruption shall not possess incorruption.” That is, the corruption of flesh and blood will not exist in the incorruption of that kingdom, because of the transformation of which he immediately went on to speak: “This corruptible must put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:50, 53).

The corruption signified by the terms “flesh and blood” will therefore not exist in the incorruption of that kingdom, because the flesh that is now corruptible will then be changed into incorruptibility.

### 23.

But if Moses, the man of God, had believed that the soul was mortal—and he certainly would have believed this if he had said that it was blood not as a sign but as a matter of its proper nature—he would not have said elsewhere:

“Everyone who touches a corpse—that is, a human person who has died—and is not purified, defiles the tabernacle of the Lord. That soul shall be cut off from Israel [Note: [Col. 0651] The editions have *exsecretur*. The manuscripts have *exteretur*, except for one Sorbonne manuscript, which reads *exterminabitur*. In the Greek of the Septuagint: *ektribēsetai*, ‘shall be destroyed.’], because the water of sprinkling was not sprinkled upon him; he is unclean, and his uncleanness remains upon him” (Num. 19:13).

He said “remains,” certainly, even after death, because the person has not been purified. Here he understands the cleansing of regeneration to have been prefigured—the cleansing now received by those who are baptized in Christ, whoever faithfully hears the words: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

# CHAPTER VII

### 24.

What wonder is it if this unhappy man, turned away from the light of truth and therefore hostile to the light of truth, directs against the Old Testament the things he does not understand in the New Testament?

Consider also the passage from the Apostle Paul where he says to the Corinthians:

“If the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, came in glory” [Note: [Col. 0651] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “for glory.”], “so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is being brought to an end, how will the ministry of the Spirit not be rather in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more will the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. For even that which was glorified in this respect was not glorified, because of the surpassing glory. For if that which is brought to an end was in glory, much more will that which remains be in glory.”

This is how he presented the Apostle’s words, and he is not very far from a better interpretation.

Because the ministry of death was said to be “engraved in letters on stones,” he supposes from this that Moses ministered to death—that is, to the author of death, namely the evil spirit whom he thinks to be the author of this world.

He does not understand that “the ministry of death” refers to the Law, in accordance with what the Apostle says elsewhere: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6–11).

Although the Law is just, holy, and good, it brought death upon transgressors whom God’s grace did not assist in fulfilling the righteousness of the Law. For it was necessary that, under the Old Testament, the Law be imposed upon the proud and those who trusted in the power of their own will. It did not give righteousness but commanded it, so that, entangled in the death of transgression, they might flee for refuge to grace—not merely commanding but also helping—which has been revealed in the New Testament.

For this reason these blasphemers of the divine utterances think that the Law given through Moses was evil, because it is called “the ministry of death in letters engraved on stones.” They do not consider that this was said on account of those who thought that the Law was sufficient through their own free will and who, without the help of the Spirit of grace, were held guilty of transgression under the letter of that same Law.

Hence the Apostle says elsewhere, “The Law produces wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). By this he shows why he said, “The Law produces wrath.” For transgression would not be evil unless the Law itself were good.

### 25.

It would be too much, and far too lengthy, to collect everything that the blessed Apostle says in this connection, distinguishing the Law from grace: under the Law the proud are cast down, while under grace those who have been cast down are raised up; the Law is so good that it commands good things, whereas grace is so good that it bestows good things [Note: [Col. 0652] The editions have “grace is so good.” But most and better manuscripts have “grace only,” without *in tantum*.].

The Law makes one a hearer of righteousness; grace makes one a doer of it.

Therefore under the Law the sinner lies convicted, and even as a transgressor, deprived of the excuse of ignorance. Under grace, however, which both spares and assists, even the person who has done evil is not destroyed but is kindled to do good [Note: [Col. 0652] The editions have “and because he has done evil.” The better manuscripts have “even the one who has done evil.”].

What wonder is it, then, if the Law is called “the ministry of death,” where the letter kills by prohibiting the evil that is done and commanding the good that is not done; while grace is called “the ministry of the Spirit,” who gives life, so that we may rise from the death of transgression and have righteousness, not as persons guilty reading it on tablets, but as free persons in our hearts and conduct?

This is how the New Testament differs from the Old: there the old person is confined within the narrow limits of fear; here the new person walks freely in the breadth of love.

### 26.

What was said about Moses, the minister of the Old Testament—that the children of Israel could not gaze upon his face because of the glory of his countenance—was a sign that they would not understand Christ in the Law.

Therefore a veil was placed between Moses’ face and them, so that they would not gaze, as it is written: “The children of Israel, to the end” [Note: [Col. 0653] In Greek, *eis to telos*, “to the end.”] (2 Cor. 3:13).

But what is the end of the Law? Let not I but the Apostle himself answer: “For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

He is the end that perfects, not the end that destroys. “End” is used of the purpose for which everything is done through some function. The difference between a function and an end is that a function concerns the things we ought to do, while the end is the purpose for which we do them.

Since all those things were done for Christ, whom the children of Israel did not understand in the things that were being done, the veil signified that they were not able to gaze to the end—that is, to the face of Moses, which signified Christ.

But it was said that this glory would be brought to nothing because all the shadows that signify something are brought to nothing when the reality signified arrives. Just as the knowledge that exists now will be brought to nothing, as the same Apostle says, when that which he calls “face to face” arrives [Note: [Col. 0653] Several manuscripts: “face toward face,” in accordance with the Greek, *prosōpon pros prosōpon*] (1 Cor. 13:10, 12), so too the things given to the Jews under the Old Testament in shadows [Note: [Col. 0653] Several manuscripts: “in words.”] necessarily had to be brought to nothing by the revelation of the New Testament.

### 27.

Nor is it true that no one among that people understood Christ as prefigured through those shadows of the Old Testament. Moses himself and the other Prophets surely understood these things, since they foretold him to their descendants.

For in the very Epistle to the Corinthians, where these statements are made—statements that this man, not understanding them, presented as opposed and hostile to the Old Testament—why does the Apostle say:

“But having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, I believed, and therefore I spoke; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13)?

Where is it written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:10)? Certainly in the Psalms, which belong to those utterances of God entrusted to the Jews.

“Having the same spirit of faith,” he says. What does “the same” mean except the Spirit possessed also by those through whom these things were administered?

Why also, in the same Epistle, did he introduce testimony from the Law, after first saying, “Let your abundance be for their want, and their abundance become for your want, so that there may be equality,” and then adding, “As it is written: He who gathered much did not have too much, and he who gathered little did not lack” (2 Cor. 8:14–15)?

Why does he invoke the authority of the Law, which he says was “the ministry of death,” if he understood it in the way this pestilence understands it?

### 28.

And so that all ambiguity may be removed, let us recall the passage in the Epistle to the Romans that shows how the Law can rightly be called the ministry of death and yet remain holy, just, and good.

After saying, “so that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter,” a statement very similar to the one this man, not understanding it, introduced, the Apostle immediately anticipated the future verbose and blasphemous people who would think that the Law had thereby been criticized. He promptly added:

“What shall we say?” [Note: [Col. 0653] In the manuscripts: “What shall we say?”] “Is the Law sin? Certainly not. But I did not know sin except through the Law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the Law said, You shall not covet. But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of covetousness. For without the Law sin was dead. I was once alive without the Law; but when the commandment came, sin revived. I died, and the commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Therefore the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Did what is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not. Rather, sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what is good” (Rom. 7:6–13).

Here is what “the ministry of death” means; here is what “the letter kills” means (2 Cor. 3:6). Here is how the Law is not sin, how the commandment was intended for life, and how the Law and the commandment are holy, just, and good. Yet because the disobedient soul is killed by that very good, where God’s grace does not assist, the Law became the ministry of death in the Old Testament because of the killing letter; and grace became the ministry of life in the New Testament because of the life-giving Spirit.

The following statements all mean the same thing as “the ministry of death” and “the ministry of condemnation”:

“Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of covetousness”;

“When the commandment came, sin revived”;

“The commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death”;

“Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me”;

“The Law entered so that transgression might abound” (Rom. 5:20);

“The Law produces wrath” (ibid. 4:15);

“The strength of sin is the Law” (1 Cor. 15:56).

For the prohibition of sin, which is the Law, certainly increases the desire to sin. That desire is not extinguished except by the contrary desire to do what is right, where faith works through love (Gal. 5:6).

The letter that commands does not provide this; the Spirit that assists does. It is therefore not the Law but grace; not the Old Testament, which generates slavery and is represented by Hagar, but the New Testament, in which the children are not those of the slave woman but of the free woman, with whose freedom Christ has set us free (ibid. 4:24, 31).

And yet the Law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good.

Through this holy, just, and good commandment, sin works every kind of covetousness in those who do not have the Spirit of Christ. The Apostle himself shows that he was such a person under the Old Testament when he says, “Sin, taking occasion, worked in me every kind of covetousness through the commandment.”

Through which commandment, except the one he mentions: “I would not have known covetousness unless the Law said, You shall not covet”?

Is it evil not to covet? On the contrary, it is supremely good [Note: [Col. 0654] Better manuscripts: “the greatest good.”].

The Law, therefore, is good when it says this. But where the life-giving Spirit is absent, this same Law, which declares what is good [Note: [Col. 0654] Thus the Ambrosian manuscript and other manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain have “which declares it to be good.”], kills, because it is the strength of sin when, through it, sin works every kind of covetousness by inflaming desire through prohibition [Note: [Col. 0654] The editions have “inflaming the prohibition.” The reading is corrected from the manuscripts.].

This is not extinguished by the commanding letter through fear of punishment, but by the assisting Spirit through love of righteousness.

Therefore he says, “Sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what is good.” He does not say, “through what is evil,” but “through what is good.”

Let those who criticize the Law of God and its minister Moses with blind and furious hearts awaken here, if they can.

The Law is therefore the ministry of death because sin worked death through what is good; and it is the ministry of condemnation because sin worked condemnation through what is good.

29. But not all who are called Christians pass over to Christ; only those from whom the veil is removed—the veil that remains when the Old Testament is read. For those who are in the Old Testament, because the veil obstructs them, understand neither the Old nor the New; but those who pass over to Christ, when the veil is removed through the New Testament, understand both the Old and the New (II Cor. 3:14–16). Would that these blind opponents of the Law and the Prophets might likewise pass over to Christ, so that they would not be among those in whom the Gospel itself is veiled. For the Apostle says that it is veiled in those who are perishing: “In whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, might not shine upon them” (ibid. 4:4).

Here this wretched man wants “the god of this age” to be understood as the evil one—as though Moses had served him in the Old Testament, as though that were what the Apostle had said. If it were necessary to understand “the god of this age” as the god of the impious, that is, the devil—for “all the gods of the nations are demons,” and especially their prince, the ruler of demons—there would be nothing surprising in this, since even the belly of certain people is called their god. For the Apostle says, “whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19), yet the belly is not thereby a god. Thus, if the devil can be called the god of this age, the devil is not thereby God; nor are demons gods, although “the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95:5).

For “age” can indeed be understood in an evil sense. Hence the Apostle Peter says, “Rescue yourselves from this present evil age” (II Pet. 1:4). But when another interpretation is evident, why is it necessary here to think that the devil is meant, rather than the true, just, and good God, who has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age? The phrase should not be divided as though it read, “among whom the god of this age, and thereafter, blinded the minds of unbelievers”; rather, it should be understood thus: “among whom God, and thereafter, blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age”—that is, he blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age.

## CHAPTER VIII

30. But these people do not accept that the good God blinds the minds of some. They do not attend to the words of the Savior, who says: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). Therefore, he who according to the Apostle’s statement “has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills,” beyond doubt illuminates whom he wills and blinds whom he wills. Yet there is no injustice with God (Rom. 9:18, 14), to whom the Church says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1). Thus he illuminates by mercy and blinds by judgment—certainly by judgment that is most just, even if most hidden. For “his judgments are unsearchable” (Rom. 11:33). Yet to him it is said: “You sat upon the throne, you who judge equity” [Col. 0656] (Ps. 9:5).

31. Moses served this God, as did the other Prophets, whom the Lord himself undoubtedly testifies to have been righteous. For the Jews were building their tombs and adorning the monuments of these men, to whom he says: “You build the tombs of the Prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous” (Matt. 23:29).
