But all of them, although in accordance with the dispensation of the time they ministered through the figures of the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0656] Am., Er., and several manuscripts: “they ministered figures.”], nevertheless belonged to the New Testament, although it had not yet been revealed, just as Abraham belonged to it.

If these people would read with the veil removed, they would understand that the Gospel is no more hostile to the Law given through Moses than Abraham and Moses themselves are hostile to one another. These people themselves confess that both worshiped the same God, although they blaspheme him so greatly that they deny him to be God. Yet the Apostle sets the promises made to Abraham—which signified the New Testament—in opposition to the Law given through Moses, so that these two appear to be hostile to one another.

For what else does he say to the Romans? “For the promise to Abraham or to his seed that he would be heir of the world did not come through the Law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise has been annulled. For the Law produces wrath; but where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:13–15).

Let them observe how he argues as though against the Law, so that from that earlier promise made to Abraham he may prove that whoever are heirs of God are heirs not through the Law but through the promise [Note: [Col. 0656] So the principal manuscripts. The printed editions have: “so that he may prove it from the promise.”].

Likewise, to the Galatians he says: “Brothers, I speak according to human standards: even a humanly confirmed testament no one annuls or adds a provision to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ. Now this is what I mean: the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul a testament previously confirmed by God, so as to abolish the promise. For if the inheritance comes through the Law, it no longer comes through the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through a promise. Why, then, the Law? It was added because of transgressions [Note: [Col. 0656] Several manuscripts: “It was placed.” Some manuscripts below, where the same passage is repeated and where Lov. also reads “it was placed,” have “it was added.”], until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made” (Gal. 3:15–19).

I do not know whether these people, who accuse the Law because they do not understand it, can find anything in the Gospel or in the Apostolic Letters that appears as hostile and contrary to that same Law as does this passage, in which the Apostle sets against the Law the promises made to Abraham. If, then, they hate the Law, let them love Abraham.

## CHAPTER IX

32. But they do not want to do even this. For they also bring against the father of the nations—the one to whom we now see the promises fulfilled among all nations—the charge of fornication. This man to whom we are replying clearly shows himself to be one of those about whom it was foretold when the Apostle said: “The Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the [Col. 0657] faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are branded, forbidding marriage” (I Tim. 4:1–3).

Abraham is not found to have defiled himself with any adultery. He did not love the slave woman through the slippery impulse of lust; rather, he received her from his wife, when his wife did what she wished with her marital right, desiring to have children by her husband, although from another woman’s womb (Gen. 16:2–4). There was no motive of wantonness at all, but only the intention of procreation.

This man, however, charges Abraham with fornication even into extreme old age, evidently because after Sarah’s death he took another wife (ibid. 25:1). Even if no hidden sacramental meaning were understood in this, Abraham ought to have done it for this one reason: so that heretics would not think, against the Apostle—while Tertullian also supports them—that taking a wife after the death of one’s wife is a crime.

But just as this man thinks he can find in the Apostolic Letters something that speaks against the Law given through Moses or against the Old Testament, let him also find something against Abraham that appears to be proclaimed by the evangelical writings. He will find absolutely nothing. Wherever Abraham is named in the books of the New Testament, he is named with due honor, so much so that the Lord himself said to the Jews: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). Consequently, this man who blasphemes Abraham is certainly blaspheming Christ, who gives such testimony to Abraham.

33. But let him say, if he can, which of those five persons the Apostle represented [Note: [Col. 0657] Above, chapter 2] when he preached in this manner about Abraham. If he had become as one without the Law to those who had been without the Law, they did not know Abraham. Therefore he ought to have found some ruler—Roman or Greek—or some philosopher whom he could preach to such people, so that, by pretending to become like them, as this man wishes, he might suit them. He should not have chosen Abraham, some foreigner whom they did not know, the father of the Hebrew nation, utterly distant from their customs, their rites, and their kinship.

But if he had become as a Jew to the Jews, or as one under the Law to those who were under the Law, why did he say that heirs do not come through the Law? Why did he say, “The Law produces wrath”? Why did he say, “The Law was placed because of transgressions”—something those who gloried in the Law could not endure with equanimity?

And if he was speaking as a weak man to the weak, and, by deceiving them as deceivers approve, was feeding them with milk through deception, why did he drive them so violently away from the old shadows in which the weak were resting that he said: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2)?

But if, in that fifth role, he was speaking wisdom to the perfect—whom alone this man considers worthy not to be deceived—why does this man, on the contrary, want to be perfect in order to blaspheme Abraham, whom the Apostle praises in this manner to the perfect [Note: [Col. 0657] So the old German manuscript. The Remigian, Corbie, and Colbert manuscripts read: “Why does he want to be contrary to the perfect, so as to blaspheme Abraham, whom the perfect Apostle praises in this manner?” The printed editions have: “Why does he want to be perfect in opposition, so as to blaspheme Abraham, whom the Apostle praises as perfect?”], especially in those two sons of his, [Col. 0658] one born of a slave woman and the other of a free woman? If the Old Testament displeases him in Ishmael, let the New Testament please him in Isaac.

34. Or is he also going to set up the chair of pestilence against the Apostle and debate the character of figures, saying that he ought not to have drawn figures of honorable things from dishonorable things? For this man considers even conjugal intercourse with Sarah herself a dishonorable matter, although the Teacher of the Gentiles testifies that she signifies our free mother, the eternal Jerusalem (Gal. 4:22–26). He wrinkles his nose and furrows his brow, and, with a contorted face, the teacher of pestilence recoils from this parable. [Col. 0659] He recoils still more strongly and shamefully when he hears the same Teacher of the Gentiles add to what is written about male and female, “The two shall become one flesh,” the words: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32).

Was this man aware that the sacraments of so great a matter—that is, its sacred signs—were to be recognized in a matter of shame, and in words to which modesty is owed, while the blessed Apostle was unaware of it? Let this man go back, then, with his like-minded companions, who said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:61).

But let us hear and understand the two Testaments in the two sons of Abraham, born from the union with his two women. Against the wishes of these people, we recognize without any obscenity the two in one flesh—Christ and the Church. In the same way, we receive with faithful heart and mouth Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings (I Tim. 2:5), who gives us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink, although it seems more horrifying to eat human flesh than to kill it, and to drink human blood than to shed it.

In all the holy Scriptures, whenever anything said or done figuratively is explained according to the rule of sound faith, let us hear that explanation wisely and without contempt, whatever the things and words contained in the sacred writings may be from which it is drawn. And let us leave this man babbling emptiness, treating the character of figures with a kind of ignorant expertise, if such a thing may be said, because he does not know what he is saying.

When he says that something ought to be signified by things that correspond to it rather than by contrary things, this foolish man could say that God must always be written in bright gold and never in black ink, because “God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all” (I John 1:5).

For this is a man who thinks that the Apostle, in order to accommodate himself to the weak and imperfect, said many false and reprehensible things, although his Letters show, from the testimonies he cites from the Law and the Prophets, how reverently he receives those Scriptures. He does not consider that, by such a perverse reasoning, even those things in the ancient books of God which he, unclean and impious though he pretends to be pious and pure, shudders at could be defended.

For if someone like him were to say to him, “The things that offend you in the Law and the Prophets are false, but the Holy Spirit wished them to be presented in that way for the sake of the weak and imperfect,” what answer could this empty-minded man give his counterpart against such an argument? He is refuted by the false rule—his own rule—not by the hand of a wise and learned person, but of a fool and an ignorant man like himself; nevertheless, he is slaughtered by his own sword.

## CHAPTER X

35. After these sacrilegious ravings of a sacrilegious and empty-minded man, to which I think I have replied sufficiently, they concern the beginning of Genesis; the making of light; the day or the sun; the reason for creating humanity; Adam’s sin; the making of humanity; the serpent’s persuasion; the curse upon humanity and the tree of life; God’s repentance; the Flood; the rainbow in the clouds; the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart; the lying spirit according to the prophet Micah; the testimony of the prophet Isaiah, because he says, “I begot sons and exalted them,” and then says to them again, “Wicked sons, evil offspring”; and what he also said is written in Isaiah, “I am God, making good things and creating evil things”; the destruction of the people at Moses’ command [Note: [Col. 0659] Am. and the manuscripts: “the commands of Moses.” This is no less suitable, as is clear from Book 1, chapter 16, no. 28]; the curse which he considers shameful; the cruelty of God, which he thinks God confessed; the supposed pursuit of evil according to King David; the statement written, “It repents me that I made Saul king”; the spirit of Moses, whose Scriptures he thinks the Apostle called old wives’ tales; the character of figures; Abraham; the sons of Eli the priest; the sacrifices, which he thinks are offered only to demons; the Prophets of God, whom he thinks did not exist before the Lord’s coming; the statement in the Law that blood is the soul; the God whom Moses served, whom he thinks was not the true God; and the variety of persons in whom he thinks the Apostle spoke deceitfully.

I have pursued all these matters not in the order in which they occur in his book, but as the interconnected sequence of our discussion required.

## CHAPTER XI

36. After all this he placed a heading, which reads: “The distinction between spirits of wickedness and goodness” [Note: [Col. 0659] Several manuscripts: “of the wicked and of goodness.” Perhaps this should be “of the wicked and of the good.”].

He then began, in brief and frequent opposing statements, to praise Christ and accuse the God of the Law, in the following manner, as though exhorting the person to whom he was writing:

“Why, then, brother,” he says, “turning away from the wickedness of our former error, should we not attend to Christ, the true and supreme God, not the ruler of this age and maker of the world, in which we have been very often shown to be exiles? Let us attend, I say, to him who is compassionate and gentle, who, showing us to be of his kindred, called us the light of the world; not to him who, according to the Jewish Scriptures, assigning us an earthly beginning, imposed upon us an end in the earth. Let us attend to him who, calling us brothers, persuaded us to keep watch and to think divine thoughts; not to him who did not even permit us to possess a sense of discernment.” In this manner he wove together many other statements.

37. I thought that the appropriate reply to this passage of his book should be made in such a way that I too would exhort you:

“Let us attend to Christ, the true and supreme God, the only Son of the true and supreme [Col. 0660] God—not the wicked ruler of this age, but nevertheless the maker of the world, that is, of heaven and earth—who commanded us to live as exiles during our temporal life in this mortality.

Let us attend, I say, to him who is merciful and gentle, who made us his brothers by grace, not by nature. For he is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who according to the Scriptures gave us an earthly body but a soul by his breath, making both, rather than begetting either of them.

He is himself, and no other, who commanded and enabled us to keep watch and to think divine thoughts. For he is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who warned us not to learn by sinning the distinction between good and evil.

He is himself, and no other, who, calling us to immortality, promised us heavenly kingdoms.

He is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who, after we sinned, separated us, as guilty, from the happiness of eternal life and punished us with earthly labor.

He is himself, and no other, who commanded us—not, as this man says, to know nothing, but to know what is useful. Nor did he, as this man thinks and as his view dissents from the truth, condemn in us the knowledge that comes from practicing righteousness, but rather the knowledge that comes from experiencing sin.

He is himself, and no other, who took pity on us because we were dying through error.

He is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who consigned us to death—not from the time when we began to acquire knowledge, as this man says, but from the time when we sinned.

He is himself, and no other, who urges us to despise our possessions—or rather, to store them in a safer place (Matt. 6:19–20). Yet he is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who, showing himself to be Lord not only of heavenly but also of earthly things, either commanded or permitted his own people—when this was appropriate for the time—to take away and possess the goods of the impious, as a punishment inflicted through their spoliation [Note: [Col. 0660] The Vatican manuscript: “punishing through spoliation.”].

He is himself, and no other, who grants forgiveness to those who turn back. Yet he is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who repays the perversely according to their deserts to the third and fourth generation.

He is himself, and no other, who forgives the sins not of everyone, as this man says, but of those whom he foreknew and predestined.

He is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who avenged certain people’s sins through bodily deaths—not spiritual deaths—for the greater punitive anguish and terror of the soul, even among those who had not committed those sins, so that the mortal condition in which the living would shortly have to die might in this way also serve God’s providence and become useful for discipline.

He is himself, and no other, who did not forbid us to be angry altogether, since he himself was angry where it was appropriate; but he commanded us to be angry without sinning.

He is himself, and no other—not one who, as this man claims, investigates the reasons for vengeance, but one who, when he knows the time, takes notice of the causes that are to be judged [Note: [Col. 0660] Several manuscripts: “the causes that are to be judged.”].

He is himself, and no other, who warned us never to swear, so that, since we can be deceived, we might be far from perjury by not swearing.

He is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion, who, when he judged it necessary for rebuking unbelievers, confirmed the truth of his judgment even by swearing. Just as a human being, when swearing, calls upon God as witness, so God calls upon himself.

He is himself, and no other, who commanded us to stand firm in faith in the true word.

He is himself, and no other, contrary to this man’s opinion—not one who changed his will, as this man blasphemes, but one who changed the things he willed without changing his will.

He is himself, and no other, who taught us the way of truth. He is himself also the God of the Prophets, [Col. 0661] who never, as this man falsely accuses him, deceives his own people with false promises.

He is himself, and no other, who commanded us to be blameless. He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who never, as this man accuses him, reproached himself, nor did anything ever cause him repentance as it does a human being. Rather, he foretold, in human speech addressed to human beings, the future alteration of things which he had foreknown from eternity he would alter, without any alteration in himself.

He is himself, and no other, who also commended to us in the Gospel that God’s anger is to be feared. He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who called not an emotional disturbance of his mind but a just and severe vengeance by the name of anger or indignation.

He is himself, and no other, who did not wish one person merely to be harmed by another, but to be harmed unjustly. He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who, whether through human beings or through holy angels, usefully punished or terrified those whom he willed, even by temporary bodily deaths.

He is himself, and no other, who taught that a woman should not be looked upon in order to desire her (Matt. 5:28). For he is the one who also said in the Law, ‘You shall not covet’ (Exod. 20:17). Nor did he, as this man accuses him, impose seven wives upon each man; he permitted chaste marriages for the sake of procreation. He himself not only did not make fathers marry their daughters, but also prohibited it, as he prohibited other incestuous unions.

He is himself, and no other, who taught us that, according to the inner renewal of the spirit of the mind, there are in him neither males nor females, and promised that we would be with him forever like the angels.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who joined male and female in marital chastity for the propagation of the race and showed that second marriages, which are also permitted in the New Testament, are lawful. He commanded men to take in marriage the wives of brothers who had died without children, in order to raise up offspring for the deceased—not from lust but from pious devotion. But he altogether prohibited fathers from entering into marriage with their daughters [Note: [Col. 0661] Perhaps: “for the deceased.”].

He is himself, and no other, who commanded us spiritually to tread upon every kind of serpent.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who, to signify the sins by whose poison the unbelieving people were dying invisibly, sent visible serpents to warn them, and represented the corrective plague of deaths of the soul by deaths of the body.

He is himself, and no other, who said, ‘Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you’ (Luke 11:41). He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who commanded such things through the voice of the Prophets.

He did not wish the firstborn sons of human beings to be sacrificed to him, but to be consecrated, signifying the Firstborn from the dead, in whom all were destined to be freed from perpetual death.

He is himself, and no other, who preferred incorruptible things to corruptible foods.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who willed that sacrifices he did not need should precede as shadows of the future sacrifice, and who, with the severity of discipline, avenged sacrileges committed by bodily deaths—deaths far milder than the eternal punishments of Gehenna.

He is himself, and no other, who did not, as this man says, command earthly riches to be condemned, but placed spiritual and heavenly riches above them.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who makes some rich by giving most generously and others poor most justly, either by not giving or by taking away.

He is himself, and no other, who commanded us to pray for our enemies. [Col. 0662]

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who, contrary to this man’s accusation, not only never wished children to be sacrificed to him by the hands of their parents, but also established in the Law that this should not be done.

He is himself, and no other, who made known that everyone should be treated well without respect of persons.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who, whenever he commanded people to be killed without distinction of age or sex, knows what compensation in good he granted them after death. Who knows what he granted them, when by their deaths he either corrected or terrified the living?

He is himself, and no other, who commanded us to endure injuries with equanimity and to forgive them.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who established eye for eye and tooth for tooth as the limit of punishment, so that no one would think that more vengeance was owed than the injury he had suffered. This was because it is said of God’s wisdom that she carries Law and mercy upon her tongue. We would not knowingly forgive our debtors their due debts through mercy unless through the Law we discerned those very debts [Note: [Col. 0662] Several manuscripts: “unless we learned those very debts.”].

He is himself, and no other, who, humbling himself in such great power in order to convert us, became human and spoke with human beings.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who spoke with the first fathers. For this reason he said that there is no other God besides him: because the highest Trinity also is one God, while the distinction of the persons remains [Note: [Col. 0662] In the same manuscripts: “the individuality of the persons.”].

He is himself, and no other, who commanded his Apostles to give freely what they had received freely. Yet, for their support, he decreed that they should not take another tunic with them because he immediately added: ‘For the laborer is worthy of his wages’ (Matt. 10:8–10), so that those who proclaimed the Gospel might live from the Gospel (I Cor. 9:14). He also showed that offerings ought to be made to God, who needs nothing, and that by accepting offerings he contributes more.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who forbids his own people to accept gifts by which the eyes of judges are blinded, and who himself, although he has no need, accepts gifts in order to enrich the souls of those who offer them through their piety.

He is himself, and no other, who healed a man on the Sabbath, showing that the time had already come for the day to breathe forth according to the prophecy of the Song of Songs and for the shadows to be removed (Song 2:17).

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who commanded that the man gathering wood on the Sabbath be stoned, because he had not yet distinguished the times of the two Testaments [Note: [Col. 0662] Several reliable manuscripts: “not because he had distinguished the times of the two Testaments”], but had contemptuously and impiously despised God’s Law. Through his bodily death—which, who could doubt, would shortly come to every human being—God established a fear of obedience that would benefit the others.

He is himself, and no other, who said that he had come for the salvation of human beings.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who in just judgment hardens whom he wills, as in the Gospel: ‘He came for judgment, not only so that those who do not see may see, but also so that those who see may become blind’ (John 9:39) [Note: [Col. 0662] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “who, as he says in the Gospel, came into the world not only…”].

He is himself, and no other, who gave us commandments of eternal life.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who gave holy, just, and good commandments to the proud, who trusted not in his grace but in their own strength—not commandments by which they would live, but by which they would die, [Col. 0663] so that they might be convicted.

Thus, as one of the Apostles says, they were the good odor of Christ both among those who were being saved and among those who were perishing: to some an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death (II Cor. 2:15–16).

He is himself, and no other, who appeared as the salvation of the diseased, giving movement to the lame, speech to the mute, hearing to the deaf, and light to the blind.

He is himself also the God of the Prophets, who not only heals these same disorders with the greatest mercy, but also most justly inflicts them. No one should therefore, through an equally impious folly, think him contrary to Christ and call this one good but Christ evil, because this one caused dry wood, supported by no root, to produce flower and fruit on Aaron’s staff, whereas Christ dried up a tree by a curse because he found no fruit on it, although it was not yet the season for figs.”

## CHAPTER XII

38. When he says that one is the father of peace and charity and another the author of war and anger—wishing Christ to be understood as the former and the God of the Law and the Prophets as the latter—this foolish man can say that Christ himself is contradictory, or that there were two Christs rather than one, opposed to each other: one who said, “I give you peace” (John 14:27), and another who said, “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). This is especially so because he is displeased when good things are represented by the names of evil things.

But when he says that one is privy to incest and adulteries while another is the lord of chaste purity and holiness, let him understand the devil as the former. Let him know that the God of the Prophets is no less the lord of chastity and holiness than Christ, because the God of the Apostles is himself also the God of the Prophets—earlier than them in time but their companion in faith. He is the God, in both Testaments, of righteous actions and pious prayers; he is the author, in both, of religious sacrifices.

39. Consider, then, how he has wanted to prove that the disorders of human bodies belong not to God the creator but rather to the devil. For in the Gospel the Lord says of the woman whom he healed that Satan had bound her for eighteen years; therefore she was bent over and could not straighten herself (Luke 13:11–16). This is as though Satan, although he always desires to do harm, could harm anyone unless he had received power from the Almighty.

For what else has been revealed—not only in the Book of Job, which this man certainly does not accept, but more clearly in the Gospel itself—where the unclean spirits would not even enter the pigs unless the gracious Savior himself, at their request, granted them this, although he could have sent them into the abyss (Matt. 8:31–32)? He wished to teach us something necessary: namely, that they have much less power to harm human beings by their own authority when they could not harm even animals of whatever kind.

The good God can grant them this power through a hidden justice; he cannot grant it unjustly.

40. Next, this man wants to twist to his purpose what the Apostle said about the coming and impious exaltation of the Antichrist, so that we should understand the God of the Prophets himself to be meant. Rather, he is thereby refuted, because the Apostle said that the man of sin, the son of destruction, who exalts himself above every god and above everything that is worshiped, will [Col. 0664] sit in the temple of God (II Thess. 2:3–4). That temple belongs to the true God, in whose temple that false one will sit.

This man also belongs to him, for under the name of Christ—which is the name of God—he wishes to appear to be a Christian while exalting himself against Christ. He shows himself to be an antichrist, not the one great Antichrist above all others, but one of those about whom the evangelist John says: “Now many antichrists have arisen” (I John 2:18).

He was speaking of heretics who had already begun to exist in the times of the Apostles. They began to arise after the Lord Jesus Christ’s ascension into heaven, beginning with that magician Simon whom we read of as having been baptized in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 8:13). After him there were several of his disciples, later successors following earlier ones in the same impiety. The fourth in their succession was Basilides [Note: [Col. 0664] The old Remigian manuscript: “Bassilides.”], who was the first to dare to say more openly that the God worshiped by the Jewish nation was not the true God.

After these there was also a certain Carpocrates, who denied that this visible world was created by the supreme God, saying instead that it was created by certain demonic powers [Note: [Col. 0664] In the manuscripts: “powers of gods.”]. He also denied that God had given the Law through Moses.

Later Cerdon arose, who is found to have been the first to say that there were two gods, one good and the other evil, long before the heresy of the Manichaeans emerged, whose error in this frenzied delirium is better known. Marcion was a disciple of this Cerdon. Apelles also taught such things.

There were also certain Patricians, or are still [Note: [Col. 0664] Lov.: “who still exist.” Other printed editions: “or are.” The manuscripts agree, but in place of “Patricians” they read “Patricians” with a variant spelling.], deriving from a certain Patricius and similarly opposing the ancient divine books.

All these people openly hold opinions against the God of the Law and the Prophets—that is, against the true God, by whom the world was made. This man belongs to some heresy of theirs, for I do not think that he is a Manichaean.

41. But whatever heretical error he or some Fabricius—whose disciple he boasts of being—belongs to, as far as the book you sent is concerned, I think he has been answered sufficiently. The supports of his madness have been thrown down, and from those supports all the blasphemies he wrote in that volume had sprouted, branching out in varied loquacity with most impious curses and insults against God.

To strike all their branches one by one would have taken too long; the roots themselves had to be cut away. If you review what we wrote against the Manichaean Faustus and against Adimantus, who is said to have been a follower of Mani while Mani was alive, you will find much there that is equally effective against this man. Perhaps, if those writings were read, it would have been not at all, or at least not very much, necessary to write this.

42. After the end of the book, in which, at its conclusion, he commends the small number of people who share his error—because wisdom evidently belongs to only a few, a claim common to all heretical opponents of the Catholic Church, which is spread throughout all lands in abundant fertility—for all of them glory in their small numbers, and seek the multitude so that they may be able to seduce it [Col. 0665] [Note: [Col. 0665] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “and seek the multitude if they can seduce it.”]—after this conclusion of the book, another beginning appears, perhaps by the same author, but certainly belonging to the same error.

He had begun to argue that the flesh had a creator other than God. Since he said very little, however, what had been begun was brought to an end at the very outset. But whether the author himself or the copyist of the manuscript was unable to complete what he had begun, I do not know.

Nevertheless, we have already written much against the Manichaeans about this madness of people who do not consider what they are saying. At the beginning of this very work, moreover, foundations have been laid which, as I think, are sufficient for a prudent and devout reader to understand that the flesh should not be removed from God’s works because the nature of the spirit is superior; nor should these temporal things be considered evil because eternal things are rightly preferred to them; nor should earthly goods be detested because heavenly goods are better. God created all things good: great in great things, [Col. 0666] but not small in small things.

The other work that had begun to be written in the same manuscript is the work of Adimantus, that disciple of Mani who was called Addas by his personal name [Note: [Col. 0666] So the older manuscripts. The printed editions have: “who was called Addas by his proper name.”]. In it, testimonies from both Testaments are produced as though they were mutually contrary, through a slippery deceitfulness, as though this were thereby demonstrated: that both could not come from one God, but that one came from another.

Against this wicked contrivance we wrote long ago, as I mentioned shortly before, and I believe you possess the work itself. There are, however, a few passages at the end of Adimantus’s work to which I did not reply. For certain matters arose, as commonly happens, which seemed more urgent, and those passages consequently remained interrupted. But, as I said, there are only a very few at the end, and, if the Lord wills, I shall take care to explain them as soon as possible.

## [AGAINST THE PRISCILLIANISTS AND ORIGENISTS]

[Col. 0665]

# CONSULTATION, OR OROSIUS’S MEMORANDUM TO AUGUSTINE ON THE ERROR OF THE PRISCILLIANISTS AND ORIGENISTS

[Note: [Col. 0665] “For the subsequent writings,” see Book 2, chapter 44 of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 648, beginning with the words “Among these”—these matters, whether periods or little works, including Orosius’s *Consultation* on the Priscillianists and Origenists, which Augustine testifies that he answered, fall approximately in the year of Christ 415—through col. 649, beginning with the words “Son Orosius.” M.] (C, S)

To the most blessed father, Bishop Augustine, Orosius.

1. I had indeed already brought this matter to Your Holiness’s attention, but I was planning to present a memorandum concerning it when I perceived that your mind was free from the other necessities of dictation. But since my lords, your sons, the bishops Eutropius and Paul, moved by the same concern for the salvation of all as I, your young servant,

[Note: [Col. 0665] Perhaps “presbyter.”]

have already submitted a memorandum concerning several heresies, though they did not indicate them all, it was necessary for me to publish this hurriedly, gather together in one place all the trees of destruction, with their roots and branches, and offer them to your fiery spirit, so that, when you have seen the multitude and examined the wickedness, you may determine what arrangement of strength you can apply.

[Note: [Col. 0665] The Vatican codices read: “what disposition you can employ in applying your zeal for virtue.”]

You, most blessed father, must only tear out and cut down the evil plantings or grafts of others, and scatter the true seed, which we shall water from your springs. I call God to witness and hope for the growth of your work, because that soil which, now cultivated insincerely, produces ungrateful fruits will, if you visit it by dispensing and filling it with that stored manna which you possess,

[Note: [Col. 0665] The printed editions read: “produces [them] in sincere cultivation, if, by dispensing to it that stored [reading uncertain] which you possess.” This is corrected with the aid of the Sigiramnensis, or Saint-Cyran, manuscript.]

[Col. 0666]

eventually advance toward a hundredfold fruit through a more freely poured abundance.

Through you, our Lord God—through you, I say, blessed father—may those whom he chastised with the sword be corrected by the word. I was sent to you by God; from you, through him, I hope for help, as I consider how it came about that I should come here. I recognize why I came: without desire, without necessity, without consent, I left my homeland, driven by some hidden force, until I was brought to the shore of this land. Only here did I recover the understanding that I had been commanded to come to you.

Do not judge me presumptuous if you receive me as one who confesses. Make me a capable merchant for my beloved mistress,

[Note: [Col. 0666] The printed editions read “my beloved master.” The manuscripts, however, read “my beloved mistress”: namely, his homeland, to which he longs to return.]

having found the pearl (Matt. 13:46), so that I may not return as a fugitive slave after having squandered my substance. We have been torn apart more grievously by wicked teachers than by the most bloodthirsty enemies. We confess the offense; you see the wound. Grant us, with the Lord’s help, the medicine that alone remains.

I shall therefore briefly show both what, having previously been badly planted, has recovered, and what, later grafted in more wickedly, has prevailed.

2. Priscillian was more pitiable than the Manichaeans in this respect first of all:

[Col. 0667]

he confirmed his heresy from the Old Testament as well, teaching that the soul, which was born from God, comes forth from some storehouse, declaring before God that it would fight, and being equipped through the encouragement of angels. Then, descending through certain circles, it is seized by evil principalities and forced into different bodies according to the will of the victorious prince, with a bond written against it.

Hence he also maintained the power of astrology, asserting that Christ had dissolved this bond and fastened it to the cross through his Passion. Priscillian himself says in one of his letters:

> “This is the first wisdom: to understand, in the forms of souls, the natures of the divine powers and the arrangement of the body. In this arrangement heaven and earth appear bound, and all the principalities of the age appear constrained to overcome the arrangements of the saints. For the Patriarchs hold the first circle of God and the divine bond of souls to be sent into the flesh, fashioned by the agreements of angels, God, and all souls; they possess it against the work of the formal army”—and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0667] Only the Lovaniensis edition has “which.”]

He further taught that the names of the Patriarchs were members of the soul, because Reuben was in the head, Judah in the chest, Levi in the heart, and Benjamin in the thighs—and similar things. Conversely, he arranged the signs of the zodiac among the members of the body: the ram in the head, the bull in the neck, the twins in the arms, the crab in the chest, and so on.

He wanted it to be understood that the eternal darknesses existed and that the prince of the world proceeded from them. He also confirmed this from a certain book entitled *The Memoirs of the Apostles*, where the Savior seems to be secretly questioned by the disciples and to show that, concerning the Gospel parable which says, “A sower went out to sow his seed” (Matt. 13:3), the sower had not been good. He argued that, if he had been good, he would not have been negligent, and the seed would not have fallen either beside the road, among the rocky places, or in uncultivated ground. He wished it to be understood that this was the sower who scattered captured souls into whatever different bodies he wished.

That same book also contains many statements about the prince of the waters and the prince of fire, with the intention of making it understood that all good things are accomplished in this world by craft, not by God’s power. For he says that there is a certain virgin light, which God, wishing to give rain to human beings, displays to the prince of the waters. When the latter desires to seize it, he is agitated, sweats, and produces rain; and when deprived of it, he arouses thunder with his bellowing.

He spoke of the Trinity in word alone. For while asserting a union without any existence or distinct property, he said that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were one Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0667] The Vatican manuscripts read: “with the Father removed, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.]

3. Then two fellow citizens of mine, Avitus and another Avitus, when the truth itself had already exposed such shameful confusion unaided, sought foreign lands. One went to Jerusalem, the other to Rome. On their return, one brought back Origen, the other Victorinus. Of these two, one yielded to the other; nevertheless, both condemned Priscillian.

We know little about Victorinus, because, almost before his works had been published,

[Col. 0668]

a follower of Victorinus yielded to Origen. Many impressive claims from Origen therefore began to be put forward, which the truth itself would soon surpass on the basis of a small opportunity.

For we learned a sufficiently sound doctrine concerning the Trinity; that everything that was made was made by God; that everything was very good; and that everything was made from nothing. Then came sufficiently sober explanations of the Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 0668] In the same codices: “a sufficiently sober explanation of all these matters,” and so forth.]

All these teachings were immediately accepted by the wise, after a faithful cleansing of the earlier errors. Only the offense concerning creation from nothing remained. They had been persuaded to believe that the soul exists; yet they could not be persuaded that it had been made from nothing, arguing that a will could not come from nothing.

This position remains almost to the present.

[Note: [Col. 0668] The Vatican codices read: “remains even now.”]

But these two Aviti, together with the holy Greek Basil, who taught these things most blessedly,

[Note: [Col. 0668] The Sigiramnensis manuscript reads: “taught these most blessed things.”]

transmitted certain incorrect doctrines from Origen’s own books, as I have recently come to understand.

[Note: [Col. 0668] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “as they now understand very clearly.”]

First, they said that all things had always existed as made in God’s wisdom, before they appeared in their actual forms and particular modes, using this expression: “For God did not begin to make whatever he made by making it.”

Next, they said that angels, principalities, powers, souls, and demons have one origin and one substance; and that a place was assigned to an archangel, a soul, or a demon according to the quality of its merits, using this expression: “A lesser fault earned a greater place.”

They said that the world was finally made for the purpose of purifying the souls that had previously sinned. They further preached that the eternal fire by which sinners are punished is neither real fire nor eternal, saying that “fire” meant the punishment of one’s own conscience.

They also said that “eternal,” according to the Greek etymology, does not mean everlasting, adding Latin testimony because Scripture says “unto eternity” and “unto the age of the age” (Ps. 9:6 and elsewhere), and places these expressions after “eternal.” Thus, they asserted that all sinful souls would return, after the purification of their consciences, into the unity of Christ’s body.

They also wished to make this claim about the devil, though they did not prevail in doing so: since the good substance created in him cannot perish, once his wickedness had been completely burned away, the devil’s substance would eventually be saved.

Concerning the Lord’s body they taught the following: when the Son of God came down to us after so many thousands of years, he had not been idle until then, but had preached the remission of sins to angels, powers, and all the higher beings. By assuming the quality of the form of those whom he visited, he passed through to the palpability of flesh in the appearance of an assumption.

[Note: [Col. 0668] The editions of Amerbachius and Erasmus read: “in a more substantial appearance, by this Passion,” and so forth.]

They concluded this by his Passion and Resurrection, and then said that, as he ascended until he came to the Father, he again became more tenuous. Thus, they said, his body was never laid aside,

[Note: [Col. 0668] The Vatican manuscripts, together with Amerbachius and Erasmus, read “anywhere.”]

nor was God, reigning in any body, confined within it.

They also said that the creature subject to corruption, though unwillingly so, should be understood to include the sun, moon, and stars; and that these are not elemental lights but rational powers. They render service to corruption “because of him who subjected it in hope” (Rom. 8:20).

4. This, insofar as I have been able, I have briefly set forth, so that, once all the diseases have been surveyed, you may hasten to apply the medicine. The truth of Christ is in me: because of the venerable reverence I bear Your Holiness, I would not dare to be presumptuous unless I recognized, by the evident judgment and arrangement of God,

[Col. 0670]

that you had been chosen to bring remedies to that great and remarkable people, upon whom, as a sinful people, a wound has been imposed and for whom, after the wound, a cure is owed; and that I had been sent.

Be mindful of me, most blessed father, and of the many who, like dew, await your word to descend upon them. Deign to remember us.

[Col. 0669]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ADDRESSED TO OROSIUS AGAINST THE PRISCILLIANISTS AND ORIGENISTS

[Note: [Col. 0669] Written in the year of Christ 415.]

[Note: [Col. 0669] The book *To Orosius against the Priscillianists and Origenists* has been corrected from two Vatican manuscripts, five Gallican manuscripts—the Colbertinus, Sorbonicus, Sigiramnensis, two Victorini—and from the older editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0669] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

## CHAPTER ONE

1. In answering you, my beloved son Orosius, I neither ought to address everything that you set forth in your memorandum, nor ought I to address nothing at all. Otherwise I might appear to have despised your zeal, which is most pleasing to me, and thereby offend through lack of restraint.

In some of our little works, which you have either read or will be able to read, many things have been said that can stand against the heresy of the Priscillianists, although I did not set out specifically to refute them. Rather, while engaged in another task, I now understand that I dealt with this matter as well, since I have learned from you what they think.

For what I have discussed in many places against the Manichaeans concerning the soul—that, although it is immortal in a certain respect proper to it, it is nevertheless shown to be changeable, declining toward what is worse and advancing toward what is better—and by this is most clearly shown not to be of God’s substance, at the same time overturns the doctrine of Priscillian.

Once this single point is established most firmly—for it is utterly true, and each person, when reminded of it, readily recognizes it in himself—neither the one group nor the other can find material from which to weave its fables.

What need is there to go through the branches of a most talkative error that must be cut off, when it is a shorter task to dig up and eradicate its root? Especially since you yourself rejoice that those most fabulous ravings have already been refuted among you.

## CHAPTER TWO

2. But the question concerning the soul still continues to be debated: whether God should be said to have created it from nothing—since it is now established that it is neither a particle nor an emanation of him—because it seems harsh and impious to say that God’s will is nothing, by whose willing it was created.

This question does not, in fact, concern the refutation of Priscillian’s sacrilegious folly. For whether the soul was made from nothing, or whether this should not be said because it was made by God’s will, which certainly is not nothing, nevertheless, because it was made and is not God’s nature,

[Note: [Col. 0670] The manuscripts read: “because it has been made, it is not God’s nature.”]

that heresy is certainly refuted which insists that the soul was originally God’s nature, so that it may have a basis for composing whatever other falsehood it adds there.

[Note: [Col. 0670] In the Victorini and several other codices: “connecting whatever other falsehood it adds there.”]

Yet since we ought not to disregard or leave undiscussed this question as well, we must ask those who refuse to believe that the soul was made from nothing because they would thereby assert that God’s will, by which it was made, is nothing. We must therefore ask them whether they admit that no creature at all was made from nothing.

For if they think this, we must fear that they are attempting to introduce some other nature that is neither God nor nothing. Unless God had this nature as a kind of material subject to him, he could not find from what to make whatever he made.

When one asks, then, from what God made his creature, some material is being sought—just as a carpenter requires wood, or any body of material; if he does not have it, he will be entirely unable to make the things demanded by his craft.

When the answer is, “From nothing,” what is being answered except that no material was subject to him—material that he himself had not made—from which he might make something if he wished, and without which he would be unable to make it?

The material of the world, insofar as it can in some way be discerned among mutable things, was established by the one by whom the world was established. Therefore, even if God made or makes something from some other thing, he did not and does not make it from something that he himself did not make.

Accordingly, setting aside for a little while the nature of the soul, if they admit that God made something from nothing, let them observe and see that, whatever it is, he made it by his will. For he would not have made anything unwillingly. Yet they must not therefore say that this same will is nothing, simply because something was made from nothing by his will.

Why then are they afraid to say of the soul what they do not hesitate to say of other things? Or if they assert that only the soul was made by God’s will, while maintaining that he made the rest not by his will, what could be said more absurdly or more insanely? If everything he made he certainly made by his will, and yet, when we say this, we do not say that this will is nothing, let them accept the same point concerning the soul.

## CHAPTER THREE

3. For when it is said, “God made from nothing,” nothing else is being said except: “There was nothing from which he could make it, and yet, because he willed, he made it.”

So far is it from being the case that, in what he made from nothing, the will is called nothing, that it is especially commended. For Scripture says: “You have power whenever you will” (Wis. 12:18). Whether there is something from which a thing may be made or there is not, will is sufficient where power is supreme.

How, then, in the creation of something from nothing, can the will of the creator be declared to be nothing, when something can be created from nothing precisely because the creator’s will is sufficient for itself even without material?

If perhaps they wish to admit that no creature at all—not merely the soul—was made from nothing, on the grounds that whatever God made he made by his will, which certainly is not nothing, let them consider from what man was made with respect to the body.

Certainly, as Scripture testifies, God made him from clay or from the dust of the earth (Gen. 2:7), and without doubt he did so by his will. Yet God’s will is not dust or clay.

Therefore, just as in what was made from clay, although it was made by the will, the will is not clay, so in what was made from nothing,

[Note: [Col. 0671] Thus the manuscripts: “from nothing, although it was made by the will.”]

although it was made by the will, the will is not nothing.

## CHAPTER FOUR

4. As for the sorrowful matter you added—that people among you had slipped from the heresy of Priscillian into the error of Origen, and could not be healed of the former plague without the medicine itself introducing something diseased—this sorrow is not to be condemned. Truth ought to have driven out falsehood, not falsehood driven out falsehood; for changing an evil is not avoiding it.

Nevertheless, since you mention that those who brought Origen’s books to your region transmitted from them teaching concerning God himself, the creator of all creatures—that is, concerning the coeternal and immutable Trinity itself—which accords with the truth, consider that Priscillian restored against this truth the ancient Sabellian doctrine, in which the Father himself is said to be the Son and also the Holy Spirit.

He is worse in this respect as well: concerning the soul he thinks that it should not possess a nature of its own, but should flow down from God himself like a particle, and he dares to assert, with the Manichaeans, that it is so shamefully polluted and changed for the worse.

Your province therefore received no small benefit from those books, especially in the matter in which the gravest error is committed. For the false and wicked opinions concern the Creator, not the creature.

Whether, then, those who had strayed were restored to this faith,

[Col. 0672]

or whether those who did not yet know it learned it by reading those discussions, let them rejoice that they have learned what is sound.

As for the error that is also present in those books, although I now see that you have recognized it, you will nevertheless be able to learn better how to argue against such things in the place where the error itself both arose long ago and was exposed not long ago.

## CHAPTER FIVE

5. Nevertheless, insofar as I can, I also warn you not to presume to hold any opinion concerning the correction of the devil and his angels or their restoration to their former state.

This is not because we envy the devil and the demons, repaying their malevolence as though in kind, since they attempt to disrupt the paths by which we journey toward God, driven by no other motive than the goad of envy. Rather, it is because we must add nothing, on the strength of our own presumption, to the final judgment of the supreme and most truthful Judge.

For he himself foretold that he would say to those like them: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Nor should the fact that elsewhere it is written, “unto eternity and unto the age of the age” (Ps. 9:6), move us to take “eternal” here as meaning merely “long-lasting.”

The Latin translator did not wish to say, “unto eternity and unto the eternity of the eternal.” For since what is called αἰών (*aiōn*) in Greek can be translated both as “age” and as “eternity,” other translators more suitably rendered it, “unto the age and unto the age of the age.”

But this is not what was said where it says, “Go into the eternal fire.” For the word there is not αἰῶνα (*aiōna*), but αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*). If the latter had been derived from *saeculum* (“age”), it would be called *saeculare* in Latin, not *aeternum* (“eternal”); no translator has ever dared to say this.

Therefore, although in Latin *saeculum* may be understood as having some end, whereas *aeternum* is ordinarily applied only to what is without end; and although the Greek word αἰών (*aiōn*) is understood sometimes to mean “eternal” and sometimes “age,” nevertheless what is derived from this noun and called αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*) is not, in my judgment, ordinarily understood even by the Greeks as anything other than what has no end.

We, however, do not ordinarily use either αἰῶνα (*aiōna*) or αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*) except for “eternal.” We use αἰῶνα to mean “age” as well, but αἰώνιον only to mean “eternal.” Although some occasionally dare to say *aeternale* (“eternal” as a derived adjective), so that the Latin language may not appear to lack a derivative from the same noun.

6. Perhaps these people may indeed find, according to the usage of Scripture, something called αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*) that is not without end, just as God repeatedly says in the books of the Old Testament: “This shall be your eternal ordinance” (Exod. 28:43; Lev. 16:34, and elsewhere). The Greek text has αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*), although he often gave this command concerning such rites as were destined to have an end.

Yet, if the words are understood more carefully, perhaps the things signified by those rites were not destined to have an end. Thus, not to go farther afield, we call God eternal—not, of course, these two very short syllables, but what they signify.

The Apostle also spoke of “eternal times, previous and ancient” (2 Tim. 1:9), which in Greek reads πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων (*pro chronōn aiōniōn*, “before eternal ages”).

Writing to Titus, he says: “The hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal times” (Titus 1:2).

But since times viewed backward from the foundation of the world appear to have a beginning, how are they eternal unless he called “eternal” those things that have no time before them?

## CHAPTER SIX

7. Whoever prudently observes what was said—“Go into the eternal fire”—to mean that which has no end proves the point from the opposite side, in that same Gospel passage, by reference to the eternal life that the righteous will receive. For that life also has no end.

The passage concludes: “They will go into eternal burning; but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:41, 46). In both places the Greek has αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*).

If mercy urges us to believe that the punishment of the wicked will not be without end, what are we to believe about the reward of the righteous, when eternity is pronounced in both cases, in the same passage, in the same sentence, and with the same word?

Are we again to say that the righteous will fall from that sanctification and eternal life into the impurity and death of sinners? Far be this from the soundness of Christian faith.

Both, therefore, are called eternal—without end—that is, αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*), lest, while we grieve over the punishments of the devil, we should doubt the kingdom of Christ.

Finally, if “eternal” and “eternal” as a derivative—namely, αἰών (*aiōn*) and αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*)—are customarily used in Scripture in both senses, sometimes without end and sometimes with an end, what shall we answer concerning the prophet’s words: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24)?

Whatever punishment is signified by the names “worm” and “fire,” certainly, if it will not die and will not be extinguished, it has been foretold as without end. The Prophet was doing nothing else when he said this than foretelling it as without end.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

8. Concerning the kingdom of Christ as well—not according to the fact that in the beginning the Word was God with God (John 1:1), for no one has ever doubted that he is the King of all ages—but according to the assumption of humanity, the sacrament of the Mediator, and his incarnation from the Virgin, it is stated most openly that it will have no end.

The angel, speaking to Mary, the mother-to-be who would remain a virgin, says among other things:

> “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33).

In what respect will his kingdom have no end, except in respect of the fact that he will reign over the house of Jacob? For, because of the ambiguity of the word “forever,” he explained it by adding, “of his kingdom there will be no end,” lest anyone should understand “forever” here in the way that an age may at some time have an end.

Can the kingdom over the house of Jacob and on the throne of David be understood as anything other than the Church and that people who are his kingdom? Concerning this the Apostle also says: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15:24)—that is, when he has brought his saints to the contemplation of the Father, and certainly also to contemplation of himself, insofar as he is God, equal to the Father.

For he does not hand it over in such a way as to lose it himself, since the Father also granted the Son to have life in himself (John 5:26), and certainly the Father did not thereby lose it.

Accordingly, if his kingdom will have no end, surely his saints, who are his kingdom, will reign with him without end.

When the Apostle says in that passage, “Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father,” he signifies by “end” not something that destroys but something that perfects. Thus it is said: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4)—the point at which the law is perfected, not abolished.

He signifies the same thing where he says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17).

## CHAPTER EIGHT

9. As for their claim concerning rational creatures—that is, holy angels, unclean demons, and the souls of human beings—that “a lesser fault earned a greater place,” I do not see with what immodesty they attempt to persuade the Church of Christ of this.

We therefore more rightly believe that God was not driven by the sins of rational spirits to construct the world, lest the absurd consequences follow: that we would have to possess two suns, or three, or four, or however many would be required,

[Note: [Col. 0674] The editions of Amerbachius and Erasmus have a great lacuna here, omitting more than sixty subsequent lines, which all our manuscripts nevertheless contain.]

if the free will of a great number of spirits had been preceded by a degree of guilt so great that they had to be enclosed in similar globes of heavenly bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0674] Thus the Vatican manuscripts. The Lovaniensis edition reads: “that two suns, or three, or four, or however many, would be necessary for you.”]

Rather, we believe that the world was made by God’s goodness: great and good, by the supreme and uncreated Good. In it all things were made very good according to their nature, with some things better than others, arranged in distinct degrees from the highest creatures to the lowest, so that everything might exist in this way, while the superior things would not exist alone, and might possess the number and limit that God, the creator of all natures, saw should be established in his own design. He did not learn that these things had been made; he knew that they were to be made.

Accordingly, what they say—that all things had already been made in his wisdom before they were brought forth into these forms and particular modes and appeared in their proper orders—is not soberly stated.

When would they have been made, before they were made? In God’s wisdom there could have been the principles or plans of all the things that were to be made, but the things themselves had not yet been made.

“All things were made through it”; it itself was not made as well, because it is the Word of whom it is said, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3).

God therefore knew all the things he made before he made them. We cannot say that he made things he did not know, and learned them only after they had been made; that he did not know what he was making, but knew what he had made. If we said this of any human craftsman, we would display the greatest foolishness.

He therefore knew them as things to be made, not as things already made; he knew them in order to make them, not because he had made them. Thus, although they were already known—for nothing can be made except by one who knows it—they did not begin to be made when they were known in order to be made, but only afterward, when those things were made that had been known beforehand so that they might be made correctly.

[Note: [Col. 0674] This passage has been restored from the Sigiramnensis manuscript: “that had been known beforehand so that they might be made.”]

10. Since the truth—which neither forms opinions about what it does not know nor deceives anyone—promises that our purification, or rather our perfection, will take place even after the resurrection of spiritual bodies, unto equality with the angels (Luke 20:36), how can those very holy angels, to whom we shall be equal when fully purified, be said still to require purification from their sins?

And since God promises a new heaven and a new earth as the dwelling place of the saints, purified from every stain of this age (Isa. 66:22), with what audacity can it be asserted that the world—that is, heaven and earth—would not have existed except for the necessity of purifying rational spirits, who would be in heaven or on earth only on account of the merits of their sins?

What need, then, do those who have been purified have of a new heaven and a new earth, if they are restored to be as they were before, without heaven and earth?

If this were altogether true, we ought to direct our hope toward what Scripture promises, even until that time. And if from there we were to be transferred to something better, we would learn this much more reasonably after having already been placed there than we would now rashly believe it and even presumptuously attempt to teach it.

What could be more absurd than to say, “Heaven and earth would not exist unless the structure of the world were necessary for the purification of spirits,” when Scripture promises another heaven and another earth for those who have been purified?

11. As for the sun, moon, and the other stars, we see that they are heavenly bodies; we do not see that they are animate. Let this be read in the divine books, and we shall believe it.

For the testimony from the Apostle’s Epistle that you said they commonly cite can also be understood as referring to human beings alone. For every kind of creature exists in each human being—not universally, as heaven and earth and all that is in them do, but in a certain generic way.

For there is in each person the rational element, which angels are either proved to possess or are believed to possess; and, so to speak, the sensory element, which beasts also possess—for they use both their senses and sensory impulses to seek what is useful and avoid what is harmful; and there is the vital element deprived of sensation, such as can be observed in trees.

For bodily growths occur in us without our sensation: even hair does not feel when it is cut, and yet it grows.

The bodily creature itself is even more evident in us. Although it has been made and formed from earth, it nevertheless contains certain particles from all the elements of this bodily world, in a proportion suitable to health.

Our limbs are invigorated by heat, which comes from fire, whose light also flashes through the eyes. The passages of the veins—which are called arteries—and the breathing passages of the lungs are filled with air. If there were no moisture, no secretions would gather, and dryness would consume life.

Even the blood itself, flowing in a moist stream and filling other veins, is spread through the whole body like channels and rivers.

Thus there is no kind of creature that cannot be recognized in a human being. And so the whole creation groans and suffers in him, awaiting the revelation of the children of God (Rom. 8:22–23). Through the resurrection of the body, the whole creation—though not in every human being—will nevertheless be freed from slavery to corruption, because the whole is present in each individual.

And if this passage of the Apostle’s letters can be understood in some other and better way, it still does not follow from the same words that we should believe the sun, moon, and stars groan together until, at the end of the age, they are freed from slavery to corruption.

[Col. 0676]

## CHAPTER NINE
12. Indeed, since I said, “Let it be read in the divine Books, and we believe it,” perhaps what those who assert these things customarily produce from the Book of holy Job may mislead you, where it is written: “How can a human being be righteous before the Lord, or how can one born of a woman cleanse himself? If he commands the moon, and it does not shine, and the stars are not pure before him, how much more is a human being corruption, and the son of man a worm?” (Job 25:4–6). From this they wish it to be understood that the stars possess rational spirits and are not free from sin, but that they are in the heavens because a lesser fault earned a greater or better place.

I do not think this opinion should be accepted as possessing divine authority. For Job himself did not utter it—Job to whom a singular testimony is given by God, namely, that “he did not sin with his lips before the Lord” (ibid. 1:22)—but one of his friends, who are all called “comforters of evils” (ibid. 16:2) and were rejected by the divine judgment. Just as in the Gospel, although it is entirely true that certain things were said, not everything that is reported as having been said is therefore believed to be true—for the truthful Scripture of the Gospel testifies that many false and impious things were said by the Jews—so also in this book, where many persons are reported to have spoken, we must consider not only what is said but also by whom it is said. Otherwise, by accepting indiscriminately whatever has been written in any part of the holy book, we would be compelled to confess—God forbid—that the things which the foolish woman suggested to her holy husband were true and just, when she urged him to say something against God so that he might be freed by death from that intolerable punishment (ibid. 2:9).

I do not say this because those friends, rejected by the Lord and rightly reproved by that holy servant of God, could not have spoken anything true, but because not everything they said should be considered true. Although they said nothing true against Job [Note: [Col. 0676] Manuscripts: “Although, therefore, they said nothing true against Job.”], someone who knows how to distinguish wisely what has been said can nevertheless take even from their words some sound opinion as a testimony to the truth. But when, in seeking confirmation for something, we wish to have the testimony of the holy Scriptures, we must not be told that we should also believe what is written in the Gospel merely because the evangelist happens to report that it was said by someone who is not worthy of belief.

For there the Jews said to the Lord Christ: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8:48). We abhor this voice all the more because Christ is dearer to us; nevertheless, we cannot doubt that it was uttered by the Jews, since we believe the Gospel narrative to be altogether truthful. Thus we neither detract from the evangelist’s credibility in writing this nor fail to execrate the blaspheming voice of the Jews.

Nor do we grant canonical authority even to impious and wicked people alone, but also not to those who are little more than children in faith—still inexperienced and uneducated—who may happen to be recorded as speaking there. For when the man whose eyes the Lord had opened, though born blind, says, “We know that God does not hear sinners” (ibid. 9:31), we must not therefore accept this statement as having evangelical authority in such a way that we resist the Lord’s own words in the Gospel. By a divine utterance he confirmed that the man who said, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner,” went down from the Temple more justified than the Pharisee who recounted and vaunted his own righteousness (Luke 18:10–14).

Nor should this newly enlightened man in the flesh be angry that we have said that, at the beginning of his faith—when he still did not know who had healed him—he uttered the less carefully considered statement that “God does not hear sinners.” For the Apostles themselves, chosen above the rest, clinging to the Lord’s side [Note: [Col. 0677] Thus with the manuscripts: “the Apostles themselves, chosen above the rest of the Lord and clinging to his side.”] and hanging upon his words, are found to have said many things that must be rejected. To recount them would be lengthy; indeed, blessed Peter deserved not only to be reproved for some of his words but even to be called Satan (Matt. 16:23).

## CHAPTER X

13. As for the comparison with God’s righteousness, if even the holy angels in heaven are said not to be righteous, the opinion does not seem to me inappropriate—not because they fell away from righteousness in order to become what they are, but because they were made, and are not God, and therefore cannot possess as much spiritual light as the one by whom they were made. For supreme righteousness is where there is supreme wisdom; and this is God, of whom it is said, “To the only wise God” (Rom. 16:27). But it is a different question how much of his righteousness the angels apprehend and how much they do not apprehend. For by participation in him they are righteous, but in comparison with him they are not righteous.

## CHAPTER XI

14. But, as I said, that is one question; another concerns the stars, the sun, and the moon—whether they possess rational spirits within those visible and luminous bodies. Anyone who doubts that these are bodies does not understand what a body is at all. Nor does this matter greatly to us, so that we should investigate with the utmost diligence things remote from our senses and from the understanding of human weakness, and not so set forth in the Scriptures that knowledge of them has been entrusted to us.

Indeed, lest through rash suspicion we rush into sacrilegious fables, divine Scripture cries out: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too strong for you; but what the Lord has commanded you, think upon always” (Ecclus. 3:22). Thus reckless presumption seems more deserving of blame in these matters than cautious ignorance.

Certainly the Apostle says: “Whether Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or Powers” (Col. 1:16). I therefore firmly believe that Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers exist among the heavenly orders, and I hold with unquestioning faith that they differ from one another in some respect. But, lest you despise me—the person you think a great teacher—I do not know what these are or how they differ from one another.

Nor do I think that this ignorance places me in danger in the same way as disobedience would, if I were to neglect the Lord’s commands. For this reason, I think that through the authors of our faith, the writers of the holy Scriptures, these matters were not fully explained but only touched upon and briefly indicated, so that if something of this kind should perhaps be revealed through a higher revelation to someone such as we are, he would not think that those through whom the holy proclamations of the canonical Scriptures were supplied to us had been inferior.

For the more anyone advances in knowledge, the more he will find himself beneath those Scriptures which God has established like a firmament above all human hearts. It is therefore not necessary to be wise beyond measure, but to be wise with moderation, according as God has apportioned to each one a measure of faith (Rom. 12:3).

Perhaps more learned men will teach you these things, if you bring to them as great a desire to learn as you have concern for knowing, lest you suppose unknown things to be known, and lest you believe what ought not to be believed or fail to believe what ought to be believed. Rather, that one Teacher—the true one—will teach you, whether through them or by whatever means he wishes: he who sees inwardly that you labor for his Church, and who has also bestowed this upon you within. He will disclose the truth more fully, since he perceives the one who knocks with the love he has deigned to grant.

[Note: [Col. 0678] Here the treatise ends in the better manuscripts. The approximately thirty verses added thereafter in the printed editions had been transferred here from the end of Augustine’s letter to Jerome, formerly number 28, now 166.]

[Col. 0677]

# THE OTHER WRITINGS OF AUGUSTINE AGAINST THE PRISCILLIANISTS ARE AS FOLLOWS:

## IN VOLUME II

Letter 237, to Bishop Ceretius.

## IN VOLUME VI

The book *Against Lying*, addressed to Consentius.

## [AGAINST THE SERMON OF THE ARIANS]

[Col. 0677]

# The Sermon of the Arians (C, S)

The numbers have therefore been marked at the individual passages so that, when the response begins to be read, whoever wishes may attend to whether an appropriate and careful answer has been given to each passage; for the response itself also contains the same numbers, by which it becomes clear to which passage each answer is directed.

[Col. 0677] 1. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God, the firstborn of the whole creation.

[Col. 0678] 2. Established by the will of God and his Father before all ages.

[Col. 0679] 3. By the will and command of that same one, he made heavenly and earthly things, visible and invisible things, bodies and spirits, from things that did not exist, so that they might exist, by his own power.

4. And before he made the universe, he had been established as God and Lord, king and creator of all things that were to be, possessing in his nature foreknowledge of all future things, and, in making them, awaiting the Father’s command in everything. By the Father’s will and command he descended from heaven and came into this world, as he himself says: “For I did not come of my own accord, but he sent me” (John 8:42).

5. And because, on account of the quality [Note: [Col. 0679] Thus the manuscripts.
