The printed editions instead read, “weakness.”] and frailty of the body, the human being appeared to have been made a little lower than the angels, inferior to all the spiritual and rational orders (Ps. 8:6), so that he would not consider himself worthless and despair of his salvation, the Lord Jesus, honoring his own work, deigned to assume human flesh and showed [Note: [Col. 0679] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions: “to show.” Manuscript reading.] that the human being is not worthless but precious, as it is written: “A great human being and a precious man” (Prov. 20:6, according to the Septuagint). And therefore he deigned to make the human being alone heir to his Father and co-heir with himself, so that what he had received to a lesser degree in nature he might possess to a greater degree in honor.

6. “When,” he says, “the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman” (Gal. 4:4). He who by the Father’s will assumed flesh also by his will and command lived in the body, as he himself says: “I have descended from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). By the Father’s will he was also baptized at the age of thirty and manifested by the Father’s voice and testimony (Luke 3:21–23). By the Father’s will and command he preached the Gospel of the kingdom of heaven, as he himself says: “I must preach the Gospel to the other cities also; for this is why I was sent” (ibid. 4:43); and, “He himself gave me a command concerning what I should say or what I should speak” (John 12:49). And thus by the Father’s will and command he hastened toward his passion and death, as he himself says: “Father, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. 26:39). And as the Apostle asserts and says: “He became obedient,” he says, “to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

7. While hanging on the cross, by the Father’s will and command he left the human flesh which he had assumed from the holy virgin Mary in the hands of human beings, and entrusted his divinity into the Father’s hands, saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). For Mary gave birth to a body destined to die, whereas the immortal God begot an immortal Son. Therefore Christ’s death is not a diminution of his divinity but a laying aside of the body. Just as his birth from the virgin was not a corruption of his deity [*dealitatis* in the text], but an assumption of a body, so also in his death there was not suffering or failure of his deity, but a separation of his flesh. For just as one who tears a garment does injury to the person wearing it, so also those who crucified his flesh inflicted an insult upon his divinity.

8. He who by the Father’s will and command fulfilled the whole dispensation also by the Father’s will and command raised his body from the dead; and with that same body, as a shepherd with his sheep, a priest with his offering, a king with his purple robe, and God with his temple, he was taken up by the Father into glory.

9. He who by the Father’s will descended and ascended, by the Father’s will and command sits [Note: [Col. 0680] Here and below the manuscripts read “sat.”] at his right hand, hearing the Father say to him: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1). He who by the Father’s will and command sits at his right hand will by the Father’s will and command come at the consummation of the age, while the Apostle cries out and says: “The Lord himself,” he says, “will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thess. 4:15).

He who by the Father’s will and command will come will by the Father’s will and command judge the whole world in righteousness and repay each person according to his faith and works, as he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”; and again: “As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:22, 30). Hence, even in judging, he places the Father’s presence first and sets his own divine dignity and power second, saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34). Therefore the Son is the just judge; but the honor and authority of the one judging consist in the imperial laws of the Father, just as the Spirit’s dutiful advocacy and consolation consist in the dignity of the only-begotten God, the just judge.

10. Therefore the Son was begotten by the Father; the Holy Spirit was made through the Son.

11. The Son proclaims the Father; the Holy Spirit announces the Son.

12. The Son’s first and principal work is to reveal the glory of the one who begot him; the first and principal work of the Holy Spirit is to manifest Christ’s dignity in human souls.

13. The Son is the Father’s witness; the Spirit is the Son’s witness.

14. The Son is sent by the Father; the Spirit is sent by the Son.

15. The Son is the Father’s minister; the Holy Spirit is the Son’s minister.

16. The Son is commanded by the Father; the Holy Spirit is commanded by the Son.

17. The Son is subject to the Father; the Holy Spirit is subject to the Son.

18. The Son does what the Father commands; the Holy Spirit speaks what the Son orders.

19. The Son worships and honors the Father; the Holy Spirit worships and honors the Son. The Son himself says: “Father, I have glorified you upon the earth; I have completed the work that you gave me” (John 17:4). And concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:14).

20. “The Son can do nothing of himself” (ibid. 5:19), but in everything awaits the Father’s nod. The Spirit does not speak of himself, but in everything awaits Christ’s command: “He will not speak of himself,” he says, “but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come” (ibid. 16:13).

21. The Son intercedes with the Father for us; the Spirit petitions the Son for us.

22. The Son is the living and true, proper and worthy image of the Father’s entire goodness, wisdom, and power; the Spirit is the manifestation of the Son’s entire wisdom and power.

23. The Son is not a part or portion of the Father, but his proper and most beloved, perfect and complete only-begotten Son. The Spirit is not a part or portion of the Son, but the first and principal work of the only-begotten God, above all the rest of the universe.

24. The Father is greater than his Son; the Son is incomparably greater and better than the Spirit.

25. The Father is God and Lord of his Son; the Son is God and Lord of the Spirit.

26. The Father begot the Son willingly, without movement or suffering; the Son made the Spirit by his own power alone, without labor or fatigue.

27. The Son, as a priest, worships his God, and is worshiped by all as God and creator of all things. The Father alone worships no one, because he has neither a greater nor an equal whom he should worship. He gives thanks to no one, because he has received a benefit from no one; in his goodness he gave to all that they might exist, while he himself received what he is from no one.

Therefore this is the distinction of three substances—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and the difference of three realities: the unbegotten God, the only-begotten God, and the Spirit who is the Advocate. The Father is God and Lord of his Son, and of all things that were made through the Son’s power by the Father’s will. The Son is his Father’s minister and high priest, but is Lord and God of all his own works, the Father willing.

28. And just as no one can pass to the Father without the Son, so no one can worship the Son in truth without the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Son is worshiped in the Holy Spirit.

29. Through the Son the Father is glorified.

30. The work and care of the Holy Spirit are to sanctify and preserve the holy; and not merely rational beings, as some think, but also to sanctify many irrational beings; to restore those who have fallen through their own negligence to their former state; to teach the ignorant; to admonish those who forget; to reprove sinners; to encourage the sluggish; to make them think about their salvation and act diligently for it; to lead those who have gone astray back to the way of truth; to heal the weak; to restrain the frailty of the body through the vigor of the soul; to strengthen them in the love of piety and chastity; and to enlighten all.

Above all, he grants faith and love to each person, distributing grace for the benefit of each according to zeal and diligence, sincerity and simplicity of mind, the measure of faith, and the merit of one’s manner of life; and he assigns each person to that work in which and to that purpose for which he is suited.

31. He is other than the Son in nature and order, rank and affection, dignity and power, might and operation, just as the Son, in nature and order, rank and affection, divine dignity and power, the only-begotten God, is other than the unbegotten God.

32. It is therefore impossible for the Father and the Son to be one and the same—the one generating and the other being born; the one to whom testimony is given and the one who gives testimony; the greater and the one who confesses that he is greater; the one who sits and stands at the right hand and the one who grants the honor of sitting; the one who was sent and the one who sent him; the disciple and the teacher, as he himself taught, saying, “As the Father taught me, so I speak” (John 8:28); the like and imitator and the one whose likeness he is and whom he imitates [Note: [Col. 0682] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice editions: “and the one whom he imitates.” Manuscript reading.]; the one who prays and the one who hears; the one who gives thanks and the one who blesses [Note: [Col. 0682] Erasmus, Lyons, and Louvain editions give the passage as follows: “And the one who prays to the one who hears; and the one who gives thanks to the one who blesses.” Manuscript reading.]; the one who received a command and the one who gave a command; the minister to the one who commands; the supplicant to the eminent; the subject to the superior; the firstborn to the eternal; the only-begotten to the unbegotten; the priest to God.

33. But God, without beginning, also knew beforehand that he would become the Father of the only-begotten God, his servant. He never knew beforehand that he would become God, because he is unbegotten, and never began either to know beforehand or to know. For what is foreknowledge except knowledge of future things? The Father, by begetting the Son, was himself named by the Son; and when the Son revealed him, he was known by all Christians as the God and Father of the only-begotten God, and was shown to be greater than the great and better than the good.

34. And because the Homoousians say that our Savior spoke all these things concerning the Father’s foreknowledge and his own subjection by way of humility, whereas we Christians believe that he spoke all these things because the Father commanded and the Son obeyed, we say and prove that the heretics are convicted and reproved by their own statements.

For if he humbled himself, that very humility demonstrates his obedience; and that obedience declares that one is above in eminence and the other subsists in subjection, as the Apostle says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. 2:8). His very humility is truth, not falsehood. For who, or when, among the wise is content to humble himself unless he has someone greater and better whom he hastens to please through humility? “And I,” he says, “always do the things that please him” (John 8:29). Once, before all ages, he was born by the will of God; he performs all things according to his will.

But if he humbled himself and lied—God forbid—and if the truth lies—which is impossible—where would anyone seek the truth? Yet the truth neither lies nor changes; for he came for this purpose, to teach the truth. He is not a teacher of ignorance but a master of truth, as he himself said: “Do not call yourselves masters upon the earth; for one is your master, Christ” (Matt. 23:10).

But if they say that, because of his incarnation, he humbled himself upon the earth and spoke these things for the sake of human beings, let us show them that the testimonies concerning the Son’s subjection found in the Scriptures are greater and firmer than those concerning what takes place in the Gospel.

If he humbled himself upon earth for the sake of human beings, and did not, as an obedient and subject son, serve his Father with incomparable love and thanksgiving—for to the degree that he is exalted in power, to that degree he is humble in service—why did he obey when commanded before he assumed flesh? And why, now sitting at the right hand of God, does he intercede for us (Rom. 8:34)? And why, while present in the body upon earth, did he promise that he would ask the Father in heaven on our behalf, saying, “And I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Advocate” (John 14:16)?

And if, despite all this, they still refuse to believe because of the hardness and blindness of their hearts, and dare to say that all these things are done for the sake of humility, then after the consummation of the age—if he did not know himself by nature and will to be subject and obedient—why would he humble himself, when humility is not necessary for the sake of human beings?

Moreover, after the consummation of the age, when all things have been subjected to him (1 Cor. 15:28)—for now, in nature, all things are indeed subject to him, as creation is subject to the Creator, but by their will, on account of free choice, we see that not all things are subject to him—then, on the day of judgment, when at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue will confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:10–11) [Note: [Col. 0684] Manuscripts: “to the glory of God the Father.”], all things will be subject to him forever, both by will and by nature.

And he himself, after all things have been subjected to him, remaining in that subjection and love in which he has always remained, will himself, as Son, be subject to the one who subjected all things to him. No Christian who hears this is ignorant that “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10:17). Thus God may be all in all, always possessing monarchy and power over all things—to him be glory and honor, praise and thanksgiving, through his only-begotten Son, our Lord [Note: [Col. 0684] Manuscripts: “God.”] and Savior, in the Holy Spirit, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0683]

# THE ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST THE SERMON OF THE ARIANS [Note: [Col. 0683] Written in the year of Christ 418.]

[Note: [Col. 0683] We have seen eight Gallican manuscript codices of this little work: the Sorbonicus, Cermanensis, Corbeiensis, Pratellensis, Michaelinus, Sagiensis, one belonging to the Church of Reims, and one belonging to the lord of Maran of Toulouse, in addition to four Vatican manuscripts. We also consulted the variant readings of three Belgian manuscripts and the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0683] We further compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. In this treatise I answer the preceding argument of those who, although they do indeed confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is God, refuse to confess that he is true God and one God with the Father. They introduce for us two gods of different and unequal nature: one true, the other not true—contrary to what is written: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6:4).

If they wish this to be understood as spoken of the Father, it follows that Christ is not our Lord God. But if it is spoken of the Son, the Father will not be our Lord God. If it is spoken of both, then plainly the Father and the Son are our one Lord God.

Accordingly, what is written in the Gospel, “That they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3), must be understood as though he had said: “That they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent as one true God.” For the Apostle John also says of Christ: “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

2. Again, when they say that Christ was established by the will of God and his Father before all ages, they are compelled to confess that the Son is coeternal with the Father. For if there was once a time when the Father existed without the Son, there was some time before the Son during which the Father alone existed. And how could the Son have existed before all ages, if there was a time before him when the Father existed without him?

Furthermore, if the Son existed before all times—for otherwise the words “In the beginning was the Word” and “All things were made through him” cannot be understood (John 1:1, 3), since time itself cannot exist without some movements of creation, and therefore we confess that times too were made through the one through whom all things were made—then without doubt the Son is coeternal with the Father.

But they say that he was established by the Father’s will, refusing to say that he is God from God, equal, begotten, and coeternal. Nowhere, however, do they read that the Son was established by the Father’s will before all ages. They say this for the purpose of making the Father’s will, by which they wish him to have been established, appear prior to him.

Their argument is usually as follows: they ask whether the Father begot the Son willingly or unwillingly. If the answer is that he begot him willingly, they say, “Then the Father’s will is prior.” But who could say that he begot him unwillingly? Yet, so that they may recognize how empty their words are, they themselves should also be asked whether God the Father is God willingly or unwillingly. For they will not dare to say that he does not wish to be God.

If, then, they answer that he is God willingly, their own absurdity must be brought back upon them, since it could be said that his will is prior to him. What could be more foolish than that?

## CHAPTER TWO

3. Next they say that, by the will and command of the Father, he made heavenly and earthly things, visible and invisible things, bodies and spirits, from things that did not exist, so that they might exist, by his own power. Here we ask them whether he himself was also made by the Father from things that did not exist—that is, from nothing.

If they will not dare to say this, then he is God from God, not made by God from nothing. This fact indicates that the Father and the Son have one and the same nature. For human beings, cattle, birds, and fish can beget offspring of their own nature, but God could not?

But if, in so great a plunge into impiety, they will dare to rush headlong into saying that the only-begotten Son too was established by the Father from nothing, let them ask through whom the Son was made by the Father from nothing. For he could not have been made through himself, as though he already existed before he was made, so that he himself might be the one through whom that same self was made. And what need was there to make him who already existed? Or how was he being made so that he might exist, when he already existed before he was made?

Furthermore, if he was made by the Father through some other being, who is that other being, since all things were made through him? But if he was made by the Father through no one, how was anything made by the Father through no one, when all things were made through the Son—that is, through his Word?

## CHAPTER THREE

4. “And before he made,” they say, “the universe, he had been established as God and Lord, king and creator of all things that were to be, possessing in his nature foreknowledge of all future things, and, in making them, awaiting the Father’s command in everything. By the Father’s will he descended from heaven and came into this world, as he himself says: ‘For I did not come of my own accord, but he sent me’” (John 8:42).

I wish they would say whether they establish two creators. If they do not dare to do so—for there is one, since “from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36), and the Trinity itself is one God, just as it is one Creator—what do they mean when they say that the Son created all things at the Father’s command, as though the Father did not create but commanded the Son to create?

Let those who think carnally consider in what other words the Father gave a command to the one Word. In the fantasy of their hearts they fashion for themselves something like two beings, positioned close to one another but nevertheless established in their own places: one commanding and the other obeying. They do not understand that the Father’s very command that all things should be made is nothing other than the Father’s Word, through whom all things were made.

That the Father sent the Son cannot be denied. But let them consider, if they can, how he sent him while he himself came with him. Or did he lie who said, “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32)?

But however they wish to understand the sending, does the Father’s sending and the Son’s being sent make their nature different? Unless perhaps a human father can send a human son of one and the same substance, while God cannot—although a human being sent by another human being is separated from the one who sends him, whereas God cannot be separated.

Yet fire sends forth its radiance, and the radiance that is sent cannot be separated from the fire that sends it, although even this comparison, since it concerns visible creation, is not in every respect comparable to the matter at hand. For when fire sends forth its radiance, the radiance travels farther than the fire itself reaches. Thus, if the radiance sent forth by the fire in a lamp could speak, it could not truthfully say on a wall, where it reaches without the fire of the lamp, “The fire that sent me is with me.” But the Son, sent by the Father, could say, “The Father is with me.”

Since, therefore, the Father’s sending of the Son is wholly ineffable and cannot be grasped by any thought, they cannot show from it that the Son is of another and inferior essence. Indeed, not even a human being sent by another human being demonstrates that the nature of the sender and the one sent is different.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Here, however, this too can be understood: the Son is said to have been sent by the Father precisely because the Son appeared to human beings in the flesh, whereas the Father did not. For who is sent to a place where he is? But where is the Wisdom of God—which is Christ—not present? Of this Wisdom it is written: “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

Since, therefore, the Son too is everywhere, where was he to be sent, where he was not already present, except by appearing as one who was not appearing? Yet we also read that the Holy Spirit was sent, although certainly he did not assume human nature into the unity of his person.

Nor was he sent by the Son alone, as it is written, “When I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7), but also by the Father, as it is written, “Whom the Father will send in my name” (ibid. 14:26). This shows that neither the Father without the Son nor the Son without the Father sent the Holy Spirit, but that both sent him together. For the works of the Trinity are inseparable.

The Father alone is not read of as having been sent, because he alone has no author by whom he was begotten or from whom he proceeds. Therefore, not because of a diversity of nature—for there is none in the Trinity—but because of that very authority, the Father alone is not said to have been sent.

For radiance or heat does not send fire; rather, fire sends either its radiance or its heat. Although these things are very dissimilar, nothing is found either among spiritual or bodily creatures that can rightly be compared with that Trinity which is God.

## CHAPTER FIVE

5. They also say: “And because, on account of the quality and frailty of the body, the human being appeared to have been made a little lower than the angels, inferior to all the spiritual and rational orders (Ps. 8:6), so that he would not consider himself worthless and despair of his salvation, the Lord Jesus, honoring his own work, deigned to assume human flesh and to show that the human being is not worthless but precious, as it is written: ‘A great human being and a precious man’ (Prov. 20:6, according to the Septuagint). And therefore he deigned to make the human being alone heir to his Father and co-heir with himself, so that what he had received to a lesser degree in nature he might possess to a greater degree in honor.”

By saying these things, they wish it to be understood that Christ assumed human flesh without a human soul. This is the particular heresy of the Apollinarians. But in the arguments of these people also—that is, the Arians—we have discovered that they hold not only that the natures of the Trinity are different, but also that Christ does not possess a human soul. This will become more evident in what follows in the present discussion.

For now, we answer the words of theirs that we have set forth by asking them to recall that, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, the statement “You made him lower than the angels for a little while” (Heb. 2:7) is understood of Christ. Let them see that the words “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28) do not apply to a diversity or inequality of the nature of the Father and the Son, but rather to the fact that, in the form of a servant, because of the weakness in which he was able to suffer and die, he was made lower even than the angels.

## CHAPTER SIX

6. They also say: “‘When,’ he says, ‘the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman’ (Gal. 4:4). He who by the Father’s will assumed flesh also by his will and command lived in the body, as he himself says: ‘I have descended from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’ (John 6:38). By the Father’s will he was also baptized at the age of thirty and manifested by the Father’s voice and testimony (Luke 3:21–23). By the Father’s will and command he preached the Gospel of the kingdom of heaven, as he himself says: ‘I must preach the Gospel to the other cities also; for this is why I was sent’ (ibid. 4:43); and, ‘He himself gave me a command concerning what I should say or what I should speak’ (John 12:49). And thus by the Father’s will and command he hastened toward his passion and death, as he himself says: ‘Father, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will’ (Matt. 26:39, 59). And as the Apostle asserts and says: ‘He became obedient,’ he says, ‘to the Father unto death, even death on a cross’ (Phil. 2:8).”

What do they attempt to persuade us by these testimonies of the holy Scriptures except that the Father and the Son have different natures because the Son is shown to be obedient to the Father? Yet they certainly would not say this of human beings. For if a human son is obedient to his human father, the nature of the two is not therefore different.

## CHAPTER SEVEN
Although this very statement of Jesus—“I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38)—may be referred to that first man, Adam (of whom the Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” [Rom. 5:12]), who, by doing his own will and not the will of him by whom he was made, made the entire human race, through a corrupted succession, subject to guilt and punishment. Therefore, conversely, he through whom we were to be liberated did not do his own will, but the will of him by whom he was sent. For in this passage “his own will” is spoken of in such a way that it is understood to be a will opposed to God’s will. For when we obey God, and by that obedience are said to do his will, we do not do so unwillingly but willingly; and therefore, if we do it willingly, how do we not do our own will? Only because Scripture calls that our will which it understands to be a will opposed to God’s will.

Adam possessed this will, so that in him we might die; Christ did not possess it, so that in him we might live. For this can rightly be said of human nature, [Col. 0688] in which, through disobedience, there arose a will of its own that was opposed to God’s will. But as regards the Son’s divinity, the Father and the Son have one and the same will; it cannot in any way be different where the whole nature of the Trinity is immutable.

But in order that Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, himself human (1 Tim. 2:5), might not do a will of his own that is opposed to God, he was not merely human but God and human: by that marvelous and unique grace, human nature could exist in him without any sin. For this reason, then, he says, “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me”: the reason for such great obedience was that the human being whom he bore was entirely without sin, because he had come down from heaven—that is, he was not merely human but also God.

He thus shows that there is one person in both natures, that is, in the nature of God and of the human being, lest, if one makes them two, a quaternity should begin to exist instead of a Trinity. Since, therefore, there is a dual substance but one person, the statement “I came down from heaven” refers to the excellence of God; while what is added, “not to do my own will,” refers, because of Adam who did his own will, to human obedience. Christ, that is, God and human, is both of these; yet the obedience in him, which is contrary to the disobedience of the first human being, is commended according to the fact that he is human. Hence the Apostle says: “For just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one human being the many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19).

## CHAPTER VIII

Nor, because he said “of a human being,” did he separate God, who assumed the human being; for, as I said—and this deserves very emphatic affirmation—there is one person. For that one Christ is always the Son of God by nature, and the Son of a human being, assumed in time by grace. He was not assumed in such a way that he was first created and then assumed; rather, he was created through the very act of assumption.

Accordingly, because the unity of the person in both natures must be understood, the Son of Man is also said to have descended from heaven, although he was assumed from the Virgin who had been on earth; and the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he suffered these things not in that divinity by which he is the Only-begotten, coeternal with the Father, but in the weakness of human nature.

For we read that the Son of Man himself said that he had descended from heaven: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John 3:13). We all also confess in the Creed that the Only-begotten Son of God was crucified and buried. Hence there is also the Apostle’s statement: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

The blessed Apostle demonstrates this unity of the person of Christ Jesus our Lord, constituted from both natures—divine, of course, and human—in such a way that either nature shares its designation with the other, the divine with the human and the human with the divine. He was exhorting us to merciful humility by the example of Christ:

“Have this mind among yourselves,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:5–8).

Since the name “Christ” belongs to him on account of what is written in prophecy, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8), and since what pertains to his becoming human is expressed in the words “taking the form of a servant” and “found in appearance as a human being”—an appearance that certainly began in time—nevertheless it was of this same Christ that it was said, “Although he was in the form of God.” Clearly, before he received the form of a servant from him, he was already in the form of God. At that time he was not yet the Son of Man but the Son of God, for whom equality with the Father was not something seized but his nature.

He was not exalted by usurpation; he was born as this, and therefore it was true. Christ, then, was not yet what he began to be when he emptied himself—not by losing the form of God, but by taking the form of a servant.

But if we ask, “Who is the one who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized?” the apostolic voice answers us: “Christ Jesus.” Therefore that divinity also received the name of this humanity.

Likewise, if we ask who was made obedient unto death, even death on a cross, the most correct answer is: “The one who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized.” Therefore this humanity also received the name of that divinity.

Yet it is evident that the same Christ, a giant of two substances, is obedient in one respect and equal to God in another; in one respect the Son of Man and in another the Son of God; in one respect he says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and in another, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); in one respect, “He does not do [Note: According to the editions of Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, “does”; M.], his own will, but the will of him who sent him” (John 6:38), and in another, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (John 5:21).

## CHAPTER IX

7. They continue and say:

“While hanging on the cross, he, by the will and command of the Father, left in the hands of human beings the human flesh that he had assumed from the holy virgin Mary, and commended his divinity into the hands of the Father, saying, ‘Father, into your hands I commend my spirit’ (Luke 23:46). Since Mary gave birth to a body destined to die, while the immortal God begot an immortal Son, Christ’s death is not a diminution of divinity but a laying aside of the body. For just as his birth from the virgin was not a corruption of his deity [*dealitas*] but an assumption of a body, so in his death there was not suffering and diminution of his deity [*dealitas*] but a separation of his flesh. For just as one who tears a garment does injury to the person wearing it, so those who crucified his flesh inflicted insult upon his divinity.”

[Note: In this passage and the next, as well as above in the *Sermo Arianorum*, the printed editions generally have *deitatis* (“of deity”), whereas the old manuscripts consistently have *dealitatis* (“of deality”).]

Behold how plainly, in these words of theirs, they altogether reveal that they deny that the human soul also belongs to the unity of Christ’s person, confessing in Christ only flesh and divinity. For when he was hanging on the wood, in the statement “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” they want us to understand that he commended divinity itself to the Father, not a human spirit, that is, a soul.

[Col. 0690] Rightly, then, in this very discussion above, when they wanted Christ to be understood as having done the Father’s will, not his own, and therefore thought him to be of a lesser and different nature, they recalled his statement, “Father, let this cup pass from me; yet not what I will, but what you will”; but they did not want to recall his statement, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:39, 38).

Let them therefore hear these passages when we recall them: “My soul is sorrowful unto death”; “I have authority to lay down my soul” (John 10:18); “No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his soul for his friends” (John 15:13); and what the Apostles understood to have been prophesied about him: “For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld” (Ps. 15:10; Acts 2:31; 13:35).

Let them not resist these and similar testimonies of the holy Scriptures, but admit that Christ united not only flesh but also a human soul to the Only-begotten Word, so that there might be one person—what Christ is: Word and human being; and the human being himself, soul and flesh; and therefore Christ, Word, soul, and flesh. Thus he must be understood as having two substances, divine and human, so that the human substance itself consists of soul and flesh.

Or, if they are troubled by the fact that it is written, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and that the soul is not mentioned there, let them understand that “flesh” is used in place of “human being,” with the whole signified by a part, as in the expression, “To you all flesh will come” (Ps. 64:3); likewise, “By works of the Law no flesh will be justified” (Rom. 3:20). In another place he stated this more plainly: “No one will be justified by the Law” (Gal. 3:11); and elsewhere, “A human being is not justified by works of the Law” (Gal. 2:16). Thus he said “all flesh” as if he had said “every human being.” In the same way it was said, “The Word became flesh,” as if it had been said, “The Word became a human being.”

Nevertheless, since these people want Christ the human being to be understood as possessing only human flesh—for they will not deny that he is a human being, of whom it is stated most plainly, “There is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5)—I am astonished that they do not agree that, because of this human nature in whatever sense, it could have been said, “The Father is greater than I,” and not because of that nature of which it was said, “I and the Father are one.”

For who could tolerate it if some human being, however great, were to say, “I and God are one”? And who would not accept it if a human being said, “God is greater than I”? What of the blessed John’s statement: “God is greater than our heart” (1 John 3:20)?

## CHAPTER X

8. They also say:

“He who fulfilled the whole dispensation by the will and command of the Father raised his body from the dead by the will and command of the Father; and with that body he was taken up by the Father into glory, as a shepherd with a sheep, a priest with an offering, a king with a purple robe, and God with a temple.”

Those who say these things must be asked what sort of sheep the shepherd brought back to the Father. For if the flesh he brought back is without a soul, what is this sheep except earth without sensation, which cannot even give thanks? For what can flesh accomplish without a soul?

## CHAPTER XI

9. They continue and say:

“He who descended and ascended by the will of the Father sat at his right hand by the will and command of the Father, hearing the Father say to him, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’” (Ps. 109:1).

“He who sat at his right hand by the will and command of the Father will come at the consummation of the age by the will and command of the Father,” as the Apostle cries out and says: “The Lord himself,” he says, “will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thess. 4:15).

“He who will come by the will and command of the Father will, by the will and command of the Father, judge the whole world in righteousness and repay each person according to his faith and works,” as he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”; and again, “As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous, because I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:22, 30).

Therefore, even in judging, he places the Father’s presence first and postpones his own divine dignity and power to a secondary position, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34). Thus the Son is the righteous judge; but the honor and authority of the one judging belong to the Father’s imperial laws, just as the Spirit’s dutiful advocacy and consolation belong to the dignity of the righteous judge, the Only-begotten God.

What we answered above is similarly valid against these claims. For the Son’s obedience to the Father’s will and command does not even among human beings demonstrate a different and unequal nature between the commanding father and the obedient son.

Moreover, Christ is not only God, by which nature he is equal to the Father; he is also human, by which nature the Father is greater, since he is not only his Father but also his Lord. Hence there is also that prophetic statement: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son’” (Ps. 2:7). There is the inferior substance by which the Father is greater, and the form of a servant whose Lord he is.

This form of his humanity, which he received while remaining in the form of divinity, so that he might be made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being (Phil. 2:6–7), will also appear in the judgment by which he will judge the living and the dead.

Therefore it was said of the Father that he will judge no one but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The ungodly will then see in Christ the form of the Son of Man by whom they are to be judged; of them it was said, “They will look upon the one whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10; John 19:37). But they will certainly not see the form of God in that same Christ, by which he is equal to the Father. Hence the prophecy preceded: “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10). For this also pertains to the statement, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Finally, he testifies to this most plainly when he says, “He gave him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27). Not because he is the Son of God—for according to this he is coeternal with the Father, and he and the Father have one and the same power—but because he is the Son of Man, which he began to be in time, so that authority might be given to him in time.

This is not said as though he himself had not also given it to himself—that is, as though the divine nature in him had not given authority to the human nature in him. Far be it from us to believe this. For how could the Father do anything except through the Only-begotten Son? Nor could he do so without the Holy Spirit, because the works of the Trinity are inseparable.

Accordingly, when he gave authority to the Son because he is the Son of Man, he gave it through that same Son to him because he is the Son of God. For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

Yet he honorably and appropriately attributes to the Father what he himself also does as God, because God is from the Father. He himself is God from God; the Father, however, is God, but not God from God.

## CHAPTER XII

“They heard from the Father,” they say, “‘Sit at my right hand’; and therefore he sat at the Father’s right hand,” as though he did this by the Father’s command and not also by his own power.

Unless this is understood spiritually, the Son will have the Father on his left. What, then, is the Father’s right hand except that eternal and ineffable blessedness to which the Son of Man also attained by receiving immortality of the flesh?

For if we wisely and faithfully understand the hand of God the Father—not according to bodily features, which do not exist in God, but according to effective power—what will we understand except the Only-begotten himself, through whom all things were made? Of him the prophet also said: “And the arm of the Lord—to whom has it been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1).

But how does the Son hear the Father? How are many words spoken by the Father to the one Word? How does he speak transiently to one whom he speaks steadily? How does he say something to him temporally when, in the one who is coeternal with him, all the things he says at their appropriate times already existed? Who would dare to ask such questions? Who could discover the answers?

And yet: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109:1); and because it was said, it was done. Therefore this already existed in the Word, which “became flesh” (John 1:14). And because it already truly existed in the Word before the flesh, it was effectively completed in the flesh; because it already existed timelessly in the Word, it was completed in the flesh at its appointed time.

In this flesh he ascended into heaven—the one who did not depart from heaven even when he descended from it; and in this flesh he sits at the right hand of the Father, the Father’s arm; and in this flesh he will descend for judgment, with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4:15).

## CHAPTER XIII

Here they want the Son’s power to appear lesser because he is said to descend at a command. But they must be asked: at whose command? If at the Father’s, they must again be asked by what temporal words the Father commands his eternal Word to descend from heaven.

For the very command of God, which will occur at its appointed time, already existed before all times in the Word of God himself. But if the Son of God descended from heaven by virtue of being the Son of Man, then by virtue of being the Word he is commanded, through himself, to descend from heaven.

For if the Father does not command through him, then the Father does not command through his Word—or else there will be another Word through whom the Only-begotten Word is commanded. And I wonder whether that Word would still be the Only-begotten if there is another.

There were indeed certain voices of the Father addressed to the Son in time, as when a sound came from the cloud: “You are my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17). Yet it was not so that the Only-begotten Son might learn anything through those words; rather, it was those who needed to hear in this way who learned.

Accordingly, even that sound of passing words was made for the Son by the Son; otherwise not all things were made through him. But when he is commanded to descend from heaven, will sounds and voices of this sort be necessary, through which the Son might learn the Father’s will? Far be it from us to believe this.

[Col. 0693] Whatever, then, it will be that must be done for the Son, the Father will do only through that same Son. It will be for him, certainly, because he is the Son of Man and was made among all things; but through him, because he is the Son of God, and through him all things are made by the Father.

But if, in the phrase “with a command, with the voice of an archangel,” they want the command to be understood as the archangel’s command, as the words themselves seem to sound, what remains for them except to call the Only-begotten Son even lesser than the angels, whose commands he is said to obey, if he is lesser because he is commanded by one who commands him?

Although the words “with a command, with the voice of an archangel” can also be understood in this way: the archangel’s voice itself is understood to be produced at God’s command; that is, the angel who is to be understood as the trumpet of God is commanded by the Lord God to emit his voice, which the lower creation will need to hear when the Son of God descends from heaven.

This is the trumpet of which he says elsewhere: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. 15:52).

## CHAPTER XIV

The Son therefore said, “As I hear, I judge” (John 5:30), either from the standpoint of human subjection, because he is also the Son of Man, or according to that unchangeable and simple nature which is the Son’s, yet is from the Father. In our case, when we hear, it is like receiving a word; for him, being the Word from the Father is equivalent to this.

For one may say that the Father gave the Word to the Son—that is, made him be the Word—in the same way that he is said to have given the Son life—that is, made him be life. For he himself says: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

This does not mean that he himself is one thing and the life that is in him another, but that the same person is the same life. Nor is the Father anything other than the life that is in him; but the Son did not give this to the Father, because he did not beget the Father. The Father, however, gave life to the Son by begetting him as life, just as he himself is also life.

But he did not beget the Word as though he himself were also the Word. When we say “life,” it can exist from no other source, as the Father’s life does—or, more explicitly, the Father is life, and he does not exist as life from another. But when “Word” is said, it can in no way be understood except as the Word of someone, specifically of the one from whom it is.

Therefore, just as the Son is God from God, light from light, life from life, so it cannot be said that he is Word from Word, since he alone is the Word. And just as it is proper to the Father to beget the Word, so it is proper to the Son to be the Word.

Thus he judges as he hears: because the Word is begotten so that the same Word may be truth, he judges according to truth.

## CHAPTER XV

For the works of the Father and the Son are the same—not because the Son is himself the same person as the Father, but because there is no work of the Son which the Father does not do through him, nor any work of the Father which he does not do through the Son working with him. “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does these same things” (John 5:19, 22). This too is an evangelical declaration, consequently uttered by the mouth of the Son himself.

Therefore the works of the Son are not one thing and those of the Father another, but these very same works; nor are they done dissimilarly by the Son, but similarly. But when not different yet similar works, but these very same works, are done by the Son as are done by the Father, what does “similarly” mean except with no unequal facility [Note: The printed editions read “capacity” (*facultate*); the manuscripts, however, “facility” (*facilitate*).] and no unequal power? For if both do these same things, but one does them more easily and powerfully than the other, the Son certainly does not do them similarly. But since they are both these same works and are done similarly, the Son’s works are certainly not other than the Father’s, nor is the power of those working different.

Nor, certainly, are they done without the Holy Spirit; for the Spirit is in no way separated from the works done by both. Accordingly, in a marvelous and certainly divine manner, the works of all are done by all, and even the works of each one by all. For heaven and earth and every creature are works of all. For it is said of the Son: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). But who would dare exclude the Holy Spirit from the works of any creatures whatever, when he sees him work the gifts of the saints, of which it is written: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing his own gifts to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11)? Finally, since Christ is Lord of all (1 Cor. 8:6) and God blessed above all for ever (Rom. 9:5), what work among all things can be denied also to the Holy Spirit, who wrought Christ himself in the Virgin’s womb? For when the Virgin said to the angel announcing the future birth, “How will this be, since I do not know a man?” she received the answer: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:34–35).

The works of each one, however, are said to be those which are manifestly related to each person. Thus none but the Son was born of the Virgin (Matt. 1:20–25); and the voice from the cloud, “You are my beloved Son,” belongs to the person of the Father alone; and the Holy Spirit alone appeared in bodily form, like a dove (Matt. 3:16–17). Yet the whole Trinity wrought both that flesh of the Son alone, that voice of the Father alone, and that form of the Holy Spirit alone. This is not because any one of them is incapable of completing without the others what he works, but because the operation cannot be divided where the nature is not only equal but also indistinguishable. Thus, although there are three and each of them is God, they are nevertheless not three gods. For the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; nor is the Son the same person as the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit the same as either Father or Son. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Spirit of both is never either Father or Son to either of them, but always the Spirit of both; yet the whole Trinity is one God.

Who, then, would deny that it was not the Father or the Holy Spirit, but the Son, who walked upon the waters (Matt. 14:25)? For it is the flesh of the Son alone [Note: The word “Son” is absent from the manuscripts.] whose feet were placed upon and borne over the waters. But far be it from us to believe that he did this without the Father, since he says universally of his works: “But the Father who abides in me does his works” (John 14:10); or without the Holy Spirit, since the casting out of demons was likewise a work of the Son. For it was the tongue of that flesh, belonging to the Son alone, by which the demons were commanded to depart; and yet he says: “In the Holy Spirit I cast out demons” (Matt. 12:28).

Likewise, who except the Son alone rose again? For he alone, having flesh, could die; yet the Father was not excluded from this work by which the Son alone rose again, concerning whom it is written: “Who raised Jesus from the dead” (Gal. 1:1). Or perhaps did he not raise himself? Then where is what he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19); and his statement that he has authority to lay down and take up again his soul (John 10:18)? And who would be so foolish as to think that the Holy Spirit did not cooperate in the resurrection of the man Christ, when he wrought the man Christ himself?

## CHAPTER XVI

There is something similar in the human being, although by no means comparable to the excellence of that Trinity which is God; for that is God, this a creature. Yet this too has something by which, in some fashion, what is said of that ineffable nature of God may be understood. For it was not said without reason, “Let us make man in your image,” as though the Father were speaking to the Son, or “in my image”; rather, it was said, “in our image” (Gen. 1:26). This is most rightly understood as spoken from the person of the Trinity itself.

Let us therefore consider these three things in the human soul: memory, understanding, and will. Everything we do is done by these three. And when these three are rightly and well ordered, everything we do is good and right—if forgetfulness does not deceive memory, error does not deceive understanding, and iniquity does not deceive will. For in this way we are reformed in the image of God. Every work of ours, therefore, is done by these three; for we do nothing which these three do not do together.

Further, when we speak of each separately, even what pertains to each is done by all. For the discourse we make about memory alone is not made by memory alone; understanding and will cooperate in it, although it pertains to memory alone. It is very easy to see the same thing in the other two. For whatever understanding says about itself, it does not say without memory and will; and whatever will says or writes about itself, it does not do without understanding and memory.

But to explain with the greatest precision how these are similar, and again how greatly dissimilar, to that immutable Trinity which is God would take long. I thought it necessary to mention this only so that I might draw something even from the creature, by which these people may understand, if they can, how not absurd it is to say concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit that inseparable works are done by all, not only works pertaining to all, but also those pertaining to each individually.

## CHAPTER XVII

Therefore the Son judges as he hears, whether because he is also the Son of Man, or because he is not from himself but is the Word of the Father. For what it is for us, when we hear, to receive a word, that is for him to be the Word from the Father. For one may say that the Father gave the Word to the Son—that is, that he might be the Word—in the same way as he is said to have given life to the Son—that is, that he might be life. For he himself says: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26). This certainly does not mean that he himself is one thing and the life in him another, but that he himself is that same life.

Likewise, the Father is not other than the life in him; but the Son did not give life to the Father, because he did not beget the Father. The Father, however, gave life to the Son by begetting him as life, just as he himself is life. But he did not beget the Word as though he himself were also the Word. For when we say “life,” it can be from no other, as is the Father’s life—or, more expressly, the Father is life, who does not exist from another. But when “Word” is said, it can in no way be understood except as someone’s word, namely, of the one from whom it is.

Therefore, just as the Son is God from God, light from light, life from life, so he cannot be said to be Word from Word, because he alone is the Word. And just as it is proper to the Father to beget the Word, so it is proper to the Son to be the Word. Therefore he judges as he hears, because just as the Word was begotten so that the same Word might be truth, so he judges according to truth.

## CHAPTER XVIII

His judgment is certainly just, because he does not seek his own will but the will of him who sent him (ibid., 30). By saying this, he wanted our attention to be directed to that human being who, by seeking his own will and not the will of him by whom he was made, did not have a just judgment concerning himself, but was himself subjected to a just judgment.

For he, while doing his own will and not God’s, did not believe that he would die; but this judgment of his was not just. Finally, he acted, and he died, because God’s judgment is just.

The Son of God exercises this judgment by not seeking his own will, although he is also the Son of Man. This does not mean that he has no will at all in judging—for what most foolish person would say that? Rather, his own will is not separate from the Father’s will.

If these people considered this, they would not, with carnal thoughts, arrange the powers or offices of the Trinity in unequal degrees, as though they were making three human beings of unequal and dissimilar dignity—as though the Father were an emperor, the Son a judge, and the Holy Spirit an advocate.

For they assert that the laws according to which the Son judges, as though they were imperial laws, belong to the Father. In these they establish the honor and authority of the Son as judge, while they say that the Holy Spirit’s dutiful advocacy and consolation belong to the dignity of the judge, that is, of the Only-begotten God—as though it were the dignity of a judge to have an advocate, just as it is the dignity of an emperor to send a judge who will judge according to his imperial laws.

Yet by this carnal conception they cannot demonstrate in these three persons the difference of nature, which is the subject of our greatest dispute with them. For when they refer these matters to human customs and do not depart from what they can grasp by thinking according to human practice—for “the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14)—what else do they remind us of except that an emperor, a judge, and an advocate are all human beings?

Accordingly, even if a judge is less powerful than an emperor, he is no less human. Nor is an advocate less human than a judge, even if by his office he appears subject to the judge.

Therefore, even if they conceive of a different power in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let them at least confess an equal nature. Indeed, what is more: they fabricate them as being in a condition even worse than the human condition.

For in human affairs it can happen that someone who has been a judge also becomes an emperor; but these people do not deign to grant this even to the unique Son of the Emperor in that Trinity. If perhaps, on the basis of human law or custom, they are excessively afraid of the charge of treason even in the case of the Son, surely they should concede to the advocate that he may at some point attain judicial power. They do not even want this.

The condition in that Trinity, then—far be such a thing—is worse than that of mortal human beings.

## CHAPTER XIX
Moreover, Holy Scripture, which measures these divine acts not by differences of powers but by the ineffable character of their works, also knows our advocate himself as judge, as the apostle John says: “If anyone should sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). He himself also indicates this when he says: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another advocate” (John 14:16). For the Holy Spirit would not be another advocate unless the Son also were one. Yet, to demonstrate that his works and the Father’s are inseparable, he says: “When I have gone, I will send him to you” (John 16:7), although elsewhere he says: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). Here it is shown that both the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit. Just as it is shown through the prophet that both the Father and the Holy Spirit sent the Son.

For who other than the Son, announcing his coming through Isaiah, says:

> “Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I shall call: I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heavens. I shall call them, and they shall stand together; all shall assemble and hear. Who announced these things to them? Loving you, I did your will concerning Babylon, so that the offspring of the Chaldeans might be removed. I spoke, I called, I brought him, and I made his way prosperous. Gather before me and hear these things; for I have not spoken in secret from the beginning. When they were happening there, I was present. And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:12–16).

What could be clearer? Behold, he himself says that he was sent by the Holy Spirit—the one who founded the earth and established heaven. Here the Only-Begotten is recognized, through whom all things were made.

As for the title “Comforter,” an office which these people assign to the Holy Spirit as though he were the lowest person in that Trinity, the Apostle says that the Spirit is God, as we read in his Epistle to the Corinthians: “The God who comforts the humble has comforted [Col. 0698] us through the presence of Titus” (2 Corinthians 7:6). God, therefore, is the comforter of the saints. They are indeed the humble; hence those three men in the furnace say: “Bless, you holy and humble of heart, the Lord” (Daniel 3:87). The Holy Spirit, then, who comforts the humble, is God. Accordingly, these people must either confess what they do not wish to confess—that the Holy Spirit is God—or, if they wish the Apostle’s statement to be understood as referring to the Father or the Son, they must cease separating the person of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son as though consolation were his distinctive function.

## CHAPTER XX

Now, when they try to show that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son because he is the Son’s advocate, as the Son is judge, they also, with astonishing blindness, place holy human beings above him. Concerning these the same Lord says: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). Let them answer there what the Holy Spirit will be: a judge alongside the Son, or an advocate before judges who are human beings.

But may such folly be absent from a faithful heart—that the Holy Spirit should be an advocate less than those judges—since those men, in order to be judges, are filled with the Holy Spirit, and by living according to him become spiritual. “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2:15). How, then, is the one who makes judges less than a judge, when he makes them members of that judge and his temple? The Apostle says: “Your bodies are members of Christ”; and again: “Your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you” [Note: [Col. 0698] Am. Er. and manuscripts: “the temple in you is the Holy Spirit,” omitting “who is in you.”] (1 Corinthians 6:15, 19).

And yet, if they read plainly in the holy Scriptures that King Solomon, at God’s command, built a temple of wood and stone for the Holy Spirit, they could not doubt that the Holy Spirit is God—to whom that great religious service, called *latria* (λατρεία), was legitimately offered among God’s people, so that a temple was even built for him—since the Lord says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13), where the Greek has *λατρεύσεις* (*latreuseis*, “you shall render latria/service”).

And they dare to deny that he is God who has not wood and stones but the members of Christ as his temple! For in this way they subject the Holy Spirit to Christ’s power, since Christ’s members are his temple—just as they subject the Son himself to imperial laws, although he is God’s Word, and in no way is an emperor’s word subject to laws, but rather makes laws [Note: [Col. 0698] Compare *Collation with Maximianus*, Augustine, no. 14.].

## CHAPTER XXI

**10.** These people, whose argument I received and to whom I am replying, do not dare to say that being made is the same as being begotten. They distinguish the two in such a way that they say the Son was begotten by the Father, but that the Holy Spirit was made by the Son. Yet they nowhere read this in the holy Scriptures, although the Son himself says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father.

**11.** “The Son,” they say, “proclaims the Father; the Holy Spirit announces the Son.” As though the Son had not announced that the Holy Spirit would come, or as though the Father had not also proclaimed the Son by saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5).

**12.** Accordingly, the Son reveals not only the Father’s glory, but the Father also reveals [Col. 0699] the Son’s glory; and the Holy Spirit manifests not only the Son’s dignity, but the Son also manifests the dignity of the Holy Spirit.

**13.** Therefore, just as the Son bears witness to the Father, so the Father bears witness to the Son; and just as the Holy Spirit bears witness to the Son, so the Son bears witness to the Holy Spirit.

**14.** The Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son; and the Son was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXII

**15.** “The Son,” they say, “is the Father’s minister; the Holy Spirit is the Son’s minister.” They do not notice that in this way they make the holy Apostles superior to the Holy Spirit. For when the Apostles say that they are ministers of God, these people surely will not deny that they are also ministers of God the Father. They became ministers of the one in whose name they baptized, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, according to their empty talk, the ministers of the Trinity will be superior if the Holy Spirit is less because he is the minister of the Son alone.

**16.** “The Son,” they say, “is commanded by the Father; the Holy Spirit is commanded by the Son.” They nowhere read this in the holy Scriptures. We do indeed read of the Son’s obedience according to the form of a servant, in which the Father is greater; not according to the form of God, in which he and the Father are one.

**17.** Thus the Son is read in the holy Scriptures as subject to the Father. For there is the form of a servant, in which he was also subject to human parents, as the Gospel says: “And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51). But nowhere does Holy Scripture say that the Holy Spirit is subject to the Son.

**18.** Accordingly, the Son performs what the Father commands because of the form of a servant; and the Son also performs what the Father performs because of the form of God. For he does not say, “Whatever the Father commands, the Son does”; rather, he says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John 5:19).

Moreover, if they say that the Holy Spirit speaks these things because the Son commands them, since it is written, “He will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:14), why does the Son not also speak the things commanded by the Holy Spirit, when the Apostle says: “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11), and when Jesus himself confirms that what is written about him was fulfilled: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me to evangelize the poor” (Luke 4:18, 21)?

For if he was anointed to evangelize the poor because the Spirit of the Lord was upon him, what did he evangelize to the poor except what he possessed from the Spirit with which he had been filled? For this too is written about him: that he was filled with the Holy Spirit (Luke 4:1).

## CHAPTER XXIII

**19.** “The Son,” they say, “worships and honors the Father; the Holy Spirit worships and honors the Son.” Here there is no need to distinguish scrupulously what difference there is between honoring and worshiping: these things are said of the Son because of the form of a servant. Let them say, if they can, where they have read that the Son is worshiped by the Holy Spirit.

For the evidence they introduce in an attempt to prove this—that it is written, “Father, I glorified you on earth; I completed the work that you gave me,” and, concerning the [Col. 0700] Holy Spirit, “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 17:4; 16:14)—has no bearing on the matter under discussion.

Everyone who worships honors, but not everyone who honors worships. For, according to the Apostle, brothers “outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12:10), yet they do not worship one another. Otherwise, if “to glorify” means “to worship,” let them say, if they please, that the Father also worships the Son—and this at the Son’s command, since the Son says to the Father: “Glorify me” (John 17:4, 5).

But when he said concerning the Holy Spirit, “He will receive from what is mine,” he himself resolves the question, lest anyone suppose that the Holy Spirit is from the Son in some sort of graduated manner, as the Son himself is from the Father, since both are from the Father—one being born and the other proceeding—and it is altogether difficult to distinguish these two within the sublimity of that nature.

Therefore, lest this be supposed, as I have said, he immediately added: “All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is mine’” (John 16:14–15). He clearly wished this to be understood as meaning that the Spirit receives from the Father. But he receives from what belongs to the Son because everything the Father has belongs to the Son. This is not a commendation of a difference in nature, but of one principle.

**20.** In this respect, the Holy Spirit does not speak from himself because he is not from himself but proceeds from the Father, just as the Son cannot do anything from himself because he too is not from himself, as I have already explained above. This does not mean that he waits in every matter for the Father’s nod; for he does not say, “Unless he sees the Father signaling,” but “what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19), in accordance with what we have already discussed.

But as for their claim that in all things the Holy Spirit waits for Christ’s command, let them read it, if they can. For what was said was, “He will not speak from himself”; it was not said, “Whatever he hears from me,” but, “Whatever he hears, he will speak” (John 16:13).

The reason for this statement has already become clear from the Lord’s explanation that I mentioned shortly before, where he says: “All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is mine.’” From where he will receive, from there unquestionably he will speak, because he hears from the source from which he proceeds. For the Word of God knows that the Spirit proceeds from the source from which the Word is born, so that the Spirit is jointly the Spirit of the Father and of the Word.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Nor should the future-tense verb “he will receive” trouble us, as though he did not yet possess it. Verbs of different tenses are used indifferently, although eternity is understood to remain without time. Thus he both received, because he proceeded from the Father; receives, because he proceeds from the Father; and will receive, because he will never cease proceeding from the Father. In the same way, God both is, was, and will be; yet he neither has had, nor has, nor will have any beginning or end of time.

## CHAPTER XXV

**21.** “The Son,” they say, “intercedes with the Father for us; and the Spirit makes petition to the Son for us.” Just as they read that the Son intercedes with the Father, in accordance with what we ourselves discussed above while recalling these passages, so let them find a source from which to produce the claim that the Spirit makes petition to the Son.

For when the Apostle says: “We do not know what we ought to pray for as we should, but the Spirit himself intercedes with inexpressible groanings; and he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to [Col. 0701] God” (Romans 8:26–27), however these people understand it—for it greatly concerns them to understand it as it ought to be understood—it was not said, “He intercedes with Christ,” or, “He intercedes with the Son.” Rather, “the Holy Spirit intercedes” was said because he makes us intercede.

Thus God says, “Now I know” (Genesis 22:12), as though he had previously been unaware. What else does this mean except, “I have made you know”? Hence also the Apostle’s statement: “But now that you have come to know God—or rather, to be known by God” (Galatians 4:9), lest they attribute to themselves the fact that they had come to know God.

According to this manner of speaking, it is said: “And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30)—that is, “Do not grieve us, who are grieved by you according to the Spirit of God.” They were grieved by love, which the Holy Spirit poured into their hearts (Romans 5:5), and through this love he himself made them sorrow over their brothers’ evils.

Finally, the same Apostle says: “You received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15); and elsewhere, recalling the same meaning, he says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6). How can the phrase “in whom we cry” and here “crying” have the same meaning, unless “crying” here means “making us cry”?

But let us accept “crying” according to their interpretation—as though the Spirit does not make us cry but cries himself. Behold: by saying “Abba, Father,” he does not intercede with the Son but with the Father. For they will certainly not dare to say that the Holy Spirit is Christ’s son. Indeed, to avoid saying this, they preferred to call him not begotten by the Son but made by him.

Therefore, we do not know of ourselves what we ought to pray for as we should; but the Spirit himself intercedes—that is, he makes us intercede for the things that are according to God. Unless he does this, we do not pray except according to this world, to satisfy the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition, which are not from the Father but are from the world (1 John 2:16).

Some, however, think that the statement “the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings” is to be understood of the human spirit.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**22.** They call the Son the living and true, proper and worthy image of the Father’s entire goodness, wisdom, and power. But the Apostle Paul says that he is not an image of God’s power and wisdom; he says that he himself is God’s power and God’s wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24). Therefore, precisely because the Son is the Father’s image, he is his Power and Wisdom.

A full and perfect image—that is, one not made by him from nothing but begotten from him—has nothing less than the one whose image it is. The Only-Begotten is the Father’s supreme image: so perfectly similar that there is nothing dissimilar in it.

They nevertheless did not dare to call the Holy Spirit the Son’s image, but his manifestation. For this reason they said that the Spirit was not begotten by the Son but made by him. They do not read this anywhere at all in the holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0701] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “do not understand.”].

## CHAPTER XXVII

**23.** What Catholic would say that the Son is a part of the Father, or that [Col. 0702] the Holy Spirit is a part of the Son? They thought this had to be denied as though there were any dispute between us and them on that point. We say that the Trinity is of one nature; we do not call any person within it a part of anything.

But since they deny that the Son is a part of the Father while nevertheless calling him the Father’s proper and most beloved, perfect and full Only-Begotten Son, they should be asked this: those whom God makes his sons by his will, begetting them through the word of truth—when they have reached such perfection that they cannot be more perfect—are they themselves also God’s proper and most beloved, perfect and full sons?

If they will be, that one will no longer be the Only-Begotten, since he will have many equals, but merely the firstborn. If they will not be, how is his fullness and perfection to be understood except as making him wholly equal to the one who begets him and in every respect entirely undissimilar from him? To put it more briefly and clearly [Note: [Col. 0702] The German manuscript reads, “more fully and clearly.”]: let these be sons by grace, but let him be Son by nature, because in them there is participation in divinity, while in him there is fullness.

Yet even his assumption of humanity—“and the Word became flesh” (John 1:14)—is not nature but grace, while the nature of the Word, which is equal to the Father, remains.

Furthermore, since they say that the Holy Spirit is not a son but the Son’s first and chief work above all the rest, let them answer whether those sons whom the Father voluntarily begot through the word of truth (James 1:18) will be better than the Holy Spirit.
