For how are they not compelled to say this, when surely it is better to be the Father’s sons than the Son’s work?

Let them consider these matters and correct their empty and impious blasphemies. Let them confess that within that Trinity no person is a creature, nor anything made by God, except that the Son, while remaining God, became human; rather, whatever the whole of it is, it is the supreme, true, unchangeable God.

**24.** Far be it from us to say that, according to their understanding, the Father is greater than his Son insofar as he is his Only-Begotten Word; he is greater only insofar as the Word became flesh. But what wonder is this, when in that same flesh he was also made lower than the angels?

Far be it from us to believe, as they blaspheme, that the Son is incomparably greater and better than the Holy Spirit—and, what is most insane to believe, that the members of the greater are the temple of the lesser.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**25.** The Father is indeed God and Lord of his Son, because the form of servitude exists in the Son—the form prophesied when it was said: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son’” (Psalm 2:7). In the same prophecy the same Son says to him: “From my mother’s womb, you are my God” (Psalm 21:11). From his mother’s womb, where he assumed humanity, he has God as his God.

Because the Father begot him coeternal before not only his mother’s womb but before all ages, the Father is his Father. But where, even in dreams, did they hear Holy Scripture say that the Son is God and Lord of the Holy Spirit?

**26.** “The Father,” they say, “begot the Son by an unchanging and impassible will; the Son, by his own power alone and without labor or fatigue, made the Spirit.” What particular praise of the Son and the Holy Spirit!

As though the Father unwillingly begot us through a changeable and [Col. 0703] passible act, when he voluntarily begot us through the word of truth; or as though the Son created heaven and earth with labor and fatigue! According to their reasoning, then, let these works be made equal either to the Son or to the Spirit. But if they are in no way equal, what purpose was served by saying this, when no question is involved—namely, that the Father begets and the Son makes without any labor or fatigue?

Let them carefully consider how they can say that the Son made the Holy Spirit by his own power alone. For in this way they are compelled to admit that the Son made something which he did not see the Father making. Or do they approve of saying that the Father too made the Holy Spirit? Then the Son did not make him by his own power alone [Note: [Col. 0703] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain editions: “the Son made him.” Manuscript M.].

Or did the Father first make one thing, so that the Son could make the one whom he made—even though he can do nothing except what he sees the Father doing? And what becomes of the statement not that the Son does other similar things, but that “whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise”?

If they try to consider these matters, everything they construct through carnal reasoning will unquestionably be thrown into confusion.

## CHAPTER XXIX

**27.** It is true that the Father gave to all things that exist the gift of existence, while he received his own existence from no one. But he gave his equality to no one except the Son, who was born from him, and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him.

Since these things are so, the difference within the Trinity that these people want does not exist. For nature in the Trinity admits no distinction, and power in the Trinity admits no distinction, so that everyone may honor the Son just as they honor the Father, as the Son himself says (John 5:19, 23).

Those who wish to live piously should worship the Lord their God and serve him alone, as was also commanded to the ancient fathers by God’s law. Nor can it in any way be otherwise: we must serve the Lord our God alone with the service owed to God. This is the service called *latria* (Greek *λατρεία*, “worship/service”). The word is used where it says: “You shall serve him alone” (Deuteronomy 6:13).

I say that this cannot possibly be the case unless the Trinity itself is our one Lord God. Otherwise, this service, called *latria*, which servants do not owe to those whom they have as lords according to the flesh, but which all human beings owe to the Lord their God alone—this service, then, we will not offer to the Son if the statement “and him alone you shall serve” was spoken of the Father; nor will we offer it to the Father if it was spoken of the Son.

Now, if we were to build a temple for the Holy Spirit out of earthly masses, who would doubt that we should serve him with *latria*, that is, with this service of which I am now speaking? How, then, do we not offer him the service called *latria*, when we do not build a temple for him but are ourselves that temple?

Or how is he not also our God, of whom the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” And shortly afterward: “Therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). He says that our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within us.

Since, therefore, we serve the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit with this service called *latria*, and hear God’s law commanding us to offer it to no other but the Lord our God alone, unquestionably our one and only Lord God is the [Col. 0704] Trinity itself, to which alone and uniquely we owe such service by the right of piety.

## CHAPTER XXX

**28.** “Just as no one can pass to the Father without the Son,” they say, “so no one can worship the Son in truth without the Holy Spirit.” As though anyone could come to the Son without the Father, when the Son himself says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44); or as though we could reach the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son, who confer him upon us by their grace.

For what else does it mean to come to them except to have them dwelling within us? In this way they too come to us, since God is everywhere and is contained by no bodily place. The Savior himself says concerning himself and the Father: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23); and concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “Unless I go away, the advocate will not come to you” (John 16:7).

What, then, do they mean when they say, “Just as no one can pass to the Father without the Son, so no one can worship the Son in truth without the Holy Spirit,” and then add, “Therefore the Son is worshiped in the Holy Spirit”?

Do these statements indicate the difference of natures over which the dispute between us and them is being conducted? For if no one can worship the Son in truth without the Holy Spirit, and the Son is worshiped in the Holy Spirit, then the Holy Spirit is certainly also truth, since, when the Son is worshiped in him, he is worshiped in truth, as they themselves have said.

But the Son himself says: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Therefore he is also worshiped in himself, since he is worshiped in truth. Accordingly, the Son is worshiped both in himself and in the Holy Spirit.

Who, however, could be so impious as to separate the Father from this? For how do we not also worship in him [Note: [Col. 0704] Thus Am., Er., and our better manuscripts. But Louvain, with some manuscripts, reads, “and worship him.” Less well.] in whom “we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28)? Accordingly, we too say that the Son is worshiped in the Holy Spirit; but let them read, if they can, that the Son is worshiped by the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXI

**29.** Who denies that the Father is glorified through the Son? But who would dare deny that the Son is also glorified through the Father, to whom the Son himself says, “Glorify me,” and to whom he also says, “I have glorified you” (John 12:28; 17:5, 4)?

“To glorify,” “to honor,” and “to make glorious” are three words, but they signify one thing, expressed in Greek by *δοξάζειν* (*doxazein*). Because of the variety among translators, however, the word has been rendered in different ways in Latin.

## CHAPTER XXXII

**30.** “The work and care of the Holy Spirit,” they say, “is to sanctify and preserve the saints; and to sanctify not only rational beings, as some think, but also many irrational beings; to restore those who have fallen through their own negligence to their former state; to teach the ignorant; to admonish those who forget; to reprove sinners; to urge the sluggish to think about their salvation and act diligently; to lead the erring to the way of truth; to heal the weak; to restrain bodily frailty through the soul’s vigor; to strengthen them in the love of piety and chastity; to enlighten everyone; and, above all, to provide each person with faith and love, distributing grace [Note: [Col. 0705] The printed editions add “of giving,” which is absent from the manuscripts.] for usefulness according to zeal and diligence, according to simplicity and sincerity of mind, according to the measure of faith and [Col. 0705] the merit of one’s conduct, and assigning each person to whatever work and purpose he is suited for.”

The Holy Spirit does indeed do these things, but far be it from us to say that he does them without the Son. Who could stray so far from the way of truth as to deny that the saints are preserved by Christ; that those who have fallen are restored to their former state; that the ignorant are taught; that those who forget are admonished; that sinners are reproved; that the sluggish are urged; that the erring are led back to the way of truth; that the weak are healed; that the blind are enlightened; and all the other things which they thought should be attributed to the Holy Spirit as though he alone did them?

To say nothing of the rest, lest the discussion become too long, how will they deny that the saints are taught by Christ, when he himself says to them: “Do not be called rabbi by human beings, for one is your teacher, Christ” (Matthew 23:8)? How will they deny that the blind are enlightened by Christ, of whom they read: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being” (John 1:9)?

Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit teaches or enlightens no one without Christ, so he sanctifies nothing without Christ.

But regarding what God says through the prophet, “So that they may know that I am the one who sanctifies them” (Exodus 31:13), let them choose whom they wish to believe spoke these words.

If they say the Father spoke them, why do they separate from him the works of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0705] Here the Louvain edition reads: “of the sanctifying Holy Spirit”], when they think that the saints are sanctified by the Holy Spirit as though by his own distinctive and separable action?

If they say the Son spoke them, at least let them not separate from him the works of the sanctifying Holy Spirit.

If they say the Holy Spirit spoke them, then the Holy Spirit too is God—the one who said through the prophet, “So that they may know that I am the one who sanctifies them.” This is what they do not wish to admit.

But if, as is better understood, that voice through the prophet belongs to the Trinity itself, then without any doubt the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, “from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11:36).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**31.** Although, then, we acknowledge that the things they mentioned are done by the Holy Spirit, it does not follow from this that the further claim they add is true: “The Holy Spirit is other than the Son in nature and order, rank and disposition, dignity and power, ability and operation.”

Even human beings do not have different natures merely because their works can be separate—something that cannot be said of the Trinity. Order, rank, and disposition, which are found in the inequality and weakness of creatures, have no place in that coeternal, equal, and impassible Trinity.

As for dignity, power, and ability, how could they not be equal in all, since all act in the same way and perform the same works? We have shown decisively that their claim that the persons differ in operation is entirely false.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

**32.** In this discourse they go on to say: “It is impossible that the Father and the Son should be one and the same, the begetter and the one born; the one to whom witness is borne and the one who bears witness; the greater and the one who confesses the greater; the one who sits or stands at the right hand and the one who gives the honor of sitting; the one who was sent and the one who sent; nor disciple and teacher, as he himself taught when he said, ‘As the Father taught me, so I speak’ (John 8:28); the one who is like and imitates, and the one to whom he is like and whom he imitates; the one who prays and the one who hears; the one who gives [Col. 0706] thanks and the one who blesses; the one who receives a command and the one who gave the command; minister and commander; petitioner and exalted one; subject and superior; Only-Begotten and Unbegotten; priest and God.”

In part they speak with complete truth, but they should say these things against the Sabellians, not against Catholics. The Sabellians say that the one who is the Father is the very same Son; we say that the Father who begets and the Son who is begotten are two persons, but not two different natures.

Therefore the Father and the Son are not one and the same, but the Father and the Son are one. That the Father is greater does not concern the nature of the begetter and the begotten, but the human being and God. According to the form of the humanity he assumed, the Son sits or stands at the Father’s right hand, prays, gives thanks, is a priest, a minister, a petitioner, and subject. According to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, he is the Only-Begotten and coeternal with the one who begets him.

Although he is the firstborn of all creation, because all things were established in him and he was begotten before these things were created, he is nevertheless everlasting like the Father and did not begin in time. We rightly say that the Father is prior to all the things he created, although he was not begotten. For nothing is more first than that before which nothing exists.

But just as nothing exists before the Father, so nothing exists before the Only-Begotten Son, who is of course coeternal with the Father. The fact that one begot and the other was begotten does not make the Father temporally earlier. For if there were any period of time between the begetting Father and the begotten Son, then time would exist before the Son, and he would no longer be the firstborn of all creation, since time too is a creature. Nor would all things be through him if time existed before him. But all things are through him (Colossians 1:15–16); therefore no time exists before him.

Accordingly, just as fire and the radiance begotten from fire and diffused all around it begin to exist together, and the begotten does not precede the begetter, so God the Father and God the Son, God from God, begin to exist together, because they exist equally without any beginning of time, and the begotten does not precede the begetter.

And just as begetting fire and begotten radiance are coeval, so God the Father who begets and God the Son who is begotten are coeternal.

But because the Son is from the Father, and the Father is not from the Son, the Son receives a command from the Father, although he himself is the Father’s command; and the Father teaches him, although he himself is the Father’s teaching. Thus he receives life from the Father, although, like the Father, he himself is life. He is also so like the Father that he is in no respect at all dissimilar.

Yet since the Father and the Son bear witness to each other, I do not know how these people make one of them the witness-bearer and the other the one to whom witness is borne. Does the Father not say, “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17)? Does the Son not say, “The Father who sent me bears witness about me” (John 8:18)?

Why, then, do they distinguish them in such a way that they call the Father the one to whom witness is borne and the Son the one who bears witness? Why are they foolish, deaf, and blind to this extent? The matter of the Father as sender and the Son as sent has already been discussed sufficiently and fully in the earlier parts of this argument.

## CHAPTER XXXV

**33.** It was never the case, as this impiety [Col. 0707] crazily imagines, that the Father foreknew that he would become the Father of the Only-Begotten God. For he was never not the Father, possessing a coeternal Son and begetting, without time, the one through whom he established the ages.

And just as he did not foresee that he would become God, since he was always God, so he did not foresee that he would become Father, since he was always with the Son. Nor is he greater than the Son in greatness, nor better in goodness, because it was said not only of the Father but of the whole Trinity: “You alone are the great God” (Psalm 85:10).

Nor is the Son’s statement, “No one is good except the one God” (Mark 10:18), rightly understood of the Father alone but of the whole Trinity. He called the one who did not yet understand that he was God a good teacher, as though saying: “If you call me good, understand that I am God; for no one is good except the one God.”

The Trinity, therefore, is the one God, alone great and good. To him alone and uniquely, as his law commands, we render the service called *latria*.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**34.** Far be it from us to say that the Son sometimes speaks in such a way as to subject himself to the Father and testify that the Father is greater for the sake of humility rather than truth. For we know the form of a servant in the Son—not fictitious or feigned, but true. Because of this human condition, and because he himself is God from the Father, whereas the Father is not God from him, he says all those things which these people use as an opportunity to believe and proclaim that the Father and the Son have different natures.

Although they plunge themselves into such a vast abyss of impiety, they call us, as though it were a reproach involving a novel name, “Homoousians.” For the antiquity of Catholic truth has this characteristic: all heretics impose different names upon it, while they themselves retain their individual names by which everyone calls them.

The Arians and Eunomians—not other heretics—call us Homoousians because, against their error, we defend the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit with the Greek term *ὁμοούσιον* (*homoousion*), that is, “of one and the same substance,” or, to express it more precisely, “of one and the same essence,” which is called *οὐσία* (*ousia*) in Greek. Put more plainly, they are of one and the same nature.

And yet if one of those who call us Homoousians were to say that his son was not of the same nature as himself but of a different nature, the son would prefer to be disinherited by him rather than have this believed of him.

How great, then, is the impiety that blinds these people! Although they confess the Only-Begotten Son of God, they refuse to confess that he is of the same nature as the Father. Instead, they claim that he is of a different and unequal nature, dissimilar in many ways and respects—as though he had not been born from God but had been created by him from nothing—and consequently that he too is a creature, a son by grace and not by nature.

Behold those who call us Homoousians [Col. 0708] as though the name itself were a stain [Note: [Col. 0707] The word “novel” is absent from the manuscripts]; yet, while holding these opinions, they do not observe that they themselves are insane.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

But since they confess that the Son was born before all ages, how are they not contradicting themselves when they say that he was born before all ages, while placing something temporal before his birth—as though either the ages themselves or any parts of the ages were not times?

But as for what the Apostle says—that in the future age also the Son will be subject to the Father, when he says, “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15:28)—what wonder is that, since that human form in the Son will remain, in which the Father is always greater? Although there have been some who thought that the Son’s subjection at that time should be understood as the transformation of his human form into the divine substance, as though each thing is subjected to whatever it is converted and changed into. But we have shown what we think of this: the Apostle said that even then the Son would be subject to the Father chiefly so that no one might suppose that the human spirit and body would perish through some transformation; so that God might be “all things,” not merely in that human form of his, but in everything—that is, so that the divine nature might suffice for possessing life and satisfying our desire for good things. For then God will be all in all, when we begin to want to possess absolutely nothing apart from him. Indeed, he himself will be everything to us when, because he suffices, nothing will be lacking.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

But where these people get the idea that the Son obeyed an order before he assumed flesh, I do not know. Was he ordered to assume flesh, so that he may seem to have done by command what he did as one sent? Let them therefore return again to what was argued above, and ask—and, if they can, discover—by what other word the Father commanded the one Word, and whether it would have been fitting for the eternal Word to be subjected to the temporal word of one giving orders. From this let them understand that he did not obey the Father’s command as though it had not been within his own power, but that “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” But when “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:7–8), he had of course already assumed flesh.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

I think that I have answered everything contained in the Arian statement that was sent to us by certain brothers so that we might answer it. So that it might be examined by those who read these things and wish to determine whether every point has been answered, we thought that it should be placed before this discussion of ours, so that it might first be read, and then our response. Since we have not inserted its wording everywhere, lest we make this work of ours excessively long, we finally conclude it with this ending.

## [CONCERNING MAXIMINUS, BISHOP OF THE ARIANS]

[Col. 0707]

## PREFATORY NOTE ON THE CONFERENCE AND THE TWO BOOKS AGAINST MAXIMINUS

You will look in vain for these short works in Augustine’s *Retractions*, since they were composed later, namely in either the year of Christ 427 or 428. Prosper writes in his *Chronicle* that the comes Segisvultus, by whom Maximinus declares at the beginning of the subsequent *Conference* that he had been sent to Hippo, came to Africa against Boniface during the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur—that is, in the year of Christ 427. The title of Sermon 140 (formerly number 16 among the Sirmondian sermons) refers to this in the following terms: “Against a certain statement of Maximinus, the Arian bishop, who, having been stationed in Africa with the comes Segisvultus, was blaspheming.” In that sermon Augustine criticizes Maximinus for maliciously interpreting the Lord’s saying in John, chapter 10, verse 30, “I and the Father are one,” as referring to agreement of wills, and for replying that the Apostles themselves were also one with the Father and the Son because they obeyed the will of the Father and the Son. Thus he blasphemes in this *Conference*, his final discussion, no. 22.

Possidius speaks of the same *Conference* in chapter 17 of his *Life of Augustine*:

> When a certain Arian bishop, Maximinus, also came to Africa with the Goths, he held a conference at Hippo, at the request and insistence of very many people, with distinguished men taking part; and it has been written down what each side asserted. If diligent readers take care to read these things attentively, they will undoubtedly discover either what that crafty and irrational heresy professes in order to seduce and deceive, or what the Catholic Church holds and proclaims concerning the divine Trinity. But because that heretic, returning from Hippo to Carthage, boasted that, because of his great loquacity in the conference, he had departed from the conference as its victor—and he lied—and because these matters could not easily be examined and judged by those ignorant of divine law, the venerable Augustine, in a later work, made a recapitulation of the entire conference, treating each objection and response; and he demonstrated no less clearly how little Maximinus had been able to offer in reply to the objections, adding supplements that could not at all be introduced and written down during the limited time of the conference. For the man’s wickedness had brought it about that, in his final and exceedingly long speech, he occupied all the time that remained in the day.

And in the *Index*, chapter 5, there is listed “The Conference with Maximinus, Bishop of the Arians,” followed immediately by “The two books addressed to him above.” Here Possidius separates from the *Conference* the books which, in earlier editions, were so closely attached to it that the *Conference* was read as the first book, and the other two books as the second and third. The ancient manuscripts, both ours and those seen by Bede or Florus, were free from this error: they clearly distinguish the *Conference* from the books against Maximinus, in the commentary on Romans, chapter 8. Pope Agatho also cites the later book with praise of Augustine at the sixth synod, session 4.

[Col. 0709]

## THE CONFERENCE OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, WITH MAXIMINUS, BISHOP OF THE ARIANS

[Note: [Col. 0709] Held in the year of Christ 427 or 428. Elsewhere, *Against Maximinus, Bishop of the Arians*, book one.]

[Note: [Col. 0709] We have corrected the *Conference with Maximinus* and the two books against him with the assistance of two Vatican manuscripts and eleven Gallican manuscripts: the Sorbonic, Fossatensis, Arnulphian, Michaelian, Cistercian, Remigian, Corbie, Laon Cathedral, Paris Saint-Martin-des-Champs, another Paris manuscript of the Bernardine College, and that of the lord of Maran.]

[Note: [Col. 0709] In addition, we compared all those editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

[Col. 0709] **1.** When Augustine and Maximinus had assembled together in Hippo-Regius, with many people present, both clergy and laity, MAXIMINUS said:

“I did not come to this city for the purpose of proposing a dispute with Your Reverence, but I came, having been sent by the comes Segisvultus [Note: [Col. 0709] Earlier editions read *Comite regis multa*; some manuscripts, *Comite Fegisvulto*; others, more correctly, *Comite Segisvulto*.], for the sake of peace.

“For in fact, when the presbyter Heraclius was dealing with me in a friendly agreement, I gave the answer as best I could, although he himself had provoked me; and he became so inflamed that he even provoked your arrival against me. And because Your Reverence has deigned to do yourself an injury [Note: [Col. 0709] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read, ‘to do me an injury.’], if you ask questions, I will give an answer insofar as I am able. If you say anything reasonable, I must follow it.

“For if you bring forward anything from the divine Scriptures that is shared with everyone, we must listen; but statements outside Scripture are accepted by us under no circumstances. Moreover, the Lord himself warns us and says, ‘In vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and precepts of men’ (Matt. 15:9).”

**2. AUGUSTINE said:**

“If I should wish to answer all these points, I too will seem to be acting so as to prevent us from reaching the matter at issue. Therefore, so that we may quickly deal with what is pressing, tell me your faith concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“If you ask for my faith, I hold that faith which was not only expounded by three hundred and thirty bishops at Ariminum [Note: [Col. 0710] The manuscripts read *Arimino*.], but also confirmed by their subscriptions.”

**3. AUGUSTINE said:**

“I have already said this, and I repeat it because you refused to answer: tell me your faith concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“Since I have not failed to answer, why am I accused by Your Reverence as though I had not given an answer?”

**4. AUGUSTINE said:**

“That is why I said that you refused to answer: when I asked you to tell me your faith concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—which I ask again now—you did not tell me your faith, but named the Council of Ariminum. I wish to know your faith: what you believe and what you think concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If you will graciously do so, I wish to hear it from your own mouth. Do not send me to writings that are not now at hand or whose authority I do not accept. Say what you believe concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“I did not wish to introduce the decree of the Council of Ariminum as an excuse for myself, but to show the authority of the Fathers, who, according to the divine Scriptures, handed down to us the faith that they themselves learned from the divine Scriptures.

“But if it pleases you—since ‘with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ (Rom. 10:10), and since we have been instructed and prepared ‘to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning the faith and hope that is in us’ (1 Pet. 3:15); and moreover since the Lord Jesus himself says, ‘Whoever confesses me before men, him I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven; and whoever denies me before men, him I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. 10:32–33)—fearing this danger, although I am not unaware of the imperial laws, yet instructed by the Savior’s command, who warned us and said, ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul’ (ibid., 10:28), I answer clearly:

“‘I believe that there is one God, the Father, who received life from no one; and that there is one Son, who received from the Father what he is and that he lives, in order that he might exist; and that there is one Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who is the illuminator and sanctifier of our souls.’

“And this I assert from the divine Scriptures. If you command it, I will continue with the testimonies. If Your Reverence finds fault with anything, I will answer concerning those matters in which I appear to have been found blameworthy.”

**5. AUGUSTINE said:**

“It troubles me that you specifically described the Holy Spirit as our illuminator, as though Christ were not our illuminator. On this point I first wish to hear from you what you think.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“We acknowledge one author, God the Father, from whom all illumination descends by degrees. Indeed, the Apostle Paul also gives testimony concerning himself in the *Acts of the Apostles*, saying, ‘For thus God commanded us’; and among other things, ‘I have set you as a light to the Gentiles’ (Acts 13:47).

“If the Apostle was set as a light to the Gentiles as a teacher, how much more the Holy Spirit, who is the Apostle’s illuminator, in whom the Apostle also spoke, according to the Apostle’s own words: ‘No one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit’ (1 Cor. 12:3). The Holy Spirit is certainly the illuminator who illuminated the Apostle.

“But the Holy Spirit received from Christ, according to Christ’s own testimony, as Christ says in the Gospel: ‘I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you’ (John 16:12–14). Therefore, according to Christ’s testimony, the Holy Spirit received from Christ.

“Christ himself unquestionably confesses that ‘my teaching is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me’ (John 7:16), and, ‘What I have seen and heard with my Father, I speak’ (ibid. 8:38).

“Therefore, whether Christ teaches and illuminates us, the Father who sent him illuminates; or whether the Holy Spirit illuminates, the illumination returns to its author, who is the source of goodness. From him, whether the blessed Apostle or all the saints have received it, they do indeed illuminate believers, but this illumination returns to one author.

“And for this reason the prophet said, ‘The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?’ (Ps. 26:1).”

**6. AUGUSTINE said:**

“I do not deny that the Holy Spirit illuminates; but what I asked was whether Christ also illuminates by himself, and whether the Father illuminates by himself, or whether they illuminate only through the Holy Spirit. This is what I asked briefly; this is what I ask.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“Your Reverence cannot be unaware that the blessed Apostle Paul said: ‘When the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, not from works of righteousness that we performed, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior’ (Titus 3:4–6).

“According to this rule I say and profess that the Holy Spirit is the illuminator through the Son, as was stated earlier: ‘Whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior.’

“I have already given my answer: whether Paul illuminates, the illumination returns to God the Father, its author; whether the Holy Spirit illuminates, the illumination returns to its author; whether Christ illuminates, the illumination returns to its author.

“And instructed by Christ’s teaching, I continue, as Christ himself says: ‘My sheep hear my voice and follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish forever, and no one shall snatch them from my hand. What my Father gave me is greater than all, and no one can snatch it from the hand of my Father.’ And again he says: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:27–30).

“Therefore, for defending the sheep and illuminating them, the Father and the Son are one, concordant and unanimous, according to this explanation that you have heard: ‘No one can snatch from my hand the sheep whom the Father gave me’; likewise, no one can snatch them from the Father’s hand.”

**7. AUGUSTINE said:**

“You are speaking about matters that are indeed necessary, but not about the issue. You have not answered my question, and yet you have said many things. If you wished, leaving aside the question that is being disputed between us, to recite the whole Gospel, how many days would suffice? How much time would be required?

“Answer me briefly, since I asked you whether Christ illuminates by himself or whether he illuminates only through the Holy Spirit. You not only refused to answer this, but, if I am not mistaken about what I heard, you said rather that the Holy Spirit illuminates through Christ.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“It is not fitting, especially when we are speaking about God, to bring an accusation. I have given an answer; and if what we have said is not sufficient, we add testimonies, because the Holy Spirit was poured out through Jesus Christ upon all believers.

“For we read that the blessed Peter said: ‘God raised up this Jesus, of which we all are witnesses. Therefore, exalted by the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this gift, which you now both see and hear’ (Acts 2:32–33).

“I said that everything the Holy Spirit communicates to us he received from Christ. Return to the testimonies brought forward earlier, and you will find that this is so.”

**8. AUGUSTINE said:**

“When you try to prove what I myself do not deny, you spend necessary time on superfluous matters. I do not deny that the Holy Spirit was poured out through Christ upon believers. You wished without cause to prove with so many delays and testimonies what I myself confess.

“This is what I said, this is what I asked, and this is what I say again: does Christ illuminate through the Holy Spirit, or does the Holy Spirit illuminate through Christ? For earlier you said that the Holy Spirit illuminates through Christ. If you do not remember, let your words be read aloud from the official record, so that it may be clear that we ordered them to be read; and I will prove that you said what I am asking.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“Proof would have been necessary if you had not yourself been satisfied. For in the testimonies I brought forward, or in the explanation I gave, you have already shown that you yourself hold the same view. Since this question has therefore been concluded, propose another to which I may answer. For you have already professed that you were satisfied in this question.”

**9. AUGUSTINE said:**

“Did you say that the Holy Spirit illuminates through Christ, or did you not say so? I ask you to answer me briefly with one of these two alternatives. Did you say it, or did you not say it?”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“I professed the Holy Spirit according to the Savior’s teaching: whether he illuminates, he received it from Christ; whether he teaches, he received it from Christ; everything the Holy Spirit does he received from the only-begotten God. And if the testimonies are insufficient, I will add more.”

**10. AUGUSTINE said:**

“Let his words be read aloud, so that he may not say that we are bringing an accusation.”

Antonius the notary read aloud the following passage:

> “I say and profess that the Holy Spirit is the illuminator through the Son, as was stated earlier, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior.”

When this had been read aloud:

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“As it appears, you yourself are rather intent on delay, so that we do not return to the principal matter, but you wish to keep us occupied with arguments on one question throughout the whole day.

“For we are reading that the Holy Spirit was poured out through the Son, and we have produced as a witness not only the blessed Paul but also Peter, the foremost of the Apostles. Our argument includes the fact that the Holy Spirit received from Christ, according to the preceding testimony: ‘He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.’

“Again, compelled to do so, I say that whether the Holy Spirit illuminates, teaches, or instructs, he received everything from Christ, because ‘all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made’ (John 1:3).

“Christ says that he received all these things from his Father, and that he lives because of the Father, and ‘every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father’ (Phil. 2:11).

“And because [Note: [Col. 0714] The manuscripts read: “What is ‘and because,’ etc.”] ‘the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is man, and the head of Christ is God’ (1 Cor. 11:3); and because the Holy Spirit is subject to the Son; and because the Son is subject to the Father—as beloved, obedient, and good, begotten from the good.

“For the Father did not beget one contrary to himself, but begot one who also cries out and says, ‘I always do the things that please the Father’ (John 8:29).”

**11. AUGUSTINE said:**

“If Christ illuminates through the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit illuminates through Christ, their power is equal. But you read to me the passage in which you just said that the Holy Spirit is subject to Christ.

“As for your claim that the Lord said of the Holy Spirit, ‘He will receive from what is mine,’ this was said because he received from the Father, and without doubt everything that belongs to the Father also belongs to the Son. For after saying this, he added, ‘Therefore I said, “He will receive from what is mine,” because everything that the Father has is mine’ (ibid. 16:14–15).

“Now say what I asked, and prove with testimonies that the Holy Spirit is subject to Christ, whereas we rather read Christ himself saying, ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor’ (Luke 4:18) [Note: [Col. 0714] The printed editions add, “he sent me.” It is absent from the manuscripts here, and also from the printed editions in the preceding book, *Against the Arian Sermon*, chapter 22.]. If he himself said that the Holy Spirit was upon him, how can you say that the Holy Spirit is subject to Christ?

“Christ said that the Holy Spirit was upon him, not because the Spirit is upon the Word of God, which is God, but because he was upon the man who was the Word made flesh. For where it is written, ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1:14), it means nothing other than, ‘The Word became man.’

“Likewise, ‘All flesh shall see the salvation of God’ (Isa. 40:5) means nothing other than, ‘Every human being.’ And, ‘By the works of the law no flesh shall be justified’ (Rom. 3:20) means nothing other than, ‘Every human being.’

“Therefore, because the Word became flesh and ‘he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’ (Phil. 2:7), it was in that form of a servant that he said, ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.’

“For their power is equal; there is one substance; there is one divinity. Thus, although we worship the Trinity—because the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit either the Father or the Son—we nevertheless worship one God, because that ineffable and exalted union of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0714] Several manuscripts read *Trinitas* (“the Trinity”).] shows one God and one Lord.

“Therefore it was said: ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one’ (Deut. 6:4).

“What do you wish to do by making two gods and two lords for us? You call the Father Lord and God; you call Christ Lord and God. I ask whether the two together are one. You answer, ‘Two gods.’ What remains is for you to make temples and idols for them as well.”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“The authors of the faith must never be turned into an accusation. You asked for testimonies so that I might demonstrate by testimonies what I professed; yet you yourself profess three equal beings, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“Moreover, after professing three equal beings, you then brought forward a testimony from the divine Scriptures—not one pertaining to equality, but to the uniqueness of the omnipotent God, namely, that he is the one author of all things.

“Therefore, since you surpass me in age and are greater in authority, first produce and establish by testimonies that there are three equal beings, three omnipotent beings, three unbegotten beings, three invisible beings, three incomprehensible beings; and only then must we submit to the testimonies.

“If you are unable to give an account from the divine Scriptures, I must nevertheless bring forward as many testimonies as you wish concerning everything I said previously: concerning the Father alone, who receives the life he lives from no one; concerning the Son [Note: [Col. 0715] The manuscripts read, “concerning the Son.”], as I professed, that he received life from the Father; and concerning the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what I said.”

**12. AUGUSTINE said:**

“You have not said what I asked you to say, namely, by what testimony you would prove that the Holy Spirit is subject to Christ. Nevertheless, I will answer the points you have raised.

“We do not say ‘three omnipotent beings’ any more than we say ‘three gods.’ For if we are asked individually whether the Father is God, we answer, ‘God’; whether the Son is God, we answer, ‘God’; whether the Holy Spirit is God, we answer, ‘God.’

“But when we are asked about all of them, whether they are three, we refer to the divine Scripture, which says, ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.’ And in this divine rule [Note: [Col. 0715] The older books read *et ex* (“and from”).] we learn that the Trinity itself is one God.

“Likewise, if each one is asked about individually, whether the Father is omnipotent, we answer, ‘Omnipotent’; if the Son, we give the same answer; if the Holy Spirit, we do not deny that he too is omnipotent.

“Yet we do not say ‘three omnipotent beings,’ just as we do not say ‘three gods.’ Rather, just as those three together are one God, so those three together are one omnipotent being; and the one invisible God is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“Therefore you suppose without cause that we are constrained by number, since the power of divinity surpasses even the account of number. For if the souls of many human beings, having received the Holy Spirit and somehow fused together by the fire of love, made one soul—of which the Apostle says, ‘For they had one soul and one heart’ (Acts 4:32)—love made one heart out of so many hearts, so many thousands of hearts; the Holy Spirit called so many thousands of souls one soul, the one soul that he himself made.

“How much more, then, do we call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit one God, always and inseparably and ineffably joined to one another in love?”

**MAXIMINUS replied:**

“And by this you have said that they are equal and coequal, something that you were unable to establish by testimonies; and for this reason you turned aside to another matter.

“We do not doubt, but know with certain faith, that there was one heart and one soul among all the believers. For this does not prejudice our faith; rather, it agrees with it. Indeed, if all believers had one heart and one soul, why should the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit not also be said to be one in agreement, harmony, love, and unanimity?

“For what did the Son do that did not please the Father? What did the Father command in which the Son did not obey? When did the Holy Spirit deliver commands contrary to Christ or the Father?

“And it is established according to the Savior’s saying, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), that they are one in harmony and agreement.

“Moreover, as you yourself professed, the Father is the Father, who was never the Son; the Son is the Son, who always remains the Son; and the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit. This is what he is, and this is what we read and profess concerning the Holy Spirit—a Spirit so great and such that even the angels themselves desire to look into him (1 Pet. 1:12).

“This Holy Spirit is so great that he is sufficient everywhere to receive the petitions of all and to perform the office of advocate [Note: [Col. 0716] The manuscripts read, ‘and to perform advocacy.’ Likewise below, ‘and the Holy Spirit performs advocacy.’].

“And on this point I produce the blessed Paul as a witness, for he says: ‘For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings’ (Rom. 8:26).

“What I read, I believe: the Holy Spirit intercedes with unspeakable groanings. Therefore, instructed by this teaching, I say that the Holy Spirit is so subject that he intercedes for us with groanings.

“Yet I profess one God—not that the three are one, but that there is one God, incomparable, immeasurable, infinite, unbegotten, invisible, whom the Son himself both prayed to and prays to, and with whom the Holy Spirit performs the office of advocate.

“For since the Son prays to the Father—although you are accustomed to apply all those testimonies that we read in the holy Gospel to the body—it is nevertheless our task to show, by searching the divine Scriptures, that even now, seated at the right hand of the Father, he intercedes for us.

“For this reason I said that he both prayed and prays: because he now intercedes for us, as the Apostle says: ‘Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies? Who is he who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, rather, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us’ (ibid., 8:33–34).

“Likewise, while Christ was with the disciples, he promised that he would pray in this way, saying: ‘If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another advocate, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him. But you have seen him and know him, because he remains with you and is in you’ (John 14:15–17).

“If these things are sufficient, that is well; if not [Note: [Col. 0716] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read: ‘Are these sufficient? If not,’ omitting ‘these things, that is well.’], I will add as many testimonies as you command.”

**13. AUGUSTINE said:**

“You do not need to prove to us the things that we profess. By doing this, as I said earlier, you are doing nothing other than wasting necessary time.

“We know that the Son of God is the Son of God; we know that he is not from himself, but was begotten by the Father. We know that the Father himself is unbegotten, that he is from no one, and that he received life from no one. We know that the Son received life from the Father, but not as though he had once been without life and then received life.

“For he gave him life by begetting life: by begetting him with life, he gave him life. He demonstrated equality by saying, ‘As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself’ (John 5:26).

“The Father has life in himself; the Son has in himself a life equal to the Father’s life. Yet the Son did not receive life from himself, because he was not born from himself; he was born from the Father.

“He gave life by begetting—not because the Son already existed without life and the Father then gave him life, as we sinners became without life and received life through pardon and grace. The Son received life from the Father because he was born as life from the Father.

“Accordingly, you could not say that the Holy Spirit is subject to the Son except because he intercedes for us with groanings. It seems to you that the perfection of holiness is always in groaning and never draws breath from groaning. O eternal misery! Understand the expression, and you will avoid blasphemy.

“For it was said, ‘He intercedes with groanings,’ so that we might understand, ‘He causes us to intercede with groanings.’ He is present with us, and by pouring love into us he causes us to intercede with groanings.

“Finally, in another passage, when the Apostle says, ‘Crying, “Abba, Father”’ (Gal. 4:6), elsewhere he says, ‘In whom we cry, “Abba, Father”’ (Rom. 8:15). He explained what ‘crying, “Abba, Father”’ means by saying, ‘In whom we cry.’

“Accordingly, what does ‘crying’ mean except ‘causing us to cry’?

“I will give an example of this kind of expression. Is God not the foreknower of all future things? What madman would deny this? Yet the Apostle says, ‘But now, knowing God—or rather, being known by God’ (Gal. 4:9).

“If God knew them only now, he had not known them, chosen them, or predestined them before the foundation of the world. But he said, ‘Now knowing God—or rather, being known by God,’ so that they might understand that God had brought about his knowledge in them.

“‘Knowing God’: what does ‘knowing God’ mean? Do not claim this for yourselves; do not become proud. You have been known by God. What does ‘you have been known by God’ mean? God made you knowers of him; God gave you the ability to know.

“Likewise, what does the Lord’s statement mean: ‘Now I know,’ the Lord says to Abraham, ‘now I know that you fear God’ (Gen. 22:12)? When Abraham brought his son to be offered as a burnt offering, God said to him, ‘Now I know.’

“Is that the whole of God’s foreknowledge? Did he know only then, when he said, ‘Now I know’? But what does ‘now I know’ mean? It means, ‘Now I have caused you to know.’

“Therefore, if you recognized these expressions as one instructed by the divine books, you would not make the Holy Spirit miserable by those groanings of which it was said that the Spirit intercedes with groanings.

“For what else is one who is always groaning than one who is always miserable? We groan because we are miserable.

“And thanks be to the Holy Spirit, because by the love of the eternal age he causes us to groan, for which reason he is called ‘groaning.’ He causes us to cry out, for which reason he is called ‘crying out.’ He causes us to know God, for which reason it was said, ‘Rather, being known by God.’ God makes Abraham one who knows, for which reason he said to him, ‘Now I know.’”

**MAX. replied:** In the very matters for which you reproach us, you yourself are exposed. For it is certain—and divine Scripture warns us—that “you will not escape sin through much speaking, but, sparing your lips, you will be wise” (Prov. X, 19). Even if someone should produce testimonies from divine Scriptures throughout the entire day, this would not truly be charged to him as verbosity [Note: Some manuscripts read, “as a true matter.”]. But if anyone, whether using literary skill or composing words through the expression [Note: Lov. reads, “exposition.”] of his own spirit, fashions statements that are not contained in Holy Scripture, they are both idle and superfluous.

It is enough for me—since I have brought you to this rule—that you profess that the Father is Father, because he is unborn, because he received life from no one; and that the Son received life from the Father; and that the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit. In saying, however, “one God,” you would do well if, while confessing one God, you did not call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit one God, thereby contradicting your own position.

We worship one God: unborn, uncreated, invisible, who did not descend into human contagion or human flesh. Yet, according to the Apostle, the Son also is not a little god but a great God, as blessed Paul says: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Tit. II, 13). For this great God, Christ, says that “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX, 17). He established one God with respect to his own subjection.

This, then, is the one God whom we have already proclaimed through our testimonies, whom Christ and the Holy Spirit adore, and whom every creature venerates and worships. For this reason we confess one God—not because the joining or mingling of the Son with the Father, or of the Holy Spirit with the Son or with the Father, makes one God. Rather, that one alone is the perfect God who—as you yourself have argued—received life from no one, and who, by his own example, gave the Son to have life in himself. We say that they are joined in love and harmony.

As we have already explained above, the Savior himself teaches us that the Father is another and not the Son, saying: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is not true; there is another who bears witness concerning me.” And lest anyone, in a presumptuous spirit, think that by “another” he meant John the Baptist, or perhaps the apostle Peter or Paul, he continued: “You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. But I do not receive testimony from a human being; I say these things so that you may be saved. He was a burning and shining lamp; but you wished for a time to rejoice in his light. I have testimony greater than John’s. The works which the Father gave me to accomplish—the very works that I do—bear witness concerning me, that the Father sent me. And the Father who sent me himself bears witness concerning me” (ibid. V, 31–37).

Who is so foolish as not to understand that one bore witness concerning another—the Father concerning the Son—the Father who also said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. XVII, 5)? I read “beloved,” and I believe that the Father is the one who loves and the Son the one who is loved. I hear “only-begotten” concerning Christ, and I do not doubt that one was begotten from one.

Paul proclaims him “firstborn,” saying: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Col. I, 15). And, in accordance with the teaching of the divine Scriptures, I profess that he is the firstborn Son and not unborn; and that in him all things were created that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers. All things were made through him and created in him; and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him (Col. I, 15–17). This Son of God, the only-begotten God, exists before all things.

For he himself says: “What I have seen with my Father, I speak” (John VIII, 38). This Son also says in the holy Gospel concerning what you ascribe to the flesh: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28). Reading these things, we believe and confess, in accordance with the Apostle, that all things have been subjected to him as the great God (I Cor. XV, 25).

This great God, whom the Father begot as such—as you yourself have argued—certainly confessed the Father to be greater, in order to establish him as the one God, in whose bosom he is described by the evangelist John. Hear him crying out and saying concerning the invisibility of almighty God: “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John I, 18).

Instructed by this, Paul cries out and says: “Blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see; to whom belong honor and power forever. Amen” (I Tim. VI, 15–16). Again he says of him: “To the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory forever. Amen” (Rom. XVI, 27).

Therefore we proclaim one God, because there is one God above all, unborn and uncreated, as we have argued. But if you do not believe Paul when he says that the Son is “the firstborn of all creation,” believe the Son himself when he says to Pilate, who asked him, “So you are a king?” Christ replied: “For this I was born” (John XVIII, 37). I read “born”; I profess what I read. I read “firstborn”; I do not deny it [Note: Am. Er. and the manuscripts read thus. Lov. has “I do not differ.”]. I read “only-begotten,” and even if I were suspended on the rack, I would say nothing else. I profess what the holy Scriptures teach us.

You, who say that the Father and the Son are one, call the Father “only-begotten”; call him “firstborn.” State what belongs to the Father in the Son. Call the Son only-begotten; call him unborn; say that no one has ever seen him, nor can see him. Speak similarly about the Holy Spirit, as we read concerning the Father, so that you may show the Holy Spirit to be equal to the Father. Tell me, I ask, and consider me your disciple. Argue concerning the Son that the Son is unborn, that he is without origin. If he is equal, then he is such; if he is such, then he is unborn; if he is unborn, then no human being has seen him. Give testimonies, instruct and teach me, and you will have me as your disciple.

### 14. AUGUSTINE said:

You said that one God is worshiped by you, as I was able to understand from your speech. It follows either that you do not worship Christ, or that you do not worship one God but two. You also said of the Father that he did not descend into human contagion or human flesh. [Col. 0720] If perhaps you do not know, when “contagions” are mentioned, some contamination is signified. You therefore intended it to be understood that Christ came into human contagions; consequently you professed that Christ was defiled by human flesh.

But I say—and indeed the catholic faith, which I hold with the Church of Christ, says—that our Lord Jesus Christ became the Word flesh in such a way that he suffered no contagion from the human race or from human flesh. He came to cleanse, not to be polluted. He therefore assumed a human soul and human flesh without any disease of contamination, and he graciously saved both—that is, the human soul and the human flesh—in himself.

But since, as far as I see, you are unwilling to accept the truth concerning his invisibility, I ask you to consider that Christ was visible according to the flesh and according to his humanity. For according to that which he is as the Word, God with God, he too is invisible. Christ is the Wisdom of God. Human wisdom is invisible; will the Wisdom of God be visible? Therefore, as regards that nature in which he is equal to the Father, he is equally God, equally almighty, equally invisible, and equally immortal.

You also said, as I understood, that the Apostle’s statement, “who alone possesses immortality” (I Tim. VI, 16), should be understood so that in this passage the Father alone is meant. Do you therefore wish the Word of God to be mortal? According to you, is the Wisdom of God not immortal? Do you not understand that the Son could in no way have died unless he had assumed mortal flesh from us? In him the flesh died; he himself did not die insofar as this pertains to God, insofar as it pertains to the divinity by which he is equal to the Father.

Thus he says to human beings: “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do” (Luke XII, 4), because the soul cannot die. Can the Word of God die? Can the Wisdom of God die? Could the only-begotten Son have died without assuming flesh? But after assuming flesh, by which he became human, just as he knows himself to be equal when he says, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), so he knows himself to be lesser, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid. I, 14).

He did not regard it as a prize to be equal with God. It was his nature, not a prize; he did not usurp this, but was born with it. Nevertheless, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and, “being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II, 6–7), he humbled himself. You have recognized him as equal; now begin to recognize him as lesser: he took the form of a servant.

See in what form the Father is greater. Distinguish the dispensation of the humanity he assumed from the divinity that remains immortal, and you will not err in the words that you love to repeat but do not deign to understand.

I profess, as you say, that the Father is unborn and the Son born. But they are not therefore different in nature and substance because one is unborn and the other born. For if he is born, he is the Son; if he is the Son, he is the true Son, because he is the only-begotten.

We too are called sons; but are so many sons of us only-begotten? The one is the only-begotten Son; he is Son by nature, while we are sons by grace. He is born from the Father as only-begotten; by nature and substance he is what the Father is. Whoever says that he is therefore of another nature because he is born denies that he is the true Son.

We have Scripture: “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; he is the true God and eternal life” (I John V, 20). Why is he the true God? Because he is the true Son of God. If he gave animals the power to beget only what they are—human begets human, dog begets dog—does God not beget God?

If, then, he is of the same substance, why do you call him lesser? Perhaps because, when a human father begets a son, although a human begets a human, the greater nevertheless begets the lesser? Let us then wait for Christ to grow, as human beings whom humans beget grow. But if Christ, from the moment he was born—which was not in time but from eternity—was what he is and yet is lesser, the human condition is better: a human being can at least grow and eventually attain the age and strength of his father, whereas Christ never can. How, then, is he a true son [Note: Serm. 139, no. 3, vol. 5]?

So thoroughly do we acknowledge the Son as the great God that we say he is equal to the Father. Therefore you wished, without cause, to prove to us through testimonies and much speaking what we very strongly profess.

He says, “My God and your God” (John XX, 17), with attention to the form of the human being in which he existed. But as regards what John said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (ibid. I, 1), the Father is not God of God; rather, God is the God of Christ, because Christ became human.

Hence he himself says in the Psalms why God is his Father: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. XXI, 11). When he says that he is his God from his mother’s womb, he shows that God is Father to the Son for this reason: because the Son is human, and in this respect the Father is greater than the Son. Hence he says, “My God and your God.”

This also explains the subjection rendered to the Father according to his humanity, which we ought not to find astonishing, since, as it is written, he was subject even to his parents (Luke II, 51). It is also written of him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII, 6).

I would like you to teach us this also through some testimonies of Scripture: where is it written that the Father is worshiped by the Holy Spirit? From the Son I accept it, even if you produce no testimonies, because a human being worships God. It is easily admitted as spoken according to his humanity, although you do not read even this. Nevertheless, I specifically demand of you that you read to us or recall a divine testimony that the Father was worshiped by the Holy Spirit. Perhaps such a passage exists and has escaped me; if you find it, I shall explain how it should be understood, just as I explained the scriptural “groanings” according to customary language.

But when you say that through that ineffable union the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not one God, do you wish to know how powerful this union is? It is certainly clear, not from our expressions but from the divine utterances, that one thing is the spirit of a human being and another the Spirit of the Lord. Hence it is said, “The Lord is Spirit” [Note: The printed editions read, “the Spirit of God; hence it is said, ‘God is Spirit.’” The manuscripts read, “the Spirit of the Lord,” and then, “hence it is said”—namely, II Cor. 3—“the Lord is Spirit.”] (II Cor. III, 17), that is, because he is not a body.

And yet the Apostle says: “He who joins himself to a prostitute is one body; but he who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 16–17). If, then, this attachment of spirits of different natures—for one is human and the other divine—made one spirit, do you not wish the Son to be so closely attached to the Father that they are one God? Understand this also concerning the Holy Spirit, who is God.

Otherwise, if the Holy Spirit were not God, we ourselves would certainly not be his temple. For it is written in the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (I Cor. III, 16). And again: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple within you of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God?” (ibid. VI, 19).

If we were to build a temple of wood and stone for some holy and most excellent angel, would we not be condemned by the truth of Christ and by the Church of God, because we would be offering to a creature the service that is owed to God alone? If, then, we would be sacrilegious by building a temple for any creature, how is he not the true God for whom we do not build a temple, but of whom we ourselves are the temple?

As for how Christ said, “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John V, 26), I answered above.

But concerning harmony and love, which you say caused the Father and Son to be one: when you produce a statement that things of different substances are one, then I shall consider what I ought to answer. For we read, “He who plants and he who waters are one” (I Cor. III, 8); but both were human beings and were of the same substance, not different substances.

Likewise, we read Christ himself saying: “That they may be one, as we also are one” (John XVII, 11). He did not say, “That they and we may be one,” but, “That they may be one”—united and fused, in a certain manner, in their own nature and substance by harmonious equality—just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one because of their undivided and identical nature.

For one thing is “they are one” [Note: Here the manuscripts add, “and another thing is, ‘we are one.’”]; another is “he is one.” When it is said, “They are one,” even if what they are one in is not stated, one substance is understood. When it is said, “He is one,” with respect to two different substances, it is necessary to ask what the one is.

For example, soul and body are different substances, yet they are one human being. The spirit of a human being and the Spirit of God are different substances, yet when the human being adheres to the Lord, “he is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17). The text adds “spirit”; it does not say, “They are one.” Where it says, “They are one,” one substance is signified. This you refuse to accept, while daring to say that you confess the true Christ, the Son of God.

The Father is not therefore greater because he bears witness to the Son. The prophets also bore witness to the Son. The one who bears witness is indeed another from the one to whom witness is borne, because the Father is Father and the Son is Son—not because they are not one, or are not one God, when they are joined and united, as they always are.

You say that there is a difference between the Father and the Son because the Father loves and the Son is loved, as though you could deny that the Son loves the Father. If they love one another, why do you deny that they are of one nature?

What I said concerning why the Father is called greater—namely, because of the form of a servant—I also say concerning invisibility: the Son is called visible because of that same form of a servant. But as regards the divine substance itself, whether of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, it is altogether invisible.

When the divinity revealed itself to the fathers, it demonstrated its invisibility through a subordinate creature. For by its very nature it is so invisible that Moses, to whom it spoke face to face, said to it: “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me openly” (Exod. XXXIII, 11, 13). He wished to see God as God is seen by the eyes of the heart. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

Thus Moses wished to see the one to whom he said, “Show yourself to me openly,” just as “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made.” For the Apostle says: “His invisible things are clearly perceived through the things that have been made, and likewise his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. I, 20). The invisible things of God, then, are perceived through understanding, and yet they are called invisible.

All things were made through Christ (John I, 3), both visible and invisible; and yet can he himself be believed by us to be visible?

You also say that the Apostle’s statement, “To the only wise God” (Rom. XVI, 27), should be understood of the Father alone. Is the Father, then, the only wise God, and is the very Wisdom of God—which is Christ—not wise? Of him the Apostle says: “Christ the power of God and the Wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24). It remains for you to say—for what will you not dare to say?—that the Wisdom of God is foolish.

You speak of the Father as uncreated, as though the Son were created, through whom all things were made. Understand that the Son was made in the form of a servant. For in the form of God he was not made to such an extent that all things were made through him. If he himself were made, all things were not made through him, but only the rest.

I do not therefore call the Son unborn; rather, I call the Father the begetter and the Son begotten. Yet the Father begot what he is; otherwise the Son is not a true Son if the Son is not what the Father is, just as we said above concerning the offspring of animals, because true sons are, in substance, what their parents are.

But what is this that you demand—that I show the Holy Spirit to be equal to the Father—as though you had shown the Father to be greater than the Holy Spirit, just as you were able to show concerning the Son because of the form of a servant?

For we know that the Father was said to be greater than the Son because the Son was in the form of a servant; and the Son is still in human form, which he raised into heaven. Therefore it was said of him that even now “he intercedes for us” (Rom. VIII, 34). And this same immortal form will be eternal in the kingdom; hence it is said: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him” (I Cor. XV, 28).

But concerning the Holy Spirit, who assumed no creature into the unity of his person, although he too graciously chose to manifest himself visibly through a subordinate creature, whether in the form of a dove or through fiery tongues (Matt. III, 16; Acts II, 3), the Father was never said to be greater than him. The Holy Spirit was never said to have worshiped the Father, and was never said to be less than the Father.

But you say of the Son, “If he were equal, then he would be such”—that is, because he is not unborn, he does not appear to be such. You could say that the human being whom Adam begot is not a human being, because Adam himself was not begotten but made by God. But if Adam could exist without being begotten and yet beget what he himself was, do you not wish God to have been able to beget God equal to himself?

I think I have answered you on all points. But if you do not wish to be a disciple, do not be verbose.

### 1. MAX. said:

You speak as though fortified by the support of rulers, with nothing according to the fear of God. I endured long hours while you explained matters as you wished. With God’s help we shall respond to everything—not with bare speech, but fortified by testimonies of the divine Scriptures.

But just as we were patient while your Religion was explaining, you too must show patience with your companions, so that we may respond to each of your statements, just as you responded to ours in whatever way pleased you.

### 2.

We worship Christ as the God of every creature. For he is worshiped and honored not only by human nature but also by all the heavenly Powers. Hear blessed Paul crying out: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard it as a prize to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him above all and gave him the name that is above every name.”

This is precisely what you thought should be removed in your arguments, although you knew that it contradicted your profession and that the reading would convict you. For concerning every knee bending to Christ, Paul himself continues in this way after saying, “He gave him the name that is above every name”: “so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 5–11).

By saying, “so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth,” he included everything. There is nothing in heaven that does not bend the knee to Christ; nothing remains on earth that does not bend the knee to Christ; nothing in the underworld fails to bend the knee to Christ. And the Father gave this to him.

Those who read can determine whether I have made this argument from my own authority or from verbosity, as you accuse me, or whether I am responding on the authority of the divine Scriptures.

### 3.

You say that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Son. Give testimonies showing where the Holy Spirit is worshiped, where those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bend the knee to him.

We learned that God the Father is to be worshiped when the blessed apostle Paul cries out: “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. III, 14–15). By the authority of the holy Scriptures we worship the Father. Likewise, instructed by those same divine Scriptures, we honor and worship Christ as God.

If there is anywhere a command that the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped; if the Father bore witness to him in this way; if the Son did so; if the Holy Spirit himself embraced such claims concerning himself, read it from the divine Scriptures beyond what we have already stated.

### 4.

Concerning Christ’s being at the right hand of God and interceding for us (Rom. VIII, 34), Paul also argues in another passage, saying: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. III, 1). Likewise, writing to the Hebrews, he says: “Having made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Heb. I, 3).

The Holy Spirit had already foretold this through the prophet, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.” The Son himself likewise confessed it in the Gospel (Ps. CIX, 1; Matt. XXII, 44).

Furthermore, when that ruler adjured him, saying, “Tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the Blessed,” he himself replied, “I am,” or, at any rate, “You say so”; and: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Mark XIV, 61–62; Matt. XXVI, 63–64).

### 5.

We appropriately honor the Holy Spirit as teacher, guide [Note: Lov. alone reads, “leader.”], enlightener, and sanctifier. We worship Christ as creator. With sincere devotion we adore the Father as author, whom everywhere and to everyone we proclaim to be the one author.

These accusations arise from instruction in philosophical disciplines. I do not think you have failed to read what the Apostle says: “For Christ, although he was not a sinner, was made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God” (II Cor. V, 21) [Note: Er. Lugd. and Ven. and Lov. read, “I do not think you have read.” M. reads, “For I think you have read.”].

Nor, surely, has this escaped you, that Scripture said [Note: Er. Lugd. and Ven. and Lov. read, “Scripture had said.” M.]: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Interpreting this, the blessed apostle Paul says: “He was made a curse for us, so that the blessing might be fulfilled among the nations” (Deut. XXI, 23; Gal. III, 13).

Nor, surely, has this escaped you, that Paul himself says: “The first human being, Adam, was from the earth, earthly; the second human being, the Lord, came from heaven, heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 47). Therefore Christ also assumed a human being, as you yourself explained. For this reason we said that he descended into earthly contagions.
