We do not ignore what we read concerning him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly” (I Pet. II, 22–23) [Note: Am. and Lov. read, “to the one who judges unjustly.” Er. and the more authoritative manuscripts read, “justly.”].

Nor do we ignore what John the Baptist said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29).

This is established, as you yourself have argued. Nor should we be so obstinate in everything that we fail to praise what you say well. Your argument is indeed entirely just: Christ came for this purpose, so that he might cleanse us from sins and iniquities, not so that he himself might be contaminated, as you yourself have argued.

It is certain that, according to the substance of his divinity—that blessed nature which he possessed before the foundation of the world, before the ages, before times, before days, months, or years, before anything existed [Note: The manuscripts read, “before anything whatever existed.”], before any conception had arisen—in that blessed nature God was born from the Father [Note: Most manuscripts read, “he was begotten as such by the Father.” The Corbie manuscript, corrected, reads, “as such.”].

### 6.

In speaking of God, one ought to use worthy comparisons. This is what displeased me, and I was deeply troubled in your argument: when you said that a human being begets a human being and a dog a dog, such a foul comparison ought not to have been extended to that immense greatness.

### 7.

Who does not know that God begot God, that the Lord begot the Lord, that the King begot the King, that the Creator begot the Creator, that the good begot the good, that the wise begot the wise, that the merciful begot the merciful, and that the powerful begot the powerful?

The Father withheld nothing in begetting the Son. For he was not envious; rather, as the fountain of goodness, he begot so great a good. Every creature bears witness to this goodness, according to your own argument, which I greatly praise, where you brought forth from the divine Scriptures the statement: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are perceived through understanding in the things that have been made, and likewise his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. I, 20).

### 8.

I add something further—not saying anything contrary to what has been rightly said, but expressing agreement: the Creator is worthily known and worshiped from the greatness of the beauty of his works.

I think we have answered these matters, since blessed Paul also argues as follows: “The record that stood against us, he removed from our midst, nailing it to the cross; and stripping himself of the flesh, he openly led away the Powers and Principalities, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. II, 14–15).

Nevertheless, since I am a human being who has not practiced the liberal arts or the art of rhetoric, if I had made some fault in speech, you ought to have attended to the meaning rather than focusing on a fault of expression and bringing a charge against us.

Far be it, far be it: the only-begotten God is the God of every creature, pure, undefiled, holy, and secure, possessing no impurity in himself. For “he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V, 23).

That “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” the evangelist testifies: “And we saw his glory,” he says, “glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (ibid. I, 14).

The Old Testament had already foretold this concerning him, saying: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his covering in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX, 11) [Note: The ancient codices read here and above, col. 725, no. 4, “had foretold.”].

What I read, I believe: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Again, I read that blessed Paul said: “He will transform the body of our humiliation, making it conform to the image of the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 21).

For I believe that Christ God, begotten by the Father before all the ages, himself built for himself, according to Solomon, a perfect house [Note: Am. Er. and the manuscripts read, “a prophet.”], in accordance with what we read: “Wisdom itself built a house for itself” (Prov. IX, 1), and that he received this house in place of a temple.

### 9

For you yourself also gave the explanation according to which he is visible and according to which he is invisible—unless, as I think, this teaching has only recently reached the ears of Your Reverence. For in the argument you advanced, taking the soul as a comparison, you showed that it is a pious and just principle that we should believe and understand this: if the human soul, placed within the body, cannot be seen by bodily eyes, how much less can the Creator of the soul be seen by bodily eyes?

For if angels are considered invisible according to the substance of their nature, how much more is the Creator of angels invisible—the one who made such and so many beings: Angels, Archangels, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers, Cherubim, and Seraphim? Compared with their multitude, as we read in the Gospel, he likened the entire human race to a single sheep, saying: “Leaving the ninety-nine on the mountains, he came to seek the one that had gone astray.” For finally he says: “So there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:4, 7).

Who, then, are those who have no need of repentance, except those heavenly powers who have nothing in common with human nature? We must consider the power of the only-begotten God, and in him we must admire the greatness of the omnipotence of God the Father, who begot so great and such a Son, so powerful, so wise, so full—he who made such and so many heavenly powers.

[Editorial notes (col. 727): The printed editions, Am. and Er., and the manuscripts read *quarum* (“of which”) rather than *quorum* (“of whom”). Some manuscripts omit “omnipotence”; others, with Am. and Er., read “of almighty God” in its place.]

And so that we may not be found long-winded, just as you have already seen fit to point out about us—something which indeed, and may it come to pass, would allow us also to say: “We are fools for Christ”; and, “We have become as the refuse of this world” (1 Corinthians 4:10, 13)—and whatever else Your Reverence may wish to judge concerning us: we know the one who said, “For your sake I have endured reproach all day long” (Psalm 68:8). To this example Paul urged us when he said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4:16). Peter likewise says: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21).

[Editorial note (col. 727): B. reads “we can say”; Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read “that we may be able to say.”]

According to the substance of his divinity, the Son is seen not only by human beings but not even by the heavenly powers. For an archangel can see an angel, and an angel can both see and penetrate our spiritual souls: that is, the greater can both see and penetrate the inferior.

[Editorial note (col. 727): The manuscripts read *archangelum* (“an archangel,” accusative) rather than *archangelus* (“an archangel,” nominative).]

And according to the Savior’s declaration, when he said at that time to the man who boasted of his wealth, “Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you” (Luke 12:20), it is the angel’s duty to restore the soul before the presence of the Lord.

[Editorial note (col. 727): Am., Er., and the manuscripts omit “of you.”]

Yet the soul cannot see or exhibit the angel.

Proceed upward through this order, and you will discover how there is one invisible God the Father, who has no superior by whom he might be surveyed. Whatever his magnitude, he is infinite; he can neither be delimited by words nor conceived by the mind. Concerning his greatness, not only the human tongue but also all the heavenly powers gathered together speak as they are able, yet they do not express him as he is. He is full beyond everything that is said of him.

Only the Son honors and praises him worthily, all the more because he has received from his progenitor more than any thought can conceive. For although the four Gospels testify that he honors, praises together with, and glorifies his progenitor, I shall now, setting aside the passages you are accustomed to apply to the flesh, present testimonies in which he worships his Father in heaven.

For Paul says to the Hebrews: “Christ did not enter into temples made with hands, representations of the truth, but into heaven itself, where he now appears before the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24). This, plainly, occurred after Christ’s return to heaven. For after he had spoken from heaven, saying, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), and after the Holy Spirit had said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work of the ministry to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2), Paul, having been called, says: “Jesus did not enter into temples made with hands, representations of the truth, but into heaven itself, where he now appears before the presence of God on our behalf.”

And because Your Reverence suggested that we should answer the question whether the Son sees the Father, we read in the Gospel: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father” (John 6:46). Therefore he saw the Father, but he saw the incomprehensible One. The Father, however, sees the Son in such a way that he holds and possesses him in his bosom; for, according to the testimony already cited, “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John 1:18).

The Father sees the Son as Son; the Son sees the Father as the immeasurable Father.

Your Reverence declares human wisdom invisible. I think the saying of Isaiah is sufficient: “Is it a small thing for you to contend with men? And how will you contend with the Lord?” (Isaiah 7:13). It is certain, however, that it is not a small thing to contend with human beings, since, however wise someone may be, he has someone wiser who sees him. Moreover, is not this person’s wisdom discerned in his work? Is it not proved in his disciples? Human wisdom, therefore, is not invisible: it can be grasped, it can be seen, and it can also be criticized.

For the rest, it is fitting—and accords with good order—that you use comparisons worthy of the subject, since you are speaking about God, about that immeasurability. Even if a comparison is offered to him, insofar as this can be done according to human thought, or at least according to the authority of the divine Scriptures, no comparison is found in every respect worthy of him who is incomparable.

### 10

I say, on the basis of the testimonies cited above, that the Father alone is God—not “one” together with another and a third, but that he alone is the one God. If he is not the one alone, then he is a part. Nor do I call God “one” as something composed of parts; rather, he is what he is: an unbegotten, simple power. The Son also, before all ages, is himself a begotten power.

[Editorial note (col. 729): Another reading is “begotten” in the feminine, agreeing with *power*.]

Concerning this power of the Son, the blessed Apostle said: “When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 5:4).

For I say and profess what the holy Gospels teach us. And because the Holy Spirit also is a power in his own distinct identity, the Lord bears witness concerning him, saying: “But you remain in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49).

### 11

If for this reason you pronounce the Son invisible—because he cannot be contemplated by human eyes—why do you not likewise pronounce the heavenly powers invisible, since they too cannot be seen by human sight?

I have indeed produced testimony without any interpretation of my words, saying: “Blessed and only powerful one, King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). If I recited Scripture, I ought not to have been criticized. But if you examine the meaning of Scripture, I shall give the explanation.

### 12

The Apostle says: “Blessed and only powerful one, King of kings.” He calls the Father alone powerful, not because the Son is not powerful. Hear, then, testimony concerning the Son, the Holy Spirit himself crying out and saying: “Lift up your gates, you princes”; and, “Be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter.” Then it follows: “Who is this King of glory?” Understand the answer: “The Lord, strong and mighty” (Psalm 23:7–8).

[Editorial note (col. 729): The printed editions read “your” in the feminine plural; the manuscripts read “you princes,” as does Augustine, *Expositions on the Same Psalm* 23.]

How can he not be powerful, whose power every creature proclaims?

### 13

How can he not be wise, of whom the Holy Spirit, extolling his wisdom, cries out and says: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24)?

Since all things were made through Christ, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit, praising him, said: “You have made all things in wisdom.” And since this is so, we must ask how the blessed Paul says: “Blessed and only powerful one.” I think he calls him alone powerful because he alone is incomparable in his power. Concerning his incomparability the prophet, in wonder, said: “O God, who will be like you?” (Psalm 82:2).

Do you wish to know that he alone is powerful? Look upon the Son and admire the Son’s power. In him observe that the Father alone is powerful, since he begot one so powerful. For the Father, in that immeasurable power, begot a powerful Creator.

[Editorial note (col. 729): Only the Lov. edition omits “Creator.”]

The Son, in the power he received from the Father—for he himself says, “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matthew 11:27)—did not create a creator but established a creature.

Admiring this power of God the Father, Paul said: “Blessed and only powerful one.”

For if a human being is also powerful and genuine—as we read concerning Job, “That man was genuine and righteous, a worshiper of God,” and, describing his region, he says that he was powerful and great among all the people of the East (Job 1:1, 3)—how, then, is the Father alone powerful? He says “alone” for this reason: because no one is compared with him, because he alone possesses such greatness, such authority, and such power.

In the same way, the blessed Apostle Paul also proclaims the Father alone wise, saying: “To the only wise God” (Romans 16:27). But we must ask how he is alone wise—not because Christ is not wise. You have already presented Christ as “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24); and we too have given testimonies that he established all things in wisdom.

Yet the Father is truly alone wise. We believe the Scriptures and venerate the divine Scriptures themselves. We do not wish to pass over even one letter, fearing the danger contained in those divine Scriptures: “Woe to those who take away or add!” (Deuteronomy 4:2).

Do you wish to know how great the Father’s wisdom is? Look upon the Son, and you will see the Father’s wisdom. For this reason Christ himself said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). That is, in me he sees the Father’s wisdom; he praises the Father’s power; he glorifies the one who begot me, so great and such a one, before all ages—one begetting one, alone begetting alone.

He did not seek material from which to make him, nor did he receive anyone’s assistance; rather, by his own power and wisdom, as he himself knows, he begot the Son. It is not as you say in your accusations: that just as every other creature was made from nothing, so we confess that he too was made from nothing, as though he were one of the creatures.

Hear, indeed, the authority of the synodical reading, for at Ariminum our fathers said, among other things, this also: “If anyone says that the Son is from nothing and not from God the Father, let him be anathema.”

If you wish, I shall offer further testimonies. For the blessed Apostle John says: “Whoever loves the one who begot loves also the one who has been born from him” (1 John 5:1).

### 14

I am astonished, dearest brother. Since you also say that the Holy Spirit is from the substance of the Father, if the Son is from the substance of God the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the substance of the Father, why is one the Son and the other not a son? What has he done against you, since he is from the same substance, since, as you say, he is equal to the Son? Why, then, is he not also constituted heir of all things? Why is he not also a son? Why is he not also called by the name by which Christ is called, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15)?

Or, if he is equal, then the Son is no longer the only-begotten, since he has another begotten with him, and one who is moreover from the same substance of the Father, from which you also say that the Son exists.

This, indeed, is painful to hear. You do not compare that immense magnificence with the soul’s unbegottenness (*ingenuitas*), but with the frailty of the body. From the body, flesh is born—a bodily son; yet soul is not born from soul.

If, therefore, our soul generates incorruptibly and without suffering, experiencing no diminution and no defilement, but legitimately, according to the divine laws, generates a son, contributing wisdom’s consent to the body while itself remaining whole, how much more does almighty God do so?

[Editorial note (col. 730): Am. reads “a son, wisdom”; Lov. reads “and wisdom”; Er. reads “a begotten son, by the consent of the wise”; Lugd. and Ven. read “generates a son by the consent of the wise”; other readings are “and the consent of wisdom.”]

I said a little earlier that every human comparison must fall silent before him; nevertheless, insofar as we can, we attempt to speak: how much more did God the incorruptible Father incorruptibly beget the Son? He did beget him—hold fast to my assurance, which has the testimonies of the holy Scriptures: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8).

He begot him as he willed, as one who is powerful; subtracting nothing, with no envy intervening, he begot one who is powerful.

[Editorial note (col. 731): Several manuscripts read “as he willed, as one who is powerful,” with *he willed* repeated.]

I have said that it is not fitting for the religious to make accusations. I profess the Word of God, the Word of God—not mortal, not corruptible. For concerning the body he assumed for our salvation, Scripture cries out: “My flesh will rest in hope,” that is, in the hope of resurrection; “for you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15:9).

If the one who was called the Son of God did not see corruption because he rose from the dead on the third day, how much more does the divinity that assumed the body remain incorruptible?

Why do you say what you do not understand? If I do not answer you concerning everything, I shall rightly be judged to lack understanding. Nevertheless, it is not religious to attack with insults.

For I assert not only that the wisdom of the Son of God is immortal, but I shall also prove that the wisdom of God’s saints is immortal. For if they themselves—that is, their bodies—are recalled to immortality, how much more does their living wisdom, which flourishes in all believers until the consummation of the age, remain immortal?

Although in the length of my discourse I passed over the immortality of almighty God, concerning which the blessed Apostle Paul said, “Who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16), I shall return to the passage; and, God favoring and granting grace, I shall also follow with its interpretation.

For he is described as possessing immortality alone in the same way as he is described as alone powerful and alone wise. What spiritual person, however, is unaware that the human soul is immortal? Moreover, since it is the Savior’s declaration, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28), the soul is immortal.

Since, then, the soul is immortal, we see much more clearly that all the heavenly powers are immortal. For when the Savior says, “Whoever keeps my word will never see death” (John 8:51), if one who keeps Christ’s word will never see death, how much more is he immortal according to the power of his divinity, whose word possesses such force?

In the statement, “Who alone possesses immortality,” we have already given the explanation. The Son does possess immortality, but he receives it from the Father. All the heavenly powers also possess immortality, but they receive it through the Son, because all things are through him.

The Father, however, truly alone possesses immortality: he did not obtain immortality from elsewhere; he has no progenitor and no origin. The Son, as you yourself have argued, was begotten from the Father.

You frequently assert that the Son is equal to the Father, although the only-begotten God himself always and in everything proclaims the Father as his author, from whom, as I said a little earlier, he also confesses that he received life, saying: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

Observe, therefore, that he received immortality, incorruptibility, and inaccessibility from the Father together with life. The Father, however, has life in himself, receiving it from no one; and therefore he is truly “blessed and only powerful one.”

Who emptied himself (Philippians 2:7)—the Father or the Son? Who hastened to please whom through obedience, except the one who said, “I always do what is pleasing to him” (John 8:29)?

Who is the one who, coming to Lazarus’s tomb, said: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but because of the crowd standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me” (John 11:41–42)?

Who is the one who, when he was shaping the eyes of the man born blind, and the disciples asked, “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” answered: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him. I must work the works of the one who sent me” (John 9:2–4)?

This is the beloved Son of the Father, who, after receiving the loaves, did not break them first, but first looked toward heaven, gave thanks to his progenitor, and then broke and distributed them. So also in the Passion—or rather, when the Passion was already near, as the evangelist reports (Matthew 26:26): “The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it” (1 Corinthians 11:23–24).

This is the Son. I shall not now weary you with eloquence of speech or by producing a multitude of testimonies, but shall conclude briefly with the one who taught that nothing occurs, even to the death of a sparrow, without the Father’s permission, saying: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? And not one of them will fall to the ground without the will of your Father” (Matthew 10:29).

[Editorial note (col. 732): Some manuscripts read “that I may not weary the saint … producing many things”; Am. and Er. read “that I may not weary the holy one with eloquence … producing many things”; Lov. reads “that I may not now, because of so much eloquence of speech or a multitude of testimonies, produce many things.”]

He also spoke concerning his own authority, which he received from the Father: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again. This commandment I received from my Father” (John 10:18).

If the Gospels report these things, let what we read be retained. If, however, I have perhaps said something else, or spoken less carefully because of forgetfulness, let me be criticized. For I am not such a person that I would refuse correction.

Moreover, since the blessed Apostle Paul commands that a bishop be teachable (1 Timothy 3:2), and the teachable person is one who learns daily and advances by teaching better things, we do not reject anything better that may be said. We are prepared for everything, even though we are subjected to insults.

Nevertheless, so that truth may not be obstructed, we do not complain about our own injury but proclaim the glory of God.

### 15

It is certain what the Apostle says: “Who, being in the form of God” (Philippians 2:6). For who denies that the Son is in the form of God? That he is God, Lord, and King, I think we have already explained at sufficient length.

And that “he did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God,” the blessed Apostle Paul teaches us. He did not seize it, nor do we say that he did; but because “he emptied himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8), we proclaim this with all our strength.

We are called sons by grace; we were not born so by nature. Therefore he is the only-begotten Son, because according to what he is by the nature of his divinity, as Son he was born.

If you bring the Holy Spirit in as his brother, since you assert that the Holy Spirit is comparable and equal to the Son, and likewise profess that he is from the substance of the Father, then the Son is no longer the only-begotten, since another also exists from the same substance.

We have not received the nature of the unbegotten Father God; we believe what Christ said: “God is spirit” (John 4:24).

[Editorial notes (col. 733): Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read “we receive.” Lov. reads “the Father, Spirit, begot the Son, Spirit.” The same edition reads “the Son before all ages.”]

The Son was born, as we have said. We both profess the true Son and do not deny that he is like the Father, being instructed moreover by the divine Scriptures.

Since we are accused of saying that there are different natures, know this: we say that the Father, who is spirit, begot a spirit before all ages; God begot God—and the other points that have already been stated above. The true unbegotten Father begot the true Son.

But when the Lord says in the Gospel, “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), he calls the Father alone true in the same way as he calls him alone good, alone powerful, and alone wise.

I think not even the devil himself dared to say that the Father did not beget a perfect Son before all ages.

[Editorial note (col. 733): Lov. reads “the Son before all ages.”]

He did not beget one who was progressing toward perfection. A human being, whose example you accepted, if he were able to generate a perfect son immediately, would not generate a little child who, after the years had been assembled, might finally fulfill his father’s will. But the Father, who is truly blessed and alone powerful, begot a Son such as he is now and such as he remains without end—not one who is progressing, but one who is perfect. He received perfection from his progenitor, from whom he also received life.

The Savior’s declaration is: “Every word will be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18:16). You brought forward the apostolic testimony, “Who, being in the form of God, did not regard it as robbery”—which you interpreted according to your own judgment; and we, likewise, responded according to what we understood.

It will be for the judgment of the hearers to choose one of two alternatives: either let them approve, according to the sequence of the reading, the Son obedient to the Father, who emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and to whom the Father also gave, as we have said, the name that is above every name; or let each person accept your interpretation.

### 16

You assert, I think, as you say, that when the Lord said, “I ascend to my God and your God” (John 20:17), he spoke on account of the form of a servant that he assumed.

If, while he was humbling himself in a human body—even after he had conquered death and triumphed over the devil—he uses this expression after his resurrection, saying, “I ascend to my Father and your Father,” then, as you say, the humility of the flesh was no longer necessary on account of the Jews; rather, the complete rule of faith was being handed down.

[Editorial note (col. 733): The manuscripts read “he uses these expressions.” In the same codices, at col. 726, no. 6, and col. 728, no. 9 near the end, Maximinus likewise construes *uti* (“to use”) with the accusative.]

Likewise, in another place after his resurrection, when he had taken his disciples up onto the Mount of Olives, he said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:18–20).

And if the Son said this because of humility and not because of truth, why did the Apostle dare to repeat the same thing and say: “The God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory” (Ephesians 1:17)? Or again: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ knows, he who is blessed forever” (2 Corinthians 11:31); and: “That with one mind and one mouth you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 15:6); and he adds further: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 1:3)?

Why, even before Christ’s incarnation, did the Holy Spirit say to the Son: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 44:8)?

Although you may wish to argue about this anointing, you will not be able to prove that it occurred in the body. For we read that he was baptized (Matthew 3:16), but we do not read that he was anointed in the body.

From the reading itself, however, when it says, “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions,” it is plainly shown that “the oil of gladness,” in place of the designation “oil,” signifies that gladness of which he spoke through Solomon: “I was beside him, rejoicing daily; I rejoiced before his face at all times, when he rejoiced over the completed world and rejoiced in the children of men” (Proverbs 8:30–31).

In the statement, “I was beside him, rejoicing daily,” we read in the book of Genesis that the Father rejoiced at all the works of the Son, as we read: “And God saw, and behold, everything was very good” (Genesis 1:31). Praising the work of his Son, he rejoiced and was glad in the Son; likewise, the Son rejoiced before his progenitor with the Father’s perfect will.

“Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching” (2 Timothy 3:16). For this reason, not one iota or one letter-stroke will pass away (Matthew 5:18). The Lord said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35).

### 17

It is established that in the beginning the Son existed, that he was with the Father, and that he was God; and “he was in the beginning with God, as the firstborn of all creation. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3). This cannot be attributed to the person of the Holy Spirit.

For you will not find such things reported in the divine Scriptures as would allow you to assert that he is equal to the Son. Indeed, the Son was in the beginning; but the Father is before the beginning and without beginning, as unbegotten and unborn.

He was in the beginning as “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). He existed before every creature, before anything whatever existed; he was with God, and he was God, and he was in the beginning with God.

### 18

What if you hear the Father saying: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3)?

You profess that he was born from the womb of a mother—which even the Jews do not doubt—according to the flesh. Why, then, should these testimonies not be brought forward, which demonstrate that birth in the beginning, just as the preceding testimony instructs us?

If, because of the body in which he emptied himself—he who, though rich, became poor for our sake, as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 8:9)—he considers himself indebted to his progenitor, how much more must he who begot him, so great and such a one, always offer his progenitor the reverence and obedience that are due, as his beloved Son?

You have argued very well that he was subject to his parents on account of the form of a servant (Luke 2:51). If he is found subject to the parents whom he himself created, since all things were made through him—for we know that the Son was begotten by the Father not after the ages but before the ages—if he was subject to his parents, as the authority of the divine Scriptures proclaims with the clearest light, how much more is he subject to his own progenitor, who begot him so great and such a one, according to what the Apostle Paul says: “When all things have been subjected to the Son, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Corinthians 15:28)?

Do you wish this also to be said by us: that all things were subjected to the body—or rather, to the dispensation—which he assumed for our salvation? Indeed, the body was subjected to the Father, not the only-begotten Son himself who is God.

For we know and believe that the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father (John 5:22–23).

This is what we profess: that even in the resurrection, when all things have been subjected to the Son, when all honor, revere, and worship him, the Son does not then exalt himself. Rather, even with all things subjected to him, he is found subject to the Father in this way, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

### 19

It has already been said that you too appeared, according to your own judgment, to estrange this statement from its meaning. The apostolic declaration nevertheless stands: “We do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings.”

And because you appeared to object on the basis of an argument, saying, “Is the Holy Spirit therefore so pitiable that he groans?”, we do not call the Holy Spirit pitiable. Indeed, the glory of the Holy Spirit is shown by the very reading, because he does not groan for himself. Hear the reading: he groans “for the saints” (Romans 8:26–27).

[Editorial note (col. 735): Most manuscripts read “but hear the reading”; others read “but by love”; the printed editions read “but for love.”]

Likewise, the Son does not plead for himself, but certainly pleads and intercedes for us, as I have already presented above.

“Whoever is faithful in a very little is also found faithful in much” (Luke 16:10).

### 20

Nor can it otherwise be asserted that the Father and the Son are one except in precisely the way that you yourself—and we also—can prove from the very examples you used.

For if, as you say and the Apostle confirms, “Whoever joins himself to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17), then there is one spirit in agreement, fulfilling the will of God, according to the Savior’s teaching. He taught us to pray in this way also, so that among the other things in our prayers we may say: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matthew 6:10).

We are the earth. Therefore, just as God’s will is done in the heavenly beings, so may it be fulfilled in us, who pray for this and accomplish it by our deeds, so that we may become one spirit with God when we desire what God desires.

The Son himself, when his Passion was near, cried out to his progenitor, saying: “Abba, Father, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36).

By saying, “Not what I will, but what you will,” he truly showed that his will was subject to his progenitor, on account of whose will he descended from heaven, as he says: “I descended from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me” (John 6:38).

Therefore the will of the Son is harmonious and concordant with the will of the Father. Insofar as the Son, as God, is greater than every creature, he is found that much more harmonious with the Father’s will and that much more closely attached to his progenitor.

I say that he is attached to his progenitor as a beloved son—in love, affection, unanimity, agreement, and concord.

Everything presented by the holy Scriptures must be received with complete reverence. For the divine Scripture did not come under our authority so that it might receive correction from us. Would that we might also be found worthy to be approved as disciples of the Scriptures!

### 21

I accept what you brought forward: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

For God does not dwell in a human being whom the Holy Spirit has not first sanctified and purified. Finally, it was also said to that blessed virgin Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you”—plainly, in order to sanctify and purify her. Then it follows: “And the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

That the power of the Most High is Christ, you yourself have already presented.

Truth is not inferred from an argument but established by certain testimonies. For this reason you ought to produce testimonies that the Holy Spirit is God, that he is Lord, that he is King, that he is Creator, that he is Maker, that he sits with the Father and the Son, and that he is worshiped—if not by the heavenly beings, at least by earthly beings; or perhaps you will show that he is worshiped even by those below.

We say these things without detracting from the Holy Spirit. For, as we have already explained above, he is the Holy Spirit without whom no one can say, “Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

This is the Holy Spirit in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). This is the Holy Spirit so great and such a one that even angels long to look into him (1 Peter 1:12).

He is so great and so powerful that everywhere, in every creature—whether in the east, the west, the north, or the south—whoever worships God cannot say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit.

Such is his nature: he is present everywhere to all who call upon God in truth (Psalm 144:18). He is so great and such a one that wherever anyone is baptized—whether in the east, the west, or anywhere at all—the Holy Spirit is present at that very moment.

Observe how great the power of the Holy Spirit is. For if anyone detracts from the Holy Spirit, he certainly detracts from the only-begotten God, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3), just as one who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him (John 5:23).

## 22.

You say that our Savior Christ did not say, “that they and we may be one,” but rather, “that they may be one in their nature and substance,” united and fused together, as it were, in harmonious equality [Note: Some manuscripts read “in harmony, equality” (*concordia, aequalitate*); others, “by equality of harmony” (*concordiae aequalitate*)]; and that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one because of their indivisible and identical nature. I shall read the passage, so that those who read it may establish what Christ said. For in the Gospel he speaks thus while praying to his Father for the disciples:

> “Father, make them one, as we also are one: as I am in you and you in me, so that they too may be one in us; so that the world may know that you sent me, and loved them as you loved me” (John 17:21–23).

I believe what I read: he mentioned love, not substance. It is certain, moreover, that the Savior himself said:

> “Whoever hears my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him; and we shall come and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:21, 23).

If, then, that great sublimity and majesty of the Father, and likewise of the Son, is received within the single little dwelling of our mind, how much more is it certain and beyond doubt that the Son will be in the Father! Yet the Son is nevertheless another than the Father. As you yourself explained, the Father and the Son “are one,” but are not “one person”: “one” pertains to concord, while “one person” pertains to singular number.

You also brought forward the testimony of the blessed Paul, which we gladly accepted, since truth is firmly established when it is produced even by those who contradict it. For you recited that Paul said:

> “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one; but each shall receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Corinthians 3:6–8).

Observe, therefore, that although they are one in concord, each shall nevertheless receive his own reward according to his labor. Consider, then, also what the Lord says:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

This we believe and accept with certain faith. The one who says “I” is the Son; the one who says “and the Father” indicates another Father. He says “one,” not “one person.” It has often been stated that “one” pertains to concord.

How are the Father and the Son not one, when the Son cries out, “I always do the things that please the Father” (John 8:29)? He would not then be one with the Father if he ever did things contrary to the Father. In the same way, the Apostles are one with the Father and the Son, insofar as in all things they look toward the will of God the Father and, in imitation of the Son, are found subject to the one God the Father, and themselves are likewise so subject. [Note: See Augustine, Sermon 140, no. 4, volume 5.]

We read that the Savior prayed not only for the Apostles, that they might be one, but also for those who would believe through their word, saying:

> “I ask not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us; so that the world may know that you sent me, and loved them as you loved me.”

As we said, he mentioned love, not divinity. Who, moreover, does not know that Paul is Paul, and Apollo is Apollo, when Paul himself says, “I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10)? For the one who labors more attains more. Nevertheless, they are one in agreement, harmony, and love, when they do what God wills.

## 23.

You say that there is one God. Establish whether, if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, the one God is to be called the Father alone, whose Son, our Christ, is God. In Jewish fashion, are you urging us to profess one God? Or is one God rather shown through the Son’s subjection, according to the Christian faith—that is, the one whose Son, our Christ, is God, as we have said?

Since the Father and the Son are not one person, believe at least Paul, who declares this in nearly every Epistle, saying:

> “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7; 1 Corinthians 1:3; 2 Corinthians 1:2; Galatians 1:3; Ephesians 1:2).

Again:

> “One God the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we in him” (1 Corinthians 8:6). [Note: The printed editions have “through him” (*per ipsum*). The manuscripts have “in him” (*in ipso*); and Augustine, in Book 2, chapter 23, no. 3, observes that Maximinus cited the passage less correctly in this form.]

This is the one God whom we Christians proclaim: the one whom the Son declares to be uniquely good, saying:

> “No one is good except one God” (Mark 10:18).

Not that Christ is not good, for he himself says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). Not that the Holy Spirit is not good: hear the prophet crying out, “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path” (Psalm 142:10). Hear also the Savior’s testimony:

> “The good person brings forth good things from the treasure of his heart” (Luke 6:45).

Indeed, every creature of God is very good. If the creature is good, if the human being is good, if the Holy Spirit is good, if Christ is good, we must ask in what sense there is one who is good. The Savior says, “No one is good except one God,” because he himself is the fountain of goodness, and, being good, received his goodness from no one.

Christ, insofar as he is good, received from his begetter that he should be good; and every creature of God received through Christ that it should be good. But whether the Son or those who were made through him, each according to the measure of his faith, received from that one fountain of goodness what made them good. The Father, however, being good, received this from no one. Therefore Christ says, “No one is good except one.”

Thus there is one God because there is one who is incomparable and one who is immeasurable, as we have already explained.

## 24.

We do not deny that the Son loves the Father, since we also read:

> “So that the world may know that I love the Father, and just as the Father commanded me, so I do” (John 14:31).

It is clear that the Son is both loved and loves, and that he fulfills the Father’s command, as he himself asserts. Therefore they are one, according to his saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

When he says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), we must believe with certain faith that whoever sees the Son sees and understands the Father through the Son.

## 25.

Because of the form of a servant, you have professed the Father to be greater; this seems to me exceedingly foolish. For we know—and you yourself also stated it—that in the form of a servant he was made lower even than the angels.

Nor have you been sufficiently lavish in glorifying God [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and Venice edition have “you have advanced” (*provectus es*). Manuscript M has the same reading.], since you profess the Father to be greater according to the form of a servant. According to the form of a servant, the angels too are greater.

Christ did not come to teach us that the Father is greater according to the form of a servant. Rather, Truth came to us in order to teach and instruct us that the Father is greater than the Son—and greater than that Son who is the great God. For we glorify the Father in such a way that we profess him greater than the great God and proclaim him higher than the lofty one.

Whether this is the proper honor owed to God—that the Father should be greater than the form of a servant—you must decide.

## 26.

You say that the divinity showed itself to the patriarchs, and shortly before you maintained that the divinity is invisible. It did indeed show itself, but not the Father, who is invisible. For if we say that the Father was seen, we make the Apostle a liar, since he says:

> “No human being has seen him or can see him” (1 Timothy 6:16).

We are then found not only to resist the New Testament, but likewise to contradict the Old. For Moses says:

> “No one can see God and live” (Exodus 33:20).

Moses himself described in the book of Genesis that from the first human being, Adam, up to the very Incarnation, it was always the Son who was seen.

If you seek testimonies, you certainly have the Father saying to the Son:

> “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.”

The text continues:

> “And God made the human being” (Genesis 1:26–27).

Which God, surely, except the Son? You yourself explained this in your treatises.

This Son, therefore, who is the prophet of his begetter and who also said, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make for him a helper corresponding to him” (Genesis 2:18), was seen by Adam, according to what we read Adam saying:

> “I heard your voice as you walked in the garden, and I hid myself because I was naked.”

You also have what God said to him:

> “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat?” (Genesis 3:10–11).

This God was also seen by Abraham (Genesis 18:1). And that it was the Son who was seen by Abraham, if you wish to believe it, the only-begotten God himself affirms in the holy Gospel, saying:

> “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

This Son was also seen by Jacob. In the figure in which he was to come—that is, in the form of a human being—he is found to have previously wrestled with Jacob. Hence Jacob said:

> “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved.”

The name of that place was therefore called “Vision of God.” God himself, who wrestled with Jacob in anticipation of what was to come, confirms this, and we see it fulfilled in Christ’s Passion. For he said to Jacob:

> “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Genesis 32:23–30),

that is, “a human being seeing God.”

We demonstrate that this one was also seen in the New Testament. The Apostles said of him:

> “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

But if, as you attempt to assert, the Father is said to have been seen, then all the Scriptures are liars among you [Note: The printed editions have “according to us” (*apud nos*).].

For Paul proclaims the Father invisible (1 Timothy 6:16), and the Lord affirms this in the Gospel (John 1:18). You accuse us repeatedly of speaking boldly and presumptuously of things that we ought not say; the readers may decide whether this is so.

We do not speak in this way to obtain anyone’s praise [Note: The manuscripts have “to obtain praise from your followers” (*ut a tuis laudem consequamur*).], but out of a desire to gather together the brotherhood that is with us [Note: The American and Erasmus editions have “that is with you” (*quae vobiscum est*).]—or perhaps on account of which you yourself deigned to provoke us, so that we would give a reply, and so that those marked out among us might agree with your profession, as I have said. Because of the fear of God, it was necessary for me to give you a reply.

You attempted not merely to strip me by your words of discipleship among them; you also delivered your treatise, to which I must respond with what I have set forth concerning the invisibility of almighty God.

You yourself, although occupied with another purpose [Note: The Louvain edition adds here, “being occupied” (*occupatus*).], nevertheless affirmed in your own words that the Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove and also in the form of fire (Matthew 3:16; Acts 2:3); the Son, certainly, in human form; but the Father neither in the form of a dove nor in human form. He has never changed himself into forms, nor will he ever change, concerning whom it is written:

> “I am who I am,” and “I do not change” (Exodus 3:14; Malachi 3:6).

The Son, already existing in the form of God, as you yourself stated, took the form of a servant; the Father did not. Likewise, the Holy Spirit assumed the form of a dove; the Father did not.

Know, therefore, that there is one who is invisible, and one who is also beyond comprehension and immeasurable. I ask and desire to be a disciple of the divine Scriptures. For I believe that Your Reverence remembers what I said in reply above: if you produce from the divine Scriptures that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one power, one substance, one divinity, one majesty, and one glory—if you affirm this from the divine Scriptures, if you produce a passage written somewhere to that effect—we desire to be found disciples of the divine Scriptures.

*I, Maximinus, bishop, have subscribed.* [Note: The Louvain edition alone has “has subscribed” (*subscripsit*).]

*And after the conclusion of the present proceedings Augustine dictated the following:*

You have said that I speak fortified by the assistance of the authorities, not according to the fear of God. But it is sufficiently clear to people whom God grants understanding who speaks according to the fear of God: whether it is the one who obediently hears the Lord saying, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4)—which we hear obediently and proclaim faithfully—or the one who refuses to hear this in such a way that he contends that there are two lords and two gods.

By introducing two gods and two lords, he shows that he does not fear the one Lord God who says, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.”

You know that your extremely lengthy speech used up the time in which we could have replied, leaving only as much of the day as was altogether insufficient even for us to have the things you said read back to us.

Nevertheless, you should know that everything you brought forward to prove that the Son is God, the great God, born from the Father, and another than the Father—since the Father himself is not the Son—belonged to lengthy delays by which you consumed the necessary time, as though it were necessary for you to prove to us something that we also confess to be true.

For we do not say that the one who is the Father is the Son, or that the one who is the Father or the Son is the Holy Spirit within the Trinity. One is one person, another another, and another yet another; but all together they are one Lord God.

If we were to say that there are two lordly gods—one great, the other greater; one good, the other better; one wise, the other wiser; one merciful, the other more merciful; one powerful, the other more powerful; one invisible, the other more invisible; one true, the other truer—and anything else that you have shown yourself to think in this way, so as to persuade us that we have two lordly gods, then God himself would accuse us, saying what I have already recalled:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.”

As though he were saying to us:

> “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4:3).

Why do you make two lordly gods for yourselves? Why do you refuse to hear me crying out, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” and instead cry out against me, “Our lords and gods are two lords”?

Would you do this if you wished to be Israel? Since this name is interpreted as “a human being seeing God,” I ask you to forgive me if you do not wish to be Israel: I do wish to be Israel. I wish to be counted among those who are granted the sight of God.

We give thanks to him because he makes us see now through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face, as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 13:12). Thus, by his gift, we see—even if for now through a mirror in a riddle—how these two propositions are not opposed to one another: that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, and yet these three together are one Lord God.

I did what I could so that you too might see this. But you preferred to resist because you did not wish to be Israel.

Yet if perhaps you still cannot see this, believe, and you will see. These things are seen by understanding, not by looking with the eyes of the flesh. You surely know that the prophet said:

> “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9).

Therefore, when you hear, “The Lord your God, the Lord is one,” do not make two lords and gods, the Father and the Son.

And when you hear:

> “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” and in the same place [Note: The manuscripts have “and in another place” (*et alio loco*):] “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:19, 15),

when you hear these things, do not deny that the Holy Spirit is God, lest you make the members of the Creator a temple of a creature.

First believe that these three are three in their individual persons, and yet together are not three lordly gods but one Lord God. The Lord himself will give the believer and petitioner understanding, so that you may be worthy also to see—that is, to understand—what you believe.

For carefully consider everything you said in your lengthy disputation, and you will see that it proceeds from this error: that you make two lords and gods, contrary to the Lord God’s most clear declaration, “The Lord your God, the Lord is one.” And you deny that the Holy Spirit is God, although you cannot deny that his temple is holy.

For the present, after our Conference, in which we spoke in turn in one another’s presence, it will be enough that I have admonished you of these matters. But if the Lord wills—since the work is lengthy and you are eager to return—I shall set out our arguments before the eyes of those who wish to read them, with as much clarity as I can, and I shall show, whether you wish it or not, that you attempted to prove your false doctrines by true divine testimonies.

*And in another hand: I, Augustine, bishop, have subscribed.*

*Again, in another hand, Maximinus:*

When you have completed this little book and sent it to me, if I have not replied to everything, then I shall be blameworthy.

*The Proceedings have been completed. I have compared them.* [Note: The Louvain edition has “Antonius: I have compared the genuine Proceedings.” The American and Erasmus editions, after “if I have not replied,” have “then the blame will be explained” (*culpa explicaberis*). Antonius has “I have compared the Proceedings.” But the ancient codices have “then I shall be blameworthy.” The very ancient Corbie manuscript has “The genuine Proceedings have been completed; I have compared them.” All the manuscripts lack the name “Antonius.”]

[Col. 0743]

# Two Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Against Maximinus, the Heretic, Arian Bishop [Note: Written around the year 428.] (C)

## Book One [Note: Elsewhere, “Book Two.”]

Augustine shows that Maximinus was unable to refute what he himself had said at the Conference.

In replying as was due to the disputation of Maximinus, the Arian bishop, whose lengthy speech consumed the time of day during which we were conferring in one another’s presence, I must address him directly—whether he still thinks contradiction necessary when he reads this, or whether, with the Lord working wonderfully in his heart, he may agree with the truth that has been made manifest [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venice edition have “manifest truth” (*manifestae*). M has the same reading.].

What moved you, Arian, to say so much while saying nothing about the matter at issue between us, as though being unable to stop speaking were the same as being able to reply? I shall first show that you were unable to refute what I said; then, insofar as it seems necessary, I shall refute what you yourself said.

## Chapter One

### On Two Gods

Concerning the two gods whom you yourself mentioned, I certainly replied to your words when you said that one God is worshiped by you:

> “It follows,” I said, “that either you do not worship Christ, or you do not worship one God, but two.”

Attempting to answer this, you spoke at length, asserting that you also worship Christ as God. Although you did not deny that two gods are worshiped by you, you nevertheless did not dare to confess it. You realized that Christian ears could not endure the claim that two gods are to be worshiped.

How promptly you would correct yourself if you feared believing what you feared to say! For since the Apostle cries out, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10), if you think that what you believe pertains to righteousness, why do you not also confess it with your mouth unto salvation? But if confessing that two gods are to be worshiped does not pertain to salvation, then undoubtedly believing it does not pertain to righteousness either.

Since you do not wish your mouth to be held guilty by such a confession, why do you not cleanse your heart of such a belief? Hold fast, with the Catholic Church, to the right faith; do not be ashamed to correct what is perverse.

Hold fast, with the Catholic Church, that the Father is not the one who is the Son, and the Son is not the one who is the Father; that the Father is God and the Son is God; yet that both together are not two gods but one.

Only in this way will you worship both the Father and the Son, while not saying that two gods are to be worshiped but one. Thus your conscience will not be pierced by the guilt of impiety when the divine declarations sound in your ears:

> “There is no God except one” (1 Corinthians 8:4);

and:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one”;

and when you hear:

> “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deuteronomy 6:4, 13),

you will be able, without fear, to serve not the Father alone but also the Son with the service owed to the one God.

Remember, therefore, that you did not answer what I had objected: that one God is not worshiped by you, but two.

## Chapter Two

### On Human Contamination

Secondly, I dealt with you concerning your words in which you had said that God the Father did not descend into human contamination, as though Christ had suffered those things in the flesh. I explained how “contamination” is ordinarily understood: certainly as referring only to some vice, and we know that Christ was free from all such vices.

You could give no answer to this either. The divine testimonies that you yourself cited could not help you, for you could not prove from them that Christ had been contaminated by any human defilement.

As for what you recall the Apostle saying—“Although Christ was not a sinner, he made sin for us”—read more carefully. Perhaps you have encountered a corrupt manuscript, or perhaps the Latin translator has erred; consult the Greek, and you will find that Christ did not himself commit sin for us, but that God the Father made Christ himself “sin,” that is, a sacrifice for sin.

The Apostle says:

> “We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He made the one who knew no sin to be sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:20–21).

Therefore he himself did not commit sin; rather, God made him “sin” for us—that is, as I said, a sacrifice for sin. For if you recall or reread the books of the Old Testament, you will find that sacrifices for sins are called “sins.”

The likeness of sinful flesh in which he came to us was itself also called “sin”:

> “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and through sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3).

That is, from the likeness of sinful flesh—which was his own—he condemned sin in sinful flesh, which is ours.

For this reason it is also said of him:

> “For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6:10).

He died to sin once because he died to the likeness of sinful flesh when, by dying, he was stripped of the flesh. Through this mystery he signified that those who are baptized into his death die to sin in order to live to God.

Likewise, through the cross he was made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Hanging on the wood, he suspended on the wood the death that had come from God’s curse; and thus our old self was crucified together with him (Romans 6:6), so that the statement in the Law, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deuteronomy 21:23), might not be understood as false.

What is “cursed” except “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19)? And what is “everyone” except that Christ himself, although he was life, nevertheless died a true death, not an imagined one?

If you understand these mysteries, you will understand at the same time that they are not contaminations. But what does it matter to us if, speaking in your customary manner, you wished perhaps to call the touch of mortals “contamination,” when nevertheless you agree with us that the Lord Jesus had no sin either in spirit or in flesh?

## Chapter Three

### On the Invisible God

Thirdly, when I was discussing the invisible God, I urged you to believe that not only the Father but also the Son is invisible according to his divinity, though not according to the flesh in which he appeared visibly to mortals—who denies this? I discussed this afterward in another place as well.

You, however, yielding to the most evident truth, agreed that the Son is invisible; and thereby you destroyed what you had said, namely, that the Father alone is invisible.

But then, disturbed by your own agreement because you had conceded that the Son too is invisible, you dared to say that lesser beings can be seen by greater beings, but greater beings cannot be seen by lesser ones. You said that angels are seen by archangels, souls by angels, but angels are not seen by souls.

From this you further asserted that Christ, according to the substance of his divinity, is seen neither by human beings nor even by the heavenly Powers. Thus you said that the Father alone is invisible because he has no superior by whom he might be surveyed on every side.

Tell us, I beg you: when did the archangels inform you that they see angels but are not seen by angels? From which angels did you learn that they see souls, while souls do not see them? From whom did you hear these things? Where did you learn them? Where did you read them?

Would it not be better to devote your attention to the divine Books, where we read that angels were seen even by human beings, whenever they wished and in whatever manner they wished to be seen, at the command or permission of the Creator of all?

Nevertheless, although you had said that only the Father should be called invisible because he has no superior by whom he might be surveyed, you later confessed that he is visible to the Son, producing against yourself the Gospel testimony in which the Son himself says:

> “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father” (John 6:46).

Here the truth defeated you most openly. But because you did not wish to be freed from error, you did not wish to be beneficially defeated.

For after you had recalled against yourself the Gospel testimony by which it became clear that the Father is seen by the Son, when the Son himself said, “The one who is from God has seen the Father,” you immediately added from your own resources, “But he saw the incomprehensible one.”

For the moment, you have forfeited what you had said: that the Father alone is invisible because he has no superior. For, overcome by the truth, you confessed that he is seen by an inferior.

You say that the Son is inferior, and yet you said—compelled by the Son’s testimony—that the Father is seen by him [Note: The Louvain edition adds here “by the truth” (*veritate*)]. We shall discuss “incomprehensible” later, so that there too the truth may defeat you.

Our dispute was not about what is comprehensible or incomprehensible, but about what is visible and invisible. In that dispute, if you yourself are visible to yourself, you see that you have been defeated.

## Chapter Four

### On the Immortal God

Fourthly, I dealt with you concerning the immortal God, the Son also. For you wished the Apostle’s words, “who alone has immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16), to be understood as though they were spoken of the Father alone; whereas he said this not of the Father, but of God, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I therefore showed that the Son too possesses immortality according to the substance of his divinity. For according to the flesh, who denies that he was mortal?

But when you wished to reply to me on this point, hemmed in by evident truth, you confessed that God the Son too possesses immortality. You were therefore defeated in maintaining that the Apostle said only of the Father that he alone has immortality. Nor do you escape the bonds of truth by saying, “The Son indeed has immortality, but receives it from the Father.” The question is not from whom he has it, but whether he has it. For you wish what is written, “He alone has immortality,” to be understood of the Father alone.

The Father possesses immortality received from no one, and the Son possesses immortality received from the Father; nevertheless, both Father and Son possess immortality. Otherwise, if the Son does not possess it, either the Father did not give it to the Son, or the Son lost what he received. But the Father gave it to the Son, and the Son did not lose it; nor did the Father, by giving, lose what he gave by begetting. Therefore both Father and Son possess immortality, not the Father alone.

You are consequently compelled to confess that “who alone has immortality” was not said of the Father alone, since you have already been compelled to confess that the Son too has immortality. Yet God possesses this alone; but the Father is not God alone, since the Son is this also, and the two, together with the Holy Spirit, are one God. But why God alone is said to possess immortality, although the soul too is immortal in its own manner, as are other spiritual and heavenly creatures, we shall see later. For now, it is enough that you could answer nothing to what I said, and that you were compelled to confess that not the Father alone, but the Son too, though from the Father, nevertheless possesses immortality.

## Chapter Five

### In What Respect the Father Is Greater

Fifthly, I showed in what respect the Father is greater than the Son: not greater than God, in respect of whom the Son is coeternal with him, but greater than the human being, because the Son was made in time. There I recalled the apostolic testimony: “Because, being in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a robbery.” For equality with God was his by nature, not by robbery.

In reply you said: “For who denies that the Son is in the form of God? That he is God, that he is Lord, that he is King, I think we have already explained at greater length. And the blessed Apostle Paul teaches us by the words, ‘he did not consider equality with God a robbery,’ that he did not seize it; nor do we say that he did.” These words of yours not only contain nothing against us; rather, they appear to be for us. For if you confess the form of God, why do you not openly confess that the Son of God is equal to God?

Especially since, concerning the Apostle’s words, “He did not consider equality with God a robbery,” you could find nothing to say for your side. And because you could not deny that the Apostle said this, you therefore said, “he did not seize it; nor do we say that he did,” as though “he did not seize it” meant “he did not have it,” that is, equality with God; and as though the statement, “He did not consider equality with God a robbery,” meant, “He did not consider that equality with God was to be seized,” because it was foreign to him. For a robber is one who usurps another’s property, as though the Son, though able to do so, had been unwilling to seize it. You see how foolish this view is.

Understand, then, that the Apostle said, “He did not consider equality with God a robbery,” because he did not consider foreign what he was born with. Yet although he did not consider equality with God foreign but his own, he emptied himself, seeking not what was his own but what was ours. To know that this is so, observe how the Apostle came to say this. For when he was enjoining on Christians the humility of charity, he said: “each esteeming the other superior to himself, not each attending to his own interests, but also to those of others” [Note: Louvain reads “but those of others”; the manuscripts read “but also those of others,” in accordance with the Greek *alla kai*.]. Then, in order to exhort them by Christ’s example not to seek or attend to their own interests, but also those of others, he says: “Let each of you have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God”—which was his own—“did not consider it robbery,” that is, did not consider it foreign, “to be equal with God”; yet, seeking what was ours, not what was his own, “he emptied himself,” not by losing the form of God, but by taking the form of a servant.

For that nature is not mutable, so as to empty itself by losing what it was, but by receiving what it was not; not by consuming what was its own, but by assuming what was ours; and then, in the form of a servant, by obeying as a human being even to death on a cross. “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:6–9), and so forth. These things were given to the human being, not to God. For when he was in the form of God, he was not without exaltation, nor did heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings fail to bend the knee to him. But when it is said, “Therefore he exalted him,” it is sufficiently apparent on account of what he exalted him: namely, on account of obedience even to death on a cross.

Thus the form in which he was crucified was itself exalted; to it was given the name above every name, so that that same form of a servant might be called the only-begotten Son of God [Note: The printed editions add “may be understood,” wrongly and against the manuscripts.]. Therefore do not make the form of God unequal to God, something which cannot even be said of human beings. For when it is said, “This human being is in the form of that human being,” no one understands anything except that they are equal [Note: The American, Erasmus, and manuscript readings have “except equal,” singular.].

Or perhaps you do not wish to understand the phrase, “being in the form of God,” in this way—namely, that the Son is in the form of God the Father, where nothing appears but the equality of both—but think that “in the form of God” means in his own form, because he himself is certainly God. I do not much mind if you understand it in this way as well. For where growth does not bring about the fullness of the form of age, but the Son was born perfect because God begot him, undoubtedly, if the form of the Son is not equal to the form of the Father, he is not a true Son. But it is written: “That we may be in his true Son, Jesus Christ” (1 John 5:20). Therefore the form of the true Son cannot be unequal to the form of God the Father. Accordingly, even at this point in my argument, where I proved from the Apostle’s words that the Son is equal to the Father, you were unable to answer anything for your own contention.

## Chapter Six
### On the True Offspring of Animals

In the sixth place, to show that the Son is of the same nature as the Father, I even set before you the offspring of mortal animals, in all their brutishness, confronting your heart with its error: you deny that the Son who is God is of the same nature as the Father, although you do not deny that he is truly the Son. Yet God himself has granted animals to reproduce what they themselves are. Thus I named not only a human being the son of a human being, but also a dog the son of a dog—not to compare them with God, but to confound those who disparage the Son of God. For they see that corruptible and mortal natures nevertheless possess unity of nature with their parents, yet they refuse to grant to the Son of God that he shares with the Father the one nature, although he is inseparable from the Father and incorruptible and eternal with the Father.

For this reason I also said that, in your view, the human condition is the better one, since it is allowed to grow, so that by growing sons may attain the strength of their parents. But the Son of God, as you say and teach, was begotten less than the Father and remained so; and, lest he be able to attain the Father’s form, he did not grow.

Here, to make clear how heavily the great weight of truth pressed upon you, you gave no answer whatever to the point. Rather, as though you were gasping with failing breath [Note: [Col. 0748] The manuscripts read, “with failing breath.”], you thought me worthy of reproach, saying that so foul a comparison—of the son of a human being or of a dog—ought not to have been extended to that immeasurable greatness.

Is this an answer, or rather an admission of your inability to answer? It is as though I had introduced these examples from earthly natures in order to equate corruption with incorruption, mortality with immortality, visible things with invisible things, and temporal things with eternal things. Surely I did so instead to convict you, who err in matters great and supreme, by means of small and lowly things: you do not see the good which the supremely good Creator granted even to the most lowly and insignificant creatures—that although they are vastly different from him, they nevertheless generate what they themselves are.

Nor do you consider how evil is what you say: that although human beings and dogs and other creatures of this kind have true offspring, whom Truth creates through their begetting, the Truth itself is not the true Son of God. Or, if the authority of holy Scripture compels you to allow that he is the true Son, then we ask you to allow that he is not degenerate.

And how is he degenerate? Let Catholics hear, and let heretics blush. If the son of a strong man does not possess strength, he is called degenerate; yet he is a human being, as his father is, and although his manner of life is unlike his father’s, his substance is not alien. You want the only-begotten Son of God to be so degenerate that you deny him the very substance of the Father. You assert that he was born less than the Father and remained less; you grant him no age in which he could grow, and no equal form by which he could be made equal. Since you subtract so much from his nature, I marvel with what face you call him the true Son—unless, in your most wretched error, you think that you cannot attain the glory of the one Father except through the humiliation of the only Son [Note: [Col. 0749] See Sermon 139, sections 4 and 5, volume 5.].

### CHAPTER VII

### On the Greatness of the Son

In the seventh place I said: “We acknowledge the Son to be so great a God that we call him equal to the Father.” Therefore, I said, you tried in vain, by testimonies and by lengthy argument, to prove to us what we very emphatically profess.

To these words of mine I added an argument in which I explained why, although the Son is equal to the Father, he nevertheless calls him his God, when he says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). You had recalled this Gospel testimony, by which you thought you had proved that the Son was not equal to the Father.

In answer to this, I said that the Father is also the God of the only-begotten Son because he became human and was born of a woman. This is what he says in the Psalm, where he foretold what was to come: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm 21:11), showing that the Father is his God because he became human.
