A human being was born from his mother’s womb, and God was born, in respect of his humanity, from a virgin; so that the Father would be not only the one who begot him from himself, but also his God, since he created him as a human being from his mother’s womb.

When you wished to answer this, you said many things and brought forward many testimonies that do not help you at all. Yet although you had recalled the very words of holy Scripture, you could not in any way discover how the statement “From my mother’s womb you are my God” was to be understood.

Nor do I see at all why you inserted at that point a testimony from another Psalm, where it is written: “With you is dominion on the day of your strength, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3). It is not the person of the Son who says, “From your womb,” or, “From your belly, you are my God.” Even if that ineffable generation is understood as being from the Father’s womb, what is signified is that God begot God from himself—that is, from his own substance—just as, from his mother’s womb, when he was born, a human being begot a human being. Thus we understand that in both generations the substance of the one who was born and of those from whom he was born is not different.

The substance of God the Father and of the human mother is indeed different; yet the substance of God the Father and of God the Son is not different, just as the substance of the human mother and the human son is not different.

But hear what this Son says in prophecy: “From my mother’s womb,” he says, “you are my God.” Do not try to conceal clear matters beneath many words unnecessary to the point. The one who is the Father to the Son from his own womb is his God from his mother’s womb, not from his own.

To this point, therefore, you were wholly unable to offer any answer.

### CHAPTER VIII

### On the Son’s Subjection

In the eighth place I answered you concerning the subjection by which the Son is subject to the Father, since you had said: “By his subjection he established one God.” I replied that this too is rightly understood in respect of his humanity: the Son is subject to the Father. Nor is this surprising, since he is read to have been subject even to his parents in the very form of a servant (Luke 2:51), and it is written of him: “You made him a little less than the angels” (Psalm 8:6).

To this, as though answering, you said that I had argued very well, since he was subject to his parents on account of the form of a servant. Then, wishing to present as being in your favor what you saw was actually against you—and thus to make yourself appear to be answering before unwary and inattentive people, whoever might read these things, when you had nothing to say—you added these words:

“For if he is found subject to his parents, whom he himself created, since all things were made through him—for we know that the Son was begotten by the Father before the ages, not after the ages—if, then,” you say, “he was subject to his parents, as the authority of the divine Scriptures proclaims with the clearest light, how much more is he subject to his own begetter, who begot him so great and such a one, according to what Paul says: ‘When all things have been subjected to the Son, then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him’” (1 Corinthians 15:28)?

I might have thought these words of yours had been spoken by me, and were wholly mine, if it were not perfectly evident to those who heard you say them and to those who later read all these things that you yourself had said them. For who would believe that you could agree with us that Christ is subject according to the form of a servant, and therefore not according to the form of God?

### CHAPTER IX

### Whether the Holy Spirit Worships the Father

In the ninth place we asked you to show from the divine Scriptures, if you could, whether the Holy Spirit worships the Father. You had said this, but, as your own argument to which I replied sufficiently indicates, you had not proved it.

See, then, what you answered to this question in your later argument. After saying as much as you wished about the judgment of the Son—which we too believe with complete faith—and about the subjection by which we do not deny that the Son, according to the form of a servant, will be subjected to the Father, when you came to prove that the Father is worshiped by the Holy Spirit, you returned to those “groanings” about which I had already answered you: according to the manner of expression used by the holy Scriptures, what is meant by the statement, “The Spirit himself intercedes with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8:26).

Otherwise, we might believe that the Holy Spirit can never be without groanings, since there is no day, no hour, no moment of time in which prayers are not poured out to God by the saints somewhere—by some here, by others elsewhere. Since no time is free from the prayers of the saints—for day and night, while some are refreshed by food and drink, others do whatever else they may be doing, and others sleep, there are certainly always some whom holy desire compels to pray—it would follow that the Holy Spirit, who is present everywhere with everyone, is not permitted to cease from groaning even for a little while. This would be a state of utter misery, since he would be compelled to groan on behalf of all who pray.

Unless “to intercede with inexpressible groanings” is understood in the way I explained: namely, that by the groanings of holy desires he causes the saints to intercede, infusing in them the pious affection of spiritual grace.

I also recalled similar modes of expression, in which what is effected is signified by the one who effects it. Thus we say “sluggish cold,” because it makes people sluggish, and “a sad” or “joyful day,” because it makes people sad or joyful. I also cited examples from the holy Scriptures, where God says to Abraham, “Now I know” (Genesis 22:12)—which means nothing other than, “Now I have made you know.” For God should not then be said to have learned what, before it happened, he could never have been ignorant of.

Since you found no other way to interpret these modes of expression from the divine utterances that I had brought forward, you certainly should not have returned to those groanings. No one thinks in this way about the Holy Spirit unless he thinks according to the flesh and not according to the Spirit.

Yet even if you were granted the view you hold—that the Holy Spirit intercedes for the saints in the manner you understand—interceding or praying is one thing, and worshiping is another. Everyone who prays asks; not everyone who worships asks, nor does everyone who asks worship. Recall the custom of kings, who are often worshiped without being asked for anything; and sometimes are asked for something without being worshiped.

Thus you were entirely unable to demonstrate that the Father is worshiped by the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER X

### How the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit Are One God

In the tenth place I dealt with you so that you might understand how, through an ineffable union, the Trinity itself is one God, which we say is of one substance. For we find even different substances—namely, the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of the Lord—called one spirit through the union by which a human being clings to the Lord, as the Apostle says: “But the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

In answer to this—or rather, without remaining silent—you tried to show how the Father and the Son are one, not by unity of nature but of will. You are accustomed to say this, but especially when you are confronted with the Lord’s statement, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Here, however, I did not wish to prove that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one—which, because of the unity of substance, we certainly and most faithfully believe—but that the same Trinity is one God. “They are one” is one thing; “he is one God” is another. Distinguish between “is” and “are.”

The Apostle does not say, “Those who cling to the Lord are one,” because their substance is different. Rather, he says: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

If, when it is said of two, “One is,” and what that one is is specified—as the Apostle says, “he is one spirit”—you think this means the same as when it is said of two, “They are one,” without specifying what they are—as the Savior says, “I and the Father are one”—why do you not say, “The Father and the Son are one God”?

Why, when you hear, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), do you want this understood of the Father alone? Surely the Father is the Lord God, and the Son is the Lord God. Why are the two not, among you, one Lord God, just as, in the blessed Apostle, the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of the Lord are one spirit? [Note: [Col. 0752] Some manuscripts read, “the Lord.”]

What benefit does it bring your case that you say this occurs through agreement of will? It does occur in that way, but where nature is different, as the nature of a human being is different from that of the Lord. Yet the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit, certainly through agreement of will.

If, therefore, you do not want to say this through unity of substance, then at least say it through agreement of will. Say it sometime—say it somehow: “The Father and the Son are one God.”

But you do not say it, lest you be forced to confess that what you have never wished to acknowledge is said of both, and not of the Father alone: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.” For you do not wish to confess the Holy Spirit to be God; you do not wish to confess him to be Lord.

Say, I repeat, in whatever manner you wish: “The Father and the Son are one Lord God,” so that, serving the Father and the Son, you may serve one Lord, not two gods and two lords contrary to God’s command [Note: [Col. 0752] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read, “and serve one Lord.”].

But let enough now have been said on this matter. I think that, when you have read these things, if you have laid aside contentiousness, you will not deny that you were unable to answer what I recalled from the Apostle: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

### CHAPTER XI

### On the Temple of the Holy Spirit

In the eleventh place I demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is God from the fact that we ourselves are his temple, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). And again: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (ibid. 6:19).

You, however, answered nothing to this. For you said: “I accept what you have brought forward: ‘Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?’ For God,” you say, “does not dwell in a human being whom the Spirit has not first sanctified and purified.”

In this way you wanted it understood that the Holy Spirit had not been called God, and that we are not the temple of the Holy Spirit but of God; and that this is what was meant by the statement, “You are the temple of God.” But, you said, “The Spirit of God dwells in you” was added because the Holy Spirit purifies God’s temple, not his own; and once he has purified it, God then dwells there.

I do not wish to speak now of the absurdity that follows from this understanding of yours. For now I must show how, although you said much, you said nothing relevant to the matter. You abandoned the issue and proceeded to praise the Holy Spirit, elaborating that praise at length against yourself.

I said “against yourself” because you do not wish to call him God, although by praising him so greatly you were compelled to confess his divinity: that, although he is one, he is present everywhere and is absent from no one whom he sanctifies; wherever any Christian wishes to be and to pray to God, he presents himself to all at once, whether they are baptized into Christ in the East or in the West. This is what we too say.

But since we say that he is such and so great, far be it from us to deny that he is God. This is also demonstrated most readily and easily by his temple, which we ourselves are. For unless he were our God, he could not have us as his temple.

To conceal this, and in your speech to turn people’s minds away from the light of truth, you said whatever you said about the temple of God, refusing to have the Holy Spirit understood as God; but about the temple of the Holy Spirit, which is demonstrated with complete clarity, you were entirely silent.

For when I set before you two testimonies of the Apostle Paul—one in which he says, “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” and another in which he says, “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?”—why did you act so deceitfully as to mention only one of them, the one that says, “You are the temple of God,” and remain silent about the other, which says, “Your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you”? Why did you do this, I ask, unless you could in no way argue that our God was not the one who had us as his temple? We would certainly recognize him as God if the divine Scripture commanded us to make a temple for him of wood and stone.

### CHAPTER XII

### On the Father and the Son Being One

In the twelfth place I urged you to produce, if you could, the divine authority by which it is said that things of different substances are one. When you wished to answer this, you could produce nothing of the kind. Instead, driven by great straits, you dared to assert that the Apostles are one with the Father and the Son.

Christ certainly did not say this. For you spoke as though the Father, the Son, and the Apostles were one. Christ did not say, “That they and we may be one,” but said, “That they may be one, as we also are one.”

To give the very words of the Gospel: “Holy Father,” he says, “keep them in your name, whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we also are one.” Did he say, “That they may be one with us,” or, “That they and we may be one”?

Again, a little later: “I do not pray for these alone,” he says, “but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one.” Here too he did not say, “That they may be one with us.”

Then it follows: “As you, Father, are in me and I in you, so may they also be one in us.” Here too he did not say, “Let us be one,” or, “Let them be one with us,” but, “Let them be one in us.” Thus those who are one by nature, because they are human beings, may also be one in the Father and the Son—not one with them, that is, not so that they and the Father and Son should be one.

He adds further and says: “That the world may believe that you sent me, and I have given them the glory that you gave me, that they may be one as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:11–23).

Although, therefore, he repeatedly said, “That they may be one,” he never said anywhere, “That they and we may be one,” that is, “That they may be one with us.” Rather, he said either “in us” or “as we are”—that is, they according to their nature, and we according to ours.

For he wished those who were one by nature to be perfected in the very thing in which they were one. When he says, “Therefore you also must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), he does not wish to unite them to God by unity of nature, as though their nature and his were one and the same. He wishes them to be perfect in their own nature, just as God is perfect in his, although the natures are different and not one—which cannot happen unless we are in him.

This is not as everything is in him, since he contains everything he created. For this reason he is said not to be far from each one of us, because “in him we live and move and exist” (Acts 17:27–28). Rather, it is as those who are such as were told: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). Hence also the statement: “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39).

You were therefore unable to produce any passage saying, “They are one,” when their substance is not one but different. Yet you wished to creep upon us in an obscure passage, saying that the Apostles are one with the Father and the Son, as though the Apostles, the Father, and the Son were one, although it is evident that the substance of the Apostles is different from that of the Father and the Son.

Since it is evident that Christ nowhere said, “That they and we may be one,” or, “That they may be one with us,” it is likewise evident that you were unable to answer us and wished to employ deceit.

### CHAPTER XIII

### On the Testimony the Father Gave to the Son

In the thirteenth place I reminded you that the Father is not greater than the Son because the Father bore testimony to the Son. I also recalled that the prophets bore testimony to him, and you cannot say that they were greater than he.

You had said that the Father bore testimony to the Son. I understood this as though you wished to prove from this that the one who bore testimony was greater than the one to whom he bore it. But since in your later argument you were entirely silent on this point, I took your silence as agreement—although it is possible that you mentioned the Father’s testimony to the Son simply to show that one is one person and the other another, not to prove that the former is greater than the latter.

That the Father is one and the Son another, since the Father himself is not the Son, is a doctrine shared by you and us against the Sabellians. They say that the Son is not another but the same one who is the Father. We, however, say that the Father is one and the Son another, while nevertheless maintaining that the Son is what the Father is.

### CHAPTER XIV

### On the Love of the Father and the Son

In the fourteenth place, responding to what you had said—“I read of one who is loved, and I believe that it is the Father who loves and the Son who is loved”—I said:

“You claim that there is a distinction between the Father and the Son because the Father loves and the Son is loved, as though you could deny that the Son also loves the Father.”

Then I added: “If they both love one another, why do you deny that they are of one nature?”

I said this so that you would not deny their one nature on the grounds that, as you yourself said, one loves and the other is loved.

In response, you did agree that the Son also loves the Father, but you refused to agree that they are of one nature—as though the Son loved the Father as a creature loves the Creator, and not as the only-begotten Son loves the one who begot him, whom you want to make him degenerate by a difference of substance.

### CHAPTER XV

### On the Invisibility of the Trinity

In the fifteenth place I said that the Trinity is equally invisible, not the Father alone. Yet I said that the Son had appeared visibly in the form of a servant, on account of which he said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Since the divinity was also displaying itself to the patriarchs, I said that this occurred through a created thing subject to it, not through its own nature, by which the Trinity is invisible.

To prove this, I recalled Moses, to whom God spoke face to face, saying: “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me openly” (Exodus 33:11, 13). You were to understand how Moses saw the one whom he desired to be shown to him: if he saw God in the substance in which he is God, he certainly would not have asked him to show himself.

I also said that Christ is the Creator of visible and invisible things, thereby proving that he is not visible in his own substance, since through him not only visible but also invisible things could be created.

In attempting to answer this, see how many things you said that have nothing to do with the matter. Yet concerning Moses—why he wished God, with whom he was speaking, to be shown to him if he perceived God’s nature and substance—you dared to say absolutely nothing.

Nevertheless, you continued to assert that the Son of God, the Creator of invisible things, had been visible in the form of God even before he took the form of a servant, although earlier you yourself had already confessed that he could be seen in the form of a servant but was invisible in the substance of his divinity.

### CHAPTER XVI

### On God Alone Being Wise

In the sixteenth place, because you had said that the Apostle spoke of the Father alone when he wrote, “To the only wise God” (Romans 16:27), I said:

“Then the Father alone is the wise God, and the very Wisdom of God, who is Christ, is not wise, although the Apostle says of him: ‘Christ the Power of God and the Wisdom of God’” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

Then I added: “It remains for you to say—for what will you not dare?—that the Wisdom of God is foolish.”

To this you replied: “The blessed Apostle Paul proclaims the Father alone to be wise, saying: ‘To the only wise God.’ But,” you say, “we must seek the explanation of how he alone is wise—not because Christ is not wise.”

You then proceed and explain how you confess Christ also to be wise. For, after weaving together many things irrelevant to the matter in order to prolong your speech and consume time, you inserted these words into your argument: “But truly the Father alone is wise,” as though the Apostle had said, “To the only wise Father.”

But he said, “To the only wise God,” because the Son too is God—which you also wish to affirm—and the Holy Spirit too is God, although you do not wish to affirm it. This Trinity is the one wise God, who could never have been foolish and never will be: he is not wise by participation in wisdom through grace, but wise through the immobility and unchangeability of his nature.

For if I say to you: “Is it really so, O man who boast in the Christian name? Is Christ wise in such a way that he is not truly wise? Is Christ, who is the true God, not truly wise?”—would you not be so confounded by this question that you would immediately answer that Christ is truly wise?

What, then, is the meaning of your statement, “But truly the Father alone is wise”? Surely you now perceive where you have arrived and from how great a blasphemy you must turn back.

### CHAPTER XVII

### On God’s Being Unmade

In the seventeenth place I dealt with you concerning the fact that the Son too, and not the Father alone, is unmade—that is, was not made [Col. 0756].

You had said that you proclaim one God because there is one who is above all, unbegotten and unmade. In answer to this audacity of yours, I said:

“You speak of the Father as unmade as though the Son had been made, through whom all things were made.”

Then I added: “Know that the Son was made, but in the form of a servant. In the form of God, however, he was so far from being made that all things were made through him. For if he himself was made,” I said, “then all things were not made through him, but only everything else.”

When, with all the length of your discourse, you tried to answer this, you found nothing whatever to say. You simply remained silent about it, as though you had not heard it at all.

### CHAPTER XVIII

### On the Unbegotten Father

In the eighteenth place I thought I should also deal with you concerning the unbegotten Father—that is, the Father who was not begotten—since you had said this as well. I said:

“I do not, therefore, call the Son unbegotten; rather, I call the Father the begetter and the Son begotten. Yet the Father begot what he is. Otherwise the Son is not the true Son, if the Son is not what the Father is, just as we have already said above concerning the offspring of animals.”

To this also you offered nothing, either true or false.

### CHAPTER XIX

### On the Holy Spirit’s Equality with the Father

In the nineteenth place, because you had demanded that I show the Holy Spirit to be equal to the Father, I answered you:

“What is this that you demand—that I show the Holy Spirit to be equal to the Father—as though you had shown the Father to be greater than the Holy Spirit, just as you were able to show this concerning the Son on account of the form of a servant?”

“We know,” I said, “that the Father was said to be greater than the Son because the Son was in the form of a servant. The Son still possesses the human form that he raised into heaven; for this reason it was said of him that even now ‘he intercedes for us’ (Romans 8:34). This same immortal form will remain forever in the kingdom; for this reason it was said: ‘Then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him’ (1 Corinthians 15:28).”

But concerning the Holy Spirit, who took no creature into the unity of his person, although he too deigned to display himself visibly through a created thing—whether in the form of a dove or through fiery tongues (Matthew 3:16; Acts 2:3)—the Father was never said to be greater than he. The Spirit was never said to have worshiped the Father, and was never said to be less than the Father.

Although you seemed to answer this, you did not in fact answer it. You could not show that the Father had anywhere been called greater than the Holy Spirit, as the Son, on account of the form of a servant, said: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

When I said that the Holy Spirit had taken no creature into the unity of his person, you said that the Holy Spirit had appeared in the dove and in the fire in the same way that Christ appeared in a human being—as though the dove and the Spirit, or the fire and the Spirit, were one person, as the Word and the human being are one person.

Those forms appeared for a time to display visibly what the Holy Spirit, who is invisible, signified: the dove on account of holy love, and the fire on account of the light and fervor of charity. Once their symbolic function had been completed, those bodily forms passed away and ceased to exist thereafter, like the pillar of cloud—cloudy by day and luminous by night (Exodus 13:21–22).

Finally, lest anyone think that the dove or the flame belonged to the substance of the Holy Spirit, or that the nature of such great majesty had changed itself into these visible forms, or had taken them into the unity of its person, the Holy Spirit is never afterwards read to have appeared in this manner.

Christ, however, did not take human form for a time, in which he would appear to human beings and then allow that form to pass away. Rather, while the invisible form of God remained, he took the visible form of a human being into the unity of his person [Note: [Col. 0757] The Lov. edition reads: “but, while the unity of his person remained, the invisible form of God received,” and so forth.]. He was not only born in that form from a human mother, but also grew in it, ate and drank in it, slept in it, was killed in it, rose again in it, ascended into heaven in it, and sits at the right hand of the Father in it. In it he will come to judge the living and the dead, and in his kingdom he will be subject in it to the one who subjected all things to him.

You refused to attend to and consider these points, which had been stated briefly in my answer and which I have now explained at somewhat greater length so that you might understand them even in this form. Instead, you rushed into such great blasphemy that, shamefully, you called the divine nature of God and of the Holy Spirit changeable and mutable.

For these are your own words:

“The things that I argued concerning the invisibility of almighty God” [Note: [Col. 0757] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read, “of the all-sustaining God.”], “although with another purpose, you too have affirmed in your own words: that the Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove and also in the form of fire; the Son, certainly, in the form of a human being; but the Father neither in the form of a dove nor in the form of a human being. He has never changed himself into forms, nor will he ever change himself into them. Of him it is written: ‘I am who I am, and I have not changed.’”

Then you add and say:

“The Son, established in the form of God, as you yourself have stated, took the form of a servant, which the Father did not. Likewise, the Holy Spirit assumed the form of a dove, which the Father did not assume. Know, therefore,” you say, “that one is invisible, and one also is incapable of being contained and immeasurable.”

Would you say such things if you were able to think according to the spirit and not according to the flesh about what you were saying? You are a human being who reads in the holy Scriptures: “I am who I am, and I have not changed” (Exodus 3:14; Malachi 3:6).

Although these words belong not to the Father alone but to the Trinity itself, which is one God, you attribute them to the Father alone and believe the Son to be changeable. You believe the only-begotten Son, through whom all things were made, to be changeable. You believe him to be changeable of whom the Gospel says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; and, “All things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3).

What shall I now say about the Holy Spirit, when you believe the one whom you confess to be the true Son of God and true God to be changeable?

You certainly would not believe this if, as a Catholic, you believed that the form of a servant was taken from the form of God, rather than that the form of God was changed into the form of a servant. If you spiritually rather than carnally considered that, when the visible human being was assumed, the invisible God remained, you would not stubbornly resist through contention but would perceive the truth through understanding.

You could also faithfully consider that the Holy Spirit appeared through a created thing, as he willed, visibly (Acts 2:3; Matthew 3:16), while his invisible nature remained unchanged and in no way became or was transformed into the form of fire or of a dove.

Remember, nevertheless, that you were unable to demonstrate from any divine testimonies, against my argument, either that the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit or that the Father is worshiped by the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER XX

### The Father Is Unbegotten, Yet the Son Is Equal

In the twentieth place, because you had said concerning the Son, “If he is equal to the Father, then he is certainly such; and if he is such, then he is certainly unbegotten,” I answered you:

“But you say of the Son, ‘If he is equal, then he is certainly such’—that is, since he is not unbegotten, he does not appear to be such.”

You could say that the human being whom Adam begot was not a human being, because Adam himself was not begotten but made by God. Yet if Adam could be unbegotten and nevertheless beget what he himself was, do you not think that God could beget God equal to himself?

I am not surprised that you found no answer to this. Rather, I plainly commend you for not attempting to answer. If only you had done this everywhere! Nowhere in our discussions could you find anything appropriate to say in reply, and yet you refused to remain silent almost everywhere [Note: [Col. 0758] Lov. has “fully” instead of “almost.”].

But since in other places you said so many things unnecessary to the case being argued between us and consumed time in speaking, thanks are due to you wherever you recognized that you could not refute certain points and preferred to pass them over in complete silence.

## BOOK TWO [Note: [Col. 0757] Elsewhere, “Book Three.”]

The final arguments spoken by Maximinus in his debate are refuted one by one; through the length of that debate he then deprived Augustine of the time needed to reply.

[Col. 0757]

### PREFACE
What remains now requires that, with the Lord’s help, I fulfill my promise concerning it. At the beginning of this work I said: “First, I shall show that you were unable to refute what I said; then, insofar as it seems necessary, I shall refute what you yourself said.” Since, therefore, with God’s help, I have shown that you were unable to refute what I said, it remains for me to refute what you said, as I shall be able with God’s help. Accordingly, I shall not go back over your earlier arguments, to which I immediately [Col. 0758] replied in this discussion that I have now undertaken; but I shall answer that final and very lengthy one, which on that day took away the time available to me for replying, if he who governs us wills it, in such a way that you may yield to the light of truth, if you have not loved the darkness of contention.

First, then, I shall remove from your argument what is irrelevant to the necessity of my reply. The issue between us is whether the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are, as you say, of different substance, or rather, as we say, of one and the same substance, and whether the [Col. 0759] Trinity itself is one God. We agree that the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father, nor is the Father or the Son the Holy Spirit. Therefore, whatever you said in the great length of your argument to show that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another—recognize that, when you are dealing with us, it is entirely superfluous. If you encounter Sabellians whom you must defeat, direct against them, if you please, those weapons that are common to us and to you.

You also said many things to prove that the Lord Jesus Christ is the great God. What does that have to do with us, when we say the same? You poured forth great and true praises of the Holy Spirit; but we can increase them, not deny them. Thus there was no need for you to say against us what we say with you. Do we not equally confess that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father? Yet you wished to prove this by testimonies of the divine utterances, as though we denied it somewhere. We both know and hold that Christ came in the flesh; yet you introduced the divine testimonies to teach this, as though we resisted it. These and other matters, which I shall point out in their proper places, where you wasted effort in doing what was unnecessary in order to create delays and prolong the time, I must mention, but not refute in argument.

## CHAPTER ONE

You say that I am protected by the support of the authorities and do not speak according to the fear of God, although you know that we have been commanded to pray for kings, so that they may come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:2, 4). We give thanks to God that this has been fulfilled in some cases; you are grieved by it. But our words show, to those who understand them correctly, which of us speaks according to the fear of God: whether the one who praises God the Father in such a way as to attribute to his praise that he generated for himself a Son equal to him, or the one who dishonors both the begetter and the begotten, saying that the former could not beget a son altogether like himself, and that the latter did not become degenerate after being born, but was born degenerate.

## CHAPTER TWO

You say that you worship Christ as the God of every creature, before whom every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Yet you do not wish him to be equal to God the Father, because the Father gave this to him. For the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” and so forth (Phil. 2:8–9). Nor do you ask to whom he gave it—whether to a human being or to God.

How [Note: At Col. 0759, the manuscripts read “When.”] he gave it is clearly apparent. “He humbled himself,” he says, “even to death, and death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:8–9). If, then, he gave him the name that is above every name because he became obedient even to death on a cross, was he not, before this happened, the exalted Son of God, God, the Word of God, God with God? Or did he begin to be the exalted Son of God, the only-begotten of God, God, and to possess the name that is above every name only after he was exalted for becoming obedient even to death on a cross? [Col. 0760] What utterly foolish person would say this? What was given to him, therefore, was given to him as a human being—the one according to whom the Son became obedient even to death on a cross—whereas that same Son of God, God born from God, equal to God, already possessed it.

## CHAPTER THREE

You object to me that I say the Holy Spirit is equal to the Son. I plainly do say so. “Give,” you say, “testimonies where the Holy Spirit is worshiped.” As I understand you, you wish him to be shown equal to Christ on the ground that he is worshiped as Christ is.

Then acknowledge that Christ is equal to the Father, whom you yourself confess is worshiped as the Father. What sort of people are you, and how religiously humble, that you do not wish to worship the Holy Spirit, although you read: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6)? You do not wish, therefore, to worship the one whom you do not deny gives life to souls, even though the patriarch Abraham worshiped human beings because they granted him a burial place in which to lay the body of his dead wife.

For it is written:

> “Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to lament her. And Abraham rose from beside his dead wife and said to the sons of Heth: ‘I am a stranger and sojourner among you; therefore give me possession of a burial place, that I may bury my dead.’ The sons of Heth answered Abraham, saying: ‘By no means, my lord; hear us now. You are a king from God among us; bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will forbid you his tomb, so that you may bury your dead there.’ Then Abraham rose and worshiped the people of the sons of Heth” (Gen. 23:2–7).

And you do not allow the Holy Spirit to be worshiped, so that you may remain ungrateful toward the grace of God itself!

“But give,” you say, “testimonies where the Holy Spirit is worshiped,” as though from what we read we could not also understand certain things that we do not read. But, so that I may not be forced to seek many examples, where have you read that God the Father is unbegotten or unborn? And yet it is true. But what you have said more than once—that the Father is also incomparable to the Son—you have neither read, nor is it true.

If you would consider the religion by which God is worshiped, as is fitting, you would see that it is much more significant that the Holy Spirit has a temple than that you should read of him being worshiped. For, as I have shown above, we know that human beings have been worshiped by holy people; but a temple is not made by human beings except either for the true God, as Solomon made one, or for those who are regarded as gods, as by nations that do not know God.

But the Holy Spirit—of whom it was said with great honor concerning God that he “does not dwell in temples made with hands” (Acts 17:24)—dwells in our body, which is the temple of the Holy Spirit. And lest you despise our bodies, they are members of Christ (1 Cor. 6:19, 15). What sort of God, then, is he for whom a temple is built both by God and from the members of God?

## CHAPTER FOUR

You say that Christ is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us (Rom. 8:34). Why do you bring this against us, if you acknowledge him not only as God but also as human? What, then, does it help you that it is repeatedly read that he sits at the right hand of the Father? What are you trying to prove to us—though not with empty testimonies, yet vainly—when we confess it?

## CHAPTER FIVE

You say that you honor the Holy Spirit appropriately as teacher, guide, illuminator, and sanctifier; that you worship Christ as creator; [Col. 0761] and that you adore the Father with sincere devotion as author.

If you call the Father “author” because the Son is from him, while he himself is not from the Son; and because the Holy Spirit proceeds from him and from the Son in such a way that he himself gave this to the Son by begetting him such that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from him; if you call the Son “creator” in such a way that you do not deny that the Father and the Holy Spirit are creators; and finally, if you call the Holy Spirit teacher, guide, illuminator, and sanctifier in such a way that you do not dare to take these works away from either the Father or the Son—then these words of yours are also ours.

But if you set up such idols in your heart that you make two gods, one greater, namely the Father, and another lesser, namely the Son; and if you imagine the Holy Spirit as the least of all three, so that you do not even deem him worthy to be called God—this is not our faith, because it is not the Christian faith, and therefore it is not faith at all.

We also forgive you for this: through your unskilled use of language, you indicated that Christ descended into earthly contagions. When I wished to correct this in you, so that you would know what we ought to call “contagions,” you say that these are calumnies and suppose that they arise from instruction in philosophical art. It is enough for me that you thought Christ descended into earthly contagions while nevertheless confessing that he had no sin.

## CHAPTER SIX

As for what I mentioned about the offspring of animals—that although they are earthly and mortal, they nevertheless beget what they themselves are, so that a human being begets a human being and a dog a dog—I think you were not disgusted and horrified by it, but pretended to be, saying that so foul a comparison ought not to have been extended to that immense reality.

Why did you say this, unless because you feared that the truth, through these very corruptible births, would press upon your throat and not allow you to breathe, as indeed it does? You see a corruptible creature begetting offspring that is what it itself is, yet you believe that God the almighty Father could beget his only-begotten Son only by allowing his nature to degenerate.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

But you say: “The Lord begot the Lord; God begot God; the King begot the King; the Creator begot the Creator; the good begot the good; the wise begot the wise; the merciful the merciful; the powerful the powerful.”

If, by these words, you think you are guarding against the charge brought against you—namely, that you do not believe God could beget what he himself is—and therefore say, “The Lord begot the Lord; God begot God,” and so forth, why then, as you said “the powerful begot the powerful,” do you not say “the almighty begot the almighty”?

If you wish to say what you think, say: “The greater Lord begot a lesser lord; the greater God a lesser god; the greater King a lesser king; the greater Creator a lesser creator; the better one the good; the wiser one the wise; the more merciful one the merciful; the more powerful one the powerful.”

But if you do not say these things, and agree that the Son possesses nothing less than the Father, why do you not say “equal”? And why do you not run through all those expressions in this way: “The Lord begot an equal Lord; God an equal God; the King an equal King; the Creator an equal Creator; the good one an equally good one; the wise one an equally wise one; the merciful one an equally merciful one; the powerful one an equally powerful one”?

But if you deny that he is equal, openly say that he is degenerate. [Col. 0762] For the one whom you say was born as a lesser god from the greater God, you do not even allow to grow, as an infant, so that at some time he might be equal to his Father. You say that he was born perfect for this purpose—not so that his praise might increase from that point onward, but so that his lesser nature might remain.

And although you hold these views, you nevertheless go on to say: “The Father took nothing away in begetting the Son.” How did the Father take nothing away in begetting the Son, whom he did not beget equal but lesser? Or did he take nothing away because he did not remove from the begotten one any of the things he gave by begetting him?

Certainly, he took nothing away. But the Creator also takes nothing from human children who are born in prosperity; rather, he adds, so that what was lacking at birth may accrue to those who grow. What great thing, then, have you said about the Father in relation to his only Son, who was not made from nothing or from some matter, but born from the Father himself? What is so great about his not taking away what he gave, if by not giving what he could give he took it away?

Where is the fact that you said he was not envious? Or perhaps he could not give it? Where is the omnipotence of God the Father? The matter comes down entirely to this point: God the Father either could not or would not beget a Son equal to himself. If he could not, he is weak; if he would not, he is envious. But both alternatives are false. Therefore the Son is truly equal to God the Father.

If, then, as you praise it, you approve what I quoted—“His invisible attributes are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20)—then, through what has been made in visible creation, namely that parents beget what they themselves are, understand the invisible birth of the true Son of God, lest you say that God the Father begot what he is not. But if he begot what he himself is, do not deny that the Father and the Son have one substance.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

As for the following matters, which you connected in such a way as to wish to prove to us from Christ’s cross or incarnation what we equally believe, you have followed your usual practice. But since I give no response to you concerning these matters, I too keep my promise.

## CHAPTER NINE

### 1

When we were discussing the invisible Son, whom you agreed to be invisible according to his divinity, whereas earlier you had presumed that only the Father was invisible, you said many things about invisible creatures that have no bearing on the matter. Those who read them will be able to judge.

The issue between us concerns the invisible God. This is what creates the question, because you think that the Father alone is called invisible where the Apostle says: “To the immortal, invisible, only God” (1 Tim. 1:17). If he had said “to the Father alone,” the question might perhaps be more difficult to solve. But because he said “to God alone,” it is certainly not against us. The Only-begotten, too, in the form of God, and the Holy Spirit in his own nature, is invisible. For we proclaim that the one and only God is the Trinity itself.

Whether we understand this correctly has been demonstrated by us in other places, and wherever it is still necessary, it will be demonstrated. For now, in this question, it may reasonably be asked how it was said of the one God, who is the Trinity itself, “to the invisible, only God,” since there is also an invisible creature. For this reason it was said of Christ that in him “all things were created, visible and invisible” (Col. 1:16).

Since, therefore, there are false visible gods, it was said: “To the invisible, [Col. 0763] only God, be honor and glory.” For although there is an invisible creature, it is not God for us. Even if it had not said “to God alone,” but had said, “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, alone, be honor and glory,” who would he be except God?

Honor and glory, therefore, belong to God alone, who is the invisible God—not to the one who alone is invisible, since, as we have said, there is also an invisible creature.

Again, it may be asked how it was said, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), when the words of that same Lord are: “Do you not know that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven?” (Matt. 18:10). This statement refutes you, since you do not know how to say that the Father is invisible.

But the statement, “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father” (John 6:46), can be referred to human beings, insofar as the word “anyone” is understood to mean any human being. And because the one who was speaking then was himself human in the flesh, he said this as though he had said: “Not that any human being has seen the Father, except me.” It is like the statement: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Ps. 106:43). This cannot be understood of the holy angels as well.

Therefore the Apostle spoke more explicitly about the invisible God: “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). He did not say “No one,” but “No human being.” Here he shows how “No one has ever seen God” ought to be understood—namely, no human being. It is like “No one has ascended into heaven” (John 3:13), although angels commonly ascend there, since they also commonly descend from there.

Nor did the Apostle say, “No human being will be able to see God,” but “No one can.” A human being will be able to do so, but then, when seeing God will be the eternal reward of the faithful. Therefore the Apostle John says:

> “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

What, then, is the meaning of your saying that the Father alone is invisible? You would say this in vain even if he were seen by the Son alone. But now, since the divine utterances testify that he is seen by the angels and will also be seen by human beings when they have become equal to the angels (Matt. 22:30), what do you mean by saying it?

Where is the claim you dared to establish—that lesser beings are seen by greater beings, but greater beings are not seen by lesser ones? You later abandoned this position when you confessed that the Father is seen by the Son, although you also say that the Son is lesser in the very substance of his divinity and that the Father is greater.

But what will you say about the angels, who always see the face of God the Father? Are the angels, because of the rule you established without consideration, to be thought greater than God the Father?

### 2

But you think you have cleverly found something to say when you said of the Son: “Therefore he saw the Father, but he saw one who is incapable of being contained.” You do not attend to the fact that, even if he saw one who is incapable of being contained—one whom, as you suppose, he could not contain—he nevertheless did not see one who is invisible, since he was able to see him.

Yet when you said these things, you were disputing with us not about what can or cannot be contained, but about what is visible and invisible. For the Apostle did not say “incapable of being contained,” but “to the invisible, only God.” Thus you thought this testimony could be brought forward on your behalf, so that by it you might also degrade the Son, as though he himself were not invisible [Col. 0764] in the form of God.

But since you were overcome by the truth and confessed that the Son is invisible, you prepared for yourself, as I suppose, the argument: “The invisible begot the invisible,” just as you said, “the powerful begot the powerful.” Then, when questioned about what you meant, you would answer: “The more invisible begot the invisible,” just as “the more powerful begot the powerful,” “the wiser the wise,” and the rest of your expressions.

How wisely, then, you showed the Father to be incapable of being contained by the Son, but the Son capable of being contained by the Father! For you said: “Therefore he saw the Father, but he saw one who is incapable of being contained. But the Father,” you say, “sees the Son in such a way that he holds him in his bosom and possesses him.”

Only those who think carnally understand matters in this way. You imagine, as I see it, a bosom as some capacity belonging to the greater Father, by which he contains and holds the lesser Son—just as a house physically contains a human being, or as a nurse’s bosom contains an infant.

Then this, too, will be counted among Christ’s marvels: that, although he grew in the form of a servant and became greater than he had been in the form of God, he was once carried in the bosom of the Father but now sits at the right hand of the Father.

Cast these childish or old-womanish fantasies out of your heart. Understand “the bosom of the Father” as indicating that one is begotten and the other begets, not that one is greater and the other lesser.

For if the Father is incapable of being contained, while the Son is capable of being contained, then the statement “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15) was not spoken truthfully. Someone could answer him: “Look, the Father has the incapacity of being contained, which you do not have.” But because what the Truth said was said truthfully, and everything the Father has belongs to the Son, the Son cannot lack whatever the Father’s incapacity of being contained may be.

We must often bring this statement of the Lord—“All that the Father has is mine”—to bear upon you, whether to convict you or, what we desire more, to correct you, using it as a perfectly straight rule. Whenever you attribute something to the Father that you deny to the Son, we shall produce this most faithful witness against your errors—or, rather, against your lies.

Why do you resist me on the point that you insist human wisdom is visible, when you have conceded that the human soul itself, in which human wisdom certainly exists, is invisible? Whatever you may think about the whole invisible creation, with regard to God, which is the matter at issue between us, it has been sufficiently demonstrated to you that the Father alone is not invisible.

## CHAPTER TEN

### 1

You think that God the Father cannot be one God with the Son and the Holy Spirit. You fear that the Father alone is not one God, but a part of one God composed of three.

Do not fear. There is no division into parts within the unity of the Godhead. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God—that is, the Trinity itself. There is one God, of whom it is said, “There is no God but one” (1 Cor. 8:4), and who said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.”

We acknowledge without any hesitation that we must serve this one and only God when we hear and read: “You shall worship the Lord [Col. 0765] your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:4, 13). We must not, because of these words, refuse to serve Christ, whose members we are (1 Cor. 6:15), or the Holy Spirit, whose temple we are (ibid. 3:17), if we understand “You shall serve the Lord your God alone” as though it were said of the Father alone and not of the Trinity itself.

But when you are asked whom you believe to be meant by the words “The Lord your God, the Lord is one,” you answer: “God the Father.” Likewise, when you are asked of whom it was said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve,” you again answer: “Of God the Father.”

Then you are told: If the Lord our God is one Lord, and this one is the Father, why do you make two Lord Gods by saying that Christ too is the Lord God? Again, if it is the Father to whom alone one must serve, how do you obey this command when you serve Christ as though he were the Lord God? For the one who serves both him and Christ does not serve him alone.

According to the right faith, however, we have learned that the Trinity itself is one Lord our God. Therefore, when we serve him alone with the service owed to God, we are confident that we serve the Lord God alone.

### 2

“So,” you say, “God the Father is a part of God.”

By no means. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons; and because these three are of one substance, they are one—indeed, supremely one—where there is no difference of natures and no difference of wills.

If they were one by nature but not by agreement, they would not be supremely one. If they were different in nature, they would not be one. These three, therefore, who are one because of the ineffable union of the Godhead by which they are ineffably joined together, are one God.

Christ, moreover, is one person of two substances, because he is both God and human. Yet God cannot be called a part of this person. Otherwise, before the Son of God assumed the form of a servant, he was incomplete, and he became greater when humanity was added to his divinity.

If it is absurd to say this of one person, since God cannot be a part of anything, how much more can he not be a part of the Trinity, since he is one among the three?

Furthermore, when the Apostle says, “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17), is the Lord a part of this one spirit? If we say this, what else do we appear to be saying except that the Lord is increased when a human being is joined to him and diminished when a human being withdraws?

In the Trinity, therefore, which is God, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and together these three are one God. Nor is one a third part of this Trinity, nor are two a greater part there than one, nor are all of them something greater than each individually, because the greatness is spiritual, not bodily.

“Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matt. 19:12). But whoever cannot receive it should believe and pray that he may understand what he believes. For what is said through the prophet is true: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9).

### 3

You yourself said that one God is not composed of parts. And because you want this to be understood of the Father, you say: “He is what he is: an unbegotten, simple power.”

Yet consider how many things you mentioned in this simple power. Your earlier words are: “God begot God; the Lord begot the Lord; the King begot the King; the Creator begot the Creator; the good begot the good; [Col. 0766] the wise begot the wise; the merciful the merciful; the powerful the powerful.”

Why, then, in the simple power that is God, were you not afraid to mention so many powers? To pass over the four you listed in the earlier passage and mention four others that we can express by familiar names, are goodness, wisdom, mercy, and power parts of the one power that you said is simple?

If you say, “They are parts,” then simple power consists of parts, and this simple power, by your definition, is one God. Are you therefore saying that one God is composed of parts?

“I do not say that,” you reply.

Then they are not parts; yet there are four of them, and there is one power, which is likewise simple. If, therefore, in the one person of the Father you find plurality without finding parts, how much more are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their undivided divinity, one God; because of the property of each, three persons; and because of the perfection of each, not parts of one God?

The Father is power, the Son is power, and the Holy Spirit is power. This you say truly. But when you refuse to allow the power begotten from power and the power proceeding from power to have the same nature, you speak falsely; you speak against the right and catholic faith.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

You return to ask me how the Son is invisible. I already said above what should be said about this. “But if,” you say, “the Son is pronounced invisible by you because he cannot be contemplated by human eyes, why do you not likewise pronounce the heavenly powers invisible, since they too cannot be seen by human sight?”

You speak as though a human being could comprehend the manner in which the heavenly powers are invisible, or as though we ought to be intent on investigating this, when Scripture says: “Do not seek what is too difficult for you” (Sirach 3:22).

Yet, disregarding this command, you dared to say that an angel is seen by an archangel, while an archangel is not seen by an angel.

It is enough that I have shown that it does not follow that we should believe the Son visible in the form of God merely because it is written, “To the invisible, only God” (1 Tim. 1:17). You demonstrated that you understood this of the Father in such a way that the Son was not invisible, even though Scripture testifies that he is also the creator of invisible things.

Nevertheless, you still have the option of saying: “Both are invisible, that is, the Father and the Son, but the Father is more invisible.” In this way, by attributing something to the Father that does not belong to the Son, you make the same Son a liar when he says: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

## CHAPTER TWELVE

### 1

You think the same way about power: the Son is indeed powerful, but the Father is more powerful than the Son. Thus, according to your authority and teaching, the powerful could beget the powerful, but the almighty could not beget the almighty.

Accordingly, if the Father has omnipotence that the Son does not have, the Son’s statement “All that the Father has is mine” is false. Furthermore, if the Father does something that the Son cannot do, the Father is rightly called more powerful than the Son. But when the Son says, “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John 5:19), should we not listen to him rather than [Col. 0767] to you, and believe the teacher rather than you who deceive?

“But the Father,” you say, “received power from no one, whereas the Son received it from the Father.”

We too confess that the Son received power from him of whom he was born powerful. But no one gave power to the Father, because no one begot him. By begetting the Son, the Father gave him power, just as by begetting him from his substance he gave him everything that he has in his substance.

But the question is whether the Father gave the Son as much power as he himself has, or less. If as much, then he should be said, believed, and understood to have begotten not merely the powerful from the powerful, but the almighty from the almighty. If less, how are all that the Father has the Son’s?

If the Father’s omnipotence does not belong to the Son, how does the Son do everything that the Father does? Surely he cannot do so if he is not almighty.

### 2

Accordingly, when the Apostle says, “Blessed and only Sovereign” or “only powerful,” I am not compelled to understand this of the Father alone, but of God, who is the Trinity itself.

Speaking to Timothy, he says:

> “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who gave testimony to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, to keep the commandment without stain, irreproachable, until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he will display at the proper times—the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see; to him be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen” (1 Tim. 6:13–16).

I see nothing here that does not apply to the Trinity.

But, for the moment, let us say nothing about the Holy Spirit, whom you do not even wish to acknowledge as God, much less as lesser than the Son, since you do not wish to call him God at all. It is enough to convict you concerning the Father and the Son.

When the Apostle says, “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things,” does the Father alone give life to all things, and not the Son? If you say that the Father alone gives life to all things, how then does the Son do everything that the Father does? According to your view, the Father gives life to all things, whereas the Son does not.

Moreover, where he says, “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21), how can this be true if the Father gives life to all things without the Son?

Therefore, when he added, “and before Christ Jesus, who gave testimony to the good confession before Pontius Pilate,” he wished to speak specifically of the Son. For the Son, like the Father, gives life to all things; but we know that, in the form of a servant, the Son suffered under Pontius Pilate, not the Father.

Then follows: “To keep the commandment without stain, irreproachable, until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only Sovereign will display at the proper times.” The one whose appearance he will display is, of course, the appearance of the Lord Christ. God will display it; and God is not the Father alone, because according to the truth, and not according to your error, the Trinity is one God: “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords.”

Would even you dare to say that the Son is not the King of kings and Lord of lords? Of him, among other things, it is written in the Apocalypse of John: “He himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fierce wrath of almighty God, and on his robe and on his thigh he has a name written: [Col. 0768] King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:15–16).

But lest you perhaps say that the Son has the Father’s name written on his robe and thigh, elsewhere earlier in the same book we read: “And the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings” (ibid. 17:14).

According to you, therefore, there are two kings of kings and lords of lords. And you are refuted if the Apostle said of the Father alone, “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords.”

But according to the right faith, the Trinity itself is one God, the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.

And how will the statement “Come to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6) be true, unless it is because no one can do this by presuming upon himself, but only if God himself grants it?

God is said alone to possess immortality because he alone is unchangeable. For in every changeable nature, change itself is a kind of death, because it causes something that was to cease to be.

Thus the human soul itself, which is called immortal because, in whatever manner and according to its own mode, it never ceases to live, nevertheless has, according to its own mode, a certain death of its own. If it was living justly and sins, it dies to righteousness; if it was sinful and is justified, it dies to sin. I say nothing of its other changes, since it would take too long to discuss them.

The nature of the heavenly creatures could also die, because it could sin. For the angels sinned and became demons, whose prince is the devil. Those who did not sin were nevertheless able to sin. And to whatever rational creature it is granted not to be able to sin, this is not proper to its nature but comes from the grace of God.

Accordingly, God alone possesses immortality: not through the grace of anyone else, but by his own nature. He neither could nor can be changed by any turning, nor could nor can he sin through any change.

According to the nature by which he is God, no human being has seen him or can see him. Yet a human being will be able to see him someday if he belongs to that number of human beings of whom it was said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

To this God—that is, to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are the Trinity, one God—be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

### 3

Far be it that, as you think, the Father is more powerful than the Son because the Father begot the Creator, whereas the Son did not beget the Creator. For the Son was not unable to do so, but it was not fitting. [Note: At Col. 0768, most and the better manuscripts read, “For the Son was able to do so.” Nevertheless, the Master of the Sentences, I, distinction 7, cites, “For the Son was not unable to do so”: that is, the Son’s not begetting did not arise from incapacity, but from the nature of the matter. Nor are we compelled to understand that the Son could have begotten another son, an opinion Petavius believes Augustine held in Book 7, chapter 13, section 6, of *Theological Dogmas on the Trinity*.]

Divine begetting would be without limit if the begotten Son were to beget a grandson for the Father. For then that grandson too, unless he begot a great-grandson for his grandfather, would, according to your remarkable wisdom, be called powerless.

Likewise, if he did not beget a grandson for his grandfather and a great-grandson for his great-grandfather, you would not call him almighty. The succession of begetting would never be completed if one were always born from another; [Col. 0769] nor would anyone complete it if one were not sufficient.

The almighty, therefore, begot the almighty Son, since whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. The Son himself was begotten by the Father’s nature; he was not made.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN
1. In that testimony also, where the Apostle says, “To the only wise God,” your error is no different; but what we answered you concerning power, we answer also concerning wisdom. For if the Apostle had said, “To the only wise Father,” even then he would not have separated the Son from him. For does the fact that in the Apocalypse it is written of the Son, “Having a name written that no one knows except himself” (Rev. 19:12), mean that the Father does not know this name, from whom the Son is inseparable? Therefore, just as the Father also knows what is said to be known by no one except the Son, because they are inseparable, so even if it had been said, “To the only wise Father,” the Son too ought to be understood together with him, because they are inseparable.

Since, however, it was not said, “To the only wise Father,” but “To the only wise God”—and the one God is the Trinity itself—the solution to this question is much easier for us. We should understand “the only wise God” in the same way as we understood “the only powerful one”: namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who is the one and only God, whom alone we have been commanded to serve. Otherwise, by misunderstanding—or rather, by failing to understand—we might appear to act against this command, since we serve the Lord Christ with the service due to God.

For it was not said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, the Father, and serve him more,” so that we might be permitted to serve the Son also, but the Father more as the greater and the Son less as the lesser God. Rather, it was said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:13)—that is, the only omnipotent, the only wise God. Thus you are refuted: unwilling to accept that the one and only God is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and saying that the one Lord God whom alone one must serve is none other than God the Father, while nevertheless confessing the Son also as God and Lord, you most plainly assert two gods and two lords, one greater and the other lesser. According to your own error, you thus show yourselves guilty of violating this command, because you serve not only the greater but also the lesser with the service due to the Lord God.

2. When the Apostle said, “To the only wise God,” he was writing to the Romans; at the end of the Epistle he speaks as follows:

“Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times but now manifested through the writings of the Prophets, according to the command of the eternal God, made known for the obedience of faith among all the nations—to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory for ever and ever” (Rom. 16:25–27).

This means: “To him who is able to strengthen you, to the only wise God, be glory for ever and ever.” But the phrase inserted, “through Jesus Christ,” is ambiguous. Should “to the only wise God through Jesus Christ” be understood so that the only wise God is understood to be wise through Jesus Christ—not by participating in wisdom but by begetting Wisdom, who is Christ [Col. 0770] Jesus? Or should it be taken not as “to the wise God through Jesus Christ,” but as “through Jesus Christ be glory to the only wise God”?

Who, however, would dare to say that God the Father is made wise through Jesus Christ, when there can be no doubt that he is wise according to his own substance, and when the substance of the Son exists through the begetting Father rather than the substance of the Father through the begotten Son? It remains, therefore, that glory is given to the only wise God through Jesus Christ—that is, the clear and laudatory knowledge by which God the Trinity was made known to the nations. It is “through Jesus Christ” because, among other things I shall omit, he himself commanded the nations to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19), where the glory of this undivided Trinity was especially commended.

God, therefore—that is, the Trinity itself—is rightly called “the only wise one” because he alone is wise according to his substance, not through an accidental or acquired participation in wisdom, as every rational creature is wise. As for the addition “to whom”—so that it says “to whom be glory,” when “to him be glory” would have been sufficient—it indicates an expression unusual in our language, not some meaning that we need to seek or about which we should be uncertain. What meaning is lost if we say, “To him be glory, to whom through Christ be glory”? For “through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory” means the same as “to whom through Jesus Christ be glory.” One of these, however, is an unusual order of words, the other a customary one.

## CHAPTER XIV

1. You ask me: If the Son is from the substance of the Father, then the Holy Spirit is also from the substance of the Father; why is one the Son, while the other is not a son? I will answer, whether you understand or do not understand.

The Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from the Father. But the one is begotten, while the other proceeds. Therefore the one is the Son of the Father, from whom he was begotten; while the other is the Spirit of both, because he proceeds from both. Yet when he was speaking of the Spirit, the Son said, “He proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), because the Father is the source of his procession: the Father who begot such a Son and, by begetting him, granted him that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him.

For unless the Spirit proceeded also from the Son, the Son would not have said to the disciples, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and then given him by breathing upon them (John 20:22). By thus signifying that the Spirit proceeds also from himself, he openly demonstrated by breathing what he secretly gave by the act of breathing forth.

Therefore, if the Spirit were begotten, he would certainly be begotten not only from the Father, nor only from the Son, but from both; and without doubt he would be called the son of both. Since, then, he is in no way the son of both, he ought not to have been begotten from both. He is therefore the Spirit of both, proceeding from both.

But who can explain, when speaking of that most exalted nature, what difference there is between being born and proceeding? Not everything that proceeds is born, although everything that is born proceeds—just as not everything that is two-footed is human, although everyone who is human is two-footed. This much I know; but I do not know, nor can I explain or understand, how to distinguish between that generation and this procession.

Therefore, since both are ineffable, just as the prophet, speaking of the Son, says, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8), so it is most truly said of the Holy Spirit, “Who shall declare his procession [Col. 0771]?”

Let it be enough for us, then, that the Son is not from himself but from him of whom he was born; and that the Holy Spirit is not from himself but from him from whom he proceeds. And because he proceeds from both, as we have already shown, he is called both the Spirit of the Father—where it is written, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you”—and the Spirit of the Son—where it is written, “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:11, 9).

There are not two Holy Spirits, as though each belonged separately to one of them, one the Father’s and the other the Son’s; rather, there is one Spirit of the Father and of the Son. Concerning this one Spirit it is written: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and we were all given one Spirit to drink” (1 Cor. 12:13). And elsewhere: “One body and one Spirit” (Eph. 4:4).

2. What, then, is this Trinity except of one and the same substance? The Son is not from some material or from nothing, but from him from whom he was begotten. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is not from some material or from nothing, but from where he proceeds.

Yet you do not wish the Son to have been begotten from the substance of the Father, while you nevertheless concede that he is neither from nothing nor from any material, but from the Father. Do you not see how necessary it is that what is not from nothing must be from God, since it cannot be from anything else, and that it can be what God is from whom it is—that is, God from God?

Therefore, God born from God, because he is not something that previously existed separately but is coeternal by nature with God, is not other than he from whom he is—that is, he is of one and the same nature, or of one and the same substance.

When you hear this, I do not know what kind of heart you have, since you suppose that we say the Son was born from the Father in the same way that bodies are born from bodies. Because such things are born corruptibly, you accuse us as though we attributed bodily suffering and corruption to the generation of the Only-Begotten, which is from the Father.

Filled with carnal thoughts, you do not think that the substance of God can beget a Son from itself unless it undergoes, when begetting, what bodily substance undergoes in the act of begetting. You are in error, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God (Matt. 22:29).

When you read, “that we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 5:20), think of the true Son of God. You cannot in any way regard this Son as the true Son of God if you deny that he was born from the substance of the Father.

Was he already the son of a human being and, by God’s gift, made the Son of God—born from God by grace, not by nature? Or perhaps, although not a human son, was he already some sort of creature and then transformed by God into the Son of God? If neither of these is the case, then he was born either from nothing or from some substance.

But lest we should believe that you think the Son of God is from nothing, you have already freed us from this concern: for you affirmed that you do not say that the Son of God is from nothing. He is therefore from some substance. If not from the Father’s, from what substance? Say so. But you cannot find one.

Let it no longer displease you, then, to confess with us that the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, is from the substance of the Father.

[Col. 0772] 3. The Father and the Son, therefore, are of one and the same substance. This is the *Homoousion*—“of the same substance”—which, at the Council of Nicaea, was established against the heretics, the Arians, by the authority of truth and the truth of authority among the Catholic Fathers.
