Later, at the Council of Ariminum, because the novelty of the word was understood less adequately than it should have been [Col. 0772; manuscripts: “understood less adequately than it could have been,” followed by “which nevertheless …”], that which the ancient faith had brought forth was attacked by heretical impiety under the heretical emperor Constantius, after many had been deceived through the fraud of a few.

But after not a long time, when the freedom of the Catholic faith prevailed and the force of the word had been understood as it ought, that *Homoousion* was defended far and wide with the soundness of the Catholic faith.

For what is *Homoousion* except “of one and the same substance”? What, I ask, is *Homoousion* except, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)?

But now neither should I bring forward the Council of Nicaea as though I were prejudging the case, nor should you bring forward the Council of Ariminum. I am not bound by the authority of the former, nor are you bound by that of the latter. Let the matter contend with matter, cause with cause, and reason with reason, by the authoritative testimonies of the Scriptures—not by the private assertions of either side, but by witnesses common to both.

We both read: “that we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; he is the true God and eternal life.” Let us both yield to the weight of such mighty evidence.

Tell us, then, whether this true Son of God, distinguished by a certain special property from those who are sons by grace, is from no substance or from some substance. “I do not say ‘from none,’” you reply, “lest I say ‘from nothing.’” Then he is from some substance. I ask: from which? If not from the Father’s, seek another. If you find no other—because there is absolutely no other—acknowledge the Father’s substance and confess the Son to be *Homoousion* with the Father.

Flesh is born from flesh; a son of flesh is born from the substance of flesh. Remove corruption from the discussion; cast carnal passions away from the light of the mind; and contemplate the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20).

Believe in the Creator, who gave flesh the ability to beget flesh, who gave parents the ability to generate true children of flesh from the substance of flesh, so that children and parents might be of one substance. How much more could he beget a true Son from his own substance and have one substance with his true Son, while spiritual incorruption remained and carnal corruption was kept entirely at a distance!

4. What you will say about the soul, I do not know. For these are your words, where you say: “You do not compare that great magnificence with the nobility of the soul, but with the frailty of the body.” “Certainly,” you say, “flesh is born from the body, and a bodily son from the body; yet a soul is not born from a soul.”

After this apparent definition of yours, you again affirm that the soul begets children. For you add and say:

“If, then, our soul generates incorruptibly and without suffering, experiencing neither diminution nor any defilement, but lawfully generates a son according to the divine laws, wisely accommodating consent to the body [Erasmus’s edition, here and above in its comparison with Maximinus, reads: “generating a son, adapting him to the body by the agreement of the wise”; less correctly. Louvain consistently reads “and wisdom,” but the particle “and” is absent from the manuscripts], it itself remains whole: how much more so does the omnipotent [Col. 0773] God?”

And shortly afterward you say: “How much more did God the incorruptible Father incorruptibly beget the Son?”

I have already said that I do not know what you intend us to understand about the soul, concerning which you first said that a soul is not born from a soul and afterward that the soul incorruptibly begets a son. If it begets a soul, how is a soul not born from a soul? If it begets flesh, you must explain how flesh is the true son of the soul.

For Christ, on account of whom you thought this comparison should be introduced, is the true Son of God. But if you wished “to generate a son incorruptibly” to be understood as referring to the soul, how is it that the Apostle says, “For in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15)? Why do you not consider that those souls already existed in their former life, and that the Apostle, renewing them through the gospel, begot them?

But the Word of God, the only-begotten Son, as we have already argued, was not previously something else and then generated by the Father through renewal. Rather, he was always with the Father, begotten eternally and coeternally with him in a wondrous and ineffable manner, as he always is and always will be.

If, however, you introduced this dissimilar comparison in order to assert that God the Father begot incorruptibly, do not trouble yourself. I entirely confess that God the Father begot incorruptibly—but he begot what he himself is.

For here again I say what must often be said to you: The Son of God was born either from some substance or from none. If from none, then from nothing; and we have already established that you do not say this. If from some substance, yet not from the Father’s, he is not the true Son. If from the Father’s, then the Father and the Son are of one and the same substance.

But how, as you say, did the Son lose nothing, if he is of the same substance and yet is lesser, unable to grow like an infant?

5. Concerning God’s immortality, since the Apostle said that immortality is possessed not by the Father but by God, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I have discussed this sufficiently above, when I both quoted the entire apostolic testimony and explained it.

6. You object that we assert the Son to be equal to the Father, as though one who is the true Son could be unequal: he was not born in time but is coeternal with the one who begot him, just as the radiance generated from fire is manifested as coeval with the fire that generates it.

“But,” you say, “the Son of God has the Father as his source.”

If you call God the Father the source of God the Son because the Father begot him, the Son was begotten; because the Son is from the Father, the Father is not from the Son, I confess and concede this. But if, under the name “source,” you wish to make the Son lesser and the Father greater, and to deny that the Son is of the same substance as the Father, I will detest and reject it.

For a human son, insofar as he is a son, has as his source the one from whom he was born, his father; yet for that reason he is not of a different substance from his father. And although the son is lesser and the father greater, the son can nevertheless attain, by growing, the father’s form and strength. He does not find his father entirely such, however, because the father too has declined through aging.

Thus mortality must necessarily vary with age where birth is temporal rather than eternal. But it is not so there, where the Son does not grow and the Father does not grow old. Therefore their ages are not unequal, because where there is eternity there is no age. Their form, therefore, is not unequal [Col. 0774], because the true Son—who was not born in order to be increased, lest he remain degenerate—was born equal.

Let divine birth, then, be far better and more excellent than human birth, through its incorruptible and inviolable generation; yet let it not be worse through a difference of nature.

7. “But,” he says, “the Son received life from the Father.”

He received it as one begotten from the one who begets. “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). Therefore, all that the Father has, he gave by begetting, and the Son received by being born.

The Father did not lose what he had by giving it, nor did the Son receive something that previously existed without it and then came to possess it. Rather, just as the Father remained possessing all things when he gave all that he has to the Son, so the Son was never without all the things that he received—not from need, but by being born as the Son. He could never have been unborn; and the things without which he would not be born, and as born is immutable, he has always possessed, because he has always been born.

For if the Father did not give the Son some of the things that he has, the Son’s statement, “All that the Father has is mine,” would be false. But because it is true, the Father gave absolutely all that he has, as we have said, by begetting, and the Son received it by being born.

Thus the Father gave life because he begot life; the Son received life because he was born as life. If the Son is lesser, pale (*decolor*) [the editions read *discolor*, “of a different colour,” whereas the manuscripts read *decolor*], or different, then the Father did not give him the life that the Father has. And how is it true that “All that the Father has is mine”? But who would dare say that what the Truth said is not true?

Therefore, “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). As he has it, so he gave it; what he has, he gave; what kind he has, he gave that kind; as much as he has, he gave that much. All that the Father has belongs to the Son.

The Father therefore did not give the Son anything less than what he has, nor did the Father lose the life that he gave to the Son. By living, he retained what he gave by begetting.

The Father himself is life, and the Son himself is life. The one and the other have what he himself has [so the manuscripts; the editions read “what he is himself”]. But the Father is life from no one, while the Son is life from life—of the same kind, of the same greatness, altogether the same as that life. For he is the true Son; he is the perfect Son; the only-begotten Son is not degenerate from the one God the Father.

The Son, therefore, is equal to the Father. Whatever you say he received from the Father, we too confess: the Father truly gave it, and the Son received it. But when the Father gave all that he has by begetting, he begot an equal, since he gave nothing less.

How, then, do you say that because the Father gave and the Son received, the Son is not equal to the Father, when you see that the one to whom everything was given received even equality itself?

It is indeed written, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). But this applies to the present life, where there is poverty, and where abundance is certainly better. It is better to possess than to lack; better to give than to receive; better to distribute than to beg [the Amiens, Erasmus, and manuscript witnesses omit “than to receive; to distribute”].

But where the giver gave by begetting and the recipient received by being born, the needy person was not assisted; rather, abundance itself was generated. Nor can the one who received be unequal to the one who gave [Col. 0775], since he also received the gift of being equal.

The one who says, “All that the Father has is mine,” has nothing less than the Father. He is therefore equal.

But because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, not losing the form of God, he became obedient in that same form of a servant even unto death, the death of the cross (Phil. 2:7–8). In that form he was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:6), while remaining equal to the Father in the form of God, because that form is not subject to change.

8. What wonder is it, then, if he says the things you mention: “I always do what pleases the Father” (John 8:29); and at the tomb of Lazarus, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but because of the crowd standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me” (John 11:41–42); and again, “I must work the works of him who sent me” (John 9:4); and before he broke the loaves, he first gave thanks to the Father (Matt. 26:26; Mark 8:6; John 6:11)?

If you had wished to show by these and similar testimonies that, in the form of a servant, the Son is lesser than the Father, while in the very form of God the Son is from the Father and not the Father from the Son—a point he often signifies, speaking in such a way that those who do not understand him suppose him lesser even in his divinity—then you would have held to the right rule of faith and would not have contradicted the truth. You would not have attacked the Gospel by such testimonies but would have taught it.

For what things please the Father that do not also please the Son? Or from where can the Son do anything except the things that please the Father, from whom he has everything in which he is equal to the Father?

How could he not give thanks to the Father from whom he is, especially in the form of a servant, in which he is lesser than the Father? How could he not petition the Father as a human being, when together with the Father he hears prayer as God?

What Christian is unaware that the Father sent the Son and that the Son was sent? It was not the begetter who had to be sent by the one whom he begot, but the begotten by the begetter. Yet this is not an inequality of substance, but an order of nature—not that one existed before the other, but that one was from the other.

It was therefore fitting that the one who was sent should perform the works of the one who sent him. But what works of the Father are not also the Son’s, since the same Son says, “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19)?

Nevertheless, he calls them the Father’s works; for he does not forget from whom he is. It is from the Father that he is the one who performs such works.

You, however, understand these matters in such a way that you even think the Father is greater than the Son because he said that a sparrow does not fall to the ground without the Father’s will (Matt. 10:29), as though it could fall without the Son’s will. Do you wish to make the Son so much lesser that he has no authority even over sparrows?

But if you are unwilling to accept this rule—that whenever you read in the authority of the divine Scriptures something [the editions read *quibus*, “by which”; the manuscripts more aptly read *quo*, “by which”] that appears to show the Son as lesser than the Father, you should either understand it as spoken according to the form of a servant, in which he truly is lesser than the Father, or understand it as spoken so that neither is shown to be greater or lesser than the other, but so that one is shown to be from the other—if, I say, you are unwilling to accept this entirely correct rule, then at least you will in no way call him the true Son of God if you do not say that he is of the same substance as the Father.

To speak of something human, for the sake of the weakness of carnal minds [Col. 0776]: when there are two human beings, a father and a son, and the son obeys his father, and for some reason asks his father, gives thanks to his father, and is finally sent by his father, saying that he did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him, does this show that he is not of the same substance as his father?

Why, then, whenever you read such things concerning the Son of God, do you immediately plunge in heart and speech into such great sacrilege that you believe and say that the true Son of God is not of one and the same substance with the Father?

9. What of the fact that you also thought it necessary to mention what he says most clearly as a human being: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again. I received this command from my Father” (John 10:18)?

How does this assist your case? Did he say anything other than, “I have authority to die and to rise again”? When he says, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again,” what did he wish to be understood except that he would not have died unless he himself had willed it?

Yet could he have died and risen again unless he were a human being?

You introduced this testimony by first saying: “Here indeed he was speaking also of the authority that he received from the Father: ‘I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again,’” as though, if he were not human, he would have been going to lay down his life.

As a human being, therefore, not as God, he received this authority. Yet he did not say, “I received this authority,” but, “I received this command from my Father.”

Who does not know that a command is one thing and authority another? We have in our power whatever we can do when we wish. A command, however, directs us to do what is already within our power; if it is not yet within our power, we pray that power may be granted to us so that we may fulfill what has been commanded.

Therefore, if you are willing to attend to what is clear, he received this authority as a human being. But for the sake of the contentious, I will conclude in both directions.

If he received this authority as a human being, you yourself see that this testimony does not help you. For if, on the basis of this authority received from the Father, you wish to prove that the Son is lesser than the Father, we too do not doubt that, insofar as Christ is human, he is lesser than the Father.

But if you wish to say that he received this authority as God, then the Father, by begetting him equal to himself, gave him authority over all things as great as the Father’s own authority [the manuscripts read “as great as the Father’s authority itself”].

For if he has less authority over something than the Father, then all that the Father has is not his. But because all that the Father has is his, he undoubtedly has as much authority as the Father.

The command also he received either as a human being or as God. If as a human being, there is no question, because as a human being he is lesser than the Father. If as God, this does not show him to be lesser, because he received it by being born, not from need.

In the one Word of God are all the commands of God. The Father, by begetting, gave them to the one being born; he did not add them to one in need after he had begotten him. Thus he begot him as great as he himself is, because he begot from himself a true Son and begot him perfect in the fullness of divinity, not one to be perfected [Col. 0777] by the advance of age [the Amiens, Erasmus, and manuscript witnesses read this; Louvain reads, “and begot the fullness of divinity perfect, not to be perfected by the advance of age”].

But I ask you more humbly: Why do you not say that any human son who receives a command from his father is of a different substance, while you dare to deny that the Son of God is of the Father’s substance merely because he received a command from the Father?

Certainly, he received a command from the Father and is of the same substance as the one who gave it. Who could tolerate your contradiction, if human fathers and sons, both of the same substance, should gather to hear you, and you nevertheless claimed that the sons were degenerate because their fathers gave them commands?

Perhaps you will say that learned fathers gave commands to ignorant sons. Now turn your attention to the Son of God, God born from God the Father. He would certainly have been born imperfect if he received a command as one who was ignorant.

But because he was born perfect, the Father gave the command by begetting, and the Son received it by being born. The true Son of God was never ignorant; indeed, he was never not the Son.

## CHAPTER XV

1. You do not deny that the Son exists in the form of God, yet you deny that he is equal to God the Father, thinking that the Father’s form is greater than the Son’s—as though the Father did not have the means to complete his own form in the Son, whom he begot from himself, not making him from nothing or from something else.

Or, if he could beget his own form fully in the only-begotten Son but nevertheless begot him not fully, but lesser, consider what follows and return to the right path, lest you be forced to call the Father envious.

You call the Son God; you call him Lord. Yet, in order to make two gods and two lords, you speak against Scripture, which cries out, “Hear, Israel: The Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6:4).

What does it benefit you in this sacrilege that you give the Father as great a form as you do not give the Son? If one is greater and the other lesser, are they not thereby still two gods and two lords?

If you wish to escape this error, say that the Father is one and the Son another, but nevertheless do not call them two together; call them one Lord God.

You say that the Son is a king born from the King Father. Yet you do not observe that in the human race the sons of kings, even when they are not kings born from kings, are nevertheless human beings born from human beings; they do not possess royal power together with their fathers, and yet they retain the same nature.

You grant the Son of God, the King, royal sovereignty with the Father, but in impious folly you deny him the paternal nature. You call him unequal to God the Father, although he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized—that is, as something belonging to another—but, not seeking the things that were his own, rather the things that were ours, he emptied himself, not losing the form of God but taking the form of a servant, in which he became obedient to the Father even unto death, the death of the cross (Phil. 2:6–8).

You do not wish to recognize him in this form as lesser than God the Father in such a way that you do not deny him equal to the Father in the form of God.

“We,” you say, “are called sons by grace; we were not born this way by nature. The Son is therefore the only-begotten because, according to the nature of his divinity, he is what the Son was born to be.”

These words are not yours alone; they are ours as well. Why, then, when you confess that the Son of God is Son by nature and not by grace, do you insist that he is not of the same nature as the Father? Do you not consider what evil you are saying?

Would you not more tolerably take away the paternal kingdom from the Son of the King God than take away his nature?

2. Concerning the Holy Spirit—how he too is from God and yet is not himself a son, because Scripture says that he is from God by proceeding rather than by being born—I have already discussed above as much as seemed sufficient.

“We,” you say, “did not receive nature in the unbegotten God, the Father.”

And as though giving a reason why you do not say that God the Father is nature [Col. 0778], you immediately add and say: “We believe what Christ said: ‘God is Spirit’” (John 4:24). As though Christ, according to that by which he is God, were not Spirit, while you have nevertheless said that he is the Son by nature.

The Father, then, is not for that reason not nature because he is Spirit. Perhaps, however, because he was not born, you do not wish him to be nature; for you suppose that “nature” (*natura*) derives from being born (*nasci*).

Know, therefore, that every thing is said to exist through its substance; and to exist in this way is certainly to exist by nature.

If you truly do not think one should say that the Son is of the same nature as the Father, say that he is of the same substance as the Father. That is sufficient for the case being argued between us.

Nevertheless, you should be reminded to observe what the Apostle says: “You served those who by nature are not gods” (Gal. 4:8). There he clearly showed that we serve the God who is God by nature.

You, therefore, who do not believe that God the Father is God by nature, consider where you are placing him; and if you have any sense of shame, be ashamed.

We say to you: We do not serve a god who is not God by nature, lest we be like those of whom it was said, “You served those who by nature are not gods.” If you wish to be such people, we ask you not to do so, but to say that God the Father is God by nature.

And do not deny that his Son, whom you already say is Son not by grace but by nature, is of the same nature as the Father. Otherwise you deny nothing less than that he is truly the Son.

For how can you say that you confess him to be the true Son and do not deny that he is like the Father, when you deny that he is of one substance with the Father?

Just as one substance indicates a true son, so a different substance indicates that he is not a true son. How, then, do you call the Son like the Father when you refuse to grant him the Father’s substance?

Is not a painting or statue like a human being, and yet it cannot be called his son because it is of a different substance?

Human beings were made in the likeness of God; yet because they are not of one and the same substance, they are not true sons. For that reason they become sons by grace, because they are not sons by nature.

If, then, you wish to confess the Son of God as true, first and above all say that he is of one and the same substance, so that you may say that, as the true Son and Son of God, he is in every respect like the Father.

For when you think that he has a different substance, you call him more unlike than like the Father, and you altogether deny that he is the true Son.

For you wish to know [Col. 0779] how much one and the same substance contributes to demonstrating a true son [Louvain alone reads, “And you do not wish”]; consider this: even if a human son, himself a human being, is in some respects like his father and in others unlike him, nevertheless, because he is of the same substance, he cannot be denied to be the true son. And because he is the true son, he cannot be denied to be of the same substance.

But you call the true Son of God like the Father while insisting that they have different substances—the very thing by which alone a true son can be demonstrated.

Two true human beings, even if neither is the son of the other, are nevertheless of one and the same substance. But a human being cannot in any way be the true son of another human being unless he is of the same substance as his father, even if he is not entirely like his father.

Therefore, the true Son of God is of one substance with the Father because he is the true Son, and he is in every respect like the Father because he is the Son of God.

For it is not permissible to say, as can occur among human sons or the offspring of any animals, that the true Son of God is indeed of one substance with the Father but is not in every respect like the Father.

Hold with us, then, to the Council of Nicaea, if you wish to call Christ the true Son of God.

3. “We are accused,” you say, “of saying that there are different natures.” And what else do you say about God the Father and God the Son? What else do you say? Do you think that you are cleared of this accusation because you immediately add: “Know this: what we say is that the Father, Spirit, begot Spirit before all ages; God begot God”? You do indeed say this, and you say what is true; but you have kept silent about the false and execrable thing that you say. “Spirit begot Spirit”: you speak truly; but you say this truth with the intention that “spirit” may also be understood as referring to different natures. For the Spirit of God—or God the Spirit—and the spirit of a human being are different in nature; yet both are called spirit. Likewise, the spirit of a human being and the spirit of an animal are different in nature; yet both are nevertheless called spirit. Again, “God” is said of God, and “god” is said of a human being, as it is written: “You are gods” (Ps. 81:6). And just as Moses was given as god to Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1) [Note: [Col. 0779] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “was called.”] Although the substance of God and of a human being is different, both are nevertheless called “God.”

You are therefore plainly and truthfully convicted, even though you say of God the Father and God the Son, “Spirit begot Spirit,” while nevertheless asserting that their natures are different; and although you say, “God begot God,” you still do not depart from difference of nature, because you say that the Son is not like the Father in every respect. For if you said that he was like him in every respect, you would consequently be understood to say that they were also of one and the same nature, or substance. Therefore, if you are considering how to clear yourselves of the charge brought against you—that you say that the natures of God the Father and God the Son are different—then, just as you say, “Spirit begot Spirit,” say also, “Spirit of the same nature or substance begot Spirit.” Likewise, just as you say, “God begot God,” say also, “God of the same nature or substance begot God.” If you believe and say this, you will no longer be accused concerning this matter. But if you do not say this, what benefit is there in your saying, “The true unborn Father begot the true Son,” when, without doubt, the Son is not truly a son if he is not of one and the same substance with the one who begot him?

4. The Son does indeed say to the Father: “Now this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3)—that is, “that they know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the only true God.” When, in these words, you understand the Father alone to be the true God, not together with the Son, what else do you do but deny that the Son is true God? Since the Father and the Son are not two gods but one God, without doubt the Son also is true God; and, with the Holy Spirit joined to them, he is the only God.

Nor should it trouble us that the Holy Spirit is not named here, as though he were not God or were not true God. The case is analogous to someone saying that Christ does not know the things that belong to God, because the Apostle says: “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11). “No one knows except the Spirit of God” means that the Spirit of God alone knows those things. Just as Christ is not excluded from that knowledge, which is said to be possessed by none except the Spirit of God, so the Holy Spirit is not excluded from the statement that the Father and Christ are the only true God.

Likewise, the name in the Apocalypse which is said to be known by no one except the one who had it written upon him (Rev. 19:12)—that is, Christ—was certainly also known by the Father, which you cannot deny; and it was known by the Holy Spirit as well, even if you deny it. For “the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2:10). Unless, perhaps, because he is called the Searcher, you deny that he comprehends. Then deny that God comprehends the hearts and kidneys of human beings; for it is written: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. 7:10).

Thus the Father and Jesus Christ are called the only true God in such a way that the Holy Spirit is in no way alienated from this truth of deity. Nor does the Son, as you suppose, say that the Father alone is powerful, alone wise, and alone good God. The one and only God is the Trinity itself, as the passages we have already cited so frequently demonstrate.

5. You speak truly when you say that God the Father begot God the Son not as one progressing toward perfection, but as one already perfect. But when you refuse to make the Son’s perfection equal to the Father’s perfection, you speak falsely and contradict the truth by which he is truly the Son.

“You say,” you object, “that if a human being could immediately beget a perfect son, he would not beget a little child who, after growing through the years, would at last fulfill the will of his begetter.” You are speaking entirely against yourself, and speaking most truly. [Note: [Col. 0780] The printed editions read, “Most truly the truth,” etc.; the manuscripts omit “the truth.”] But so that what you say may not be against you, acknowledge the equality of the Father and the Son. For if a human being could immediately beget an equal son, he would beget him at once and would not wait for the years through which the son might fulfill his will by attaining the son’s form.

Why, then, did God not beget an equal Son, for whom neither years were necessary to bring this about nor omnipotence lacking? Did he perhaps not wish to? Then—God forbid—he was envious. But he was not envious; therefore he begot an equal Son. Consequently, the Son is of one and the same substance with him. A human being, who begets an unequal son only because he cannot beget an equal one, nevertheless begets a son of the same substance as himself. If this were not so, the child could certainly not be a true son.

What, then, do you mean when you say: “The Father begot such a Son as he is now and as he remains without end”? You would speak well if you did not deny that the true Son is equal to the Father. But when you call him perfect, deny him equality, and do not deny that he remains forever such as he was born, you plainly declare that the Son remains forever less than the Father.

Consequently, a human son is born less than his father; and because he is born imperfect, he reaches his father’s form by growing. The Son of God was born less than the Father; and because he was born perfect and immortal, he receives no increase, but that very perfection makes him forever alien from the Father’s form.

Behold what you believe; behold what you say; behold what, worse still, you teach.

“But it lies with the judgment of the hearers,” you say, “to choose one of two alternatives: either the Son obedient to the Father, who ‘emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,’ and to whom the Father ‘gave the name that is above every name’ (Phil. 2:7, 9), or your interpretation.”

The hearers to whom the Lord grants understanding certainly do not choose one of these two, but both: both the Son obedient to the Father and my interpretation—or rather, my exposition—in which I have shown that he was obedient in the form of a servant in such a way that he did not lose the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father.

But consider how insultingly you attribute obedience to the Son of God, while diminishing his nature in respect of divinity.

## CHAPTER XVI

1. When did you ever hear me say that, on account of the Jews and for the sake of humility rather than truth, the Son said that his Father was his God? You could never have heard me say this, just as I never said it. I plainly said that it was spoken on account of the form of a servant.

Just as that very form of a servant is real, not false, so he truthfully said that the Father was his God also on account of that form; he did not feign this out of humility. For what fruit of humility is there where truth suffers loss?

You tried to refute this most certain truth by saying that the words with which the Lord said, “My God and your God,” did not pertain to the form of a servant because the Lord used these words after the resurrection—as though the resurrection had destroyed the form of a servant rather than transformed it for the better; as though the one who died were not himself also the one who rose again; as though the form that was put to death had not itself come back to life; as though it were not itself taken up into heaven; as though the Son of God did not sit in that very form at the right hand of the Father; as though in that form he were not going to come to judge the living and the dead.

Is not the testimony of the angels perfectly clear when they say: “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11)? Why, then, would he not say after the resurrection, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17), when he was going to ascend in that same form, on account of which God is his God in time, while the Father is his Father outside of time?

On account of that form, he will be subject even after the judgment to the one who subjected all things to him (1 Cor. 15:28). Therefore, although you have brought forward many testimonies to prove that the one who is Christ’s Father is called Christ’s God, I consider it unnecessary to examine how those statements were made. I think that you have recalled them to no purpose, something of which you yourself ought not to be uncertain.

2. As for the passage in which the Lord, established in the same flesh that he had raised and bearing the same human being, said to his disciples: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me; go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:18–20)—I really do not know why you recalled it or what you wanted to prove from it.

For did he say, “Authority has been given to me by my God”? If he had said this, there could be no doubt that it was spoken on account of the human form. But since he did not say it, I do not understand what you wished to accomplish with this testimony. Indeed, I do understand: you wanted to speak at greater length.

If this authority was given to him as God, the Father gave it to him at his begetting, not because he was in need of it; he gave it by begetting, not by increasing. If this authority was given to him as a human being, what question is there? Perhaps you wished to remind us that the Lord commanded the nations to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. There you hear one name, yet you refuse to understand one divinity.

3. You also say that, even before Christ’s incarnation, the Father was called his God, because it is written: “God, your God, has anointed you”—long before Christ came in the flesh. Do you really not understand that this was foretold in prophecy, as though what was future had already taken place?

Does not the Lord himself say in prophecy: “They pierced my hands and feet” (Ps. 21:18), along with the other things by which he announced his passion so long beforehand and expressed what was going to happen as though it had already happened?

Thus the words, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation above your companions,” were spoken in prophecy concerning future events as though in the language of past events. By “his companions” he signified those who would become his servants, his associates, his friends, and his brothers and members.

It was therefore foretold that God would anoint the man Christ; yet he was made human in such a way that he remained God. He would be anointed not with visible and bodily oil, but with the Holy Spirit, whom Scripture designates figuratively, as it commonly does, by the name “oil of exultation.”

It said, “He has anointed,” not “He will anoint,” because in predestination what was going to happen in its own time had already taken place.

Here you feared that the Holy Spirit, by whom Christ was anointed, might appear greater than Christ, because he is indeed greater than Christ as a human being: for the one who sanctifies is greater than the one who is sanctified. Fearing this, you wanted “the oil of exultation” to be understood as signifying the joy with which the Son rejoiced with the Father when creation was made.

And, as is your custom, you cited testimonies unnecessary to your case concerning the joy of the Father and the Son. But what will you do? Where will you go? How will you deny or twist into something else what is clearer than light, when the blessed Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10:38)?

There is what was prophesied when it was said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation,” or “with the oil of gladness,” above your companions.

The God to whom it was said in the same Psalm, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. 45:7–8)—the Son was anointed by God the Father. He was made human in such a way that he remained God, and he was full of this anointing, that is, of the Holy Spirit.

For this reason it is written of him: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1).

## CHAPTER XVII

1. You say that what was said about the Son—“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3)—cannot be accepted as referring to the person of the Holy Spirit.

You say this so that you may persuade as many as you can of what has been wrongly impressed upon you: that the Holy Spirit is not the Creator. It is as though you had read, “All things were made through him, without the Holy Spirit”; or, “All things were made by no one except him.”

Even if you had read something of this kind, we ought not therefore to believe that the Holy Spirit was excluded from the work by which creation was established, just as the Son is not excluded from the knowledge of which it was said: “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11).

But if, because the Holy Spirit was not named when it was said of the Son, “All things were made through him,” you therefore think that the Spirit of God is not the Creator, then surely you will not be able to say that those baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus were baptized in his name, since Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38), but did not say, “and of the Holy Spirit.” Nor can you say that they were baptized in the name of the Father, since he too was not named there.

But if, even without the Father and the Holy Spirit being named, they were commanded to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, and yet they are understood to have been baptized only in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, why do you not hear the statement concerning the Son—“All things were made through him”—in such a way that you also understand the unnamed Holy Spirit to be included there?

2. For what is more excellent among created things than the powers of heaven? Yet it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 33:6).

You had said that I could not find such things in the divine Scriptures by which I might assert the Holy Spirit’s equality with the Son. Behold, I have found one in which he might even appear greater, unless piety recalls us to the truth that he is equal.

For certainly the powers of heaven, which were established by the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth—that is, by the Holy Spirit—are something greater than the heavens, which were established by the word of the Lord—that is, by the only-begotten Son.

But if you consult the truth, both things were established by both. What is said of one and not said of the other is understood of both.

What could be more thoughtless than to deny that the Spirit of God is the Creator, when it is said to the Lord: “You take away their spirit, and they fail and return to their dust; you send forth your Spirit, and they are created, and you renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 104:29–30) [Note: [Col. 0783] The printed editions read “send forth”; the manuscripts read “you will send forth”; Augustine likewise has the latter reading in his exposition of Psalm 103.]?

Unless, perhaps, the Holy Spirit was less capable of creating things destined to perish, though he is capable of creating things destined to remain forever.

A little earlier I asked: “What is more excellent among created things than the powers of heaven?” What shall I say about the flesh of the Creator? Since the Creator himself, through whom all things were made, says: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52).

What then? The world was made through the Son, and the Son is Creator; his flesh, which was given for the life of the world, was made through the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is not Creator?

When the virgin Mary said to the angel who promised her a son, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” the angel replied: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:34–35).

Here, as I noticed in a later passage of your argument, you tried to assert that the Holy Spirit came first, in order to cleanse and sanctify the virgin Mary; then the Power of the Most High—namely, the Wisdom of God, which is Christ (1 Cor. 1:24)—would come, and that Wisdom, as it is written, would build a house for itself (Prov. 9:1), that is, would create flesh for itself, not the Holy Spirit.

What, then, does the holy Gospel mean when it says: “She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18)? Surely “the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped” (Ps. 63:12).

If, therefore, you intend to open your mouth truthfully, confess not only the Son but also the Holy Spirit as the Creator of the Son’s flesh.

3. Perhaps you will say that the things I have mentioned were made through the Holy Spirit: that the whole host of heaven was established through him; that through him human beings will be created anew, although at first they are created in such a way that they return to their dust; that he himself worked Christ’s flesh—for I do not wish to say anything about the soul, which involves a very difficult question—and that anything else that may be found to have been created through the Holy Spirit was made through him.

But perhaps you will say that not all things were made through him, as they were through the only-begotten Son, of whom it was said: “All things were made through him.”

If you say this, are you not afraid that someone will say to you that the Holy Spirit is superior to the Son because he chose for himself the better things to make and did not deign to make the inferior ones?

But who would think this except one who is out of his mind?

All things, therefore, were made through the Son. Far be it from us to separate the Holy Spirit from this work, just as it is said of those great works: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:11); yet the Son is not separated from this work.

4. You seem to yourself to be saying something important when you say: “The Son was in the beginning before anything existed; but the Father was before the beginning.”

Where did you read this, that you should believe it? From where did you presume to say it, when there is neither authority nor reason for it?

For what does “before the beginning” mean, since whatever existed before would itself be the beginning? If, therefore, the Father is before the beginning, he is before himself, because he himself is also the beginning. [Note: [Col. 0784] Here the Louvain edition omits “before.”]

What else does “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1) mean except “In the Father was the Son”? When the Jews asked this same Son who he was, he replied: “The Beginning, because I am also speaking to you” (John 8:25).

The Father, therefore, is beginning not from a beginning; the Son is beginning from beginning. Yet both together are not two beginnings but one beginning, just as the Father is God and the Son is God, while both together are not two gods but one God.

Nor will I deny that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, is also the beginning. But these three together, just as I say that they are one God, so I say that they are one beginning.

## CHAPTER XVIII

1. “What if you hear the Father saying,” you ask, “‘With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you’” (Ps. 110:3)?

What do you promise, or what do you threaten, if I hear what I hear so often and faithfully believe? I am greatly surprised that you do not see how this helps you not at all.

Whether the prophet speaks this in his own person to the Lord Jesus, or in the person of the Father to the Son, since I accept, venerate, and proclaim both generations of Christ—the generation from God the Father outside of time and the generation from his human mother in the fullness of time—this testimony is not against me.

But you indicate that you wanted to delay the matter, whereas I understand more readily why he said, “From the womb I begot you,” because you too accept this as spoken in the person of the Father.

God does not have a womb in the way the members of the human body are arranged; rather, the word has been transferred from bodily to incorporeal substance, so that we might understand the only-begotten Son to have been begotten from the substance of the Father. Consequently, what else does this mean but that he is of one and the same substance?

I ought therefore to have brought this testimony against you, but I give thanks that you reminded me of it.

Consider, then, how great an evil it is that you deny the Son to be of the same substance as the Father, although you confess that he was begotten from the Father’s womb, inflicting the gravest insult upon God—as though he could beget from his womb something that was not himself.

Do you not perceive that you believe God’s generation to be defective and proclaim it monstrous, when you dare to say that a different nature proceeded from God’s womb?

But if, as you ought, you shudder at and reject this together with us, then at last praise and hold with us the Council of Nicaea and the *Homoousion*—the doctrine that the Son is of the same substance.

2. Who does not see your failure when, after hearing me mention that Christ said in prophecy to his Father, “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. 22:10)—so that we might understand that he is God of the nature which the Son received in time from his mother’s womb, while the Father is Father of that nature which he himself generated from himself—you found nothing to answer, yet, so as not to remain silent, said:

“You profess Christ to have been born from his mother’s womb according to the flesh,” and you added that even the Jews do not doubt this.

Then you asked: “Why are these testimonies not brought forward, which demonstrate that birth which occurred in the beginning, just as the preceding testimony,” you say, “also instructs us?”

You speak as though I did not believe, proclaim, and embrace that eternal birth of Christ—not temporal—for which it was said, “In the beginning was the Word,” but asserted only that Christ was born from his mother’s womb.

Behold, I say that God the Son was begotten from God the Father outside of time. I have shown how he is also the God of the one who is his Father, on account of the human being whom he assumed and in whom he was born from his mother’s womb without intercourse with a human father.

To prove this I cited the testimony in which he says in prophecy to his Father: “From my mother’s womb you are my God.”

You, who say that I profess Christ to have been born from his mother’s womb—a fact even the Jews do not doubt—as though I professed only this birth of Christ, should not try to escape through empty arguments. Instead, say why you did not answer me when Christ says to the Father, “From my mother’s womb you are my God.”

Because you saw that you had nothing to say in response, you thought that another birth—the birth of God from God—had to be introduced so that you might escape.

I ask you: when you have no answer, how much better would it be for you to remain silent?

3. “If,” you say, “on account of the body in which he emptied himself, he recognizes himself as indebted to his begetter, much more must he revere and always offer obedience to the one who begot him so great and so exalted.”

Whatever carnal notion you hold about the Son’s reverence and obedience toward the Father, his Father is not his God except on account of his mother’s womb.

And however greatly God the Son obeys God the Father, since I see that you do not understand how great is the equality of begetter and begotten in that generation, is the nature of a human father and a human son therefore different because the son obeys his father?

This is wholly intolerable in you: from the Son’s obedience you want to prove that the substance of the Father and the Son is different.

One question is whether the Father and the Son are of one and the same substance; another question is whether the Son obeys the Father.

For the present, let us not deny that he is a true Son, since in no way is he a true Son if he does not share one and the same nature with his Father.

Therefore say that God the Father and God the Son are of one and the same substance. Let divinity itself force you to acknowledge what divinity itself granted to humanity.

A human being obeys his father, from whom the human being was born; yet by obeying, he does not cease to be a human being. And if the son were not merely equally honored but more honored, the father would rejoice, not be envious. The son would nevertheless honor his father, even if he had been born equal to him rather than as a little child needing to grow with advancing age.

If a human father could beget an equal son, he would certainly beget one, without any doubt. Who, then, would dare to say, “The Almighty could not do this”? I add that if a human being could do so, he would beget a son greater and better than himself; but nothing can be greater or better than God. Therefore let us believe that God’s true Son is equal to him.

If you say that the Father is greater than the Son precisely because, though begotten by no one, he nevertheless begot an equal, I shall answer at once: rather, the Father is not greater than the Son because he begot an equal, not an inferior.

The question of origin is: who is from whom? The question of equality is: what sort or what greatness does each possess?

Therefore, if the reasoning of truth permits an equal Son to obey an equal Father, we do not deny the obedience. But if you want to believe that the Son is inferior in nature because of his obedience, we forbid it. [Note: [Col. 0786] Am. and Er. read “born inferior”; most manuscripts read “inferior in nature.”] God the Father in no way wanted to deny the nature of his only Son in order that he might have the Son’s obedience.

4. Christ’s subjection to his parents was not a matter of divine majesty but of human age. Therefore you said in vain: “If he was subject to the parents whom he created” (Luke 2:51), “how much more to his begetter, who begot him so great and so exalted?”

The answer to you is: if he was subject to his parents on account of childhood, how much more was he subject to God on account of the very form of a human being?

When God made that form immortal and did not cause him to lose it through death, why are you surprised if, even after the end of this age, he will be subject in that form to the one who subjected all things to him?

You, however, do not say that the Son is subject to the Father on account of the form of a servant, but because the Father begot him so great and so exalted—that is, as a great God, though less than the Father himself.

In this you derogate both from the Father, who either could not or did not wish to beget an equal only Son for himself, and from the Son, who was not begotten equal to the Father as his only Son, and who was therefore born perfect, lest he should ever become through growth what he could not be by birth.

5. We say that not only the Son’s body—that is, the body of a human being—but also his human spirit is subject to the Father. And we understand the statement, “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15:28), according to the fact that he became human.

This is according to Christ as head and body: the head being the Savior himself, who rose from the dead and sits at the right hand of the Father; and the Church being his body, his fullness, as the Apostle states most explicitly (Col. 1:18).

Consequently, when all things have been subjected to Christ, they will undoubtedly be subject both to the head and to the body. For insofar as he was born God outside of time, nothing could ever have failed to be subject to him.

6. We know that you thought it necessary to remind us of the statement: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

I wish, however, that you would tell us how the Father judges no one, when the Son himself repeatedly says: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges” (John 8:50).

Thus you may understand why it was said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”: because, when the living and the dead are judged, the form of a human being will appear, a form that the Father does not possess. For this reason the prophet says: “They will look upon the one whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10).

Yet the Father will also be invisibly present with him, because he is inseparable from him. If the Son, while about to die, said, “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32), how much more will he have the Father with him when he judges the dead and the living?

The Holy Spirit will also be with him. For how will the Holy Spirit abandon him on the royal throne, when he returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit (Luke 4:1)?

What is written to the Hebrews—“But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him; but we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death” (Heb. 2:8–9)—should teach us how to understand what is written to the Corinthians: “When all things have been subjected to him.” The latter was said according to the fact that he became human, not according to the fact that he is God.

Thus, appearing in human form—in which, through the suffering of death, he was made a little lower than the angels—he will judge the living and the dead when he says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34).

You wanted to use this testimony to prove that it was not a human being but God who was less than his Father. But, as is clear to those who understand, you did not prove this.

## CHAPTER XIX

Concerning the groanings of the Holy Spirit—that he himself does not groan, but, by inspiring us with holy desire, makes us groan as long as we are away from the Lord—I believe that I have already answered you sufficiently.

I also showed, as far as seemed adequate, how such expressions occur in the Holy Scriptures: the Holy Spirit is said to groan because he makes us groan, just as God said, “Now I know” (Gen. 22:12), when he caused a human being to know.

For the one who knows everything before it happens had not then come to know what he said he had then come to know.

What benefit is it that you perceive that you could not answer this, when you do not agree with it?

## CHAPTER XX

1. I have already shown that you were unable to answer anything concerning the Lord’s words, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

But if here too you want to prove, by the examples you say I used, how the words “I and the Father are one” should be understood, and for this reason you recall the apostolic testimony that I cited—“Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17)—then you too should say: “When the Son clings to the Father, he is one God.”

The Apostle did not say, “Whoever clings to the Lord, they are one,” as it is said, “I and the Father are one”; rather, he said, “He is one spirit.”

Since you do not say, “When the Son clings to the Father, he is one God,” why do you also bring forward this testimony of the Apostle, “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit,” unless it is so that I may convict you even by the witness you yourself produced?

At least now distinguish these two things, which you were unable to distinguish in our discussion when we were together.

Pay close attention, therefore, to what I say. When it is said of two or more things, “He is one” or “it is one,” and it is added what the one thing is, this can be said both of things that are different and of things that are of one substance.

The spirit of a human being and the Spirit of the Lord are different in substance [Note: Earlier manuscripts read, “and the Spirit the Lord.”]; yet it is said, “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

The souls of human beings and the hearts of human beings are of one substance; and of them it is said: “They had one soul and one heart” (Acts 4:32).

But when it is said of two or more things, “They are one,” and it is not added what they are one in, they are understood not to be different but to be of one substance. Thus it is said: “The one who plants and the one who waters are one” (1 Cor. 3:8); and, “I and the Father are one.”

You, who want the Father and the Son to be different in substance, could not find a passage in which it is said of things of different substances, “They are one.”

And because you do not want to say, “When the Son clings to the Father, he is one God,” you too brought forward the apostolic testimony that I had used, but you brought it forward against yourself, where it says: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

If it could rightly be said of those who are of different substances, “He is one spirit,” how much more rightly is it said of those who are of one substance, “He is one God”?

If you understand this, do you not now see that you have not answered these matters, and do you not recognize that you have spoken at such length and to no purpose about agreement of will?

We too confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to possess an incomparable agreement of will and indivisible love; for this reason we say, “This Trinity is one God.”

But we also say what you do not say: “These three are one,” on account of their one and the same nature and substance.

If you distinguish these things and refuse to be contentious, you will now see that you have offered no answer to the matters at issue, and you will undoubtedly fall silent concerning this question.

2. When the Son said to the Father, “Not what I will, but what you will,” what help do you receive from adding your own words and saying, “He truly showed his will to be subject to his begetter”? Do we deny that the will of a human being ought to be subject to the will of God?

Anyone who looks more carefully at the passage in the holy Gospel quickly sees that the Lord said this according to the nature of a human being. For there he said: “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. 26:38–39).

Could this have been said according to the nature of the only-begotten Word? But you, who think that the nature of the Holy Spirit groans, why do you not also say that the nature of the only-begotten Word of God could have been sorrowful?

Yet, so that nothing of this kind might be said, he did not say, “I am sorrowful.” Even if he had said this, it would necessarily have had to be understood according to the nature of a human being. Instead he said, “My soul is sorrowful,” and as a human being he certainly possessed a human soul.

Moreover, by saying, “Not what I will,” he showed that he willed something other than the Father. He could not have done this except with a human heart, when he transformed our weakness into his own—not divine, but human—feeling.

If the human being had not been assumed, the only-begotten Word would in no way have said to the Father, “Not what I will.” For that unchangeable nature could never will anything other than what the Father wills.

If you distinguished these things, you would not be Arians, the heretics.

### 3.

For that statement also, “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38), can indeed be understood according to what he is as the only-begotten Word: he said that the will was not his own but the Father’s because whatever the Son is, he is from the Father, whereas whatever the Father is, he is not from the Son. The same applies to the statement, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16), because the Father’s teaching is himself who is the Father’s Word, and he is certainly not from himself but from the Father. Again, when he says, “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15), he shows himself equal to the Father.

Nevertheless, it is not absurd to understand this statement also according to what he became as a human being: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” For the second Adam, who takes away the sin of the world, distinguished himself in this way from the first Adam, through whom sin entered the world (Romans 5:12): this one did not do his own will, but the will of him by whom he was sent, whereas the first did his own will, not the will of him by whom he was created.

Nor should it trouble us how Christ, according to what he is as a human being, came down from heaven, since he became human from a mother who was on earth. This was said because of the unity of the person, since Christ is one person, God and man. For this reason he also says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

If, then, you consider the distinction of substances, the Son of God descended from heaven, while the Son of Man was crucified; but if you consider the unity of the person, the Son of Man descended from heaven, and the Son of God was crucified. For he is the Lord of glory, of whom the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

Because of this unity of person, therefore, he not only said that the Son of Man had descended from heaven, but also said that he was in heaven while he was speaking on earth. He did not, then, do his own will because he committed no sin; rather, he did the will of him who sent him. A human being does God’s will when he does the righteousness that comes from God.

### 4.

Nor should we suppose that the Son was sent by the Father in such a way that he was not sent by the Holy Spirit, since it is the Son’s own voice through the prophet: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” That the Son said this is indicated by what was stated above. For the passage reaches these words in the following way:

“Listen to me, Jacob, and Israel whom I will call. I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heavens. I will call them, and they will stand together; all will assemble and hear. Who announced these things to them? Loving you, I have done your will concerning Babylon, so that the offspring of the Chaldeans may be removed. I spoke; I called; I brought him, and made his way prosperous. Assemble yourselves to me and hear these things. For from the beginning I have not spoken in secret: when they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:12–16). [The reading is materially uncertain.]

What could be clearer? Nor was he sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit in such a way that he did not send himself, just as he is shown to have been handed over by the Father where we read, “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32); while elsewhere the Son himself is said to have been handed over: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Galatians 2:20).

How, moreover, does he not do his own will, when he says, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21), and when someone said to him, “If you will, you can cleanse me,” he replied, “I will; be cleansed,” and immediately what he said he willed was accomplished (Matthew 8:2–3)?

Just as the Son does the will of the Father, so also the Father does the will of the Son. For the Son says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). He did not say, “I ask,” or “I beseech,” but “I will”—so that the Father would act because the Son willed it, just as the Son acted because the Father willed it. Nor did the Father do one thing and the Son another; rather, whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does (John 5:19). These are his words; they are words of truth and cannot be false.

## CHAPTER XXI

### 1.

You say that you accept what I brought forward: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). You proposed [Note: [Col. 0790] Thus several manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “what you were able.”] that this was said because God dwells in no one whom the Holy Spirit has not first sanctified and purified—as though the Holy Spirit sanctifies and purifies a temple for God, who is going to dwell there, and not for himself. Yet the Apostle showed by this very statement that the one whose temple he had said we are is himself God, because he did not say, “The Spirit of God sanctifies and purifies you so that God may dwell in you,” but, “The Spirit of God dwells in [Col. 0791] you” (1 Corinthians 3:16). God certainly dwells in his own temple. For what is God’s temple except God’s dwelling place?

You too consequently saw that the one whose temple we are is our God, and you did not wish to mention another testimony that I brought forward: “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Confess, then, that the Holy Spirit is God. For unless he were God, he would not have a temple—and not a temple made by human hands, but one built from the members of God. For “Christ is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5), and our bodies are his members. The one who said, “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?” also said, “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:19, 15).

Is the one for whom Solomon built a temple from wood and stones God, while the one for whom a temple is built from the members of Christ—that is, from the members of God—is not God? The blessed martyr Stephen, speaking of God, said: “Solomon built him a house; but the Most High does not dwell in temples made by hands” (Acts 7:47–48).

And yet the members of Christ, whose head is above all the heavens, are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom it is certain came from heaven. What is it to deny that he is God except not to be, and not to wish to be, his temple?

The Apostle addresses us, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1). The bodies of the faithful are therefore a sacrifice to God, members of Christ, and the temple of the Holy Spirit—and the Holy Spirit is not God? Who says this except one in whom he does not dwell? For in the one in whom he dwells, that person is certainly his temple.

Finally, after the Apostle had said, “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price,” he immediately added, “Therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Here he clearly showed that the Holy Spirit is God, who is to be glorified in our body as in his own temple.

And when the Apostle Peter said to Ananias, “Have you dared to lie to the Holy Spirit?”—then, showing that the Holy Spirit is God, he added, “You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:3–4).

### 2.

I marvel at your state of mind—more than I can express in words—that although you praise the Holy Spirit in such a way that everywhere you assert him to be present for the sanctification of the faithful, you nevertheless dare to deny that he is God.

Is he not God who has filled the whole world? Scripture says: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7). But what shall we say of the one who filled the world, when he also filled the Redeemer of the world? For the Lord Jesus, “full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1). Yet you presume to say that the Lord Jesus himself was God, while the Holy Spirit with whom he was filled was not God.

You think so poorly of the Holy Spirit that you do not grant him even what was granted to Moses, the servant of God. Moses, through the same Holy Spirit—for he is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19)—inflicted upon the Egyptians not gifts of grace but miraculous plagues, and yet he was a god to Pharaoh.

[Col. 0792] In one place he was present to afflict the Egyptians, and he was a god to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1); the Holy Spirit is present everywhere to regenerate human beings for eternal life, and he is not their God!

Indeed, he is God, and he is the true God, because the members of the true God are his temple. The temple is certainly subject to the one whose temple it is. How, then, is he not God to whom the members of God are subject?

Accordingly, he is also the Lord of his own temple. Who could deny this? Who could be so foolish as to say that someone is not lord of his own house? How, then, is the Holy Spirit not Lord, when he is Lord of the members of the Lord?

He is the Spirit of the Lord, of whom it is said in one and the same passage: “But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:16–17).

### 3.

Above I have already demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is Creator. How, then, is he not king, whose temple is made up of the members that belong to the King? How could he not sit with the Father and the Son, when he filled the Son and possesses as his own house the members of the Son?

Unless perhaps, when the Son returned from the Jordan, he was full of the Holy Spirit, but when he began to sit at the right hand of the Father, he expelled the Holy Spirit from himself!

Furthermore, since he proceeds from the Father, how could he not sit with the Father? This sitting is certainly not to be imagined in a physical way. Otherwise we would suppose that the Son sits more honorably than the Father, since sitting at the right hand is more honorable; and it would follow that the Father sits at the left.

Finally, you must decide what kind of spirit persuaded you to deny the Holy Spirit what holy Scripture grants to holy human beings. The Apostle says: “When we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace we have been saved; and he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:5–6).

The saints, therefore, whom the Holy Spirit sanctifies, were made alive together with Christ and predestined to sit together with him, so that the Apostle already says has been accomplished what is certainly yet to come. Yet you withhold from the Holy Spirit whatever this sharing of the seat may be, as though the one who makes others worthy to sit with the Father or the Son were unworthy to sit with them himself.

You also raise the question of why he is not worshiped, and you do this through the very same kind of error, even though—as I have already shown—you read that human beings themselves have been worshiped by holy people.

Nevertheless, to avoid the charge that you are blaspheming, you praise the Holy Spirit in such a way that you attribute to him what no creature possesses, while taking away from him what even a human creature can attain.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 1.

I admit that I said what you recall, and I say it again now: our Savior did not say, “That they and we may be one,” but, “That they may be one.” I remember that I already gave an adequate answer concerning these Gospel words when I showed that you had been unable to refute what I said.

I asked you to produce a passage where you had read that the expression “they are one” was used of things that were not of one and the same substance, but you did not produce one. What helps you that you assert it was said of Paul and Apollos in the sense of agreement in love—“The one who plants and the one who waters are one” (1 Corinthians 3:8)—when you do not show that they were of different substance? [Col. 0793] Both were human beings.

If they did not love one another, they would be one by nature but not by love; but if they were not one by nature, they could not be called one through love.

The Son therefore asks that they may be one in the way that he and the Father are one: not only by nature, which they already possessed, but also by the perfection of love and righteousness, insofar as their nature could contain this within the kingdom of God. Thus they too may be supremely one in their own nature, just as the Father and the Son are supremely one, although in their own nature, which is more excellent and incomparably better.

The Son therefore said to the Father: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are” (John 17:11). He did not say, “So that they may be one with us,” or, “So that we and they may be one.”

A little later he says: “I ask not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, so that they also may be one in us” (John 17:20–21). Here too he did not say, “So that they and we may be one,” but, “so that they may be one in us.”

Human beings, who are one by nature, cannot be supremely and perfectly one according to their own measure through the fullness of righteousness unless they are perfected in God, so that they may be one in the Father and the Son—that is, one in them, not one with them.

He continues and adds: “So that the world may believe that you sent me, and I have given them the glory that you gave me, so that they may be one, as we are one: I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:21–23). Here too he did not say, “So that they may be one with us,” or, “So that they and we may be one.”

Then, after he had added, “So that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me,” he continued: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). “Where I am,” he says, “let them be with me.” He did not say, “Let them be one with me.” [Note: [Col. 0793] The Lovaniensian edition and some manuscripts omit: “He did not say, ‘Let them be one with me.’”]

This, then, was his will: that they should be with him, not that they and he should be one.

What did you mean when you said, “He made mention of love, not of substance”? Even though you did not place these words of the Lord where he himself placed them, what does that matter to us? He did not say or will that they and he, or they and the Father, should be one; rather, he willed that those whom he knew to be of one substance should be one.

“As we are one,” he says—of those whom he likewise knew to be of one substance.

### 2.

If you wish to offer any reply, show from holy Scripture that the expression “they are one” is used of things whose substance is different. Christ did not say this, although you dared to say that the Apostles are one with the Father and the Son in that, looking in all things to the will of God the Father, they too are found subject to the one God the Father in imitation of the Son [Note: [Col. 0793] See Sermon 140, §4, vol. 5.].

By saying this, you have made God and holy human beings one. Can any of the saints therefore say, “I and God are one”? Far be this from holy hearts and mouths.

I think that you too, whoever you may hear saying this, shudder and cannot tolerate any human being—however distinguished by the gift of holiness—saying, “I and God are one.”
