[Col. 0794] But perhaps it would seem arrogant if someone said this about himself. Does any one of you, then, even if he does not dare to say, “I and God are one,” at least dare to say, “Paul and God are one,” just as we confidently say, “Paul and Apollos are one,” and, “God the Father and God the Son are one”?

If you do not dare to say, “Any holy man, any prophet, any apostle, and God are one,” who compelled you, who pushed you, who drove you headlong [Note: [Col. 0794] In the Erasmus, Lyon, and Venetian editions: “who compelled you, who drove you headlong?” M.] into saying, “The Apostles are one with the Father and the Son”?

“The Father and the Son,” you say, “are one, yet are not one [*unus*].” Immediately you add: “‘One’ [*unum*] pertains to agreement; ‘one’ [*unus*], to the number of singularity.” You meant to say, “‘They are one’ pertains to agreement; ‘there is one’ pertains to the number of singularity,” but the force of the argument carried you away from considering your own words.

For both “one” as a neuter and “one” as a masculine certainly refer to a singular number. But what is true [Note: [Col. 0794] In the Lovaniensian edition and some manuscripts: “word.”] is this: “They are one,” because of the added verb “are,” indicates a plural number joined together in a certain unity; while “there is one” most plainly indicates a singular number.

Would the Apostle, however, say, “The one who clings to the Lord, they are one”? What else would he say, if he said this, except, “A holy human being and God are one”? But far be it—far be it—from that wisdom to hold such an opinion.

Yet he did say, “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17), so that you may understand that “they are one” is said of those who are of one and the same substance. Thus it was said of certain human beings: “For all of you are one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28); and Christ himself said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

When “one” is said of someone [Note: [Col. 0794] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and what is one by nature, and what is added, one.”], however, it can be said both of different substances—as in, “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit”—and of things of one substance, as in, “They had one soul and one heart” (Acts 4:32). It says “there was,” not “there were,” because it also stated what there was: namely, “soul and heart.”

So also we say of the Father and the Son, “They are one,” because the two are of one substance; and we say, “There is one,” but we add what the one is: one God, one Lord, one Almighty, or something similar.

I think I have impressed upon you sufficiently the distinction between these two expressions. Search the canonical Scriptures, both Old and New, and find, if you can, where anything is said to be one when the things involved are of different nature and substance.

### 3.

I do not want you to be deceived concerning the Epistle of the Apostle John, where he says: “There are three witnesses: the spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three are one” (1 John 5:8). Do not perhaps say that the spirit, the water, and the blood are different substances and yet that it is said, “The three are one.” I warned you about this so that you would not be deceived.

These are sacraments, in which attention is always directed not to what they are but to what they signify, since they are signs that exist as one thing and signify another.

If, then, the things signified by these are understood, they are found to be of one substance. [Col. 0795] It would be as though we said, “The rock and the water are one,” intending by the rock to signify Christ and by the water the Holy Spirit. Who doubts that the rock and the water are different in nature?

But because Christ and the Holy Spirit are of one and the same nature, when it is said, “The rock and the water are one,” it can rightly be understood in the respect that these two things, whose nature is different, are also signs of other things whose nature is one.

We know, then, that three things came forth from the Lord’s body while he hung upon the wood: first, the spirit, as it is written, “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit”; then, when his side was pierced with a spear, blood and water (John 19:30, 34).

If we consider these three things in themselves, each has a different substance, and therefore they are not one. But if we seek what was signified by them, the Trinity itself not unreasonably presents itself: the one, only, true, supreme God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of whom it could most truly be said, “There are three witnesses, and the three are one.”

By the name “spirit,” we may understand God the Father, since the Lord was speaking of him as the one to be worshiped when he said, “God is Spirit” (John 4:24). By the name “blood,” we may understand the Son, because “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). By the name “water,” we may understand the Holy Spirit, since when Jesus was speaking of the water that he would give to those who thirst, the Evangelist said, “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:39).

Whoever believes the Gospel and hears the Son say, “I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me” (John 8:18), can doubt that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are witnesses? Although the Holy Spirit is not mentioned there, he is not thereby understood to be separated.

Nor was he silent about the Spirit elsewhere; he clearly showed that he too is a witness. For when he promised him, he said: “He himself will bear witness about me. These are the three witnesses, and the three are one” (John 15:26)—because they are of one substance.

The fact that the signs by which they were signified came forth from the Lord’s body foreshadowed the Church, which proclaims the one and same nature of the Trinity. For these three, who were signified in a threefold manner, are one; and the Church that proclaims them is the body of Christ.

If, then, the three things by which they were signified came forth from the Lord’s body, this corresponds to the sound that came forth from the Lord’s body when he commanded the nations to be baptized “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19)—in the name, not in the names. For these three are one, and these three are one God.

If this profound mystery of so great a sacrament, which is read in John’s Epistle, can be explained and understood in any other way according to the catholic faith—which neither confuses nor separates the Trinity, neither rejects three persons nor believes them to be different substances—then it should not be rejected for any reason.

For when something is placed obscurely in the holy Scriptures to exercise the minds of the faithful, we should rejoice if it is explained in many ways, provided that it is not explained foolishly.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 1.

What is the point of your asking me to establish that “the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0796] are one God,” when divine Scripture establishes this in the clearest voice by saying: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4)?

You too would hear this if you wished to be Israel—not carnally, as the Jews are, but spiritually, as Christians. Whoever does not wish faithfully to hear what was said, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” has only to believe that the one who said it is a liar.

But if he is not a liar, this statement is true; and if this statement is true, the question is settled. Truth unquestionably compels you to confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one Lord God.

Yet you deny that the Holy Spirit is God, although his temple is not made by human hands but is our body, and his temple is not wood and stones but the members of Christ. What, then, will you say about Christ himself, whom you confess to be God and Lord?

Answer us, then: are the Father and the Son one Lord God? If they are not one, there are two. If there are two, then the one who says, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” is lying; and the one who says, “See now that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deuteronomy 32:39), is lying.

But because you do not dare to call him a liar, why do you hesitate to correct yourselves and come—or return—to the catholic faith, which believes that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three lord gods but one Lord God, and hears him crying out to his people, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” and, “See now that I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me”?

If I called you deaf and blind because you neither hear nor see these things, you would undoubtedly regard me as insulting you. Look: I will not say that. Explain to us how you understand, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.” Is Christ to be understood as included there, or not?

If you say that he is included, you will confess with me that the Father and the Son are one Lord God. But if you answer that Christ is not to be understood there, you will introduce two lord gods contrary to the divine statement, since you do not deny that Christ too is Lord God.

I ask you similarly how you understand, “See now that I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me.” Is Christ included there, or not? If he is included, then the Father and the Son are one Lord. But if he is not included, and yet is Lord, then the one who says, “There is no other besides me,” is lying. For there is another Lord, the Son, if the Father and the Son are not one Lord.

However much you praise the Father as greater and place the Son beneath him, you make them unequal, not prevent them from being two. Cry out as much as you wish, “The Father is greater, the Son lesser”; the answer is: nevertheless there are two, the greater and the lesser.

It was not said, “The Lord your God is greater; the Lord is one,” but, “The Lord your God, the Lord is one.” Nor was it said, “There is no one equal to me,” but, “There is no other Lord besides me.”

Therefore either confess that the Father and the Son are one Lord God, or openly deny that Christ is Lord God, just as openly as you deny that the Holy Spirit is Lord God.

If you do this, I will not press you with these divine statements; [Col. 0797] rather, I will produce other divine testimonies by which I will prove you even more detestable in this error [Note: [Col. 0797] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read, “I will prove you even more detestable”; M.].

But even if you deny that the Holy Spirit is Lord God, it is sufficient to crush you with these divine statements that you confess Christ to be Lord God. For if he is not one Lord God with the Father, there will be two lord gods, and those statements of God will be false: “The Lord your God, the Lord is one,” and, “There is no other besides me.”

But how much better it is that your words should be corrected than that God’s words should be lies!

### 2.

You ask me whether I am urging you, in the Jewish manner, to confess one God, or whether the unity of God is instead demonstrated according to Christian faith through the Son’s subordination, whose Son is our God.

You speak as though the statement, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” or, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me,” were a Jewish utterance. God himself said this. Acknowledge it and be silent—or rather, explain how he spoke truly, since none of us dares to assert that he lied.

Explain, I say, how it is true that “the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” if, as you say, there are two lord gods, one greater and the other lesser. Explain how it is true: “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me.”

Who said this, I ask: the Father or the Son? If the Father said, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me,” he did not speak truly, because there is another Lord, the Son. If the Son said this, he too did not speak truly, because there is another Lord, the Father.

But if the Trinity said this, then it both spoke truly and showed that you are speaking falsely. For according to the true faith, the Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in whose name we are baptized—is one Lord God, and there is no other besides it.

This is the God of whom the Apostle says: “There is no God except one” (1 Corinthians 8:4). For if you understand this as spoken of the Father, Christ will not be God for you, since Scripture cannot be set aside when it says, “There is no God except one.” I say nothing here about the Holy Spirit, whom we have already shown to be Lord God, although you deny it.

Therefore, if you were Macedonian heretics, who refuse to agree with the catholic faith concerning the Holy Spirit alone, but consent that the Father and the Son are indeed two—that is, one is the Father and the other the Son—and that they are equal and of one and the same substance, while nevertheless not being two lord gods but together one Lord God, then I would not press you with these divine statements.

You would at least affirm that the Father and the Son together said, “There is no other besides me.” If only I did not have to deal with you about anything except your adding the Holy Spirit and saying not a duality but a Trinity to be one Lord God!

But now, since you assert that the Father is Lord God and the Son is Lord God in such a way that you do not say that they together are one Lord God but two—one greater and the other lesser—you are thoroughly pierced by the sword of truth, which says, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” and cries out, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides [Col. 0798] me.”

For God the Father would not have wished to turn the Israelites away from the worship of many false gods by lying to them about the one God and Lord, saying that there was no other Lord besides himself, while knowing that his Son too was God and Lord.

Far be it from us to think that truth and the Father of truth deceived his people with a lie. Such a horrifying and detestable blasphemy belongs to heretics, not to Catholics.

God certainly speaks the truth when he says, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one,” because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God, nor three lords but one Lord.

He certainly speaks the truth when he says, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me,” because it is not the Father alone but the Trinity itself that says this. This is the one Lord, and there is no other besides him.

For if the Father said, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me,” he would certainly deny that the only-begotten Son is Lord. And who among us would dare to confess him as Lord when the Father contradicted him by saying, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me”?

According to the true faith, therefore, this is not the voice of the Father alone but of the Trinity, and therefore of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Let the tongues of those who do not know the truth be silenced: this Trinity is one God. Of this one God it is said, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.” This one God says, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me.”

The Son is subject to the Father according to the form of a human being; nevertheless, according to the form of God, there are not two gods and two lords. Rather, together with his Spirit, the Father and the Son are one Lord.

### 3.

The testimonies you brought forward from the Apostle Paul speak against you, and you do not know it. He says: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7; 1 Corinthians 1:3; 2 Corinthians 1:2; Galatians 1:3; Ephesians 1:2).

How, then, is Jesus Christ Lord, if the Father says, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me”? This statement, as I said, is therefore not the voice of the Father alone but of the Trinity.

You add another testimony, also against yourself, where the Apostle says: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6), as you quoted it. But the Apostle says “we through him,” not “we in him.”

What does this have to do with the issue? Such things often happen when people recite testimonies from memory rather than reading them from a manuscript. Pay attention instead to what concerns the matter.

Look: the Apostle said, “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

He distinguished two persons altogether—one of the Father and the other of the Son—without any confusion and without any error. For there are not two God the Fathers, but one God the Father; nor are there two Lord Jesus Christs, but one Lord Jesus Christ.

In that Trinity which is God, there is one Father, not two or three; and one Son, not two or three; and one Spirit of both, not two or three. That one Father is certainly God; that one Son, even you admit, is also God; and that Spirit of both, even though you deny it, is also God.

If you ask about Lordship in the same way, I answer concerning each individually; but all [Col. 0799] together I call them not three lord gods but one Lord God.

This is our faith, because this is the true faith, which is also called catholic.

But you, who contradict this faith, explain to us how Jesus Christ is Lord, when you assert that the statement, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me,” belongs not to the Trinity but to the Father alone.

Surely you are confused; surely you cannot find what to answer, except that you refuse to remain silent when you are refuted.

For if not God the Trinity but the Father alone said, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me,” he certainly denied that the Son is Lord. For if the Son too is Lord, then the statement, “There is no other Lord besides me,” was false.

The issue is not the kind of lords who are human beings, masters of human servants, whom the Apostle calls lords according to the flesh (Ephesians 6:5). The issue is the Lord to whom the service called in Greek *latreia* (λατρεία)—that is, religious worship—is owed, according to the statement, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13).

If this Lord God is not the Trinity but the Father alone, then we are forbidden to serve Christ the Lord with that kind of service when we hear, “You shall serve him alone,” if this was said as though it meant, “You shall serve God the Father alone.”

If the Father alone, and not the Trinity itself, said, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me,” then he denied that the Son is such a Lord as deserves the service by which God alone is served in true religion.

For he did not say, “I am the Lord who is greater or better, and there is no one besides me who is as great or as such.” Rather, wishing that the service owed to the Lord God alone should be offered to him alone, he said, “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me.”

But if this statement, as the catholic faith teaches, belongs to the one God who is the Trinity, then without any doubt this Trinity alone must be served with the service owed only to the Lord God, because he is the Lord, and there is no other besides him.

### 4.

Next I ask how you understand the statement: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him.” Are not all things also from the Son, since he himself says, “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19)? But if you distinguish the matter in such a way that all things are not through the Father but from the Father, and that all things are not from the Son but through the Son, which of them do you think is meant by the same apostle when he says:

> O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen. (Romans 11:33–36)

Is the Father to be understood, or the Son? For he first called him “God,” saying, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” Then he called him “Lord,” where he says, “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” But this presents no difficulty: you too assign both names to the Father and to the Son. For you do not call the Father God in such a way as to deny that the Son is God; nor do you call the Son God in such a way as to deny that the Father is God.

[Col. 0800] Although, in the apostolic testimony you cited, the Father is called God and the Son Lord: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” But pay attention to where it says, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” For whether this is the Father or the Son, “from him and through him and in him are all things.” How, then, are all things from the Father and not from the Son, and through the Son and not through the Father, when the apostle says—whether he wished the Father or the Son to be understood here—“From him and through him and in him are all things”?

Therefore, whether the statement concerns the Father or the Son, it is nevertheless most truly said that all things are from him, through him, and in him. Without doubt, then, the equality of the Father and the Son is being demonstrated. But if, because he did not name the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but “God” and “Lord”—which can also be said of the Trinity itself—he wished each of these three expressions to refer to one of the three, saying “from him” with reference to the Father, “through him” with reference to the Son, and “in him” with reference to the Holy Spirit, why do you refuse to acknowledge this Trinity as one Lord God? For he did not say, “From them, and through them, and in them are all things,” but, “From him, and through him, and in him are all things.” Nor did he say, “To them be glory,” but, “To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

### 5.

You are certainly mistaken in thinking that the statement “No one is good except one, God” was spoken of the Father alone. For if he had said, “No one is good except one, the Father,” even then he would not have wished the Son and the Holy Spirit to be understood as excluded from this unity of goodness. For that other statement, expressed in a similar form, which I mentioned above—“No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11)—does not exclude the Son of God from this knowledge.

How much broader, then, is the scope of our understanding, since he did not say, “No one is good except one, the Father,” but, “No one is good except one, God,” which is the Trinity itself. The man to whom Jesus replied was seeking not just any kind of good, but the good by which he might become blessed; indeed, he desired true blessedness, that is, eternal life. He had addressed Christ as though he were merely a human being, not knowing that he was also God. For he had said, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Then Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:17–18). Or, as it is read in another evangelist, with the same meaning, “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19).

It was as though he were saying: “You will rightly call me good if you know me to be God. But when you think of me as nothing other than a human being, why do you call me good? Nothing makes you good or blessed except the immutable good that God alone is. An angel is good, a human being is good, and other creatures are good; but they are not so good that whoever obtains them thereby becomes blessed. Nor is there any blessed life unless it is eternal.”

How, then, is the true Son of God not such a good, since he is true God and eternal life, which the man who questioned him desired to attain?

### 6.

Since I maintain that “No one is good except the one and only God” was spoken of the Trinity itself, which is the one and only God, while you maintain that it was spoken of God the Father alone, because he is God from no other and good from no other, whereas the Son is God from the Father and great and good from the Father, consider carefully which of us thinks rightly about God the Father and God the Son.

Is it I, who say that God the Father is not God from another God, while God the Son is God from God the Father—but that the Son is as great from the Father as the Father is great from no one; and that the good Father is not good from another good, while the Son is good from the good Father—but that the Son is as good from the Father as the Father is good from no one?

Or is it you, who say that the Father alone is the good God because he is neither God from another God nor good from another good, while the Son is not to be equated with the Father because he is God from the Father and good from the Father?

In this position you blaspheme both: the Father, because he did not beget one as great as he himself is, nor one of the same nature as himself; and the Son, because he was not worthy to be born such and so great as the one who begot him.

Finally, the very two matters under discussion—namely, divinity and goodness—fail in this opinion of yours, since it is said, “No one is good except one, God.” For if the Father could not beget one as great as he himself is and of the same nature as himself, how is he God? If he did not wish to do so, how is he good?

### 7.

“The Father,” you say, “is the fountain of goodness, since he received from no one what he is as good.”

Is the Son therefore less good because he received his goodness from that Father who was able to give the Son, at his birth, as much goodness as belongs to him because he is God—and gave it because, being good, he could not be envious? For if he gave his only Son less goodness than he himself possesses, then he himself is less good than he ought to be. To think this is madness.

Therefore, as much goodness as the Father possesses, so much he gave to the Son [Note: [Col. 0801] Some manuscripts read, “so much he gave to his Only-begotten.”]. And because the Son is Son by nature, not by grace, the Father gave it to one being born, not to one in need; and, being full, he begot one full: the fountain of goodness begot the fountain of goodness.

Thus the Son did not increase in himself what he received, nor did the Father diminish in himself what he gave [Note: [Col. 0801] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions, however, read: “what he gave.”]: immutability has no point from which it can decline, and fullness has no point to which it can grow.

What, moreover, is goodness itself except life that gives life? Therefore, because the fountain begot the fountain, “as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). The Son himself said this, not I.

Accordingly, it is rightly said to God the Father, “For with you is the fountain of life.” What, then, is this fountain of life with the Father except the one of whom it is said:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God;

and of whom shortly afterward it is also said:

> And the life was the light of human beings. (John 1:1–2, 4)

This life is the fountain of life, and this light is the light of light. Therefore, after it was said, “With you is the fountain of life,” it immediately continues, “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10)—that is, in your Son, the Holy Spirit, whom you too acknowledged to be the illuminator in the first part of our Discussion.

The fountain, therefore, from the fountain—the Son from the Father—and together they are one fountain; light from light—the Son from the Father—and together they are one light; just as God from God, and together they are certainly one God—and all this not without the Spirit of them both.

From this fountain of goodness, from this fountain of life, from this immutable light, from this unfailing fullness—that is, from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one Lord God alone—all who truly believe, according to the measure of their faith, receive what makes them good, gives them life, illuminates them, and fills them.

To these you have joined the only-begotten Son—if I may say so without offending your peace—with an astonishing recklessness whose nature I cannot understand. These, indeed, are your words:

> “Whether the Son,” you say, “or those who were made through the Son, each of them received from that one fountain of goodness, according to the measure of his faith, in order to be good.”

Where, then, is what you had previously confessed: that he is the Son by nature, not by grace [Note: [Col. 0802] Several manuscripts read, “not by grace”?]? Behold, you contradict your own position; behold, you now reveal the wicked secret of your heresy: you profess that the only-begotten, true Son of God, true God, is Son not by nature but by grace.

For if he too, as your words loudly proclaim, received according to the measure of his faith in order to be good, then the Son is by grace, not by nature. At some time, therefore, he was not good, and by believing he became good; because, as you say, in order to be good he received according to the measure of his faith from him who is the Father, the fountain of goodness.

We do indeed read that “Jesus increased in age and wisdom, and the grace of God was in him” (Luke 2:52), but this refers to the form of a human being which he accepted for our sake from us, not to the form of God, in which he did not regard equality with God as something alien to him (Philippians 2:6).

Nevertheless, even in that human form we read that he increased in age and wisdom; but not that by believing he earned the status of becoming good from being not good. The dispute between us now is not about the nature of the Son of Man, in which the Son of God is inferior to the Father, but about the nature of the Son of God, in which, as we say and you deny, he is equal to the Father.

For the true Son, the only Son, the true God from the true God, has in no respect degenerated from the Father. Thus you could nowhere read in the holy Scriptures that the Father is incomparable to the Son. Nor did you speak with sound faith when you called the Father “immeasurable,” since you say this in order to regard the Son as not equally immeasurable, but bounded by measure.

Keep your measure, then, by which you measure your false lord and lie about the true Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIV

You rightly confess that the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father. But you should also confess that the Father’s love is not greater than the Son’s. Since they are equal in the nature of divinity, they love one another equally.

The Son, in the manner of a human being, carries out the Father’s command. But as God, the Son himself is the Father’s command, because he himself is the Father’s Word. Hence elsewhere, speaking of the Father’s command—that is, of himself—he says, “I know that his commandment is eternal life” (John 12:50).

That the Son of God himself is eternal life is attested by divine Scripture. When he says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), who does not understand that this was said because whoever sees the Son through understanding sees him as equal to the Father? You refuse this because you do not see the Son with the eyes of the heart, insofar as he can be seen in this life.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0803]

You think that I was wrong to say that, because of the form of a servant which the Son assumed (Philippians 2:7), the Father is greater. Yet according to your heresy you want the Father to be greater than the Son even in the form of God. You so begrudge him the paternal form that you want the Son to have been born perfect with eternal perfection precisely so that, even by growing, he might never be able to attain the paternal form.

But a human being vainly begrudges the Son of God the Father’s form, which the Father did not begrudge him, since he begot his only Son equal to himself. You say, however, that the Father’s glory would not be great if the form of a servant were greater, since angels too are greater in that form.

See whether you are attempting anything other than to reach the glory of the one Father through the dishonor of his only Son—that is, to increase the Father in glory only by diminishing the Son in nature.

Restrain yourself. You do not understand that you bring dishonor upon both Father and Son if the Father either could not or would not beget one equal to himself, and if the Son could not be born equal to the Father. God does not wish the Father to be praised in such a way that the Son is said to have generated from himself a degenerate offspring. The good lover of the Son does not wish his own form to be proclaimed in such a way that his only Son could neither receive it by being born nor attain it by growing.

As for your view that nothing great is said about God the Father if the form of a servant is greater, since angels too appear greater in that form, you are not thinking correctly about the place occupied among created things by human nature, which was made in the image of God.

Angels can be called greater than human beings because they are greater than the human body. They are also greater in spirit, but in that form in which the body, rendered corruptible by the penalty of original sin, weighs down the spirit. Yet human nature as such—such as the nature assumed by Christ’s human mind, which could not be corrupted by any sin—has only God as its superior.

Finally, Scripture has made clear why it was said, “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6), where we read: “We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9).

Therefore, it was not because of the nature of the human being, but because of the suffering of death. The nature of the human being, which surpasses all other creatures by its rational and intellectual mind, has only God as its superior. No insult was done to him when it was written, “God is greater than our heart” (1 John 3:20).

When, therefore, the Son of God was about to raise the human being he had assumed to the Father, he said, “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). He was presenting God the Father as superior not merely to his flesh, but also to the human mind he bore. This whole reality is unquestionably recognized as the form of a servant, since every creature serves the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### 1.

Your final argument concerned how God was seen by the patriarchs when Christ had not yet assumed the human body in which he would be seen, since the divine nature in itself is invisible.

Although you too had confessed this, saying among other things that not only the Father, but also the Son himself, in the substance of his divinity, was invisible not merely to human beings but even to the heavenly powers, you later changed your position and now say that he appeared even before his incarnation to mortal observers. You assert that the apostle’s statement, “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Timothy 6:16), was spoken of God the Father alone, while the Son had been accustomed to be seen by human beings from the beginning of the human race.

When you wished to prove this, you brought forward many testimonies from the holy Scriptures, but they could not help you. Nowhere, as you claim, do you read that Moses wrote that from the first human being, Adam, up to the incarnation itself, the Son was always seen. You declare that Moses described this in the book of Genesis, but this is so false that it is even ridiculous.

Does the book of Genesis contain everything that happened from Adam to Christ’s incarnation? Or did Moses himself live until the time of Christ’s incarnation, or write about events that took place then? You say these things and think you are saying something—or you may be regarded as saying something by those who are unable to recognize statements so plainly false.

### 2.

Next, concerning your citation of the Father saying to the Son, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness,” I ask you: what does this have to do with the matter? What does it have to do with the matter?

Did you have so much leisure for speaking that, without paying attention to what you had undertaken to prove, you could rehearse the text of Genesis to us from memory and to no purpose? Is Christ proved to have been seen by human beings before assuming flesh merely because the Father said to the Son, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness”?

Then you add, “And God made the human being” (Genesis 1:26–27), and ask, “Which God, except the Son?” And, as though you wished to forestall me by appealing to my own work, you say, “You too have explained this in your treatises.”

I do not wish to ask how truthful you are speaking, since I see that what you are saying has no bearing on the case. The question between us is whether Christ appeared to human eyes through the substance of his divinity. You say, “God made the human being,” and add, “Which God, except the Son?”—as though it were therefore necessary that the human being should see with bodily eyes the God who made him.

If this were so, all human beings would see God. For who else makes them in their mothers’ wombs?

You go on to say:

> “This Son, then, who is the prophet of his father, was saying: ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper corresponding to him’” (Genesis 2:18).

If I ask who told you that it was the Son who said this, what difficulties will you find yourself in? The Scripture that said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” without specifying whether the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself made them—for the Trinity is the one God—continues throughout to mention God in the same way, saying, “And God made,” “And God said,” in connection with each of his works, and asserting that he was their creator.

In the same manner, therefore, it says, “And God said, ‘Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.’ And God made the human being.” It spoke no differently when it said, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper corresponding to him.”

Where, then, did you get the conviction that the Father spoke all the preceding words, but the Son this one? Where, I ask, do you distinguish and separate the Father as the one who said, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:1–27), and the other words, and finally, “Let us make the human being,” while the Son said, “Let us make him a helper,” when Scripture everywhere says only, “God said”?

What is this recklessness? What is this presumption?

Moreover, since you customarily assert that the Father is greater because he said, “Let this be,” or “Let that be,” as one commanding the Son, while the Son is lesser because he carried out the commands, what will you say where it is written, “Let us make the human being”?

For it does not say, as in the preceding passages, “Let the human being be,” as though he had commanded the Son. Rather it says, “Let us make the human being.”

I will not ask whom you think said this, since we already have your own words: the Father said this to the Son. Why, then, did he not say, “Let it be,” or “Make it,” but, “Let us make”?

Did God command in the other cases and the Son make them, while in the case of the human being both made him—but the Father both commanding and cooperating, and the Son neither commanding but merely carrying out what was commanded [Note: [Col. 0805] The printed editions read, “and the Son cooperating, but the Son not commanding,” and so on. The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.]?

But if you understand the Father as commanding because it is written, “God said, ‘Let us make the human being,’” then the Son also commanded, since you yourself do not take the Father to have said, but the Son to have said, “Let us make him a helper.”

And just as, where it is said, “And God made the human being,” you want the Son to appear to have obeyed the commanding Father because the Father had said, “Let us make the human being,” so too, when we read, “And the Lord cast Adam into a deep sleep and took one of his ribs” (Genesis 2:21), and the rest of the passage by which it is shown that a helper was made for the human being, let us understand—on your authority—that the Father obeyed the commanding Son, since you assert that it was not the Father but the Son who said, “Let us make him a helper.”

### 3.

But I speak in this way as though anything at all belonging to what you may wish to believe or suspect here had any bearing on the case before us.

By all means, let the Father have commanded, as you say, when it was stated, “Let us make the human being,” and let the Son have obeyed when it was stated, “And God made the human being.” By all means, let the Son have said, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper,” while, as you wish, he did not command when he said this.

How do you show that the Son who made the human being was seen by the human being? How do you show that the Son who said, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper,” was seen by the human being—or by the woman herself, if you do not want her to have been made by the Father, lest the Father appear to have obeyed the Son, but instead want the Son himself, as one commanding and obeying himself, both to have said that she should be made and to have made her?

Show that the Son was seen by the man; show that he was seen by the woman. You had promised that you would demonstrate this—that the Son was seen by human observers before he was incarnate. Produce what you promised.

Why do you continue at such length without substance? Why do you deceive our expectation and fail to deliver your promise? You multiply unnecessary words in order to consume the time needed for necessary matters.

[Col. 0806]

### 4.

“But this Son,” you say, “was seen by Adam, according to what we read Adam saying: ‘I heard your voice as you were walking in the garden, and I hid myself because I am naked’” (Genesis 3:10).

This, then, is where you should have begun, good sir; from this point you should have started displaying what you promised. Yet here too Adam says, “I heard your voice”; he does not say, “I saw your face” or “your appearance.” And when he says, “I hid myself because I am naked,” he feared that he would be seen by God; he did not show that God had been seen by him.

For if hearing a voice is followed by seeing, then God the Father was also seen whenever he bore witness to the Son by a voice. We know the words of the Father sounding forth in the Gospel and saying, “You are my beloved Son,” and so forth (Mark 1:11): he was heard by human beings but was not seen.

Accordingly, in those words that you add—where he says, “Who told you that you were naked?” and what follows—God could have been heard without being seen.

You have not yet said anything from what you promised. Say at last something that we ought to examine, or that we can acknowledge as supporting your case.

### 5.

“This God,” you say, “was also seen by Abraham.”

We cannot deny that God was seen by Abraham. The most trustworthy Scripture speaks of this with complete clarity, saying, “God appeared to him by the oak of Mamre.”

But here too it is not stated whether the Father or the Son was meant. When Scripture narrates how God appeared to him, it declares that three men appeared to him. In them the Trinity itself, which is the one God, can more appropriately be understood.

Abraham sees three, yet calls them not “lords” but “Lord,” because the Trinity consists of three persons but is one Lord God.

This is how Abraham’s vision is narrated:

> Looking up with his eyes, he saw, and behold, three men were standing before him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the door of his tent, bowed to the ground, and said, “Lord, if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant.”

Here we see that three men appeared and that one Lord is named; one Lord is asked not to pass by his servant, since it is fitting for God to visit his servants.

Then he addresses the three persons in the plural:

> “Let water now be brought, and wash your feet; rest under the tree, and I will bring bread, and eat; afterward you shall continue on your way, since you have turned aside to your servant.”

It is clear that they are being invited as human beings. Such service, by which bodies in need would be refreshed, would not be offered to them unless they were thought to be human beings.

Scripture also records that they answered him in the plural. For it says, “And they said, ‘Do as you have said.’” It does not say, “And he said,” but “they said.”

Then, when the meal had been prepared, Scripture says, “And he set it before them, and they ate.” It does not say, “He set it before him, and he ate.”

But when the narrative reaches the point at which Abraham’s son is promised through Sarah, because a divine benefaction was being offered rather than human service being rendered to human beings, Scripture recounts one speaking: “Where is Sarah your wife?” It does not say, “And they said to him,” but, “And he said to him, ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’”

Who this was is revealed afterward. When Sarah laughed, the same Scripture says:

> “And the Lord said to Abraham, ‘Why did Sarah laugh within herself?’”

and continues to the end as though one Lord were speaking in the singular.

After this, when the men are said to depart in the plural, the narrative says:

> “The men, having risen from there, looked toward the face of Sodom and Gomorrah; but Abraham was walking with them, accompanying them.”

Again Scripture returns to the singular and says:

> “But the Lord said, ‘Shall I hide from my servant Abraham what I am about to do?’”

Then a splendid and abundant posterity is promised to Abraham, and the destruction of Sodom is announced.

The following passage says:

> “And the men, turning from there, came to Sodom; but Abraham was still standing before the Lord. And Abraham approached and said, ‘Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? And will the righteous be like the wicked?’”

After the conversation between the Lord and Abraham, Scripture continues:

> “And the Lord departed when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.”

Then:

> “Two angels came to Sodom in the evening.”

These are the ones of whom it had said shortly before, “The men, turning from there, came to Sodom.” But it had not specified that there were two, although at the beginning it had said that three men appeared to Abraham, that he received them hospitably, and that he accompanied them as they departed, walking with them.

### 6.

Perhaps, then, you are already eager to declare that one of them was the Lord Christ, who was making promises and answering Abraham in the singular, while the other two were his angels, who came to Sodom as angels sent by their Lord.

But wait. Why are you in such a hurry? Let us consider everything carefully, and first examine the words of the Lord speaking to Abraham:

> “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has become great, and their sins are very grievous. Therefore I will go down and see whether they have completed their deeds according to the outcry that has come to me.”

Here he said that he himself would go down to Sodom, yet it was not he himself who went down there, but two angels. For he himself departed when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.

As it was said, two angels came to Sodom in the evening. What if one Lord is also found in those two angels, who, according to his word, descended in those angels to Sodom? Will it not be clear that one Lord was seen in those three men, in which nothing other than the Trinity itself was symbolized?

But let us see whether Holy Scripture demonstrates to us that, in those two angels as I have said, one Lord was found, lest we appear to have asserted this merely from our own thoughts.

Two angels therefore came to Sodom in the evening. Lot, as it is written, was sitting by the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed with his face to the ground.

You see that here angels were worshiped by a righteous man, yet you do not want the Holy Spirit to be worshiped, whom you too place without ambiguity above all the angels [Note: [Col. 0807] The Louvain edition omits “above all angels.”]?

But you will say, “He thought they were human beings, for he invited them into his house as human beings.”

This is even more against you, since you say that the Holy Spirit, who is to be preferred to all angels, is not to be worshiped, while you see righteous human beings worshiping human beings who are inferior to angels.

You will still say, “He worshiped the Lord; for he recognized him as being in those two whom he thought were human beings, just as he is in prophets.”

It has now been proved, then, what I promised to demonstrate from Holy Scripture: that the same Lord who was said to have departed when he ceased speaking with Abraham descended into Sodom in those two angels, as he had said, and was recognized in them by a righteous man.

Lot therefore offered them hospitality as he would to holy men of God, in whom he recognized that God was present, although, like Abraham himself, he did not know that they were angels, yet recognizing—as far as he could, with the Lord himself showing him—who was in them. These patriarchs are signified in the Letter to the Hebrews, where, speaking of hospitality, it says, “Through it some, without knowing it, received angels as guests” (Hebrews 13:2).

After Lot had received them, not knowing that they were angels but recognizing—through the Lord himself showing him, as far as he could—that one was present in them, and leaving aside what happened in the meantime, he went out with them from Sodom.

Before this took place, as Scripture says, the men said to Lot:

> “Do you have here a son-in-law, or sons, or daughters? Or anyone else belonging to you in the city, bring them out of this place, because we are destroying this place; for their outcry has become great before the Lord, and the Lord has sent us to destroy it.” [Note: [Col. 0808] The manuscripts read, “we are destroying”; the printed editions read, “we shall destroy.”]

Behold where that burning of Sodom appears to have been carried out through the angels whom the Lord sent, yet he himself was also in them. For he does not send his own in such a way that he departs from them.

In them, therefore, he descended to Sodom, as he had said he would do when he spoke with Abraham. After he had done this, he himself is said to have departed, and the angels to have come to Sodom in the evening.

Then, shortly afterward, as soon as they had led Lot outside and said, as the same Scripture narrates:

> “Save your life. Do not look back, and do not remain in the whole region. Save yourself on the mountain, lest you be caught,”

Lot said to them:

> “I beg you, Lord, because your servant has found mercy before you,”

and so forth.

When he had finished speaking and had chosen for himself a small city in which he might be saved, Scripture follows and says that he received this answer:

> “Behold, I have regarded your face [Note: [Col. 0808] The printed editions read, “I have shown mercy.” The manuscripts read, “I have regarded,” as does Book 16, chapter 29, of *The City of God*, following the Greek Septuagint, *ethaúmasa*, which may be rendered “I have respected” or “I have regarded with favor.]. I will not destroy the city concerning which you have spoken. Hurry, save yourself there; for I cannot carry out the matter until you have entered it” (Genesis 18–19).

Who answered him except the one to whom he had said, “I beg you, Lord”? He had said this to both, not to one, as is stated most explicitly: “Lot said to them, ‘I beg you, Lord.’”

Lot therefore recognized one Lord in the two angels, just as Abraham recognized one in the three.

### 7.

There is no reason to say, “The one who was Lord and had spoken with Abraham had departed; the other two were his angels, who came to Sodom after he had departed” [Note: [Col. 0808] Almost only the Louvain edition reads, “after he had commanded.”].

All three men who appeared to Abraham are called men, just as Scripture customarily calls angels men. Abraham did not serve any one of them more readily or humbly than the other two; rather, he washed the feet of all equally and served a meal to all equally.

[Col. 0809] Therefore he saw God in them all. For this reason Scripture had stated beforehand that God had appeared to Abraham by the oak of Mamre, beneath whose shade he fed the three men whom he saw with the eyes of his body. In them, however, he saw God not with bodily eyes but with the eyes of his heart—that is, he understood and recognized him—just as Lot did in the two, with whom he spoke and who answered him not in the plural but in the singular, as though they were one.

At first Abraham heard him through the three men; afterward, through the one who remained behind while the other two went to Sodom and who spoke with him. Lot, however, heard him through the two, yet he too recognized one Lord, whom he asked for deliverance and who answered him.

Both Abraham and Lot thought that those who were angels were human beings; but they understood that the God who truly was present in them was there, and did not suppose that he was what he was not.

What, then, is the meaning of this visible Trinity and intelligible unity, except that it was intended to suggest to us that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were three in such a way that together they were nevertheless not three gods and lords, but one Lord God?

Yet you said, “This God was seen by Abraham,” knowing that you had read that it was written that God appeared to Abraham by the oak of Mamre. And wishing, as it were, to prove that the Lord Son was seen by that patriarch, you passed over those three men and said nothing at all about them, although Scripture narrates that God was seen by Abraham in them.

You did this so that you yourself would not remind us that the Trinity is one in substance, just as the three men whom Abraham saw were one in substance. Scripture had stated beforehand, “God appeared to Abraham,” yet it did not say that there were three gods, because it says, “God appeared,” not “gods appeared.” Abraham himself saw three and worshiped one. He did not wish to pass that one by; from the one he received divine answers.

Nor did he perceive two of them as two gods, but one in them all, since Lot too saw two and nevertheless recognized one Lord.

It seems to me that the Son and the Holy Spirit are signified through the angels, since those angels said that they had been sent. Of the Trinity that is God, the Father alone is not read to have been sent; the Son and the Holy Spirit, however, are read to have been sent. Their nature is not thereby different, for the men through whom they were signified were also of one and the same nature.

You therefore avoided this Scripture, by which you could have been refuted, through a crafty silence. And after saying, “This God was seen by Abraham,” wishing it to be thought that the Son alone was seen in the statement of Genesis that God appeared to Abraham, you did not wish to say how he was seen, lest God should be recognized there not as the Son alone but as the Trinity.

### 8.

You said:

> “If you wish to believe that the Son was seen by Abraham, the only-begotten Son himself affirmed it in the holy Gospel in these words: ‘Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and rejoiced’” (John 8:56).

What an argument! What a proof of your promise! It is as though the Son of God had said, “Abraham desired to see me, and he saw me and rejoiced.”

Even this could still be understood to mean that the holy patriarch saw the Son of God with the eyes of his heart, not with the eyes of his flesh—which is precisely the question between us.

But since Christ said, “Abraham desired to see my day; and he saw it and rejoiced,” why should we not understand Christ’s day as the time of Christ, when he was to come in the flesh, which Abraham, like the other prophets, was able to see in the spirit and rejoice over?

Here too, therefore, you could not prove what you had proposed and promised.

### 9

After this you came to Jacob, who wrestled with an Angel—whom Scripture itself in Genesis calls both a man and God. For it is read as follows:

> “Jacob remained alone, and a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the breadth of his thigh, and the breadth of Jacob’s thigh became numb [Note: [Col. 0810] In the manuscripts, “obstipuit.”] while he wrestled with him. And he said to him, ‘Release me, for dawn has risen.’ But he said, ‘I will not release you unless you bless me.’ And he said to him, ‘What is your name?’ He answered, ‘Jacob.’ And he said, ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, because you have prevailed with God, and you are powerful with men.’ Jacob asked him, saying, ‘Tell me your name.’ And he said, ‘Why do you ask my name?’ And he blessed him there. Jacob called the name of that place ‘The Appearance of God,’ for, he said, ‘I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved.’” (Genesis 32:24–30)

From this passage you attempt to demonstrate that the only-begotten Son of God appeared visibly even before he came in the flesh. Here Christ may indeed not unreasonably be understood as represented, on account of the prophecy announcing future events: for it was to come about that Jacob would appear to have prevailed over Christ in his descendants who crucified Christ; and in his descendants he would see Christ face to face, and the soul of the Israelites who saw this faithfully would be saved.

Nevertheless, Hosea the prophet clearly calls this man who wrestled with Jacob an angel. For this is what is written concerning Jacob:

> “In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his labor he prevailed with God; he was strengthened with the angel, and he prevailed.” (Hosea 12:3–4)

Therefore, just as in Genesis the one who wrestled with Jacob is called both man and God—[Note: [Col. 0810] In the manuscripts, “and is known as God.”]—so by this prophet he is called both God and angel. Accordingly, the one who was an angel was called a man in the same way as those who appeared to Abraham were called men, when both Abraham and Lot, without knowing it—[Note: [Col. 0810] In the manuscripts, “when seeing them.”—] received angels as guests.

God, therefore, was in the angel, just as God is in a man, especially when he speaks through a man. Christ, however, was represented through this angel just as he was represented through a man. For Isaac, Abraham’s son—what was he in representation except Christ, when he was led like a sheep to be sacrificed (Isaiah 53:7), and when, like the Lord carrying his cross, he too carried the wood on which he was to be laid?

Finally, why should we be surprised that Jesus was represented through an angel, if he was represented not only through a man but also through an animal? For who was that ram caught by its horns in the thicket except Christ crucified, or even crowned with thorns? Abraham sacrificed this ram in place of his son, whom he had been commanded to spare (Genesis 22:6–13). God therefore commanded that the man be spared, while nevertheless, [Col. 0811] through an animal, on account of Christ’s passion—which was foretold in that manner—the mystery of the sacred blood was fulfilled.

If, then, you think that Christ was the angel who wrestled with Jacob literally, and not figuratively, you can also say that the ram whom the patriarch Abraham sacrificed was Christ literally, and not figuratively. Finally, you can say that Christ was literally, and not figuratively, the rock which, when struck with wood, poured out abundant drink for the thirsty people (Exodus 17:6). For the Apostle says:

> “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” (1 Corinthians 10:4)

These figures were not the realities themselves; rather, through the figures that preceded them, the realities that were to come were signified. These figures were presented to mortal eyes through a creature subject to God, especially through the ministry of angels: God’s power was at work, but his nature remained concealed—whether it was the Father’s, the Son’s, or the Holy Spirit’s.

### 10

You therefore assert in vain that the Son of God was seen by human beings, whereas the Father was not seen. For through a creature subject to him the Father could be seen, as could the Son and the Holy Spirit; but in their own substance none of them was seen.

God, therefore, was signified rather than displayed, in accordance with the weakness of human senses. He was not seen as he is; for this is promised to the saints in the life to come. Thus the Apostle John says:

> “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” (1 John 3:2)

The Apostles, then, also saw the Lord in this world; they saw him, but not as he is. Finally, Moses desired that he be shown to him, although Scripture says that he spoke with him face to face (Exodus 33:13, 11). When I had said this earlier in my discussion, you passed over it as though you had not heard it, even though I had wished the whole of that same discussion to be read aloud to you from the tablets.

Failing to distinguish between seeing God through his substance and seeing God through a creature subject to him, you fell into such great blasphemy that you said that the only-begotten Son of God was mutable precisely in that he is God. You thought that what was written, “I am who I am, and I have not changed,” must be attributed to the Father alone—as though the Son or the Holy Spirit had changed when he appeared visibly, or as though the one who was certainly born from a woman had changed, or the one who showed himself to human eyes in the form of a dove or in fiery tongues.

I have already answered you on this point in the discussion in which I showed that you had not refuted what I said. Now, however, so that you may understand how God said, “I am who I am, and I have not changed,” or, as it is more fully found written, “For I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Exodus 3:14; Malachi 3:6)—since it was not the Father alone but the one God, who is the Trinity itself, who said this—consider the Psalm where we read:

> “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you shall remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment. You will change them like a covering, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail.” (Psalm 101:26–28)

[Col. 0812] Holy Scripture testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews that this was said of the Son of God (Hebrews 1:10–12). Who, then, does not understand that where it says, “The heavens shall be changed, but you are the same,” nothing else is meant than, “You do not change”?

Therefore it is also fitting for the Son of God to say, “I am who I am, and I have not changed,” or, “For I am the Lord, and I do not change.” You assigned this to the Father alone so that the Son might be believed to be mutable in his substance—as though he had assumed a human being in such a way that he was changed into a human being.

You will not correct this great blasphemy unless you believe that, in the assumption of humanity, something that was not there was added to the Son, while what was there neither departed nor failed.

### 11

Next I ask: who appeared to Moses in the fire when the bush was burning without being consumed? Scripture itself declares that an angel appeared there also, saying:

> “The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the bush.”

Who would doubt that God was in the angel? But which God was it—the Father or the Son?

You will say, “The Son,” for you do not wish the Father to have appeared in any way to mortal eyes, even through a creature subject to him. But whichever of the two you choose, I answer with respect to both.

If it was the Father, then the Father also appeared to human beings. If it was the Son, then the Son did not change. For when Moses asked who it was that was sending him, he replied:

> “I am who I am.”

What else does this mean than, “I am not mutable,” just as you yourself cited the prophetic testimony, “I am who I am, and I have not changed”?

Again he said to Moses:

> “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” (Exodus 3:2, 14, 6, 15)

Dare, if you can, to deny that the Father is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, if it was not he but the Son who was speaking from the bush. If it was the Father, then confess also that the Father was seen by human beings.

But if both are the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—which you acknowledge to be so—why do you hesitate to say that both are the one God? For Jacob himself is Israel, whose children are told:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.” (Deuteronomy 6:4)

### 12

Recognize, therefore, that what I said is true: divinity appeared to mortal eyes not through its own substance, in which it is invisible and immutable, but through a creature subject to it, whenever it willed to appear.

I did not say—although you wished to understand or represent my words in this way—that divinity had shown itself to the fathers [Note: [Col. 0812] Several manuscripts read “of the Father.”] as though I wanted it to be believed visible, after I had previously said that it was invisible. Rather, I said that, when divinity showed itself to the fathers, it made itself visible through a creature subject to it.

For through its own nature it is so completely invisible that Moses himself said to the one with whom Scripture says he spoke face to face:

> “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself openly.” (Exodus 33:11, 13)

There is what I said. Read it again, and you will find that I speak the truth; but you either did not wish or were not able to understand what I said.

Listen, then, to my explanation of the very same matter in somewhat plainer terms. I say that the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is invisible to mortal eyes in its own nature and substance. But that it changes itself into visible [Col. 0813] forms—far be it from me to say this, since I also say that it is immutable.

It remains, therefore, that whenever it showed itself to human eyes as it willed, it did so through a creature subject to it, which can appear to mortal eyes.

### 13

But what is this that, after you had said concerning the Father, “He alone is invisible”—a matter that has now been sufficiently discussed—you added, “He alone is uncontainable and immeasurable”?

We do not, indeed, read that God is uncontainable. Why you should call him uncontainable, I do not know. For if he cannot be contained, how do not only the Son but also the Father come to a human being, as the Son himself says, and make their dwelling with him (John 14:23)? I suppose that the one with whom they make their dwelling contains them.

Or perhaps you say that they are contained not wholly but in part? Say whatever you wish; the answer to you is: then they are not uncontainable, since they can be contained at least in part.

Or is it not enough for you to call him uncontainable, so that you added “and immeasurable” in order to explain the extent to which you called him incomprehensible—that is, because human nature cannot contain the whole of him, he is immeasurable?

But this can also be said of the Son. No one, after all, contains the only-begotten Word in such a way that he would dare to claim that he contains him in every respect. We certainly do not doubt that he too is immeasurable.

For I ask you: of whom do you understand it to be written:

> “He is great and has no end; exalted and immeasurable”?

For shortly afterward it says of him:

> “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings.” (Baruch 3:26, 36–38)

Who is this? Answer me. Who is he, I ask, who is great and has no end, exalted and immeasurable, who appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings?

I see what agitation and distress you are suffering. You fear saying, “It is the Father,” when you hear, “He appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings.” For you insist that the Father, invisible in his substance, was not seen by human beings even through a creature subject to him.

You fear saying, “It is the Son,” when you hear, “He has no end, exalted and immeasurable.” For you contend that only the Father is immeasurable.

You fear saying, “It is the Holy Spirit,” when you hear, “This is our God.” For you do not even wish the Holy Spirit to be God.

What will you do, what will you answer, you who do not wish to be catholic? What will you do, what will you answer, you who do not wish to be catholic, if you do not receive Christ as seen upon the earth and living among human beings in the form of a servant, while nevertheless confessing him to be immeasurable in the form of God, in which he remained invisible.

> “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him.”

Who is the other, except the Antichrist, whom true faith does not reckon as the true Christ, but whom the detestable error of the Jews awaits as the true Christ?

### 14

If you pray and ask, as you say, to be a disciple of the divine Scriptures, consider the divine testimonies relevant to the matter. Do not wander through many passages that help you nothing. Choose wisely to remain silent rather than speak emptily when you cannot find an answer to the clearest truth.

You show that you fear being exposed [Col. 0814] naked before your disciples. Would that you were so clothed with Christ that you would wish your disciples to be his disciples rather than yours. For my part, insofar as the Lord grants me the ability, I do not regret laboring so that you and your disciples may be fellow disciples with me under one teacher.

As for my treatise, to which even after so long a time you promise that you will reply: if you are going to reply to it as you have just replied, whether to my questions or to my discussions, you will not really answer anything; but, so as to deceive in some fashion those who do not understand, you will not remain silent.

From all these matters, therefore, which I have discussed as best I could, it is sufficiently clear that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit possess one power, one substance, one divinity, one majesty, and one glory; for the Trinity itself is our one Lord God, concerning whom it was said:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.” (Deuteronomy 6:4)

This was said when the Lord alone was leading them, and there was no foreign god among them. For Christ too was leading them, since the Apostle says:

> “Nor let us test Christ, as some of them tested him.” (1 Corinthians 10:9) [Note: [Col. 0814] The printed editions read “whom Christ”; the manuscripts, more correctly, read “or Christ.”]

Either Christ is not God, or Christ is a foreign god.

This, then, is the God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the Trinity, one God. We are commanded to serve this one God with the service owed to God alone, when we hear:

> “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” (Deuteronomy 6:13)

For we do not fail to serve Christ with this service, whose members we are; nor do we fail to serve the Holy Spirit, whose temple we are.

This Trinity, one God, says:

> “I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me.” (Deuteronomy 32:39)

For Christ is not thereby excluded from being Lord, whom you too confess to be God and Lord; nor is the Holy Spirit not Lord of his own house, that is, of his temple. He is the Spirit of the Lord, of whom it is said:

> “The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” (2 Corinthians 3:17)

This is the Trinity, one God, of whom the Apostle says:

> “There is no God except one.” (1 Corinthians 8:4)

For when you hear these things, you do not dare to deny that the only-begotten is God.

This God, the Trinity, says:

> “I am who I am, and I have not changed.” (Exodus 3:14; Malachi 3:6)

Christ has not changed, to whom it is said:

> “You will change the heavens, and they will be changed; but you are the same.” (Psalm 101:27–28)

Nor will the Spirit of truth change, since he is immutable truth. Christ himself gives him such great honor that he says:

> “It is expedient for you that I go away; for unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you.” (John 16:7)

And:

> “Whoever speaks blasphemy against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.” (Matthew 12:32)

And when he said of himself:

> “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” (Matthew 28:20)

he said of the Holy Spirit:

> “That he may be with you forever.” (John 14:16)

If you peacefully accept these and similar testimonies—which would take too long to seek out and collect in their entirety—you will be, as you say you pray and desire to be, a disciple of the divine Scriptures, so that we may rejoice in your brotherhood.

## [On the Trinity]

[Col. 0815]

## Preface to the Books on the Trinity

[Col. 0815]

Augustine kept his lengthy work on the Trinity in hand for many years. As he himself writes to Aurelius, he began it when young and published it when old. He readily interrupted it whenever he had to undertake another work that he thought would benefit more people, considering this work more laborious and less useful than most others, since it contained matters less necessary and intelligible to fewer readers.

He undertook this labor especially for the benefit of those who did not accept the authority of faith and wished the truth of the mysteries to be demonstrated to them by reason. For as the holy man, in Book 1, chapter 3, declares that he was especially devoted to meditation on sacred matters, and as he discovered more and deeper things each day through divine illumination, charity did not permit him to deny to others what he had received through God’s gift.

He hoped, therefore, that by ministering to others what they might read, he himself would also make progress; and, wishing to answer others who asked questions, that he too might find what he was seeking. “Therefore,” he says (Book 1, chapter 5), “with the command and help of the Lord our God, I have undertaken this work, not so much to discuss known things with authority as to come to know them by discussing them piously.”

At the beginning of Book 3 he testifies that he would gladly have suppressed his writing if works of this kind had been found in Latin already explained, or if the Greeks who had treated these matters had been translated into Latin, or finally if others had been willing to undertake the task of answering the questions proposed to him—which, he says, in view of the position I hold in Christ’s service, I must endure.

He treats his subject, together with the various questions and difficulties proposed concerning it, in the following order.

**I.** In Book I he demonstrates from Scripture the unity and equality of the supreme Trinity. He shows how the testimonies that are wrongly brought forward against the Son’s equality are to be interpreted according to the catholic faith.

**II.** He asserts the same equality of the Trinity, proving that nothing said in Scripture about the Son’s mission, about the Holy Spirit’s mission, or about God’s various appearances stands in its way. For the whole Trinity, immutable in its nature, invisible, and present everywhere, works inseparably in every mission or appearance.

**III.** He asks whether, in the aforementioned appearances of God, only a corporeal creature was formed through which God might be shown to human eyes; or whether angels who already existed were sent in such a way that they spoke in the person of God, either through a bodily appearance assumed from a corporeal creature or through their own bodies transformed into whatever forms they wished—so that the essence of God itself was never seen by itself.

**IV.** He teaches for what purpose the Son of God was sent. In addition, although the Son of God was made lesser by his mission, he is not lesser because the Father sent him; nor is the Holy Spirit lesser because both the Father and the Son sent him.

**V.** He proceeds to refute those arguments of the heretics which they now produce not from the divine books but from their own reasoning. First he refutes their objection that, since begetting and being begotten, or being begotten and being unbegotten, are different, the substances must be different, showing that these terms are said of God not according to substance but relationally.

**VI.** To those who argue against the Son’s equality on the ground that Christ was called by the Apostle the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, he proposes the question whether the Father himself is not also wisdom. He postpones the solution of this question for a time, while continuing to prove the unity and equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and that God ought to be called and believed not as three Gods but as the Trinity. He then explains Hilary’s statement: “Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift.”

**VII.** He resolves the question that had been postponed and teaches that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one power and one wisdom, just as they are one God and one essence. He then asks how the Latins say “one essence, three persons,” while the Greeks say “one essence, three substances or hypostases.”

**VIII.** Having also supplied a rational explanation, he shows that not only is the Father not greater than the Son, but that the two together are not something greater than the Holy Spirit; nor are any two together in the same Trinity something greater than one; nor are all three together something greater than each individually. He advises that God’s nature be understood through the apprehension of truth, knowledge of the highest good, and innate love of justice; and especially that knowledge of him be sought through charity, in which he observes three elements, as it were a trace of the Trinity.

**IX.** He teaches that a certain trinity is found in human beings, who are the image of God: the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves both itself and its knowledge. These three are equal to one another and of one essence.
