**X.** He finds a more evident trinity in the human mind: memory, understanding, and will.

**XI.** He also detects certain traces of the Trinity in the outer human being, as in bodily vision.

[Col. 0817]

**XII.** Having first distinguished wisdom from knowledge, he shows that a certain trinity exists in what is properly called knowledge. Although this already belongs to the inner human being, it should not yet be called the image of God.

**XIII.** He explains the trinity found in knowledge through a commendation of the Christian faith.

**XIV.** He speaks of the true wisdom of human beings—namely, that by which a person remembers, understands, and loves God. He shows that in this very respect the human being is the image of God according to the mind. This image is renewed here in the knowledge of God, but then the likeness to God in that image will be perfect, when the vision of God is perfect.

**XV.** He gathers into a brief discourse whatever he explained above. Finally, he shows that the Trinity, in whose perfect vision blessed life is promised to us, is here seen by us “through a mirror and in a riddle,” insofar as it is seen through the image of God that we are.

Augustine places these books in the *Retractations* among the shorter works written around the year of Christ 400, because he began them at that time. In Letter 120, sent to Consentius in 410, section 13, he mentions a work on the Trinity that he had in hand but had not yet been able to complete because of the excellence and difficulty of its subject. In Letter 162, to Evodius, which belongs to the year 414, he writes in section 2 that he had not yet published the books on the Trinity. In Letter 169, also to him, written toward the end of 415, he testifies in section 1 that he had not yet completed them.

From Letter 143, sent to Marcellinus toward the end of 412, it may be understood (section 4) that friends had demanded that he publish these books, while he had kept them back longer than they wished or could tolerate. Hence one may infer that the first publication, which took place before the work was complete, did not precede the year 412.

It is clear, however, that the second publication took place only much later, since in Book 13 he cites what he had written in Book 12 of *The City of God*, which was not completed before 416. In Book 15 he cites Treatise 90 on John. Prosper refers to this work in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8, believing that it was already available in Gaul.

Cassiodorus the senator, in *Institutions*, chapter 16, praises the fifteen books which Augustine wrote on the holy Trinity with marvelous profundity and which are to be meditated upon with attentive intellectual effort.

The monk Maximus Planudes, who lived under the elder Andronicus, around the year 1350, translated these books from Latin into Greek. Demetrius Cydonius, under John Cantacuzenus, translated several chapters from Augustine’s discourses. Possevinus testifies in his *Apparatus* that these translations are preserved at Rome in the Vatican Library.

We saw the catalogue of the Greek manuscripts of the Vatican Library, which is in the possession of the distinguished scholar Antonio Faure, Doctor of Theology in Paris, and a similar catalogue in Codex 5125 of the Colbert Library. In them the following entries are found:

> “The fifteen books on the Trinity of the most blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, which the wisest and most honored of monks, Maximus Planudes, translated from the Latin language into Greek.”

And also:

> “Demetrius Cydonius translated from the Latin language into Greek certain chapters taken from the discourses of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo.”

See Allatius, Book 2 of *On the Agreement of the Two Churches*, chapter 17, section 4.

## Augustine’s Letter to Aurelius

To the most blessed Lord and most sincerely revered in charity, the holy brother and fellow priest, Pope Aurelius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

I began these books on the Trinity, which is the supreme and true God, when I was young and published them when I was old. I had set the work aside after I discovered that they had been taken or stolen from me before I had completed and revised them, polishing them as I had intended.

For I had decided to publish them all together, not individually, because the later investigations are linked to the earlier ones as the inquiry advances. Since, however, my plan could not be fulfilled because these books were able to reach certain people before I wished them to, I abandoned the interrupted dictation, thinking that I would complain of this very matter in some of my writings, so that those who could understand might know that the books had not been published by me but had been taken away before they seemed worthy of publication in my edition.

Nevertheless, compelled by the most urgent requests of many brothers, and especially by your command, I have taken care, with the Lord’s help, to complete this work, which was so laborious. I have sent the books, corrected not as I wished but as I was able, so that they would not differ too greatly from those already stolen and circulated among people, to Your Reverence through our beloved son, the subdeacon. I have permitted anyone who wishes to hear, copy, or read them to do so.

If my plan could have been preserved in them, they would certainly have had the same ideas but would have been much more thoroughly worked out and clearer, as far as the difficulty of explaining such great matters and our ability would have allowed.

There are copies that contain the first four, or rather even the first five, books without their prefaces, and Book 12 without a substantial final portion. But if this edition becomes known to them, they will correct everything, if they wish and are able.

I ask that you order this letter to be placed separately, but nevertheless at the beginning of those same books.

Farewell. Pray for me.

[Col. 0819]

## The Fifteen Books of the Trinity of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo

[Note: [Col. 0819] Begun around the year 400, completed around the year 416.]

[Note: [Col. 0817] On the books on the Trinity, see Book 2, chapter 15, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 635, from the words “The books on the Trinity,” section 1, through the words “We discuss the Trinity,” section 3, column 636. M.]

[Note: [Col. 0819] The fifteen books on the Trinity were carefully collated and corrected against thirty Gallican manuscripts: the Tours manuscript of the Church of Saint Gratian; two from the Abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres; the manuscript from the Abbey of Saint Albin at Angers; two from Laon, namely from the major church and from Saint Vincent; three from Reims, one from the cathedral and two from the Church of Saint Remigius; and the manuscripts of Thérouanne, Saint-Bénigne, Fleury, Vendôme, Saint-Michel, Pratellis, Bec, Lyre, Germain-des-Prés, Cîteaux, Bigot, three from the College of Navarre, five from the Sorbonne, one from the Dominican Grand Convent of Paris, and one from the Augustinian Grand Convent; eleven Vatican manuscripts; five Belgian readings preserved at Leuven; and finally the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and the theologians of Leuven.]

[Note: [Col. 0819] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

# Book One

In this book the unity and supreme equality of the Trinity are demonstrated according to the sacred Scriptures, and certain passages brought forward against the Son’s equality are refuted.

## Chapter One

[Col. 0819]

### 1. He writes against those who abuse reason and slander faith in the Trinity. The error of those who discuss God arises from three causes. Holy Scripture, removing falsehoods, gradually raises the mind to divine things. True immortality. We are nourished by faith so that we may become capable of grasping divine things.

Those who are going to read this discussion of the Trinity must first understand that our writing is directed against the slanders of those who despise the beginning supplied by faith and are deceived by an immature and perverse love of reason.

Some of these people attempt to transfer to incorporeal and spiritual realities what they know through bodily things—either what they have learned by experience through the bodily senses [Note: [Col. 0819] Nineteen manuscripts read “have observed.”], or what they have grasped through the nature of human ingenuity and the vigor of diligence, with the assistance of art—so that they wish to measure and form opinions about those realities on the basis of these things.

There are also others who think about God according to the nature or feeling of the human mind, if indeed they think anything about him; and from this error, when they discuss God, they establish distorted and deceptive rules in their speech. [Note: [Col. 0819] Five manuscripts read *figunt*, “they establish”; the printed editions read *fingunt*, “they invent.”] [Note: [Col. 0819] Two Vatican manuscripts read *sermone*, “in speech,” instead of *sermoni*, “for their speech.”]

There is also another class of people: those who indeed strive to transcend the whole of creation, which is certainly mutable, so that they may raise their attention to the immutable substance that is God. But weighed down by the burden of mortality, while wishing to appear to know what they do not know and being unable to know what they wish to know, they block the paths to understanding for themselves by asserting their speculative opinions with excessive boldness. They prefer not to correct a perverse judgment of their own rather than change one that they have defended.

This is the disease common to all three classes that I have described: those who think about God according to the body; those who think about him according to a spiritual creature, such as the soul; and those who think falsely about God according to neither body nor spiritual creature. They are farther from the truth because what they think is found neither in the body, nor in a created and fashioned spirit, nor in the Creator himself.

For example, someone who thinks that God is white or ruddy is mistaken; nevertheless, these qualities are found in a body. Again, someone who thinks that God sometimes forgets and sometimes remembers, or anything similar, is likewise in error; nevertheless, these things are found in the mind. But someone who thinks that God has such power that he generated himself errs still more, because not only is God not such, but neither is any spiritual or bodily creature. For absolutely nothing exists that generates itself in order to exist.

### 2. Scripture uses language drawn from every kind of thing in order to raise the mind gradually to divine realities. True immortality belongs to God alone.

In order, then, that the human mind might be cleansed of such falsehoods, holy Scripture, accommodating itself to little ones, avoided no class of words. Through these words our intellect might, as it were, rise gradually, nourished toward divine and sublime realities.

It used words taken from bodily things when it spoke about God, as when it said:

> “Protect me in the shelter of your wings.” (Psalm 16:8)

It also transferred many things from spiritual creation to signify something that was not actually so but needed to be spoken of in that way, as in:

> “I am God who am jealous.” (Exodus 20:5)

And:

> “It repents me that I made humankind.” (Genesis 6:7)

But from things that do not exist at all, it did not derive terms with which it might either construct figurative expressions or thicken its riddles. [Note: [Col. 0821] The printed editions read *spiraret*, “might breathe forth”; most manuscripts read *spissaret*, “might thicken.”]

Hence those who are cut off from the truth by that third kind of error vanish away more dangerously and emptily, imagining about God something that can be found neither in him nor in any creature.

For with things found in creation, divine Scripture is accustomed to fashion, as it were, childish amusements, through which the disposition of the weak might be moved according to its capacity, like steps, toward seeking higher things and abandoning lower ones.

But Scripture rarely uses expressions that properly concern God and are found in no creature, such as what was said to Moses:

> “I am who I am,”

and:

> “He who is has sent me to you.” (Exodus 3:14)

Since a body and a mind are also said to exist in some manner, Scripture would not have said this unless it wished the words to be understood in a manner proper to God.

Likewise, when the Apostle says:

> “Who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16),

although the soul too is said, and is, in a certain sense, immortal, he would not have said “alone possesses” unless true immortality were immutability, which no creature can possess, since it belongs to the Creator alone.

James says the same:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.” (James 1:17)

David says the same:

> “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same.” (Psalm 101:27–28)

3. Therefore, to contemplate and fully know the substance of God, which makes mutable things without undergoing any change in itself and creates temporal things without any temporal movement of its own, is difficult. Hence the purification of our mind is necessary, so that what is ineffable may be seen in an ineffable manner. Since we do not yet possess this purification, we are nourished by faith and led along paths that are more bearable, so that we may become suited and capable of grasping it.

Thus the Apostle says that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3). Yet, although they had already been reborn by his grace, he commended Christ to those who were still carnal and natural, like little children in Christ—not from the divine power by which he is equal to the Father, but from the human weakness in which he was crucified. For he says: “For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” Then he continues: “And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling” (1 Cor. 2:2–3). A little later he says to them: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able” (ibid. 3:1–2).

When this is said to certain people, they become angry and think that it has been said insultingly to them. Often they would rather believe that those who say this have nothing to say than admit that they are unable to grasp what has been said. Sometimes we offer them an explanation—not the one they seek when they inquire about God, since neither are they able to receive it nor perhaps are we able either to grasp or express it, but an explanation showing them how unprepared and wholly unfit they are to understand what they demand. Yet because they do not hear what they want, they either think that we are acting craftily to conceal our ignorance or maliciously withholding our knowledge from them; [Col. 0822] and so they depart angry and disturbed.

## CHAPTER II

### 4. How the doctrine of the Trinity is to be discussed in this work

Therefore, with the help of the Lord our God, we shall undertake, as far as we can, to provide the very explanation they demand: that the Trinity is one and only one true God, and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are rightly said, believed, and understood to be of one and the same substance or essence. Thus they will not be mocked by what they regard as our excuses, but will actually discover both that this supreme good is seen by the purest minds and that it cannot therefore be seen and grasped by them because the sight of the human mind is too weak to remain fixed upon so great a light unless it is nourished and strengthened by the righteousness of faith.

First, however, it must be demonstrated, according to the authority of the holy Scriptures, whether the faith is in fact as we have stated. Then, if God wills and helps us, we shall perhaps serve these talkative reasoners—more elevated than capable, and therefore afflicted with a more dangerous disease—in such a way that they may find something about which they cannot doubt. Consequently, concerning what they have been unable to discover, they will complain of their own minds rather than of the truth itself or of our arguments.

In this way, if they possess any love or fear toward God, they may return to the beginning and order of faith, now perceiving how salutary is the medicine of the faithful established in the holy Church: observant piety keeps the weak mind attentive to the perception of immutable truth, lest reckless disorder plunge it into an opinion of harmful falsehood. I shall not be reluctant to inquire wherever I am uncertain, nor ashamed to learn wherever I am in error.

## CHAPTER III

### 5. What Augustine asks of his readers; errors of slower readers are not to be attributed to the author

Therefore, whoever reads this, where he is equally certain, should proceed with me; where he is equally uncertain, should inquire with me; where he recognizes his own error, should return to me; and where he recognizes mine, should recall me from it. Let us enter together the way of charity, making our way toward him of whom it is said: “Seek his face continually” (Ps. 104:4).

I have entered into this devout and safe agreement before the Lord our God with all who read what I write, and in all my writings—especially in those where the unity of the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is sought—because nowhere is error more dangerous, nothing is sought with greater difficulty, and nothing is found with greater fruitfulness.

[Note: In Lovaniensis, *interim* (“meanwhile”); other manuscripts have *inierim* (“I have entered into”).]

[Note: Thus more than twenty manuscripts. The printed editions have *Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus* (“the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit”).]

Whoever, then, says while reading, “This has not been well said, because I do not understand it,” is criticizing my manner of expression, not my faith; and perhaps it could truly have been stated more clearly. Nevertheless, no human being has spoken in such a way that everyone understood everything.

Let the person who is displeased with this in my speech therefore consider whether, when he does not understand me, he understands others who are engaged in such matters and questions. If so, let him set aside my book—or even throw it away, if he thinks that best—and devote his effort and time instead to those whom he understands. Yet he should not therefore think that I ought to have remained silent because I could not express myself as readily and clearly as those whom he understands. Not everything written by everyone comes into everyone’s hands. It may happen that some who are able to understand even these writings of ours do not find those clearer books, and at least happen upon these.

It is therefore useful for many works to be produced by many people, in different styles but with the same faith, even on the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach a greater number—one way to some, another way to others. [Col. 0823]

But if the person who complains that he has not understood these matters has never been able to understand anything carefully and incisively argued about such subjects, let him deal with himself through prayers and study, so that he may make progress, rather than with me through complaints and abuse, so that I may be silent.

Whoever, however, says while reading, “I do understand what has been said, but it is not true,” should, if he wishes, assert his own position and refute mine, if he can.

[Note: Sixteen manuscripts have *asserat ut placet* (“let him assert it, if he wishes”).]

If he does this with charity and truth, and takes care to make me recognize it also—if I remain in this life—

[Note: The printed editions have *si dum in hac vita maneo* (“if, while I remain in this life”). *Dum* is absent from the manuscripts.]

—I shall reap abundant fruit from this labor of mine. If he cannot do this for me, let him do it for those who can, with my willing and glad consent.

For my part, I meditate on the law of the Lord, if not day and night (Ps. 1:2), at least during such portions of time as I can; and I bind my meditations to writing, lest they escape through forgetfulness. I hope from God’s mercy that he will make me persevere in all truths that are certain to me; but if I think otherwise about anything, he will also reveal that to me (Phil. 3:15), whether through hidden inspirations and admonitions, through his manifest utterances, or through conversations with the brethren.

This I ask, and this is the desire I have entrusted to him, who is fully able to guard what he has given me and to restore what he has promised.

### 6. Slower readers may misunderstand Augustine’s meaning

I believe, indeed, that some slower readers will suppose in certain passages of my books that I have thought what I did not think, or have not thought what I did think. Who does not know that their error ought not to be attributed to me if, following me as though they were following a guide but failing to grasp me, they have strayed into some falsehood while I am forced to cut a path through dense and obscure places?

For no one would rightly attribute the many and various errors of heretics to the sacred authorities of the divine Books themselves, although all heretics strive to defend their false and deceptive opinions from those same Scriptures.

The law of Christ—that is, charity—clearly admonishes me and commands me with most gracious authority that, when people suppose I have thought something false in my books which I did not think, and that same falsehood displeases one person but pleases another, I should prefer to be criticized by the critic of falsehood rather than praised by its admirer. For although I am wrongly criticized by the former, since I did not hold this view, the error itself is rightly condemned. By the latter, however, neither am I rightly praised—since he thinks I held what the truth condemns—nor is the opinion itself rightly praised, since the truth condemns it.

Therefore, in the name of the Lord, let us undertake the work we have begun.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0824]

### 7. What the Catholic faith teaches concerning the Trinity

All the Catholic interpreters of the old and new divine Books whom I have been able to read, who wrote before me about the Trinity, which is God, have intended to teach, in accordance with the Scriptures, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit signify the divine unity through the inseparable equality of one and the same substance. Therefore they are not three gods, but one God.

Although the Father begot the Son, and therefore the Son is not the Father; and although the Son was begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the Son; and although the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, he too is coequal with the Father and the Son and belongs to the unity of the Trinity.

Nevertheless, it was not this same Trinity that was born of the Virgin Mary, was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven, but only the Son. Nor was this same Trinity that descended in the form of a dove upon Jesus after he had been baptized (Matt. 3:16); nor, on the day of Pentecost after the Lord’s ascension, when a sound came from heaven as of a mighty rushing wind, did this same Trinity sit upon each of them in divided tongues as of fire, but only the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:2–4).

Nor was it this same Trinity that spoke from heaven, “You are my Son” (Mark 1:11), either when he was baptized by John or on the mountain when three disciples were with him (Matt. 17:5); nor when the voice sounded, saying, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12:28). It was only the voice of the Father addressed to the Son, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, likewise work inseparably.

This is also my faith, since this is the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER V

### 8. Difficulties concerning the Trinity: how the three are one God, and how, while working inseparably, they perform certain acts without one another

Some people are troubled by this when they hear of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, and yet hear that this Trinity is not three gods but one God. They ask how they are to understand this, especially when it is said that the Trinity works inseparably in everything God does, while nevertheless a certain voice sounded which was the Father’s and not the Son’s; and in the flesh it was only the Son who was born, suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven; while in the form of a dove it was only the Holy Spirit who came.

They want to understand how the Trinity made that voice, which belonged only to the Father; how that flesh, in which only the Son was born of the Virgin, was created by the same Trinity; and how that form of a dove, in which only the Holy Spirit appeared, was produced by that same Trinity.

Otherwise the Trinity does not work inseparably, but the Father does some things, the Son others, and the Holy Spirit others; or, if they do some things together and some things separately, the Trinity is no longer inseparable.

They are also troubled about how the Holy Spirit belongs to the Trinity, since neither the Father nor the Son, nor both together, begot him, although he is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son.

Since people ask these questions, and they weary us, let us explain to them, as we are able, whatever our weakness understands here by God’s gift, “and let us not faint on the way through envy” (Wis. 6:25).

If we say that we do not usually think about such matters, we lie. But if we admit that these matters dwell in our thoughts, since we are carried along by our love of investigating the truth, they rightly demand, in the spirit of charity, that we tell them what we have been able to devise.

This is not because I have already received the answer or am perfect. For if the Apostle Paul did not consider that he had already grasped it, how much less should I, lying far beneath his feet? Rather, according to my measure, if I forget what lies behind, stretch forward to what lies ahead, and pursue the goal according to my intention, toward the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. 3:12–14), I desire to disclose how far I have traveled along this same way, where I have arrived, and how much of the remaining journey is left for me to complete. I desire this for those who desire it of me, whom free charity compels me to serve.

It is necessary—and God will grant it—that, while ministering to them what they may read, I myself should also make progress; and, desiring to answer those who ask, I myself should also find what I was seeking.

Therefore, at the command and with the help of the Lord our God, I have undertaken these matters—not so much to discuss what is already known with authority as to come to know it by discussing it with piety.

## CHAPTER VI

### 9. The Son is true God, of the same substance as the Father; not only the Father but the Trinity is called immortal; all things are not from the Father alone but also from the Son; the Holy Spirit is true God, equal to the Father and the Son

Those who have said that our Lord Jesus Christ is not God, or is not true God, or is not one and only one God with the Father, or is not truly immortal because he is mutable, have been refuted by the clearest testimonies of the divine Scriptures and by their harmonious voice. Among these are the following:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

It is clear that we understand this Word of God to be the only Son of God, of whom he later says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” referring to his incarnate birth, which took place in time from the Virgin.

Here he declares not only that the Word is God, but also that he is of the same substance as the Father. For after saying, “And the Word was God,” he continues: “He was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1, 14, 2–3).

He does not say “all things” except those that were made—that is, the whole creation. It is therefore plainly evident that he himself was not made through whom all things were made. If he was not made, he is not a creature; and if he is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father. For every substance that is not God is a creature, and what is not a creature is God.

If the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, then he is a made substance. If he is a made substance, not all things were made through him. But all things were made through him. Therefore he is of one and the same substance as the Father. Consequently, he is not merely God but true God.

The same John says this most clearly in his Epistle: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

[Col. 0826]

### 10. “Who alone has immortality” refers not only to the Father but to the one God, the Trinity

From this it follows that the Apostle Paul did not say, “Who alone has immortality,” only of the Father, but of the one and only God, who is the Trinity itself.

For eternal life itself is not mortal according to any mutability. Accordingly, since the Son of God is eternal life, he too is understood with the Father where it is said, “Who alone has immortality.” We too, having become participants in that eternal life, are made immortal according to our measure.

But the eternal life of which we become participants is one thing, and we, who live forever through participation in it, are another.

Even if he had said, “Whom the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, will display at the proper times, who alone has immortality,” the Son should not for that reason be understood as separated from him.

For the Son himself, speaking elsewhere in the voice of Wisdom—for he is the Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24)—says, “Alone I traversed the circuit of heaven” (Sirach 24:8); yet he did not separate the Father from himself. How much less, then, is it necessary to understand the statement “Who alone has immortality” as referring only to the Father apart from the Son, when the passage says:

“Keep the commandment without stain, irreproachable, until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, will display at the proper times; he alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see; to him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen” (1 Tim. 6:14–16).

In these words the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not specifically named. Rather, “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords” is the one and only true God, the Trinity itself.

### 11. “Whom no human being has seen” does not exclude Christ according to his divinity

Perhaps what follows will disturb this understanding, because he says, “Whom no human being has seen or can see.” Yet this too may be understood as applying to Christ according to his divinity, which the Jews did not see, although they saw and crucified his flesh.

Divinity cannot in any way be seen by human sight. It is seen by that sight through which those who see are no longer human beings but something beyond human beings.

The blessed and only Sovereign is therefore rightly understood as the God of the Trinity, who displays the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ at the proper times.

The statement “He alone has immortality” is like the statement, “He alone works wonders” (Ps. 71:18). I should like to know of whom they understand this to be said. If of the Father alone, how is it true that the Son himself says, “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise”?

Is anything among wonders more wondrous than raising and giving life to the dead? Yet the same Son says: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whomever he wishes” (John 5:19, 21).

How, then, does the Father alone work wonders, when these words allow us to understand neither the Father alone nor the Son alone, but rather the one true God alone—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

[Col. 0827]

### 12. All things are from the Father, through the Son, and in the Holy Spirit

Likewise, when the same Apostle says, “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we are for him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we are through him” (1 Cor. 8:6), who could doubt that he means all created things, just as John says, “All things were made through him”?

I therefore ask about whom he speaks elsewhere: “For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

If this is said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that each person is assigned one expression—“from him,” from the Father; “through him,” through the Son; “in him,” in the Holy Spirit—it is clear that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, since he concludes in the singular: “To him be glory forever and ever.”

For when he began this thought, he did not say, “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of the Father,” or “of the Son,” or “of the Holy Spirit,” but “of the wisdom and knowledge of God.” “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:33–36).

But if they wish to understand this of the Father alone, how then are all things through the Father, as it says here, and all things through the Son, as he says to the Corinthians, “And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things,” and as it says in John’s Gospel, “All things were made through him”?

If some things were through the Father and other things through the Son, then not all things were through the Father, nor all things through the Son. But if all things were through the Father and all things were through the Son, the same things were through the Father as through the Son.

The Son, therefore, is equal to the Father, and the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable. For if the Father made the Son, while the Son himself did not make him, then not all things were made through the Son. But all things were made through the Son. Therefore he himself was not made, so that together with the Father he might make all things that were made.

The Apostle has not been silent even about the phrase itself, but has said most plainly: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). Here he specifically calls the Father “God,” just as elsewhere: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3).

### 13. The Holy Spirit is true God, not a creature, and equal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son

Testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit have likewise been collected, and those who before us discussed these matters used them more abundantly, because the Holy Spirit too is God and not a creature.

If he is not a creature, then he is not merely called “god” in the way human beings also have been called gods (Ps. 81:6), but is true God. Therefore he is entirely equal to the Father and the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with them in the unity of the Trinity.

It is especially clear that the Holy Spirit is not a creature in the passage where we are commanded not to serve the creature but the Creator (Rom. 1:25). This is not in the sense in which we are commanded to serve one another through charity (Gal. 5:13), which in Greek is δουλεύειν (*douleuein*), but in the sense in which service is offered to God alone, which in Greek is λατρεύειν (*latreuein*).

Hence idolaters are so called because they offer images the service that is owed to God. It is according to this service that it is said: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13). This distinction is also found more clearly in the Greek Scripture, which has λατρεύσεις (*latreuseis*, “you shall serve”).

But if we are forbidden to serve a creature with this kind of service—for it is said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve”—and if the Apostle condemns those who “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator,” then the Holy Spirit is certainly not a creature, since all the saints offer him this kind of service. The Apostle says: “For we are the circumcision, serving the Spirit of God” (Phil. 3:3), which in Greek is λατρεύοντες (*latreuontes*).

Many Latin manuscripts also have: “who serve the Spirit of God.” All, or almost all, the Greek manuscripts have this reading. In some Latin copies, however, we find not “we serve the Spirit of God,” but “we serve God in spirit.”

[Note: Augustine again reports three readings of this passage in *Against Boniface*, book 3, chapter 7. Ambrose notes in *On the Holy Spirit*, book 2, chapter 6, that the same passage was altered in Latin manuscripts through the fraud of falsifiers.]

But those who err in this and refuse to yield to the more authoritative reading—do they also find the following variation in the manuscripts? “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple within you”—

[Note: The printed editions have: “a temple of him who is in you.” The manuscripts have: “a temple within you.” Augustine consistently quotes it in this form in his earlier books *Against the Sermon of the Arians* and *Against Maximinus*.]

—of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God?

What could be more insane and sacrilegious than for anyone to dare say that the members of Christ are the temple of a creature whom, according to their own view, they regard as inferior to Christ? Elsewhere he says: “Your bodies are members of Christ.”

If, then, those bodies that are members of Christ are the temple of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit is not a creature. For whoever is offered our body as a temple must necessarily be owed that service which is to be offered to God alone, and which in Greek is called λατρεία (*latreia*).

Accordingly he says: “Therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19, 15, 20).

[Note: The printed editions add “and bear him,” but this is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.]

## CHAPTER VII

### 14. How the Son is less than the Father and less than himself

By these and similar testimonies of the divine Scriptures, which, as I said, our predecessors used more extensively to overthrow such accusations and errors of heretics, the unity and equality of the Trinity are commended to our faith.

But because many things in the holy Books are said on account of the incarnation of the Word of God—which took place for our restoration and salvation, so that the man Christ Jesus might be the mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5)—in such a way as to signify or even plainly show that the Father is greater than the Son, people have gone astray by examining or considering the whole sequence of the Scriptures less carefully. They have tried to transfer to Christ’s substance, which was eternal before the incarnation and is eternal still, things said about Christ Jesus according to his humanity.

They say that the Son is less than the Father because it is written, in the Lord’s own words, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

But truth shows that, in this respect, the Son is also less than himself. For how could he not also have been made less than himself, who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”? He did not take the form of a servant in such a way as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father.

If, then, the form of a servant was taken without the form of God being lost, and if the only-begotten Son of God the Father is the same person in both the form of a servant and the form of God—in the form of God equal to the Father, and in the form of a servant the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and human beings—who can fail to understand that in the form of God he is greater even than himself, while in the form of a servant he is less even than himself?

Scripture therefore rightly says both that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The former is understood with reference to the form of God, the latter with reference to the form of a servant, without any confusion.

This rule for resolving the question is drawn for us from one chapter of the Apostle Paul’s Epistle, where this distinction is presented more clearly. He says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:6–7).

The Son of God is therefore equal to God the Father by nature, but less in appearance. In the form of a servant, which he took, he is less than the Father; but in the form of God, which he possessed even before taking the form of a servant, he is equal to the Father.

In the form of God he is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3); in the form of a servant he was made from a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law (Gal. 4:4–5).

Thus, in the form of God he made the human being; in the form of a servant he was made a human being. For if the Father alone, without the Son, had made the human being, it would not have been written, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

Therefore, because the form of God took the form of a servant, he is both God and human being: both God because God is the one who assumed, and both human because a human being was assumed.

For in that taking, neither of the two was changed and transformed into the other. Divinity was not changed into a creature so as to cease to be divinity, nor was the creature changed into divinity so as to cease to be a creature.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 15. Explains passages about the Son’s subjection to the Father, wrongly understood; Christ will not hand the kingdom over to the Father in such a way as to deprive himself of it; the promised contemplation is the end of all actions; the Holy Spirit is sufficient for our blessedness, just as the Father is

As for what the Apostle says, “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him,” this was said either to prevent anyone from thinking that Christ’s form, which was taken from a human creature, would later be transformed into divinity—or, to express the matter more precisely, into the deity, which is not a creature but the incorporeal, immutable, consubstantial, and coeternal unity of the Trinity.

Or, if someone argues—as some have understood it—that the words “the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him” mean that the subjection will be the future transformation and conversion of the creature into the very substance or essence of the Creator, so that what had been the substance of a creature will become the substance of the Creator, then surely he at least concedes what admits of no doubt: this had not yet happened when the Lord said, “The Father is greater than I.”

He said this not only before he ascended into heaven, but even before he suffered and rose from the dead.

Those who think that the human nature in him is to be changed and transformed into the substance of divinity, and that the words “Then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him” mean that then the Son of Man, and the human nature assumed by the Word of God, will be changed into the nature of the one who subjected all things to him, think that this will happen when, after the day of judgment, he hands the kingdom over to God the Father.

According to this view, therefore, the Father is still greater than the form of a servant assumed from the Virgin. If some also assert that the man Christ Jesus has already been changed into the substance of God, they certainly cannot deny that the human nature still remained in him when, before his passion, he said, “The Father is greater than I.”

There can therefore be no doubt that this statement means that the form of a servant is less than the Father, while in the form of God the Son is equal to him.

Nor should anyone, on hearing the Apostle say, “When he says that all things have been subjected to him, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15:28, 24, 27), think that the Father subjected all things to the Son in such a way that the Son himself did not subject all things to himself.

The Apostle shows this in his Epistle to the Philippians: “Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the operation by which he is able also to subject all things to himself” (Phil. 3:20–21).

The operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable. Otherwise the Father himself did not subject all things to himself, but the Son subjected them to the Father, who hands the kingdom over to him and abolishes every principality, authority, and power. These things are said of the Son: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality and every authority and power.” The one who abolishes them is the one who subjects them.

### 16. Christ will not hand the kingdom over to the Father in such a way as to deprive himself of it

Nor should we think that Christ will hand the kingdom over to God the Father in such a way as to deprive himself of it. Some foolish talkers have believed this.

When it is said that he will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father, he is not separated from him, because together with the Father he is one God.

But the word “until” deceives those who are careless about the divine Scriptures and eager for disputes.

The passage continues: “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Cor. 15:24–25), as though, once he has done this, he would no longer reign. They do not understand that this is like the statement: “His heart is established; he will not be moved until he sees his enemies” (Ps. 111:8). He will not, after seeing them, be moved.

What, then, does “When he has handed the kingdom over to God and the Father” mean? Is God the Father not now in possession of the kingdom?

Rather, because he will lead all the righteous—in whom the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, now reigns through their living by faith—to the form which the same Apostle calls “face to face” vision (1 Cor. 13:12), it is said, “When he has handed the kingdom over to God and the Father,” as though it meant, “When he has brought believers to the contemplation of God and the Father.”

For he says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

Then the Father will be revealed by the Son, when he has abolished every principality, authority, and power—that is, when the dispensation of likenesses through angelic principalities, authorities, and powers is no longer necessary.

In the person of these powers it is not inappropriately understood that the Song of Songs says to the bride: “We shall make likenesses of gold for you, with points of silver, until the king is at his reclining place” (Song of Songs 1:11, according to the Septuagint). This means, “Until Christ is in his hidden place,” because “your life is hidden with Christ in God; when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4).

Before this happens, “we now see through a mirror in an enigma,” that is, in likenesses; but then, “face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

17. For this vision is promised to us as the end of all our actions and the eternal perfection of our joys. For we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). What he said to his servant Moses—“I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14)—this we shall contemplate when we live forever. For he says: “Now this is eternal life, that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

This will happen when the Lord comes and “brings to light the things now hidden in darkness” (1 Cor. 4:5), when the darkness of this mortality and corruption has passed away. Then our morning will come, of which the Psalm says: “In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall contemplate” (Ps. 5:5). I understand “when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father” to refer to this contemplation—that is, when he has led the righteous, among whom the mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus, now reigns through those who live by faith, to the contemplation of God and the Father.

If I am foolish here, let the one who understands better correct me; I see no other interpretation. For we shall seek nothing else when we have reached that contemplation, which is not yet ours so long as our joy is in hope. “Now hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25), until “the king is on his couch” (Song 1:12, according to the Septuagint). Then what is written will be fulfilled: “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Ps. 16:11). In that joy nothing further will be sought, because there will be nothing further to seek. For the Father will be shown to us, and he will be sufficient for us.

Philip had understood this well when he said to the Lord, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” But he had not yet understood that he could say the same thing in another way: “Lord, show us yourself, and it is enough for us.” To make him understand this, the Lord answered him: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” But because he wanted Philip to live by faith before he could see that reality, he continued: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:8, 10).

For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord. “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7). Contemplation is the reward of faith, and through faith hearts are cleansed for that reward, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). That hearts are cleansed for this contemplation is proved especially by the saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). And because this is eternal life, God says in the Psalm: “With length of days I shall satisfy him, and I shall show him my salvation” (Ps. 91:16).

Whether, therefore, we hear “Show us the Son” or “Show us the Father,” it means the same thing, because neither can be shown without the other. For they are one, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Finally, because of this inseparability, sometimes the Father alone is named, or the Son alone, as the one who will fill us with joy in his presence.

18. Nor is the Spirit of both—the Spirit of the Father and of the Son—separated from them. This Spirit is properly called the Holy Spirit, “the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive” (John 14:17). For this is our full joy, beyond which there is no greater: to enjoy the triune God, in whose image we were made.

For this reason Scripture sometimes speaks of the Holy Spirit as though he alone were sufficient for our blessedness. And he is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Son. Likewise, the Father alone is sufficient because he cannot be separated from the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the Son alone is sufficient because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

What, then, does he mean when he says: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive” (John 14:15–17)—that is, those who love the world? “For the natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14).

Yet it might still seem that the words “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate” were spoken as though the Son alone were not sufficient. But elsewhere the Spirit is spoken of as though he alone were altogether sufficient: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13). Is the Son, then, separated from this, as though he himself did not teach all truth, or as though the Holy Spirit fulfilled what the Son had been less able to teach?

Let them say, then, if they please, that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son, whom they are accustomed to call less than him. Or do they allow the Son to be believed to teach together with the Spirit because it was not said, “He alone,” or “No one but he will teach you all truth”?

The Apostle, therefore, separated the Son from knowledge of the things belonging to God when he said: “Thus no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11). From this these perverse interpreters could now say that the Spirit alone teaches even the Son the things of God, as though the greater taught the lesser. Yet the Son himself attributed so much to the Spirit that he said: “Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you” (John 16:6–7).

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0833]

### Sometimes all are understood in one person

He said this not because the Word of God and the Holy Spirit are unequal, but because the presence of the Son of Man among them was, as it were, an impediment to the coming of one who was not lesser, since he had not emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, as the Son had (Phil. 2:7). It was therefore necessary that the form of a servant be removed from their eyes; for, looking at it, they thought Christ was nothing more than what they saw.

This is also the meaning of what he said: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). That is: I must go to the Father because, while you see me in this way, you judge from what you see that I am less than the Father. Occupied as you are with the creature and the form I have assumed, you do not understand the equality that I possess with the Father.

This also explains the saying: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20:17). Touching seems to establish the limit of knowledge. Therefore he did not want the final aim of the heart’s attention to rest in him in such a way that what was seen would be regarded as all that he was. His ascent to the Father meant that he should be seen as one who is equal to the Father, so that there the vision sufficient for us might reach its end.

Again, it is sometimes said of the Son alone that he is sufficient, and the whole reward of our love and desire is promised in his vision. For he says: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” Since he did not say here, “I will manifest the Father to him,” did he therefore separate the Father?

But because the saying “I and the Father are one” is true, when the Father is shown, the Son who is in him is also shown; and when the Son is shown, the Father who is in him is also shown. Therefore, just as “I will manifest myself to him” is understood to mean that he manifests the Father as well, so in the statement “when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father,” it is understood that he does not exclude himself.

For when he leads believers to the contemplation of God and the Father, he will surely lead them to the contemplation of himself, who said, “I will manifest myself to him.” And therefore, when Judas said to him, “Lord, what has happened, that you are going to manifest yourself to us and not to the world?” Jesus answered him: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” Behold: he does not manifest himself alone to the one who loves him, because he comes to him together with the Father and makes his dwelling with him.

19. Or will it perhaps be thought that, when the Father and the Son make their dwelling in the one who loves them, the Holy Spirit is excluded from that dwelling? What, then, does he mean by what he said earlier about the Holy Spirit: “Whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him; but you know him, because he remains with you and is in you”?

He is therefore not separated from this dwelling, of whom it was said, “He remains with you and is in you.” Unless someone is so absurd as to imagine that, when the Father and the Son come to make their dwelling with the one who loves them, the Holy Spirit will depart from there and, so to speak, yield his place to his superiors.

But Scripture confronts this carnal thought. A little earlier he says: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, so that he may be with you forever” (John 14:16–23). He will not, then, depart when the Father and the Son come; rather, he will be with them in the same dwelling forever, because neither comes without them, nor do they come without him.

But, to reveal the Trinity, certain things are spoken separately with the individual persons named. [Note: The word “separately” is absent from the manuscripts.] Nevertheless, they are not understood as separated from the others, because of the unity, the one substance, and the one divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER X

20. How Christ will hand over the kingdom to God the Father. Once the kingdom has been handed over to God the Father, Christ will no longer intercede for us.

Our Lord Jesus Christ will therefore hand over the kingdom to God the Father, without being separated from it, nor the Holy Spirit either, when he leads believers to the contemplation of God, where there is the end of all good actions, eternal rest, and joy that will never be taken from us.

This is signified by what he says: “Again I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22). Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet and intent upon his word, prefigured the likeness of this joy: resting, that is, from every activity and intent, in a certain manner, upon the truth—a manner of which this life is capable, yet which prefigures what will be eternal.

While her sister Martha was occupied in an activity necessary, and indeed good and useful, but destined to pass away when rest should come, Mary herself was resting in the Lord’s word. Therefore, when Martha complained to the Lord that her sister was not helping her, he answered: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:39–42).

He did not call what Martha was doing a bad part, but he called Mary’s part the better one because it would not be taken away. For the part devoted to ministering to need will be taken away when need itself has passed. The reward of good work that will pass away is rest that will remain.

In that contemplation, therefore, God will be all in all, because nothing else will be required from him; to be illumined by him alone and to enjoy him will be sufficient. Hence he in whom the Spirit intercedes with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8:26) says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord” (Ps. 27:4).

For we shall contemplate God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit when the mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus, has handed over the kingdom to God the Father. Then our mediator and priest, the Son of God and Son of Man, will no longer intercede for us. Rather, he himself, insofar as he is a priest, will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him and to whom he subjected all things; while, insofar as he is God, he will have us subjected together with him, and, insofar as he is a priest, he will be subject with us to that one (1 Cor. 15:24–28).

Therefore, since the Son is both God and human being, “human being” is another substance in the Son rather than the Son another substance in the Father. [Note: So the better manuscripts. The printed editions have: “one substance God, another human being; human being rather in the Son,” and so forth.] It is like flesh in relation to my soul: flesh is another substance in relation to my soul, although both are in one human being, just as the soul of another human being is another substance in relation to my soul.

21. When, therefore, he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father—that is, when he has led to contemplation those who believe and live by faith, for whom he now intercedes, and for whose reception of that contemplation we sigh and groan—when labor and groaning have passed away, he will no longer intercede for us, the kingdom having been handed over to God the Father.

Signifying this, he says: “I have spoken these things to you in figures; the hour will come when I shall no longer speak to you in figures, but shall announce the Father to you plainly” (John 16:25). [Note: Six manuscripts read: “I have spoken these things to you,” omitting “in.”] That is, there will no longer be figures when the vision is face to face.

For this is what he means by “I shall announce the Father to you plainly,” as though he were saying, “I shall show the Father to you plainly.” He says “announce” because he is his Word. For he continues: “On that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I shall ask the Father for you; for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father and came into this world; again, I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:25–28).

What does “I came forth from the Father” mean, except that I appeared not in the form in which I am equal to the Father, but otherwise—that is, in the assumed creature, in which I appeared as lesser? And what does “I came into this world” mean, except that I displayed the form of a servant, which I received by emptying myself, also to the eyes of sinners who love this world?

And what does “Again, I leave the world” mean, except that I remove from the sight of those who love the world what they saw? And what does “I go to the Father” mean, except that I teach my believers to understand me as one who is equal to the Father?

Those who believe this will be considered worthy to be led from faith to sight—that is, to the vision itself—which is what he is said to bring about when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father.

For his faithful, whom he redeemed by his blood, are called his kingdom; for them he now intercedes. But then, making them cleave to himself there where he is equal to the Father, he will no longer ask the Father for them. “For the Father himself,” he says, “loves you.”

He asks insofar as he is lesser than the Father; but insofar as he is equal, he is heard together with the Father. Therefore, by saying “the Father himself loves you,” he certainly does not separate himself from the Father. Rather, in accordance with what I mentioned above and sufficiently explained, he makes us understand that one person of the Trinity is often named in such a way that the others are understood there as well.

Thus he says, “The Father himself loves you,” so that the Son and the Holy Spirit are consequently understood also. This does not mean that he who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (Rom. 8:32) does not love us now. Rather, God loves us as we shall be, not as we are.

For those whom he loves, he preserves forever as they are to be. This will happen when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father, he who now intercedes for us, so that he will no longer ask the Father, because the Father himself loves us.

And on what merit, except that of faith, by which we believe before seeing what is promised? Through faith we shall arrive at sight, so that he may love us as those whom he loves us to become, not as those whom he hates because we are such; and he exhorts us and enables us not always to wish to remain such. [Note: The printed editions read “because we are evil”; “evil” is absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XI

22. The rule by which the Son is understood in Scripture sometimes as equal, sometimes as lesser.

Therefore, having learned this rule for understanding the Scriptures concerning the Son of God, so that we distinguish what in them sounds according to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, from what sounds according to the form of a servant, which he assumed and in which he is less than the Father, we shall not be disturbed as though the statements of the sacred books were contradictory and opposed to one another.

According to the form of God, the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father, because neither of them is a creature, as we have already shown. According to the form of a servant, however, he is less than the Father, because he himself said: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). He is less than himself, because it is said of him: “He emptied himself” (Phil. 2:7). He is less than the Holy Spirit, because he himself says: “Whoever speaks a blasphemy against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven” (Matt. 12:32).

He also performed miracles in the Holy Spirit, saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has certainly come upon you” (Luke 11:20). And in Isaiah he says—as he himself read this passage in the synagogue and showed without hesitation that it had been fulfilled concerning him—“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives” (Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:18–19), and so forth. He says that he was sent to do these things because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him.

According to the form of God, “all things were made through him” (John 1:3). According to the form of a servant, “he was made from a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. 4:4).

According to the form of God, “he and the Father are one” (John 10:30). According to the form of a servant, “he did not come to do his own will, but the will of him who sent him” (John 6:38).

According to the form of God, “as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). According to the form of a servant, his soul is sorrowful unto death; and he says, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:38–39).

According to the form of God, “he is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). According to the form of a servant, “he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

23. According to the form of God, all that the Father has belongs to him (John 16:15); and he says: “All my things are yours, and your things are mine” (John 17:10). [Note: In manuscript B: “All my things are yours, he says, and my things are yours.” The reading is better in Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition: “All your things are mine, he says, and mine are yours.” But the Greek and the Vulgate seem to preserve the true reading: “All my things are yours, he says, and your things are mine.”]

According to the form of a servant, “the teaching is not his, but that of him who sent him” (John 7:16).

## CHAPTER XII

By what reasoning the Son is said not to know the day and hour that the Father knows. Statements about Christ according to the form of God and according to the form of a servant. How the kingdom is both Christ’s and not Christ’s. How Christ will both not judge and judge.

“And concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father” (Mark 13:32). He does not know what he makes others not know—that is, he did not know it in such a way as to disclose it to the disciples at that time. This is like the statement made to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12), meaning, “Now I have caused you to know it,” because Abraham himself became aware of this through being tested in that trial.

He was also certainly going to say to the disciples at the appropriate time something about the future, speaking of it as though it had already happened: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends. For the servant does not know his master’s will; but I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). He had not yet done this, but because he was certainly going to do it, he spoke as though he had already done so.

For he said to them: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). Among these things, “the day and hour” is understood to be included. The Apostle likewise says: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). He was speaking to people who could not grasp higher things concerning Christ’s divinity. To them he also says shortly afterward: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as fleshly” (1 Cor. 3:1).

Therefore, among them he did not know what they could not know through him. And he said that he knew only what it was necessary for them to know through him. Finally, among the mature he knew what among the little ones he did not know; for there he says: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (1 Cor. 2:6).

A person is said not to know, in this manner of speech, what he conceals—just as a hidden pit is called “blind” because it is concealed. Scripture does not speak in any manner that is absent from ordinary human usage, since it speaks to human beings.

24. According to the form of God, it is said: “He begot me before all the hills” (Prov. 8:25), that is, before all the heights of created things; and, “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 110:3), that is, before all times and temporal things.

According to the form of a servant, however, it is said: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22). According to the form of God he said, “I am the truth”; according to the form of a servant, “I am the way” (John 14:6).

Because he himself, as “the firstborn from the dead” (Rev. 1:5), made for his Church a way to the kingdom of God and to eternal life, and is its head even unto the immortality of the body, he was created at the beginning of God’s ways, in his works.

According to the form of God, he is the Beginning who also speaks to us (John 8:25), in whom God made heaven and earth (Gen. 1:1). According to the form of a servant, however, he is “the bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 19:5).

According to the form of God, he is “the firstborn of all creation”; he is before all things, and all things hold together in him. According to the form of a servant, “he is the head of the body, the Church” (Col. 1:15, 17–18).

According to the form of God, he is “the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). From this it is clear that he glorifies his saints. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30).

It is of him that it is said that he justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5); it is of him that it is said that he is just and justifies (Rom. 3:26). If, therefore, those whom he justified he also glorified, then the one who justifies also glorifies—the one who, as I have said, is the Lord of glory.

According to the form of a servant, however, when the disciples were eagerly discussing his glorification, he answered: “To sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matt. 20:23).

25. What has been prepared by his Father has also been prepared by the Son himself, because he and the Father are one (John 10:30). We have already shown that, in this Trinity, through many modes of divine speech, what belongs to all is said even of individual persons, because of the inseparable operation of one and the same substance.

Thus he also says of the Holy Spirit: “When I have gone, I shall send him to you” (John 16:7). He did not say, “We shall send him,” but spoke as though the Son alone were going to send him and not the Father. Yet elsewhere he says: “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you; but the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will declare all things to you” (John 14:25–26).

Here again the statement is made as though the Son would not send him, but only the Father. Therefore, just as with these statements, so also with the words “for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father”: he wished it to be understood that he prepared the seats of glory together with the Father for whomever he willed.

Someone may say: In the passage where he spoke of the Holy Spirit, he said that he would send him in such a way as not to deny that the Father would send him; and elsewhere he spoke of the Father in such a way as not to deny that he himself would send him. Here, however, he plainly says, “It is not mine to give,” and then says that these things have been prepared by the Father.

But this is what we established at the outset: that the statement was made according to the form of a servant. Thus we should understand “It is not mine to give” as though he had said, “It is not within human power to give this.” By this, it is understood that he gives it according to that nature in which he is God and equal to the Father.

“It is not mine,” he says, “to give”—that is, “I do not give these things by human power, but they have been prepared by my Father.” But understand now that if everything the Father has is mine (John 16:15), this too is mine; and I prepared these things together with the Father.

26. For I also ask how we should understand the statement: “If anyone does not hear my words, I shall not judge him.” Perhaps he meant here “I shall not judge him” in the same way as there, “It is not mine to give.”

But what follows? “For I did not come,” he says, “to judge the world, but to save the world.” Then he adds: “Whoever rejects me and does not receive my words has one who judges him.” At this point we would understand the Father, unless he added: “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.”

What, then? Will neither the Son judge, because he said, “I shall not judge him,” nor the Father, but the word that the Son has spoken?

Listen further to what follows: “For I,” he says, “have not spoken from myself; but the Father who sent me gave me a commandment concerning what I should say and what I should speak. And I know that his commandment is eternal life. Therefore, the things I speak, I speak just as the Father told me” (John 12:47–50).

If, then, the Son does not judge, but the word that the Son has spoken judges—and the word that the Son has spoken judges because the Father who sent him gave him a commandment concerning what he should say and speak—then surely the Father judges, whose word is what the Son has spoken. And the very Word of the Father is the Son himself.

For the Father’s commandment is not one thing and the Father’s Word another. He called it both “word” and “commandment.” Let us see, then, whether perhaps by saying “I have not spoken from myself” he wished to be understood as saying, “I was not born from myself.”

For if the Word of the Father speaks, he speaks himself, because he is the Word of the Father. He often says, “The Father gave me,” by which he wishes it to be understood that the Father begot him—not that the Father gave something to one who already existed and did not possess it, but that giving him possession of it was begetting him so that he might exist.

For, unlike a creature, the Son of God—before the incarnation and before the assumed creature—was not one thing and possessed something else. Rather, he is himself what he possesses.

This is expressed more clearly in the passage, if anyone is capable of grasping it, where he says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). He did not give life in himself to one who already existed without possessing life, since by the very fact that he is, he is life. [Note: Some ancient codices read: “he is eternal life.”]

Therefore, “he gave the Son to have life in himself” means that he begot the Son to be unchangeable life, which is eternal life. Since the Son is the Word of God, and the Son of God is the true God and eternal life, as John says in his Epistle (1 John 5:20), what else do we recognize here when the Lord says, “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day”? He says that this word is the Father’s word and the Father’s commandment, and he calls that commandment eternal life: “I know,” he says, “that his commandment is eternal life.”

27. I therefore ask how we should understand the statement: “I shall not judge; but the word that I have spoken will judge.” From what follows, it appears to have been said as though he meant: “I shall not judge; but the Father’s Word will judge.” The Father’s Word, however, is the Son of God himself.

Is this how we should understand it: “I shall not judge, but I shall judge”? How can this be true unless the meaning is: “I shall not judge by human authority, because I am the Son of Man; but I shall judge by the authority of the Word, because I am the Son of God”?

Or, if “I shall not judge, but I shall judge” seems contradictory and opposed to itself, what shall we say where he declares: “My teaching is not mine”? How is it mine, and how is it not mine? He did not say, “This teaching is not mine,” but “My teaching is not mine.” The teaching he called his own, he also called not his own.

How is this true except that it is his according to one aspect and not his according to another: his according to the form of God, not his according to the form of a servant?

For when he says, “It is not mine, but that of him who sent me” (John 7:16), he directs us back to the Word himself. The Father’s teaching is the Father’s Word, who is his only Son.
