What, likewise, does he mean by: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me” (John 12:44)? How does one believe in him, and how does one not believe in him? How can the statement be understood as contrary to and opposed to itself?

Unless it is understood in this way: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in what he sees, so that our hope may not be in a creature, but in the one who assumed a creature in which he might appear to human eyes and thus cleanse hearts by faith for the contemplation of himself as equal to the Father.”

Therefore, by directing the attention of believers to the Father and saying, “He does not believe in me, but in him who sent me,” he certainly did not wish to separate himself from the Father, that is, from the one who sent him. Rather, he wished people to believe in him as they believe in the Father, to whom he is equal.

Elsewhere he states this openly: “Believe in God, and believe in me” (John 14:1)—that is, “As you believe in God, so believe in me, because I and the Father are one God.”

Therefore, just as here he seems to remove human faith from himself and transfer it to the Father by saying, “He does not believe in me, but in him who sent me,” though he certainly did not separate himself from the Father, so also in saying, “It is not mine to give, but for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” I think it is clear in what respect each statement should be understood.

The same is true of the statement, “I shall not judge,” although he himself will judge the living and the dead (2 Tim. 4:1). But because he will not judge by human authority, he turns back to his divinity and raises human hearts upward, for the sake of raising which he descended.

## CHAPTER XIII

28. Different things are declared of the same Christ because of the different natures of his hypostasis. Why the Father is said not to judge, but to have given judgment to the Son.

If he were not himself the Son of Man because of the form of a servant that he assumed, while being the Son of God because of the form of God in which he exists, the Apostle Paul would not have said of the rulers of this age: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

He was crucified according to the form of a servant, and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For the assumption was of such a kind as to make God human and a human being God.

What is said because of what, and according to what aspect, the prudent, attentive, and devout reader will understand with the Lord’s assistance. For we have said that, according to what he is as God, he glorifies his own—that is, precisely as he is the Lord of glory. And yet the Lord of glory was crucified, because God is rightly said to have been crucified—not by the power of divinity, but through the weakness of the flesh (2 Cor. 13:4).

Similarly, we say that, according to what he is as God, he judges—that is, by divine authority, not human authority. And yet he himself, as a human being, will judge, just as the Lord of glory was crucified.

For he says this plainly: “When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then all the nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. 25:31–32), followed by the other statements concerning the future judgment, extending to the final sentence, which are proclaimed in that passage.

And the Jews, who will be punished in that judgment because they persist in wickedness, will “look upon him whom they pierced,” as it is written elsewhere (Zech. 12:10).

Since both the good and the wicked will see the judge of the living and the dead, without doubt the wicked will be able to see him only according to the form in which he is the Son of Man. Yet they will see him in the glory in which he will judge, not in the humility in which he was judged.

As for the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, the ungodly will certainly not see it. For they are not pure in heart; yet it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

This is the vision face to face (1 Cor. 13:12), which is promised as the supreme reward to the righteous. It will take place when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father. In that event, the vision of his own form is also understood to be included: the whole creation being subjected to God, including the form in which the Son of God became the Son of Man.

For according to this form the Son himself will then be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:24, 28).

Otherwise, if the Son of God will appear even to the ungodly as judge in the form in which he is equal to the Father, when he comes to judge them, what is the meaning of the great promise he makes to the one who loves him: “I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21)?

Therefore, the Son of Man will judge, yet not by human authority, but by that authority according to which he is the Son of God. And again, the Son of God will judge, yet he will not appear in the form in which, as God, he is equal to the Father, but in the form in which he is the Son of Man.

29. Accordingly, both statements can be made: “The Son of Man will judge,” and “The Son of Man will not judge.” For the Son of Man will judge, so that what he said may be true: “When the Son of Man comes, then all the nations will be gathered before him”; and the Son of Man will not judge, so that what he said may be true: “I do not judge” (John 12:47); and, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges” (John 8:50). For, insofar as in the judgment it will not be the form of God but the form of the Son of Man that appears, the Father himself will not judge either; for in this sense it was said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” Whether this was said according to the expression we mentioned above, where he says, “He has granted the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:22, 26), thereby signifying that he thus begot the Son; or according to that of which the Apostle speaks [Note: The manuscripts read, “or according to that by which he speaks,” omitting “of.”], saying, “For this reason he raised him up” [Note: shortly afterward the Vulgate has “exalted”; according to the Greek, *hyperypsōsen* (“highly exalted”).] “and granted him the name that is above every name”—this was said of the Son of Man, according to whom the Son of God was raised from the dead.

For he, being in the form of God and equal to the Father, in that he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant [Note: The printed editions read “from which”; some manuscripts, more fittingly, read “from whom”], acts and suffers in that very form of a servant and receives what the Apostle then sets forth: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:6–11).

Whether, then, the statement “He gave all judgment to the Son” was made according to the former expression or according to the latter is sufficiently clear from this: if it had been said according to the sense of “He granted the Son to have life in himself,” it certainly would not have been said, “The Father judges no one.” For insofar as the Father begot the Son equal to himself, he judges together with him. Thus it was said because in the judgment it will not be the form of God but the form of the Son of Man that appears. This does not mean that the one who gave all judgment to the Son will not judge, since the Son says of him, “There is one who seeks and judges.” Rather, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” means as much as this: No one will see the Father in the judgment of the living and the dead, but all will see the Son—for he is also the Son of Man, and so he can be seen even by the wicked, since they too will see the one whom they pierced.

30. So that we may not seem to be conjecturing rather than demonstrating this plainly, let us produce a definite and explicit statement of the same Lord, by which we may show that this was the very reason he said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”: namely, that the judge will appear in the form of the Son of Man. That form is not the Father’s but the Son’s; nor is it the Son’s form in which he is equal to the Father, but the form in which he is less than the Father, so that he may be visible in the judgment to both the good and the wicked.

For shortly afterward he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.” This eternal life is that vision which does not belong to the wicked. Then he continues: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour will come, and now is [Note: Most manuscripts read “comes.”], when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.”

This belongs properly to the godly, who hear concerning his incarnation in such a way that they believe that he is the Son of God; that is, they receive him, for their sake made less than the Father in the form of a servant, while believing that he is equal to the Father in the form of God. Therefore he continues, commending this very point: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.”

Then he comes to the vision of his glory, in which he will come to judgment—a vision that will be shared by the wicked and the righteous. For he continues and says: “And he has given him authority to exercise judgment” [Note: the printed editions omit the conjunction “and,” which is found here in the manuscripts and in the Greek] “because he is the Son of Man.”

I think nothing could be clearer. Because the Son of God is equal to the Father, he does not receive this authority to exercise judgment; he possesses it with the Father in secret. But he receives it so that the good and the wicked may see him judging, because he is the Son of Man. The vision of the Son of Man will indeed be presented even to the wicked; for the vision of the form of God is granted only to the pure in heart, because “they shall see God”—that is, only to the godly, to whose love he promises this very thing: that he will show himself to them.

And therefore see what follows: “Do not marvel at this,” he says. What prevents us from marveling except that which truly astonishes everyone who does not understand—namely, that he said the Father had given him authority to exercise judgment because he is the Son of Man, when one might rather have expected him to say, “because he is the Son of God”? But because the wicked cannot see the Son of God insofar as he is equal to the Father in the form of God, while it is necessary that the judge of the living and the dead be seen by both the righteous and the wicked when they are judged before him, he says: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:22–29).

It was therefore necessary that he receive this authority because he is the Son of Man, so that, when all rise, they may see him in a form that can be seen by everyone—but some to condemnation, others to eternal life.

And what is eternal life except this: “that they know you,” he says, “the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3)? And how are they to know Jesus Christ himself except as the one true God, who will show himself to them—not in the manner in which he will also show himself to those who are to be punished, in the form of the Son of Man?

31. He is good according to that vision by which God appears to the pure in heart: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!” (Psalm 72:1). But when the wicked see the judge, he will not appear good to them, because they will not rejoice in him in their hearts; rather, then “all the tribes of the earth will mourn” (Revelation 1:7)—that is, in the number of all the wicked and unbelieving.

For this reason also, when the man who had called him “Good Teacher” asked him for counsel about attaining eternal life, he replied: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except one, God” (Matthew 19:17). Yet the Lord himself says elsewhere that a human being is good: “A good person,” he says, “brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart; and an evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12:35).

But because that man was seeking eternal life—and eternal life consists in that contemplation in which God is seen not for punishment but for everlasting joy—and because he did not understand with whom he was speaking, regarding him only as the Son of Man, he said: “Why do you ask me about the good?” That is: Why do you ask about the good in this form that you see, and call me a good teacher according to what you see?

This is the form of the Son of Man; this is the form he assumed; this form will appear in the judgment, not only to the righteous but also to the wicked. The vision of this form will not be beneficial to those who do evil. But there is also the vision of my form, in which, although I was present, I did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied myself in order to assume this form (Philippians 2:6–7).

That one God, then—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—will appear only for the joy that will not be taken away from the righteous. It is for this future joy that the one who says longs: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord” (Psalm 27:4).

That one God, then, is alone good for this reason [Note: the manuscripts have “for this purpose”]: no one sees him for mourning and lamentation, but only for salvation and true gladness.

If you understand me according to that form, I am good; but if according to this form alone, why do you ask me about the good?—if you are [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “will be.”] among those who “will see the one whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10); and that vision itself will be evil for them, because it will be punitive.

It is probable, on the basis of the considerations I have mentioned, that the Lord said, “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except one, God.” [Note: the printed editions read, “From this statement you may recognize that the Lord said”; “you may recognize” is absent from the manuscripts.]

For that vision of God by which we shall contemplate the immutable substance of God, invisible to human eyes, promised only to the saints, which the Apostle Paul calls “face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12); of which the Apostle John says, “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2); of which it is said, “One thing I have asked of the Lord, that I may behold the delight of the Lord”; and of which the Lord himself says, “I will love him and show myself to him” (John 14:21); and for the sake of which alone we purify our hearts by faith, so that we may be blessed in being pure in heart, because “they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8)—and whatever else has been said about this vision, which anyone who directs the eye of love toward seeking it will find scattered abundantly throughout all the Scriptures—that vision alone is our supreme good, and for the sake of attaining it we are commanded to do whatever we rightly do.

But that vision of the Son of Man which was foretold, when all the nations will be gathered before him and will say to him, “Lord, when did we see you hungry and thirsty?” and so forth, will be neither a good for the wicked, who will be sent into eternal fire, nor the supreme good for the righteous. For he is still calling them to the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

For just as he will say to the wicked, “Go into eternal fire,” so to these he will say, “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matthew 25:37, 41, 34). And just as the wicked will go into eternal burning, so the righteous will go into eternal life.

And what is eternal life except this: “that they know you,” he says, “the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent”? But this will be in that glory of which he says to the Father, “the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:3, 5).

For then “he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father” (1 Corinthians 15:24), so that the good servant may enter into the joy of his Lord (Matthew 25:21, 23), and so that God may hide those whom he possesses in the secrecy of his face, away from the disturbance of human beings—namely, those who will then be disturbed when they hear that sentence. From that evil report the righteous will not be afraid (Psalm 112:7), provided that he is protected in the tabernacle—that is, in the right faith of the catholic Church—from the contradiction of tongues (Psalm 31:21), that is, from the slanders of heretics.

If, however, there is another interpretation of the Lord’s words, “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except one, God,” provided that it is not for this reason believed that the substance of the Father possesses greater goodness than that of the Son, according to which the Word is he through whom all things were made, and provided that it in no way departs from sound doctrine, let us confidently use not merely one interpretation but as many as can be found. For the more avenues open for avoiding their snares, the more forcefully are the heretics refuted.

But let us now take up what remains to be considered from another beginning.

# BOOK TWO

Augustine again defends the equality of the Trinity. Treating of the mission of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and of the various manifestations of God, he demonstrates that the one who is sent is not for that reason less than the one who sends, because one sent and the other was sent; rather, that the Trinity is equal in all things, equally immutable and invisible in its nature, and everywhere present, operating inseparably in every mission or manifestation.

[Col. 0845]

## PREFACE

1. When human beings seek God and direct their minds toward understanding the Trinity according to the capacity of human weakness, after experiencing arduous difficulties—whether in the very effort of the mind striving to contemplate the inaccessible light, or in the manifold and diverse language of the sacred Scriptures, where it seems to me that the soul is worn down only so that, glorified by the grace of Christ, it may become sweet [Note: several manuscripts read, “so that Adam may be worn down.”]—when they have reached something certain after every ambiguity has been examined, they ought very readily to pardon those who err in the investigation of so great a secret.

But there are two things in human error that are endured with the greatest difficulty: presumption before the truth has been revealed, and, once it has been revealed, the defense of a falsehood that had been presumed. If God, as I pray and hope, protects and fortifies me against these two vices, which are exceedingly hostile to the discovery of truth and to the interpretation of the divine and holy books, with the shield of his good will (Psalm 5:13) and the grace of his mercy, I will not be sluggish in seeking the substance of God, whether through his Scripture or through creation.

Both of these are set before us for contemplation so that he himself may be sought and loved [Note: the Michaelinus manuscript reads, “understood”]—the one who inspired the former and created the latter. Nor will I be afraid to express my judgment, in which I will prefer to be examined by the upright rather than fear being bitten by the perverse.

The most beautiful and modest charity gladly welcomes the eye [Note: most manuscripts read, “kiss”] of the dove; cautious humility either avoids the dog’s tooth or the most solid truth blunts it. And I shall prefer to be reproved by anyone rather than praised either by someone who is mistaken or by a flatterer. No critic is to be feared by one who loves the truth.

For the critic will be either an enemy or a friend. If an enemy insults, he must be endured; but if a friend errs, he must be instructed, and if he instructs, he must be heard. A flatterer, however, both confirms error when he is himself mistaken and entices one into error when he flatters.

“Let the righteous correct me in mercy and reprove me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Psalm 141:5).

## CHAPTER ONE

2. A twofold rule for understanding the scriptural expressions concerning the Son of God. Three kinds of expressions.

Although we hold most firmly, as a canonical rule disseminated throughout the Scriptures and demonstrated by learned Catholic interpreters of those Scriptures, how the Son of God is to be understood as equal to the Father according to the form of God in which he exists, and as less than the Father according to the form of a servant that he assumed (Philippians 2:6–7)—in which form he was found to be less not only than the Father but also than the Holy Spirit, and not merely less than his former self but less than his present self, because, having assumed the form of a servant, he did not lose the form of God, as the testimonies of Scripture cited in the preceding book have shown—nevertheless, certain statements in the divine words are so placed that it is ambiguous to which rule they should rather be referred: whether to the rule by which we understand the Son to be less in the creature he assumed, or to the rule by which we understand that the Son is not less but equal to the Father, though he is God from God, light from light, from him.

For we call the Son “God from God,” but the Father “God” only, not “from God.” Hence it is clear that the Son has another from whom he is, and to whom he is Son; whereas the Father does not have a Son from whom he is, but only has one to whom he is Father. Every son is what he is from his father, and is a son to his father; but no father is what he is from his son, though he is a father to his son.

3. Accordingly, certain statements are made in Scripture about the Father and the Son in such a way as to indicate unity and equality of substance, as: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and, “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6); and whatever other statements are of this kind.

Others, however, are expressed in such a way as to show the Son to be less because of the form of a servant—that is, because of the assumed creature of mutable and human substance—as when he says, “Because the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); and, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” For shortly afterward he appropriately says, “And he has given him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

Still others are expressed in such a way that he is shown at that time to be neither less nor equal, but only that he is from the Father is intimated, as in: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself”; and: “The Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:22, 27, 26, 19).

If we understand this as having been said because the Son is less in the form he assumed from the creature, it will follow that the Father first walked upon the waters, or opened the eyes of some other man born blind with spittle and mud, and performed the other things that the Son, appearing in the flesh among human beings, did (Matthew 14:26; John 9:6–7), so that the one who said that the Son could do nothing of his own accord except what he had seen the Father doing could perform them. But who, except someone deranged, would think so?

It remains, therefore, that these statements were made because the life of the Son is immutable, as is the Father’s, and yet he is from the Father; and because the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable, yet for the Son to operate in this way is from the one from whom he himself is—that is, from the Father.

The Son sees the Father in such a way that, by the very fact that he sees him, he is Son. For being from the Father—that is, being born from the Father—is not something different for him from seeing the Father; nor is seeing him at work something different from working together with him. But he cannot act from himself precisely because he is not from himself.

Therefore, whatever the Son sees the Father doing, these same things the Son also does likewise, because he is from the Father. It is not that he does other things in the same manner, as a painter paints other panels in the way he sees other panels painted by someone else; nor that he does the same things differently, as the body produces the same letters that the mind has conceived. Rather, he says: “Whatever the Father does, these same things the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19).

He said both “these same things” and “likewise.” Consequently, the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable and equal, but for the Son it is from the Father. Therefore the Son cannot do anything from himself except what he has seen the Father doing.

On the basis of this rule—according to which Scripture speaks not in order to make one less than another, but only to show who is from whom—some have conceived the meaning as though the Son were being called less. Some of our own people, however, less educated and inexperienced in these matters, attempt to understand these statements according to the form of a servant; when a correct understanding does not follow, they become confused.

To prevent this from happening, this rule must be retained: the Son is not less, but it is being intimated that he is from the Father. These words show not inequality but his birth.

## CHAPTER TWO

4. Certain expressions concerning the Son can be understood according to either rule.

There are therefore certain statements in the holy books, as I began to say, which are so placed that it is ambiguous to what they should be referred: whether to the fact that the Son is less because of the creature he assumed, or to the fact that, although he is equal, it is nevertheless indicated that he is from the Father.

It seems to me that if the ambiguity is such that it cannot be explained and distinguished, the statement may safely be understood according to either rule. Such is what he says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16).

For this can be understood according to the form of a servant, as we have already discussed in the preceding book (above, Book 1, chapter 12), and according to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father in such a way that he is nevertheless from the Father.

In the form of God, just as the Son is not one thing and his life another, but the Son himself is life, so the Son is not one thing and his teaching another, but the Son himself is teaching. Thus, just as the statement “He gave life to the Son” means nothing other than “He begot the Son who is life,” so also when it is said, “He gave teaching to the Son,” it is properly understood as “He begot the Son who is teaching.”

Thus the statement, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me,” may be understood as though it said: “I am not from myself, but from him who sent me.”

## CHAPTER THREE

5. Certain statements concerning the Holy Spirit are understood according to only one of the rules.

Concerning the Holy Spirit also, of whom it was not said, “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” the Lord himself nevertheless says: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you.”

After these words, unless he had immediately added, “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said, He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:13–15), it might perhaps have been believed that the Holy Spirit was born from Christ in the same way that Christ was born from the Father.

For Christ had said of himself, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me”; but of the Holy Spirit he said, “He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak,” and, “Because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you.”

But because he gave the reason why he said, “He will receive from what is mine”—for he says, “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said, He will receive from what is mine”—it remains to be understood that the Holy Spirit also has from the Father, just as the Son does. [Note: The printed editions read “from the Father”; the manuscripts have *de Patris*. Augustine customarily uses this expression—that is, “of the Father’s,” or “of his own”—when citing the Son’s words, “He will receive from what is mine.”]

How else can this be understood except according to what we said above: “When the Paraclete whom I will send to you from the Father comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26)?

Proceeding from the Father, he is therefore said not to speak from himself. And just as the Son is not thereby made less because he said, “The Son cannot do anything from himself except what he sees the Father doing”—for he did not say this according to the form of a servant but according to the form of God, as we have already shown; and these words do not indicate that he is less but that he is from the Father—so the Holy Spirit is not thereby made less because it was said of him, “He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” This was said because he proceeds from the Father.

But since the Son is from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, why are they not both called sons, nor both begotten, but one is the only-begotten Son, while the other is neither son nor begotten? For if he were begotten, he would certainly be the Son. We shall discuss this elsewhere, if God grants it and to the extent that he grants it (below, Book 15, chapter 25).

## CHAPTER FOUR

6. The Son’s glorification by the Father does not demonstrate inequality.

Let those who thought that this too supported their position, as though it demonstrated that the Father is greater than the Son, now rouse themselves if they can, because the Son said, “Father, glorify me.”

Behold, the Holy Spirit also glorifies him. Is the Holy Spirit therefore greater than he? Moreover, if the Holy Spirit glorifies the Son because he will receive from what is the Son’s, and receives from what is the Son’s because everything the Father has belongs to the Son, it is clear that when the Holy Spirit glorifies the Son, the Father glorifies the Son.

From this it is understood that everything the Father has belongs not only to the Son but also to the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is able to glorify the Son whom the Father glorifies.

If the one who glorifies is greater than the one whom he glorifies, let them allow those who glorify one another to be equal.

It is also written that the Son glorifies the Father: “I have glorified you,” he says, “on earth” (John 17:1, 4).

Let them take care, however, lest the Holy Spirit be thought greater than both, because he glorifies the Son whom the Father glorifies, while the Holy Spirit himself is not written to be glorified either by the Father or by the Son.

## CHAPTER FIVE

7. The Son and the Holy Spirit are not less because they are sent. The Son was also sent by himself. Concerning the mission of the Holy Spirit.

Having been refuted on these points, they turn to the claim that the one who sends is greater than the one who is sent. Accordingly, they say that the Father is greater than the Son because the Son repeatedly declares that he was sent by the Father; and that the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit because Jesus said of him, “The Father will send him in my name” (John 14:26).

The Holy Spirit, they say, is less than both, because the Father sends him, as we have mentioned, and the Son also sends him when he says, “But if I go, I will send him to you.”

In this question I first ask: From where and to where was the Son sent? “I came forth from the Father,” he says, “and came into this world” (John 16:7, 28). Therefore to come forth from the Father and to come into this world is to be sent.

What, then, does the same evangelist mean when he says of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him”? Then he adds: “He came to his own” (John 1:10–11).

He was certainly sent to the place to which he came. But if he was sent into this world because he came forth from the Father and came into this world, while he was already in this world, then he was sent to the place where he was.

The prophet also records God as saying, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24). If this was said of the Son—for some want it understood that he spoke either to the prophets or in the prophets—to what place was he sent except to the place where he was? For he was everywhere who said, “I fill heaven and earth.”

If, however, this was said of the Father, where could he be without his Word and his Wisdom, which “reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things gently” (Wisdom 8:1)? Nor could he be anywhere without his Spirit [Note: the printed editions read, “without the Holy Spirit”; the manuscripts have, “without his Spirit”].

Therefore, if God is everywhere, his Spirit is also everywhere. The Holy Spirit, then, was sent to the place where he was.

The one who found no place to which he could go [Note: in manuscript B, “to which he might go”; Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, “to which he could go”] from the face of God, and says, “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present,” wishing to indicate that God is present everywhere, first named his Spirit. For he says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? And where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 139:8, 7).

8. Therefore, if both the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent to the place where they were, we must ask how this mission of either the Son or the Holy Spirit is to be understood. For the Father alone is nowhere read to have been sent.

Concerning the Son, the Apostle writes: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4:4–5).

He says, “He sent his Son, born of a woman.” What Catholic does not know that by this expression he intended to signify not the loss of virginity but the distinction of sex, according to the Hebrew manner of speaking?

When he says, “God sent his Son, born of a woman,” he sufficiently shows that the Son was sent precisely insofar as he was born of a woman.

Insofar as he was born from God, he was in this world; but insofar as he was born from Mary, he came into this world as one sent.

Accordingly, he could not have been sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit—not only because, when he sent him, the Father is understood to have made him from a woman, and certainly did not do this without his Spirit, but also because the Gospel says this most plainly and explicitly to the virgin Mary when she asks the angel, “How will this happen?”: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:34–35). Matthew likewise says: “She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:18).

Moreover, in the prophet Isaiah, Christ himself is understood to speak of his future coming: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16).

9. Perhaps someone may compel us to say that the Son was also sent by himself, because that conception and birth from the Virgin is an operation of the Trinity, by which all things are created.

“But how,” he asks, “did the Father send him if he sent himself?”

I first answer by asking him to say, if he can, how the Father sanctified him if he sanctified himself. The same Lord says both things: “The one whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world—you say, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (John 10:36). Elsewhere he says: “For their sake I sanctify myself” (John 17:19).

I ask further: How did the Father hand him over if he handed himself over? The Apostle Paul says both things. He says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32). Elsewhere he says of the Savior himself: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Galatians 2:20).

I believe that anyone who understands these matters properly will answer that the Father and the Son have one will and an inseparable operation.

Let him therefore understand that incarnation and birth from the Virgin, in which the Son is understood to have been sent, were accomplished by one and the same inseparable operation of the Father and the Son, and certainly not with the Holy Spirit separated from it, of whom it is plainly said, “She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.”

Even if we ask the question in this way, what we are saying may perhaps appear more clearly: How did God send his Son? Did he order him to come, and did he come in obedience to the one who ordered him? Or did he ask him, or merely admonish him?

Whatever the case may be, it was certainly done by a word; and the Word of God is himself the Son of God. Therefore, when the Father sent him by a word, it was accomplished by the Father and his Word that he should be sent.

Thus the same Son was sent by the Father and by the Son, because the Son himself is the Word of the Father. Who would clothe himself in so sacrilegious an opinion as to think that a temporal word was made by the Father so that the eternal Son might be sent and appear in the flesh in time?

Rather, in the very Word of God, which was in the beginning with God and was God—in the very Wisdom of God—there was, without time, the time at which it was fitting for him to appear in the flesh.

Therefore, although the Word was in the beginning without any temporal beginning, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, within that very Word, without any time, there was the time at which the Word would become flesh and dwell among us (John 1:1–2, 14).

When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4)—that is, made in time—so that the incarnate Word might appear to human beings. The time at which this would occur was already present without time in the Word itself.

For the order of times exists without time in the eternal Wisdom of God.

Since, then, it was accomplished by the Father and the Son that the Son should appear in the flesh, he who appeared in that flesh was appropriately said to have been sent; and the one who did not appear in it was said to have sent him.

For the things that occur outwardly before bodily eyes arise from the inward arrangement of spiritual nature, and therefore are appropriately called “sent.”

The form of the human being assumed is the person of the Son, not also of the Father. Therefore the invisible Father, together with the invisible Son who was with him, is said to have sent the same Son by making him visible.

If he had become visible in such a way that he ceased to be invisible with the Father—that is, if the invisible substance of the Word had been changed and transformed into a visible creature—then the Son would be understood to have been sent by the Father in such a way that he was merely sent and was not also found to be sending together with the Father.

But since the form of a servant was assumed in such a way that the form of God remained immutable, it is clear that what became visible in the Son was accomplished by the Father and the Son, who did not appear: namely, that the same Son might be sent visibly by the invisible Father together with the invisible Son.

Why, then, does he say, “I did not come of my own accord”? This was said according to the form of a servant, according to which he also said, “I do not judge anyone” (John 8:42, 15).

10. If, then, one is said to be sent insofar as he appeared outwardly in bodily creation, while inwardly he is always hidden from mortal eyes in spiritual nature, it is now readily understood why the Holy Spirit is also said to have been sent.

For a certain created form was made in time in which the Holy Spirit might be visibly displayed: either when he descended upon the Lord himself in bodily form, like a dove (Matthew 3:16); or when, ten days after his ascension had been completed, on the day of Pentecost, suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a powerful rushing wind, and tongues appeared divided as though of fire, which also rested upon each of them (Acts 2:2–4).

This operation, visibly expressed and presented to mortal eyes, was called the mission of the Holy Spirit—not because his very substance, by which he too is invisible and immutable, like the Father and the Son, appeared, but so that, by the external appearances presented to them, human hearts might be moved from the temporal manifestation of the one who was coming toward the hidden eternity of the one who is always present.

## CHAPTER SIX
### 11. The Creature Was Not Assumed by the Holy Spirit as Flesh Was Assumed by the Word

The creature was not assumed by the Holy Spirit in the way that flesh was assumed by the Word. For this reason it is nowhere written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is less than God the Father: the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed in the same way as the Son of Man was assumed, in whose form the person of the very Word of God was manifested. This was not that he might have the Word of God as other holy and wise men have it, but above his companions (Heb. 1:9); certainly not because he had the Word in a greater measure, so as to be wiser than the others by a more excellent wisdom, but because he himself was the Word.

For “the Word in flesh” is one thing, and “the Word made flesh” another; that is, “the Word in a human being” is one thing, and “the Word a human being” another. For “flesh” is used in place of “human being” when it is said, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), just as in the saying, “All flesh together shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6). This does not mean without a soul or without a mind; rather, “all flesh” is as if it said, “every human being.”

Therefore the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed in the same way as that flesh and that human form from the Virgin Mary were assumed. The Spirit did not make blessed the dove, or that breath, or that fire, and join it to himself [Col. 0852] and to his person in an everlasting unity and indwelling. Nor is the nature of the Holy Spirit mutable and convertible, so that these things would not have been made from a creature, but that he himself would have been changeably transformed into one thing and then another, like water into ice.

Rather, these things appeared as they ought suitably to appear: the creature serving the Creator, who remains unchangeably in himself at his command, was changed and transformed in order to signify and demonstrate him as it was necessary for mortals that he be signified and demonstrated.

Accordingly, although that dove is called “the Spirit” (Matt. 3:16), and although it was said of that fire, “There appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire, which also rested upon each one of them, and they began to speak with tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:3–4)—so that it might show that the Spirit was signified through that fire just as through the dove—we nevertheless cannot say that the Holy Spirit is both God and a dove, or both God and fire [Note: [Col. 0852] Several manuscripts read: “Nevertheless, we cannot say that the Holy Spirit, one person, is the Holy Spirit and God and a dove.”], in the way that we say that the Son is both God and human being. Nor can we say this in the way that we call the Son “the Lamb of God,” not only because John the Baptist said, “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John 1:29), but also because the Evangelist John saw a slain Lamb in the Apocalypse (Rev. 5:6).

That prophetic vision was not displayed to bodily eyes through bodily forms, but in the spirit through spiritual images of bodies. The dove, however, and the fire were seen by the eyes by whoever saw them. Nevertheless, concerning the fire it may be debated whether it was seen by the eyes or by the spirit, because of the wording used. For it does not say, “They saw divided tongues like fire,” but, “They appeared to them.” We do not usually say “It appeared to me” with the same meaning as “I saw.” In those spiritual visions of bodily images, one may indeed say both “It appeared to me” and “I saw”; but in those things that are displayed to the eyes through an expressly bodily form, one does not usually say “It appeared to me,” but “I saw.”

Thus the question may be raised concerning that fire: in what manner was it seen? Was it inwardly in the spirit, as though outwardly, or truly outside, before the eyes of the flesh? But concerning the dove which is said to have descended in bodily form, no one has ever doubted that it was seen by the eyes.

Nor, in the way that we call the Son “the rock”—for it is written, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4)—can we call the Spirit “the dove” or “the fire.” That rock already existed in creation and was named through the manner of its action after Christ, whom it signified; just as that stone which Jacob placed at his head and anointed [Note: [Col. 0852] Thus Am., Er., and the manuscripts; Lov. reads, “placed at his head, and also the anointing.”], taking it up to signify the Lord (Gen. 28:18); and just as Isaac was Christ when he carried the wood for his own sacrifice (ibid. 22:6). A certain signifying action was added to things that already existed; but the dove and the fire suddenly came into being solely for the purpose of signifying these things.

These seem rather to me to be like the flame that appeared to Moses in the bush (Exod. 3:2), and like the pillar that the people followed in the wilderness (ibid. 13:21–22), and like the lightning and thunder [Col. 0853] that occurred when the Law was given on the mountain (ibid. 19:16). The bodily form of those things came into being for this purpose: that it might signify something and then pass away.

### CHAPTER VII

#### 12. Doubt Concerning Divine Appearances

Because of these bodily forms, which came into being temporarily in order to signify him and to demonstrate him as was appropriate to human senses, the Holy Spirit is also said to have been sent. Yet he was not called less than the Father, as the Son was on account of the form of a servant. For the form of a servant adhered to the unity of the person, whereas those bodily appearances appeared temporarily in order to demonstrate what was necessary, and afterwards ceased to exist.

Why, then, is the Father not also said to have been sent through those bodily appearances—the fire of the bush, the pillar of cloud or fire, the lightning on the mountain, and whatever similar things appeared at that time—when we learn from Scripture that he spoke openly to the patriarchs? If he himself was demonstrated through those modes and forms of creation, bodily expressed and presented to human sight, why is he not said to have been sent?

But if the Son was demonstrated through them, why is he said to have been sent only much later, when he was made from a woman, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. 4:4), since he was also sent earlier, when he appeared to the patriarchs through those mutable forms of creation?

Or, if it could not rightly be said that he was sent except when the Word was made flesh, why is the Holy Spirit said to have been sent, since no such embodiment took place in him?

But if, through those visible things commended in the Law and the Prophets, neither the Father nor the Son but the Holy Spirit was displayed [Note: [Col. 0853] Nearly only Lovaniensis reads, “nor the Holy Spirit.”], why is he himself now also said to have been sent, since he had already been sent through those means?

#### 13. The Problem of the Question

In the perplexity of this question, with the Lord’s help we must first inquire whether it was the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit; whether at one time the Father, at another the Son, and at another the Holy Spirit; or whether, without any distinction of persons, just as God is said to be one and alone—that is, the Trinity itself—appeared to the patriarchs through those forms of creation.

Next, whatever conclusion may be discovered or seem apparent, we must ask whether creation was formed solely for this purpose: that God might be displayed to human sight in the manner that he then judged appropriate; or whether angels, who already existed, were sent so that they might speak in the person of God, assuming a bodily form from bodily creation for the use of their ministry, as each occasion required; or whether they changed and transformed their own bodies—over which they are not subject, but which they rule as subjects—into appearances suited and appropriate to their actions, according to the power assigned to them by the Creator.

Finally, we shall consider the question we originally undertook to investigate: whether the Son and the Holy Spirit were also sent earlier; and, if they were sent, what difference there is between that mission and the one we read of in the Gospel; or whether none of them was sent except when either the Son was made from the Virgin Mary or the Holy Spirit appeared in visible form, either as a dove or in fiery tongues [Note: [Col. 0853] See below, book 3, chapter 1, §4.].

### CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0854]

#### 14. The Whole Trinity Is Invisible

Let us therefore set aside those who, with excessive carnality, have thought that the nature of the Word of God and of Wisdom—which remains in itself and renews all things, and which we call the only Son of God—is not merely mutable but also visible. In investigating divine matters, they have brought to the task a heart exceedingly gross, more audacious than reverent.

For the soul, although it is a spiritual substance, and although it too was made and could not have been made except by him through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3), is nevertheless mutable; it is not visible. This is what they believed concerning the Word itself and the Wisdom of God, by whom the soul was made. Yet that Wisdom is not only invisible, as the soul also is, but immutable, which the soul is not.

Its immutability is recalled when it is said, “Remaining in itself, it renews all things” (Wis. 7:27).

These men, attempting as it were to prop up the collapse of their error with testimonies from the divine Scriptures, bring forward a statement of the Apostle Paul. What was said of the one God alone, in whom the Trinity itself is understood, they take to have been said only of the Father and not also of the Son and the Holy Spirit: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory for ever and ever” (1 Tim. 1:17). They likewise appeal to the other passage: “Blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” (ibid. 6:15–16). I think we have already discussed sufficiently how these passages are to be understood.

### CHAPTER IX

#### 15. Against Those Who Believed That Only the Father Was Immortal and Invisible. Truth Must Be Sought in a Peaceful Spirit

But those who wish these statements to be understood not of the Son or the Holy Spirit, but only of the Father, say that the Son was visible—not through the flesh assumed from the Virgin, but also previously, through himself. “He himself,” they say, “appeared to the eyes of the patriarchs.”

If you say to them, “How, then, was the Son visible through himself? In that case he was also mortal through himself, so that what you wish to understand only of the Father may be established—namely, the statement, ‘Who alone possesses immortality.’ For if the Son is mortal on account of the flesh he assumed, allow him on account of that same flesh to be visible,” they reply that they do not call the Son mortal on account of the flesh, but that, just as he was visible before the flesh, so also he was mortal before the flesh.

For if they say that the Son is mortal on account of the flesh, then the Father alone, without the Son, no longer possesses immortality, because his Word, through whom all things were made, also possesses immortality. The Son did not lose his immortality merely because he assumed mortal flesh. Indeed, this could not happen even to a human soul, so that it would die together with the body, since the Lord himself says, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

Or, in fact, the Holy Spirit also assumed flesh? They will certainly be perplexed by this. If the Son is mortal on account of the flesh, how will they understand that the Father alone, without the Son and without the Holy Spirit, possesses immortality, when the Holy Spirit did not assume flesh? If the Holy Spirit does not possess immortality, then the Son is not mortal on account of the flesh. But if the Holy Spirit possesses immortality, then the statement “Who alone possesses immortality” was not said only of the Father.

[Col. 0855]

Accordingly, they think they can prove that the Son was mortal through himself even before the incarnation, because mutability itself may not improperly be called mortality, according to which the soul too is said to die—not because it is changed and transformed into a body or into some other substance, but because, in its own substance, whatever is now otherwise than it was is found to be mortal in proportion as it has ceased to be what it was.

Therefore, they say, before the Son of God was born from the Virgin Mary, he himself appeared to our fathers—not in one and the same form, but in many forms, differently and variously. He is visible through himself because, before flesh was assumed, his substance was perceptible to mortal eyes; and he is mortal insofar as he is mutable. So too the Holy Spirit, who appeared at one time as a dove and at another as fire.

Hence, they say, the statement “To the immortal, invisible, only God” and “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” applies not to the Trinity but exclusively and properly to the Father.

#### 16. Truth Is to Be Sought Peacefully

Let us therefore set aside these people, who were unable even to recognize the substance of the soul as invisible. It was consequently far beyond them to recognize that the substance of the one and only God—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—not only remains invisible but also immutable, and therefore exists in true and complete immortality.

We, who say that God—neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit—has ever appeared to bodily eyes except through a bodily creature subject to his power, should seek the truth in the peace of the Catholic faith and in a peaceful spirit. We should be ready to be corrected if we are reproved fraternally and rightly; ready also, even if we are wounded by an enemy, provided that he speaks the truth.

We must ask whether God appeared to our fathers indiscriminately before Christ came in the flesh; or whether some one person of the Trinity appeared; or whether the persons appeared separately, as it were in succession.

### CHAPTER X

#### 17. Whether God the Trinity Appeared Indiscriminately to the Patriarchs, or Some Person of the Trinity Appeared. God’s Appearance to Adam. The Same Appearance. Abraham’s Vision

First, concerning what is written in Genesis—that God spoke with the human being whom he had formed from clay—if, setting aside figurative meaning, we are considering the matter so that faith in the event may also be maintained literally, God appears at that time to have spoken with the human being in human form.

This is not expressly stated in the book, but the context of the reading [Note: [Col. 0855] The printed editions read “of the speech”; the manuscripts read “of the reading.”] suggests it, especially where it is written that Adam heard the voice of God walking in the garden toward evening, and hid himself among the trees in the garden, and that when God said, “Adam, where are you?” he replied, “I heard your voice, and I hid myself from your presence, because I am naked” (Gen. 3:8–10).

For I do not see how such a walking and conversation of God can be understood literally except in human form. [Col. 0856] It cannot be said that only a voice occurred where God is said to have walked, or that the one who was walking in the place was not visible, since Adam also says that he hid himself from the face of God.

Who, then, was that one? Was it the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit? Or was God—the Trinity itself, without distinction—speaking to the human being in human form?

The actual continuity of Scripture nowhere seems to pass from one person to another. The one who appears to speak to the first human being is the one who said, “Let there be light,” and “Let there be a firmament” (Gen. 1:3, 6), and the other commands throughout the individual days—the one whom we customarily understand as God the Father, saying that whatever he wished to make should come into being.

For he made all things through his Word, and according to the rule of right faith we know that this Word is his only Son. If, then, God the Father spoke to the first human being, and he himself walked in the garden toward evening, and the sinner hid himself from his face among the trees of the garden, why should we not understand that he himself appeared to Abraham, Moses, and whomever he wished, and in whatever manner he wished, through a mutable and visible creature subject to him, while he himself remained in himself and in his substance, which is immutable and invisible?

Yet it could have happened that Scripture secretly passed from one person to another. After narrating that the Father said, “Let there be light,” and the other things which he is said to have made through the Word, it might then indicate that the Son was speaking to the first human being [Note: [Col. 0856] Thus read by many manuscripts. The printed editions read, “indicates through the Son.”], without explaining this openly, but intimating it to those who could understand.

#### 18. The Matter Remains Hidden

Whoever, therefore, possesses the strength to penetrate this secret with the mind’s keen insight, so that it may become clear to him whether the Father too can appear through a visible creature to human eyes, or whether only the Son and the Holy Spirit can do so, may proceed, if he can, to investigate, express, and discuss these matters.

Nevertheless, insofar as this testimony of Scripture is concerned—where God spoke with the human being—the matter seems to me hidden. For it is not even evident whether Adam was accustomed to see God with bodily eyes, especially since there is a major question concerning what kind of eyes were opened for them when they tasted the forbidden food (ibid. 3:7); for those eyes had been closed before they tasted it.

This, however, I would not rashly assert: if that Scripture suggests some bodily place called paradise, God could in no way have walked there except in some bodily form. It can indeed be said that only voices occurred, which the human being heard, without his seeing any form. Nor, because it is written that “Adam hid himself from the face of God,” does it immediately follow that he was accustomed to see God’s face.

For what if Adam himself could not see God, but feared that he would be seen by the one whose voice he had heard and whose presence he had perceived as he walked? Cain likewise said to God, “I shall hide myself from your face” (ibid. 4:14). Yet we are not thereby compelled to admit that Cain was accustomed to see God’s face with bodily eyes in any visible form, even though he had heard the voice of the one who questioned him and spoke with him about his crime.

What sort of speech God then caused to sound in the external ears of human beings—especially when speaking to the first human being—is difficult to discover, [Col. 0857] and this is not the subject we have undertaken in this work.

Nevertheless, if only voices and sounds occurred by which a certain sensible presence of God was offered to those first human beings, I do not know why I should not understand the person of God the Father to have been present there. His person is also displayed in the voice that occurred when Jesus appeared in glory on the mountain before three disciples (Matt. 17:5); and in the voice when a dove descended upon the baptized Jesus (ibid. 3:17); and in the voice when he cried out to the Father concerning his glorification, and the answer was given to him, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28).

This is not because the voice could have occurred without the work of the Son and the Holy Spirit—for the Trinity works inseparably—but because that voice occurred which displayed the person of the Father alone. In the same way, the human form from the Virgin Mary was brought about by the Trinity, but it belongs to the person of the Son alone: the invisible Trinity brought about the visible person of the Son alone.

Nothing prevents us from understanding those voices made to Adam not only as having been made by the Trinity, but also as displaying a person of that same Trinity. For in the passage where it was said, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17), we are compelled to understand the Father alone. Jesus cannot be believed or understood to be the son of the Holy Spirit, or his own son.

Likewise, where the voice sounded, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again,” we acknowledge the person of the Father alone. For this was the answer to the Lord’s voice in which he had said, “Father, glorify your Son,” which he could have said only to God the Father, not to the Holy Spirit, whose son he was not.

But where it is written, “And the Lord God said to Adam,” there is no reason why the Trinity itself should not be understood.

#### 19. Abraham’s Vision

Similarly, when it is written, “And the Lord said to Abraham, ‘Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house,’” it is not clear whether only a voice was made for Abraham’s ears, or whether something also appeared to his eyes.

A little later, however, it is said somewhat more plainly: “And the Lord appeared to Abraham, and said to him, ‘To your seed I will give this land’” (Gen. 12:1, 7). But even there it is not stated in what form the Lord appeared to him, or whether it was the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit who appeared to him.

Perhaps some think that the Son appeared to Abraham because it is not written, “God appeared to him,” but, “The Lord appeared to him.” They suppose that the Son is properly called “Lord,” since the Apostle says: “Although there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:5–6).

But God the Father is also found called Lord in many places, as in the passage, “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. 2:7), and, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109:1).

The Holy Spirit too is found called Lord, where the Apostle says, “The Lord is the Spirit.” And lest anyone suppose that the Son was meant, and that he was called “Spirit” because of his incorporeal substance, he continues: “But where the Spirit [Col. 0858] of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). No one will doubt that the Spirit of the Lord is the Holy Spirit.

Here, therefore, it is not evident whether some person of the Trinity, or God himself—the Trinity, concerning whom it was said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13)—appeared to Abraham.

Under the oak of Mamre he saw three men. He invited them, received them as guests, and served them while they ate. Yet Scripture begins to narrate the event in such a way that it does not say, “Three men appeared to him,” but, “The Lord appeared to him.”

Then, explaining how the Lord appeared to him, it adds the account of the three men whom Abraham invites in the plural number to receive as guests. Afterwards he addresses them in the singular, as one person, and as one person promises him a son through Sarah. Scripture calls him “Lord,” just as at the beginning of the same account it says, “The Lord appeared to Abraham.”

Abraham therefore invites them, washes their feet, and escorts them as they depart, as though they were human beings. Yet he speaks as with the Lord God, both when a son is promised to him and when the destruction impending over Sodom is announced (Gen. 18).

### CHAPTER XI

#### 20. Concerning the Same Vision

This passage of Scripture requires no slight or passing consideration. If one man had appeared, what else would those who say that the Son was visible in his substance even before he was born from the Virgin have proclaimed him to be but the Son himself? “For,” they say, “it was said of the Father, ‘To the invisible only God’” (1 Tim. 1:17).

Yet I could still ask how, before assuming flesh, he was found in the form of a human being, since his feet were washed and he ate human food. How could this have happened while he was still in the form of God, not considering equality with God something to be seized? Had he already emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being (Phil. 2:6–7)? We know that he did this through the birth from the Virgin.

How, then, before he had done this, did one man appear to Abraham? Or was that form not real?

I could raise these questions if one man had appeared to Abraham and were believed to be the Son of God. But when three men appeared, and none of them was said to be greater than the others in form, age, or power, why should we not understand that the equality of the Trinity was visibly intimated through visible creation, and that in the three persons there was one and the same substance?

#### 21. The Three Men and the Two Angels

For, lest anyone should think that one among the three had been indicated as greater and that he should be understood as the Lord, the Son of God, while the other two were his angels [Note: [Col. 0858] Most manuscripts read, “the other two, those angels of his”], since three had appeared but Abraham there spoke to one as Lord, Holy Scripture did not fail to forestall and contradict such future thoughts and opinions.

A little later it says that two angels came to Lot, and that this righteous man, who deserved to be rescued from the destruction of Sodom, also spoke to one of them as Lord.

Scripture continues in this way:

“And the Lord departed after he had ceased speaking to [Col. 0859] Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.”

### CHAPTER XII

#### Lot’s Vision Examined

“Two angels came to Sodom in the evening.”

Here we must consider more attentively what I set out to demonstrate. Abraham was certainly speaking with three, and he addressed one of them individually as Lord.

Perhaps someone will say [Note: [Col. 0859] Erasmus, Lugdunensis, Veneta, and Lovaniensis read, “Perhaps someone will say”; manuscript M reads, “Perhaps someone will inquire”]: “He recognized one of the three as Lord, and the other two as his angels.”

What, then, does Scripture mean when it subsequently says, “The Lord departed after he had ceased speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place; but two angels came to Sodom in the evening”?

Had the one who was recognized as Lord among the three perhaps departed and sent the two angels who had been with him to destroy Sodom?

Let us therefore examine what follows.

“Two angels,” it says, “came to Sodom in the evening. Lot was sitting at the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed with his face to the ground, and said, ‘Behold, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant.’”

Here it is clear that they were two angels, that they were invited as guests in the plural, and that they were honorably addressed as “lords,” even though perhaps they were thought to be human beings.

#### 22. The Two Angels Called “Lord”

Yet another difficulty arises. If they were not recognized as the angels of God, why would Lot bow with his face to the ground? Why, then, are hospitality and food offered to them as though they needed such human kindness?

Whatever may be hidden here, let us now pursue the matter we have undertaken.

Two appear, both are called angels [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “Two angels appear, and both are called lords”], they are invited in the plural, as though Lot speaks with both in the plural, until they leave Sodom.

Then Scripture continues:

“And it happened that, after they had brought them outside, they said, ‘Save your life; do not look back, and do not remain in all this region. Go to the mountain, and there you will be saved, lest you be caught.’ But Lot said to them, ‘I beg you, Lord, because your servant has found mercy in your sight’” (Gen. 19:1–19), and so forth.

What does he mean by saying to them, “I beg you, Lord,” if the one who was Lord had already departed and sent the angels? Why does he say, “I beg you, Lord,” and not, “I beg you, lords”?

Or, if he wished to address one of them, why does Scripture say, “Lot said to them, ‘I beg you, Lord, because your servant has found mercy in your sight’”?

Should we understand here also two persons in the plural number, while the same two are addressed as one, as one Lord God of one substance?

Which two persons should we understand here: the Father and the Son, the Father and the Holy Spirit, or the Son and the Holy Spirit? Perhaps the last possibility is more fitting.

For they said that they had been sent, which is what we say of the Son and the Holy Spirit. We never encounter the Father being sent in the Scriptures.

### CHAPTER XIII

#### 23. The Vision in the Bush

When Moses was sent to lead the people of Israel out of Egypt, it is written that the Lord appeared to him in this way:

“He was tending the sheep of Jethro, the priest of Midian, his father-in-law. He drove the sheep into the wilderness and came to the mountain of God, Horeb. The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame [Col. 0860] of fire from the bush. He saw that the bush was burning with fire, but the bush was not consumed. Moses said, ‘I will go and see this great sight, why the bush is not consumed.’ When the Lord saw that he had come to see, the Lord called to him [Note: [Col. 0860] The editions read, “called to him”; the particle *to* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint.] from the bush, saying, ‘I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’” (Exod. 3:1–6).

Here too he is first called “the angel of the Lord,” and then “God.” Is the angel, then, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?

It may rightly be understood as the Savior himself, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Whose are the patriarchs, and from whom, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom. 9:5). Since he is God over all, blessed for ever, he may also rightly be understood here as the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.

But why was he first called the angel of the Lord when he appeared in a flame of fire from the bush? Was it because he was one of the many angels, but through an administrative arrangement represented the person of his Lord? Or was some creature assumed which would appear visibly for the present matter, and from which sensible voices would be produced, so that the presence of the Lord might be displayed through the creature subject to him even to the bodily senses of human beings, as was appropriate?

If he was one of the angels, who could easily affirm whether the person of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, or of God the Father, or of the Trinity itself—the one and only God—had been entrusted to him to announce, so that he might say, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”?

We cannot say that the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is the Son of God while the Father is not; or that he is the Holy Spirit; nor will anyone dare deny that the Trinity itself, which we believe and understand to be one God, is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.

For he is not the God of those patriarchs who is not God.

Moreover, if not only the Father is God, as even all heretics concede, but the Son also—which, whether they wish it or not, they are compelled to confess, since the Apostle says, “who is over all, God blessed for ever”—and if the Holy Spirit is also God, since the same Apostle says, “Therefore glorify God in your body,” after saying, “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6:20, 19); and if these three are one God, as Catholic soundness of faith believes, it is not sufficiently clear which person in the Trinity that angel represented, or whether he represented any particular person or the Trinity itself, if he was one of the other angels.

But if a creature was assumed for the use of the present matter—one that would appear to human eyes, sound in human ears, and be called both the angel of the Lord and Lord and God—then this God cannot be understood as the Father, but either as the Son or as the Holy Spirit.

I do not recall, however, that the Holy Spirit is called an angel anywhere, though this may be understood from his work. For it is said of him, “He will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 16:13); and certainly the Greek word *angelos* means “messenger” in Latin.

Concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, however, we read most clearly in the prophet that he was called “the Angel of the Great Counsel” (Isa. 9:6), although both the Holy Spirit and the Son of God are God and Lord of the angels.

### CHAPTER XIV

#### 24. The Vision in the Pillar of Cloud and Fire

Likewise, at the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, it is written:

“God went before them: by day in a pillar of cloud, to show them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not fail to remain before the people” (Exod. 13:21–22).

Who could doubt here also that God appeared to mortal eyes through a creature subject to him, and likewise bodily, not through his own substance? But whether it was the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself, the one God, is likewise not apparent.

Nor, as I understand it, is this distinguished in the passage where it is written:

“And the majesty of the Lord appeared in the cloud, and the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, ‘I have heard the murmuring of the children of Israel’” (ibid. 16:10–12), and so forth.

### CHAPTER XV

#### 25. The Vision on Sinai. Whether the Trinity or Some Particular Person Spoke in That Vision

As for the clouds, voices, lightning, trumpet, and smoke on Mount Sinai, it is said:

“Mount Sinai was entirely covered with smoke because God had descended upon it in fire, and its smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace. The sound of the trumpet grew exceedingly strong. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice” (ibid. 19:18–19).

A little later, after the Law had been given in the Ten Commandments, it is said accordingly:

“All the people saw the voices, the lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking.”

And shortly afterward:

“All the people stood far off; but Moses entered into the cloud where God was, and the Lord spoke to Moses” (ibid. 20:18, 21), and so forth.

What can I say about this except that no one is so foolish as to believe that smoke, fire, cloud, mist, and things of this kind are the substance of the Word and Wisdom of God, which is Christ, or of the Holy Spirit? As for God the Father, not even the Arians have ever dared to say this.

All those things, therefore, came about while creation served the Creator, and were presented to human senses in accordance with an appropriate dispensation.

Unless, perhaps, because it is said, “Moses entered into the cloud where God was,” carnal thought should suppose that the people saw the cloud, while within the cloud Moses saw with bodily eyes the Son of God, whom the delirious heretics wish to have been seen in his own [Col. 0861] substance [Note: [Col. 0861] One Vatican manuscript reads, “visible.”].

Let Moses indeed have seen him with bodily eyes, if not only the Wisdom of God, which is Christ, but even the soul of any human being, and of any wise person whatsoever, can be seen with bodily eyes.

Or, because it is written concerning the elders of Israel that “they saw the place where the God of Israel had stood, and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the appearance of the firmament of heaven” (ibid. 24:10), must we therefore believe that the Word and Wisdom of God stood in its own substance within the space of an earthly place—he who “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)?

Must we believe that the Word of God, through whom all things were made (John 1:3), is mutable, so that it now contracts itself and now stretches itself out? May the Lord cleanse the hearts [Col. 0862] of his faithful from such thoughts.

Rather, as we have often said, all these visible and sensible things are displayed through a creature subject to God, in order to signify the invisible and intelligible God—not the Father only, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit—“from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things” (Rom. 11:36).

Although the invisible things of God are perceived and understood, from the creation of the world, through the things that have been made, so too are his eternal power and divinity (ibid. 1:20).

26. But as regards what we have now undertaken, even on Mount Sinai I do not see how, through all those things that were terrifyingly displayed to mortal senses, it can be determined whether the Trinity as a whole, or the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit in particular was speaking.
