Nevertheless, if we may modestly and hesitantly conjecture something here without rashly asserting it, if one Person of the Trinity may be understood, why should we not understand the Holy Spirit in preference, since the Law itself, which was given there on tablets of stone, is said to have been written by the finger of God (Exod. 31:18)—a name by which we know the Holy Spirit to be signified in the Gospel (Luke 11:20)? Moreover, fifty days are counted from the slaying of the lamb and the celebration of Passover until the day on which these things began to take place on Mount Sinai; just as, after the Lord’s Passion, fifty days are counted from his resurrection, and the Holy Spirit promised by the Son of God came.

At his very coming, which we read about in the Acts of the Apostles, fire appeared through the division of tongues and came to rest upon each of them (Acts 2:1–4). This corresponds to Exodus, where it is written: “Now Mount Sinai was entirely smoking, because God descended upon it in fire”; and somewhat later: “The appearance of the majesty of the Lord was like a burning fire upon the summit of the mountain before the children of Israel.” Or, if these things happened because neither the Father nor the Son could there be presented in that manner without the Holy Spirit, in the manner in which the Law itself had to be written, we recognize that God appeared there—not through his substance, which remains invisible and unchangeable, but through that form of created being. Yet, insofar as my understanding permits, we do not see any one Person of the Trinity indicated by some distinctive sign of its own.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 27. How Moses Saw God

There is also a point by which many are accustomed to be troubled, because it is written: “And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as one speaks to his friend”; while shortly afterward the same Moses says: “If therefore I have found favor before you, show yourself plainly to me, that I may see you; so that I may find favor before you, and know that this people is your nation.” A little later Moses said again to the Lord: “Show me your majesty.”

What is this? In all the events described above, God was thought to have been seen through his substance; hence, in their wretchedness, some have believed that the Son of God was visible not through a creature but through himself. And Moses, who had entered into the cloud, seemed to have entered it for this purpose: that a dark cloud might indeed be displayed to the eyes of the people, while he, within, heard the words of God as though contemplating his face. And how was it said, “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as one speaks to his friend,” when the same man says, “If I have found favor before you, show yourself plainly to me”?

Certainly he knew what he was seeing bodily, and was spiritually seeking the true vision of God. For that speech which took place through voices was modulated as though it were a friend speaking to a friend. But who sees God the Father with bodily eyes? And who sees with bodily eyes “the Word which was in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” through whom all things were made (John 1:1, 3)? And who sees the Spirit of wisdom with bodily eyes?

What else is “Show yourself plainly to me, that I may see you” than “Show me your substance”? If Moses had not said this, fools who think that God’s substance was made visible to his eyes through the things described or enacted above might somehow be endured. But when it is shown here most plainly that this was not granted even to one who desired it, who would dare to say that, through forms like those that had also visibly appeared to him, it was not a creature serving God but that very thing which God is that appeared to the eyes of any mortal?

28. And indeed, as to what the Lord says afterward to Moses—“You cannot see my face and live; for no human being shall see my face and live”—the Lord also said: “Behold, there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock. As soon as my majesty passes by, I will place you in a cleft [Note: [Col. 0863] The printed editions have *in the cave* here. But in the passages below, as in most of the old manuscripts throughout, the reading is *in the cleft*.] of the rock; and I will cover you with my hand until I pass by. Then I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back; but my face shall not appear to you” (Exod. 33:11–23).

## CHAPTER XVII

### How God’s Back Was Seen. Faith in Christ’s Resurrection. The Catholic Church Alone Is the Place from Which God’s Back Is Seen. God’s Back Seen by the Israelites. The Opinion That God the Father Alone Was Never Seen by the Fathers Is Rash

It is not incongruous to understand this as prefigured in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that his “back” is taken to mean his flesh, in which he was born of a Virgin, died, and rose again—whether it was called “back” because of the later position [Note: [Col. 0863] Most manuscripts have *lastness* or *finality*.] of mortality, or because he deigned to assume it near the end of the age, that is, later. His “face,” however, is that form of God in which he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God the Father (Phil. 2:6), and which no one can see and live.

Or perhaps it is because, after this life, in which we are exiles from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), and in which “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15), we shall see him face to face, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 13:12). For of this life it is said in the Psalms: “Yet every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38:6); and again: “For no living person shall be justified before you” (Ps. 143:2). In this life also, according to John, “it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know,” he says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). He clearly wished this to be understood as occurring after this life, when we have paid the debt of death and received the promise of resurrection.

Or perhaps it is because, even now, insofar as we spiritually understand the Wisdom of God through whom all things were made, we die to carnal affections, reckoning this world dead to us and ourselves also dead to this world, and saying what the Apostle said: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Of this death he likewise said: “But if you have died with Christ, why, as though you were still living in the world, do you make judgments concerning it?” (Col. 2:20).

Therefore, not without reason will no one be able to see the face—that is, the very manifestation—of God’s Wisdom and live. For this is the appearance for which everyone longs who seeks to love God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind. In order to contemplate it, the person who loves his neighbor as himself also builds up his neighbor as much as he can; upon these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:37–40).

This too is signified in Moses himself. For after he had said, out of his love for God, with which he burned above all else, “If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself plainly to me, so that I may find favor before you,” he immediately added, out of love for his neighbor: “And so that I may know that this people is your nation.”

That appearance, then, is what draws every rational soul toward itself by desire—one made more ardent the purer it is, and purer the more it rises toward spiritual things; and the more it rises toward spiritual things, the more it dies to carnal things. But while we are exiles from the Lord and walk by faith, not by appearance (2 Cor. 5:6–7), we must see Christ’s back—that is, his flesh—through faith itself: standing upon the solid foundation of faith, which the rock signifies, and contemplating it from such a very secure vantage point, namely, in the Catholic Church, of which it was said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18).

For the more certainly we love Christ than we desire to see his face, the more we recognize in his back how greatly Christ first loved us.

29. But faith in his resurrection, in that very flesh, saves and justifies us. “If you believe,” he says, “in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:9). And again: “He was delivered up,” he says, “for our offenses, and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25).

Therefore the resurrection of the Lord’s body is the merit of our faith. Even his enemies believe that this flesh died in the suffering of the cross, but they do not believe that it rose again. Firmly believing this, we contemplate it as though from the solidity of the rock. From there we await with certain hope the adoption, the redemption of our body (Rom. 8:23), because we hope for this in the members of Christ, which we ourselves are; and we recognize, through the soundness of faith, that it has already been perfected in him as in our head.

For this reason he does not wish his back to be seen until he has passed by, so that people may believe in his resurrection. *Pascha* is said to be a Hebrew word, translated “Passage.” Hence the evangelist John also says: “Before the festival of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13:1).

30. But those who believe this, yet believe it not in the Catholic Church but in some schism or heresy, do not see the Lord’s back from the place that is beside him. For what does the Lord’s statement mean: “Behold, there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock”?

What earthly place is beside the Lord, unless that which touches him spiritually is meant? For what place is not beside the Lord, who “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1); of whom it is said, “Heaven is my throne, and earth is the footstool of my feet”; and who said, “What house will you build for me? Or what is the place of my rest? Did not my hand make all these things?” (Isa. 66:1–2).

But clearly the place beside him is understood to be that in which one stands upon the rock: the Catholic Church itself, where one sees the Lord’s Passover—that is, the Lord’s passing over—and his back—that is, his body—salvifically, if one believes in his resurrection.

“And you shall stand,” he says, “upon the rock, as soon as my majesty passes by.” Indeed, as soon as the Lord’s majesty passed by in the Lord’s glorification, when, rising again, he ascended to the Father, we were established upon the rock. Peter himself was then made firm, so that he could preach with confidence the one whom, before he was made firm, he had denied three times out of fear (Matt. 26:70–74). He had indeed already been placed, by predestination, in the cleft of the rock, but the Lord’s hand was still placed over him, so that he could not see. He was going to see the Lord’s back, but the Lord had not yet passed over—from death to life—and had not yet been glorified through the resurrection.

31. For what follows in Exodus also says: “I will cover you with my hand until I pass by; and I will remove my hand, and then you shall see my back.” Many Israelites, of whom Moses was then a figure, believed in him after the Lord’s resurrection, as though they were now seeing his back, his hand having been removed from their eyes.

Thus the evangelist recalls such a prophecy from Isaiah: “Make the heart of this people fat, and stop up their ears, and weigh down their eyes” (Isa. 6:10; Matt. 13:15). Finally, in the Psalm it is not improperly understood as being spoken in their person: “For day and night your hand was heavy upon me.”

Perhaps “day” refers to the time when he performed manifest miracles and was not recognized by them; “night,” however, to the time when he died in his Passion, when they more certainly thought that he had been killed and extinguished like any other human being.

But after he had passed over, so that his back might be seen, and the Apostle Peter preached to them that Christ had to suffer and rise again, they were pierced with the pain of repentance (Acts 2:37, 41). Thus what is said at the beginning of that Psalm came to pass in those who were baptized: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.”

Therefore, after it had been said, “Your hand was heavy upon me,” as though the Lord were passing over so that he might now remove his hand and his back might be seen, there follows the voice of one grieving and confessing, and receiving forgiveness of sins through faith in the Lord’s resurrection: “I turned in my anguish, while the thorn was being fastened into me. I acknowledged my sin, and I did not cover my iniquity. I said, ‘I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Ps. 32:1–5).

We must not be so enveloped in the dense cloud of the flesh that we suppose the Lord’s face to be invisible but his back visible. In the form of a servant, both appeared visibly; but in the form of God, far be it that anything of this sort should be imagined. Far be it that the Word of God and the Wisdom of God should have a face on one side and a back on the other, like a human body, or that they should be changed at all by any form, motion, place, or time.

32. Therefore, if the Lord Jesus Christ was displayed in those voices that occurred in Exodus and in all those bodily manifestations—or Christ on some occasions, as consideration of this passage suggests, and the Holy Spirit on others, as what we said above indicates—this does not establish that God the Father was never seen by the Fathers in some such form.

For many such visions occurred in those times without the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit being explicitly named and identified in them. Yet, because certain highly probable indications were present through various signs, it would be exceedingly rash to say that God the Father never appeared to the Fathers or Prophets through any visible forms.

That opinion was produced by those who could not understand, within the unity of the Trinity, what was said: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God” (1 Tim. 1:17); and, “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). Sound faith understands these statements as referring to the very highest and wholly divine, unchangeable substance, in which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and only God.

Those visions, however, were made through changeable creation subject to the unchangeable God. They displayed God not as he properly is, but symbolically, in the manner required by the circumstances and times of the things concerned.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Daniel’s Vision

Although I do not know how these people understand the fact that the Ancient of Days appeared to Daniel, from whom the Son of Man—whom he deigned to be for our sake—is understood to have received the kingdom; that is, from the one who says to him in the Psalms: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:7–8), and who placed all things under his feet (Ps. 8:8).

If, then, both the Father, who gave the kingdom, and the Son, who received it, appeared to Daniel in bodily form, how do these people say that the Father was never seen by the Prophets, and that only the one whom no human being has seen or can see should be understood as invisible?

For Daniel narrated as follows: “I was watching,” he says, “until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels were blazing fire, and a stream of fire drew [Note: [Col. 0866] The printed editions have *passed by*. Nearly all manuscripts have *drew*; so also the Septuagint, *heilken*.] before him. A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and the books were opened,” and so forth.

A little later he says: “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming with the clouds of heaven. He reached the Ancient of Days, and was presented before him. And to him were given dominion, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7:9–14). Behold: the Father giving, and the Son receiving, an everlasting kingdom; and both are visible in bodily form before the prophet who is seeing.

Therefore it is not incongruous to believe that God the Father too is accustomed to appear to mortals in such a manner.

34. Unless perhaps someone should say [Note: [Col. 0867] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and the Louvain edition have *unless perhaps someone should say*. Manuscript M has *unless perhaps someone says*.] that the Father is not visible for this reason: because he appeared before a sleeping person; whereas the Son and the Holy Spirit are visible because Moses saw all those things while awake.

As though Moses saw the Word and Wisdom of God with bodily eyes! Or as though a spirit—even a human spirit, which gives life to this flesh—or the very bodily thing called wind could be seen! How much less, then, can the Spirit of God be seen, who surpasses the minds of all human beings and angels by the ineffable excellence of the divine substance?

Would anyone be driven into such an error as to dare say that the Son and the Holy Spirit are visible even to people who are awake, but that the Father is visible only to those who are dreaming? How, then, do they understand the statement concerning the Father alone: “Whom no human being has seen or can see”? Do human beings cease to be human beings when they sleep?

Or can he who is able to form a bodily likeness to signify himself through the visions of sleeping people not form bodily creation itself to signify himself to the eyes of those who are awake? His very substance, by which he is what he is, cannot be displayed to the sleeping through any bodily likeness or to the waking through any bodily form—not only the substance of the Father, but also that of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

And certainly, those who are moved by the visions of people who are awake so as to believe that not the Father but only the Son or the Holy Spirit appeared bodily to human sight—without mentioning the great breadth of the sacred Scriptures and their manifold interpretation, from which no sane person should assert that the Person of the Father was nowhere displayed to the eyes of the awake through some bodily form—what, I ask, do they say about our father Abraham?

While he was certainly awake and serving, Scripture first says, “The Lord appeared to Abraham”; then not one or two but three men appeared, and none of them is said to have stood out above the others, shone more honorably, or acted with greater authority (Gen. 18:1).

35. Therefore, since in our threefold division we first undertook to ask (above, chap. 7) whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit; or at one time the Father, at another the Son, and at another the Holy Spirit; or, without any distinction of Persons, the one and only God—that is, the Trinity itself—appeared to the Fathers through those forms of creation, after examining as many passages of the sacred Scriptures as we could, and insofar as seemed sufficient, the modest and cautious consideration of the divine mysteries persuades me of nothing other than this: we should not rashly say which Person of the Trinity appeared to any Father or Prophet in some bodily form or likeness, unless the context of the reading places around it some probable indications.

For that very nature, substance, essence—or whatever other name should be given to that which God is, whatever it may be—cannot be seen bodily. But through created beings subject to him, we must believe that not only the Son or the Holy Spirit but also the Father could give mortal senses a sign of himself through bodily form or likeness.

Since this is so, let the length of this second book not advance too far; let us examine what remains in what follows.

# BOOK THREE

In this book it is asked whether, in those appearances of God made through bodily forms of which the preceding book spoke, only a created thing was formed, in which God was displayed to human sight in whatever manner he then judged appropriate; or whether angels who already existed were sent in such a way that they spoke in the person of God, assuming a bodily form from corporeal creation, or transforming their own bodies into whatever forms were suited to their actions, according to the power given to them by the Creator; while God’s own essence itself was never seen through itself.

[Col. 0867]

## PROEM

### 1. Why He Writes About the Trinity. What He Desires from His Readers. What Was Said in the Preceding Book

Let those who wish believe that I would rather labor by reading than by dictating what is to be read. Those who do not wish to believe this, but both can and desire to test it, should provide whatever, through reading, may be offered in response either to my investigations or to the questions of others—questions which, because of the office I bear in Christ’s service and because of the zeal with which I burn to fortify our faith against the error of carnal and merely animal human beings, I must endure.

Let them see how easily I can abstain from this labor, and with what joy I could keep my pen at rest. But if what we have read on these matters either has not been sufficiently published in the Latin language, or cannot be found, or can at least be found by us only with difficulty; and if we do not possess such a command of Greek that we can in any way be found capable of reading and understanding books on such subjects—although I do not doubt that, in this kind of literature, all that we can profitably seek is contained in what has been translated for us, little though it is—and if I cannot resist the brothers when, by the right through which I became their servant, they insist that I should serve their praiseworthy pursuits in Christ with my tongue and pen, those two steeds driven within me by charity; and if I myself confess that by writing I have learned many things that I did not know, then no lazy person or highly educated person should regard my labor as superfluous, since it is to no small extent necessary for many diligent people and many unlearned people, among whom I too am included.

Accordingly, supported and assisted greatly by what we have already read that others have written on this subject, I have undertaken to seek and discuss what I judge may piously be sought and discussed concerning the Trinity, the one supreme and supremely good God—seeking with his encouragement and discussing with his help. If no other writings of this kind exist, let there be something for those who wish and are able to have and read; but if they already exist, then the more easily may some be found, the more such writings there may be.

2. Certainly, in all my writings I desire not only a devout reader but also a free critic—especially in these writings, where I wish the magnitude of the question itself could find as many discoverers as it has opponents.

Nevertheless, just as I do not want my reader devoted to me, so I do not want my critic devoted to himself. Let the reader love me no more than the Catholic faith; let the critic love himself no more than the Catholic truth.

To the reader I say: “Do not serve my writings as though they were canonical Scriptures. But whenever you find in them something you did not previously believe, believe it without hesitation; whereas, if something was not certain to you in them, do not hold it firmly unless you understand it to be certain.”

To the critic I say: “Do not correct my writings according to your own opinion or contentiousness, but according to divine reading or unshaken reason. If you grasp something true in them, it is not mine merely by its existence; but by understanding and loving it, let it be both yours and mine. If, however, you convict me of something false, it was mine through error; but once it is avoided, let it be neither yours nor mine.”

3. Let this third book, then, take its beginning from the point at which the second had arrived. When we had reached the point at which we wished to show that the Son is not therefore less than the Father because the Father sent him and he was sent, nor the Holy Spirit less than both because the Gospel says that he was sent both by one and by the other, we undertook to ask the following.

Since the Son was sent to the place where he already was—for he came into this world, and he was in this world (John 1:10); and since the Holy Spirit too was sent to the place where he himself already was, because “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,” and “that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice” (Wis. 1:7)—was the Lord sent for this reason: that he was born in the flesh from what was hidden, and appeared to human eyes as though he had gone forth from the bosom of the Father in the form of a servant?

And was the Holy Spirit sent for this reason: that he too was seen in bodily form, as a dove (Matt. 3:16), and in divided tongues, like fire (Acts 2:3)? Was their being sent, then, their proceeding from spiritual secrecy into the sight of mortals in some bodily form? Since the Father did not do this, is he said only to have sent, and not also to have been sent?

Next it was asked why the Father too was not at some time said to have been sent, if it was he who was displayed through those bodily forms that appeared to the eyes of the ancients. But if the Son was then being displayed, why would he be said to have been sent only so much later, when the fullness of time came for him to be born of a woman (Gal. 4:4), since he was already being sent when he appeared bodily in those forms?

Or, if it is not rightly said that he was sent except when the Word became flesh (John 1:14), why is the Holy Spirit read to have been sent, since no such incarnation took place in his case?

But if, through those ancient manifestations, neither the Father nor the Son but the Holy Spirit was being displayed, why would he himself now also be said to have been sent, since he had already been sent in those ways?

Next we subdivided the question so that these matters might be treated with the greatest care, and we made the inquiry threefold. One part was explained in the second book; two remain, and I shall now undertake to discuss them.

For it has already been asked and treated whether, in those ancient bodily forms and visions, it was not only the Father, nor only the Son, nor only the Holy Spirit who appeared, but either the Lord God without distinction—understood as the Trinity itself—or any Person of the Trinity whom the indications surrounding the text of the reading signified.

## CHAPTER I

### 4. What Must Be Said Next

Now, then, let us first ask what follows. For in the second place in that division was the question whether only a created thing was formed for this work, in which God was displayed to human sight in whatever manner he then judged appropriate; or whether angels who already existed were sent in such a way that they spoke in the person of God, assuming a bodily form from corporeal creation for the use of their ministry; or whether they changed and transformed their own body—which they are not subject to, but rule as subject to them [Note: [Col. 0870] The printed editions have *which they carry*. Most manuscripts have *which they rule*.]—into whatever forms they wished, forms suited and adapted to their actions, according to the power given to them by the Creator.

After this part of the question has been treated as far as the Lord grants, we must finally examine what we had undertaken to investigate: whether the Son and the Holy Spirit were also sent previously; and, if so, what difference there is between that mission and the one we read about in the Gospel; or whether none of them was sent until either the Son was made from the Virgin Mary or the Holy Spirit appeared in visible form, whether as a dove or in tongues of fire (above, book 2, chap. 7, §13).

5. But I confess that it exceeds the powers of my intention to determine whether angels, while retaining the spiritual quality of their bodies, work through it in a more hidden manner and assume from the lower, more corporeal elements something which, when fitted to them, they change and transform like a garment into whatever bodily forms they wish—even real forms themselves, just as real water was changed by the Lord into real wine (John 2:9)—or whether they transform their own proper bodies into whatever they wish, adapting them to what they do [Note: [Col. 0870] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *adapted*.]

But whichever of these may be the case, it does not pertain to the present question. And although, since I am human, I cannot comprehend these matters by experience, as the angels who do these things can and know them better than I do—just as I know, from what I have experienced in myself or in others, how my body is changed according to the feeling [Note: [Col. 0871] Ten manuscripts have *into the feeling*.] of my will—there is no need now to say what I should believe about these matters on the authority of the divine Scriptures, lest I be compelled to prove it and the discussion become longer concerning something the present question does not require.

6. What must now be seen is whether the angels were then responsible both for the bodily forms that appeared to human eyes and for the voices that sounded in human ears, while sensible creation itself, serving the Creator at his command, was changed into whatever work was required at the appropriate time, as it is written in the Book of Wisdom:

“For creation, serving you who made it, exerts itself against the unjust as a punishment, and becomes gentler in doing good to those who trust in you. Therefore even then, transforming itself into everything, it served your grace, the nourisher of all, according to the will of those who desired you” (Wis. 16:24–25).

For the power of God’s will extends through spiritual creation to the visible and sensible effects of corporeal creation. Where does the wisdom of almighty God not work according to his will—he who “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)?

## CHAPTER II

### 7. The Will of God Is the Higher Cause of Every Bodily Change. This Is Demonstrated by an Example

There is, however, another natural order in the conversion and mutability of bodies. Although this order too serves at God’s command, through the persistence of habit it has lost its capacity to astonish. Such are the things that change, at very short or at least not lengthy intervals of time, in heaven, on earth, and in the sea, whether through things coming into being or passing away, or through things appearing now in one way and now in another.

Other things, although they arise from that same order, are less familiar because they occur at longer intervals of time. Though many people are amazed by them, investigators of this age have understood them; and, as generations proceed and they are repeated more often and become known to more people, they are less astonishing.

Such are eclipses of the heavenly bodies, certain kinds of stars that appear rarely, earthquakes, monstrous births of animals, and whatever similar phenomena there are. None of these occurs except by the will of God, but this is not apparent to most people.

Thus the vanity of philosophers has been permitted to attribute these things to other causes—whether true but proximate causes, since they could not see the higher cause above all others, namely, the will of God; or false causes, produced not even by careful investigation of bodily things and movements but by their own suspicion and error.

8. I shall state, if I can, something by way of example that may make these matters clearer. Certainly, in the human body there is a mass of flesh, a visible form, an arrangement and distinction of the limbs, and a balance of health. This body is ruled by an infused soul, and that soul is rational. Therefore, although changeable, it can nevertheless become a participant in that unchangeable wisdom, so that its participation is in the same thing, as it is written in the Psalm concerning all the saints, from whom, as from living stones, that Jerusalem which is our eternal mother in heaven is built.

For thus it is sung: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing” (Ps. 122:3). Here “the same thing” is understood to mean that supreme and unchangeable good which God is, together with his wisdom and will.

To him it is sung elsewhere: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Ps. 102:27–28).

## CHAPTER III
## On the Same Argument

Let us therefore conceive in our minds such a wise man whose rational soul already participates in immutable and eternal truth, consulting it concerning all his actions and doing absolutely nothing that he has not recognized in it as something that ought to be done, so that, subject and obedient to it, he acts rightly.

Suppose that, after consulting the supreme reason of divine justice, which he heard in the secrecy of his heart’s ear, and at its command, this man fatigued his body through some act of mercy and contracted an illness. Having consulted physicians, one of them might say that the cause of the disease was bodily dryness, while another might say that it was an excess of moisture. One of them would state the true cause and the other would be mistaken, yet both would be pronouncing upon proximate causes—that is, bodily causes.

But if the cause of that dryness were sought and voluntary labor were discovered, one would already have arrived at the higher cause, which proceeded from the soul to affect the body it governs. Yet even that would not itself be the first cause. For undoubtedly the higher cause lay in immutable Wisdom itself, which the wise man’s soul, serving in love and obeying its ineffable command, had undertaken the voluntary labor. Thus the will of God alone would most truly be found to be the first cause of that illness.

Now suppose that, in his dutiful and pious labor, this wise man employed assistants working with him in the good undertaking, but who served God not with the same intention, wishing instead to attain the reward of their carnal desires [Note: [Col. 0872] Several manuscripts read “of their carnal intentions.” Two read “of their pleasures.”], or to avoid bodily hardships. Suppose also that he employed animals, if the execution of that work required it—animals that would certainly be irrational creatures and would therefore move their limbs under burdens not because they thought about some aspect of that good work, but from their natural desire for pleasure and avoidance of discomfort. Finally, suppose that he employed material bodies themselves, entirely lacking sensation, which were necessary for the work: grain, wine, oil, clothing, money, a book, and anything of that kind.

In all these bodies engaged in that work—whether animate or inanimate—whatever was moved, worn down, repaired, destroyed, or reshaped, and whatever was affected and changed in different ways according to places and times: could the cause of all these visible and mutable events be anything other than that invisible and immutable will of God, working through the just soul as the seat of Wisdom, using all things—both rational and irrational souls [Note: [Col. 0872] The printed editions read “both rational and irrational souls.” In the manuscripts, the word “rational” is left to be understood.]—and finally [Col. 0873] bodies, whether those into which souls were breathed and which were animated, or those entirely lacking sensation? And all this while He first used the good and holy soul which He had subjected to Himself for pious and religious service?

# CHAPTER IV

### 9. God uses all creatures as He wills, and makes visible things serve to reveal Him

What we have proposed by way of example concerning a single wise man—although he still bears a mortal body and sees only in part—may also be conceived concerning a house in which a number of such people live together, or concerning a city, or even the whole world, if the government and administration of human affairs were in the hands of wise people who were holily and perfectly subject to God.

But since this is not yet the case [Note: [Col. 0873] The Louvain edition reads: “But this indeed is not yet the case”; and, after the word “instructed,” adds the particle “so that,” connecting the following words as: “so that we may contemplate that very ….” The text has been corrected from the manuscripts.]—for in this pilgrimage we must first be trained through mortal experience and instructed by the disciplines of gentleness and patience under chastisements—let us contemplate that very heavenly and celestial homeland from which we are pilgrims.

There the will of God, who makes His angels spirits and His ministers a blazing fire (Ps. 103:4), presides as if in an exalted, holy, and secret dwelling, in His own house and temple. In spirits joined together in supreme peace and friendship, fused into one will by a kind of spiritual fire of charity, He diffuses Himself from there through all things by certain perfectly ordered movements of creation—first spiritual, then bodily—and uses everything according to the immutable judgment of His decision: incorporeal or corporeal things, rational or irrational spirits, those made good by His grace or those made evil by their own will.

And just as denser and lower bodies are governed in an ordered manner by subtler and more powerful bodies, so all bodies are governed by the spirit of life; irrational spirit of life by rational spirit of life; rational spirit of life that has deserted and sinned by pious and righteous rational spirit of life; and that spirit by God Himself. Thus the whole creation is governed by its Creator, from whom, through whom, and in whom it was also created and established (Col. 1:16).

Accordingly, the will of God is the first and supreme cause of all bodily forms and movements. Nothing takes place visibly and perceptibly that is not either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Ruler, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments, graces and recompenses, in this exceedingly vast and immeasurable commonwealth of the whole creation.

### 10

Therefore, if the apostle Paul—although he still bore the burden of a body that is subject to corruption and weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), although he still saw only partially and in a riddle (1 Cor. 13:12), longing to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23), and groaning within himself while awaiting adoption, the redemption of his body (Rom. 8:23)—could nevertheless proclaim the Lord Jesus Christ by signifying Him in one way through his tongue, in another through a letter, and in another through the sacrament of His body and blood, then what is surprising if God also makes whatever sensible and visible things He wills in the creation of heaven and earth, sea and air, in order to signify and demonstrate Himself through them as He Himself knows ought to be done?

For we do not call his tongue [Col. 0874], his parchment, his ink, the meaningful sounds uttered by his tongue, or the written letters on sheets of parchment the body and blood of Christ. Rather, we call that body and blood only what, taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by mystical prayer, we duly receive for spiritual salvation in remembrance of the Lord’s passion on our behalf.

When this is brought by human hands to that visible form, it is not sanctified so as to become so great a sacrament unless the Spirit of God works invisibly. For God performs all the things that take place through bodily movements in that act, first moving the invisible beings who minister—whether human souls or the hidden spiritual servants subject to Him.

God does not signify and demonstrate Himself through His own substance as it appears, since He is altogether immutable and more inwardly and secretly exalted than all the spirits He created.

# CHAPTER V

### 11. Why miracles are not customary works

The divine power governs the whole spiritual and bodily creation. By it, on fixed days throughout the years, the waters of the sea are summoned and poured over the face of the earth.

But when this happened at the prayer of the holy Elijah, because such a long and uninterrupted period of clear weather had preceded it that people were perishing from hunger, and because at the hour when that servant of God prayed the air itself had not displayed any sign, through a moist appearance, of rain about to come, the divine power became evident through the great and rapid rains that followed, by which that miracle was granted and administered (1 Kings 18:45).

Thus God produces the customary flashes of lightning and peals of thunder. But because these occurred on Mount Sinai in an unusual manner, and because those voices were not produced as confused noise but clearly appeared to convey certain signs through the most definite indications, they were miracles (Exod. 19:16).

Who draws moisture through the root of the vine to the grape and makes wine, if not God, who gives growth when a person plants and waters (1 Cor. 3:7)? But when, at the Lord’s command, water was changed into wine with extraordinary rapidity, divine power was declared even to fools who admitted it (John 2:9).

Who regularly clothes the trees with leaves and blossoms, if not God? Yet when Aaron’s priestly staff blossomed, divinity in a certain way entered into dialogue with doubting humanity (Num. 17:8).

Certainly, the earthly material common to all wood and to the flesh of all animals is the same. And who makes these things, if not the One who commanded the earth to produce them (Gen. 1:24), and who by that same word governs and directs what He created?

But when He recently and rapidly changed the same material from Moses’ staff into the flesh of a serpent, it was a miracle (Exod. 4:3): a change of a mutable thing, certainly, but an unusual change. And who gives life to every living thing that is born, if not the One who also gave life for a time to that serpent, as the work required?

# CHAPTER VI

### Variety alone makes a miracle

And who restored souls to corpses when the dead rose again (Ezek. 37:1–10), if not the One who animates [Col. 0875] flesh in the wombs of mothers so that those who will die may come forth? [Note: [Col. 0875] The printed editions add: “Similarly, from the common material that exists in the causes of the world, He suddenly and temporarily causes a ram and a dove to emerge; in them a single fleshly vigor appeared, not different in the time and manner of its coming and going, but unusual.” This is absent from nearly all the manuscripts.]

When such things occur in what may be called a continuous stream of flowing and issuing events, passing by the customary route from the hidden into the manifest and from the manifest into the hidden, they are called natural. But when they are introduced to admonish people through an unusual alteration, they are called mighty works.

# CHAPTER VII

### 12. Great miracles through magical arts

Here I see what might occur to a weak understanding: namely, why these miracles are also performed through magical arts. For the magicians of Pharaoh likewise made serpents, along with other similar things.

But what is more astonishing is how that power of the magicians, which could make serpents, utterly failed when it came to the tiniest flies. For *sciniphes* are very small insects, by which the proud people of Egypt were struck in the third plague. There the magicians, when they failed, said: “This is the finger of God” [Note: [Col. 0875] The printed editions read “This is here”; but the manuscripts read “This is this,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint.] (Exod. 7 and 8).

From this it may be understood that not even the transgressing angels themselves and the aerial powers—who were thrust down from the habitation of that lofty ethereal purity into this deepest darkness as into a prison of their own kind, and through whom magical arts can do whatever they can—have any power unless power is granted from above.

This power is granted either to deceive the deceitful, as it was granted to the Egyptians and to the magicians themselves, so that those by whom these things were performed might appear wondrous in the seduction of their spirits, though condemned by the truth of God; or to admonish the faithful, so that they would not desire to perform such things as something great—on account of which they have also been handed down to us by the authority of Scripture; or to exercise, test, and reveal the patience of the righteous.

For it was not through any small power of visible miracles that Job lost everything he possessed, his children, and even the health of his body (Job 1–2).

# CHAPTER VIII

### 13. God alone creates even those things that are transformed through magical arts

Nor should it therefore be thought that the material of visible things serves these transgressing angels at their command. Rather, it serves God, from whom this power is granted to the extent that He judges immutably in His lofty and spiritual dwelling.

For water, fire, and earth serve even condemned wrongdoers in the mines, so that they may make from them what they wish—but only insofar as they are permitted.

Nor should those evil angels be called creators because, through them, the magicians resisting God’s servant made frogs and serpents. They did not create them themselves.

For in the bodily elements of this world there lie hidden certain seeds of all things that are born bodily and visibly. Some are already visible to our eyes, arising from fruits and living creatures; others are the hidden seeds of these seeds, from which, at the Creator’s command, the primal water produced swimming and flying creatures, while the earth produced the first shoots of its kind [Note: [Col. 0875] Some manuscripts omit “of its kind” at this first occurrence.] and the first animals of their [Col. 0876] kind (Gen. 1:20–25).

For these things were not then produced in such a way that the power in them was exhausted in what was produced. Rather, suitable combinations of conditions are often lacking by which they might burst forth and complete their forms.

Consider, for example, a very small shoot: it is a seed, since, when properly entrusted to the earth, it produces a tree. But a subtler seed of this shoot, of the same kind, is a grain—and this far it remains visible to us.

Now, although we cannot see with our eyes the seed even of that grain, we can nevertheless infer it by reason. For unless some such power existed in these elements, things not sown there would not often arise from the earth. Nor would so many animals be born, whether on land or in water, without the prior union of males and females—animals that nevertheless grow and reproduce by union, although they themselves arose without parents joining together. Bees, certainly, conceive the seeds of their offspring not through union, but as though they gathered them with their mouths after they had been scattered over the earth.

The Creator of invisible seeds is Himself the Creator of all things. For whatever emerges through birth into our sight receives the beginnings of its development from hidden seeds, and derives the growth appropriate to its size and the distinctions of its forms from original patterns, as from rules.

Therefore, just as we do not call parents the creators of human beings, nor farmers the creators of crops, although God’s power works inwardly to create these things through the outward movements they apply, so it is not right to think that either evil or good angels are creators if, according to the subtlety of their sense and body, they know seeds of these things that are more hidden from us, secretly scattering them through suitable combinations of the elements and thus providing opportunities for things to be generated and their growth to be accelerated.

Yet the good do not do these things except insofar as God commands; nor do the evil do them unjustly except insofar as He Himself justly permits them. For the wicked possess an unjust will through their wickedness, but receive power only justly [Note: [Col. 0876] This is the reading of most and the better manuscripts. The printed editions read: “They possess an unjust will, but receive power only justly”], whether for their own punishment, or for the punishment of others who are evil, or for the praise of those who are good.

### 14

Accordingly, the apostle Paul distinguished between God’s inward act of creating and forming and the works of creation applied externally. Drawing an illustration from agriculture, he said: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. 3:6).

Thus, just as God alone can form our mind by justifying it in the life itself, while people too can preach the Gospel outwardly—not only the good through truth, but also the evil through opportunity (Phil. 1:18)—so God works inwardly to create visible things. The outward operations of either good or evil angels or human beings, or even of any animals whatsoever, He employs in the nature of things [Col. 0877], in which He creates all things, according to His command and the distributions of powers and appetites for appropriate things that He has granted, just as one employs the cultivation of the earth.

Therefore I cannot say that evil angels summoned by magical arts were the creators of frogs and serpents, any more than I can say that evil human beings are the creators of the crop which I see arising through their labor [Note: [Col. 0877] Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read “which I see”; manuscript reading].

### 15

Nor was Jacob the creator of the colors in the flocks, because he placed before the mothers, while they were drinking and conceiving, variegated rods for them to look upon (Gen. 30:41).

Nor were the animals themselves creators of the variety of their offspring, because a variegated image had adhered to their souls, impressed upon them through their eyes by the sight of the various rods. Through the sympathy of their mingling, this image could affect only the body animated by a spirit so influenced, so that the color was sprinkled upon the tender beginnings of the offspring [Note: [Col. 0877] Only two manuscripts read: “so that the color was externally sprinkled.”].

For the appropriate principles that make the soul be affected by the body, or the body by the soul, live immutably in the very supreme Wisdom of God, which no spatial dimensions contain. And although that Wisdom itself is immutable, it abandons nothing of the things that are mutable, because nothing of them was created except through it.

The fact that animals, rather than rods, gave birth to animals was accomplished by the immutable and invisible rational principle of God’s Wisdom, through which all things were created. But the fact that the color of the rods caused something to be drawn into the color of the animals conceived was accomplished by the soul of the pregnant animal, affected externally through the eyes and inwardly drawing with itself, according to its limited capacity, the pattern by which it formed the offspring—a pattern it had received from the inner power of its Creator.

How great is the power of the soul to affect and change bodily matter—although it cannot be called the creator of the body, since every cause of mutable and sensible substance, and every measure, number, and weight by which it comes to exist and to be this or that kind of nature, proceeds from the intelligible and immutable life that is above all things and reaches down to the furthest and earthly things—is a subject requiring much discussion and not necessary here [Note: [Col. 0877] On this, see below, book 11, chapter 2; and *The City of God*, book 12, chapter 25, and book 18, chapter 5.]

I have thought it worthwhile to recall Jacob’s deed concerning the animals for this reason: if the man who placed those rods in that manner cannot be called the creator of the colors in the lambs and goats, and if the souls of the mothers themselves—which, as far as nature allowed, sprinkled the image of variety conceived through the eyes of the body upon the fleshly seeds conceived within them—cannot be called creators, then evil angels, through whom Pharaoh’s magicians performed those things at that time, can much less be called creators of frogs and serpents.

# CHAPTER IX

### 16. The original cause of all things is God

It is one thing to establish and administer creation from the innermost and supreme hinge of causes—something only God, who does it, is the Creator. It is another thing, in accordance with the powers and capacities distributed by Him, to apply some operation externally so that what is created may emerge at this or that time and in this or that way.

All things have already been created originally and primordially in a certain fabric of the elements [Col. 0878], but they emerge when the appropriate opportunities are received. For just as mothers are pregnant with offspring, so the world itself is pregnant with the causes of things that are born. These causes are not created within it except by that supreme essence in which nothing arises or dies, begins to exist or ceases to exist.

External causes that approach may be applied—although they are not natural, they are nevertheless applied according to nature—so that what is contained hidden in the secret bosom of nature may burst forth and, in a certain sense, be created outwardly by unfolding the measures, numbers, and weights that it received in secret from Him who arranged all things in measure, number, and weight (Wis. 11:21). This can be done not only by evil angels but also by evil human beings, as I have shown above by the example of agriculture.

### 17

But lest the case of animals move us as though it involved a different principle because they possess the spirit of life, with the capacity to desire what is according to nature and avoid what is contrary to it, consider also this fact, which many people know: from which herbs, meats, or juices and liquids of any kind, placed, buried, crushed, or mixed in particular ways, particular animals commonly arise. Who would be so foolish as to dare call himself their creator?

What is surprising, then, if just as any utterly wicked person can know from what particular worms and flies arise, so evil angels, according to the subtlety of their sense, know in the more hidden seeds of the elements from what frogs and serpents arise, and, by applying these through hidden movements at definite and known opportunities of combination, cause them to be created rather than creating them?

People do not marvel at the things that are customarily produced by human beings. If someone happens to marvel at the speed of their growth, because those animals were made so quickly, let him observe how such things are also produced by human beings according to the measure of human ability.

Why, for example, do the same bodies become worm-infested more quickly in summer than in winter, and more quickly in warmer places than in colder ones? Such conditions are applied by human beings with proportionately greater difficulty because they lack subtle senses and the mobility of bodies in earthly and sluggish limbs.

Accordingly, since it is easier for whatever angels there may be to draw proximate causes from the elements, according to their nature, their rapidity in such works is all the more wondrous.

### 18

But no one is a creator except the one who forms these things in the primary sense. Nor can anyone do this except the One with whom the measures, numbers, and weights of all things exist originally. He alone is the one Creator, God. By His ineffable power it also comes about that what these angels could do, if they were permitted, they cannot do because they are not permitted.

There is no other apparent reason why they could not make the tiniest flies, when they made frogs and serpents, except that the greater dominion of God, who prohibited them, was present [Note: [Col. 0878] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions read “of the one prohibiting,” omitting “God”].

The magicians themselves also confessed this, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 7:12; 8:7, 18–19).

But what they can do by nature, yet cannot do because of prohibition, and what they are prevented from doing by the condition of that very nature of theirs, is difficult—indeed impossible—for a human being [Col. 0879] to investigate except through that gift of God which the Apostle mentions when he says: “To another, the discernment of spirits” (1 Cor. 12:10).

We know that a human being can walk, yet cannot do even that if not permitted; but cannot fly even if permitted. So those angels can do certain things if more powerful angels permit them by God’s command, but they cannot do other things even if those angels permit them, because the One from whom they have such a limitation of nature does not permit them. He also often does not permit those things through His angels which He has granted them the ability to do.

### 19

Leaving aside, therefore, those things that occur bodily in the order of nature through the customary passage of time—such as the risings and settings of the stars, the generations and deaths of animals, the innumerable varieties of seeds and shoots, mists and clouds, snow and rain, flashes of lightning and thunder, lightning bolts and hail, winds and fires, cold and heat, and all such things—and leaving aside also those that are rare within that same order, such as eclipses of the lights, unusual appearances of the stars, monsters, earthquakes, and similar events:

leaving aside, then, all these things, whose first and supreme cause is nevertheless nothing other than the will of God—for in the Psalm, when certain things of this kind had been mentioned, “Fire and hail, snow and ice, storm-wind,” lest anyone should believe that they were brought about either by chance, or merely by bodily causes, or even by spiritual causes existing apart from the will of God, it immediately adds: “Which do His word” (Ps. 148:8).

# CHAPTER X

### The ways in which creation is taken up for signification. The Eucharist

Apart from these things, then, as I had begun to say, there are others which, although they arise from the same bodily matter, are brought before our senses by divine arrangement in order to announce something. These are properly called miracles and signs.

Yet in everything announced to us by the Lord God, the person of God Himself is not assumed. When He is assumed, He is sometimes manifested in an angel; sometimes in a form that is not an angel, although it is arranged and administered through an angel.

Again, when He is assumed in a form that is not an angel, sometimes the body already existed and is taken up into some transformation in order to demonstrate this; sometimes the form comes into existence for this purpose and, once the matter has been accomplished, disappears again.

Likewise, when human beings announce something, they sometimes speak the words of God in their own person, as when it is prefaced by “The Lord said” or “Thus says the Lord” (Jer. 31:1–2), or something similar. At other times, without any such prefatory statement, they assume the person of God Himself in themselves, as in: “I will give you understanding and set you on the way in which you shall go” (Ps. 32:8).

Thus, not only in words but also in deeds, the person of God is imposed upon a prophet to be represented by him in the ministry of prophecy. This was the case with the man who divided his garment into twelve parts and gave ten of them to the servant of King Solomon, the future king of Israel (1 Kings 11:30–31).

Sometimes a thing that was not a prophet and already existed among earthly things was taken up for this kind of signification, as when Jacob, having seen the dream [Col. 0880], awoke and made a stone—which he had had beneath his head while sleeping—into something of this kind (Gen. 28:18).

Sometimes the same form is made for this purpose, either to remain for a while, as with the bronze serpent raised up in the wilderness (Num. 21:9), or as letters may remain; or to pass away once the ministry has been completed, as bread made for this purpose is consumed when the sacrament is received.

### 20

But because these things are known to human beings, since they are performed through human beings, they may receive honor as religious things, but they cannot produce astonishment as wondrous things.

Thus, the things performed through angels are more wondrous to us the more difficult and unknown they are; to the angels themselves, however, they are familiar and easy actions.

An angel speaks to a human being in the person of God, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” although Scripture had first said: “The angel of the Lord appeared to him” (Exod. 3:2, 6).

A human being also speaks in the person of the Lord, saying: “Hear, O my people, and I will speak to you; O Israel, and I will testify to you: I am God, your God” (Ps. 81:9, 11).

A staff was taken up for signification and changed into a serpent by angelic power (Exod. 7:10). Yet because such power is lacking to a human being, a stone was nevertheless taken up by a human being for a similar signification (Gen. 28:18).

There is a great difference between the deed of an angel and the deed of a human being. The former is both to be marveled at and understood; the latter is merely to be understood. Perhaps what is understood from both is one and the same, but the things from which it is understood are different—just as if the name of the Lord were written both in gold and in ink: one would be more precious, the other cheaper, yet what is signified in both would be the same.

Although the serpent made from Moses’ staff signified the same thing as Jacob’s stone, Jacob’s stone nevertheless signified something better than the magicians’ serpents. For just as the anointing of the stone signified Christ in the flesh, in which He was anointed with the oil of gladness above His companions (Ps. 45:8), so Moses’ staff changed into a serpent signified Christ made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8).

Hence He said: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:14–15), just as those who looked upon the serpent lifted up in the wilderness did not perish from the bites of the serpents.

For “our old man was crucified with Him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed” (Rom. 6:6). The serpent signifies death, which was brought about by the serpent in paradise (Gen. 3), in a mode of expression that indicates the effect through its efficient cause.

Thus, the staff becoming a serpent signifies Christ unto death; and the serpent becoming a staff again signifies Christ in the resurrection, whole with His body, which is the Church (Col. 1:24). This will occur at the end of time, which is signified by the serpent’s tail, which Moses grasped so that it might return to a staff (Exod. 4:4).

The serpents of the magicians, as dead things of the world, will not be able to rise again in Christ unless, by believing in Him, they enter His body as though they had been swallowed up by it (Exod. 7:12).

Jacob’s stone, then, as I have said, signified something better than the magicians’ serpents; yet the magicians’ deed was much more wondrous. But these facts do not prejudice the things to be understood, as though the name of a human being were written in gold and [Col. 0881] the name of God in ink.

### 21

Even if the Lord or the Holy Spirit was manifested in those bodily forms, which human being knows how the angels made or assumed those clouds and fires in order to signify what they announced?

It is like infants who do not know what is placed on the altar and consumed after the celebration of the religious rite, or from what it is made, or how, or from where it is taken for religious use. If they never learn through their own experience or that of others, and never see that kind of thing except during the celebration of the sacraments, when it is offered and given to them, and if they are told with the highest authority whose body and blood it is, they will believe nothing other than that the Lord Himself appeared to mortal eyes in that form and that the liquid flowed entirely from His pierced side (John 19:34).

It is wholly useful for me to remember my own powers and to remind my brothers that they too should remember theirs, lest human weakness advance farther than is safe.

For how the angels do these things—or rather, how God does these things through His angels—and to what extent He may wish to do so even through evil angels, whether by permitting, commanding, or compelling them, from the hidden seat of His supreme rule: I am unable to penetrate this with the sharpness of my eyes, unravel it with confidence in reason, or comprehend it through the advancement of my mind, so as to speak about all the questions that may be asked concerning these matters with the certainty I would have if I were an angel, prophet, or apostle.

“For the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our foresight is uncertain. The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks about many things. We can scarcely judge what is on earth, and we discover with labor what is before our eyes; but who can investigate what is in heaven?”

But the passage continues and says: “Who has known Your counsel, unless You give wisdom and send Your Holy Spirit from on high?” (Wis. 9:14–17).

We do not investigate the things that are in heaven with regard to the kind of reality in which the angelic bodies according to their proper dignity, and certain bodily activity of theirs, are contained. Yet, according to the Spirit of God sent to us from on high and the grace imparted by Him to our minds, I dare confidently say that neither God the Father, nor His Word, nor His Spirit [Col. 0882]—who together are the one God—is in any way mutable in respect of what He is and precisely as what He Himself is, and therefore is much less visible.

For there are some things that, although mutable, are nevertheless not visible, such as our thoughts, memories, and wills, and every incorporeal creature. But nothing visible exists that is not mutable.

# CHAPTER XI

### God’s essence has never appeared by itself. The divine appearances to the Fathers were made through the ministry of angels. An objection drawn from the manner of speaking is refuted. God’s appearance to Abraham, like that to Moses, was made through angels. The same is proved from the law given to Moses through angels. What has been said in this book and what is to be said in the next

Therefore, the substance—or, if it is better said, the essence—of God, inasmuch as according to our capacity we understand from even the smallest portion something of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, since it is in no way mutable, can in no way itself be visible through itself.

22. Accordingly, it is clear that all those things which were seen by the Fathers, when God presented himself to them according to his dispensation and in a manner appropriate to those times, were accomplished through a creature. And if it is hidden from us how he accomplished these things through angelic ministers, nevertheless we do not assert on the basis of our own judgment that they were accomplished through angels, lest we seem wiser than we ought; rather, we are wise unto moderation, according as God has apportioned to us the measure of faith (Rom. 12:3), and we believe, and therefore speak (2 Cor. 4:13).

For there exists the authority of the divine Scriptures, from which our mind must not deviate, nor, abandoning the firm foundation of divine speech, plunge headlong over the precipices of its own suspicions, where neither bodily sense provides guidance nor clear reason illuminates the truth. It is written most plainly in the Epistle to the Hebrews that, when the dispensation of the New Testament was distinguished from that of the Old Testament according to the fittingness of ages and times, not only those visible things but the very utterance itself was made through angels. For it says:

> “But to which of the angels did he ever say, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’? Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are destined to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:13–14)

Here it shows that all those things were accomplished not only through angels but also for our sake—that is, for the sake of the people of God, to whom the inheritance of eternal life is promised. As it is also written to the Corinthians:

> “All these things happened to them figuratively; but they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

Then, because at that time the word was spoken through angels, but now through the Son, he demonstrates this consequently and plainly:

> “Therefore we must pay much closer attention to the things we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?”

And, as though one might ask what salvation he meant, to show that he was now speaking of the New Testament—that is, of the word spoken not through angels but through the Lord—he says:

> “Which, having first been declared through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard it, God bearing witness with signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will” (Heb. 2:1–4).

23. But someone may say: Why, then, is it written, “The Lord spoke to Moses,” rather than, “The angel spoke to Moses”? Because when a herald announces the words of a judge, the official record does not say, “That herald spoke,” but, “That judge spoke.” In the same way, when a holy prophet speaks, even if we say, “The prophet spoke,” we intend nothing other than that the Lord spoke. And if we say, “The Lord spoke,” we do not remove the prophet; rather, we indicate who spoke through him.

Indeed, that Scripture often discloses that the angel is the Lord, while the words “The Lord said” are repeatedly used of him as he speaks, we have already demonstrated.

[Note: Most manuscripts read *Domini* (“of the Lord”) rather than *Dominum* (“the Lord”).]

But because some, when Scripture names an angel in that passage, wish the Son of God himself to be understood—on the ground that, because he announces the Father’s will and his own, he was called an angel by the prophet—I therefore wished to provide a clearer testimony from this Epistle, where it does not say “through an Angel” but “through Angels.”

24. Stephen, too, recounts these matters in the manner in which they were written in the ancient Books. “Men, brothers, and fathers, hear me,” he says:

> “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia” (Acts 7:2).

[Note: Ambrose and some manuscripts read “in Mesopotamia of Syria.”]

But lest anyone suppose that the God of glory, in what he is in himself, appeared to the eyes of any mortal, Stephen says in what follows that an angel appeared to Moses:

> “Moses fled at this word and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons. And when forty years had been completed there, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he marveled at the sight. As he approached to examine it, the voice of the Lord came, saying: ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ And Moses, trembling, did not dare to examine it. Then the Lord said to him, ‘Remove the sandals from your feet’” (Exod. 2:15–3:7), and so forth.

Here he certainly speaks both of an angel and of the Lord, and calls him the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, just as it is written in Genesis.

25. Or perhaps someone will say that the Lord appeared to Moses through an angel, but to Abraham by himself? Let us not ask Stephen about this; let us question the very book from which Stephen recounted these things.

Because it is written, “And the Lord God said to Abraham” (Gen. 12:1), and shortly afterward, “And the Lord God appeared to Abraham” (Gen. 17:1), does it follow that these things were not accomplished through angels? In another place Scripture likewise says:

> “And God appeared to him at the oak of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent at midday”;

yet it immediately adds:

> “And when he lifted his eyes, he saw, and behold, three men were standing above him” (Gen. 18:1–2).

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis here read “standing before him.” But the manuscripts consistently read “above him,” as also in Book 2 against Maximinus, ch. 26, §5. In Greek, according to the Septuagint, ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ (*epanō autou*, “above him”).]

We have already spoken about these men. How will those who either refuse to rise from words to their meaning, or easily plunge from meaning back into words, explain that God appeared in three men, unless they acknowledge—as the sequel also teaches—that they were angels? Or, because it is not said, “An angel spoke to him,” or “appeared to him,” will they therefore dare to say that the vision and voice were made to Moses through an angel because this is what is written, but that, since no mention of an angel is made in Abraham’s case, God appeared and spoke to Abraham through his own substance?

Moreover, even in Abraham’s case Scripture does not remain silent about the angel. For thus we read when his son was commanded to be sacrificed:

> “And it came to pass after these words that God tested Abraham, and said to him, ‘Abraham, Abraham.’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’ And he said to him, ‘Take your beloved son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the high land, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall tell you.’”

[Note: Most manuscripts read “when his son was requested” rather than “when his son was to be sacrificed.”]

Certainly here God, not an angel, is mentioned. Shortly afterward, however, Scripture reads:

> “But Abraham stretched out his hand and took the sword, intending to kill his son.”

[Note: The printed editions read “wishing to kill.” *Wishing* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint.]

> “And the angel of the Lord called to him from heaven and said, ‘Abraham, Abraham.’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’ And he said, ‘Do not lay your hand upon the boy, nor do anything to him.’”

What answer can be given to this? Will they say that God ordered Isaac to be killed, while the angel forbade it; and that the father, contrary to God’s command—who had ordered him to kill him—obeyed the angel and spared him? This interpretation deserves ridicule and rejection.

But Scripture does not allow even this crude and base interpretation any place, immediately adding:

> “For now I know that you fear God, and you have not spared your beloved son for my sake.”

[Note: The manuscripts read “so crude” rather than “so gross.”]

What does “for my sake” mean except “for the sake of him who had commanded that he be killed”? Is the God of Abraham the same as the angel—or rather, was God speaking through the angel?

Consider what follows. The angel has now been expressed most clearly; nevertheless, observe what is woven into the account:

> “And Abraham lifted his eyes and saw, and behold, a ram was caught by its horns in a tree of sabech. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son Isaac. And Abraham called the name of that place, ‘The Lord saw,’ so that they say to this day, ‘On the mountain the Lord was seen.’”

Just as earlier God said through the angel, “For now I know that you fear God”—not because God is to be understood as having then acquired knowledge, but because he acted so that Abraham himself might come to know how great was the strength of his heart for obeying God even to the sacrifice of his only son—in that mode of speech by which what is accomplished is signified through the one who causes it, as when we speak of “lazy cold,” meaning cold that makes people lazy. Thus he was said to have known because he had caused Abraham himself to know; the firmness of his faith might have remained hidden from him unless it had been tested by such an experiment.

So here also Abraham called the name of that place, “The Lord saw”—that is, “the Lord caused himself to be seen.” For immediately afterward he says:

> “So that they say to this day, ‘On the mountain the Lord was seen.’”

Here the same angel is called the Lord. Why, unless because the Lord was speaking through the angel?

Now, in what follows, the angel speaks wholly in a prophetic manner and makes entirely clear that God speaks through an angel:

> “And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: ‘By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your beloved son for my sake’” (Gen. 22), and so forth.

These are certainly the kinds of words that prophets also use when the one through whom the Lord speaks says, “Thus says the Lord.” Or does the Son of God say of the Father, “The Lord says,” and is he himself that Angel of the Father?

What, then, of those three men? Do they not see how they are pressed by the evidence—those who appeared to Abraham when it had been said, “The Lord appeared to him”? Or, because they were called men, were they not angels? Let them read Daniel, who says, “Behold, the man Gabriel” (Dan. 9:21).

[Col. 0885]

26. But why do we delay any longer in closing their mouths with another most evident and weighty proof, where they are called neither a single angel nor plural men, but angels without qualification? Through these angels, it is most clearly shown, a word was spoken—not just any word, but the Law itself was given. Certainly no believer doubts that God gave this Law to Moses for the subjection of the people of Israel; nevertheless, it was given through angels.

Thus Stephen speaks:

> “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become—those who received the Law by decrees of angels and did not keep it” (Acts 7:51–53).

What could be clearer? What could be stronger in such authority? The Law was indeed given to that people by decrees of angels; but through it the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ was arranged and foretold. And he himself, as the Word of God, was in the angels in a wondrous and ineffable manner, in whose decrees the Law itself was given.

Hence he says in the Gospel:
