> “If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

Thus the Lord was then speaking through angels; through angels the Son of God, who was destined to become the mediator between God and human beings from the seed of Abraham, arranged his coming, so that he might find people ready to receive him—people confessing themselves guilty, whom the unfulfilled Law had made transgressors.

Hence the Apostle also says to the Galatians:

> “What, then, is the Law? It was added because of transgressions”;

[Note: Several manuscripts read “it was proposed” rather than “it was added.” The Greek is προσετέθη (*prosetethē*).]

> “until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, arranged through angels in the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3:19).

[Note: The printed editions read *disposita* (“arranged,” feminine), but most manuscripts read *dispositum* (“arranged,” neuter), referring it to *semen* (“offspring”).]

That is, it was arranged through angels in his hand. For he was not born by the condition of nature but by power.

That the Apostle does not call one of the angels a mediator, but the Lord Jesus Christ himself, insofar as he graciously consented to become human, is shown elsewhere:

> “There is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

Hence that Passover in the sacrifice of the lamb (Exod. 12); hence all those things that are portrayed in the Law concerning Christ, who was to come in the flesh, suffer, and also rise again. This Law was given in the decrees of angels, among whom were certainly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. At one time the Father, at another the Son, at another the Holy Spirit, and at another God without any distinction of person was figuratively represented through them—even though he appeared in visible and perceptible forms through his creature, not through his substance, for the sight of which hearts are purified through all those things that are seen by the eyes and heard by the ears.

27. But by now, I think, we have argued and demonstrated sufficiently, so far as our capacity permits, what we undertook to show in this book. It has been established both by the probability of reasoning—as far as a human being, or rather as far as I, could establish it—and by the firmness of authority, insofar as the divine utterances have made it clear from the holy Scriptures, that to our ancient fathers before the Savior’s incarnation, when God was said to appear, those bodily voices and appearances were produced through angels.

This happened either when the angels themselves spoke or performed something in the person of God, as we have also shown the prophets to have been accustomed to do; or when they assumed from creation something that they themselves were not, through which God was figuratively displayed to human beings. Scripture teaches by many examples that the prophets, too, did not omit this kind of signification.

It remains, therefore, for us now to see what difference there is between those manifestations and these manifestations of the Son of God and the Holy Spirit—although these, too, were made through visible creation—since, after the Lord was born of a virgin, the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove (Matt. 3:16), and fiery tongues appeared, with a sound coming from heaven, on the day of Pentecost after the Lord’s ascension (Acts 2:1–4). It was not the Word of God himself, through that substance by which he is equal and coeternal with the Father, nor the Spirit of the Father and the Son, through that substance by which he too is equal to both [Note: [Col. 0886] Venetus reads “equal to either”; Lovaniensis, “equal to either,” with this marginal annotation: “Elsewhere, equal to both.” M.] and coeternal with them, that appeared; rather, it was certainly a creature that could be formed and exist in those bodily ways and could appear to mortal senses.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “but certainly through a creature.”]

We shall begin this discussion more suitably in another volume.

# BOOK FOUR

Explains for what purpose the Son of God was sent: namely, that by Christ’s death for sinners we might first be persuaded both of how much God loved us and of the kind of people whom he loved. It was also fitting that, so that we might be cleansed for contemplating God and clinging to God, the Word should come in the flesh. By his single and simple death our double death was dissolved. Here he explains how the simple measure of our Savior corresponds to our double measure for salvation, and he discusses at greater length the perfection of the number six, to which the very ratio of one to two is reduced. He teaches that all are gathered from many into one through the one mediator of life, Christ, through whom alone the true purification of the soul takes place. Finally, he demonstrates that although the Son of God was made lesser by his mission because of the form of a servant that he assumed, he is not for that reason lesser than the Father according to the form of God, because he was sent by him; and that the same principle applies to the mission of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0885]

# PROEM

## 1. Knowledge of God must be sought from God

The human race is accustomed to value highly the knowledge of earthly and heavenly things. In this respect those are certainly better who place self-knowledge before such knowledge; and more worthy of praise is the mind that knows even its own weakness than one which, disregarding this, examines the courses of the stars in order to learn them—or which, already knowing them, remains ignorant of the path by which it should proceed toward salvation and its own stability.

But the person who has already awakened to God, roused by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, and who, in God’s presence, has come to regard himself as worthless through love of him—who wishes to enter into him but cannot, and, as God’s light shines upon him, attends to himself and finds himself, and recognizes that his sickness cannot be brought into harmony with God’s purity—takes delight in weeping and in pleading that God may have mercy on him again and again, until he lays aside all misery. He prays with confidence, having already received the free pledge of salvation, through God’s one Savior and illuminator of humanity.

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “acting and suffering need” rather than “acting and grieving.”]

Such a person is not puffed up by knowledge, because love builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). He has placed one knowledge before another: he has preferred to know his own weakness rather than to know the walls of the world, the foundations of the earth, and the heights of the heavens. And by adding this knowledge, he has added sorrow (Eccl. 1:18): the sorrow of his pilgrimage, arising from desire for his homeland and for its creator, his blessed God.

Among such people, in the household of your Christ, Lord my God, if I groan among your poor, grant me bread from you with which to answer those who neither hunger nor thirst for righteousness (Matt. 5:6), but are filled and overflowing. Their own phantom has filled them, not your truth, which they reject and recoil from, falling into their own vanity.

I certainly sense how many fantasies the human heart produces; and what is my heart except a human heart? But this I ask of the God of my heart: that I may not spew from those fantasies anything in these writings as solid truth, but that whatever can come through me into them may come from the place whence the breath of his truth is sprinkled upon me—even though I have been cast away from the sight of his eyes (Ps. 30:23) and am attempting to return from afar, by the road which the divinity of his Only-Begotten has paved through his humanity.

[Note: The oldest manuscript reads “and attempting from afar,” omitting “to return.”]

[Note: The printed editions read *humanitati* (“for humanity”); the manuscripts more appropriately read *humanitate* (“through humanity”).]

I drink in this truth, mutable as I am, insofar as I see nothing mutable in it: neither in place and time, as with bodies; nor in time alone and, as it were, place, as with the thoughts of our spirits; nor in time alone, with no image even of place, as with certain reasonings of our minds. For the essence of God, by which he is, possesses nothing mutable—neither in eternity, nor in truth, nor in will. For there truth is eternal, and love eternal; there love is true, and eternity true; there eternity is beloved, and truth beloved.

# CHAPTER ONE

## 2. We are perfected through recognition of our weakness. The incarnate Word dispels our darkness

But because we have gone into exile from unchangeable joy, yet have not been cut off and torn away from it so completely that we would not seek eternity, truth, and blessedness even amid these mutable and temporal things—for we do not wish either to die, or to be deceived, or to be disturbed—there were divinely sent to us manifestations suited to our pilgrimage. Through them we might be reminded that what we seek is not here, but that we must return from here to that place from which, unless we depended upon it, we would not seek these things here.

First, it was necessary to persuade us how much God loved us, lest through despair we should not dare to rise toward him. But it was also necessary to show what kind of people he loved, lest, as though growing proud of our merits, we should recoil from him still more and fail more completely in our own strength. Accordingly, he dealt with us so that we might advance instead through his strength, and so that the power of love might be perfected in the weakness of humility.

This is signified in the Psalm, where he says:

> “Separating a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance; and it was weakened, but you perfected it” (Ps. 68:10).

By “voluntary rain” he wishes nothing other than grace to be understood—not something repaid according to merits, but something given freely; hence it is called grace. For he gave it not because we were worthy, but because he willed to give it.

When we recognize this, we shall not put our confidence in ourselves; and this is what it means to be weakened. But he himself perfects us, who also said to the Apostle Paul:

> “My grace is sufficient for you; for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

It was therefore necessary to persuade human beings both how much God loved us and what kind of people he loved: how much, so that we would not despair; what kind, so that we would not become proud.

The Apostle explains this indispensable point as follows:

> “But God demonstrates his love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved in his life” (Rom. 5:8–10).

Likewise, in another passage:

> “What, then, shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all—how will he not also, together with him, freely give us all things?” (Rom. 8:31–32).

But what has been announced as having happened for us was also shown as destined to happen to the righteous of ancient times, so that through the same faith they too might be humbled and weakened, and, having been weakened, perfected.

## 3. All things are life in the Word

Since there is therefore one Word of God through whom all things were made, who is unchangeable truth, all things exist there principally and unchangeably together—not only the things that now exist in this whole creation, but also those that have existed and those that will exist.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “there principally.” The printed editions read “where principally.” Again, a little later, they read “where” in place of “there.”]

But there things neither have existed nor will exist; they simply exist. And all things are life, and all things are one; indeed, they are more truly one, and there is one life.

For all things were made through him in such a way that whatever was made in them is life in him and was not made. For in the beginning the Word was not made, but the Word was with God, and God was the Word; and all things were made through him. Nor would all things have been made through him unless he had existed before all things and had not been made.

Among the things made through him is also the body, which is not life. Yet it would not have been made through him unless, before it was made, it had been life in him. For what was made was already life in him—and not just any kind of life. The soul too is the life of the body, but it was made, since it is mutable; and through what was it made except through the immutable Word of God? For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

What, therefore, was made was already life in him—and not merely any kind of life, but “the life was the light of human beings”: clearly, the light of rational minds, through which human beings differ from animals and are therefore human beings.

It was not bodily light—the light of flesh—whether it shines from heaven or is kindled by earthly fires. This light is seen not only by human flesh but also by the flesh of animals, even down to the tiniest worms. All these things see that light; but that life was the light of human beings, and it was not far from any one of us. For in it we live and move and exist (Acts 17:27–28).

[Col. 0889]

# CHAPTER TWO

## 4. How through the incarnate Word we are made capable of receiving the truth

But “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” The darkness is the foolishness of human minds, blinded by wicked desire and unbelief. In order to heal and restore these minds, the Word through whom all things were made became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1–14).

Our illumination is participation in the Word—that is, in the life which is the light of human beings. But we were wholly incapable and unfit for this participation because of the uncleanness of sins. We therefore had to be cleansed.

Now the one cleansing of the wicked and proud is the blood of the righteous and the humility of God: so that, in order to contemplate God—which we are not by nature—we might be cleansed through him who became what we are by nature and what we are not through sin.

By nature we are not God; by nature we are human beings; through sin we are not righteous. Thus God, having become a righteous human being, interceded with God for the sinful human being. For the sinful person does not correspond to the righteous, but a human being corresponds to a human being.

By joining to us the likeness of his humanity, he removed the unlikeness of our iniquity.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “the likeness” rather than “the unlikeness.”]

And, having become a participant in our mortality, he made us participants in his divinity. For death deservedly comes upon the sinner through the necessity of condemnation; but it was dissolved through the death of the righteous, which came through the will of mercy, since his single measure corresponds to our double measure.

This correspondence, or suitability, or harmony, or consonance—or whatever more fitting name may be given to that which is one in relation to two—is of great importance in every joining together or, more suitably, fitting together of creation. I now wish to call this fitting together what the Greeks call ἁρμονία (*harmonía*, “harmony”).

Nor is this the place to show how much the consonance of one to two is worth—the consonance that is found most fully in us and is naturally implanted in us.

[Note: Several manuscripts omit “in us.” After “is found,” the printed editions formerly read “so that it may be for us.” This is corrupt.]

From whom, indeed, could it come except from the one who created us? Even the uneducated cannot fail to perceive it, whether they themselves are singing or are listening to others. Through it, high and low voices harmonize, so that whoever departs from it violently offends not the knowledge of music—for many lack that—but the very sense of our hearing.

To demonstrate this, however, would require a long discussion. It can nevertheless be displayed directly to the ears by one who understands the regular monochord.

# CHAPTER THREE

## 5. The one death and resurrection of Christ’s body corresponds to our double death and resurrection of body and soul for salvation. How Christ’s single death was expended for our double death

What now presses upon us must be explained, insofar as God grants it: how the single measure of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ corresponds to our double measure and in a certain way harmonizes with it for salvation.

Certainly, as no Christian doubts, we are dead both in soul and in body: in soul because of sin; in body because of the punishment of sin—and therefore also in body because of sin. Both aspects of our condition, that is, both soul and body, needed a remedy and resurrection, so that what had been changed for the worse might be renewed for the better.

The death of the soul is impiety; the death of the body is corruptibility, through which separation of the soul from the body also occurs. For just as the soul dies when abandoned by God, so the body dies when abandoned by the soul. Hence the soul becomes foolish, while the body becomes lifeless.

The soul is raised again through repentance, and in the still-mortal body the renewal of life begins through faith—faith by which one believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5). This life is increased and strengthened by good conduct from day to day, as the inner person is renewed more and more (2 Cor. 4:16).

But the body, as the outer person, becomes increasingly corrupt the longer this life lasts, whether through age, illness, or various afflictions, until it reaches the final affliction that everyone calls death.

[Note: Erasmus, Lugdunensis, Venetus, and Lovaniensis add “affliction”; in the B manuscript this word is absent but is noted in the margin: “understand ‘affliction.’”]

Its resurrection, however, is postponed until the end, when our justification itself will also be completed ineffably. For then we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

But now, as long as the corruptible body weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), and the whole of human life upon earth is temptation (Job 7:1), no living person will be justified in his sight (Ps. 143:2), when compared with the righteousness by which we shall be made equal to the angels, and with the glory that will be revealed in us.

Why should I mention further proofs that the death of the soul must be distinguished from the death of the body, when the Lord, in a single Gospel saying, set forth both deaths so that anyone could easily distinguish them? He said:

> “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22).

The dead body was to be buried; but he wished those who buried it to be understood as dead in soul through the impiety of unbelief. Such people are roused when it is said:

> “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you” (Eph. 5:14).

The Apostle also condemns a certain kind of death when he says of a widow:

> “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6).

Thus the soul, once impious but now devout, is said to have come back to life from death and to live because of the righteousness of faith.

The body, however, is not only destined to die because of the separation of the soul that will occur, but also because of the great weakness of flesh and blood. In one passage of Scripture it too is called dead, when the Apostle says:

> “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.”

This life has come through faith, because:

> “The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17).

But what follows?

> “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11).

## 6. Christ’s single death was offered for our double death

For this double death of ours, therefore, our Savior offered his single death; and, in order to accomplish both our resurrections, he set forth and presented his own single resurrection in sacrament and example.

For he was neither a sinner nor impious, so that, as though dead in the spirit, he would need to be renewed in the inner person and, as though coming to his senses, be recalled to the life of righteousness. Rather, clothed in mortal flesh, dying in it alone and rising again in it alone, he made that flesh correspond to both our deaths, since in it there was provided the sacrament of the inner person and the example of the outer person.

As a sacrament of our inner person, that voice was given to signify the death of our soul—not only in the Psalm but also on the cross:

> “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 22:1; Matt. 27:46).

To this voice the Apostle’s words correspond:

> “Knowing that our old person was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we should no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6:6).

The crucifixion of the inner person is understood as the pains of repentance and a certain health-giving suffering of self-restraint. Through this death, the death of impiety is destroyed—the death in which God left us.

[Note: The printed editions read, “the death in which God did not leave us.” But the better manuscripts read, “the death in which God left us” or “leaves us”—that is, in the death and crucifixion of our inner person, namely, in the pains of repentance and the suffering of self-restraint.]

And therefore, through such a cross, the body of sin is destroyed, so that we may no longer present our members to sin as weapons of iniquity (Rom. 6:6, 13). For if the inner person is indeed renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16), then before being renewed it was old.

What takes place within is what the same Apostle says:

> “Put off the old person and put on the new.”

He explains this consecutively:

> “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth” (Eph. 4:22–25).

But where is falsehood put away except within, so that the person who speaks truth in his heart may dwell on God’s holy mountain (Ps. 15:1, 3)?

The Lord’s bodily resurrection is shown to pertain to the sacrament of our inner resurrection when, after rising, he said to the woman:

> “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17).

To this mystery the Apostle’s words correspond:

> “If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things above” (Col. 3:1–2).

For this is what it means not to touch Christ until he has ascended to the Father: not to think of Christ in a carnal manner.

But the death of the Lord’s flesh pertains to the example of the death of our outer person, because through such suffering he especially urged his servants not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matt. 10:28). Hence the Apostle says:

> “That I may complete in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ” (Col. 1:24).

The resurrection of the Lord’s body is also found to pertain to the example of the resurrection of our outer person, because he said to his disciples:

> “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

And one of the disciples, also touching his scars, exclaimed:

> “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

When the full integrity of that flesh was evident, it was demonstrated in him what he had said when exhorting his own:

> “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18).

Why, then, did he first say, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” and why was he touched by the disciples before he ascended to the Father? It was because in the former passage the sacrament of the inner person was being signified, while in the latter the example of the outer person was being provided.

Or is anyone so absurd and so turned away from the truth that he would dare to say that men touched him before he ascended, but women touched him after he had ascended?

Because this example of our future bodily resurrection preceded us in the Lord, the Apostle says:

> “Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ” (1 Cor. 15:23).

That passage concerned the resurrection of the body, for which reason he also says:

> “He will transform the body of our humiliation to conform to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21).

[Note: Several manuscripts read “He will transform” rather than “He transforms.”]

Thus our Savior’s one death brought salvation to our two deaths. And his one resurrection provided us with two resurrections, since his body, both in death and in resurrection, was administered to us through a certain medicinal correspondence as both the sacrament of our inner person and the example of our outer person.

# CHAPTER FOUR
7. The ratio of the simple to the double, derived from the perfection of the number six. The perfection of six commended in Scripture. The year possesses the power of the number six.

This ratio of the simple to the double does indeed arise from the number three: for one compared with two makes three. But the whole matter I have described reaches the number six: one, two, and three together make six. This number is therefore called perfect because it is completed by its parts: it has three such parts—the sixth, the third, and the half—and no other part that can be described as a specified fraction is found in it. Its sixth, then, is one; its third, two; its half, three. One, two, and three together complete that same number six.

Holy Scripture commends its perfection to us, especially in the fact that God perfected his works in six days, and that on the sixth day the human being was made in the image of God (Gen. 1:27). In the sixth age of the human race the Son of God came and became the Son of Man, so that he might reform us according to the image of God.

That age is now in progress, whether a thousand years are assigned to each age, or whether we trace in divine Scripture the memorable and notable divisions of time, so that the first age is found to extend from Adam to Noah, and the second from Noah to Abraham; and thereafter, as the evangelist Matthew distinguished them, from Abraham to David, from David to the deportation to Babylon, and from there to the birth of the Virgin’s child (Matt. 1:17). These three ages, joined to the preceding two, make five. Accordingly, the Lord’s birth began the sixth age, which is now in progress until the hidden end of time.

That this number six bears a figure of time we also recognize [Col. 0893] in that threefold division by which we reckon one period before the Law, a second under the Law, and a third under grace. In this period we have received the sacrament of renewal, so that at the end of time, renewed in every respect also by the resurrection of the flesh, we may be healed from every infirmity—not only of the soul but of the body as well.

Hence we understand that the woman whom the Lord healed and raised up was a type of the Church; infirmity had bent her down, with Satan binding her. Of such hidden enemies the voice of the Psalm laments: “They have bent down my soul” (Ps. 56:7). This woman had been ill for eighteen years, which is three times six. The months of eighteen years are found in the number that is the solid square of six—that is, six times six, and that result six times again.

In the same passage of the Gospel there is also, nearby, that fig tree whose wretched barrenness was condemned even by its third year. Yet intercession was made for it, so that it might be spared that year: if it bore fruit, well; otherwise, it was to be cut down (Luke 13:6–17). The three years likewise belong to the same threefold division, and the months of three years make the square of six, which is six times six.

8. The year, too, if its twelve complete months are considered—months completed by thirty days each, for the ancients observed such a month as the lunar circuit reveals—possesses the power of the number six. For what six is worth in the first order of numbers, which consists of units and reaches ten, sixty is worth in the second order, which consists of tens and reaches one hundred. The number sixty days, therefore, is one-sixth of a year.

Accordingly, it is multiplied by six of the first order, as though by six tens of the second order, and six times sixty makes three hundred and sixty days, which are the twelve complete months. [The editions read “are multiplied”; the manuscripts, better, “is multiplied,” namely the number six.]

But since, just as the moon’s circuit reveals the month to human beings, the year is observed through the sun’s circuit, five days and a quarter of a day remain for the sun to complete its course and conclude the year. For four quarters make one day, which must be intercalated after four years have elapsed—a period they call a leap year—so that the order of the seasons is not disturbed.

If we consider those five days and a quarter themselves, the number six has great force in them. First, because it is customary to reckon the whole from a part, there are no longer five days but rather six, with the quarter being taken as a day. Then, because within those five days there is one-sixth of a month; and the quarter itself contains six hours. For the whole day, that is, together with its night, consists of twenty-four hours, and its fourth part—the quarter of a day—is found to be six hours. Thus the number six has great force in the course of the year.

## CHAPTER V

9. Six commended likewise in the building of Christ’s body and of the Jerusalem temple.

Nor without reason, in the building of the Lord’s body—of which the temple destroyed by the Jews was a figure, when he said that he would raise it up in three days—is the number six [Col. 0894] understood as standing for a year. For they said: “Forty-six years was this temple in building.” And forty-six times six makes two hundred and seventy-six.

That number of days completes nine months and six days, which are reckoned, as it were, as ten months for women giving birth—not because all of them reach the sixth day after the ninth month, but because the perfection of the Lord’s body is found to have been brought to birth in that number of days, as the Church’s authoritative tradition, received from the elders, preserves.

For he is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which day he also suffered. Thus the new tomb in which he was buried, where no dead person had been laid (John 19:41–42), corresponds exactly—neither before nor afterward—to the Virgin’s womb in which he was conceived, where no mortal seed had been sown.

He is traditionally said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. Reckoned from that day to this one [the Venetian edition reads “to be reckoned”; M. reads “reckoned”], two hundred and seventy-six days are found, and that number contains six forty-six times. The temple was built over that number of years because the Lord’s body was perfected through that number of sixes; destroyed by the suffering of death, he raised it up in three days.

For he was speaking of the temple of his body (John 2:19–21), as the Gospel’s clearest and strongest testimony declares when it says: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. 12:40).

## CHAPTER VI

10. The three days of the resurrection, in which the ratio of the simple to the double also appears.

Scripture bears witness that this three-day period was not wholly and completely comprised of three full days. Rather, the first day was counted in full from its final portion; the third day likewise in full from its first portion; while the day between them—that is, the second day—was entirely complete, with its twenty-four hours, twelve nocturnal and twelve diurnal.

He was first condemned by the voices of the Jews at the third hour, when it was the sixth day of the week. Then he was hung upon the cross at the sixth hour, and gave up his spirit at the ninth hour (Matt. 27:23–50). He was buried when it had already become evening, as the words of the Gospel indicate (Mark 15:42–46), which is understood to be at the end of the day.

Therefore, wherever one begins—even if another explanation can be given for how it is not contrary to John’s Gospel (John 19:14) to understand him as having been hung upon the wood at the third hour—you do not include the whole first day [the Lovaniensian edition reads “if you do not include the whole day”; “if” is absent from the other books and should be absent]. It will therefore be counted in full from its final portion, just as the third day is counted from its first portion.

For the night up to dawn, when the Lord’s resurrection was revealed, belongs to the third day. God, who said that light should shine out of darkness (2 Cor. 4:6), so that through the grace of the New Testament and participation in Christ’s resurrection we might hear, “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8), indicates to us in a certain way that the day takes its beginning from the night.

For just as the first days, because of the future fall of humanity, are reckoned from light to night (Gen. 1:4–5), so these days, because of humanity’s restoration, are reckoned from darkness to light.

From the hour of his death to the dawn of the resurrection [Col. 0895] there are therefore forty hours, with the ninth hour itself also included. To this number there also corresponds his life on earth after the resurrection, lasting forty days.

This number occurs very frequently in Scripture to signify the mystery of perfection in the four-part world [the editions read “in the fourfold manner,” erroneously]. For ten possesses a certain perfection, and multiplied four times it makes forty.

From the evening of the burial to the dawn of the resurrection there are thirty-six hours, which is the square of six. This is related to the ratio of the simple to the double, in which there is the greatest harmony of correspondence. For twelve and twenty-four correspond as the simple to the double, and together they make thirty-six: the whole night with the whole day and the whole night again—and this, too, not without the sacramental meaning I mentioned above.

For it is not absurd to compare the spirit to the day and the body to the night. In his death and resurrection the Lord’s body bore both the figure of our spirit and the example of our body. Thus, too, the ratio of the simple to the double appears in the thirty-six hours, when twelve are compared with twenty-four.

As for the reasons why these numbers have been placed in Holy Scripture [the editions read “have been placed” in the feminine], another person may investigate other explanations, or determine whether those I have offered ought to be preferred, or whether others are equally probable or even more probable. Nevertheless, no one so foolish and senseless would contend that they were placed in Scripture without purpose, and that there are no mystical reasons why these numbers are mentioned there.

The explanations I have offered I have gathered either from the authority of the Church, handed down from the elders [most manuscripts read “handed down” in the singular], or from the testimony of the divine Scriptures, or from the reasoning supplied by numbers and their correspondences. No sober person will think contrary to reason, no Christian contrary to the Scriptures, and no peaceful person contrary to the Church.

## CHAPTER VII

11. How, through the one Mediator, we are gathered into one.

This sacrament, this sacrifice, this priest, this God, before he was sent and came, having been made from a woman—all things that appeared to our fathers in sacred and mystical ways through angelic miracles, or that were performed through them, were likenesses of this reality. Through its works, all creation was in a certain manner proclaiming the one who was to come, in whom there would be salvation for all who were to be restored from death.

For because, through the iniquity of ungodliness, we had recoiled and fallen away from the one true and supreme God, and had vanished into many things—torn apart among many things and clinging to many things—it was necessary, by the command and decree of the merciful God, that these many things themselves should proclaim with one voice the One who was to come; that the One proclaimed by many should come; that many things should testify that the One had come; that, released from many things, we should come to the One; that, dead in soul through many sins and destined to die in the flesh because of sin, we should love the One who, without sin, died in the flesh for us; and that, believing in him who was raised and rising with him in spirit through faith, we should be justified in the One and made one in the just One.

Nor should we despair of rising in that same flesh, since we see that many members have preceded us in the One Head. In him we are now cleansed through faith, and then restored through vision [Col. 0896]; reconciled to God through the Mediator, we cling to the One, enjoy the One, and remain one.

## CHAPTER VIII

12. How Christ wills all to be one in him.

Thus the Son of God himself, the Word of God, and that same Mediator of God and human beings, the Son of Man (1 Tim. 2:5)—equal to the Father through the unity of divinity, and sharing our condition through the assumption of humanity [Erasmus and Lovaniensian editions: “sharing our condition”—the manuscripts read “sharing in us”]—interceding for us by virtue of what he was as a human being (Rom. 8:34), yet not concealing that as God he was one with the Father, speaks among other things as follows:

“But I ask not for these only,” he says, “but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me I have given them, so that they may be one, as we are one” (John 17:20–22).

## CHAPTER IX

The discussion continues on the same subject.

He did not say, “I and they are one,” although, because he is the Head of the Church and the Church is his body (Eph. 1:22–23), he could have said, “I and they”—not “are one,” but “are one person,” since the Head and the body are one Christ.

But showing that his divinity is consubstantial with the Father [the printed editions add “he said this”; those words are absent from the manuscripts], for which reason he also says elsewhere, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), he wills his own to be one in their own mode—that is, in the consubstantial equality of the same nature—but in him. For they could not be one in themselves, separated from one another by different pleasures [several manuscripts: “wills”] and desires and the uncleanness of sins.

Therefore they are cleansed through the Mediator, so that they may be one in him—not only through the same nature, by which all who come from mortal human beings become equal to the angels [the editions read “all human beings from human beings,” less well], but also through the same concordant will, converging upon the same blessedness, fused in a certain manner into one spirit by the fire of charity [some manuscripts: “fused”; the editions read: “through the same charity, converging upon the same blessedness with a most concordant will”].

For this is the force of what he says, “That they may be one, as we are one”: just as the Father and the Son are one not only through equality of substance but also through unity of will, so those between whom the Son is Mediator and through whom we are reconciled to God may be one not only because they are of the same nature, but also through the fellowship of the same love.

Then he indicates in this way the very fact that he is the Mediator through whom we are reconciled to God: “I in them,” he says, “and you in me, that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:23).

## CHAPTER X

13. As Christ is the Mediator of life, so the devil is the mediator of death.

This is true peace and our firm union with our Creator: we are purified and reconciled through the Mediator of life, just as, stained and alienated, we had withdrawn from him through the mediator of death.

For just as the proud devil led the proud human being to death, so the humble Christ led the obedient human being back to life. As the one, exalted, fell and cast down the one who consented to him, so the other, humbled, rose and raised up the one who believed.

Because the devil had not reached the place to which he himself had led us [Col. 0897]—for he carried the death of the spirit in ungodliness, but had not undergone the death of the flesh, since he had not assumed a body—he appeared to humanity as a great prince among the legions of demons through whom he exercises his kingdom of deception. He held human beings subject to him, inflating them through the swelling of pride, making them more desirous of power than of justice, whether by a false philosophy or by ensnaring them through sacrilegious rites.

In those rites he also plunges souls that are more curious and proud into the deceptions of magic, deceived and mocked by them. He promises the purification of the soul through what they call *τελεταί* (“initiatory rites”), transforming himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14) through manifold contrivance in lying signs and wonders.

## CHAPTER XI

14. The miracles performed by demons are to be despised.

It is easy for wicked spirits, through aerial bodies, to do many things that souls weighed down by earthly bodies—even souls of better disposition—admire.

For if earthly bodies themselves, shaped by various arts and exercises, display such great marvels to human beings in theatrical spectacles that those who have never seen such things scarcely believe them when they are reported, what great thing is it for the devil and his angels, through aerial bodies and from corporeal elements, to do things that the flesh marvels at? Or what great thing is it for them, through hidden inspirations, to devise images and phantasms for deceiving human senses—deceiving people awake or asleep, or driving the frenzied into agitation?

Yet just as it can happen that a person superior in life and character watches utterly wicked people walking on a rope or performing many incredible feats through manifold movements of their bodies, without desiring in any way to do such things or thinking that they should therefore be considered better than himself, so a faithful and devout soul—even if it sees the miracles of demons, or, because of the frailty of the flesh, recoils from them—will not on that account grieve that it cannot do such things, nor judge the demons to be better.

This is especially so since the company of the saints includes those who, through the power of God, to whom all things are subject, and without any deception, have done things far greater—whether human beings or good angels [the printed editions read “since they are”; the manuscripts read “since it is,” referring to the devout soul].

## CHAPTER XII

15. The devil is the mediator of death; Christ is the Mediator of life.

Souls are by no means purified and reconciled to God through sacrilegious imitations, impious curiosities, and magical consecrations. The false mediator does not convey them to higher things; rather, by occupying the way, he blocks it through the affections he inspires in his fellowship—affections all the more evil because they are more proud.

These affections cannot grow wings of virtue for flying upward; instead, they increase the weights of vices for sinking downward. The soul will fall all the more heavily the higher it seems to itself to have been raised.

Therefore, just as the Magi acted when divinely warned (Matt. 2:12)—the star having led them to worship the Lord’s humility—we too must return to our homeland not by the way we came, but by another way, which the humble King taught and which the proud king, the adversary of the humble King, cannot blockade.

For the heavens also have declared [Col. 0898] the glory of God to us, so that, as we worship humble Christ, their sound has gone out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. 18:2, 5).

Our way to death was through sin in Adam. “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). The mediator of this way was the devil, persuading us to sin and hurling us into death.

For, to bring about our double death, he brought his own simple death. He died in spirit through ungodliness, but did not die in the flesh. To us, however, he persuaded ungodliness and through it caused us to deserve entry into the death of the flesh [nearly all manuscripts: “and because of it”].

Thus we desired one death through an unjust persuasion, and another followed us through a just condemnation. For this reason it is written, “God did not make death” (Wis. 1:13), because he himself was not the cause of death; yet through his most just retribution death was inflicted upon the sinner [the manuscripts read “death was justly inflicted”; the editions read “most just death”].

A judge inflicts punishment upon the guilty person, but the cause of the punishment is not the judge’s justice; it is the merit of the crime.

Therefore, to the place to which the mediator of death transmitted us—and to which he himself did not come, namely, the death of the flesh—there our Lord God inserted the medicine of correction, which the devil did not deserve, by the hidden and exceedingly mysterious ordering of divine and exalted justice.

Thus, just as through one human being came the death of the dead, so through one human being might come the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. 15:21–22). For human beings were more concerned to avoid what they could not avoid—the death of the flesh—than the death of the spirit; that is, they were more concerned with the punishment than with the merit that deserved punishment. Not to sin is either not cared about or cared about little; not to die, although it cannot be achieved, is pursued with great eagerness.

The Mediator of life, showing us that the death which can no longer be escaped through human nature is not to be feared, but rather the ungodliness that can be avoided through faith, came to meet us at the end to which we had arrived, but not by the way by which we had arrived.

We came to death through sin; he came through justice. And therefore, since our death is the punishment of sin, his death became a sacrifice for sin.

## CHAPTER XIII

16. Christ’s death was voluntary. How the Mediator of life conquered the mediator of death. How the devil leads his followers to despise Christ’s death.

Since the spirit is superior to the body, and since the death of the spirit is abandonment by God while the death of the body is abandonment by the spirit—and since the punishment in the death of the body is that the spirit, having voluntarily abandoned God, abandons the body involuntarily, so that, although the spirit abandoned God because it willed to do so, it abandons the body even if it does not wish to do so, and does not abandon it when it wishes unless it has inflicted upon itself some force by which the body is destroyed—the spirit of the Mediator demonstrated that no punishment of sin extended to him even as far as the death of the flesh.

For he did not abandon it unwillingly, but because he willed to, when he willed to, and in the manner he willed to. Joined to the Word of God in unity [the editions read, incorrectly, “the human being was joined; then he says”], he says [Col. 0899]: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John 10:18).

Those who were present were especially astonished at this, as the Gospel relates, when, immediately after that utterance in which he expressed the figure of our sin, he gave up his spirit.

For those hung upon the cross suffered a prolonged death. Accordingly, the legs of the criminals were broken so that they might die and be taken down from the cross before the Sabbath. But when he was found already dead, this was a miracle. We also read that Pilate was astonished at it when the Lord’s body was requested from him for burial (Mark 15:37, 39, 43–44; John 19:30–34).

17. That deceiver, who was the mediator of death for humanity and falsely presents himself as the way to life under the name of purification through sacrilegious rites and sacrifices by which the proud are deceived, could neither share in our death nor possess a resurrection of his own. He could bring his simple death to bear upon our double death, but he could not bring his simple resurrection, in which there would be both the sacrament of our renewal and the example of the awakening that is to occur at the end.

Therefore, the one who, alive in spirit, raised his dead flesh—the true Mediator of life—drove out from the spirits of those who believe in him that one who was dead in spirit and the mediator of death. Thus the devil would not reign within them, but would attack from outside, without conquering them.

Christ also offered himself to be tempted by him, so that he might be the Mediator for overcoming his temptations—not only through assistance but also through example.

But when the devil first attempted to creep in through every entrance to the inner person and was expelled, after the baptism, in the wilderness, when every alluring temptation had been completed (Matt. 4:1–11), he could not invade the One who was alive in spirit, since he himself was dead in spirit. In his greed for human death, he turned in whatever way he could to inflict the death that was within his power, and he was permitted to act against that mortal element which the living Mediator had received from us [one Vatican manuscript: “the Mediator of life received”].

Where he was able to do something, there he was defeated in every respect; and from the place where he received external power to kill the Lord’s flesh, there his inner power—the power by which he held us—was itself killed.

For it came to pass that the bonds of the sins of many, in many deaths, were loosed through the one death of One whom no sin had preceded. The Lord therefore rendered on our behalf a death that was not owed, so that the death owed by us might not harm us.

He was not stripped of his flesh by the lawful authority of anyone; he stripped himself of it. For one who could not die if he had not wished to die certainly died because he wished to. And therefore he made a public example of principalities and powers, triumphing over them confidently in himself (Col. 2:15).

By his death, offered for us as one true sacrifice, he cleansed, abolished, and extinguished whatever guilt there was by which principalities and powers were lawfully holding us for punishment. By his resurrection he called those predestined to new life, justified those called, and glorified those justified (Rom. 8:30).

Thus the devil had possessed humanity, deceived into consenting to him, as though by a fully valid right. Although he himself was not enclosed by any corruption of flesh and blood, through the frailty of this mortal body [Col. 0900] he dominated one who was exceedingly poor and weak, becoming all the prouder because he seemed, as it were, richer and stronger. But he lost humanity in the very death of the flesh.

For to the place where he had driven the falling sinner without following him, he pursued and compelled the descending Redeemer. Thus, in sharing our death, the Son of God deigned to become our friend, in the very realm which the enemy thought made him better and greater than us because he could not reach it.

For our Redeemer says: “No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

Accordingly, the devil even believed himself superior to the Lord, insofar as the Lord yielded to him in his sufferings. For of the Lord too was understood what is read in the Psalm: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6). Thus, though the wicked one acted against us as though by an equal right, the innocent One, having been killed, might overcome him by the most equitable right; and so he might lead captivity captive, captivity brought about because of sin (Eph. 4:8), and free us from that captivity which sin had justly imposed, by erasing the record of death with his just blood unjustly shed and redeeming sinners who were to be justified [the editions read “with his own blood … redeeming sinners by justifying them”].

18. The devil still deceives his followers in this way. He presents himself to them as a false mediator through his rites, supposedly to purify them, but in reality to entangle and plunge them further. For he easily persuades the proud to mock and despise Christ’s death. The more alien he himself is from that death, the more holy and divine they believe him to be.

Yet very few remain with him, as the nations recognize and drink their price with devout humility, abandoning their enemy in confidence in Christ and hastening to their Redeemer.

For the devil does not know how the supremely excellent wisdom of God makes use of him, even while he lies in wait and rages, for the salvation of God’s faithful—extending strongly from the higher end, which is the beginning of spiritual creation, to the lower end, which is the death of the body, and ordering all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1).

For wisdom reaches everywhere because of its purity, and nothing defiled enters into it (Wis. 7:24–25).

But for the devil, who is alien to the death of the flesh and therefore proceeds in excessive pride, a death of another kind is prepared in the eternal fire of Tartarus, where spirits can be tormented not only with earthly bodies but also with aerial bodies.

But proud human beings, to whom Christ seemed worthless because he died, though he purchased us at so great a price (1 Cor. 6:20), will undergo this death together with human beings, as due to the miserable condition of nature drawn from the first sin; and with the devil they will be plunged into that death.

They therefore placed the devil before Christ because he cast them down into the state into which he himself did not fall through a different nature, and into which Christ descended for their sake through immense mercy. Yet they do not hesitate to believe themselves better than demons, and they never cease to pursue and detest them with every curse, although they know that the demons are strangers to the suffering of that death because of which they despise Christ.

Nor do they wish to consider how it could happen that the Word of God, remaining in himself and incapable of being changed in any respect [Col. 0901], could nevertheless, through the assumption of a lower nature, suffer something lower—something that an unclean demon cannot suffer because he does not possess an earthly body.

Thus, although they themselves are better than demons, because they carry flesh they can die in a way in which demons, who do not carry flesh, cannot die.

And although they greatly pride themselves on the deaths of their sacrifices [the editions read “the rites of their sacrifices”], they do not perceive that they are sacrificing themselves to deceitful and proud spirits; or, if they do perceive it, they imagine that the friendship of faithless and envious beings benefits them. Such spirits have no concern except to obstruct our return.

## CHAPTER XIV

19. Christ is the most perfect victim for cleansing our sins. Four things to be considered in every sacrifice.

They do not understand that even those most proud spirits could not have rejoiced in the honors of sacrifices unless a true sacrifice were owed to the one true God in whose place they wish to be worshipped; nor that it could properly be offered except through a holy and just priest; nor that what is offered can be received except from those for whom it is offered; nor that it can be offered for the cleansing of the sinful unless it is itself without defect.

Certainly all who wish a sacrifice to be offered to God on their behalf desire these things.

Who, then, is so just and holy a priest as the only Son of God, who had no need to cleanse his own sins through sacrifice—neither original sins nor those added through human life (Heb. 7)?

And what could be taken from human beings and offered for them so fittingly as human flesh? What could be so suitable for this immolation as mortal flesh? What could be so pure, for cleansing the sins of mortals, as flesh born without any contamination of carnal desire in and from a virgin’s womb?

And what could be offered and received with such favor as the flesh of our sacrifice, which became the body of our priest?

Since four things are considered in every sacrifice— to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—the same one true Mediator, reconciling us to God through the sacrifice of peace, remained one with the one to whom he offered; made those for whom he offered one in himself; and was himself both the one who offered and what he offered.

## CHAPTER XV

20. The proud believe that they can be purified by their own power to see God.

There are some who think that by their own power they can be purified so as to contemplate God and cling to God. Pride itself stains them most of all. For there is no vice that the divine law resists more strongly, nor over which that supremely proud spirit—the mediator to the depths and the blocker of the way to the heights—receives a greater right of domination [the editions read “receives more greatly”], unless it is secretly avoided through another route; or unless, raging openly through the failing people signified by Amalek, and resisting and denying passage to the promised land, it is overcome through the cross of the Lord, prefigured by Moses with his hands extended (Exod. 17:8–16).

These people promise themselves purification by their own power because some of them have been able [Col. 0902] to send the mind’s gaze beyond every creature and touch, however slightly, the light of unchanging truth. They mock many Christians who meanwhile live by faith alone and have not yet been able to do this.

But what does it profit the proud person, who is ashamed for that reason to climb the wood, to gaze from afar upon a homeland across the sea? Or what harm does it do the humble person not to see it from so great a distance, while coming to it on that wood by which the proud person disdains to be carried?

## CHAPTER XVI

21. The ancient philosophers are not to be consulted about the resurrection and future events.

These philosophers also criticize us for believing in the resurrection of the flesh and wish people to believe them instead concerning such matters. As though, because they were able to understand the lofty and unchanging substance through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20), they should therefore be consulted about the transformation of mutable things or the woven order of the ages.

Because they argue with the greatest truth and persuade us through the most certain proofs that all temporal things are made according to eternal principles, were they therefore able to perceive within those principles—or derive from them—the number of species of living creatures; the seeds of each at their beginnings; the manner of their growth; the numerical patterns in conception, birth, the stages of life, and decline; and the movements involved in pursuing what accords with nature and fleeing what is contrary to it?

Did they not investigate all these matters not through that unchanging wisdom, but through the history of places and times, and believe the reports of things experienced and written down by others?

It is therefore much less surprising that they were entirely unable to trace the sequence of longer ages and determine a certain limit to this course through which the human race runs like a river, and from there its return to the end owed to each.

Historians could not write about things far in the future, experienced and narrated by no one. Nor did these philosophers, better than others, contemplate such matters intellectually in those highest and eternal principles. Otherwise they would not inquire into the past of the same kind—past events that historians could investigate [the editions read “historically”; the manuscripts, better, “historians”]—but would instead foresee the future as well.

Those who were able to do this were called *vates* (“seers”) by them and Prophets by our people.

## CHAPTER XVII
### 22. In what ways the future is foreknown

Philosophers—including those who excelled among the ancients—are not to be consulted about the resurrection of the dead. Although the name “prophets” is not altogether foreign to their writings, there is a very great difference between conjecturing the future from experience of the past—as physicians, by foreseeing many things, have even committed to writing what they themselves observed through experience; and as farmers, or even sailors, predict many things (for such predictions, when they arise from long intervals of time, are considered divinations)—and the case in which things already on the way have advanced and what is coming is announced as having been seen from far off [Note: [Col. 0902] Almost the only edition, that of Louvain, reads, “they have anticipated, and they announce what they see coming from afar.” Less correctly.], on account of the keen perception of those who see; when aerial powers do this, they are believed to divine—as if someone from the summit of a mountain saw someone approaching from far away and announced him beforehand to those living nearby on the plain [Col. 0903]—or between these and the case in which such things are disclosed by the holy Angels, to whom God makes them known through his Word and Wisdom, in whom future and past things stand; or in which they are foretold to certain human beings, or, having been heard by them, are transmitted again to other human beings; or in which the minds of certain human beings are so raised up by the Holy Spirit that they see, not through Angels but by themselves, the standing causes of future things [Note: [Col. 0903] The printed editions read, “imminent causes.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “standing causes.” One Vatican manuscript subsequently has, “they behold them in the very summit of the art of all things.”] in the very summit of the order of things.

For aerial powers also hear these things, whether Angels announce them or human beings do so; and they hear only as much as he judges necessary to whom all things are subject. Many things are also foretold through a certain impulse and prompting of the spirit by those who do not know what they are saying: thus Caiaphas did not know what he said, but, because he was high priest, he prophesied (John XI, 51).

### 23.

Therefore, concerning the succession of the ages and the resurrection of the dead, we ought not to consult philosophers—not even those who, as far as they were able, understood the eternity of the Creator, in whom we live and move and have our being (Acts XVII, 28). For although they knew God through the things that have been made, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, claiming to be wise, they became fools (Rom. I, 20–22).

And because they were not capable of fixing the eye of the mind steadily enough upon the eternity of a spiritual and immutable nature to see, in the very wisdom of the Creator and Ruler of the universe, the cycles of the ages—which there already were and always would be, whereas here they would be future and would not yet exist—and to see there the transformations toward a better state, not only of souls but also of human bodies, each to the perfection proper to it: since, then, they were altogether incapable of seeing these things there, they were not even deemed worthy to have them announced to them through the holy Angels, whether outwardly through the bodily senses or through inward revelations impressed upon the spirit.

Such things were shown to our fathers, who were endowed with true piety. By proclaiming them, and by having their predictions confirmed through present signs or events soon to occur, they gained credibility; and thus they deserved to possess an authority that would be believed concerning things far in the future, even to the end of the age.

But the proud and deceitful aerial powers—even if they are found to have spoken through their own prophets certain things heard from the holy Prophets or Angels concerning the fellowship and city of the saints and concerning the true Mediator—acted in such a way that, through these truths belonging to others, they might, if possible, draw even God’s faithful people over to their own falsehoods. God, however, brought it about through those who did not know what they were saying that the truth should resound everywhere: for the help of the faithful and as a testimony against the impious.

### CHAPTER XVIII

### 24. The Son of God became incarnate so that, purified through faith, we might be raised to immutable truth

Since, therefore, we were not capable of attaining eternal things, and the filth of sins weighed us down—filth contracted through love of temporal things and, as it were, naturally ingrained through our mortal descent—we had to be purified. But in order to be purified so that we might be conformed to eternal things, we could be purified only through temporal things, since we were already held fast by things of that kind.

Health is very far removed from sickness; but an intermediate treatment, unless it corresponds to the illness, does not lead to health [Note: [Col. 0904] The printed editions read, “the treatment of a physician.” This is corrected from the manuscripts.]. Useless temporal things deceive the sick; useful temporal things are received by those who are to be healed and carry the healed over to eternal things. As the rational mind, when purified, ought to contemplate eternal things, so, while being purified, it ought to place its faith in temporal things.

One of those who were once regarded as wise among the Greeks said: “As great as eternity is in relation to what has come into being, so great is truth in relation to faith.” And this is certainly a true statement. For what we call temporal, he called “what has come into being.” We too belong to this category, not only with respect to the body but also with respect to the mutability of the soul. For what changes in any respect is not properly called eternal.

To the extent, therefore, that we are mutable, to that extent we are distant from eternity. Eternal life is promised to us through truth, from whose clarity our faith is again as far removed as mortality is from eternity. Now, therefore, we place our faith in things accomplished temporally for our sake, and through that faith we are purified, so that when we have come to the vision, eternity may succeed mortality just as truth succeeds faith.

Since, therefore, our faith will become truth when we arrive at what is promised to us who believe—and eternal life is promised to us—and since Truth spoke, not the truth that will come into being as our faith will, but the Truth that always is, because eternity is there, Truth said: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII, 3). When our faith becomes truth through seeing, eternity will possess our mortality after it has been changed.

Until this occurs, and so that it may occur, because we attach the faith of belief to things that have come into being, just as we hope for the truth of contemplation in eternal things, so that the faith of mortal life may not be discordant with the truth of eternal life, Truth itself, coeternal with the Father, arose from the earth (Ps. LXXXIV, 12), when the Son of God came in such a way as to become the son of man. He himself received in his own person our faith, by which he would lead us to his truth; and he assumed our mortality in such a way that he did not lose his eternity.

“For as great as eternity is in relation to what has come into being, so great is truth in relation to faith.” We therefore had to be purified in such a way that he who would remain eternal might become for us one who had come into being, lest one be ours in faith and another in truth [Note: [Col. 0904] Louvain reads, “and lest another.”]. Nor could we pass from the state into which we had come into being to eternal things unless, through our coming into being, the Eternal had been joined to us, and we were transferred to his eternity.

Thus our faith has in a certain way followed him there where the one in whom we have believed ascended—having come into being, died, risen again, and been taken up. Of these four things, we knew the first two in ourselves, for we know that human beings come into being and die. But the remaining two, namely, rising again and being taken up, we rightly hope will occur in us, because we have believed that they occurred in him.

Therefore, because in him what had come into being passed over into eternity, so will what is ours pass over when faith reaches truth. He already speaks thus to those who believe, so that they may remain in the word of faith and from there be led to truth, and through truth to eternity, and thus be delivered from death: “If you abide in my word, you will truly be my disciples” [Note: [Col. 0905] The manuscripts read, “you are.”]. And as though they asked, “With what result?” he continues: “And you will know the truth.” And again, as though they said, “What benefit is truth to mortals?” he replies: “And the truth will set you free” (John VIII, 31–32).

From what, if not from death, corruption, and mutability? For truth remains immortal, incorruptible, and immutable. True immortality, true incorruptibility, and true immutability are eternity itself.

### CHAPTER XIX

### 25. In what way the Son was sent and foretold. How, through the mission of his birth in the flesh, he became less without detriment to his equality with the Father

See, then, for what he was sent—the Son of God; or rather, see what it means for the Son of God to have been sent. Whatever was temporally accomplished, for the sake of producing the faith by which we might be purified to contemplate the truth, among things that had come into being, brought forth from eternity and referred back to eternity, was either testimony to this mission or was itself the mission of the Son of God.

Some testimonies foretold that he would come; others testified that he had come. For he through whom every creature was made, having been made a creature, ought to have every creature as his witness. For unless the One had been proclaimed through the sending of many, the One would not be held fast through the dismissal of many.

And unless the testimonies were such that great things might seem great to the little, it would not be believed that the Great One, who was sent little to the little, makes them great [Note: [Col. 0905] After “it would not be believed,” the printed editions add, “that he, being so great”; the addition is rightly absent from the manuscripts.].

For heaven and earth and all that is in them—because all things were made through him—are incomparably greater works of the Son of God than the signs and wonders that burst forth in testimony to him. Yet human beings, though small, trembled at those small things as though they were great, so that they might believe that these great things had been made through him [Note: [Col. 0905] Ambrose, Erasmus, and nearly all the manuscripts read, “so that they might be believed.”].

### 26.

When, therefore, the fullness of time came, “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. IV, 4)—so far made little that he was made; and therefore sent in the same condition in which he was made. If, then, the greater sends the lesser, we too confess that he was made lesser, lesser to the extent that he was made, and made to the extent that he was sent.

For he sent his Son, made of a woman, through whom, nevertheless, all things were made. We confess him equal to the One who sent him—not only before he was made and sent, but before all things existed—although we call him, as sent, lesser.

How, then, before that fullness of time when he ought to be sent, could he have been seen by the fathers, when certain angelic visions were displayed to them, if, even after he had been sent, he was not seen as the equal of the Father? Why else does he say to Philip—by whom, as by the others, and by those who crucified him in the flesh, he was evidently seen—“Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” unless it is because he was seen and was not seen?

He was seen as the one he had been made when sent; he was not seen as the one through whom all things had been made.

Or why else does he say: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 9, 21), when he was manifest before the eyes of human beings—unless it is because he offered the flesh, which the Word had become in the fullness of time, to be received by our faith, while reserving the Word itself, through which all things had been made, for contemplation in eternity by the mind purified through faith?

### CHAPTER XX

### 27. The sender and the one sent are equal. Why the Son is said to be sent by the Father. How and by whom the Holy Spirit was sent. The Father is the source of the whole Godhead

If the Son is said to have been sent by the Father because the one is Father and the other Son, this in no way prevents us from believing that the Son is equal to the Father, consubstantial and coeternal with him, and yet sent by the Father.

It is not because the one is greater and the other lesser, but because the one is Father and the other Son; the one begets and the other is begotten; the one is the source of the one who is sent, and the other is from the one who sends. The Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son.

In this way it can now be understood that the Son is said to have been sent not only because the Word became flesh (John I, 3, 18, 14), but also because he was sent so that the Word might become flesh and might accomplish through his bodily presence the things that are written. That is, it is not only the man who is understood to have been sent, because the Word was made [Note: [Col. 0906] Erasmus and Louvain read, “the Word was made flesh.” “Flesh” is absent from the other books.], but the Word was also sent so that he might become man.

He was not sent according to an inferior power, substance, or anything in which he is unequal to the Father, but according to the fact that the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son. The Son is the Father’s Word, and he is also called his Wisdom.

What wonder, then, if he is sent—not because he is unequal to the Father, but because he is “a certain pure emanation (manatio) of the brightness of the almighty God” [Note: [Col. 0906] The manuscripts consistently read here and below, “pure.”]? What emanates and that from which it emanates are of one and the same substance. It does not emanate as water flows from an opening in the earth or in a stone, but as light comes from light.

For what else is meant by the statement, “For she is the brightness of eternal light,” than “She is the light of eternal light”? What is the brightness of light except light? And therefore she is coeternal with the light from which she is.

But he preferred to say “the brightness of light” rather than “the light of light,” lest what emanates should be thought darker than that from which it emanates. When it is heard that this is its brightness, it is more readily believed that the light from which it emanates shines through it than that this emanating light shines less brightly.

But since there was no need to guard against anyone’s thinking that the light which generated this one was lesser—for no heretic has ever dared to say this, nor should we believe that anyone will dare to do so—Scripture anticipated the thought by which this emanating light might appear darker than that from which it emanates. It removed this suspicion when it said, “She is its brightness,” that is, the brightness of eternal light, and thus showed that she is equal.

If she is lesser, she is its darkness, not its brightness. If she is greater, she does not emanate from it, for she could not surpass that from which she was begotten. Therefore, because she emanates from it, she is not greater than it; but because she is not its darkness but its brightness, she is not lesser. Therefore she is equal.

Nor should it disturb us that she is called “a certain pure emanation of the glory of the almighty God,” as though she herself were not almighty but merely an emanation of the Almighty. For immediately it is said of her: “And although she is one, she can do all things” (Wis. VII, 25–27). Who is almighty except the one who can do all things?

She is therefore sent by the one from whom she emanates. Thus she is sought from the one who loved and desired her: “Send her,” he says, “from your holy heavens, and send her from the seat of your greatness, that she may be with me and labor with me” (Wis. IX, 10)—that is, that she may teach me to labor, lest I labor. For her labors are her virtues [Note: [Col. 0907] Louvain adds here, “of which it has already been said.”].

But she is sent in one way so that she may be with a human being, and in another way she was sent so that she herself might be man. She transfers herself into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets (Wis. VII, 27), just as she also fills the holy Angels and accomplishes through them everything appropriate to such ministries.

But when the fullness of time came, she was sent (Gal. IV, 4), not to fill the Angels, nor to be an Angel—except insofar as she announced the Father’s plan, which was also her own—nor to be with human beings or in human beings, for this had already occurred in the fathers and prophets. Rather, she was sent so that the Word itself might become flesh, that is, become man.

In this future sacrament, once revealed, there would also be the salvation of those wise and holy people who were born from women before he himself was born from a virgin; and in the sacrament accomplished and proclaimed, there is the salvation of all who believe, hope, and love.

“For this is the great mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to Angels, was preached among the nations, was believed on in the world, and was taken up in glory” (1 Tim. III, 16).

### 28.
