The Word of God is therefore sent by the one whose Word he is; he is sent by the one from whom he was born. The one who begot sends; what was begotten is sent.

And he is sent to each person when he is known and received by that person, to the extent that he can be known and received according to the capacity either of a soul progressing toward God or of a rational soul perfected in God.

The Son is therefore not said to have been sent simply because he was eternally born from the Father. Rather, he is said to have been sent either because he appeared to this world as the Word made flesh—whence he says, “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John XVI, 28)—or because he is received in the mind of someone at a particular time, as it is said: “Send her, that she may be with me and labor with me.”

What was born from eternity is eternal: “For she is the brightness of eternal light.” But what is sent in time is known by someone.

When the Son of God was manifested in the flesh, he was sent into this world, in the fullness of time, made of a woman. For since the world could not know God through the wisdom of God—because “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it”—it pleased God “through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. I, 21), so that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 5, 14).

When, however, he is received in the mind of someone at a particular time as that person progresses, he is indeed said to be sent, but not into this world. For he does not appear sensibly—that is, he is not present to the bodily senses.

We too, insofar as we grasp something eternal with the mind, as far as we are able, are not in this world; and the spirits of all the righteous, even while they still live in this flesh, insofar as they savor divine things, are not in this world.

But when the Father is known by someone at a particular time, he is not said to be sent. For he does not have anyone from whom he could be [Note: [Col. 0908] The printed editions read, “from whom he could be sent.” “Sent” is absent from the manuscripts.], or from whom he might proceed. Wisdom says, “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. XXIV, 5); and it is said of the Holy Spirit, “He proceeds from the Father” (John XV, 26). But the Father proceeds from no one.

### 29.

As, therefore, the Father begot and the Son was begotten, so the Father sent and the Son was sent. But just as the one who begot and the one who was begotten are one, so also the one who sent and the one who was sent are one, because “the Father and I are one” (John X, 30).

The Holy Spirit is likewise one with them, because these three are one. For just as, for the Son, being born means being from the Father, so for the Son, being sent means being known as being from him. And just as, for the Holy Spirit, being the gift of God means proceeding from the Father, so being sent means being known as proceeding from him [Note: [Col. 0908] Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain read, “so being sent means being known as proceeding from him.” M.].

Nor can we say that the Holy Spirit does not also proceed from the Son, for the same Spirit is not called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son without reason. Nor do I see what else he wished to signify when, breathing upon the faces of the disciples [Note: [Col. 0908] The manuscripts do not have “upon the faces of the disciples.”], he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22).

For that bodily breath, proceeding from the body and perceptible to bodily touch, was not the substance of the Holy Spirit; rather, it was a demonstration through an appropriate sign that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son.

Who, except someone utterly insane, would say that the Spirit whom he gave by breathing was different [Note: [Col. 0908] Most manuscripts read, “that the Holy Spirit whom he gave was different.”] from the Spirit whom he sent after his ascension (Acts II, 1–4)? For there is one Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, the Holy Spirit, who works all things in all (1 Cor. XII, 6).

But the fact that he was given twice was certainly an arrangement of signification, concerning which we shall discuss in its proper place, as the Lord grants.

When the Lord says, “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John XV, 26), he shows that the Spirit belongs to both the Father and the Son. For even when he had said, “Whom the Father will send,” he added, “in my name” (John XIV, 26); yet he did not say, “Whom the Father will send from me,” as he said, “Whom I will send to you from the Father.” In this he evidently showed that the Father is the source of the whole divinity—or, if it is better expressed, of the whole Godhead.

Therefore, the one who proceeds from the Father and the Son is referred back to the one from whom the Son was born.

And when the Evangelist says, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 39), how is this to be understood except that the particular giving or sending of the Holy Spirit was to occur after Christ’s glorification, in a form such as had never existed before? It does not mean that previously there had been no giving at all, but that there had not previously been one of this kind.

For if the Holy Spirit was not given before, by what Spirit did the prophets, when filled, speak? Scripture plainly says, and demonstrates in many passages, that they spoke through the Holy Spirit. It is also said of John the Baptist, “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” And his father Zechariah is found filled with the Holy Spirit, so that he might say such things about him. Mary too was filled with the Holy Spirit, so that she might proclaim such things about the Lord whom she carried in her womb (Luke I, 15, 41–79). Simeon and Anna were filled with the Holy Spirit, so that they might recognize the greatness of the infant Christ (Luke II, 25–38).

How, then, had the Spirit not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified, unless this giving, donation, or sending of the Holy Spirit was to possess a particular feature in that very coming—a feature such as had never existed before?

For nowhere do we read that people spoke in languages they did not know when the Holy Spirit came upon them, as happened then, when it was necessary that his coming be demonstrated by perceptible signs. This was so that it might be shown that the whole world and all the nations established in different languages would believe in Christ through the gift of the Holy Spirit, and that what is sung in the Psalm might be fulfilled:

“There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard; their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 4–5).

### 30.

Thus, when the fullness of time came, a human being was joined and in a certain way united to the Word of God in the unity of person, when the Son of God, made of a woman, was sent into this world, so that he might also be the son of man for the sake of the sons of human beings.

The angelic nature could previously represent this person in order to foretell him; it could not appropriate him to itself so as itself to be that person.

### CHAPTER XXI

### On the perceptible manifestation of the Holy Spirit and on the coeternity of the Trinity. What has been said and what remains to be said

Concerning the perceptible manifestation of the Holy Spirit, whether through the form of a dove (Matt. III, 16) or through fiery tongues (Acts II, 3), when a created nature, subject and serving, displayed his substance—coeternal and equally immutable with the Father and the Son—through temporal movements and forms, and when that created nature was not joined to the unity of his person as was the flesh which the Word became (John I, 14), I would not dare to say that nothing of this kind had ever occurred before.

But I would say with complete confidence that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one God and Creator, the omnipotent Trinity, work inseparably. Yet this cannot be demonstrated inseparably through a creature that is so greatly inferior and especially bodily, just as, through our words—which certainly sound bodily—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be named except with a definite separation according to their proper intervals of time, which the syllables of each word occupy.

In the substance in which they are, the three are one: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Without any temporal movement, above every creature, they are the same, without any intervals of time or place, simultaneously one and the same from eternity to eternity, as eternity itself—which does not exist without truth and love.

But in my words the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are separated; they cannot be spoken simultaneously, and in visible letters they occupy separate spaces in separate places.

And just as, when I name my memory, understanding, and will, each name refers to an individual thing, yet each of the three is produced by all three together—for none of these three names exists without my memory, understanding, and will working together—so the Trinity worked together in producing the Father’s voice, the Son’s flesh, and the dove of the Holy Spirit, although each of these is properly referred to one person.

Through this analogy, it is possible to understand to some extent that the Trinity, inseparable in itself, is demonstrated separately through the form of visible creation, and that the inseparable operation of the Trinity exists even in individual things said to belong particularly to the demonstration of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit.

### 31.

If, then, I am asked how voices or perceptible forms and appearances were produced before the incarnation of the Word of God, so as to prefigure what was to happen, I answer that God produced them through Angels. This also, as I think, has been sufficiently demonstrated by the testimony of the holy Scriptures.

If, however, it is asked how the incarnation itself occurred, I say that the Word of God became flesh, that is, became man, but was not changed or transformed into what he became. He became man in such a way that there is there not only the Word of God and the flesh of man, but also the rational soul of man; and this whole person is called God because of God and man because of man.

If this is difficult to understand, let the mind be purified by faith, increasingly abstaining from sins, doing good works, and praying with the groaning of holy desires, so that, progressing through divine assistance, it may both understand and love.

If, however, it is asked how, after the incarnation of the Word, the Father’s voice or the bodily appearance through which the Holy Spirit was demonstrated was produced, I do not doubt that these things were produced through a creature. But whether the creature was merely bodily and perceptible, or whether a rational or intellectual spirit was also employed—for some have preferred to call this what the Greeks call νοερόν (*noeron*, intellectual)—not for the unity of person (for who would say that whatever creature it was through which the Father’s voice sounded was God the Father, or that whatever creature it was in which the Holy Spirit was demonstrated through the form of a dove or through fiery tongues was the Holy Spirit in the same way as the man who was made from the virgin is the Son of God?), but only for the carrying out of the signification, as God judged necessary: whether something else should be understood is difficult to discover, and it is not expedient to affirm it rashly.

Yet how these things could have occurred without a rational or intellectual creature, I do not see. Nor is there yet an opportunity to explain why I think this, as far as the Lord grants me strength. First, the arguments of the heretics must be examined and refuted—arguments that they produce not from the divine Books but from their own reasoning, by which they imagine themselves to compel us to understand the testimonies concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the way they themselves wish.

### 32.

It has now been sufficiently demonstrated, as I think, that the Son is not lesser because he was sent by the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit lesser because both the Father and the Son sent him [Col. 0911].

Whether these statements in Scripture are understood with reference to the visible creature, or rather with reference to the affirmation of the source, they are not placed there on account of inequality, inferiority, or dissimilarity of substance. For even if God the Father had wished to appear visibly through a subject creature [Col. 0912], it would nevertheless be utterly absurd to say that he was sent either by the Son whom he begot or by the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him.

Let this, then, be the limit of this volume. In what follows, with the Lord’s help, we shall examine what those extremely subtle arguments of the heretics are and how they are refuted.

## BOOK FIVE

He comes to those arguments of the heretics which they produce not from the divine Books but from their own reasoning, and refutes those who therefore think that the substance of the Father and the Son is not the same: because they suppose that everything said of God is said according to substance, and consequently contend that begetting and being begotten, or being begotten and being unbegotten, since these are different, indicate different substances.

He demonstrates that not everything said of God is said according to substance. “Good” and “great,” and anything else said of him in relation to himself, are said according to substance; but things are also said relatively—that is, not in relation to himself but in relation to something that he himself is not—as “Father” is said in relation to the Son, or “Lord” in relation to the creature that serves him.

When something relative—that is, in relation to something that he himself is not—is said of him with reference to time, as in “Lord, you have become our refuge,” nothing happens to him by which he is changed; rather, he remains wholly immutable in his nature or essence.

[Col. 0911]

### CHAPTER I

### 1. What the author asks of God and of the reader. Nothing mutable or corporeal is to be conceived in God

Beginning now to discuss those things that cannot be spoken as they are thought, either by any human being or certainly by us in every respect—although even our thought, when we think about the Trinity of God, feels itself far unequal to the one about whom it thinks and does not grasp him as he is, but, as it is written, is seen “through a mirror and in an enigma” even by those as great as the Apostle Paul was here (1 Cor. XIII, 12)—I first ask from the Lord our God himself, of whom we ought always to think but whom we cannot think of worthily, to whom blessing must be rendered at all times (Ps. XXXIII, 1), and to whom no expression is adequate when he is declared, both the help necessary for understanding and explaining what I intend and forgiveness wherever I offend.

For I am mindful not only of my will but also of my weakness. I also ask those who will read these things to forgive me whenever they perceive that I wished to say more than I was able to say—whether they themselves understand it better or, because of the difficulty of my speech, do not understand it—as I forgive them whenever they cannot understand because of their own slowness.

### 2.

We more readily forgive one another, however, if we know—or at least hold firmly through faith—that what is said about an immutable, invisible, supremely living nature, which is sufficient to itself, must not be measured according to the customary patterns of visible, mutable, mortal, or needy things.

Although we labor to comprehend even those things that lie close to our bodily senses, or that we ourselves are in the inner person, and are not sufficient for this task, faithful piety nevertheless burns without presumption toward those divine and ineffable things that are above us—not inflated by the arrogance of its own powers, but kindled by the grace of the Creator and Savior himself.

For with what understanding does a human being grasp God, when he does not yet grasp the understanding itself by which he wishes to grasp him? If he already grasps this understanding, let him carefully consider that nothing in his nature is better than it [Col. 0912], and let him see whether he finds there any outlines of forms, brilliance of colors, extended magnitude, distance between parts, expansion of bulk, movements across intervals of place, or anything of this kind.

Certainly we find none of these things in that by which we find nothing better in our nature: namely, in our understanding, by which we grasp wisdom to the extent of our capacity.

What, therefore, we do not find in what is better in us, we ought not to seek in him who is far better than what is better in us. Thus, if we can, and to the extent that we can, let us understand God as good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, presiding without location [Note: [Col. 0912] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “present.”], containing all things without posture, wholly present everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing.

Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet discover in every respect what he is, nevertheless piously guards, as far as he can, against thinking of him as something he is not.

### CHAPTER II

### 3. God alone is immutable essence

There is nevertheless no doubt that he is a substance—or, if this is a better designation, an essence, which the Greeks call οὐσία (*ousia*). For just as wisdom is named from “to be wise,” and knowledge from “to know,” so essence is named from “to be.”

And who exists more truly than the one who said to his servant Moses, “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14)?

But other things that are called essences or substances admit accidents, through which great changes, or changes of whatever extent, may occur in them. Nothing of this kind can happen to God; and therefore he alone is immutable substance or essence, who is God, to whom being itself—the source of the name “essence”—belongs most fully and most truly.

For what changes does not preserve being itself; and what can be changed, even if it is not changed, can cease to be what it was. Accordingly, only that which not only does not change but cannot change at all presents itself without hesitation as what can most truly be said to be.

### 4. The Arians’ argument drawn from the terms “begotten” and “unbegotten” is refuted

Therefore, in order that we may now begin to answer the adversaries of our faith concerning matters that are neither spoken as they are conceived nor conceived as they are, it seems that, among the many arguments which the Arians usually advance against the catholic faith, they devise this especially subtle contrivance. They say:

“Whatever is said or understood concerning God is said according to substance, not according to accident. Therefore, for the Father to be unbegotten is something according to substance, and for the Son to be begotten is something according to substance. But to be unbegotten and to be begotten are different; therefore the substance of the Father and of the Son is different.”

We answer them:

If whatever is said concerning God is said according to substance, then what was said—“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—was said according to substance. Therefore the substance of the Father and the Son is one.

Or, if this was not said according to substance, then something is said concerning God otherwise than according to substance; and consequently we are no longer compelled to understand “unbegotten” and “begotten” according to substance.

Again, it was said of the Son, “He did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized” (Philippians 2:6). We ask: in what respect is he equal? For if “equal” is not said according to substance, they admit that something may be said concerning God otherwise than according to substance; let them therefore admit that “unbegotten” and “begotten” are not said according to substance. But if they do not admit this because they wish everything concerning God to be said according to substance, then according to substance the Son is equal to the Father.

### CHAPTER IV

#### 5. An accident always implies some change in a thing

An accident, moreover, is not ordinarily said to be anything except what can be lost through some change in the thing to which it belongs. For even though certain things are called inseparable accidents—called *achōrista* (ἀχώριστα) in Greek—such as the black color of a raven’s feather, the feather nevertheless loses it, not indeed so long as it remains a feather, but because it is not always a feather. Accordingly, the matter itself is mutable; and when that animal or that feather ceases to exist, and the whole body is changed and transformed into earth, it necessarily loses that color as well.

Although an accident called separable is likewise lost not by separation but by change—such as the blackness of human hair, which is called a separable accident because, while the hair remains hair, it can become white—yet to those who observe carefully it is sufficiently evident that, when the hair turns gray, something does not, as it were, depart from the head by separation, so that blackness leaves it, succeeded by whiteness, and goes somewhere else. Rather, that quality of color is altered and changed there.

There is therefore no accident in God, because nothing in him is mutable or capable of being lost. But if one also wishes to call that an accident which, although it is not lost, is nevertheless diminished or increased—such as the life of the soul—for as long as the soul exists, so long does it live, and because the soul always exists, it always lives; yet because it lives more fully when it is wise and less fully when it is foolish, some change occurs even here—not so that life ceases, as wisdom is absent from the foolish, but so that it is diminished—nothing of this kind occurs in God, because he remains wholly immutable.

### CHAPTER V

#### 6. Nothing is said of God according to accident, but according to substance or relation

Therefore nothing in him is said according to accident, because nothing happens to him; yet not everything that is said of him is said according to substance.

For among created and mutable things, whatever is not said according to substance remains to be said according to accident. For everything happens to them that can either be lost or diminished: quantities and qualities; and whatever is said in relation to something else, such as friendships, relationships, servitudes, likenesses, equalities, and things of this kind; as well as position and state, places and times, actions and passions.

In God, however, nothing is said according to accident, because nothing in him is mutable; yet not everything that is said of him is said according to substance. Something is said relationally, such as “Father” in relation to “Son,” and “Son” in relation to “Father.” This is not an accident, because the one is always Father and the other always Son—not “always” in the sense that the Father began to be Father when the Son was born, so that, if the Son never ceased to be Son, the Father would not cease to be Father; rather, the Son was always born and never began to be Son.

If the Son had begun at some time to exist, or if at some time he were to cease to be Son, then this would be said according to accident.

If, however, “Father” were said in relation to himself, not to the Son, and “Son” were said in relation to himself, not to the Father, then both “Father” and “Son” would be said according to substance. But because the Father is called Father only because he has a Son, and the Son is called Son only because he has a Father, these terms are not said according to substance. They are said not of each in relation to himself, but of them mutually and reciprocally. Nor are they said according to accident, because both what is called “Father” and what is called “Son” are eternal and immutable for them.

Therefore, although being Father and being Son are different, the substance is not different, because these terms are not said according to substance but according to relation. Yet this relation is not an accident, because it is not mutable.

[Note: The printed editions have *haec* (“these things”); the manuscripts have *hoc* (“this”).]

### CHAPTER VI

#### 7. He answers the heretics’ sophistries concerning the same terms “begotten” and “unbegotten”

But if they think that this argument must be resisted by saying that “Father” is spoken in relation to “Son” and “Son” in relation to “Father,” whereas “unbegotten” and “begotten” are spoken in relation to themselves, not to one another—for “unbegotten” does not mean the same as “Father,” since, even if he had not begotten a Son, nothing would prevent him from being called unbegotten; and if anyone begets a son, he is not thereby himself unbegotten, since begotten human beings themselves beget others—then they say:

“Father” is said in relation to the Son, and “Son” in relation to the Father; but “unbegotten” is said in relation to itself, and “begotten” in relation to itself. Therefore, if whatever is said in relation to itself is said according to substance, while being unbegotten and being begotten are different, the substance is consequently different.

If they say this, they do not understand that, with respect to “unbegotten,” they are saying something that requires more careful examination. For no one is a father because he is unbegotten, nor is anyone unbegotten because he is a father; and for this reason “unbegotten” is thought to be said not relationally but in relation to itself.

Yet, with astonishing blindness, they do not notice that “begotten” cannot be said except relationally. He is a son precisely because he is begotten, and because he is a son he is certainly begotten. Just as “son” is referred to “father,” so “begotten” is referred to “begetter”; and just as “father” is referred to “son,” so “begetter” is referred to “begotten.”

Accordingly, the concept by which “begetter” is understood is one thing, and that by which “unbegotten” is understood is another. Although both are said of God the Father, the former is said in relation to the begotten one, that is, to the Son—which they themselves do not deny. But they claim that “unbegotten” is said in relation to itself.

They therefore say:

“If the Father is said in relation to himself in a way in which the Son cannot be said in relation to himself; and if whatever is said in relation to itself is said according to substance; and if ‘unbegotten’ is said in relation to itself, whereas the Son cannot be called this—then ‘unbegotten’ is said according to substance. Since the Son cannot be called unbegotten, he is therefore not of the same substance.”

This trickery is answered by compelling them to say in what respect the Son is equal to the Father: whether according to what is said in relation to himself, or according to what is said in relation to the Father.

It cannot be according to what is said in relation to the Father, since the Son is called Son in relation to the Father, whereas the other is not Son but Father. For “father” and “son” are not said in relation to themselves in the same way as “friends” or “neighbors.”

A friend is said relationally in relation to a friend; and if they love one another equally, the same friendship exists in both. A neighbor is said relationally in relation to a neighbor; and because they are equally neighbors of one another—for this one is as near to that one as that one is to this one—the same nearness exists in both.

But because the Son is not called Son relationally in relation to a Son, but in relation to the Father, the Son is not equal to the Father according to what is said in relation to the Father. It remains, therefore, that he is equal according to what is said in relation to himself.

Whatever is said in relation to itself is said according to substance. It remains, therefore, that he is equal according to substance. The substance of both is therefore the same.

When the Father is called “unbegotten,” however, what he is not is being stated, not what he is. When a relation is denied, it is not denied according to substance, because the relation itself is not said according to substance.

### CHAPTER VII

#### 8. The addition of a negation does not change the category

This must be made clear by examples. First, we must observe that what is signified by “begotten” is what is signified by “son.” He is a son because he is begotten, and because he is a son he is certainly begotten.

Therefore, when “unbegotten” is said, it is shown that he is not a son. “Begotten” and “unbegotten” can conveniently be said; but although “son” is said in Latin, ordinary usage does not permit the form *in-filius*. Nothing is nevertheless taken away from the understanding if one says “not a son.” Likewise, if one says “not begotten” instead of “unbegotten,” nothing else is said.

Thus “neighbor” and “friend” are both said relationally, yet one cannot say *un-neighbor* in the way one says “enemy.” Therefore, in considering things, we must not ask what the usage of our language permits or does not permit us to say, but what understanding of the things themselves is made clear.

Let us therefore no longer say “unbegotten,” although it can be said in Latin, but instead say “not begotten,” which has exactly the same force. Are we then saying anything different from “not a son”?

This negative particle “not” does not cause what is said relationally without it to be said substantially when it is prefixed. It merely denies what was asserted without it, just as occurs in the other categories.

For example, when we say, “A human being exists,” we designate substance. Whoever says, “It is not a human being,” does not state another kind of category, but merely denies that one. Therefore, just as I affirm according to substance when I say, “It is a human being,” so I deny according to substance when I say, “It is not a human being.”

When it is asked how large it is, and I say, “It is four-footed,” that is, “of four feet,” I affirm according to quantity. Whoever says, “It is not four-footed,” denies according to quantity.

“It is white”: I affirm according to quality. “It is not white”: I deny according to quality.

“It is near”: I affirm according to relation. “It is not near”: I deny according to relation.

I affirm according to position when I say, “It is lying down”; I deny according to position when I say, “It is not lying down.”

I affirm according to state when I say, “It is armed”; I deny according to state when I say, “It is not armed.” The same thing is conveyed if I say, “It is unarmed.”

I affirm according to time when I say, “It is yesterday’s”; I deny according to time when I say, “It is not yesterday’s.”

When I say, “It is in Rome,” I affirm according to place; and I deny according to place when I say, “It is not in Rome.”

I affirm according to the category of action when I say, “He is striking”; but if I say, “He is not striking,” I deny according to the category of action, showing that he is not doing this.

When I say, “He is being beaten,” I affirm according to the category called passion; and I deny according to that category when I say, “He is not being beaten.”

In short, there is no category according to which we wish to affirm something without being compelled to acknowledge that we deny according to that same category if we choose to prefix the negative particle.

Since this is so, if I were affirming substantially by saying “son,” I would be denying substantially by saying “not a son.” But because I affirm relationally when I say, “He is a son”—for I refer him to the father—I deny relationally if I say, “He is not a son,” for I refer the same denial to the parent, wishing to show that he is not his parent’s son.

But if “begotten” has the same force as “son,” as we stated above, then “not begotten” has the same force as “not a son.” We deny relationally when we say “not a son”; therefore we deny relationally when we say “not begotten.”

What, then, is “unbegotten” except “not begotten”? The relational category is therefore not abandoned when “unbegotten” is said.

For just as “begotten” is not said in relation to itself, but indicates that someone is from a begetter, so when “unbegotten” is said, it is not said in relation to itself, but indicates that someone is not from a begetter.

Both meanings nevertheless belong to the same category, which is called Relation. What is pronounced relationally does not indicate substance. Thus, although “begotten” and “unbegotten” are different, they do not indicate different substances, because just as “son” is referred to “father,” and “not a son” to “not a father,” so “begotten” must be referred to “begetter,” and “not begotten” to “not a begetter.”

### CHAPTER VIII

#### 9. Whatever is said substantially of God is said of each person individually and of the Trinity together

In God there is one essence, three *hypostases* in Greek, and three persons in Latin.

Let us therefore hold this above all: whatever is said of that supreme and divine sublimity in relation to itself is said substantially; whatever is said in relation to something else is not said substantially but relationally.

The force of the same substance in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is so great that whatever is said of each individually in relation to himself is understood not plurally in the totality but singularly.

For just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God—which no one doubts is said according to substance—we nevertheless do not say three gods, but one God, namely that same supreme Trinity.

Likewise, the Father is great, the Son is great, and the Holy Spirit is great; yet we do not say three great ones, but one great one. For it was not written of the Father alone, as they perversely think, but of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: “You alone are the great God” (Psalm 85:10).

The Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good; yet there are not three good ones, but one who is good, of whom it was said, “No one is good except one God.”

Indeed, the Lord Jesus, so that the one who had said to him “Good Teacher” (Luke 18:19, 18), addressing him as a human being, would not understand him merely according to his humanity, did not say, “No one is good except the Father alone,” but, “No one is good except one God.”

In the name “Father,” the Father himself is designated by himself; but in the name “God,” both the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are designated, because the Trinity is one God.

Position, state, places, and times are spoken of God not properly, but figuratively and by way of likeness. For he is said to sit upon the cherubim (Psalm 79:2), which pertains to position; and to be clothed with the abyss as with a garment (Psalm 103:6), which pertains to state; and, “Your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101:28), which pertains to time; and, “If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Psalm 138:8), which pertains to place.

As for action, perhaps it can be said most truly of God alone: God alone acts and is not made, nor does he suffer, insofar as this concerns his substance, by which he is God.

Thus the Father is omnipotent, the Son is omnipotent, and the Holy Spirit is omnipotent; yet there are not three omnipotent beings, but one Omnipotent, “from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things; to him be glory” (Romans 11:36).

Whatever, therefore, is said of God in relation to himself is said individually of each person—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and is also said of the Trinity itself together, not plurally but singularly.

[Note: Several manuscripts read *similiter dicitur* (“is likewise said”); some read *ter dicitur* (“is said three times”).]

Since being God is not one thing for God and being great another, but being God is the same for him as being great, just as we do not say three essences, so we do not say three greatnesses, but one essence and one greatness.

By “essence” I mean what is called *ousia* (οὐσία) in Greek, which we more commonly call “substance.”

#### 10.

They also use the term *hypostasis* (ὑπόστασις), but I do not know what distinction they wish to make between *ousia* and *hypostasis*. Thus many of our people who discuss these matters in the Greek language have become accustomed to saying μίαν οὐσίαν, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις—“one essence, three substances” in Latin.

### CHAPTER IX

#### The three persons are not properly so called

But because our customary usage has now established that what we understand by “essence” is what we understand by “substance,” we do not dare to say “one essence, three substances.” Instead, we say “one essence” or “substance,” but “three persons,” just as many Latins of authority who have treated these matters have said, since they found no more suitable way of expressing in words what they understood without words.

For in fact, since the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit—who is also called the gift of God—is neither the Father nor the Son, there are certainly three.

For this reason it was said in the plural, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He did not say, “There is one,” as the Sabellians say, but, “We are one.”

Nevertheless, when it is asked what the three are, human speech suffers from utter poverty. Yet “three persons” has been said—not so that this would be expressed adequately, but so that nothing would be left unsaid.

### CHAPTER X

#### 11. What properly belongs to God as essence is said of the Trinity in the singular, not in the plural

Therefore, just as we do not say three essences, so we do not say three greatnesses or three great ones.

Among things that are great by participation in greatness, whose being is one thing and whose being great is another—such as a large house, a great mountain, and a great soul—greatness is one thing, and what is made great by that greatness is another. The greatness of the house is not the same as the large house itself.

There is, however, a true greatness by which not only the house that is large is large, and not only the mountain that is great is great, but by which everything else called great is great. Thus greatness itself is one thing, and the things called great by it are another.

This greatness is itself great in the first place, and far more excellently so than those things that are great by participation in it.

God, however, is not great by a greatness that is other than what he himself is, as though God were a participant in it when he is great; otherwise that greatness would be greater than God, and nothing is greater than God. He is therefore great by the greatness that he himself is.

Accordingly, just as we do not say three essences, so we do not say three greatnesses. For being God is the same for him as being great.

For the same reason we do not say three great ones, but one great one, because God is not great by participation in greatness, but is great through his own greatness; he himself is his greatness.

The same may be said of God’s goodness, eternity, omnipotence, and absolutely every category that can be predicated of God: whatever is said in relation to himself is said properly, not figuratively or by way of likeness—if indeed anything can be properly said of him by human speech.

### CHAPTER XI

#### 12. What is said relationally in the Trinity

[Note: Nearly the sole Louvain edition reads *Quae* (“the things which”) for *Quod* (“that which”).]

Whatever is properly said of the individual persons in this same Trinity is in no way said in relation to themselves, but in relation to one another or to creation. It is therefore clear that such terms are said relationally, not substantially.

Just as the Trinity is called one God, great, good, eternal, and omnipotent—and can likewise be called its own deity, its own greatness, its own goodness, its own eternity, and its own omnipotence—the Trinity cannot in the same way be called “Father,” unless perhaps figuratively in relation to creation, on account of the adoption of sons.

For when it is written, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), this must not be understood as excluding the Son or the Holy Spirit, whom we rightly call one Lord and our God, and also our Father, because by his grace he regenerates us.

The Trinity cannot in any way be called “Son.”

The Holy Spirit, however, according to what is written, “God is spirit” (John 4:24), can indeed be called so universally, because the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy.

Thus, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, and because God is certainly holy and God is spirit, the Trinity may be called “the Holy Spirit.” Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit who is understood not as the Trinity but as existing in the Trinity, insofar as he is properly called “the Holy Spirit,” is spoken of relationally, since he is referred both to the Father and to the Son: the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son.

The relation itself is not apparent in this name, but it becomes apparent when he is called “the gift of God” (Acts 8:20). He is the gift of the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from the Father (John 15:26), as the Lord says; and when the Apostle says, “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9), he is speaking of this same Holy Spirit.

When we say “the gift of the giver” and “the giver of the gift,” we speak of both relationally, each in relation to the other.

The Holy Spirit is therefore an ineffable communion of the Father and the Son. Perhaps he is called this because the same name can apply to both the Father and the Son. For he is properly called what they are called jointly: the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit; the Father is holy and the Son is holy.

Thus, so that the communion of both might be signified by a name that applies to both, he is called the Holy Spirit, the gift of both.

This Trinity is one God, alone, good, great, eternal, and omnipotent; he is his own unity, deity, greatness, goodness, eternity, and omnipotence.

### CHAPTER XII

#### 13. In mutually relational terms, corresponding names are sometimes lacking

Nor should it trouble us that we said that the Holy Spirit is spoken of relationally—not the Trinity itself, but the one who is in the Trinity—because the name of the one to whom he is referred does not seem to answer reciprocally to his name.

For just as we say “the servant of the master” and “the master of the servant,” “the son of the father” and “the father of the son,” because these are said relationally, so we cannot say the same here.

We say “the Holy Spirit of the Father,” but we do not correspondingly say “the Father of the Holy Spirit,” lest the Holy Spirit be understood to be his son.

Likewise, we say “the Holy Spirit of the Son,” but we do not say “the Son of the Holy Spirit,” lest the Holy Spirit be understood to be his father.

In many relational expressions this occurs: no term is found by which the things referred to one another might reciprocally answer each other.

For what is said more manifestly in relation to something else than “pledge”? A pledge is referred to the thing of which it is the pledge, and a pledge is always the pledge of something.

When we say “the pledge of the Father and the Son” (2 Corinthians 5:5; Ephesians 1:14), can we reciprocally say “the Father of the pledge” or “the Son of the pledge”?

When we say “the gift of the Father and the Son,” we cannot indeed say “the Father of the gift” or “the Son of the gift.” But, so that these may answer one another reciprocally, we say “the gift of the giver” and “the giver of the gift.” In the former case a customary term could be found; in the latter it could not.

### CHAPTER XIII

#### 14. In what sense “principle” is said relationally in the Trinity

The Father is spoken of relationally, and he is likewise spoken of relationally as “principle,” and perhaps in some other way as well. But “Father” is said in relation to the Son, whereas “principle” is said in relation to all things that are from him.

Likewise, the Son is spoken of relationally; he is also called “Word” and “Image,” and in all these terms he is referred to the Father. The Father is not called any of these things.

The Son is also called “principle.” For when he was asked, “Who are you?” he answered, “The Beginning, who am also speaking to you” (John 8:25). But is he the Father’s principle? By calling himself “principle,” he wished to show that he is the Creator, just as the Father is the principle of creation, since all things are from him.

“Creator” too is said relationally in relation to creation, just as “master” is said in relation to “servant.”

Therefore, when we call both the Father and the Son “principle,” we do not speak of two principles of creation. The Father and the Son together are one principle in relation to creation, just as they are one Creator and one God.

If whatever remains in itself and begets or performs something is the principle of what it begets or performs, we cannot deny that the Holy Spirit too is rightly called principle, because we do not separate him from the designation “Creator.” It is written of him that he acts, and he certainly acts while remaining in himself; he is not himself changed or transformed into any of the things he performs.

Observe what he performs:

“To each,” he says, “the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good. To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another various kinds of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills”—certainly as God does.

For who could perform such great things except God? “It is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:6–11).

If we are asked separately about the Holy Spirit, we answer with complete truth that he is God; and together with the Father and the Son he is one God.

God is therefore called one principle in relation to creation, not two or three principles.

### CHAPTER XIV

#### 15. The Father and the Son are the one principle of the Holy Spirit

In relation to one another within the Trinity, if the one who begets is the principle of the one begotten, the Father is the principle in relation to the Son, because he begets him.

[Note: The manuscripts have *quia genuit eum* (“because he begot him”).]

Whether the Father is also the principle in relation to the Holy Spirit, since it was said, “He proceeds from the Father,” is no small question.

For if this is so, he will no longer be the principle only of what he begets or makes, but also of what he gives.

[Note: The printed editions read *utpote* (“as being”); the manuscripts read *ut potest* (“insofar as possible”).]

Here too it becomes clear, insofar as possible, what often troubles many: why is the Son not also the Holy Spirit, since he too proceeds from the Father, as is read in the Gospel (John 15:26)?

He proceeds not in the manner of being born, but in the manner of being given. Therefore he is not called Son, because he was neither born as the Only-Begotten nor made so that, through God’s grace, he might be born into adoption, as we are.

What is born from the Father is referred solely to the Father when it is called “Son”; hence he is the Son of the Father, but not also our son.

[Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions have *et non noster* (“and not our [son]”); manuscript M has *et non noster* likewise.]

But what is given is referred both to the one who gave it and to those to whom he gave it. Thus the Holy Spirit is called not only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, who gave him, but also our Spirit, since we have received him.

Just as “the Lord’s salvation” is said of the one who gives salvation (Psalm 3:9), that same salvation is also ours, since we have received it, so the Spirit is both God’s, because he gave him, and ours, because we have received him.

He is not our spirit in the sense of that spirit by which we exist, since that is the human spirit which is in the human being; but he is ours in another sense, in which we say, “Give us our bread” (Matthew 6:11).

Although even that spirit which is called the human spirit we have certainly received. For what do you have, he says, that you did not receive? (1 Corinthians 4:7).

[Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions have *inquit Apostolus* (“the Apostle says”); manuscript M has simply *inquit* (“he says”).]

But what we received in order to exist is one thing, and what we received in order to be holy is another.

Thus it is also written of John that he would come in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). He is called Elijah’s spirit, namely the Holy Spirit whom Elijah received.

The same must be understood of Moses when the Lord says to him, “I will take from your spirit and give to them” (Numbers 11:17)—that is, “I will give them some of the Holy Spirit whom I have already given to you.”

If what is given also has as its principle the one from whom it is given, because it did not receive from elsewhere what proceeds from him, then we must acknowledge that the Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit—not two principles. Rather, just as the Father and the Son are one God, and in relation to creation are one Creator and one Lord, so in relation to the Holy Spirit they are one principle.

In relation to creation, however, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one principle, just as they are one Creator and one Lord.

### CHAPTER XV

#### 16. Whether the Holy Spirit was a gift even before he was given

[Note: The Amiens edition and most manuscripts read *interius* (“more deeply”); three other manuscripts read *interim* (“meanwhile”).]

A further question is raised: just as the Son possesses not merely the fact of being Son through being born, but through being born possesses existence altogether, so whether the Holy Spirit, by the fact that he is given, possesses not merely the fact of being a gift, but existence altogether.

Was he therefore in existence before he was given, but not yet a gift? Or, at the very moment when God was going to give him, was he already a gift even before he was given?

But if he proceeds only when he is given, he would certainly not proceed before there was someone to whom he could be given. How, then, was the substance itself already present if he exists only because he is given—just as the Son possesses through being born not only the fact of being Son, which is said relationally, but existence altogether?

[Note: Most manuscripts have *ipsa substantia* (“the substance itself”).]

Or does the Holy Spirit always proceed, proceeding not in time but from eternity; and, because he proceeded in such a way that he would be able to be given, was he already a gift even before there was someone to whom he could be given?

For “gift” is understood in one way, and “thing given” in another. A gift can exist even before it is given; but a thing given cannot in any way be called “given” unless it has been given.

### CHAPTER XVI
17. What is said of God in time is said relatively, not accidentally

Nor should it disturb us that, although the Holy Spirit is coeternal with the Father and the Son, something is nevertheless said of him in time—for example, this very thing which we have called “given.” For the Spirit is eternally a gift, but temporally he is given. Likewise, if “lord” is not said until someone begins to have a servant, this designation too is relative and temporal as applied to God: for the creature of which he is Lord is not eternal.

How, then, shall we maintain that these relative terms themselves are not accidents, since nothing happens to God temporally, because he is not mutable, as we discussed at the beginning of this inquiry? Behold, he does not possess being Lord eternally, lest we be forced to say that the creature too is eternal, since he could not eternally rule as Lord unless that creature also eternally served him. But just as there cannot be a servant who has no lord, so neither can there be a lord who has no servant.

And suppose someone should arise who says that God alone is eternal, while times are not eternal because of their variation and mutability, but that times nevertheless did not begin to exist in time—for there was no time before times began, and therefore it did not happen to God in time that he became Lord, since he was Lord of the times themselves, which certainly did not begin to exist in time. What will he answer concerning the human being, who was made in time and whose Lord God certainly was not before there was someone of whom he could be Lord? Certainly, then, for God to be Lord of a human being, this happened to him in time. And, to remove every possible dispute, certainly for him to be your Lord or mine—for we have only recently begun to exist—this happened to God in time.

Or, if even this seems uncertain because of the obscure question concerning the soul, what about God becoming Lord of the people of Israel? For although the nature of the souls possessed by that people already existed—which is not what we are asking now—that people itself did not yet exist, and it is clear when it began to exist. Finally, for God to be Lord of this tree or of this crop happened to him in time, since these have only recently begun to exist.

For even if the material itself already existed, it is nevertheless one thing to be lord of the material and another to be lord of a nature already formed. At one time, for example, a human being is lord of wood, and at another time he is lord of a chest, although the chest was made from that very wood, which certainly did not yet exist as a chest when he was already lord of the wood.

How, then, shall we maintain that nothing is said of God according to accident, except because nothing happens to his own nature by which it is changed? For those relative predicates are accidents which arise together with some change in the things of which they are predicated. Thus “friend” is said relatively: one does not begin to be a friend until one begins to love. Some change of will therefore takes place, so that one may be called a friend.

But when a coin is called a price, it is said relatively, although it has not changed when it began to be a price; nor has it changed when it is called a pledge, or by any similar designation. If, then, a coin can be called relatively by so many terms without any change in itself—so that neither when it begins to be called by such a term nor when it ceases to be called by it does any change occur in its nature or form as a coin—how much more readily should we understand that, in the unchangeable substance of God, something can be said relatively to a creature so that, although it begins to be said in time, nothing is understood to have happened to God’s own substance, but rather to the creature to which the term is applied?

“Lord,” he says, “you have become our refuge” (Psalm 89:1). God is therefore called our refuge relatively; the term refers to us, and he becomes our refuge when we flee to him. Does something then occur in his nature that was not there before we fled to him? A change therefore takes place in us. We were worse before we fled to him, and by fleeing to him we become better; but no change takes place in him.

So also he begins to be our Father when, by his grace, we are regenerated, since “he gave us power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Our substance is therefore changed for the better when we become his children; at the same time, he begins to be our Father, but without any change in his substance.

What, then, begins to be said of God in time which was not previously said is clearly said relatively. Yet this is not according to an accident of God—as though something had happened to him—but plainly according to an accident of that to which God begins to be said relatively.

And when a just person begins to be called God’s friend, that person is changed. But far be it from us to say that God loves someone temporally [Note: The manuscripts read thus. The printed editions read, “ever loves someone.”] as though with a new love that was not previously in him—he with whom past things have not passed away and future things have already become present. Accordingly, he loved all his saints before the foundation of the world, just as he predestined them. But when they are converted and find him, they are said to begin to be loved by him, so that what is said may be expressed in a manner that human feeling can grasp.

Likewise, when he is said to be angry with the wicked and peaceful toward the good, they are changed, not he—just as light is harsh to weak eyes and gentle to sound ones: the change is in their eyes, not in the light.

# BOOK SIX

In this book the proposed question is discussed: how Christ was called, in the words of the Apostle, “the power of God and the wisdom of God”; whether the Father is not himself wisdom but only the Father of wisdom, or whether wisdom has begotten wisdom. After postponing the solution for a short time, the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are established, and it is shown that one should believe not in a threefold God but in the Trinity. Finally, Hilary’s statement, “Eternity in the Father, form (*species*) in the Image, use in the Gift,” is explained.

[Col. 0923]

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. The Son, according to the Apostle, is the power and wisdom of God the Father. The reasoning of Catholics against the earlier Arians. The difficulty whether the Father is not himself wisdom but only the Father of wisdom

Some people think that the equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is prevented from being understood by the fact that Scripture says that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God”: thus, they suppose, the Father is not himself power and wisdom, but the begetter of power and wisdom, and consequently equality does not appear to obtain. Indeed, the question of how God is called the Father of power and wisdom is commonly raised with no small degree of attention.

For the Apostle says that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). On this basis, some of our people reasoned in this way against the Arians—specifically, against those who first rose up against the Catholic faith. Arius himself is said to have declared: “If he is a son, he was born; if he was born, there was a time when he was not a son,” not understanding that being born from God can nevertheless be eternal, so that the Son is coeternal with the Father, just as the radiance generated and emitted by fire is coeval with it and would be coeternal with it if the fire were eternal.

For this reason, some later Arians rejected that position and admitted that the Son of God did not begin in time. But in the debates our people held against those who said, “There was a time when the Son was not,” some also introduced the following argument: “If the Son of God is the power and wisdom of God, and God was never without power and wisdom, then the Son is coeternal with God the Father. The Apostle says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; and it is the statement of a madman to say that God at some time lacked power or wisdom. Therefore, there was no time when the Son was not.”

### 2. This reasoning compels us to say that God the Father is not wise except by possessing the wisdom he begot, rather than existing through himself as wisdom itself

This reasoning compels us to say that God the Father is wise only by possessing the wisdom he begot, and not by existing as wisdom itself [Note: Several manuscripts read, “he himself.”]

Next, if this is so, then, just as the Son is called God from God and light from light, we must consider whether he can be called wisdom from wisdom, if God the Father is not wisdom itself but only the begetter of wisdom.

But if we accept this, why should he not also be the begetter of his own greatness, goodness, eternity, and omnipotence, so that he himself is not his own greatness, goodness, eternity, or omnipotence, but is great by the greatness he begot, good by the goodness, eternal by the eternity, and omnipotent by the omnipotence born from him—just as he is not himself his own wisdom [Note: Some manuscripts read, “just as he himself is not his very wisdom.”] but is wise by the wisdom born from him?

There is no need to fear that we would then be forced to speak of many sons of God, apart from the adoption of the creature—sons coeternal with the Father—if he is the begetter of his own greatness, goodness, eternity, and omnipotence. The charge is easily answered: the fact that many names are mentioned does not make him the Father of many coeternal sons, just as he is not thereby the Father of two when Christ is called “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” For the same power is wisdom, and the same wisdom is power.

The same applies to the other attributes, so that the same thing is greatness as power, and likewise with any other attributes mentioned above or still capable of being mentioned [Note: The printed editions read, “Is it therefore so?” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3. What is said of the Father and the Son together, and what is not

But if nothing is said of the Father in himself except what is said in relation to the Son—that is, “father,” “begetter,” or “his principle”—and if the one who begets is consequently the principle of the one begotten from himself, then whatever else is said is said together with the Son, or rather in the Son [Note: We restore here the particle *autem* (“however”), which the earlier printed editions had rashly deleted.]: whether the Father is great by the greatness he begot, just by the justice he begot, good by the goodness he begot, powerful by the power or strength he begot, or wise by the wisdom he begot.

Greatness itself, however, is not called “Father,” but “the generator of greatness.” The Son, on the other hand, is called “Son” in himself—a designation not spoken together with the Father but in relation to the Father. He is not similarly called “great” in himself, but together with the Father, whose greatness he is. So too he is called wise together with the Father, whose wisdom he is; just as the Father is wise together with the Son, because he is wise by the wisdom he begot.

Therefore, whatever is said of them with reference to themselves is not said of one without the other. That is, whatever is said of them that reveals their substance is said of both together.

If this is so, then the Father is not God without the Son, nor the Son God without the Father; rather, both together are God.

And when it is said, “In the beginning was the Word,” it is understood that the Word was in the Father. Or, if “in the beginning” was said as though it meant “before all things,” what follows—“and the Word was with God”—is understood as follows: the Word, who is the Son alone, was with God, who is not the Father alone but the Father and the Son together as God.

The Son alone is understood as the Word, not the Father and the Son together as one Word. For the Word is like the Image: the Father and the Son together are not both the image, but the Son alone is the image of the Father, just as he is the Son. They are not both together “son.” But when it is added, “and the Word was with God,” it is too much to understand it as saying that the Word, who is the Son alone, was with God, who is not the Father alone but the Father and the Son together as God.

But what surprise is there if this can be said of two things that are very different from each other? What is as different as mind and body? Yet one can say, “The mind was with the human being,” that is, in the human being, even though the mind is not the body, while the human being is mind and body together.

Thus, too, what is subsequently written, “and the Word was God” (John 1:1), may be understood as follows: the Word, who is not the Father, was God together with the Father.

Are we therefore to say that the Father is the generator of greatness—that is, the generator of his own power or wisdom—while the Son is greatness, power, and wisdom, and God is great, omnipotent, and wise in the two together?

How, then, is it “God from God, light from light”? For the two together are not God from God; the Son alone is from God, namely, from the Father. Nor are the two together light from light; the Son alone is from the light that is the Father.

Unless these expressions—“God from God,” “light from light,” and anything else said in this manner—were used to indicate and impress upon us, in the briefest possible way, that the Son is coeternal with the Father. It would then be as though one were saying: “That which is not the Son without the Father is from that which is not the Father without the Son”; that is, “this light, which is not light without the Father, is from that light—the Father—which is not light without the Son.”

Thus, when it is said, “God, who is not the Son without the Father, from God, who is not the Father without the Son,” we should perfectly understand that the begetter did not precede what he begot.

If this is so, the only thing that cannot be said of them is “one from the other” when the two together are not that thing. Thus, “Word from Word” cannot be said, because the two together are not the Word, but the Son alone. Nor can “image from image” be said, because the two together are not the image. Nor can “Son from Son” be said, because the two together are not the son. This is in accordance with the statement, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). For “we are one” means: “What he is, I also am,” according to essence, not according to relation.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 4. The unity of the Father’s and the Son’s essence established from the words “We are one.” The Son is equal to the Father in wisdom and in all other respects

I do not know whether Scripture contains the expression “they are one” when the things in question have different natures. But if several things are of the same nature and hold different opinions, they are not one to the extent that they hold different opinions.

For if the disciples were already one by virtue of being human beings, he would not have said, “that they may be one, as we are one” (John 17:11), when he commended his disciples to the Father.

Paul and Apollos, however, were both human beings and held the same opinion. “He who plants,” he says, “and he who waters are one” (1 Corinthians 3:8).

Therefore, when “one” is said without adding what they are one in, and several things are called one, the meaning is that they have the same nature and essence, without disagreement or dissent.

When what they are one in is added, however, it can signify that one thing has been made from several things, even though their natures differ. Soul and body, for example, are certainly not one—what is more different than they are?—unless what they are one in is added or understood: one human being or one animal.

Thus the Apostle says: “He who is joined to a prostitute is one body.” He did not say, “They are one,” or “It is one,” but added “body,” as though one body had been composed by the joining of two different beings, male and female.

And he says: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:16–17). He did not say, “He who is joined to the Lord is one,” or “They are one,” but added “spirit.” For the human spirit and the Spirit of God differ in nature [Note: Several manuscripts read, “and God is Spirit.”] Yet through attachment, one spirit is made from two different spirits, so that the Spirit of God is blessed and perfect without the human spirit, while the human spirit is blessed only with God.

Nor, as I think, is it without reason that, although in the Gospel according to John the Lord repeatedly and so often speaks of unity—either his unity with the Father or our mutual unity with one another—he never says, “that we and they may be one,” but rather, “that they may be one, as we also are one” (John 17).

The Father and the Son, therefore, are one, specifically according to the unity of substance. There is one God, one great being, and one wise being, as has been discussed.

### 5. In what sense, then, is the Father greater?

If the Father is greater, he must be greater in greatness. But since his greatness is the Son, the Father is not greater than the one he begot; nor is he greater than the greatness by which he is great. Therefore they are equal.

For how could they be equal if not in that by which he is what he is, since for him being and being great are not different? Or if the Father is greater in eternity, the Son is not equal to him in any respect. In what respect, then, could he be equal? If you say “in greatness,” the greatness is not equal, since it is less eternal—and so with the other attributes.

Perhaps he is equal in power but not equal in wisdom? But how can a power that is less wise be equal? Or is he equal in wisdom but not equal in power? But how can a wisdom that is less powerful be equal?

It follows, then, that if he is unequal in any respect, he is unequal in all respects. Yet Scripture cries out: “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6).

Therefore every opponent of the truth who is at least held by apostolic authority is compelled to confess that the Son is equal to God in at least one respect [Note: The printed editions read, “who is in some way held.” The manuscripts read, “who is at least held,” that is, “who is held by apostolic authority in any degree.”]

Let him choose whichever respect he wishes; from it he will be shown to be equal in all the things said of his substance.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 6. Continuation of the same argument

The virtues that exist in the human mind, although each is understood in its own way, cannot in any manner be separated from one another. Thus, whoever is equal in courage is also equal in prudence, temperance, and justice.

For if you say that these people are equal in courage but that one surpasses the other in prudence, it follows that the courage of the former is less prudent. Consequently, they are not equal even in courage, since the courage of one is more prudent.

You will find the same concerning the other virtues if you examine them all by the same reasoning. For this concerns not bodily strength but strength of mind.

How much more, then, must this be so in that unchangeable and eternal substance, incomparably simpler than the human mind? In the human mind, being is not the same as being courageous, prudent, just, or temperate; for the mind can exist without possessing any of these virtues.

In God, however, being is the same as being courageous, just, or wise—and the same applies to anything else that may be said of that simple multiplicity, or multiple simplicity, by which his substance is signified.

Therefore, whether “God from God” is said in such a way that the name applies to each individually, yet not so that there are two gods together but one God, they are joined together in the same way that the Apostle testifies can occur even in substances that are separate and different [Note: Most manuscripts read, “which can occur even in substances that are separate and different.”].

The Lord alone is spirit, and the spirit of a human being is also certainly spirit; yet if it clings to the Lord, it is one spirit. How much more, then, is this true where there is an entirely inseparable and eternal union?

Otherwise it might seem absurd to speak of the Son of both when he is called the Son of God, if the term “God” is said only of the two together. Or perhaps whatever is said of God that indicates his substance is said only of the two together—indeed, of the Trinity itself together.

Whether this or that is the case—a matter that must be examined more carefully—it is enough for the present argument to see that the Son could not possibly be equal to the Father if he were found unequal in any respect pertaining to the signification of his substance, as we have already shown.

The Apostle, however, said that he was equal. Therefore the Son is equal to the Father in all respects, and they are of one and the same substance.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 7. The Holy Spirit is also equal to the Father and the Son in all respects

Accordingly, the Holy Spirit too exists within the same unity of substance and equality.

For whether he is the unity of the two, or their holiness, or their love, or whether he is unity because he is love and love because he is holiness, it is clear that he is not one of the two by whom each is joined to the other: by whom the begotten is loved by the begetter and loves his begetter, and by whom they preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3), not by participation in something else but by their own essence, and not by the gift of some superior being but by their own.

We are commanded to imitate this by grace, both toward God and toward one another. “On these two commandments,” the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew 22:37–40).

Thus those three are one God: alone, great, wise, holy, and blessed. We, however, are blessed from him, through him, and in him, because by his gift we are one among ourselves and, with him, one spirit, since our soul is joined to him.

It is good for us to cling to God, because “he destroys everyone who commits fornication away from him” (Psalm 77:28, 27).

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is something common to the Father and the Son, whatever that may be. This communion is itself consubstantial and coeternal. If it can appropriately be called friendship, let it be called that; but “love” is the more suitable term.

This too is substance, because God is substance and “God is love,” as it is written (1 John 4:16).

And just as he is substance together with the Father and the Son, so he is great, good, holy, and whatever else is said of them according to themselves, together with them. For, as we showed above, being God is not one thing and being great or good another.

If love there were less great than wisdom, then wisdom would be loved less than it is. Love is therefore equal, so that it is loved as much as wisdom is great. Wisdom, however, is equal to the Father, as we argued above. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is also equal; and if equal, equal in all respects, because of the supreme simplicity existing in that substance.

Consequently, there are no more than three: one loving the one who is from him, one loving the one from whom he is, and love itself.

If this love is nothing, how is God love? If it is not substance, how is God substance?

## CHAPTER SIX

### 8. How God’s substance is simple and multiple

If it is asked how that substance can be both simple and multiple, we must first observe why creation is multiple, while in no way truly simple.

First, the whole bodily universe certainly consists of parts, so that one part is larger and another smaller, and the whole is greater than any part, however large.

Heaven and earth are parts of the entire structure of the world. Earth alone and heaven alone consist of innumerable parts; a third of either is smaller than the remainder, and half is smaller than the whole. The entire body of the world, which is usually said to consist of two parts—heaven and earth—is certainly greater than heaven alone or earth alone.

In every body, moreover, magnitude is one thing, color another, and shape another. The same color and shape can remain while magnitude is diminished; the same shape and magnitude can remain while color is changed; and the same magnitude and color can remain even when the shape no longer remains.

Whatever else is said together of a body can likewise be changed both together and in several respects without the others. Thus the nature of body is shown to be multiple and in no way simple.

The spiritual creature too, such as the soul, is indeed simpler in comparison with the body; but apart from comparison with the body, it is multiple and itself not simple.

It is simpler than the body because it is not spread out through space by bulk, but is whole in any given body, whole in its entirety, and whole in each part of it. Therefore, when something happens in any small part of the body that the soul perceives, although it does not happen throughout the body, the soul nevertheless perceives it wholly, because it is not hidden from the whole soul.

Yet even in the soul, being skillful is one thing and being unskilled another; being sharp another, being capable of remembering another; desire is one thing, fear another, joy another, sadness another. These and countless other things can exist in the soul independently of one another, and some to a greater and others to a lesser degree.

It is therefore clear that the soul’s nature is not simple but multiple. For nothing simple is changeable, whereas every creature is changeable.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### The Triune God, but not a threefold God

God is indeed called, in various ways, great, good, wise, blessed, true, and whatever else may seem worthy to say of him. Yet his greatness is the same as his wisdom; for he is not great by bulk but by power. His goodness is the same as his wisdom and greatness, and his truth is the same as all of these. In him, being blessed is not one thing and being great, wise, true, or good another, nor is being itself something different.

### 9. Why he should not be thought threefold simply because he is Trinity

Nor, because he is Trinity, should he therefore be thought threefold. Otherwise the Father alone or the Son alone would be less than the Father and the Son together.

Indeed, it is difficult to see how one could speak of the Father alone or the Son alone, since each is always and inseparably with the other: not so that both are the Father or both the Son, but because they are always in one another and neither is alone.

We also call the Trinity itself alone God, although it is always with holy spirits and souls. We call it “alone” because it is God, whereas they are not God with him.

Similarly, we call the Father alone “Father,” not because he is separated from the Son, but because both together are not the Father.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### No addition is made to God’s nature

Since the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is as great as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, God must in no way be called threefold.

Bodies grow through addition. Although the one who is joined to his wife is one body, the body is nevertheless larger than it would be if it consisted of the husband alone or the wife alone.
