In spiritual things, however, when something lesser clings to something greater—as creation clings to the Creator—the lesser becomes greater than it was, not the greater. In things that are not great by bulk, to be greater is to be better.

The spirit of a creature becomes better when it clings to the Creator than when it does not; and therefore it also becomes greater, because it becomes better.

“He who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17). Yet the Lord does not thereby become greater, although the one who clings to the Lord does become greater.

When, therefore, the Son, equal to the Father, clings to God, or when the Holy Spirit, equal to the Father and the Son, clings to them, God does not become greater than any one of them, because that perfection has no capacity for increase.

The Father is perfect, the Son is perfect, and the Holy Spirit is perfect; and the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are perfect God. Therefore they are a Trinity rather than something threefold.

## CHAPTER NINE

### 10. Whether the one God is called God by one person or by three persons together

Since we have shown how the Father alone can be called Father, because only he is Father there, we must consider the statement that the one true God is not the Father alone but the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

If someone asks whether the Father alone is God, how should one answer that he is not—unless perhaps we say that the Father is indeed God, but is not the only God, whereas the only God is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together?

What, then, shall we do with the Lord’s testimony? He was speaking to the Father and had named the Father to whom he was speaking when he said: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God” (John 17:3).

The Arians customarily understand this as though the Son were not true God. Once that interpretation has been excluded, must we understand that, when he said to the Father, “that they may know you, the only [Note: The Greek has *monon*, “only.”] true God,” he wished to indicate that the Father alone is the true God, lest we understand God to be only the three together—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

Are we therefore to say, on the basis of the Lord’s testimony, that the Father is the one true God, the Son is the one true God, and the Holy Spirit is the one true God, and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together—that is, the Trinity itself together—are not three true gods but one true God?

Or, since he added, “and Jesus Christ whom you sent,” should “the one true God” be understood with this as well, so that the order of the words is: “that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the one true God”?

Why, then, did he remain silent about the Holy Spirit? Perhaps because wherever one is named who clings in such peace to another that the two are one by that union, the peace itself is understood from this, even if it is not mentioned.

At one place the Apostle also seems to omit the Holy Spirit, yet he is understood there as well, when he says: “All things are yours; you are Christ’s; Christ is God’s” (1 Corinthians 3:22–23). And again: “The head of a woman is man; the head of a man is Christ; and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

But if God is only all three together, how is God the head of Christ—that is, how is the Trinity the head of Christ—when Christ is in the Trinity, so that the Trinity exists?

Or is that which the Father is with the Son the head of that which the Son alone is? The Father with the Son is God, while the Son alone is Christ—especially since the Word has now become flesh and is speaking. According to this humility, the Father is also greater than he, as he says: “For the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). [Note: Most manuscripts read “humanity.”]

Thus God himself—that which he is one with the Father—is the head of the human Mediator, who is himself alone (1 Timothy 2:5).

If we rightly call the mind the ruling principle of a human being, that is, as the head of the human substance, even though the human being is a human being together with the mind, why should we not much more appropriately and properly say that the Word with the Father, which together is God, is the head of Christ, although Christ as human cannot be understood apart from the Word who became flesh?

But, as we have already said, we shall consider this somewhat more carefully later.

For now, the equality of the Trinity and its one and the same substance has been demonstrated as briefly as we could, so that, whatever the proper solution to this question may be—the question we postponed for more intense examination—nothing prevents us from confessing the supreme equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER TEN

### 11. The attributes assigned by Hilary to the individual persons. The Trinity is represented in created things

Someone wishing to indicate very briefly what is proper to the individual persons of the Trinity said: “Eternity in the Father, form (*species*) in the Image, use in the Gift.”

Because Hilary was a man of no small authority in the interpretation of Scripture and the defense of the faith—he placed this statement in his books (*On the Trinity*, Book 2)—I have searched out, as far as I am able, the hidden meaning of these words: Father, Image, and Gift; eternity, form, and use.

I do not think that he followed this line of thought in the word “eternity” except insofar as the Father has no Father from whom he is, whereas the Son is from the Father in order to exist and in order to be coeternal with him.

For if an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, the image itself is made equal to it, not that thing to its image.

In the Image, Hilary named form, I believe, because of its loveliness: there is perfect correspondence, primal equality, and primal likeness—no disagreement in any respect, no inequality in any way, and no dissimilarity in any part—but a complete correspondence with that of which it is the image.

There is primal and supreme life, for which living is not one thing and being another, but being and living are the same. There is also primal and supreme understanding, for which living is not one thing and understanding another; rather, what understanding is, that is living and being—everything one.

This is like a perfect Word, lacking nothing, a kind of art of the almighty and wise God, full of all living and unchangeable principles [Note: Several manuscripts read, “and of unchangeable principles.”] All things are one in it, just as it is itself one from the One with whom it is one.

In it God knows all the things he made through it. Therefore, although times pass away and succeed one another, nothing passes away or succeeds in God’s knowledge.

For created things are not known by God because they have been made; rather, they were made and are mutable because they were immutably known by him.

That ineffable union of the Father and the Image is therefore not without enjoyment [Note: The manuscripts read “perfection” or “fulfillment.”], love, and joy.

That love, delight, happiness, or blessedness—if it can worthily be expressed in any human word—Hilary briefly called “use.” In the Trinity it is the Holy Spirit: not begotten, but the sweetness of the Begetter and the Begotten, pouring over all creatures with immense generosity and abundance, according to their capacity, so that they may preserve their order and rest content in their proper places.

### 12. Unity, form, and order in created things

All these things, therefore, which have been made by divine art, display within themselves a certain unity, form (*species*), and order.

Whatever exists is one thing, as are the natures of bodies and the dispositions of souls. It is formed according to some form (*species*), as are the shapes or qualities of bodies and the teachings or arts of souls. And it seeks or maintains some order, as do the weights or arrangements of bodies and the loves or pleasures of souls.

We must therefore contemplate the Creator through the things that have been made and understand the Trinity, whose trace appears in creation in a manner appropriate to it (Romans 1:20).

For in that supreme Trinity is the highest origin of all things, the most perfect form, and the most blessed delight.

These three appear to be defined in relation to one another, and they are infinite in themselves. [Note: The manuscripts read “from themselves” (*a se*).] But here, in bodily things, one thing is not as much as three together, and two things are something more than one thing. In that supreme Trinity, however, one is as much as three together, and two are not something more than one.

They are infinite in themselves.

Thus each is in each, all are in each, each is in all, all are in all, and all are one.

Whoever sees this, whether in part or through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Corinthians 13:12), should rejoice in knowing God, honor him as God, and give thanks. Whoever does not see it should strive through devotion to see it, not through blindness to slander it.

For God is one, yet he is Trinity. And we must not understand confusedly the words, “From him and through him and in him are all things”; “to him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11:36).

# BOOK SEVEN

In this book the question deferred from the preceding book is explained: namely, that God the Father, who begot the Son as Power and Wisdom, is not only the Father of his Power and Wisdom, but is himself also Power and Wisdom; and likewise the Holy Spirit. Yet it is shown that there are not three Powers or three Wisdoms, but one Power and one Wisdom, just as there is one God and one essence. Next it is asked how it is said in God that there is one essence and three persons among the Latins, but one essence and three substances or hypostases among the Greeks; and both expressions are shown to be required by the necessities of language, so that we might not remain entirely silent when asked what the three are whom we truthfully confess to be three—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0931]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0931]

### 1. Whether each person of the Trinity is wisdom in himself; the difficulty of the question and the manner in which it is resolved

Let us now inquire more carefully, insofar as God grants it, into what we deferred a little earlier: whether each individual person in the Trinity can, by himself and without the other two, be called God, or great, or wise, or true, or almighty, or just, or anything else that can be said of God—not relatively, but with reference to himself—or whether such terms are spoken only when the Trinity is understood.

[Col. 0932]

[Col. 0933] This is what makes the question difficult, because it is written that Christ is “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). Is the Father therefore the Father of his own Wisdom and Power in such a way that he is wise by the Wisdom he begot and powerful by the Power he begot? And because he is eternally powerful and wise, did he eternally beget Power and Wisdom? For we had said that, if this is so, why is he not also the Father of his own greatness, by which he is great, and of his goodness, by which he is good, and of his justice, by which he is just, and of whatever else there may be?

Or, if all these things are understood under several names in the same Wisdom and Power, so that the greatness is the Power, the goodness the Wisdom, and again the Wisdom the Power, as we have already discussed, let us remember that whenever I name one of these, it should be understood as though I were mentioning them all.

The question, then, is whether the Father alone is also wise and is himself Wisdom to himself, or whether he is wise in the same way as he is one who speaks. For he is one who speaks by the Word whom he begot—not by a word that is uttered, sounds, and passes away, but by the Word who “was with God, and the Word was God,” and “all things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3): by the Word equal to himself, through whom he eternally and unchangeably speaks himself.

He himself is not the Word, just as he is neither the Son nor the Image. Yet he is one who speaks—apart from those temporal words of God that take place in creation, for they sound and pass away—by that coeternal Word. He is not understood as speaking alone, but together with the Word, without whom he certainly would not be one who speaks.

Is he therefore wise in the same way as he speaks, so that Wisdom is what the Word is, and being the Word is the same as being Wisdom, and also being Power, so that Power, Wisdom, and Word are the same, and are spoken of relatively, as are Son and Image? Is he therefore not powerful or wise alone, but together with the Power and Wisdom whom he begot, just as he is not one who speaks alone, but by and with the Word whom he begot? And is he thus great by and with the greatness whom he begot?

If he is not great in one way and God in another, but is great by that whereby he is God, because for him being great is not one thing and being God another, it follows that he is not God alone, but by and with the Godhead whom he begot. Thus the Son is the Father’s Godhead, just as he is the Father’s Wisdom and Power, and just as he is the Father’s Word and Image.

And because for him being is not one thing and being God another, the Son is likewise the Father’s essence, just as he is his Word and Image. Accordingly, apart from the fact that he is Father, the Father is nothing except because he has a Son. Thus not only is the name “Father”—which plainly is not said with reference to himself but relatively to the Son—applied to him because he has a Son; rather, he is what he is with reference to himself because he begot his own essence.

For just as he is great only by the greatness he begot, so he is only by the essence he begot, because for him being is not one thing and being great another. Is he therefore the father of his own essence just as he is the father of his own greatness, and just as he is the father of his own Power and Wisdom? For his greatness is the same as his Power, and his essence the same as his greatness.

### 2. The origin of this discussion in the statement that Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God

This discussion arose from the fact that it is written that Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God. Consequently, when we wish to speak of things ineffable, our discourse is constricted [Col. 0934] by such difficulties that we must either say that Christ is not the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, and thus shamelessly and impiously resist the Apostle; or confess that Christ is indeed the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, but deny that his Father is the father of his own Power and Wisdom—which is no less impious. For in that case he would not be Christ’s Father either, since Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God.

Or must we say that the Father is not powerful by his own Power, nor wise by his own Wisdom? Who would dare say that? Or must we understand that being in the Father is one thing and being wise another, so that he is not what he is by the very fact that he is wise—as is usually understood of the soul, which is at one time foolish and at another wise, being a mutable nature and not supremely and perfectly simple?

Or must we say that the Father is nothing with reference to himself, and that not only what he is called as Father, but absolutely everything he is, is said relatively to the Son? How, then, is the Son of the same essence as the Father, when with reference to himself the Father is neither essence nor anything at all with reference to himself, but even his being is with reference to the Son? [Note: Two manuscripts read “whom” rather than “whose essence” in the following clause.]

Indeed, he is all the more of one and the same essence with the Son, because the Father and the Son are one and the same essence. For the Father’s being is not being with reference to himself, but with reference to the Son, whose essence he begot, and by whose essence he is whatever he is.

Neither, therefore, is either of them with reference to himself, and both are spoken of relatively to each other. Or is the Father alone—apart from the fact that he is called Father—called relatively to the Son in absolutely everything that is said of him, while the Son is also spoken of with reference to himself? And if so, what is said of him with reference to himself? [Note: Printed editions read: “with reference to the Father and with reference to himself? And if so, what is said in the Son with reference to himself?” The manuscripts lack “with reference to the Father” and “in the Son.”]

Is it the essence itself? But the Son is the Father’s essence, just as he is the Father’s Power and Wisdom, the Father’s Word and the Father’s Image. Or, if the Son is called essence with reference to himself, while the Father is not essence but the begetter of essence, and is not with reference to himself but is by that very essence which he begot, just as he is great by that very greatness which he begot, then the Son as Greatness is also said with reference to himself, and likewise as Power, Wisdom, Word, and Image.

But what could be more absurd than to say that the Image is spoken of with reference to itself? Or, if Image and Word are not the same as Power and Wisdom, but the former are spoken of relatively while the latter are spoken of with reference to themselves rather than to something else, then the Father begins not to be wise by the Wisdom he begot, because he himself cannot be spoken of relatively to it while it is not spoken of relatively to him. For all things that are spoken of relatively are spoken of reciprocally.

It therefore remains that the Son too is spoken of relatively to the Father as essence. From this an entirely unexpected conclusion follows: that essence itself is not essence—or at least that when “essence” is said, it indicates not essence but a relative term.

This is like the case in which, when “lord” is said, essence is not indicated, but a relative term referring to a servant; whereas when “man” or something similar is said—something said with reference to itself and not to another—essence is indicated. Thus when a man is called “lord,” the man himself is essence, while “lord” is said relatively: “man” is said with reference to himself, “lord” with reference to a servant. But in the matter under discussion, if essence itself is said relatively, essence itself is not essence.

[Col. 0935] Moreover, every essence that is spoken of relatively is also something apart from the relative term. Thus there are a man who is a lord, a man who is a servant, a horse that is a beast of burden, and money that is earnest-money. “Man,” “horse,” and “money” are said with reference to themselves and are substances or essences; but “lord,” “servant,” “beast of burden,” and “earnest-money” are said relatively to something else.

If there were no man—that is, no substance—there would be no one who could be called lord relatively. If there were no horse, which is a certain essence, there would be nothing that could be called a beast of burden relatively. Likewise, if money were not a substance, it could not be called earnest-money relatively.

Therefore, if the Father is nothing with reference to himself, he is not at all something that can be spoken of relatively to anything. For the color of something colored is referred to what is colored; color itself is not spoken of with reference to itself, but is always the color of something. Yet the thing whose color it is, although it is referred to color by being called colored, is nevertheless called a body with reference to itself.

We must not therefore suppose that the Father is not something with reference to himself, but that everything said of him is said with reference to the Son, while the same Son is said both with reference to himself and with reference to the Father when he is called great in greatness and powerful in Power—plainly with reference to himself—and is called the greatness and Power of the great and powerful Father, by which the Father is great and powerful. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain corrupt the sense by adding “therefore” and wrongly punctuating the passage.]

It is not so. Both are substance, and both are one substance. Just as it is absurd to say that what is white is not whiteness, so it is absurd to say that the wise is not Wisdom. And just as whiteness is called white with reference to itself, so Wisdom is called wise with reference to itself.

But the whiteness of a body is not its essence, since the body itself is the essence and whiteness is its quality. Hence the body is called white because of that quality; being a body is not the same for it as being white. For form is one thing there and color another, and neither exists in itself but in some mass; and that mass is neither form nor color, but formed and colored.

True Wisdom is both wise and wise in itself. And since every soul becomes wise by participating in Wisdom, if it should again become foolish, Wisdom nevertheless remains in itself, nor is it changed when the soul has been changed into folly. [Note: Perhaps the reading should be “into a foolish soul.”] It is not in the one who becomes wise through it as whiteness is in a body that becomes white through it. When a body is changed into another color, that whiteness will not remain, but will altogether cease to exist.

But if the Father who begot Wisdom becomes wise through it, and for him being is not the same as being wise, then the Son is his quality, not his offspring, and supreme simplicity will no longer exist in him. But far be it from us to suppose this, since there is truly supremely simple essence there. Therefore, there being is the same as being wise.

If there being is the same as being wise, the Father is not wise through the Wisdom he begot; otherwise he himself would not have begotten it, but it would have begotten him. For what else do we mean when we say, “For him being is the same as being wise,” except, “He is by that whereby he is wise”?

Therefore, the cause that makes him wise is itself [Col. 0936] the cause that makes him be. Accordingly, if the Wisdom he begot is the cause of his being wise, it is also the cause of his being. This could happen only by its begetting or making him. But no one would call Wisdom the mother or creator of the Father. What could be more insane?

Therefore the Father himself too is Wisdom. [Note: Many manuscripts read “himself” (ipse); printed editions read “itself” (ipsa).] And the Son is called the Wisdom of the Father as he is called the Light of the Father: that is, just as Light is from Light and both are one Light, so Wisdom is understood to be from Wisdom and both are one Wisdom. Therefore there is also one essence, because there being is the same as being wise.

For what being wise is to Wisdom, being able is to Power, being eternal is to eternity, being just is to justice, and being great is to greatness—that being itself is to essence. And because in that simplicity being wise is not one thing and being another, the Wisdom there is the same as the essence.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3. The Father and the Son together are one Wisdom, as they are one essence, although they are not together one Word

The Father and the Son together are one essence, one greatness, one truth, and one Wisdom. But the Father and the Son together are not one Word, because together they are not one Son.

For just as the Son is referred to the Father and is not spoken of with reference to himself, so the Word is referred to the one whose Word he is when he is called Word. He is Son precisely insofar as he is Word, and Word precisely insofar as he is Son.

Since, therefore, the Father and the Son together are certainly not one Son, it follows that the Father and the Son together are not one Word belonging to both. And for this reason the Word is not the same as Wisdom in the same respect, because Word is not said with reference to itself but only relatively to the one whose Word it is, just as Son is said relatively to the Father. Wisdom, however, is spoken of with reference to itself, because it is essence. Hence, because there is one essence, there is one Wisdom.

Yet the Word too is Wisdom, although the Word is not Word in the same respect in which he is Wisdom. [Note: Louvain adds “and” here.] For Word is understood relatively, while Wisdom is understood essentially. Let us therefore understand “Word” when it is said as though “begotten Wisdom” were said, so that he is both Son and Image.

When these two are named—that is, “begotten Wisdom”—then in one of them, namely in the fact that it is begotten, let Word, Image, and Son be understood; and in all these names essence is not shown, because they are said relatively. But in the other, namely Wisdom, since it is also said with reference to itself—for it is wise in itself—let essence also be indicated, and let its being be understood as the same as its being wise.

Hence the Father and the Son together are one Wisdom because they are one essence; and individually there is Wisdom from Wisdom, just as essence is from essence.

Therefore it is not because the Father is not the Son and the Son is not the Father, or because the one is unbegotten and the other begotten, that they are not one essence, since these names indicate their relative distinctions. Together they are one Wisdom and one essence, where being is the same as being wise. But together they are not Word or Son, because being is not the same as being Word or being Son, as we have already sufficiently shown that these terms are spoken relatively.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 4. Why the Son is especially signified in Scripture by the name “Wisdom,” although the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0937] are also Wisdom; the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son is one Wisdom

Why, then, is almost nothing ever said in Scripture about Wisdom except to show that it was begotten or created by God? It is begotten insofar as all things were made through it; created or made insofar as this occurs in human beings, when they turn toward and are illuminated by that Wisdom which was not created and made but begotten. For in them something comes to be that is called their wisdom.

Or it may refer to what Scripture foretold or narrated: that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). In this way Christ became made Wisdom, because he became man.

Is it therefore because that Wisdom was the one we had to commend and imitate, by whose imitation we are formed, that these books do not speak of Wisdom or say anything about it except what shows it to have been born from God or made, even though the Father himself is also Wisdom? [Note: Almost only the Louvain edition reads ipsa, “itself,” rather than ipse, “himself.”]

The Father speaks it so that it may be his Word—not as a word uttered from the mouth, sounding, or conceived before pronunciation. The former is completed within intervals of time, whereas the latter is eternal. Through it he speaks to us, illuminating us, both about himself and about the Father, what must be said to human beings.

Therefore he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27), because the Father reveals through the Son, that is, through his Word.

If this temporal and passing word that we utter both reveals itself and reveals that about which we speak, how much more does the Word of God, through whom all things were made?

He reveals the Father as the Father truly is, because he himself is such as the Father is, and in respect of being Wisdom and essence he is what the Father is. But in respect of being Word he is not what the Father is, because the Word is not the Father, and Word is said relatively, just as Son is said—obviously, the Son is not the Father.

Thus Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God because, being from the Father’s Power and Wisdom, he himself is also Power and Wisdom, just as he is Light from the Father who is Light, and the fountain of life with God the Father, who is himself the fountain of life. [Note: Louvain reads “the Light of God”; “of God” is absent from the other books.]

“For with you,” he says, “is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10), because “as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). And “he was the true Light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world,” and this Light was the Word who was with God; “and the Word was God” (John 1:9, 1).

God is Light, and “in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). This Light, however, is not bodily but spiritual; nor is it spiritual in the sense that it came to be through illumination, as it was said to the Apostles, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). Rather, it is the Light that enlightens every human being: God himself, supreme Wisdom, which is the subject of our present discussion.

The Son is therefore Wisdom from the Father who is Wisdom, just as Light is from Light and God from God. Thus the Father individually is Light and the Son individually is Light; the Father individually is God and the Son individually is God. Therefore the Father individually is Wisdom and the Son individually is Wisdom.

And just as together they are one Light and one God, so together they are one Wisdom. Yet the Son “became for us [Col. 0938] Wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification” (1 Cor. 1:30), because we turn toward him in time—that is, from a certain point in time—in order to remain with him forever. And he himself, at a certain point in time, became flesh and dwelt among us.

### 5. Why Scripture chiefly presents the Son whenever it speaks of Wisdom

Therefore, whenever something is pronounced or recounted in Scripture concerning Wisdom, whether Wisdom itself is speaking or something is said about it, the Son is chiefly presented to us.

Following the example of this Image, let us too not depart from God, because we too are the image of God—not indeed an equal image, since we were made by the Father through the Son, not born from the Father as that Image was.

We too are illuminated by the Light; but that Image is itself the Light that illuminates. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “And we too are light, because …”] Thus it is an example for us without itself having an example.

For it does not imitate anyone preceding it in relation to the Father, from whom it can never be separated at all, because it is the very same thing as he from whom it is. We, however, striving, imitate the one who remains; following the one who stands, and walking in him, we press toward him. For he became for us a temporal way through humility, while through divinity he is our eternal dwelling. [Note: Louvain gives the variant “humanity” for “humility.”]

Since God, in the form of God, equal to God and himself God, provides an example to pure intellectual spirits who did not fall through pride, he emptied himself in order to provide the same example of return to fallen humanity. Humanity, because of the uncleanness of sins and the punishment of mortality, could not see God. He emptied himself not by changing his divinity, but by assuming our mutability; and “taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), he came to us in this world (1 Tim. 1:15).

He was already in this world, because “the world was made through him” (John 1:10). Thus he became an example above to those who see God, and below to those who marvel at the human being; an example to the healthy for remaining, to the weak for recovering, to the dying for not being afraid, and to the dead for rising again—holding primacy in all things (Col. 1:18).

Since the human being ought to follow none other than God toward blessedness, but could not perceive God, by following God made man he would follow both the one whom he could perceive and the one whom he ought to follow.

Let us therefore love him and cling to him through the love poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

It is therefore not surprising that, because the equal Image of the Father offers us an example so that we may be reformed according to the image of God, when Scripture speaks of Wisdom it speaks of the Son, whom we follow by living wisely, although the Father too is Wisdom, just as he is Light and God.

### 6. The Holy Spirit too is Wisdom

How, then, could the Holy Spirit not also be Wisdom, whether he is the supreme Love joining the two together and joining us to them—a designation that is not unfitting, since it is written, “God is love” (1 John 4:8)—or whether the essence of the Holy Spirit must be named individually and properly in another way? [Note: Louvain reads: “Whether, therefore, in this way or in another way …”]

Since he is God, he is certainly Light; and since he is Light, he is certainly Wisdom.

Scripture proclaims [Col. 0939] that the Holy Spirit is God through the Apostle, who says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple?” Immediately he adds: “And the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16). For God dwells in his temple.

The Spirit of God does not dwell in the temple of God as a minister, since elsewhere he says more plainly: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a great price; therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20). [Note: The printed editions add here, “and bear”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]

What is Wisdom except spiritual and unchangeable Light? This sun too is light, but it is bodily; and a spiritual creature is light, but not unchangeable.

The Father is therefore Light, the Son Light, and the Holy Spirit Light; yet together they are not three lights but one Light. Thus the Father is Wisdom, the Son Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit Wisdom; yet together they are not three Wisdoms but one Wisdom.

And because being is the same as being wise there, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one essence. Nor is being there anything other than being God. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 7. Why the Greeks said “three hypostases” and the Latins “three persons”; Scripture nowhere says “three persons” in God

Thus, for the sake of speaking about ineffable things, so that we might in some way say what we cannot express at all, our Greek brethren have said “one essence, three substances,” while the Latins have said “one essence or substance, three persons.” For, as we have already said, in our language, that is, Latin, essence is ordinarily understood in the same way as substance (Book 5, chapters 2 and 8).

Since what is said could at least be understood in an enigma, it seemed preferable to speak in this way, so that something might be said when it was asked what the three are—those three whom true faith declares to be three—since it says that the Father is not the Son, and that the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of God, is neither the Father nor the Son.

When we are asked what the three or who the three are, we apply ourselves to finding some specific or general name by which to embrace these three, but none occurs to the mind, because the transcendence of the Godhead surpasses the capacity of ordinary speech.

For God is more truly thought than spoken, and more truly is than he is thought.

When we say that Jacob is not the same as Abraham, and that Isaac is neither Abraham nor Jacob, we certainly confess that there are three: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But when we are asked what the three are, we answer, “three men,” calling them by a plural name that is specific. By a general name, however, we might say “three animals,” since, as the ancients defined it, man is a rational mortal animal; or, as our Scriptures usually speak, “three souls,” when it is preferred that the whole be named from its better part—that is, from the soul—although the whole human being consists of body and soul. [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “since body and soul are the whole human being.” Manuscript reading: “and body and soul, which is the whole human being.”]

Thus it is said that seventy-five souls went down into Egypt with Jacob, in place of the same number of human beings (Gen. 46:27; Deut. 10:22).

Likewise, when we say that your horse is not the same as mine, and that a third horse belongs to someone else and is neither mine nor yours, we confess that there are three. When asked [Col. 0940] what the three are, we answer “three horses” by the specific name, and “three animals” by the general name.

Again, when we say that an ox is not a horse, and that a dog is neither an ox nor a horse, we speak of three things. When asked what the three are, we no longer name them specifically as three horses, three oxen, or three dogs, because they are not contained under the same species; but generally as three animals, or by a higher genus as three substances, three creatures, or three natures.

Whatever things are stated in the plural under one specific name can also be stated under one general name. But not everything that is called by one general name can also be called by one specific name.

For we call three horses, which is a specific name, three animals; but a horse, an ox, and a dog we call only three animals or substances, which are general names, or by any other general term that can be applied to them. We cannot call them three horses, three oxen, or three dogs, which are specific terms.

Although we name things with one plural name, we do so because they commonly possess what that name signifies. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob commonly possess what “man” signifies; therefore they are called three men. A horse, an ox, and a dog likewise commonly possess what “animal” signifies; therefore they are called three animals.

Thus we call three laurel trees three trees; but a laurel, a myrtle, and an olive we call only three trees, three substances, or three natures. Likewise, three stones are also three bodies; but a stone, wood, and iron we call only three bodies, or by some still higher general name if one is available.

The Father, then, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since they are three, require us to ask what the three are and what they have in common.

They do not have in common what the Father is, so that they could be fathers of one another, as friends can be called three friends when they are named relatively to one another, since they are mutually friends.

That is not the case here, because only the Father is Father; nor is he the father of two, but of one Son. Nor are there three sons, since the Father is not a son, nor is the Holy Spirit. Nor are there three Holy Spirits, because the Holy Spirit, in the proper sense in which he is also called the gift of God, is neither the Father nor the Son.

What, then, are the three?

If they are three persons, what “person” signifies is common to them. Thus, if we attend to ordinary speech, this is either a specific or a general name for them.

Where there is no difference of nature, several things are so named generally that they can also be named specifically. Difference of nature makes it impossible to call a laurel, a myrtle, and an olive three laurels, or a horse, an ox, and a dog three horses; but generally we call the former three trees and the latter three animals.

Here, however, where there is no difference of essence, these three ought to have a specific name, yet none is found. For “person” is a general name, to such an extent that even a human being can be called a person, although there is so great a difference between a human being and God.

### 8. Why we do not say “three gods” if we say “three persons”

Furthermore, in the very general term, if we say “three persons” because what “person” signifies is common to them—otherwise they could not be called this, [Col. 0941] just as they are not called three sons because what “son” signifies is not common to them—why do we not also say “three gods”?

Certainly, because the Father is a person, the Son is a person, and the Holy Spirit is a person, we say “three persons.” Since, therefore, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, why do we not say “three gods”?

Or, since through the ineffable union these three together are one God, why do we not also say “one person,” so that we could not say “three persons,” although we call each one individually a person, just as we cannot say “three gods,” although we call each one individually God, whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit?

Is it because Scripture does not say “three gods”? But nowhere do we find Scripture mentioning “three persons” either.

Or is it because Scripture says neither “three” nor “one person” of these three—for we read of the Lord’s person, not “the Lord person”? For this reason, by the necessity of speaking and arguing, were we permitted to say “three persons,” not because Scripture says so, but because Scripture does not contradict it? If we said “three gods,” however, Scripture would contradict us when it says: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6:4).

Why, then, is it not also permissible to say “three essences,” since Scripture likewise neither says nor contradicts this?

If essence is a specific name common to the three, why are they not called three essences, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called three men, because “man” is a specific name common to all human beings?

But if essence is not a specific name but a general one, because a man, an animal, a tree, a star, and an angel are all called essences, why are these three not called three essences, just as three horses are called three animals, three laurels three trees, and three stones three bodies?

Or if, because of the unity of the Trinity, they are not called three essences but one essence, why, because of that same unity of the Trinity, are they not called three substances or three persons but one substance and one person?

The name “essence” is as common to them, so that each individually is called an essence, as the term “substance” or “person” is common to them. What we have said concerning persons according to our usage must be understood concerning substances according to Greek usage.

For they say “three substances, one essence” in the same way that we say “three persons, one essence or substance.”

### 9. These terms arose from the necessity of speaking

What, then, remains except to confess that these terms were produced by the necessity of speaking? [Note: Several manuscripts: “divided.”] This necessity arose when an extensive argument was required against the plots and errors of heretics.

When human poverty of speech attempted to express to human senses what it holds in the sanctuary of the mind, according to its capacity, concerning the Lord God, its Creator—whether through devout faith or through whatever understanding it might possess—it feared saying “three essences,” lest any difference be understood in that supreme equality.

Yet it could not say that there were not three in some sense, because Sabellius fell into heresy by saying this.

For Scripture establishes with complete certainty what must be devoutly [Col. 0942] believed and what the mind grasps in an undoubting perception: that there is the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that the Son is not the same as the Father; and that the Holy Spirit is not the same as either the Father or the Son.

It sought a way to say what the three are, and it said “substances” or “persons.” By these names it did not intend to understand difference, but it did not wish singularity to be understood either. Thus not only unity would be understood from the phrase “one essence,” but also Trinity from the phrase “three substances” or “persons.”

For if, in God, being is the same as subsisting, then “three substances” ought no more to be said than “three essences.” Just as, because in God being is the same as being wise, we say neither three essences nor three Wisdoms, so, because in him being God is the same as being, it is not lawful to say either three essences or three gods.

But if being in God is one thing and subsisting another, just as being in God is one thing and being Father or Lord another—for being is said with reference to itself, while Father is said with reference to the Son and Lord with reference to the serving creature—then he subsists relatively, just as he begets relatively and rules relatively.

In that case substance will not be substance, because it will be relative. For just as essence is named from being, so substance is named from subsisting. But it is absurd for substance to be spoken of relatively: everything subsists with reference to itself, and how much more does God?

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 10. In God “substance” is said improperly, while “essence” is said properly

Yet this assumes that it is fitting to say that God subsists. For subsistence is properly understood of things in which there are properties that are in some subject, such as color or form in a body.

A body subsists and is therefore a substance. But the things that are in the subsisting and subject body are not substances but are in a substance. If either that color or that form were to cease to exist, they would not deprive the body of being a body, because for the body being is not the same as retaining this or that form or color.

Mutable and non-simple things, therefore, are properly called substances.

But if God subsists in such a way that he can properly be called a substance, then something is in him as in a subject, and he is not simple. In that case being would not be the same for him as whatever else is said of him with reference to himself, such as being great, almighty, or good, or anything of this kind that is appropriately said of God.

But it is impious to say that God subsists and is subject to his goodness, and that this goodness is not substance—or rather essence—and that God himself is not his own goodness, but that it exists in him as in a subject.

It is therefore clear that God is called substance improperly, so that by the more familiar name essence may be understood—the name that is truly and properly said. Perhaps, indeed, only God ought to be called essence.

For he alone truly is, because he is unchangeable. He proclaimed this name to his servant Moses when he said, “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to them: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14).

Nevertheless, whether essence is said—the proper term—or substance—the improper term—both are said with reference to themselves, [Col. 0943] not relatively to something else. [Note: Printed editions read “and whatever else”; “and” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Hence for God being is the same as subsisting. Therefore, if the Trinity is one essence, it is also one substance.

Perhaps, then, “three persons” is more suitably said than “three substances.”

## CHAPTER SIX
## 11. Why in the Trinity one person and three essences are not said

What one ought to believe about the Trinity if one does not grasp what has been said above. The human being is both according to the image and the image of God.

But lest I seem to be supporting our side, let us investigate this as well. [Note: So Am., Er., and some manuscripts; Lov. reads “lest it seem.”] Although they too, if they wished, could, just as they say “three substances” and “three hypostases,” say “three persons,” *tria prosopa*. But they preferred the expression that perhaps was more suitably used according to the custom of their language.

For the same reasoning applies to persons: for it is not one thing for God to be, and another thing for him to be a person; rather, they are entirely the same. For if “to be” is said absolutely, whereas “person” is said relatively, let us say “three persons”—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—in the same way that some say “three friends,” or “three relatives,” or “three neighbors,” meaning that they are related to one another, not that each of them is related to himself. Therefore each one of them is the friend, relative, or neighbor of the other two, because these names have a relative meaning.

What then? Shall we be willing to say that the Father is the person of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, or that the Son is the person of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is the person of the Father and of the Son? But neither is “person” customarily said in this way anywhere, nor, when in this Trinity we speak of the person of the Father, do we mean anything other than the substance of the Father.

Accordingly, just as the substance of the Father is the Father himself—not insofar as he is Father, but insofar as he is—so also the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself. For “person” is said absolutely, not in relation to the Son or the Holy Spirit, just as “God,” “great,” “good,” “just,” and anything else of this sort are said absolutely. And just as for him to be is the same as for him to be God, to be great, and to be good, so for him to be is the same as for him to be a person.

Why, then, do we not call these three together one person, just as we call them one essence and one God, but call them three persons, while we do not call them three gods or three essences? Is it not because we wish one term to serve this meaning by which the Trinity is understood, so that we would not remain completely silent when asked what the three are, while confessing that they are three? [Note: Several manuscripts read “preserve” (*servare*) for “serve” (*servire*).]

For if essence is the genus, and substance or person the species, as some maintain, I pass over what I have already said: that we ought to call them three essences, just as they are called three substances or persons, in the same way that we call them three horses, and three animals, since “horse” is the species and “animal” the genus. For the species is not there expressed in the plural and the genus in the singular, as if one were saying “three horses, one animal”; rather, just as “three horses” is said by a specific name, so “three animals” is said by a general name.

But if they say that the name “substance” or “person” does not signify a species, but something singular and individual—so that “substance” or “person” is not said in the way “human being” is said, which is common to all human beings, but in the way one says “this human being,” such as Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, or someone else who could even be pointed out as present with a finger—then the same reasoning will apply to them. For just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called three individuals, so they are called three human beings and three souls.

Why, then, if we also discuss these things according to genus, species, and individual, are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not called three essences, just as they are called three substances or persons? But I pass over this, as I said. I say this: if essence is a genus, then one essence no longer has species, just as, because “animal” is a genus, one animal no longer has species. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, therefore, are not three species of one essence.

If, however, essence is a species, as “human being” is a species, and the three whom we call substances or persons share that same species in common, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob share the species called “human being,” then just as “human being” is not divided into Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so one human being cannot be divided into several individual human beings. It cannot be so at all, because one human being is already an individual human being.

Why, then, is one essence divided into three substances or persons? For if essence is a species, as “human being” is, then one essence is like one human being. Or is it as when we say that three human beings of the same sex, the same bodily constitution, and the same soul have one nature? There are three human beings, but one nature. Do we therefore say in that case also that three substances are one essence, or that three persons are one substance or essence?

This is in some measure similar, because the ancients who spoke Latin, before they had these terms—which have only recently come into use, namely, “essence” and “substance”—used to say “nature” instead. We do not therefore speak of these things according to genus and species, but as though according to a common and identical material.

If three statues were made from the same gold, we would say “three statues, one gold,” yet we would not call gold the genus and statues the species, nor gold the species and statues the individuals. For no species extends beyond its own individuals so as to include something outside them. When I define what a human being is, and “human being” is a specific name, each individual human being is included under the same definition, and nothing that is not a human being belongs to it.

When I define what gold is, however, not only statues, if they are made of gold, but also rings and anything else made of gold belongs to gold; and even if nothing is made from it, it is still called gold. Likewise, even if they are not made of gold, they will not for that reason cease to be statues.

Again, no species exceeds the definition of its genus. When I define “animal”—since horse is a species of this genus—every horse is an animal, but not every statue is gold. Therefore, although in the case of three golden statues we rightly say “three statues, one gold,” we do not say this in such a way that we understand gold as the genus and statues as the species.

Nor, then, do we say of the Trinity “three persons” or “three substances, one essence and one God” as though three things subsisted from one material, even if whatever that material is had been fully expressed in these three. For there is nothing else belonging to that essence apart from this Trinity. Nevertheless, we say “three persons of one essence,” or “three persons, one essence”; but we do not say “three persons from one essence,” as though one thing there were what essence is and another what person is, as we can say “three statues from the same gold.” For there it is one thing to be gold and another to be statues.

And when three human beings are said to have one nature, or to be of the same nature, they can also be said to be three human beings from the same nature, because from the same nature three other human beings of the same kind can also exist. In the case of that essence of the Trinity, however, no other person of any kind can exist from the same essence.

Moreover, in these other things one human being is not as much as three human beings together; two human beings are more than one human being. In the case of equal statues, too, there is more gold in the three together than in any one of them, and less gold in one than in two. But it is not so in God. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are not a greater essence than the Father alone or the Son alone. Rather, those three substances or persons together—if they are to be called that—are equal to each one individually. The animal human being does not grasp this.

For such a person cannot think except in terms of masses and spaces, whether small or great, with phantasms flitting in the mind like images of bodies.

## 12. Until cleansed from this impurity, let him believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God

Until he is cleansed from this impurity, let him believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, alone, great, almighty, good, just, merciful, creator of all visible and invisible things, and whatever else can worthily and truly be said about him according to human capacity.

And when he hears that the Father alone is God, let him not separate the Son or the Holy Spirit from him. For he is the sole God together with him with whom he is also one God; likewise, when we hear that the Son is sole God, we ought to understand this without any separation from the Father or the Holy Spirit.

Let him therefore say “one essence” in such a way that he does not suppose one to be greater or better than another, or different from another in any respect. [Note: Some manuscripts read “or greater, or less”; many others read “or greater, or less, or better.”]

Yet this is not to say that the Father himself is the Son and the Holy Spirit, or that each of the things said individually in relation to one another is identical; for example, “Word,” which is said only of the Son, or “Gift,” which is said only of the Holy Spirit. For this reason they also admit the plural number, as it is written in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

He said “one,” and he said “are”: “one” according to essence, because they are the same God; “are” according to relation, because the one is Father and the other Son.

Sometimes the unity of essence is entirely left unmentioned, and only the relative terms are expressed in the plural: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (ibid. 14:23). “We will come” and “we will make our dwelling” are plural, because what preceded was “I and the Father,” that is, the Son and the Father, who are spoken of relatively to one another.

Sometimes this is expressed altogether implicitly, as in Genesis: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26). “Let us make” and “our” are expressed in the plural, and they ought to be understood only from relative terms. [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “and cannot be understood except from relative terms.”]

For it was not so that gods might make the human being, or that he might be according to the image and likeness of gods; rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit might make the human being according to the image of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that the human being might subsist as the image of God. God, however, is Trinity.

But because that image of God was not made altogether equal—since it was not born from him but created by him—it is an image in such a way that it is “according to the image,” to signify this fact: it does not equal him by parity but approaches him by a certain likeness. For God is approached not by intervals of place but by likeness, and one departs from him by unlikeness.

There are some who distinguish the matter in this way: they want the image to be the Son, while the human being is not the image but “according to the image.” The Apostle refutes them, however, when he says: “A man indeed ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7). He did not say “according to the image,” but “the image.”

Yet when this same image is elsewhere called “according to the image,” it is not said as though it were directed toward the Son, whose image is equal to the Father. Otherwise he would not have said “our image.” For how could it be “our,” when the Son is the image of the Father alone?

But on account of the unequal likeness, as we said, the human being is said to be “according to the image.” It is therefore said to be “our image,” so that the human being might be the image of the Trinity—not equal to the Trinity as the Son is equal to the Father, but approaching it, as was said, by a certain likeness. Thus, among things that are distant, a certain nearness is signified—not of place, but of a certain imitation.

For this reason it is also said: “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). To them he likewise says: “Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Ephesians 5:1). For it is said to the new human being: “Who is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of him who created him” (Colossians 3:10).

Or, if for the sake of argument it is now acceptable, even apart from relative terms, to admit the plural number, so that one term may be given in response when it is asked what the three are, and we may say “three substances” or “three persons,” then no masses or intervals should be imagined, no distance involving even the slightest unlikeness, lest one be understood to be less than another, even by a little, in whatever way one thing can be less than another. [Note: Many manuscripts read “or there”; some read “or where.”] In this way there is neither confusion of the persons nor a distinction of such a kind that anything is unequal.

If this cannot be grasped by understanding, let it be held by faith until the one who spoke through the prophet shines in our hearts: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9).

# BOOK EIGHT

In this book he demonstrates by reason that not only is the Father not greater than the Son, but that the two together are not greater in any respect than the Holy Spirit; nor are any two together in the same Trinity greater than one; nor are all three together greater in any respect than each individually. He then proceeds so that the very nature of God may be understood both from the understanding of truth, from knowledge of the highest good, and from the innate love of justice, on account of which even a not-yet-just soul loves a just soul. Above all, he urges that the knowledge of God be sought through charity, which is called God in the Scriptures; and in this charity he observes that a certain trace of the Trinity is also present.

## PREFACE

### 1. Summary of the foregoing. The rule to be observed in more difficult questions of faith

We have said elsewhere that, in that Trinity, those things are properly said distinctly of the individual persons which are said relatively to one another, such as “Father” and “Son,” and the “Gift” of both, the Holy Spirit. For the Father is not the Trinity, nor is the Son the Trinity, nor is the Trinity the Gift.

But whatever is said of each absolutely is not expressed in the plural as three, but as one—the Trinity itself. [Note: So most manuscripts. The printed editions read: “but as one Trinity itself.”] Thus: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; good Father, good Son, good Holy Spirit; almighty Father, almighty Son, almighty Holy Spirit. Yet we do not say “three gods,” or “three good ones,” or “three almighty ones,” but one God, good and almighty—the Trinity itself—and whatever else is said of each individually, not relatively to one another but absolutely.

These things are said according to essence, because in that reality to be is the same as to be great, to be good, to be wise, and whatever else each person there, or the Trinity itself, is said to be absolutely.

Therefore “three persons” or “three substances” is said not so that any diversity of essence may be understood, but so that one term may serve as an answer when one asks what the three or what the three things are; and so great is the equality in that Trinity that not only is the Father not greater than the Son with respect to divinity, but the Father and the Son together are not greater in any respect than the Holy Spirit, nor is any individual person of the three in any respect less than the Trinity itself.

These things have been said, and although they become more familiar when repeated by frequent consideration, some restraint must also be observed. We must entreat God with the deepest devotion to open our understanding and remove the zeal for contentious argument, so that the essence of truth may be perceived by the mind without any mass and without any motion. [Note: The manuscripts read “without any changeability.”]

Let us now, therefore, insofar as the Creator himself, wondrously merciful, assists us, attend to these matters, which we shall treat in a more inward manner than the preceding ones, although they are the same. [Note: The printed editions read “which are now so much more inward.” The manuscripts read “which are now more inward,” that is, “in a more intimate and subtler manner than before.” The manuscript of Reims reads “which are now more inward than before.”] Let that rule be preserved: whatever has not yet become clear to our understanding must not be abandoned from the firmness of faith.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 2. It is demonstrated by reason that in God three persons are not greater than one person

For we say that in this Trinity two or three persons are not greater in any respect than one of them. The carnal habit of thought does not grasp this for any other reason than that it perceives created things as it is able, while it cannot behold the truth itself by which created things were made. For if it could, this bodily light would in no way be more manifest than what we have said.

In the substance of truth—for it alone truly is—nothing is greater except what is more truly so. [Note: Four manuscripts read “what is truer.”] Whatever is intelligible and unchangeable is not truer in one case than another, because it is equally and unchangeably eternal. Nor is what is called great there great from anything other than that by which it truly is. [Note: Most manuscripts read “than by what truly is.”]

Therefore, where greatness itself is truth, whatever has more greatness must necessarily have more truth. Whatever does not have more truth does not have more greatness either. Moreover, whatever has more truth is certainly truer, just as what has more greatness is greater. Therefore, there what is greater is what is truer.

The Father and the Son together are not truer than the Father alone or the Son alone. Therefore the two together are not greater in any respect than either of them individually.

And since the Holy Spirit is equally true, the Father and the Son together are not greater in any respect than he, because they are not truer. The Father and the Holy Spirit together likewise do not surpass the Son in truth—for they are not truer—and therefore they do not surpass him in greatness.

Thus the Son and the Holy Spirit together are as great as the Father alone, because they are equally true. The Trinity itself is likewise as great as each individual person there. For that which is not truer is not greater where truth itself is greatness.

In the essence of truth, to be true is the same as to be; and to be is the same as to be great. Therefore to be great is the same as to be true. Whatever is equally true there must consequently also be equally great.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3. All bodily thinking must be rejected if God is to be grasped as he is, namely, as truth

In bodily things, however, it can happen that this gold and that gold are equally true gold, while this is greater than that, because greatness and truth are not the same there; for it is one thing for it to be gold and another thing for it to be great.

Likewise, in the nature of the soul, when a soul is called great, it is not on that account called true. Even someone who is not magnanimous has a true soul, since the essence of body and soul is not the essence of truth, as the Trinity is: one God, alone, great, true, truthful, truth.

When we try to think of him, insofar as he permits and grants it, let us not imagine any contact or interconnection through intervals of place, as though there were three bodies; nor any structure formed by joining, such as the myths report in the case of three-bodied Geryon. Whatever of this sort occurs to the mind, in which something is greater in three than in one, and less in one than in two, must be rejected without any hesitation. For in this way everything bodily is rejected.

In spiritual things, whatever changeable thing occurs should not be thought to be God. It is no small part of knowledge when, as we breathe upward from this depth toward that summit, we can already know what God is not before we are able to know what he is.

Certainly he is not earth, nor heaven, nor something like earth and heaven, nor anything such as we see in heaven, nor whatever of this sort we do not see and perhaps exists in heaven. [Note: So Am. and the manuscripts; Er. and Lov. read, “nor anything of the sort that we do not see.”] Even if by the imagination of thought you increase the light of the sun as much as you can—whether in size or brightness—a thousand times, or innumerably many times, even that is not God.

Nor is God like the angels of the world as they are imagined: spirits animating heavenly bodies and, at the will by which they serve God, changing and moving them. [Note: Perhaps: “Nor even if angels are imagined.”] Nor would he be anything of that sort even if all of them, since they are “thousands of thousands” (Revelation 5:11), were brought together into one and became one.

Nor is God anything of that sort even if you think of those same spirits without bodies—something exceedingly difficult for carnal thought.

Look, then, if you can, O soul weighed down by the body that is corrupted and burdened with many and varied earthly thoughts; look, if you can: God is truth (Wisdom 9:15).

For it is written, “God is light” (1 John 1:5)—not as these eyes see, but as the heart sees when you hear the words, “He is truth.” [Note: The printed editions read “when it hears”; the manuscripts read “when you hear.” The German manuscript reads, “For when you hear,” etc.] Do not ask what truth is. Immediately the darkness of bodily images and the clouds of phantasms will rise before you and disturb the serenity that flashed upon you at the first stroke when I said “truth.”

Remain, if you can, in that first stroke by which, as though by a flash of lightning, you are struck when “truth” is spoken. But you cannot. You slip back into what is familiar and earthly.

Under what weight, I ask, do you slip back, except under the glue of accumulated filth—that is, desire—and the errors of your wandering?

## CHAPTER THREE

### 4. How it is known that God is the highest good. The soul becomes good only by turning toward God

Look again, if you can. Certainly you love only what is good, because the earth is good with the height of its mountains, the moderate elevation of its hills, and the level expanse of its plains; a pleasant and fertile estate is good; a house is good when arranged with balanced proportions, spacious and bright; living animals are good; a mild and healthy atmosphere is good; food is good when pleasant and suitable for health; health without pain or weariness is good; a human face is good when proportionately formed, cheerfully disposed, and brightly colored; the soul of a friend is good in the sweetness of agreement and the fidelity of love; a just man is good; riches are good because they readily provide what is needed; the heavens with their sun, moon, and stars are good; the angels are good in their holy obedience; speech is good when it teaches pleasantly and admonishes the hearer appropriately; and a song is good when it is melodious in rhythm and weighty in meaning. [Note: Many manuscripts read “moves the hearer appropriately.”]

Why say more and more? This is good and that is good. Take away this and that, and behold the good itself, if you can. In this way you will see God—not good through another good, but the good of every good.

For among all these good things, whether those I have mentioned or others that are perceived or thought of, we would not say that one is better than another when we judge truly unless the knowledge of good itself had been impressed upon us, according to which we approve one thing and prefer another to it.

God must be loved in this way—not this good or that good, but the good itself. The good of the soul must be sought, not that over which it may hover in judgment, but to which it may cling in love. And what is this but God?

Not a good soul, nor a good angel, nor a good heaven, but the good that is good.

Perhaps what I mean will be noticed more easily in this way. When, for example, I hear the words “good soul,” just as there are two words, so I understand two things from those words: one by which it is a soul, and another by which it is good.

Certainly, in order for it to be a soul, it did not itself do anything; for it was not already there to do anything in order to exist. But in order for the soul to be good, I see that something must be done by the will. This is not because that by which it is a soul is not itself something good—for why, then, is it called, and most truly called, better than the body? Rather, it is not yet called a good soul because an action of the will remains by which it may become more excellent. If it neglects that action, it is rightly blamed, and it is rightly called a bad soul.

For it differs from the soul that performs this action; and because the latter is praiseworthy, the one that does not perform it is certainly blameworthy.

But when the soul performs this action with zeal and becomes good, it cannot achieve this unless it turns toward something that it itself is not. Toward what, then, should it turn in order to become good, except toward the good, since it loves, desires, and attains it?

If it turns away from it again and becomes bad, then, by the very fact that it turns away from the good, unless that good from which it turned away remains, it has nowhere to turn again if it wishes to correct itself.

### 5. Mutable goods could not exist unless there were an immutable good

Therefore there would be no mutable goods unless there were an immutable good.

When, then, you hear “this good” and “that good”—things that can sometimes also be called not good—if you can, apart from those things that are good through participation in the good, perceive the good itself through whose participation they are good, then you perceive the good itself at the same time as you hear “this good” or “that good.”

If, having removed those things, you can perceive the good itself through itself, you will have perceived God. And if you cling to him in love, you will immediately be blessed.

It ought to bring shame that, while other things are loved only because they are good, the good itself from which they are good is not loved by clinging to it.

Consider also that the soul, simply because it is a soul—even though it is not yet good in the way that turns toward the immutable good—is nevertheless so pleasing to us merely as a soul that, when we understand correctly, we prefer it even to every bodily light. It is not pleasing to us in itself, however, but in the art by which it was made. For it is approved as something made where it is seen that it ought to have been made.

This is truth, and the simple good. For it is nothing other than the good itself, and therefore also the highest good. The good cannot be diminished or increased except insofar as it is good from another good.

The soul therefore turns toward that by which it has its being as a soul, in order that it may be good. The will is then in harmony with nature, so that the soul may be perfected in the good, when that good is loved by a turning of the will from which it also has that which is not lost through a turning away of the will. [Note: Some manuscripts read “when it is directed toward that good.”]

For by turning away from the highest good, the soul loses its being a good soul; but it does not lose its being a soul, since this too is already better than the body. Thus the will loses what the will attains.

The soul already existed and could wish to turn toward that from which it had its being; but one who wished to exist before existing did not yet exist.

And this is our good: in it we see whether whatever we comprehend ought to have been or ought to be, and in it we see that whatever we do not comprehend how it ought to be could not have existed unless it ought to have existed. [Note: The printed editions read “we comprehend,” omitting the negative particle found in the manuscripts.] [Note: The printed editions read “we comprehend”; the negative particle found in the manuscripts is omitted.]

This good, therefore, is not far from each one of us: “for in it we live and move and are” (Acts 17:27–28).

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 6. God must first be known by an unfailing faith so that he may be loved

But we must stand by love toward that good and cling to it, so that we may enjoy the presence of him from whom we are, without whom we could not even exist.

For while we still walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7), we certainly do not yet see God face to face, as the same apostle says (1 Corinthians 13:12). Yet unless we love him now, we shall never see him.

But who loves what he does not know? Something can be known and not loved; but whether what is unknown can be loved, I ask. For if it cannot, no one loves God before knowing him.

And what is it to know God except to behold him with the mind and grasp him firmly? For he is not a body, to be sought with bodily eyes.

Yet before we are able to behold and grasp God as he can be beheld and grasped—which is granted to the pure in heart, for “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8)—unless he is loved through faith, the heart cannot be cleansed so as to be fit and capable of seeing him.

Where else are those three things for whose construction all the elaborate structures of the divine books arise in the soul—faith, hope, and love (1 Corinthians 13:13)—except in the soul that believes what it does not yet see, and hopes for and loves what it believes?

Therefore one who is unknown is also loved, but he is nevertheless believed. Yet the believing soul must certainly take care that, while believing what it does not see, it does not imagine for itself something that does not exist and hope for and love what is false.

If that happens, it will not be the love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, which is the goal of the commandment, as the same apostle says (1 Timothy 1:5).

### 7. Bodily images formed by the mind are not themselves the object of faith

When we believe certain bodily things that we have read or heard about but have not seen, the mind necessarily forms for itself something in the outlines and shapes of bodies, according to what occurs to its thought. This image may not be true; or, even if it is true, that can happen only very rarely.

Yet it is not useful for us to hold anything by faith merely because of this image; rather, it is useful because something else is conveyed through it.

For who among those reading or hearing what the Apostle Paul wrote, or what has been written about him, does not form in the mind both the face of the Apostle himself and the faces of all whose names are mentioned there?

And when, among so great a multitude of people familiar with those writings, one person imagines the outlines and appearance of their bodies in one way and another in another way, it is certainly uncertain who imagines them more closely and more accurately.

Our faith is not occupied with what bodily appearance those people had, but only with the fact that they lived in the way God’s grace enabled them to live and did the things that Scripture attests. It is useful to believe this, and it should not be despaired of, but desired.

Even the bodily face of the Lord himself is varied and imagined through the innumerable diversity of human thoughts, although it was one face, whatever it was.

In the faith we have concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, what is salutary is not what the mind imagines for itself—perhaps far differently from the way the matter really is—but what we think about the human being according to the form.
