For we possess, as it were, a rule firmly implanted in us, a knowledge of human nature according to which, whenever we see something of this sort, we immediately recognize it as a human being or as the form of a human being.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### How the unknown Trinity is loved

According to this knowledge our thought is formed when we believe that, for our sake, God became a human being, as an example of humility and to demonstrate God’s love toward us.

It is useful for us to believe this and to retain it firmly and unshakably in our hearts: that the humility by which God was born from a woman and, by mortal human beings, led through such great insults to death is the supreme medicine by which the swelling of our pride was healed, and the profound mystery by which the bond of sin was loosened.

Likewise, because we know what omnipotence is, we believe in the power of his miracles and his resurrection on the basis of the omnipotent God. And according to the forms and kinds of things, whether implanted in nature or gathered through experience, we think about deeds of this kind, so that our faith may not be fictitious.

For we do not know the face of the virgin Mary, from whom he was miraculously born, without contact with a man and without injury even in the act of birth. We have not seen the bodily features of Lazarus, or Bethany, or the tomb and the stone that he ordered removed when he raised Lazarus; nor the new monument hewn in rock from which he himself rose; nor the Mount of Olives from which he ascended into heaven.

Indeed, whoever has not seen these things does not know whether they are as we imagine them; rather, it is more probable that they are not.

For when the face of some place, person, or body appears to our eyes exactly as it had appeared to our mind when we imagined it before seeing it, we are moved by no small wonder. It happens so rarely, almost never.

Nevertheless, we believe these things most firmly because we think of them according to the specific and general knowledge that is certain for us. For we believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from a virgin called Mary.

But what a virgin is, what birth is, and what a proper name is, we do not believe; we know these things completely. Whether Mary’s face was the face that occurred to our mind while we are speaking or remembering these things, however, we neither know nor believe at all.

Thus, without compromising the faith, one may say here: “Perhaps she had such a face; perhaps she did not.” But no one can say, without compromising the Christian faith: “Perhaps Christ was born from a virgin.”

### 8. How the Trinity may be loved before it is known

Since we desire, insofar as it is granted, to understand the eternity, equality, and unity of the Trinity, but must believe before we understand, we must be vigilant lest our faith be fictitious.

For we must enjoy that same Trinity in order to live blessedly. But if we believe something false about it, our hope will be empty and our love impure.

How, then, do we love by believing the Trinity that we do not know?

Is it according to a specific or general knowledge, in accordance with which we love the Apostle Paul? Even if he did not have the face that occurs to us when we think about him—and if we are entirely ignorant of that face—we nevertheless know what a human being is.

To avoid going far afield: this is what we are. It is clear that he too was this, and that his soul was joined to his body and lived a mortal life.

Thus we believe about him what we find in ourselves, according to the form or genus that encompasses all human nature equally.

What, then, do we know about that transcendent Trinity, either specifically or generally, as though there were many such trinities, some of which we had experienced, so that through a rule of similarity impressed upon us, or through a specific or general knowledge, we might believe that Trinity too to be of such a kind? Could we therefore love, on the basis of the likeness of something known, the thing that we believe but do not yet know?

Certainly this is not the case.

Or, just as we love in the Lord Jesus Christ the fact that he rose from the dead, although we have never seen anyone rise from the dead, so can we love through believing the Trinity that we do not see and whose like we have never seen?

But we certainly know what it is to die and what it is to live, because we live and have at some time seen and experienced the dead and the dying.

What else is resurrection, then, except coming back to life—that is, returning from death to life?

When, therefore, we say and believe that there is a Trinity, we know what “Trinity” means, because we know what “three” means. But this is not what we love. For whenever we wish to have it, we can easily do so—even leaving other things aside—by counting on three fingers.

Do we perhaps love not every trinity, but the fact that the Trinity is God?

This, then, is what we love in the Trinity: that it is God. But we have seen or known no other God, because there is one God, the one whom we have not yet seen and whom we love by believing.

The question, then, is from what likeness or comparison with known things we can believe so as to love God, who is not yet known.

## CHAPTER SIX
9. How one who is not yet just can know the just person whom he loves

Return, then, with me, and let us consider why we love the Apostle. Is it because of the human appearance that we know so well, on the grounds that we believe him to have been a human being? Certainly not. Otherwise, there is no longer anyone for us to love, since that human being no longer exists: his soul has been separated from his body. But what we love in him we believe still lives even now: for we love a just soul.

From what general or particular rule, then, unless it is because we know both what a soul is and what it is to be just? As for what a soul is, we rightly say that we know it because we too have a soul. For we have never seen it with our eyes and, from the similarity of several things seen, acquired a general or particular conception of it; rather, as I have said, we know it because we too possess a soul. What is known so intimately, and is so conscious of its own existence, as that by which all other things are also sensed—that is, the soul itself?

We also recognize the movements of bodies, by which we perceive that others besides ourselves are alive, from their likeness to our own: for we too move our bodies while living, just as we observe those bodies to move. When a living body moves, no passage is opened for our eyes by which we might see the soul—a thing that cannot be seen with the eyes. But we sense that something like what exists in us for moving our body is present in that mass: this is life and soul. Nor is this peculiar to human prudence and reason. Animals too perceive that not only they themselves are alive, but also one another, each of them perceiving the others and us. They do not see our souls, but they recognize them from the movements of the body, immediately and with the greatest ease, through a kind of natural mutual attunement.

We therefore know the soul of anyone both from our own soul and, from our own experience, believe in one whom we do not know. For we not only sense the soul; by reflecting upon ourselves we can also know what the soul is, since we have a soul.

But how do we know what it is to be just? We had said that we love the Apostle for no other reason than that he is a just soul. We therefore know what it is to be just, just as we know what a soul is. But, as has been said, we know what a soul is from ourselves, because the soul is present in us. How, then, do we know what it is to be just, if we are not just?

If no one knows what it is to be just except one who is just, no one loves the just person except one who is just. For someone cannot love the person whom he believes to be just, precisely because he believes him to be just, if he does not know what “just” means—according to what we demonstrated above: no one loves what he believes and does not see except from some general or particular rule of knowledge.

Accordingly, if no one loves the just person except one who is just, how will someone who is not yet just wish to be just? No one wishes to be what he does not love. But in order that one who is not yet just may become just, he will certainly wish to be just; and in order to wish this, he loves the just person. Therefore even one who is not yet just loves the just person. But no one can love the just person if he does not know what it is to be just.

Therefore even one who is not yet just knows what it is to be just. Where, then, does he know it? Has he seen it with his eyes? Or has he seen some just body, like something white, black, square, or round? Who could say that? Yet the eyes see only bodies. But in a human being, the just is nothing other than the soul; and when a human being is called just, this is said on account of the soul, not the body.

For there is a certain beauty of the soul—justice—by which human beings are beautiful, including many who are twisted and deformed in body. But just as the soul is not seen with the eyes, neither is its beauty.

Where, then, does one who is not yet just know what it is to be just, and love the just person in order to become just? Do certain signs shine forth through bodily movement, by which this or that human being appears to be just? But how does he know that those signs belong to a just soul, if he does not know at all what “just” means? He does know, then.

But where do we know what it is to be just, even when we are not yet just? If we know it outside ourselves [Col. 0954] *Most manuscripts*: “If we know it other than in ourselves,” then we know it in some body. But this is not a bodily reality. Therefore we know within ourselves what it is to be just. For when I seek to express it, I find it nowhere else but within myself; and if I ask another person what it is to be just, he searches within himself for what he should answer. Whoever is able to give a true answer to this question finds within himself what he should say.

When I wish to express “Carthage,” I search within myself for how to express it, and within myself I find the image of Carthage. I received it through the body—that is, through bodily sensation—because I was bodily present there, and saw and sensed it, and retained it in my memory, so that I could find within myself a word concerning it when I wished to speak of it.

For the image of Carthage in my memory is its word—not this three-syllable sound when “Carthage” is pronounced, nor even the name itself silently thought through temporal intervals, but what I see in my mind when I utter this three-syllable word, or before I utter it.

So too, when I wish to express “Alexandria,” which I have never seen, its image is present within me. For when I had heard from many people and believed that it was a great city, I fashioned in my mind an image of it as best I could. This is its word within me when I wish to speak of it, before I utter aloud its five syllables—the name being familiar to almost everyone.

Yet if I could bring this image forth from my mind before the eyes of people who knew Alexandria, surely they would all say, “That is not it.” Or, if they said, “That is it,” I would be greatly surprised; and, looking into my mind at Alexandria itself—that is, at its image as though it were a painting—I would nevertheless not know whether it was really Alexandria, but would believe those who had seen it and retained the memory of it.

I do not seek to know what it is to be just in this way, nor do I find it in this way, nor do I contemplate it in this way when I express it. Nor am I approved in this way when I am heard, nor do I approve it in this way when I hear it, as though I had seen something of that kind with my eyes, or learned it through some bodily sense, or heard it from people who had learned it in that way.

For when I say, knowingly, “A just soul is one that, with knowledge and reason, distributes to each person what is his or hers in life and conduct,” I am not thinking of some absent thing, as with Carthage, nor imagining one as best I can, as with Alexandria, whether it is so or not. Rather, I see something present; I see it within myself, although I am not myself what I see, and many who hear me will approve it.

Anyone who hears me and approves knowingly sees this same thing within himself, even though he is not himself what he sees. But when a just person says this, he sees and speaks what he himself is. And where does he see it, if not within himself? But this is not surprising: where else would he see himself except within himself?

What is marvelous is that the soul sees within itself what it has nowhere else seen; that it sees the truth; that it sees the just soul itself, which is the truth; and that it is itself a soul, yet is not the just soul that it sees within itself.

Is there another just soul within a soul that is not yet just? Or, if there is not, what does it see there when it sees and says what a just soul is, seeing it nowhere but within itself, although it is not itself a just soul? Or is what it sees the inner truth, present to the soul that is capable of contemplating it?

Not everyone is capable of this. And those who are capable of contemplating it are not all themselves what they contemplate—that is, they are not themselves just souls, although they can see and say what a just soul is.

How could they become this [Col. 0955] *Editions*: “could become”; the manuscripts, more aptly: “will they be able to become,” unless by cleaving to the very form that they contemplate, so that they may be formed by it and become just souls—not merely seeing and saying that a just soul is one that, with knowledge and reason, distributes to each person what is his or hers in life and conduct, but also living justly and conducting themselves justly by distributing to each person what is his or hers, so that they owe nothing to anyone except mutual love (Rom. 13:8)?

And how does one cleave to that form except by loving it? [Col. 0956] Why, then, do we love another person whom we believe to be just, and not love the very form in which we see what a just soul is, so that we too may be able to be just?

Indeed, unless we also loved this form, we would in no way love the person whom we love because of it. But perhaps, while we are not just, we love it less than is sufficient for us to become just?

The human being who is believed to be just is therefore loved on account of that form and truth which the person who loves sees and understands within himself. But the form and truth itself cannot be loved on account of something else. For we find nothing like it apart from it, so that, while it is unknown, we might love it by believing, on the basis of something similar that we already know.

Whatever such thing you have looked upon is itself; and there is nothing such, because it alone is such as it is.

Therefore whoever loves human beings ought to love them either because they are just or in order that they may become just. In the same way, he ought to love himself either because he is just or in order that he may become just. Thus he loves his neighbor as himself without danger.

For whoever loves himself in any other way loves himself unjustly, since he loves himself in order that he may be unjust; that is, in order that he may be evil—and consequently he no longer loves himself. “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

## CHAPTER VII

### 10. True love, by which one arrives at knowledge of the Trinity

God is to be sought not outwardly, by desiring to perform wonders with the angels, but inwardly, by imitating the piety of the good angels.

Accordingly, in this question that concerns the Trinity and the knowledge of God, we must chiefly consider what true love is—or rather, what love is. For only that love which is true ought to be called love; otherwise it is desire. Thus those who desire are improperly said to love, just as those who love are improperly said to desire.

True love is this: by cleaving to the truth, we live justly, and therefore, out of love for human beings—for we want them to live justly—we despise all mortal things [Col. 0956] *Mss.*, “temporal things.” In this way we can also be usefully prepared to die for our brothers and sisters, as the Lord Jesus Christ taught us by his example.

Since there are two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend—the love of God and the love of one’s neighbor (Matt. 22:37–40)—Scripture quite properly often gives one commandment in place of both.

Sometimes it mentions only love of God, as in: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Rom. 8:28); and again: “Whoever loves God is known by him” (1 Cor. 8:3); and: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5); and many other passages.

For whoever loves God necessarily does what God has commanded, and loves him to the extent that he does so. It follows, therefore, that he also loves his neighbor, because God has commanded this.

At other times Scripture mentions only love of one’s neighbor, as in: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2); and: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (ibid. 5:14); and in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish that people would do to you, do so to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 7:12).

We find many other passages in the sacred Scriptures in which only love of one’s neighbor seems to be commanded as leading to perfection, while love of God is not mentioned—even though the Law and the Prophets depend upon both commandments.

But this is also because whoever loves his neighbor necessarily loves love itself above all. “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God” (1 John 4:16). It follows, therefore, that he loves God above all.

### 11. God must be sought inwardly, not through powers that rule the world

Therefore those who seek God through those Powers that rule the world or its parts are carried far away from him and scattered—not by distances of place, but by differences of affection. For they try to go outward and abandon their inner selves, where God is more inward than they are.

Even if they hear of some holy heavenly Power or in some way imagine it, they desire chiefly the deeds of that Power, which human weakness admires, rather than imitating the piety by which divine rest is obtained. They prefer proudly to possess the power that an angel has rather than devoutly to be what an angel is.

No holy being rejoices in its own power, but in the one from whom it has the ability to do whatever it appropriately can. It knows that it is more powerful to be joined to the Almighty by a devout will than to be able, by one’s own power and will, to do what those who cannot do such things tremble at. [Col. 0957] *Earlier editions* omitted “by power and will.”

Thus the Lord Jesus Christ himself performed such deeds in order to teach those who marveled at them about greater things, and to turn those who were absorbed and suspended by unusual temporal events toward eternal and inward things.

“Come to me,” he said, “all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest; take my yoke upon you.” He did not say, “Learn from me because I raise the dead after four days”; rather, he said, “Learn from me because I am gentle and humble in heart.”

The most solid humility is more powerful and safer than the most inflated exaltation. Therefore he continues: “And you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

“For love does not puff itself up” (1 Cor. 13:4), and “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and the faithful “will rest in him through love” (Wis. 3:9), recalled from the noise that is outside to the silent joys [Col. 0957] *Editions*, “to the joys of silence”; but several *Mss.*, “to silent joys.” Others read, “to the silence of joy.”

Behold, God is love. Why, then, do we go and rush into the heights of heaven and the depths of the earth, seeking the one who is with us, if only we are willing to be with him?

## CHAPTER VIII

### 12. Whoever loves a brother loves God, because he loves the love itself that is from God and is God

Let no one say, “I do not know what I should love.” Let him love his brother, and he will love that same love. For he knows the love with which he loves better than the brother whom he loves.

Behold, he can now have a knowledge of God clearer than that of his brother—clearly clearer, because God is more present; clearer, because he is more inward; clearer, because he is more certain.

Embrace love, which is God, and embrace God through love. This is the love that unites all good angels and all servants of God in the bond of holiness; it joins them and us to one another and subjects us to itself.

The less we are swollen with pride, the fuller we are of love. And who is full of love unless he is full of God?

But I see love, and, as far as I can, I contemplate it with the mind; I believe the Scripture that says, “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God” (1 John 4:16). Yet when I see love, I do not see the Trinity in it.

On the contrary, you see the Trinity if you see love. But, if I can, I will remind you to see that you are seeing. Let love itself be present, so that we may be moved by love toward some good.

For when we love love, we love something that loves, precisely because it loves something. What, then, does love love, so that love itself can also be loved? Love is not love if it loves nothing.

But if it loves itself, it must love something in order that it may love itself as love [Col. 0958] *The Louvain edition alone, nearly*: “as love” (*ut charitate*). For just as a word signifies something and also signifies itself—but the word does not signify itself unless it signifies that it signifies something—so love does love itself, but unless it loves itself as loving something, it does not love itself as love.

What, then, does love love except what we love through love? To advance from the neighbor, that thing is a brother. Let us consider how highly the Apostle John commends brotherly love:

“He who loves his brother,” he says, “remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him” (ibid. 2:10).

It is clear that he placed the perfection of justice in love of one’s brother: for one in whom there is no cause of stumbling is certainly perfect.

Yet he seems to have remained silent about love of God. He would never have done this unless he wished God to be understood in that very brotherly love. For shortly afterward, in the same Letter, he says most explicitly:

“Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God; and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.”

This sequence of thought makes it sufficiently and plainly clear that the very brotherly love—for brotherly love is the love with which we love one another—is proclaimed with such authority to be not only from God but also God [Col. 0958] *Editions* add after “but also God”: “whom we see.” These two words are absent from the *Mss.*

Therefore, when through love we love our brother, we love our brother from God; and it cannot happen that we do not especially love that same love by which we love our brother.

From this it follows that those two commandments cannot exist without each other. Since God is love, whoever loves love certainly loves God; and whoever loves his brother must love love. Therefore shortly afterward he says:

“Whoever does not love the brother whom he sees cannot love God whom he does not see” (ibid. 4:7, 8, 20).

For this is the reason he does not see God: he does not love his brother. Whoever does not love his brother is not in love; and whoever is not in love is not in God, because God is love.

Moreover, whoever is not in God is not in the light, because God is light and there is no darkness in him at all (ibid. 1:5). Therefore, whoever is not in the light—what wonder is it if he does not see the light, that is, does not see God, because he is in darkness?

He sees his brother with human sight, by which God cannot be seen. But if he loved with spiritual love the one whom he sees with human sight, he would see God, who is love itself, with the inward sight by which God can be seen.

Thus, whoever does not love the brother whom he sees—how can he love God, whom he therefore does not see because God is love, and the one who does not love his brother lacks that love?

Nor should the question now trouble us how much love we ought to give our brother and how much to God. We owe incomparably more to God than to ourselves, but to our brother as much as to ourselves. We love ourselves more, however, the more we love God.

Therefore, by one and the same love we love God and our neighbor; but we love God for God’s sake, and ourselves and our neighbor for God’s sake.

## CHAPTER IX

### 13. We are inflamed to love the just by love of the immutable form of justice itself

What is it, I ask, that makes us burn when we hear and read:

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. We give no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed; but in everything we commend ourselves as servants of God: in great endurance, in afflictions, in necessities, in hardships, in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; with weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left; through honor and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers, and yet truthful; as unknown, and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined, and yet not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:2–10)?

What is it that inflames us to love the Apostle Paul when we read these things, except that we believe he lived in this way?

Yet we do not believe, on the basis of having heard about certain people, that God’s servants ought to live in this way. Rather, within ourselves—or rather, above ourselves—we see it in the truth itself.

Therefore we love the one whom we believe lived in this way because of what we see. And unless we especially loved this form, which we always perceive as stable and unchangeable, we would not love him because we retain by faith the conviction that, while living in the flesh, his life was adapted and conformed to this form.

But somehow we are stirred to love the form itself even more through the faith by which we believe that someone lived in this way; and through the hope by which, because some human beings have lived in this way, we do not at all despair that we too, who are human beings, can live in this way. Thus we desire it more ardently and pray for it more confidently.

In this way, love of that form causes us to love the lives of those people as well, because they are believed to have lived according to it; and belief in their lives kindles a more fervent love of that same form. The more fervently we love God, therefore, the more certainly and serenely we see, because in God we contemplate the unchangeable form of justice according to which we judge that a human being ought to live.

Faith therefore contributes to the knowledge and love of God—not as though he were wholly unknown or wholly unloved, but so that he may be known more clearly and loved more firmly.

## CHAPTER X

### 14. Three things in love, as a trace of the Trinity

What is love, or charity—which divine Scripture praises and proclaims so greatly—except love of the good? But love belongs to one who loves, and something is loved by love.

Behold, there are three: the one who loves, what is loved, and love.

What, then, is love except a kind of life joining, or seeking to join, two things—the one who loves and what is loved?

This is also the case in external [Col. 0960] *Am., Er., and the manuscripts*: “outermost” (*in extremis*) and carnal loves. But in order that we may draw something purer and clearer, let us trample down the flesh and ascend to the soul.

What does the soul love in a friend except the soul? Here too, then, there are three: the one who loves, what is loved, and love.

There remains a further ascent, and we must seek these things higher still, as far as is granted to a human being. But let our attention rest here for a little—not so that it may now think it has found what it seeks, but just as one sometimes finds the place where something must be sought: the thing itself has not yet been found, but the place where it is to be sought has already been found.

Let it therefore be enough to have said this, so that from what may be called the beginning of an argument we may weave together what follows.

# BOOK NINE

The Trinity exists in some manner in the human being, who is the image of God: namely, the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves both itself and its knowledge. These three are shown to be equal among themselves and to be of one essence.

[Col. 0959]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0959]

### 1. How the Trinity is to be sought

Certainly we seek the Trinity—not just any trinity, but that Trinity which is God, the true, supreme, and only God.

Wait, then, whoever you are who hears these things. We are still seeking; and no one rightly reproaches someone who seeks such things, provided that he seeks in the firmest faith what is exceedingly difficult either to know or to express. But whoever asserts something is rightly and promptly reproved if another sees or teaches it better.

“Seek God,” he says, “and your soul shall live” (Ps. 69:33). And lest anyone rashly rejoice as though he had grasped him: “Seek his face continually” (Ps. 105:4).

The Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But whoever loves God is known by him” (1 Cor. 8:2–3).

Here too he did not say, “He has known God,” which is a dangerous presumption, but “He is known by him.”

Likewise, elsewhere, after saying, “But now that you have come to know God,” he immediately corrects himself: “Or rather, to be known by God” (Gal. 4:9).

And especially in that passage: “Brothers,” he says, “I do not consider that I have apprehended it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus. Let all who are perfect think this way” (Phil. 3:13–15).

By perfection in this life he means nothing other than forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward, with determination, toward what lies ahead. The determination of one who seeks is safest until that toward which we strive and stretch ourselves is apprehended.

But the right determination is the one that proceeds from faith. For sure faith begins knowledge in some fashion; but certain knowledge will not be perfected until after this life, when we shall see face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

Let us therefore think in this way, so that we may know that the disposition of one who truly seeks is safer than the presumption that unknown things are known.

Let us seek, then, as though we are going to find; and let us find as though we are going to seek. “When a human being has finished, then he begins” (Ecclus. 18:6).

Let us not doubt with unbelief what is to be believed; let us not assert with rashness what is to be understood. In the former, authority must be held; in the latter, truth must be sought.

Therefore, as far as this question is concerned, let us believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, the creator and ruler of the whole creation; that the Father is not the Son, nor the Holy Spirit either the Father or the Son; but that there is a Trinity of mutually related persons and a unity of equal essence.

Let us seek to understand this, praying for help from the one whom we wish to understand, and desiring with such care and devout concern to explain as much as he grants us to understand [Col. 0961] *We have supplied* the word “desiring” from sixteen *Mss.*, so that even if we say one thing instead of another, we may nevertheless say nothing unworthy.

For example, if we say something about the Father that does not properly belong to the Father but belongs to the Son, or to the Holy Spirit, or to the Trinity itself; or if we say something about the Son that does not properly belong to the Son but at least belongs to the Father, or to the Holy Spirit, or to the Trinity; likewise, if we say something about the Holy Spirit that does not suit the distinctive property of the Holy Spirit, it should nevertheless not be alien to the Father, the Son, or the one God who is the Trinity itself.

At present, for example, we wish to see whether that most excellent love is properly the Holy Spirit. If it is not, then either the Father is love, or the Son, or the Trinity itself, since we cannot resist the most certain faith and the strongest authority of Scripture, which says, “God is love” (1 John 4:16).

Nevertheless, we must not deviate through sacrilegious error by saying something of the Trinity that belongs not to the Creator but rather to the creature, or that is fabricated by empty speculation.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The three things found in love

Since this is so, let us consider these three things which we seem to have found. We are not yet speaking of heavenly things, not yet of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but of this unequal image—nevertheless an image—that is, the human being. The weakness of our mind perhaps contemplates this more familiarly and easily.

Behold, I who am seeking this: whenever I love something, there are three things—I, what I love, and love itself. For I do not love love unless I love one who loves; there is no love where nothing is loved.

There are therefore three: the one who loves, what is loved, and love.

But what if I love only myself? Will there not then be two: what I love and love? For the one who loves and what is loved are the same thing when someone loves himself, just as loving and being loved are the same thing in the same case.

The same thing is said twice when one says, “He loves himself” and “He is loved by himself.” In that case, loving and being loved are not different things, just as the one who loves and the one who is loved are not different.

Yet love and what is loved are still two. For when someone loves himself, there is no love unless love itself is loved. But loving oneself is one thing, and loving one’s love is another.

Love is not loved unless one is already loving something, because where nothing is loved there is no love. Thus when someone loves himself, there are two: love and what is loved. At that point the one who loves and what is loved are one.

It therefore seems that it does not follow that wherever there is love, three things must already be understood. Let us remove from this consideration all the other things, which are many, of which a human being consists; and, in order that we may clearly find what we are now seeking, as far as this is possible in such matters, let us consider the mind alone.

When the mind loves itself, therefore, it reveals two things: the mind and love. But what is it to love oneself except to wish to be present to oneself in order to enjoy oneself?

When the mind wishes itself to be only as much as it is, its will is equal to the mind, and love is equal to the one who loves. And if love is some substance, it is certainly not a body but a spirit; nor is the mind a body, but a spirit.

Yet love and mind are not two spirits but one spirit; nor are they two essences but one essence. Nevertheless, two things are one: the one who loves and love—or, as you may put it, what is loved and love.

These two are spoken of relatively to one another. The one who loves is related to love, and love to the one who loves. For the one who loves loves with some love, and love belongs to someone who loves.

But mind and spirit are not spoken of relatively; they signify essence. For mind and spirit do not exist as mind and spirit because they belong to some human being. [Col. 0962] *The manuscripts read thus.* The editors read, “and the spirit remains.”

If what is called “human” because of the addition of the body is withdrawn—if, therefore, the body is withdrawn—the mind and spirit remain. But if the one who loves is withdrawn, there is no love; and if love is withdrawn, there is no one who loves.

Therefore, insofar as they are related to one another, they are two; but insofar as they are spoken of in themselves, each is a spirit, and together they are one spirit; each is a mind, and together they are one mind.

Where, then, is the Trinity? Let us attend as much as we can, and invoke the eternal light, so that it may illumine our darkness and we may see within ourselves, as far as we are permitted, the image of God.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. The image of the Trinity in the mind of a human being who knows and loves itself

The mind knows itself through itself. For the mind cannot love itself unless it also knows itself. How can it love what it does not know?

Or if someone says that the mind, from a general or particular conception, believes itself to be such as the other minds it has experienced, and therefore loves itself, he speaks most foolishly.

For how can the mind know any mind if it does not know itself? The mind does not know other minds while remaining ignorant of itself, as the bodily eye sees other eyes but does not see itself.

Through the eyes of the body we see bodies, because we cannot cause the rays that shine forth through the eyes and touch whatever we see to be refracted and turned back upon the eyes themselves—except when we look into mirrors. [Col. 0963]

This matter is discussed with the greatest subtlety and obscurity until it is demonstrated most clearly whether it is so or not. But whatever may be the nature of the power by which we see through our eyes—whether it consists of rays or something else—we cannot see that power itself with our eyes. We seek it with the mind, and, if possible, comprehend it with the mind as well.

Therefore, just as the mind gathers knowledge of corporeal things through the senses of the body, so it gathers knowledge of incorporeal things through itself. Thus it also knows itself through itself, because it is incorporeal. For if it did not know itself, it would not love itself.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. Three things that are one and equal: the mind itself, its love, and its knowledge

The three are substantially the same and are spoken of relatively. The same three are inseparable. The same three are not joined and mixed together like parts, but are of one essence and are relative to one another.

Just as there are two things—the mind and its love—when the mind loves itself, so there are two things—the mind and its knowledge—when the mind knows itself.

Therefore the mind itself, its love, and its knowledge are three things; and these three are one. When they are perfect, they are equal.

For if the mind loves itself less than it is—for example, if the human mind loves itself only as much as the human body ought to be loved, although the mind itself is more than the body—it sins, and its love is not perfect.

Likewise, if it loves itself more than it is—for example, if it loves itself as much as God ought to be loved, although it is incomparably less than God—it also sins excessively and does not possess perfect love of itself.

It sins with still greater perversity and injustice when it loves the body as much as God ought to be loved.

Likewise, if knowledge is less than the thing that is known and can be fully known, it is not perfect. But if knowledge is greater, then the nature that knows is superior to the nature that is known, just as knowledge of a body is greater than the body itself that is known by that knowledge.

For knowledge is a kind of life in the reasoning subject; but the body is not life. And every kind of life is greater than any body—not in bulk, but in power.

When the mind knows itself, however, it does not surpass itself by its knowledge, because it is itself the knower and itself the thing known. When, therefore, it knows itself in its entirety, and nothing else along with itself, its knowledge is equal to it, because its knowledge does not arise from another nature when it knows itself.

And when it perceives itself wholly and nothing more, it is neither less nor greater. We were therefore right to say that these three, when perfect, are consequently equal.

### 5. The three exist substantially, not as qualities inhering in a subject

We are also reminded that, if we can somehow see these things, they exist in the soul and, as though unfolded from something wrapped up, become apparent so that they may be perceived and counted as substantially—or, so to speak, essentially—existing, not as qualities existing in a subject, like color or shape in a body, or any other quality or quantity.

For whatever is of this kind does not exceed the subject in which it exists. This color or shape of this body cannot belong also to another body.

But the mind, through the love by which it loves itself, can love something besides itself. Likewise, the mind does not know only itself, but many other things as well.

Therefore love and knowledge do not exist in the mind as in a subject; they too exist substantially, just as the mind itself does. For although they are spoken of relatively to one another, each is nevertheless a substance in itself.

Nor are they related to one another as color and the colored object are, so that color exists in the colored subject without possessing its own substance in itself—for the colored body is a substance, whereas color exists in a substance—but rather as two friends are also two human beings, who are substances, since “human beings” is not said relatively, while “friends” is said relatively.

6. But although the substance that loves or knows is a substance, and knowledge is a substance, and love is a substance, and although “one who loves” and “love,” or “one who knows” and “knowledge,” are spoken of relatively to one another, like “friends,” while “mind” or “spirit” are not relative terms, just as “human beings” are not relative terms, nevertheless a lover and love, or one who knows and knowledge, cannot exist apart from one another in the way that human friends can.

Indeed, friends may appear to be separated bodily, though not in spirit insofar as they are friends. Yet it can happen that one friend begins to hate the other and, by that very fact, ceases to be his friend, while the other remains unaware of this and continues to love him. But if the love by which the mind loves itself should cease to exist, then the mind itself would simultaneously cease to be a lover. Likewise, if the knowledge by which the mind knows itself should cease to exist, then the mind would simultaneously cease to know itself.

Just as the head of something that has a head is certainly its head, and “head” and “that which has a head” are spoken relatively to one another, although they are also substances—for the head is a body, and that which has a head is also a body—so, if there were no head [Note: [Col. 0964] The printed editions read, “if there were no body.” But the manuscripts read “head.”], there would be nothing that had a head. Yet these things can be separated from one another by division; those others cannot.

7. And even if there are some bodies that cannot be cut or divided at all, nevertheless, unless they consisted of parts, they would not be bodies. A part, therefore, is spoken of relatively to a whole, since every part is a part of some whole, and a whole is a whole by all its parts. But since both the part and the whole are bodies, they are not spoken of merely relatively; they also exist substantially.

Perhaps, then, the mind is the whole, and the love by which it loves itself and the knowledge by which it knows itself are, as it were, its parts, so that this whole consists of those two parts? Or are there three equal parts by which one whole is completed? Yet no part embraces the whole of which it is a part. But when the mind knows itself wholly—that is, knows itself perfectly—its knowledge extends through its whole being; and when it loves itself perfectly, it loves itself wholly, and its love extends through its whole being.

Are we therefore to think that these three—mind, love, and knowledge—exist together in something like the following way? From wine, water, and honey one drink is made; each ingredient is present throughout the whole, and yet there are three ingredients. For no part of the drink lacks these three—not joined together as water and oil might be, but thoroughly mingled—and all are substances, while the entire liquid is one substance formed from the three. Is something of this kind to be supposed in the simultaneous existence of these three: mind, love, and knowledge?

But water, wine, and honey are not of one substance, although their mixture produces one substance, namely, the drink. I do not see how those three could fail to be of one and the same substance, since the mind itself loves and knows itself, and since these three are so constituted that the mind is not loved or known by any other thing. These three, therefore, must necessarily be of one and the same essence. And consequently, if they were confused by something like a mixture, they would in no way be three, nor could they be related to one another.

It is like making three similar rings from one and the same gold. Although they are joined together, they are related to one another because they are similar; for everything similar is similar to something. Thus there is a trinity of rings and one gold. But if they were mixed together, so that each was scattered throughout the entire mass, that trinity would disappear and cease altogether to exist. It would then be called not merely one gold, as it was called in the case of the three rings, but there would no longer be three golden things.

## CHAPTER V

8. These three exist each in itself, and each wholly in the others.

But in those three, when the mind knows and loves itself, the trinity remains—mind, love, and knowledge—and is not confused by any mixture. Yet each exists in itself, and each exists wholly in the others: whether each is in the two, or the two are in each. Thus all are in all.

The mind is certainly in itself, since the mind is spoken of in relation to itself. It is spoken of relatively to its knowledge when it is knowing, known, or knowable; and it is spoken of relatively to its love when it is loving, loved, or lovable, in relation to the love by which it loves itself.

Knowledge, although it is related to the mind that knows or is known, is also called known and knowing in relation to itself. For the knowledge by which the mind itself knows itself is not unknown to itself.

Likewise, although love is related to the loving mind, whose love it is, love is also love in relation to itself, so that it is also in itself. For love is loved, and it can be loved by nothing other than love itself—that is, by itself.

Thus each of these exists in itself. They exist in one another because the loving mind is in love, love is in the knowledge of the one who loves, and knowledge is in the knowing mind.

Each is in the other two in this way: the mind that knows and loves itself is in its love and knowledge; the love of the loving and knowing mind is in the mind and its knowledge; and the knowledge of the mind that knows and loves itself is in the mind and its love, because the mind loves itself as knowing and knows itself as loving.

For the same reason, the two are in each: the mind that knows and loves itself is with its knowledge in love, and with its love in knowledge. Love itself [Note: [Col. 0965] The printed editions read, “love indeed”; the Conctunius manuscripts read, “love also.”] and knowledge together are in the mind that loves and knows itself.

We have already shown how each is wholly in the others, when the mind loves itself wholly, knows itself wholly, knows its love wholly, and wholly loves its knowledge, when these three are perfect in relation to themselves.

In a wondrous manner, therefore, these three are inseparable from one another, and yet each of them is a substance; and together they are one substance or essence, although they are spoken of relatively to one another.

## CHAPTER VI

9. One kind of knowledge is knowledge of a thing in the thing itself, another is knowledge in eternal truth. Judgments about bodily things are made according to the rules of eternal truth.

But when the human mind knows and loves itself, it does not know or love something unchangeable. In one way each person declares what is happening in his own mind when he speaks, attending to what is taking place within himself; in another way he defines the human mind by a particular or general understanding.

Thus, when someone tells me about his own mind—whether he understands this or that, or does not understand it, whether he wants or does not want this or that—I believe him. But when he speaks truly about the human mind in particular or in general, I recognize and approve what he says.

It is therefore clear that one person sees in himself something which another, hearing him speak, may believe without seeing it himself; but he sees something else in truth itself, which another person also can behold. The former changes through time; the latter abides in unchangeable eternity.

For we do not derive a general or particular knowledge of the human mind by looking with bodily eyes at many minds and gathering their likeness. Rather, we contemplate inviolable truth, from which we define, as perfectly as we can, not what the mind of each individual is, but what it ought to be according to eternal principles.

10. For this reason, when we rightly approve or disapprove something, we are also compelled either to approve or to disapprove, by other rules that remain unchangeably above our mind, the images of bodily things drawn in through bodily sensation and, in a certain manner, poured into memory—images from which even things not seen are thought through fabricated representations, whether otherwise than they are or, by chance, as they are.

When I recall the walls of Carthage, which I have seen, and when I imagine the walls of Alexandria, which I have not seen, and rationally prefer some imagined forms to others, the judgment of truth above remains vigorous and clear, firm in its incorruptible rules and subject to its own authority. Even if it is overlaid by something like a cloud of bodily images, it is not thereby enveloped or confused.

11. But it makes a difference whether I am shut off by that darkness, beneath or within it, as though from a clear sky, or whether, as often happens on lofty mountains, I enjoy the open air between the two and look upon the clearest light above and the thickest clouds below.

For what is the source of the ardor of brotherly love that is kindled in me when I hear that some man has endured severe tortures for the beauty and steadfastness of the faith? If that man is pointed out to me, I strive to join myself to him, make him known to me, and bind him to me in friendship. If opportunity is given, I approach him, address him, converse with him, express my affection for him in whatever words I can, and in turn wish that he should experience and express toward me the spiritual embrace that I have toward him. Since I cannot so quickly investigate and see through his inner being, I construct this spiritual embrace through faith.

Thus I love the faithful and courageous man with a chaste and genuine love. But if, in the course of our conversation, he should admit to me, or inadvertently reveal in some way [Note: [Col. 0966] Lovaniensis reads, “more inadvertently.”], that he believes something inappropriate about God, or that he desires something carnal in relation to Him, and that he endured those sufferings on account of such an error, or from desire for hoped-for money, or from a vain hunger for human praise, then that love by which I was carried toward him is immediately offended and, as it were, thrown back. Taken away from an unworthy man, it remains in the form in which I had loved him while believing him to be such. [Note: [Col. 0966] The printed editions read, “it does not remain in that form,” adding a negating particle contrary to Augustine’s meaning; all our manuscripts lack it.] [Col. 0967] Unless, perhaps, I now love him in order that he may become such, once I have discovered that he is not such.

Nothing, however, has changed in that man. He can nevertheless change, so that he may become what I had already believed him to be. In my mind, on the other hand, the judgment I had formed about him has certainly changed: it was one way before and is another now. The same love has been redirected, at the command of the unchangeable justice above, from the intention of enjoying him to the intention of helping him.

The form of unshaken and stable truth itself—the form in which I would enjoy the man by believing him good, and in which I would help him to become good—bathes, in the light of incorruptible and most pure reason, both the gaze of my mind and that cloud of imagination which I see below, when I think of the same man whom I had seen, with an undisturbed eternity. [Note: [Col. 0967] So read Ambrosianus and the manuscripts by strong agreement. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “it bathes with equity.”]

Likewise, when I mentally recall an arch beautifully and evenly curved, which I saw, for example, at Carthage, a certain thing announced to the mind through the eyes and transferred into memory produces an imaginary vision. But I behold something else in my mind according to which that work pleases me; and if it displeased me, I would correct it. Thus we judge these things according to that form [Note: [Col. 0967] Understand: “the form of eternal truth.”], and we perceive that form by the intellectual vision of the rational mind.

As for the bodily things themselves, we either touch them as present through bodily sensation, or recall images of absent things fixed in memory, or fabricate from their likeness such things as we ourselves would make in reality if we wished and were able. In one way we shape images of bodies in the mind, or see bodies through the body; in another way, by simple understanding, we grasp the principles and the ineffably beautiful art of such forms above the mind’s field of vision.

## CHAPTER VII

12. We conceive and bring forth within ourselves a word from things seen in eternal truth. The word is conceived through love, whether of a creature or of the Creator.

In that eternal truth, therefore, from which all temporal things have been made, we behold with the mind’s vision the form according to which we exist and according to which we do something, whether within ourselves or in bodies, by true and right reason. From this we conceive a truthful knowledge of things, and we hold it within ourselves as a word; by speaking, we bring it forth inwardly, yet it does not depart from us by being born.

When we speak to others, we add to the word that remains within us the service of the voice or of some bodily sign, so that through a kind of sensible remembrance something may be produced in the mind of the hearer corresponding to what does not depart from the speaker’s mind.

In all our actions and words through the bodily members, by which human conduct is either approved or disapproved, we do nothing that we have not first anticipated by a word brought forth within us. For no one willingly does anything that he has not first said in his heart.

13. This word is conceived through love, whether of a creature or of the Creator—that is, whether of a mutable nature or of unchangeable truth.

## CHAPTER VIII

The difference between desire and charity.

Thus it is either through desire or through charity—not because the creature is not to be loved, but because, if that love is referred to the Creator, it is no longer desire but charity. [Note: [Col. 0968] Lovaniensis reads, “not that it is not.”]

Desire exists when the creature is loved for its own sake. Then it does not assist the user but corrupts the one who enjoys it.

Since, therefore, a creature is either our equal or inferior, what is inferior must be used in relation to God; what is equal must be enjoyed, but in God. Just as you ought to enjoy yourself not in yourself but in Him who made you, so also you should enjoy the one whom you love as yourself—not in that person, but in God.

Let us therefore enjoy both ourselves and our brothers in the Lord, and from there let us not dare to turn back toward ourselves or, as it were, relax downward.

The word is born when what has been thought out pleases us, whether for sinning or for acting rightly. Our word, therefore, and the mind from which it is begotten are joined by love as an intermediary; and love binds itself together with them as a third in an incorporeal embrace, without any confusion.

## CHAPTER IX

14. In the love of spiritual things, the word born is identical with the word conceived; otherwise in the love of carnal things.

The word conceived and the word born are identical when the will comes to rest in the knowledge itself, as happens in the love of spiritual things. For someone who perfectly knows and perfectly loves justice is already just, even if no external necessity exists of performing an action according to it through the bodily members.

In the love of carnal and temporal things, however, as in the offspring of animals themselves, conception is one thing and birth another. There, what is conceived through desire is born through attainment.

For it is not enough for avarice to know and love gold unless it also possesses it; nor is it enough to know and love eating or sexual intercourse unless one also engages in them; nor is it enough to know and love honors and commands unless they are obtained. Yet none of these things is sufficient even when attained. “Whoever drinks from this water,” he says, “will thirst again” (John 4:13).

Therefore the Psalm also says: “He conceived pain and brought forth iniquity” (Psalm 7:15). It speaks of pain or labor being conceived when things are conceived which it is not enough merely to know and desire; the mind burns and languishes from want until it reaches them and, as it were, gives birth to them.

Hence, elegantly, in the Latin language things acquired are called parta, “brought forth,” as well as reperta and comperta, “found” and “discovered”—words that sound as though derived from partus, “birth.” For “when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin” (James 1:15).

Therefore the Lord cries out: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened” (Matthew 11:28); and elsewhere: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (ibid. 24:19).

When, therefore, he referred all deeds—whether rightly done or sinful—to the birth of the word, he said: “By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned” (ibid. 12:37), intending “mouth” to mean not this visible mouth but the inward and invisible mouth of thought and heart.

## CHAPTER X

15. Whether only loved knowledge is the word of the mind.

It is rightly asked, therefore, whether every knowledge is a word, or only loved knowledge. We know even the things we hate; but things that displease us should not be said to be conceived or brought forth in the mind.

For not everything that touches us in any way is conceived. Some things [Note: [Col. 0968] The words “but some” had been wrongly omitted in the printed editions.] are merely known and yet are not called words, such as those with which we are now concerned. In one sense, words are things that occupy intervals of time in syllables, whether they are pronounced or thought; in another sense, everything known is called a word impressed upon the mind, so long as it can be brought forth from memory and defined, even if the thing itself displeases us; and in yet another sense, the word is what is conceived when what is in the mind pleases us.

It is according to this last sense of “word” that we should understand what the Apostle says: “No one says, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). For, according to another meaning of “word,” even those of whom the Lord Himself says, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21), say this.

Nevertheless, when the things we hate rightly displease us and are rightly condemned, the condemnation of them is approved, pleases us, and is itself a word. It is not our knowledge of vices that displeases us, but the vices themselves.

For I am pleased that I know and define what intemperance is; and this is its word. In an art, too, the vices are known, and knowledge of them is rightly approved when the expert distinguishes the form and privation of virtue, as in affirming and denying, being and not being. Yet being deprived of virtue and falling into vice is blameworthy.

To define intemperance and state its word belongs to the art of morals; to be intemperate belongs to what that art condemns. Similarly, knowing and defining what a solecism is belongs to the art of speaking; committing one, however, is a vice censured by that same art.

The word that we now wish to distinguish and make clear is therefore knowledge together with love. When the mind knows and loves itself, its word is joined to it by love. And since it loves its knowledge and knows its love, the word is in love and love is in the word, and both are in the one who loves and speaks.

## CHAPTER XI

16. The image or begotten word of the mind knowing itself is equal to the mind itself.

Every knowledge according to form is similar to the thing that it knows. There is also a knowledge according to privation, which we express when we disapprove something. This disapproval of privation praises the form, and for that reason it is approved.

The mind therefore possesses some likeness of the known form, whether the form itself pleases it or its privation displeases it. Accordingly, insofar as we know God, we are like Him; but we are not like Him in equality, since we do not know Him as much as He knows Himself.

Just as, when we speak of bodies through bodily sensation, some likeness of them is produced in our mind, which is the imagination in memory—for the bodies themselves are not wholly in the mind when we think of them, but their likenesses—so, when we approve these likenesses in place of the bodies, we err. For error is the approval of one thing in place of another.

Nevertheless, the imagination of a body in the mind is better than the bodily form itself, insofar as the former exists in a better nature, namely, in a living substance, as the mind is. Likewise, when we know God, although we become better than we were before knowing Him, and especially when that knowledge, being pleasing and worthily loved, is also a word, and that knowledge becomes in some way a likeness of God, it is nevertheless inferior because it exists in an inferior nature. The mind is a creature, whereas God is the Creator.

From this it follows that when the mind itself knows and approves itself, its knowledge is its word in such a way that it is altogether equal and identical to the mind. For its knowledge is not of an inferior essence, as in the case of the body, nor of a superior essence, as in the case of God.

Since knowledge bears a likeness to the thing it knows—that is, to the thing whose knowledge it is—this knowledge has a perfect and equal likeness by which the mind itself [Note: [Col. 0970] Lovaniensis reads, “because the mind itself”; incorrectly.] that knows is known. It is therefore both image and word, because it is expressed from the mind and, in knowing, is made equal to it; what is begotten is equal to the one who begets.

## CHAPTER XII

17. Why knowledge is the offspring of the mind, but love is not likewise its offspring. The solution of the question. The image of the Trinity: the mind together with its own knowledge and love.

What, then, of love? Is it not an image? Is it not a word? Is it not begotten? For why does the mind beget its knowledge when it knows itself, but not beget its love when it loves itself?

If it is the cause of its knowledge because it is knowable, it is also the cause of its own love because it is lovable. Why, then, has it not begotten both? It is difficult to say.

This question is also accustomed to trouble people concerning the supreme Trinity, God the almighty Creator, in whose image human beings were made. The truth of God invites them to faith through human speech: why is the Holy Spirit not also believed or understood to be begotten by God the Father, so that He too might be called a son?

We are now attempting, as best we can, to investigate this in the human mind, so that from the lower image—one in which our own nature responds to us more familiarly, as though questioned—we may exercise the mind’s vision and direct it from illuminated creation toward unchangeable light, if truth itself persuades us that, just as no Christian doubts that the Word of God is the Son, so charity is the Holy Spirit.

Let us therefore return to that image, which is a creature—that is, to the rational mind—and examine and question it more carefully concerning this matter. Its temporal existence, the knowledge of certain things that was not present before, and its love of certain things that were not previously loved, disclose to us more distinctly what we should say. For in a discourse that must proceed through time [Note: [Col. 0970] Most manuscripts read, “that must be arranged.”], it is easier to explain things that can be grasped in temporal sequence.

18. First, then, let it be clear that something can be knowable—that is, capable of being known—and yet not be known; but it cannot happen that something is known which was not knowable. Hence we must firmly hold that every thing whatsoever that we know generates knowledge of itself in us. Knowledge is begotten from both—the knower and the known.

Thus, when the mind knows itself, it alone is the parent of its own knowledge, since it is both the thing known and the knower. It was knowable to itself even before it knew itself, but knowledge of itself was not in it while it did not know itself.

When, therefore, it knows itself, it begets knowledge of itself equal to itself, because it knows itself no less than it is, and its knowledge is not of another essence—not only because it knows, but also because it knows itself, as we said above.

What, then, should be said about love? Why does the mind not seem to have begotten its own love when it loves itself, just as it begot its own knowledge when it knew itself?

It was lovable to itself even before it loved itself, because it was able to love itself, just as it was knowable to itself even before it knew itself, because it was able to know itself. For if it were not knowable to itself, it could never have known itself; likewise, if it were not lovable to itself, it could never have loved itself.

Why, then, is it said not to have begotten its love by loving itself, as it begot its knowledge by knowing itself? Or is the beginning of love manifestly shown by the source from which it proceeds? It proceeds from the mind itself, which is lovable to itself before it loves itself, and thus is the beginning of the love by which it loves itself.

But it is not rightly said to be begotten by the mind, as is the knowledge by which it knows itself, because knowledge is something already found, which is called something born or discovered; inquiry often precedes it and comes to rest in that result. Inquiry is the desire to find, which amounts to the same as saying “to discover.”

What is found is, as it were, born; hence it is similar to offspring. But where is it born except in knowledge itself? For there it is formed as though expressed.

Although the things we discover by seeking already existed, the knowledge itself did not exist; and it is this knowledge that we regard as a newly born offspring.

Moreover, that desire which exists in seeking proceeds from the seeker and, in a certain way, hangs in suspense. It does not rest at the goal toward which it is directed unless what is sought is found and joined to the seeker.

Although this desire—that is, inquiry—may not seem to be love, since what is known is loved, while what is being sought is not yet known but is being pursued in order to be known, nevertheless it belongs to the same genus in some way.

For it may already be called will, since everyone who seeks wishes to find; and if what is sought concerns knowledge, everyone who seeks wishes to know. If he wishes ardently and persistently, he is said to be eager or devoted—something especially said of those who pursue and acquire various forms of learning.

A certain desire, therefore, precedes the offspring of the mind. Through seeking and finding what we wish to know, the offspring itself—knowledge—is born. Consequently, that desire by which knowledge is conceived and brought forth cannot rightly be called either the birth or the offspring. Yet the same desire by which one yearns to know a thing becomes love of the thing known when it holds and embraces the pleasing offspring, namely, knowledge, and joins it to the one who begot it.

This is a certain image of the Trinity: the mind itself, its knowledge—which is its offspring and its word proceeding from itself—and love as the third. These three are one and one substance. The offspring is not less, since the mind knows itself to the extent that it is; nor is love less, since it loves itself to the extent that it knows itself and to the extent that it is.

# BOOK TEN

In this book it is shown that another trinity exists in the human mind, and that it appears far more clearly in memory, understanding, and will.

## CHAPTER I

1. The love of the mind that is studying—that is, desiring to know—is not love of the thing it does not know.

Let us now approach with more refined attention the matters that follow, explaining them more clearly in due order.

First, since no one can love something entirely unknown, we must carefully consider what kind of love belongs to those who are studying—that is, not those who already know, but those who still desire to know—a particular discipline.

Even in matters where the word “study” is not ordinarily used, loves often arise from hearsay: the reputation of some beauty kindles the mind to see and enjoy it, because the mind knows bodily beauty in general from having seen many beautiful bodies, and has within itself something by which the beauty sought outwardly may be approved.

When this happens, love is not aroused for something wholly unknown, since its kind is already known.

When we love a good man whose face we have not seen, we love him because of the knowledge of his virtues, which we know in truth.

In the pursuit of learning, the authority of those who praise and commend a discipline often kindles us. Yet unless we possessed in our mind some brief impression of what each discipline is, we would not burn with any desire to learn it.

Who, for example, would devote any care or effort to learning rhetoric unless he already knew that it was the science of speaking?

Sometimes we also marvel at the ends of the disciplines themselves, having heard of them or experienced them, and from this we become inflamed with the desire to acquire, by learning, the ability by which we may reach those ends.

Suppose someone who does not know letters were told that there is a discipline by which a person can send words, even to someone far away, made by the hand in silence, and that the person to whom they are sent can gather them not with his ears but with his eyes, and can see that this is being done. Would he not, while desiring to know how this could be accomplished, be moved with every effort toward the end that he already knows?

In this way the studies of learners are kindled. For no one can love what he is wholly ignorant of.

2. The same is true if someone hears an unfamiliar sign, such as the sound of a word whose meaning he does not know. He wants to know what it is—that is, what thing that sound was established to recall.

Suppose, for example, that he hears the word temetum and, not knowing what it means, asks about it.

He must already know that it is a sign: that is, that the sound is not empty, but signifies something. Otherwise this trisyllabic word is already known, and through the sense of hearing it has impressed its articulated form upon the mind. What more can be sought in it to make it better known, when all its letters and all the intervals of its sound are familiar, except that it has simultaneously become known as a sign and has aroused the desire to know what it signifies?

The more something is known but not fully known, the more the mind desires to know what remains.

If he knew only that this was a sound, and did not know that it was the sign of something, he would seek nothing further, since he had perceived the sensible thing as far as he could by sensation. But because he already knows not only that it is a sound but also that it is a sign, he wants to know it perfectly.

No sign is perfectly known unless the thing of which it is a sign is known.

Can someone who seeks this with ardent care and persists in the pursuit, inflamed by study, be said to be without love? What, then, does he love? Certainly nothing can be loved unless it is known.

He does not love these three syllables, for he already knows them. If he loves them because he knows that they signify something, that is not what is presently at issue; he is not seeking to know this. We are asking what he loves in what he is striving to know, which he certainly does not yet know.

We are therefore surprised that he loves it, since we know with complete certainty that nothing can be loved unless it is known.

What, then, does he love, except that he knows and contemplates in the principles of things what beauty belongs to the discipline that contains knowledge of all signs, and what usefulness belongs to the skill by which human beings communicate their thoughts to one another? Without conversation, human society would be worse than any solitude, since people would not mingle their thoughts by speaking.

The soul therefore sees, knows, and loves this beautiful and useful form. Whoever investigates any of the meaningful words he does not know strives, as far as he can, to perfect this form in himself. [Note: [Col. 0973] So read Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads, “whatever signification he does not know.”]

What the soul sees in the light of truth is one thing; what it desires in its own ability is another.

For in the light of truth it sees how great and good it is to understand and speak all the languages of all peoples, to hear none as a foreigner, and to be heard by no one as a foreigner. The beauty of this knowledge is already perceived in thought, and the known thing is loved. It is seen in this way and inflames the studies of learners, so that they are moved toward it and yearn for it in all the work they devote to acquiring such an ability, until through practice they also embrace what they had foreseen in reason.

Thus each person burns with more fervent love for the ability toward which he draws nearer in hope.

People devote themselves more intensely to disciplines that they do not despair of being able to master. For what someone has no hope of attaining, he either loves lukewarmly or does not love at all, even though he sees how beautiful it is.

Since almost everyone despairs of mastering all languages, each person studies his own language most earnestly in order to know it. And even if he feels unable to master it perfectly, no one is so sluggish in this pursuit that, when he hears an unfamiliar word, he does not want to know what it is and, if he can, seek and learn it.

While he seeks it, he is certainly engaged in study; and he appears to love an unknown thing. But this is not so.

That form touches the mind which the mind already knows and considers: the form in which the beauty of joining minds is evident through hearing and returning meaningful words. This form kindles the one who seeks what he does not know, while contemplating and loving the known form to which the unknown word belongs.

Suppose, for example, that when someone asks what temetum means—the example I introduced for this purpose—he is told, “What does it matter to you?” He will reply: “What if I hear someone speaking and do not understand, or happen to read it somewhere and do not know what the writer meant?”

Who would then say to him, “Do not understand what you hear; do not know what you read”? For the beauty of this skill is readily apparent to nearly every rational mind: through the utterance of meaningful words, the thoughts of human beings become known to one another.

Because of this known beauty, and because it is loved as known, that unknown word is sought with diligence.

When he hears and learns that temetum was the ancient word for wine, but that the term has now died out of ordinary usage, he may judge it necessary on account of certain ancient books. But if he has no use for those books either, he may perhaps no longer consider the word worthy of being committed to memory, since he sees that it has no connection with the form of learning which he contemplates and loves as known in his mind.

3. Therefore, all the love of a studying mind—that is, of one who wishes to know what it does not know—is not love of the thing it does not know, but of the thing it knows, on account of which it wishes to know what it does not know.

Or, if someone is so curious that he is drawn not by some other known reason but solely by the love of knowing what is unknown, then this person should indeed be distinguished from the name “student.” Yet he too does not love unknown things. More appropriately, one might say that he hates the unknown, since he wants nothing to remain unknown while he wants everything to be known.

But lest anyone raise a more difficult objection against us, asserting that no one can hate what he does not know any more than he can love what he does not know, we do not resist the truth [Note: [Col. 0974] So read most of the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “we do not resist words.”]. It must be understood, however, that “he loves to know unknown things” does not mean the same as “he loves unknown things.”

It can happen that someone loves to know unknown things; but he cannot love unknown things. The word “to know” has not been inserted without reason. For the person who loves to know unknown things does not love the unknown things themselves, but loves knowing.

If he did not already know what knowing is, no one could confidently say either that he knows or that he does not know.
