For not only must someone who says, “I know,” and speaks truthfully know what it is to know; even someone who says, “I do not know,” and says this confidently and truthfully, knows that he is speaking the truth and therefore knows what it is to know. He distinguishes the one who knows from the one who does not know when, truthfully attending to himself, he says, “I do not know.” And when he knows that he is speaking the truth, how could he know this if he did not know what knowing is?

## CHAPTER II
## 4. No One at All Loves What Is Unknown

Therefore no student, no curious person, loves what is unknown, even when he presses forward with the most ardent desire to know what he does not know. For either he already has as known the kind or general class of what he loves, and desires to know it in some particular instance or in particular instances that perhaps are not yet known to him and are being praised; and he forms in his mind an imaginary image by which he may be stirred to love. But from where does he form it, except from things he already knew? If, however, he finds the thing praised unlike that image formed in his mind and thoroughly familiar in thought, perhaps he will not love it. But if he does love it, he will begin to love it from the moment when he learned it. For shortly before, the thing loved was different from what the mind had been accustomed to present to itself in forming that image. If, on the other hand, he finds it like the image that report had proclaimed, he can truly say to it, “I already loved you”; yet even then he was not loving an unknown thing, since he knew it in that likeness.  

Or we see something in the form of eternal Reason and love what, when expressed in the likeness of some temporal thing, we both believe and love because those who have experienced it praise it. We do not love something unknown; I have already discussed this sufficiently above. Or we love something known, on account of which we seek something unknown. It is not the unknown thing’s love that holds us, but the love of that known thing, which we know the unknown thing belongs to, so that we may come to know also what we are still seeking as unknown—just as I spoke shortly before about an unknown word. Or each person loves knowledge itself, which cannot be unknown to anyone who desires to know something.  

For these reasons those who wish to know something they do not know seem to love unknown things, and because of their more ardent desire to seek, they cannot be said to be without love. But how the matter stands otherwise, and that absolutely nothing unknown is loved, I think I have persuaded those who examine the truth carefully. Yet since the examples we gave concern people who desire to know something other than themselves, we must see whether perhaps a new kind of case appears when the mind itself desires to know itself.

## Chapter III

### 5. The Mind Does Not Love Itself as Unknown to Itself

What, then, does the mind love when it ardently seeks to know itself, while it is unknown to itself? For behold, the mind seeks itself in order to know itself, and is inflamed by this pursuit. It therefore loves—but what does it love? Itself? How can that be, when it does not yet know itself, and no one can love what he does not know? Has report proclaimed its appearance to it, as we are accustomed to hear about absent persons? Perhaps, then, it does not love itself, but loves what it imagines about itself—perhaps something altogether different from what it is. Or, if the mind imagines itself as like that image, and therefore loves itself when it loves this fiction, it loves itself before knowing itself, because it observes something like itself. It therefore knows other minds from which it forms this image, and is familiar with itself in that general kind.  

Why, then, when it knows other minds, does it not know itself, when nothing can be more present to it than itself? If, just as other eyes are more familiar to the bodily eyes than the eyes are to themselves, the mind cannot know itself, then it should never seek itself, since it will never find itself. For the eyes will never see themselves except in mirrors. Nor should we in any way suppose that something similar is employed in contemplating incorporeal realities, so that the mind may know itself as though in a mirror.  

Or does it see in the Reason of eternal truth how beautiful it is to know oneself, and love what it sees, striving to bring this about in itself? For although it is not known to itself, it nevertheless knows how good it is for it to be known to itself. And this is indeed astonishing: not yet to know itself, and already to know how beautiful it is to know itself.  

Or does it see, through a certain hidden memory that has not abandoned it even when it has advanced into the distance [Note: Most manuscripts read “into the far distance” (*in longinquum*)], some supreme end—that is, its security and blessedness—and believe that it cannot reach that same end unless it knows itself? Thus, while it loves that, it seeks this; and it loves what is known on account of which it seeks what is unknown. But how could the memory of its blessedness endure, while the memory of itself along with it could not endure, so that it might know itself as fully as it knows what it wishes to reach?  

Or, when it loves to know itself, does it love not itself, which it does not yet know, but knowledge itself, and does it bear more painfully that it is absent from its own knowledge, by which it wishes to comprehend all things? Yet it knows what it is to know, and while it loves what it knows, it also desires to know itself. Where, then, does it know its own knowing, if it does not know itself? For it knows that it knows other things but does not know itself; from this, therefore, it also knows what it is to know. How, then, does it know itself as knowing something, when it does not know itself? For it does not know another mind as knowing, but knows itself. It therefore knows itself.  

Moreover, when it seeks to know itself, it already knows itself as seeking. It therefore already knows itself. Consequently, the mind cannot altogether fail to know itself, since, while it knows itself as not knowing itself, it certainly knows itself. But if it did not know itself as not knowing itself, it would not seek itself in order to know itself. Consequently, by the very fact that it seeks itself, it is shown to be more known to itself than unknown. For it knows itself as seeking and not knowing, while it seeks to know itself.

## Chapter IV

### 6. How the Mind Knows Itself Not Partially but as a Whole

What, then, shall we say? Does it know itself in part and not know itself in part? But it is absurd to say that it does not know wholly what it knows. I do not say, “It knows the whole”; but whatever it knows, it knows as a whole. Therefore, when it knows something about itself that it cannot know except as a whole, it knows itself as a whole [Note: Some manuscripts read: “it knows itself wholly”]. It knows, however, that it knows something, and it cannot know anything except as a whole. It therefore knows itself as a whole.  

Furthermore, what is so known to it as the fact that it lives? But the mind cannot both exist and not live, since it has even more in that it understands. For the souls of animals also live, but they do not understand. Therefore, just as the mind is wholly mind, so it lives wholly. It knows that it lives. It therefore knows itself as a whole.  

Finally, when the mind seeks to know itself, it already knows that it is a mind; otherwise it would not know whether it were seeking itself, and might perhaps be seeking one thing in place of another [Note: Following the Louvain edition: “seeks.”]. For it is possible that it is not itself a mind, and thus, while it seeks to know a mind, it is not seeking itself. Consequently, since, when the mind seeks what a mind is, it knows that it is seeking itself, it plainly knows that it is a mind. Moreover, if it knows in itself that it is a mind, and the whole of it is a mind, it knows itself as a whole.  

But suppose it does not know that it is a mind, while, when it seeks itself, it knows only that it is seeking itself. Even so, it can seek one thing in place of another if it does not know this; but, in order not to seek one thing in place of another, it undoubtedly knows what it is seeking. If it knows what it is seeking, and is seeking itself, then it certainly knows itself. What, then, does it still seek?  

But if it knows itself in part and is still seeking itself in part, it is not seeking itself but a part of itself. For when it is called “itself,” it is called as a whole. Moreover, because it knows that it has not yet found itself as a whole, it knows how great the whole is. And thus it seeks what is lacking, just as we are accustomed to seek that what has slipped from memory may come to mind, although it has not completely departed, since, when it comes, it can be recognized as the very thing that was being sought.

But how can the mind come to mind, as though the mind could not be in the mind? In addition, even if, after one part has been found, it does not seek itself as a whole, still it seeks itself as a whole. Therefore the whole of it is present to itself, and there is nothing further to seek. For what is lacking is what is sought, not the one who seeks.  

If, however, it does not seek itself as a whole, but the part that has been found seeks the part that has not yet been found, then the mind is not seeking itself, since no part of it is seeking itself. The part that has been found is not seeking itself; and the part that has not yet been found is not itself seeking itself, since it is being sought by the part that has already been found. Therefore, since neither the mind as a whole seeks itself, nor any part of it seeks itself, the mind does not seek itself at all.

## Chapter V

### 7. Why the Soul Is Commanded to Know Itself; The Source of the Mind’s Errors about Its Own Substance

Why, then, is it commanded to know itself? I believe it is so that it may think about itself and live according to its nature—that is, so that it may desire to be ordered according to its nature: beneath that to which it ought to be subject, above those over which it ought to be placed; beneath the one by whom it ought to be governed, above those which it ought to govern.  

For through perverse desire it does many things as though it had forgotten itself. It sees certain things inwardly beautiful in the more excellent nature that is God. When it ought to remain in order to enjoy them [Note: The printed editions read “press on”; the manuscripts read “remain,” to which the later phrase “and falls into what is less” corresponds], it turns away, wishing to attribute them to itself and to be what He is—not from Him, by being like Him, but from itself. It is moved and falls into what is less and less, which it supposes to be more and more, because nothing is sufficient either for itself or for it as it departs from the one who alone is sufficient. Accordingly, through poverty and difficulty it becomes excessively intent upon its own activities and upon the restless pleasures it gathers through them. Thus, through its desire to acquire knowledge from external things—things whose known kind it loves and senses may be lost unless held by diligent care—it loses security, and thinks of itself less and less the more secure it is that it cannot lose itself.  

Thus, since not knowing oneself is one thing and not thinking about oneself another—for we do not say that someone skilled in many disciplines is ignorant of grammar when he is not thinking about it, because at that moment he is thinking about the art of medicine—since, then, not knowing oneself is one thing and not thinking about oneself another, the force of love is so great that the things one has long thought about with love, and to which one has clung through the glue of attention, draw along with them even the one who returns in some way to thinking about himself.  

And because those things are bodies, which it has loved externally through the senses of the flesh, and with which it has become entangled through a kind of long familiarity, it cannot bring those bodies inward with itself, as though into the region of incorporeal nature. Instead, it gathers their images together and carries into itself images formed within itself from itself. For it gives them something of its own substance by which they are formed, but it preserves something by which it may freely judge the appearance of such images. This latter is more properly the mind—that is, rational understanding—which is preserved in order to judge. For we recognize that those parts of the soul which are formed by the likenesses of bodies are shared by us even with animals.

## Chapter VI

### 8. The Mind’s Deceptive Estimate of Itself

The mind errs, however, when it joins itself to these images with such love that it even supposes itself to be something of this kind. For it is conformed to them in a certain way—not by being what they are, but by thinking that it is so. It does not suppose itself to be an image, but supposes itself to be the very thing whose image it carries with itself.  

For judgment is active in it, distinguishing the body that it leaves outside from the image that it carries within itself—except when those same images are represented as though they were perceived externally rather than thought internally, as commonly occurs in sleepers, the delirious, or those in some state of ecstasy.

## Chapter VII

### 9. The Philosophers’ Opinions about the Substance of the Soul

The error of those who think that the soul is corporeal does not arise because the soul is absent from their knowledge, but because they add something foreign to it. What “to find” means. [Note: The printed editions add, “as Empedocles and Ericates thought”; this is wholly absent from the manuscripts.]】【”】【

When, therefore, the soul supposes itself to be something of this kind, it supposes itself to be a body. And because it is well aware of its own sovereignty, by which it governs the body, some people therefore sought what in the body had greater power over the body, and considered this to be the mind; or they considered the whole soul to be such a thing.  

Accordingly, some thought it to be blood, others the brain, others the heart—not in the sense in which Scripture says, “I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart,” and “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart” (Psalm 9, 110, and 137; Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37). For in this usage the word is transferred from the body to the soul, through misuse or transference. Rather, they thought the soul to be precisely that small bodily part which we see when the viscera are torn apart.  

Others believed that it was composed of the tiniest and indivisible particles, which they call atoms, coming together and cohering. Others said that air was its substance; others, fire. Others held that it was no substance at all, because they could conceive no substance except a body, yet could not find it to be a body. They therefore supposed it to be the arrangement of our body or the structure of the elements from which this flesh is, as it were, joined together.  

For this reason all of them judged it mortal, since, whether it were a body or some composition of body, it could not remain immortal. Those, however, who argued as best they could that its substance was a certain life, altogether incorporeal—for they found that life animates and gives life to every living body—consequently argued that it was immortal, because life cannot be without life.  

As for that fifth kind of body—I know not what—which some join to the four familiar elements of this world and from which they say the soul derives, I do not think it necessary to discuss it at length here. For either they call “body” what we call body, whose part in the space of a place is smaller than the whole; and they must be counted among those who believed the mind corporeal; or, if they call every substance, or every mutable substance, body, while recognizing that not every substance is contained within spatial extension having length, breadth, and height, there is no need to quarrel with them over a question of terminology.

In all these opinions, whoever sees that the nature of the mind is a substance and is not corporeal—that is, that it does not occupy a smaller spatial extension through a smaller part of itself and a larger extension through a larger part—must at the same time see that those who think it corporeal do not err because the mind is absent from their knowledge, but because they add things without which they are unable to conceive any nature.  

For without images of bodies, they think that whatever they may be commanded to think of is absolutely nothing. [Note: The printed editions read “seen”; the manuscripts read “commanded.”] Therefore the mind should not seek itself as though it were absent from itself. For what is so present to knowledge as that which is present to the mind? Or what is so present to the mind as the mind itself?  

Hence even the word commonly translated “discovery,” if we trace its origin, says nothing other than this: to discover is to come upon what is being sought. For this reason things that come into the mind, as it were, of their own accord are not ordinarily said to have been “discovered,” although they may be called known, because in seeking them we were not directing ourselves toward them so as to come upon them—that is, so as to discover them.  

Therefore, just as the mind itself seeks things that are sought through the eyes or through any other bodily sense—for it is itself also what directs the bodily sense, and it discovers when that same sense comes upon the things being sought—so it discovers other things that it must know not through the mediation of bodily sense but through itself, when it comes upon them: either in the higher substance, that is, in God, or in the other parts of the soul, as when it judges those very images of bodies. For it discovers within the soul the images impressed there through the body.

## Chapter VIII

### 11. How the Soul Seeks Itself; The Source of the Soul’s Error about Itself

How, then, it seeks and finds itself is a remarkable question: toward what does it extend itself in seeking, or to what does it come in order to find? For what is so much in the mind as the mind itself?  

But because it is among the things it thinks about with love, and has become accustomed through love to sensible things—that is, bodily things—it cannot exist within itself without their images. From this arises the disgrace of error, because it cannot separate from itself the images of sensed things so as to see itself alone. For they have become wonderfully attached to it by the glue of love. This is its uncleanness: while it endeavors to think of itself alone, it supposes itself to be that without which it cannot think of itself.  

Therefore, when it is commanded to know itself, it should not seek itself as though it had been taken away from itself, but remove what it has added to itself. For it is more inward than not only these sensible things that are plainly external, but also their images, which are in a certain part of the soul shared even by animals, although they lack the understanding proper to the mind.  

Since, then, the mind is inward, it in a certain way goes out from itself when it extends the affection of its love toward these things as though toward traces of its many acts of attention. These traces are, as it were, impressed upon memory when the bodily things outside are sensed, so that even when those things are absent, their images are nevertheless present to those who think about them.  

Let it therefore know itself, and not seek itself as though absent; rather, let it direct toward itself the intention of the will by which it had been wandering among other things, and let it think about itself. [Note: Most manuscripts read “in itself.”] Thus it will see that it has never failed to love itself and has never failed to know itself, but that, by loving something else along with itself, it has confused and in a certain way fused itself with that other thing. Thus, while it embraces different things as though they were one, it supposed that different things were one.

## Chapter IX

### 12. The Mind Knows Itself by Understanding the Command to Know Itself

Let it not, then, seek to perceive itself as though it were absent, but take care to distinguish itself as present. Let it not know itself as though it did not know itself, but distinguish itself from that other thing which it knows. [Note: The manuscripts read thus; the printed editions read “from that by which.”]  

For when it hears, “Know yourself,” how will it take care to do this if it does not know either what “know” means or what “yourself” means? But if it knows both, it also knows itself. For the mind is not told, “Know yourself,” in the same way that it is told, “Know the Cherubim and Seraphim.” We believe that those are absent, according to what is proclaimed about them, namely, that they are certain heavenly powers.  

Nor is it told in the same way as, “Know that man’s will,” which is in no way present to us either for perception or understanding except through bodily signs that have been produced—and even then we believe rather than understand. Nor is it told as a person is told, “Look at your face,” which cannot be done except in a mirror. For our own face too is absent from our sight, because it is not located where the gaze can be directed.  

But when the mind is told, “Know yourself,” by the very stroke by which it understands the words “yourself,” it knows itself, and for no other reason than that it is present to itself. If it does not understand what was said, it certainly does not carry it out. Therefore, it is commanded to do that which it does when it understands the command itself.

## Chapter X

### 13. Every Mind Knows with Certainty Three Things about Itself: Understanding, Being, and Living

When it hears that it should know itself, therefore, let it not add something else to what it knows about itself. For it certainly knows that this is said to it—to it, namely, which exists, lives, and understands. A corpse exists, and an animal lives, but neither a corpse nor an animal understands. Thus it knows that it exists and lives in the manner in which it exists and lives as understanding.  

For example, when the mind supposes itself to be air, it supposes that air understands, but it knows that it understands. It does not know that it is air, however; it supposes this. Let it distinguish what it supposes from what it knows. Let it retain what remains to it—that which even those who supposed the mind to be one body or another did not doubt.  

For not every mind supposes itself to be air: some suppose it to be fire, others the brain, others some other body, and still others something else, as I mentioned above. Yet all know that they understand, and that they exist and live. But they refer understanding to that which they understand, whereas they refer existing and living to themselves.  

No one doubts that no one understands who does not live, nor that no one lives who does not exist. Therefore, what understands exists and lives—not in the manner of a corpse, which does not live, nor in the manner of a soul that lives but does not understand, but in a certain proper and more excellent manner.  

Likewise, they know that they will, and they know equally that no one can will who does not exist and live. They also refer the will itself to something that they will by that will. They know, too, that they remember, and at the same time they know that no one would remember unless he existed and lived. But we also refer memory itself to something that we remember by it.  

Within two of these three—memory and understanding—are contained the knowledge and awareness of many things; but the will is present by which we either enjoy or use them. For we enjoy known things, in which the will, delighted by them for their own sake, rests; but we use things that we refer to something else that is to be enjoyed. To use is to take something into the power of the will; to enjoy is to use with joy, not still in hope, but already possessing the thing itself. Consequently, everyone who enjoys also uses, for he takes something into the power of the will with the end of delight. But not everyone who uses enjoys, if he desires what he takes into the power of the will not for its own sake but for the sake of something else.

### 14.

Since, then, the subject is the nature of the mind, let us remove from our consideration all knowledge acquired externally through the bodily senses, and attend more carefully to what we have stated: that all minds know and are certain about themselves.  

For people have doubted whether air possesses the power of living, remembering, understanding, willing, thinking, knowing, and judging; or fire, or the brain, or blood, or atoms; or some fifth body of unknown kind beyond the customary four elements; or whether the structure or temperament of our flesh itself could accomplish these things. One person tried to assert one possibility, another another.  

Yet who would doubt that he lives, remembers, understands, wills, thinks, knows, and judges? Even if he doubts, he lives. If he doubts the source of his doubt, he remembers. If he doubts, he understands that he doubts. If he doubts, he wishes to be certain. If he doubts, he thinks. If he doubts, he knows that he does not know. If he doubts, he judges that he ought not to give assent rashly.  

Therefore, whoever doubts anything else ought not to doubt these things. If they did not exist, he could not doubt anything at all.

### 15.

Those who think that the mind is either a body or a composition or temperament of body wish all these things to appear in a subject, so that the substance may be air, fire, or some other body which they take to be the mind, while understanding inheres in this body as its quality: the subject is one thing, and the quality inheres in the subject. The subject, they say, is the mind, which they suppose to be a body; understanding, or whatever else among the things we have stated to be certain for us, inheres in it.  

Those who deny that the mind itself is a body but say that it is a structure or temperament of body hold a similar opinion. The difference is that the former say that the mind itself is the substance in which understanding inheres, whereas the latter say that the mind itself inheres in a subject—namely, the body whose composition or temperament it is. Consequently, they too suppose that understanding is something existing in that same subject, the body.

### 16.

None of them notices that the mind knows itself even while it seeks itself, as we have already shown. But it is in no way correctly said that something is known while its substance is unknown. Therefore, when the mind knows itself, it knows its substance; and when it is certain about itself, it is certain about its substance. It is certain about itself, as the things said above establish.  

Yet it is not at all certain whether it is air, fire, some body, or something belonging to a body. It is therefore none of these. Everything that it is commanded to know about itself pertains to this: that it should be certain that it is not any of the things about which it is uncertain, and that it should be certain that it is only what it is certain that it is.  

For it thinks of fire or air, and of whatever other body it thinks of, in one way. It could not in any way think of what it itself is in the same manner as it thinks of what it is not. For it thinks of all these things—fire, air, this or that body, or some part, structure, or temperament of body—through an imaginary representation. Yet it is not said to be all these things, but to be one of them.  

If it were any of them, it would think of that one differently from the others—not through an imaginary fiction, as absent things are thought of that have been touched by bodily sense, whether those very things or others of the same kind, but through a certain inward presence that is not fabricated but real. For nothing is more present to it than itself. In this way it thinks that it lives, remembers, understands, and wills.  

For it knows these things in itself, and does not imagine them as though it had touched them outside itself through sense, as every bodily thing is touched. If, from its thoughts of these things, it does not attach to itself anything by which it supposes itself to be something of that kind, then whatever remains to it concerning itself is itself alone.

## Chapter XI

### 17. In Memory, Understanding, and Will, Talent, Learning, and Use Are Observed

Memory, understanding, and will are one essentially, and three relatively. Let us therefore set aside for a little while the other things of which the mind is certain about itself, and consider and discuss above all these three: memory, understanding, and will.  

For these three are also commonly examined in children to determine what sort of disposition they display. The more tenaciously and easily a child remembers, the more sharply he understands [Note: The manuscripts read “more keenly understands”], and the more ardently he applies himself, the more praiseworthy is his talent.  

But when one asks about someone’s learning, the question is not how firmly or easily he remembers, or with what keenness he understands, but what he remembers and what he understands. And since a mind is judged praiseworthy not only for how learned it is but also for how good it is, attention is paid not only to what it remembers and understands but also to what it wills—not how fervently it wills, but first what it wills, and then how greatly it wills.  

For a mind that loves vehemently is to be praised when what it loves is something that ought to be loved vehemently. When, therefore, these three are mentioned—talent, learning, and use—the first is considered in those three faculties: what each person is capable of through memory, understanding, and will. [Note: Seven manuscripts omit “understanding and will.”] The second is considered in what each person possesses in memory and understanding, and in what he has reached through devoted willing. The third, use, is found in the will, as it handles what is contained in memory and understanding, whether it refers these things to something else or rests delighted in their end.  

To use is to take something into the power of the will; to enjoy is to use with joy, not still in hope, but already possessing the thing itself. Therefore everyone who enjoys uses, for he takes something into the power of the will with the end of delight; but not everyone who uses enjoys, if he has desired what he takes into the power of the will not for its own sake but for the sake of something else. [Note: The manuscripts read “if it”; the printed editions read “but it.”]

### 18.

These three—memory, understanding, and will—are not three lives but one life, nor three minds but one mind. Consequently, they are not three substances but one substance.  

Memory, which is called life, mind, and substance, is said in relation to itself; but when it is called “memory,” it is said relatively to something. The same must be said of understanding and will: understanding and will too are spoken of relatively to something. Each, however, is life, mind, and essence in relation to itself.  

Therefore these three are one insofar as they are one life, one mind, and one essence. Whatever else the individual things are said to be in relation to themselves is also said of them together, not plurally but singularly. They are three insofar as they refer to one another. If they were not equal, not only would each contain each, but neither would each contain all, nor would they contain one another.  

For each contains not merely each individually, but all together. I remember that I have memory, understanding, and will; I understand that I understand, will, and remember; and I will that I will, remember, and understand. I remember my entire memory, understanding, and will together. For what I do not remember from my memory is not in my memory. Nothing is so much in memory as memory itself. I therefore remember it wholly.  

Likewise, whatever I understand, I know that I understand; and I know that I will whatever I will. Whatever I know, I remember. I therefore remember my entire understanding and my entire will. Similarly, when I understand these three, I understand all three together.  

For I do not fail to understand any intelligible thing except what I do not know. What I do not know I neither remember nor will. Therefore, whatever intelligible things I do not understand, I consequently neither remember nor will. Whatever intelligible things I remember and will, I consequently understand.  

My will also contains my entire understanding and my entire memory, since I use all that I understand and remember. Therefore, since each wholly contains all through each and all together, each whole is equal to each whole, and each whole together is equal to all wholes. These three are one: one life, one mind, one essence.

## Chapter XII

### 19. The Mind Is an Image of the Trinity in Its Memory, Understanding, and Will

Must we now ascend, with whatever powers of attention we possess, to that supreme and most exalted essence, of which the human mind is an unequal image, but nevertheless an image? Or must these same three still be explained more distinctly in the soul through those things we apprehend externally by bodily sense, where knowledge of bodily things is impressed temporally?  

We found the mind itself in its memory, understanding, and will to be such that, since it was understood always to know itself and always to will itself, it was also understood always to remember itself, always to understand itself, and to love itself. Yet it does not always think of itself as distinct from those things that are not what it is. Consequently, it is difficult in it to distinguish its memory of itself from its understanding of itself.  

For in a matter where these are very closely joined, and one is not preceded by the other at any time, they appear as though they were not two things but one thing called by two names. Love itself does not appear to be present in the same way when need does not reveal it, since what is loved is always present. [Note: The printed editions read “is not always present”; the negative is to be removed, since it is absent from the manuscripts.]  

Therefore these matters can also become clear to slower minds when we consider things that come to the soul in time and things that happen to it temporally: when it remembers what it had not remembered before, when it sees what it had not seen before, and when it loves what it had not loved before. But this discussion now requires a different beginning, because of the limits of this little book.

# BOOK ELEVEN

A certain image of the Trinity is also shown in the exterior human being: first, in those things perceived externally—namely, the body that is seen, the form impressed from it upon the vision of the one who sees, and the intention of the will that joins the two together—although these three are neither equal to one another nor of one substance.  

Then, in the mind itself, another trinity, or three things of one substance, is observed as though introduced by those things sensed externally: the imagination of the body that is in the memory, the formation arising from it when the vision of the thinker turns toward it, and the intention of the will joining the two together. This second trinity is also said to belong to the exterior human being, because it has been brought in from bodies that are sensed externally.

## Chapter I

### 1. A Trace of the Trinity Also in the Exterior Human Being

No one doubts that, just as the interior human being is endowed with understanding, so the exterior human being is endowed with bodily sense. Let us therefore strive, if we can, to investigate in this exterior human being also some kind of trace of the Trinity—not because it is itself an image of God in the same manner.  

For the apostolic statement is clear: it declares that the interior human being is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of the one who created him (Colossians 3:10), while it also says elsewhere, “Even if our exterior human being is being corrupted, nevertheless the interior is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).  

Let us therefore seek, as best we can, some likeness of the Trinity in this human being who is being corrupted; if not a more exact likeness, perhaps one easier to discern. For it is not without reason that this too is called “human,” unless some likeness of the interior human being is present in it.  

And by that very order of our condition through which we have become mortal and carnal, we handle visible things more easily and, as it were, more familiarly than intelligible things: the former are external, the latter internal; we perceive the former through bodily sense, and understand the latter through the mind. We ourselves, however, as souls, are not sensible—that is, bodily—but intelligible, since we are life.  

Nevertheless, as I have said, such a great habit has been formed in bodies, and our attention, falling outward into them in such a remarkable way, has projected itself into them, that when it has been removed from the uncertainty of bodies so that it may be fixed in the spirit through a much more certain and stable knowledge, it recoils toward these things and seeks rest there from which it drew weakness.  

We must accommodate ourselves to this sickness, so that whenever we attempt to distinguish and explain spiritual inward realities more suitably and easily, we may take from external bodily things examples of likeness.  

The exterior human being, then, endowed with bodily sense, senses bodies. This sense is divided into five parts, as is readily observed: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. But it would be both excessive and unnecessary to question all five senses about what we seek. What one of them reports to us is also valid in the others. Let us therefore make use especially of the testimony of the eyes. For this bodily sense is preeminent and, by the difference proper to its kind, is closer to the vision of the mind.

## Chapter II
## 2. A Certain Trinity in Vision. The Three Things Present in Vision Differ in Their Nature. How Vision, or the Image of the Thing Seen, Arises from the Visible Object. The Matter Is Demonstrated More Clearly by an Example. How Those Three Coalesce into One

When, therefore, we see some body, these three things—which is very easy—must be considered and distinguished. First, the thing itself that we see, whether a stone, some flame, or anything else that can be seen with the eyes; this could certainly already have existed before it was seen. Second, the vision, which did not exist before we sensed that object presented to our sense. Third, the attention of the mind, which, in the object being seen, holds the sense of the eyes for as long as the object is seen.

In these three, then, there is not only an evident distinction but also a distinct nature. For that first body, the visible object, is of a nature far different from the sense of the eyes, upon whose encountering it vision arises. And what else does vision appear to be than a sense informed by the thing that is sensed? Although, when the visible object is removed, vision no longer exists, and although no such vision can exist at all unless there is a body capable of being seen, nevertheless the body by which the sense of the eyes is formed, when that body is seen, is in no way of the same substance as the very form impressed by it upon the sense, which is called vision.

For the body seen [Note: [Col. 0985] Some manuscripts: “by the sight.”] is separable in its own nature. But the sense, which already existed in the living creature even before it saw what it could see, when it encountered something visible—or vision, which comes to be in the sense from the visible body when the two have already been joined and the object is seen: this sense, then—or vision, that is, the sense formed from outside—belongs to the nature of the living creature, which is entirely different from that body which we sense by seeing and by which the sense is not formed so as to be a sense, but so as to be vision.

For unless the sense had existed in us before the sensible object was presented, we would not differ from the blind while seeing nothing, whether in darkness or with our eyes closed. The difference is that there is in us, even when we do not see, something by which we can see, and this is called the sense; but it is not present in the blind. They are called blind for no other reason than that they lack it.

Likewise, the attention of the mind—which holds the sense upon the thing we see and joins the two—not only differs in nature from that visible object, since this is mind and that is body, but also differs from the sense and vision itself, because this attention belongs to the mind alone. The sense of the eyes is called a bodily sense for no other reason than that the eyes themselves are also members of the body. And although an inanimate body does not sense, the soul, mingled with the body, senses through a bodily instrument, and that instrument is called the sense.

When this instrument is intercepted and extinguished by a bodily affliction, as when someone is blinded, the mind and its attention nevertheless remain. Having lost the eyes, the mind no longer has that bodily sense by which it might join itself externally to a body through seeing and fix its gaze upon the object seen; yet by that very effort it shows that, when the bodily sense has been taken away, it could neither perish nor be diminished. For a certain desire to see remains intact, whether seeing can take place or cannot.

These three, then—the body that is seen, vision itself, and the attention that joins the two—are evident for distinguishing, not only because of the properties of each, but also because of the difference of their natures.

## 3.

Although, among these, the sense does not proceed from that body which is seen but from the body of the sentient living creature, with which the soul is harmonized in a certain wondrous manner, vision nevertheless arises from the body that is seen; that is, the sense itself is formed. Thus not only is there the sense that can remain intact even in darkness, so long as the eyes are healthy, but there is also the informed sense called vision.

Vision therefore arises from the visible thing, but not from that thing alone, unless a viewer is also present. Accordingly, vision arises from the visible and the viewer, in such a way that the sense of the eyes and the attention of the one looking and gazing come from the viewer; yet that informing of the sense which is called vision is impressed by the body alone that is seen, that is, by some visible thing. When it is removed, no form remains that had been present in the sense while the object seen was there; nevertheless the sense itself remains, the sense that existed even before anything was sensed.

It is like a footprint in water, which remains as long as the body making the impression is present. Once that body is removed, the footprint no longer exists, while the water remains—the water that existed before it received the form of the body.

Therefore we cannot indeed say that the visible thing generates the sense; yet it does generate a form resembling itself, which arises in the sense when we sense something by seeing. But through the same sense we do not distinguish the form of the body that we see from the form produced in the sense of the viewer by that body. Their conjunction is so close that there is no opportunity for distinguishing them.

Nevertheless, by reasoning we conclude that we could not have sensed anything unless some likeness of the body seen had been produced in our sense. When a ring is impressed into wax, the fact that the image cannot be distinguished until the ring has been separated does not mean that no image has been made. Since, after the wax has been separated, what was made remains so that it can be seen, it is therefore easily understood that the wax already contained a form impressed by the ring before it was separated from it.

But if a ring were placed in a liquid, when the ring was removed no image would appear. Yet reason should not for that reason fail to distinguish that, before the ring was removed, there had been in the liquid a form made from the ring—[Note: [Col. 0987] The word “not” appears redundant. Perhaps the passage should be read, with the words transposed, as follows: “Reason should not for that reason fail to distinguish that there had been in that liquid, before it was removed, a form of the ring made from the ring,” etc. M.]—a form that must be distinguished from the form in the ring itself, from which the other form was produced. When the ring is removed, the latter form will no longer exist, although the form in the ring remains, from which the other was made.

Thus the sense of the eyes does not fail to contain an image of the body that is seen for as long as it is seen merely because, when the body is removed, the image does not remain. Consequently, it is extremely difficult to persuade less capable minds that, when we see a visible thing, an image of it is formed in our sense, and that this same form is vision.

## 4.

But those who perhaps notice what I am about to recall will not struggle so much with this inquiry. Often, when we have gazed for a fairly long time at some lights and then closed our eyes, certain bright colors seem to move before our sight, changing into various forms and becoming progressively less and less bright until they disappear altogether. We should understand these to be remnants of the form that had been produced in the sense when the luminous body was seen, gradually and, in a certain manner, step by step, changing and fading away.

The latticework of the inserted windows, too, if we happened to be looking at it, often appeared among those colors. This makes it clear that this affection had been impressed upon our sense by the thing that was seen. It was therefore present even while we were seeing, and at that time it was brighter and more distinct; but it was so closely joined to the appearance of the thing being observed that it could not be distinguished at all. And it was vision itself.

Moreover, when the little flame of a lamp, in a certain way, is doubled for our eyes by rays spreading apart, two visions arise even though the thing seen is one. The same rays, issuing from each eye, are affected separately, since they are not allowed to converge together upon the body being viewed, so that one act of looking might arise from both. Therefore, if we close one eye, we see not a double flame but one, just as it is.

Why, when the left eye is closed, the appearance that belonged to the right eye ceases to be seen, and conversely, when the right eye is closed, the appearance that belonged to the left eye dies away—this would take too long to investigate and discuss, and it is not necessary for the matter immediately before us. What is sufficient for the question undertaken is this: unless a certain image, extremely like the thing we see, were produced in our sense, the appearance of the flame would not be doubled according to the number of the eyes when a certain manner of seeing had been introduced that could separate the convergence of the rays. For once either eye is withdrawn, pressed upon, or twisted in any manner, while the other is closed, it is in no way possible for one thing to be seen as two.

## 5.

Since this is so, let us remember how these three things, although different in nature, are harmonized into a kind of unity: namely, the appearance of the body that is seen; its image impressed upon the sense, which is vision, or the formed sense; and the will of the mind, which applies the sense to the sensible thing and holds vision itself upon it.

The first of these—the visible thing itself—does not belong to the nature of the living creature, except when we see our own body. The second belongs to it in such a way that it occurs in the body and, through the body, in the soul; for it occurs in the sense, which exists neither without the body nor without the soul. The third, however, belongs to the soul alone, because it is the will.

Although these three are substances of such different kinds, they nevertheless come together in so great a unity that the first two can scarcely be distinguished except by the intervention of judgment—namely, the appearance of the body that is seen and its image produced in the sense, that is, vision. The will, however, possesses such power to join these two that it applies the sense to be formed to the thing being seen and holds it there once it has been formed.

And if the will is so violent that it can be called love, desire, or lust, it also powerfully affects the rest of the living creature’s body; and where the slower and harder material does not resist, it changes that body into a similar appearance and color. One may observe how readily the little body of the chameleon changes in response to the colors it sees.

Because the bodies of other animals are not so readily susceptible to change, their offspring generally reveal the lusts of their mothers when they have looked upon something with great pleasure. For the more tender and, so to speak, malleable are the beginnings of the seeds, the more effectively and receptively they follow the attention of the mother’s soul and the phantasy formed in it through the body at which she gazed with desire.

There are examples that could be recalled at length, but one from the most trustworthy Books is sufficient: Jacob caused the sheep and goats to give birth to offspring of various colors by placing variegated branches before them in the channels of water, where they could look at them while they were conceiving (Gen. XXX, 37–41).

## CHAPTER III

### 6. The Unity of Three Things in Thought: Memory, Inner Vision, and the Will That Joins the Two

The rational soul lives deformedly when it lives according to the trinity of the outer man; that is, when it applies to those things that externally form the bodily sense not a praiseworthy will, by which it refers them to something useful, but a shameful desire by which it clings to them.

For even when the appearance of the body that was sensed bodily has been removed, its likeness remains in memory. The will can again turn its gaze toward this likeness, so that it may be formed inwardly from it, just as the external sense was formed from the bodily object presented to the senses. Thus that trinity arises from memory, inner vision, and the will that joins the two.

When these three are driven together into one, the result of that compulsion is called thought. In these three there is no longer a difference of substance. For neither is the sensible body present there—that body is entirely distinct from the nature of the living creature—nor is the bodily sense formed there so as to become vision, nor does the will act there by applying the sense to be formed to a sensible body and holding it there once formed.

Instead of the appearance of the body that was sensed externally, memory succeeds, retaining the appearance that the soul absorbed through the bodily sense. Instead of the vision that existed externally when the sense was formed by the sensible body, a similar inner vision succeeds, when the mind’s gaze is formed from what memory retains and absent bodies are thought of. And just as the will externally applied the sense to be formed to the presented body and joined it once formed, so it turns the gaze of the remembering mind toward memory, so that from what memory has retained the gaze may be formed and there may be [Note: [Col. 0989] Most manuscripts: “and it becomes.”] in thought a similar vision.

Just as reason distinguished the visible appearance by which the bodily sense was formed from its likeness, which arose in the formed sense so that it might be vision—although otherwise the two were so closely joined that they would be thought entirely one and the same—so this phantasy, when the mind thinks of the appearance of a body seen, consists of the likeness of the body retained by memory and of that which is formed from it in the gaze of the remembering mind. Yet it appears so single and undivided that the two elements cannot be found except by the judgment of reason.

By reason we understand that one thing is what remains in memory even when we are thinking of something else, and another is what comes into being when we remember—that is, when we return to memory and find there the same appearance. If it were no longer there, we would say that we had forgotten it so completely that we could not recall it at all.

But if the gaze of the remembering person were not formed from what was in memory, the vision of one thinking would in no way arise. The conjunction of the two—that is, of what memory retains and of what is expressed from it so that the gaze of the remembering person may be formed—makes them appear as one because they are extremely similar.

When the gaze of the thinker turns away from that object, and ceases to look upon what was being seen in memory, none of the form that had been impressed upon that gaze will remain. It will instead be formed from whatever the gaze turns toward again so that another thought may arise. Yet what it left in memory remains; when we remember it again, the gaze turns toward it, is formed, and becomes one with that from which it is formed.

## CHAPTER IV

### 7. How This Unity Arises

The will that carries and brings back the gaze to be formed, and joins it once formed, if it flows entirely into the inner phantasy, turns the gaze of the mind completely away from the presence of the bodies surrounding the senses and from the bodily senses themselves, and turns it wholly toward the image seen within. The likeness of the bodily appearance expressed from memory then affects it so strongly [Note: [Col. 0989] Several manuscripts: “is poured over it.” Others: “is confused.”] that even reason itself is not allowed to distinguish whether the actual body is being seen outside or something of that kind is being thought within.

At times people, either enticed or terrified by excessive thought about visible things, have suddenly uttered sounds as though they were truly engaged in the midst of such actions or undergoing such experiences. I remember hearing from someone that he was accustomed, in thought, to see such a vivid and almost solid image of a woman’s body that, feeling as though he were mingling with it, he even experienced an emission from his genitals.

So great is the power of the soul over its own body, and so great its ability to turn and alter the quality of its bodily covering, according to how a clothed person is affected, when the person is joined to the clothing.

The fact that in dreams we are deceived by images also belongs to this same kind of affection. Yet it makes a great difference whether the mind’s attention, through some necessity, falls upon images that present themselves when the bodily senses are asleep, as in sleepers; when they are disturbed by an inner disorder, as in the insane; or when they are alienated in some other way, as in diviners or prophets, whether these images arise from memory or from some other hidden power through certain spiritual mixtures of spiritual substances; or whether, as sometimes happens to those who are healthy and awake, the will, occupied with thought, turns away from the senses and thus forms the mind’s gaze with various images of sensible things, as though the sensible things themselves were being sensed.

These impressions of images do not arise only when the will is directed toward such things in desire; they also arise when the mind is drawn, for the purpose of avoiding and guarding against something, to look upon what it is fleeing. Thus, not only through desire but also through fear, either the sense is brought to the sensible things themselves, or the mind’s gaze is formed by images of sensible things.

Accordingly, the more intense fear or desire is, the more distinctly the gaze is formed—whether that of one sensing, formed from the body present in the place, or that of one thinking, formed from the image of the body contained in memory.

What a body located somewhere is in relation to bodily sense, the likeness of a body in memory is in relation to the mind’s gaze. What the vision of one looking is in relation to the bodily appearance from which the sense is formed, the vision of one thinking is in relation to the image of the body established in memory, from which the mind’s gaze is formed. And what the attention of the will is in relation to joining the body seen to vision, so that there may be a certain unity of three things although their natures differ, the same attention of the will is in relation to joining the image of the body in memory to the vision of the thinker—that is, to the form received by the mind’s gaze when it returns to memory—so that here too there may be a certain unity of three things, no longer distinguished by a diversity of nature but belonging to one and the same substance, because the whole of it is within and the whole is one mind.

## CHAPTER V

### 8. The Trinity of the Outer Man, or of External Vision, Is Not the Image of God. The Likeness of God Is Sought Even in Sins. In External Vision, the Bodily Form Is as Parent, Vision as Offspring, and the Will Joining Them Suggests the Holy Spirit

Just as, when the form and appearance of the body have perished, the will cannot recall the sense of the viewer to that form, so, when the image carried by memory has been erased by forgetfulness, there will be nothing toward which the will can turn back the mind’s gaze in remembering so as to form it.

But because the mind is powerful, it often fabricates and imagines not only things forgotten but also things neither sensed nor experienced, enlarging, diminishing, changing, and composing at will what has not vanished, so that something appears to be as it either knows it is not or does not know to be so.

In this kind of activity one must beware lest one either lie in order to deceive or suppose in order to be deceived. Once these two evils have been avoided, imagined phantasms do no harm, just as experienced sensible things retained in memory do no harm, provided that things which please are not eagerly desired and things which offend are not shamefully shunned.

But when the will, having abandoned better things, greedily rolls about among these, it becomes unclean. Thus these things are harmful when present and even more harmful when absent but thought of.

One therefore lives badly and deformedly according to the trinity of the outer man, because that trinity—which, although imagined inwardly, nevertheless imagines external things—was produced for the sake of using sensible and bodily things. No one could use these things even well unless the images of things sensed were retained in memory. And unless the greater part of the will dwells among higher and inner things, and unless whatever part of the will is applied either to bodies externally or to their images internally refers whatever it grasps in them to a better and truer life and rests in the end with a view to which it judges these things ought to be done, what else are we doing but what the Apostle forbids us to do when he says, “Do not be conformed to this age” (Rom. XII, 2)?

Therefore this trinity is not the image of God. It arises in the soul through the bodily sense from the lowest creature, namely, the bodily creature, which is inferior to the soul. Yet it is not entirely unlike God. For what does not possess some likeness of God according to its own kind and measure, since God made all things very good (Eccli. XXXIX, 21), for no other reason than that he himself is supremely good?

Whatever exists is good to the extent that it exists; to that extent, although at a great distance, it nevertheless has some likeness of the supreme Good. If the likeness is natural, it is right and ordered; but if it is vicious, it is shameful and perverse.

For even in their very sins souls pursue nothing but a certain likeness of God—an arrogant and disordered likeness and, so to speak, a servile freedom. Thus sin could not have been persuaded upon our first parents unless it had been said, “You will be like gods” (Gen. III, 5).

Yet not everything in creatures that is in some way like God should also be called his image. Only that creature in which he alone is superior should be called his image. For that image is wholly expressed from him, and between it and him no intervening nature exists.

### 9.

Of that vision, then—that is, of the form produced in the sense of the viewer—the bodily form from which it arises is as a kind of parent. But that parent is not a true parent; hence this is not a true offspring either. For vision is not generated from it alone, since something else is applied to the body so that vision may be formed from it, namely, the sense of the viewer.

Consequently, to love that body is to become estranged. [Note: [Col. 0991] Book II of the Retractions, chapter 15.]

The will, therefore, which joins the two as a kind of parent and a kind of offspring, is more spiritual than either of them. For that body which is seen is not spiritual at all. The vision produced in the sense contains something spiritual, because it cannot arise without the soul. Yet it is not wholly spiritual, since what is formed is the bodily sense.

The will, therefore, which joins the two is recognized as more spiritual, as I have said, and for this reason begins to suggest the person of the Holy Spirit in that trinity. Yet it belongs more to the formed sense than to the body from which the sense is formed. The sense of the living creature and the will belong to the soul, not to the stone or to any body that is seen.

The will therefore does not proceed from that body as from a parent, nor from the sense as from an offspring—that is, from the vision and form existing in the sense. For before vision arose, the will already existed and had applied the sense to be formed to the body in order to see it; but it was not yet pleased.

For how could it have been pleased by what had not yet been seen? Pleasure is a tranquil will. Therefore we cannot call the will the offspring of vision, since it existed before vision; nor can we call it the parent, since it was formed and expressed not from the will but from the body seen.

## CHAPTER VI

### 10. How the Will’s Rest and End in Vision Should Be Understood

Perhaps we may rightly call vision the end and rest of the will, but only with respect to this one thing. [Note: [Col. 0992] The printed editions add: “namely, the body to be seen.”] For the will does not thereby cease to desire anything else merely because it sees something that it wanted to see.

It is therefore not the whole will of a human being—whose end is nothing other than blessedness—but, for the time being, the will to see has no end except vision, whether it refers that vision to something else or does not refer it to anything else. For if it does not refer vision to something else but wanted only to see, there is no need to discuss how it can be shown that vision is the end of the will; this is evident.

If, however, it refers vision to something else, then it certainly wills that other thing, and it will no longer be the will to see—or, if it is the will to see, it is not the will to see this particular thing.

It is like someone who wants to see a scar in order thereby to establish that there had been a wound, or who wants to see a window in order through the window to see passersby. All such wills, and others like them, have their own proper ends. These ends are referred to the end of that will by which we wish to live happily and attain a life that is not referred to anything else but is sufficient in itself to the one who loves it.

The will to see therefore has vision as its end; and the will to see this thing has the vision of this thing as its end. Thus the will to see a scar seeks its own end, namely, the vision of the scar, and extends no farther. For the will to prove that there had been a wound is another will, although it is linked to the former; and its end is likewise the proof of the wound.

The will to see a window has the vision of the window as its end. For the will that is linked to this one—the will to see passersby through the window—is another will, and its end is the vision of the passersby.

These wills are rightly ordered, and all are linked to one another, if the will to which they are all referred is good. If it is perverse, they are all perverse.

The connection of rightly ordered wills is therefore a kind of road by which those ascending to blessedness proceed, as if by definite steps. But the entanglement of perverse and distorted wills is a chain by which the one who acts in this way will be bound, so as to be cast into the outer darkness (Matt. XXII, 13).

Blessed, then, are those who in their deeds and conduct sing the Song of Ascents; and woe to those who drag iniquity like a long rope (Isa. V, 18).

Such is the rest of the will that we call its end if it is still referred to something else: it is like the rest of a foot in walking, when it is placed where another foot may lean and by which one proceeds step by step. [Note: [Col. 0992] In the manuscripts: “by which one proceeds with steps.”]

But if something pleases in such a way that the will rests in it with some delight, it is nevertheless not yet that toward which one is advancing. It too is referred to something else, so that it is reckoned not as a citizen’s homeland but as a traveler’s refreshment or even stopping-place.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0993]

### 11. Another Trinity in the Memory of One Recalling a Vision

There is now another trinity, indeed an interior one, than that which exists in sensible things and the senses, yet one conceived from it. Here the mind’s gaze is formed not from the body by the bodily sense but from memory, once the appearance of the body sensed externally has taken hold in memory.

We call the appearance in memory a kind of parent of the appearance produced in the phantasy of one thinking. For it was in memory before we thought of it, just as the body was in its place before it was sensed and vision arose.

But when it is thought of, the appearance is expressed in the gaze of the thinker from what memory retains, and by remembering the appearance is formed that is, as it were, the offspring of the appearance retained by memory.

Yet neither is a true parent nor is the other a true offspring. For the mind’s gaze, which is formed from memory when we recall and think of something, does not proceed from the appearance of the thing we remember having seen. [Note: [Col. 0993] Louvain: “of it.” But the other editions and the manuscripts read “of them,” that is, of both the body seen and the appearance committed to memory.] We could not remember those things unless we had seen them; but the mind’s gaze that is formed in remembering existed even before we saw the body that we remember—and how much more before we committed it to memory?

Although, therefore, the form produced in the gaze of the remembering person arises from that which exists in memory, the gaze itself does not originate from it; it existed before this form. [Note: [Col. 0993] Some manuscripts: “before these things.”]

It follows that, if the one is not a true parent, the other is not a true offspring either. Nevertheless, the one as a kind of parent and the other as a kind of offspring suggest something by which interior and more genuine realities may be seen with greater practice and certainty.

### 12.

It is now more difficult to discern whether the will that joins vision to memory is not the parent or offspring of one of them. The difficulty of this distinction is caused by their similarity and equality of nature and substance.

For just as externally the formed sense could easily be distinguished from the sensible body, and the will from both, because of the diversity of nature belonging to all three—about which we have discussed sufficiently above—so it cannot be distinguished here.

Although the trinity now under investigation was brought into the mind from outside, it is nevertheless active within, and none of it exists apart from the nature of the mind itself. How, then, can it be shown that the will is neither the parent nor the offspring of either the bodily likeness contained in memory or the likeness expressed from it when we remember, when it joins the two in thought so that they appear as one single thing and cannot be distinguished except by reason?

The first point to be seen is that there can be no will to remember unless we retain in the inner recesses of memory either the whole thing we wish to remember or some part of it. For what we have forgotten entirely and in every respect does not give rise even to a will to remember; for whatever we wish to recall, we have already recalled as being or having been in our memory.

For example, if I want to remember what I had for dinner yesterday, I have either already remembered that I dined, or, if I have not yet remembered even that, I have certainly remembered something concerning the time itself—if nothing else, at least yesterday, and that part of yesterday in which people usually dine, and what it means to dine. For if I had remembered nothing of this kind, I could not want to remember what I had for dinner yesterday.

From this it can be understood that the will to remember proceeds from those things contained in memory, together with those things that are expressed from them by seeing through recollection—that is, from the conjunction of some thing we have remembered and the vision produced from it in the gaze of the thinker when we remembered.

But the will itself, which joins the two, also requires something else that is, as it were, near and contiguous to the person remembering.

There are therefore as many trinities of this kind as there are acts of remembering, since none exists in which these three things are not present: what is stored in memory even before it is thought of; what arises in thought when it is seen; and the will joining the two and, from the two together with itself as the third, completing one thing.

Or should we rather understand one trinity of this kind in such a way that we call one general thing whatever bodily appearances lie hidden in memory, and another general vision of the mind recalling and thinking of such things? To the conjunction of these two, the will that joins them is added as a third, so that the whole is one thing composed of three?

## CHAPTER VIII

### Various Modes of Thinking

Since the mind’s gaze cannot contemplate all that memory holds in a single view at the same time, trinities of thoughts alternate [Note: [Col. 0994] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “alternates.”], yielding and succeeding one another; thus this trinity becomes innumerably numerous. Yet it is not infinite, provided that the number of things stored in memory is not exceeded.

From the time each person began to sense bodies by any bodily sense, even if the things forgotten could be added, the number would certainly be fixed and determinate, though beyond counting. For we call things “innumerable” not only when they are infinite but also when they are so finite that they exceed the capacity of the one counting them.

### 13.

From this point it can be observed somewhat more clearly that what memory stores is one thing and what is expressed from it in the thought of the remembering person is another, although, when the two are joined, they appear to be one and the same.

For we cannot remember the appearances of bodies except in the number in which we sensed them, to the extent that we sensed them, and as we sensed them. The mind absorbs them into memory from the bodily sense. [Note: [Col. 0994] Some manuscripts: “into memory.”]

The visions of those who think [Note: [Col. 0994] According to one edition: “the visions of thoughts.”] do indeed arise from the things in memory, but they are multiplied and varied innumerably and altogether without limit.

I remember one sun because I saw one, just as it is. But if I wish, I think of two, or three, or as many as I wish; and the gaze of one thinking of many is formed from the same memory by which I remember one.

I remember only as much as I saw. For if I remember it as larger or smaller than I saw it, then I do not remember what I saw—and therefore I do not remember it at all. But because I do remember it, I remember it only as much as I saw it. Nevertheless, by my will I think of it as larger or smaller. I remember it as I saw it, but I think of it as running wherever I wish, standing where I wish, and coming from wherever and going wherever I wish.

It is also readily possible for me to think of something square when I remember something round, and of any color, even though I have never seen a green sun and therefore do not remember one. The same applies to the sun and to other things.

But because these forms of things are bodily and sensible, the mind errs when it supposes that they exist externally in the manner in which it thinks of them internally; or when, although they have already perished externally, they are still retained in memory; or when what we remember is formed otherwise, not through the fidelity of remembering but through the variety of thinking.

14. Although we very often believe even those who report truths that they themselves have perceived through their senses. When we think about these things at the very moment they are being recounted to us, the mind’s attention does not seem to be turned back toward memory so that visions of the thinking mind may be formed. For we do not think about them as we recall them, but as another person recounts them. Nor does that trinity seem to be completed here which arises when the form lying hidden in memory and the vision of the person remembering are joined by a third element, the will. For when something is recounted to me, I do not think about what was hidden in my memory, but about what I hear. I am not referring to the speaker’s actual words, lest anyone think that I have entered into that trinity which takes place externally, among sensible things and the senses; rather, I think about the forms of bodies which the narrator signifies by words and sounds. I think about these not by remembering them, but by hearing them.

Yet if we consider the matter more carefully, even then the limits of memory are not exceeded. For I could not understand the narrator if, although I were hearing for the first time the things he says and their connected sequence, I did not nevertheless remember each of them in a general way. For example, someone who tells me about a certain mountain stripped of forest and clothed with olive trees tells this to one who remembers the forms both of mountains and of forests and of olive trees. If I had forgotten these, I would have no idea at all what he was saying, and therefore could not think about his narration. Thus it comes about that everyone who thinks about bodily things—whether he himself invents something, or hears or reads someone recounting past events or foretelling future ones—returns to his own memory, and there finds the mode and measure of all the forms which he beholds while thinking.

For no one can think at all of a color he has never seen, or of a bodily shape, or of a sound he has never heard, or of a taste he has never tasted, or of a smell he has never smelled, or of any bodily contact he has never experienced. But if no one thinks about something bodily except what he has sensed because no one remembers anything bodily except what he has sensed, then just as the mode of sensing is found in bodies, so the mode of thinking is found in memory. For the sense receives a form from the body which we sense; memory receives it from the sense; and the mind’s thinking attention receives it from memory.

15. Moreover, just as the will joins the sense to the body, so it joins memory to the sense, and the thinking attention to memory. Yet that which brings these together and unites them also separates and sunders them: namely, the will.

The will separates the bodily senses from bodies to be sensed by means of bodily movement, so that we do not sense something or cease to sense it—for example, when we turn our eyes away from something we do not wish to see, or close them. In the same way we turn our ears away from sounds and our nostrils from smells. Likewise, by closing the mouth or spitting something out of it, we turn away from tastes. In the case of touch also, we either withdraw the body so that we do not touch what we do not wish to touch, or, if we were already touching it, cast it away or push it back. Thus by bodily movement the will acts so that the bodily sense is not joined to sensible things. It does this as far as it can; for when, because of the condition of our servile mortality, it encounters difficulty in this action, suffering follows, so that nothing remains to the will except endurance.

The will turns memory away from the sense when, being intent on something else, it does not allow memory to remain attached to what is present. This is easy to notice when, although someone is often speaking to us in our presence, we seem not to have heard him because we were thinking about something else. That is false: we did hear him, but we do not remember, since the words slipped through the sense of hearing while the will’s attention was turned elsewhere, even though it is ordinarily through that attention that things are fixed in memory. It would therefore be more accurate to say, when something of this kind happens, “We do not remember,” than, “We did not hear.”

The same thing happens to readers—and it happens to me very often—when, after reading through a page or letter, I do not know what I have read and read it again. For when the will’s attention is directed to something else, memory has not been applied to the bodily sense in the way that the sense itself was applied to the letters. Likewise, people walking with their attention fixed on something else do not know where they have passed. Yet if they had not seen the places, they would not have walked, or would have walked by feeling their way with greater attention, especially if they were proceeding through unfamiliar regions. But because they walked easily, they certainly saw; and because memory was not joined to the sense itself in the way that the sense of sight was joined to the places through which they were proceeding, they could in no way remember what they had seen, even though it had just occurred. Furthermore, to wish to turn the mind’s attention away from what is in memory is nothing other than not thinking about it.

## CHAPTER IX

16. One form is generated in turn from another.
