In this arrangement, then, when we begin with the form of the body and proceed all the way to the form produced in the thinking person’s act of contemplation, four forms are found, as it were, born successively, one from another: the second from the first, the third from the second, and the fourth from the third.

From the form of the body that is seen arises the form produced in the sense of the person seeing; from this arises the form produced in memory; and from this arises the form produced in the thinking mind’s attention. Accordingly, the will joins what is, as it were, parent to offspring three times: first, the form of the body to the form which it generates in the bodily sense; then that form again to the form which arises from it in memory; and third, that form also to the form which is born from it in the thinking person’s act of contemplation.

But the middle joining, which is the second, although it is nearer, is not as similar to the first as the third is [Note: [Col. 0996] Many manuscripts read “the third” (tertiae). M.] For there are two visions: one belonging to the person sensing, the other belonging to the person thinking. In order that a thinking person’s vision may exist, something similar to the vision of the person sensing is produced in memory; this enables the mind’s attention to turn itself in thinking just as the eyes’ attention turns itself toward the body in seeing.

For this reason I wished to emphasize two trinities in this category: one, when the vision of the person sensing is formed from the body; the other, when the vision of the person thinking is formed from memory. I did not wish to emphasize the middle one, because when the form produced in the sense of the person seeing is entrusted to memory, it is not usually called a vision. Yet everywhere the will appears only as the element that joins what is, as it were, parent and offspring. And therefore, whatever its point of origin, it can be called neither parent nor offspring.

## CHAPTER X

17. Imagination adds what we have seen elsewhere even to things not seen. But if we remember only what we have sensed, and think only what we remember, why do we so often think falsely, when we certainly do not falsely remember the things we have sensed? Is it not because the will—which, as far as I have been able, I have already taken pains to show to be the joiner and separator of such things—leads the thinking mind’s attention through the hidden recesses of memory as it pleases, and urges it to take, from among the things we remember, one element from here and another from there, in order to think about things we do not remember? These elements, coming together in a single vision, produce something that is called false either because it does not exist externally in the nature of bodily things, or because it does not seem to have been drawn from memory, since we remember having sensed nothing of the kind.

For who has seen a black swan? Hence no one remembers one. Yet who cannot think of one? It is easy to cover with black the form which we have come to know by seeing, a color which we have likewise seen in other bodies; and because we have sensed both, we remember both. Nor do I remember a four-footed bird, because I have not seen one; yet I can very easily behold such an image by attaching two additional feet, of the same kind that I have also seen, to some flying form like one that I have seen (Retractations, book 2, chapter 15, section 2).

Accordingly, when we think of things joined together which we remember sensing individually, we seem not to be thinking about what we remember, although we are doing precisely that under the guidance of memory, from which we take everything that we combine in multiple and varied ways according to our will.

For we do not think even of the very magnitudes of bodies which we have never seen without the assistance of memory. The amount of space which our sight usually occupies by reason of the world’s magnitude is the measure by which we extend any bodily masses when we think of them as immense. Reason indeed proceeds toward greater things, but imagination does not follow. For reason even declares the infinity of number, which no vision of a person thinking about bodily things can grasp.

The same reason teaches that even the tiniest bodies can be divided infinitely. Yet when we have reached those subtleties or minute dimensions which we remember seeing, we can no longer behold imaginations more slender and smaller than these, although reason does not cease to pursue and divide them. Thus we think of no bodily things except either those which we remember or things formed from those which we remember.

## CHAPTER XI

8. Number, weight, and measure. But because things impressed individually upon memory can be thought of in numerical multiplicity, measure seems to belong to memory, and number to vision. For although the multiplicity of such visions is innumerable, an insurmountable limit has nevertheless been prescribed for each one in memory.

Thus measure appears in memory and number in visions. Just as in visible bodies there is a certain measure to which the sense of those who see is adapted in countless numerical ways [Note: [Col. 0998] Most manuscripts read “the sense of seeing” (sensus videndi).], and from one visible object the sight of many observers is formed—so that even one person, because of the number of his two eyes, often sees one thing with a doubled appearance, as we explained above—in the things from which visions are expressed there is therefore a certain measure, while in the visions themselves there is number.

The will, however, which joins and orders these things and unites them by a kind of unity, and which places the desire for sensing or thinking nowhere except in the things from which visions are formed, resembles weight. Therefore, for the moment, I will briefly note that these three—measure, number, and weight—are also to be observed in all other things.

For the present, I have shown, as best I could and by whatever means I could, that the will, which joins the visible thing and the vision as parent and offspring, whether in sensing or in thinking, can be called neither parent nor offspring. Hence the time has come to seek this same trinity in the inner human being, and to turn inward from that animal and carnal being of whom I have spoken for so long, who is called the exterior human being.

There we hope to be able to find the image of God according to the Trinity, with our efforts aided by the very one whom, as the things themselves indicate, Holy Scripture also testifies to have ordered all things in measure, number, and weight (Wisdom 11:21).

# BOOK TWELVE

In this book, after distinguishing wisdom from knowledge, a certain trinity of its own kind is first demonstrated in what is properly called knowledge, and what is inferior. Although this trinity already belongs to the inner human being, it is not yet to be called or considered the image of God.

[Col. 0997]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0997]

1. The character of the exterior and interior human being. Come, then, let us see where there is, as it were, a boundary between the exterior and interior human being. Whatever we possess in the mind in common with animals is still rightly said to belong to the exterior human being.

For the exterior human being is not to be understood as the body alone, but also as the life attached to it, by which the bodily structure and all the senses with which it has been equipped for sensing external things are active. When the images of these senses, fixed in memory, are revisited through recollection, the activity still belongs to the exterior human being.

In all these respects we differ from animals only in that our bodily form is not bent forward but upright. In this we are admonished by the one who made us not to be like animals in the better part of ourselves—that is, in the mind—from which we differ by the uprightness of our bodies.

This does not mean that we should cast the mind toward those things which are exalted among bodies; for even to desire the repose of the will in such things is to cast down the mind. But just as the body is naturally upright toward those things which are lofty among bodies, that is, toward heavenly things, so the mind, which is a spiritual substance, must be raised toward those things which are lofty among spiritual realities—not through the exaltation of pride, but through the devotion of righteousness.

## CHAPTER II

2. Among living creatures, only the human being perceives eternal principles in bodily things. Animals can sense bodily things externally through their bodily senses, recall them when fixed in memory, desire what is useful in them, and avoid what is harmful. But to note these things, and to retain them in memory not merely because they are naturally seized upon but because they have been deliberately entrusted to memory; to impress them again through remembering and thinking when they are already slipping into oblivion; so that, just as thought is formed from what memory holds, what is in memory itself may also be strengthened by thought; and likewise to compose fictitious visions by taking various remembered things from here and there and, as it were, sewing them together; to inspect how, in this class of things, the plausible may be distinguished from the true—not in spiritual matters, but in bodily ones themselves: although these and similar activities take place and move among sensible things and among those which the mind has drawn from them through bodily sensation, they are nevertheless not without reason, nor are they common to human beings and animals.

But it belongs to a higher reason to judge bodily things according to incorporeal and eternal principles. Unless these principles were above the human mind, they would certainly not be unchangeable; and unless something of ours were joined to them, we could not judge bodily things according to them [Note: [Col. 0999] The printed editions read “in these” (in his). Most manuscripts omit “in.”]

We do judge bodily things according to the rational principles of dimensions and shapes, which the mind knows to remain unchangeably constant.

## CHAPTER III

3. The higher reason, which belongs to contemplation, and the inner reason, which belongs to action, in one mind. But that part of ours which is occupied with handling bodily and temporal matters in such a way that it is not shared by us with animals is indeed rational; yet from that rational substance of our mind by which we cling to intelligible and unchangeable truth, it has been, as it were, drawn off and assigned to the handling and governing of lower things.

For just as among all the animals a helper comparable to the man was not found until what had been taken from him was formed into a woman for marriage, so for our mind, by which we consult the higher and inner truth, there is no comparable help for the use of bodily things, insofar as human nature requires it, from those parts of the soul which we share with animals.

And therefore one rational element of ours, not separated by a divorce from unity but, as it were, diverted to assist in their fellowship, is distributed among the duties of its own work [Note: [Col. 0999] Nearly all manuscripts read “in its work” (officio). Some read “duties” (officia).]

And just as the two, male and female, are one flesh, so our understanding and action, or counsel and execution, or reason and rational appetite—or whatever more meaningfully they may be called—are embraced by one nature of the mind. Thus, just as it was said of the former, “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), so it may be said of the latter, “Two in one mind.”

## CHAPTER IV

4. The Trinity and the image of God exist only in that part of the mind which belongs to the contemplation of eternal things. When, therefore, we discuss the nature of the human mind, we are discussing one particular thing, and we divide it into the two aspects mentioned only according to their functions.

Accordingly, when we seek the Trinity in it, we seek it in the whole mind. We do not separate rational action in temporal matters from contemplation of eternal things in order to seek some third element by which the Trinity might be completed.

Rather, the Trinity must be found throughout the nature of the mind in such a way that, even if temporal action were absent—an activity requiring assistance and on account of which some part of the mind is diverted to administer lower things—the Trinity would still be found in the one, nowhere divided mind. Once this division has been made, however, not only the Trinity but also the image of God is found solely in that which belongs to the contemplation of eternal things. In that which has been diverted to action in temporal matters, the Trinity may perhaps be found, but the image of God cannot.

## CHAPTER V

5. An opinion that imagines the image of the Trinity in the union of male and female and their offspring. Accordingly, those do not seem to me to offer a probable opinion who think that the Trinity of the image of God, insofar as it concerns human nature, can be found in such a way that it is completed in the union of male and female and in their offspring.

On this view, the man himself would, as it were, signify the person of the Father; the Son would be that which proceeded from him in order to be born; and they say that the woman is the third person, like the Spirit, since she proceeded from the man in such a way that she was not herself his son or daughter (Genesis 2:22), although offspring was born when she conceived.

For the Lord said of the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the Father (John 15:26), and yet he is not the Son. In the error of this opinion, the only point that can plausibly be advanced is that, in the origin of the woman’s creation, the authority of Holy Scripture sufficiently shows that not everything which proceeds from a person in such a way as to constitute another person can be called a son. For the woman’s person proceeded from the man’s person, yet she was not called his daughter.

The rest, however, is so absurd—indeed, so false—that it is very easily refuted. I set aside how objectionable it is to think of the Holy Spirit as the mother of the Son of God and the spouse of the Father. Perhaps someone might answer that such things are offensive in bodily contexts, when bodily conception and childbirth are being imagined.

Yet even these matters are imagined in the most chaste way by those to whom all things are clean; but to the unclean and unbelieving, whose mind and conscience are polluted, nothing is clean (Titus 1:15), so that some of them are even offended by Christ’s birth from a virgin according to the flesh.

Nevertheless, in those highest spiritual realities, where there is nothing violable or corruptible, nothing born in time and nothing formed from what was formless, if such things are said—things in whose likeness even the forms of this lower creation, though made at an immeasurably remote distance, have been fashioned—they should not disturb anyone’s sober judgment. Let no one, while avoiding a vain horror, fall into a destructive error.

One should become accustomed to finding traces of spiritual realities in bodily things, so that when reason begins to lead one upward from them toward the highest things, until one reaches the unchangeable truth through which these things were made, one does not drag along to the heights what one despises in the lowest things.

For someone was not ashamed to choose Wisdom as his wife because the name “wife,” when one is thinking of the begetting of offspring, introduces the idea of corruptible intercourse. Nor indeed is Wisdom herself female in sex [Note: [Col. 1001] The printed editions read “feminine” (feminea).], because she is expressed by a noun of feminine gender in both Greek and Latin.

## CHAPTER VI

6. Why that opinion must be rejected. We do not reject this opinion, then, because we are afraid to think of holy, inviolable, and unchangeable love as the spouse of God the Father, existing from him but not in the manner of offspring for the generation of the Word through whom all things were made. We reject it because divine Scripture clearly shows it to be false.

For God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”; shortly afterward it is said, “And God made man in the image of God” (Genesis 1:26–27). “Our” certainly would not rightly be said, since it is plural, if man were made in the image of one person, whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. But because he was made in the image of the Trinity, it was therefore said, “in our image.”

Again, so that we would not suppose three gods to be believed in the Trinity, since the same Trinity is one God, Scripture says, “And God made man in the image of God,” as though it had said, “in his own image.”

7. Such expressions are common in those Scriptures, although some who defend the Catholic faith do not pay close attention to them and therefore think that “God made man in the image of God” means something like “the Father made him in the image of the Son.” They wish to assert that the Son is also called God in the sacred Scriptures, as though there were not other documents that are entirely true and unmistakable, in which the Son is called not merely God but true God.

In this testimony, while they intend to resolve one difficulty, they entangle themselves so that they cannot extricate themselves. For if the Father made man in the image of the Son, so that man is not the image of the Father but of the Son, then the Son is unlike the Father. But if pious faith teaches—and it does teach—that the Son is like the Father in equality of essence, then what was made in the likeness of the Son must necessarily also have been made in the likeness of the Father.

Furthermore, if the Father made man not in his own image but in the image of the Son, why did he not say, “Let us make man in your image and likeness,” but instead say, “in our image,” unless it is because the image of the Trinity was being made in man, so that in this way man would be the image of the one true God, since the Trinity itself is the one true God?

There are countless such expressions in Scripture, but it will be sufficient to have cited these. In the Psalms it is said, “The Lord’s is salvation, and your blessing is upon your people” (Psalm 3:9), as though it had been said to someone other than the one of whom he had said, “The Lord’s is salvation.”

Again, “From you,” he says, “I shall be delivered from temptation, and hoping in my God I shall leap over a wall” (Psalm 17:30) [Note: [Col. 1002] Several manuscripts omit “hoping” (sperans).], as though he had said to someone else, “From you I shall be delivered from temptation.”

Again, “The peoples shall fall beneath you in the heart of the king’s enemies” (Psalm 44:6) [Note: [Col. 1002] The printed editions read “in the hearts” (in corda). The manuscripts read “in the heart” (in corde), as does Augustine in his exposition of the same Psalm 44.], as though he had said, “in the heart of your enemies.” For he had said to that king—that is, to our Lord Jesus Christ—“The peoples shall fall beneath you.” He intended him to be understood as the king when he said, “in the heart of the king’s enemies.”

Such expressions are found less often in the writings of the New Testament. Nevertheless, in the Epistle to the Romans the Apostle says, “concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 1:3–4), as though he were speaking above of someone else.

For what is “the Son of God predestined by the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ” except the same Jesus Christ who was predestined to be the Son of God in power? Therefore, when we hear here “the Son of God in the power of Jesus Christ,” or “the Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification of Jesus Christ,” or “the Son of God by the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ,” although it could have been expressed in the usual manner, “in his power,” or “according to his Spirit of sanctification,” or “by his resurrection from the dead,” or “by the resurrection of his dead,” we are not compelled to understand another person, but one and the same person, namely, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus, when we hear, “God made man in the image of God,” although it could have been expressed more customarily as “in his own image,” we are not compelled to understand another person in the Trinity, but the one and same Trinity, which is one God and in whose image man was made.

8. Since this is so, if we understand the same image of the Trinity to exist not in one person but in three human beings—the father, mother, and son—then man was not made in the image of God before he had a wife and before they produced a son, because the Trinity did not yet exist.

Does someone say, “There was already a trinity, because although they did not yet have their proper form, the woman was already in the man’s side by original nature, and the son was already in the father’s loins”? Why, then, when Scripture had said, “God made man in the image of God,” did it continue, saying, “God made him; male and female he made them, and he blessed them” (Genesis 1:27–28)?

Or, if the passage is to be distinguished in this way—“And God made man,” followed by “he made him in the image of God,” and then, as a third clause, “male and female he made them”—why did some fear to say, “He made him male and female,” lest something monstrous should be understood, such as those whom they call hermaphrodites? Even in that form, however, it could be understood without falsehood that both were included in the singular number, because of what was said, “The two shall be one flesh.”

Why, then, as I had begun to say, when Scripture speaks of human nature made in the image of God, does it mention only male and female and not the son? To complete the image of the Trinity, it ought to have added the son, even though he was still present in the father’s loins, just as the woman was in his side.

Or perhaps the woman had already been made, and Scripture had compressed into a brief account what it would later explain more carefully; and for that reason the son could not be mentioned, because he had not yet been born? As though the Holy Spirit could not also have included this in that brief account, intending to narrate the son’s birth later in its proper place, just as he later narrated the woman’s being taken from the man’s side in its proper place (Genesis 2:24, 22), and yet did not omit naming her here.

## CHAPTER VII

9. How man is the image of God. Whether the woman too is the image of God. How the Apostle’s statement that the man is the image of God, while the woman is the glory of the man, is to be understood figuratively and mystically. We must not therefore understand man’s being made in the image of the highest Trinity—that is, in the image of God—in such a way that the same image is understood to exist in three human beings, especially since the Apostle says that the man is the image of God and for that reason removes the covering from his head, while he instructs the woman to wear one. He speaks as follows: “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God. But the woman is the glory of the man” (1 Corinthians 11:7).

What, then, shall we say to this? If the woman, in her own person, completes the image of the Trinity, why, after she was taken from the man’s side, is he still called the image? Or if even one human person out of three can be called the image of God, just as in the highest Trinity each person is God, why is the woman not also the image of God? For it is precisely for this reason that she is commanded to cover her head: because he, being the image of God, is forbidden to do so (1 Corinthians 11:7, 5).

10. But we must see how the Apostle’s statement—that it is not the woman but the man who is the image of God—does not contradict what is written in Genesis: “God made man; he made him in the image of God; male and female he made them, and he blessed them.”

For he says that human nature itself was made in the image of God, and this nature is completed in both sexes; he does not separate the female from the image of God. After saying that God made man in the image of God, he says, “He made him male and female,” or, according to another division, “male and female he made them.”

How, then, have we heard through the Apostle that the man is the image of God, for which reason he is forbidden to cover his head, while the woman is not, and is therefore commanded to do so? Unless, I believe, it is what I have already said when discussing the nature of the human mind: that the woman with her husband is the image of God, so that the whole of that substance is one image. But when it is distributed for the purpose of assistance, that which pertains to the woman alone is not the image of God, whereas that which pertains to the man alone is the image of God, as fully and completely as when the woman is joined to him as one.

We said the same regarding the nature of the human mind: when the whole mind contemplates truth, it is the image of God; and when something is distributed from it and diverted by a certain act of attention toward the performance of temporal affairs, it is nevertheless the image of God insofar as it contemplates and consults the truth, but insofar as it is directed toward carrying out lower activities, it is not the image of God.

And because the more it extends itself toward what is eternal, the more it is formed according to the image of God, it must not therefore be restrained so that it withdraws and limits itself from that; hence the man ought not to cover his head.

But because excessive advance into lower things is dangerous for that rational activity which is occupied with bodily and temporal matters, it must have authority over the head, which is indicated by the covering, signifying that this activity is to be restrained. For this is a pleasing, sacred, and pious sign to the holy angels. God does not see in time, nor does anything new occur in his vision and knowledge when something happens temporally and transiently, as bodily senses—whether of animals and human beings or even of heavenly angels—are affected by such events.

11. That the Apostle Paul signified a mystery of some more hidden matter in this manifest distinction of male and female can also be understood from the following. In another passage he says that a true widow is desolate, without children and grandchildren, and yet ought to hope in the Lord and persist in prayers night and day (1 Timothy 5:5). Here, however, he indicates that the woman who was deceived and brought into transgression will be saved through the bearing of children; and he adds, “if they continue in faith, love, and sanctification with sobriety” (ibid. 2:15).

As though it could harm a good widow if she had no children, or if those she had did not wish to continue in good works. But because the works that are called good are like the children of our life, according to which it is asked what kind of life each person has—that is, how he conducts these temporal affairs, a life which the Greeks call not ζωήν (*zōēn*) but βίον (*bion*)—and because these good works are especially practiced in duties of mercy; while works of mercy are of no benefit either to pagans, or to Jews who do not believe in Christ, or to any heretics or schismatics among whom faith, love, and sober sanctification are not found—it is clear what the Apostle intended to signify.

He intended it figuratively and mystically because he was speaking about the woman’s head being covered; unless this is referred to some secret sacramental meaning, it will remain pointless.

12. For, as not only the most truthful reason but also the authority of the Apostle himself makes clear, man was made in the image of God not according to the form of the body but according to the rational mind. It is shamefully empty thinking to suppose that God is bounded and confined by the outlines of bodily limbs.

Moreover, does not the same blessed Apostle say, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God” (Ephesians 4:23–24)? And elsewhere, more explicitly: “Having put off the old man with his deeds, put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” (Colossians 3:9–10).

If, then, we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and the new man is the one who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, no one doubts that man was made in the image of the one who created him not according to the body, nor according to any other part of the soul, but according to the rational mind, where the knowledge of God can exist.

Through this renewal we also become children of God through the baptism of Christ; and by putting on the new man, we put on Christ through faith. Who, then, would exclude women from this fellowship, since they are fellow heirs with us of grace, and since the same Apostle says elsewhere, “For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:26–28)?

Have faithful women, then, lost the sex of their bodies? Rather, because they are renewed there according to the image of God where no sex exists, man was made in the image of God there where no sex exists—that is, in the spirit of his mind.

Why, then, ought the man not to cover his head because he is the image and glory of God, while the woman ought to do so because she is the glory of the man? Is it because the woman is not also renewed in the spirit of her mind, which is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created it?

But because she differs from the man in bodily sex, that part of reason which is diverted toward governing temporal matters could rightly be represented by her bodily covering, so that the image of God remains only in that part by which the human mind clings to the contemplation or consultation of eternal principles [Note: [Col. 1005] The edition of Louvain reads “has adhered” (adhaeserit).], and it is clear that women possess this part no less than men.

## CHAPTER VIII

13. Deflection from the image of God. Thus the common nature is recognized in their minds, while in their bodies the distribution of the one mind itself is represented.

As certain steps of reflection ascend inward through the parts of the soul, from the point at which something begins to appear that we do not share with beasts, reason begins there, and the interior human being can now be recognized.

But even this interior human being, if through that reason to which the administration of temporal matters has been delegated it advances without measure and slips too far into external things, with its own head consenting—that is, with that portion which presides in the mirror of counsel, as it were the masculine part, failing to restrain and check it—it grows old among its enemies (Psalm 6:8), the demons who envy virtue together with their prince, the devil.

Then the vision of eternal things is withdrawn from the head itself when, together with his spouse, it eats what was forbidden, so that “the light of his eyes is not with him” (Psalm 37:11). Thus both, stripped of that illumination of truth and with the eyes of conscience opened to see how dishonorable and indecent they have remained, weave together good words without the fruit of good works, like leaves of sweet fruits but without the fruits themselves; and, while living badly, they conceal their ugliness as though by speaking well (Genesis 3).

## CHAPTER IX
14. The same subject continued. For the soul, loving its own power, slips away from the common whole into a private part; and that apostate pride—which is called the beginning of sin (Ecclus. 10:15)—although, by following God as ruler within the universe of creation, it could have been governed most rightly by his laws, desires something beyond the universe and attempts to govern it by its own law. Since nothing is greater than the universe, it is thrust into a partial concern, and thus, by desiring something greater, is diminished. Hence avarice is also called the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10). Everything in which it attempts to act privately against the laws by which the universe is administered, it carries out through its own body, which it possesses as a part. And so, delighting in bodily forms and movements, because it does not possess them inwardly with itself, it becomes entangled with the images of them that it has fixed in memory and is shamefully polluted by a phantasmal fornication. It refers all its activities to those ends by which it eagerly seeks bodily and temporal things through the bodily senses; or, in swollen arrogance, it strives to be superior to other souls devoted to bodily senses; or it plunges into the muddy whirlpool of carnal pleasure.

## CHAPTER X

15. The steps toward the most shameful things. When, therefore, with a good will one provides either for oneself or for others in the apprehension of inward and higher things—which are possessed, not privately, but in common by all who love such things, in a chaste embrace without constraint or envy—and if one is deceived in some matter through ignorance of temporal things, because one is also acting temporally and does not maintain the manner of acting that one ought, this is human temptation. It is a great thing to live this life in such a way—which, as we return, we tread as a road—that temptation does not overtake us except as human (1 Cor. 10:13). This sin is outside the body, is not counted as fornication, and is therefore very easily forgiven.

But when, in order to attain what is perceived through the body, out of a desire to experience, excel, or handle such things, one does something so as to place the end of one’s good in them, whatever one does, one does shamefully. One fornicates against one’s own body by sinning (1 Cor. 6:18), inwardly dragging in the deceptive images of bodily things and arranging them through empty meditation, so that nothing divine seems pleasing to it unless it appears to be of this kind [Note: [Col. 1006] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “so that nothing divine pleases it unless it appears to be of this kind.” Ambr. and the manuscripts are better, with the word “pleases” deleted: “so that nothing divine, unless it is of this kind”—that is, unless it belongs to the class of which he is speaking—“appears to it.”]. Privately it becomes pregnant with errors through avarice, and privately is drained of strength through prodigality [Note: [Col. 1006] Retractations II.15.3.]. Nor would it leap all at once into so shameful and miserable a fornication from the beginning; but, as it is written, “He who despises small things will fall little by little” (Ecclus. 19:1).

## CHAPTER XI

16. The image of a beast in man. For just as a serpent does not creep with open strides but crawls by the tiniest movements of its scales, so the slippery movement of decline gradually takes possession of the negligent. Beginning with a perverse desire for the likeness of God, it arrives at the likeness of beasts. Hence, having been stripped of their first garment, they earned tunics of skins through mortality (Gen. 3:21).

The true honor of man is the image and likeness of God, and this is preserved only by turning toward the one by whom it is impressed [Note: [Col. 1006] Several manuscripts read: “only from the one by whom it is impressed.”]. The more one clings to God, therefore, the less one loves what is one’s own. But through the desire to experience its own power, the soul plunges by a kind of inclination toward itself, as toward a center. Thus, when it wishes to be like him who is under no one, it is driven downward in punishment from the very center of itself—that is, toward those things in which beasts rejoice. And so, although man’s honor is the likeness of God and his disgrace the likeness of a beast, man, placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and made like them (Ps. 48:13).

By what route could he pass so far from the heights to the depths except through his own center? For when, neglecting the love of wisdom, which always remains the same, he desires knowledge gained from experience of changing and temporal things, he is puffed up and does not build up (1 Cor. 8:1). Thus the soul, weighed down as though by its own burden, is driven from blessedness; and through that experience of its own center it learns by its punishment what difference there is between the good it abandoned and the evil it committed. It cannot return with its powers poured out and lost unless the grace of its Creator calls it to repentance and forgives its sins. For who will free the unhappy soul from this body of death except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord? (Rom. 7:24–25). Concerning this grace we shall speak in its proper place, insofar as he himself grants it [Note: [Col. 1007] Most manuscripts and the edition of Ambr. read: “when he himself grants it.”].

## CHAPTER XII

17. A certain secret marriage in the inner man. Illicit pleasures of thought. Let us now, insofar as the Lord assists, complete our consideration of that part of reason to which knowledge belongs—that is, the cognition of temporal and mutable things necessary for carrying out the activities of this life.

For just as, in the manifest marriage of the two human beings who were first made, the serpent did not eat from the forbidden tree but merely persuaded the woman to eat; while the woman did not eat alone but gave some to her husband, and they ate together—although she alone spoke with the serpent and was deceived by him (Gen. 3:1–6)—so also in what takes place and is discerned within a single human being there is a certain hidden and secret marriage. The carnal—or, so to speak, sensual—movement of the soul, which is directed toward the bodily senses and is common to us and beasts, is separated from the reason of wisdom.

Through bodily sensation, bodily things are perceived; eternal and unchangeable things, however, are understood spiritually through the reason of wisdom. The appetite is close to the reason of knowledge, since it reasons about the very bodily things perceived through the bodily sense—this is what is called the knowledge of action—either rightly, so that it refers that awareness to the end of the highest good, or wrongly, so that it enjoys them as goods of such a kind in which it may rest in a false happiness.

When, therefore, that carnal or animal sense brings to the mind’s attention—which is occupied with temporal and bodily things through the vitality of reasoning for the sake of action—a certain enticement to enjoy it, as though it were some private and personal good rather than the public and common good that is unchangeable, then the serpent, as it were, speaks to the woman. To consent to this enticement is to eat from the forbidden tree.

But if this consent is satisfied with the pleasure of thought alone, while the authority of the higher counsel restrains the members so that they are not offered as weapons of unrighteousness to sin (Rom. 6:13), I think it should be understood as though the woman alone had eaten the forbidden food. If, however, in consenting to misuse the things perceived through bodily sensation [Note: [Col. 1008] The Lovaniensis edition reads: “into consent”], whatever sin is decided upon is determined in such a way that, if there is power to do so, it is also carried out bodily, then the woman must be understood to have given her husband the illicit food to eat together with her.

For sin cannot be decided upon not merely to be thought about pleasantly but also to be effectively committed unless that intention of the mind—which possesses supreme power to move the members into action or restrain them from action—also yields and submits to the evil deed.

18. Indeed, when the mind is pleased by illicit things in thought alone, not deciding that they should be done, but nevertheless gladly holding and turning over what ought to have been rejected as soon as it touched the mind, it must not be denied that this is sin—although it is far less than if it were also decided that the deed should be carried out. Therefore forgiveness must also be sought for such thoughts, the breast must be struck, and one must say, “Forgive us our debts”; and what follows must be done and joined to the prayer: “as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

For just as, in those first two human beings, each bore his own person, and therefore, if the woman alone had eaten the illicit food, she alone would certainly have been punished with the penalty of death, so it cannot be said that, in a single human being, if thought alone gladly feeds on illicit pleasures from which it ought immediately to turn away, and if evils are not decided upon for execution but are merely held pleasantly in memory, the woman could be condemned without the man. Far be it from us to believe this. This is one person, one human being, and the whole person will be condemned unless, through the grace of the Mediator, these things—which are felt as sins of thought alone, without the will to perform them but nevertheless with the will to delight the mind in such things—are forgiven.

19. This discussion, then, in which we have sought within the mind of each individual a certain rational marriage of contemplation and action, with their functions distributed among particular aspects but with the unity of the mind preserved in both, must be heard only for the following purpose: without compromising the truth of that history which divine authority transmits concerning the first two human beings—the man and his wife, from whom the human race was propagated—we are to understand that the Apostle, by attributing the image of God to the man alone and not also to the woman, nevertheless wished to signify something in the two persons of different sex that was to be sought within one human being.

## CHAPTER XIII

20. The opinion of those who understood the mind to be signified by the man and bodily sense by the woman. I am not unaware that certain distinguished defenders of the Catholic faith and interpreters of divine Scripture who lived before us, when they sought these two things within one human being—whose entire good soul they understood to be a kind of paradise—said that the man signified the mind and the woman bodily sense.

According to this distribution, in which the man is identified with the mind and the woman with bodily sense, everything seems to fit appropriately if the passages are considered carefully, except that it is written concerning all the beasts and birds that no helper like the man was found for him, and then the woman was made for him from his side (Gen. 2:20–22).

For this reason I did not think that bodily sense should be assigned to the woman, since we see that it is common to us and to beasts. Rather, I wished to identify something that beasts do not possess; and I thought that bodily sense should more properly be understood as the serpent, who is said to be wiser than all the beasts of the earth (Gen. 3:1). Among those natural goods that we see to be common to us and to irrational animals, the serpent excels by a certain liveliness of sensation.

This is not the sense of which it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where we read that solid food belongs to the mature, who through practice have their senses trained to distinguish good from evil (Heb. 5:14). Those senses belong to rational nature and pertain to understanding. Rather, this is the fivefold sense in the body, through which not only we but also beasts perceive bodily form and movement.

21. But whether the saying of the Apostle—that the man is the image and glory of God, while the woman is the glory of the man (1 Cor. 11:7)—is to be understood in this way, in that way, or in some other way, it nevertheless appears that, when we live according to God, our mind, directed toward his invisible things, ought progressively to be formed from his eternity, truth, and love.

Some part, however, of our rational intention—that is, of the same mind—must be directed toward the use of mutable and bodily things, without which this life cannot be conducted. This is not so that we may be conformed to this age (Rom. 12:2) [Note: [Col. 1009] Several manuscripts read: “that it may be conformed”], by making such goods our end and twisting toward them the desire for blessedness, but so that whatever we rationally do in the use of temporal things, we may do for the contemplation of attaining eternal things: passing through the former, clinging to the latter.

## CHAPTER XIV

The difference between wisdom and knowledge. The worship of God and love of him. How intellectual cognition of eternal things takes place through wisdom. Knowledge also has its own proper good, provided that whatever in it does or usually does puff up is overcome by the love of eternal things, which does not puff up but, as we know, builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). For without knowledge even the virtues by which one lives rightly cannot be possessed—virtues by which this miserable life is so governed that one may arrive at that eternal life which is truly blessed.

22. There is nevertheless a difference between contemplation of eternal things and action by which we make good use of temporal things: the former is assigned to wisdom, the latter to knowledge. Although what is wisdom can also be called knowledge—as the Apostle says: “Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Cor. 13:12)—and by “knowledge” he certainly wishes the contemplation of God to be understood, which will be the highest reward of the saints, nevertheless, when he says, “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:8), he unquestionably distinguishes these two, although he does not explain there what the difference is or how each can be recognized.

Yet, after examining the abundant variety of the holy Scriptures, I find it written in the book of Job, spoken by that holy man himself: “Behold, piety is wisdom; but to abstain from evil is knowledge” (Job 28:28). In this distinction we should understand wisdom to pertain to contemplation and knowledge to action.

For in this passage he calls the worship of God “piety,” which in Greek is θεοσέβεια (*theosebeia*). This is the word found in the Greek manuscripts. And what is more excellent among eternal things than God, whose nature alone is unchangeable? And what is his worship except love of him—the love by which we now desire to see him, believe and hope that we shall see him, and, to the extent that we progress, now see through a mirror in an enigma, but then in manifestation?

This is what the Apostle Paul says: “face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). It is also what John says: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). The discourse concerning these and similar matters seems to me to be the discourse of wisdom [Note: [Col. 1010] Some manuscripts read: “the discourses concerning these and similar matters.”].

But to abstain from evil, which Job said is knowledge, plainly concerns temporal things. For in the present time we are among evils from which we must abstain in order to reach those eternal goods. Therefore whatever we do prudently, courageously, temperately, and justly belongs to that knowledge or discipline in which our action is occupied with avoiding evils and pursuing goods. The same applies to whatever we gather through historical knowledge for the sake of examples to avoid or imitate, and for the sake of necessary instruction concerning any matters adapted to our uses.

23. When discourse concerns these things, therefore, I think it is the discourse of knowledge, to be distinguished from the discourse of wisdom. To wisdom belong things that neither were nor will be, but are; and because of the eternity in which they are, they are said to have been, to be, and to be going to be, without any change of times.

They were not such that they ceased to be, nor will they be such as though they do not now exist. Rather, they have always possessed and will always possess that same being. They remain, not as bodies fixed in spatial intervals, but in incorporeal nature they are intelligibly present to the mind’s sight, just as visible or tangible things are present in places to the bodily senses.

Not only do the incorporeal and intelligible principles of sensible things situated in places remain without spatial dimensions; the principles also of movements passing through time stand without temporal passage. They too are intelligible, not sensible.

To reach them with the mind’s sharp vision belongs to few. And when one reaches them, insofar as this is possible, the one who has reached them does not remain in them; rather, as though the very sharpness of vision were thrown back, he is repelled, and a transitory thought of a non-transitory reality arises [Note: [Col. 1010] Several manuscripts read *acies*, “the sharpness” or “edge,” rather than *acie*, “by the sharpness.”].

Nevertheless, this passing thought, through the disciplines by which the mind is educated, is entrusted to memory, so that it has somewhere to return when it is compelled to pass away from there. Even if the thought did not return to memory but found there what it had entrusted to it, it would be led back as though untrained to the very place to which it had first been led, and it would find it where it had first found it—in that incorporeal truth from which it would again be fixed in memory as though copied out.

For the mind of man does not remain in the incorporeal and unchangeable principle of a square body in the same way that that principle remains—provided, of course, that the mind was able to reach it without the phantasy of spatial extension. Or if the numerical structure of some artistic and musical sound passing through temporal intervals is grasped as standing without time in a certain secret and profound silence, it can at least be thought for as long as that song can be heard.

Nevertheless, whatever the mind’s vision, even though passing, snatches from it and, as though swallowing it into its belly, stores in memory [Note: [Col. 1011] The manuscripts read: “in its belly”], it can, by recollecting, ruminate in a certain way and transfer into discipline what it has learned in this manner.

If it has been completely erased by oblivion, one will again arrive, under the guidance of instruction, at what had entirely slipped away; and it will be found as it was.

## CHAPTER XV

24. Against the recollection-theory of Plato and Pythagoras. Pythagoras of Samos. The difference between wisdom and knowledge, and the search for a trinity in knowledge of temporal things. That famous philosopher Plato attempted to persuade people that human souls had lived here before they inhabited these bodies, and that this explains why what is learned is remembered as previously known rather than learned as something new.

He reported that a certain boy, questioned about some matter of geometry [Note: [Col. 1011] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “about geometry.”], answered as though he were highly skilled in that discipline. For, questioned gradually and skillfully, he saw what was to be seen and said what he had seen.

But if this were a recollection of things previously known, surely not everyone—or nearly everyone—would be able to do this when questioned in that manner. For not everyone had been a geometer in the former life, since geometers are so rare among the human race that scarcely one can be found. Rather, we should believe that the nature of the intellectual mind was created in such a way that, according to the natural order established by the Creator, it sees intelligible things in a certain incorporeal light peculiar to itself, just as the eye of the flesh sees the things that surround it in this bodily light—a light for which it was created capable and suited.

Nor does the eye distinguish white from black without a teacher because it already knew these things before it was created in the flesh. Finally, why is it possible for someone, when properly questioned, to answer correctly concerning intelligible matters belonging to any discipline, even if he is ignorant of that discipline? Why can no one do this concerning sensible things unless he saw them while established in this body, or believed someone who knew them—whether through that person’s writings or words?

We should not accept the claim that Pythagoras of Samos remembered certain things that he had experienced when he had previously been in another body [Note: [Col. 1012] The printed editions read: “things that he had not experienced.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts]. Others, too, are said by others to have undergone something similar in their minds. These were false memories, such as we often experience in dreams, when we seem to remember having done or seen something that we did not do or see at all.

It can be inferred that the minds of those people, even while awake, were affected in the same way by the prompting of evil and deceptive spirits, who are concerned to establish or sow among human beings the false belief in the revolutions of souls as a means of deceiving them. For if they truly remembered what they had previously seen while inhabiting other bodies here, this would happen to many, indeed almost all, since they suppose that the living continually become dead, and the dead living—just as the sleeping become wakeful and the wakeful sleeping—without interruption.

25. If, then, this is the correct distinction between wisdom and knowledge—that intellectual cognition of eternal things belongs to wisdom, while rational cognition of temporal things belongs to knowledge—it is not difficult to judge which should be placed before or after the other.

But if another distinction must be applied by which these two are recognized—two things that the Apostle unquestionably teaches to be different when he says, “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit”—there is nevertheless also this most evident difference between the two that we have proposed: one is intellectual cognition of eternal things, the other rational cognition of temporal things; and no one doubts that the former should be preferred to the latter.

As we leave behind the things belonging to the outer man and desire to ascend inwardly from those things we have in common with beasts, before we reach cognition of intelligible and supreme things that are eternal, rational cognition of temporal things presents itself.

In this cognition, therefore, let us also find, if we can, some trinity, just as we found one in the bodily senses and in those things that entered imaginally into our soul or spirit through them. In the case of bodily things that we touch outside us by bodily sensation, we have inwardly impressed in memory likenesses of bodies, from which thought is formed, while a third element, the will, joins the two together.

Thus, outside us, the sharpness of the eyes was formed; the will directed it toward the visible thing so that vision might occur, and joined the two together, itself also moving toward the object as a third element.

But this subject must not be compressed into this book, so that in the one that follows it may, with God’s help, be investigated appropriately and whatever is discovered may be explained.

## BOOK THIRTEEN

This book continues the discussion of knowledge, in which, insofar as it is distinguished from wisdom, the preceding book began to seek a certain trinity. On this occasion, commending the Christian faith, it explains how the faith of believers is one and common. It then shows that all desire blessedness, yet not all possess the faith by which blessedness is attained. It defines this faith as being in Christ, who rose in the flesh from the dead, and maintains that no one is freed from the dominion of the devil except through him, by the forgiveness of sins. It demonstrates at length that the devil had to be conquered by Christ not through power but through justice. Finally, while the words of this faith are committed to memory, it shows that a certain trinity exists in the mind, because the sounds of the words are in memory even when a person is not thinking about them; from these sounds the focus of recollection is formed when he thinks about them; and finally the will of the person remembering and thinking joins the two together.

[Col. 1013]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1013]

1. He undertakes to distinguish the functions of wisdom and knowledge from Scripture. From the opening of John, some statements pertain to wisdom and others to knowledge. Certain matters are known only with the help of faith. How we see the faith that is in us. In the same narrative of John, some things are known through bodily sense and others only through the mind’s reason.

In the twelfth book of the preceding part of this work we have sufficiently distinguished the function of the rational mind in temporal things—where not only our cognition but also our action is involved—from the more excellent function of the same mind, which is devoted to contemplating eternal things and is completed in cognition alone.

I think it more appropriate, however, to insert something from the holy Scriptures, so that the two may be distinguished more easily.

2. The evangelist John began his Gospel as follows:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came for a testimony, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but he came to bear witness to the light.

“There was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name—who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:1–14).

Everything I have quoted from the Gospel contains, in its earlier portions, what is unchangeable and eternal, the contemplation of which makes us blessed; in its later portions, however, eternal things are recalled intermixed with temporal things. Accordingly, some matters there pertain to knowledge and others to wisdom, as our distinction in the twelfth book established beforehand.

For the words, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; what was made in him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it,” require the contemplative life and must be perceived by the intellectual mind [Col. 1014]. The more anyone progresses in this matter, the wiser he will undoubtedly become.

But because it says, “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it,” faith was needed, by which what was not seen could be believed. By “darkness” he intended human hearts that had turned away from this kind of light and were less capable of contemplating it. Therefore he adds and says:

“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came for a testimony, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him.”

This had already taken place temporally and belongs to knowledge, which is contained in historical cognition.

We think of the man John in the imagination, which has been impressed upon our memory from our knowledge of human nature. Those who do not believe these things and those who do believe them think of him in the same way. For both know what a human being is; they learned his outward part, that is, his body, through the bodily lights—the eyes. They know and retain his inward part, that is, the soul, within themselves, since they too are human beings and have learned it through human association. Thus they can think what is said: “There was a man whose name was John,” since they also know names through speaking and hearing.

But the statement “sent from God” is held by faith by those who hold it. Those who do not hold it by faith either hesitate in doubt or mock it in unbelief. Nevertheless, if they are not among those who are exceedingly foolish, who say in their hearts, “There is no God” (Ps. 13:1), then, hearing these words, both groups think about both matters: what God is and what it means to be sent by God—even if they think of them not as the realities themselves are, but at least according to their capacity.

3. We know the faith itself, which each person sees to be in his own heart if he believes, or not to be there if he does not believe, in a different way. We do not know it as we know bodies, which we see with bodily eyes and think about when absent through the images of them that we retain in memory.

Nor do we know it as we know things that we have not seen but form in some way in thought from things that we have seen and entrust to memory, so that we may return to them whenever we wish and there see again in recollection either those things or, rather, whatever images of them we have fixed there.

Nor do we know it as we know a living human being, whose soul, even if we do not see it, we infer from our own soul, and whom we contemplate in thought as a living human being on the basis of bodily movements, just as we have learned by seeing [Note: [Col. 1014] Several manuscripts read: “by living.”].

Faith is not seen in the heart in this way by the person whose faith it is. Rather, the most certain knowledge holds it, and conscience proclaims it.

Although we are commanded to believe precisely because we cannot see what we are commanded to believe, nevertheless, when faith is present within us, we see faith within us. For faith is present to absent things; faith concerning things outside is within us; faith concerning things that are not seen is itself seen; and yet faith itself comes to be temporally in human hearts. If believers become unbelievers, it perishes from them.

Sometimes faith is also given to false things. We speak in this way, saying, “He was trusted, and he deceived.” Faith of this kind, if indeed it is still to be called faith, does not culpably perish from hearts when the truth discovered drives it out.

It is desirable, however, that faith in things that are true should pass over into those very things. For it must not be said to perish when the things that were believed are seen. Surely faith should no longer be called faith when faith has been defined in the Epistle to the Hebrews as the conviction of things that are not seen (Heb. 11:1)?

4. Next comes the statement, “He came for a testimony, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him.” As we said, this is a temporal action. Testimony is borne temporally even concerning an eternal reality, namely, the intelligible light. John came to bear witness to it; he was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light.

For he adds:

“There was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.”

All who know the Latin language understand these words from things that they know. Some of those things became known to us through bodily senses—for example, a human being, the world itself, whose evident magnitude we see, and the sounds of these same words, since hearing too is a bodily sense.

Others became known through the mind’s reason—for example, the statement, “And his own did not receive him.” This is understood to mean, “They did not believe in him,” and what this means we know not through any bodily sense but through the mind’s reason.

We learned not only the sounds of the words themselves but also their meanings, partly through bodily sense and partly through the mind’s reason. Nor are we now hearing these words for the first time. We had heard them before; and not only the words themselves but also what they signified had been known and retained in memory, and we recognized them here.

When the two-syllable word *mundus* (“world”) is spoken, its sound, since it is a body, entered our awareness through the body—that is, through the ear. But what it signifies also became known through the body—that is, through the eyes of the flesh. For, insofar as the world is known, it is known to those who see it.

The four-syllable word *crediderunt* (“they believed”), however, enters through its sound, since it is bodily, by the ear of the flesh. What it signifies is known not through any bodily sense but through the mind’s reason. Unless we knew through the mind what *crediderunt* means, we would not understand what those concerning whom it is said, “His own did not receive him,” failed to do.

The sound of the word therefore resounds outwardly in the ears of the body and reaches the sense called hearing.

The appearance of a human being is also known to us in ourselves, and outwardly it is present to the other bodily senses: to the eyes when it is seen, to the ears when it is heard, and to touch when it is held and touched. It also has its image in our memory—incorporeal, certainly, but resembling a body.

Finally, the wondrous beauty of the world itself is outwardly present both to our sight and to the sense called touch, if we touch any part of it. It too has inwardly in our memory its own image, to which we return when we think of it either enclosed by walls or even in darkness.

We have already spoken sufficiently in the eleventh book about these images of bodily things—incorporeal indeed, but possessing likenesses of bodies and belonging to the life of the outer man.

Now, however, we are dealing with the inner man and his knowledge, which concerns temporal and mutable things. When something belonging to the outer man is taken up into the mind’s attention, it must be taken up so that something may be learned from it that assists rational knowledge.

Accordingly, the rational use of the things we share with irrational animals belongs to the inner man. It cannot rightly be said that the inner man is common to us and irrational animals.

## CHAPTER II
### 5. Faith is a matter of the heart, not of the body; how the faith of all believers is common and one

The faith of believers is one, just as the will of those who will is one. The faith, however, about which in this book we are compelled, for a definite reason in the arrangement of our discussion, to argue at somewhat greater length—the faith by which those who possess it are called faithful, and those who do not possess it unfaithful, as were those who did not receive the Son of God when he came to his own—although it has been produced in us through hearing, nevertheless does not belong to that bodily sense which is called hearing, since it is not a sound. Nor does it belong to the eyes of this flesh, since it is neither a color nor a bodily form; nor to what is called touch, since it has nothing corporeal; nor to any bodily sense whatever, since this is a matter of the heart, not of the body. It is not outside us, but within our inmost being [Note: [Col. 1016] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have *in intimis nostris*, “within our inmost being,” with *nostris* instead of *nobis*.]. Nor does anyone see it in another person, but each person sees it in himself. Finally, it can be fabricated by pretence and can be thought to exist in someone in whom it does not exist.

Each person, therefore, sees his own faith within himself; in another, however, he believes that it exists but does not see it—and he believes this the more firmly, the more he knows its fruits, which faith ordinarily produces through love (Galatians 5:6). Accordingly, to all those of whom the Evangelist goes on to say, “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God,” this faith is common—not in the way that some bodily form is common to be seen by the eyes of all for whom it is present, since from that one form the sight of all who see is, in a certain manner, formed; but in the way that one may say that a human face is common to all human beings. For this is said in such a way that each individual nevertheless has his own face.

Certainly, we may most truly say that the faith of individual believers is impressed upon the hearts of each of them by one and the same teaching, since they believe the same thing. But the things that are believed are one thing, and the faith by which they are believed is another [Col. 1017]. The former exist in realities which are said either to exist, to have existed, or to be going to exist; the latter exists in the mind of the believer and is visible only to the one whose it is. Although it exists in others also, it is not the same faith but a similar one. It is not one in number, but in kind; nevertheless, because of its likeness and its complete lack of difference, we call it one rather than many. For when we see two people who are very much alike, we say that they have one face, and we marvel at the face of both.

It is therefore easier to say that there were many souls, each belonging to an individual, of whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles that they had “one soul” (Acts 4:32), than, when the Apostle says “one faith” (Ephesians 4:5), for anyone to dare to say that there are as many faiths as there are believers. And yet when he says to one woman, “Great is your faith” (Matthew 15:28), and to another, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (ibid. 14:31), he indicates that each has her own faith.

Yet the faith of believers is called one and the same in the way that the will of those who will is called one and the same. For even among those who will the same thing, each person’s own will is visible to him, while another’s remains hidden, although that other person wills the same thing; and if the will reveals itself through certain signs, it is believed rather than seen. Each person, however, being conscious of his own mind, does not merely believe that this is his will, but clearly sees it.

### Chapter III.

### 6. Certain wills are known by all individually. The poet Ennius

There is, indeed, such great harmony among living beings of the same nature and endowed with reason that, although one person is unaware of what another wants, nevertheless some desires of all people are known to each individual. Although each person does not know what one particular other person wants, in certain matters he can know what everyone wants.

Hence that exceedingly witty saying of a certain mime is celebrated. He had promised that at another theatrical performance he would say what everyone had in mind and what everyone wanted. When the appointed day arrived, a much larger crowd than usual gathered in eager expectation. When all were waiting in suspense and silence, he is said to have declared: “You want to buy cheaply and sell dearly.” In this saying, though it was the jest of a very frivolous stage performer, everyone found his own conscience, and they applauded with remarkable enthusiasm the man who had set the truth before everyone’s eyes, yet had said something unexpected.

Why, moreover, did such great expectation arise when he promised that he would state everyone’s desire, unless it is because one person’s desires are hidden from another? But was this hidden from the mime? Is it hidden from anyone? For what reason, except that there are certain things which each person may, not unreasonably, infer about others from himself, whether by sympathy or by a common defect or nature? Yet seeing one’s own will is one thing; inferring another’s, even by the most certain conjecture, is another.

I am as certain that Rome was founded as a fact of human history as I am that Constantinople exists, although I have seen Rome with my own eyes and know nothing of Constantinople except what I have believed on the testimony of others. That mime, then, either by observing himself or by testing others as well, believed that everyone shared the desire to buy cheaply and sell dearly. But since this is truly a vice, a person may acquire a kind of justice, or may fall into the plague of some other vice contrary to this one, by which he resists and conquers it.

For I myself know a man who, when a book was offered for sale, saw that the seller, unaware of its value and therefore asking a small sum, had named a price far below what was just; and he gave him a fair price, much larger than the seller expected [Col. 1018]. What if someone were so possessed by wickedness that he sold cheaply what his parents had left him, and bought dearly what his lusts would consume? This extravagance is not, I think, unbelievable. If such people are sought, they may be found—or perhaps they may even appear without being sought—people whose wickedness is greater than that of the theater, who mock the theatrical proposition or declaration by buying sexual debauchery at a high price while selling estates cheaply.

We have also known some people who, out of generosity, bought grain at a higher price and sold it more cheaply to their fellow citizens.

That saying also which the old poet Ennius uttered,

> All mortals desire to be praised [Note: [Col. 1018] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Louvain have *laudari exoptant*, “desire to be praised,” incorrectly. M.],

he evidently inferred from himself and from those whom he had tested that this was true of others, and he seems to have pronounced the desires of all human beings. Finally, if that mime had also said, “You all want to be praised; none of you wants to be blamed,” he would likewise seem to have stated something common to everyone’s will.

There are, however, people who hate their own vices and are displeased with themselves, and who do not want others to praise them; rather, they thank the goodwill of those who rebuke them, when they are blamed in order that they may be corrected. But if the mime had said, “You all want to be happy; you do not want to be miserable,” he would have said something which everyone would recognize in his own will. For whatever else anyone may secretly want, he does not depart from this desire, which is sufficiently known to all and in all human beings.

### Chapter IV.

### 7. The will to possess happiness is one in all; but there is great variety in people’s wills concerning happiness itself

It is remarkable that, although the will to attain and retain happiness is one in all people, such great variety and diversity of wills concerning happiness itself should arise—not because anyone does not want it, but because not everyone knows it. If everyone knew it, it would not be thought by some to consist in virtue of soul, by others in bodily pleasure, by others in both, and by still others in one thing or another, in one place or another. For whatever thing most delighted them, they established life’s happiness in that thing.

How, then, can all love most ardently what not all know? Who can love what he does not know, as I have already discussed this matter in the earlier books (Book 8, chapters 4 and following, and Book 10, chapter 1, etc.)?

Why, then, is happiness loved by everyone but not known by everyone? Perhaps everyone knows what it is, but not everyone knows where it is, and this is the source of the dispute? As though the question concerned some place in this world where one who wishes to live happily ought to wish to live, rather than asking where happiness is in the same way as we ask what it is.

For certainly, if happiness consists in bodily pleasure, the happy person is the one who enjoys bodily pleasure; if it consists in virtue of soul, the happy person is the one who enjoys that; and if it consists in both, the happy person is the one who enjoys both. When one person says, “To live happily is to enjoy bodily pleasure,” while another says, “To live happily is to enjoy virtue of soul,” do they not either both fail to know what the happy life is, or else not both know it? How, then, do both love it, if no one can love what he does not know?

Or perhaps what we have accepted as most true and certain—that all human beings want to live happily—is false? For if living happily means, for example, living according to virtue of soul, how can the person who does not want this want to live happily? Shall we not more truly say, “This man does not want to live happily, because he does not want to live according to virtue,” since living according to virtue alone is living happily?

Therefore not everyone wants to live happily. Indeed, only a few want this, if living happily means living according to virtue of soul, which many do not want. Will it then be false—that proposition about which even that Academic, Cicero, did not doubt, although everything was doubtful to the Academics—when, wishing in his dialogue *Hortensius* to take the beginning of his discussion from some certain matter about which no one would disagree, he said, “Certainly, we all want to be happy”?

Far be it from us to say that this is false. What, then? Should we say that, even if living happily means nothing other than living according to virtue of soul, the person who does not want this nevertheless wants to live happily? This seems excessively absurd. It is as though we were saying, “Even the person who does not want to live happily wants to live happily.” Who could listen to such a contradiction, or endure it?

And yet necessity drives us to this conclusion if both of the following are true: that everyone wants to live happily, and that not everyone wants to live in the manner in which alone one lives happily.

### Chapter V.

### 8. The same subject

Perhaps what can rescue us from these difficulties is this: since we said that each person established the happy life in whatever most delighted him—pleasure for Epicurus, virtue for Zeno, and something else for someone else—we might say that living happily means nothing other than living according to one’s own pleasure.
