Thus it would not be false that everyone wants to live happily, because everyone wants to live in the way that pleases him. If this had been proclaimed in the theater to the assembled people, everyone would have found it in his own will.

But Cicero, having proposed this very position to himself as an objection, refuted it in such a way that those who hold it ought to be ashamed. He says:

> “And yet, not philosophers indeed, but people ready to argue, all say that those are happy who live as they themselves wish”—that is precisely what we said: “in the way that pleases each person.”

But he immediately added:

> “That is false. To want what one ought not to want is itself the greatest misery; nor is it as miserable not to obtain what you want as to obtain what one ought not to want.”

This is altogether most excellent and most true. Who could be so blind in mind, so estranged from every light of moral beauty, and so enveloped in the darkness of disgrace, that he would call the person who lives wickedly and disgracefully, with no one preventing him, no one punishing him, and no one even daring to rebuke him, but with many people praising him—since, as divine Scripture says, “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who practices iniquity is blessed” (Psalm 9:3)—happy because he fulfills all his most criminal and shameful desires [Note: [Col. 1019] Thus Ambrosian manuscripts, Erasmus, and several manuscripts. The Louvain edition has *voluptates*, “pleasures.”], when surely, although he would still be miserable in this condition, he would be less miserable if he could not possess any of the things he wrongly desired?

Even an evil will alone makes a person miserable; but he is more miserable because of the power by which the desire of the evil will is fulfilled.

Since, therefore, it is true that all human beings want to be happy, and that they seek this one thing with the most ardent love, and seek all other things because of it; and since no one can love what he is entirely unaware of—nor can anyone be unaware of what he knows himself to want—it follows that all people know the happy life.

All happy people have what they want, although not everyone who has what he wants is immediately happy. Those who either do not have what they want, or have what they wrongly want, are immediately miserable. No one, therefore, is happy except the person who both has everything he wants and wants nothing wrongly.

### Chapter VI.

### 9. Why, although all want happiness, people choose what takes them farther from it

Since, then, the happy life consists of these two things, and both are known and cherished by everyone, what do we think is the reason why, when people cannot have both, they choose to have everything they want rather than to want everything rightly, even if they do not have what they want?

Is this perhaps the perversity of the human race: although people are not unaware that neither the person who does not have what he wants nor the person who has what he wrongly wants is happy, but that the happy person is the one who both has whatever good things he wants and wants nothing evil—yet, when both are not granted, they choose the one of these two things by which they depart farther from the happy life? For the person who obtains what he wrongly desires is farther from it than the person who does not obtain what he desires.

Rather, the good will ought to have been chosen and preferred, even when it has not obtained what it seeks. For the person who rightly wants whatever he wants is close to happiness, and when he has obtained those things, he will be happy. Certainly, it is not evil things but good things that make a person happy, whenever they do so. The person who desires to rejoice in the good things of which human nature is capable, not in the commission or attainment of any evil, already possesses something of these goods—a thing that must not be regarded as insignificant: namely, a good will itself.

He pursues and, insofar as it is granted, attains the kinds of good things that can exist even in this miserable life, with a prudent, temperate, courageous, and just mind, so that even amid evils he is good; and when all evils have ended and all good things have been fulfilled, he is happy.

### Chapter VII.

### 10. Faith is necessary if a person is ever to be happy; this will be attained only in the future life. The happiness of proud philosophers is ridiculous and pitiable

Accordingly, in this mortal life, which is filled with errors and afflictions, faith is especially necessary—the faith by which one believes in God. For no good things whatsoever, especially those by which a person becomes good and those by which he will become happy, can be found unless they come to human beings from God and are granted to them.

When, however, the person who is faithful and good amid these miseries has departed from this life and reached the happy life, then what is now in no way possible will truly occur: that a person will live as he wishes. In that happiness he will not want to live wrongly; he will not want anything that will be lacking, nor will anything he wants be lacking. Whatever is loved will be present; what will not be present will not be desired [Col. 1021]. Everything that exists there will be good, and the supreme God will be the supreme good, present for the enjoyment of those who love him. And what is altogether most blessed is that it will be certain that this will always remain so.

For now, however, philosophers have indeed fashioned happy lives for themselves, each according to his own preference, as though by their own virtue they could live as they wished—something they could not do under the common condition of mortals [Note: [Col. 1021] The printed editions have *quidam* (“some”) in place of *quidem* (“indeed”).]. For they believed that no one could be happy except by having what he wanted and suffering nothing he did not want.

Who, however, would not want whatever kind of life delights him, and therefore is called happy by him, to be so entirely in his power that he could possess it perpetually? And yet who is in such a condition? Who wants to suffer troubles which he endures courageously, although, if he suffers them, he may be willing and able to endure them? Who would want to live amid torments—even one who can live commendably amid them by preserving justice through endurance?

Those who have endured these evils have considered them transitory, whether they desired to possess or feared to lose what they loved, whether their love was wicked or praiseworthy. For many have courageously pressed through transitory evils toward lasting goods. Such people are happy in hope even while they are in transitory evils, through which they reach goods that will not pass away. But the person who is happy in hope is not yet happy; for he awaits through patience the happiness he does not yet possess.

The person who is tortured without any such hope and without any such reward, whatever endurance he applies, is not truly happy but courageously miserable. He is not therefore not miserable because he would be more miserable if he endured his misery impatiently.

Moreover, if he does not suffer the things he would not want to suffer in his body, he should not even then be considered happy, since he does not live as he wishes. To omit other things which, even when the body is unharmed, concern the injuries of the soul—things without which we would wish to live, and which are innumerable—he would certainly, if he could, want to keep his body safe and sound in such a way as to suffer no troubles from it, so that he might have it under his control, or possess it in incorruptible condition. Since he does not have this, and since his condition hangs in uncertainty [Note: [Col. 1021] The manuscripts have *pendet incerto*, “hangs in uncertainty,” omitting *in*.], he plainly does not live as he wishes.

Although through courage he is prepared to receive and bear with an even mind whatever adversity may occur, he nevertheless prefers that it not occur, and, if he can, he acts to prevent it. Thus he is prepared for either outcome: insofar as it lies within him, he desires one and avoids the other; and if what he avoids overtakes him, he bears it willingly because what he wanted could not happen.

He endures so that he may not be overcome; but he would not want to be pressed down. How, then, does he live as he wishes? Is it because he is willingly courageous in bearing what he would not want inflicted upon him? He therefore wants what he can, because he cannot have what he wants.

This is the whole happiness—whether it should rather be ridiculed or pitied—of proud mortals, who boast that they live as they wish because they willingly endure patiently what they do not want to happen to them. This, they say, is what Terence wisely said:

> Since what you want cannot happen,  
> Want what you can [Note: [Col. 1021] Terence has *possit*, “may be possible,” rather than *possis*, “you may be able.”].

(*Andria*, act 2, scene 1, lines 5–6.) [Col. 1022]

Who denies that this saying is apt? But it is advice given to a miserable person so that he may not be more miserable. To the happy person, whom everyone wants to be, it is neither rightly nor truly said, “What you want cannot happen.” For if he is happy, whatever he wants to happen can happen, because he does not want what cannot happen.

But this life does not belong to our mortality, nor will it exist except when immortality also exists. If immortality could in no way be given to human beings, the pursuit of happiness would likewise be futile, because there can be no happiness without immortality.

### Chapter VIII.

### 11. Happiness cannot exist without immortality

Since, then, all human beings want to be happy, if they truly want this [Note: [Col. 1022] Ambrosian manuscripts have *si verum volunt*, “if they truly want this.”], they certainly also want to be immortal; otherwise they could not be happy. Indeed, when questioned about immortality, just as about happiness, they all answer that they want it.

Yet any kind of happiness—something that is called happiness rather than truly is happiness—is sought, or rather imagined, in this life while immortality is despaired of, although true happiness cannot exist without it.

The person lives happily, as we said above and established sufficiently by argument, who lives as he wishes and wants nothing evil. No one wants immortality wrongly, if human nature is capable of it by God’s gift; and if it is not capable of immortality, it is not capable of happiness either.

For in order that a person may live happily, he must live. When life itself abandons a dying person, how can the happy life remain with him? When it abandons him, it certainly abandons him either unwillingly, willingly, or neither unwillingly nor willingly.

If it abandons him unwillingly, how is that a happy life which is so subject to his will that it is not in his power? Since no one is happy who wants something but does not possess it, how much less happy is the person whom the happy life itself abandons unwillingly—not honor, not property, not any other thing, but the very happy life—when no life will remain for him?

Thus, even if no consciousness remains by which he could be miserable—for the happy life departs because all life departs—he is nevertheless miserable as long as he has consciousness, because he knows that, against his will, he is being consumed on account of what he loves above all other things [Note: [Col. 1022] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *nolentem*, “the unwilling person,” less correctly.].

Life therefore cannot both be happy and abandon the unwilling person; for no one becomes happy unwillingly. Accordingly, the more the happy life makes a person miserable by abandoning him unwillingly, the more it would make him miserable if it were present to him against his will.

But if it abandons him willingly, then too how was it a happy life, when the person who possessed it wanted it to perish [Note: [Col. 1022] The manuscripts have *finire*, “to end.”]?

It remains for them to say that neither unwillingness nor willingness exists in the mind of the happy person; that is, that when the whole of life departs through death, he is abandoned by the happy life neither unwillingly nor willingly, but remains prepared and even-minded toward either possibility. But this too is not a happy life, since it is such that the person whom it makes happy is unworthy to love it.

For how is that a happy life which the happy person does not love? Or how is something loved when it is accepted indifferently whether it flourishes or perishes? Unless perhaps the virtues, which we love solely for the sake of happiness, dare to persuade us not to love happiness itself. But if they do so, we also cease to love the virtues themselves, when we do not love that for whose sake alone we loved them.

Moreover, how will that thoroughly examined, thoroughly tested, thoroughly purified, and thoroughly certain judgment be true—that all human beings want to be happy—if those who are already happy neither refuse nor desire to be happy [Col. 1023]? Or if they do desire it, as truth cries out and nature compels—nature into which the supremely good and immutable Creator implanted this desire—if, I say, the happy desire to be happy, then surely they do not want not to be happy.

But if they do not want not to be happy, they certainly do not want their happy state to be consumed and perish. And they can be happy only while they are living; therefore they do not want the life in which they are happy to perish.

All who truly are happy, or desire to be happy, therefore want to be immortal. But no one lives happily if what he wants is not present to him. Therefore a life cannot in any way be truly happy unless it is everlasting.

### Chapter IX.

### 12. We say, with the help of faith rather than human arguments, that happiness will truly be everlasting. Through the incarnation of the Son of God, the immortality of happiness becomes credible

Whether human nature can receive this immortality—which it nevertheless acknowledges to be desirable—is no small question. But if faith is present, the faith possessed by those to whom Jesus gave power to become children of God, there is no question.

For those who have attempted to discover this by human arguments, only a very few, endowed with great intelligence, possessing abundant leisure, and trained in the most subtle disciplines, have been able to investigate the immortality of the soul alone. Yet they did not find a stable—that is, a true—happy life for that soul. They said that even after happiness the soul would return to the miseries of this life.

Those among them who were ashamed of this view and thought that the purified soul should be placed in everlasting happiness without the body nevertheless hold such views about the world’s recurring eternity that they themselves refute their position concerning the soul. It would take too long to demonstrate this here, but in Book 12 of *The City of God* we have explained it sufficiently, as I think, in chapter 20.

Faith, however, promises by divine authority, not by human argument, that the whole human being will become immortal—for the human being consists of soul and body—and therefore truly happy.

Accordingly, after the Gospel had said that Jesus gave power to those who received him to become children of God, and after it had briefly explained what it means to receive him by saying, “To those who believe in his name,” and had added how they become children of God—“who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”—then, lest this weakness of human beings, which we see and bear within us, should despair of so great an excellence, it immediately added: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:12–14).

Thus, by contrast, it was suggested that what seemed incredible was nevertheless believable. If the Son of God, by nature, became the son of man through mercy for the sake of the sons of men—for this is what “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us human beings” means—how much more credible is it that, by nature, the sons of men should by the grace of God become sons of God and dwell in God, in whom alone and from whom alone they can be happy, made participants in his immortality? It was precisely to make this believable that the Son of God became a participant in our mortality [Col. 1024].

### Chapter X.

### 13. No other way was more fitting for freeing the human race from the misery of mortality through the incarnation of the Word. What are called our merits are God’s gifts

When people say, “Was there no other way by which God could free human beings from the misery of this mortality, except that he should will his only-begotten Son, God coeternal with himself, to become human by assuming a human soul and flesh, and, having become mortal, to suffer death?”—it is not enough to refute them merely by asserting that this manner by which God, through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, deigns to free us is good and fitting for the divine dignity.

We must also show that another possible way was not lacking to God, to whose power all things are equally subject, but that there was not, nor ought there to have been, another way more fitting for healing our misery.

For what was so necessary for raising our hope and freeing minds cast down by the condition of mortality from despair of immortality as for it to be demonstrated to us how highly God valued us and how greatly he loved us? What sign of this could be clearer and more glorious than that the Son of God, immutably good, remaining in himself what he was and accepting from us, for our sake, what he was not, deigned to enter into fellowship with our nature without any detriment to his own nature [Note: [Col. 1024] Erasmus and Louvain have *praeter animae suae naturae detrimentum*, “without detriment to the nature of his soul.” *Animae* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Ambrosian edition.]?

Before any merits of ours, he first endured our evils without any evil merit of his own; and thus, when we already believed how greatly God loves us and hoped for what we had despaired of, he bestowed upon us his gifts with gratuitous generosity, without any good merits of ours—indeed, despite and in advance of our evil merits.

#### 14. For what are called our merits are his gifts

For “so that faith may work through love” (Galatians 5:6), “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). He was given when Jesus was glorified through the resurrection. For then he promised that he would send him, and then he sent him (John 20:22; 7:39; and 15:26), because then, as it is written of him and was foretold earlier, “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4:8 and Psalm 67:19).

These gifts are our merits, by which we reach the supreme good of immortal happiness [Note: [Col. 1024] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “of immortality and happiness.”].

The Apostle says, “God demonstrates his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, now that we have been justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.” He adds further:

> “For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved in his life.”

Those whom he first called sinners he afterward called enemies of God; those whom he first called justified in the blood of Jesus Christ he afterward called reconciled through the death of the Son of God; and those whom he first called saved from wrath through him he afterward called saved in his life.

Before this grace, therefore, we were not merely sinners in some ordinary sense; we were in sins of such a kind that we were enemies of God.

Earlier, however, the same Apostle had called us sinners and enemies of God by two corresponding names, one seemingly very mild and the other plainly most severe, saying: “For while we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6–10). He called the same people weak and ungodly.

Weakness seems to be something slight, but at times it is of such a kind that it is called ungodliness. Yet if there were no weakness, there would be no need of a physician. In Hebrew his name is Jesus; in Greek, Σωτήρ (*Sōtēr*), “Savior”; in our language, *Salvator*, “Savior.” The Latin language did not previously possess this word, but it could possess it, just as it did when it wished.

This preceding statement of the Apostle—“While we were still weak, at the appointed time he died for the ungodly”—is connected with the two following statements, in one of which he called us sinners and in the other enemies of God, as though he had matched each term with its corresponding counterpart, referring “sinners” to “the weak” and “enemies of God” to “the ungodly.”

### Chapter XI.

### 15. The difficulty of how we have been justified in the blood of the Son of God

But what does “justified in his blood” mean? What power, I ask, does this blood possess, that believers should be justified in it? And what does “reconciled through the death of his Son” mean?

Was it really that, when God the Father was angry with us, he saw the death of his Son on our behalf and was appeased toward us? Was his Son, then, already so favorably disposed toward us that he even deigned to die for us, while the Father was still so angry that he would not be appeased unless the Son died for us?

And what does the same teacher of the Gentiles mean elsewhere when he says:

> “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also, together with him, freely give us all things?” (ibid. 8:31–32)

Would the Father have delivered up his own Son for us, not sparing him, unless he were already appeased? Does this not seem contrary to the other statement? In that passage, the Son dies for us, and the Father is reconciled to us through his death; in this passage, however, it is as though the Father loved us first, and, for our sake, did not spare the Son but delivered him up to death.

But I see that the Father loved us even before this—not only before the Son died for us, but before he created the world—the Apostle himself bearing witness when he says, “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4).

Nor was the Son delivered up, as though unwilling, because the Father did not spare him for our sake, since it was also said of the Son himself: “He loved me and delivered himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

The Father, therefore, and the Son and the Spirit of both together perform all things simultaneously and harmoniously. Nevertheless, we have been justified in the blood of Christ and reconciled to God through the death of his Son. How this happened I shall explain here too, insofar as I am able and as far as seems sufficient.

### Chapter XII.

### 16. Because of Adam’s sin, all human beings were handed over to the power of the devil

By a certain just judgment of God, the human race was handed over to the power of the devil, because the sin of the first human being passed originally into all who are born through the union of the two sexes, and the debt of our first parents bound all their descendants.

This handing-over was first signified in Genesis. When it had been said to the serpent, “You shall eat earth,” it was said to the human being, “You are earth, and you shall return to earth” (Genesis 3:14, 19).

By the words “You shall return to earth,” the death of the body was foretold, since he would not have experienced even this if he had remained as he was created—in a right condition. But by saying to the living human being, “You are earth,” he showed that the whole human being had been changed for the worse.

For “You are earth” is like this statement: “My Spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (ibid. 6:3). At that point, therefore, he demonstrated that the human being had been handed over to the one to whom it had been said, “You shall eat earth.”

The Apostle proclaims this more openly when he says:

> “And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of unbelief, among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of our inclinations; and we were by nature children of wrath, as were the others” (Ephesians 2:1–3).

The children of unbelief are unbelievers. And who is not such before becoming a believer? Accordingly, from their origin all human beings are under the ruler of the power of the air, who works in the children of unbelief.

What I called “from their origin” is what the Apostle means when he says that he too was “by nature” like the others: by nature, that is, as nature has been corrupted by sin, not as it was created right in the beginning.

The manner in which the human being was handed over to the power of the devil must not be understood as though God had done this or commanded it to be done, but as meaning that he permitted it—yet permitted it justly. For when God abandoned the sinner, the author of sin immediately seized him.

God did not, of course, abandon his creature in such a way as not to show himself to be the God who creates and gives life, and who, even amid punitive evils, bestows many good things upon the wicked. For “he has not restrained his mercies in his anger” (Psalm 76:10).

Nor did he lose the human being from the law of his own power when he permitted him to be under the power of the devil, because the devil himself is not outside the power of the Almighty, just as he is not outside his goodness. For from whom would the evil angels have received even their limited existence and life, except from the one who gives life to all things?

If, then, the commission of sins subjected the human being to the devil through God’s just anger, surely the remission of sins rescues the human being from the devil through God’s gracious reconciliation.

### Chapter XIII.

### 17. Man was to be rescued from the devil’s power not by power, but by justice

The devil was not to be overcome by God’s power, but by justice. For what is more powerful than the Almighty? Or what creature’s power can be compared with the power of the Creator? But since the devil, through the vice of his perversity, became a lover of power and a deserter and assailant of justice—for human beings imitate him all the more as they increasingly neglect, or even hate, justice and pursue power, rejoicing in possessing it or inflamed by the desire for it—it pleased God that, in order to rescue humanity from the devil’s power, the devil should be conquered not by power but by justice. Thus human beings, imitating Christ, would seek to conquer the devil through justice, not through power.

This is not because power, as though it were something evil, should be avoided; rather, the proper order must be maintained, in which justice comes first. For how great can the power of mortals be? Let mortals therefore hold fast to justice; power will be given to immortals. Compared with it, however great may be the power of those human beings who are called powerful on earth, it is found to be ridiculous weakness; and there the pit is dug for the sinner where the wicked seem to have the greatest power.

But the just person sings and says:

> Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord,  
> and teach from your law,  
> that you may give him relief from the evil days,  
> until the pit is dug for the sinner.  
> For the Lord will not reject his people,  
> nor abandon his inheritance,  
> until justice is turned into judgment,  
> and all who possess it are upright in heart.  
> (Psalm 93:12–15)

Therefore, during this period in which the power of God’s people is deferred, “the Lord will not reject his people, nor abandon his inheritance,” however many harsh and undeserved things that humble and weak people may suffer, “until justice,” which the weakness of the devout now possesses, “is turned into judgment”—that is, receives the power to judge. This is reserved for the just at the end, when power has followed the justice that preceded it in its proper order.

For power joined to justice, or justice added to power [Note: [Col. 1027] Am. and many manuscripts read *accedente potentiae*, “with power being added”; some read *accedente potentia*, “with power added.”], produces judicial authority.

Justice pertains to the good will; hence it was said by the angels at Christ’s birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Power, however, ought to follow justice, not precede it. For this reason it is also called “success” (*secunda*), that is, prosperity; and *secunda* derives from following (*sequendo*).

Since, as we discussed above, two things make people blessed—willing what is good and being able to do what one wills—there must not be that perversity which was identified in the same discussion: that, of the two things which make a person blessed, someone should choose to be able to do what he wills while neglecting to will what he ought. He ought first to have a good will, and only afterward great power.

Moreover, the good will must be cleansed of vices. If a person is overcome by those vices, he is overcome so that he wills evil; and how then will his will still be good? It is therefore to be desired that power now be granted—but power against the vices on account of which those who are powerful do not wish to be powerful for the purpose of conquering them, but wish to be powerful for the purpose of conquering other people. Why is this, except that those who are truly defeated may falsely conquer, and be victors not in truth but in opinion?

Let the prudent person wish to be prudent; let him wish to be courageous, temperate, and just. And, so that he may truly be able to be these things, let him clearly desire and seek power: let him be powerful in himself, and, in a marvelous way, against himself for his own sake. As for the other things he rightly wills but cannot yet possess, such as immortality and true and complete happiness, let him not cease to desire them, but await them patiently.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 18. Christ’s undeserved death freed those subject to death

What, then, is the justice by which the devil was conquered? What justice except the justice of Jesus Christ? And how was he conquered? Because, although he found nothing in Christ deserving death, he nevertheless killed him. It is altogether just that the debtors whom the devil held should be released, if they believe in the one whom he killed without any debt of his own.

This is what is meant when we are said to be justified by Christ’s blood (Romans 5:9). For that innocent blood was poured out for the remission of our sins. Hence, in the Psalms, Christ says that he is “free among the dead” (Psalm 87:6). For he alone who died was free from the debt of death.

For this reason he says in another Psalm: “Then I restored what I had not stolen” (Psalm 68:5). By “theft” he wished sin to be understood, since sin is something usurped against what is permitted. Hence, through the mouth of his own flesh, as we read in the Gospel, he says: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me”—that is, no sin—“but so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, arise, let us go from here” (John 14:30–31).

From there he proceeds to his passion, so that on behalf of us debtors he might pay what he himself did not owe. Would the devil have been conquered by this most equitable right if Christ had chosen to deal with him by power rather than by justice? But he set aside what he could do in order first to do what he ought to do.

For this reason it was necessary that he be both human and divine. If he were not human, he could not be killed; if he were not God, we would think that he had not wished to do what he could do, but had been unable to do what he wished. We would not think that he had preferred justice to power, but that he had lacked power.

Now, because he was human, he suffered human things for us. But if he had not wished to suffer them, he could not have suffered them, because he was also God [Note: [Col. 1028] The manuscripts read *noluisset*, “had not wished.” The printed editions read *voluisset*, “had wished.”]. Thus justice became more worthy of love in his humility, because such was the power of his divinity that, if he had not wished to do so, he could have avoided enduring humility. And so, through one who died while possessing such power, justice was commended and power promised to us mortal and powerless human beings.

Of these two things, he accomplished one by dying and the other by rising again. For what is more just than to go forth on behalf of justice even to death on a cross? And what is more powerful than to rise from the dead and ascend into heaven with the very flesh in which he was killed?

Thus justice first, and power afterward, conquered the devil: justice, because Christ had no sin and was killed by the devil with the greatest injustice; power, because, having died, he came back to life, never afterward to die (Romans 6:9).

The devil would have been conquered by power even if he had not been able to kill Christ. Yet it is a greater display of power to conquer death by rising again than to avoid it by remaining alive. But there is another reason why we are justified by Christ’s blood, when we are rescued from the devil’s power through the remission of sins. This belongs to the fact that the devil is conquered by Christ through justice, not through power.

Christ was crucified from the weakness he assumed in mortal flesh, not from immortal power. Yet the Apostle says of this weakness: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

## CHAPTER XV

### 19. On the same subject

It is not difficult to see that the devil was conquered when the one whom he killed rose again. It is greater, and more profound to understand, to see that the devil was conquered when he seemed to himself to have conquered—that is, when Christ was killed.

For that blood, since it belonged to one who had absolutely no sin, was poured out for the remission of our sins. The devil rightly held those whom he had bound as guilty of sin under the condition of death; therefore it was right that he should release them through the one whom, though guilty of no sin, he undeservedly subjected to the punishment of death.

By this justice the strong man was conquered, and by this bond he was bound, so that his possessions might be taken away (Mark 3:27)—those who, together with him and his angels, had been vessels of wrath in his possession, and might be transformed into vessels of mercy (Romans 9:22–23).

The Apostle Paul recounts these words of our Lord Jesus Christ, spoken from heaven to him when he was first called. Among the other things he heard, he says that this also was spoken to him:

> For this purpose I appeared to you, to appoint you as a servant and witness of the things that you see from me, and of those in which I also go before you, delivering you from the people and from the nations, to which I am sending you to open the eyes of the blind, so that they may turn from darkness and from the power of Satan to God, in order that they may receive the remission of sins, and the lot that is among the saints, and faith that is in me.  
> (Acts 26:16–18)

For this reason the same Apostle, exhorting believers to give thanks to God the Father, says:

> He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the remission of sins.  
> (Colossians 1:13–14)

In this redemption, Christ’s blood was given as a price on our behalf. When the devil received it, he was not enriched but bound, so that we might be released from his bonds. He was not to drag any of those whom Christ, free from every debt, had redeemed by the undeserved shedding of his blood, still entangled in the nets of sins, along with himself to the destruction of the second and eternal death (Revelation 21:8).

Those who belong to Christ, foreknown, predestined, and chosen before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), would die only to this extent: Christ himself died for them with the death of the flesh alone, not of the spirit.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 20. The remnants of death and the evils of this age are turned to the good of the elect. Why Christ’s death was appropriately chosen, so that we might be justified by his blood. What the wrath of God is

Although death itself in the flesh also came originally from the sin of the first human being, its good use nevertheless produced the most glorious martyrs. Therefore not only death itself, but all the evils of this age—the sufferings and labors of human beings—which arise from the consequences of sins, and especially of original sin, from which life itself has also been made subject to the bond of death, nevertheless ought to remain even after sins have been forgiven. Human beings must contend with them for the sake of truth, and through them the virtue of the faithful must be exercised.

Thus the new human being, through the New Testament, is prepared for the new age amid the evils of this age: wisely enduring the misery deserved by this condemned life, prudently rejoicing because it will end, and faithfully and patiently awaiting the blessedness that the liberated life of the future will possess without end.

For the devil, cast out from dominion over and from the hearts of the faithful—over whose condemnation and unbelief he once reigned, although he too had been condemned—is permitted to oppose them only to the extent that he knows is beneficial for them, according to the condition of this mortality. Of this the sacred Scriptures resound through the mouth of the Apostle:

> God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.  
> (1 Corinthians 10:13)

These evils, which the faithful devoutly endure, are beneficial either for correcting sins, or for exercising and testing justice, or for demonstrating the misery of this life, so that the life in which there will be true and perpetual blessedness may be desired more ardently and sought more earnestly.

These things, however, are reserved for those of whom the Apostle says:

> We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed [Note: [Col. 1030] The printed editions add *fieri*, “to become”; it is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.] to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.

None of these predestined people will perish with the devil [Note: [Col. 1030] The manuscripts read *perit*, “perishes,” rather than the printed *peribit*, “will perish.”]; none will remain under the devil’s power until death.

Then follows what I already quoted above (Chapter 11):

> What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also give us all things with him?  
> (Romans 8:28–32)

### 21. Why, then, should Christ’s death not have taken place?

Indeed, why should it not have been chosen above the countless other ways by which the Almighty could have used to free us? In it, nothing of his divinity was diminished or changed; and such great benefit was bestowed upon human beings through the humanity he assumed that a temporal and undeserved death, inflicted upon the eternal Son of God and likewise the Son of Man, might free them from the eternal death they deserved.

The devil held our sins, and through them rightly fixed us in death. Christ, who had no sins of his own, dismissed them, and was undeservedly led by the devil to death. That blood was of such value that the devil ought not to have been able to hold in the eternal death they deserved anyone clothed with Christ, since he had killed Christ, though Christ did not deserve death, even if only for a time.

“God demonstrates his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having now been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him.”

“Having been justified,” he says, “by his blood”: plainly justified in that we have been freed from all sins. We have been freed from all sins because the Son of God, who had none, was killed for us.

Therefore we shall be saved through him from wrath—namely, from the wrath of God, which is nothing other than just punishment. For God’s wrath is not, as it is in a human being, a disturbance of the mind. Rather, God’s wrath is that of the one to whom Holy Scripture says elsewhere: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wisdom 12:18).

If, then, just divine punishment has received this name, what else is God’s reconciliation rightly understood to be except the ending of such wrath? We were not enemies of God except in the sense in which sins are enemies of justice. When those sins are forgiven, such enmity ends, and those whom God himself justifies are reconciled to the just one [Note: [Col. 1031] The manuscripts read *justo*, “to the just one.” The printed editions have *Deo*, “to God.”].

Yet he loved them even as enemies, since he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all while we were still enemies.

The Apostle therefore rightly continues:

> For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son—which brought about that remission of sins—much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.

We who were reconciled through his death shall be saved by his life. Who could doubt that he will give his life to his friends, for whom, as enemies, he gave his death?

“Not only this,” he says, “but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.”

Not only, he says, shall we be saved, but we also glory—not in ourselves, but in God; not through ourselves, but through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation, in accordance with what was discussed above.

Then the Apostle adds:

> Therefore, just as through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.  
> (Romans 5:8–12)

And so forth, where he discusses at greater length the two human beings: the one, the first Adam, through whose sin and death we, his descendants, have been bound as though by hereditary evils; the other, the second Adam, who is not merely human but also God, through whom we have been freed from both inherited and personal debts, since he paid on our behalf what he did not owe.

Accordingly, since on account of that one man the devil held all who were generated through his corrupted carnal desire, it is just that on account of this one man he release all who have been spiritually regenerated through his immaculate grace.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 22. Other benefits of the incarnation

There are many other things concerning Christ’s incarnation—which displeases the proud—that ought beneficially to be observed and considered. One of them is that humanity was shown what place it has among the things God created. Human nature could be joined to God in such a way that, from two substances, one person would be formed, and thus already from three—God, soul, and flesh.

Therefore those proud and wicked spirits who insert themselves between God and humanity, as though to deceive rather than to help, should not dare to put themselves above human beings merely because they do not possess flesh. And especially because the Son of God deigned to die in that flesh, they should not persuade human beings to worship them as gods merely because they appear to be immortal.

Moreover, this was done so that God’s grace might be commended to us without any preceding merits in the man Christ. For Christ himself did not attain, through any preceding merits, such union with the true God that he became, together with him, one person and the Son of God. Rather, from the moment he began to be human, he was also God. Hence it is said: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14).

There is also this benefit: the pride of human beings, which is the chief obstacle to their clinging to God, could be rebuked and healed by such great humility on God’s part.

Humanity also learns how far it has withdrawn from God and what value this has for its healing through sorrow, when it returns through such a Mediator—one who, as God, comes to the aid of human beings through his divinity, and, as human, meets them in their weakness.

What greater example of obedience could be offered to us, who perished through disobedience, than God the Son obeying God the Father even to death on a cross (Philippians 2:8)? And where could the reward of that obedience be shown better [Note: [Col. 1032] Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read: “Where could the reward of such great obedience be shown better?” The manuscript reading is retained here.] than in the flesh of so great a Mediator, which rose again to eternal life?

It also belonged to the justice and goodness of the Creator that the devil should be conquered through the same rational creature over whom he rejoiced that he had triumphed, and that he should be conquered by one who came from the very race which, through its corrupted origin, he held universally.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 23. Why the Son of God assumed humanity from Adam’s race and from a virgin

God could certainly have assumed humanity from elsewhere, so that there would be a Mediator between God and human beings, rather than from the race of that Adam who bound the human race through his sin—just as God created the first human being whom he made without deriving him from anyone’s race.

He could therefore have created another human being in this way, or in any other way he wished, through whom the conqueror of the first would be conquered. But God judged it better to assume humanity from the very race that had been conquered [Note: [Col. 1032] Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read the passage as *assumeret*, “that he might assume,” rather than the manuscript reading *assumere*, “to assume.”], so that through him he might conquer the enemy of the human race.

Yet he assumed humanity from a virgin, whose conception was preceded by the spirit, not by the flesh; by faith, not by lust (Luke 1:26–38). Carnal desire, through which the others who contract original sin are conceived and generated, played no part. Virginity was made fruitful through believing, not through intercourse, so that what was born from the stock of the first human being might derive from him the origin of its race, but not of its guilt.

For there was born not a nature corrupted by the contagion of transgression, but the sole remedy for all such corruptions. A human being was born, I say, who had no sin at all and would never have any, through whom those who could not be born without sin would be reborn and freed from sin.

Although married chastity makes good use of carnal desire, which is present in the genital organs, it nevertheless has involuntary movements. These show either that such desire could not have existed at all in paradise before sin, or that, if it did exist, it was not of such a kind that it ever resisted the will.

Now we experience it as being of such a kind that, resisting the law of the mind, it imposes urges toward intercourse even when there is no reason for procreation. If one yields to it, it is satisfied through sin; if one does not yield, it is restrained through dissent. Who could doubt that these two things were absent from paradise before sin? For that innocence did not produce anything dishonorable, and that blessedness did not endure anything disturbed.

Therefore this carnal desire ought not to have been present there at all when the virgin’s offspring was conceived—an offspring in whom the author of death would find nothing deserving death, yet would kill him, and by whose death he would himself be conquered by the Author of life.

The one who had conquered the first Adam and held the human race was conquered by the second Adam and lost the Christian race, which was liberated from human guilt through one who was not guilty, although he belonged to the human race. Thus the deceiver was conquered by the race which he had conquered through guilt.

This happened so that humanity might not exalt itself, but that “the one who boasts might boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17). For the one who was conquered was merely human, and he was conquered because, in his pride, he desired to be God. But the one who conquered was both human and God. For this reason he conquered in such a way, born of a virgin: as God, he ruled that human being humbly—not as he rules other holy people, but as he bore that humanity in himself.

These great gifts of God, and whatever other gifts there are concerning this matter which it would now take too long to ask about and discuss, would not exist unless “the Word became flesh.”

## CHAPTER XIX

### 24. What belongs to knowledge and what belongs to wisdom in the incarnate Word

All these things which the Word made flesh temporarily and locally did and endured for us belong, according to the distinction we have undertaken to demonstrate, to knowledge, not to wisdom.

The Word, however, exists without time and without place; he is coeternal with the Father and wholly present everywhere. If anyone can speak truthfully about him, to the extent that he can, that speech will belong to wisdom.

Thus the Word made flesh, Christ Jesus, possesses both the treasures of wisdom and of knowledge. For, writing to the Colossians, the Apostle says:

> I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you, for those who are in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh, so that their hearts may be comforted, joined together in love, and enriched with all the fullness of understanding, for knowledge of the mystery of God, which is Christ Jesus, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.  
> (Colossians 2:1–3)

Who can know how well the Apostle knew these treasures, how far he had penetrated into them, and how far he had advanced in them?

Nevertheless, according to what is written, “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:7–8). If these two things are so distinct that wisdom is attributed to divine matters and knowledge to human matters, I recognize both in Christ, and every faithful person recognizes them with me.

When I read, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” in “the Word” I understand the true Son of God; in “the flesh” I recognize the true son of a human being; and I understand both joined together into one person of God and human being through an ineffable generosity of grace.

For this reason the text continues: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

If we refer grace to knowledge and truth to wisdom, I think that we do not depart from the distinction between these two things which we have commended. For in things that arise in time, the supreme grace is that humanity has been joined to God in the unity of one person. In eternal things, the supreme truth is rightly attributed to the Word of God.

But the fact that this same one, the only-begotten from the Father, is “full of grace and truth” was brought about so that he might be the same one in the things accomplished temporally for us, through the same pure faith in whom we are cleansed, in order that we may contemplate him steadfastly in eternal things.

Those eminent philosophers among the nations who were able to perceive the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, nevertheless philosophized without a Mediator—that is, without the human being Christ. They neither believed that he would come, as the Prophets proclaimed, nor that he had come, as the Apostles proclaimed. Thus they “held the truth in unrighteousness,” as was said of them.

For, being established in these lowest regions of reality, they could do nothing but seek certain intermediaries through which they might reach the lofty things they had understood. And so they fell in with deceptive demons, through whom they exchanged “the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of a corruptible human being, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Romans 1:20, 18, 23).

They established or worshiped idols in forms such as these.

Therefore Christ is our knowledge, and Christ is also our wisdom. He implants in us faith concerning temporal things; he displays to us the truth concerning eternal things. Through him we proceed to him; through knowledge we advance toward wisdom. Yet we do not depart from the one and same Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

For now we are speaking about knowledge; later we shall speak about wisdom, to the extent that he himself grants it.

Nor should we understand these two things in such a way that it would be impermissible to call either that wisdom which exists in human matters “wisdom,” or that knowledge which exists in divine matters “knowledge.” In the broader customary use of speech, both may be called wisdom and both knowledge.

Nevertheless, the Apostle would by no means have written, “To one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge,” unless these things were also properly designated by their individual names. It is their distinction that we are now discussing.

## CHAPTER XX

### 25. What has been accomplished in this book. How we have gradually arrived at a kind of trinity found in active knowledge and true faith

Let us now see what this extended discourse has accomplished, what it has gathered together, and where it has arrived.

Everyone wishes to be happy, but not everyone possesses the faith through which, by cleansing the heart, one reaches happiness. Thus, through the faith that not everyone desires, one must strive toward the happiness that no one can fail to desire.

Everyone sees within his own heart that he wishes to be happy. Such is the agreement of human nature on this matter that a person is not deceived when he infers from his own soul what another person desires in his soul. Indeed, we all know that everyone wishes this.

Many, however, despair of being able to be immortal, although no one can be happy in any other way than by possessing what everyone wishes for—that is, happiness [Note: [Col. 1034] Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read: “Although, in what everyone wishes for, no one can be happy in any other way.” The manuscript reading is retained here.]. Yet they would also wish to be immortal if they could. But because they do not believe that they can, they do not live in such a way that they can.

Faith is therefore necessary if we are to attain blessedness with all the goods of human nature—that is, of both soul and body.

This same faith holds that blessedness is defined in Christ, who rose in the flesh from the dead, never again to die; and that no one is freed from the devil’s dominion except through him, by the remission of sins. It also holds that life under the devil’s power must be miserable and perpetual, and should rather be called death than life.

I have discussed this faith in this book as best I could, given the time available, although I also said much about it in the fourth book of this work (Chapters 19–21). There, however, I did so for one purpose, and here for another. There I wished to show why and how Christ was sent by the Father in the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4), for the sake of those who say that the one who sent and the one who was sent cannot be equal in nature. Here I discuss it in order to distinguish active knowledge from contemplative wisdom.

### 26. The trinity found in faith and in the inner human being

It pleased us, as though ascending step by step, to seek in each of the two within the inner human being a certain trinity of its own kind, just as earlier we sought one in the outer human being. In this way, according to our capacity—if indeed we are capable even of this—we may approach, with a mind more practiced in these lower things, the Trinity which is God, so as to contemplate it at least “in a mirror and enigmatically” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Suppose someone commits the words of this faith to memory through sounds alone, without knowing what they signify, as those who do not know Greek often memorize Greek words, or as those who are similarly ignorant of Latin or of any other language memorize words in it. Does this person not possess a certain trinity in his mind?

The sounds of the words are in his memory even when he is not thinking about them; from memory the focus of recollection is formed when he thinks about them; and the will of the person remembering and thinking joins the two together.

Yet we would by no means say that such a person, when doing this, is acting according to the trinity of the inner human being, but rather according to that of the outer human being. For he remembers only what belongs to the bodily sense called hearing, and, whenever and to whatever extent he wishes, he considers it; and in such thought he turns over images of nothing other than bodily things, namely sounds.

If, however, he retains and recalls what those words signify, he is indeed doing something belonging to the inner human being. But he is not yet to be said or thought to live according to the trinity of the inner human being if he does not love the things that are proclaimed, commanded, and promised there.

He may retain and consider them even in order to judge them false and attempt to refute them. That will of his, therefore, which joins together what was held in memory and what has been impressed from memory into the focus of thought, does indeed complete a certain trinity, since it is itself the third element. But one does not live according to it when the things being considered do not please one because they are regarded as false.

When those things are believed to be true, and the things there declared worthy of love are loved, one is already living according to the trinity of the inner human being. For everyone lives according to what he loves.

But how can things be loved that are unknown, and only believed? This question was already treated in the earlier books (Book 8, Chapters 8 and following, and Book 18, Chapter 1 and elsewhere). It was discovered that no one loves what he entirely does not know; rather, things that are unknown are said to be loved insofar as they are loved from among things that are known.

We now close this book by recalling that “the just person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17), and that this faith “works through love” (Galatians 5:6). Thus even the virtues by which one lives prudently, courageously, temperately, and justly are all referred to this same faith; for otherwise they could not be true virtues.

Yet in this life they are not so powerful that there is never a need for the forgiveness of whatever sins may occur here. Such forgiveness comes only through the one who, by his blood, conquered the prince of sins.

From this faith and such a life, whatever perceptions exist in the mind of a faithful person, when they are held in memory, examined through recollection, and approved by the will, produce a certain trinity of their own kind.

But the image of God, about which we shall speak later with his help, is not yet found in this trinity. This will appear more clearly when it has been shown where that image is found. Let the reader await this in the future volume.

# BOOK FOURTEEN

On the true wisdom of humanity. It demonstrates the image of God, which is the human being according to the mind. It places this image not properly in passing things—such as memory, understanding, and love, whether of temporal faith itself or of the mind turned toward itself—but in enduring realities. It teaches that the image is perfected when the mind is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created humanity in his own image, and thus perceives wisdom, where there is contemplation of eternal things.

[Col. 1035]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. What wisdom is to be discussed here. The origin of the name “philosopher.” What has already been said about the distinction between knowledge and wisdom

We must now discuss wisdom—not the wisdom of God, who is unquestionably God; for his only-begotten Son is called the Wisdom of God (Sirach 24:5; 1 Corinthians 1:24)—but human wisdom, which is nevertheless true wisdom according to God and is his true and principal worship. This worship is called by one word in Greek, *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια).

As we have already mentioned, our own writers, wishing also to translate it with a single word, have called it *piety*, although among the Greeks piety is more commonly called *eusebeia* (εὐσέβεια). Since *theosebeia* cannot be perfectly translated by one word, it is better translated by two, so that it may rather be called “the worship of God.”

That this is human wisdom, as we have already stated in the twelfth book of this work (Chapter 14), is demonstrated by the authority of Holy Scripture. In the Book of God’s servant Job, we read that God’s wisdom said to humanity:

> Behold, piety is wisdom; but to abstain from evils is knowledge.  
> (Job 28:28)

Some have translated the Greek *epistēmē* (ἐπιστήμη) as “discipline,” a word that certainly derives its name from learning and therefore can also be called knowledge. For everything is learned in order that it may be known.

Although, in another sense, the term *discipline* is commonly used for the evils that a person suffers because of his sins, so that he may be corrected. Hence the statement in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> What son is there whom his father does not discipline?

And more clearly in the same epistle:

> No discipline for the present seems to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of justice to those who have been trained by it.  
> (Hebrews 12:7, 11)

God himself, then, is supreme wisdom; but the worship of God is the wisdom of humanity, which we are now discussing.

For “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). In accordance with this wisdom, therefore, which is the worship of God, Holy Scripture says:

> The multitude of the wise is the health of the world.  
> (Wisdom 6:26)

2. But if it is the mark of the wise to discuss wisdom, what shall we do? Shall we dare to profess wisdom, lest our discussion of it be impudent? Shall we not be frightened by the example of Pythagoras? Since he had not dared to profess himself wise [Note: [Col. 1037] The printed editions read *wisdom*. The manuscripts read *wise*.], he replied that he was rather a philosopher—that is, a lover of wisdom. From him that name arose, and thereafter it pleased his successors so much that, however outstanding anyone might seem either to himself or to others in learning concerning matters belonging to wisdom, he was called only a philosopher.

Or did no one among such men dare to profess himself wise because they thought that a wise person was without any sin? Our Scripture does not say this, for it says: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9:8). Clearly, he judges the person to have sin whom he considers worthy of reproof.

But even so, I do not dare to profess myself wise. It is enough for me that even they cannot deny that philosophers—that is, lovers of wisdom—also discuss wisdom. For those who professed themselves lovers of wisdom rather than wise men did not refrain from doing this.

3. In discussing wisdom, they defined it as follows: “Wisdom is knowledge of human and divine things.” Accordingly, in the preceding book I too did not fail to say that knowledge of both kinds of things—that is, divine and human things—may be called both wisdom and knowledge (Book XIII, chapters 1 and 19).

Yet according to the distinction made by the Apostle, “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (1 Cor. 12:8), this definition must be divided, so that knowledge of divine things is properly called wisdom, while knowledge of human things properly retains the name “knowledge.” I discussed this in the thirteenth book—not assigning to this knowledge everything that human beings can know about human affairs, where there is a great deal of superfluous vanity and harmful curiosity, but only that by which the most salutary faith, which leads to true blessedness, is generated, nourished, defended, and strengthened. Many of the faithful do not possess this knowledge, although they possess faith itself in abundance.

For it is one thing merely to know what a human being ought to believe in order to attain the blessed life, which is eternal and nothing else; it is another to know how this very belief both assists the devout and is defended against the impious. The Apostle seems to call the latter by the proper name “knowledge.”

When I was speaking earlier about this, I took particular care to commend faith, briefly distinguishing eternal things from temporal things, [Col. 1038] and discussing temporal things there; but I deferred eternal things to this book. I also showed that, although faith concerning eternal things is temporal and dwells temporally in the hearts of believers, it is nevertheless necessary for attaining those very eternal things (Book XIII, chapter 7).

I likewise argued that faith concerning temporal things—which the eternal One made and endured for our sake in the human being whom He assumed temporally and brought to eternity—contributes to the attainment of those same eternal things. I also argued that the virtues themselves, by which one lives prudently, courageously, temperately, and justly amid this temporal mortality, are not true virtues unless they are referred to that same faith, temporal though it is, which nevertheless leads to eternal things (ibid., chapter 20).

## CHAPTER II

### In retaining, contemplating, and loving temporal faith there is a certain trinity, but not yet properly the image of God

4. Therefore, since, as it is written, “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7), and since “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), although he lives according to the inner person, and although through that same temporal faith he strives toward truth and presses on toward eternal things, nevertheless, in retaining, contemplating, and loving that temporal faith there is not yet such a trinity that it should already be called the image of God. Otherwise it might seem to be established in temporal things, whereas it must be established in eternal things.

For when the human mind sees its faith—by which it believes what it does not see—it does not see anything everlasting. This will not always exist, since it will certainly cease to exist when that pilgrimage by which we are away from the Lord has ended, so that it is no longer necessary to walk by faith. Then that sight will take its place by which “we shall see face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). Just as now, though we do not see, we shall deserve to see because we believe, and shall rejoice that faith has led us to sight.

For faith will no longer exist by which unseen things are believed; there will instead be sight by which the things once believed are seen. Thus, even if we remember that this mortal life has passed, and recall in memory that we once believed things we did not see, this faith will be counted among past and completed things, not among present and everlasting realities. Consequently, this trinity, which now consists in the memory, contemplation, and love of that present and abiding faith, will then be found to have passed away and become past, not to remain.

From this it follows that, if this trinity is already the image of God, it must be regarded as existing not in things that always are, but in things that pass away.

## CHAPTER III

### The difficulty concerning what was just said is resolved

But far be it from us to suppose that, since the nature of the soul is immortal and, from the beginning when it was created, never thereafter ceases to exist, that which it possesses as its greatest good does not endure together with its immortality. What has been created in its nature better than the fact that it was made in the image of its Creator (Gen. 1:27)?

Therefore, the image of God must be sought not in the retention, contemplation, and love of faith—which will not exist forever—but in that which will exist forever, and which ought to be called the image of God.

5. But shall we investigate somewhat more carefully and deeply whether the matter is really so? It may be said that this trinity does not perish even when faith itself has passed away. For just as now we retain it in memory, perceive it in thought, and love it by the will, so then also, when we retain in memory that we once possessed it, we shall recall it, and shall join both of these by a third act of the will; and the same trinity will remain.

For if it leaves behind in us no kind of passing trace, surely we shall have nothing of it in our memory to which we may return when remembering it as past and joining these two things by a third act of attention: namely, what was in the memory without our thinking of it, and what is formed from it in thought.

But the person who says this does not distinguish between the trinity that exists now, when we retain, see, and love present faith in ourselves, and the trinity that will exist then, when we shall contemplate in recollection not faith itself but, as it were, its image-like trace stored in memory, and shall join these two things—namely, what was retained in memory and what is impressed from it upon the focus of the remembering mind—by a third act of the will.

To make this intelligible, let us take an example from bodily things, about which we spoke sufficiently in the eleventh book (chapter 2 and following). As we ascend from lower things to higher, or enter from outward things into inward things, we first find a trinity in the body that is seen, in the sight of the one who sees, which is formed when he sees it, and in the intention of the will that joins the two.

Let us establish a similar trinity when the faith that now exists in us is situated in our memory, as that body was situated in its place. From the faith in our memory the thought of the person remembering is formed, just as the sight of the observer was formed from that body. To these two, in order to complete the trinity, a third element is added: the will, which connects and joins the faith established in memory with a certain likeness of it impressed upon the contemplation of recollection. This is like the way in the bodily trinity of vision the intention of the will joins the form of the body that is seen with the impression produced in the sight of the one who sees.

Let us suppose, then, that the body being observed has perished and dissolved, and that nothing of it remains anywhere to which the sight may return in order to see it. Since an image of the bodily thing, now completed and past, remains in memory, from which the gaze of the person remembering is formed [Note: [Col. 1039] The manuscripts read “the gaze of the person thinking.”], and since these two are joined by a third act of the will, is this to be called the same trinity that existed when the appearance of the body situated in its place was being seen?

Certainly not; it is altogether another trinity. For, apart from the fact that the former was outward and the latter inward, the former was produced by the appearance of the present body, whereas the latter is produced by the image of the past.

So also in the matter with which we are now concerned, and for which we thought it appropriate to introduce that example: the faith that is now in our mind, like the body in its place, produces a certain trinity while it is retained, contemplated, and loved. But that trinity will not exist when this faith is no longer in the mind, just as that body is no longer in its place.

The trinity that will then exist, when we remember that faith was in us but is no longer in us, will plainly be another. For the trinity that exists now is produced by the thing itself, present and fixed in the mind of the believer; but the trinity that will then exist, [Col. 1040] will be produced by the image of the past thing left behind in the memory of the person remembering.

## CHAPTER IV

### The image of God must be sought in the immortality of the rational soul. How the trinity in the mind has been demonstrated

6. Neither, then, will that trinity which does not now exist be the image of God; nor is this present trinity the image of God, since it will not then exist. Rather, the image of the Creator is to be found in the human soul—that is, the rational or intellectual soul—which is immortally implanted in its immortality.

For the immortality of the soul is spoken of in a certain sense: the soul also has its death, when it lacks the blessed life, which ought to be called the soul’s true life. Yet it is called immortal because, whatever its life may be, even when it is most wretched, it never ceases to live.

Similarly, although reason or understanding is now dormant in it, now appears weak, and now great, the human soul is never anything other than rational and intellectual. Therefore, if it was made in the image of God in this respect—that it can use reason and understanding to understand and behold God—then, from the beginning when this great and wondrous nature began to exist, whether this image has become so worn that it is almost nonexistent, or whether it is obscure and disfigured, or whether it is bright and beautiful, it always exists.

Finally, in pity for the disfigurement of its dignity, divine Scripture says: “Although a human being walks in the image [Note: [Col. 1040] The printed editions read “in the image of God.” The word “God” is absent from the manuscripts.], yet he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasures and does not know for whom he will gather them” (Ps. 38:7).

It would not attribute vanity to the image of God unless it saw that the image had been made disfigured. Nor does it fail to show that this disfigurement is not powerful enough to remove what is an image, when it says: “Although a human being walks in the image.”

Accordingly, this statement may truthfully be pronounced in both directions: just as it is said, “Although a human being walks in the image, yet he is troubled in vain,” so it may also be said, “Although a human being is troubled in vain, yet he walks in the image.”

Although it is a great nature, it could nevertheless be corrupted, because it is not the highest nature. And although it could be corrupted because it is not the highest nature, nevertheless, because it is capable of the highest nature and can share in it, it is a great nature.

Let us therefore seek in this image of God a trinity of its own kind, with the help of the One who made us in his image. For we cannot investigate these matters profitably in any other way or discover anything according to the wisdom that comes from him.

But if the reader retains in memory and recalls what we said in the preceding books, especially the tenth, concerning the human soul or mind, or reviews it carefully in the places where it was written, he will not here require a longer discussion of the investigation of so great a matter.

7. Among other things, then, we said in the tenth book that the human mind knows itself (chapter 7). For the mind knows nothing so well as what is present to it, and nothing is more present to the mind than the mind itself. We also supplied other evidence, as much as seemed sufficient, by which this was proved with complete certainty.

## CHAPTER V

### Whether the mind of infants knows itself

What, then, are we to say about the mind of an infant, still so small [Col. 1041] and immersed in such great ignorance of things that the mind of an adult who knows anything recoils from the darkness of that mind?

Should we believe that it also knows itself, but that, being excessively intent upon those things which it has begun to perceive through the bodily senses with a pleasure all the greater because it is so new, it cannot be unaware of itself but cannot think of itself?

How intensely it is directed toward these sensible things outside can be inferred from this alone: it is so eager to drink in the light of day that, if someone careless or ignorant of what might result from it were to place a night-light where the infant lies, on the side toward which the eyes of the one lying down could be turned while the neck could not be bent, the infant’s gaze would not be removed from it. We know that some infants have consequently become cross-eyed, their eyes retaining the shape that habit has in some way impressed upon them while they were tender and soft.

In the same way, the souls of little children, insofar as that age permits, seem to contract their attention upon the other bodily senses, so that whatever disturbs or attracts them through the flesh is the only thing they vehemently avoid or desire. They do not think about their own interior selves, nor can they be admonished to do so, because they do not yet recognize the signs of the one admonishing them—among which words hold the chief place—and they are altogether ignorant of words as of other things.

But that not knowing oneself is one thing and not thinking of oneself another, we have already shown in the same book (Book 10, chapter 5).

8. Let us leave aside, then, this age, which cannot be questioned about what takes place within it, and of which we ourselves have largely forgotten. It will be enough for us here to be certain of this: when a human being is able to think about the nature of his own soul and to discover what is true, he will find it nowhere except within himself.

He will discover not something he did not know, but something about which he was not thinking. For what do we know if we do not know what exists in our mind, since we can know everything that we know only through the mind?

## CHAPTER VI

### How a certain trinity exists in the mind when it thinks of itself. What thought contributes to this trinity

The power of thought is nevertheless so great that the mind itself, in a certain way, does not place itself before its own sight except when it thinks of itself.
