Consequently, nothing is before the mind’s sight except that of which it is thinking. Thus the mind itself, by which whatever is thought is thought, cannot be before its own sight in any other way than by thinking of itself.

But how, when it does not think of itself, is it not before its own sight, when it can never exist without itself—as though the mind itself were one thing and its sight another? I cannot discover.

This may properly be said of the bodily eye: the eye itself is fixed in its place in the body, but its sight is directed toward things outside and extends even to the stars. The eye is not before its own sight, since it does not see itself except by means of a mirror placed before it, as we have already discussed (Book 10, chapter 3).

But this does not happen when the mind establishes itself before its own sight by thinking of itself. Does it therefore see one part of itself with another part when it beholds itself in thought, just as with one of our limbs—our eyes—we behold other limbs of ours that can be before our sight? What could be more absurd to say or conceive?

From where, then, is the mind taken away, if not from itself? And where is it placed before its own sight [Col. 1042] except before itself? It will not, therefore, be where it was when it was not before its own sight, because, when it was placed here, it was removed from there.

But if it has moved in order to be seen [Note: [Col. 1042] The printed editions read “will move.” The manuscripts more appropriately read “has moved.”], where will it remain in order to see? Is it doubled, as it were, so that it is both there and here—that is, both where it can see and where it can be seen—so that it is in itself as the seeing subject and before itself as the object seen?

Truth, when consulted, gives us none of these answers. For when we think in this way, we think only of imagined images of bodies. That the mind is not such a thing is certain to a few minds, by whom the truth concerning this matter can be consulted.

It remains, therefore, that its sight is something belonging to its nature, and that, when it thinks of itself, it is recalled to itself not as through spatial distance but by an incorporeal turning. When it does not think of itself, it is not indeed before its own sight, nor is its own gaze formed from it; nevertheless, it knows itself as though it were its own memory.

Just as someone skilled in many disciplines has the things he knows contained in his memory, and nothing of them is before his mind’s sight except what he is thinking about, while the rest are stored in a certain hidden knowledge called memory, so we commended the trinity by placing in memory that from which the gaze of the person thinking is formed, the formation itself as an image impressed from it, and that by which the two are joined—love or will.

When, therefore, the mind beholds itself in thought, it understands and recognizes itself; thus it begets this understanding and knowledge of itself. An incorporeal thing is seen when understood, and is known through understanding.

The mind does not, strictly speaking, beget this knowledge of itself when it beholds itself as understood in thought as though it had previously been unknown to itself. Rather, it was known to itself in the way that things contained in memory are known, even when they are not being thought of. We say that a person knows letters even when he is thinking about other matters, not about letters.

These two—the begetting and the begotten—are joined by a third element, love, which is nothing other than the will desiring or holding something for enjoyment. For this reason, we also thought that the trinity of the mind should be indicated by these three names: memory, understanding, and will.

9. But since, toward the end of the tenth book, we said that the mind always remembers itself, always understands itself, and always loves itself, although it does not always think of itself as distinct from those things that are not what it is, we must ask in what way understanding belongs to thought, while the knowledge of each thing that is present to the mind even when it is not being thought of is said to belong to memory alone.

For if this is so, the mind did not possess these three things in such a way that it remembered itself, understood itself, and loved itself. Rather, it remembered only itself, and afterward, when it began to think of itself, it then understood and loved itself.

## CHAPTER VII

### The matter is explained by an example. How the discussion was conducted for the assistance of readers

Let us therefore consider more carefully the example we introduced [Note: [Col. 1042] The Erasmus, Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions read *ut*, as do the manuscripts.], by which it was shown that not knowing a thing is one thing and not thinking about it another, and that [Col. 1043] a person may know something he is not thinking about when he is thinking about something else rather than about that thing.

Someone skilled in two or more disciplines knows one or another even when he is thinking about one of them and not thinking about the other or others. But can we correctly say: “This musician certainly knows music, but he does not now understand it because he is not thinking about it; he now understands geometry, because he is thinking about it”?

This statement is plainly absurd. What about the following? Suppose we say: “This musician certainly knows music, but he does not now love it, since he is not thinking about it; he now loves geometry, because he is thinking about geometry.” Is this not similarly absurd?

We rightly say: “This man whom you see discussing geometry is also a fully trained musician. He remembers his musical discipline, understands it, and loves it. But although he knows and loves it, he is not now thinking about it, because he is thinking about geometry, which he is discussing.”

From this we are reminded that, hidden within the mind, there are certain kinds of knowledge of certain things. These then proceed, in a certain way, into the middle and are established more openly before the mind’s sight when they are thought about.

For then the mind discovers that it remembers, understands, and loves itself, even with respect to what it was not thinking about when it was thinking about something else. But what we have not thought about for a long time, and what we cannot think about unless reminded, we somehow—by the same wondrous process, if it may be so described—know without knowing that we know.

Accordingly, the one who reminds another person rightly says to the person whom he reminds [Note: [Col. 1043] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “to whom” (*cui*) rather than “whom” (*quem*).]: “You know this, but you do not know that you know it. I shall remind you, and you will find that you know what you thought you did not know.”

The same is done by writings composed about these matters. The reader discovers by the guidance of reason that the things discussed are true—not merely believes them to be true because the author who wrote them says so, as happens when one reads history, but discovers them to be true within himself or in the very light of truth in the mind.

But whoever cannot contemplate these things even after being admonished is sunk more deeply in the great blindness of the heart and in the darkness of ignorance, and requires more wondrous divine assistance in order to reach true wisdom.

10. For this reason I wished to introduce some kind of demonstration concerning thought, by which it might be shown how, from the things contained in memory, the gaze of the person remembering is formed, and how something is begotten when a person thinks—something like what existed in him when, before thinking, he remembered.

This is more easily recognized because what is added in time can be distinguished, and because the parent precedes the offspring by an interval of time.

For if we turn to the inner memory of the mind, by which it remembers itself; the inner understanding, by which it understands itself; and the inner will, by which it loves itself—where these three are always together and have always been together from the moment they began to exist, whether they are thought about or not—then the image of that trinity will indeed seem to belong to memory alone.

But because the word cannot exist there without thought—for we think everything that we say, even by that inner word which belongs to no language of any people—this image is recognized rather in those three: memory [Col. 1044], understanding, and will.

By “understanding” here I mean the understanding by which we understand when thinking—that is, when, from the things that were present to memory but were not being thought about, our thought is formed. By “will,” or love, or affection, I mean that which joins this offspring to its parent and is, in a certain way, common to both [Note: [Col. 1044] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read “common to each.”].

For this reason, in the eleventh book I led the slowness of readers through outward sensible things seen by the eyes of the flesh. From there I entered with them into that power of the inner person by which it reasons about temporal things, while postponing discussion of the principal and governing power by which it contemplates eternal things [Note: [Col. 1044] The printed editions read “discussing.” Corrected from the manuscripts.].

I dealt with these matters in two books, distinguishing in the twelfth both powers—one superior and the other inferior, which ought to be subject to the superior. In the thirteenth book I discussed, with as much truth and brevity as I could, the function of the inferior power, which contains salutary knowledge of human affairs, so that in this temporal life we may do what will enable us to attain eternal life.

For although this matter is so manifold and extensive, and has been celebrated in many large discussions by many great authors, I compressed it into a single brief book, showing that even in it there is a trinity, though not yet one that ought to be called the image of God.

## CHAPTER VIII

### The trinity that is the image of God must now be sought in the principal part of the mind

11. We have now reached the discussion in which we have undertaken to consider the principal part of the human mind, by which it knows God or can know him, so that in it we may find the image of God.

Although the human mind is not of the same nature as God, the image of that nature—than which no nature is better—must nevertheless be sought and found in that part of us in which our own nature has nothing better.

But first the mind must be considered in itself, before it becomes a participant in God, and his image must be found in it. For we said that, although it has become worn and disfigured through losing participation in God, it nevertheless remains the image of God (above, chapter 4).

It is precisely in this respect that it is his image: it is capable of him and can participate in him. Such a great good cannot be understood [Note: [Col. 1044] The printed editions read “cannot be understood.” The manuscripts omit “understood.”] except through the fact that it is his image.

Behold, then: the mind remembers itself, understands itself, and loves itself. If we perceive this, we perceive a trinity—not yet God, certainly, but already the image of God.

Memory did not receive from outside what it was to retain, nor did the understanding find outside itself what it was to contemplate, as the bodily eye does. Nor did the will join these two outside itself, as it joins the form of a body with the impression formed from it in the gaze of the observer.

Nor, when thought turned toward it, did it find the image of something seen outside, as though that image had somehow been snatched away and stored in memory, with the gaze of the person remembering formed from it and a third act of the will joining the two. We showed that this occurs in those trinities found in bodily things or somehow drawn inward from bodies through bodily sensation; we discussed all these matters in the eleventh book (chapters 2 and following) [Col. 1045].

Nor is it like what occurred or appeared when we were discussing that knowledge established in the operations of the inner person and needing to be distinguished from wisdom. Things that are known are, as it were, introduced into the mind from elsewhere, whether through historical knowledge—facts and sayings that take place and pass away in time—or through things established in the nature of reality in their own places and regions; or through things arising in the human being that were not there before, whether taught by others or produced by one’s own thoughts, such as faith, which we commended at length in the thirteenth book, and the virtues, by which, if they are true virtues, one lives well in this mortality in order to live blessedly in that immortality promised by God.

These things, and others of the same kind, have their own order in time, in which the trinity of memory, vision, and love appeared to us more readily.

Some of them precede the knowledge of those who learn. They are knowable and, before they are known, generate their knowledge in learners. They exist either in their own places or in things that have passed away. Yet things that have passed away are not themselves present; rather, certain signs of past things remain, and through seeing or hearing these signs we learn that the things existed and have passed away.

These signs are situated either in places, such as monuments of the dead and anything similar; or in trustworthy writings, such as all history possessing serious and approved authority; or in the minds of those who already know these things. For they are already known to those people, and are surely knowable also to others, whose knowledge they preceded and who can come to know them when instructed by those to whom they are known.

All these things, when they are learned, produce a certain trinity: their form, which was knowable even before it was known; the knowledge of the learner added to it, which begins to exist when it is learned; and a third element, the will, which joins the two.

When they have been learned, another trinity arises as they are recalled, now within the mind itself. It consists of the images impressed in memory when they were being learned, the formation of thought when the gaze of the person remembering turns toward them, and the will, which as a third element joins these two.

But things that arise in the mind where they did not previously exist, such as faith and other things of this kind, although they seem to be introduced from elsewhere when teaching implants them, are not placed or accomplished outside, as are the things that are believed. Rather, they begin to exist entirely within the mind itself.

For faith is not the thing that is believed, but that by which it is believed; the thing is believed, while faith is contemplated.

Nevertheless, because faith begins to exist in a mind that already existed before it began to exist in that mind, it appears to be something added from outside. It will be counted among past things when, with the succession of sight, it ceases to exist; and now it produces one trinity through its presence—as it is retained, contemplated, and loved—and then it will produce another through a certain trace of itself that it leaves behind in memory as it passes away, as has already been said above.

## CHAPTER IX

### Whether justice and the other virtues cease in the future life

Whether the virtues by which one lives well in this mortality—since they too begin to exist in a mind that was previously without them, although it was nevertheless a mind—cease to exist when they have led us to [Col. 1046] eternal things is a matter on which there is some question.

Some have thought that they will cease. When this is said of the three virtues—prudence, courage, and temperance—there seems to be some point to it. Justice, however, is immortal, and will then be perfected in us rather than cease to exist.

Yet the great authority on eloquence, Tully, discussing all four virtues in the dialogue *Hortensius*, says:

“If, when we have departed from this life, we were permitted, as the stories relate, to spend immortal time in the Isles of the Blessed, what need would there be for eloquence, since no judgments would be held? Or even for the virtues themselves? For we would have no need of courage, since there would be no task, labor, or danger before us; nor of justice, since there would be nothing belonging to another that could be desired; nor of temperance, which would govern desires that did not exist; nor indeed of prudence, since no choice between good and evil would be proposed.

We would therefore be blessed in one thing alone: the knowledge of nature, and the understanding by which alone the life of the gods too is worthy of praise. From this it can be understood that all the rest belong to necessity, while this one thing belongs to the will.”

Thus that great orator, while praising philosophy, recalling what he had received from philosophers and explaining it splendidly and pleasantly, said that in this life alone—which we see to be full of troubles and errors—all four virtues are necessary. But none of them would be necessary after we had departed from this life, if we were permitted to live where people live in blessedness. Rather, good minds would be blessed by knowledge and understanding alone—that is, by contemplation of the nature than which nothing is better or more lovable.

This is the nature that created all the other natures and established them. If being subject to its rule belongs to justice, then justice is altogether immortal. It will not cease to exist in that blessedness, but will be such and so great that it cannot be more perfect or greater.

Perhaps the other three virtues will also exist in that happiness: prudence, without any danger of error; courage, without the burden of enduring evils; and temperance, without resistance to desires. Prudence will consist in preferring or equating no good with God; courage, in cleaving to him with the greatest firmness; temperance, in taking pleasure in nothing through any harmful deficiency.

But what justice now does in helping the miserable, what prudence does in guarding against ambushes, what courage does in enduring hardships, and what temperance does in restraining depraved pleasures will not exist there, where there will be no evil at all.

Consequently, these works of the virtues, which are necessary for this mortal life, just as faith is to which they must be referred, will be counted among past things. Now they produce one trinity, while we retain, contemplate, and love them as present; then they will produce another, when we discover that they are no longer present but were present, through certain traces of them that they will leave behind in memory as they pass away.

For there will also then be a trinity, when that trace, whatever it may be, is retained in memory, truly recognized, and these two things are joined by a third act of the will.

## CHAPTER X

### How a trinity is formed when the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself

13. In the knowledge of all the temporal things we have mentioned, certain knowable things [Col. 1047] precede knowledge by an interval of time. Such are sensible things that already existed in reality before they were known, or all the things known through history.

Other things begin to exist simultaneously with knowledge. For example, if something visible that previously did not exist at all comes into being before our eyes, it certainly does not precede our knowledge. Or if something makes a sound while a hearer is present, the sound and its hearing plainly begin and cease at the same time.

Nevertheless, whether knowable things that precede knowledge in time or things that begin to exist simultaneously with it generate knowledge, they are not generated by knowledge.

Once knowledge has been formed, when the things we have learned are reviewed in recollection from their place in memory, who does not see that the retention in memory precedes in time the vision in recollection, and that the joining of these two is accomplished by a third element, the will?

But this is not so in the mind. For the mind is not something added to itself, as though the very thing that was not had come from elsewhere to the mind that already was; nor is it something that, without coming from elsewhere, was born within itself—the thing that was not arising in what already was—as faith, which was not present, arises in the mind that already existed [Note: [Col. 1047] At this point the printed editions add: “as things that were not arise in the human being, whether through the teaching of others or through one’s own thoughts, such as faith and the virtues.” These words have been wrongly transferred here from Chapter VIII above, §11, col. 1045, lines 8–12.].

Nor, after knowing itself, does the mind see itself in recollection as though established in its own memory, as though it had not been there before it knew itself. For, from the moment it began to exist, it has never ceased to remember itself, never ceased to understand itself, and never ceased to love itself, as we have already shown.

Consequently, when it turns toward itself in thought, a trinity is formed in which the word can now also be understood. For the word is formed from thought itself [Note: [Col. 1047] This is the reading of many manuscripts. The printed editions read “from knowledge itself.”], with the will joining the two.

It is therefore here that the image we seek must be recognized most clearly.

## CHAPTER XI
### 14. Whether memory also concerns present things

But someone may say: “The memory by which the mind is said to remember itself is not memory, since it is always present to itself. For memory concerns past things, not present ones.” Indeed, when certain writers were discussing the virtues—including Tully [Cicero]—they divided prudence into these three: memory, understanding, and foresight. They assigned memory to past things, understanding to present things, and foresight to future matters; and foresight is not certain except to those who know the future beforehand—a gift not belonging to human beings unless it is given from above, as it is to the prophets. Hence Scripture, speaking of human beings, says: “The thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our foresight is uncertain” (Wis. IX, 14). [Note: Several manuscripts read “speaking” rather than “says.”]

Memory concerning past things, and understanding concerning present things, are indeed certain—but present things that are incorporeal. [Note: Am. [Amerbach], Er. [Erasmus], and most manuscripts read “corporeal.”] For corporeal things are present to the eyes as objects of bodily sight.

But whoever says that memory does not concern present things should consider how this was expressed in secular literature, where greater care was devoted to the integrity of the wording than to the truth of the matter:

> Nor did Ulysses suffer such things,  
> nor did the Ithacan, in so great a danger, forget himself.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.628–629.)

For when Virgil said that Ulysses had not forgotten himself, what else did he intend us to understand but that he remembered himself? Since he was present to himself, he could in no way have remembered himself unless memory pertained to present things. Therefore, just as memory is spoken of in relation to past things when it makes it possible for them to be recalled and remembered, so, without absurdity, memory may be spoken of in relation to a present reality—namely, the mind—for it is present to itself, so that it can be understood by its own thought, and so that both may be joined by love of itself. [Note: Almost the sole exception is the Louvain edition, which reads “by love” rather than “by the love of itself.”]

## CHAPTER XII

### 15. The Trinity in the mind is the image of God insofar as it remembers, understands, and loves God, which is wisdom

This trinity of the mind is therefore not the image of God merely because the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, but because it can also remember, understand, and love the one by whom it was made. When it does this, it itself becomes wise. If it does not, then—even when it remembers, understands, and loves itself—it is foolish.

Let it therefore remember its God, in whose image it was made, and understand and love him. To put it more briefly: let it worship the uncreated God, by whom it was made capable of receiving him and of sharing in him. Hence it is written: “Behold, the worship of God is wisdom” (Job XXVIII, 28). It will be wise not by its own light, but by participation in that supreme light; and where eternity is, there it will reign in blessedness.

This human wisdom is called wisdom in such a way that it is also God’s. For then it is true wisdom; if it is merely human, it is vain. Yet God is not wise in this way. He is not wise by participation in himself, as the mind is wise by participation in God.

In the same way, “the justice of God” is spoken of not only as that by which he himself is just, but also as that which he gives to human beings when he justifies the ungodly. Referring to certain people, the Apostle says: “For, being ignorant of God’s justice and seeking to establish their own justice, they were not subject to the justice of God” (Rom. X, 3). So too it may be said of certain people: “Being ignorant of God’s wisdom and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the wisdom of God.”

### 16. The uncreated nature, God, made all other natures and is superior to them

There is therefore an uncreated nature that made all other natures, great and small. It is without doubt superior to the natures it made, and consequently superior also to the rational and intellectual nature of which we are speaking—namely, the human mind, which was made in the image of the one who made it.

That superior nature is God. And indeed he is not far from any one of us, as the Apostle says, adding: “For in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII, 27–28). If he were speaking according to the body, this could also be understood of the bodily world. For in that world, according to the body, we live, move, and have our being. But this must be understood according to the mind, which was made in his image, in a higher way—one that is likewise not visible but intelligible.

For what is not in him, of whom it is divinely written: “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36)? If all things are in him, in what can those things that live live, and those things that move move, except in the one in whom they are?

Yet not everyone is with him in the manner expressed by the words: “I am always with you” (Ps. LXXII, 23). Nor is he with everyone in the manner in which we say: “The Lord be with you.” Great, therefore, is the misery of a human being who is not with the one without whom he cannot be.

For in him a person is, and undoubtedly is not without him; yet if that person does not remember him, understand him, and love him, he is not with him. But whatever someone completely forgets cannot, of course, be brought back to his attention.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 17. How one can forget and remember God

Let us take an example from visible things to illustrate this matter. Someone whom you do not recognize says to you, “You know me.” To remind you, he tells you where, when, and how you came to know him. If, after all the signs have been supplied by which you might be recalled to memory, you do not recognize him, then you have forgotten him so completely that all that knowledge has been entirely erased from your mind. Nothing remains except that you believe the person who tells you that you once knew him—or perhaps not even that, if the speaker does not appear trustworthy to you.

But if you remember him, you certainly return to your own memory, and in it you find that he had not been wholly erased by forgetfulness.

Let us return to the matter for which we introduced this example from human intercourse. The ninth Psalm says: “Let sinners be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God” (Ps. IX, 18). And the twenty-first Psalm says: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI, 28).

Those nations had not forgotten God in such a way that they could not remember him when he was brought to mind. By forgetting God—as though forgetting their own life—they had turned toward death, that is, toward hell. But when they were reminded, they turned to the Lord, as though coming back to life by remembering their own life, from which forgetfulness had held them away. [Note: In printed editions, after “which forgetfulness had taken from them,” there was added: “that is, of which they had been forgetful.”]

Likewise, in the ninety-third Psalm we read: “Understand now, you who are foolish among the people; and you fools, become wise at last. He who planted the ear, shall he not hear?” (Ps. XCIII, 8–9), and so forth. These words were spoken to those who, because they did not understand God, said foolish things about him.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 18. By rightly loving itself, the mind loves God; if it does not love God, it must be said to hate itself

Even the weak and erring mind always possesses memory, understanding, and love of itself. Let it turn to God, so that by remembering him, understanding him, and loving him, it may be blessed.

The divine writings contain many testimonies concerning the love of God. In them, these two points are also understood consecutively: no one loves what he does not remember, and no one loves what he utterly does not know. Hence the most famous and principal commandment is: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. VI, 5).

The human mind was created in such a way that it never fails to remember itself, never fails to understand itself, and never fails to love itself. But since someone who hates another seeks to harm that person, the human mind is not improperly said to hate itself when it harms itself.

In ignorance, it wills evil for itself, because it does not think that what it wills will harm it. Yet it does will evil for itself when it wills what harms it. Hence it is written: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6).

Whoever therefore knows how to love himself loves God. But whoever does not love God—even if he loves himself, as has been naturally implanted in him—is nevertheless not improperly said to hate himself, since he does what is contrary to himself and pursues himself as though he were his own enemy.

This is a dreadful error: although everyone wishes to benefit himself, many do nothing except what is most harmful to them. When the poet described a similar disease among dumb animals, he wrote:

> May the gods grant better things to the good—and that error to their enemies!  
> They tore apart their limbs with bare teeth.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* 3.513–514.)

Since that was a bodily disease, why did he call it an “error”? Because every animal is naturally inclined toward itself so that it may preserve itself as far as possible; yet this disease was such that they mangled their own limbs, whose preservation they desired.

When the mind loves God and, as has been said, consequently remembers and understands him, it is rightly commanded concerning its neighbor that it love the neighbor as itself. For it no longer loves itself perversely, but rightly, when it loves God. By participation in God, that image is not only an image; it is also renewed from its old condition, reformed from its deformity, and blessed from its misery.

Although the mind loves itself so much that, if it had to choose between itself and everything else it loves beneath itself, it would prefer to lose all those things rather than perish, nevertheless, by abandoning the one above it—in whom alone it could preserve its strength and enjoy his light, to whom the Psalm sings, “I will keep my strength for you” (Ps. LVIII, 10), and elsewhere, “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 6)—it becomes so weak and dark that it falls even from itself, through loves it cannot overcome and errors from which it does not see how to return.

Therefore, now repentant through God’s mercy, it cries out in the Psalms: “My strength has abandoned me, and the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII, 11).

### 19. The mind cannot lose its natural memory, understanding, and love of itself

Yet even amid such great evils of weakness and error, the mind could not lose its natural memory, understanding, and love of itself. For this reason it was rightly said, as I recalled above (chap. 4): “Although a human being walks in the image, yet he is troubled in vain. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” (Ps. XXXVIII, 7).

Why does he store up treasure, unless because his strength has abandoned him—the strength by which, if he possessed God, he would need nothing? And why does he not know for whom he will gather it, unless because the light of his eyes is not with him? Therefore he does not see what Truth says: “Fool, this night your soul is required of you; and these things that you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20).

Nevertheless, because even such a person walks in the image, and because the human mind possesses memory, understanding, and love of itself, suppose it were revealed to him that he could not possess both of two things, and that he were permitted to choose one while losing the other—either the treasures he had accumulated or his mind. Who could be so mindless as to prefer possessing treasures to possessing a mind?

Treasures can often overthrow the mind; but a mind that is not overthrown by treasures can live more easily and freely without any treasures. Who, moreover, could possess any treasures except through the mind?

If an infant, even one born extremely wealthy, is legally the owner of everything that belongs to him, yet possesses nothing because his mind lies dormant, how could anyone possess anything after losing his mind?

But why speak of treasures, when anyone, if such a choice were offered, would prefer to lack them rather than lack a mind? No one places them before, or even compares them with, the eyes of the body. Not merely a rare person, as with gold, but every human being possesses the sky through the eyes of the body; through the bodily eyes, each person possesses whatever he willingly sees.

Who, then, if he could not retain both and were compelled to lose one, would not prefer to lose his treasures rather than his eyes? And yet, if he were similarly asked whether he would prefer to lose his eyes or his mind, who would not see with his mind that he would prefer the eyes to the mind?

A mind without bodily eyes is human; bodily eyes without a mind are bestial. Who, moreover, would not prefer to be a human being blind in body rather than a seeing beast?

### 20. The mind loves itself even when weak and erring

I have said this so that even the slower of those to whose eyes or ears these writings may come might be reminded, however briefly, how much the mind loves itself even when weak and erring—loving and pursuing badly the things beneath it.

It could not love itself if it were entirely ignorant of itself, that is, if it did not remember itself; nor could it love itself if it did not understand itself. In this image of God it is so powerful that it can cling to the one whose image it is.

It has been ordered according to the order of natures, not of places, so that above it there is no one except him. Finally, when it has clung entirely to him, it will be one spirit with him. The Apostle attests to this when he says: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17).

The mind thus approaches participation in that nature, truth, and blessedness, but God does not thereby grow in his nature, truth, or blessedness. When it has happily clung to that nature, it will live immutably [Note: The manuscripts omit “it will live immutably”] and will see everything it sees as immutable.

Then, as divine Scripture promises it, “its desire will be satisfied with good things” (Ps. CII, 5)—with immutable good things, namely, the Trinity, its God, whose image it is. And, so that it may never again be violated, “his face will be in secret” [that is, it will be sheltered in the hiddenness of God] (Ps. XXX, 21), filled with such abundance of him that it will never delight in sinning.

But when it now sees itself, it does not see anything immutable.

## CHAPTER XV

### 21. Although the soul hopes for blessedness, it does not remember a lost blessedness, but remembers God and the rules of justice

The soul does not doubt this because it is miserable and desires to be blessed. Nor does it hope that this can happen for any other reason than that it is changeable. For if it were not changeable, it could no more become blessed from misery than it could become miserable from blessedness.

And what would have made it miserable under an omnipotent and good Lord except its own sin and the justice of its Lord? And what will make it blessed except its own merit and the reward of its Lord?

Yet its merit too is the grace of the one whose reward will be its blessedness. It cannot give itself the justice it has lost, because it does not possess it. It received that justice when the human being was created, and certainly lost it by sinning. It therefore receives justice, so that by it it may deserve to receive blessedness.

Hence the Apostle truthfully says to one who is beginning to grow proud of his own good, as though it were his own: “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

When it rightly remembers its Lord, after receiving his Spirit, it recognizes fully—for it learns this through an inward teaching—that it can rise only through his gratuitous favor, and that it could fall only through its own voluntary defect.

It does not, however, remember its own blessedness. That blessedness existed but no longer exists, and it has completely forgotten it; therefore it cannot be recalled. It believes trustworthy writings of its God, written through his prophet, which tell of the happiness of paradise and indicate, through historical tradition, the first good and evil of the human being.

But it does remember its Lord God. He always is; he neither was and is not, nor is and was not. Just as he will never not be, so he never was not. He is wholly everywhere. Therefore the soul “lives, moves, and has its being in him” (Acts XVII, 28), and for this reason it can remember him.

This is not because it remembers that it knew him in Adam, or somewhere else before the life of this body, or when it was first made to be placed in this body. It remembers none of these things at all; whatever may be true of them has been erased by forgetfulness.

Rather, it is recalled so that it may turn to the Lord, as to that light by which it was touched in some way even when it was turning away from him.

For this reason even the ungodly think about eternity, and rightly condemn and rightly praise many things in human conduct. By what rules do they judge these matters, unless by rules in which they see how each person ought to live, even though they themselves do not live in that way?

Where do they see those rules? Certainly not in their own nature, since they undoubtedly see them with the mind, while their minds are clearly changeable and whoever is able to see this also sees that the rules are immutable. Nor are they seen in the settled condition of their own minds, since those rules are rules of justice, while their minds are demonstrably unjust.

Where, then, are these rules written—rules in which anyone recognizes what is just and unjust, and sees that he ought to possess what he himself does not possess? Where are they written, unless in the book of that light which is called truth? From that light every just law is copied and transferred into the heart of the human being who acts justly—not by migrating, but as though by being stamped into it, just as an image passes from a ring into wax without leaving the ring.

The person who does not act justly but nevertheless sees what ought to be done is the one who turns away from that light, although he is still touched by it.

But the person who does not even see how one ought to live sins in a more excusable way, because he is not a transgressor of a known law. [Note: This is the reading of Am. [Amerbach], Er. [Erasmus], and several manuscripts. Louvain reads “unknown law.”] Yet even he is touched at times by the splendor of the truth that is present everywhere, when, after being admonished, he confesses.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 22. How the image of God is reformed in the human being

Those who, after being reminded, turn to the Lord from that deformity by which they had been conformed through worldly desires to this world are reformed by him. They hear the Apostle saying: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Rom. XII, 2), so that the image may begin to be reformed by the one by whom it was formed.

It cannot reform itself, just as it was able to deform itself. Elsewhere he also says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth” (Eph. IV, 23–24).

What he says—“created according to God”—is expressed elsewhere as “in the image of God” (Gen. I, 27). But by sinning it lost the justice and holiness of truth; therefore this image became deformed and discolored. It receives them again when it is reformed and renewed.

When he says “in the spirit of your mind,” he does not intend two things to be understood, as though the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind another. Rather, every mind is spirit, though not every spirit is mind.

For God is Spirit (John IV, 24), and he cannot be renewed because he cannot grow old. The human being also has a spirit that is not the mind; to it belong images resembling bodies. Concerning this the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” (I Cor. XIV, 14).

He says this when what is said is not understood, since it cannot be said unless images of bodily sounds anticipate the sound of the mouth through the thought of the spirit. [Note: Printed editions read “in the thought of the spirit”; the word “in” is absent from the manuscripts.]

The human soul is also called spirit. Hence we read in the Gospel: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John XIX, 30), signifying the death of the body, as the soul departed. [Note: Printed editions add after “as the soul departed”: “from the body.”]

Even the spirit of an animal is called spirit, as is stated most clearly in Solomon’s book, Ecclesiastes, where he says: “Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of human beings goes upward and the spirit of the animal goes downward into the earth?” (Eccl. III, 21).

Spirit is also called wind, which is plainly a corporeal thing. Hence the Psalm says: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm wind” (Ps. CXLVIII, 8).

Since, then, spirit is spoken of in so many ways, by “the spirit of the mind” he intended the spirit that is called mind.

The same Apostle also says: “In the putting off of the body of the flesh” (Col. II, 11). He did not intend two things to be understood, as though flesh were one thing and the body of flesh another. Rather, because “body” is the name of many things, none of which is flesh—for there are many heavenly bodies and earthly bodies apart from flesh—he said “the body of flesh,” meaning the body that is flesh.

So too, “the spirit of the mind” means the spirit that is mind.

Elsewhere he named the image even more plainly, commanding the same thing in other words: “Putting off,” he says, “the old human being with his acts, put on the new human being, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him” (Col. III, 9–10).

What is written there—“Put on the new human being who was created according to God”—is expressed here as: “Put on the new human being, who is renewed according to the image of the one who created him.” There he says “according to God”; here, “according to the image of the one who created him.” In place of what he there called “in the justice and holiness of truth,” he here says “in the knowledge of God.”

This renewal and reformation of the mind therefore takes place according to God, or according to the image of God. It is said to take place “according to God” so that it may not be thought to occur according to some other creature. It is said to take place “according to the image of God” so that it may be understood to occur in that which is the image of God—namely, in the mind.

We speak similarly when we say that someone who departs from the body as a faithful and just person is dead “according to the body,” not according to the spirit. What else do we mean by “dead according to the body” except dead in the body or with respect to the body, not dead in the soul or with respect to the soul?

Or if we say, “He is beautiful according to the body,” or “He is strong according to the body,” not according to the mind, what else does this mean than that he is beautiful or strong in body, not in mind? We speak in this way countless times.

We must not therefore understand “according to the image of the one who created him” as though it were some other image according to which he is renewed, rather than the very image that is being renewed.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 23. How the image of God in the mind is renewed until the likeness of God is perfected in blessedness

This renewal does not occur in one moment, at the moment of conversion, as the renewal that occurs in Baptism through the forgiveness of all sins takes place in a single moment. For not even the smallest sin remains unforgiven.

But just as it is one thing to be free from fevers and another to recover from the weakness caused by fevers, and just as it is one thing to remove an embedded weapon from the body and another to heal, by a second treatment, the wound caused by it, so the first cure is to remove the cause of the sickness, which is accomplished through the forgiveness of all sins; the second is to heal the sickness itself, which takes place gradually through progress in the renewal of this image.

These two things are indicated in the Psalm, where we read: “He who forgives all your iniquities”—which takes place in Baptism—and then: “He who heals all your diseases” (Ps. CII, 3), which takes place through daily advances as this image is renewed.

The Apostle spoke most clearly about this when he said: “Although our outward human being is being corrupted, the inward human being is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV, 16).

The inward human being is renewed in the knowledge of God, that is, in the justice and holiness of truth, as the apostolic testimonies I recalled shortly before make clear.

Therefore, being renewed day by day in the knowledge of God, in justice, and in the holiness of truth, the mind transfers its love from temporal things to eternal things, from visible things to intelligible things, and from bodily things to spiritual things. It diligently strives to restrain and diminish desire for the former and to bind itself by love to the latter.

It does this only insofar as it is helped by God. For God’s sentence is: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

When the last day of this life finds someone holding fast to the faith of the Mediator amid this progress and approach, he will be led to the God whom he worshiped and received by the holy angels, to be perfected by him. At the end of the age he will receive an incorruptible body, not for punishment but for glory.

In this image, the likeness of God will then be perfect, when the vision of God is perfect. Concerning this the Apostle Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

He also says: “With unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 18). This is what happens day by day to those who make good progress.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 24. Whether John’s statement concerns our future likeness to the Son of God, including bodily immortality

The Apostle John says: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2).

From this it is clear that the complete likeness to God will come about in this image of God when it has received the complete vision of God.

Nevertheless, this statement may also be understood, according to the Apostle John, as referring to the immortality of the body. In this respect too we shall be like God, but only like the Son, because in the Trinity he alone assumed a body, in which he died, rose again, and carried it to heaven.

This image is also called the image of the Son of God. In it we shall have, like him, an immortal body, made conformable to him in this respect—not to the image of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, but only to that of the Son, because of him alone it is read and held by the soundest faith: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14).

For this reason the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII, 29).

He is certainly the firstborn from the dead, according to the same Apostle (Col. I, 18). His flesh, sown in dishonor, rose in glory.

According to this image of the Son, to which we are conformed in body through immortality, we also do what the same Apostle says: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (I Cor. XV, 43, 49). Thus, just as we were mortal according to Adam, we firmly hold by true faith and certain hope that we shall be immortal according to Christ.

For now we can bear this same image—not yet in vision, but in faith; not yet in reality, but in hope. The Apostle was speaking of the resurrection of the body when he said these things.

## CHAPTER XIX

### 25. John should rather be understood as speaking of our perfect likeness to the Trinity in eternal life

But the image of which it was said, “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26)—since it does not say “according to my image” or “according to your image”—is, we believe, the image of the Trinity. To the extent that we have been able to investigate, we have understood the human being to have been made according to this image.

Therefore, it is rather according to this image that we should understand what the Apostle John says: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” For he also spoke of the one concerning whom he had said, “We are children of God” (I John III, 2).

The immortality of the flesh will be perfected at the moment of the resurrection of which the Apostle Paul says: “In the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (I Cor. XV, 52).

In that very twinkling of an eye, before the judgment, the spiritual body will rise in power, incorruption, and glory. It is now sown as an animal body in weakness, corruption, and dishonor.

But the image that is renewed in the spirit of the mind, in the knowledge of God—not outwardly but inwardly, day by day—will be perfected by the vision that will then be face to face after the judgment. Now it progresses through a mirror in an enigma (I Cor. XIII, 12).

It is with reference to this perfection that the statement must be understood: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

This gift will be given to us when it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. XXV, 34).

Then the ungodly will be removed so that he may not see the glory of the Lord (Isa. XXVI, 10), when those on the left will go into eternal punishment, while those on the right go into eternal life (Matt. XXV, 46).

This, as Truth says, is eternal life: “That they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

### 26. Contemplative wisdom and Cicero’s account of it

I think that this contemplative wisdom is properly called “wisdom” in the sacred writings and distinguished from knowledge. It is the wisdom, specifically, of the human being; and it does not belong to him except from the one by whose participation the rational and intellectual mind can truly become wise.

Cicero commends this wisdom at the end of his dialogue *Hortensius*:

> “For us, as we consider these matters day and night, sharpening our understanding—which is the edge of the mind—and taking care that it never become dull, that is, as we live in philosophy, there is great hope. If what we feel and understand is mortal and perishable, then, having completed our human duties, our setting will be pleasant to us, and our extinction—or, as it were, the repose of life—will not be burdensome. But if, as the ancient philosophers, and those greatest and most distinguished of them, held, we possess eternal and divine souls, then we must think that the more continuously these souls have remained in their proper course—that is, in reason and the desire to investigate—and the less they have mixed themselves with and entangled themselves in human vices and errors, the easier their ascent and return to heaven will be.”

Then, adding this conclusion and bringing his discourse to an end by repeating the argument, he says: [Note: The manuscripts read “repeating, and bringing the discourse to an end.”]

> “Therefore, to bring the speech to some conclusion: whether we wish to be peacefully extinguished after having lived in these pursuits, or, without delay, to move from this dwelling into another and considerably better one, all our effort and care must be devoted to these studies.”

Here I am amazed that a man of such great talent should promise a pleasant setting, after the completion of human duties, to human beings living in philosophy—which makes people blessed through the contemplation of truth—if what we feel and understand is mortal and perishable. It is as though that which we did not love, or rather which we hated intensely, should die and perish, so that its setting might be pleasant to us.

But he had not learned this from the philosophers whom he praises so highly. Rather, the opinion bore the influence of the New Academy, where he approved even of doubting matters that were entirely evident.

From the philosophers, however, as he himself admits—those greatest and most distinguished philosophers—he had received the doctrine that souls are eternal. Eternal souls are rightly stirred by this exhortation, so that when the end of this life arrives they may be found in their proper course: in reason and the desire to investigate, and less involved in and entangled with human vices and errors, so that their return to God may be easier.

But this course, established in the love and investigation of truth, is not sufficient for the miserable—that is, for all mortals who possess only this reason, without faith in the Mediator. I have taken care to demonstrate this as far as I could in the earlier books of this work, especially in the fourth and thirteenth.

# BOOK FIFTEEN

At the beginning, he briefly and summarily explains what was said in each of the preceding fourteen books. He shows that the discussion has finally reached the point at which the Trinity, which is God, is to be sought even in those eternal, incorporeal, and immutable realities in whose perfect contemplation blessed life is promised to us.

He shows here that this Trinity is seen by us “through a mirror and in an enigma,” insofar as it is seen through the image of God, which we are, and thus in an obscure likeness that is difficult to discern.

He likewise demonstrates that the generation of the divine Word from the word of our mind can be inferred and explained, though only with difficulty, because of the very great disparity observed between the two words; and that the procession of the Holy Spirit from the love joined to the will can in some measure be conjectured and explained.

[Col. 1057]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. God is above the mind

Because we wished to exercise the reader, through things that have been made, in knowing the one by whom they were made, we have now reached his image, which is the human being, specifically in that respect in which the human being surpasses the other animals: reason or understanding, and whatever else may be said of the rational or intellectual soul that belongs to the reality called the mind or soul.

By this name, some authors of the Latin language distinguish what is superior in the human being and absent in animals from the soul that is also present in animals, according to a particular usage of speech.

If, then, we seek something above this nature—and if we seek what is true—there is God: the nature, that is, which was not created but creates.

Whether this nature is a Trinity, we must now demonstrate, if possible, not only to those who believe by the authority of divine Scripture, but also to those who understand, by some form of reasoning.

Why I have said “if possible,” the matter itself will show more clearly once the discussion has begun.

## CHAPTER II
## 2. God, Incomprehensible, Must Always Be Sought. The Traces of the Trinity Are Not Sought in Creation Without Reason

For God himself, whom we seek, will, I hope, assist us, so that our labor may not be fruitless, and so that we may understand how it was said in the sacred Psalm: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice; seek the Lord, and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:3–4).

For what is always sought seems never to be found. And how will the heart of those who seek rejoice, rather than be saddened, if they are unable to find what they seek? For he does not say, “Let the heart of those who find rejoice,” but “of those who seek the Lord.” Yet the prophet Isaiah testifies that the Lord God can be found while he is being sought, when he says: “Seek the Lord, and as soon as you have found him, call upon him; and when he has drawn near to you, let the impious man abandon his ways, and the unrighteous man his thoughts” (Isa. 55:6–7).

If, then, what is sought can be found, why was it said, “Seek his face always”? Or must what has been found perhaps still be sought? For incomprehensible things must be sought in such a way that the person who has been able to discover how incomprehensible what he was seeking is does not think that he has discovered nothing.

Why, then, does he seek in this way, if he comprehends that what he seeks is incomprehensible? Is it not because one must not cease for as long as one makes progress in the very seeking of incomprehensible things, and the seeker becomes better and better as he seeks so great a good—which is sought in order to be found, and found in order to be sought? For it is sought so that it may be found more sweetly, and it is found so that it may be sought more eagerly.

In this sense we may understand what Wisdom is said to say in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still” (Ecclus. 24:29). They eat and drink because they find; and because they hunger and thirst, they continue to seek.

Faith seeks; understanding finds. Hence the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9). And again, understanding continues to seek the one whom it has found: “For God has looked down upon the sons of men,” as it is sung in the sacred Psalm, “to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 13:2). A human being, therefore, ought to be understanding for this purpose: that he may seek God.

## 3.

# Chapter III

## 4. A Brief Summary of All the Previous Books

We shall therefore have lingered sufficiently [Note: [Col. 1058] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “we have recalled.”] over those things which God made, so that through them he himself who made them might be known: “For his invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made, are seen from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1:20).

For this reason those who, from the good things that are seen, were unable to know the one who is, are reproved in the Book of Wisdom. They did not recognize the Craftsman by attending to his works, but considered either fire, or spirit, or swift air, or the circle of the stars, or the violent waters, or the lights of heaven to be gods, rulers of the world. If, indeed, delighted by their beauty, they considered these things gods, let them know how much better than they is their Sovereign; for the author of beauty created them. Or if they were amazed at their power and activity, let them understand from them how much stronger is the one who established them. “For from the greatness of the beauty of created things their Creator may correspondingly be seen” (Wis. 13:1–5).

I have set down these words from the Book of Wisdom so that none of the faithful may think that I have sought, pointlessly and without purpose, in creation for indications of that supreme Trinity through certain triads of its own kind, proceeding, as it were, by stages until I reached the human mind, in which I might seek indications of that supreme Trinity which we seek when we seek God.

### 4. What Has Been Said Briefly in All the Previous Books

But since the necessity of discussion and reasoning compelled us throughout fourteen books to say many things, all of which we are unable to survey together, so that we may refer them by swift thought to what we wish to grasp, I shall do what I can with the Lord’s help: whatever I brought to the knowledge of the reader by discussion in the individual volumes, I shall gather together briefly, removing the discussion itself, and shall set down, as if under a single view of the mind, not the manner in which each point was established, but the conclusions that were established. This is so that what follows may not be so far removed from what preceded that consideration of the latter causes forgetfulness of the former—or, if it does cause such forgetfulness, so that what has slipped away may quickly be recovered by rereading.

In the first book, the unity and supreme equality of that Trinity are shown according to the sacred Scriptures. In the second, third, and fourth books, the same subject is treated; but careful inquiry into the mission of the Son and of the Holy Spirit occupied three books. It was shown that the one who is sent is not for that reason lesser than the one who sends, because one sent and the other was sent, since the Trinity, which is equal in all respects, operates inseparably and equally in its nature, which is immutable, invisible, and present everywhere.

In the fifth book, for those who think that the Father and the Son do not have the same substance because they suppose that everything said of God is said according to substance, and therefore argue that, since begetting and being begotten, or being begotten and being unbegotten, are different, the substances must be different, it is demonstrated that not everything said of God is said according to substance. Thus “good” and “great,” and anything else said of him in relation to himself, are said according to substance; but things are also said relatively—that is, not in relation to himself, but in relation to something which he is not. Thus “Father” is said in relation to the Son, or “Lord” in relation to the creature that serves him. If something relative—that is, in relation to something which he is not—is said of him temporally, as in “You have become our refuge, Lord” (Ps. 89:1), nothing happens to him by which he is changed; rather, he remains entirely immutable in his nature or essence.

In the sixth book, the statement made by the apostolic mouth that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24) is discussed in such a way that the same question is deferred for more careful reconsideration: whether the one from whom Christ was begotten is not himself wisdom, but only the father of his wisdom, or whether wisdom begot wisdom. Whichever of these alternatives might be the case, the equality of the Trinity nevertheless became apparent in this book also: God is not triplicate, but Trinity; nor are the Father and the Son, as it were, something double in relation to the single Holy Spirit, since the three together are not more than any one of them.

It was also discussed how the statement of Hilary, bishop [Note: [Col. 1059] The Louvain edition alone reads “holy bishop.”], may be understood: “Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift.”

In the seventh book, the question that had been deferred is explained, so that God who begot the Son is shown to be not only the Father of his own power and wisdom, but himself also power and wisdom. The same is true of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, there are not three powers or three wisdoms together, but one power and one wisdom, just as there is one God and one essence.

Next, the question was raised how they are called “one essence, three persons,” or, by certain Greeks, “one essence, three substances.” It was found that this is said out of necessity of expression, so that they might be designated by one name when the question is asked what the three are whom we truly confess to be three: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

In the eighth book, with a rational account also supplied, it is made clear to those who understand that, in the substance of truth, the Father is not greater than the Son, nor are both together something greater than the Holy Spirit alone; nor are any two in that Trinity something greater than one; nor are all three together something greater than each individually.

Next, through the truth that is perceived by understanding, and through the supreme good from which every good derives, and through the justice on account of which a just soul is loved even by a soul that is not yet just, I urged the reader, as far as possible, to understand the nature that is not only incorporeal but also immutable—which is God. And through love, which is called God in the sacred Scriptures (1 John 4:16), the Trinity began, to some extent, to appear to those who understood: namely, the one who loves, what is loved, and love.

In the ninth book, the discussion reached the image of God, which is the human being according to the mind. In it a certain trinity is found: the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves both itself and its knowledge. These three are shown to be equal to one another and to be of one essence.

In the tenth book, this same subject was treated more carefully and subtly, and the discussion was brought to the point where a more evident trinity was found in the mind: memory, understanding, and will. But since it was also discovered that the mind could never exist in such a way that it did not remember itself, understand itself, and love itself—although it did not always think of itself—and that, when it did think of itself, it did not by that same thought distinguish itself from bodily things, the discussion of the Trinity whose image it is was deferred, so that a trinity might also be found in bodily appearances themselves and the reader’s attention might be exercised more distinctly in this matter.

In the eleventh book, therefore, the sense of sight was selected, so that what was discovered in it might also be recognized, without being stated, in the other four bodily senses. Thus the trinity of the outer person first appeared in things perceived externally: the body that is seen, the form impressed by it upon the visual faculty of the one who sees, and the intention of the will that joins the two together. But these three were shown to be neither equal to one another nor of one substance.

Then, in the mind itself, introduced as it were by things sensed externally, another trinity was found, in which the same three appeared to be of one substance: the bodily image that is in the memory, the formation that occurs when the mind’s attention turns toward it, and the intention of the will that joins the two together. But this trinity was found to belong to the outer person because it was introduced from bodies that are perceived externally.

In the twelfth book, wisdom was to be distinguished from knowledge, and in what is properly called knowledge, because it is lower, a certain trinity of its own kind was first to be sought. Although it already belongs to the inner person, it should not yet be called or considered the image of God.

This is carried out in the thirteenth book through commendation of the Christian faith.

In the fourteenth book, the true wisdom of the human being—that is, wisdom bestowed as a gift of God through participation in God himself, and distinguished from knowledge—is discussed. The discussion reaches the point where a trinity appears in the image of God, which is the human being according to the mind. This image is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of the one who created the human being (Col. 3:10) in his own image (Gen. 1:27), and thus perceives wisdom, where there is contemplation of eternal things.

# Chapter IV

## 6. What the Whole of Nature Teaches Us about God

Let us therefore seek the Trinity who is God in those eternal, incorporeal, and immutable things, in the perfect contemplation of which the blessed life promised to us is found—a life that is eternal and nothing else.

For it is not only the authority of the divine books that proclaims God’s existence. The whole nature of things itself, which surrounds us and to which we also belong, declares that it has an excellent Creator. He has given us a natural mind and reason by which we see that living things are preferable to nonliving things; things endowed with sensation to things without sensation; things endowed with understanding to things without understanding; immortal things to mortal things; powerful things to powerless things; just things to unjust things; beautiful things to deformed things; good things to evil things; incorruptible things to corruptible things; immutable things to mutable things; invisible things to visible things; incorporeal things to corporeal things; and blessed things to miserable things.

Since, therefore, we unquestionably place the Creator above created things, we must confess that he supremely lives; that he perceives and understands all things; that he cannot die, be corrupted, or be changed; that he is not a body but a spirit; and that he is all-powerful, most just, most beautiful, most good, and most blessed.

# Chapter V

## 7. How Difficult It Is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason

But all these things that I have said, and whatever else seems suitably to be said of God in a similar manner of human speech, apply both to the entire Trinity, which is one God, and to the individual persons within that Trinity.

For who would dare say that either the one God, who is the Trinity itself, or the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit is not living, or perceives or understands nothing? Who would dare say that, in that nature in which they are proclaimed equal to one another, any one of them is mortal, corruptible, mutable, or corporeal? Or who would deny that any one of them is all-powerful, most just, most beautiful, most good, and most blessed?

If, then, all these and similar attributes can be said both of the Trinity itself and of the individual persons within it, where and how will the Trinity appear? Let us first reduce these many things to some small number.

Whatever life is said to be in God is his essence and nature itself. God therefore lives only by the life that he himself is. This life is not like the life present in a tree, where there is neither understanding nor sensation. Nor is it like the life present in an animal: animal life has the fivefold sense, but no understanding. That life which is God, however, perceives and understands all things; and it perceives with the mind, not with the body, because “God is spirit” (John 4:24).

God does not perceive through a body, as animals with bodies do, for he is not composed of soul and body. Thus that simple nature understands as it perceives, and perceives as it understands; and for it the same thing is both perception and understanding.

Nor did it at some time cease to exist or begin to exist, for it is immortal. Nor was it said of him without reason that he alone possesses immortality (1 Tim. 6:16), for his immortality is true immortality, in whose nature there is no change. This is also the true eternity by which God is immutable, without beginning and without end; consequently, he is incorruptible.

The same one thing, therefore, is designated whether God is called eternal, immortal, incorruptible, or immutable. Likewise, when he is called living and understanding—that is, wise—the same thing is designated. For he did not acquire wisdom by which he became wise [Note: [Col. 1062] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “For he does not perceive wisdom by which he becomes—or, by which he is—wise.”]; rather, he himself is wisdom.

This life is likewise power or might, and likewise form, by which he is called powerful and beautiful. For what is more powerful and beautiful than wisdom, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)?

As for goodness and justice, do they differ from one another in God’s nature as they differ in his works, as though there were two different qualities of God, one goodness and the other justice? Certainly not. The justice is itself goodness, and the goodness is itself blessedness.

God is called incorporeal, or without a body, so that he may be believed or understood to be spirit, not body.

## 8. The Attributes Said of God According to Substance

If, then, we say “eternal, immortal, incorruptible, immutable, living, wise, powerful, beautiful, just, good, blessed, spirit,” the last word that I have set down seems to signify substance alone, while the others seem to be qualities of this substance. But that is not how it is in that ineffable and simple nature.

Whatever seems to be said there according to qualities must be understood according to substance or essence. For it would be wrong to say that God is spirit according to substance but good according to quality; both are said according to substance. The same applies to all the other attributes we have mentioned, about which we have already said much in the earlier books.

Of the first four that we have just enumerated and arranged—eternal, immortal, incorruptible, and immutable—let us choose one, because these four signify one thing, as I have already discussed. Let us choose “eternal,” which is placed first, so that our attention may not be spread among many terms.

Let us do the same with the second four: living, wise, powerful, and beautiful. Since some kind of life is also present in an animal, which does not possess wisdom, while wisdom and power are so related in the human being that Holy Scripture says, “The wise man is better than the strong man” (Prov. 24:5; cf. Wis. 6:1), and bodies are also commonly called beautiful, let us choose one of these four: “wise” [Note: [Col. 1062] In place of “four,” “equal” may perhaps be read.].

Although these four must not be called unequal in God—the four names designate one reality [Note: [Col. 1063] Several manuscripts read “not equal.” This is preferable, if above, in place of “the one we choose,” we should read “the equal ones.”]—let wisdom be selected.

Of the final four, although in God being just is the same as being good and blessed, and being spirit is the same as being just, good, and blessed, nevertheless, since in human beings there can be a spirit that is not blessed, and someone can be just and good without yet being blessed, whereas whoever is blessed is certainly also just, good, and spiritual, let us choose what cannot exist in human beings without those other three: “blessed.”

# Chapter VI

## 9. How the Trinity Exists in God’s Very Simplicity. Whether God the Trinity Is Demonstrated by the Trinities Observed in the Human Being

When, then, we say “eternal, wise, blessed,” are these three the Trinity called God? We have indeed reduced those twelve to this small number of three. But perhaps we can also reduce these three to one of them.

For if in God’s nature wisdom and power can be one and the same thing, or life and wisdom can be one and the same thing, why could eternity and wisdom not be one and the same thing in God’s nature, or blessedness and wisdom? Thus, just as it made no difference whether we called them the twelve or these three, when we reduced the many to this small number, so it makes no difference whether we call them these three or that one to whose singularity we have shown that the other two can similarly be reduced [Note: [Col. 1063] Several manuscripts read “which we have recalled.”].

What method of discussion, then, what power of understanding, what vitality of reason, what sharpness of thought could demonstrate—even leaving other matters aside—how this one thing called wisdom, which is God, is a Trinity?

For God does not receive wisdom from something else as we receive wisdom from him. He himself is his wisdom, because his wisdom is not one thing and his essence another; for him, to be is the same as to be wise.

Christ is indeed called in the sacred Scriptures “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). But how this is to be understood, so that the Son may not seem to make the Father wise, was discussed in the seventh book (chapters 1–3). The reasoning reached the conclusion that the Son is wisdom from wisdom in the same way as light is from light and God from God.

We could find no other account of the Holy Spirit than that he too is wisdom, and that all three together are one wisdom, just as they are one God and one essence.

How, then, do we understand this wisdom, which is God, to be a Trinity? I have not said, “How do we believe?” For among the faithful this ought not to be a matter of dispute. Rather, if we can in some way see through understanding what we believe, what will that way be?

## 10.

If we recall where the Trinity began to appear to our understanding in these books, the eighth book comes to mind. There, as best we could, we attempted through discussion to raise the mind’s attention toward understanding that supremely excellent and immutable nature, which is not our mind.

Yet we contemplated it as something that was neither far from us nor above us in place, but above us through its own venerable and wondrous excellence, so that it seemed to be present with us through its present light. Nevertheless, no Trinity yet appeared to us in it, because we did not hold the firm gaze of the mind upon that radiance in order to seek the Trinity [Note: [Col. 1064] Several manuscripts read “we directed.”].
