We perceived only, to some extent, that there was no mass in which it would be necessary to believe that the magnitude of two or three was greater than that of one.

But when we came to love, which is called God in Holy Scripture (1 John 4:16), the Trinity shone forth somewhat: the one who loves, what is loved, and love.

Because that ineffable light dazzled our sight, however, and the weakness of our mind was shown, as it were, not yet able to bear it, we turned back from what we had begun and arranged, for the sake of restoring our struggling attention, to a more familiar consideration of our own mind, according to which the human being was made in the image of God (Gen. 1:27).

From there we lingered in the creature that we are, so that we might be able to understand and see “the invisible things of God through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). We remained at this task from the ninth book through the fourteenth.

And now, after our understanding has been exercised in lower matters as much as was necessary—or perhaps more than was necessary—we wish to raise ourselves to contemplate the supreme Trinity who is God, but we are unable.

Do we see, then, just as we see with complete certainty the trinities that arise externally from bodily things, or when those very things sensed externally are thought about; or when the things that arise in the mind itself and do not belong to the bodily senses—such as faith and the virtues that are arts for conducting life—are plainly discerned by reason and contained in knowledge; or when the mind itself, by which we know whatever we truthfully say that we know, is known to itself or thinks of itself; or when it contemplates something eternal and immutable that it is not itself?

Do we therefore see the Trinity of God in the same way as we see these certain trinities, because they occur in us or exist in us when we remember, contemplate, and will them? Do we see God as Trinity because, by understanding, we contemplate there something like one who speaks, and his Word—that is, the Father and the Son—and the love proceeding from them and common to both, namely the Holy Spirit?

Or do we see these trinities pertaining to our senses or to our mind rather than believe them, while we believe that God is Trinity rather than see it?

If this is so, then either we do not understand and see any of God’s invisible attributes through the things that have been made, or, if we see any, we do not see the Trinity in them. There is something there for us to see, and something that, even when not seen, we ought to believe.

The eighth book shows that we contemplate the immutable good, which we are not; and the fourteenth book, when we were speaking of the wisdom that comes to the human being from God, gave us a reminder of this.

Why, then, do we not recognize the Trinity there? Is this wisdom called God not understanding itself and not loving itself? Who would say such a thing? Or who does not see that where there is no knowledge, there can in no way be wisdom?

Should we perhaps think that wisdom, which is God, knows other things but does not know itself, or loves other things but does not love itself? Since it is foolish and impious either to say or believe this, behold the Trinity: wisdom, its knowledge of itself, and its love of itself.

For in the human being also we find a trinity: the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves itself.

# Chapter VII

## 11. The Trinity of God Cannot Easily Be Detected from the Trinities Described

But these three exist in the human being in such a way that they are not themselves the human being. For the human being is, as the ancients defined him, a mortal rational animal. Those three therefore excel in the human being; they are not themselves the human being.

And one person—that is, each individual human being—possesses those three in the mind [Note: [Col. 1065] The manuscripts add “or the mind itself.”].

Even if we define the human being in this way, saying that the human being is a rational substance consisting of soul and body, it is beyond doubt that the human being possesses a soul that is not body and a body that is not soul. Consequently, those three are not the human being, but belong to the human being or exist in the human being.

Even when the body is removed and the soul alone is considered, the mind is something belonging to it, as its head, eye, or face, so to speak. But these things are not to be conceived as bodies. It is therefore not the soul as a whole that is called mind, but what excels in the soul.

Can we say that the Trinity exists in God in such a way that something belongs to God without itself being God?

Accordingly, each individual human being, who is called the image of God not according to everything belonging to his nature but according to the mind alone, is one person and is the image of the Trinity in the mind.

That Trinity of which he is the image, however, is wholly nothing other than God; wholly, it is nothing other than the Trinity. Nothing belongs to God’s nature that does not belong to that Trinity. The three persons are of one essence—not as each individual human being is one person.

There is also a great difference in this respect: whether we speak of the mind in the human being, together with its knowledge and love, or of memory, understanding, and will, we remember nothing of the mind except through memory, understand nothing except through understanding, and love nothing except through will.

But in that Trinity, who would dare say that the Father understands neither himself, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit except through the Son; or loves either himself, the Son, or the Holy Spirit except through the Holy Spirit; while by himself he remembers only himself, the Son, or the Holy Spirit?

And similarly, who would dare say that the Son remembers neither himself nor the Father except through the Father, loves neither himself nor the Father except through the Holy Spirit, and by himself understands only the Father, himself, and the Holy Spirit?

Or that the Holy Spirit, through the Father, remembers the Father, the Son, and himself; through the Son, understands the Father, the Son, and himself; and by himself loves only himself, the Father, and the Son—as though the Father were the memory of himself, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; the Son the understanding of himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit the love of himself, the Father, and the Son?

Who would presume to think or assert such things in that Trinity?

For if only the Son understands himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1065] Here the printed editions add: “so that he is the understanding,” a reading absent from the manuscripts.], we return to the absurdity that the Father is not wise through himself, but through the Son; and that wisdom did not beget wisdom, but the Father is said to be wise through the wisdom that he begot.

For where there is no understanding, there can be no wisdom. Therefore, if the Father does not understand himself, but the Son understands for the Father, the Son certainly makes the Father wise.

And if for God to be is the same as to be wise, and his essence is the same as his wisdom, then the Son has his essence from the Father, which is true; but rather the Father would have his essence from the Son, which is utterly absurd and false.

It is certain that we examined, refuted, and rejected this absurdity in the seventh book (chapters 1 and 3).

God the Father is therefore wise with the wisdom that he himself is, and the Son is the wisdom of the Father, begotten from wisdom, which is the Father, from whom the Son was begotten.

Consequently, the Father is also understanding with the understanding that he himself is. For he would not be wise if he were not understanding. The Son, however, is the understanding of the Father, begotten from the understanding that is the Father.

The same may appropriately be said of memory. For how can one be wise who remembers nothing, or does not remember himself?

Since, therefore, the Father is wisdom and the Son is wisdom, just as the Father remembers himself, so does the Son [Note: [Col. 1066] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “remembers himself” with a reflexive form referring to himself differently.]. Just as the Father remembers both himself and the Son, with a memory that is not the Son but his own, so the Son remembers both himself and the Father, with a memory that is not the Father but his own.

And where there is no love, who would say that there is any wisdom? From this it follows that the Father is his own love, just as he is his own understanding and memory.

Behold, then: those three—memory, understanding, and love or will—in that supreme and immutable essence which is God are not the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but the Father alone.

And because the Son too is begotten wisdom from wisdom, just as neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit understands for him, but he understands himself, so neither does the Father remember for him, nor does the Holy Spirit love for him, but he himself remembers and loves himself.

For he himself is his own memory, his own understanding, and his own love. But that he is so derives for him from the Father, from whom he was born.

The Holy Spirit, too, because he is wisdom proceeding from wisdom, does not have the Father as his memory, the Son as his understanding, and himself as his love. For he would not be wisdom if another remembered for him, another understood for him, and he alone loved himself. Rather, he himself possesses all three, and possesses them in such a way that he himself is these three.

Nevertheless, that he is so derives for him from the one from whom he proceeds.

Who, then, among human beings can comprehend that wisdom by which God knows all things, so that things called past do not pass away there, nor things called future await their arrival as though they were absent, but past and future, together with the present, are all present; so that individual things are not thought of one by one, with thought passing from one to another, but all things known are simultaneously present in a single view?

Who, I ask, can comprehend this wisdom, and this prudence, and this knowledge, when we do not even comprehend our own [Note: [Col. 1066] The printed editions read “are not even comprehended.” The manuscript reading “is not even comprehended” is preferable.]?

Things that are present to our senses or to our understanding we can, to some extent, contemplate. But things that are absent, though they were present, we know through memory, provided that we have not forgotten them.

We do not infer past things from future things; rather, we infer future things from past things, though not with firm knowledge.

For some of our thoughts, which we see as future and as near at hand, almost more clearly and certainly, as though we were looking ahead at them, we bring about through the operation of memory, when we are able to act, insofar as we are able. Memory appears to relate not to things that are future [Note: [Col. 1067] Erasmus and the Louvain edition read: “which do not seem to relate to things that are future.” Vercellone reads: “which do not seem to relate to it, which is future.”], but to things that are past.

This can be tested in sayings or songs whose sequence we reproduce from memory. Unless we foresaw in thought what comes next, we would certainly not say it.

Yet memory, not foresight, equips us to foresee it. For until everything that we say or sing is finished, there is nothing that is not brought forth as having been foreseen and looked ahead to.

Nevertheless, when we do this, we are not said to sing or speak providently, but from memory. Those who are especially capable of producing many things in this way are not usually praised for their foresight, but for their memory.

We know, and are completely certain, that these things occur in the mind or through our mind. But the more attentively we wish to observe how they occur, the more both our speech fails us and the attention itself does not persist, so that our understanding may reach something clearly, even if our tongue does not.

And we suppose that we can comprehend, despite such great weakness of mind, whether God’s providence is the same as his memory and understanding—he who does not behold individual things by thinking about them one after another, but embraces all things that he knows in a single, eternal, immutable, and ineffable vision.

In this difficulty and distress, I delight to cry out to the living God: “Your knowledge has been made wondrous beyond me; it has prevailed, and I shall not be able to attain it” (Ps. 138:6).

From myself I understand how wondrous and incomprehensible your knowledge is, by which you made me, since I cannot even comprehend myself, whom you made. Yet “in my meditation the fire blazes” (Ps. 38:4), so that I may “seek your face always” (Ps. 104:4).

# Chapter VIII.

14. How the Apostle Says That God Is Now Seen by Us “Through a Mirror”

I know that Wisdom is an incorporeal substance and that it is the light in which those things are seen that are not seen by bodily eyes. Yet so great and spiritual a man says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). If we ask what this mirror is and what kind it is, surely the answer presents itself: in a mirror nothing is seen except an image. We have therefore attempted to see, through this image—that is, through what we are—something of him by whom we were made, as through a mirror.

This is also signified by what the same Apostle says: “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). He said “beholding,” that is, seeing through a mirror, not looking out from a watchtower. In the Greek language this is not [Col. 1068] ambiguous, which is why the apostolic Letters were translated into Latin. For the word meaning “mirror,” in which images of things appear, differs entirely—even in the sound of the word—from the word meaning “watchtower,” from whose height we look out upon something at a distance. It is therefore sufficiently clear that the Apostle said “beholding the glory of the Lord” from *speculum* (“mirror”), not from *specula* (“watchtower”).

When he says, “We are transformed into the same image,” he surely intends the image of God to be understood. By “the same” he means this very image, namely, the one we behold; for the same image is also the glory of God, as he says elsewhere: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:7). We have already discussed these words in Book Twelve.

Thus, when he says “we are transformed,” he means that we are changed and pass from one form into another—from an obscure form into a luminous form. For even that obscure form is the image of God; and if it is an image, it is certainly also a glory, in which we human beings were created, surpassing the other animals. For it was of human nature itself that it was said: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God.” This nature, the most excellent among created things, when it is justified from ungodliness by its Creator, is transferred from a deformed form into a beautiful form. Indeed, even in ungodliness itself, the more damnable the vice, the more certainly praiseworthy is the nature.

For this reason he added, “from glory to glory”: from the glory of creation to the glory of justification. Yet “from glory to glory” may also be understood in other ways: from the glory of faith to the glory of sight; from the glory by which we are children of God to the glory by which we shall be like him, because “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). By adding, “as by the Spirit of the Lord,” he shows that the good of so desirable a transformation is conferred upon us by the grace of God.

## CHAPTER IX

### 15. On the Enigma and Figurative Expressions

These things have been said because the Apostle says that we now see through a mirror. But since he added, “in an enigma,” many people who do not know those writings in which a certain doctrine of modes of expression is taught are unfamiliar with this. The Greeks call these modes *tropes*, and we too use that Greek word in place of the Latin term. Just as we more commonly say *schemata* than “figures,” so we more commonly say *tropes* than “modes.”

To render the names of the individual modes or tropes in Latin, so that each corresponds to its proper term, is extremely difficult and highly unusual. Hence some of our translators, when the Apostle says, “which things are allegorical” (Gal. 4:24), unwilling to use the Greek word, interpreted it by circumlocution, saying, “which things signify one thing by means of another.”

There are several kinds of this trope, that is, of allegory, among which is what is called an enigma. The general definition of the term itself must necessarily include all its kinds. Thus, just as every horse is an animal but not every animal is a horse, so every enigma is an allegory, but not every allegory is an enigma.

What, then, is allegory except a trope in which one thing is understood from another? An example is the passage addressed to the Thessalonians:

“Therefore let us not sleep, as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who become drunk, are drunk at night; but since we belong to the [Col. 1069] day, let us be sober” (1 Thess. 5:6–8).

This allegory, however, is not an enigma, since its meaning is immediately apparent except to the very slow-witted. An enigma, to explain it briefly, is an obscure allegory, as in: “The leech had three daughters” [Note: [Col. 1069] Some manuscripts read, “two daughters.”] (Prov. 30:15), and in any similar examples.

But when the Apostle named allegory, he did not find it in words but in an event. From the two sons of Abraham—one by a slave woman, the other by a free woman—he showed that the two Testaments were to be understood. This was not merely said but also enacted; before he explained it, it was obscure. Accordingly, such an allegory, although the term is general, could specifically be called an enigma.

### 16.

But since it is not only those who do not know the writings in which tropes are learned who ask what the Apostle meant by saying that we now see “in an enigma,” but also those who do know them and nevertheless wish to know what that enigma is in which we now see, one interpretation must be found from both expressions: from what he says, “We see now through a mirror,” and from what he adds, “in an enigma.” For the complete statement is one: “We see now through a mirror in an enigma.”

Therefore, so far as I understand it, just as by the name “mirror” he intended an image to be understood, so by the name “enigma” he intended a likeness that is nevertheless obscure and difficult to discern. Since, then, by the names “mirror” and “enigma” any likenesses signified by the Apostle may be understood—likenesses adapted to the understanding of God, insofar as he can be understood—nothing is more suitable than that which is not without reason called his image.

Let no one therefore be surprised that, even in this mode of seeing granted to the present life, namely, through a mirror in an enigma, we labor to see him somehow. The name “enigma” would not be heard here if vision were easy. And this is the greater enigma: that we do not see what we cannot fail to see.

For who does not see his own thought? And who sees his own thought—not with bodily eyes, but with that innermost vision? Who does not see it, and who does see it? Thought is, after all, a kind of vision of the mind, whether the things that can also be seen by bodily eyes or perceived by the other senses are present, or whether they are absent and their likenesses are discerned in thought; whether nothing of that kind is present, but things are thought that are neither bodily nor likenesses of bodily things, such as virtues and vices, and finally thought itself as it is thought; whether they are matters transmitted through the liberal disciplines and teachings; whether the higher causes and principles of all these things are thought within an immutable nature; or whether we think evil, empty, and false things, either with our judgment withholding assent or with our assent going astray.

## CHAPTER X

### 17. On the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God as in a Mirror and in an Enigma

But let us now speak of the things that we think and know, and that we retain in knowledge even when we are not thinking of them—whether they belong to contemplative knowledge, which is properly called wisdom [Note: [Col. 1069] The printed editions add here *dicimus* (“we call it”).], or to active knowledge, which I have argued ought properly to be called knowledge [Col. 1070].

Both belong simultaneously to the one mind, and there is one image of God. When the lower of the two is treated more distinctly and separately, it is not then to be called the image of God, although even then some likeness of that Trinity is found in it, as we showed in Book Thirteen (chs. 1, 20).

We are now speaking simultaneously of the whole of human knowledge, in which whatever is known to us is known. These things are certainly true; otherwise they would not be known. For no one knows false things unless he knows that they are false. If he knows that, he knows something true: it is true that those things are false.

We are therefore discussing the things that we think and that are known to us even when we are not thinking of them. Yet if we wish to speak of them, we cannot do so unless we think of them. For even if no words are uttered aloud, the person who thinks nevertheless speaks in his heart. Hence the statement in the Book of Wisdom: “They said among themselves, thinking wrongly” (Wis. 2:1). The text explains what “they said among themselves” means by adding “thinking.”

Something similar occurs in the Gospel. Certain scribes, when they heard the Lord say to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven,” said within themselves, “This man blasphemes.” What does “they said within themselves” mean except that they thought? Finally, the text continues: “And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:2–4).

This is Matthew’s account. Luke narrates the same event in this way: “The scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying: Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone? But when Jesus knew their thoughts, he answered and said to them: What are you thinking in your hearts?” (Luke 5:21–22).

What is expressed in the Book of Wisdom by “they said, thinking” is expressed here by “they thought, saying.” In both places it is shown that to speak within oneself and in one’s heart means to speak by thinking. They “said within themselves,” and they were told, “What are you thinking?” And concerning the rich man whose field produced an abundant harvest, the Lord himself says: “And he thought within himself, saying” (Luke 12:17).

### 18.

Some thoughts, then, are words of the heart, where the Lord also shows that there is a mouth, when he says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person.” In this one statement he included two mouths belonging to a human being: one of the body and the other of the heart.

What they had thought defiled a person enters the mouth of the body; but what the Lord said defiles a person proceeds from the mouth of the heart. He himself explained what he had said. Shortly afterward, speaking to his disciples about this matter, he says: “Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?” Here he very clearly showed the mouth of the body.

But in what follows he indicates the mouth of the heart: “The things that proceed from the mouth come from the heart, and they defile a person. For from the heart proceed evil thoughts” (Matt. 15:10–20), and so forth. What could be clearer than this explanation?

Yet because we call thoughts the words of the heart, it does not follow that they are not also visions arising from the visions of knowledge, when they are true. Outside, when these things are performed through the body, speech is one thing and vision another [Col. 1071]; but inside, when we think, the two are one.

Just as hearing and seeing are two distinct things among the bodily senses, but in the mind seeing and hearing are not different things, so the holy Gospel says that inner words—that is, thoughts—were seen by the Lord, not heard: “They said within themselves, ‘This man blasphemes.’” Then it adds: “And when Jesus had seen their thoughts.” He therefore saw what they had said. He saw through his own thought the thoughts that they believed only they themselves could see.

### 19.

Whoever can understand the word not only before it sounds but even before the images of its sounds are turned over in thought—for this word belongs to no language, that is, to none of the languages called the languages of the nations, among which ours is Latin—whoever, I say, can understand this can already see through this mirror and in this enigma some likeness of that Word of which it is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

For whenever we speak truthfully—that is, whenever we speak what we know—a word of precisely the same kind must arise from the knowledge that we hold in memory as is the knowledge from which it arises. A thought formed by the thing we know is the word that we speak in our heart. It is neither Greek nor Latin nor any other language. But when it is necessary to convey it to the knowledge of those with whom we are speaking, some sign by which it may be signified is adopted.

Usually this is a sound, but sometimes it is also a gesture: the former is presented to the ears, the latter to the eyes, so that through bodily signs the word we carry in the mind may become known to the bodily senses as well. For what is making a gesture except speaking visibly in a certain way?

There is testimony to this meaning in the Holy Scriptures. In the Gospel according to John we read:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain of whom he was speaking. One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining on Jesus’ breast. Simon Peter therefore gestured to him and said to him, “Who is it of whom he speaks?” (John 13:21–24).

Behold, by making a gesture he said what he did not dare to say aloud.

We present such bodily signs, whether to the ears or to the eyes, to those who are present and with whom we are speaking. Letters, however, were invented so that we might also converse with those who are absent. Yet these are signs of sounds, while the sounds themselves in our speech are signs of the things that we think.

## CHAPTER XI

### 20. Whatever Likeness of the Divine Word Exists in Our Word Is to Be Sought Not in the External and Sensible Word but in the Interior and Mental Word; the Greatest Difference between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge

The word that sounds outwardly is a sign of the word that shines inwardly, to which the name “word” more properly belongs. For what is uttered by the mouth of the flesh is the voice of the word; it is itself also called a word because of that from which it is assumed in order to appear outwardly [Col. 1072].

Thus our word becomes, in a certain way, a bodily voice by assuming a voice in which it may be manifested to human senses, just as the Word of God became flesh by assuming flesh in which he too might be manifested to human senses. And just as our word becomes a voice without being changed into a voice, so the Word of God became flesh, but—far be it from us to say that he was changed into flesh. By assuming it without being consumed into it, our word becomes a voice and that Word became flesh.

Therefore, whoever desires to approach whatever likeness of the Word of God can be attained—although it is unlike him in many respects—should not look at our word as it sounds in the ears, either when it is uttered aloud or when it is thought in silence. For the words of all sounding languages are also thought in silence, and songs are run through in the mind while the bodily mouth is silent. Not only the rhythms of syllables but also the modes of melodies, although bodily and belonging to the bodily sense called hearing, are present to those who think and silently turn all these things over in their minds through certain incorporeal images of themselves.

But these matters must be passed over, so that we may arrive at that word of the human being through whose partial likeness the Word of God may somehow be seen as in an enigma. I do not mean the word that came to this or that prophet, and of which it is said, “The word of God grew and multiplied” (Acts 6:7); nor that of which it is again said, “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10:17); nor again: “When you received from us the word of the hearing of God, you received it not as the word of human beings but, as it truly is, the word of God” (1 Thess. 2:13).

Many similar things are said in the Scriptures about the word of God that is spread through the hearts and mouths of human beings in the sounds of many different languages. It is called the word of God because divine teaching is transmitted, not human teaching.

But we are seeking, through this likeness, to see in some way that Word of God of which it is said, “The Word was God”; of which it is said, “All things were made through him”; of which it is said, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:1, 3, 14); of which it is said, “The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high” (Sir. 1:5).

We must therefore arrive at that word of the human being, the word of a rational living creature, the word of the image of God that was not born from God but made by God. It is neither uttered in sound nor thought in the likeness of sound. It need not belong to any language, but precedes all the signs by which it is signified and is born from the knowledge that remains in the mind, when that knowledge is spoken inwardly just as it is.

The vision of thought is exceedingly like the vision of knowledge. For when it is expressed through sound or through some bodily sign, it is not expressed just as it is, but as it can be seen or heard through the body. When, therefore, what is in knowledge is also in the word, then the word is true; and there is that truth which is expected from a human being, so that what is in the one may also be in the other, and what is not in the one may not be in the other. Here we recognize: “Yes, yes; No, no” (Matt. 5:37).

Thus, insofar as possible, this likeness of a made image approaches the likeness of the image that is begotten, by which the Son of God is proclaimed to be substantially like the [Col. 1073] Father in every respect.

This likeness of the Word of God must also be noticed in this enigma: just as it is said of that Word, “All things were made through him,” by which God is proclaimed to have made the universe through his only-begotten Word, so there are no works of a human being that are not first spoken in the heart. Hence it is written: “The word is the beginning of every work” (Sir. 37:20).

Yet here too, when the word is true, it is the beginning of a good work. The word is true when it is born from knowledge of how to act well, so that here also “Yes, yes; No, no” is preserved: if something is present in the knowledge by which one ought to live, it must also be present in the word through which one ought to act; if it is not, it must not be. Otherwise such a word will be false, not true, and the result will be sin, not a right action.

There is also in this likeness of our word a likeness of the Word of God, because our word may exist without being followed by an action, whereas no action can exist unless a word precedes it. In the same way, the Word of God could exist when no creature existed; but no creature could exist except through him through whom all things were made.

Therefore it was not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the Trinity itself, but the Son alone, who is the Word of God, who became flesh—although the Trinity accomplished the act—so that, with our word following and imitating his example, we might live rightly, having no falsehood in either the contemplation or the operation of our word.

But this is the perfection that this image will one day attain. To reach it, the good teacher instructs us through Christian faith and the teaching of piety, so that, with unveiled face, having removed the veil of the Law, which is the shadow of future things, and beholding the glory of the Lord—that is, looking upon it through a mirror—we may be transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18), in accordance with the foregoing discussion of these words.

### 21.

When, therefore, this image has been renewed and brought to perfection through this transformation, we shall be like God, because we shall see him not through a mirror but as he is (1 John 3:2)—which the Apostle Paul expresses as “face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

But now, in this mirror, in this enigma, in this likeness of whatever kind it may be, who can explain how great the unlikeness also is? Nevertheless, I shall touch upon certain points, as I am able, by which this may be perceived.

## CHAPTER XII

### Academic Philosophy

First, what sort or degree of knowledge can come to a human being, however skilled and learned, from which our thought is truthfully formed when we speak what we know?

For, apart from the things that enter the mind through the bodily senses—among which so many things are other than they appear that a person who is insane may think himself sane, being excessively hemmed in by their likeness to truth—apart from these, then, how much remains that we know as certainly as we know that we are alive?

In this matter we are entirely free from fear that we may perhaps be deceived by some mere likelihood, since it is certain that even the person who is deceived is alive. Nor is this knowledge [Note: [Col. 1074] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “these things are found.” Incorrect.] found among the appearances presented externally, in which the eye is deceived as when an oar appears broken in water, towers appear to move to sailors, and countless other things are other than they appear. For this knowledge is not perceived through the eye of the flesh.

There is an inward knowledge by which we know that we are alive. Here even the Academic philosopher cannot say: “Perhaps you are asleep and do not know it, and you are seeing these things in a dream.” Who does not know that the appearances of those who dream are exceedingly like the appearances of those who are awake? But the person who is certain of his knowledge of life does not say in that knowledge, “I know that I am awake,” but “I know that I am alive.” Whether he is asleep or awake, he is alive.

Nor can he be deceived by dreams in this knowledge, because both sleeping and seeing in dreams belong to one who is alive. Nor can the Academic philosopher say against this knowledge: “Perhaps you are raving and do not know it,” because the appearances of those who rave are also exceedingly like those of the sane. But the person who raves is alive.

He does not say against the Academics, “I know that I am not raving,” but “I know that I am alive.” Therefore whoever says that he knows he is alive can never be deceived or lie in that statement.

Let a thousand kinds of deceptive appearances be brought against the person who says, “I know that I am alive.” He will fear none of them, since even the person who is deceived is alive.

But if matters of this kind alone belong to human knowledge, they are very few—except that within each category they multiply so greatly that they are found not merely to be few but even to tend toward an infinite number.

For the person who says, “I know that I am alive,” says that he knows one thing. If he then says, “I know that I know that I am alive,” there are already two things. But to know these two is to know a third. He can add a fourth and a fifth, and innumerable further things, if he is able.

Yet because he cannot comprehend all the individual items by adding them one after another, nor state them in an infinite series, he most certainly comprehends and states this very fact: that it is true, and that it is so innumerable that he cannot comprehend or express its number as truly infinite.

The same point can be observed in a firm act of will. Who could respond without shamelessness to the person who says, “I want to be happy,” “Perhaps you are mistaken”? If he says, “I know that I want this,” and “I know that I know this,” he can already add a third, namely, that he knows these two; and a fourth, that he knows that he knows these two; and he can proceed similarly into infinity.

Again, if someone says, “I do not want to be mistaken,” then whether or not he is mistaken, it will still be true that he does not want to be mistaken. Who could say to him with anything but the utmost shamelessness, “Perhaps you are mistaken,” when, wherever he may be mistaken, he is not mistaken in not wanting to be mistaken?

And if he says that he knows this, he may add as many known things as he wishes, and he sees that their number is infinite. For the person who says, “I do not want to be deceived, and I know that I do not want this, and I know that I know this,” can thereby display an infinite number, even if not in an entirely convenient form of expression.

Other arguments too can be found that are effective against the Academics, who maintain that nothing can be known by a human being. But restraint is necessary, especially since this is not the subject we have undertaken here.

There are three books of ours on this subject, written at the beginning of our conversion. Whoever is able and willing to read them and understands what he reads will certainly not be disturbed by any of the many arguments they have devised against the apprehension of truth [Note: [Col. 1075] Three books *Against the Academics*, vol. 1.].

Since there are two kinds of things that are known—one consisting of things that the mind perceives through the bodily senses, the other of things that it perceives through itself—those philosophers made many foolish arguments against the bodily senses. But they could not at all call into doubt certain exceedingly firm perceptions of true things that the mind possesses through itself, such as the one I mentioned: “I know that I am alive.”

Far be it from us, however, to doubt that the things we have learned through the bodily senses are true. Through them we learned of heaven and earth, and of the things in them that have become known to us, insofar as he who made both us and them wished them to become known to us.

Nor should we deny that we know things learned through the testimony of others. Otherwise we would not know that the ocean exists; we would not know that there are lands and cities celebrated by the most widespread report; we would not know that human beings existed, nor the works they performed, which we have learned through historical reading; we would not know the things reported daily from every direction and confirmed by consistent and mutually corroborating indications [Note: [Col. 1075] Most manuscripts read *constantibusque*, “constant and corroborating.”]; finally, we would not know from what places or from what people we ourselves originated, since we have believed all these things on the testimony of others.

If it is absurd to say this, then we must acknowledge that not only the senses of our own bodies but also those of other bodies have contributed very greatly to our knowledge.

### 22.

All these things, then—those that the human mind knows through itself, those it knows through the senses of its own body, and those it has perceived through the testimony of others—it stores up in the treasury of memory. From them the true word is born when we speak what we know, but a word prior to every sound and prior to every thought of sound.

For then the word is most like the known thing from which it is born, and its image arises from that thing, since from the vision of knowledge there arises the vision of thought. This is a word belonging to no language: a true word concerning a true thing, having nothing of its own but deriving everything from the knowledge from which it is born.

It makes no difference when the person who speaks what he knows learned it. Sometimes he says it immediately upon learning it; provided only that it is a true word, that is, one arising from known things.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Again on the Difference between Our Knowledge and Mental Word and the Knowledge and Word of God

But did God the Father—from whom the Word was born, God from God—learn some things through the senses of his body and other things through himself, in that Wisdom which is himself?

Who could say this while thinking of God not as a rational animal but as one above the rational soul—as far as he can be thought of by those who place him above all animals and all souls, although they see him conjecturally through a mirror and in an enigma, not yet face to face as he is?

Did God the Father learn from somewhere else or from someone else the very things he knows not through a body—for he has none—but through himself? Or did he need messengers or witnesses in order to know them? Certainly not. For that perfection is sufficient for itself to know all that it knows.

He does indeed have messengers, namely angels, but not messengers who announce to him what he does not know. There is nothing he does not know. Rather, it is good for them to consult the truth concerning his [Col. 1076] works; and this is what it means for them to be said to announce certain things to him—not so that he may learn from them, but so that they may learn from him, through his Word and without bodily sound.

They also announce what he wills, sent by him to whomever he wills, hearing everything from him through his Word—that is, finding in his truth what they must do, what they must announce, to whom, and when.

We too pray to him, yet we do not teach him our needs. “Your Father,” his Word says, “knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. 6:8).

Nor did he come to know these things at some point in time and thereby become knowledgeable. Rather, without beginning, he foreknew all future temporal things, including what we would ask of him and when, and whom he would hear or not hear, and concerning what matters.

He knows all his creatures, spiritual and bodily, not because they exist, but because they were known by him. They exist because he knew them. For he was not ignorant of what he was going to create. Because he knew them, he created them; he did not know them because he created them.

Nor did he know them as created in a way different from how he knew them as about to be created. Nothing was added to his wisdom through them. Rather, when they existed as was fitting and when it was fitting, his wisdom remained as it was.

So it is also written in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “Before they were created, all things were known to him; so also after they were completed” (Sir. 23:29). “So,” it says—that is, not otherwise—they are known to him both before they were created and after they were completed.

Our knowledge, then, is very unlike this knowledge. God’s knowledge is also his wisdom, and his wisdom is also his essence or substance. For in the astonishing simplicity of that nature, to be wise is not one thing and to be something else; rather, what it is to be wise is also what it is to be, as we have often said in the earlier books.

Our knowledge, however, is both capable of being lost and capable of being regained in many matters precisely because being is not the same for us as knowing or being wise. We can exist even if we do not know or possess wisdom concerning the things we have learned from elsewhere.

Therefore, just as our knowledge is unlike God’s knowledge, so our word, which is born from our knowledge, is unlike the Word of God, which was born from the Father’s essence. It is as though I said, “from the Father’s knowledge, from the Father’s wisdom,” or, more precisely, “from the Father, knowledge; from the Father, wisdom.”

## CHAPTER XIV

### 23. The Word of God Is in Every Respect Equal to the Father, from Whom He Is

The Word of God, therefore, the only-begotten Son of the Father, is in every respect like and equal to the Father: God from God, light from light, wisdom from wisdom, essence from essence. He is altogether what the Father is, yet he is not the Father, because the one is the Son and the other is the Father.

Accordingly, he knows everything that the Father knows; but for him, knowing is from the Father, just as being is. For there, knowing and being are one [Note: [Col. 1076] So the manuscripts read; the printed editions have “for him they are one.”].

Therefore, just as being is not from the Son for the Father, neither is knowing. The Father, as though speaking himself, begot the Word equal to himself in every respect. For he would not have spoken himself wholly and perfectly if there were anything less or anything more in his Word than in himself.

There supremely we recognize: “Yes, yes; No, no” (Matt. 5:37). Therefore this Word is truly truth, because whatever is in the knowledge from which he was begotten is also in him, and whatever is not in that knowledge is not in him.

This Word can never contain anything false, because he remains unchangeably as does the one from whom he is. “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). He cannot do otherwise by any power—not because this is weakness, but because it is the strength by which truth cannot be false.

God the Father therefore knows all things in himself and knows them in the Son: in himself as himself, and in the Son as his Word, which is of all the things that are in himself.

The Son likewise knows all things: in himself, as things born from what the Father knows in himself; in the Father, as the things from which were born the things that the Son knows in himself.

The Father and the Son therefore know one another—but the Father by begetting and the Son by being begotten. Each of them sees simultaneously all the things that are in their knowledge, wisdom, and essence—not piecemeal or individually, as though their sight alternated from here to there, and from there back here, and again from one thing to another, so that one could not see certain things without failing to see others. Rather, as I said, he sees all things simultaneously, and there is nothing among them that he does not always see.

### 24.

Our word, however, is without sound and without a thought of sound; it is of the thing that we utter inwardly by seeing it [Note: [Col. 1077] Here the manuscripts add: “which shines inwardly, to which the name ‘word’ more properly belongs.” This is taken from the beginning of Chapter XI.], and therefore belongs to no language. In this enigma it is in some way like that Word of God, which is also God, because it is born from our knowledge in the same way that the Word was born from the Father’s knowledge.

Since, then, we find that our word is in some way like that Word, let us not shrink from considering, insofar as we can express it, how greatly it is also unlike him.

## CHAPTER XV
## How Great the Dissimilarity Is between Our Word and the Divine Word

Can our word be eternal, or even be called eternal? Does our word arise solely from our knowledge? Do we not also say many things that we do not know? We say them not while doubting, but while supposing them to be true. If they happen to be true, they are true in the things themselves about which we speak, not in our word; for a true word is only one that is generated from a thing that is known.

In this respect, then, our word is false—not when we lie, but when we are mistaken. When we doubt, there is not yet a word concerning the thing about which we doubt; rather, there is a word concerning the doubt itself. Although we do not know whether what we doubt is true, we do know that we are doubting. Accordingly, when we say this, it is a true word, because we say what we know.

What if we can also lie? When we do so, we certainly have a false word willingly and knowingly; yet there is a true word in that we are lying, for we know this. And when we confess that we have lied, we speak the truth: we say what we know, for we know that we have lied.

But that Word who is God and is more powerful than we are cannot do this. For he cannot do anything except what he has seen the Father doing; nor does he speak from himself, but everything he says is from the Father, since [Col. 1078] the Father himself uniquely speaks him. The great power of that Word is that he cannot lie, because in him there cannot be “Yes” and “No” (2 Cor. 1:19), but only “Yes, yes” and “No, no.”

Yet a word that is not true should not even be called a word.

“If that is so,” I gladly agree. [Note: [Col. 1078] Thus the Antwerp Benedictine edition, together with some printed editions; but the earlier Benedictine edition reads “sit ita.” M.]

But when our word is true and therefore rightly called a word, can we say of it “essence from essence,” just as we can say “vision from vision” or “knowledge from knowledge,” in the way in which that Word of God is most especially said—and must most especially be said—to be essence from essence?

Why not? Because for us being is not the same as knowing. We know many things that in a certain way live through memory, and in a certain way die through forgetfulness. Thus, when they are no longer present in our knowledge, we nevertheless continue to exist; and when our knowledge has slipped away from our mind and perished, we nevertheless continue to live.

### 25.

There are also things known in such a way that they can never fall from knowledge, because they are present and belong to the very nature of the mind—for example, the fact that we know we are alive. This remains as long as the mind remains; and because the mind always remains, this too always remains. If there are other things of this kind, in which the image of God should rather be contemplated, nevertheless, even though they are always known, they are not always thought of. It is therefore difficult to see how our eternal word can be spoken of them, since our word is spoken by our thought.

To live is eternal for the mind; to know that it lives is eternal. Yet it is not eternal for the mind to think of its own life or to think of its knowledge of its life. When it begins to think of one thing and then another, it ceases to think of this, although it does not cease to know it.

Hence, if there can be some eternal knowledge in the mind, while the thought of that same knowledge cannot be eternal, and if our true inner word is spoken only by our thought, we must understand that God alone has an eternal Word coeternal with himself.

Unless perhaps we should say that the very possibility of thought is a word, since what is known, even when it is not being thought of, can nevertheless be thought of truthfully; and that this possibility is as perpetual as the knowledge itself is perpetual.

But how is that a word which has not yet been formed in the vision of thought? How will it be like the knowledge from which it is born if it does not have its form—and is therefore already called a word merely because it can have one? This is like saying that something should already be called a word because it can become a word.

But what is it that can become a word and therefore is already worthy of the name “word”? What, I ask, is this formable yet unformed thing, except something belonging to our mind, which we toss about through a kind of shifting motion, thinking now this and now that as it is discovered or occurs to us?

It becomes a true word when that which, as I have said, we toss about in this shifting motion reaches what we know [Note: [Col. 1078] Printed editions read “will have reached” (pervenerit); the manuscripts, more suitably, read “reaches” (pervenit).] and is formed from it, taking on its complete likeness. [Col. 1079] Thus, just as each thing is known, so also it is thought—without sound and without the thought of sound, which certainly belongs to some language—and is spoken in the heart. [Note: [Col. 1079] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions read “if” (si).]

Accordingly, even if we concede this point, so that we may not seem to be troubled by a dispute over terminology—namely, that the thing in our mind which can be formed from our knowledge should already be called a word before it has been formed, because it is, so to speak, formable—who does not see how great is the dissimilarity here from that Word of God who exists “in the form of God”? He was not first formable before being formed, nor can he ever be formless. Rather, he is a simple form, simply equal to him from whom he is, and wondrously coeternal with him.

## CHAPTER XVI

### Our Word Will Never Be Made Equal to the Divine Word, Even When We Become Like God

For this reason that Word of God is called “the Word,” rather than “the thought of God,” lest something be believed to exist in God as a kind of shifting entity that now receives and now takes back its form in order to become a word, and that could lose it and somehow roll about formless.

The excellent speaker who knew words well and had examined the force of thought understood this perfectly when he said in his poem:

> And within himself he turns over  
> The various outcomes of war.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid, Book 10, lines 159–160.)*

That is, he thinks.

The Son of God, therefore, is not called the thought of God, but the Word of God. Our thought, when it reaches what we know and is formed from it, is our true word. Therefore the Word of God must be understood without any thought of God, so that it may be understood as the simple form itself, possessing nothing formable that could also be formless.

The holy Scriptures do indeed speak of the thoughts of God; but they do so in the manner in which they also speak of God’s forgetfulness—something that plainly does not belong to God in the proper sense.

### 26.

Since, then, there is such great dissimilarity between God and the Word of God in this riddle, although some likeness has nevertheless been discovered, we must also acknowledge that even when we become like him, when we see him as he is (1 John 3:2)—and surely the one who said this was considering the dissimilarity that exists now—we will not then be equal to him in nature.

The nature of the one who makes is always greater than that of what has been made. At that time our word will not be false, because we will neither lie nor be deceived. Perhaps our thoughts will no longer be shifting, moving from one thing to another and back again [Note: [Col. 1079] Printed editions read “to other things” (in alias); the manuscripts more suitably read “to another thing” (in alia).]; instead, we will see all our knowledge in a single simultaneous vision.

Nevertheless, even when this has happened—if indeed it does happen—the creature that was formable will have been formed, so that nothing will any longer be lacking from the form to which it ought to attain. Yet it will still not be made equal to that simplicity in which there is not something formable that has been formed or reformed, but the form itself: neither formless nor formed, but there eternally the immutable substance itself.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 27. In What Sense the Holy Spirit Is Called Love, and Whether He Alone Is So Called; the Holy Spirit Is Specifically Called by the Name of Charity in the Scriptures

We have spoken sufficiently [Col. 1080] about the Father and the Son, insofar as through this mirror and in this riddle we have been able to see. Now we must discuss the Holy Spirit, insofar as God grants us the ability to see.

According to the holy Scriptures, the Holy Spirit belongs neither to the Father alone nor to the Son alone, but to both. Therefore he makes known to us the love that the Father and the Son have for one another in common.

To exercise us, however, the divine word has made us search with greater zeal for matters that are not set plainly before us, but must be examined in secret and brought forth from concealment. Scripture did not therefore say, “The Holy Spirit is love.” Had it said this, it would have removed no small part of the present question. Instead, it said, “God is love” (1 John 4:16), leaving it uncertain—and therefore requiring investigation—whether God the Father is love, or God the Son, or God the Holy Spirit, or God the Trinity itself.

For we shall not say that God is called love, not because love itself is a substance worthy of the name “God,” but because it is a gift of God [Note: [Col. 1080] Printed editions read “because love itself is no substance” (quod ipsa charitas nulla substantia); corrected from the manuscripts.], just as it is said to God, “For you are my patience” (Ps. 70:5). It was not said for the reason that our patience is God’s substance, but because it comes to us from him, as it is written elsewhere, “For from him is my patience” (Ps. 61:6).

The very manner of expression in Scripture easily refutes this interpretation. “You are my patience” has the same sense as “You, Lord, are my hope” (Ps. 90:9), and “My God is my mercy” (Ps. 58:18), and many similar expressions.

It was not said, “Lord, my love,” or “You are my love,” or “God is my love.” Rather, it was said, “God is love,” just as it was said, “God is Spirit” (John 4:24).

Whoever does not discern this should seek understanding from the Lord, not an explanation from us. We cannot say anything more plainly.

### 28.

God, then, is love. But whether the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself is meant is the question—especially since the Trinity is not three gods but one God.

Earlier in this book I argued that the Trinity who is God should not be understood through the three things we have shown to exist in our mind in such a way that the Father is the memory of all three, the Son the understanding of all three, and the Holy Spirit the love of all three—as though the Father neither understood nor loved himself, but the Son understood for him and the Holy Spirit loved for him, while he himself merely remembered himself and the others; and as though the Son neither remembered nor loved himself, but the Father remembered for him and the Holy Spirit loved for him, while he himself merely understood himself and the others; and likewise as though the Holy Spirit neither remembered nor understood himself, but the Father remembered for him and the Son understood for him, while he himself merely loved himself and the others.

Rather, all three, and each of the three individually, possess everything in their own nature. These things are not distinct in them as memory, understanding, and love or charity are distinct in us. Instead, there is one thing capable of accomplishing everything, just as wisdom itself is; and it exists in the nature of each in such a way that whoever possesses it is what he possesses, as is fitting for an immutable and simple [Col. 1081] substance.

If this has been understood, and if it has become clear that—as far as we are permitted to see or conjecture concerning such great matters—it is true, I do not know why, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each called wisdom, while together they are not three wisdoms but one wisdom, so the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit should not likewise each be called love, while together they are one love.

For in the same way the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, while together they are one God.

### 29.

Nevertheless, it is not without reason that within this Trinity the Word of God is called “the Word” only of the Son, the Gift of God only of the Holy Spirit, and God the Father is called the one from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds principally.

I added “principally” because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. But the Father also gave this to the Son—not to one who already existed and previously lacked it, but whatever he gave to the only-begotten Word he gave by begetting him.

He begot him in such a way that the common Gift would also proceed from him, and the Holy Spirit would be the Spirit of both.

This distinction within the inseparable Trinity must therefore not be accepted superficially, but carefully contemplated. It is for this reason that the Word of God is properly also called the Wisdom of God, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are wisdom as well.

If, then, one of these three is to be called love properly, what is more fitting than that it should be the Holy Spirit? In that [Note: [Col. 1081] Printed editions read “in that Trinity”; the word “Trinity” is absent from the manuscripts.] simple and supreme nature, substance is not one thing and love another; rather, the substance itself is love, and love itself is substance—whether in the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit is properly called love.

### 30.

Sometimes the word “Law” signifies collectively all the utterances of the holy Scriptures of the Old Testament. For example, when the Apostle cites the prophet Isaiah, saying, “In other tongues and in other lips I will speak to this people,” he nevertheless prefaced it with, “It is written in the Law” (Isa. 28:11; 1 Cor. 14:21).

The Lord himself also said, “In their Law it is written, ‘They hated me without cause’” (John 15:25), although this is found in a Psalm (Ps. 34:19).

At other times “Law” properly means the Law given through Moses, as in the words, “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Matt. 11:13), and, “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40). Here “Law” plainly refers properly to the Law given on Mount Sinai.

The Psalms, however, are also included under the name “Prophets.” Yet elsewhere the Savior himself said, “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). Here again he wished the name “Prophets” to be understood as excluding the Psalms.

Thus “Law” may be used universally together with the Prophets and Psalms, and it may also be used properly for the Law given through Moses. Likewise, “Prophets” may be used collectively together with the Psalms, and properly for the prophetic books apart from the Psalms.

Many other examples could show that terms for things are used both universally and specifically, except that, where the matter is clear, a lengthy discussion should be avoided.

I have said this so that no one may think it inappropriate for us to call the Holy Spirit love merely because God the Father and God the Son can also be called love.

### 31.

Just as, therefore, we properly call the unique Word of God “Wisdom,” although the Father himself and the Holy Spirit are also universally wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called “Love,” although the Father and the Son are also universally love.

The Word of God—that is, the only-begotten Son of God—was plainly called the Wisdom of God by the Apostle, when he said, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

But we find that the Holy Spirit is called love if we carefully examine the words of the Apostle John. After saying, “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God,” he continued, “Everyone who loves is born from God; whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.”

Here he made clear that he called love “God,” the same love that he had said was “from God.” Thus love is God from God.

But since the Son too is born from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, it is rightly asked which of them we should understand to be called here “God who is love.”

The Father alone is God in such a way that he is not from God. Therefore the love that is God in such a way that it is from God is either the Son or the Holy Spirit.

But after mentioning the love of God—not the love with which we love him, but the love with which he loved us and sent his Son as a propitiator [Note: [Col. 1082] Printed editions read “deliverer” (liberatorem); the manuscripts read “propitiator” (litatorem). In Greek, 1 John 4:10: ἱλασμόν.] for our sins—and after exhorting us to love one another, so that God might remain in us, since he had called God love [Col. 1082], John immediately wished to speak more openly about the matter:

“By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.”

The Holy Spirit, then, of whom he has given us, makes us remain in God and God in us. But love does this. He, therefore, is the God who is love.

A little later, when John repeated this very point and said, “God is love,” he immediately added, “Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” This is what he had said earlier: “By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.”

He, therefore, is signified where it is written, “God is love.”

God the Holy Spirit, then, who proceeds from God, when he is given to a human being, kindles that person with love for God and neighbor; and he himself is love. For a human being has no source from which to love God except from God.

For this reason John says shortly afterward, “Let us love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:7–19).

The Apostle Paul also says, “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 32. No Gift of God Is Greater Than Love

There is no gift of God greater than this. It alone distinguishes the children of the eternal kingdom from the children of eternal destruction.

Other gifts are also given through the Holy Spirit, but without love they are of no benefit. Unless, therefore, the Holy Spirit is granted to someone in such measure that he makes that person a lover of God and neighbor, that person is not transferred from the left to the right.

Nor is the Spirit properly called [Col. 1083] “the Gift” except on account of love. Whoever does not possess love, even if he speaks in the tongues of human beings and of angels, is a sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal. Even if he has prophecy, knows all mysteries and all knowledge, and has all faith so as to move mountains, he is nothing. Even if he distributes all his possessions, and delivers his body to be burned, it profits him nothing (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

How great, then, is the good without which such great good deeds bring no one to eternal life?

But love or charity—for both are names of the same thing—if possessed by one who does not speak in tongues, does not have prophecy, does not know all mysteries and all knowledge, and does not distribute all his possessions to the poor, whether because he has nothing to distribute or because some necessity prevents him; if he does not deliver his body to be burned because no trial involving such suffering confronts him—if such a person possesses love, it brings him to the kingdom.

Indeed, love alone makes faith useful. Without love faith can exist, but it cannot benefit.

Therefore the Apostle Paul says, “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6). In this way he distinguishes it from the faith by which even the demons believe and tremble (James 2:19).

Love, then, which is from God and is God, is properly the Holy Spirit. Through him the love of God is poured into our hearts, and through that love the whole Trinity dwells in us.

Accordingly, the Holy Spirit, since he is God, is most rightly also called the Gift of God (Acts 8:20). What should this Gift properly be understood to be except love, which brings us to God, and without which no other gift of God brings us to God?

## CHAPTER XIX

### 33. The Holy Spirit Called the Gift of God in Scripture; “The Gift of the Holy Spirit” Said for “the Gift Who Is the Holy Spirit”; the Holy Spirit Properly Called Love, Although Love Is Not Found in the Trinity in Him Alone

Must this also be proved—that the Holy Spirit is called the Gift of God in the sacred Scriptures?

If this too is expected of us, we have in the Gospel according to John the words of the Lord Jesus Christ:

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The Evangelist then added:

“He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive” (John 7:37–39).

Hence the Apostle Paul also says, “We have all drunk of one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:13).

The question is whether this water was called the Gift of God—that is, whether the Holy Spirit was so called.

Just as here we find that this water is the Holy Spirit, so elsewhere in the same Gospel we find that this water was called the Gift of God.

For when the Lord was speaking with the Samaritan woman at the well, he had said to her, “Give me a drink.” When she replied that Jews did not associate with Samaritans, Jesus answered her:

“If you knew the Gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would perhaps have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

The woman said to him:

“Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep. From where, then, do you have the living water?”

And so forth.

Jesus answered and said to her:

[Col. 1084] “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never thirst. Rather, the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:7–14).

Since, therefore, this living water is the Spirit, as the Evangelist explained, there can be no doubt that the Spirit is the Gift of God of which the Lord here says:

“If you knew the Gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would perhaps have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

For where he says, “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly,” here he says, “It will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

### 34.

The Apostle Paul also says, “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” Then, to show that Christ’s gift is the Holy Spirit, he continued:

“Therefore he says: ‘He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings’” (Eph. 4:7–8).

It is well known that when the Lord Jesus, after rising from the dead, ascended into heaven, he gave the Holy Spirit. Those who believed were filled with him and spoke in the tongues of all nations.

It should not trouble us that Paul says “gifts,” not “gift,” for he took this testimony from a Psalm. In the Psalm it is read as follows:

“You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among human beings” (Ps. 67:19).

Thus many manuscripts read it, especially the Greek ones; and we have it translated in this way from the Hebrew.

The Apostle therefore said “gifts,” as did the Prophet, not “gift.” But whereas the Prophet said, “You received gifts among human beings,” the Apostle preferred to say, “He gave gifts to human beings,” so that from both expressions—one prophetic and the other apostolic—the fullest sense might be conveyed, since both bear the authority of divine speech.

Both statements are true: he gave to human beings, and he received among human beings.

He gave to human beings as their head gives to his members; and he received among human beings as the same one received in his members, on whose account his members he himself cried from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Of these same members he said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40).

Christ himself, therefore, both gave from heaven and received on earth.

The Prophet and the Apostle both used the plural “gifts” because through the Gift that is the Holy Spirit, many gifts—particular to particular members—are distributed among all the members of Christ.

Not every individual has all the gifts; some have one, others another. Yet all possess the Gift itself from which the particular gifts are distributed to each, namely, the Holy Spirit.

Elsewhere, after listing many gifts, Paul says, “One and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing them individually to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

The same expression is also found in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where it is written, “God bearing witness by signs and wonders, various powers, and a distribution of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 1084] Most manuscripts read “distributions” (divisionibus).] (Heb. 2:4).

Here, after saying, “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings,” Paul adds:

[Col. 1085] “But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things. And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as shepherds and teachers.”

This shows why the gifts were mentioned. As he says elsewhere, “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” (1 Cor. 12:29), and so forth.

Here he added, “For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. 4:7–12).

This is the house which, as the Psalm sings, is built after captivity (Ps. 126:1). Those who have been rescued from the devil, by whom they were held captive, are used to build the house of Christ; this house is called the Church. [Note: [Col. 1085] The manuscripts read “body” (corpus).]

The one who took this captivity captive was the one who conquered the devil. So that the members of the holy Head who were destined to come might not be dragged with him into eternal punishment, he first bound him with the chains of justice and then with those of power.

The devil himself, therefore, is called the captivity that was taken captive by the one who ascended on high and gave gifts to human beings—or received them among human beings.

### 35.

The Apostle Peter, as we read in the canonical book in which the Acts of the Apostles are written, was speaking about Christ to the Jews who had been moved in heart and were saying, “What, then, shall we do, brothers? Tell us.” He said to them:

“Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:37–38).

In the same book it is also recorded that Simon Magus wished to give money to the Apostles so that he might receive from them the power by which the Holy Spirit would be given through the laying on of his hands.

Peter said to him:

“May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed through money” (Acts 8:18–20).

Elsewhere in the same book, when Peter was speaking to Cornelius and those who were with him, announcing and preaching Christ, Scripture says:

“While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word. And the faithful from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the gift of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations. For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God” (Acts 10:44–46).

Later, when Peter gave an account to the brothers in Jerusalem concerning what he had done in baptizing the uncircumcised—since the Holy Spirit had come upon them before they were baptized, thereby resolving the difficulty of this question—and when those who heard this were troubled, he said, among other things:

“When I began to speak to them, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as upon us in the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ If, therefore, he gave them an equal gift as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God from giving them the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 11:15–17).

There are many other testimonies of Scripture that unanimously attest that the Holy [Col. 1086] Spirit is the Gift of God, insofar as he is given to those who love God through him. But it would be too lengthy to gather them all. And what evidence would be sufficient for those for whom what we have said is not sufficient?

### 36.

They should certainly be admonished, since they now see that the Holy Spirit is called the Gift of God, that when they hear “the gift of the Holy Spirit,” they should recognize the kind of expression found in the words, “In the stripping off of the body of the flesh” (Col. 2:11).

Just as “the body of the flesh” means nothing other than flesh, so “the gift of the Holy Spirit” means nothing other than the Holy Spirit.

He is therefore the Gift of God insofar as he is given to those to whom he is given. In himself, however, he is God, even if he is given to no one, because he was coeternal God with the Father and the Son before he was given to anyone.

Nor, because he is given by them, is he therefore inferior to them. He is given as the Gift of God in such a way that he also gives himself as God.

It cannot be said that he is not master of his own power, of whom it is written, “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8). The Apostle also says, as I have already quoted above, “One and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing them individually to each as he wills.”

There is no condition of the one given and domination by those who give, but a harmony between the one given and those who give.

### 37.

Therefore, if [Note: [Col. 1086] The manuscripts read sicut (“just as”); perhaps si (“if”).] holy Scripture proclaims, “God is love,” and love is from God and works in us so that we remain in God and he in us—and we know this because he has given us of his Spirit—the Spirit himself is God who is love.

Moreover, if among the gifts of God nothing is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit, what follows more consistently than that he is love, who is called both God and from God?

And if the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably demonstrates their common communion, what is more fitting than that the one who is the Spirit common to both should properly be called love?

It is more soundly believed or understood that the Holy Spirit alone is not love in that Trinity, but that he is not without reason properly called love on account of what has been said.
