Just as he is not the only one in that Trinity who is spirit or holy—for the Father is spirit, and the Son is spirit; the Father is holy, and the Son is holy, something piety does not doubt—nevertheless he is not without reason properly called the Holy Spirit.

Because he is common to both, he is properly called by the name that both possess in common.

Otherwise, if the Holy Spirit alone is love in that Trinity, the Son would plainly be found to be the Son not only of the Father but also of the Holy Spirit.

The only-begotten Son of God is called and read about in countless passages as the Son of God the Father. Yet what the Apostle says about God the Father would also be true:

“He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:13).

He did not say, “of his Son.” Had he said this, he would have spoken most truly, just as he spoke most truly when he said it often. But he said, “of the Son of his love” [Note: [Col. 1087] The Louvain edition reads “by his love” (charitate).].

Therefore the Son is also the Son of the Holy Spirit, if the Holy Spirit alone is the love of God in that Trinity.

Since this is utterly absurd, it remains that the Holy Spirit is not the only one who is love there, but that he is properly so called on account of the matters [Col. 1087] I have discussed sufficiently.

The expression “the Son of his love” should be understood as meaning nothing other than “his beloved Son,” or, finally, “the Son of his substance.”

For the love of the Father, which is in his ineffably simple nature, is nothing other than that very nature and substance of his, as we have often said and do not hesitate to repeat.

Accordingly, the Son of his love is no other than the one begotten from his substance.

## CHAPTER XX

### 38. Against Eunomius, Who Said That the Son of God Is the Son Not of Nature but of Will; Epilogue to the Foregoing

For this reason the dialectic of Eunomius, from whom the heretics called Eunomians arose, deserves ridicule.

Since he could neither understand nor was willing to believe that the only-begotten Word of God, through whom all things were made (John 1:3), is the Son of God by nature—that is, begotten from the substance of the Father—he said that the Son was not the Son of God’s own nature, substance, or essence, but the Son of God’s will. In doing so, he wished to assert that God’s will was something accidental to God, by which he would beget the Son.

He argued this because we sometimes will something that previously we did not will—as though it were not precisely because of such changes that our nature is understood to be mutable. Far be it from us to believe such a thing of God.

For it was written for no other reason than that we should understand or believe that, just as God is eternal, so his counsel exists eternally [Note: [Col. 1087] Thus some printed editions, including the Antwerp Benedictine edition; the earlier Benedictine edition reads “thus eternal” (ita aeternum). M.], and therefore is immutable as he himself is:

“Many are the thoughts in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Prov. 19:21).

What is said of thoughts can most truly also be said of wills:

“Many are the wills in a man’s heart, but the will of the Lord remains forever.”

Some, wishing not to call the only-begotten Word the Son of God’s counsel or will, said that the counsel or will of the Father itself was the Word.

But, in my judgment, it is better to say “counsel from counsel” and “will from will,” just as “substance from substance” and “wisdom from wisdom,” lest the absurdity we have already refuted arise—namely, that the Son is said to make the Father wise or willing if the Father does not possess counsel or will in his substance.

A certain man gave an incisive reply to a very cunning heretic who asked whether God begot the Son willingly or unwillingly.

If he answered, “Unwillingly,” an utterly absurd misery would follow concerning God. But if he answered, “Willingly,” the heretic would immediately conclude, as though by an invincible argument, that the Son was not of nature but of will.

That man, however, most alertly asked him in turn whether God the Father was God willingly or unwillingly.

If he answered, “Unwillingly,” the misery would follow that it is utter madness to believe concerning God. But if he said, “Willingly,” the reply would be made to him: “Then he too is God by his will, not by nature.”

What remained, then, except that he should fall silent and see himself bound by his own question in an insoluble knot?

But if God’s will is also properly to be called some person in the Trinity, this name belongs more fittingly to the Holy Spirit, just as does the name “love.” For what else is love than will?

[Col. 1088] **39.** In this book I see that I have discussed the Holy Spirit, according to the holy Scriptures, in a way sufficient for believers who already know that the Holy Spirit is God, neither of another substance nor lesser than the Father and the Son—which we established as true in the preceding books, according to those same Scriptures. Concerning the creature also which God made, we have, insofar as we were able, admonished those who demand an account of such matters to contemplate, as far as they could, his invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20), and especially through the rational or intellectual creature, which was made in the image of God. Through it, as through a mirror, they might, insofar as they could, discern the Trinity—God—in our memory, understanding, and will.

Whoever vigorously perceives these three, divinely and naturally established in his mind, and remembers through memory how great is that in the mind from which even an eternal and unchangeable nature can be recalled, perceived, and desired; observes it through understanding; and embraces it through love, certainly discovers the image of that supreme Trinity. [Note: [Col. 1088] The printed editions add here the word *amplecti* (“to embrace”), which the manuscripts omit.] To remember, see, and love that supreme Trinity—to remember it, contemplate it, and take delight in it—he ought to refer everything in his life. Yet I have admonished him sufficiently concerning this image, made by that same Trinity and changed for the worse by its own fault, lest he compare it with the Trinity in such a way that he considers it altogether similar; rather, in whatever similarity it possesses, let him also perceive its great dissimilarity.

## CHAPTER XXI

**40. On the proposed likeness of the Father and the Son in our memory and understanding, and on the likeness of the Holy Spirit in our will or love.**

As best I could, I have taken care to indicate—though not as something already seen face to face, but by conjecturing through this likeness as through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor. 13:12)—what might in some small measure be perceived in the memory and understanding of our mind concerning God the Father and God the Son. The Father is God the begetter who, in his coeternal Word, in a certain manner spoke everything that he possesses substantially; and his Word is itself God, possessing substantially neither more nor less than what is in him who truthfully, not deceptively, begot the Word. I assign to memory everything that we know, even when we are not thinking of it; but to understanding, in its own particular way, the formation produced by thought. [Note: [Col. 1088] The Louvain edition reads *quamdam* (“a certain”).]

For when, by thinking, we discover what is true, we are said especially to understand it, and we again leave it in memory. Yet there is a more hidden depth of our memory, where we also discovered this truth when we first thought of it; and an inner word is begotten there, belonging to no language—like knowledge from knowledge, vision from vision, and understanding appearing in thought from an understanding that was already in memory but lay hidden. Indeed, the thought itself would not return to what it had left in memory while thinking of other things, unless it retained a kind of memory of its own.

**41.** Concerning the Holy Spirit, I have shown nothing in this enigma that seemed similar to him except our will, or our love—or affection, which is a stronger form of will. For our will, naturally present in us, has various affections according as the things presented or occurring to us attract or repel us. What then? Shall we say that our will, when it is rightly ordered, does not know what it desires or avoids? But if it knows, there is certainly in it a kind of knowledge of its own, which cannot exist without memory and understanding.

Or should anyone be heeded who says that love does not know what it is doing, when it does not act wrongly? Therefore, just as understanding is present in that principal memory in which we find ready and stored what we can reach by thinking, so love is present there as well. For we find these two in it when, by thinking, we discover that we understand and love something—things which were already there even when we were not thinking of them. And just as memory is present, so love is present in that understanding formed by thought—which is the true word we say inwardly, without the language of any people, when we say what we know. For the gaze of our thought does not return to anything unless by remembering, nor does it care to return unless by loving. Thus love joins together the vision established in memory and the vision formed from it in thought, as parent and offspring. If love did not possess knowledge of what it ought to desire—a knowledge that cannot exist without memory and understanding—it would not know what it should rightly love.

## CHAPTER XXII

**42. How great is the dissimilarity between the image of the Trinity discovered in us and the Trinity itself.**

Yet when these three are in a single person, as in a human being, someone may say to us: “These three—memory, understanding, and love—belong to me, not to themselves; they act for me, not for themselves—indeed, I act through them. I remember through memory, understand through understanding, and love through love.”

When I turn the attention of my thought toward my memory [Note: [Col. 1089] The Louvain edition alone reads “through my memory.”] and thus say in my heart what I know, and a true word is begotten from my knowledge, both belong to me—both the knowledge and the word. For I know, and I say in my heart what I know. And when, by thinking in my memory, I discover that I already understand and already love something—understanding and love that were there even before I thought about them—I find my understanding and my love in my memory. It is I who understand and I who love, not they.

Likewise, when thought remembers and wishes to return to what it had left in memory, in order to behold it as understood and speak of it inwardly, it is my memory that remembers and my will that desires, not theirs. My love also, when it remembers and understands what it ought to desire and what it ought to avoid, remembers through my memory, not its own; and whatever it loves intelligently, it understands through my understanding, not its own.

This can be stated briefly: “Through all three I remember, I understand, and I love”—I who am neither memory, nor understanding, nor love, but possess these things. Thus these can be spoken of by one person who possesses the three, but who is not himself the three.

In that supreme simplicity of nature which is God, however, although God is one, there are nevertheless three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**43. The discussion continues concerning the dissimilarity between the trinity in the human being and the Trinity who is God. The Trinity is now seen through a mirror with the help of faith, so that afterward it may be seen more clearly in the promised vision face to face.**

The Trinity itself is one thing; its image in another thing is another. Because of this image, the thing in which these three exist is also called an image—just as both the panel and what is painted on it are called an image, although the panel too is called by the name of “image” because of the painting upon it.

In that supreme Trinity, however, which surpasses all things incomparably, there is such inseparability that, whereas the trinity of human beings cannot be called one human being, in that Trinity there is and is called one God. Nor, again, is that Trinity constituted as this image—which is a human being possessing these three—is one person. Rather, there are three persons: the Father of the Son, the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

Human memory—especially that memory which animals do not possess, namely, memory in which intelligible things are retained even though they did not enter it through the bodily senses—has, according to its limited capacity, an utterly unequal but nevertheless real likeness to the Father. Likewise, human understanding, formed from memory through the focused activity of thought when what is known is spoken and becomes the word of the heart belonging to no language, possesses, despite its great dissimilarity, some likeness to the Son.

And human love, proceeding from knowledge and joining memory and understanding, shared by parent and offspring and therefore understood as neither parent nor offspring, possesses in this image some likeness—although a very unequal one—to the Holy Spirit.

Yet just as in this image of the Trinity these three are not one human being but belong to one human being, so in the supreme Trinity, whose image this is, those three belong to one God; rather, there is one God, and those three are not one person but three. [Note: [Col. 1090] The manuscripts read “do not belong to one God,” with the negative particle, which is rightly omitted in the printed editions.]

This is wonderfully unspeakable, or unspeakably wonderful: although this image of the Trinity is one person, while the supreme Trinity itself is three persons, that Trinity of three persons is more inseparable than this one person. For it exists in the nature of divinity—or, more properly, of deity—and what it is, it is; it is unchangeably and always equal among its persons. It was never nonexistent or otherwise; nor will it ever be nonexistent or otherwise.

These three in the unequal image, however, although not separated by place—for they are not bodies—are nevertheless separated from one another in this present life by degrees of greatness. For although there are no masses or bodily magnitudes there, we nevertheless see that in one person memory is greater than understanding, while in another the reverse is true; and in yet another these two are surpassed by the greatness of love, whether those two themselves are equal to one another or not.

Thus, taken individually, the pairs are overcome by the single members; taken in pairs, they are overcome by the individual members; and the lesser are overcome by the greater. And when they have been healed of all weakness and become equal to one another, even then the created thing, which will not be changed by grace, will not be made equal to the unchangeable nature. [Col. 1091] For the creature is not made equal to the Creator, and when it is healed of all weakness, it will be changed. [Note: [Col. 1091] The printed editions had omitted *mutabitur* (“it will be changed”).] [Note: [Col. 1091] The manuscripts read *mutatur* (“it is changed”).]

**44.** But when the vision promised to us face to face arrives, we shall see this Trinity, which is not only incorporeal but also supremely inseparable and truly unchangeable, much more clearly and certainly than we now see its image, which is what we are.

Yet through this mirror and in this enigma those who see—as it has been granted to see in this life—are not those who merely behold in their own mind the things we have arranged and commended. They are those who see this trinity as an image, so that they may in some way refer what they see to him whose image it is, and, through the image which they see by contemplating it, may also, by conjecture, see that other reality, since they cannot yet see face to face.

For the Apostle did not say, “We now see a mirror,” but, “We now see through a mirror” (1 Cor. 13:12).

## CHAPTER XXIV

**The weakness of the human mind.**

Those, then, who see their own mind—how it can be seen—and in it this trinity, about which I have discussed in many ways as best I could, yet do not believe or understand that it is the image of God, see a mirror indeed. But they see so little through the mirror—that is, him who must now be seen through the mirror—that they do not even know that the mirror they see is a mirror, that is, an image.

If they knew this, perhaps they would also recognize that the one whose mirror it is must be sought through it and, for the present, somehow seen through it, by an unfictitious faith cleansing the heart (1 Tim. 1:5), so that he who is now seen through a mirror may be seen face to face.

When this faith, which cleanses the heart, is despised, what do they accomplish by understanding the subtle discussions concerning the nature of the human mind, except that they are condemned by their own understanding as witness? They would not labor over these matters, nor arrive with difficulty at anything certain, if they were not enveloped in punitive darkness and weighed down by a corruptible body that burdens the soul (Wis. 9:15). And for what offense was this evil inflicted, if not for sin? Therefore, warned by the magnitude of so great an evil, they ought to follow the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

## CHAPTER XXV

**In blessedness alone will it be understood why the Holy Spirit is not begotten and how he proceeds from the Father and the Son.**

Even those who belong to him and are far slower in understanding than these, when at the end of this life they are released from the body, cannot be held by the envious powers that would retain them. Those powers the Lamb—slain without owing them any debt of sin—overcame by the justice of his blood rather than by the power of might. [Col. 1092]

Thus, freed from the devil’s power, they are received by the holy angels, liberated from every evil through the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5). For, in agreement with the divine Scriptures, both the old and the new, through which Christ was foretold and through which he was announced, there is no other name under heaven by which human beings must be saved (Acts 4:12).

Purified from every contagion of corruption [Note: [Col. 1092] The Amiens edition and the manuscripts read “contagion of corruption”; Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “thought of corruption.”], they are placed in peaceful dwellings until they receive their bodies—now incorruptible bodies, which will adorn them rather than weigh them down. For it pleased the best and wisest Creator that the human spirit, piously subject to God, should have a body happily subject to it, and that this happiness should endure without end.

**45.** There we shall see the truth without any difficulty and enjoy it in the clearest and most certain manner. We shall not seek anything through a mind engaged in reasoning; rather, with a contemplative mind we shall see why the Holy Spirit is not the Son, although he proceeds from the Father.

In that light there will be no question. Here, however, experience itself has shown me that this matter is so difficult—and undoubtedly it will appear similarly so to those who read these things carefully and intelligently—that, although in the second book of this work I promised to discuss it elsewhere (ch. 3), whenever I have wished to show in the creature that we are something resembling that reality, my expression has not proved sufficient to follow even my limited understanding. Even in my understanding, I have felt that I possessed more endeavor than accomplishment.

I wished to show, in the one person who is a human being, the image of that supreme Trinity, and, in a changeable thing, to display those three—so that they might be understood more easily—especially through temporal intervals, as I did in the ninth book. But the three belonging to one person could not, as human intention demands, correspond to those three persons, as we demonstrated in this fifteenth book.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**The Holy Spirit given twice by Christ. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is without time, and he cannot be called the son of both.**

In that supreme Trinity, which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it could be shown—or even asked—whether the Son was first born from the Father and afterward the Holy Spirit proceeded from both. For Holy Scripture calls the Spirit the Spirit of both.

He is the one of whom the Apostle says: “But because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts” (Gal. 4:6). And he is the one of whom the Son himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

By many other testimonies of the divine utterances it is established that the Spirit, properly called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity, belongs to the Father and the Son. Concerning him the Son himself also says: “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26); and elsewhere: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26).

That he proceeds from both is taught as follows: the Son himself says, “He proceeds from the Father.” And when he had risen from the dead and appeared to his disciples, he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), thereby showing that he also proceeds from himself. It is this same power that went forth from him, as we read in the Gospel, “and healed them all” (Luke 6:19).

**46.** As for why, after his resurrection, he first gave the Holy Spirit on earth (John 20:22) and afterward sent him from heaven (Acts 2:4), I think the reason is that through this gift love is poured into our hearts (Rom. 5:5)—the love by which we love God and our neighbor, according to those two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40).

To signify this, the Lord Jesus gave the Holy Spirit twice: once on earth, for the love of our neighbor, and again from heaven, for the love of God. And even if some other explanation is offered for the Holy Spirit’s being given twice, we must nevertheless not doubt that the same Holy Spirit was given when Jesus breathed on them—the Spirit of whom he soon afterward said, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), where this Trinity is especially commended.

He is therefore the one who was also given from heaven on the day of Pentecost, that is, ten days after the Lord ascended into heaven. How, then, is God not the one who gives the Holy Spirit? Indeed, how great is the God who gives God!

For none of his disciples gave the Holy Spirit. They prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands; they did not themselves give him. The Church still preserves this practice in its leaders.

Finally, Simon Magus, when offering money to the Apostles, did not say, “Give me this power also, so that I may give the Holy Spirit,” but, “Whoever I lay my hands upon,” he said, “let him receive the Holy Spirit.” For Scripture had not said above, “Simon saw that the Apostles gave the Holy Spirit,” but, “Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands” (Acts 8:18–19).

For this reason the Lord Jesus himself not only gave the Holy Spirit as God, but also received him as a human being; therefore he is said to have been “full of grace” (John 1:14) and of the Holy Spirit (Luke 4:1). More plainly, it is written of him in the Acts of the Apostles: “God anointed him with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10:38).

This was certainly not with visible oil, but with the gift of grace, signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized. Nor was Christ then anointed with the Holy Spirit when, after his baptism, the Spirit descended upon him like a dove (Matt. 3:16). For then he graciously chose to prefigure his body—that is, his Church—in which the baptized especially receive the Holy Spirit.

Rather, he must be understood to have been anointed at that mystical and invisible anointing when the Word of God became flesh (John 1:14): that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to God the Word in the Virgin’s womb, so that it became one person with him.

For this reason we confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. It would be utterly absurd to believe that he received the Holy Spirit when he was already thirty years old—for he was baptized by John at that age (Luke 3:21–23). Rather, he came to baptism, just as he was entirely without sin, so too not without the Holy Spirit.

For if it is written of his servant and forerunner, John himself, “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1:15)—since, although begotten by a father, he nevertheless received the Holy Spirit while being formed in the womb—what should be understood or believed concerning the man Christ, whose very conception according to the flesh was not carnal but spiritual?

Further, in what is written of him—that he received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33)—both natures are displayed, namely, the human and the divine: he received as a human being; he poured out as God.

We, however, can receive this gift according to our limited capacity, but we cannot pour it out upon others. Rather, in order that this may happen, we invoke God upon them, from whom it is accomplished.

**47.** Can we therefore ask whether the Holy Spirit had already proceeded from the Father when the Son was born, or had not yet proceeded and proceeded from both after the Son was born—when there are no times there? We could ask such a question where we find time: whether the will first proceeds from the human mind, so that what has been discovered may be called offspring; and, once that offspring has been brought forth or begotten, whether that will is perfected, coming to rest in this goal, so that what had been the desire of the seeker becomes the love of one who enjoys, proceeding now from both—from the begetting mind and the begotten conception—as from parent and offspring.

Such questions absolutely cannot be asked where nothing begins in time in order to be completed later in time. Therefore, whoever can understand the generation of the Son from the Father without time should understand the procession of the Holy Spirit from both without time.

And whoever can understand that, when the Son says, “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26), the Father did not give life to the Son as though the Son had previously existed without life, but begot him without time in such a way that the life the Father gave the Son by begetting him is coeternal with the life of the Father who gave it—let that person understand that, just as the Father has in himself that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him, so he gave the Son that the same Holy Spirit should proceed from him also.

Both occur without time. Thus the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father is to be understood in such a way that he also proceeds from the Son, and that what proceeds from the Son is from the Father for the Son. [Note: [Col. 1094] The printed editions read “is from the Father and for the Son.” We have removed *et* (“and”) on the authority of the manuscripts.]

For if the Son has everything he possesses from the Father, then surely he has from the Father that he should also be the one from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds. But no times involving a “before” and an “after” should be imagined there, because there are absolutely no such times.

How, then, would the Holy Spirit not most absurdly be called the son of both, since, just as the generation from the Father grants the Son essence without any beginning in time and without any change of nature, so the procession from both grants the Holy Spirit essence without any beginning in time and without any change of nature?

For this reason, although we do not say that the Holy Spirit was begotten, we nevertheless do not dare to say that he is unbegotten, lest anyone should suppose from this term either that there are two fathers in that Trinity or that there are two persons who are not from another.

The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called “unbegotten”—not indeed in Scripture, but in the customary language of disputants who speak about so great a matter as best they can. The Son, however, was born from the Father; and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father, while, through the Father’s giving without any interval of time, he proceeds jointly from both.

He would be called the son of the Father and the Son if both had begotten him—which is abhorrent to the understanding of all sound minds. Therefore the Spirit of both was not begotten by both; he proceeds from both.

## CHAPTER XXVII

**48. What suffices here for solving the question of why the Spirit is not called begotten and why the Father alone is unbegotten. What those who do not understand these matters should do.**

Since in that coeternal, equal, incorporeal, ineffably unchangeable, and inseparable Trinity it is extremely difficult to distinguish generation from procession, let it suffice for the present for those who cannot extend their understanding further to repeat what we said in a sermon delivered to the ears of the Christian people and then committed to writing.

Among other things, after teaching through testimonies from the holy Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, I said:

“If, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, why did the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John 15:26)? Why, do you think, except that he is accustomed to refer to the one from whom he himself is even what belongs to him? Hence also the statement: ‘My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 7:16).

“If, then, here his teaching is understood to be the teaching which he nevertheless said was not his but the Father’s, how much more must the Holy Spirit there be understood to proceed also from him, where he says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ without saying, ‘He does not proceed from me’?

“From the one from whom the Son has his being God—for he is God from God—from that same one he surely has that the Holy Spirit should also proceed from him. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Son, as he proceeds from the Father, is something he has from the Father himself.

“Here, insofar as such people as we are can understand it, we may also understand why the Holy Spirit is not said to have been born but rather to proceed. For if he too were called the Son, he would necessarily be called the son of both—which is utterly absurd. No one is the son of two except of a father and a mother. But far be it from us to suspect anything of this sort between God the Father and God the Son.

“For even a human child does not proceed simultaneously from father and mother: when it proceeds from the father into the mother, it does not at that time proceed from the mother; and when it proceeds from the mother into this light, it does not at that time proceed from the father.

“The Holy Spirit, however, does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son to sanctify the creature; he proceeds simultaneously from both, although the Father gave the Son that, just as he proceeds from the Father, he should also proceed from the Son.

“For we cannot say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. Accordingly, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son also to have life in himself, so he gave him that the Spirit should proceed from him, just as he proceeds from the Father.” (On the Gospel of John, tractate 99, §§8–9.)

I have transferred these words from that sermon into this book, speaking to believers, not unbelievers.

**49.** But if they are not capable of contemplating this image and seeing how true these things are—things that exist in their mind, which are not three in such a way as to be three persons, but all three belong to the human being, who is one person—why do they not instead believe what is found in the sacred Scriptures concerning that supreme Trinity who is God, rather than demand that a perfectly clear account be given to them, an account that cannot be grasped by the human mind, which is naturally slow and weak?

Once they have firmly believed the holy Scriptures as utterly truthful witnesses, let them act by praying, seeking, and living well, so that they may understand—that is, so that, insofar as it can be seen, what they hold by faith may be seen by the mind. Who would forbid this? Indeed, who would not urge it?

But if they think these things must be denied because their blind minds cannot perceive them, then those who have been blind from birth ought also to deny that the sun exists.

The light therefore shines in the darkness; and if the darkness does not comprehend it (John 1:5), let them first be illumined by God’s gift so that they may become believers and begin to be light in comparison with unbelievers. Then, with this foundation laid, let them be built up toward seeing what they believe, so that eventually they may be able to see.

There are, indeed, things believed in such a way that they can no longer be seen at all. Christ will not be seen again on the cross. But unless one believes that this happened and was seen in such a way that it is not hoped for as something still future and to be seen, one does not reach Christ as he will be seen without end.

As for contemplating through understanding, insofar as possible, that supreme, ineffable, incorporeal, and unchangeable nature, the human mind never exercises its vision better—under the guidance of the rule of faith—than in that which the human being, by his nature, possesses better than the other animals and even better than the other parts of his soul: namely, the mind itself.

To it has been assigned a sight of invisible things. To it, presiding honorably as though in a higher and inner place, the bodily senses report all things to be judged. And there is nothing higher than it, to which it ought to be subject for governance, except God.

**50.** Yet amid all that I have now said—while I dare to declare that I have said nothing worthy of the ineffability of that supreme Trinity, but rather confess that his knowledge has been wonderfully made too great for me and that I cannot attain it (Ps. 138:6)—where do you feel yourself to be, O my soul? Where do you lie? Where do you stand? [Note: [Col. 1096] Some manuscripts read: “where you lie, where you dwell, or where you stand, until …” Most others read: “where you lie, where you dwell, until …”] Until the one who is gracious toward all your iniquities heals all your diseases (Ps. 102:3)?

Surely you recognize that you are in that stable to which the Samaritan brought the man whom he found half-dead from the many wounds inflicted by robbers (Luke 10:30–34). [Col. 1097] Yet you have seen many true things—not with the eyes by which colored bodies are seen, but with those for which the one who said, “Let my eyes see equity,” prayed (Ps. 16:2).

You have surely seen many true things, and distinguished them from the light by which you saw while it shone upon you. Lift your eyes toward that very light and fix them upon it, if you can. For then you will see the difference between the generation of the Word of God and the procession of the Gift of God, on account of which the only-begotten Son said that the Holy Spirit was not begotten from the Father—for otherwise he would be his brother—but proceeded from him.

Therefore, although the Spirit is a certain consubstantial communion of the Father and the Son, he is not called the son of both—far be that away. But to see this clearly and distinctly, you cannot fix your vision there; I know that you cannot.

I speak the truth; I speak to myself: I know what I cannot do. Yet that light itself shows you those three within you, in which you may recognize the image of that supreme Trinity, which you are not yet able to contemplate with fixed eyes.

It shows you that there is a true word within you when it is begotten from your knowledge—that is, when we say what we know—even though we neither utter nor think a meaningful sound in the language of any people. Rather, our thought is formed from what we know, and in the gaze of the thinker there is an image most like the cognition that memory contained. [Note: [Col. 1097] Nearly all manuscripts read “cognition” here; below, “to proceed from cognition”; and shortly afterward, “the image of cognition.”] These two—parent and offspring, as it were—are joined by a third, namely, will or love.

This will certainly proceeds from thought—for no one desires what he does not know at all, either in kind or in quality—yet it is not an image of thought. Thus, in this intelligible reality, a certain distinction between generation and procession is suggested, since whoever is capable of seeing and distinguishing understands that to behold something in thought is not the same as to desire it or even to enjoy it through the will.

You too were able to perceive this, although you have not been and are not able to explain it in sufficiently adequate language: what you scarcely saw amid the clouds of bodily likenesses, which do not cease to confront human thoughts.

But that light, which is not what you are, also showed you that those incorporeal likenesses of bodies are one thing, and that the truth which we contemplate through understanding after rejecting those likenesses is another. That light showed your inward eyes this and other things equally certain.

What, then, is the reason you cannot see that light itself with fixed vision, except weakness? And what caused that weakness in you, except iniquity? [Note: [Col. 1097] Most manuscripts read: “And who caused it in you, except iniquity?”]

Who, then, heals all your diseases except the one who is gracious toward all your iniquities? I shall therefore finally conclude this book at last more suitably with a prayer than with argument.

## CHAPTER XXVIII
## 51. Conclusion of the book, with a prayer and an apology for verbosity

Lord our God, we believe in you as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For Truth would not have said, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), unless you were Trinity. Nor would you, Lord God, command us to be baptized in the name of one who is not the Lord God. Nor would the divine voice say, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4), unless you were Trinity in such a way that you were one Lord God.

And if you yourself were God the Father, and the Son were himself your Word, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit your gift, we would not read in the Scriptures of truth, “God sent his Son” (Galatians 4:4; John 3:17); nor would you, O Only-Begotten, say of the Holy Spirit, “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26), and, “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26).

Directing my attention according to this rule of faith, I have sought you as far as I could—as far as you enabled me to do so—and I have desired, through understanding, to see what I believed. I have argued at length and labored greatly. Lord my God, my one hope, hear me, so that, wearied, I may not cease to seek you, but may always seek your face with ardor (Psalm 104:4).

Grant the strength to seek—you who have caused yourself to be found [Note: The manuscripts read, “you who have caused yourself to be discovered”—or “to be found.”], and who have given ever greater hope of finding you. Before you stand my strength and my weakness: preserve the former and heal the latter. Before you stand my knowledge and my ignorance: where you have opened the way for me, receive me as I enter; where you have closed it, open to me when I knock. May I remember you, understand you, and love you. Increase these gifts in me until you reform me completely.

I know that it is written, “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs 10:19). But would that, in proclaiming your word and praising you alone, I spoke! Then I would not merely escape sin; I would also acquire a good reward, however much I spoke in that way. For the blessed man of God would not have enjoined sin upon his brother, a son in the faith, when he wrote to him, saying, “Proclaim the word; be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2).

Must we say that he did not speak at length—he who did not keep silent about your word, Lord, not only in season but also out of season? Yet it was not “much,” because it was entirely necessary.

Deliver me, God, from the verbosity that I suffer within my soul, wretched as I am in your sight and fleeing to your mercy [Note: The printed editions read, “and fleeing”—or “as one who flees.” Most manuscripts omit the conjunction *et*, reading simply “fleeing.”]. For even when I am silent in speech, I do not keep silent in my thoughts. And if I thought only what pleased you, I would certainly not ask you to deliver me from this verbosity. But my thoughts are many, such as you know them to be—the thoughts of human beings, for they are futile (Psalm 93:11).

Grant me not to consent to them; and if at times they delight me, nevertheless enable me to condemn them and not linger among them as though drowsing. Let them not have such power over me that anything arising from them proceeds into my actions; but, with you guarding me, at least let my judgment and conscience remain safe from them.

A certain wise man, speaking of you in his book, now called by its proper name Ecclesiasticus, says: “We say many things, and do not reach the end; but the sum of all discourse is he himself” (Ecclesiasticus 43:29). Therefore, when we have reached you, these many things that we say without reaching you will cease; and you will remain one, all things in all things (1 Corinthians 15:28). Without end we shall say one thing, praising you as one, and, made one in you, we too shall be one.

Lord, one God, God Trinity, whatever I have said in these books concerning what is yours, may I recognize as yours; and if anything has come from what is mine, forgive me—and may it nevertheless be yours. Amen.

# Appendix to Volume Eight of the Works of Saint Augustine

In this appendix these works, which are not genuinely Augustine’s, are presented, namely:

- *A Treatise Against Five Heresies*.
- *A Sermon Against Jews, Pagans, and Arians*.
- *A Dialogue on the Dispute between the Church and the Synagogue*.
- *A Book on the Faith Against the Manichaeans*, attributed to Evodius.
- *A Commonitory*, commonly attributed to Augustine, on receiving converted Manichaeans.
- *Against Felicianus the Arian on the Faith of the Trinity*, a book restored to Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus.
- *Questions on the Trinity and on Genesis*, excerpted from Alcuin.
- *Two Books on the Incarnation of the Word to Januarius*, compiled from Origen.
- *A Book on the Trinity and Unity of God*.
- *On the Essence of the Divinity*.
- *A Dialogue on the Unity of the Holy Trinity*.
- *A Book on Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.

[Note: We compared all these editions at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

[Col. 1099]

# A Treatise Against Five Heresies, or Against Five Kinds of Enemies

*(C, G, S)*

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Sermon

The Leuven scholars and Bellarmine, together with others, unhesitatingly assign to Augustine the treatise *Against Five Heresies*, which Erasmus had judged to be the work of an educated, clever, and eloquent man, but not of Augustine—unless, he said, it had perhaps been written by Augustine in his youth. They do so on the authority of Bede, who cites certain passages from chapters four and five of this same treatise in his comments on the first chapter of Paul’s Letter to the Romans.

I found those words, cited under Augustine’s name, not only in Bede’s well-known longer collection, which is more properly the work of Florus of Lyon, but also in another collection of Bede’s, certainly genuine, which is preserved with us: his shorter collection on Paul, not yet published in print.

In fact, however, this sermon is found to have been delivered at a time when Africa was under Arian domination, when the orthodox shepherds had been removed—some by exile or flight, others by death—and the heretics were harassing the Catholics with disputations and attempting to corrupt them with gifts or money. In chapter 6 we read: “Where are you, fountains of tears? To what farmers am I speaking? Some are dead; others have been driven away.” And in chapter 7: “The Arian resists, shouts, quarrels, fights, gathers crowds, and battles against Christ. Christ shed blood to redeem; the Arian scatters money to destroy.”

Similar statements are found in Sermon 2 *To the Catechumens*, section 24, and in the *Sermon on the Time of the Barbarians*, section 10. We observed in volume 6 that these belong to the period of the Vandal persecution, which arose after Augustine’s death.

Furthermore, the diction is neither sufficiently precise nor as serious as Augustine’s usually is. For example, in chapter 3 the author teaches that, for God the Father to beget the Son, a good will took the place of a wife. Again, what Augustine wrote against the Donatists, the author turns against the Arians in chapter 6: “Why do we quarrel? If the inheritance is one for us, let us possess it together; we are brothers,” and so forth.

We therefore believe that Bede was deceived here—as he was also in the spurious *Conference with Pascentius*, which we relegated to the appendix of volume 2—by the error of ancient codices that assign this treatise to Augustine.

Bellarmine says that Hincmar mentions this book in his work *On the Non-Trinal Deity*. Because the statements in chapter 7 were highly inconvenient to Hincmar’s preconceived opinion—“Thanks be to you, true and one Trinity, one and triune Truth, triune and one Unity”—he argues at length, from page 450 to page 464, that these words were inserted by some forger and impostor.

Bellarmine says that the work is noted in the *Index of Possidius*, specifically in the interpolated copy published by Johannes Ulimmerius. Yet it is found nowhere in the other copies of Possidius’s *Index*, whether printed or manuscript, that we have been able to see.

We have reviewed the treatise and corrected it against ten Vatican codices, as well as one Germanensis codex, the Michaeline, Remigian, Ebrulfian, Arnulfian, Cistercian, Fossatian, and Colbertine codices, the codex of the distinguished lord of Maran of Toulouse, the Tours codex of Saint Gatianus, and another codex of the Church of Lyon. In these it is entitled *A Little Book Against Five Heresies, or Against Five Kinds of Enemies*, because it is directed against Pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians.

# Chapter One

[Col. 1101]

## 1. The five kinds of enemies

I confess that I am a debtor—not because necessity compels me, but because charity does, which is stronger. An exactor cannot be as troublesome in compelling payment as a debtor is devoted to making repayment [Note: Another reading is: “An exactor cannot be troublesome in compelling payment when the debtor is devoted to making repayment,” and so forth.].

But, in order that I may fulfill what I promised, help me with your holy prayers, so that almighty God may grant grace to my words and I may satisfy your devout minds and ears.

If you remember, you who were present at the time, we said that there were five kinds of enemies. Against these we asked for a postponement so that we might prepare the necessary weapons for their defeat. The promised day has dawned, and, with the Lord’s help, we too have advanced eagerly to battle.

“Our help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 123:8). He who gave the courage to fight will grant victory to the fighter. Let neither the multitude of the enemies nor the appearance of those engaged in battle turn us back. Let not their shining weapons frighten us, as though they were made of glass [Note: Several manuscripts read: “as though shining glass armor terrified.”].

The great and powerful Goliath, terrifying in his weapons and protected by a huge army [Note: The manuscripts read: “protected by his appearance.”], was struck down by David alone, a small and unarmed boy, with a single blow of a stone; and he threw the entire camp of the Philistines into confusion and flight (1 Samuel 17:49).

What else did the stone hurled by David’s hand against Goliath signify but Christ, who would come from David’s seed, against the devil?

## 2. The five errors

Let us now attack and set forth the five kinds of errors that we have mentioned.

The Pagans say: “Why do you shrink from us and reject us as worshipers of many gods? Behold, you too say that the God whom you proclaim must be worshiped has a son, and you invent that he was born without the union of another sex.”

The Jews say: “How do you worship one God, when you also extort from human beings that they should venerate and worship with you as the Son of God the man whom our fathers crucified, while calling him Lord [Note: Several manuscripts read: “calling him God.”]?”

The Manichaeans say that what is called the Lord Christ’s birth from a woman’s womb is a phantom. “It is not fitting,” they say, “to believe that so great a majesty passed through the filth and squalor of a woman.”

The Sabellians, who are also called Patripassians, say: “The Father and the Son are one God, because the one who is Father is himself also Son. For if we say otherwise, we shall be called worshipers of many gods.”

The Arians say: “The Father is one, and the Son is another, but the Son is lesser. For how can the one begotten be equal to the one who begot him?”

# Chapter Two

## 3. Confidence against the heretics

Behold the questions posed by these errors, like battle lines arranged by enemies. Against these destructive lines, most holy brothers, take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfected in all things.

“Gird your loins with truth.” Let no one tremble; let no one fear. There is the breastplate of righteousness; there is the shield of faith, with which the flaming arrows of the evil one may be received and extinguished. There is the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6:14–17).

Whoever among the soldiers of Christ the faithful is armed with these weapons will fear no person and will not be called back from battle by the terror of the times.

Come, brothers: the battle is at hand, the work is burning, the adversary presses upon us, prepares his darts, and attempts to cast them. Let no one be terrified. Brothers, there are more [Col. 1102] with us than with them.

With us is that great Moses, the friend of God, who, to conquer the enemy in battle, stretched out his hands toward heaven, already then displaying the figure of Christ’s cross. At the divine command, by one stroke of his staff he turned the surging waves of the swollen sea [Note: Older manuscripts read: “the waves of the most turbulent sea.”] into dry fields for the people to cross.

With us is Joshua, Israel’s leader after Moses, the strongest of warriors, whose very name indicates “Savior.” By his power and divine confidence, he stopped the day before it completed the course of its journey and commanded the night not to advance. He overcame, captured, humbled, and killed the kings of the nations—not one by one, but all together.

With us is David, strong-handed. What should I say? He was God’s servant, God’s chosen one, God’s friend, God’s ancestor. He knew—and knew well—not only how “to spare the conquered and subdue the proud” (*Aeneid* 6.853), but also how to display courage and preserve patience. When he pursued his enemies [Note: The Tours manuscript reads: “When his enemies were pursuing him”], he was not destructive; when he conquered, he was not impious.

With us are many other holy men who foresaw and foretold everything that was to come.

There is therefore nothing for you to fear. Only wait, listen, and pray; let your prayer for me be more attentive and more fervent [Note: Several manuscripts read “sharper”; others, “higher.”]. Let us not linger longer. Let us now pursue what we have proposed.

# Chapter Three

## 4. Hermes and the Sibyl against the Pagans

What do you say, Pagan? You say: “If God delighted in a son, he needed a marriage. If he recoiled from marriage, he is alone and without a son. For what could be found like God that could be joined to God and bear a son for God? Furthermore, if, as you say, God has a son, you no longer worship one God.”

What shall we do? We have received a weapon hurled by a Philistine; what shall we hurl in return? Whatever weapon we send, even if it reaches him, it is of no use. Why? Because he is hard. How hard? He is made of stone: he worships idols, and it is written, “Let all who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Psalm 113:8).

He does not accept the Holy Scriptures. Let us therefore seek a stone with which he may be struck, so that, once struck, he may be shattered; once shattered, broken into pieces; once broken into pieces, turned into dust; once turned into dust, watered; once watered, sown; and once sown, may produce fruit—not fruit to be consumed by fire, but fruit to be stored in the granary.

Hermes, who in Latin is called Mercury, wrote a book entitled *Λόγος τέλειος* (*Logos teleios*), that is, “Perfect Word.” It is a great title for this book, because the one about whom it is written is great. For what is more perfect than the Word, who alone is free among the dead (Psalm 87:6)?

Let us hear what Mercury says about the Perfect Word:

“The Lord,” he says, “and maker of all the gods, made the second Lord.”

And shortly afterward, to show what he had said, he repeated it and said:

“Since, therefore, he made this one first, and alone and one” [Note: Some manuscripts read “and true”; others, “and good”], “he appeared good to him and completely full of every good.”

How completely full? Let the evangelist John say: “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John 1:16).

“He appeared good to him and completely full of every good.” And he continues:

“He rejoiced.”

With whom, or over whom, did he rejoice? Let the Wisdom of God itself, the Son of God, say: “I was the one over whom he rejoiced” (Proverbs 8:30).

“Therefore he rejoiced and loved him greatly as his only-begotten.”

[Col. 1103]

The one whom he had first called “made” he later called “only-begotten.”

In another place he said:

“The Son of the blessed God and of good will, whose name cannot be related by human mouth.”

Were you looking, Pagan, for a wife for God? Hear Mercury: “Prepare your forehead and receive stone against stone. Fall, so that you may be raised; be broken, so that you may be strengthened; be destroyed, so that you may be built. Let the blow of the stone divide neither the skin of your forehead, nor rupture a vein of blood, nor open a pit of injury; rather, let it make the sign of the cross.”

You seek a wife for God? I beg you, let impure perversity be cast out from your heart. God’s wife is good will.

How God is Father and the Son is God, yet there are not two gods but one God, I ought not to dispute with you, because unless you believe, you will in no way be able to understand. Nevertheless, Mercury confesses the Son of God as God [Note: The manuscripts read “Lord.”]. Struck by this stone, let the stony man cease to be sacrilegious.

Let us hear what their prophetess, the Sibyl, also says about the same subject:

“God,” she says, “gave another one to the children of human beings to worship” [Note: Several manuscripts read “to faithful human beings.”].

As is evident, in these statements of Mercury and the Sibyl, Sabellius too is judged. Mercury speaks of God the Father and of the Son; the Sibyl speaks of another God. Sabellius says “not another,” because he asserts that the Father is the same one as the Son.

It is very good if, by one blow, we strike not merely one adversary but as many as possible, wherever the blow may reach.

The Sibyl also says:

“Know that your own Lord is the Son of God” [Note: Another reading is “God.”].

This verse reproves both the Pagan and the Jew.

Elsewhere she calls the Son of God *σύμβουλον* (*symboulon*), that is, “counsel” or “counselor.” And the prophet says, “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty and Powerful God” (Isaiah 9:6).

Here the Arian is condemned. When he says that the Son of God is lesser, he implies that God once did not have a son. And if he was without a son, he was without counsel.

Behold the dangers to which we are exposed. But since God was never without counsel, even in opposition to the Arian, the Father could never have been without the Son.

What are you doing, Pagan? Open your ears. Do not be like the deaf asp that stops its ear so that it may not hear the voice of the charmer (Psalm 57:5).

I am not bringing forward my own authorities to you. Mercury is yours, the one whom you honor and worship so greatly among the gods that you named a day after him. Hear him himself. Let him convict you himself; let him conquer you himself, so that when he has defeated you, you may yield to him and believe me.

Mercury said: “God loved his Only-Begotten.”

He himself said: “The Son of the blessed God and of good will.”

And lest he should endure the tedium of inquiry about his name, he continued:

“Whose name cannot be related by human mouth.”

What do you say, Mercury? You say that the name of God’s Son cannot be related by human beings. Let it be related by you, who are judged by human beings to be not a human but a god.

He speaks to his son, saying:

“But there is something.”

What is it?

“The holy, holy [Note: Another reading is “Holy Spirit”] word of wisdom of the ineffable Son.”

Is this not what is meant by “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1)?

Tell us, Hermes: does this speech of wisdom have a mother?

He continues:

“It belongs to God the Lord alone, God who rules over all mortal beings.”

And because it cannot be investigated by human beings, he adds:

“It is above human beings.”

Therefore, because it is above human beings, I cannot relate the name of the Son of God, because I am not a god. Let human beings, as human beings, say what I am not; I acknowledge what I am.

“The speech of wisdom belongs to God alone.”

Therefore, Pagan, do not imagine or invent a human marriage there. It belongs to God alone, and it is above human beings.

The Sibyl reproves you, saying:

“Know that your own Lord is the Son of God”—himself, not another; not Mars, not Jupiter, not Mercury, but the one whom Mercury confesses.

Why are you surprised, Christian, that these people say such things about the Father and the Son? Even the demons believe—and tremble (James 2:19). Indeed, when the Lord passed by in the Gospel, they said:

“We know who you are, the Son of God. You have come before the appointed time to torment us” (Mark 1:24).

Would that human beings recognized the Savior as the demons recognize the Judge!

# Chapter Four

[Col. 1104]

## 5. The Old Testament against the Jews

What does the Jew say? “We have one God; besides him we know no other. But the one whom you call Christ our fathers killed, not as God, but as a man.”

Indeed, this is what I said: Would that human beings recognized the Savior as the demons recognize the Judge!

Behold, the demons saw and trembled; human beings saw and killed. The demons confessed; human beings persecuted. What unhappiness, and how great a misery, to be found inferior even to demons?

Yet human beings believe and demons perish; human beings are saved and demons are punished. But this transformation is “the work of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11), not the presumption of a human being who trusts in his own strength.

Against this Jew I do not labor. His own books fight against him; the Law and the Prophets fight against him. Either, conquered and humbled, he will be saved, or, proud and obstinate, he will be punished.

The Lord said to Moses:

“Behold, I send my angel before you, to guard you on the way and bring you into the place that I have prepared. Pay attention to him and listen to his voice, nor think that he should be despised. You must not despise him, because he will not forgive when you sin, and my name is in him” (Exodus 23:20–21).

You have heard of an angel: recognize the Lord. Do not think that he should be despised. Hear further what you should fear: “Do not think that he should be despised.” Why? “Because he will not forgive when you sin, and my name is in him.”

Who is this one so great that God has given him both his authority and his name?

“The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Psalm 23:10).

And how do we prove that when an angel is mentioned, God ought to be understood? You have it in the book called Genesis:

“Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting before the gate of the city. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them” (Genesis 19:1).

What more need be said? He received them and served them as strangers. Through the practice of hospitality he was delivered from the danger of the city; he escaped temporal fire and obtained an eternal reward.

Learn, Christians, to show hospitality without distinction, lest perhaps the one whose house you have closed and to whom you have denied kindness should be Christ himself.

Let us not wander any longer from the action we have begun. The angels came to Lot and said—observe carefully, since angels are said to speak:

“Save your life; do not look behind you” (Genesis 19:17).

For “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

Nor should you stand anywhere in the whole surrounding region. Do not cling to earthly pleasures, but save yourself on the mountain (Genesis 19:17). Let God be your hope, lest you too perish together with the inhabitants of Sodom.

“And Lot said to them”—observe a man who sees: not blind, like the Jews and Sabellians; not bleary-eyed, like the Arians; but possessing sound eyes, like Catholic Christians. He saw angels and understood the Lord.

What did he say to the angels?

“Lot said to them: My lord, because your servant has found favor before you, and you have magnified the mercy that you have shown me in saving my life” (Genesis 19:19).

What a great thing this is! When I wish to strike the Jew in this way, Moses, that most powerful man, brandished the spear of his word and sent it through the Jew to pass over to the Sabellian and strike the Arian.

What are you doing, holy Lot? You see angels, not one but two, and you say, “My lord.” You address one; you pray to one. Do you not fear that you may seem to insult the other?

“Far from it,” he says. Depart, Jews; depart, Sabellians, because you do not see. Depart, Arians, because you see too little. I see, and because I see what I see, I neither despise nor err. I see two; I see equals. I ask one and do injury to no one, because I do not divide the Father from the Son.

For, so that you may understand that I am not deceived when I entreat two as one, observe whether two or one answers my prayers.

He asked to have refuge in a small and nearby city and to live there. He is answered. Let us see how many answer.

The words of the book follow:

“And he said to him”—as though this were a singular response.

Continue further; let us see:

“Behold, I have also received your prayers in this matter, so that I will not destroy the city for which you have spoken. Hurry and save yourself there, because I cannot do anything until you enter it” (Genesis 19:21–22).

[Col. 1105]

Do you see, Jew, that the one who is called an angel is also God? Do you hear, Arian, two—the Father and the Son—speaking, yet not the same Father as Son, as the Sabellians claim, but Father and Son?

Do you hear what is said: “I have received your prayers”? Do you hear him say: “I will not destroy the city”? Do you hear: “I cannot do anything”?

Let the Jew read “angel” and understand God. Let the Sabellian read that two came. Let the Arian read that one answered. Let them not despise these things, but flee their error, lest they reach the fire.

But to demonstrate more fully that the angel mentioned must be understood as God, let us recite what follows in this passage:

“The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven” (Genesis 19:24).

What is “the Lord from the Lord” except the Son from the Father? As in another passage:

“The Lord said to my Lord”—that is, the Father said to his Son—“Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet” (Psalm 109:1).

Again, in Exodus:

“The angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the bush. He saw that the bush was burning with fire, but the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, ‘I shall go and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned.’ When the Lord saw that he was approaching to see, the Lord called him from the bush.”

Behold: the very angel is the very Lord.

And the account continues:

“Moses, Moses.”

And he said:

“Who [Note: Another reading is “What”] are you, Lord?”

The Lord said to him:

“Do not come near here unless you remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”

Hear further what he said to him:

“I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:2–6).

Therefore, let the Jew hear “angel” in such a way that he understands “Lord” and fears God. Let the Sabellian confess the Father without denying the Son. Let the Arian confess the Father and the Son without diminishing the Son.

Joshua son of Nun also, as the book written under his name says, was fighting against enemies. While he stood in the very battle array, he saw a man standing opposite him, holding a drawn sword. He went toward him and said:

“Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?”

He replied:

“Neither; but I am the commander of the army of the Lord, and now I have come” (Joshua 5:13–14).

Then Joshua fell face down upon the earth and worshiped.

Now follow your leader, Jew. He sees, asks, and worships. Vision has communion, for both what is recognized and what is not recognized are seen. Thus vision has communion, questioning has ignorance, and worship has faith.

Whom does he see? A man.

Who is this man? He is the one whose coming against the hostile nations was foretold, desired, and awaited.

“And he is a man,” it says, “and who will recognize him?” [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the manuscripts.]

Who is the commander of the Lord’s army? Is he not the one who, when asked in the Gospel who he was, answered, “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25)?

Why are you troubled, Joshua? “Why did the nations rage and the peoples devise empty things against the Lord and against his Christ?” (Psalm 2:1).

You see an armed man; do not fear. I have not come against you but for you, because I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24).

What is this, Joshua? You see, ask, and worship. Hear the answer:

“I see a man; I ask whom I see; I hear one whom I do not see; I worship not what I see but what I believe, because faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

What, then, are you seeking? Pay attention and follow:

“I see a man, but what I understand is beyond the sons of men. I do not know what flashes before me, and something bright shines as though from hiding. I go to him because he comes to me. I will examine this great sight that I see.”

Whom do I see? He is a man, and he is not a man. Rather, he is a man on account of the Manichaean, and more than a man on account of the Jew.

Go forward, my Joshua, my leader, go forward. Why? Because, when you seek me, you acquire me.

Behold, I come; I find a man. Within I understand something, but it is obscure; I do not yet see. Moses’ face is direct, but a veil prevents clear sight (Exodus 34:33); truth lies hidden.

I do not recognize what it is; questioning is necessary. Say, you man: “Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?”

If he belongs to the adversaries, he is both man and enemy. If he is one of ours, he is both man and Savior.

“He came after me, but he was made before me” (John 1:30).

If he is Jesus, he is also Savior.

Let Jesus question Jesus; let the earlier question the later, yet the lesser question the greater; let the one who is failing question the one who is growing; let the figure question the truth—or rather, let the figure understand the truth, so that the day may shine and temporal darkness be removed.

Behold, I come. I know that a spirit does not have flesh and bones (Luke 24:39); I touch the flesh. I seek and behold the armed man. The mystery is still hidden.

I question a man; I hear the Word. I remove the veil; I worship God.

[Col. 1106]

In the fact that Joshua saw Jesus but did not recognize him, he signified the frenzied Jewish nation, which, if it had recognized what it saw, would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). But in the fact that, by hearing, he believed and worshiped, he signified the people of whom it is written:

“The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 17:45).

Hear further, you who deny that God begot the Son. Hear what the Father says through the prophet Isaiah:

“Will I, who cause others to give birth, not myself give birth? says the Lord” (Isaiah 66:9).

I, who grant generations to others, shall I remain barren? says the Lord your God, to whom it was said:

“You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7).

Why do you provoke me, Arian, and mock me when you hear the word “today”? With God there is never a tomorrow and never a yesterday, but always today. There the year does not revolve through cycles of months; the month does not pass through successive and departing days; the hours do not change; times and moments do not vary. There the day is neither enclosed by an ending nor begun by a beginning.

Let the Jew also hear what the Lord says through the prophet; let the Arian hear it; let all who say either that the Son of God does not exist or that he is lesser hear it:

“I am God, and there is no other.”

And what do you say about the Son, Lord, if you alone are God?

Hear further; why do you hurry?

“By myself I have sworn.”

Where there is an oath, there is no doubt.

“By myself I have sworn: a word of justice shall go forth from my mouth.”

Behold, you have the Son:

“A word of justice shall go forth from my mouth, and it shall not return.”

What does “it shall not return” mean? So that the Sabellian may not say that the Son is the same one as the Father, the Word that has gone forth will not return. The Father is Father; the Son is Son.

Let the verbosity of the heretics, which has no sense of shame, be silent for a while. Let the Lord fulfill his pronouncement. Either no one will oppose the Son of God, or whoever becomes his adversary will be put to shame.

“A word of justice,” he says, “shall go forth from my mouth, and it shall not return, because every knee shall bow to me and every tongue shall confess.”

And what of the Son? Hear, then, what is said in the Lord:

“To me belong the highest matters of justice and authority.”

Proceed, then. What follows?

“They shall come to him, and all who resist him shall be put to shame” (Isaiah 45:22–25).

Go now, all of you—Pagans, heretics, Jews. Oppose and resist the Son of God. You will come to him, and all who resist him will be put to shame.

# Chapter Five

## 6. Against the Manichaeans

We have spoken at some length about the Son of God according to his divinity, and, as far as we were able, we did not spare those adversaries who resist him. Now I wish to approach his incarnation, and the impure Manichaean stands in the way.

Why? Because he does not want the Son of God also to be called the son of man.

And what of what is written?

“Drop dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together. I, the Lord, created him” (Isaiah 45:8).

Again:

“Behold, a child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and the government is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

Again:

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23).

Someone may say: “You had resolved to contend with the Manichaean, not with the Jew.”

Against the Manichaean, new weapons are necessary, not old ones.

Why? Because he accepts the New Testament, not the Old.

[Col. 1107]

But since I have undertaken the battle against both, weapons are necessary from every direction—especially because these new weapons have been fashioned from the old. Therefore the old must not be cast aside, and the new must be carried.

Different adversaries fall by different weapons. The order must therefore be observed: when speaking of the Gospel, I must not remain silent about the Prophets.

7. But I, says the Manichaean, accept neither Moses nor the Prophets.

“What do you say [Note: [Col. 1107] Bede and the manuscripts read: ‘and what are you doing?’] about the Apostle Paul, who at the beginning of his Epistle to the Romans wrote: ‘Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh’ (Rom. 1:1–3)?

Do you hear that the Gospel would not have been presented through the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1107] Bede and the older manuscripts omit ‘through the Apostles’] unless it had first been promised through the Prophets? Do you hear that the Son of God according to his divinity was made the son of man from the seed of David according to the flesh?

For in what respect are the Prophets opposed to the Gospel? The Prophet said: ‘Let the heavens rain down from above, and let the clouds pour forth the Just One; let the angel come and proclaim the word. Let the earth be opened; let Mary hear; and let it bring forth the Savior; let it bear Jesus.’ The Prophet said: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son; and his name shall be called Emmanuel.’ When the evangelist said this also, he followed and explained it by saying, ‘God with us’ (Matt. 1:23).

In vain, Manichaean, do you strive against the Prophets. Behold, the Apostle says: ‘Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh’ (Rom. 1:3). What the Prophets foresaw and foretold, the Apostles saw and proclaimed. He who was became something. What was he? What did he become? He was the Word; he became flesh. He was God; he became man. He was the Son of God; he became the Son of man.

He assumed humanity; he did not lose divinity. Having become humble, he remained exalted. He was born a man, yet did not cease to be God. He was born a little child, while the Great One lay hidden. Let the one who gladly embraces God born as man not shrink in horror from the virgin’s childbirth [Note: [Col. 1107] The manuscripts read: ‘does not shrink in horror.’].

The God who created man, the Son of man, says to you: “What is it that troubles you about my birth? I was not conceived through the desire of lust. I made the mother from whom I was to be born; I prepared and cleansed the way for my journey. She whom you despise, Manichaean, is my mother; but she was fashioned by my hand. If I could be defiled [Note: [Col. 1107] The Colbertinus codex reads: ‘be wearied.’] when I made her, I could be defiled when I was born from her. Just as my passage did not corrupt her virginity, so my majesty was not stained there.

“If a ray of the sun knows how to dry the filth of sewers without knowing how to be defiled by it, how much more can the splendor of eternal light—which encounters no defilement—cleanse whatever it shines upon without itself being polluted? Fool, where is the filth in the virgin mother, where there was no intercourse with a human father? Where is the filth in her who neither conceived in lust nor endured pain in giving birth? Where is the filth in the house to which no inhabitant had come? Its Maker and Lord alone came to her, put on the garment he had not previously possessed, and left her closed just as he found her.

“As he was born alone among the dead, free” (Ps. 87:6), so the modesty of this mother from whom he was born remains alone intact.”

Eve, by disobedience, deserved punishment; Mary, by obedience, obtained grace. The former was cursed by tasting what was forbidden; the latter was blessed by believing the angel. The former brought death upon us; the latter bore life for us.

What are you doing, Manichaean? You are attacking a Christian, not defending Christ. Let unclean vanity be silent, because truth was born pure [Note: [Col. 1107] Some manuscripts read: ‘because truth was born into the world.’]

## CHAPTER VI

### 8. Against the Arians

I would still like to pursue the Manichaean, but I am confronted by the hostile Arian, who trusts in his own strength and boasts of his power (Ps. 48:7). When we answered him along with others, we did not keep silent even then; but now, while maintaining his own order of argument, let us see what darts he throws.

[Col. 1108] Let no one be frightened by the person of the powerful: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6). You see grass growing every day; you see it flowering. Why are you afraid? Such is the fruit that the desolate earth produces.

I do not accuse the farmers, but I ask: Where are you now [Note: [Col. 1108] The manuscripts read: ‘Where are you to me?’], good farmers? What are you doing? Why are you idle? You see how full this earth is of evils: here thorns, there thistles, and grass rising everywhere. Burn the thorns, uproot the thistles, cut down the grass, sow good seed. Do not let winter frighten you; and even if iniquity abounds, let your charity nevertheless burn fervently. Sow in winter what you will reap in summer.

But to whom am I speaking? Where are the springs of tears? To what farmers am I speaking? Some are dead, others have been driven away. “The earth has been given into the hand of the impious” (Job 9:24); tribulation and necessity have found us.

Lord, give us help in tribulation, so that the salvation of man may not be vain but true (Ps. 59:13).

What do you say, Arian? I ask you to answer the one questioning you. Do not despise the little one; a large appearance does not help you, nor do great weapons protect you. A blow from a single stone penetrates a helmeted forehead (1 Sam. 17:49).

Tell me, then, what I ask you. Do you believe in God the Father almighty?

“I believe,” he says.
