Do you believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, our Lord?

“I believe,” he says.

Do you believe that Jesus Christ, God and man, was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary?

“I believe,” he says.

You do well. I ask further: Just as the Father is God, so also is the Son God?

“Yes.”

Is the Father one, and the Son another?

“Certainly.”

Is the Son equal to the Father?

“Equal,” he says.

What remains? Behold, he has answered everything I asked. In saying that he believes in God the Father and God the Son, he is opposed to the pagan together with me. In believing that Christ, God and man, was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, he stands with me against the Jew and the Manichaean. In believing that the Father is one and the Son another, he stands with me against the Sabellian.

Come, then: if you are with me in everything [Note: [Col. 1108] See Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 2 on Psalm 21, no. 30; and Sermon 358, no. 2.], why do we quarrel? If we have one inheritance, let us possess it together; we are brothers. “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

Why is there a new structure before the wall? Let us keep watch together for the protection of our inheritance. “Our inheritance is glorious for us” (Ps. 16:6). We have envious people; we have enemies. They too want to possess it—not with us, but against us.

Let no one claim anything for himself. This inheritance was left to us to be possessed undivided, not scattered into portions. Let us gather its fruit together, lest we lose it by dividing it. Poverty makes me anxious; I ask you, do not gather outside without me, lest you begin to scatter. “For whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23).

It may seem that I have forgotten whom I was addressing, but I have not forgotten. I am questioning the Arian, whom I desire to be Catholic.

Someone says: “He answered everything you wanted; nothing contrary is found in his answers. What more do you seek?”

Wait, brother; do not judge too quickly. I still have something to ask. Do not entrust yourself to him too quickly: the answer is bright, but the poison lies hidden.

What did you say, brother? Is the Son equal to the Father?

“Equal,” you say.

Come now, be watchful; now what was hidden will be revealed. In what way do you say that the Son is equal to the Father? In operation, or in origin? In power, or in eternity? Or perhaps in both?

“By no means,” you say. “He is equal in operation and power, but not in eternity. For how could one who was begotten be equal to one who was unbegotten?”

Behold, the one who was walking with me as though a fellow heir has appeared; the deceit that was hidden has been exposed. He was thought to possess with me; he wants to divide. But I do not permit it; I resist utterly.

The laws require that the testator’s will be obeyed in everything. If anyone wishes to act against the testator’s will, let him be deprived of the inheritance.

“But do the laws not fall silent amid arms?” (Cicero, *Pro Milone*, 40.)

Not at all. The struggle and the battle are undertaken precisely so that the laws may be obeyed.

I produce the testament; I recite the testator’s words. If there is something to divide, I find it there; if there is nothing to divide, I resist you from the testament itself.

Hear what the testament contains: “My peace I give you; [Col. 1109] my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). This is the inheritance.

And who is the testator himself? Read the Testament, and you will find him. When the prophet was speaking about the Lord, he said: “He shall be magnified to the ends of the earth, and he himself shall be peace” (Micah 5:4–5). “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men” (Luke 2:14)—not to those who divide holy unity, but to men of good will.

He himself is the inheritance; he himself is the testator. You are seeking to divide him. Why do you divide what is one? If you divide what is one, you will possess nothing whole.

O Arian heresy, cruel and impious prostitute, blush before Solomon’s judgment. The prostitute, so as not to lose one living child—one conceived by anyone and already born—did not permit her son to be divided. And you divide the Lord your God?

Although she was a prostitute, she was nevertheless pious because she was a mother. You are both a prostitute and impious, because you are not a mother: you strangle what you give birth to, and gather what you do not bear. How can you nurse another’s child when you kill your own? Your inward parts have hardened; hers trembled.

What did she say? “Give her the child, and do not divide him” (1 Kings 3:27): “He is my son; but I would rather rejoice in seeing him alive and whole with her than mourn him dead after he has been divided. He is my son,” she said; “but what benefit will I be as a mother to the child if I take away the life I do not give? I want to drive the cruel woman’s breast away from the child, but I am compelled even more to fear the judge’s sword.

“Give her my son: he was born mine; but let him pass over whole to her, while affection remains with me. Give her the entire child; let the life of his limbs not be taken away. Let his integrity not be divided; let my piety not be stolen from me.”

What did she say? “Give her the child, and do not divide him.” Behold, I too say: Possess the whole, and do not divide God.

“No,” he says, “but if you wish to have peace without prejudice, divide the inheritance.”

And how am I to divide it? Is the Father greater and the Son lesser? O portions! O justice! O equality [Note: [Col. 1109] Several manuscripts read: ‘O equity?’] One portion is greater, another lesser.

I do not consent; I do not make a portion, because I do not divide peace. For if peace is broken, it will no longer be peace.

But how can peace remain undiminished with you, when faith is not whole in you? Since you do not wish to possess with me and wish to divide peace, you cannot obtain the inheritance.

Finally, if according to your custom you pursue not peace but faithlessness, go and appeal to the judge; let us see what he will say to you.

You have an ordinary judge. I do not want you to bring me one power after another from different quarters. I need not a man-at-arms but a lawgiver.

“And where,” you ask, “will I find him?”

Where will you not find him? Hear the prophet saying: “The Lord is our judge; the Lord is our lawgiver.” Do not think the judge contemptible; hear what follows: “The Lord is our king; the Lord himself will save us” (Isa. 33:22).

Behold, you have your judge. If that is not enough, our king too stands before you. He is in heaven in such a way that he does not abandon the earth. “I fill heaven and earth,” he says (Jer. 23:24). “I am with you always, to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

He is with us and with the Father, because he neither abandoned the Father when he descended to us nor deserted us when he ascended to the Father.

Appeal to him; say to him: “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

Hear the divine answer; hear the just judge; hear peace fleeing from litigation. What does he say? “Friend, who appointed me judge or divider between you?” (Luke 12:13–14.)

You wish to divide peace and seek to have as judge Peace himself? I do not wish to be your judge. I am peace; I do not know how to quarrel. I sit beside those who agree; I flee from those who litigate.

When you were an enemy of my Father, I reconciled you through myself. How, then, will you separate me from my Father? When you were far away, I came to bring you back. When you were wandering among mountains and forests, I sought you. I found you among stones and wood. You stumbled over the stones and clung to them, because you worshiped wood and stones.

And so that you would not be torn apart by the hungry mouths of wolves and wild beasts, I gathered you up, carried you on my shoulders, and returned you to my Father. I labored; I sweated; I placed my head beneath thorns; I offered my hands to nails; a lance opened my side. Torn apart by so many things—not to call them injuries, but hardships—I shed my blood and laid down my life [Col. 1110] so that I might unite you to myself. And you divide me?

Hear what was answered to the disciple who knew the Son and was seeking the Father. Philip said to the Lord: “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”

Was he not also separating the Son from the Father? “We already know you,” he says, “but we do not know your Father. What do you want? Show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”

And the Lord said to him: “If you wish, Arian, to hear it, you went astray with the Apostle; return with the Apostle. Let his rebuke also be your healing.”

What does the Lord say? “For so long a time I have been with you, and you have not known me? Philip, I came to bring you to my Father; do not separate me. Why are you seeking someone else besides me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.

“So great is the unity in us, so great the likeness, so great the love, that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.”

I perceive, Sabellian, what you are muttering, or how you are hastening either to trap me with the Arian or to draw me away from the Arian. But in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—not of three, but of one God—while I answer him, I do not pass you by.

What did the Lord say? “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” Did he say, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” or, “I am at once Son and Father”? Rather, he said, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:8–10).

The insertion of a single syllable—the word “and”—distinguishes the Father and also distinguishes the Son; and it shows that you possess neither Father nor Son.

Tell me, Arian: do you call the Father God?

“Certainly.”

What about the Son?

“I confess that he too is God.”

How do you recognize this?

“Because when his coming in the flesh was foretold, the prophet said of him: ‘Say to the fainthearted, “Take courage; do not fear. Behold, our God will bring vengeance and recompense; God himself will come and save us”’” (Isa. 35:4).

Recognize him in what you claim to recognize, if you do not oppose the Prophets.

What, then, do you say about the Father?

“He is God.”

What about the Son?

“He is God.”

Is the Son coeternal with the Father?

“No.”

Then, according to you, there was a time when the Son did not exist. If there was a time when the Son did not exist, then there was a time which the Son did not make. If there was a time which the Son did not make, then not everything was made through him—for there already was a time when the Son did not exist.

If there was a time when the Son did not exist, John the evangelist should not have said, “In the beginning was the Word,” but, “In the beginning was time.”

John says, “All things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3), but the Arian contradicts him.

Tell me, Arian: how do you know that there was a time when the Son did not exist? Are you perhaps going to say, “And how does John know that in the beginning was the Word?”

Because he reclined upon the Lord’s breast and drew from there what he drank at Christ’s banquet: that in the beginning was the Word.

Nevertheless, tell me: when “in the beginning was the Word” (ibid. 1), or when John reclined upon the Lord’s breast (ibid. 13:23) and learned from the Lord’s Word that the Word was in the beginning and that the Word was God—where was Arius?

I do not know whether you dare to say that he was there. For it is known and recorded at what time he was born, and rightly he was condemned. It is also known how he lived and how he died. Therefore you do not dare to say of Arius, as of the Word, “He was, and he is,” because Arius was not there then, nor is he now.

But so that the Arian may be excluded in every respect, hear what is said through Solomon: “The Lord made regions and uninhabitable boundaries under heaven. When he prepared heaven, I was there with him.” And a little later: “I was beside him, arranging everything; I was there when he made the mighty foundations of the earth; I was the one in whom he rejoiced” (Prov. 8:26–27, 30).

But you say that the question concerns time: whether the Son existed before time existed. Hear him himself speaking through the prophet: “From the time,” he says.

What does “from the time” mean? Does it mean from the moment time began to exist?

Not so, impious Arian; not so. It means: “From the time, before it was made, I was there” (Isa. 48:16). Behold, before time was made, he was there. Ask now when he did not exist who existed before time.

“In the beginning was the Word.” The Greeks more aptly say *Logos* (Λόγος). *Logos* means both “word” and “reason.” You see, therefore, that he of whom you dare to say “He did not exist” always existed.

Or if you say that God was at some time without Word or without Reason, you will be an adversary not only of the Son but also of the Father [Col. 1111].

“I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Sir. 24:5). Who says this? The Word.

And what is this Word? Let John speak: “The Word was God.” Therefore both the Word and the one whose Word it was are not two but one.

“No,” you say, “because a word is later than the one whose word it is. Hence it is clear that the Son is lesser than the Father.”

You deny, then, that the Son of God is God.

“I do not deny it,” you say. “I call the Father God, and I call the Son God; but the Father is greater and the Son lesser.”

How long is the Father greater and the Son lesser? Tell me, since I see that you wish to calculate eternity: by how many years does God the Father precede his Son?

Where did you read the birthday of the Son of God? I say the Son of God; I do not mean the Son of God and man. Where, then, did you read the day of his birth? With what astrologer did you seek and examine the constellation of the Creator of the stars? What periods, what hours, what moments, what numbers, what minute subdivisions [Note: [Col. 1111] Several manuscripts read: ‘minutiae.’] of the moments of the birth of the one who created all things have you gathered?

Let your heresy—I will not call it religion but superstition—come to rest, I beg you; let it come to rest. Calculation fails before Christ’s beginning. For when eternity without beginning is heard, no age is sought there.

If the Father is God and the Son is God, but the Father is greater and the Son lesser, then there are not one God but two gods.

If there are two gods, what then is the meaning of the Lord’s saying through the prophet: “Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none” (Isa. 43:10)?

What do you say, Arian? To whom do you assign these words?

If they belong to the Father, then by saying, “Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none,” either the Father himself will not exist, or the Son will not be God. For if he had said only, “Before me no god was formed,” and had not added, “and after me there shall be none,” you would have been free to apply these words to the Father alone. But since he continues and says, “After me there shall be none,” then, according to you, as I have said, he denies that both the Father and the Son are God.

Likewise, if these words belong to the Son, he denies both his Father and his God. For if he had not said, “Before me no god was formed,” but had said only, “After me there shall be none,” it might perhaps be said that the Son spoke those words. But now, when he says, “Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none,” he says that his Father is neither God nor Father.

Again, if these words belong to the Father, who is the one who says, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7)? Or, God forbid, is God to be accused of falsehood?

But if they are the Son’s words, who is it that says, and of whom does he say, “My Father is working until now” (John 5:17)? Or is he perhaps to be judged insulting toward his Father and ungrateful?

Yet would it be said to an ungrateful one, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8)?

Or perhaps the Prophet did not know what he was saying, or wished to deceive; or, to speak more mildly of the Prophet, should he be thought to have invented for himself two people conversing—namely, the Father and the Son—and, when the Father said, “Before me no god was formed,” added the Son’s words, “And after me there shall be none”?

Are the things we are doing theatrical and comical, or divine [Note: [Col. 1111] The manuscripts omit ‘and comical’]?

O crime! Alas for the grief! Spare us, spare us, heretical impiety. Since you cannot comprehend God, you provoke us also to blasphemy.

The holy Church does not teach this. The Father is Father; the Son is Son. The one was never not Father, and the other was never not Son. Both are eternal; neither began to be, nor does either cease to be.

What the Father speaks, the Son speaks, because he is the Father’s Word. And what the Son speaks, the Father speaks, because the Father is the Word’s Father.

The Word himself says: “The words that I speak, I do not speak from myself” (John 14:10).

Grant, I beg you, to the Creator what he himself has granted to the creature; and, if you can, comprehend the Creator through the creature.

Behold: fire and radiance are two things; one is from the other, and neither exists without the other. Fire is the father; radiance is the son. The radiance itself, if it could speak, would say: “That I shine, I do not shine from myself; rather, the one who sent me himself gave me to shine.” For fire sends forth radiance.

And just as the Son says of God the Father, “The Father is with me” (John 16:32), so radiance could say, “Fire is with me.”

Extinguish the fire, and the radiance [Col. 1112] will appear nowhere.

If, then, fire and radiance—father and son—are one father without a spouse and the other a son without a mother; if one cannot be separated from the other; and although one is from the other, the beginning of either cannot exist without the other; and if this capacity has been granted to the creature by the Creator—what can the Creator himself do?

Let the pagan approach; let the Sabellian approach; let the Arian approach. Let them contemplate a lamp, and in it see what they cannot see in God.

I do not do an injustice if, desiring in some measure to demonstrate the power of so great a Creator, I bring forward a tiny likeness from fire or a lamp. For it is written: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Ps. 118:105). And it is said of God: “A consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29).

Come, then, and carefully consider the lamp, and remove your foolish darkness.

Let the pagan look upon it and learn there that the Father and the Son exist without a spouse, and how the Son was born. And if you are not blind, look there: between fire and radiance, seek the intermediary.

If there is no intermediary, there is no marriage. Do not wish to scrutinize the intermediary, lest you suffer a great conflagration.

Let the Sabellian approach and see two existing as one: fire and radiance. Can radiance not rightly say, “I am in the fire, and the fire is in me,” just as the Son says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10)?

Let the Arian approach as well. Let him see that one is from the other, and yet that neither can come into being without the other. Neither is earlier or later; father and son, radiance and fire, are coeval. Fire cannot exist without radiance, nor radiance without fire.

Or, if you prefer, stretch out your hand and separate one from the other. Show me fire without radiance, or radiance without fire.

Far from it, far from it! You may be able to burn, but you will not be able to separate one from the other.

For just as fire and radiance are one from the other, and yet neither can exist without the other, so God the Father and God the Son are one from the other, and yet neither can exist without the other.

Their origin is not one that did not exist; rather, their eternity and substance are one. Fire and radiance are temporal; but God the Father and God the Son are eternal.

I say “they exist,” because they are Father and Son. I say “God,” because they are one. Duality is in the offspring; unity is in the divinity. The birth makes one distinct, but the divinity shows that they are one.

When I say “Son,” he is another. When I say “God,” he is one. He is another because he is the Son; he is not something else because he is God.

Be ashamed, Arians. The executioners of Pilate did not dare to tear apart the tunic of the man already condemned and hanging upon the cross (John 19:24). And you attempt to divide the love of God who sits in heaven—or rather, to divide Love itself, who is God?

Attempt it, then; attempt it as much as you can. You have already plunged into hell. For you will never tear that tunic.

Likewise, through the prophet the Lord says: “There is no God besides me; a just God and a Savior, there is none except me” (Isa. 45:21).

## CHAPTER VII
### 9. Against Sabellius

Here the Sabellian exults. For, in order to show that the Father and the Son are one and the same, he believes himself fortified by such testimonies. The Arians, on the other hand, in order to prove that the Father is one and the Son another, bring forward other testimonies and say: “The Father is one, the Son another; one is greater, the other lesser”; thus the Father says to the Son, “I have given you as a light to the nations” (Isa. XLIX, 6), and the Son says, “The Father sent me” (John VIII, 19).

As I understand it, this light of the nations is so bright and evident that the heretics, unable to grasp and perceive it, have therefore been blinded: they cannot walk in it, but rather go astray. The Arian says one thing, the Sabellian another. What a conflict! What does the Catholic say to this? “The weapons they carry are mine; they fight on my behalf. Both fight against each other, but for me. Would that both might fail, and that neither might pass over to the other, but to me!”

I too shall bring forward something by which both may be struck. You, Arian, say that the one who sends is greater, and the one who is sent lesser. I ask you in turn: Who is greater, the one who goes before or the one before whom another goes? Again, who is greater: the one for whom something is prepared as he comes, or the one who prepares it; the one to whom a service is rendered, or the one who renders it? Surely, if you ask the human race, it will answer that the one is greater before whom another goes, for whom something is prepared, or to whom a service is rendered.

You wish to prove from this that the Son is lesser because he was sent. I show that the one who sent went before the one whom he sent; yet I do not call either of them greater, because I do not dare to call either lesser. The prophet Isaiah says: “Thus says the Lord to Christ, my Lord, whose right hand I have grasped, so that I may subject nations before his face.” Behold, the Father is now the companion of the Son who was sent. Continue further: “And I will turn the backs of kings, and I will open doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut” (Isa. XLV, 1).

Behold, the one who had sent has become his forerunner. For who, being greater or higher, opens doors before one who is lesser? Or how could he do so unless he had gone a little before? Hear further: “And the gates,” he says, “shall not be shut.” How so? “I will go before you” (ibid., 2). You see that the one who sent both accompanies and precedes: he sends, yet does not depart. It is little that he does not depart; moreover, he precedes. Now discern who is greater and who is superior. I see no distinction at all, but rather perceive equality.

The Son says of the Father, “He sent me” (John VIII, 16). The Father says to the Son, “I will go before you.” Let the disastrous discord withdraw: this displays equality, not disparity. Continue further, so that it may appear more clearly who says what to whom: “I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious of the earth.”

Here you too must be present, pagan. Hear what the prophet says. I myself did not write down what I wished: the book in which these words are read is kept in a Jewish archive. My enemy is my witness; ask him himself. Open it, read, and believe. “I will turn the backs of kings,” he says, “and I will humble the glorious of the earth.” Do you not see that the kings of the earth who formerly persecuted Christians are now Christians? Do you not see those who humbled the Church now entering the Church in humility? Do you not now see that the very people whom they formerly persecuted are their defenders?

“I will go before you,” he says, “and I will humble the glorious of the earth. I will shatter bronze doors and break iron bars. And I will give you hidden treasures and secret things kept concealed, so that you may know that I am God, who call you by your name, the God of Israel” (Isa. XLV, 2–3).

Let the Sabellian hear: God speaks, and he speaks to God. Therefore there are two—the one who speaks and the one to whom he speaks. Let the Arian hear as well: “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (ibid., 5).

For a long time I have labored in contending against these two heresies, and I am almost exhausted. Come, my Lord Jesus, most valiant warrior, commander of the Lord’s army, who conquered the devil and the world: “Take up arms and shield, and rise to my help” (Ps. XXXIV, 2).

About to advance into battle and, as victor in the world, to conquer the world, he prayed—not as though he lacked power, since he was omnipotent, but in order to display to us the lesson of humility for which he had come. And what did he say? “Father, glorify your Son” (John XVII, 1).

At once the accursed Arian says: “You see that he is lesser, and that he would not possess glory unless he had asked the Father?” Wait, man—why do you hurry? You see a man, in the form of one who is lesser not only than the Father but also than the angels (Ps. VIII, 6): the man is apparent, God is hidden. You show me a humble man; open your eyes and see the exalted God, not lesser than the angels but equal to the Father.

“Father,” he says, “glorify your Son”: behold the lesser. Continue further: “so that your Son may glorify you” (John XVII, 1): behold the equal. We find the Son acknowledging the Father and praying to him, and joined to him—not, as he was thought to be, ungrateful.

Let us see what the Father also says concerning the Son. “Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother” (these are the words of the Gospel), “and led them up onto a high mountain by themselves, and he was transfigured before them. And his face shone like the sun, while his garments became white like snow. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him” (Matt. XVII, 1–3).

Moses and Elijah: the Law and the Prophets. They were speaking with him because they had spoken about him; they were displaying the one whom they had foretold, making manifest the one of whom they had prophesied. They were speaking. What do you suppose they were saying? So that the Jews might be convicted, the pagans converted, the Manichaeans confounded, the heretics restrained, and the Catholics strengthened.

The Law and grace were speaking; severity and gentleness; terror and meekness; commandment and assistance; the instrument and the physician; shadow and light; the herald and the judge; sentence and mercy.

And what happened after this? “Peter answered and said to Jesus: Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matt. XVII, 4).

What are you saying, holy Peter? The world is in labor [Note: [Col. 1114] Four manuscripts read “is perishing”], and you seek seclusion? You see so many nations coming together as one, and you seek repose? You see the darkness of the world, and you hide the light?

“No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house” (ibid. V, 15). This house is the whole world; the lighting of the lamp is the incarnation of the Word; the lampstand is the wood of the cross; the lamp shining on the lampstand is Christ hanging on the cross.

“No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house.” You have seen it; let us see it too. There is darkness: let us not stumble among the pagans or go astray among the heretics. Let the lamp shine for us; let the Word in the flesh teach us.

Let us see what the Evangelist says, and whether Peter’s proposal was accepted: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud saying” (ibid. XVII, 5).

Let us all listen; let no one close his ears. Let the pagan mockers listen; let the Jewish persecutors listen; let the Manichaean dreamers of phantoms listen; let the erring, contentious heretics listen; and let the Catholics too, above all, listen—the faithful worshipers of God. Let these listen so that they may be instructed, and those so that they may be corrected; or let these listen lest they be deceived, and those so that they may be punished.

What does the voice from the cloud say? “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid., and III, 17).

Where are you, you who oppose the Son of God? The Father says, “This is my Son,” and you say, “God does not have a Son.” You, pagan, why do you stand outside and murmur? Enter here into the school of God; open the ears of your heart; hear the voice of the Lord and learn the Son of God.

What will you do, Jews, who killed the Son of God? Where will you flee? Where will you hide yourselves? What mountains, what rocks will fall upon you? And if you hide yourselves in caves of rocks, I shall draw you out from there, says the Lord (Jer. XLIX, 16).

But you too, come in; enter; hear my counsel; do not despair, “for there is a future for the man of peace” (Ps. XXXVI, 37). You raged, you killed, you shed Christ’s blood; you are in danger, for you were unbelieving toward the Son of God. What, then, do you now have to do except be baptized as believers and drink the blood that you shed? There is no reason for you to shudder: the physician’s blood was poured out and became medicine for the delirious.

Why do you hesitate? “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9).

And you, Manichaean, how long will you dream of phantoms? Wake up and see. The clouds thunder [Note: [Col. 1114] Several manuscripts read, “The little cloud thunders.”] What do they thunder? “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III, 17; XVII, 5).

See on earth the true man; hear from heaven the true God. See on earth the son of man; hear from heaven that he is the Son of God. Recognize that both are true—that is, that the one and the same is God and man, Son of God and son of man. Acknowledge the man, and you will appease God.

Take care not to stumble against the rock and suffer the ruin of death, because what you dream is vanity, whereas what God thunders is truth.

Hear, Sabellian; hear the Father from heaven; see the Son on earth, and do not say, “The Father is the same as the Son.” Hear, Arian, and do not go astray concerning either the Father or the Son, but follow unity and behold divinity [Note: [Col. 1114] One manuscript reads, “but seek and behold divinity. Follow, Lord, etc.”].

Lord, let us hear what you say concerning your Son: “This is,” he says, “my Son.” See on earth the son of man; hear from heaven that he is the Son of God. “My beloved, in whom I am well pleased.” And what follows? “Hear him.”

Thanks be to God. The command of God thundered, and Peter’s proposal was removed. Thanks to you, God the Power; thanks to you, God the Father, who both showed me your Son and gave me a teacher [Note: [Col. 1115] Several manuscripts read, “a guide.”] [Note: [Col. 1115] Most printed editions read: “Thanks to you, God; thanks to you, true and one Trinity, one and threefold Truth, threefold and one Unity. Thanks to you, God the Father, who both showed me the Son,” etc. We have restored the passage from Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, who, after consulting very ancient codices, states that this interpolation entered in the ninth century. At that time it was found only in the falsified codex presented to Charles the Bald and in newly written quires that had flowed from the same muddy source. See Hincmar, *On the Non-Trine Deity*, and P. Germonius, *Diplomatic Disputations*, *On the Art of Discerning Documents*, chapter 3 and following.]

Let the Sabellian withdraw; let the Arian withdraw; let the remaining plagues withdraw; let every wicked doctrine withdraw. Let God teach, not Arius; let the Son of God teach, not the adversary of the Son.

Speak, my Lord Jesus; teach, and I shall learn what I am to teach.

The Sabellian says, “The Father is the same as the Son.” The Arian says, “The Father is one, the Son another; the Father is greater, the Son lesser.” He opposes, cries out, quarrels, fights, gathers crowds, and battles against Christ. One shed blood in order to redeem; the other scatters money in order to destroy.

He constructs a den [Note: [Col. 1115] This den is to be understood as the Arian church, as in the following sermon, chapter 22]; there he strangles the Catholic, and calls a Christian a pagan [Note: [Col. 1115] Because, when a person about to be baptized was asked whether he was a Christian, he answered that he was not. Hence Augustine, *Against the Donatists*, exposition on Psalm XXXIX, no. 1, and on Psalm CXLV, no. 16]. He thrusts baptism upon one who has already been baptized, contrary to what is written: “The one who has been washed once does not need to be washed again” (John XIII, 10).

The man cries out, “I am a Christian; why do you call me what I am not?” He cries out, “I am faithful.” And the other says, “Take money from me.” He cries out, “I have been redeemed.” And the other says, “Take gold from me.”

What are you giving, or what are you taking away? You give money in order to take away grace; you give money in order to take away life; you offer a price in order to take away that by which I was bought. What are you buying from one already bought?

My price is not gold but the blood of Christ. You do not seduce me; you do not deceive me. However much you may give me, you do not take away my price. “May your money perish with you” (Acts VIII, 20), for my price has no price.

The man cries out, “I am faithful,” and you perform exsufflation. He cries out, “I was baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” and you perform exsufflation. What, then, do you reserve for a Christian, in whom you exsufflate the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Have you perhaps brought from overseas a new faith, a new baptism, a new god?

Speak, my holy teacher Paul; teach, expert in divine law, friend of the Bridegroom. This man has just arrived, overturns the world, tears apart the unity of faith, divides the Trinity, and insists on rebaptizing those who do not agree with him. What shall I do? “In Jesus himself, through the Gospel, you begot me” (I Cor. IV, 15); I was baptized in Christ. Is there perhaps another baptism or another faith?

“By no means,” you say: “There is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. IV, 5–6). If, then, there is one faith—or rather, because there is one faith—one baptism, one God and Father of all, I have already believed, I have already been baptized, I already have God as my Father. Why, then, must I suffer the murderous Arian?

Come to my aid, my Lord Jesus, and gird your sword around your thigh, most powerful one (Ps. XLIV, 4). Most powerful of all, come forth; kill them in themselves, so that they may live in you and cease persecuting me.

The Sabellians diminish you by taking you away; the Arians diminish you by reducing you. What do you say about yourself? The Father said that we should hear you; when we hear you, we hear him. Strike both adversaries with a single blow.

“Let the empty talkers and deceivers of minds perish, Arian and Sabellian. For ‘I and the Father are one’” (John X, 30). He did not say, “I and the Father am one,” but, “I and the Father are one.” Let the Arian hear the word “one” that I speak; let the Sabellian hear the word “are.” Let the Arian not divide “one”; let the Sabellian not erase “are.” Rather, let both come and themselves be one in us, just as I and the Father are one (ibid. XVII, 11).

Therefore, if the Father and the Son are one—or rather, because they are indisputably one—not two gods but one God, the prophet did not write something merely imitative, but spoke the truth, when the Lord said: “Before me no God was formed, and after me there shall not be” (Isa. XLIII, 10).

Truth taught Truth, and with a two-edged sword put every error to death. If the heretics still resist, let the Catholics hear the definitive sentence that they should follow.

## Chapter VIII

### 10. Conclusion

You have heard what the Father said concerning the Son; you have heard what the Son said concerning the Father and concerning himself. “If anyone proclaims to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. I, 8).

We have said what we could, and as much as we could, concerning the Father and the Son—if indeed we have been able to say anything worthily. We have kept silent about the Holy Spirit, but we have not separated him. For whatever we have said concerning the Father and the Son, we have also said concerning the Holy Spirit. He is in them and with them, equal and one—not a lesser or third god.

What else should I say, exhausted as I am by the exhausted? Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity, substance, or communion, and whoever denies that the Holy Spirit is not of the Father and the Son, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit.

For this reason God is called love (I John IV, 8): because he does not divide unity into parts, but ineffably binds the Trinity together. For the Trinity itself is one God, “a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Ps. LX, 4), who guards those who believe in him throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1115]

# Sermon Against Jews, Pagans, and Arians on the Creed (C, G)*

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Sermon

This sermon too was delivered under Arian domination, at a time when no one dared resist those heretics as they argued and attempted to draw Catholics away from the faith—some by promises and rewards, others by force and power.

“You think yourself great,” says the preacher in chapter 7, “because you argue with no one disputing against you and with no judge presiding. And while time favors your error, you suppose yourself to be something, though you are nothing; and, having been deceived, you desire to deceive many—some by money, others by power.”

Compare this with the preceding sermon, chapter 7. There too, above, in column 1115, line 11, you will observe that the Arian church is called a den, as here in chapter 22.

The baptized are admonished to fulfill their profession of renunciation in chapters 3 and 4, just as in the spurious sermons on the Creed addressed to catechumens in volume 6. We pass over other passages similar to those sermons or to the preceding sermon.

Much, moreover, has been borrowed from Augustine. The statement in chapter 18, “If he used magical arts to cause a dead man to be worshiped, was he a magician before he was born?” comes from Book 1, chapter 11, of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*. Likewise, the statement in chapter 13, “What does ‘You are recognized in the midst of two animals’ mean, unless either in the midst of the two Testaments, or in the midst of the two thieves, or in the midst of Moses and Elijah speaking with him on the mountain?” is taken from Book 18, chapter 32, of *The City of God*.

From the same source, the Sibylline verses in chapter 23 have also been transferred here. As with Gregory in *Homily 33 on the Gospels*, the preacher uses the words “since it is more fitting to weep than to say anything” at the beginning of the sermon. Chapter 17 also contains certain passages agreeing with his *Homily 10 on the Gospels*.

In chapter 15 he says that the poet Virgil bore witness to Christ in the line,

> “Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven,”

whereas Augustine, in Letter 104 to Nectarius, no. 11, much more truthfully calls it a flattering poem addressed to a nobleman, namely Pollio.

Bernard Winding points out the barbarism of the diction in his *Augustinian Critic*, and censures some passages as inept. These, however, were defects of the editions and have here been corrected from a Remigian manuscript eight hundred years old, in which the work is entitled *Sermon of Saint Augustine on the Creed*; from three Vatican manuscripts; from one belonging to the Abbey of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais; from the Corbie manuscript; and others.

# Chapter I

### Christian Vigils

Amid the pressures and anxieties of the present time, and the duties of our servitude, we are compelled, beloved, not to remain silent, although it is more fitting to weep than to say anything. Nevertheless, lest, because too little profit has accrued to the Lord’s threshing floor, it be said to us, “Wicked and lazy servant, you should have put my money with the bankers, and when I came I would have collected it with interest” (Matt. XXV, 26–27), I ask your Charity to receive willingly what the master of the household himself has ministered to you through us.

The Apostle’s words are: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near. Therefore, laying aside the works of darkness, put on the weapons of light” (Rom. XIII, 12).

With the darkness of night therefore expelled, and the shadows of sins driven away, let the ray of true light shine in our hearts. The reason for so great an assembly demands that we render you an account both of the night that has passed and of the true and everlasting salvation received by you today from so great a sacrament.

For if we consider the works of the past night and are able, by the Lord’s gift, to explain what we have done, we shall find that during the night we have performed not the works of night but those of day [Note: [Col. 1117] So the manuscripts. Lov. reads: “if we consider the work of the past night.”]

For we did not find our senses lulled in the pleasure of sleep; our souls were not deceived by phantoms; nor did repose incline our bodies, weighed down by the warmth of bedding, into deep slumber. Rather, by keeping vigil, praying, singing psalms, and battling against the adversary the devil, we both felt a great light poured into our hearts and performed the works of day in the night.

What have we done during this night? We drove out the devil and brought in Christ. What have we done during this night? We took captive the captor. What have we done during this night? We excluded the devil’s darkness from your hearts and showed that the true light must be drawn in.

What happened during this night? The true Strength came and bound the strong man and plundered his household’s vessels (Matt. XII). What happened during this night? Pride was uprooted and humility brought in. What happened during this night? The prince of all vices was expelled, and the source of all good was received.

You see, beloved, what good things have been prepared for you, and from what burden, or from what baggage of sins, you are relieved by him who calls you to receive his easy yoke and his light burden (ibid. XI, 29).

“Therefore, laying aside the works of darkness, put on the weapons of light.” Know that the meaning of this has been explained to you from the words of the Creed that you have just received.

What does “Lay aside the works of darkness” mean except “Renounce the devil, his pomps, and his angels”? And what does “Put on the weapons of light” mean except “Believe in God the Father almighty”?

# Chapter II

### Who the Devil Is

First, however, beloved, let us examine who and what the devil is, and what his pomps are, by renouncing which we lay aside the works of darkness. Then, concerning God the Father almighty, who is the true light, we shall say to your Charity as much as he himself grants.

What is the devil? An angel separated from God through pride, who did not stand in the truth; the author of falsehood, deceived by himself, who desired to deceive another. He became the adversary of the human race, the inventor of death, the teacher of pride, the root of wickedness, the head of crimes, the prince of all vices, and also the persuader of shameful pleasures [Note: [Col. 1117] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “thoughts.”]

When he looked upon that first man, Adam, the father of us all, and saw that the man had been made from the clay of the earth in the image of God, adorned with chastity, ordered by self-control, surrounded by love, and clothed with immortality, he—an emulous and envious being—begrudged that this earthly man had received what he himself, though an angel, is known to have lost through pride.

At once, as an insatiable murderer, he envied them and stripped our first parents of those gifts and such great blessings, and moreover killed them. For, beloved, after the devil had taken such great goods from man—chastity, continence, love, and immortality—and had left him naked and shameful, he mocked him while clothed in his own rags, bound him under his dominion, and from that bond subjected all his offspring to himself.

Adam took on shameful rags when, stripped of chastity by the devil, he was girded with impurity; having lost self-control, he became uncontrolled; having forfeited love, he was found wicked; stripped of immortality, he was brought near to death.

Alas! What did he lose, and what did he receive! He bound his descendants as well to these most shameful rags of his [Note: [Col. 1118] Other printed editions read: “For to these shameful rags.”]

# Chapter III

### What It Means to Renounce Satan

Let us renounce this ruinous inheritance: we have become orphans. Before the collector comes, if anyone neglects to renounce so evil an inheritance—an inheritance in which are the devil’s rags, namely, his pomps and his angels—then, when the judge comes, as the Gospel says, the debtor will be handed over to the collector, and the collector will throw the debtor into prison.

“Amen, I say to you,” says the Lord, “you will not leave there until you have paid the last farthing” (Matt. V, 26).

Divine Scripture therefore commends the whole human race to God as poor and orphaned, saying: “To you the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan.” And, demonstrating their adversary the devil, it adds: “Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (Ps. IX, 14–15, according to the Hebrew text).

Let some pious person therefore come forward and show some mercy to this orphan and poor man. For he suffers a fierce and crafty adversary, and this orphan fails in his own case, because his adversary has bound him by wicked deeds.

Let us provide this orphan with competent defenders, and substitute for him the protection of the Apostles, as heavenly jurists [Note: [Col. 1118] The manuscripts read: “and the choir of the Apostles, as heavenly jurists, and substitute their assistance and protection.”]

What is to be done before such men on behalf of such a person? Before you, therefore, Peter, Paul, John, and the other holy counselors of the true Judge, friends of supreme power, we set forth the case of this poor and orphaned person—that is, of the human race—who, found guilty and bound as a debtor by his father’s written contract, is held captive by the adversary. There is no other way by which he can be helped except through your counsel.

What, then, does your serenity think should be done for the freedom of this wretched man? From your common deliberation, deign to issue a united sentence on his behalf [Note: [Col. 1118] Other printed editions read: “Would that you might deign to issue a sentence on his behalf.”]

For this obligation had bound you as well, unless grace had come to your aid. You have been freed: free others. Bring forth the counsel that you received from the true Judge, so that the captive may follow it and, through your defense, come from evil servitude to true freedom [Note: [Col. 1118] The manuscripts read: “to your freedom.”]

And this is the voice of all: “Let him do what we did.” What, I ask, is he to do? Let him renounce the devil, his pomps, and his angels. This is that ruinous inheritance to which we are compelled to renounce.

You see, beloved, what sentence our defenders have pronounced.

# Chapter IV

### Relapse after Baptism

Let each person therefore keep watch, lest, by not renouncing wholeheartedly after his profession, he allow the devil to recognize his rags in him and begin to be held perpetually guilty—the one whom Christ wished to free by his grace.

Nor should those flatter themselves who, after receiving grace, refuse to be corrected and return again to their former pleasures. The day of judgment is awaited. That most impartial Judge will be present, who accepts no person because of power, and whose palace no one can corrupt with gold or silver.

All souls will stand present, so that each may render an account according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil (II Cor. V, 10). The adversary the devil will also be present, and the words of our profession will be read aloud.

And if someone is found to be such that he departs this life as a debtor, that adversary will exult in the presence of the most severe Judge [Note: [Col. 1119] Other printed editions read: “most serene Judge”], claiming to be the superior, and bringing such a case before such a Judge:

“Most just Judge,” he will say, “judge with perfect justice. ‘Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne’” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 15). Judge that he belongs to me, since he did not wish to belong to you. He is mine and must be condemned with me. After his renunciation, why did he seize my rags? What was impurity doing in one who had himself renounced it? What were intemperance, greed, anger, pride, and the rest of what belongs to me doing in him?

Finally, most just Judge: when he fled from me and took refuge with you, afterward I seized him with the things he had renounced; I held him as an invader, and in a certain sense he was seized by me in my own possession.

For what was he doing in the circus, and there dividing among himself furies, quarrels [Note: [Col. 1119] The Corbie manuscript reads: “and there furious quarrels”], insane shouts, and empty victories—things already alien to him? What was the renouncer of shameful pleasures doing in the theater? What was he doing in the amphitheater, watching cruelties with his own eyes? “He stored up wrath for himself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II, 5).

He seized all these things of mine after his renunciation; he wanted to be mine and coveted what was mine. Judge, judge with perfect justice, because the one whom you deigned to free at so great a price afterward chose to bind himself to me.

Will the person who, after his profession, is found to be such that he is justly handed over to the devil be able to open his mouth?

See what you are doing, my sons, my brothers. See what you are doing; see how you guard this profession of yours. We charge you, by that Judge himself and by all the heavenly powers—who both hear us admonishing and receive you as you make your profession—not to receive the grace of God in vain (II Cor. VI, 1), but to renounce and reject with an undivided heart, with all your strength, and with perfect faith so ruinous a diabolical inheritance, lest you remain orphans or poor.

# Chapter V

### The Unity of the Trinity

“Believe in God the Father almighty.” In changing your Father, change your inheritance.

Who is this almighty Father? We indeed believe and recognize God the Father, by grace, as our Father and the Father of the whole world; but we also seek his own Son by substance, since he was Father even before the world was formed by him.

If he was Father, whose Father was he? He certainly had a Son from himself and with himself, that which he himself is, but not himself: for he is the Father, the other is the Son. For the almighty Father begot an almighty Son from himself, equal to himself in such a way that he wholly remained in himself, and was Father of the Son and Son of the Father: God from God, day from day, light from light. Yet they are not two gods, or two days, or two lights, but one God, one day, one light.

You do not grasp this by seeing; understand it by believing. Cleanse the eyes of your heart—or rather, let the very light that you desire to see cleanse your heart, so that it may be purified from the darkness of sins. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

Behold, extend the gaze of your heart’s eye and see; incline the ear of your heart and hear. “Father” and “Son” sound like two, but when the Son himself says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10)—for the Son is the Word of the Father, and the Father was never without the Word, since “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God” (ibid. I, 1)—this Word, the Son, is in the Father, and the Father is in the Son, his Word. Therefore there are not two gods, but one God.

“Day from day” appears to signify two days. But when the Son himself says to the Jews in the Gospel, “Abraham your father desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (ibid. VIII, 56), and when Abraham saw three men beneath the oak of Mamre, he did not call them three lords, but called one Lord in all of them—as though three were one day—therefore the Lord himself, wishing the Father and the Son to be understood as one day [Note: [Col. 1120] In other copies, here and in the following lines, “God” occurs instead of “day”], when Philip asked him about the Father as though he were another day, since he was already seeing the Son as day, showed with what eye he ought to seek to see the unity of God, because he had fixed the eye of the flesh upon the humanity:

“Philip,” he said, “who has seen me has seen the Father.” For I and the Father are not two days [Note: [Col. 1120] Other copies read, “gods”], but one.

If you can grasp it, grasp the eternal day.

# Chapter VI

### The Incomprehensible Trinity

“Light from light” appears to sound like two lights. But far be it from us to be seized by the error of the Manichaeans, who suppose that this sun is Christ. We believe the Sun of righteousness to be the Word of the Father, inseparable from him, equal to him, remaining with the Father, and ordering all things with him: the Father doing all things through the Son, constructing the fabric of the world through his Word; the Son coming to us without abandoning the Father, always with him, nowhere without him; illuminating, shining from himself and from the Father, radiating and flashing forth—not two lights, but one light.

“For I and the Father are one,” he says (ibid. X, 30).

Concerning this only-begotten Word the prophet David says: “God has spoken once; I have heard two things” (Ps. LXI, 12). How did God speak once, and yet sound forth a second time, unless it is because the Word, proceeding untransgressibly from the Father’s heart, assumed flesh in order to be man, from his mother’s womb? He came and remained; he came to us and did not depart from the Father.

Behold, through the fact that God spoke once, our entire structure arose; through the fact that he sounded forth a second time, he became our peace, so that he might dissolve hostilities in the flesh (Eph. II, 14).

The Arian, failing to attend to this Word, this light, dares to say that the Son whom we confess to be equal is lesser. In mad obstinacy he wishes to debate concerning the Word remaining in the Father’s heart, although he is unable to understand himself.

Mad heretic, first return to yourself; consider your whole being, if you can comprehend yourself. Then debate concerning the one who made both me and you.

See how that humble man did not seek lofty things, but sought to know God in simplicity of heart—he who with one stone brought down Goliath’s proud forehead (I Sam. XVII, 49). See how he did not seek lofty things. He considered what was taking place within himself; he considered his soul, examined his structure, searched himself inwardly to discover what he was and from what part he governed so great and beautiful a mass, and where, in an earthen vessel, the mistress soul dwelled, filled with such great treasures of wisdom, knowledge, and prudence.

Where were such great, precious, and immense things located? What places did the soul occupy, when it has no place? And how did individual virtues proceed from a single source without diminishing either the source or what flowed forth?

He saw these things, considered them, wished to comprehend them but could not, and cried out to God, saying: “Your knowledge has been made wondrous through me; it has prevailed, and I cannot attain to it” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 6) [Note: [Col. 1120] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “He wished to comprehend himself and cried out.”]

This was his meaning: “When shall I be able to comprehend you, who are so great, when I cannot even explain myself, so small and insignificant?”

Observe also another humble man seeking the measure of his weakness—not exceeding it, but inclining toward what is lowly:

“Who has counted the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss? Who has investigated the wisdom of God, which precedes all things?” (Eccli. I, 2–3).

Behold, the prophet says—or rather, the Lord himself, who was speaking through the prophet—that no one has investigated the wisdom of God. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 24).

No one, according to divinity, has been able to investigate the wisdom of God, because, insofar as the Son was born from the Father without a mother, “who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8).

# Chapter VII
Against the Arians. Tell me, heretic, who dares say that the Wisdom of God is lesser: tell me how high the heavens are, how broad the earth, how deep the abyss. Count, if you can, the drops of rain, the sand of the sea, and the days of the age; tell me also the number of your hairs, since “all the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. 10:30). Explain these small and lower things to me, and then I shall believe that you can investigate the things above. But you cannot; you are unable. The Spirit of God convicts you—the Spirit who foresaw you heretics beforehand. For those who wrote and understood the things we mentioned above were moved by the spirit of truth, not of error.

But you, heretic, unable to explain these things, dare to discuss the very Wisdom of God, which cannot be investigated. And you think yourself great because you argue when no one disputes with you and no judge presides. While time lends support to your error, you imagine yourself to be something, though you are nothing; and, deceived, you desire to deceive many—some by money, some by power. You gather such people around you that you may cause very many to perish with you. This labor of yours does not contribute to salvation, but rather to destruction.

For by teaching such things—or rather, not teaching but blaspheming—you are shown to inflict injuries not upon some powerful person, but upon God the Father himself, in his Son. “The Father is greater, the Son lesser”; “the Father is better, the Son inferior.” Let no wise man willingly accept such insults, if he claims to have a son better than himself or equal to himself. Hence there is also that prophetic saying:

> “The father rejoiced in a wise son; while he lived he saw him, and at his death he was not saddened. For the father is dead, and seems not to be dead: for he left behind him one like himself” (Ecclus. 30:5, 4).

Behold, the prophet says that a human father lives in the fact that he left behind a wise son like himself; and you, heretic, dare to say that Wisdom itself—that is, the Son of God—is unlike the Father? The prophet says that a dead human father lives in his son because he left behind one like himself; and you dare to separate the very eternal Life, who is the Son of God, from the Father who never dies?

## CHAPTER VIII

### The equality of the persons

“And what,” you ask, “am I to do?” He himself said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Because you do not understand it, what he rightly said sounds wrong to you. For he did say it—indeed, he confirmed it. He himself most certainly said, “The Father is greater than I”: the Son himself said it.

But observe when he said this: he said it while placed in the assumption of human nature. He said, “The Father is greater than I,” when he said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). He said, “The Father is greater than I,” when he wept, when he grew weary, when he was hungry, when he thirsted. He said, “The Father is greater than I,” when Scripture says that he was made “a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6).

Does your mad pride here advance so irreverently that you dare say that the Word of God, remaining with the Father, is, in that very divinity, lesser than the angels? If you do not dare say this, heretic, preserve these distinctions, and your error will perish:

The Son with the Father, and equal with the Father, because eternal with the eternal, always remaining with him who always remains; equal when sent and when coming; lesser in the assumption of humanity—not only than the Father, but also than the angels [Note: [Col. 1121] The manuscripts read, “and coming in the assumption.”]; equal in the form of God, lesser in the form of a servant; equal with the Father in creating angels, lesser than the Father in making human beings angels; equal with the Father in constructing the new world [Col. 1122] [Note: [Col. 1122] Some manuscripts read, “lesser than the Father in constructing the new world.”]; lesser than the Father in restoring the ruined world; equal with the Father in granting eternal life, lesser than the Father in accepting our death.

## CHAPTER IX

### Christ’s birth

We therefore believe that this Son of God was lesser in the assumption of humanity and equal to the Father in divinity, being made, as the Apostle says, “of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). For the virgin Mary was of the seed of David; she conceived by the Holy Spirit, and in her womb the Word, having assumed flesh, became for us the mediator, wholly man and God (1 Tim. 2:5): one Christ, Word, soul, and flesh.

The order of this sacrament also declares this to us: after we believe in God the Father almighty, we also believe in his Son Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1122] The printed editions add here, “conceived,” which is absent from the manuscripts], born of the Holy Spirit from the virgin Mary.

This birth utterly disturbs every human thought, because divine power brought it about. For when does the logic of our generation allow that a virgin should conceive, remain a virgin after childbirth, and yet a son should be seen, with her integrity preserved inviolate? No ordinary human being born could accomplish this; but he could, because he was not merely man, but God and man. For this reason he wished to be born as man: because every human being had perished.

The first great and unique miracle of this Mediator was therefore that he was born in this way. He who came to teach many to perform miracles—which he himself performed through himself and through them—nevertheless possessed something proper to himself, having appropriated nothing belonging to another. For he alone was born of a virgin, because he alone was conceived from the Holy Spirit without the embrace of man and woman. He alone filled his mother’s womb without corruption, because he alone ascended above the heavens for us, to sit at the right hand of the Father.

The disciples received from him the power to perform many great miracles, and they did so. Yet no one is proclaimed or believed to have been born of a virgin or conceived from the Holy Spirit except that one who, having been found in time, was himself also created—the creator of times—assuming the human nature that he himself had formed entire, so that through it, in a certain way, he might restore our ruin as redeemer [Note: [Col. 1122] The manuscripts omit “redeemer.”].

This one is both Son of God and son of man: Son of God in the Father’s heart, son of man in his mother’s womb; the same one Christ, who came forth from the virgin womb “like a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. 18:6). In that womb a spiritual marriage was celebrated: God was joined to flesh, and flesh adhered to God, so that there might be one Christ, God and man.

## CHAPTER X

### Herod’s cruelty

Coming forth from his chamber like a bridegroom, he caused the whole creation to appear stirred and exultant at his wedding. For the choir of angels, through these nuptials, signifies peace to people of good will: he who was the Son of God became also the Son of man, assuming what he was not and not losing what he was.

Through these nuptials the heavens produce a new star, a new and splendid light, with that very bridegroom working within them, so that they might announce that the true Light had been born for those sitting in the shadow of death and, as though with their own tongue, praise this bridegroom coming forth. They knew that he had assumed mortal humanity for this purpose: to make it immortal.

To this bridegroom the Magi come from the farthest ends of the earth. Warned, they seek him; summoned, they offer gifts. They desire to worship the king indicated by the star, although they have not yet even seen the child who was born [Note: [Col. 1122] The manuscripts read, “to see.”].

At these nuptials of the king, Herod was disturbed, and the Jews were troubled, not understanding the king of all creation. Herod seeks to destroy the infant whom he hears has been born king, lest, as he grows, he should lose his kingdom. The Jews, unwilling to have the Son of God as king, disclose to Herod where Christ would be born, and the will of both is bound together in the death of one infant.

After Herod learned from the Jews’ report where Christ might be found in order to be killed, he summoned the Magi and asked them the time of the star [Col. 1123]. Then he said to them: “Go, inquire carefully about the child, so that I too may come and worship him” (Matt. 2:8).

O deceitful lips! Why do you speak evil with a double heart? Your tongue says one thing, your conscience cries another. You deceive yourself by thinking such things; you err, you deceive, and you are deceived. Falsity keeps watch in vain for evil [Note: [Col. 1123] The Corbie manuscript reads, “you keep watch; falsity.”]; truth is not sought by you as it ought to be.

Behold, the Magi hear you saying one thing outwardly, but they do not know that you are thinking something else inwardly, and they depart in such a way that they do not return to you. For he who mocked your folly instructed the Magi to do what the true king had commanded, not what the false king had craftily persuaded them to do. “They returned,” says the Evangelist, “to their own country by another way” (ibid., 12).

But when you realized that you had been deceived by the Magi, Herod, you wished to destroy all the infants of that region, so that you might kill the one you sought. But our bridegroom, who came forth from his chamber so that praise might be perfected from the mouths of infants and nursing children, allowed you to fulfill your will, so that an age unable to confess Christ with its own tongue might confess him by the testimony of its death, your savage cruelty might be demonstrated, and a throng of infants might be gathered for the wedding of the heavenly bridegroom [Note: [Col. 1123] Some manuscripts read, “might offer the testimony of its death” (or, “by its death”), “and your savage unbelief,” and so forth.].

Tell me, Herod: if Christ offended you because you heard of his kingdom from the Magi who announced it, what offense did those people give you who, together with you, held the leading positions among the Jews and thought against Christ? By killing their children, you afflicted them with an even more atrocious punishment in their own children. For you could not find Christ. But why should I speak with you any longer? Let me address those very Jews who, because they refused to recognize the infant Christ, were compelled to lose their children with him [Note: [Col. 1123] The printed editions read, “on his account.”]. Your friend Herod killed them and delivered them to death; but Christ, whom even now you call your enemy, bestowed upon them mortality and eternal life.

## CHAPTER XI

### Against the Jews, from Isaiah and Jeremiah

I address you, I say, O Jews, who to this very day deny the Son of God. Was it not your voice when you saw him performing miracles and, while testing him, said, “How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly”?

But he directed you to consider his miracles, saying, “The works that I do themselves bear witness about me” (John 10:24–25), so that facts, not words, might bear witness to Christ.

But you, failing to recognize the Savior who was working salvation in the midst of your land (Ps. 73:12), added evil to evil and said, “You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.” But you did not wish to consider what he answered you. “Is it not written,” he said, “in your Law, that the testimony of two men is true” (John 8:13, 17)?

Transgressors of the Law, attend to the Law! You seek testimony concerning Christ: in your Law it is written that the testimony of two men is true (Deut. 17:6; 19:15). Let not merely two, but even more witnesses of Christ come forth from your Law and convict those who hear the Law but do not practice it.

Speak, Isaiah; bear witness to Christ. “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14).

Let another witness also come forward. You too, Jeremiah, bear witness to Christ. “This is our God,” he says, “and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who discovered the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38).

Behold two reliable witnesses from your Law, by whose testimony your hearts were not pierced.

## CHAPTER XII

### From Daniel

But let other witnesses of Christ, one after another, be introduced from the Law, so that the hardest foreheads of his enemies may be crushed. Let holy Daniel also come—young in age, but old in knowledge and gentleness—and convict all false witnesses. Just as he convicted the shameless elders (Dan. 13:47), so by his testimony let him crush the enemies of Christ.

Speak, holy Daniel; speak of Christ what you know. “When the Holy of Holies comes,” he says, “anointing shall cease” (ibid. 9:24).

Why, when he was present, did your anointing cease—the one whom, in mockery, you said, “You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true” (John 8:13)—unless he is the one who had come, the Holy of Holies?

If, as you say, he has not yet come, but the Holy of Holies is still awaited, demonstrate the anointing. But if, as is true, your anointing has ceased, acknowledge that the Holy of Holies has come.

For he is also that stone cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut it—that is, Christ, born of a virgin without the hands of those who embrace—who grew so greatly that he became a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth (Dan. 2:34–35).

Concerning this mountain the prophet says, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2:3). And David says of it, “The mountain of God is a fertile mountain; why do you suspect mountains covered with cheese, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell?” (Ps. 67:16–17).

When the Lord Christ himself asked his disciples whom people said the Son of man was, they answered: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets” (Matt. 16:14). And he said: “Why do you suspect mountains covered with cheese, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell”?

Peter recognized this mountain, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 17). He recognized the mountain and ascended the mountain; he bore witness to the Truth, and he was loved by the Truth. Peter was founded upon the rock so that he might accept death by loving the one whom, through fear, he had denied three times.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Further testimonies from the Law and the Prophets

You too, Moses the lawgiver and leader of the people of Israel, bear witness to Christ. “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers. Every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from his people” (Deut. 18:15, 19).

Hear Christ himself in the Gospel showing that Christ is the prophet who was spoken of: “A prophet,” he says, “is not without honor except in his own country” (Matt. 13:57).

Let holy David also come forward, a faithful witness, from whose seed came the one to whom the Law and the Prophets bear witness. Let him too speak of Christ: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:11).

Whom will they serve? Tell me—whom will they serve? Do you wish to hear whom? “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1).

And more explicitly and by name: “Why,” he says, “did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2:1).

Let another witness also come forward. You too, prophet Habakkuk, bear witness to Christ. “Lord,” he says, “I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, O God, and I was terrified” (Habakkuk 3:2).

What works of God did he marvel at and fear? Did he marvel at the construction of the world and become terrified? Certainly not. But listen to what terrified him. “In the midst,” he says, “of two animals you shall be known.” The works of God: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). “In the midst of two animals you shall be known.”

Who are you? How far have you descended? You have made me afraid, because the Word through whom all things were made lay in a manger. “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1:3).

“In the midst of two animals you shall be known.” What does “in the midst of two animals you shall be known” mean, unless it is either in the midst of the two Testaments, or in the midst of the two thieves, or in the midst of Moses and Elijah speaking with him on the mountain?

“The Word walked,” he says, “and went forth into the fields” (Habakkuk 3:3). “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Jeremiah says the same: “After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:38).

Behold how the witnesses of truth agree with one another; behold how they convict the children of falsehood.

Are these things enough for you, O Jews? Or shall we, for your confusion, introduce from the Law and from your own people still other witnesses, so that they may bear witness to the one whom, with minds lost, you insulted by saying, “You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true”?

If I wished to collect from the Law and the Prophets everything that was said about Christ, time would fail me more readily than abundance.

## CHAPTER XIV

### The testimony of Simeon and Zechariah

Nevertheless, I shall bring forward that old man born from your people but not abandoned to your error—holy Simeon—who was worthy to be kept alive in this light, though already aged, until he should see the true Light.

His age was already compelling him to depart, but he waited to receive the one whom he knew was coming. When this old man had been warned by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before he had seen the Christ of God, he recognized the one who had been born and went to the temple.

When he saw him being carried in his mother’s hands, and holy old age reverently recognized the divine infancy, he took the infant in his own arms. He was carrying the infant Christ, but Christ was guiding the old man. He guided the one who was being carried, so that he would not be released from the body before the promise.

But hear what he said and whom he confessed, you enemies—not of Christ, but of yourselves. Blessing God, that old man exclaimed and said:

> “Now you release your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:26–32).

Let the parents of John also—Zechariah and Elizabeth, young in their sterility but fruitful in old age—bear witness to Christ. Let them say what they think about Christ and raise up a reliable witness for Christ.

For they say to their little son at his birth:

> “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (ibid. 1:17).

And Elizabeth said to his mother, the virgin:

> “And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (ibid., 43–44).

Understanding that the mother of his Lord had come to his mother, John, still confined within the narrowness of the womb, greeted her by a movement that he could not yet express with his voice.

What did John himself later say—the forerunner and friend, humble and most faithful servant, made a reliable witness? He was considered greater than those born of women precisely because he was thought to be what he was not. For the Jews believed that he was the Christ, but he loudly declared that he was not, saying:

> “I am not the one you suppose me to be; but behold, one comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to loosen” (Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16; Acts 13:25).

O faithful witness and friend of the true bridegroom, how much would you have humbled yourself if you had said that you were worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal! But by saying that you were unworthy of this, you contradict the Jews, those false witnesses.

You said these things before you saw Christ. But when he himself came to you, exalted yet humble, in order to fulfill his dispensation, so that he might be baptized by you, although he had no sin whatsoever, hear what you answered, whom you recognized, and what testimony you gave. Let the enemies who refuse to hear listen:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29, 36).

And he added:

> “You come to me to be baptized, and I ought to be baptized by you” (Matt. 3:14).

The servant recognized the Lord; one bound by the chains of original sin recognized him who was free from every bond of sin; the herald recognized the judge; the creature recognized the Creator; the friend of the bridegroom recognized the bridegroom.

For this too is John’s voice:
