[Note: In the treatise *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 44, the Basel and Louvain editions have *evectationem*—incorrectly—and here *evectionem*. On the authority of the Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice editions, *rectationem* has been written throughout. M.]

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 1144]

But that which still bears the stains of the hostile race descends piecemeal through vapors and heat, mingles with trees and other plants and with all crops, and is stained with various colors.

And just as, from that great and most brilliant ship, the forms of boys and virgins submit to the hostile powers that dwell in the heavens and possess a fiery nature, and from this beautiful sight the portion of life contained in their limbs is loosened and drawn through the heat into the earth, so also that highest virtue which dwells in the ship of the vital waters appears, through its angels, in the likeness of holy boys and virgins to those powers whose nature is cold and moist and which have been arranged in the heavens.

To those among them who are female, the form of boys appears; to the males, that of virgins. Through this change and diversity of divine and most beautiful persons, the male and female rulers of the moist and cold stock are loosened, and what is vital in them flees. But whatever has settled is loosened and drawn down to earth through the cold and mingled with every kind of earth.

## CHAPTER XVII

Who would not laugh—or rather grieve and detest this man, who says such dreadful and abominable things about the divine substance?

According to your error and your doctrine, then, the substance of the eternal light, the portion of God, held captive amid disasters, calamities, afflictions, pressures, filth, and uncleanness, could receive daily assistance in no other way than that the blessed Father, who has luminous ships as inns, whom you call the third ambassador, and the highest Power should transform their virtues into the nature of different sexes.

You call these virtues undefiled, yet you say that, in the manner of prostitutes, they mutually inflame through their beauty the deadly and most foul desire of the rulers of darkness [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript and the Cistercian and Corbie manuscripts read *confusae invicem accendant*, “being confused, they inflame mutually.” Erasmus and Louvain read *confusae et invitiae accendant*, “being confused and unwilling, they inflame.”].

For you have not found a true way to express such immense beauty in more honorable terms. And why do they do this? So that, when the rulers are aroused to lust by them, the divine substance may find an opportunity for liberation.

What else does this mean except that the divine majesty finds a way of escape even through the genitals of demons?

Great God, come to the aid of souls that believe these filthy things and follow these abominations. Who, I ask you, would not shudder at this? Who is so blind, I ask you, as to believe it?

## CHAPTER XVIII

But let those who follow Manichaeus himself answer me this: If God is incorruptible, or if the whole nature of the supreme good is inviolable, immaculate, imperishable, undefiled, and incomprehensible, what could the nature of evil do to such a great nature if it did not wish to fight with it, so that it might not be brought to such disgrace?

I have said: What could the race of darkness do to God if he did not wish to fight with it?

If I am told, “Nothing,” I ask why his portion—that is, God’s portion—is today established amid calamities, pressures, captivity, and subjection, so that it may be liberated in such a shameful manner, and yet cannot all be liberated even in this way; or why the Father himself should mourn on account of the portion mentioned, a grief that Manichaeus openly proclaims in his books.

## CHAPTER XIX

Someone says: “Nothing could be done to him; but, to demonstrate that he possessed foreknowledge of the thoughts of the rulers of darkness, and to show that he feared nothing, he fought.”

To him I replied: “If he could see the thoughts of the rulers of darkness and fear no one, why did he not foresee the grief that was impending for him because of the misfortune of his portion, which he suffers today?

“He will never recover his portion intact, because something of it remains, as he himself says, which cannot be purified and will be condemned for eternity in the sphere of darkness.

“What great foreknowledge—or rather ignorance—and wretched weakness this is: that he feared no one.

“Certainly, if he could not in any way defend himself, he ought to have asked for mercy, lest that integrity and beauty of all ornaments be brought to such disgrace.”

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 1145]

Again someone said: “The race of darkness could do nothing to him, but he did not wish to suffer an evil thing near his borders, and he sent someone to defeat it.”

To him I replied: “If it is as you say, then he himself is rather found to be evil, since he wished to destroy a neighboring thing that harmed him in no way. And just as he was evil toward that thing, so he was cruel toward his own, or ignorant of the calamity that would befall it.

“For when he thinks that he can accomplish something good by extending his own region into the kingdom of evil, which did him no harm, first he did not foresee the misfortune that now presses his portion every day; and then he did not foresee that he would never be able to restore it entirely to its original freedom.”

## CHAPTER XXI

But since they are wholly unable to answer this objection, they oppose their customary ignorance:

“What would the Jews have done to Christ if he had not wished to suffer at their hands?”

Would that they could see what they would easily see if they were not blinded by the clouds of contention: the difference between being pressed by the necessity of an impending evil—which they assert that their god suffered—and the supremely merciful act that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Wisdom and Power of God, graciously chose to display to the human race through the human being whom he assumed, so that through a human being he might show human beings an example of patience.

For it was necessary, and it was just, that human beings overcome through patient humility the difficulty of the weakness of their flesh, since they had fallen into it through the exaltation of pride, as our Scripture indicates in Adam, the first man.

Can you also say that, because there were certain human beings whom God wished to teach patience, he therefore wished to suffer such evils at the hands of the race of darkness, just as the Lord suffered at the hands of the Jews?

Or can you say that God assumed some passible nature in which he would suffer from the race of darkness whatever it could do to him, while he himself remained wholly unchanged in his own substance—just as the Word of God, who is the Son of God, himself immutable like the Father, assumed mortal humanity so that, with his divinity intact and inviolate, he might teach mortals in mortal flesh to conquer death through patience, and by his resurrection demonstrate the future transformation of that weak flesh into something better?

## CHAPTER XXII

Although he was invisible in himself, he appeared visible in the human being whom he graciously chose to assume from a woman, as we read in the Gospel (Luke II). The Apostle also says, “born of a woman” (Gal. IV, 4).

And they say: “Why did he not say ‘born of a virgin’?” They do not understand that this was said conventionally, according to the proper usage of the language of Scripture, just as it was said of Eve, “He formed her into a woman” (Gen. II, 22), before she was even presented to a man.

Although Mary is not improperly called a woman because of childbirth, she is called a virgin because she had not known intercourse with a man, and because her virginity was not violated by giving birth.

As for what the Angel and Elizabeth said to Mary, “Blessed are you among women” (Luke I, 42), there is no question that the virgin truly is blessed among women.

But do not say: “Just as angels appeared, so he had a body; therefore he need not have been born of a woman.”

What if you are asked: “Where do you read that Christ came in the flesh?” Will you not say: “In the Gospel”?

Then the answer will be given to you: “There it is written that Christ was born of a virgin.”

But in your customary foulness you will say that Scripture itself is false. You do not see that someone as blind as yourselves could do the same thing: he could say that what you declare true is false, and that what you declare false is true.

Thus you open the doors to every human error and crime, so that each person may accept or reject the divine Scriptures according to his own desire or pleasure, rejecting whatever he does not understand and, offended by it, considers evil. In this way there will no longer be any rule by which those such people can be corrected from their error.

## CHAPTER XXIII
Receive the canonical Scriptures in their entirety, if you desire to be complete. For if you understood—or certainly believed—what the Apostle said, that our race was deceived through a woman—for he says, “[Col. 1146] I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (II Cor. 11:3)—you could understand that our race ought to have been redeemed through a woman: so that, since death came through a woman, life might be recovered through a woman. In this way it would be shown that the female creature itself is not to be blamed, since God is its creator, but rather the will by which Eve sinned.

Yet you fear to believe that the majesty, that undefiled and ineffable power, was present in a virgin’s womb, lest it be polluted by her blood—even though it has dwelt, and now dwells, in the Apostles and in many worthy women, who certainly have bodies and blood. For if it could be polluted in Mary, it could be polluted in everyone; but if it could not be polluted in them, then certainly it could not be polluted in Mary, in whose womb the Wisdom of God effected the assumption of a body.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Certainly they will not deny that Manichaeus himself was born of a father and a mother; nor, according to their error, will they deny that his soul is God, likewise almighty. He boasts, with marvelous pride, that he was taken up by his own genius—that is, by the Holy Spirit. And certainly, if his genius is the Holy Spirit, then the Holy Spirit himself is also holy, and he himself is God almighty, just as the Holy Spirit is. Yet this Manichaeus had flesh; and if the Holy Spirit, or his soul as the genius of the Holy Spirit, was polluted in that flesh, they worship a pollutable God.

But if God is nowhere polluted—just as the light of the heavenly bodies reaches even to the earth without being polluted, although it is evident that this sun, before which they bow the knee, spreads its rays over every dungheap and foul place and is nowhere polluted by them—then let them cease blaspheming and ask God to free them from their error.

An undefiled substance is not undefiled because it touches nothing, but because it remains in its own purity, whatever the thing may be that it touches. For example, do we call a body invulnerable or impenetrable one that is not struck by iron, or rather one that, even when struck, is not penetrated? Thus the Son of God is shown all the more clearly to be incapable of pollution by a woman’s blood because he was born through a woman, rather than if he had not been born through a woman and had avoided those bodily members. For then he would seem to have judged that he could be polluted by them, and we would speak less confidently of him as undefiled.

He consecrated virginity because he chose to be born of a virgin. And on earth he had to choose as mother the one who was to receive the human being, while he already had a Father in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXV

But they say: “Why, then, did he deny his mother when he said to her, ‘What have I to do with you, woman?’ (John 2:4); and when, having been told that she wished to see him, he replied, ‘Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?’ (Matthew 12:48), counting instead as belonging to this relationship those who did the will of his Father?”

Because by his own example he was already teaching that earthly parents must be denied for God’s sake. For earthly affection ought not to obstruct one who was carrying out divine works. Indeed, if he had no mother for the reason that he denied his mother, then neither Peter nor the other Apostles had fathers, because he instructed them, saying: “And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (ibid. 23:9). What, therefore, he instructed them concerning an earthly father, he first did concerning his mother.

This, then, is what we say: in assuming a human being, the Wisdom of God was not polluted; rather, out of mercy, for the salvation of human beings, he assumed a human being, so that, as the Apostle says, he might become “the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (I Timothy 2:3).

He could not have lied to his doubting disciple when he said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and offered the scars of his wounds for him even to touch with his hand (ibid. 20:27). For how could we trust him securely in anything if he had lied in this way to his disciple? Far be such blasphemy! And may it not hold even those who dare to assert or believe this guilty forever; rather, let them awaken at last and understand with what unspeakable perversity such things are believed.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 1147]

We believe that the Lord truly assumed a human being, and that in this human being he appeared visibly to human beings, though invisible; that in this human being he lived among human beings; that in this human being he endured human treatment at human hands; and that in this human being he taught human beings what they should leave behind, what they should endure, and toward what they should strive.

He did all this without any necessity. Hence he himself says: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, in order to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:17–18). He therefore did not lose it under compulsion from evil. He wished everything that happened in his passion to happen for the instruction of human nature, not for his own protection.

Just as we, who consist of soul and body, are invisible in respect of the soul but visible in respect of the body, so everything that we visibly receive, whether honors and benefits, or endure, whether insults or injuries, must necessarily be referred to the invisible soul as to the ruling principle, because the soul governs the body. And although in respect of the soul we are immortal, when we have died in the body we are called dead. So also the Lord, according to the flesh and the form of a servant that he deigned to assume, is shown to have suffered insults, bonds, scourging, and death, so that the Truth might be believed to have done everything truthfully and nothing falsely.

For by power and will the Word became flesh, was born, suffered, died, and rose again—not from any necessity of his own, but by will and power. No part of him was ever despoiled, and no part remains captive to this day—not only no part of his divine nature, but not even of the mortal nature he assumed. Nor can any part ever be captured except by those who, through faith, wish to be joined to him with pure hearts.

This is not like the god of the Manichaeans, who, pressed by the evil of necessity, is today—something they cannot deny—in part still wallowing in misery and calamity.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Understand, if you can, even among human beings themselves how great the difference is between necessity and will. Suppose, for example, that someone is sent to prison by the command of justice on account of his deserved punishment, and that another, a holy man, enters the same prison for that person’s consolation or liberation. Are both of them in prison for the same reason? One was sent there; the other entered. One suffers punishment; the other performs an act of mercy.

The latter entered when he wished and left when he wished. The former cannot lawfully be freed unless pardon intervenes. Human beings can do even this, freely bestowing a benefit when at times they themselves desire no benefit in return.

Consider, then, whether God can suffer any necessity, when human beings can do good by their own will, hired by no reward and compelled by no necessity. God therefore suffers no necessity, nor does he do what he does from necessity, but from supreme and ineffable will and power.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

And yet, according to your error, you above all ought not to have raised this objection, in which you say: “What were the Jews going to do to Christ if he did not wish to suffer at their hands?” For according to the blasphemies of that same Manichaeus, Christ did not have flesh and suffered nothing at the hands of the Jews.

Thus he says in the Epistle of the Foundation: “For the enemy, who hoped that he had crucified that same Savior, the father of the righteous, was himself crucified, at the time when one thing was done and another displayed. Therefore the prince of darkness was fastened to the cross; he likewise wore a crown of thorns with his companions and had a scarlet garment. He also drank vinegar and gall, which some supposed the Lord had drunk. And everything that he appeared here to endure was inflicted upon the rulers of darkness, who were also wounded by nails and a spear.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

Why, then, do you raise the objection, saying, “What were the Jews going to do to Christ if he did not wish to suffer at their hands?” when you hold this view of his passion: that it was not God himself who suffered anything in his body, but that the prince of darkness suffered all those things?

How, then, do you raise these objections against our faith?

## CHAPTER XXX

We believe, as it is written in the Gospel, that Christ wished to suffer, and suffered when he wished. For the Jews did not bring about his passion when they wished. They certainly wanted to seize and kill him, and according to their will they had already accomplished the crime they were attempting; they were already guilty of the most monstrous sin, because they wanted to do it, even if they had done nothing.

Yet he who had the authority to lay down his life (John 10:17) permitted them to act when he wished. He could have commanded legions of angels so that the Jews would perish, or destroyed them all with a single word of his own (Matthew 26:53).

## CHAPTER XXXI

The Lord Christ, therefore, suffered according to the human being whom he assumed. And no member of his mortal body, which he had assumed, is held by the Jews today, as we said above.

But your god, O Manichaeans, is pressed by impending stain and devastation. He did not advance to battle by free will, but was compelled by necessity; nor did he wish to bestow anything, but tried to resist. He was swallowed up and mixed together in his own substance, not in an assumed mortal body. He is partly held captive today, and part of him will always be held in the globe.

Yet who could endure such incredible blasphemies, which these people do not hesitate to utter concerning the Lord’s very passion?

## CHAPTER XXXII

All the Apostles, all rational tongues, proclaim that the Lord Christ suffered. All sound faith confesses that Christ suffered for us. But the wicked Manichaeus asserts that those demons endured those sufferings.

For he does not say that they suffered because the Lord triumphed over them and taught us to triumph over them through endurance. Rather, he says this because they deny that the Lord Christ had mortal flesh.

To them we say: If he did not have mortal flesh, what was it that the Jews held? What was it that hung on the cross? What was fastened with nails to the wood? What was struck by the spear, from which blood and water flowed? For if these things only appeared to happen and did not happen, they were phantoms—a belief that it is impious to hold.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

But if these things truly happened, and yet happened not in mortal flesh but in the divine substance itself, then you are saying that the divine substance is changeable, visible to fleshly eyes, tangible to fleshly hands, and vulnerable to iron. This too it is impious to believe.

Thus Manichaeus fears to say that these things did not happen; and again he fears to say that they happened in the divine substance; and he does not wish to confess—nor could he understand—how the Son of God, through whom all things were made, assumed a human being with flesh without any alteration or pollution of his divine substance. He was therefore compelled to say that it was not Christ, but the prince of darkness with his companions, who suffered all those things.

Wretched people! Do you not fear that at the judgment you will be told: “I freed those for whom I suffered; go, let the one to whom you attribute my sufferings free you”?

## CHAPTER XXXIV

You say, in great error, but nevertheless you say it, that Christ is born every day, suffers every day, and dies every day. Is it perhaps in those who believe and suffer tribulations and death for his name? “No,” you reply, “but in gourds, leeks, purslane, and other such things.”

Great mockery, great blindness! Above, human beings are liberated from sins through the sufferings of demons; here, through the sufferings of vegetables.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Again, when we say to them, “What would the race of darkness have done to God if he did not wish to fight with it?” they say: “Nothing could have been done to the incorruptible God.”

For if, for example, someone wanted to tear a solid glass sphere with his fingernails, the violence of his nails could never do anything to it. But if these people imagined the divine substance to be such that all the violence of the race of darkness was toward it as the nails of one tearing are toward a glass sphere, then the god of Manichaeus would not today be suffering grief over the cutting off or loss of part of himself.

They say that this part, when it is in fruits or herbs—that is, in a melon, beet, or similar things—knows its beginning, middle, and end; but when it comes into the flesh, it loses all understanding. For this reason, they say, a teacher was sent to human beings, because a part of God had become foolish in them; and for this reason he was not sent to melons, because they have a wise soul.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Who could believe that such things were ever said either by human beings or among human beings? And yet how does the substance of your god suffer no evil, when it is bound in fruits, blinded in flesh, or, when it wishes to return, cast down to the earth by the race of darkness?

But if no evil happened or happens to it, then everything Manichaeus said in the Epistle of the Foundation—which is the head of all vain fables—or in the Treasury—which is the treasury of all disgrace and blasphemy—or in all his other books, in which with such endless verbosity he asserts nothing other than the misery of the substance of God, which he says has been mixed with the princes of darkness, and grief among the divine powers because of their great anxiety to be liberated—all of this is false.

For truly the substance of God neither could have suffered, nor can suffer, nor will be able to suffer any evil. Nor does it have an enemy who can corrupt its ungenerated part. Rather, human beings are enemies of God—or, more accurately, of themselves—because they do not obey God’s commandments and corrupt themselves through their desires, not God.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

If you wished, O Manichaeans, to regard the harmony of the two Testaments with a simple eye, you would see it very easily.

You are violently agitated by what is written: “The Spirit of God was moving over the water” (Genesis 1:2); “God saw that it was good” (ibid. 1:10); “Adam, where are you?” (ibid. 3:9); “God who is jealous” (Exodus 20:5); “devouring fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24); “my sword” (ibid. 32:42), and other such expressions.

You do not consider that if someone else were so blind as to criticize what the Lord said in the Gospel—“You shall not swear by heaven, because it is the throne of God; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet” (Matthew 5:35)—and were to say what you habitually say in your astonishing madness, “Where was God before heaven and earth existed?”; or if he criticized what is written, “Jesus was amazed” (Luke 7:9), since no one is usually amazed except at something previously unknown to him—then one could answer that seeing that something is good is not the action of one who is ignorant, but of one who approves what he has made.

Or consider what is written when the Lord says, “Who touched me?” (ibid. 8:45); and concerning Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:34); and, “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34); and, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49); and, “I have come so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39); and, “Sell your possessions and buy swords for yourselves” (Luke 22:36); and the Apostle, “I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God” (II Corinthians 11:2); and, “The wrath of God will be revealed from heaven against all ungodliness” (Romans 1:18); as well as countless other things said or done by the Lord himself or by the Apostles, which people may most irrationally accuse because they do not understand them.

For greedy or immoral people can also interpret in another way what the Lord said: that if someone abandons what he possesses, he will receive sevenfold, or even a hundredfold, in this age (Matthew 19:29)—or that if someone wishes to abandon a wife, a female slave, or even prostitutes for the Lord’s sake, he should do so in hope of that multiplication, rather than from love of righteousness.

They can also be horrified, through misunderstanding, by what he said: “If anyone does not eat my flesh and drink my blood, he will not have life in himself” (John 6:54).

And concerning what he said, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:22), if fools say, “Look: the one whom you call merciful and forgiving sins threatens Gehenna for an insult,” do they not fail to know where they stand, while nevertheless imagining that they are saying something?

Or how did he hand over so many souls to demons in pigs to be killed (Luke 8:32), when you say that the souls of pigs are of the same kind as those of human beings?

Or how did he make a tree on which he found no fruit—because it was not the season—dry by a word (Mark 11:13), when you say that it possesses an intelligent soul?

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 1150]

Behold how many things the most wicked and blind can say concerning the divine utterances. Thus you rush against the ancient Books, ignorant of the things done or said there mystically, rashly accusing what you do not understand.

But when these matters are brought forward against you from the New Testament, you say that they signify divine and spiritual things. Yet you deny that the sacred writings of the Old Testament can be understood figuratively, even though the Lord himself spoke certain things from it figuratively and the Apostle Paul writes that everything happened to that people as a figure (I Corinthians 10:11). He himself also showed the rule by explaining many things from it.

Perhaps, however, with your customary vanity and dullness of heart, speaking against God and the Apostle’s authority, you say that the sayings of the Old Testament cannot be explained at all, while only the New Testament can be explained in such matters.

You do not consider that you would have nothing to say if other impious people said to you that the Old Testament could be explained, but the New could not. A sound mind, considering both Testaments, will undoubtedly declare that whatever it finds to admit of explanation in one can be explained in the other as well.

Your ignorance—or rather your malice—is plainly evident.

Consider the Acts of Leucius, which he writes under the name of the Apostles. Consider what sort of things you accept there concerning Maximilla, the wife of Egetes. When she did not wish to render the marital debt to her husband, although the Apostle had said, “Let the husband render the marital debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (ibid. 7:3), she placed her own female slave, named Euclia, in her husband’s bed in her place. She adorned her, as it is written there, with the devices and cosmetics of prostitution, and substituted her for herself at night, so that he, not knowing, would have intercourse with her as with his wife.

It is also written there that when Maximilla and Iphidamia went together to hear the Apostle Andrew, a certain handsome little boy—whom Leucius wants understood either as God or at least as an angel—commended them to the Apostle Andrew. He then went to the praetorium of Egetes, entered their bedroom, and imitated a woman’s voice, as though Maximilla were murmuring about the pains of the female sex and Iphidamia were answering her. When Egetes heard these conversations, believing that they were there, he departed.

What do you say to this, I ask you? Why was Maximilla not afraid to bind souls in the flesh through the most disgraceful prostitution of her slave? Yet when you believe that the little boy lied so shamefully, who will believe you when you speak, since, if you lie, you say that you are imitating the Lord?

## CHAPTER XXXIX

But, filled with rashness, continue to rush upon the ancient Books, striving to accuse what you do not know rather than to learn it.

Consider what miracles are found there. If you delight in the miracles of the New Testament, the dead were first raised there, lepers were first cleansed there, and many other things became known there to those who diligently and devoutly seek them, for the building up of faith.

If you delight in good commandments, the two commandments praised so highly by the Lord—concerning love of God and of one’s neighbor—were first written there (Matthew 22:37, 39). There too are the abandoning of houses, parents, children, and other things for the Lord’s sake (ibid. 19:29); not repaying evil with evil (Romans 12:17); praying for enemies (Matthew 5:44); forgiving an enemy; and offering the cheek to receive a slap (Luke 6:27; Matthew 5:39). Whatever commandments are found in the New Testament were not only commanded there, but also fulfilled with complete vigilance by holy men.

Will your malice also be able to say that whatever good and magnificent things are written there are false and added, while only those things that you, through not understanding them, think evil are true?

You ought to realize that certain similarly impious people could treat the New Testament in the same way: they could criticize whatever they thought evil because they did not understand it, and say that these alone were true there; while declaring all the things openly praised there false and inserted by lovers of the Lord, lest everything seem worthy of avoidance. Thus, struck by such blindness, both you and they may be shunned as already judged and condemned.

At last, wake up, cease from blasphemies, and, if you intend to be Christians, accept the authority of all the holy canonical Scriptures. Do not accuse what you do not understand; rather, desire to understand it.

## CHAPTER XL

For what of that matter as well, that you deny the resurrection of the flesh? The Apostle Paul cries out: “It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (I Corinthians 15:42–44).

And you protest in opposition that human flesh cannot rise and that it has the prince of darkness as its creator, although the Apostle says that this same flesh is the members of Christ and the temple of the Holy Spirit. “Do you not know,” he says, “that your bodies are members of Christ?” (ibid. 6:15).

He does not mean this according to the weakness of present corruption, which descends from the punishment of original sin, but according to the adoption of the future resurrection, as he says elsewhere: “And we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the resurrection of our body” (Romans 8:23).

Elsewhere also, when speaking of marriage, he compared this same flesh to the Church, saying: “No one has ever hated his own flesh; rather, he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church” (Ephesians 5:29).

Therefore, when he says in another place, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17), he does not condemn the flesh, so that we should regard it as an enemy. Rather, he admonishes us to bring it under our control, so that it may conceive and bear good works and, like a wife, serve the spirit. He says that this cannot be done except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

For it is not the nature of the flesh, but its punishment, that resists us, because through sin we deserved to be mortal. Again he says: “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you” (I Corinthians 6:19).

And yet, although this flesh is called grass because of its present weakness (Isaiah 40:6), do you believe that John made gold from grass, and do you not believe that God almighty can make a spiritual body from an animal body?

Because of this very transformation of the flesh that is to come—for God will make a heavenly body from this flesh, when we shall be equal to the angels of God (Matthew 22:30)—the same Apostle most truthfully says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Corinthians 15:50).

## CHAPTER XLI

But it is no wonder that you are so blind as to think that these things cannot be done by almighty God, since you also say that God could not have made the world, or anything that was made, otherwise than through a great and pitiable necessity, and that, unless there were matter to assist him in making the world, he could not have liberated his own part from it.

Choose now, then, which you wish to follow: a god who is less powerful and weak, who, because of the necessity imposed by his part placed in misery, was assisted in making the world by matter that he himself had not made; or almighty God, who, without any necessity but by his own will and supreme power, said—and they came to be; commanded—and they were created (Psalm 32:9; Genesis 1:3); who calls those things that are not as though they were (Romans 4:17).

## CHAPTER XLII

You, therefore, human beings who have been deceived by the impiety of Manichaeus, flee; hasten while you may, lest you deserve eternal condemnation from that just Judge.

Repent of your sins if you desire to be liberated. Do not listen to the Manichaeans when they say, “We do not sin; we are souls of light. The race of darkness sins.”

For if this is so, why do they frighten us so that we should believe them? They cannot say that unbelief is not a sin, since it is written: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18).

## CHAPTER XLIII

If, therefore, unbelief is a sin, and no one sins except the race of darkness, it follows that the part of light is found free from every sin.

Then all return to the kingdom, because they themselves do not sin; and no soul has anything to fear, because it commits no sin. The things Manichaeus says are therefore false: that the remnant part of the light—that is, sinful souls—is condemned to guard the globe, so that some security may eventually be obtained for the divine kingdoms placed in danger.

It is therefore necessary either that the part of light sin or that the part of darkness sin. But if the part of light sins, God sins—which it is impious to say. If, however, the part of darkness sins, it is called to the kingdom by him who said, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, because those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:13).

That divinity, then, from divinity, and that light from light, degenerating into the race of darkness, is joined to it forever.

## CHAPTER XLIV

O hateful error of mind in those who believe such things! Yet I wish that you would pay attention and desire to see that the one whom you naturally call the supreme evil cannot be evil.

For if whatever he does he does in such a way that he cannot depart from his nature or act otherwise, then he commits no sin at all. If he commits no sin, he does no evil. And if he does no evil, he is certainly not evil.

It therefore remains that the part of God—which is understood to be God, and which you call the soul—is alone guilty of all sins, and that you attribute to your god all those things that you madly think must be condemned.

But what does the truth proclaim? When the body is lifeless, it cannot sin, although sin can be committed through it. An irrational soul cannot sin, because it can neither receive rational commandments nor attain blessedness; but it preserves, at its own level, the order of nature that it has received.

A rational soul, however, because it can receive rational commandments concerning right actions and attain eternal blessedness through right actions, is justly condemned to lower things if it refuses this by sinning, because nothing separates it from God except a perverse will.

## CHAPTER XLV

Read, O Manichaeans, and examine these things with complete vigilance; read and examine them more and more—but with a calm mind, not a hostile one.

Read them with this in mind: at the future judgment this Scripture will be a witness against you, if, recognizing the truth of what has been said, you do not hasten with all speed to the bosom of the mother, the Catholic Church, which alone teaches the truth.

## CHAPTER XLVI

At last judge, or choose, O Manichaeans, whom you wish to follow: the ungenerated Father, the only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, common in the unity of the Father and the Son; one almighty God, incorruptible, inaccessible, immutable, true, good, holy, merciful, just, who has no parts because he is one; from whom no fragment can be separated because he is inseparable; of whom nothing can be changed because he is wholly immutable; none of whose substance can even slightly be corrupted because he is wholly incorruptible.

He willed, and all things that exist, all things that live, and all things that understand came to be. For he himself is supreme substance, supreme life, and supreme truth. He commanded, and all things were ordered in their places and times, good.

He deigned to place the rational creature above every other creature. When that creature, through pride, had fallen by its will from his laws and pursued visible things, he mercifully deigned to speak to it through his ministers and through himself, by means of certain visible signs, examples, and commandments, so that it might rise again and be renewed for eternal life.

This is the God proclaimed by the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XLVII

Or do you wish to follow that god who is falsely called incorruptible, because afterward he is found to have been overwhelmed by the evil of necessity; timid, because, when stain and devastation threatened, he was compelled to go to war; full of ignorance, because he could not foresee what might happen to his own part; cruel, because, foreseeing the future misery of his own part and being able to remain secure with it, he nevertheless sent it into a wretched battle; evil, because, although nothing could be done to him by the nature of evil, he nevertheless tried to destroy it himself; reckless, because he dared to engage with the one by whom his part was to be held captive and eternally defiled; changeable, because he has already been changed in part; corruptible, because he has already become in part a fornicator, in part a liar, in part a blasphemer, and in part a perpetrator of every crime, since he has been mixed in part with all these things; a mourner, covered with a mourning veil; subjected to demons like clay to a potter; and driven by necessity even to an obscene disguise, so that, transformed into boys and virgins, he might arouse the lust of demons?

This is the god proclaimed by Manichaeus.

Or, if you can, let your conscience deny one of these things before the true eternal God, who will judge everyone. Deny one of them to yourselves.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

But if what we say is true, look back at last; see at last in what death you are placed.

Be humble if you desire to be liberated. Do not proudly and impiously say that you yourselves are God almighty. For this is what you say when you assert that your souls are his parts. God is not greater in one part and lesser in another.

Rather, say to yourselves: “God is immutable; we are changeable. God is incorruptible; we are corrupted by our desires. God is undefiled; we are polluted by our sins. God is wisdom itself; we are foolish and strive to attain wisdom. God is eternal and blessed life itself; we are wretched through our sins and desire to become blessed. We are therefore not part of his substance.”

For if you are his parts and suffer all these things, it follows that he too already suffers all these things in part and could have suffered still more, whatever happens to his part, unless he provided for himself through your misery.

See, then, what you are. If you are his parts, you are God. If you were begotten by him, likewise you are God. Why, then, are you disgraced by such great corruption of sins? But if you were made by him, confess this, and you will no longer be Manichaeans.

## CHAPTER XLIX

Manichaeus says that there are two natures, one good and the other evil: the good one made the world, and the evil one is the one from which the world was made.

But if God made you, Manichaeus has no explanation of what God made you from. If he made you from himself, then you are what he himself is. You ought not, therefore, to have been disgraced by such great corruption of sins, as has already been said.

If he made you from something foreign, then you do not belong to him, because he made you in the same way as he made the world.

But if he made you neither from himself nor from something foreign, and simply willed by his omnipotence, and you came to be, say this to Manichaeus and renounce his error. For it is fitting that the Omnipotent make whatever he wills, as the Catholic faith says: “He spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 32:9).

Say to yourselves: “We are not his parts, but his works.”

Say to yourselves: “If God suffered necessity and could not escape in any other way except by suffering the loss of his own part, who could ever be freed from such necessities? Or who will be protected by a God unable to protect himself? Or when will he be able to free me from this necessity of captivity, who could not protect himself in his intact kingdoms?

“For he did not send me away from there because I was sinning, but sent me into sins themselves.” [Note: [Col. 1154] Cistercian Manuscript: “he himself sent me.”]

“Or when will he be able to help me, miserably situated among foreign things, who, in order to help himself, handed me over to such destruction rather than fight?

“If God himself is incorruptible, what would that evil nature have done to him if he had not wished to fight with it, so that I would not now be tortured in this way?

“Or what sort of injustice is this, that I should be condemned to the globe, while I endure such great suffering so that he may be somewhat secure for the moment?

“Certainly, since I am what he is and since I am his part, let us suffer this misery in turn, with no one in need or weakness in his glorious kingdoms, so that I too may rest for a while and those kingdoms may remain at peace without danger.

“Although there is reason to fear that this evil nature cannot be kept confined even within the globe itself. For if it corrupted the incorrupt kingdoms and violated the undefiled substance of God, how will that part of the light—that is, sinful souls—which, weakened and enfeebled, are fixed in the globe for its preservation, not be swallowed up by it, so that those divine kingdoms will again be thrown into complete disorder, with no one now able to resist?

“For who would dare to go to war when the citizens of the part that had gone forth were treated so unjustly that, for the sake of its repose, they were condemned to the eternal guardianship of the globe?” [Note: [Col. 1154] The same manuscript: “so that, for its repose, [its] citizens … to eternity,” etc. Other manuscripts: “so that, for its repose, none of its citizens …”]

“Or if it cannot break through the globe to reach that bright covering of condemned souls, why must it be enclosed by the condemned members of the divine being?

“But if it can break through the globe, who will resist it, wounded as he is, when he wounded those who were whole?”

Far be such grave and abominable blasphemy! Do not admit such wickedness into your ears. Do not entangle yourselves in such a deadly affair. Flee from Manichaeus, and hasten with all desire to the breasts of Catholic truth.

[Col. 1153]

# Commonitorium, Commonly Attributed to Saint Augustine, Bishop of the Catholic Church: How One Should Deal with Manichaeans Who Are Converted (C, G, S)

## Editorial Notice Concerning the Following *Commonitorium*

This work was published under Augustine’s name in the Appendix to the tenth volume of the works of Saint Augustine in the complete edition of 1586. Around the same time it was also published, through Baronius’s efforts, in the Appendix to the fifth volume of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, from an old manuscript of the Gervasian College in Paris. It now appears at last, more carefully revised against the copy preserved in the library of Queen Christina, as well as against the Anathemas of a certain Prosper, a convert from Manichaeism, which Sirmond published in the first volume of the Councils of Gaul.

[Col. 1153] When Manichaeans who are converted, and who repent of this most abominable error, have anathematized the same heresy according to the formula written below, and each of them has submitted a written statement of his confession, repentance, and anathema, asking in the Church [Col. 1154] for either the place of a catechumen or that of a penitent; if his written statement pleases the bishop and he receives him, let the bishop give him a letter bearing the date and the name of the consul, so that he may suffer no harassment on account of the earlier period, either under the public laws or under ecclesiastical discipline. But after that [Col. 1155] date, if the man should appear to be a Manichaean on the basis of any evidence, let him experience the severity of justice that ought to be applied to such people: namely, that Christians abstain from his companionship, friendship, or any association with him, in accordance with apostolic discipline [Note: [Col. 1155] Elsewhere, “authority.”] (Titus 3:10).

Those who have received letters from the bishop should be commended to devout Catholic neighbors or fellow residents, whether clergy or laypeople, through whose care toward them they may frequently attend the hearing of the word of God [Note: [Col. 1155] Elsewhere, “through whose care toward them they may securely and frequently attend the hearing of the word of God.”], and through whose testimony they may become known. They should not readily be admitted to Baptism if they are catechumens, nor to reconciliation if they have received the place of penitents, unless the danger of death is pressing, or unless the bishop has learned, through the testimony of those to whom they have been commended, that they have been tested for a considerable period of time.

The formula, therefore, according to which those who are being corrected must anathematize this heresy is as follows:

**I.** Let him be anathema who believes that there are two natures, existing from different principles: one good, which is God; the other evil, which God did not create, possessing its own rulers and its own evils, which God did not create.

**II.** Let him be anathema who believes that the two natures waged war against each other, and that a part of God’s nature was mixed in that same war with the rulers of darkness and with all the peoples belonging to the evil nature, and was held captive by them, bound together [Note: [Col. 1155] Elsewhere it reads, “and bound together with them in darkness.”], oppressed, and polluted—thereby also causing it to be believed that God’s nature is changeable and capable of being polluted.

**III.** Let him be anathema who believes that a part of God is held bound and polluted in demons, in all animals, and in every kind of shrub [Note: [Col. 1155] Elsewhere, “and every kind of fruit.”], and that it is released and cleansed through the foods of the Manichaean Elect; so that it is believed that a polluted part of God is held in cucumbers, melons, radishes, leeks, and every kind of most worthless herb, and that it is aided when these things are eaten by the Manichaean Elect.

**IV.** Let him be anathema who believes that the first human being, who was called Adam, was not made by God but begotten by the rulers of darkness, so that the part of God held captive in their limbs might be held on earth more copiously and abundantly; and that he was created in this manner after the male and female rulers of darkness had lain together, given their offspring to the chief ruler of darkness, and he had eaten them all and lain with his consort, and thus generated Adam from her, binding in him a large part of God that had been bound in all the offspring of the rulers of darkness whom they gave him to eat.

**V.** Let him be anathema who believes that the rulers of darkness were bound in heaven, holding within themselves the vital substance—that is, a part of God—bound amid anguish and distress; and that it was liberated from their limbs in this way: when the blessed Father, who possesses luminous ships as lodgings and dwelling places—that is, the sun and the moon—transforms his powers into beautiful females whom he sets before the male rulers of darkness as objects of desire, and into beautiful males [Col. 1156] whom he sets before the female rulers of darkness as objects of desire, so that through this desire the vital substance, that is, the part of God, may be released from them and, liberated from their limbs, cleansed.

**VI.** Let him be anathema who believes that the part of God which could not be liberated and cleansed from its mixture with the race of darkness is condemned and fastened eternally to a horrible globe, where the race of darkness is enclosed.

**VII.** Let him be anathema who believes that the Law given through Moses was not given by the good [Note: [Col. 1156] Elsewhere, “by the one.”] and true God, and that the Prophets who were among the people of Israel and are held in the canon of the divine Scriptures by the Catholic Church did not speak through the Spirit of the good and true God.

**VIII.** Let him be anathema who believes that the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, did not have true flesh, was not born of the Virgin Mary, did not truly suffer death, and did not rise from the dead [Note: [Col. 1156] Elsewhere, “come to life again.”], but was merely a spirit without flesh and wished to appear in such a way that what was not flesh might be thought to be flesh; and who thus contradicts the Gospel, where the Lord himself is read to have said: “See my hands and my feet; touch and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). Therefore, let him be anathema who confesses Christ as God in such a way that he denies him to be also a true and complete human being.

**IX.** Let him be anathema who believes that Manes, or Manichaeus, who proclaimed and taught all the things written above, which deserve anathema and condemnation, had the Holy Spirit as his Paraclete, since the Spirit of truth could not have taught all those things, but rather the spirit of falsehood.

**X.** And especially let Manes, or Manichaeus himself, be anathema: he taught and composed all the impieties written above [Note: [Col. 1156] Elsewhere, “who taught all the spirits of impiety.”] and other sacrilegious and damnable fables, and persuaded wretched people to believe them, giving heed to deceiving spirits and the teachings of demons that speak lies.

The formula of the letter that the bishop gives to converts is as follows:

Since you repent, as you yourself have confessed, of having been a Manichaean Hearer, anathematizing their blasphemies and their most impious and unclean heresy, from which only the Catholic faith makes you safe, you shall have this letter against those who may think that the error of your former period, insofar as it concerns that abominable sect, ought to be held against you. It was written on such-and-such a day, in the consulship of such-and-such a person.

Letters should not readily be given to their Elect who say that they are converting to the Catholic faith, even if they too have anathematized the same heresy according to the foregoing formula. Instead, they must remain with servants of God, whether clergy or laypeople, in a monastery or hospice, until it becomes clear that they have entirely abandoned that superstition. Then they should either be baptized, if they have not been baptized, or reconciled, if they have received the place of penitents. Nor should they leave too quickly the places to which they had been commended after receiving their letters.

[Col. 1155]

# One Book Against Felicianus the Arian on the Unity of the Trinity, Restored to Vigilius (C, G, S)

## Editorial Notice Concerning the Following Book

Erasmus once declared that it was not probable that this dialogue was Augustine’s, since he does not mention it in the books of the *Retractations*. “For in ecclesiastical records,” he says, “a place is customarily added, and sometimes also what the proposer or respondent did.” Moreover, Arians do not usually concede points so readily in debate as Felicianus does here. Furthermore, Augustine is more densely packed with Scriptural citations than this work is. Finally, Erasmus notes the divergence of style and concludes that some learned person fabricated the dialogue as an exercise of ingenuity—a practice that we also see in Jerome.

The Louvain scholars, however, setting aside this criticism by Erasmus, arranged for the book to be printed among the authentic works and [Col. 1157] under Augustine’s name, because the commonly circulated Bede acknowledges it as Augustine’s in his commentary on Paul at 1 Corinthians 1, and Lanfranc does so in his work against Berengarius. To these may be added Alcuin, book 1 against Elipandus, and Peter Lombard in the *Sentences*, book 3, distinction 21, chapter “Sicut,” and distinction 22, chapter “Et utique.”

As for Bede, however, the collection on Paul by the genuine Bede, which we possess in the German library and which has not yet been published, entirely lacks the passage of this book that is cited as Augustine’s in the commonly circulated collection—whose author we have often noted to be Florus. It is not surprising that this book was believed to be Augustine’s, since it is prefaced with his name in very ancient manuscripts and perhaps was attributed to him by its true author for definite reasons. We have observed that this was done by Vigilius of Tapsus in the notice concerning the *Altercation with Pascentius*, in the Appendix to the second volume.

Peter Francis Chifflet demonstrated and established that this same Vigilius was the author of the following *Altercation with Felicianus*, not only because of its similarity of style to Vigilius’s undisputed books against Eutyches, but also because an ancient manuscript of the Abbey of Dijon—which we believe was written approximately eight hundred years ago—bears the name of Vigilius. In the preface to his books against Varimadus, Vigilius himself mentions booklets on the Unity of the Trinity that he had arranged into a single work. There, he says, he responded to his opponent’s propositions not with the authority of testimonies but in rustic speech—that is, as one unskilled in sacred letters.

The name of Optatus, to whom the published editions note that the book was addressed, is absent from the Dijon manuscript and from other manuscripts of better quality. In some manuscripts, however, the title reads, “On the Unity of the Trinity, to Optatus,” and the preface begins, “You have compelled me, dearest son Optatus.”

## Chapter I

[Col. 1157]

You have compelled me, dearest son, to write something concerning the unity of the Trinity, which is perfect and supreme God always; and, mindful of my priestly duty, I have done so. Although I repeatedly excused myself, conscious of my own weakness, you pressed me in many ways, asserting that the exposition of the common faith is both received by devout people and ought not to be denied by priests to the faithful. Otherwise, while they do not receive it, they may begin to be easily deceived by unbelievers; or, when priests do not grant them what they desire, the heavenly treasure may appear not to have been expended upon Christ’s members but, in a certain sense, to have been hidden in the ground as sterile knowledge.

Thus I confess that I have been overcome by persuasive reasons, lest I seem to hand over the defenseless to opposing evils while they are not equipped with the protection of truth against unbelievers. But because in questions of this kind some obscurity frequently arises during continuous discourse, I therefore thought it appropriate to set down, in the brevity of this little book, the conversation recently held between Felicianus and me, prefacing it with the principal letters of the names for the sake of distinguishing the speakers.

## Chapter II

For when we had been sitting together a few days ago, he said:

“Among the things that frequently offend me in your disputations, I consider nothing worse than the way you hand down the precepts of faith to the uneducated, prescribing to them a method of speaking not about the reasoning by which things are to be understood, but rather about a kind of display of testimonies. To call this clever would be too much; everyone knows how rustic it is.

“First, if the person being instructed has already believed the books, he obeys you and does not resist. Otherwise he must contradict you no more than he must contradict the same testimonies that are produced in support of the assertion. For that reason, the following method seems better to me for teaching: first, the basis of the faith should be set forth without testimonies; then, once the person has been convicted by reasoning, that path should be refined with the Scriptures answering in support.

“And not without reason. If these testimonies are approved because they are not lacking in reason, then that reasoning ought to be sufficient in itself, since it appears to establish these testimonies only through itself. If, on the other hand, that is not so, who can submit the neck of rational faith to irrational testimonies, even if those testimonies are falsely represented as divine?

“As for that method of disputing, I admit that I would tolerate it in others whom necessity, arising from ignorance, compels to flee to what belongs to others because they cannot stand by themselves. But in you I tolerate it in no way at all, precisely because I see that you lack neither eloquence nor knowledge of the faith.”

Then I said:

“Do not suppose that I am so carried away by praise of myself that I would do injury to the saints who preceded me. Nor will I ever presume upon wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power (1 Corinthians 1:17; see the commonly circulated Bede on this passage). Rather, content with the authority of the Scriptures, I strive to obey simplicity rather than display.

“But you say that a person is better instructed by reasoning than by testimonies. What, then, is the reasoning you can offer if you proclaim that a virgin gave birth, if you do not deny that eyes were restored to the blind, or if you show that those buried returned from the dead? If the reasoning for these things is incomprehensible while their truth is evident, then in matters of faith it is easier to believe testimonies than to investigate the reasoning.

“Yet because you distinguish these two matters with reasonable consistency, since after presenting the reasoning you do not omit the testimonies as well, I confess that in this discussion I shall follow what you yourself have approved.”

## Chapter III

**FELICIANUS:** “Therefore, since we have leisure, let us come to the question of your *homoousios*—the consubstantial—which has often been discussed not only between us but also among our elders. And so that the discourse does not wander too far, now assume, as you are accustomed to do, the role of the one proposing the question, and ask us to return the reasoning for our faith in response to your inquiries.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “Tell me, then: is it true that, as I hear you say, the Son is not entirely *homoousios* with the Father?”

**FELICIANUS:** “It is true, and I cannot be persuaded that what is begotten is unbegotten, lest I seem to proclaim the same person as both Father and Son.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “That is not so. For I too have no intention of saying that the unbegotten is the same as the begotten; rather, that the unbegotten is the same thing as the begotten.”

**FELICIANUS:** “And how do you not say that the begotten is the same as the unbegotten, if you think that both are one and not another?”

[Col. 1159]

**AUGUSTINE:** “I perceive that you have paid no close attention to the force of the words. When I say that both are one, I do not separate at all the substance of the true Father and the true Son; and when I declare that the Father is not the same person as the Son, I distinguish the person of each while preserving the property of each. Thus, if you ask about substance, the Trinity itself is one God; if you ask about person, the Son is another.”

**FELICIANUS:** “And how can you say both that he is the same and that the Son is another?”

**AUGUSTINE:** “The same, I say, by communion of substance; another by the property of person.”

**FELICIANUS:** “I do not know how one substance can be believed when one person is not said to exist.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “The person is not one, I say, because one is said to have begotten and another to have been begotten. Yet the substance of the one who was born and the one who gave birth is not different, because that which arose from the begetter is taught not to be unlike him.”

**FELICIANUS:** “Please clarify these statements for me by an easier example.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “In matters that are incomprehensible, examples are not readily available to the debater. Nevertheless, insofar as it can be done, I shall not fail even in this respect. Consider, then: a human father has a human son. What is human is common to both, yet what belongs to one as son and to the other as father appears to be proper to each. For the person of each is distinguished in such a way that their common humanity is not denied: one begets, the other is begotten; and both the one who begot and the one who was begotten are equally called human.”

## Chapter IV

**FELICIANUS:** “I would like you to say this at least: is the begotten separated from the unbegotten at some beginning, or not?”

**AUGUSTINE:** “Even this is not admitted by the truth of spiritual understanding: the Father is not separated from the Son by an interval—not, I say, of time, which is measured by days and nights, but by any span of age or duration [Note: [Col. 1159] All manuscripts read this way. Erasmus and the Louvain editions, however, read “or of eternity.”].”

**FELICIANUS:** “If that is so, you admit two unbegotten beings. And how can one person be thought to be the Father and the other the Son, when, through the common designation ‘unbegotten,’ both seem to be confused?”

**AUGUSTINE:** “In this matter your predecessors have woven together a sophism of no slight calumny. Nevertheless, with the help of the Trinity itself, it must be undone by Catholic simplicity. I call the Father unbegotten and the Son begotten; yet I do not therefore deny that the begotten is coeternal with the unbegotten. I call the Father unbegotten only because he did not proceed from another; the Son begotten because he did not arise from himself.

“It is not common to both to be born; it is not common to both not to beget. Yet it is common to both that one is not separated from the other by the intervention of an interval of time. Thus, if you ask what is proper to the Father, it is enough that he alone has no father; if you ask what is proper to the Son, it is enough that he has no offspring. But we say that the divinity of the Father and the Son is one and coeternal.”

**FELICIANUS:** “As far as I am concerned, I do not see what you are gathering from this. For although you contend with me with Aristotelian subtlety, it is nevertheless impossible for you to distinguish the one who was begotten from the one who begot by no antiquity of an intervening age.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “I know indeed, as he says, how difficult a position the argument occupies. Yet we have nothing to fear, since through the help of the Holy Spirit we bear witness to God. What, then, shall we say? Is there something in the Father that is denied to be unbegotten, or is there not?

“If there is, then let him be called unbegotten not in his entirety but rather in part; otherwise the Son did not begin in time. For if the fatherhood of the Father did not begin, the beginning of offspring cannot be found. If a beginning is attributed to the offspring, the Father’s fatherhood will not be shown to be eternal.

“And how will your position stand, when you teach that everything in the Father is unbegotten, although you think that the very name of fatherhood has a beginning, while you say that the Son began in time—so that, since he did not yet exist, the Father could not be called Father?”

**FELICIANUS:** “I am not so foolish as to place time before the Son. But it is certain that a beginning is assigned to the begotten.”

[Col. 1160]

**AUGUSTINE:** “What, then? Do you say that there was nothing intermediate between the Father and the Son?”

**FELICIANUS:** “Precisely so.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “How, then, do you deny that the Son is coeternal with the Father, when you admit that nothing intermediate existed between the Father and the Son—lest that very absence of an intermediary be established as much as a third entity?”

## Chapter V

**FELICIANUS:** “Since you have cornered me by your skill in debate, I shall briefly explain what our predecessors said. Whenever they discuss the Son’s beginning and the Father’s eternity, they say: ‘There was when he was not, and before he was born he was not.’”

**AUGUSTINE:** “As I understand it, while the error of evil belief remains, only the words have been changed. You said, ‘There was when he was not.’ Does this ‘there was’ refer to the age, or to the Son?

“If it refers to the age—that is, to something like an interval of eternity before the Son’s birth—then necessity drives you down into the earlier blasphemy, since you introduce a third sort of time between the Father and the Son. You say that before the Son there were the Father and time; after these two came the Son; and after these three came the Spirit.

“If we admit that the Son could not have been begotten without time, see how far the consequences of what we are saying extend. For if the Son did not exist without time, he must certainly also be said to have been begotten in a place. Once this is admitted, let place in some sense be called coeval with the Father, before the Son and the Holy Spirit. If that is so, since the Son could not have been born without place and time, in what place or at what time do you say that place and time themselves were made?

“If in no place or time, then behold: time and place could have been made without time and place. If in something, that very thing appears to be time and place, at whose origin place and time are likewise required. And if something could be made so entirely without time and place that you do not say that place was made in a place or time in time, I do not know with what recklessness you insist that the Son could not have been born without these things [Note: [Col. 1160] Erasmus and the manuscripts omit ‘without these things.’], when sound faith teaches that he made both place and time.

“But enough of this. Let us now return to what you claim was said by your predecessors: ‘There was when he was not.’ If you refer this ‘there was’ to time, behold, time existed before the Son. If you refer it to the Son, then the Son was never not there; for he already existed when the Son was not, since he is said to have made time [Note: [Col. 1160] Thus the manuscripts. The Louvain editions read, ‘for the Son already existed when time did not.’].

“But you say, ‘Before he was born, he did not exist.’ Who, I ask, did not exist before he was born? If the Son, then by this very interpretation time is said to have existed before the Son. But if, before the Son was born, time did not exist, it follows that the Son is to be called coeternal with the Father, between whom and the Father no time is said to have existed—especially since, among other things, the Evangelists bear witness that the Son also made time.

“Perhaps someone may think that the statement ‘There was when the Son was not’ was said about the Father. But the words that follow do not agree with this interpretation: ‘And before he was born he did not exist.’ For the Father, who always exists in himself, cannot even by you be called born, since he is not taught to have arisen from a beginning; and the statement ‘There was when he was not begotten’ cannot apply to the Father.”

**FELICIANUS:** “Since, in my opinion, you wear me out considerably by contending with words through an unexpected subtlety, I ask you, if possible, to show by an example from some ordinary thing that what you are trying to teach is possible. For otherwise I cannot believe that the begotten is coeternal with the Father, although I am overwhelmed by the force of your argument, unless you say either that both were begotten or that both are fathers to each other.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “Since you compel me to use examples of incomparable things, let us consider the power of fire, from which radiance and vapor always arise. Both are born from it, yet fire is not found without either of them. These three do not beget one another, since neither fire and vapor arise from radiance, nor fire and radiance from vapor; rather, radiance and vapor are always begotten from fire.

“Since this is so, do you see that even among created things something can be born, while nevertheless no time can be shown at which that from which it was born could have been found without the begotten? If, then, we perceive these things through visible examples, why should we not say something similar of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, insofar as concerns their common and undifferentiated eternity?

“For it is not necessary to say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are equally unbegotten merely because we say that none is separated from another by an intervening age. Even in other things, some things are begotten, yet they are not therefore taught to be equally begetters or to exist without one another. But what benefit is there in gathering many such examples, when the rest may also be assessed from a few testimonies?”

## Chapter VI

**FELICIANUS:** “Since you disturb my opinion, founded upon the authority of the preceding fathers, by a new method of argument, I would like you to tell me what you think concerning the nature of the Son of God—that is, concerning the substance itself. For if, as you are accustomed to say, he is *homoousios* with the Father, then he is in a certain sense father to himself; otherwise he cannot be consubstantial with his begetter. One of our number used to mock the opinion of the *homoousios* in this way, saying: ‘If the Son was produced not from outside but from the very same substance, then one has been divided into two in some way, since the begetter is said to be nothing other than the begotten.’”

**AUGUSTINE:** “While you accuse us of contending by Aristotelian skill, you yourself appear to have fled to the snares of the dialecticians. But these things cannot frighten us, who trust in the truth of the faith.

“What, then? I suppose you say that the Son could not have been born from the substance of the Father, lest we appear by generation to divide the unbegotten Father [Note: [Col. 1161] Erasmus, the Lyon and Venice editions read this passage as follows: ‘What, then, do you say? I suppose that the Son could not have been born from the substance of the Father, lest by generation we appear to divide the unbegotten Father of the Son.’ Manuscript M.]. If that is so, the Son is wrongly believed in when he is proclaimed to have been made from outside rather than begotten from the Father—that is, from the same substance—as one among other things.

“To make this easier to understand, I shall explain it as far as I can [Note: [Col. 1161] Alcuin, book 1 against Elipandus.]. Among sons, some are adopted and others natural. Those who are begotten are sons from the beginning, always proper to their father; the others are strangers at first and later become sons, when they are received into the family through adoption.

“To which, then, should the Son of God be compared? If to adopted sons, he will be like us before the Father; if to natural sons, he must be said to subsist from the substance of his begetter.

“But, you say, the father’s substance is divided into two if the Son is substantially generated from the Father alone. How foolish this is, even visible things themselves teach us. For what fleshly father has ever been divided by begetting? If division does not even belong to the condition of the body—for no one begets a son in such a way as to lose himself in the process—how can you say that the Son could not be born while the Father’s integrity remained intact?

“But why say more? To those investigating the birth and origin of the Son of God, the following alternatives, unless I am mistaken, present themselves: either he is from the Father, or from nothing, or from another, or from himself. Let us consider the consequence of each.

“If he is from himself, he is not rightly called a son, since he is proclaimed not begotten but unbegotten. If from nothing, he is shown to be a creature along with the others, not the author of creatures. If from another, he is proclaimed the son not of the one in whom we believe but of some unknown father.

“If, apart from these four, a fifth possibility cannot be found, and if three of these cannot at all be affirmed because of their obvious blasphemy, it remains that he was substantially begotten from the Father. For, as we have said, no fifth possibility can be found, nor can any mode other than the first be taught among these—since he is neither a creature, nor the son of another father, nor unbegotten in the manner of the Father.”

**FELICIANUS:** “As though I had either proposed a fifth possibility beyond these or asserted one of those three! I say that the Son did not arise from the substance of the Father, while nevertheless I do not deny that he was begotten by the Father’s will.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “You are driven by the consequence itself into one of the alternatives mentioned above. For when we inquire into the substance of the Son, whom you do not acknowledge to have been substantially begotten from the Father, you undoubtedly maintain that he was made from nothing, since we do not say that corruptible creatures came into existence unless we also say that God both willed to produce them through an ineffable dispensation and was able to do so through his singular power. We know both the will by which it pleased God and the power by which the ability to act is subject to the Lord.”

**FELICIANUS:** “Then the Father’s power is not sufficient for the Son’s existence?”

**AUGUSTINE:** “As though I were arguing about the Father’s power rather than about the truth of fatherhood itself! Did he wish to be called Father of one whom he did not wish to be like himself but only similar to creatures? Therefore you must confess that the Son arose from the substance of the Father if he is both begotten and God. Otherwise you must deny that he is both Son and God, if he was created not from the Father’s substance but from nothing, by the Father’s will and power alone operating in him, just as it operates in the other creatures.”

## Chapter VII

**FELICIANUS:** “Since you compel me by necessity to make such a confession, I shall not conceal what our predecessors are accustomed to say. For they say that the Son is a creature, but a perfect one, capable of ruling over all creatures.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “I rejoice that by an open confession you have exposed the innermost poison of your irreligious proclamation [Note: [Col. 1162] The manuscripts read, ‘that at the beginning of the proclamation you exposed the innermost poison.’]. Yet you offer nothing that appears worthy of belief.

“A creature is a substance made, insofar as it depends upon itself, by the will of almighty God from that which does not yet exist or once did not exist, whatever corruptible thing it may be. Let us see whether this definition applies to the Son of God.

“For the Son, in what he is, was brought forth in the truth of an undifferentiated nature: from him who is—that is, from the begetter—he was born not dissimilar. Thus, unless I am mistaken, the first distinction between the Son and a creature is this: the Son is substantially begotten from the Father, whereas a creature is brought into being not from the substance of its maker but from his will and power alone.

“The creature is corruptible by nature unless it is preserved by grace; the Son is incorruptible, since by being born from an incorruptible Father he appears to possess an incorruptible substance. The Son is in every respect like the Father; the creature is unlike its maker.

“The Son does not pass from what is not into what is; and therefore he will never pass from what is into what is not. The creature passes from what is not into what is; and therefore, insofar as it depends upon itself, by the condition of its origin it returns from what is into what is not.”

**FELICIANUS:** “I do not see what sort of obscurity you are wrapping your meaning in. You will therefore do rightly if you explain more intelligibly what, in my opinion, you have stated incomprehensibly.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “I said concerning the Son, when I distinguished him from the definition of a creature, that he does not pass from what is not into what is. This is equivalent to saying that he was not made from nothing. Therefore he will never pass from what is into what is not—that is, he will never be dissolved into nothingness from what he is, by the property of his nature.
