“But a creature passes from what is not into what is, demonstrating that it was brought forth from nothing. Therefore, insofar as it depends upon itself, it must pass from what is into what is not—that is, into nothingness—unless perpetual grace [Note: [Col. 1162] Perhaps, “perpetual.”] preserves it, since the quality of its nature tends toward dissolution.

“Therefore the Son will never not exist, since he is taught to be perpetual in substance; and for this reason, as something proper to him, he is rightly understood to be separated from the condition of all creatures, which were made through him.”

## Chapter VIII

**FELICIANUS:** “Although you stretch my understanding with a new subtlety concerning things, I still do not know how you can say that the Son is coeternal with the Father, since both common usage and the law of nature appear to make the begetter prior to the begotten.”

**AUGUSTINE:** “If we judge the author of nature according to the laws of creatures, when we proclaim the Father to be prior to the Son, why do we not, by that same law of nature, call the Son stronger than the Father through the addition of time—since the one who is born is not without growth, while old age imposes the injury of weakness upon the Father?

“If reason itself does not admit this, let us set aside the law of bodily understanding in God, lest we say that the maker is like his works. Especially since, from what is evident among us, we can also demonstrate what is hidden.

“For just as a mother gave birth to her author without an example, so the Father is to be believed to have ineffably begotten one who is coeternal with him. The one who already existed was born from a mother; the one who was never absent was born from the Father.

“Let faith believe this; let understanding not demand an explanation. Otherwise it may judge what it has not discovered incredible, or fail to believe what it has discovered to be unique.

“Consider: Christ was born from a mother, yet the mother’s modesty was not diminished through the touch of a man. A virgin gave birth because a virgin conceived; and, without following the ordinary course of things, Christ assumed an intact body from the intact body of his mother.

“If, then, according to a new mode and without any example, he is taught to have been born according to the flesh from a body, what is surprising if he proceeded from the Father not according to the customary manner of human birth? The Son, born from her alone, did not diminish his mother’s substance; and we know that the son’s body was born without harm to the body of the woman giving birth. Yet is the incorporeal Father believed to have diminished his substance when the Son is said to have been born substantially and incorporeally from that very same substance?

“Therefore, if we examine the nature of things with understanding as our guide, let us grant a beginning if we do not deny an end. Otherwise, let us say that the Son does not have a beginning precisely because we confess him to be perpetual not by grace but by nature.

“In sum, ‘greater’ and ‘lesser’ can be said in three ways: by age, by form, and by power. By age, an elder is greater than a boy; by form, a taller person is greater than a small one; by power, a stronger person is greater than a weak one.

“Let us see whether any of these applies to the Son. He is not lesser in age, since it is established that he arose from the Father, who is the beginning; nor in form, since he may rightly be proclaimed to be nothing other than God; nor in power, since we know that everything has been perfected by him.”

## Chapter IX

**FELICIANUS:** “I want to know how the Father’s dignity passed to the Son, while the humility of the offspring did not return to the Father.”

AUG. The examples of ordinary affairs teach us that these things are not now being said according to nature. Let us suppose, for example, that some king and the king’s son, having laid aside the insignia of royal majesty, assume the clothing of a subordinate soldier and, for a definite arrangement made by the father and for the safety of his companions, endure the insults of rebels. Does it follow that, because it is certain that participation in royal power descends to the son by birth, the insult suffered by the son necessarily reaches the one who begot him—not by the affection of one who shares the son’s suffering, but by the very property of the suffering itself? It does not. For it is certain that the son was born from the father, not the father from the son.

And therefore we say that everything belonging to the communion of nature is similar between them; but that which is recognized as having happened accidentally to one person is proper to that person. Thus, by being born, the Son possesses with the Father everything that the Father is; but the Father does not possess with the Son whatever the Son himself specially endured. It is not common to both that one born from a human being is human; rather, this is a particular accident, which is generally taught not to belong to the other without prejudice to the common nature.

The Father’s substance is one thing, his person another. When the latter begot, what came forth from the former is undoubtedly recognized as not different, but as another; and this other is taught to be nothing other than the first, since it is taught to be both common and proper—common, I say, by the unity of substance; proper, by the distinction of person. Therefore, since what was born exists in itself, not everything that happens to it necessarily passes over to the begetter, just as everything proper and substantial to the begetter is plainly transmitted to the one born.

For just as the Father’s divinity was bestowed upon the Son by generation itself, so the care, suffering, poverty, death, and humiliation of the offspring are not thereby referred back to the Father. This does not happen because, although what was begotten was similar from one substance—that is, from the Father’s substance—nevertheless, since it already exists in itself, whatever is imposed upon it from outside is called not common but proper to it.

If, then, this is the condition of the human race: that the substance of sons is never so changed into something else from the one who begot them that it cannot remain the same yet be another, while many things happen externally to the son and the common nature nevertheless remains—what ought we rightly to believe about God and his Son? What ought we to proclaim? Although their nature is not dissimilar according to the simple glory of undivided majesty, a body was nevertheless specially assumed by the Son, so that he who could suffer nothing in the common divinity of the substance might be humbled in the weakness of our flesh.

A human being, the son of a human being, does not assume another nature; and although he suffers in that same nature which he shares with his father, he nevertheless does not transmit the insult to his father. Yet is God the Father believed to have been passibly humbled in the Son, when the Son is believed to have endured the Jews’ perversity not in that very nature common to both, but rather in our nature, which he alone assumed?

In sum, what, I ask, was hanging on the cross? What was it that the spear is said to have wounded? Was it passible flesh, or the substance of the Godhead? If, as a profane preacher of the incorporeal nature, you assume that it was the majesty, you appear to believe in a corruptible God. If it was passible flesh, then this flesh is not common with the Father, so that through it that cross could affect him.

## CHAPTER X

FEL. While you rush through everything we have said as though in a torrent, you proclaim two Christs rather than one. And not without reason: for if the divinity in him suffered absolutely nothing, Christ according to the human being was another; otherwise, through the participation of the common Godhead, the suffering itself also reached the Father.

AUG. It is not so. For I neither confuse nor divide our Savior. I do not confuse him, lest I proclaim either an incorporeal and imaginary flesh or a carnal and mortal divinity. I do not separate him, lest I appear to introduce one offspring of God the Father according to the flesh and another according to majesty. For the same Son of God both proceeded from the Father without beginning and deigned to be born in time from a virgin.

Impassible in what is his own, suffering in what is ours, he deigned to clothe the incomprehensible majesty, as though with a garment, in flesh from the womb [Note: [Col. 1164] Chiffletius: *dignatus est*. “From both, one,” etc.]. One person of the Mediator, not one substance: one person, I say, lest there be not one Christ; not one substance, lest, when the Mediator’s dispensation is removed, he be called either God alone or the son of a human being.

Therefore I do not extend the flesh assumed in Christ through the perpetuity of divine generation, nor do I confine the immeasurable divinity within the temporal limits of bodily birth. For the same one is the author of all things in divinity who is the redeemer of human beings in flesh; the same one is impassible in himself who suffered in the body. Thus, being born like the begetter from both natures, he truly expressed the property of each, so that it is clear both that he assumed true flesh from his mother and that he possesses undifferentiated divinity from his Father.

When these were joined into one person through the incomprehensible dispensation of the Mediator, he preserved what was proper to each but joined foreign properties to what was proper. He preserved what was proper by not abandoning the immensity of divinity and not rejecting the weakness of flesh. He joined foreign properties to what was proper because the same and inseparable Christ was killed by the proper property of flesh and was not held among the dead by the proper property of divinity. By the property of flesh, life tasted death; by the property of divinity, he restored perpetual life to the flesh.

It is therefore not rightly said, “The Father suffered in the Son,” since the Son suffered in flesh that is not common to him and the Father. Thus the flesh was glorified by majesty, while majesty is taught to have been humbled in flesh. But we are certain to proclaim both not of two Christs, as you suppose, but of one and the same Christ, whom after the virgin’s giving birth we know to be God and human being.

## CHAPTER XI

FEL. If Christ, then, was born from a virgin, how is he said to be coeternal with God the Father?

[Col. 1165] AUG. On this matter too we have a different dispute with others; and therefore, lest the explanation of the truth be more difficult, we shall first set forth the cause of the error. For, beginning from one principle of false belief, they split in two, so to speak, into delirious interpretations that differ from one another [Note: [Col. 1165] Thus several manuscripts. The printed editions have *funduntur* (“are poured out”).].

They have this in common: they proclaim one birth of Christ, not two. But some accept as the definition of their own doctrine that principal birth by which God was born from God before all things; others accept only this birth by which this Lord proceeded from the virgin. Through the consequence of a badly sown seed, they have fallen into the abyss of similar blasphemy.

For behold: those who do not believe that he was born from a virgin overturn, as though by a kind of Jewish blindness of unbelief, the entire faith of the Gospels, the entire usefulness of Baptism, the entire preaching of the Apostles, and, in sum, the whole authority of the New Testament. And therefore they must not even be thought to have recognized the majesty of the Son of God, because they rejected the mystery of the Mediator by which the Father willed him to be made known to the nations.

But those who contend that he was born not from the Father before every beginning, but in time from the virgin’s childbirth, have not learned that he is the Creator of all things, nor that he is like the Father in omnipotence and majesty. For how could he be thought to have made all things before whose birth it is certain that the universe already existed? Or how is his divinity to be confessed [Note: [Col. 1165] Some manuscripts: *probanda* (“to be approved”).] when individual things were made before he was yet born? Or how is his divinity believed to be perpetual, when it is proclaimed to have come into being not always, as the Father’s did, but in time?

These people too, then, in a certain way deny the mystery of the Mediator through the necessary consequences of their position, because they do not proclaim openly, rather than merely plausibly, that Christ was born God and human being: from eternity and in time, from power and weakness; a Son from the Father, like the Father before all things, and a true—not [Note: [Col. 1165] Here the Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Louvain editions omit *non*. Chiffletius restored it, but, leaving the later manuscripts aside, has this with the Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Louvain editions: “not from eternity, but from time; not from power, but from weakness; not a Son from the Father, like the Father before all things, but from his mother among all things; not true, but imaginary.”] imaginary—son of a human being from his mother among all things.

Consequently, they must not even be thought to know God in the flesh, since they do not think that he was begotten from the Father before assuming flesh. You see, then, how among these people, although the intervening positions differ, the same beginning and the same conclusion of error are nevertheless taught.

We, by contrast, defend both births in such a way that we remove neither by affirming the other. We neither condemn the temporal birth by the perpetuity of the first, nor confine the eternal birth by the brevity of the temporal one. We know the inseparable offspring of the true God, and afterward the most truly real flesh of this true offspring. We do not say that Christ’s divinity began when the virgin conceived, nor that the flesh began then when, by an ineffable birth, that Monad, without any interval of intervening time, begot a Monad differing in nothing except that it is taught to be a monad.

The omnipotent majesty of Christ did not shrink from voluntary weakness, nor did bodily weakness extinguish omnipotence. I know that the divinity of the Son of God descended to the dead through the property of flesh; I know that flesh ascended to heaven by the merit of divinity.

It is not proper to God that he felt hunger; but it is proper to God that with a few loaves he satisfied so many thousands of people [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscripts have *saginavit* (“fed abundantly”).]. It is not proper to flesh that he walked with dry feet upon the raging waves; but it is proper to flesh that he endured spittle, blows, and scourges.

Yet it is one and the same Christ who both endured insults so many times and was carried into the depths without sinking. In this way, in the Mediator of God and human beings, we confess that the divinity was affected by the insult suffered by the assumed body [Note: [Col. 1165] Thus the manuscripts. But the Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Louvain editions have: “I do not confess.”], just as we know that the flesh was glorified by the majesty of divinity.

Therefore Christ [Col. 1166] died, and he rose again. Yet he did not accomplish both things from one nature, but each from its own, while he himself remained perfect in both: the one and inseparable Christ accomplished such different things—by one he tasted death, by the other he raised the dead. Thus the true Mediator showed himself to be God and human being, with neither person doubled nor substance confused.

The Son of God entered the virgin’s womb in order to be born again, although he had already been born; he assumed the whole human being, while already possessing from the Father the fullness of divinity. He was not unlike his begetter when, eternal, he was born from the eternal; he was not unlike a human being when he was born from his mother in order to die.

Yet the same one was eternal in what was his own and destined to die in what was ours, containing both from himself and losing neither through the other. Thus Christ was born not imperfect but fully complete in the distinct property of each nature, just as every human being is taught to be one complete being from soul and body.

A human being is not one body and another soul, although soul is one thing and body another; nevertheless one and the same human being is taught to be both body and soul. Again, body and soul are not one and the same thing, because from both one human being has been made. For these do not either confuse substance in the unity of person or double person through the diversity of substance, since one human being is recognized to have arisen from them.

They do not lose what is proper to them; but because they have come together into one inseparable whole, what is common appears to have been made from what is proper to each. The mind is affected in the body by bodily pains, and the body is wearied by the mind’s thoughts; yet one of these belongs properly to the body and the other to the mind. When it happens to one human being, it appears common both to the body and to the mind.

Thus, after the virgin’s childbirth, Christ was not one person of God and another of a human being, but the same Christ was Son of God and of a human being. And just as in one human being soul is one thing and body another, so in the Mediator of God and human beings the Son of God was one thing and the son of a human being another; yet one Christ the Lord existed from both.

One thing, I say, by the distinction of substance; not another person [Note: [Col. 1166] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Louvain editions have *non aliud* (“not another thing”). Incorrectly.], by the unity of person.

## CHAPTER XII

FEL. In what preceded, you had indeed compelled me to believe in Christ’s birth from his mother while preserving his perpetuity. But because arguments forcibly extracted against reason cannot remain continuously in us, when I now turn with anxious attention to my original proposition, I still do not seem to have found in what you have said what I seek.

For I do not know how you teach that one was born in time whom you say already existed coeternal with the Father. To be born is, as it were, a movement of something that did not exist before it was born, by which, through the benefit of birth, it comes to exist. From this it follows that Christ, who existed, could not be born; and if he could be born, he did not exist.

AUG. You compel us to investigate incomprehensible matters with a new curiosity in questioning; and therefore what you seek can be explained only by certain outlines drawn from examples. Permit me, then, to introduce, as an affirmed proposition, a matter belonging to another question. Since I now bring it forward not for its own credibility but to illuminate another matter, do not force me to explain in it what I believe; rather, for the present, suppose that I believe it so that you may more easily understand what I shall say.

Let us suppose, then, as many people wish, that there is in the world a universal soul which, by an ineffable movement, gives life to all seeds, without being compounded with the things begotten, but itself bestowing life upon those to be born. When this soul has entered a receptive womb to shape the material for its purposes [Note: [Col. 1166] Several manuscripts: “for its births.”], it makes itself one person with that thing, although it is clear that it does not possess the same substance; and, while the soul acts and the material suffers, one human being is made from two substances, since soul is taught to be one thing and flesh another.

Thus we confess that the soul is born from the womb, although we say that, coming to the womb, it bestowed life upon what had been conceived. It is said to be born from its mother because from her it fashioned a body suitable for itself, in which it could be born—not because, before it was born, it had not existed at all in itself.

And here, if you attend as an observer to the force of words and ordinary speech, we set forth contradictory propositions and proclaim things that seem mutually opposed [Note: [Col. 1167] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and manuscript readings have *oppugnanda* (“to be opposed”).]. Yet in these statements what we say is nevertheless established as true.

We know that the soul is born from the mother’s womb together with the body; but we also see that the soul is proclaimed to precede the mother. In the son, the mother begets the soul; yet even in the mother herself it is only a soul that lives, without which she herself could not exist as the one who gives birth.

Therefore, if we seek the origin of the living power, the soul precedes the mother, and from the mother it again appears to have been born together with the offspring. The soul precedes, I say, because the mother is animated by it; the mother precedes because through her the soul appears to have been born in the son.

But the mother did not turn soul into flesh, nor did she change flesh into soul. Rather, the Creator of flesh, soul, and the whole human being brought forth from the mother’s womb animated flesh: through the dispensation of an analogy that joins diverse things in one and the same human being, he joined both in an indissoluble unity and confused neither through participation in the other.

Thus—indeed, much more incomprehensibly and sublimely—the Son of God was born through the assumption of a perfect human being from his mother. By his unique omnipotence he is, for all things begotten, not merely the capacity but also the cause of birth.

God, I say, was born from the virgin according to the human being, in the same manner in which soul is taught to be born together with the body: not because the substance of both is one, but because one person is made from both. The body is not one human being and the soul another; rather, body and soul are one human being.

Thus, after the virgin’s childbirth, the Son of God was not one and the son of a human being another, but the same Christ was Son of God and of a human being. And just as in one human being body is one thing and soul another, so in one Mediator the Son of God was one thing and the son of a human being another; yet he was the same Son of God and not another than the son of a human being, although he was Son of God for one reason and son of a human being for another.

We do not say that the Son of God began with the beginning of the flesh, lest anyone believe that his divinity is temporal; nor do we recognize the flesh of the Son of God as existing from eternity, lest we think that he assumed not the reality of a human body but some kind of image.

For the truth of flesh does not destroy the majesty of the Son of God, nor does the immensity of divinity destroy the truth of flesh. One is shown in his own powers, the other in our weaknesses.

The one and inseparable Christ is humbled in what he assumed and glorified in what is his own: he does not disdain to be affected by insults, while preserving the equality of his begetter.

Therefore Mary both gave birth to and did not give birth to the Son of God. She gave birth when Christ was born from her according to the flesh; she did not give birth when the Son existed from the Father without beginning. She gave birth when the Word proceeded from her as flesh in order to dwell among us (John 1:14); she did not give birth when, in the beginning, the Word was God, the one who gave origin to all things.

Therefore do not determine the origin of the Word of God by the virgin’s childbirth; do not say that the body born from the virgin is coeternal with the divinity. For the Mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), is coeternal with the Father in his first birth, but in his second birth shares our time: in the first he is the author of time; in the second he shares our age.

## CHAPTER XIII

FEL. Since you have treated the mystery of the Mediator with a clear argument, sufficiently for anyone to believe, I therefore ask that you explain what should also be thought concerning Christ’s soul. For our elders have always handed down that Christ’s body was animated in place of a human soul by the indwelling of the Son of God himself, and that it did not require the addition of a life-giving spirit, since the source of life dwelling within it could confer what it lived by.

AUG. We could indeed teach by testimonies from the divine books what is prescribed in this question by the definition of catholic authority. But since it has now pleased us to examine everything not by the testimony [Note: [Col. 1167] Some manuscripts: “judgment.”] of books, but by reason alone [Col. 1168], reserving the records of Scripture for another time, we shall treat the inquiry concerning the soul just as we did above.

To make this easier, let us briefly investigate, using only one passage from the Apostle, what was the reason for our Savior’s assuming a human being. Once this has been discovered, we shall pass without difficulty to the matters that follow from this preceding inquiry.

In the beginning, then, God made the human being from body and soul. After transgressing the commandment of the law and taking possession of the forbidden tree, he received, in a certain sense, the sentence of capital punishment. He could return to the state from which he had fallen only after being restored by the grace of his author, in a kind of right of restoration.

It is like someone who willingly throws himself headlong from a height: what he did was within his power, but what falls is certainly no longer subject to his own decision [Note: [Col. 1168] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Louvain editions have “what rises.”]. Therefore the one who fell rises through another’s benefit, though he fell through his own fault.

Nor should he be said not to have fallen by his own act because he is recognized to rise through another; nor, for that reason, to have risen by his own act because it is certain that he did not fall through another. But let us leave this for another time and return now to our subject.

The venerable Paul says that Christ was born according to the flesh for this reason: just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned; and shortly afterward:

“But not as the trespass, so also is the grace. For if by the trespass of one many died, much more has the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one human being Jesus Christ abounded to many. And not as through one sin, so also is the gift. For judgment from one trespass resulted in condemnation, but grace from many trespasses resulted in justification. For if death reigned through one person by the trespass of one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one human being many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:12, 15–19).

Christ therefore came to save what had perished (Luke 19:10). Let us first see, then, what it was that perished through the transgression of the first human being; from this we shall easily be able to know what the Lord was able to save by coming.

We must therefore inquire who received the Creator’s law. For undoubtedly the one who despised the commands sinned; and the one who despised the commands was the one who did what had been forbidden.

Scripture says: “The Lord commanded Adam, saying, ‘You shall eat [pl.] from every tree that is in paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat [pl.] from it. For on the day on which you eat [pl.] from it, you shall die [pl.]’” (Genesis 2:16).

Let us ask, then, whether the whole human being received this law. For if, as the Book of Genesis states, he received it already complete, consisting of body and soul, then the whole human being sinned by transgressing; and if the whole human being sinned by transgressing, then the whole human being perished at that time through the fault of his sin.

If the whole human being perished, the whole human being needed the Savior’s benefit; and if the whole human being needed the Savior’s benefit, Christ saved the whole human being by coming. If he saved the whole human being by coming, then he assumed not a body without a soul, but body and soul, which constitute the whole human being and through which he is seen previously to have sinned.

For if, when the whole human being sinned, Christ assumed only his flesh, then the soul remained even now condemned to the punishment of that first transgression, without any hope. But if this is so, I do not know what the person of the Mediator has conferred upon us: rather than redeeming us wholly, he assumed a brute body by itself, which, without a soul, could not even experience his benefit.

I would nevertheless like to ask those who preach such things why, after assuming flesh, the Mediator’s dispensation omitted the soul. Was it perhaps because, knowing it to be innocent, he did not believe that it needed healing? Or because he thought it alien to himself and therefore did not grant it the benefit of redemption? Or because he judged it altogether incurable and was unable to heal it? Or because he rejected it as worthless and seemingly useful for no purpose [Col. 1169]?

Two of these possibilities, through the unbelief of a blasphemous spirit, foolishly insult the Creator of the whole human being. In the first case they believed him impotent; in the second, not the God of all. For how is he taught to be omnipotent if he could not heal what was thought beyond hope? Or how is he the God of all if he himself did not make our soul?

In the other two cases, the cause of the soul is unknown in one, and its worth is not measured in the other [Note: [Col. 1169] Chiffletius and several manuscripts: “does not seem.”]. Can one be thought to understand the soul’s cause who tries to separate it from the sin of voluntary transgression even though it was equipped to receive the law with the character of innate reason? Or how does he recognize its nobility who says that it was despised because of the defect of lowliness, while flesh was preferred—flesh which, unlike the soul, is known to have been formed not by God’s breath but from the clay of the earth?

Since none of these opinions about the soul is correct, let us believe that our Redeemer assumed the whole human being, lest we appear in some way to allow the eternal benefit of our soul to perish.

“Alas!” they say. “Christ assumed flesh alone; he did not seek the soul.”

If you attend as an informed observer to the origin of both, the substance of the soul is more precious. If you attend to the guilt of transgression, its case is worse because of its understanding.

But I know Christ to be perfect in wisdom, and I do not doubt that he is most compassionate. In the first respect, he did not despise what was better and capable of wisdom; in the second, he assumed what had been more gravely wounded. For it is neither fitting to wisdom to love the most foolish of two equally his own more than the other, nor fitting to perfect compassion not to help the one in greater need.

## CHAPTER XIV

FEL. I admit that I understood everything you said earlier—not merely rationally but truthfully—and I do not deny that I approved it. But how Christ’s divinity is said to have experienced death, I do not know. Whether you said something obscure about this, or whether I have been unable, because of the slowness of my understanding, to grasp adequately what you said, I do not know.

For I would not dare to believe that the source of life, from which all things have whatever life they possess, during the three days in which the body lay in the tomb fell so far from the property of its nature that, if it is permissible to say so, having buried its senses, it lost every movement of its living substance [Note: [Col. 1169] Thus Chiffletius and the manuscripts. The Louvain edition has “lost its measure”; the Ambrosian and Erasmian editions, “lost its nature.”] and, for the redemption of the human race, abandoned not only the Father but also all the adornments of spiritual glory.

AUG. [Note: [Col. 1169] *Sentences*, book 3, distinction 21, chapter “Sicut”; and distinction 22, chapter “Et utique.”] Far be it, far be it from the faithful to entertain the suspicion that Christ experienced our death in such a way that, as far as he himself was concerned, life lost life.

For if this were so, how can we say that anything could have lived during those three days if we believe that the source of life had dried up? The divinity of Christ therefore experienced death by participating in the human condition that he had voluntarily assumed; it did not lose the power of its own nature, through which it gives life to all things.

Thus in the tomb he did not abandon his flesh by dying with it, just as in the virgin’s womb he formed it by being born with it. In both cases the Lord willed to be born and to die not under compulsion from another but voluntarily, so that it is clear that he endured what he himself brought about: not that he was not suffering because he himself was acting, nor that he was not acting because someone else was enduring it.

For if you consider the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation while preserving the cooperation of the undivided Trinity, the same one is both author and work in this humiliation. He is the same author because he is born voluntarily and suffers voluntarily; he is the same work because, although no other compels either event, he alone endures both.

He made the flesh in his mother’s womb: here you have the author of the work. He himself deigned to be born in this flesh: here you have the work of the author. Yet there is one person, while the distinct property of both substance—the author and the work—is preserved.

Thus he died without life departing, just as he suffered without power perishing. “No one takes his soul from him, because he has power to lay it down and power to take it up again.” Here too you have the author of the work. “He lays down his soul for his friends” (John 10:18, 17): here you have the work of the author.

To conclude this by a general definition: whenever Christ suffers something in the flesh [Col. 1170], it is the work of the author. But because he endures that very thing by his own power and not under compulsion from another, he himself is the author of the work.

Therefore divinity did not come to Mary by a local movement; rather, by the ineffable manifestation of its power it filled his mother’s womb in order to be born, without being deprived of the fullness of its substance.

He did not abandon the Father when he came to the virgin. He was wholly everywhere and perfect everywhere, because the simplicity of the incorporeal does not admit division, and fullness knows nothing of the name “part.”

Thus at one and the same time he himself was wholly in the realm of the dead and wholly in heaven: there suffering the injury of flesh, here not abandoning the glory of divinity. Among the dead he was the resurrection of the dead; above the heavens he was the life of the living.

He was truly dead and truly alive: in him the assumption of mortality underwent death, while the divinity that remained preserved did not lose life.

Whenever, therefore, you consider those things that Christ endured in humility, recognize him as the author of voluntary suffering. In this way, while humility is attributed to the one who suffers and power to the one who acts, the same Christ is taught to be weak while suffering and omnipotent while acting, at one and the same time.

But lest you still think that we accept some insensibility in the death of the Son of God, it is not out of place to investigate what was experienced in death. In death, without doubt, the body was abandoned, but our life did not perish [Note: [Col. 1170] Thus Chiffletius and the manuscripts. The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Louvain editions have: “the soul does not destroy our life when the body has been abandoned.”]. As the departing soul does not lose its power, but leaves what it had made alive, it causes the death of another while it does not itself receive death.

It causes death, I say, by no longer giving life to what it abandons, not by losing what lives. Therefore human death is nothing other than the falling away of the flesh. When the power of the life-giving force has departed from it, the flesh returns to the earth from which it was taken, having lost the senses that it did not possess through itself.

“But death,” you say, “is contrary to life.”

I admit it. But it is not one of those contraries that destroy one another by the opposition of existing substances. Rather, it belongs to those things which, while occurring to something, cannot indeed exist simultaneously, but arise through the presence and privation of one substance alone.

Consider, for example, night and day. These too are taught to be contraries of the same kind, although the substance appears to belong not to both but to one alone. We say that it is day when the sun is above the earth; and it is clear that the sun is a substance. When, after the course of the daytime has been completed, the sun withdraws from human sight, by departing it immediately makes night.

It makes night, I say, by withdrawing the availability of light, not by receiving the substance of night into itself. Thus one substance of light appears to make both night and day, but not in the same way. When it comes, it makes day; when it departs, it makes night.

For this reason we often refute the Manichaeans’ division—which is not merely irreligious but also foolish—by which they attempt to separate good and evil as substances existing equally. We point out to them the greater light by which we know that day is made, and compel them likewise to explain what, if it is permissible to say so, would be the greater darkness by which they believed that night too was made substantially [Note: [Col. 1170] The Erasmian edition has *tenebrare majus*. Manuscript M.].

But let these matters be treated elsewhere. They concern those who, through the foolishness of a blasphemous doctrine, seem to affirm either nonexisting things in place of existing things, or consequences in place of first principles, or common things in place of contraries. If anyone examines these matters with the eyes of faith still intact, he easily overturns all their schemes.

Therefore, as we began to say, the soul gives life to the flesh in no other way than the sun does: when it comes, it bestows life; when it departs, it causes death.

But lest anyone think that the soul is consumed by the body’s death, let him hear how the Lord defines this matter in the Gospels with universal authority: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in the Gehenna of fire” (Matthew 10:28).

Therefore, while the soul survives, it is established that the body can be killed; and for this reason it does not necessarily follow that souls are consumed by the destruction of bodies. If this is so, then even after the body’s death we nevertheless live in our minds [Col. 1171].

If this is rightly believed of each one of us, how can it be asserted that the source of life lost the power of giving life through participating in human death?

“But,” you say, “the soul and body can be killed in the Gehenna of fire.”

This does not initially work against us, because that death appears to belong not to the condition of nature but to guilt. Apart from guilt, we are commanded not to fear human beings, who, although they can kill the body, are nevertheless denied the power to kill the soul.

Furthermore, since this is said to be possible for God alone, we do not believe that the Son of God, by communion of nature and equality of power, failed to possess this capability.

The Savior therefore assumed the condition of our death, but not in such a way as to make it worse by allowing it, contrary to custom, to dominate the soul. Rather, he did so to demonstrate that death could harm neither the soul nor the life of all the righteous.

## CHAPTER XV

But let us suppose, although the Gospels protest against it, that souls perish. Does our Savior not nevertheless possess a third and distinctive majesty which, although he did not repel death in these matters, human death could not touch?

In sum, let us see what he promised while hanging on the cross. “Today,” he said, “you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). “Today,” he said—not after three days, when I shall raise my flesh from the repose of the tomb; not when I shall display in myself the first fruits of the future resurrection.

Whose voice do we think this is—the voice of majesty? Of the mind or of the body? No one is unaware that the body was in the tomb [Note: [Col. 1171] Chiffletius and the manuscripts: “in the cave.”]. It remains, then, that this voice belongs either to the divinity or to the soul.

But someone may say: “We believe this to be the voice of the divinity, not of Christ’s soul.”

And what do we understand by it in the case of the one to whom the promise was made? “Today,” he says to the thief, “you will be with me in paradise”—although common death enclosed the thief’s body until the future resurrection.

It is therefore the soul to which the Lord made and fulfilled this promise. If, then, after the body has died, the soul is immediately called to paradise, can we still believe anyone so impious as to dare say that during those three days our Savior’s soul was consigned to custody among the dead because of bodily death?

“And who else,” you ask, “is there who, as his passion approached, groaned as Christ did, saying, ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death’ (Matthew 26:38)?”

It was sorrowful unto death because of the feeling of the flesh he had assumed—not after death, when the fellowship of divinity promises blessedness. Death is not the beginning of sorrow but its end. Nor do the scourges of the righteous begin after death; they cease, when they both lay aside the impediments of fluctuating matter [Note: [Col. 1171] The Louvain edition alone has “put down”] and already grasp their author through the contemplation of fuller understanding.

## CHAPTER XVI
Therefore, you ask, did the Son of God neither undergo death in his soul nor experience it in his majesty? [Col. 1172] What, then, did you say that he underwent? He certainly experienced and underwent it, but by participation in an alien sickness, not through the wound proper to himself. He experienced it as all experience it who live in mind while the flesh is dying—not as the impious do, who, as the same author says, are destroyed by the fires of Gehenna in both respects. Some, indeed, define common death in this way also, saying that it is nothing other than this: when, through the agreement of the various things that constitute life, a kind of dissension has arisen between them through separation from one another. If this is the death of a human being, which does not consume the things joined together but divides them, restoring each to its origin, what shall we now say about the Savior’s soul? Even if I do not mention the indwelling divinity or his singular righteousness, certainly by reason of the common lot of dying it could leave the body during those three days in such a way that it could not itself perish utterly.

## CHAPTER XVII

“Therefore,” you say, “Christ’s soul, but not his divinity, was among the dead.” It was, I reply. Otherwise I cannot see how he could have raised his own flesh, if I were to maintain that among the dead there had been no power of the absent God, as it were. Yet no one should therefore suppose that we proclaim a local presence of God. We say these things to indicate a certain work, because he was in one place who was absent from no place. As far as the flesh was concerned, he lay dead in the tomb; in the underworld he raised the dead; in heaven he gave life to all. He did not leave the world when he ascended to the heavens, nor did he abandon heaven when he came to earth; rather, wholly present, he filled all things at one and the same time. In one place he manifested his works more fully and withheld knowledge of his presence from the unworthy, but he did not thereby bring about the absence of his boundless divinity.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Do you wish to know what I think about this death of the Mediator? It is precisely the following judgment, gathered from all that I have scattered above because of the necessity of the questions that arose: I believe that the Son of God died, not according to the punishment of injustice—which he did not possess at all—but according to the law of nature, which he assumed for the redemption of the human race: that death of which it is said, “Who is the human being who shall live and not see death?” (Psalm 88:49); not that death of which Isaiah says, “But the dead shall not see life” (Isaiah 66). It was the death that, according to nature, is common to all, not the death that is peculiar to the wicked.

Let us therefore suppose that in this there is, in a certain manner, the force and power of a seed, by which the soul restores souls and, through the flesh of us all, raises our flesh when judgment is imminent. For, by the operation of his own divinity, giving life to all things, from the single grain of the humanity he assumed he will return an innumerable harvest to the Father. Then he will separate the crop from the weeds (Matthew 13:30), when he begins to repay the righteous their reward.

[Col. 1171]

# QUESTIONS ON THE TRINITY AND ON GENESIS, TRANSCRIBED FROM ALCUIN [Note: [Col. 1171] Alcuin’s Twenty-Eight Questions on the Trinity to Fredegisus.] (G)

[Col. 1171] **QUESTION ONE.** How is God truly unity and truly Trinity?

**ANSWER:** Unity in substance, Trinity in persons.

**II. QUESTION.** What is proper to each person in the holy Trinity?

**ANSWER:** It is proper to the Father that he alone is Father and that he is from no other but himself. It is proper to the Son that he alone is begotten from the Father alone, coeternal and consubstantial with the one who begets him. It is proper to the Holy Spirit that he is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds equally from the Father and the Son.

**III. QUESTION.** Why should the Holy Spirit not be called either unbegotten [Col. 1172] or begotten?

**ANSWER:** Because if he were called unbegotten, like the Father, two fathers could be thought to exist in the holy Trinity; if begotten, two sons.

**IV. QUESTION.** Should the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit be called, in himself, fully God and perfect?

**ANSWER:** Certainly the Father in himself is fully God; likewise the Son is fully God, and the Holy Spirit is believed to be fully God.

**V. QUESTION.** If each person can in himself be called fully God, why do we not call the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three gods?

**ANSWER:** Because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, and not [Col. 1173] three substances. Therefore the unity of substance prevents us from calling or believing them three gods.

**VI. QUESTION.** Since we speak of three persons—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—why is it not lawful to speak of three gods, three almighty beings, three good beings, or three great beings?

**ANSWER:** Because “God,” “almighty,” “great,” “good,” and “eternal” are substantial names and are said of a thing in itself. Therefore it is not lawful to use them in the plural, but in the singular. Every name that signifies God’s substance or essence must always be uttered in the singular. “Father,” however, “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are relative names, and therefore three persons are rightly spoken of.

**VII. QUESTION.** How are they relative?

**ANSWER:** According to dialectic, relative names are those that refer to something else, as master to servant and servant to master, father to son and son to father. Whenever I say “father,” I signify “son,” because there is no father unless there is a son to whom he is father; likewise, there is no son unless there is a father to whom he is son.

**VIII. QUESTION.** Is the Holy Spirit spoken of relatively or substantially?

**ANSWER:** Certainly relatively, because the spirit is the spirit of someone; but the rule of relation is not maintained in him as it is in the Father and the Son.

**IX. QUESTION.** Why does the Holy Spirit not have an equal rule of relation, as the Father and the Son do?

**ANSWER:** Because the names “Father” and “Son” can be mutually related, so that we may say “Father of the Son” and “Son of the Father.” A reciprocal turning of the relation cannot be found in the name “Holy Spirit” in the same doubled manner.

**X. QUESTION.** By what necessity does it happen that the relation of the Holy Spirit cannot be turned in this way?

**ANSWER:** We can rightly say “the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son”; but in the reverse order we cannot say “Father of the Holy Spirit,” as we say “Father of the Son,” lest two sons be understood in the holy Trinity. Likewise, we cannot say “Son of the Holy Spirit,” as we say “Son of the Father,” lest two fathers be understood in the holy Trinity. Thus we say “the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son,” without reciprocal reversal of the relative names.

**XI. QUESTION.** Are the works of the holy Trinity inseparable?

**ANSWER:** Certainly, whatever the holy Trinity does, it does inseparably, because the Trinity’s operation is one, just as its substance, essence, and will are one.

**XII. QUESTION.** Is the holy Trinity to be called separable or inseparable in its persons, since the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another?

**ANSWER:** The Father is truly another person than the Son, just as the Son is another person than the Father, and the Holy Spirit is another person than the Father and the Son. Yet he is not something other in nature, divinity, or essence. For you cannot say “Father” without understanding “Son,” nor “Holy Spirit” without understanding whose Spirit he is. Therefore the holy Trinity must be called entirely inseparable, both in its works and in its persons.

**XIII. QUESTION.** Does the statement “who alone does great wonders” (Psalm 71:18), and the Apostle’s statement “who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16), apply only to the person of the Father?

**ANSWER:** In no way does it apply only to the person of the Father, when God is called “alone,” whether in the New or the Old Testament, or when God alone is said to possess or do this or that. It refers to the whole holy Trinity, which is the one almighty God, doing all things in heaven and on earth.

**XIV. QUESTION.** How does blessed John the Evangelist say, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), while the Lord himself says elsewhere, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), and the Apostle calls God invisible (1 Timothy 1:17)?

**ANSWER:** God can indeed be seen—that is, understood—according to the gift of his grace, whether by angels or by the souls of the saints. But no angel, nor any of the saints, will be able perfectly to understand the full nature of divinity. Therefore God is called incomprehensible.

[Col. 1174] **XV. QUESTION.** Since the highest reward promised to the saints is the eternal vision of God, will all see or understand him equally?

**ANSWER:** In no way will all angels or all the souls of the saints see or understand God equally, either now or after the resurrection, but according to the dispensation of the giver and the quality of their merits. Nevertheless, each will possess, in the vision of him, the blessedness sufficient for his merits; he will neither seek more than he has nor grieve at having less than he wishes to have.

**XVI. QUESTION.** Is there any difference in God between being, living, understanding, and being able?

**ANSWER:** In God, being is in no way one thing, living another, understanding another, or being able another. God lives by the very fact that he is; by the fact that he lives, he understands; by the fact that he understands, he is able; and by the fact that he is able, he is. The simple nature of divinity has one being, one life, one understanding, and can do all things. It is not so in us, since in our nature living is one thing, understanding another, and being able another. In God, however, all these are one and the same.

**XVII. QUESTION.** With respect to the Son, may we say, just as we say “light from light” and “God from God,” “almighty from almighty,” “good from good,” “great from great,” and other such expressions?

**ANSWER:** We must certainly hold as a rule that all names of nature can be said equally of the Son as of the Father. That is, just as we say “God from God” and “light from light,” so we should say “almighty from almighty,” “good from good,” and “great from great”—but not so with relative names.

**XVIII. QUESTION.** But how should we speak with relative names?

**ANSWER:** We cannot say “Word from Word,” because “Word” is a relative name and the Son alone is Word, whereas we say “God from God,” since “God” is not the Son’s name alone. Nor can we say “Image from Image,” because the Son alone is Image (2 Corinthians 4:4; Colossians 1:15), whereas we say “light from light,” since “light” is not the Son’s name alone but a substantial name.

**XIX. QUESTION.** Is the Father one light and the Son another?

**ANSWER:** Not at all: the Father and the Son are one light, just as they are one substance. Therefore “light from light” is rightly said, just as “God from God.” For just as the Father and the Son are one God, so they are one light.

**XX. QUESTION.** We read the Apostle saying that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Does the Father not possess wisdom or power in himself, except in the Son whom the Apostle called the wisdom and power of God?

**ANSWER:** Many people destroy the impiety of Arianism in this way, saying that it is impious to believe that God the Father was ever without his wisdom or without his power. But it is better to understand the Father himself as wisdom and power—and indeed the Holy Spirit also as wisdom and power. Yet there are not three powers or three wisdoms, because “wisdom” is a substantial name, as is “power.” In God, being is not one thing, knowing another, and being able another; rather, for God being, knowing, and being able are one.

**XXI. QUESTION.** Does love belong only to the person of the Holy Spirit, since the Apostle says, “God is love” (1 John 4:16), and he is read to be the love of the Father and the Son?

**ANSWER:** The Holy Spirit is in no way understood as love in such a way that the Father and the Son are not also love. Just as the Holy Spirit is love, so the Father is love and the Son is love. Yet there are not three loves, but one love. But because the Holy Spirit is properly called the gift of God (Acts 2:38; 8:20), and no gift of God is greater than love—indeed, without it no gift can lead a human being to everlasting blessedness—the Holy Spirit is therefore properly called love (Romans 5:5).

**XXII. QUESTION.** Do the wicked possess the gifts of God?

**ANSWER:** Certainly they possess them through him who enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9). For in him “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28). The gifts of God are good for those who use them well. Therefore love is a singular gift among the saints, by which the children of God are distinguished from the children of impiety.

**XXIII. QUESTION.** If God is wholly everywhere, why is he said to dwell more in heaven than on earth?

**ANSWER:** [Col. 1175] Because knowledge of divinity is greater among the holy angels and the souls of the saints when they are with God in heaven than it is on earth. For just as in this mortal body some understand the divine substance more and others less, so God is said to be more in heaven than on earth because the inhabitants of heaven understand that substance more fully than do the inhabitants of earth.

**XXIV. QUESTION.** If the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, why is the Son alone said to have become incarnate?

**ANSWER:** Because the person of the Son is one, that of the Father another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. The person of the Son alone became incarnate, although the whole holy Trinity performed the same incarnation, whose works are inseparable.

**XXV. QUESTION.** In the Catholic Creed, God’s Son is customarily sung as having become incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. Why is he not called the Son of the Holy Spirit, as he is called the Son of the Blessed Virgin?

**ANSWER:** The Son of God was not born from him in the same way as from her. He was born from her—that is, from the holy Virgin—as from a mother; not from him—that is, from the Holy Spirit—as from a father, lest two fathers be said to exist in the holy Trinity.

**XXVI. QUESTION.** If the Father and the Son have one nature, and the incarnate Son is fully and perfectly God, how is it that the Father did not become incarnate?

**ANSWER:** The Son is fully and perfectly God; he alone became incarnate and became human. For fire has one substance, but heat performs one function in fire and light another. Light illuminates, heat warms; nevertheless, the one nature of fire produces both heat and light.

**XXVII. QUESTION.** Was the divinity conceived, born, and subjected to suffering together with the flesh, as well as undergoing the other things known to belong properly to humanity?

**ANSWER:** Certainly the divinity was conceived in the conception of its flesh and born in its birth; it experienced death through participation in human feeling, a death which it had freely assumed, without losing the power of its nature by which it gives life to all things. The same author who was born willingly also suffered willingly. And it is the same work, because he is both [God and human]: although not compelled by another, he alone undergoes it, while the impassibility of the divinity remains unharmed.

**XXVIII. QUESTION.** With respect to which nature does he say, “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10:18)?

**ANSWER:** The authority for all the works that are in Christ comes from the divinity. Nevertheless, it belongs to the flesh to say, “I have power to lay down my life,” not to the divinity. For the divinity did not abandon the soul after assuming it in the Virgin’s womb; Christ, in the flesh, laid it down when he released his spirit on the cross.

**XXIX.** [Note: [Col. 1176] The remaining questions of the same Alcuin concern Genesis.]

**QUESTION.** How is it consistent that Genesis says, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works” (Genesis 2:2), while the Gospel says, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17)?

**ANSWER:** He rested from creating new creatures, not from governing those already created. Therefore God is to be regarded then as creator, in the creation of the six days, but now as governor in the natures of the whole world.

**XXX. QUESTION.** How many rational creatures did God create?

**ANSWER:** Two: the angelic and the human. He gave heaven as a dwelling to the angels and earth as a dwelling to human beings.

**XXXI. QUESTION.** Why is the angelic sin concealed in silence in Genesis, while the human sin is disclosed?

**ANSWER:** Because God did not predestine the angelic wound to be healed, but predestined the human wound to be healed.

**XXXII. QUESTION.** Why was the sin of the highest angel incurable, while the human sin was curable?

**ANSWER:** Because the angel was the inventor of his own crime, whereas the human being was deceived by another’s fraud. Moreover, the more exalted the angel in glory, the greater his fall; while the more fragile the human being in nature, the easier the way to pardon.

**XXXIII. QUESTION.** Why was the human being created as the author of his own power?

**ANSWER:** So that he himself might be the author of his own life or death. If he were subject to necessity, he would possess neither the glory of a good work nor the punishment of an evil one, but would be like one of the animals.

[Col. 1175]

# TWO BOOKS ON THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD TO JANUARIUS, COMPILED FROM ORIGEN’S WORK *ΠΕΡΙ ΑΡΧΩΝ* [*On First Principles*], ACCORDING TO RUFINUS’ TRANSLATION (G)

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

## He Reviews What the Apostles Proclaimed about God

[Note: [Col. 1175] From the prologue of Book 1 of *On First Principles*.]

The forms indeed [Note: [Col. 1175] Here we add *indeed* (*vero*) from the Vatican and Victorinus manuscripts; it is also found in Origen.] of those things that are manifestly handed down through apostolic preaching are these. First, there is one God who created and ordered all things, and who, when they did not exist, brought the universe into being. He is the God of the first creation and founding of the world, the God of all the righteous: Adam, Abel, Seth, Enos, Enoch, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the twelve Patriarchs, Moses, and the Prophets.

And this God, in the last days, as he had previously promised through his Prophets, sent the Lord Jesus Christ, first to call Israel, and afterward also the Gentiles, following the unbelief of the people of Israel.

This just and good God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, himself gave the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels. He is also the God of the Apostles and of both the Old and the New Testament.

Then, next, because Jesus Christ, who existed before every creature, was born from the Father—for he had ministered to the Father in every creation, since through him all things were made (John 1:3)—in the last [Col. 1176] times he emptied himself and became human. He became incarnate while he was God, and, having become human, he remained what he was: God. He assumed a body like our body, differing in this one respect: it was born from a virgin and from the Holy Spirit.

And since this God, Jesus Christ, was truly born and suffered, not in appearance, he truly died this common death. [Note: [Col. 1176] The Victorinus Manuscript reads: “He suffered in truth, and not in appearance; he shared this death and truly died. For truly …”] For he truly rose from the dead, and after the resurrection, having lived among his disciples, he was taken up.

Finally, it handed down that the Holy Spirit is joined to the Father and the Son in nature, honor, and dignity. [Note: [Col. 1176] The manuscripts omit “to the Father and the Son.”] It is plainly proclaimed in the Church that this Holy Spirit inspired each of the saints, whether Prophets or Apostles, and that there was not one spirit among the ancients and another among those inspired at Christ’s coming.

### CHAPTER TWO

## The Soul’s Free Will and Origin

After these matters comes the teaching that the soul, since it already possesses its own substance and life, will, when it departs from this world, be allotted according to its merits: either it will obtain the inheritance of eternal life and blessedness, if its actions have earned this for it, or it will be consigned to eternal punishment, if the guilt of its crimes has turned it toward this fate.

There will also be a time of the resurrection of the dead, when this body, which is now sown in corruption, will rise in incorruption, and what is sown in dishonor will rise in glory (1 Corinthians 15:42–43).

It is also established in ecclesiastical preaching that every soul is rational and possesses free choice and will. It also has a struggle against the devil, his angels, and opposing powers, because they try to burden it with sins, while we, if we live rightly and prudently, try to free ourselves from such defilement.

Hence it follows that we are not subject to necessity, so that we are compelled to do good or evil even if we do not wish to do so. [Note: [Col. 1177] The Victorinus Manuscript reads “if we wish.”] For if we possess free choice, certain powers may perhaps attack us toward sin, while others may help us toward salvation; nevertheless, we are not compelled by necessity either to act rightly or to act wrongly.

This is what those people suppose who say that the course and movements of the stars are the cause of human actions—not only of those things that occur outside the freedom of choice, but also of those placed within our power.

As for the soul, whether it is derived from the transmission of the seed, so that its reason or substance is contained within the bodily seeds themselves; or whether it has some other beginning; and whether that beginning itself is generated or ungenerated; or, certainly, whether it is inserted into the body from outside or not—this is not distinguished in sufficiently clear teaching.

### CHAPTER THREE

## The Devil’s Condition

Ecclesiastical preaching has also taught concerning the devil, his angels, and the opposing powers that these beings do indeed exist, but it has not explained sufficiently clearly what they are or how they exist.

Nevertheless, among very many people this opinion is held: that this devil was an angel, and that, having become an apostate, he persuaded very many angels to fall away with him. These are still called his angels.

### CHAPTER FOUR

## The Beginning and End of the World

There is also this teaching in ecclesiastical preaching: that this world was made, that it began at a definite time, and that, because of its own corruption, it will be dissolved.

What existed before this world, however, or what will exist afterward, has not become known to many as an established fact. No clear statement about these matters is put forward in ecclesiastical preaching.

### CHAPTER FIVE

## The Hidden Meaning of Scripture

Finally, there is the teaching that the Scriptures were written through the Spirit of God and possess a meaning—not only the one that is manifest, but also another meaning hidden from very many.

For the things that are described are forms of certain mysteries and images of divine realities. On this the whole Church has one judgment: the whole Law is indeed spiritual, but the things breathed by the Law are not known to human beings except those alone to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit is granted in the word of wisdom and knowledge. [Note: [Col. 1177] Some material from Origen has been omitted here.]

### CHAPTER SIX

## The Good Angels

There is also this teaching in ecclesiastical preaching: that there are certain angels of God and good powers who minister to him for the completion of the salvation of human beings. But when these beings were created, or what kind they are, or how they exist, is not sufficiently distinguished in the manifest teaching.

### CHAPTER SEVEN

## How Truth Is to Be Investigated

Therefore one ought to use such teachings as elements and foundations, according to the command that says, “Illuminate for yourselves the light of knowledge.” Anyone who desires to construct a certain sequence and a unified body from the reasoning of all these things should investigate what is true concerning each matter by means of manifest and necessary assertions, and should form, as we have said, one body from examples and affirmations—whether those he has found in the holy Scriptures or those he has discovered through subsequent investigation and the course of sound reasoning.

### CHAPTER EIGHT

## The Son Born Without Beginning

[Note: [Col. 1177] From chapter 2 of Book 1 of *On First Principles*.]

We have always known God as the Father of his only-begotten Son, who was indeed born from him and draws from him what he is, yet without any beginning—not merely because he cannot be separated by intervals of time, but not even by that beginning which the mind alone usually observes within itself and, so to speak, contemplates with bare understanding and thought.

Therefore it must be believed that Wisdom was generated beyond every beginning that can either be spoken or understood. In this very subsistence of Wisdom, since every power and formation of the future creature was present—whether of those that exist primarily or of those that subsequently arise—preformed and arranged by the power of foreknowledge, Wisdom said through Solomon that, on account of those creatures that had been depicted and prefigured in her, she herself had been created as “the beginning of God’s ways” (Proverbs 8:22). In herself she contained the beginnings, reasons, and forms of the whole creation.

In what manner, then, do we understand Wisdom to be the beginning of God’s ways, and how is she said to have been created—namely, as preforming and containing in herself the forms and reasons of the whole creation? In this same way we must understand the Word of God to be Wisdom: because she opens to all other things, that is, to the whole creation, the reason of the mysteries and secrets contained within God’s Wisdom. The Word is therefore called “Word” because it is, as it were, the interpreter of the secrets of the mind.

At the beginning of his Gospel, John, properly defining the Word to be God, says: “And the Word was God, and this was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1). But whoever gives a beginning to the Word of God or to the Wisdom of God, beware lest he cast his impiety more directly against the unbegotten Father himself, by denying that he was always Father, that he generated the Word, and that he possessed Wisdom throughout all earlier times or ages—or whatever else it may be called.

### CHAPTER NINE

## Exemplary Reasons in the Word

This Son, therefore, is also the truth, the life, and the way of all things that exist (John 14:6). And rightly so. For how could the things that were made live unless they came from life? Or how could the things that exist be established in truth unless they descended from truth? Or how could rational substances exist unless the Word or reason preceded them? Or how could they be wise unless wisdom existed?

The Word and Wisdom of God became the way. It is called “the way” because it leads to the Father those who walk along it.

Therefore, whatever we say about the Wisdom of God will also appropriately be applied and understood in relation to the Son of God’s being life, Word, truth, way, and resurrection. For all these names are derived from his works and powers. In none of them can anything corporeal be understood, even in the slightest opinion, nor anything that appears to indicate magnitude, shape, or color.

### CHAPTER TEN

## The Inconceivable Birth of the Word

But since those who among us are called human children, or the offspring of other animals, correspond to the seed of those who sowed them, or even to those in whose wombs they are formed and nourished, receiving from them whatever it is that they assume and carry into this light when they come forth, it is unspeakable and unlawful to equate God the Father, in the generation and substance of his only-begotten Son, with any human or other animal that generates.

Yet something exceptional and worthy of God must be involved—something for which no comparison whatsoever can be found, not merely in things but not even in thought or perception—so that human thought might apprehend how the unbegotten God the Father becomes the Father of the only-begotten Son.

His generation is therefore eternal and everlasting, as splendor is generated from light. The Son does not become one from outside through adoption by the spirit; he is Son by nature.

Let us nevertheless see how what we are saying is fortified by the authority of divine Scripture. The Apostle Paul says that the only-begotten Son is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15). Writing to the Hebrews about him, he says [Col. 1179] that he is “the splendor of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3).

We also find, in the Wisdom that is called Solomon’s, a certain description of God’s Wisdom written in this way: “For she is,” it says, “a vapor of the power of God and an emanation [ἀπόρροια, *aporrhoia*] of the pure glory of the Almighty. Therefore nothing defiled can enter into her. For she is the splendor of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s operation, and the image of his goodness” (Wisdom 7:25–26).

As we said above, we call the Wisdom of God a subsistence existing nowhere except in the one who is the beginning of all things, from whom she was born. Since this Wisdom is the one who alone is Son by nature, she is therefore also called the Only-Begotten.

### CHAPTER ELEVEN

## The Word as the Image of the Father

Let us examine what should also be understood by the statement that he is called the image of the invisible God, so that through it we may perceive how God is rightly called the Father of his Son.

Let us first consider the things that, according to human custom, are usually called images. Sometimes an image is something painted or carved in some material, that is, in wood or stone. Sometimes the one who is born is called the image of the one who begot him, when the features of the one who begot reproduce a likeness in the one who was born. [Note: [Col. 1179] The manuscripts read: “no likenesses”; Origen: “in no respect.”]

I think, then, that the first example can be applied to the human being who was first made according to the image and likeness of God. With God’s favor, we shall examine this more carefully when we begin to expound the relevant passage in Genesis.

The second comparison can be applied to the image of the Son of God, about whom we are now speaking, including in this respect that he is the invisible image of the invisible God. Just as, according to the historical account, we say that Seth, his son, is the image of Adam, so it is written: “And Adam begot Seth according to his image and according to his likeness” (Genesis 5:3).

This image also contains the unity of the nature and substance of the Father and the Son. For if the Son does everything that the Father does (John 5:19), then, in the fact that the Son does all things as the Father does, the Father’s image is formed in the Son, who was born from him as a kind of will proceeding from the mind. [Note: [Col. 1179] The manuscripts add “his.”]

Therefore I think that the Father’s will ought to be sufficient for the subsistence of what the Father wills. For when he wills, he uses no other way than that which proceeds through the deliberation of his will.

Thus the Son’s subsistence is also generated from him. This must first be accepted by those who confess that nothing is unbegotten—that is, unborn—except God alone, the Father.

One must be careful lest anyone fall into those absurd fables of people who depict for themselves certain emanations, thereby dividing the divine nature into parts and, as far as they can, dividing God the Father. To suspect this even slightly of an incorporeal nature is not only the height of impiety but also the utmost folly; nor does it follow at all from understanding that a substantial division of an incorporeal nature could be conceived.

Rather, just as a will proceeds from the mind without cutting off or separating any part of the mind, so the Father should be thought to have begotten the Son in such a form—as his own image—that, just as he himself is invisible by nature, he likewise begot an invisible image.

For the Son is the Word, and therefore nothing sensible is to be understood in him. He is Wisdom, and nothing corporeal is to be suspected in Wisdom. He is the true Light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9), but he has nothing in common with the light of this sun. [Note: [Col. 1179] These words are translated differently in Jerome’s Letter 59 to Avitus, chapter 1, and in Augustine, *On Heresies* 43.]

Our Savior, therefore, is the image of the invisible God the Father. In relation to the Father himself, he is truth; but in relation to us, to whom he reveals the Father, he is the image through which we know the Father—whom no one else knows except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him (Matthew 11:27).

He reveals him by being himself understood. For whoever has understood him consequently understands the Father also, in accordance with what he himself said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also” (John 14:9).

### CHAPTER TWELVE
### Christ, the Image of the Father’s Substance

But since we have introduced Paul’s statement about Christ, in which he says that he is “the radiance of God’s glory and the express image of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3), let us examine what should be understood by this. God is light, according to John (1 John 1:5). The only-begotten Son, therefore, is the radiance of that light, proceeding inseparably from it, as radiance proceeds from light, and illuminating the whole creation.

For in this connection we explained above how he is the way and leads to the Father; how he is the Word, interpreting and proclaiming to rational creation the mysteries hidden in wisdom and knowledge; and how he is also truth, life, and resurrection [Note: [Col. 1180] Manuscripts read “prayer.” Perhaps for “reason.”]. Consequently, we must also understand the function of radiance. Through radiance, the light itself is recognized and perceived. This radiance presents itself more gently and mildly to the fragile and feeble eyes of mortals, gradually teaching them and accustoming them to endure the brightness of the light. When it removes from them everything that covers and obstructs their sight, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, “Take the beam out of your eye” (Matthew 7:5), it makes them capable of receiving the glory of the light. In this respect it also becomes, as it were, a mediator between human beings and the light.

But since the Apostle says not only that he is the radiance of glory, but also “the express image of his substance or subsistence” (Hebrews 1:3), it does not seem to me an idle exercise of understanding to consider how something other than God’s own substance or subsistence—whatever that substance or subsistence is called—can be said to be the image of his substance. Consider whether perhaps the Son of God, who is also called his Word and Wisdom, who alone knows the Father and reveals him to those whom he wishes (Matthew 11:27)—that is, to those who are capable of his Word and Wisdom—is said to express the image of his substance or subsistence precisely insofar as he causes God to be understood and known. In this way, Wisdom first describes in itself what it wishes to reveal to others, through which God is known and understood by them; and this is called the express image of God’s substance.

To make it still clearer how the Savior is the image of God’s substance or subsistence, let us also use an example. Although it does not fully or properly signify the matter under discussion, it may nevertheless be taken for this one purpose: that the Son, who was in the form of God, “emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6), and through this very self-emptying undertook to demonstrate to us the fullness of divinity.
