For example, suppose a statue had been made so large that, by its magnitude, it occupied the entire globe of the earth, and because of its immensity could be contemplated by no one. Suppose another statue were then made identical in the arrangement of its limbs and the lines of its face, in appearance and in material, but without the former statue’s immensity of size, so that those who could not contemplate or behold the immense statue might, on seeing this one, consider themselves to have seen the former—since it preserved everything, namely, the lines of the limbs and face, as well as the very appearance and material, with an altogether indistinguishable likeness.

By a somewhat similar likeness, the Son of God, emptying himself of equality with the Father and showing us the way to know him, becomes “the express image of his substance.” Thus, since we could not gaze upon the glory of the pure light situated in the greatness of his splendor [Note: [Col. 1180] Manuscripts read “the greatness of his divinity”], through the fact that he becomes radiance for us, we gain, by contemplating the radiance, a way of beholding the divine light.

The comparison concerning statues, being drawn from bodily [Note: [Col. 1180] Manuscripts read “material”] things, should be accepted for no other purpose than this: that the Son of God, briefly inserted into the form of a human body, signified in himself, through the likeness of his works and virtue, the immense and invisible greatness of God the Father, in accordance with what he said to his disciples: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), and, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). The following saying should likewise be understood as analogous: “The Father is in me, and I am in him” (John 14:10).

### CHAPTER XIII

#### The Son, the Vapor of Divine Power

Let us now examine how we should understand what we read in the Wisdom of Solomon, which speaks of Wisdom in this way: “She is a certain vapor of the power of God, and *aporrhoia*—that is, a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty—and the radiance of eternal light, and an immaculate mirror of the working or power of God, and the image of his goodness” (Wisdom 7:25).

By defining these five things concerning God, Scripture indicates through each one that a particular quality belongs to God’s Wisdom. It names God’s power, glory, eternal light, working, and goodness. It says, however, that Wisdom is the vapor not of the glory of the Almighty, nor of eternal light, nor of the Father’s working, nor of his goodness. Indeed, it would not have been appropriate to ascribe a vapor to any of these. Rather, with complete precision, it says that Wisdom is the vapor of God’s power.

God’s power must therefore be understood as that by which he is vigorous and active; by which he either establishes, sustains, or governs all visible and invisible things; because it is sufficient for everything over which he exercises providence, and because it is present to all things as though united with them.

The vapor of this entire power, so great and immense—or, as I might say, its very vigor—having come to subsist in its own proper subsistence, proceeds from that power as the will proceeds from the mind. Nevertheless, the will of God itself also becomes God’s power. Thus another power comes to subsist in its own proper subsistence, as Scripture’s statement says: a certain vapor of God’s first and ungenerated power. In its being, it draws its origin from that power.

There was never a time when it did not exist. If someone wishes to say that it did not exist previously but afterward came into subsistence, let him explain why the Father, who caused it to subsist, did not do so earlier. And if he assigns some beginning at which this vapor proceeded from God’s power, we shall again ask why it did not proceed before the beginning he has proposed. Continuing in this way to inquire about what preceded each supposed beginning, and ascending by the force of our questions, we shall arrive at the conclusion that, since God always had both the power and the will, there was never a fitting occasion or any cause by which he could have failed to possess eternally what he eternally willed as good.

It follows that this vapor of God’s power has always existed, having no beginning except God himself. For it was not fitting that it have any other beginning than the one from whom it is and from whom it is born, namely God.

According to the Apostle’s statement that “Christ is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), he should now be called not merely the vapor of God’s power, but power from power. [Note: [Col. 1181] Some words of Origen have been omitted here.]

Lest anyone suppose that the title “Almighty” precedes the birth of Wisdom in God, through which the Father is called the Almighty—since Wisdom, who is the Son of God, was said to be the purest *aporrhoia* of the glory of the Almighty—let anyone who wishes to hold this view hear what divine Scripture plainly declares: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24). The Gospel also teaches: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

From this he will understand that the title “Almighty” cannot be earlier in God than the title “Father.” For the Father is Almighty through the Son.

But since Wisdom is said to be the *aporrhoia* of the glory of the Almighty, this glory being the glory from which she proceeds, it is shown that Wisdom also shares in the glory of omnipotence, through which God is called Almighty. Through Wisdom, who is Christ, God holds sovereignty over all things, not only by the authority of one who rules, but also through the willing service of those who are subject to him.

To understand that the Father and the Son possess one and the same omnipotence, just as the Father and the Son are one and the same God and Lord, hear John speaking in the Apocalypse: “Thus says the Lord God, who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” (Revelation 1:8). Who is the one “who is to come” if not Christ?

And just as no one should be offended that, although the Father is God, the Savior also is God, so too, when the Father is called Almighty, no one should be offended that the Son of God is also called Almighty. In this way what he says to the Father will be true: “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them” (John 17:10).

If, therefore, everything belonging to the Father belongs to Christ, and among everything that the Father is there is also omnipotence, then undoubtedly the only-begotten Son of God must also be Almighty, so that the Son may possess everything the Father possesses.

“And I have been glorified,” he says, “in them.” For “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10–11).

Accordingly, the *aporrhoia* of God’s glory, insofar as he is Almighty, is Wisdom herself, pure and clear, glorified as the *aporrhoia* of omnipotence or glory.

To make the glory of omnipotence still more evident, we shall add the following. God the Father is Almighty because he holds sovereignty over all things—that is, over heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them. He exercises sovereignty over these things through his Word, because “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth.”

If every knee bows to Jesus, then without doubt Jesus is Almighty [Note: [Col. 1182] Manuscripts omit “Almighty”], to whom all things are subject. He is the one who exercises sovereignty over all things, and through whom all things are subject to the Father. For they are subjected through Wisdom—that is, through word and reason—not through force or necessity.

Therefore, in the very fact that he possesses all things, his glory is present. This is the purest and clearest glory of omnipotence: that all things are subjected through reason and wisdom, not through force or necessity.

### CHAPTER XIV

#### Glory, Radiance, and Working (*energeia*). What Is Called Everlasting. What God’s Working Is

The phrase “the purest and clearest glory of Wisdom” is entirely appropriate as a distinction from that glory which is called neither pure nor sincere glory. Every nature that is changeable and capable of alteration, even if it is glorified in works of justice or wisdom, cannot have its glory called sincere and clear, precisely because it possesses justice or wisdom as an accident, and whatever is accidental can also depart.

But the Wisdom of God, who is the only-begotten Son, is in every respect unchangeable and immutable; and every good in him is substantial, something that can never be changed or altered. Therefore his glory is proclaimed pure and sincere. [Note: [Col. 1182] From the same passage of Origen, with several lines omitted.]

That which is properly called everlasting or eternal is what had no beginning in order to exist and can never cease to be what it is. This is indicated by John when he says, “God is light” (1 John 1:5). The radiance of his light is his Wisdom—not only insofar as it is eternal light, so that his Wisdom is the radiance of the eternal and of eternity.

If this is understood fully, it plainly declares that the substance of the Son descended from the Father himself, but not temporally, nor from any beginning other than, as we have said, God himself.

Wisdom is also called the immaculate mirror of the Father’s working [Note: [Col. 1182] Manuscripts read “of the power of the working”] of God. We must therefore first understand what the working of God’s power is. It is, so to speak, a certain vigor through which the Father works, whether when he creates, provides, judges, or arranges and dispenses each thing at its proper time.

Just as in a mirror every movement and every action by which the person looking into the mirror moves or acts causes the image formed in the mirror to be moved or to act through those same movements and actions, without deviating in anything whatsoever, so Wisdom wishes herself to be understood when she is called the immaculate mirror of the Father’s power and God’s working.

Likewise, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Wisdom of God, declares concerning himself: “The works that the Father does, the Son also does likewise.” And again he says: “The Son cannot do anything of himself except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19).

Since, therefore, the Son in no respect differs from the Father in the power of his works, and the work of the Son is not different from the work of the Father, but there is, so to speak, one and the same movement in all things, he therefore called him the immaculate mirror. By this it is understood that there is no dissimilarity between the Son and the Father, since in the Gospel the Son is not said merely to do similar things, but to do the very same things in the same way.

### CHAPTER XV

#### The Son, the Image of Divine Goodness

It remains to inquire what is meant by “the image of his goodness.” In this matter, I think, the same understanding should be adopted that we expressed above concerning the image formed in a mirror.

The original goodness is undoubtedly the Father, from whom the Son was born and who is said to be his image in every respect. There is no other, secondary goodness in the Son apart from the goodness that is in the Father. Hence the Savior himself rightly says in the Gospel: “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18).

By this, it is evidently understood that the Son does not belong to some other goodness, but only to that goodness which is in the Father. He is rightly called its image because he comes from nowhere other than that original goodness; no goodness other than the goodness in the Father is seen in the Son; and there is no dissimilarity or difference of goodness in the Son.

For this reason, what was said—“No one is good except one, God”—should not be regarded as any kind of blasphemy, as though Christ or the Holy Spirit were thereby denied to be good. Rather, as we said above, the original goodness is to be understood as residing in God the Father, from whom the Son is born and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds. Without doubt, the Son and the Holy Spirit carry within themselves the nature of that goodness which is in the source from which the Son is born and from which the Holy Spirit proceeds.

Moreover, whenever Scripture calls an angel, a human being, a servant, a treasure, the human heart, or a tree “good,” all these expressions are used figuratively. They contain in themselves goodness that is accidental, not substantial.

### CHAPTER XVI

#### The Dignity of the Holy Spirit

It would require a great deal of work, and a separate treatment or occasion, to gather together all the names attributed to the Son of God—for example, how he is the true light, the door, righteousness, sanctification, redemption, and countless other things—and to explain the reasons, virtues, or relations on account of which each of these names is applied.

But, satisfied with what we have discussed above, let us proceed to investigate the remaining matters.

[Note: [Col. 1183] Beginning of chapter 2 of book 1 of *On First Principles*.]

It follows that we must now inquire, as briefly as we can, into the Holy Spirit.

All who in any way acknowledge providence confess that there is an ungenerated God who created and ordered all things, and they understand him to be the parent of the universe. We are not alone in proclaiming that he has a Son, although this may seem sufficiently astonishing and incredible to those who appear to philosophize among Greeks or barbarians. Nevertheless, the same opinion seems to have been held by some among them, since they confess that all things were created by the Word of God or by reason.

But, according to the faith of his teaching—which we firmly hold to be divinely inspired—we believe that no one is able to set forth and make known to human understanding a more eminent and divine account of the Son of God than the Scripture alone that was inspired by the Holy Spirit: that is, the apostolic and evangelical Scriptures, as well as the Law and the Prophets, as Christ himself affirmed.

As for the substance of the Holy Spirit, no one could even have a suspicion of it except those who have occupied themselves with the Law and the Prophets, or those who profess to believe in Christ.

For although no one can speak worthily about God the Father, some understanding can nevertheless be grasped from the visible creatures and from what the human mind naturally perceives; and it is also possible for this understanding to be confirmed by the holy Scriptures.

Likewise, although “no one knows the Son except the Father,” the human mind is formed by the divine Scriptures to understand how the Son should be regarded—not only from the New Testament but also from the Old, through the things performed by the saints that are interpreted figuratively with reference to Christ. From these things it is possible to discern either his divine nature or the human nature assumed by him.

But concerning the Holy Spirit, Scripture has taught us what he is in many passages. Thus David says in the fiftieth Psalm: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 50:13). And in Daniel it is said: “The Holy Spirit who is in you” (Daniel 4:5, 6, 15; 5:11).

In the New Testament, we are instructed by abundant testimonies: it is written that the Holy Spirit descended upon him (Matthew 3:16); and after the resurrection the Lord himself breathed upon the Apostles, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). The angel says to Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35).

Paul teaches: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). And in the Acts of the Apostles, the Holy Spirit was given in baptism through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands (Acts 8:17).

From all this we have learned that the substance of the Holy Spirit possesses such authority and dignity that saving baptism is completed only through the authority of the most excellent Trinity, that is, through the naming of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that the name of the Holy Spirit is joined to the ungenerated God the Father and to his only-begotten Son. [Note: [Col. 1184] Origen reads “of the whole Trinity.”]

Who, then, would not be astonished at how great the majesty of the Holy Spirit is, when one who speaks a word against the Son of Man may dare to hope for forgiveness, whereas whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit is said to have no forgiveness, either in the present age or in the age to come?

### CHAPTER XVII

#### The Word “Spirit” in the Scriptures

[Note: [Col. 1184] Eleven lines of Origen have been omitted here.]

Nevertheless, up to the present we have not been able to find any statement in the holy Scriptures by which the Holy Spirit is said to be a work or a creature—not even in the manner in which we were taught above to understand Solomon’s statement concerning Wisdom, or the passages we discussed concerning life, the Word, and the other names of the Son of God.

The Spirit of God, therefore, which “was borne over the waters,” as it is written, at the beginning of the creation of the world (Genesis 1:2), I think is none other than the Holy Spirit, insofar as I am able to understand it. We also demonstrated this when we explained those passages—not according to the historical sense, however, but according to the spiritual understanding.

Some of our predecessors observed in the New Testament that wherever “spirit” is mentioned without an addition specifying what kind of spirit it is, the Holy Spirit should be understood. For example: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” (Galatians 5:22), and so forth. Likewise in the passage: “Having begun with the Spirit, are you now being perfected in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3).

We think that this distinction can also be maintained in the Old Testament, as when it says: “He who gives spirit to the people upon the earth, and Spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isaiah 42:5). Without doubt, everyone who treads upon the earth—that is, upon earthly and bodily things—is a participant in the Holy Spirit, receiving him from God.

[Note: [Col. 1184] Ten lines are omitted here.]

Just as it is said of the Son, “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27), so the Apostle teaches the same concerning the Holy Spirit when he says: “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

Again, in the Gospel, when the Savior speaks of divine and deeper teachings that his disciples were not yet able to grasp, he says to the Apostles: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” [Note: [Col. 1184] Manuscripts read “you cannot understand them now”]. “But when the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, comes, he will teach you all things and remind you of everything I have said to you” (John 16:13).

### CHAPTER XVIII

#### The Influxes and Various Operations of the Holy Spirit

[Col. 1185]

It must therefore be understood [Note: [Col. 1185] Manuscripts read “it must therefore be considered”] that just as the Son, who alone knows the Father, reveals him to whomever he wishes, so the Holy Spirit, who alone searches even the depths of God, reveals God to whomever he wishes. “The Spirit blows where he wishes” (John 3:8).

We must not suppose that the Spirit knows the Father because the Son reveals him. For if the Holy Spirit knows the Father because the Son reveals him, then the Holy Spirit has passed from ignorance to knowledge. This would be both impious and foolish: to confess the Holy Spirit and at the same time attribute ignorance to him.

For the Spirit did not first exist as something else and then, through progress, arrive at being the Holy Spirit, so that anyone could dare to say that, when he was not yet the Holy Spirit, he was ignorant of the Father, but that afterward, when he received knowledge, he also became the Holy Spirit.

If this were so, the Holy Spirit would never be included in the unity of the Trinity—that is, with God the Father, who is unchangeable [Note: [Col. 1185] Manuscripts omit “unchangeable”], and with his Son—unless he too had always been the Holy Spirit.

What we say here—whether “always,” “was,” or any other term of temporal signification—must be accepted simply and with indulgence. The meanings of these names are temporal, but the realities of which we speak, although they are named temporally in the course of our discourse, in their nature transcend every understanding of temporal sense.

[Note: [Col. 1185] After many omissions, the remainder is transcribed from chapter 3 of book 1 of *On First Principles*.]

God the Father grants to all things that they exist. Participation in Christ, insofar as he is the Word or Reason, makes them rational. Consequently, they are capable either of praise or of blame, because they are capable of virtue and vice.

For this reason, the grace of the Holy Spirit is also present, so that those things which are not holy in their substance may become holy through participation in him.

Thus, first, they receive from God the Father that they exist; second, they receive from the Word that they are rational; third, they receive from the Holy Spirit that they are holy. Again, those who have already been sanctified by the Holy Spirit become capable of Christ, insofar as he is the righteousness of God.

Those who have advanced to this degree through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit likewise obtain the gift of wisdom according to the power of the working of God’s Spirit. I think this is what Paul means when he says that to some is given the word of wisdom, and to others the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit.

In distinguishing the various gifts, he refers them all to the source of the universe and says: “There are divisions of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:8, 6).

Hence the working of the Father, which grants existence to all things, is found to be clearer and more magnificent. Each person advances through participation in Christ, insofar as he is wisdom, knowledge, and sanctification, and reaches higher stages of progress.

Through the fact that a person has been sanctified by participation in the Holy Spirit, he becomes purer and more sincere and receives more worthily the grace of wisdom and knowledge. Thus, with every stain of pollution and ignorance driven away and cleansed, he receives such an increase of sincerity and purity that what he has received from God in order to exist becomes such as is worthy of God, who granted him existence purely and perfectly. What exists becomes as worthy as the one who caused it to exist.

In this way, the one who is such as the one who made him wished him to be will also receive from God the power to exist forever and to remain eternally.

For this to happen, and so that the things made by him may attend unceasingly and inseparably upon him who is, it is Wisdom’s task to instruct and educate them and bring them to perfection by the strengthening and unceasing sanctification of the Holy Spirit, through which alone they can receive [the unstated object].

Thus, through the unceasing work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, renewed in each successive stage of progress [Note: [Col. 1185] Origen reads “with the heart renewed”], we may perhaps at last behold the holy and blessed life.

When, after many struggles, we have been able to reach it, we must persevere in it so that no satiety of that good may ever seize us. Rather, the more we partake of that blessedness, the more our desire for it should expand and increase within us, while we receive or hold the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit with ever greater ardor and capacity.

But if satiety should at some time seize one of those who have stood at the highest and most perfect stage, I do not think that he would suddenly be emptied and fall away. Rather, he must decline gradually and little by little. It may therefore happen that, if a brief lapse occurs and he quickly comes to his senses and returns to himself, he will not fall completely, but will withdraw his foot, return to his former state, and once again restore what had slipped away through negligence.

[Note: [Col. 1186] From this point onward, taken from chapter 5 of book 3 of *On First Principles*.]

The only-begotten Son of God, who was the Word and Wisdom of the Father, while he was in that glory with the Father which he possessed before the world existed, “emptied himself,” and, taking the form of a servant, became obedient unto death. In this way he taught obedience to those who could obtain salvation in no other way than through obedience, first fulfilling in himself what he wished others to fulfill.

For this reason, he became obedient to the Father not only unto the death of the cross, but also through the consummation of the age, embracing in himself all those whom he subjects to the Father and who come through him to salvation. Since they themselves are subject, and he is subject in them, he too is said to be subject to the Father. All things subsist in him; he is the head of all things; and he is the fullness of those who attain salvation.

This, then, is what the Apostle says concerning him: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

Yet somehow the heretics, failing to understand the Apostle’s meaning contained in these words, disgrace the term “subjection” when applied to the Son. If the proper meaning of this term is sought, it can easily be discovered from its opposite. For if being subject is not good, then what is contrary to it—being unsubjugated—must be good.

According to their interpretation, the Apostle’s statement seems to show this when it says: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him.” It would seem that the one who is not now subject to the Father will then become subject when the Father has first subjected everything to him.

But I am astonished how this can be understood: that the one who is not subject while all things have not yet been subjected to him should be thought to become subject when all things have been subjected to him, when he has become king of all and holds power over everything—although he was not subject beforehand.

They do not understand that Christ’s subjection to the Father shows the blessedness of our perfection and declares the completion of the work he undertook. He offers to the Father not only the supreme authority of ruling and reigning, which he had set right throughout the whole creation, but also the restored and corrected order of obedience and subjection belonging to the human race.

If, therefore, this subjection, by which the Son is said to be subject to the Father, is understood as good and salutary, it is entirely consequential and consistent that the subjection of enemies, which is said to belong to the Son of God, should likewise be understood as salutary and beneficial.

Just as the statement that the Son is subject to the Father (ibid.) declares the perfect restoration of the whole creation, so when the enemies are said to be subject to the Son of God (ibid., 25), the salvation of those who are subject and the restoration of the lost are to be understood in that subjection.

This subjection, however, will be completed through particular means, teachings, and times. The whole world will not be compelled to subjection by any necessity, nor will it be subjected to God by force. Rather, it will be brought to subjection by word, reason, instruction, the encouragement of better things, excellent institutions, and also by fitting and appropriate threats, which justly confront those who disregard the care and healing of their own salvation and welfare.

Indeed, even we human beings, when we educate slaves or children while they are still too young to understand reason, restrain them by threats and fear. But when they have grasped what is good, useful, and honorable, then, once the fear of blows has ceased, they obey every good thing after being persuaded by word and reason.

How, while the freedom of choice of all rational creatures is preserved, each person is to be dealt with—that is, whom the Word of God finds already prepared and capable and instructs; whom it temporarily postpones; from whom it entirely conceals itself and arranges that its hearing be kept far from them, until again, when they despise the Word of God that has been shown and proclaimed to them, it drives them toward salvation through certain corrections and punishments and in a certain way exacts and extorts their conversion—[Col. 1188] and for what reasons or on what occasions these things occur; what divine Wisdom sees within them, or what movements of their purpose it observes when it orders all these things—this is known only to God, and to his only-begotten Son, through whom all things were created and restored, and to the Holy Spirit, through whom all things are sanctified. He proceeds from the Father himself and the Son [Note: [Col. 1188] The manuscripts do not have “and the Son”; neither does Origen]. To him be glory forever and ever.

## BOOK TWO

### Likewise Extracted from the Books of Origen

[Col. 1187]

[Col. 1187] [Note: [Col. 1187] From Origen, chapter 6 of book 3 of *On First Principles*, shortly after the beginning.]

Everywhere and in all things, we say that God is present, because nothing can be empty of God. We do not, however, say that he is now everything in the things in which he is. We must therefore examine more carefully what this means when it signifies the perfection of blessedness and the end of things: namely, that God is said not only to be in all things, but also to be all things.

Let us inquire, then, what these “all things” are in which God will be all things.

I think that the statement that God is all things in all things also means that he is all things in each individual. He will be all things in each person in this way: whatever a rational mind, cleansed of every dreg of vice and completely wiped clean of every cloud of wickedness, is able to feel, understand, or think—that will all be God.

Such a mind will no longer feel anything except God, think of anything except God, see anything except God, or possess anything except God; every movement of it will be God. There will no longer be any distinction between good and evil, because evil will exist nowhere. God will be everything to the one to whom evil no longer clings.

Nor will such a person any longer desire to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, since he is always in the good and God is everything to him.

Thus the end, restored to the beginning, and the outcome of things brought back to their origins, will restore the state that rational nature possessed at the time when it did not need to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. When every perception of wickedness has been removed and cleansed away into sincerity and purity, God alone, who is the one good, will become everything to that nature—not merely in a few or in many things, but so that he himself is everything in all things.

And when death is nowhere, the sting of death nowhere, and evil nowhere at all, then truly God will be all in all.

### CHAPTER XIX
# How the Son Is to Be Subjected to the Father

[Note: [Col. 1187] Beginning of Origen’s Summary of the First Book of *On First Principles*.]

Now that we have, as best we could, gone through these matters that were discussed above, it is time, for the sake of recollection, to recapitulate each of them separately as we mentioned them in various places, and first of all to repeat what concerns the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Although God the Father is indivisible and inseparable from the Son, the Son was not generated from Him by an act of emission, as some suppose. For if the Son is an emission, and “emission” denotes a generation of the sort by which the offspring of animals or human beings usually comes into existence, then necessarily both the one who emits and the one emitted are bodies. We do not say, as the heretics suppose, that some portion of God’s substance was changed into the Son, or that the Son was created by the Father from things that had no subsistence—that is, outside His substance—so that there was a time when He did not exist. Rather, with every bodily conception removed, we say that the Word and Wisdom were begotten from the invisible and incorporeal God without any bodily passion, as though a will proceeds from the mind.

Nor will it seem absurd to speak of the Son as the Son of love, if He is understood in this way also as the Son of will. John likewise indicates that “God is light” (1 John 1:5), and Paul declares that the Son is “the radiance of eternal light” (Hebrews [Col. 1188] 1:3). Just as light could never exist without radiance, so the Son cannot be understood without the Father. He is also called the exact expression of His substance, the Word, and Wisdom.

How, then, can it be said that there was a time when the Son did not exist, or that He once existed when He did not exist? For this means nothing other than saying that there was once a time when truth did not exist, when wisdom did not exist, when life did not exist, although the substance of God the Father is perfectly designated by all these things. They cannot ever be separated from Him or divided away from His substance. Although these are said to be many in thought, in reality and substance they are one, and in them is the fullness of divinity.

Even the statement we make—that there was never a time when He did not exist—must be accepted with indulgence, lest these very words carry the meaning of temporal terminology, namely, “when” or “never.” What is said about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit must be understood as above all time, above all ages, and above all eternity. For this is the one Trinity that surpasses every power of understanding—not only temporal understanding but even eternal understanding. Everything else outside the Trinity must be measured within ages and times.

No one, therefore, should consequently suppose that this Son of God, insofar as He is God the Word “who was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1), is contained in some place—neither insofar as He is Wisdom, nor insofar as He is Life, Justice, Sanctification, or Redemption. For none of these requires a place in order to act or accomplish anything. Rather, each of these must be understood with reference to those who participate in His virtue and activity.

But if someone says that, because those who participate in the Word of God, His Wisdom, His truth, or His life see these things, the Word and Wisdom themselves must also be understood as being in a place, he must be answered as follows: there is no doubt that Christ, insofar as He is the Word and Wisdom, and all the other things named above, was in Paul. For this reason Paul said, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). And again: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

When He was therefore in Paul, who would doubt that He was likewise in Peter, in John, and in each of the saints—not only in those who are on earth but also in those who are in heaven? It would be absurd to say that Christ was in Peter and Paul but was not in the archangels Michael and Gabriel.

From this it is plainly evident that the divinity of the Son of God was not enclosed in any place. Otherwise He would have been in one person alone and not in another. Rather, according to the majesty of His incorporeal nature, since He is enclosed in no place, He is understood to be absent from no place.

Only this distinction must be understood: although He is in different persons—as we have said, in Peter, Paul, Michael, or Gabriel—He is not present in all of them in the same way. For He is more fully, more clearly, and, so to speak, more openly in the archangels than in other holy men. This is evident from the fact that, when the saints have reached the highest perfection, they are said, according to the Gospel’s teaching, to become like or equal to the angels (Matthew 22:30).

It is therefore clear that Christ becomes in each person to the extent permitted by the measure of that person’s merits.

Having briefly recalled these matters concerning faith in the Trinity, it is appropriate also to point out that all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible—whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers—are said to have been created through the Son. Everything was created through Him and in Him. He is before all things, and all things have their existence in Him, who is the Head.

John says something corresponding to this in his Gospel: “All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1:3). David, signifying the mystery of the whole Trinity in the creation of all things, says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of His mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6).

After this we shall appropriately discuss the bodily coming and incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God. We must not understand this in such a way that the entire majesty of His divinity was enclosed within the confines of a very small body, so that the whole Word of God, His Wisdom, His substantial Truth and Life, was either separated from the Father or confined and circumscribed within the smallness of that body, and supposed to have ceased from operating elsewhere.

Rather, between these two positions there must be such a confession of piety that we neither believe that anything of the divinity was lacking in Christ nor suppose that any division whatsoever took place from the Father’s substance, which is everywhere.

John the Baptist indicates something of this kind when, although Jesus was bodily absent, he said to the crowds: “Among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie” (John 1:26). This could not have been said of one who was absent, insofar as bodily presence is concerned, if he were standing among those among whom he was not bodily present.

Thus it is shown that the Son of God was wholly in the body and wholly everywhere.

Yet no one should think that by this we mean to affirm that one portion of the Son of God’s divinity was in Christ, while the remaining portion was elsewhere or everywhere. Only those could think this who are ignorant of the nature of incorporeal and invisible substance. For it is impossible for any division to occur in what is incorporeal.

Rather, He is in all things, through all things, and above all things, in the manner we explained earlier: that is, in the sense in which He is understood as Wisdom, Word, Life, or Truth. By this understanding every local confinement is unquestionably excluded.

Since the Son of God, who is God, wished to appear to human beings for the salvation of the human race and to live among human beings, He assumed not only a human body, as some suppose, but also a soul. This soul was like our souls in nature, but in purpose and virtue it was like Him, and it was such that it could unfailingly fulfill all the will and dispensations of the Word and Wisdom.

That He possessed a soul is most clearly indicated in the Gospel by the Savior Himself, who says: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of my own accord”; and again: “I have authority to lay down my soul, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18). Again He says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38), and: “Now my soul is troubled” (John 12:27).

For the sorrowful and troubled soul cannot be understood as the Word of God, which, by the authority of His divinity, says, “I have authority to lay down my soul.”

Nevertheless, we do not say that the Son of God was in that soul in the same way that He was in the soul of Peter, or Paul, or the other saints, in whom Christ is likewise believed to have spoken, as He did in Paul.

Concerning all those souls, we must accept what Scripture says: “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life is but one day” (Job 25:4).

But this soul that was in Christ, before it knew evil, chose good (Isaiah 7:15). Because it loved righteousness and hated iniquity, God therefore anointed it with the oil of gladness above its companions (Psalm 45:8).

It is anointed with the oil of gladness when it is joined to the Word of God in an undefiled union. For this reason alone among all souls it was incapable of sin, because it was fully and rightly capable of receiving the Son of God. Therefore it is one with Him, is called by His names, and is named Jesus Christ, through whom all things are said to have been made (John 1:3).

Concerning this soul, because it had received within itself the whole Wisdom, Truth, and Life of God, I believe the Apostle also said: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory” (Colossians 3:3).

For what other Christ is to be understood here—He who is said to be hidden in God and afterward to appear—than the one who was anointed with the oil of gladness, filled, that is, substantially filled with God, and in whom He is now said to be hidden?

For this reason Christ is also presented as an example to all believers. Just as He always chose good, even before He knew evil at all, loved righteousness, hated iniquity, and was therefore anointed by God with the oil of gladness, so each person, whether after a fall or after error, should cleanse himself from stains, follow the example set before him, and, with a guide for the journey, walk the difficult road of virtue. Thus, if possible, insofar as it can be achieved, he may through imitation become a participant in the divine nature, as it is written: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as He walked” (1 John 2:6).

This Word and this Wisdom, through imitation of whom we are called wise or rational, becomes all things to all people, so that He may win them all, and becomes weak to the weak, so that He may win the weak.

And because He becomes weak, it is said of Him: “Although He was crucified through weakness, yet He lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

Of this Christ, Paul indicates that he knew nothing among the Corinthians, who were weak, except “Jesus Christ, and Him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).

Some, however, wish even this statement of the Apostle to be understood as spoken of that very soul: when it first assumed a body from Mary, He “who was in the form of God did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7), so that He might undoubtedly restore it to the form of God by better examples and teachings and recall it to that fullness from which it had emptied itself.

Just as, through participation in the Son of God, someone is adopted as a son, and through participation in Wisdom becomes wise in God, so through participation in the Holy Spirit someone becomes holy and spiritual. For to receive participation in the Holy Spirit—the Spirit who belongs to the Father and the Son—is one and the same thing, since the Trinity has one incorporeal nature.

[Note: [Col. 1190] From Chapter 6 of Book 2 of *On First Principles*.]

The preceding discussion has taught, according to the judgment of Scripture, that the only-begotten Son of God, through whom all visible and invisible things were made, both made all things and loves what He made.

For although He Himself is the invisible image of the invisible God, He invisibly granted participation in Himself to all rational creatures, so that each one received as much participation in Him as the affection of love with which it clung to Him permitted.

But because, in accordance with the freedom of the will, variety and diversity of dispositions had affected each person—so that one was held by a more ardent love for his Creator, another by a weaker and more feeble love—that soul of which Jesus said, “No one takes my soul from me” (John 10:18), clung to Him inseparably and indissolubly, as to the Word and Wisdom of God, to the Truth and the true Light. Receiving the whole of Him in its entirety, and itself yielding wholly into His light and radiance, it became with Him, in the primary sense, one spirit.

In the same way the Apostle promises this to those who ought to imitate it: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

Through this substance of the soul, therefore, mediating between God and flesh—for it was not possible for God’s nature to be united with a body without a mediator—the God-man was born, as we have said, with that intermediate substance in place, for which it was not contrary to nature to assume a body.

Nor, again, was it contrary to nature for that soul, being a rational substance, to receive Him into whom, as we said above, it had already wholly yielded, as to the Word, Wisdom, and Truth.

Therefore, deservedly, because it was either wholly in the Son of God or wholly received the Son of God within itself, it too, together with the flesh that it had assumed, is called the Son of God, the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God.

Again, the Son of God, through whom all things were created, is named Jesus Christ and the Son of Man. The Son of God is said to have died, clearly with reference to that nature which could receive death; and He is called the Son of Man, who is proclaimed as coming in the glory of God the Father with the holy angels.

For this reason, throughout all Scripture, divine nature is called by human names, while human nature is adorned with the insignia of divine names.

More than of anyone else, it can be said of Him that which is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), and, “They are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:5).

The Word of God must be thought of as being one flesh with the soul more truly than a man is one flesh with his wife. And with whom is it more fitting to be one spirit with God than with this soul, which joined itself to God through love so completely that it is deservedly called one spirit with Him, as the Prophet says: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:8)?

Because of its love, therefore, it is anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, the soul becomes Christ together with the Word of God. For to be anointed with the oil of gladness means nothing other than to be filled with the Holy Spirit.

The words “above your companions” indicate that the grace of the Spirit was not given to Him as it was to the prophets; rather, the substantial fullness of the very Word of God was present in Him, just as the Apostle says: “In Him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Finally, for this reason the Psalm does not merely say, “You have loved righteousness,” but adds, “and hated iniquity.” To hate iniquity is what Scripture says of Him: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth” (Isaiah 53:9; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). It is also what is meant by: “Tempted in every respect according to our likeness, without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). And He Himself says of Himself: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30).

All these statements indicate that no awareness of sin ever existed in Him.

To make this clearer, the prophet says that no awareness of iniquity had ever entered Him: “Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he turns away from iniquity” (Isaiah 8:4).

If this should seem difficult to anyone because we have shown above that Christ possessed a rational soul, while throughout our discussions we have often demonstrated that the nature of souls is capable of good and evil, the difficulty can be explained in the following way.

I believe, indeed, that the prophet Jeremiah, understanding what the nature of God’s Wisdom in Him is, said this also of the soul that He had assumed for the salvation of the world: “The breath of our face is Christ the Lord, of whom we said, ‘Under His shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lamentations 4:20).

Just as the shadow of our body is inseparable from the body and unfailingly receives and reproduces the body’s movement and gestures, so, I think, the prophet wished to indicate the work and movement of Christ’s soul, which clung to Him inseparably and accomplished everything according to His direction [Note: [Col. 1191] Manuscripts: “according to its movement.”] and will. He therefore called this soul the shadow of Christ the Lord, under whose shadow we would live among the nations.

For in the mystery of this assumption the nations live: through faith they imitate it and come to salvation.

David likewise seems to me to indicate something similar when he says: “Remember my reproach, Lord, with which they reproached me in exchange for your Christ” (Psalm 89:51).

And what else does Paul mean when he says, “Our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3)? And what does he mean elsewhere when he says, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3) [Note: [Col. 1191] Manuscripts: “Do you seek instruction.” Origen: “Do you seek a demonstration.”]

He now says that Christ is hidden in God. The meaning of this is difficult unless it is understood in the way we explained above, namely, that the Prophet signified it by the shadow of Christ.

Perhaps even this exceeds the capacity of the human mind. Indeed, what is more accurate is that we say that the mass of metal, as we have often observed with our eyes in furnaces, becomes entirely fire, since nothing but fire can be seen in it. And if someone attempts to touch or handle it, he will feel not the force of iron but the force of fire.

In this way, then, that soul—which was like iron in fire—was always placed in the Word, always in Wisdom, always in God. Everything it does, feels, and understands is God.

Therefore it cannot be called convertible or changeable, since, through its union with the Word of God, it possesses an unceasing fiery steadfastness.

Finally, we must suppose that some heat of the Word of God has reached all the saints. But in this soul the divine fire itself must be believed to have dwelt substantially, from which some heat has passed to the others.

Finally, the statement, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:8), shows that this soul is anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Word of God and Wisdom—in one way, while its companions, namely, the holy prophets and apostles, are anointed in another.

They are said to have run in the fragrance of His ointments (Song of Songs 1:3). But this soul was the vessel of His ointment, from whose fragrance the worthy prophets and apostles became participants.

Just as the odor of an ointment is one thing and the substance of the ointment another, so Christ is one thing and those who participate in Him another.

And just as the vessel itself that contains the substance of the ointment cannot in any way receive anything foul, while those who participate in its fragrance can receive a foul odor if they withdraw a little farther from its perfume, so it was impossible for Christ’s soul, like a vessel containing the substance of the ointment, to receive an opposing odor. But the closer those who participate in Him are to the vessel, the more they will share in and be capable of its fragrance.

In this way the difficulty of the matter can be explained.

There can be no doubt that the nature of that soul was the same as the nature of all souls. Otherwise it could not truly have been called a soul if it had not really been a soul.

But because the ability to choose good and evil is available to everyone, this soul, which belongs to Christ, chose to love righteousness in such a way that, because of the immensity of its love, it clung to Him immutably and inseparably. Thus the firmness of its purpose, the immensity of its affection, and the unquenchable heat of its love cut off every possibility of change, so that what had originally rested in the will was, through the long practice of affection, transformed into nature.

Thus we must believe both that a human and rational soul truly existed in Christ and that it had no awareness or possibility of sin.

For a fuller explanation of the matter, it does not seem absurd to use an analogy, although in a matter so difficult and profound there is scarcely freedom even to employ suitable examples. We may nevertheless say, without prejudice:

The metal iron is capable of both cold and heat. If, then, some mass of iron were always placed in fire, receiving fire through all its pores and veins and becoming entirely fire, and if the fire never ceased from it and it were never separated from the fire, would we say that this object—which by nature is a mass of iron, but has been placed in fire and burns without interruption—could ever receive cold?

[Note: [Col. 1192] Final words of Chapter 6 of Book 2 of *On First Principles*.]

We also find many other references to the significance of shadow inserted in the divine Scriptures. For example, in the Gospel according to Luke, Gabriel says to Mary: “The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

And the Apostle says of the Law that those who have a carnal circumcision “serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5).

Elsewhere it is said: “Is not our life a shadow upon the earth?” (Job 8:9).

If, therefore, the Law that is upon the earth is a shadow, and all our life that is upon the earth is a shadow, and we live among the nations under the shadow of Christ, we must consider whether the truth of all these shadows will be recognized in that revelation when the saints will be deemed worthy to contemplate, no longer through a mirror and in a riddle but face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12), both the glory of God and the causes and truth of things.

Having already received a pledge of that truth through the Holy Spirit, the Apostle said: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him no longer in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

For the present, these are the matters that have occurred to us as we discuss such difficult subjects, namely, the incarnation and the divinity of Christ. If anyone can discover something better and confirm what he says with clearer assertions from the holy Scriptures, let that be accepted rather than what we have written here.

[Col. 1193]

# One Book on the Trinity and Unity of God (C, G, S)

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Book

This work was formerly divided into thirteen chapters. The last nine contained an abridged and interpolated version of almost the entire book of Augustine *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, with the sayings of those heretics inserted without distinction.

The earlier chapters, however, reproduce, in shortened and corrupted form, several questions from the dialogue of Orosius, which appears in the Appendix to the sixth volume. It is therefore more probable that this book was taken from the Dialogue than that the Dialogue was enriched from this book.

In that portion of the Dialogue which has been transferred here, one finds several words of Augustine. For example, the statement found here in Chapter 3 and in Question 9 of the Dialogue—“If the Spirit were called the Son, He would be called the Son of both; but no one is the son of two, unless …”—is copied from Treatise 99 on John and from Book 15 *On the Trinity*.

Another portion of the same third chapter presents some shorter excerpts from Book 2 *On the Trinity*. Finally, the fourth chapter is taken from Book *Questions on the New Testament*, Question 93. That book of *Questions* is found in the Appendix to the third volume.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1193]

[Note: [Col. 1193] From Question 1 of the dialogue between Orosius and Augustine.]

The opening of Genesis clearly reveals the person of the begotten Son. For it says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). What other beginning should we understand except the Son? For when the Jews asked Him who He was, He answered concerning Himself: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25). Therefore the Beginning is the Son.

Through the Son God made heaven and earth, as John the Evangelist relates: “All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

The Son of God is Son by nature, not by adoption, as it is written: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Psalm 110:3).

God the Father does not have a womb as we do, nor should He be thought to be corporeal. Rather, by “womb” He wished substance to be understood, from which the Son was born.

Whatever the Father is, that He begot: God begot God, light begot light, just as a human being begets a human being and a dog a dog. It has never been seen that a human being begot a dog.

Accordingly, the Father begot the Son neither from nothing nor from some other substance, but from Himself.

[Note: [Col. 1193] From Question 2 of the same dialogue.]

Right faith declares that the Holy Spirit is neither unbegotten nor begotten. For if we say that He is unbegotten, we will seem to affirm two fathers; but if we say that He is begotten, we will be accused of believing in two sons.

What the certain faith maintains is that He is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from both—that is, from the Father and the Son.

To establish this by testimonies, hear our Lord Jesus Christ Himself speaking to His disciples: “When the Paraclete comes,” He says, “whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, He will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

Again, after His resurrection, the Lord Jesus Christ showed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him just as He does from the Father. Breathing upon His disciples, He said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

There is therefore one Spirit of the Father and the Son, the one Spirit of them both.

That He is the Spirit of the Father, the Lord and Savior Himself says to His disciples: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

And that He is also the Spirit of the Son, the Apostle Paul bears witness: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ,” he says, “that person does not belong to Him” (Romans 8:9).

# CHAPTER II
[Note: [Col. 1194] From Question 1 of the dialogue between Orosius and Augustine.] In the name of God, without a doubt, the Father is to be understood; in the name of “the beginning,” the Son. Certainly, after saying, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” he immediately added, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:1–2): he who is the third Person in the Trinity. Therefore, if there were not three Persons, our Lord Jesus Christ would never have said to his disciples, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Nor, when the Lord was baptized by John in the Jordan, would a voice from heaven have been heard saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid. 3:17). Nor would the Holy Spirit have been said to descend upon him in the form of a dove and remain there. Therefore, according to the holy Scriptures, we understand three Persons: that the Father is one, the Son another, who was begotten by the Father, and the Holy Spirit another—not something else, because they are one in substance. We distinguish the Persons; we do not separate the divinity.

[Note: [Col. 1194] From Question 3 of the same dialogue.] That the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, blessed Paul the Apostle demonstrates when writing to the Romans concerning the Son: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9:5). And again in the Gospel according to John: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3)—that is, that you and Jesus Christ whom you sent are the one true God. And again Scripture says, “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; he is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). And to show his equality, the Lord himself said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—that is, in nature, not in Person. And again he says, “For this reason the Jews sought to kill Jesus, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (ibid. 5:18). And again Paul says, “Who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). It could not be seizure where the nature was equal; it was not usurped, but innate; he did not seize it, because he truly possessed it.

[Col. 1195] The Acts of the Apostles most plainly teach that the Holy Spirit is God. “Ananias,” Peter says, “why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” And below: “You have not lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). And in the Gospel according to John he says, “The Lord is Spirit” (John 4:24). Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says, “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?” The same Paul says, “For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20).

The Father is God, I say; the Son is God; the Holy Spirit is God—not three gods, but one God, as Moses says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). Accordingly, just as we say that there are not three gods and not three essences, so neither are there three wisdoms or three spirits. When we are asked individually concerning the Persons whether the Father is wisdom, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, we answer: the Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, the Holy Spirit is wisdom—not three wisdoms or three spirits, but one wisdom and one spirit, just as there is one substance and one essence; for what it is for the Father to be is what it is for the Son, the Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit to be.

[Note: [Col. 1195] From Question 4 of the dialogue between Orosius and Augustine.] Although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are equal, the Son nevertheless says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); and, “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (ibid. 6:38, 40); and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39); and, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16). All these statements, and others that the Son makes, are to be understood and interpreted according to the form of a servant that he assumed.

Therefore, when the first man had been created by God and endowed with free will, and a command had been given to him that, if he kept what God had commanded him, he would not die either bodily or in his soul, he nevertheless disobeyed God’s command, was lifted up in pride, obeyed the serpent’s persuasion, and disregarded the commandments. This became the cause by which he incurred the danger of death; and from that one man the whole of human nature, corrupted and subjected to sin, became mortal. Hence the Apostle Paul says, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all human beings sinned. For just as through one man all human beings fell into condemnation, so also through the justice of one all human beings rose to the justification of life” (Rom. 5:12, 18); and again, “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47).

Thus I call him heavenly because he was not conceived from human seed, but was taken from the Virgin Mary for our salvation by the Son of God, as John testifies: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). “The Word became flesh,” not “was changed into flesh,” as though he ceased to be what he was, but he began to be what he was not: for he assumed flesh; he was not converted into flesh. By “flesh” we understand the whole human being, by a part standing for the whole—that is, flesh and a rational soul. Just as the first man had died in both flesh and soul, so it was necessary that through the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, he should be made alive in both flesh and soul. Therefore, as we said above, the statement “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28) was spoken according to the form of the flesh assumed.

[Note: [Col. 1195] From Question 5 of the same dialogue.] It must not be believed that the Son of God and the Son of Man are two sons, because they are not two sons, but one. For he who was the Son of God became the son of man in the unity of Person. Just as soul and flesh are one human being, so the Word and the human being are one Christ. We accept two substances in the one Son of God: one of divinity, the other of humanity—not two Persons. And if we say two Persons, we shall also introduce two sons of God; and then there will no longer be a Trinity, but a quaternity—which God forbid.

Certainly, in that by which he is God and equal to the Father, he is present everywhere; he is wholly in heaven and wholly on earth, and is contained in no place. In that by which he is human, he suffered and died, rose again and ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father; and thus he will come to judge the living and the dead, in the same manner as he was seen to go into heaven, in the same form and substance of flesh. To that flesh he indeed gave immortality; he did not take away its nature.

[Note: [Col. 1196] From Question 6 of the dialogue between Orosius and Augustine.] Though there is one substance, it was neither the Person of the Father nor that of the Holy Spirit, but the Person of the Son alone, that assumed flesh. To make this understood, I shall use comparisons. Certainly, so that you may understand the Creator from the creature: in the soul there is reason, and although they are one, the soul does one thing and reason another; by the soul we live, by reason we understand. So also, although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one substance, the whole Trinity brought about the human being, but the whole Trinity did not assume him; only the Person of the Son did so.

[Note: [Col. 1196] From Question 7 of the same dialogue.] The Father begot the Son neither by will nor by necessity. Not by necessity, because there is no necessity in God; not by will, because the will cannot precede wisdom, which is the Son. Therefore, rationally to know is prior to rationally to will. Hence the Father begot the Son neither by will nor by necessity, but naturally, by wisdom alone.

[Note: [Col. 1196] From Question 8 of the same dialogue.] “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26). We know that the Son of God is not from himself, but was begotten by the Father; the Father, however, was begotten by no one and received life from no one. The Father gave life to the Son by begetting the life that the Father had in himself. This does not mean that the Son first existed without life and afterward received life, as we, who lost life through sin, received life again through the grace of the Savior. Therefore it is said of him that the Son received life from the Father because he was not begotten from himself: the Father did not give life to one who already existed, but gave it by begetting.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 1196] From Question 9 of the same dialogue.] Since by both argument and testimonies we have established the Son’s subordination—that he is not lesser according to substance, but according to the form of a servant that he assumed—we nevertheless wish to say something about his being called “sent.” We know that, just as the Son is not said to have been sent or to be lesser according to substance, so neither is the Holy Spirit said to have been sent because of the dove or the fire: namely, because he did not appear in that substance in which he is equal to the Father, but, as has been said, through an assumed creature.

For just as the Son assumed a human being so that he might remain forever, the Holy Spirit did not assume a dove or fire. Rather, those manifestations made from a lower creature, serving to reveal the Spirit, afterward ceased to exist. For that incomprehensible and immutable divinity which is God the Trinity can never be seen by bodily eyes except, as has been said, through an assumed creature.

There is this difference between the begotten Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit: the Son is from the Father as one born, not as one given; the Holy Spirit, however, is from the Father and the Son not as one born, but as one given. The Son who was born belongs to the Father alone, not to the Holy Spirit. The Spirit belongs to both—that is, to the Father and the Son—because [Note: [Col. 1196] Words of Augustine in Treatise 99 on John, no. 9.] if the Spirit were called “Son,” he would be called the Son of both. No son, however, belongs to two except to a father and a mother—which God forbid anyone should imagine between God the Father and the Son. For even a human son does not proceed simultaneously from father and mother: when he proceeds from his father, he does not then proceed from his mother; and when he proceeds from his mother into this light, he does not then also proceed from his father. The Holy Spirit, however, does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son to sanctify the creature, but proceeds simultaneously from both.

[Note: [Col. 1196] From Questions 11 and 12 of the dialogue of Orosius, and from Augustine’s On the Trinity, Book 2, chapters 5–7.] Concerning what is said by John, that the Holy Spirit “does not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak” (ibid. 16:13): he does not speak from himself because he is not from himself. For the Father is begotten by no one; the Son is begotten from the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore he does not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak. For “to hear” is his being: he is not from himself, but from the Father; therefore whatever he hears, he will speak.

What does it mean that the Holy Spirit is said to intercede for us, as Paul says in writing to the Romans: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with ineffable groanings. And he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God” (Rom. 8:26)? This mode of expression, which is frequently found in the holy Scriptures, is like what God says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12)—that is, “I have made you know.” Thus the Apostle says, “Now knowing God, or rather, being known by God” (Gal. 4:9). Indeed, all things are present before God before they happen; future things are present as though they had already happened. How does he say “known by God,” unless God makes us know God? So also it is written here that the Holy Spirit groans for us—that is, makes us groan, by pouring into us love for God and neighbor. Thus one reads of “a joyful day,” because it makes people joyful.

The Father alone is nowhere said to have been sent, but the Apostle describes the sending of the Son thus: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (ibid. 4:4–5). That the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, came into the world, the evangelist testifies, saying, “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:10). And he himself says, “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (ibid. 16:28). Likewise the Evangelist says, “And the world did not know him.” Then he adds, “He came to his own” (ibid. 1:10–11). He was sent, certainly, to the place to which he came; but he was sent into this world, where he was. Nevertheless, no Catholic should doubt that this sending is the work of the holy Trinity.

Nowhere is it written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is lesser than God the Father, because this is not so. The Person of his divinity was assumed by the Son of God from the Virgin Mary, and he joined it to the person and condition of his humanity in an eternal unity. Although the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove or fire, we nevertheless cannot say that the Holy Spirit is God and a dove, or God and fire, as we say that the Son is God and human. Because of these bodily forms in which the Holy Spirit appeared, he is said to have been sent; he cannot on account of them be called lesser than the Father, as the Son can be called lesser because of the form of a servant that adhered to him permanently in the unity of Person. Those bodily forms, however—such as that of a dove or of fire—appeared temporarily in order to demonstrate what was necessary, and afterward ceased to exist.

Should not creatures have appeared as was fitting, serving the Creator at his command—he who remains immutable in himself—in order to signify and demonstrate him as he needed to be signified and demonstrated to mortals, being changed and transformed for that purpose?

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Col. 1197] From Questions on the New Testament, Question 93.] Some people are accustomed to ask whether the Apostles possessed the Holy Spirit at the time when they were with Christ the Lord, in accordance with what the Evangelist says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (ibid. 7:39). And in another passage he says, “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him. But you see him and know him, because he remains with you and is with you” (ibid. 14:15–17). And even after his resurrection he is read to have breathed upon the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (ibid. 20:22). At Pentecost, however, the Holy Spirit is read to have descended upon the Apostles (Acts 2:1).

The answer to this is that there is one Spirit, but he has many gifts. There is no doubt that the Holy Spirit was with them, because wherever Christ is, the Holy Spirit is. And because Christ had promised that the Holy Spirit would come from the Father, his divinity was not absent from this matter.

Three forms of the Spirit’s gift were manifested in the Apostles, of which the first pertains to ecclesiastical authority in the regeneration of believers. Ecclesiastical power is understood to reside in the offices of bishops and priests, who ought to perform all things according to the Lord’s tradition through the Holy Spirit. Hence Jesus says to them, “Whose sins you retain, they shall be retained; and whose you remit, they shall be remitted” (John 20:23).

The second form is that which was given at Pentecost and is universal: for the Holy Spirit fell not only upon the Apostles, but also upon all believers. The third form is that which was granted at the beginning only to the Apostles or to those ordained, for the performance of signs and powers, until they had sown the seeds of faith for its increase. For the seeds of faith are the mighty works performed through the Apostles; the Apostles themselves were appointed overseers of this kind of truth, and through signs and wonders they testify that our faith is reasonable.

Therefore the Holy Spirit is given generally to all believers, provided that he remains in them; but through signs and wonders they are proved to be sons of God. Sometimes, however, the Holy Spirit does not remain in a person, but comes when called, to suggest what is necessary, and departs. Likewise, in transmission or ordination, he grants from outside grace and protection to the faithful who are devoted, so that through his inspiration they may be held in higher esteem.

## CHAPTER V

[Note: [Col. 1198] From the book Against the Sermon of the Arians, chapters 1, 2, etc.] The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one true God, according to what is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4). And it is written in the Gospel, “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). And John the Apostle says of Christ, “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

Before all times the Son existed, as is to be understood in the words, “In the beginning was the Word,” and, “All things were made through him.” For time itself cannot exist without some movements of creation. Therefore we confess that the times also were made through the Son, through whom all things were made; and therefore the Son was undoubtedly begotten equal to and coeternal with the Father.

It is said that the Son of God, by the will and command of the Father, made the heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible things, bodies and spirits, from things that did not exist—that is, from nothing, so that they might exist, by his own power [Note: [Col. 1198] Words of the Arians.]—although he himself was not made from things that did not exist, that is, from nothing, but was God from God the Father. This fact indicates one and the same nature of the Father and the Son. The Son could not have made himself, as though he did not exist before he was made, so that he himself might be the one through whom he himself was made. Furthermore, if the Son was made by someone other than the Father, who is that other, since all things were made through him—that is, through his Word?

“Before he made all things, he had been established as God and Lord, king and creator of all future things, possessing in his nature foreknowledge of all future things, and awaiting in the making of everything the Father’s command. By the Father’s will he himself descended from heaven and came into the world, as he himself says: ‘For I have not come of myself, but he sent me’” [Note: [Col. 1198] Likewise, words of the Arians.]

The Trinity itself is one, since from him, through him, and in him are all things. We say that the Son created all things at the Father’s command; he is nothing other than the Word through whom all things were made. That the Father sent the Son, who came with him, is testified by the Son himself, who says, “I am not alone, because the Father is with me.” Therefore the nature is never different because the Father sends and the Son is sent.

A human father can send a human son, who is not of one and the same substance, since a human being sent by a human sender is separated from him; this cannot happen with God. Fire, however, sends forth its radiance, and the radiance cannot be separated from the fire that sends it. When fire sends forth its radiance, the radiance reaches farther than the fire itself reaches.
