Thus, when radiance is sent from the fire that is in a lamp, [Note: [Col. 1198] Augustine, in his book Against the Sermon of the Arians, wrote: “He certainly could not truly say on the wall, to which the fire of the lamp reaches without the lamp’s fire, ‘The fire that sent me is with me’; but the Son sent by the Father could say, ‘The Father is with me.’ The copyist has shamefully disfigured the sentence and adds nothing further except excerpts from the same book of Augustine, Against the Sermon of the Arians, badly joined together and rendered unfit to read by severely truncated or interpolated sentences.”] [Col. 1199] it can truly be said that the fire is on the wall, although the fire of the lamp itself has not reached there.

Concerning this the Son says, “He who sent me is with me” (John 8:42, 16:29)—something the Son could truly say: “The Father is with me.” Since, therefore, this sending of the Son by the Father is altogether ineffable and cannot be grasped by any thought, it can also be understood here that he is said to have been sent by the Father because the Son appeared to human beings in the flesh, not the Father. For where is the Son sent, where he is not? And where is the wisdom of God not? Etc.

[Col. 1199]

# ONE BOOK ON THE ESSENCE OF THE DIVINITY (G,S)*

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

This work was falsely attributed, not only to Augustine but equally to many other authors: Ambrose, Jerome, Anselm, and Bonaventure. Although it does not survive in its entirety under Jerome’s name, but only up to the words “All these things that have been mentioned,” etc., in col. 1208, chapter 2; there it is entitled *On Those Things That Are Attributed to God in Scripture*. In Anselm it is entitled *On the Garments, Members, and Actions Attributed to God*. In Bonaventure it is entitled *On the Essence, Invisibility, and Immensity of God*. In the Vatican and Victorine manuscripts, under Augustine’s name, it bears the title *On the Essence of the Divinity and on the Invisibility and Immutability of God*. The first and largest part of the book is taken from Eucherius of Lyon’s work *On Forms of Spiritual Understanding*; it contains the whole of the first chapter of that work, which concerns the divine names.

## I.

Almighty God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one and triune—one, namely, in nature, but existing as three in persons—is alone invisible, alone immeasurable and incomprehensible, alone uncircumscribed, alone unchangeable, incorporeal and immortal, present everywhere yet hidden; wholly everywhere, yet immeasurable.

He is invisible because he cannot be seen in his essence, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Whom no human being has seen, nor can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). And in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

He is incorporeal because he exists composed or constituted by no outlines of bodily members, just as the Truth says in the Gospel: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

He is immeasurable because his quantity or quality can be measured by none of the creatures. Solomon, pleading with him in his prayer, says: “If heaven and the heaven of heavens do not contain you, how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27).

He is uncircumscribed because he cannot be circumscribed. He is not confined to a place, because he does not pass from place to place, nor is he held within any particular place [Note: [Col. 1199] The Vatican manuscript reads: “contained.”], as he himself bears witness concerning himself through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). And through Jeremiah: “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jer. 23:24).

The prophet, confessing his immensity in the Psalm, says to God himself: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into the underworld, you are present” (Ps. 138:8). Concerning his immensity it is also written in the book of blessed Job: “He is higher than heaven—what can you do? He is deeper than the underworld—how will you know?” (Job 11:8). “Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.”

For he who fills heaven and earth is certainly such that no place is absent from his presence. He presides over every creature, governing and commanding; he is beneath all things, sustaining and carrying them—not by the burden of labor, but by tireless power—for no creature made by him can subsist by itself unless it is sustained by him who created it. He is outside all things, but not excluded; within all things, but not enclosed.

He is unchangeable because he cannot be changed at all from what he is, as he himself says through the prophet Malachi: “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6). God is called unchangeable because anger, wrath, repentance, forgetfulness, remembrance, and other things of this kind in no way occur in his nature. For his nature is simple, unchangeable, and undisturbed; he is not one thing and what he possesses another, but he is himself what he possesses and what he is.

He is immortal because he cannot die in any way, as the Apostle attests, saying: “He alone possesses immortality, dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen, nor can see” (1 Tim. 6:16).

Whenever sacred Scripture, scattered throughout the divine books, describes in God the movements of the soul or human members—that is, the head, hair, eyes, eyelids, ears, nostrils, mouth, lips, tongue, heart, image, womb, hands, right hand, left hand, fingers or finger, arm, wings, shoulders, back parts, and feet; and likewise the movements of the soul—anger, wrath, forgetfulness, remembrance, repentance, and others of this kind, these are not to be understood by those who interpret correctly in a carnal manner according to the historical sense [Note: [Col. 1200] Jerome has “to be understood”], as they are by Jews and by most heretics who think carnally and suppose God to be corporeal and confined to a place. Rather, everything concerning him is to be understood and confessed spiritually.

If anyone believes that human members or movements of the soul exist in God in a human manner, he undoubtedly fashions idols in his heart.

Therefore, as has been said, when we read figuratively of God’s head, we must understand it as his very divine essence, which precedes all things and to which everything is subject. His head’s hair, however, must be understood typologically as the holy angels or all the elect.

Concerning this mystery it is written in the book of the prophet Daniel: “I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool” (Dan. 7:9). The white clothing and the hair of his head signify the holy angels and the multitude of whitened saints. Or certainly his hair is compared to clean wool so that by this he may be believed to be the Ancient of Days.

God is said to have eyes because he sees everything and nothing is hidden from him. In his sight, as the Apostle says, no creature is invisible: “For all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4:13).

In another sense, the eyes of the Lord are understood as the regard of his grace, as in the Psalm: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33:16).

Again, in another sense, the eyes of the Lord are mystically understood as his commandments, through which the light of knowledge is supplied to us, as in the Psalm: “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9).

The eyelids of the Lord indicate his hidden and incomprehensible judgments, or his spiritual speech in the divine books. Concerning these hidden and incomprehensible mysteries and judgments it is written in the Psalm: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. 10:5)—that is, they test them.

God is said to have ears because he hears everything and nothing escapes him in silence. Concerning this it is written in the book of Wisdom: “The ear of jealousy hears all things, and the tumult of murmuring will not be hidden” (Wis. 1:10).

The nostrils of God signify his inspiration in the hearts of the faithful, as in the book of Kings: “Smoke rose from his nostrils” (2 Kings 12:9)—that is, the tearful compunction of repentance through his inspiration [Note: [Col. 1201] The Sorbonne manuscript reads “by inspiration”; Jerome has “through the inspiration of him.”].

The face of God signifies the knowledge of his divinity among human beings. Concerning this knowledge it is written in the Psalm: “Show us, Lord, your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:4)—that is, “Give us knowledge of you.” This knowledge became known to human beings through the Son, who says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

In another sense, the face of God signifies the invisible essence of the divinity of the Son of God. Concerning this the Lord himself, answering Moses through the angel, says: “You shall see my back parts, but my face you cannot see” (Exod. 33:23), as though he were saying: “You will see my incarnation in the last days, but you will not be able to see my divinity.”

The mouth of God is the Son of God the Father, that is, Christ the Lord. Concerning him the prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Jews, says: “For we provoked his mouth to anger” (Lam. 1:18).

In another sense, the mouth of the Lord is understood as his speech or command. Concerning this speech of the Lord the aforementioned prophet says: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 58:14)—that is, the Word of God, the Son of the Father, through whom all things were made. Concerning him it is said in the Psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 33:6). And elsewhere: “He sent his Word and healed them” (Ps. 106:20). And in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

The tongue of God mystically signifies the Holy Spirit, through whom God the Father revealed his secret to human beings. Hence in the Psalm: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44:2).

The lips of the Lord signify the agreement of the two Testaments. Concerning these two Testaments it is written in Proverbs: “Divination is on his lips; his mouth shall not err in judgment” (Prov. 16:10).

The arms of God the Father are understood as his Son and the Holy Spirit, as in the prophet Isaiah: “And my arms shall judge the peoples” (Isa. 51:5).

The arm of God the Father in the singular is understood as his Son. Concerning him the prophet Jeremiah says to God himself: “And now, Lord God, who brought out your people from the land of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm” (Jer. 32:21). The Son of God the Father is called his arm because every elect creature is held together by him.

The right hand of God the Father is understood as the same only-begotten Son. Concerning him the Psalm says in the person of the assumed human being: “The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. 117:16).

In another sense, the right hand of the Lord signifies the glory of the Father, that is, eternal blessedness. Concerning this the Psalm says, in the person of the Father to the Son: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

The right hand of God is also said to be every elect creature in heaven and on earth, just as by his left hand is understood the reprobate creation: that is, the demons and all the impious, who, placed on the left, will endure eternal punishments.

The hand of God the Father is understood as the Son of God, because through him all things were made, as in the prophet Isaiah: “All these things my hand has made” (Isa. 66:2), and all things came into being.

In another sense, the hand of God is understood as his power. Concerning this power it is written in the book of Jeremiah: “As clay is in the hand of the potter, so you are in my hand, house of Israel” (Jer. 18:6).

The hand of God is also understood as a scourge. Concerning its striking it is written in the prophet Zephaniah: “I will stretch out my hand against Judah and against the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and I will destroy from this place the remnants of Baal, etc.” (Zeph. 1:4). Concerning this striking of the Lord blessed Job says of himself: “The hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job 19:21).

The finger of God in the singular is understood as the Holy Spirit. By that Holy Spirit the Law is said to have been written on two stone tablets on Mount Sinai. He himself wrote who dictated what was to be written—that is, the Holy Spirit. Concerning this Holy Spirit the Lord says in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20). Another Evangelist explains this openly, saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28).

For just as the finger together with the hand or arm, and the hand or arm together with the body, are one in nature, so the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are indeed three persons, but one substance of divinity.

The fingers of God in the plural are understood as the holy prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit, by his inspiration, wrote the books of the Law and the Prophets. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm: “I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8:4). By the heavens he mystically signified the books of the Law and the Prophets; by the fingers, the holy prophets, as has been said.

The image of the invisible God the Father is his only-begotten Son, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Who is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15).

The image of God the Father in his Son is one thing: he begot him not from elsewhere but from himself—that is, from his own substance—wholly like himself and equal to him. It is another thing in the human soul, which he did not beget from himself, that is, from his substance, as many heretics have supposed, but created from nothing.

It is like the difference between the image of any king in his son, whom he begot from himself, like himself—namely, a human being from a human being—and the image of that king impressed upon his ring or in wax. The latter is not what he himself is, whereas the son, naturally, is what the father is.

The heart of God the Father mystically indicates the secret of his wisdom, from which he begot the Word, that is, his Son, impassibly and without beginning. He himself says through the prophet: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44:2).

God is read to have wings because, like a bird, he gathers his elect beneath himself as chicks, cherishes them, and protects them from the snares of the devil and wicked people. Concerning this protection the Prophet says to him in the Psalm: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:8).

God is said to have shoulders because he patiently carries the weak members of the Church, as though upon his shoulders, and protects them by carrying them. Concerning this it is said of the righteous man in the Psalm: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you will hope” (Ps. 90:4).

The belly of God the Father is understood as the secret origin of his substance, from which origin he ineffably begot his Son before every creature. He himself bears witness through the prophet, saying—that is, the Father to the Son: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

In another sense, the womb of God mystically indicates his incomprehensible and hidden judgments, which cannot be investigated. Concerning these hidden judgments it is written in Job: “From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who gave birth to the frost from heaven?” (Job 38:29).

The back parts of the Son of God are understood as his incarnation, which took place at the end of time for the redemption of the human race. Concerning this posterior part the Son of God, speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai through the angel, says: “You shall see my back parts, but you cannot see my face” (Exod. 33:23), as though he were saying to him: “You shall see my incarnation, but you shall not be able to see my deity.”

The feet of God are the foundation of his power and might, because he is present everywhere and all things are subject to him. He himself says through the prophet Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1).

In another sense, the feet of the Son of God are understood as his incarnation, which is subject to the divinity, like feet to the head, or because the incarnation itself took place toward the end of the world. For just as the head signifies the divinity, as has been said, so by the feet human nature is figuratively expressed. Concerning this humanity it is written in Exodus: “They saw the God of Israel”—that is, Moses and Aaron and Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of the people—“and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. 24:10).

Just as by the sapphire stone he wished to signify the heavenly creatures, that is, the holy angels, so by the clear sky he figuratively wished to signify the holy Church of the elect, taken from among human beings. Over these two creatures the human being assumed by the Son of God reigns forever.

Concerning him the Psalm says: “He has put all things under his feet” (Ps. 8:8).

In another sense, the feet of the Lord, that is, of Jesus Christ, signify the holy preachers, concerning whom it is written in Deuteronomy: “Those who approach his feet shall receive instruction from him” (Deut. 33:3).

The clothing of the Son of God is sometimes understood figuratively in the divine books as his flesh, which was assumed by the divinity. Concerning this garment of his flesh the prophet Isaiah prophesies: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1).

Again, the clothing of the same Lord is understood as the holy Church, which is joined to him through faith and love. Concerning it it is written in the Psalm: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Ps. 92:1). And in another Psalm addressed to the Lord himself: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothed in light as with a garment” (Ps. 104:2).

The cloak of Christ is rightly understood as the Church already mentioned. Concerning it it is written in the book of Genesis: “He shall wash his robe in wine”—that is, his flesh in the blood of his passion—“and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49:11)—that is, his Church.

The footwear of our Lord Jesus Christ mystically signifies his incarnation, which he deigned to assume from the mortality of the human race. Concerning this incarnation he himself says through the Prophet in the Psalm: “I will stretch out my shoe over Edom” (Ps. 59:10)—that is, “I will manifest my incarnation to the people of the Gentiles.”

The steps of God signify the coming of the Son of God into the world and his return to the Father. Concerning these steps the Psalmist sings: “Your steps have been seen, O God, the steps of my God and King who is in the sanctuary” (Ps. 67:25).

For he came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb; from the womb, by being born, he was placed in a manger. After he had fulfilled everything for which he had come, sent by the Father, he was hung upon the wood of the cross. Taken down from the cross, he was buried according to the flesh, but according to the soul he descended to the underworld. On the third day, by the power of his divinity, he raised his flesh from the tomb. After the days of his resurrection—namely, on the fortieth day—he ascended into heaven in the sight of the Apostles (Acts 1:9), and sits at the right hand of the Father, that is, in his glory.

These are the steps of the Son of God: his descent and ascent, which are frequently mentioned in the sacred Scriptures.

God is said to ascend when the Son of God carried into heaven, as a captive, the flesh assumed from us, as in the Psalm: “He ascended on high; he led captivity captive” (Ps. 67:19). For when he assumed the nature of the human race, which was held captive in the world by the devil, he carried it with himself into heaven, where it had never previously been, as though carrying it captive.

God is read to hide his face when, because of the guilt of certain reprobates, he hides his knowledge from them. We now see this fulfilled among the Jewish people: by denying the Son of God, they lost knowledge of the true God and became like the Gentiles who did not know God.

God is said to show his face when, by the regard of his grace, he secretly introduces himself into the hearts of those whom he wills—namely, his elect—through hidden inspiration, and pours his love into them so that they may love him.

God is said to sit not bodily in the human manner, but by his power to preside over every rational creature [Note: [Col. 1203] Jerome has: “to preside by reigning over every creature”], as in the Psalm: “The Lord has reigned over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne” (Ps. 46:9).

God is also said to sit upon the cherubim. “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” or “multitude”; by this are signified the holy angels or the minds of spiritual men, in whom God invisibly presides and reigns. He sits in those who are filled with his knowledge and love. For in Solomon’s Proverbs it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” The Wisdom of God the Father is Christ, who is said to sit in the souls of the righteous.

God is read to descend into the world when he works something new in human creation that had not existed before. Thus the Son of God is said to have descended when he assumed true flesh from the Virgin Mary for our redemption and deigned to become a true human being—not by losing what he was, but by assuming what he was not.

Concerning this descent, that is, his incarnation, it is written in the Psalm: “He inclined the heavens and descended, and darkness was beneath his feet” (Ps. 17:10). He inclined the heavens because before his coming he sent angels or prophets as heralds, who announced his coming to human beings. Darkness was beneath his feet because impious people, blinded by their own wickedness, could not recognize his incarnation—and still cannot.

God is said to stand when he patiently sustains us in our weakness—that is, his creature—in repentance and conversion of life. Thus in the prophet Habakkuk: “He stood and measured the earth, and dissolved the nations” (Hab. 3:6)—that is, he stood to give help and released believers in him from the bonds of sins.

God is said to pass over when, from the hearts of certain people in whom he was previously believed to dwell through faith, he later departs because faithlessness or some sin has secretly crept in, and passes over to others.

Thus God is said to have departed from the Jews to the Gentiles, and from heretics to Catholics, or to depart from any irreligious or negligent people on account of their vice and to pass over to others. He does this not locally or visibly, but invisibly, by a hidden and just judgment.

God is said to walk not by passing from place to place—for it is impious to believe this—but his walking consists in delighting in the hearts of the saints, as it is written: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God” (Lev. 26:12). Or certainly God’s walking consists in his passing from place to place in his holy preachers.

God’s speaking consists in his invisibly and secretly inspiring his will and right understanding into the minds of the saints, without the sound of a voice or any noise [Note: [Col. 1204] Alternatively: “secret”], or in revealing future things, as he did to the holy prophets.

According to some, this speaking of God is understood in three ways.

First, it occurs through a created intermediary, as when he appeared to Moses in the bush and in the fire; or as when he deigned to appear to Abraham, Jacob, the Moses already mentioned, and the other saints to whom he wished to appear—in angels.

Second, it occurs in dreams, as to Jacob, the prophet Zechariah, Joseph the husband of Mary, and other saints to whom he wished to reveal secrets.

Third, it occurs neither through a visible creature nor through a dream, but by invisibly touching the hearts of the saints with hidden inspiration and causing them to speak [Note: [Col. 1204] Jerome has: “affecting them by touching them”]. Thus it is read in the books of the prophets, when the prophets themselves, suddenly inspired by the divine Spirit, exclaimed, saying: “Thus says the Lord.”

God’s seeing consists in approving good deeds, as in Genesis: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. 1:31)—that is, he demonstrated that they were good to those who understand.

In another sense, God’s seeing consists in rejecting human evils by knowing them, as in the prophet Isaiah: “The Lord saw, and it appeared evil in his eyes” (Isa. 59:15).

Again, in another sense, God’s seeing consists in making us see—that is, making us know—as in the Psalm: “Test me, Lord, and know my heart; question me, and know my paths, and see whether there is any way of iniquity in me, etc.” (Ps. 138:23).

This mode of speaking is likewise found in the book of blessed Job. After saying many remarkable things about the wisdom of God the Father, he added: “Then he saw it, and declared it; he investigated it and prepared it” (Job 28:27)—that is, he made people see, proclaim, investigate, and announce it to others.

God’s knowing consists in making people know, as he himself says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12). For he did not come to know this at that moment, since he knows all things before they happen. Rather, God is said to know when he makes people know, so that those who were previously unknown to themselves in regard to what they were might, through his questioning—that is, his testing—become manifest to themselves.

The same is true of what is said in the Law of Moses concerning the Israelite people: “I will test them,” he says, “whether they will keep my commandments or not” (Deut. 13:3).

God’s not knowing consists in rejecting certain reprobates, as in the Gospel: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27; Ps. 6:9).

God is said to be jealous when he often chastises, reproves, and scourges his creature, whom he does not wish to perish, and by scourging brings it back to himself. Or certainly God is said to be jealous when he does not wish to leave any sin unpunished. For he is just, and therefore every injustice is detestable to him; as has been said, he in no way permits it to go unpunished.

God is said to be angry not because of any movement of the soul or disturbance, which cannot occur in him at all, but because he is said to inflict just vengeance upon the sinful creature—that is, upon impious and sinful human beings. This means that he gives them what they deserve; and this divine vengeance is called his anger or wrath.

God is said to repent not because he regrets his past works in the human manner—for he knows all things before they happen and therefore cannot repent of his past deeds—but God’s repentance consists in changing his decrees and changing into something else what had previously been begun in another way.

This may be from good to evil because of the demands of guilt, as God is read to have repented that he had made Saul king (1 Kings 15:11); or as we now see to have happened among the Jewish people, who, having been God’s people, became, because of their impiety, the synagogue of Satan.

It may also be from evil to good, as happened among the Gentile peoples, who previously were not God’s people but have now, through the grace of Christ, become God’s people.

In this way, by God’s hidden judgment, Judas the traitor fell from the rank of apostleship and was plunged into the abyss of hell, while the thief, after the crime of robbery, was transferred from the cross to paradise.

This change from good to evil, as has been said, or from evil to good—whether it takes place by God’s hidden and just judgment, through the severity of justice or through his mercy—we call God’s repentance.

This is expressed more clearly in the book of the prophet Jeremiah.

God’s not repenting consists in not changing his decrees in any way, as in the Psalm: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent”—that is, the Father says to the Son: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

The Son of God is called the priest of the Father not according to his divinity but according to his humanity, in which he offered himself to God the Father as an acceptable sacrifice for us through his passion and death, so that he himself might be both the priest and the sacrifice.

God is said to forget when he does not show mercy to certain impious and sinful people. He does this not through cruelty, which does not exist in God, but through his hidden and just judgment.

God is said to harden the hearts of certain evil people, as it is written concerning Pharaoh, king of Egypt—not because almighty God hardens their hearts by his power, for it is impious to believe this, but because, in response to their guilt, he does not remove the hardness of heart that they themselves foster by committing evil. Thus he seems to harden them because, by a just judgment, he permits them to be hardened.

God’s sleeping consists in the occasion when the only-begotten Son of the Father deigned to die for us in the flesh he had assumed. His death was rightly proclaimed a sweet sleep, as he himself says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Therefore, as one awakened from sleep, I arose; and I saw, and my sleep was sweet to me” (Jer. 31:26).

In another sense, God is said to sleep when faith in him does not remain vigilant amid the prosperity of this world in the hearts of certain believers, but sleeps [Col. 1206]. Our Savior signified this sleep in himself when he slept in the boat amid the waves of the sea (Matt. 8:24).

Or certainly God’s sleeping consists in his coming slowly to the aid of his elect when they are placed in the tribulations of this world, as in the Psalm: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. 43:23).

God’s vigilance consists in showing himself manifestly for the defense of his elect and the vengeance of his enemies [Note: [Col. 1206] Here this book ends in the Sorbonne manuscript and in Jerome.].

## II.

All these things that have been mentioned, and others like them, which sacred Scripture narrates about God according to the historical sense, are not to be understood according to the letter, as has been said, but as meaningful expressions. For almighty God in the essence of his divinity is spirit, not flesh; invisible and incorporeal, composed of no human members. Therefore he is to be contemplated not with the eyes of the flesh but with the eyes of the heart.

God is wisdom, truth, love, and justice. Therefore he is to be seen with those same eyes with which all these things are contemplated. For this reason the faithful must behold him not with bodily sight, as has been said, but with a pure heart.

It is written in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

This is the reward promised to the saints—not only in this life, but especially in the life to come. Blessed John the Apostle says: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. For we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

This promise, as has been said, is reserved for the saints in the future age, after the resurrection of the flesh and the judgment of God.

In the present life, however, there has never been and never can be any saint so holy, nor anyone among God’s elect so perfect, that he has seen or will be able to see the Lord himself in the essence of his divinity as he is. He himself testifies to Moses: “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20), as though he were saying: “No one, so long as he lives as a mortal, will be able to see God as he is.”

The saints do see God in the present life, but not as he is in his substance; rather, they see him “through a mirror and in a riddle, but afterward face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). In this life they see him by believing, not by perceiving him with bodily eyes.

To see God is to believe rightly in him and love him from the heart. This is signified by the name Israel, which is interpreted as “a man seeing God.”

But because the Son of God, who is one with the Father in the substance of divinity, came down near the end of the world into the womb of the Virgin Mary for the restoration of the human race, which had fallen in Adam, and created true flesh from her substance and united it in the singularity of his person in such a way that he was equally God and human being; and because he was born from that same Virgin in one person, as has been said, but with a twofold substance and in incorrupt virgin modesty—so that he who was and is true God in divinity, begotten from the true Father, invisible, incorporeal, and incomprehensible like the Father, might himself also be a true, visible, corporeal, and circumscribed human being; and so that he himself, not one God and another human being, but God and human being, one Christ, the Son of God, might suffer for our salvation, die and be buried in the flesh alone, rise from the tomb in that same flesh on the third day by the power of his divinity, ascend into heaven, and sit at the right hand of the Father—

and because the universal Church awaits him coming from there to judge the living and the dead in that same flesh in which he ascended, but glorified, as all the faithful proclaim in the Creed, therefore the same Son of God must be believed and confessed, according to the substance of his divinity, to be invisible, incorporeal, immortal, and uncircumscribed, just as the Father and the Holy Spirit are.

According to his humanity, however, it is right to believe and confess him to be visible, corporeal, local, and truly possessing all human members.

For just as it is impious not to believe the same Son of God and our Redeemer, according to his divinity, to be invisible and incorporeal, as are the Father and the Holy Spirit, so after the resurrection it is profane not to believe and confess the same Son of God in the human being he assumed to be visible, corporeal, and local.

As for what is written in Genesis, when God the Father says to the Son: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), this is not to be understood as though God were corporeal and composed of the outlines of limbs, and had made our exterior human being—that is, the human body—according to that bodily composition as though according to his likeness, as Jews and many other unbelievers have supposed. To believe this is impious.

God, as has often been said, is spirit, not flesh; he is wisdom [Note: [Col. 1207] Thus the Victorinus manuscript. The printed editions read: “substance.”], not body.

God made the human being in his image not in the body but in the soul; not in the body but in understanding; not in the exterior human being but in reason.

The human soul, as has been said, is said to have been made in the image of God because it is a spiritual, invisible, incorporeal, and immortal creature. It does not derive its origin from God’s substance, as the heretics Manichaeans and Priscillianists falsely supposed, but was created by God from nothing.

It has a beginning but has no end.

The human soul is called the image of God because God made it rational and intellectual. For it possesses by nature rational understanding, through which it understands, knows, and distinguishes between good and evil. It possesses memory, through which it recalls past things; it possesses will, through which it chooses what it wishes; it possesses sensation, through which it perceives; it possesses reason, through which it contemplates both hidden and invisible things [Col. 1208], through which it understands God its creator, through which it distinguishes truth from falsehood, and through which it contemplates or beholds invisible things and God with the eyes of the heart [Note: [Col. 1208] The Victorinus and Vatican manuscripts read: “and beholds through the eyes of the heart.”].

In all these respects the human soul is said to have been made in the image of God. It shares all these things with the angels, but shares the body with brute animals that lack understanding.

The origin of this soul is hidden and known to God alone.

The human soul itself, because it is a spiritual creature, is sometimes called “spirit” in sacred Scripture; at other times “nature” [Note: [Col. 1208] The Vatican and Victorinus manuscripts read: “sometimes soul”]; sometimes also “life,” and occasionally “heart.” Although it is one in its nature, it has acquired different names because of its various effects [Note: [Col. 1208] The Victorinus manuscript reads: “different affections.”].

The likeness of God, however, is referred to the work of righteousness, as the Lord says in the Law: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 19:2).

Concerning this holiness blessed Paul the Apostle instructs us: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who has been created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:23).

And again he himself says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1).

Blessed John likewise exhorts us: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2:6).

And the Truth says in the Gospel: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

For just as the image of God pertains to the nature of the soul, so the likeness refers to the work of righteousness.

# A Dialogue on the Unity of the Holy Trinity

[Note: [Col. 1207] By an unknown but very ancient author. It is not extant in manuscripts eight hundred years old, namely in two Remigian manuscripts. One of these prefaces this very title without Augustine’s name: “Here begins a little book, or dialogue, on the Unity of the Holy Trinity”; the other attributes the dialogue to Augustine with this inscription: “Here begins the treatise of Saint Augustine, bishop, by himself ‘to himself.’” This is certainly false, as is sufficiently clear from the manner of expression, although this very codex is thought to have been written about eight hundred years ago and copied from a still older exemplar. This is shown by the writing at the end of the dialogue, made by exactly the same pen: immediately after the word “may obtain,” on the same line, follows: “I have compared it, as I was able, with every care; you who read, pray for me.”]

(C,G,S)

[Col. 1207] When sleepless concern for the faith had made me wakeful, I questioned myself with these inquiries and kindled the light of our school with such diligence. Let the reader judge whether this is useful to him; for me, however, if he neglects it, it takes nothing away.

**QUESTION.** “The Father,” they say, “is God?”

**ANSWER.** No profane person is ignorant of that.

**Q.** Is the Son God?

**A.** The Apostle is witness.

**Q.** What does he say?

**A.** “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom. 9:5).

**Q.** What do you affirm concerning the Holy Spirit?

**A.** A great brevity in teaching that he is God supports me.

**Q.** I desire to know what that is.

**A.** That he proceeds from the Father. I shall prove only that he also forgives sins.

**Q.** Where do you read that?

**A.** In John, when the Lord breathed upon the face of the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22–23).

**Q.** Nothing could be stronger.

**A.** Do you know nothing else?

**Q.** What?

**A.** That he creates Christ in the womb; that he came upon Christ in the river; that he gives life to all things; that he consecrates Baptism; that he directs Christ; that he fills the world; that he is joined to the Trinity; that he knows, embraces, and governs all things, not only earthly but heavenly things also; that he chooses and commissions the Apostles; that he bestows his gifts and prophecies upon whomever he wills; and many other things which are set forth in the Holy Scriptures [Col. 1208] but do not occur to me at this moment. And if these things do not move you, for me the single fact that he is from the Father would have sufficed as proof of his deity.

There are also particular statements that support this truth, such as those of Paul: “There are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:5–6). And among other statements, that of Peter: “In truth,” he says, “I understand that God is not a respecter of persons.” When the Holy Spirit had spoken to him while he was pondering and hesitating about the vision, saying, “Arise and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them to you” (Acts 10:20, 34).

For David very often calls him the “upright Spirit” in the fiftieth Psalm. In the ninety-first he calls him Lord God: “For the Lord our God is upright,” he says, “and there is no unrighteousness in him.” And in the twenty-eighth Psalm he declares, “The Lord is over many waters,” those waters over which Genesis at its beginning proclaims the Spirit of God to have moved (Gen. 1:2).

Although I clearly know that the Holy Spirit could never have been numbered with the Father, or even with the Son, unless he reigned with them in a shared deity, since it is said, “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

**Q.** What then? Are there three Gods?

**A.** Far be it from us: “He who sacrifices to gods shall be exterminated,” unless it be to the Lord alone.

**Q.** Are there two?

**A.** Certainly not, because “no one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24).

**Q.** May one be proved?

**A.** There is no God except one.

**Q.** I read that; but I wish to know how it is true of the whole Trinity.

**A.** You will know if you fix your mind upon the words. The Father is an appellative name, the Son is an appellative name, and likewise “Holy Spirit” is both an appellative and a natural name. Although “Father” is said in relation to the Son and “Son” in relation to the Father, these names are called relative names. But “God” is the proper name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Psalm: “According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 47:11). Therefore the appellative names are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the proper name is God, God, God.

**Q.** Then there are three gods?

**A.** I ask you to recall something else: “Hear, O Israel; the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6:4). Do you see, I ask, a certain royal elevation of meaning in this statement?

**Q.** Explain it briefly; I shall listen.

**A.** “The Lord,” it says, “your God, the Lord is one.” Unless I am mistaken, here he has united a threefold designation of God: “the Lord,” he says, “and your God, and the Lord.” You have what the Father, what the Son, and what the Holy Spirit are. And immediately he added, “is one.” O clear light of unity!

**Q.** Where, then, is the Trinity?

**A.** In the one who begets, the one begotten, and the one proceeding; that is, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, namely in appellative or relative names.

**Q.** What of the proper names—God, God, and God? Is a threefold repetition not admitted?

**A.** No.

**Q.** Why?

**A.** Because he is one; proper terms are not tripled.

**Q.** Therefore the Trinity is understood in relative names.

**A.** It is.

**Q.** In which names?

**A.** In the distinction of persons and names: of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Finally, Christ himself does not say, “Go, baptize the nations in the name of gods,” but “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” so that he might teach the Trinity in the relative names of the persons, while showing the name of God—which is not tripled—in its singularity.

**Q.** Do the proper names therefore not run together with the appellative ones?

**A.** They do run together.

**Q.** Then are they also counted together?

**A.** Far be it from us; for if we triple them, we introduce a plurality of gods.

**Q.** Then the Father is not God?

**A.** He certainly is God.

**Q.** Then the Son is not God?

**A.** He most certainly is God.

**Q.** Then the Holy Spirit is not God?

**A.** He is God without ambiguity.

**Q.** You see three; do you dare to call them gods? But, as I see it, the Trinity is believed in relative terms.

**A.** Certainly in natural terms and persons, and in relative names.

**Q.** Why then, “God, God, and God”?

**A.** They are natural names. “God” is natural to each, but it is a proper name. For we cannot say “three gods,” but we speak of the Trinity in the relative terms of nature and in the persons—that is, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But we speak of unity in “God, God, and God.”

**Q.** Then do you not say three persons?

**A.** We do.

**Q.** And do you believe that in each individual person there is God, God, and God?

**A.** It is plainly evident that this must be believed without hesitation.

**Q.** Then, just as you say three persons, do you also say three gods?

**A.** Far be it from us.

**Q.** Why?

**A.** Because there is distinction in the persons, but none in the deity.

**Q.** What is this distinction?

**A.** The Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit.

**Q.** Do you maintain that you worship the Trinity through diversity?

**A.** Through diversity of persons and names, not of nature, because it is one.

**Q.** Certainly, you said earlier that these names too were natural and appellative; repeat which are the proper ones [Note: [Col. 1209] Another reading: “find”].

**A.** “God, God, and God”: therefore, when tripled, these do not create a difference [Note: [Col. 1209] The manuscripts read: “create a difference of names”].

**Q.** Therefore proper names are not tripled along with natural appellatives.

**A.** By no means.

**Q.** Then Father and God, Son and God, or Holy Spirit and God are not joined together.

**A.** They certainly are joined together: the same Father is God, the same Son is God, and the same Holy Spirit is without doubt united to his deity.

**Q.** Deity will be tripled.

**A.** That is the fault of sacrilege [Col. 1210] [Note: [Col. 1210] Another reading: “is known”], because number is under God, not within God.

**Q.** Then the Father is not called God, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit?

**A.** We are taught, and we believe, precisely so that we deprive neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit of his deity.

**Q.** Yet you seem to do that when you say, “The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God,” since the conclusion is that together they are other gods.

**A.** Would human ears really hear this without all being smeared with spittle? Nevertheless, in the appellative names—that is, in the persons—I understand the Trinity; but I firmly believe that the deity cannot in any way be tripled [Note: [Col. 1210] Another reading: “I concede.”], because I find no variety or distinction in the nature.

**Q.** How many names do you believe there are?

**A.** Three relative names in the persons.

**Q.** How many proper names?

**A.** I have already endured you several times as you ask, in the plural, about the proper name; but the proper name of the deity is one.

**Q.** You have removed a great *macheria* [Note: [Col. 1210] Another reading in the second Remigian manuscript: *macaeria*.], but tell me: is this name natural?

**A.** Certainly.

**Q.** And are the relative names that you call appellative natural?

**A.** They are also natural, but through the efficacy of generation and procession, not through the property of the undivided deity.

**Q.** Therefore, unless the Son were Son of God, he could not be God?

**A.** Why do you doubt it?

**Q.** Because he is Son of God, therefore he is God.

**A.** I agree.

**Q.** And if there were no efficacy of generation that conferred the appellative name upon the Son, he would neither have the proper name of deity nor be God.

**A.** Certainly. Through generation the Son is the Son, and “God” is truly the proper name of the Son of God. He did not receive it later, when previously he did not have it; rather, when he was begotten, he received it timelessly from the timeless one.

**Q.** What of the Holy Spirit?

**A.** Unless he too proceeded from the Father and possessed his substance, he would not be God.

**Q.** Did procession therefore confer deity upon him?

**A.** In the Holy Spirit there are both name and nature; but because he proceeded from the Father, he therefore obtained the proper name of deity. For nothing other than what the Father himself is could proceed from the Father; yet the Father was neither exhausted nor divided. Thus “Holy Spirit” is a natural and personal appellative; “God,” however, is the proper name.

**Q.** What account does the name you call proper contain, so that it applies equally to three persons and yet is not tripled? In the same way, verbally, we can designate several persons as Statius, Sallust, or Horace.

**A.** I shall unravel the reasoning as best I can, if you attend carefully.

**Q.** I am attentive.

**A.** We read Paul saying of Christ that he is our peace, “who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). Let this support for our invincible case serve this purpose: that it may more easily be believed that Christ was designated under the name of “peace” because he can neither be cut apart nor divided nor in any way doubled.

Now he who made both one is much more himself one with the Father and the Holy Spirit; but he is not one if he is divided. Therefore he is both one with the Father and the Holy Spirit and one himself, because he joins others together and admits no division at all.

**Q.** I accept this strongest weapon against rebels; but I wish to know how far this proposition extends.

**A.** May God be peace, as we desire, and lead us on a prosperous course.

**Q.** So be it; continue now.

**A.** This very “Peace,” then, because it is written with three letters, does it receive a plural number?

**Q.** No.

**A.** Consider, then, that P signifies the Father and A the Son; and do not think this was said without the most subtle reasoning. For A is the beginning of the letters, and no element is known to precede it, so that you may understand that nothing exists before the Son. Nor will I leave this without the testimony of divine Scripture: when the Jews questioned him, he himself declared that he was the beginning (John 8:25).

No other letter precedes this one; and since every letter has a time, time too was absent. Nevertheless, this syllable is both long and first. Its being long signifies the eternity of the Son of God, not temporality. Its being a syllable signifies that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and that they are one. Its being first signifies that the Son is not second.

In the Apocalypse, John too, expressly placing this very letter, says: “I am α and ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8). But accept “the last” for this reason: because he deigned humbly to be born and die at the end of time, and himself to undergo the final judgment.

X is the third letter, placed at the end. Here you should understand that the Holy Spirit does not tend toward an end, but proceeds always in the majesty above. Thus the Apostle Paul also says, “Set your minds on the things above” (Col. 3:2), so that we may have our hearts above, toward God; and certainly the Lord is Spirit. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

I therefore do not doubt that, inviting us to the glory of this most exalted reality, the Apostle spoke as follows: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to my intention toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling” (Phil. 3:13–14).

Thus, for “Peace” to be formed, A, the vowel, is joined to P, lest P remain mute, because God the Father is always joined to his voice and Word. But in order that there may be Peace, X is added, which is placed as a double letter in place of consonants; here you may see also the consonance and participation of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, and recognize his fellowship [Note: [Col. 1211] In the manuscripts, “his linkage.”] in the heavenly and perfect Trinity.

These letters differ from one another in their designations and persons, because this is called and written P, that A, and the other X; yet, in order that there may be Peace, these letters are joined together. P is substantial as a letter, A is substantial as a letter, and X is substantial as a letter; just so, the Father is naturally God, the Son is naturally God, and the Holy Spirit is naturally God.

That difference of characters produces a difference of appellations and persons, not of nature, because the whole is a letter. Just as “Peace” is written through these three letters, called by different names, and is not held in the plural number, so the appellation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is proof of the Trinity; but, like “Peace,” “God” retains the singular number of deity.

In this joining of the three letters [Col. 1212], therefore, division is not admitted, so that Peace may be complete. For if you remove even one, there will be neither Trinity nor Peace.

**Q.** Repeat this more clearly, I ask.

**A.** Pay attention. P, I said, is a letter, A is a letter, and X is a letter; likewise, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. Yet the appellations and persons are different, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are incorporeal.

What, nevertheless, are P, A, and X? Peace, certainly, which does not admit a plural number within itself. O the foolishness of unbelievers, which does not attend to what is placed before its eyes! For, as I think, the impious person understands this least of all because he does not seek God in simplicity of heart.

**Q.** It is true, entirely true, what you say. What example is closer than this? What is found clearer than this reasoning?

**A.** But I shall repeat it to you and demonstrate it with even greater pleasure. Thus, just as Peace is formed from three persons and the different names of these letters—but you should take this as referring to the concord and fellowship of the persons—it also shows that this letter, that letter, and the other letter each exist, while Peace is singular.

Here, then, behold one God demonstrated in God, God, and God. Although P has one name and one person, A another name and another person, and X another name and another person, just as the Father has one name and one person, the Son another name and another person, and the Holy Spirit another name and another person, nevertheless this letter, this letter, and that letter are each called a letter; likewise this God, this God, and that God are unquestionably believed to be God, yet one God is acknowledged, because Peace is not held in the plural number.

Unless you have something to say against this.

**Q.** I would not want others even to hesitate over this, so brightly has the light of this manifestation shone upon me. But, as I understand it, it is even more delightful to believe this delicately [Note: [Col. 1212] The manuscripts read “more subtly.”] and not to waver in the least; so that what human beings, blinded by carnal concerns, cannot see, they may at least obtain through the shortcut of faith.

[Col. 1211]

# A Book on Ecclesiastical Dogmas Attributed to Gennadius

(C,G,S)*

## Notice Concerning the Following Book

It is clear that this work is not Augustine’s, although it is attributed to him in many manuscripts and is cited under his name by the Master of the Sentences: Book 2, Distinction 35, chapter “Therefore”; Book 3, Distinction 1, chapter “Diligently”; and Book 4, Distinction 12, chapter “Established.”

Trithemius assigns it to Alcuin in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers* and in Book 2 of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 26. John Bale likewise assigns it to him in the second century of his *Writers of Britain*. Gratian assigns it to Bishop Paterus in *On Consecration*, Distinction 2, chapter 13. Algerus attributes it to Gennadius in Book 1 of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 22; and Saint Thomas does so in *Quodlibet* 12, article 11, and in the *Catena* on the first chapter of Matthew. The Master of the Sentences himself does so in Book 2, Distinction 8, of the Louvain edition, as do many others, supported by certain manuscripts.

Among these, one of the Colbertine manuscripts, of excellent quality, has at the beginning of the book: “Here begins Gennadius’s Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas”; and at the end: “Here ends Gennadius’s Definition of Ecclesiastical Dogmas.”

Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, says in Book 3, chapter 5, of *Against the Opposing Statements of the Greeks*: “Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, a man skilled through extensive reading of the ancients, speaks as follows concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit in his book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.”

Some of the words indeed have the flavor of a Greek writer—for example, those read in chapter 14—which certain presumptuous Latins affirm. Nevertheless, others praise it under the name of Gennadius of Marseilles: namely, Platina in his account of Symmachus, where he wrongly calls him a bishop; and Walafrid Strabo in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 20, in these words: “Gennadius of Marseilles, presbyter, in the *Ecclesiastical Dogma*, and so forth.”

A manuscript from Padolirone attributes it to Faustus with this inscription: “Here begin the definitions of the Ecclesiastical Dogmas of Faustus, bishop of the Church of Marseilles,” from the *Italian Literary Journey* of 24 May 1686, p. 208.

In the oldest of all the Colbertine manuscripts, written nearly nine hundred years ago, it stands without an author’s name under this title: “Here begins the dogma of the holy Fathers and of the three hundred and eight bishops assembled [or, according to the manuscript, ‘who were assembled’] at Nicaea.”

The following is prefixed to the first chapter: “In the Father, unity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, unity and equality of substance; and these three are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, joined because of the Holy Spirit. We believe there is one God the Father,” and so forth, as in the other manuscripts, except that this manuscript has a better arrangement of the chapters, placing together consecutively everything pertaining to Baptism, [Col. 1213] the Eucharist, and Penance. The book is also fuller, containing there an additional chapter on Baptism and a chapter on Penance, besides certain other matters at the end of the book.

Moreover, after chapter 21, the material that followed in the printed editions up to the chapter now numbered 22, “On Baptism,” is absent from all the manuscripts. It had been transferred here in opposition to certain errors in the preceding chapters from Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, from the Council of Carthage against the Pelagians, and from the Second Council of Orange; all of these materials are found in a more authentic form at the end of the tenth volume.

We have therefore removed these thirty chapters, as well as three others inserted before the present chapter 30 contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts. The older codices, however, do not all end at our chapter 55; different manuscripts add still other chapters.

It is worthwhile finally to append the judgment of the Louvain theologians. “This book,” they say, “is not by a Catholic writer, but by Gennadius of Marseilles, a presbyter in Gaul . . . . . . . . . of the party of the Gauls, against whom Prosper and Hilary write to Augustine, and against whom the Second Council of Orange was assembled. Moreover, just as he often contains serious errors in his catalogue of illustrious men, so in these *Ecclesiastical Dogmas* he contains certain things against which the reader must be on guard.

“Indeed, this author nowhere in the book mentions original sin or the baptism of infants for the remission of sins. Although he names many heretics, he nowhere mentions Pelagius or the Catholic doctrine promulgated against him. On the contrary, he carefully insists that souls are not transmitted by generation, because he knew that Pelagius established his doctrine on that point.”

## Chapter One

[Col. 1213]

We believe that there is one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Father, because he has a Son; the Son, because he has a Father; the Holy Spirit, because he is from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 1213] The printed editions add: “proceeding, coeternal with the Father and the Son”; this is absent from the manuscripts].

The Father, therefore, is the beginning of the deity: just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit proceeds—not born, because he is not the Son; nor unbegotten, because he is not the Father; nor made, because he is not from nothing, but proceeds as God from God the Father and God the Son.

The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, whose eternal Father he is. The Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father. The Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son.

The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says; nor is the divinity separated or divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes [Note: [Col. 1213] Several manuscripts read “different”]; but the Father is one in person, the Son another in person, and the Holy Spirit another in person; while the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in nature [Note: [Col. 1213] The manuscripts read “one in nature”] in the holy Trinity.

## Chapter Two

The Father did not assume flesh, nor did the Holy Spirit, but only the Son: so that he who was the Son in the divinity of God [Note: [Col. 1213] The printed editions add “of the Father”] might himself become, in humanity, the son of man; lest the name “son” pass to another who would not be the Son of God by birth [Note: [Col. 1213] The printed editions read “the Son by eternal birth,” omitting “of God”].

Therefore the Son of God became the son of man, born according to the truth of nature from God as the Son of God, and according to the truth of nature from a human being as the son of man. Thus the truth of the one begotten would possess the name “son” by birth, not by adoption or designation, in both births; and there would be one Son, true God and true man.

We therefore do not confess two Christs or two sons [Note: [Col. 1213] The printed editions add “we confess”], but one Son, God and man—whom for that reason we also call the Only-Begotten—remaining in two substances, as the truth of nature conferred upon him: the natures not confused or mixed, as the followers of Timothy wish, but united by fellowship.

God therefore assumed man, and man passed into God—not by a changeability of nature, as the Apollinarists say, but by God’s condescension—so that God was not changed into human substance by assuming man, nor man into divine substance by being glorified into God. For a change or mutability [Col. 1214] of nature produces both diminution and abolition of substance [Note: [Col. 1214] Here the printed editions insert: “We believe that the holy Trinity is joined without confusion and distinguished without separation.” This is absent from the manuscripts].

The Son of God was therefore born from a human being, not through a human being—that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says—but drawing flesh from the Virgin’s body, and not bringing it with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen, and Eutyches affirm [Note: [Col. 1214] Several manuscripts read: “as Marcion, Origen, and their followers”].

Nor was he born in appearance—that is, without flesh—as Valentinus says; nor by *dokēsei* (δοκήσει) [Note: [Col. 1214] See Cyril, *Catechetical Lecture* 4], that is, merely as an imagined or supposed reality; but with a true body. He is not merely flesh from flesh, as Marcianus says, but true God from divinity and true man from flesh, one Son: in divinity, the Word of the Father and God; in humanity, soul and flesh.

The soul was not without sensation and reason, as Apollinaris says, nor the flesh without a soul, as Eunomius says; rather, there was a soul with its reason and flesh with its senses, through which true senses he endured the pains of his flesh both in the Passion and before the Passion.

## Chapter Three

He was not born from the Virgin in such a way that, by being born, he received the beginning of his deity as a man—as though, before he was born from the Virgin, he had not been God, as Artemon, Berillus, and Marcellus taught. Rather, he was born as eternal God and as man from the Virgin.

## Chapter Four

[Note: [Col. 1214] Nicetas, in his work on Gregory of Nazianzus’s *Holy Baptism*.]

Nothing created or servile is to be believed in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the source of Arius, wishes; nothing unequal, as Eunomius says; nothing equal by grace, as Aetius maintains; nothing earlier or later, or less, as Arius teaches; nothing foreign or functioning officially for another, as Macedonius teaches; nothing inserted by invasion [Note: [Col. 1214] Another reading: “by persuasion”] or stealth, as Manichaeus says; nothing corporeal, as Melito and Tertullian say; nothing bodily represented, as the Anthropomorphist [Note: [Col. 1214] Perhaps “Anthropomorphites”] and Vadianus say; nothing invisible to itself [Note: [Col. 1214] The printed editions add “to creatures”], as Origen says; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus says; nothing different in conduct or will, as Marcion says; nothing drawn from the essence of the Trinity into the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian say; nothing singular in function or incommunicable to another, as Origen says; nothing confused, as Sabellius says.

Rather, everything is perfect, because everything is from one and is one [Col. 1215] [Note: [Col. 1215] The printed editions add “from the whole”]. Yet it is not solitary, as Praxeas and Silvanus presume—that condemnable doctrine of Pentapolis.

## Chapter Five

The Son is therefore *homoousios*, that is, coessential with the Father in divinity; the Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son; and one Son, God and man, is *homoousios* with God and man, remaining God in his humanity, in the glory of the Father, desirable to be seen by the angels.

He is worshiped by the angels and by every creature just as the Father and the Holy Spirit are worshiped—not a man apart from God [Note: [Col. 1215] The printed editions read “not a man made apart from God.” Some manuscripts read “not a man made for God.” Some add afterward “or Christ without God.”], or Christ with God, as Nestorius blasphemes, but man in God and God in man.

## Chapter Six

There will be a resurrection of all the dead, but one resurrection, together and at one time—not first of the righteous and second of sinners, as the fable of dreamers has it [Note: [Col. 1215] The manuscripts read “as the fable is dreamed”], but one resurrection of all.

And if that is said to rise which falls, then our flesh will truly rise, just as it truly falls. There will not be, according to Origen, a transformation of bodies—that is, another new body in place of the flesh. Rather, the same corruptible flesh that falls, both of the righteous and of the unrighteous, will rise incorruptible: able either to suffer punishment for sins or to remain in eternal glory according to its merits.

## Chapter Seven

The resurrection will be of all human beings. If it will be of all, then all die, so that the death derived from Adam may rule over all his children, while that privilege remains in the Lord which is said specifically of him: “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). His flesh did not see corruption.

We have accepted this interpretation because the greatest multitude of the Fathers transmitted it. But since there are also other equally Catholic and learned men who believe that those who will be found alive at the Lord’s coming will be changed to incorruption and immortality while their souls remain in their bodies, and that this will be reckoned to them as a resurrection from the dead because they lay aside mortality [Note: [Col. 1215] Some manuscripts add here “of the present life”] through transformation rather than death, whoever agrees with either view is not a heretic—unless he becomes a heretic through contentiousness.

For it is enough, according to the law of the Church, to believe that the resurrection of the flesh will come from death.

## Chapter Eight

When we say in the Creed that, at the Lord’s coming, the living and the dead will be judged, we do not mean only the righteous and sinners, as Diodorus thinks. We also believe that “the living” means those who will be found in the flesh, who are believed still to be destined to die—or, as others hold, to be transformed—so that, raised immediately or restored, they may be judged together with those who died earlier.

## Chapter Nine

After the resurrection and judgment, let us not believe that there will be a restoration, as Origen deliriously imagines: that demons or impious human beings, after torments—as though purified by punishments—will either return to the angelic dignity in which they were created, or that the latter [Note: [Col. 1215] Several manuscripts read “the unjust”] will be granted fellowship with the righteous, on the grounds that this would accord with divine mercy, so that nothing rational might perish from creation but everything might somehow be saved.

Rather, let us believe in the very Judge of all and just Requiter, who said: “The impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46), so that they may receive the fruit of their works.

## Chapter Ten

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth and water” out of nothing. While darkness still concealed the water itself and the water hid the earth, the angels and all the heavenly Powers were made, so that God’s goodness would not be idle but would have beings in whom he could display his goodness through many ages beforehand. Thus this visible world was made and adorned from the things that had been created.

## Chapter Eleven

Nothing incorporeal and invisible by nature is to be believed in except God alone—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is believed to be incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills and embraces all things; and therefore he is invisible to all creatures because he is incorporeal.

## Chapter Twelve

Every creature is corporeal. The angels and all the heavenly Powers are corporeal [Note: [Col. 1216] Several manuscripts read “corporeal” in the singular], although they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual natures to be corporeal because they are bounded by locality, just as the human soul is enclosed by flesh, and demons, who in substance belong to the angelic nature, are likewise bounded.

## Chapter Thirteen

We believe intellectual natures to be immortal because they lack flesh and have no place by which they can fall and therefore need resurrection after a ruin.

## Chapter Fourteen

Human souls did not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created simultaneously, as Origen invents. Nor were they sown along with bodies through sexual intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain presumptuous Latins affirm, as though maintaining the succession of nature [Note: [Col. 1216] Six manuscripts read “serving the consequence”; three others, “with the consequence serving”].

Rather, we say that the creation of the soul is known only to the Creator of all things. Only the body is sown through the marital union; by God’s judgment it is joined together, compacted, and formed in the womb. Once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that the human being, consisting of soul and body, may live in the womb and emerge alive from the womb, complete in human substance.

## Chapter Fifteen

Nor do we say that there are two souls in one human being, as James and certain other Syrians write: one animal soul by which the body is animated and which is mixed with the blood, and another spiritual soul that supplies reason. Rather, we say that there is one and the same soul in a human being, which both gives life to the body through its association with it and governs itself through its reason. It possesses freedom of choice, so that in the thought of its substance [Note: [Col. 1216] All manuscripts read “in its substance”] it may choose what it wills.

## Chapter Sixteen

We believe that only the human being possesses a substantial soul, which lives when separated from the body and vigorously retains its senses and faculties. It does not die with the body, as Aratus asserts [Note: [Col. 1216] All manuscripts read “the Arab”], nor after a short interval, as Zeno says, because it lives substantially.

## Chapter Seventeen

The souls of animals, however, are not substantial [Note: [Col. 1216] Several manuscripts read “substances”; others “subsisting”], but are born together with the flesh through the vitality of the flesh itself and end with the death of the flesh. Therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, but are driven toward everything by the impulse of nature.

## Chapter Eighteen

The human soul does not die with the flesh, because, as we said above, it is not sown with the flesh. Rather, once the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, the soul is created and infused by God’s judgment, so that the human being may live within the womb and thus come forth through birth into the world.

## Chapter Nineteen

The human being consists of only two substances: soul and flesh—the soul with its reason and the flesh with its senses. Yet the flesh does not move these senses without the soul’s association with it. The soul, however, retains its rational faculty even without the flesh.

## Chapter Twenty

There is no third substance in the human being, a spirit, as Didymus contends. Rather, the spirit itself is the soul, called “spirit” because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes within the body. The soul, however, is so called because it animates the body for living or gives it life.

But the third element that the Apostle introduces along with soul and body should be understood as the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle prays may remain whole in us, lest through our fault it be diminished or driven away from us (1 Thess. 5:23), because “the Holy Spirit will flee from deceit” (Wis. 1:5).

## Chapter Twenty-One
Man was entrusted to the freedom of his will from the very beginning of his creation, so that, with the mind’s vigilance alone assisting him, he might remain in obedience to the commandment, if he wished to continue in the state in which he had been created. [Col. 1217] But after he fell through the serpent’s seduction by way of Eve, he lost the good of nature and, likewise, the strength of free choice—not, however, the power of choosing, lest what he had to correct should not be his own sin, and lest what had not been washed away by his own free choice should not rightly be forgiven. Thus the freedom of choice remains for seeking salvation [Note: [Col. 1217] This is how several manuscripts read. But the printed editions have *evitaret*, “might avoid.” Some codices continue as follows: “Yet not for attaining it without him who makes those who seek find, opens to those who knock, and gives to those who ask. Therefore, just as we believe that we have the beginning through God’s mercy and inspiration, so we freely confess that the free choice of our nature follows divine inspiration. Therefore, lest we fall, etc.” They judge this to have been inserted by a Catholic writer because of the Pelagians’ error latent there.]—that is, rational willing—but only after God first admonishes and invites him to salvation, so that he may either choose, follow, or undertake an action in response to the opportunity for salvation, that is, through God’s inspiration. But that he should attain what he chooses, follows, or undertakes in response to that opportunity, we freely confess to be God’s work. Thus we have the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy; to assent to the saving inspiration lies within our power; to obtain what we desire by assenting to the admonition is a divine gift; not to fall away from the gift of salvation once acquired depends upon our vigilance and, at the same time, heavenly assistance; to fall away depends upon our own power and negligence.

**CHAPTER XXII (also 52).**

There is one baptism, but it is in the Church, where there is one faith, and where it is administered in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if some have been baptized among those heretics who baptize with the confession of the Holy Trinity and come to us, they are indeed to be received as baptized, lest the invocation or confession of the Holy Trinity be nullified. But they must first be taught and instructed regarding the sense in which the mystery of the Holy Trinity is held in the Church; and if they consent to believe, or agree to confess it, then, already cleansed by the integrity of faith, they are to be confirmed by the laying on of hands. If they are children or simple-minded persons incapable of understanding the teaching, those who present them should answer on their behalf according to the custom of baptism; and thus, strengthened by the laying on of hands and chrism, they are to be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist.

But those who have not been baptized among heretics with the invocation of the Holy Trinity and who come to us, we declare ought to be baptized, not rebaptized. For we must not believe that those have been baptized who were not immersed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit according to the rule established by the Lord. Such are the Paulianists [Note: [Col. 1217] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have *Paulini*, “Paulinians.”], Proclians, Borborites, Siphorites—now called Bonosians—Photinians, Montanists, and Manichaeans, various offshoots of impiety; or the other plagues arising from their origin or order, which introduce two principles unknown to themselves, as do Cerdo and Marcion; or contrary principles, as does Manichaeus; or three and barbarous principles, as do the Sethian and Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1217] The manuscripts read *Theodotus*, or *Theudotus*.]; or many principles, as does Valentinus; or the belief that Christ was a man without God, as do Cerinthus, Ebion, Artemon, and Photinus. If any of these, I say, come to us, they are not to be asked whether they have been baptized or not; they are to be asked only whether they believe in the faith of the Church, and then they are to be baptized with ecclesiastical Baptism.
