**CHAPTER XXIII (also 53).**

I neither praise nor condemn receiving communion in the Eucharist every day. Nevertheless, I advise and urge that communion be received on every Sunday, provided that the mind is not disposed toward sinning [Note: [Col. 1217] The manuscripts read this way. The printed edition has: “provided that there is no disposition toward sinning.”]. For one who still has the will to sin, I say, is burdened more by receiving the Eucharist than purified by it.

Therefore, even if someone is troubled by sin, provided that he no longer has the will to sin, and, intending to receive communion, makes satisfaction with tears and prayers, let him approach the Eucharist without fear and securely, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, which is accustomed to forgive sins when they are confessed devoutly. But I say this concerning one who is not weighed down by grave and mortal sins. For one oppressed by mortal crimes committed after Baptism, I urge first to make satisfaction through public penance and then, reconciled by the priest’s judgment, to be joined to communion, if he wishes to receive the Eucharist not for his judgment and condemnation.

Nor do we deny that mortal crimes may be absolved through private satisfaction; but first the secular habit must be changed, and devotion to religion confessed through the correction of one’s life, together with continual—or rather perpetual—mourning, God in his mercy assisting. This must be done in such a way that one performs deeds contrary to those for which one is penitent, and receives the Eucharist humbly and submissively on every Sunday until death.

**CHAPTER XXIV (also 54).**

True repentance is not to admit sins for which one must repent, and to mourn those that have been admitted. The satisfaction of repentance is to cut off the causes of sins and not to grant access to their suggestions.

**CHAPTER XXV (also 55).**

In the divine promises, let us expect nothing earthly or transitory, as the Meletians hope. Let us not expect sexual union, as Cerinthus and Marcion deliriously claim [Note: [Col. 1218] The manuscripts read *delectantur*, “take delight.”]. Nor anything relating to food or drink, as Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Lactantius accept on the authority of Papias [Note: [Col. 1218] See Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.].

Nor should we hope that Christ’s kingdom will exist on earth for a thousand years after the resurrection, and that the saints will reign with him in delights, as Nepos taught: namely, that there would be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of the impious; that between these two resurrections of the dead, nations ignorant of God would be preserved in the flesh in the corners of the earth; that after the thousand-year reign of the righteous on earth, these nations, instigated by the devil, would be stirred up to war against the righteous who were reigning; that, while the Lord fought on behalf of the righteous, they would be restrained by a fiery rain; and that, having thus been killed, they would be resurrected with the others who had previously died in impiety, in incorruptible bodies, for eternal punishments.

**CHAPTER XXVI (also 56).**

We believe that no one comes to salvation unless invited by God. No one who has been invited works out his salvation unless God assists him. No one merits assistance unless he prays. We do not believe that anyone perishes by God’s will, but by his permission, in accordance with the choice of free will, lest the innate freedom of power once bestowed upon human beings be forced into slavish necessity.

**CHAPTER XXVII (also 57).**

Evil, or wickedness, was not created by God but invented by the devil, who himself was created good by God. But because he was entrusted with free choice, as a rational creature, and had received the ability to think, he turned his knowledge of good toward evil. By thinking many things he became the inventor of evil; and what he had lost in himself he envied in others. Not content to perish alone, he persuaded others, so that he who had been the inventor of his own wickedness might also become the author of wickedness in others. From him, therefore, evil or wickedness spread to the other rational creatures.

**CHAPTER XXVIII (also 58).**

From this we understand that nothing is immutable by nature except God alone—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—who cannot be changed from the good, because he possesses the good by nature and cannot be anything other than good.

**CHAPTER XXIX (also 59).**

The angels, however, who persevere in the blessedness in which they were created, do not possess the good by nature, as though they were not changed along with the others. Rather, by preserving the good will of their free choice, the goodness of their condition, and faith in their Lord, they remained faithful. Hence the Lord himself rightly calls them holy angels: they preserved the holiness of their free choice and did not deviate from the good following the example of their companions [Note: [Col. 1218] In earlier editions, the following three chapters, which are absent from the manuscripts, had been added:

“True faith, which is catholic, confesses the good substance of all creatures, whether spiritual or bodily, and that evil has no nature, because God, who is the creator of the universe, made nothing that was not good. Hence the devil too would have been good if he had remained in what he was made. But because he used his natural excellence badly and did not remain in the truth, he did not pass over into a contrary substance; rather, he departed from the supreme Good to which he ought to have adhered.

“The angelic powers that remained fixed in divine love, when the proud angels had fallen, received this gift as a reward: they would no longer be gnawed by any rust of creeping [Col. 1219] sin, but would remain without end of blessedness in contemplation of the Creator and would persist in the eternal stability for which they had been created. The angels were created in such a way that, if they wished, they could remain in the light of blessedness; but, if they wished, they could also have fallen. Hence Satan fell with the legions that followed him. But after his fall, the angels who remained were so strengthened that they could not fall at all, because, so that they might no longer fall altogether, they received the power of immutability.”]

**CHAPTER XXX (also 63).**

Marriage is good, but for the sake of children and for the purpose of restraining fornication [Note: [Col. 1219] Some manuscripts read: “not for the sake of concupiscence and fornication.”].

**CHAPTER XXXI (also 64).**

Continence is better. But it is not sufficient in itself for blessedness if it is maintained solely for the love of chastity; rather, it must also be chosen with this disposition for the sake of having leisure for the Lord. Otherwise, it will appear to be the dissolution of marriage rather than chastity.

**CHAPTER XXXII (also 65).**

Virginity is superior to both goods, because it conquers both nature and struggle: nature through bodily integrity, and struggle through the peace of chastity.

**CHAPTER XXXIII (also 66).**

It is good to receive as food, with thanksgiving, whatever God has commanded to be eaten. To abstain from certain things—not as though they were evil, but as though they were unnecessary—is not evil. To regulate their use [Note: [Col. 1219] The manuscripts read: “To regulate the use of meat.”] according to necessity and the proper time is characteristic of Christians.

**CHAPTER XXXIV (also 67).**

To call marriages evil, or to compare them with fornication or adultery; and to believe that foods are evil, or that they cause evil in those who receive them [Note: [Col. 1219] The printed editions have: “or that they cause wickedness in those who receive them”], is not characteristic of Christians but specifically of the Encratites [Note: [Col. 1219] The printed editions have “Hieracites.”] and Manichaeans.

**CHAPTER XXXV (also 68).**

To equate marriage with virginity consecrated to God, or to believe that those who abstain from wine or meat for the sake of disciplining the body gain no increase of merit, is not Christian but Jovinian.

**CHAPTER XXXVI (also 69).**

It must be believed with complete faith that blessed Mary, the mother of God Christ, conceived while a virgin, gave birth while a virgin, and remained a virgin after childbirth. Nor should we accept the blasphemy of Helvidius, who said: “A virgin before childbirth, not a virgin after childbirth.”

**CHAPTER XXXVII (also 70).**

We do not believe that the elements—that is, heaven and earth—will be destroyed by fire, but that they will be changed for the better. We also believe that the form of the world—that is, its appearance, not its substance—will pass away.

**CHAPTER XXXVIII (also 71).**

It is good to distribute one’s resources to the poor with proper stewardship. It is better, with the intention of following the Lord, to give them away once for all [Note: [Col. 1219] The printed editions have *insimul donare*, “to give together,” rather than “to give once for all.”] and, freed from anxiety, to endure poverty with Christ.

**CHAPTER XXXIX (also 72).**

A cleric who, after Baptism, has married two matrons is not to be ordained. Nor is one who has had one woman, but a concubine rather than a matron. Nor one who has taken a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute in marriage. Nor one who, overcome by anger or by a reasonable or unreasonable fear [Note: [Col. 1219] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “by a reasonable or unreasonable judgment.”], has mutilated himself in any member of his body. Nor one who is convicted of having accepted interest, or is known to have performed on the stage. Nor one who publicly mourns mortal crimes through penance. Nor one who at some time, having been seized by madness, became insane, or was afflicted by the assault of the devil. Nor one who, out of ambition, offers money in imitation of Simon Magus.

**CHAPTER XL (also 73).**

We believe that the bodies of the saints, and especially the relics of the blessed martyrs, are to be honored with the utmost sincerity as members of Christ; and that the basilicas called by their names, as places dedicated to divine worship, are to be approached with the most devout affection and the most faithful devotion [Note: [Col. 1219] The word *credimus*, “we believe,” is absent from the manuscripts.]. Anyone who opposes this opinion is considered not a Christian but an Eunomian and a Vigilantian.

**CHAPTER XLI (also 74).**

We believe that the way of salvation is open only to the baptized. We do not believe that any catechumen, even one who has died in good works, possesses eternal life, except through martyrdom, in which the entire sacrament of Baptism is completed.

The person about to be baptized confesses his faith before the priest and, when questioned, answers. The martyr does the same before his persecutor: he confesses his faith and, when questioned, answers. After his confession, the former is either sprinkled with water or immersed; the latter is either sprinkled with blood or touched by fire [Note: [Col. 1220] The manuscripts read: “or immersed in fire.”]. The former receives the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands; the latter becomes a mouthpiece [Note: [Col. 1220] The manuscripts read *locutorium*, “mouthpiece”; the printed editions have *habitaculum*, “dwelling-place.”] of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he himself who speaks but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in him. The former shares in the Eucharist in remembrance of the Lord’s death; the latter dies together with Christ himself. The former confesses that he will renounce the deeds of the world; the latter renounces life itself. The former has all sins forgiven; in the latter, they are extinguished.

**CHAPTER XLII (also 75).**

In the Eucharist, pure water ought not to be offered, as some are deceived by an appearance of sobriety; rather, wine mixed with water should be offered. For wine too was part of the mystery of our redemption, when he said, “I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine any longer” (Matthew 26:29); and, mixed with water, it was what was given after the meal. Moreover, when water mixed with blood flowed from his side, which had been pierced by a lance, this showed that wine had been pressed from the vine of his true flesh together with water.

**CHAPTER XLIII (also 76).**

Our flesh is good, and very good, since it was created by the good and by God alone. It is not evil, as the Sethian, Ophian [Note: [Col. 1220] The manuscripts read *Ophinianus*.], and Patrician maintain; nor the cause of evil, as Florinus taught [Note: [Col. 1220] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *Florianus*.]; nor composed from evil and good, as Manichaeus blasphemously claims. But although it is good by creation, through the choice of the soul it becomes good or evil for us—not through a change of substance, but through the reward of its deeds [Note: [Col. 1220] Some manuscripts read “through the excuse of the transaction”; others, “through the execution of the transaction.”]. For it is the flesh itself that will stand before the tribunal of Christ, in which each soul will receive what belongs to its body according to what it has done, whether good or evil.

**CHAPTER XLIV (also 77).**

At the resurrection from the dead, the form of the sexes will not be changed. A dead man will rise in the form of a man, and a woman in the form of a woman, though free from the condition of sex belonging only to this life, not from its natural appearance. Otherwise the resurrection would not be true if what rises were not what falls.

**CHAPTER XLV (also 78).**

Before the Lord’s Passion, all the souls of the saints were held in hell under the debt of Adam’s transgression, until they were freed from their servile condition by the Lord’s authority through his undeserved death.

**CHAPTER XLVI (also 79).**

After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, the souls of all the saints are with Christ, and, when they depart from the body, they go to Christ, awaiting the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with him they may likewise be changed into complete and everlasting [Note: [Col. 1220] Some manuscripts read “perfect.”] blessedness. In the same way, the souls of sinners, placed in hell under fear, await the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with them they may be thrust into eternal punishment [Note: [Col. 1220] The manuscripts read “may be turned.”].

**CHAPTER XLVII (also 80).**

We confidently believe that sins are abolished through repentance, even if a person repents of what he has committed at the final breath of life and his sins are disclosed through public lamentation. For God’s purpose, by which he decreed to save what had perished, stands immovable. Therefore, since his will does not change, whether through correction of life, if time is granted, or through humble confession, if life is immediately ended, forgiveness of sins is to be faithfully expected from him who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back from destruction through repentance (Ezekiel 18:32; 33:11), and, saved by the Lord’s mercy, live.

If anyone thinks otherwise concerning God’s most just compassion [Col. 1221], he is not a Christian but a Novatian.

**CHAPTER XLVIII (also 81).**

We are certain that the devil does not see the inward thoughts of the soul. But we have learned by experience that he infers them from bodily movements and indications of the emotions. The secrets of the heart are known only to him of whom it is said: “You alone know the hearts of the children of humankind” (3 Kings 8:39).

**CHAPTER XLIX (also 82).**

Not all our evil thoughts are always aroused by the devil’s prompting; at times they emerge from the movement of our own free choice. Good thoughts, however, are always from God.

**CHAPTER L (also 83).**

We do not believe that demons enter the soul substantially through energetic operation [Note: [Col. 1221] The manuscripts have “through energy” and omit “operation.”]; rather, we believe that they are united to it through attachment and oppression. To enter the mind is possible only for him who created it, who, existing incorporeally by nature, is capable of reaching his own creature.

**CHAPTER LI (also 84).**

We have learned from God himself that even sinners can perform signs, wonders, and healings in the Lord’s name. When, through this presumption, they help others, they harm themselves through ambition for human glory, because they glory in a false gift—that is, one not owed on the basis of their merits.

**CHAPTER LII (also 85).**

We rightly believe that a person may be made renowned as a Christian through signs and wonders, yet not holy, if he acts through uncontrolled and harsh impulses [Col. 1222]. But through disciplined and peaceful impulses, even without the efficacy of signs, a person may rightly become holy, perfect, and a man of God.

**CHAPTER LIII (also 86).**

No saint or righteous person is without sin. Yet for this reason he does not cease to be righteous and holy, when he holds fast to holiness in his disposition. We acquire holiness not through the powers of nature but through the assistance of our purpose and the grace of God. Therefore all the saints truly declare themselves sinners, because in truth they have something to mourn—if not the reproach of conscience, then certainly the instability of their transgressive nature.

**CHAPTER LIV (also 87).**

Easter—that is, the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection—cannot be celebrated before the passage of the spring equinox and the completion of the fourteenth day of the moon [Note: [Col. 1222] In the manuscript codices: “and the beginning of the fifteenth moon” or “of the sixteenth moon” cannot be celebrated], though it must be celebrated in the same month in which they occur.

**CHAPTER LV (also 88).**

Against the novel legislators who say that the soul alone was created in the image of God, so that, because God is rightly believed to be incorporeal, the soul too may be believed to be incorporeal, we freely confess that the image is found in eternity and the likeness in conduct.

**ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE TWO SOULS, AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS.**—The Manichaean heretics say that there are two souls in every human being: one good, from the substance of God, and the other evil, from the race of darkness and not created by God. Augustine regrets that he once adhered to this doctrine so closely that he paid no attention to arguments so obvious and manifest by which this delusion is overthrown. For, in the first place, it readily appears to anyone who considers the matter that every soul, since it is a kind of life and an intelligible thing, and therefore superior to visible light—which the Manichaeans acknowledge to be from God—must be attributed to God its creator. The passages of Scripture by which they argue that evil things are not from God are better explained by comparison with other passages. Thereafter, from the definition of sin and of the will, from the forgiveness of sins granted to sinners in the Church, and finally from the pious and beneficial disposition of repentance, it is shown with complete clarity that sinful souls are not evil by nature. 93–94

**CHAPTER ONE.** How the Manichaeans’ error concerning two souls, one of which is not from God, is overthrown. Every soul, since it is a kind of life, can come only from God, the source of life. Ibid.

**VI.** Whether even vices, as intelligible things, should be preferred to sensible light and attributed to God as their author. A vice of the soul is a certain deficiency and should rightly not be counted among intelligible things. Even deficiencies, if they were counted among intelligible things, would never be preferred to sensible things. If visible light is from God, much more is the soul from him, since, insofar as it lives, it is an intelligible thing, even when vicious. **VII.** The question concerning divine manifestations. 853

**XVI.** How Moses saw God. 862

**XVII.** How the “back parts” of God were seen. Faith in Christ’s resurrection. The Catholic Church alone is the place from which God’s back parts are seen. The Israelites saw God’s back parts. To suppose that only the Father was ever seen by the Fathers is a rash opinion. 863

**XVIII.** Daniel’s vision. 866

**BOOK THREE.**—It is asked whether, in those manifestations of God made through bodily forms that were discussed in the preceding book, only a created form was produced in which God was shown to human eyes as he then judged possible; or whether angels who already existed were sent in such a way that they spoke in the person of God, assuming a bodily form from corporeal creation, or changing their own bodies into forms suited to their actions according to the power granted them by the Creator; while the very essence of God was never seen in itself. 867–868

**PROOEMIUM.** Why he writes about the Trinity. What he desires from his readers. What was said in the preceding book. Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.** What must be said next. 870

**VIII.** God alone also creates the things that are transformed by magical arts. Ibid.

**X.** In how many ways a creature is assumed for signification. The Eucharist. 879

**XI.** The essence of God never appeared in itself. Divine manifestations to the Fathers were made through the ministry of angels. An objection drawn from the manner of speaking is dispelled. God’s manifestation to Abraham, just as to Moses, was made through angels. The same is proved from the Law given to Moses through angels. What was said in this book and what remains to be said in the next. 881

**BOOK FOUR.**—He explains for what purpose the Son of God was sent: namely, that through Christ’s death for sinners we might be persuaded above all both of how much God loved us and of what sort of people he loved. It was also fitting that, so that we might be cleansed for contemplating God and adhering to God, the Word should come in the flesh. By his one and simple death our double death was annulled; here he explains how the Savior’s single [death] corresponds to our double [death] for salvation, and discusses at greater length the perfection of the number six, into which number the ratio of the single to the double is brought. He teaches that all are gathered from many into one through the one Mediator of life, Christ, through whom alone true purification of the soul takes place. Finally, although the Son of God was made lesser by his mission because of the form of a servant which he assumed, he was not therefore lesser than the Father according to the form of God because he was sent by him; and he demonstrates that the same reasoning applies to the mission of the Holy Spirit. 885–886

**PROOEMIUM.** Knowledge of God must be sought from God. Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.** We are perfected through recognition of our weakness. The incarnate Word dispels our darkness. 887

**BOOK FIVE.**—He turns to those arguments of the heretics which they produce not from the divine books but from their own reasoning. He refutes those who think that the substance of the Father and the Son is not the same because they suppose that everything said of God is said according to substance; and consequently argue that begetting and being begotten, or being begotten and being unbegotten, since they are different, imply different substances. He demonstrates that not everything said of God is said according to substance: goodness and greatness, for example, and whatever else is said of him in relation to himself, are said according to substance; but things are also said relatively—that is, not in relation to himself but in relation to something that he is not—as when he is called Father in relation to the Son, or Lord in relation to the creature that serves him. If something relative, that is, in relation to something that he is not, is said of him temporally—as in “Lord, you have become our refuge”—nothing happens to him by which he is changed; rather, he remains altogether immutable in his nature or essence. 911–912

**CHAPTER ONE.** What the author asks from God and what he asks from the reader. Nothing mutable or bodily is to be conceived in God. [Col. 1229] Ibid.

**II.** God is the one immutable essence. 911–912

**III.** The Arians’ argument drawn from the terms “begotten” and “unbegotten” is dissolved. Ibid.

**IV.** An accident always implies some change in a thing. 913

**VII.** The addition of a negation does not change the category. 915

**VIII.** Whatever is said substantially of God is said individually of each person and simultaneously of the Trinity itself. In God there is one essence, three *hypostases* in Greek, and three persons in Latin. 916

**IX.** The three persons are not properly so called. 917

**X.** What belongs absolutely to God as essence is said of the Trinity in the singular, not in the plural. 918

**XII.** In mutual relations, terms are sometimes lacking. 919

**XIV.** The Father and the Son are the one principle of the Holy Spirit. Ibid.

**XV.** Whether the Holy Spirit was a gift even before he was given. 921

**XVI.** What is said of God temporally is said relatively, not accidentally. 922

**BOOK SIX.**—The question is proposed how Christ was called in the apostolic utterance “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” It is discussed whether the Father is not wisdom itself but only the Father of wisdom, or whether wisdom begot wisdom. After postponing the solution for a while, the unity and equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are proved, and it is shown that one must believe not in a triplex God but in the Trinity. Finally, Hilary’s statement is explained: “Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift.” 923–924

**CHAPTER ONE.** The Son, according to the Apostle, is the power and wisdom of God the Father. From this follows the reasoning of Catholics against the earlier Arians. The difficulty is whether the Father is not wisdom itself but only the Father of wisdom. Ibid.

**IV.** The same subject follows. 927

**V.** The Holy Spirit too is equal in all things to the Father and the Son. Ibid.

**VI.** How God is simple and multiple in substance. 928

**VIII.** No addition is made to God’s nature. Ibid.

**X.** The attributes assigned by Hilary to the individual persons. The Trinity is represented in created things. 931

**BOOK SEVEN.**—The question postponed from the preceding book is explained: namely, that God the Father, who begot the Son as power and wisdom, is not only the Father of power and wisdom but is himself power and wisdom; and the same is true of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, it is shown that there are not three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom, just as there is one God and one essence. It is then asked how it is said in God that there is one essence and three persons among the Latins, but one essence and three substances or *hypostases* among the Greeks. Both expressions are shown to be used out of necessity of speech, so that when asked what the three are we would not remain entirely silent, while we truthfully confess that there are three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 931–932

**CHAPTER ONE.** He returns to the question whether each person of the Trinity is wisdom in himself. How difficult the proposed question is and by what method it is solved. Ibid.

**II.** The Father and Son together are one wisdom, just as they are one essence, although they are not together one Word. 936

**III.** Why the Son is especially indicated by the name “Wisdom” in Scripture, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom. The Holy Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, is one wisdom. 936–937

**BOOK EIGHT.**—Having supplied the reasoning, he shows not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but also that both together are not something greater than the Holy Spirit, that any two together in the same Trinity are not something greater than one, and that all three together are not something greater than each individually. He then proceeds so that God’s very nature may be understood both from the apprehension of truth, from knowledge of the supreme good, and from the implanted love of justice, on account of which even a not-yet-just soul loves a just soul. Above all, he admonishes us to seek knowledge of God through love, which Scripture calls God; and he observes that in this love there is also a certain trace of the Trinity. 945–946

**PROAEMIUM.** Recapitulation of the preceding discussion. The rule to be observed in more difficult questions of faith. Ibid.

## BOOK NINE

The Trinity is shown to exist in some manner in man, who is the image of God: namely, the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves both itself and its knowledge. These three are shown to be equal to one another and to be of one essence. 959–960

How the Trinity is to be investigated. Ibid.

## BOOK ELEVEN

A certain image of the Trinity is also shown in the outer man: first, in what is perceived externally—namely, the body that is seen, the form impressed from it upon the vision of the one seeing, and the intention of the will joining the two together. Yet these three are neither equal to one another nor of one substance. Then, in the mind itself, another trinity is observed as though introduced by things sensed externally: three things of one substance, namely, the bodily image that is in memory, the formation of that image when the vision of the one thinking turns toward it, and the intention of the will joining the two together. This latter trinity is said also to belong to the outer man because it has been introduced from bodies that are sensed externally. 983–984

A vestige of the Trinity also exists in the outer man. Ibid.

What the outer and inner man are like. Ibid.

## BOOK THIRTEEN

He continues his discussion of knowledge, in which, while distinguishing it from wisdom, he began in the preceding book to investigate a certain trinity. On this occasion, commending the Christian faith, he explains how the faith of believers is one and common. He then shows that everyone desires blessedness, though not everyone possesses the faith by which blessedness is attained. He defines this faith as being in Christ, who rose bodily from the dead, and teaches that no one is liberated from the dominion of the devil except through him, by the remission of sins. He extensively demonstrates that the devil had to be conquered by Christ not through power but through justice. Finally, when the words of this faith are committed to memory, a certain trinity exists in the mind: the sounds of the words are in memory even when a person is not thinking about them; from them the vision of recollection is formed when he thinks about them; and the will of the person remembering and thinking joins the two together. 1013–1014

## BOOK FIFTEEN

At the beginning, he briefly and summarily explains what was said in each of the preceding fourteen books, and teaches that the discussion has finally reached the point at which the Trinity, which is God, is sought in those very eternal, incorporeal, and immutable realities whose perfect contemplation promises us the blessed life. He shows that this Trinity is now seen by us as through a mirror and in an enigma, insofar as it is seen through the image of God, which we are, in an obscure likeness difficult to discern. Likewise, he demonstrates that from the word of our mind the generation of the divine Word can be inferred only with difficulty, because of the very great disparity observed between the two words, and that from the love joined to the will the procession of the Holy Spirit can in some manner be inferred and explained. 1057–1058
